units.la: VAE mihi adhuc, Generosi & Amplissimi viri, vos unicé amandi & colendi causse fuerunt: eadem me nunc ad hoc, qua lecunq; meum, opusculum, volui potissimum dedicandum, imo pulerunt. Erat autem sunt, ut uno quasi verbo dicam, & Generis vestri vetustas ac nobilitas, et auitæ eximiaq; vestræ virtutes, & clara splendidaq; vestra dignitas, et denique egregia ac prope singularis vestra erga me Meosq; humanitas atq; benevolentia, & quæ inde promanarunt, multa magnaq; vestra in me, Meosq; merita atq; beneficia. Hæc autem uon mihi tantum, sed quibus/suis etiam aliis vos amandi et observandi iustissimæ sane sunt grauissimæq; causæ. Nam primum quidem quàm amabili, quamq; veneranda sit Nobilitas inter omnes, qui sana sunt mente præditi, satis superq; constat. Unde sapientissimus & eloquentissimus ille quondam Reip. Rom. Consul, qui primus nouum & obscurum suum genus virtute suâ nobilitauit, Nobilitatem scitè admodum et verè BLANDAM CONCILIATRICVLAM appellauit, grauissima hac addita ratione: Omnes enim, inquit, boni semper Nobilitati fauemus, & quia utile est Reipub. nobiles esse homines dignos Maioribus suis; & quia ualet apud nos clarorum hominum, & bene de Rep. meritorum memoria, etiam mortuorum, O egregiū luculentumq; Nobilitatis encomiū, omnes ferè eius laudes uno quasi fasciculo complectens! O præclarū & eximium Nobilitatis præconē; qui etiā primus Nobilitatis suigeneris autor fuit! At Nobilitate quidē clarūq; Natalibus ortos plurimi esse faciendos, magniq; afficiendos honoribus docet ratio, docet natura, docet omnium gentium consensio, quæ lex naturæ est putanda. Cunctis enim Mortales vel ipsius naturæ ductu & instinctu plurimum generis splendori tribuunt, & eum summis honoribus decorandum existimant: unde Aristoteles in Politicis: H & γένεια, inquit, παρ' ἰκέτοις οἱ ηὑοι τιμῶσι, hoc est, Nobilitas (quam Græci generis bonitatem seu præstantiam vocant) apud singulos magno domi est in pretio: &, ut idem ait, Πολίται μᾶλλον οἱ ἀγαθοὶ γενέσει ἀγαθοῖ τιμῶσιν, quod est, Cuncti magis sunt habendi homines nobiles et generosi, quàm ii, qui humili genere et obscuro loco sunt nati; quia, ut addit, verisimile est apud Francos obtinebant (quæ admodum norunt omnes, quinque parum in Germanicu, & Francicu præsertim, historiæ sunt vel fati) Rutboldi, Clerboldi, Diethboldi, Guthboldi, Gelboldi, Grunboldi, Hildeboldi, Himboldi, Ramboldi, Sembol di, Sigboldi, Luthboldi, Amboldi, Archamboldi; et hu similibus nominib, fuerunt insigniti. Hæc, inquâ, & alia his similia nomina apud Francos, non hominum vulgarium et plebeiorum, sed nobilium, equitum, heroum, ducum, virorum illustrium apud Francos fuerunt nomina in Bold siue Bolt terminantia: quæ vox ipsa bellicam virtutem atq; celeritatē videtur sonare. Sed idem testatur alterum quoq; illud nomen vestrum gentilitium VMSTAT: quod Francica olim fuit ditionis oppidum: in quo multa adhuc hodie vsisuntur gentis familiaq; vestræ vestigia atq; monimenta illustria, multaq; ibi loca atque prædia a Vuamboldis Maioribus vestris nomina sua sunt sortita, quæ non opus est hic enumerare.
units.tr: Up to now, distinguished gentlemen, you have been the sole reasons for my loving and honouring you, and the same reasons have now moved me, or rather compelled me, to dedicate this little work of mine to you above all others. To put it in a word: your family's antiquity and nobility, your ancestors' outstanding virtues, your bright and splendid rank, and finally your rare and almost unique kindness and goodwill towards me and mine, with the many great services and favours you have done for me and mine, all these are very just and weighty reasons for loving and respecting you, and not for me alone but for others too. First, how lovable and how worthy of reverence nobility is, in the judgement of all who have sound minds, is quite plain. That is why that most wise and eloquent consul of the Roman Republic, who by his own virtue first ennobled his new and obscure family, rightly and very neatly called nobility a flattering little conciliator, adding this weighty reason: all good men, he says, always favour nobility, both because it is useful to the commonwealth that noblemen be worthy of their ancestors, and because among us the memory of famous men who have deserved well of the state, even of the dead, carries weight. What an excellent and brilliant encomium of nobility, embracing almost all its praises in one bundle! O distinguished and remarkable herald of nobility, who was also the first author of his own kind of nobility! Reason teaches, nature teaches, and the agreement of all nations, which must be considered a law of nature, teaches that those born of noble stock are to be held in high regard and honoured greatly. For all mortals, by the very guidance and instinct of nature, grant much to the splendour of birth and think it worthy of the highest honours. Hence Aristotle says in the Politics: "Nobility" (which the Greeks call the goodness or excellence of birth) "is held in great esteem among individuals at home" [ἡ εὐγένεια παρ' ἑκάστοις μέγα ἐν τιμῇ]; and, as the same writer says, "citizens rather honour those who are good by birth" [πολῖται μᾶλλον οἱ ἀγαθοὶ γενέσει ἀγαθοὶ τιμῶσιν], that is, all men should be regarded as noble and well-born rather than those who are born of humble stock and obscure place. This, he adds, is likely to have been the case among the Franks. (As all know, who are at all acquainted with German, and especially Frankish, history or legend, names such as Rutbold, Clerbold, Diethbold, Guthbold, Gelbold, Grunbold, Hildebold, Himbold, Rambold, Sembold, Sigbold, Luthbold, Ambold and Archambold were borne by men of distinction.) These names, I say, and other names like them among the Franks, which end in -bold or -bolt, were the names not of common and plebeian men, but of nobles, knights, heroes, dukes and illustrious men; the word itself seems to suggest martial courage and swiftness. The same writer also bears witness to your other family name, Umstadt, which was once a town in Frankish territory, where many traces and famous monuments of your family and race survive even today, and many places and estates there took their names from your ancestors the Wamboldts. There is no need to list them here.

units.la: Familiam deniq; vestram Francorum esse propaginem, argumento non le- vi sunt illa ipsa vestra insignia, nimirum panes illi dimidiati (quos vulgo Germani vocant: quia voce Phryges quoq; ut testu est Herodotus, usi sunt) siue, ut alii ea appellant, Pinne: cuiusmodi antiqua & Caroli Magni, & Francica gentis insignia fuisse tradunt. Bauaria certè & Teccensis familia (quæ & ipsa Francu sunt oriunda) panes integros habent pro suu insignibus. Sed de gentu familiaq; vestra paterna antiquitate, dignitate, splendore, Maiorumq; vestrorum virtutibus malo, ut de Carthagine olim Salustius dixit, silere, quàm nimu pauca dicere.
units.tr: Finally, that your family is a shoot of the Franks is shown by no slight evidence: those same arms of yours, namely the halved loaves (which the Germans commonly call Weck, since the Phrygians too used that word, as Herodotus testifies), or, as others call them, pinnes. Such were, they report, the ancient arms of Charlemagne and of the Frankish people. Bavaria, and the family of Teck (which is also of Frankish origin), certainly bear whole loaves for their arms. But concerning your paternal family's ancient lineage, rank and splendour, and the virtues of your ancestors, I prefer, as Sallust once said of Carthage, to keep silent rather than say too little.

units.la: Quantum vero ad maternum vestrum genus, GEMMINGENSI VMnumirum (quod & ipsum multorum Heroum seminarium exstitit) attinet; illius quoq; tanta est claritas, tantumq; splendor in utriusq; Germania, ut, si quis il- lud laudibus illustrare conetur, u ipsi Soli, fonti omnu luminis, ut est in Prouebio, lumen adferre velle videatur.
units.tr: As for your maternal line, namely the Gemmingen family (which has itself been a nursery of many heroes), its brightness and splendour are so great throughout both Germanies that anyone who tries to illustrate it with praise would seem to be bringing light to the sun itself, the fountain of all light, as the proverb goes.

units.la: Secunda vero, viri Generosi & Amplissimi, quæ mihi, ut uos amandi & obseruandi: sic labores hosce meos glorioso potissimum vestro nomini inscribendi caussa fuit vestra Virtus. Virtute enim, ut rectè vereq; Cicero dixit, sic ut nihil est formosius, nihil pulchrius, nihil præstabilius: ita nihil amabilius. Virtus optima est efficacissimaq; amoris amicitiaq; conciliatrix: cuiusquidem tantavis est, ut ad hostes quoq; & inimicos nostros, in quibus illa conspiciatur, diligendos ac saspiciendos nos inuitet & alliciat. Hæc Nobilitatis, de qua paullo ante dixi, & genitrix est, & altrix atque nutrix: unde Nobilitatem Aristoteles definiuit generis virtutem: & quidam eam definiunt dignitatem generis; in quo maxime virtutes exstiterunt, vita communi salutares et fructuosa. Hinc Poeta illa: Nobilitas sola est & unica virtus.
units.tr: The second reason, distinguished gentlemen, which moved me to love and honour you, and which made your virtue the chief cause of my inscribing these labours of mine to your glorious name, is virtue. For virtue, as Cicero rightly and truly said, is such that nothing is more beautiful, nothing more splendid, nothing more excellent, and therefore nothing more lovable. Virtue is the best and most effective bringer together of love and friendship; indeed it is so great that it invites and draws us to love and esteem even our enemies and adversaries in whom it is seen. This is the mother, nurse and foster-mother of that nobility of which I spoke a little while ago. That is why Aristotle defined nobility as the virtue of a family, and some define it as the dignity of a family in which virtues have especially flourished, wholesome and profitable for common life. Hence that line of the poet: nobility alone is also the only virtue.

units.la: Non mirum igitur est, Romanos Virtutem olim, tanquam Deam coluisse, eiq; templum consecrasse, post quod erat Honoru templum: quo ipso situ significabant teste Plutarcho, nemini aditum ad Honorem, nisi per Virtutem patere. At nos Christiani Virtutem non Deam: sed Dei donū atq; munus esse credimus, contra impiam illam Ciceronu sententiam & orationem: ubi Virtutem, inquit, nemo nostrum acceptam Deo retulit; & recte. Propter Virtute enim iure laudamur, & in virtute gloriamur. De vestris
units.tr: It is no wonder, then, that the Romans once worshipped Virtue as a goddess and consecrated a temple to her, next to which stood a temple of Honour. By this very arrangement, as Plutarch tells us, they signified that no one has access to Honour except through Virtue. But we Christians believe that Virtue is not a goddess but the gift and bounty of God, against that impious opinion and saying of Cicero's, where he says that none of us has referred virtue to God as its source; and rightly so. For it is on account of virtue that we are justly praised, and in virtue that we glory. Concerning your

units.la: De vestru autem virtutibus, Generosi & Amplissimi viri, multa hoc tempore verba facere primum vester pariter meusq; pudor prohibet, ne vos, quasi in os laudando, adulatorem potius, quàm laudatorem agere videar. Deinde quod non tantum meum ingenii est, nec tanta mea est dicendi aut scribendi vu & facultas, qua inclytas virtutes vestras vel solum enumerare, nedu pro dignitate exornare possim. Hu adde, quód, ut vino or vendibili non opus est hedera: sic vestra virtutes nullius indigent laudatione atq; praeconio. Ipsa etenim, tanquam actuosa, seipsas laudant & praedicant, seq; in plurimu grauissimiuq; ve stru actionibus conspiciendas quotidie, atq; etiam imitandas praebent. Non enim Principes vestri illustrissimi: non etiam alii viri clari & illustres in rebus atq; negociis maximis momenti atq; ponderis, & ad publicam salutem dignitatemq; pertinentibus vestrá potissimum uterentur operá atq; ministerio: non, inquam, vobis tam honorifica quidem, augusta & magnifica, sed ardua valde, dissicilia atq; gravia imponerent munera quasiq; onera: nisi cognita probe perspectaq; illu esset vestra sapientia, prudentia, eloquentia, iustitia, fortitudo, temperantia, continentia, vigilantia, industria, fides, pietas & integritas: ac nisi vos hu & alii praclari virtutibus instructos tot tantiq; muneribus sustinendu ac tuendu pares esse persuasum exploratumq; haberent.
units.tr: Concerning your virtues, distinguished gentlemen, my own modesty and yours alike forbid me to say much about them at this time, lest I seem to be flattering you to your face rather than praising you. Besides, I have neither such talent nor such ability in speaking or writing that I could enumerate your famous virtues, let alone adorn them as they deserve. Add to this that, as wine that is good needs no ivy bush, so your virtues need no praise or proclamation. For they, being active, praise and proclaim themselves, and offer themselves daily to be seen, and even imitated, in your most serious and most numerous actions. For your most illustrious princes, and other famous and distinguished men, would not employ your help and service in matters of the greatest importance and weight that pertain to the public welfare and dignity, nor would they impose on you such honourable, august and splendid, yet very arduous, difficult and burdensome offices, unless your wisdom, prudence, eloquence, justice, fortitude, temperance, self-restraint, watchfulness, industry, faithfulness, piety and integrity had been well known and clearly perceived, and unless they were persuaded and certain that you and others like you, famous for such virtues, were equal to sustaining and discharging so many and such great duties.

units.la: Harum igitur vestrarum virtutum quasi theatrum quoddam est uniuersus Palatinatus, patriaque vestra charißima, seq; ille, tanquam palatium et campus quidam amplissimus: in quo virtutes hae vestrae egregiae quotidie excurrunt atq; conspiciuntur. Nec vero Palatinatus tantum, sed alia quoq; orbi Christiani partes virtutum vestrarum spectatrices adhuc fuerunt atq; testes propter peregrinationes, legationesq; vestras honorificentissimas, quas hinc inde ad Imperatores, ad Reges & ad Principes externos, in Gallia, Bohemia & Germania, ma imá cum vestrá laude obiistis.
units.tr: The whole Palatinate, your most beloved fatherland, is in a sense a theatre of these virtues of yours. It is like a palace and a broad field, where your outstanding virtues daily come forward and are seen. Nor is the Palatinate alone a witness to them. Other parts of the Christian world have also watched your virtues and borne witness to them, because of your most honourable journeys and embassies, which you have undertaken here and there to emperors, kings and foreign princes, in France, Bohemia and Germany, to your very great praise.

units.la: Sed & illa ipsa generosissima stirpu familiaq; vestra insignia, quae mihi semper ante mentu oculos obuersantur, cum Maiorum, tum vestra quoq; Nobilita tu pariter atq; virtutum symbola sunt insignia valde et illustria. Non temeré enim & promiscue olim (ut hodie pro seculi nostri more atque licentia fieri consueuit) sed singulari consilio atque iudicio huiusmodi scuta, insignia atque stemmata ab Imperatoribus, Regibus atque Principibus non nisi viris, virtutu rerum ἡ gestarū gloria florentibus optime ἡ de patria & genere humano, domi militi ἡ meritis, tanquam virtutum rerumq; gestarum praemia atq; monumenta perpetua tributa fuerunt atque concessa. Sic igitur ille ipse Canu, qui vestro suto insistit, exserta lingua suo quasi latratu atque clamore virtutes laudesq; ue ras canit quodammodo et decantat. Huius autem animalis imaginem non slum priscis seculis Alani, gens fortissima & bellicosissima, sed etiam hodie nobili simae et uetustissime quedá familia, ut Delfeldensium, Heussensteinorum, atque ad o Comitum quoq; Teccensium, Zollerensium, Ottingensium, pro suis habent im nibus. Est autem Canis in sacris & profanis litteris & prudentia, solertia atque vigacitatis, & fortitudinis, & vigilantiae, & denique fidei atque charitatis symbolum: quae virtutes quoniam in iis, quae vel sacra, vel profana munera gerunt & administrant, maxime requiruntur: idcirco idem animal apud Aegyptios, ⟨ɛ⟩ iudicis, ⟨ɛ⟩ magistratum, ⟨ɛ⟩ vatu, ⟨ɛ⟩ scribae sacri quam maxima ad pudeos erat dignitas hieroglyphica. Pra cateru autem virtutibus in Canibus maxima solet esse admirationi illorum fides atq; charitas erga dominos et amicos: unde Plinius: Fidelissimi, inquit, ante omnia (animalia) hominis Canes ⟨ɛ⟩ Equi: ubi etiam multa admiranda, imo stupenda fidelitatis canum erga dominos suos exempla recensent. Sic etiam inter omnes vestras virtutes nulla ut rarior (hoc praesertim nostro seculo, perfidia et infidelitatus plenissimo) ita pra clarior est, quam vestra erga patriam, tanquam matrem vestram charissima, patriaq; vestra patres, hoc est, Principes ac Dominos vestros illustrissimos, constantissima fides atque pietas. Sed nimis imprudenter forsan facio, quasi falcem in alienam immittens segetem, insignibus hisce vestris explicandis nimis diu immoror, cum CASPARVS VVASERVS, lingua Hebraea apud nos doctor publicus, illa elegantissimo carmine descripserit, ⟨ɛ⟩ suis quasi coloribus de pinxerit: quae vir vobis probe notus propter eximiam multarum linguarum, artium disciplinarumq; liberalium scientiam, ⟨ɛ⟩ rerum multarum, quam Germanicus, Belgicus, Sabaudicus, Anglicus, Scoticus, Hibernicus et Italicus suo peregrinationibus consecutus est, experientiam, magno patriae nostrae cæpit esse usui ⟨ɛ⟩ ornamento.
units.tr: Your family's most noble arms, which always stand before my eyes, both those of your ancestors and your own, are most distinguished symbols of both your nobility and your virtues. For formerly such shields, arms and coats of arms were not granted rashly or indiscriminately, as is commonly done today according to the custom and licence of our age. They were granted by emperors, kings and princes with singular counsel and judgement, only to men who flourished in virtue and the glory of their deeds, and who had deserved well of their country and the human race at home and in war. They were bestowed as rewards and as perpetual monuments of virtues and deeds performed. Thus the dog that stands on your shield, its tongue thrust out, sings and, as it were, chants your virtues and praises with its barking and shouting. The image of this animal was used as a device not only in ancient times by the Alani, a very brave and warlike people, but even today by very noble and most ancient families, such as those of Delfeld and Heussenstein, and also by the counts of Teck, Zollern and Oettingen, who have it as their own arms. In sacred and profane letters the dog is a symbol of prudence, shrewdness, watchfulness, strength, vigilance, and finally of faith and charity. Since these virtues are chiefly required in those who perform and administer sacred or profane offices, for this reason the same animal was held in the highest honour among the Egyptians as a hieroglyph for judges, magistrates, prophets and sacred scribes. Among the other virtues of dogs, their faith and affection towards their masters and friends is usually the greatest object of admiration. Hence Pliny: "Of all animals, the most faithful to man," he says, "are dogs and horses." There they also recount many wonderful, indeed astonishing, examples of the fidelity of dogs towards their masters. So too among all your virtues, none is as rare (especially in our age, so full of perfidy and faithlessness), yet none is more distinguished than your constant faith and devotion towards your fatherland, which is like your dearest mother, and towards your fathers, that is, your most illustrious princes and lords. But perhaps I am acting too imprudently, putting my sickle into another's crop, in lingering so long over the explanation of your arms. CASPAR WASER, public teacher of the Hebrew language among us, has already described them in most elegant verse and painted them, as it were, in his own colours. This man is well known to you for his outstanding knowledge of many languages, arts and liberal disciplines, and for the experience he gained through his travels in Germany, Belgium, Savoy, England, Scotland, Ireland and Italy. He has begun to be of great use and ornament to our fatherland.

units.la: Inter alias autem virtutes laudesque vestras, ut ad vos redeam, hæc fere iam propria clarissima splendidissimaque vestra familiae laus est, quod cum generis vestri splendore, cum civili, politico et militari quoque vitae vestrae gerere ⟨ɛ⟩ instituto, ut etiam reliqui vestri fratres, Musarum, hoc est, linguarum ⟨ɛ⟩ artium disciplinarumque ingenuarum ac liberalium studia vebu consungenda duxistis. Multorum hodie animi stulta stoldaque hoc opinione sunt imbuti, ut Musas atque litteras Regibus, Principibus, virusque nobilibus ac politicis fraudi magis, quam laudi ⟨ɛ⟩ dedecori potius, quam decori · denique damno potius ⟨ɛ⟩ impedimento, quam usui ⟨ɛ⟩ adiumento, ad munera juna, pacis bellique temporibus, bene ac feliciter administranda, esse arbitrentur. Verum insanam, barbarorum ac brutorum istorum hominum opinionem omnes omnium fere gentium historiae refellunt ac refutant, quae manifeste testantur, nobilissimos ⟨ɛ⟩ generosissimos quosque viros: immo ipsos Reges, Imperatores ac Principes potentissimos ⟨ɛ⟩ celeberrimos in studia artium atque scientiarum liberalium omnibus animi viribus incubuisse, in plurimum fuisse delectatos, iuq; tanquam admirandum ⟨ɛ⟩ fabulidus optimum, multos doctos res admiratione praedicationeq; perpetuo dignissimas gestisse, ⟨ɛ⟩ Republicas, regna ⟨ɛ⟩ imperia fuanon domi solum ⟨ɛ⟩ in pace optime felicissime gubernasse ac cum feruasse, sed etiam bellica sua virtute amplificasse, ⟨ɛ⟩ longe late propagasse.
units.tr: Among your other virtues and praises, to return to you, this is almost already the particular, most bright and splendid praise of your family: that, along with the splendour of your birth and your civil, political and military way of life, you have also judged that the studies of the Muses, that is, of languages, arts and the liberal and gentlemanly disciplines, should be pursued together. Today the minds of many are imbued with the foolish and stupid opinion that the Muses and letters are a source of deceit rather than praise for kings, princes, and noble and political men; that they are a disgrace rather than an ornament, a loss rather than a help; and that they hinder rather than aid the good and successful performance of their duties in times of peace and war. But the histories of almost all nations refute and confute this insane opinion of these barbarous and brutish men. They clearly testify that the most noble and generous men, indeed kings, emperors and the most powerful and renowned princes themselves, have devoted all the powers of their minds to the study of the arts and liberal sciences, have greatly delighted in them, and, as something admirable and most excellent, have accomplished many things worthy of perpetual admiration and praise from learned men. They have governed and preserved their commonwealths, kingdoms and empires most well and happily, not only at home in peace, but also by their martial virtue have enlarged them and spread them far and wide.

units.la: Verissime igitur Platonis, Philosophorum facile princeps, non dubitavit ac firmare, eas demum Respublicas felices esse ac beatas, quae a Philosophis regantur vel quorum rectores ac moderatores philosophi sunt. Unde Alphonsus, illamus ille Rex Aragonum, cum quendam audiuisset dicentem, Principem literas non decere, exclamasse fertur: Bovu, non hominis illam esse vocem. Ad quemadmodum Diogenes olim hominem opulentum, qui litterarum rudis fit ⟨ɛ⟩ imperitus, ἀγυνόμνορος esse, quem aureum ⟨ɛ⟩ gestantem vellus: Socrates autem mancipium tipium aureum appellauit: sic nos talem hominem idolum, seu simulacrum aut reum vere appellabimus: quo etiā nomine vernacula nostra lingua vuleo hoc minem stolidum ac stupidum vocitamus. Nā quemadmodū idolum aureum, assabre pꝛæsertim artificioseq; effictum & elaboratum, speciosissimam quidem vel Dei, vel hominu alicuius speciem pꝛæse ferticum nihil vel diuinitatis, vel humanitatis in se contineat: sic multos videre licet passim homines diuitiis & opibus abundantes, qui magnifica pompa sese inferunt, ac splendidissimo corpore habitu atq; cultu hominum oculos ita perstringunt, ut quasi Du quidā esse viu deantur: qui tamē, cum artium disciplinarumq; liberalium non modo sint ignari, sed etiā ab iis abhorreāt, uel ipsis idolis stupidiores merito uiliores q; sunt censendi.
units.tr: Therefore Plato, easily the prince of philosophers, did not hesitate to affirm most truly that those commonwealths are happy and blessed which are ruled by philosophers, or whose rulers and governors are philosophers. Hence Alfonso, that famous king of Aragon, when he had heard someone say that letters were not becoming to a prince, is said to have exclaimed: "That is the voice of an ox, not of a man." Just as Diogenes once called a wealthy man who was unlearned and untaught a donkey carrying gold, and Socrates called him a golden image, so we shall truly call such a man an idol, or a simulacrum, or a mere figure. In our own vernacular we also call such a man a dolt and a blockhead. For just as a golden idol, skilfully and artfully fashioned and wrought, presents a most splendid image of God or of some man, yet contains nothing of divinity or humanity in itself, so one may see many men everywhere abounding in riches and wealth. They make a magnificent display and dazzle the eyes of men with their splendid bearing, dress and manner, so that they seem to be some kind of gods. Yet since they are not only ignorant of the arts and liberal disciplines but even shun them, they are rightly judged more stupid than idols and more worthless.

units.la: Quam utilu autem, immo necessaria sit Principi ad bene regendā Rempu blicam doctrina atq; eruditio Plutarchus, qui Philosophus fuit, peculiarium ea de reconscripto libro egregie demonstrauit. Ide Cicero in aurea ele gantissimaq; illa sua oratione pro Archia Poeta, antiquu pꝛæstantissimorum & celeberrimorum Regum, Imperatorum atq; Principum Reipubl. Romana, atq; etiam aliorum testimonia & exemplu comprobauit. Sed, ut exemplorum antiquorum, quorum pleuas sunt omnes historiæ, cōmemoratione super sedeam, nostra quidem hac aetate palma in hoc laudu genere videtur deferenda. Principibus Palatinis quorum non Academia solum atq; Scholæ, sed Aulæ quoq; vi ru eruditissimi, liberalissimiq; studia assiduunt. Viru enim doctu atq; litterati plurimum delectantur, illoru familiaritate, consuetudine atq; colloquiis magna cum voluptate fruuntur, illorum potissimum opera atq; consilio in legationibus, & quibusuis vel difficillimis muneribus & actionibus utuntur, illos liberalis sime munificentissime q; foueunt, alunt, honoribus ac dignitatibus augent atque or nant, ut quottidiana testatur experientia.
units.tr: How useful, indeed how necessary, learning and erudition are for a prince in governing the commonwealth well, Plutarch, who was himself a philosopher, has admirably demonstrated in his special book on this subject. Cicero, in his golden and most elegant speech for the poet Archias, confirmed the same by the testimonies and examples of the most excellent and renowned kings, emperors and princes of the Roman commonwealth, and of others. But, to pass over the recollection of ancient examples, of which all histories are full, in our own age the palm in this kind of praise seems due to the Palatine princes. Their academy and schools, and also their courts, are full of the most learned and most liberal men who pursue the studies. For these princes take great delight in learned and literary men and enjoy their familiarity, companionship and conversation with great pleasure. They use their work and counsel especially in embassies and in all kinds of the most difficult offices and business. They cherish, nourish, honour and adorn them most generously and munificently with dignities, as daily experience attests.

units.la: Præalui autem quasi lumen quoddam atq; columen Reipub litterariæ hisce nostru temporibus appellare possumus illustrissimum Principem ac Dominum, Dn. IOHANNEM, Bipontinum Ducem, qui & ipse est litteratissimus, & in hi storiis pꝛæsertim versatus, & Scholas in sua ditione, omnium q; artium & scientiarum doctores munificentissime foueat, & bibliotheca habet optimorum librorum suppelleētile instructissimam, & filios deniq; suos, tanquam carissima sua pignora, ab ipsis quasi incunabulis cum pietate & religione, tum linguu litterariq; humanioribus diligentissime curat informari atq; institui, adhibita ad id doctis simorum quorumq; virorum opera. Aulam itaq; illam vere cum pietatis atq; religionis, tum litterarum disciplinarumq; liberalium gymnasium atq; scholam dixerimus. Similis fere de MAVRITIO, illustrissimo Hlassiæ Principe, littera tissimi doctissimiq; patris gloriosissima memoria filio doctissimo & litteratissi mo, fama est, laudis atque gloriæ plenissima. Tales Principes suo exemplo lau dabilimo erroris atq; mendacii aperte conuincunt omnes eos, qui doctrinam atque eruditionem a viro principe, nobili, politico ac militari alienam esse, eosq; minime docere existimant.
units.tr: Among these, one may call the most illustrious prince and lord, Lord JOHN, Duke of Zweibrücken, a kind of light and pillar of the literary commonwealth in our times. He is himself most learned, especially versed in history, and most munificently favours the schools in his territory and the teachers of all arts and sciences. He has a library furnished with a very rich supply of the best books. Finally, he diligently takes care that his sons, as his dearest pledges, are trained and instructed from their very cradle, both in piety and religion and in languages and the humane letters, employing the work of the most learned men for this purpose. We may therefore rightly call that court a gymnasium and school of piety and religion as well as of letters and the liberal disciplines. There is a similar report, full of praise and glory, about MAURICE, most illustrious prince of Hesse, a most learned and literate son of a most learned and literate father of glorious memory. Such princes, by their example, clearly convict of error and falsehood all those who think that learning and erudition are foreign to a prince, a noble, a politician or a soldier, and who believe that such men should in no way be taught.

units.la: Est igitur ut ad vos redeam, Generosi & Amplssimi viri, quod maximas cum Deo immortali, tu Principib. nestris illustrissimis, cū patri nestro beatæ memoria, agatu (g) habeatu gratias, qui nullu parcendo vel curu atq laboribu, v. lfumptibu, vos catero q fratres vestros ab meunte atate,domi foru, omnilinguarum, doctrinarum, difciplinarumq talium genere excolu atq exornari curauit, ut Patria ac Principibus veftru illuftriffimu magno aliquando pof-fetu esse emolumento simul (y) ornamento. Qua quidem spes ip/um minime fefellit, ita ut operam fumptuq suos non perdiderit, sed optime collocarit. Nam adearum potissimum artium difciplinarumq studium vos applicaftis, quibus instrucți Patria (y) Principibus veftru illuftriffimu nunc maximu cum summa vestra laude adfertu fructu : nec vos ita litteri abdidistis, ut nihil possitis ex hu ad communem adferre utilitatem (y) in lucem afpectumq proferre.
units.tr: It remains, therefore, for me to return to you, noble and most distinguished gentlemen, and to give the greatest thanks to the immortal God, to your most illustrious princes, and to your father of blessed memory. Sparing neither care, labour nor expense, he saw to it that you and your other brothers were educated from your earliest youth, at home and abroad, in all languages, learning and disciplines of this kind, so that you might one day be of great benefit and ornament to your country and your illustrious princes. This hope did not disappoint him in the least; he did not waste his effort and expense but invested them well. For you have devoted yourselves especially to those arts and disciplines by which, being equipped, you now bring the greatest fruit to your country and your illustrious princes, to your own great praise. Nor have you so buried yourselves in your studies that you cannot bring anything from them into the light and view of the common good.

units.la: Ac patru quidem vestri, beata memoria, quoniam hic a me fada est memorio, laudes eius nequaquam sunt silentio pratermittenda: quarum hac no est minima, quod xl. fere annorum spatio quattuor Electoribus Palatinis, (y) VVOLFGANGO Principi Palatino Bipontino, illustrissimae memoria Principibus domi militiaq (Militauit enim in Vngaria sub FRIDERICO, Principe Palatino, Germanici exercitus ductore) honorificentiffimu fuuctus muneribus, tanta inseruiuit fide atque diligentia, ut sibi fuuq perpetuam pepererit gloriam. Sed vita, morum, virtutum rerumq gestarum eius quasi compendium quoddam est egregium (y) elegans illud Epitaphium, quod in templo Birckens heimenfi (ubi in Maiorum suorum monumentu sepultus iacet) ad perpetuam eius nominis memoriam fixum est, atque legitur; quod mihi hic fubiuciena duxi putaui. Hac terra requiesco, fatus genitore PHILIPPO, VVOLFGA Q S VVAMBOLDT: quifiemmate dicorabvm stat. Inelytan arer erat Dvrnensis gloria stirpis. Gnaru iterque parens statim puerisbus annis Moribus institui me jbisir, & arte poli Crescebam pietate & oc itate paterna. Deinde Palatinus claram FRIDERICV in Aulam, Iudicium mirans juvenile, recepit & auxit Me variis donis. Tunc Marte valente feroces Me duxit contra Turcas ubi fortis rmis Pugnabam. Tandem victrici Marte reverso ANNA thoro mihi juncta fuit d minima nata De GEMMINGENSI praeclara stirpe, ipo avit Deinde LVDOIVS, FRIDERI s Magnus & OTTO HENRICVS: necnon FRIDERI tertius Heros, A me Dueatus perfecta negotia mu ti. Summa Palatinae VVOLFE gloria stirpis Aux ioq meo est fretus. Nam rebus amplis Iuft eram simili poe simili e favore Afficiebantur fine fuco. C & Iesus. Multa tu vici, Christ e,cunda,rel is Sex Natis, Patris q la exemplafequuntur. Hos decorat pietas,innataque gloria summis Principibus chari, omm ffa negotia tractant. In coelis merces latitat: victrici tandem Dona reportabunt, elhgia nostra sequentes. In lacrymis natu lacrymarum in valle morabar: In lacrymis Mundi mortalia funera clausi. Quid reauror? Vella vice nunc exsulto triumphans,
units.tr: As for your father of blessed memory, since I have mentioned him here, his praises must by no means be passed over in silence. Not the least of them is that for nearly forty years he served four Electors Palatine and the illustrious Prince Wolfgang of Pfalz-Zweibrücken, and held honourable offices at court and in war (for he served in Hungary under Frederick, Count Palatine, leader of the German army). He served with such faith and diligence that he won for himself and his house lasting glory. But a kind of excellent and elegant summary of his life, character, virtues and deeds is that epitaph, which is fixed and read in the church at Birkenfeld (where he lies buried in the tomb of his ancestors) in perpetual memory of his name. I thought it fitting to add it here: Here I rest, the son of Philip and Wolfgang Wambolt, who in his own time was of an ancient line. My family was the glory of Dürn. Taught by a wise and careful father from my boyhood, I was trained in good morals and in the arts of war, and I grew in piety and in the zeal of a father's care. Then the Palatine Frederick received me into his famous court, admiring my youthful judgement, and advanced me with various gifts. Then, when Mars was strong, he led me, a fierce fighter, against the Turks, where I fought bravely in arms. At last, Mars returning victorious, I was joined in marriage to Anna, a daughter of the famous house of Gemmingen. After her came Ludwig, Frederick the Great, and Otto Henry, and also the third hero Frederick, to whom I carried out the business of the duchy perfectly. The glory of the Palatine Wolfgang's line rested on my support, for I was held in high esteem and favour by great men, without pretence. Christ and Jesus, you have conquered many things; six sons and a father's example follow you. Piety adorns them, and glory innate to the highest princes, dear to all, they handle affairs. Their reward lies hidden in heaven; following our elegy, they will at last bring back victory's gifts. I dwelt as a child of tears in the valley of tears; I shut away mortal burials in the tears of the world. Why do I grieve? Now in turn I exult triumphant,
Angelic

units.la: Angelicâ laetus post mille pericla phalange, Aspecstâque fruor sancto solamine Christi.
units.tr: Joyful with the angelic host after a thousand dangers, and I enjoy the sight and holy solace of Christ.

units.la: Harum paternarum virtutum cum vos strenui sitis & fideles imitatores, qui vos non amore & obseruantia merito complectendos summis laudibus effe-rendos censeat? O felicem igitur vestrum patrem, qui tales vos post se reliquit filios, paterna nimirum & auita virtutu imitatores & cultores strenuos! O vos felices filios, qui talem habuistis patre, virum scilicet immortali laude dignifsimum, unde omnium virtutum exempla vobis liceat petere!
units.tr: Since you are vigorous and faithful imitators of these paternal virtues, who would not think you worthy of love and respect and deserving of the highest praise? O happy father, then, who left behind him such sons, surely imitators and vigorous cultivators of paternal and ancestral virtues! O you happy sons, who had such a father, a man most worthy of immortal praise, from whom you may draw examples of every virtue!

units.la: Non minor est virtus, quam quaerere parta tueri: inquit Poeta ille. Maxima igitur haec vestra est virtus, & maxima laus, ab omnibus merito praedicanda, quod & Nobilitatis & virtutis, & nominis atq; gloriae patrimonium atque hereditatem, vobis a parentibus & Maiorib[us] vestris, per longa annorum seriem, relictam atq; traditam non retinere solum atq; conseruare, verum etiam augere atq; amplificare egregiu uestris uirtutibus, & ad liberos atq; posteros uestros trāsmittere ac propagare seduló studetu. Si enim laude dignissimi sunt, quā pecuniarũ patrimonia sibi a parentib. suis reliĉta nō modo seruant atq; tuentur, verum etiā honestis artib.augent & amplificant (ut contrā vituperatione grauissimam illi merentur, qui suâ uel neglIgentiā & incuriā, uelprodigalitate atq; luxuria patrimonia sua perdunt & amittunt, liberiq; suis as alienu, & paupere tatem ignominiosissimâ relinquunt:) quanto maiori laude digni sunt ii, qui virtutu, laudu atq; gloriā patrimonii (quod lautissimis & locupletissimis quibusq; pecuniarū patrimonio atq; thesauri loge est pretiosis) suis uirtutib. facilq; egre giū nō solum seruant, sed etiā id magna auctu cumulatumq; accessione liberiū posteriq; suis relinquunt ac tradunt? Atq; haec quoq; sunt pia, religiosaq; uestra susta atq; parētalia, quae parentib. Maioribus uestris facitu assiduē, dum nimirum laudabile gloriosamq; illoru memoriam, quam nulla unquā delebit obliuio, constanti uirtutu ipsorū imitatione, quasi refricare assiduē & innouare conamini.
units.tr: "It is no less a virtue to keep what has been won than to seek it," says that poet. This, then, is your greatest virtue and greatest praise, rightly proclaimed by all: that you not only keep and preserve, but also strive diligently to increase and enlarge by your own virtues, and to pass on and propagate to your children and descendants, the patrimony and inheritance of nobility, virtue, name and glory, handed down and left to you by your parents and ancestors through a long series of years. For if those are worthy of praise who not only keep and guard the money-patrimony left them by their parents, but also increase and enlarge it by honest arts, (just as those deserve the gravest reproach who, through their own negligence and carelessness, or through prodigality and luxury, lose and squander their patrimony, leaving their children burdened with debt and in most shameful poverty), how much greater praise do they deserve who, by their own virtues, easily keep and not only keep but also hand down to their children and posterity this patrimony of virtue, praise and glory, which is more precious than any wealthy and abundant money-patrimony or treasure, and increase it with great accession? And these too are your pious and dutiful rites, your parental observances, which you perform for your ancestors constantly, since you strive, by the steady imitation of their virtues, to refresh and renew as it were the praiseworthy and glorious memory of them, which no oblivion will ever destroy.

units.la: Tertia porrō ut iuste debitaq; mea ergā uos, Viri generosi & amplifs,beneuoe lentiæ & obseruantiæ: sicnuncupationu huiusce mea caussa est uestra dignitas, uester honos atq; gloria, qua Deus uos ornauit. Hoc enim ipsa pietatis, æquitatis iustitiaq; ratio postulat, ut eos, quos Deus in excesso & sublimi dignitatis potestatisq; loco collocauit, amore, honore & obseruantia prosequamur: quos etiā ipse suo dignatur nomine, eos ח ח ח Aelohim, id est, Deos appellādo, Vobis aut Deus prouestris uirtutibus, quæ & ipse gratuita eius dona sunt atq; munera, uiā aditumq; ad maximos honores atq; dignitates patefecit, uosq; Casarum, Regū atq; Principū officiarios, sosilarios, aulamagistros, legatos, oratores, uicarios et pro principes costituit, quod nemo, quantūuis inuidus atq; maleuolus inficiari potest. In his ipsis autē summis uestris dignitatib. & honorib. qui magnos plæriq; hominib. spiritus afferut, eosq; arrogantes & insolentes reddūt, maximæ veræq; Christiane uestræ cernūtur uirtutes. Easunt, humilitas, humanitas, modestia, facielitas, lenitas, comitas ac benignitas uestra, quæ quidē uirtutes uos merito quibus uis amabiles carosq; reddunt, Vos etenim uitæ rerumq; humanarū imbecillitatis, fragilitatis, ac uicissitudinis perpetuæ memores; memores etiam Christianæ imprimis pietatis, quo in maiori dignitatis gradu estis positi, tato humiliores vos
units.tr: Thirdly, as is justly owed from me to you, noble and most distinguished gentlemen, of goodwill and respect: this dedication has as its cause your dignity, your honour and glory, with which God has adorned you. For the very reason of piety, equity and justice demands that we pursue with love, honour and respect those whom God has placed in a high and exalted position of dignity and power; those whom he himself deigns to call by his own name, calling them Elohim, that is, gods. And God has opened the way and access to the greatest honours and dignities for you, through your virtues, which are themselves his free gifts and benefits, and has appointed you officers, stewards, court masters, envoys, orators, vicars and even princes of Caesars, kings and princes, which no one, however envious and ill-disposed, can deny. In these very high dignities and honours of yours, which bring great pride to most men and make them arrogant and insolent, your greatest and truest Christian virtues are seen: your humility, humanity, modesty, affability, gentleness, courtesy and kindness. These virtues rightly make you lovable and dear to everyone. For you, mindful of the weakness, frailty and constant change of human life and affairs, and mindful above all of Christian piety, the higher the rank of dignity in which you are placed, the more humble and modest you conduct yourselves.

units.la: modestioresq; geritis, ac non modo nemine mprae vobis cotemnitis atq; despicitis, verum etiam, patris vestri, piae memoria, exemplo {&} imitatione, ad quibusuis vel infime fortunae hominibus ac peregrinis, pauperib. vidui, pupillis gratificandum, commodandi, operam, ope, confilioq; vestro subueniendi propensi semper estis {&} parati: quo pacto firma stabilemq; non ab hominibus solum, sed ab ipso Deo in situ gratiam. Nam quemadmodum inter omnes diuinas virtutes nulla Deo quasi magis est propria, quam Clementia {&} Misericordia: sic nulla virtute, quam hac ipsa homines propius ad Dei similitudinem accedunt, eiusq; gratiam sibi facilius {&} efficacius conciliant.
units.tr: Not only do you despise and look down upon no one, but also, following the example and imitation of your father of blessed memory, you are always inclined and ready to oblige, to lend, and to help with your work, resources and counsel any people, even those of the humblest fortune, strangers, the poor, widows and orphans. In this way you gain firm and stable favour not only from men, but from God himself. For just as among all the divine virtues none is more proper to God than clemency and mercy, so by no other virtue do men come closer to the likeness of God, and more easily and effectively win his favour for themselves.

units.la: Postremo, me, ut ad vos magnopere amandos {&} colendos sic ad lucubratio nem hanc meam nouam vobis potissimum dicandam quasi consecrandam incitauit ac impulit singularis vestra erga me, Meosq; amor atq; fauor, quae quidem multis magnisq; vestris in nos beneficiis satis declarastis. Nec enim me tantum, sed etiam fratrem meum charissimum, SEBASTIANVM nomine (quem Deus superiori anno, IV.KL. Mart. ex hu terris, {&} ex Altofladiana illa praefectura ad se {&} ad superas caelestes, illas suas sedes euocauit) eximia quadam humanitate, benevolentia ac beneficentia per annos aliquot est prosecuti: quo certe nomine me Meosq; plurimum vobis deuinctos {&} obstrictos, atque adeo tos in are vestro esse conspicor.
units.tr: Finally, it was your singular goodwill towards me and my family, and your love and favour, which greatly moved me to dedicate to you, as it were consecrate, this new work of mine, to love and honour you, and which you have sufficiently shown by your many great kindnesses to us. For you have shown exceptional kindness, benevolence and generosity over several years not only to me but also to my dearest brother, named Sebastian, whom God called last year, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, from this earth and from that Altdorf prefecture to himself and to the heavenly heights, those his seats. Truly, by this I see that I and my family are very much bound and obliged to you, and indeed that we are in your debt.

units.la: Huc accedit singularis vestra nō erga me Meosq; tatum, sed etiam erga uniuersam patriam meam charissimam charitas, quam cum alius signis, tum eo certe manifestissime declarastis, quod unus vestrum, tu nimirum, VVOLFGANGE generose, cum familia tua in illa migrare, {&} sedem domiciliumq; tuum in illa figere atq; collocare non dubitauisti. Selegisti autem tu tibi locum ad habitandum in amplissimo nostro Comitatu Turgoiensi, non obscurum {&} ignobile, sed antiquissimum {&} clarissimum, quae antiquitus a Romanis, bellis in his nostris oris gerentibus, cultu {&} habitatu fuisse cum Annales nostri, cum prater alia oppidi agri illius antiqua rudera atq; vestigia, plurima, quae quotidie fere ibi effodiuntur atq; reperiuntur, numismata Romana arca {&} argentea, tum denique ipsum oppidi agri illius nomen PFINAD FINES antiquitus dictum, clarissime testatur. Hic idem locus adhuc nobilissimarum {&} elarissimarum quarumq; familiarum sedes fuit. Quoniam autem inter Palatinatum {&} Heluetiam, hoc est, inter vestram meamq; patriam per multos annos egregia intercessit necessitudo {&} amicitia, multisofficiis utrinq; culta, diuinitus profectio nunc accidit, ut tu, generose {&} amplissime, Dn. VVOLFGANGE, hac tua migratione in nostram patriam, hoc tuo incolatu: sed inprimis tua pietate, iustitia, aequitate, benignitate et que beneficentia, qua tua iurisdictionis hominibus praefuisti adhuc, {&} profuisti, plurimum antiquam illam tuam noftraq; patria necessitudinem {&} amicitiam tuendi atq; fouendi optimam nactus sis occasionem.
units.tr: Moreover, your singular affection is not only for me and mine but also for my most dear fatherland as a whole. You have declared this by many signs, and most plainly by this: one of you, you indeed, noble Wolfgang, did not hesitate to migrate with your family into that land and to fix and establish your home and dwelling there. You chose for your residence a place in our most ample county of Thurgau, not obscure or ignoble but most ancient and most renowned. Our annals attest that in former times the Romans inhabited and cultivated it while waging war in these our regions. Besides other ancient ruins and traces of the town and its fields, very many Roman coins of bronze and silver are dug up and found there almost every day, and the very name of that town and district, once called PFINAD, FINES, clearly bears witness to this. The same place was also the seat of the most noble and most distinguished families. Since a remarkable bond and friendship, cherished by many mutual services, has existed for many years between the Palatinate and Helvetia, that is, between your country and mine, it has now come about by divine providence that you, noble and most ample Sir Wolfgang, through this migration of yours into our country and this residence of yours, and above all through your piety, justice, equity, kindness and beneficence, by which you have hitherto presided over and benefited the people under your jurisdiction, have found the best opportunity to preserve and foster that ancient bond and friendship of yours with our fatherland.

units.la: Propter has igitur commemoratas causas, {&} inprimis propter summam ac prope singularem vestram cum erga uniuersam meam patriam charissimam, tum erga me Meosq; benevolentiam ac beneficetiam nouum hoc meum opusculum sub honorifico gloriosoq; vestro nomine in publicum, lucemq; prodire volui, ut hoc qualicunque argumento, etsi non referenda, at saltem predicanda publice gratia gratam memoremq; vicissim meam in vos voluntatem & animum, amoru obferuantiaq; erga vos plenissimum declararem. Non me quidem fallit, quam opus hoc meum sit exiguum, & quam minime non motto vestra dignitati, doctrina atque iudicio, sed etiam incredibili meo erga vos studio & obseruantia respondeat. Sed non debent, qui magna praestare nequeunt, parua negligere, & qui magna merita atque beneficia magnu muneribus remunerare nequeunt, ob id etiam in parua & leuioribus muneribus apud eos, quibus plurimum debent, collocandus negligentes esse: praesertim cum in omni officii genere pluris animi voluntas, quam in muneris magnitudo sit facienda. Quemadmodu igitur (ut illa Plinii verbi & simili, operi huic meo accommodato, utar) Duo olim cre debantur non minus propitii, imo etiam placatiores lacte, aut mola falsa, quam ture supplicantibus: sic vos quoq; generosi & amplissimi viri, [pero pro incredibili vestra humanitate, & natura ingeniq; bonitate, proq; eximia vestra erga me beneuolentia, hoc tenue & exiguum meum munusculum, vestra licet dignis tate longe inferius: at ex animo, dignitatu vestra amantissimo profectum, non minus beneuolu animu acceptur, ac si amplum esset atque splendidum. Cogitabitis etiam liberalitatem non in dando tantum, sed etiam in accipiendo confistere, nec minus splendidu & magnificum iudicari, parua & exigua hilariter accipere, quam interdum magna dare. Id exemplo ARTAXERXIS, maximi potentissimi Persarum Regis, cui Mvvaus, id est, MEMOR, fuit cognomentum, Plutarchus docet. Nullum enim huic tam paruum afferebatur unquam munus, quin id libenti alacriq; animo acciperet. Quod vos quoque facturos, & qualecunque hoc meum scriptum aequi boniq; con/ulturos, vestra fretus humanitate persuasum habeo. Sed ut scribendi grauisimasq; vestras occupationes interpellandi finem faciam, rogo vos maximu in modum, ut me Mcosq;, ut adhuc fe ciftu, humanitati, beneuolentiae fideliq; vestr a commendatos semper habeatis.
units.tr: For these reasons, then, and above all because of your great and almost unique affection and goodwill, both toward my most dear fatherland as a whole and toward me and mine, I wished to bring this new little work of mine out into public light under your honoured and glorious name. In this way, though I cannot repay you with words, at least I may publicly proclaim my gratitude and, in return, show you my grateful and mindful will and spirit, full of love and devotion toward you. I am certainly not unaware of how small this work of mine is, and how far it falls short of your dignity, learning and judgement, and of my own great zeal and devotion toward you. But those who cannot render great services ought not to neglect small ones, and those who cannot repay great merits and benefits with great gifts should not, for that reason, be negligent in offering small and lighter gifts to those to whom they owe so much. This is especially so, since in every kind of duty the willingness of the mind counts for more than the size of the gift. Therefore, to borrow Pliny's words and comparison, which suit my present work: long ago, the gods were thought to be no less propitiated, indeed even more placated, by milk or salted meal than by incense offered by those who prayed to them. So you too, noble and most ample sirs, out of your incredible courtesy, your natural goodness of character and your remarkable kindness toward me, will receive this slight and small little gift of mine, though it is far below your worthiness, with no less goodwill than if it were large and splendid, since it comes from the heart and is most affectionately dedicated to your dignity. You will also consider that liberality consists not only in giving but also in receiving, and that to accept small and meagre gifts cheerfully is judged no less generous and magnificent than sometimes to give large ones. Plutarch teaches this by the example of Artaxerxes, the greatest and most powerful king of the Persians, whose surname was Mnemon, that is, Mindful. For no gift, however small, was ever brought to him that he did not receive with a willing and cheerful mind. I am persuaded, trusting in your courtesy, that you too will do the same and will receive this writing of mine, whatever it may be, with a fair and kindly judgement. But to bring to an end my interruption of your weighty occupations, I earnestly beg you to keep me and mine, as you have done hitherto, commended to your courtesy, goodwill and faithful favour always.

units.la: Postremo precor toto pectore non lanum, nescio quem bicipitem ac bifrontem (quem annorum atq; temporum praesidem [superstitio]fa finxit Antiquitas:) sed Christum Θεανθρωπον, qui unica tæli atq; salutis nostrae ianua simulefta atq; ianitor: ut annum hunc ineuntem nouum, qui tribus istis prodigiosis, Solis Lunaq; defectibus, ne/cio quae nobu mala (quae Deus pro sua misericordia auertat) portendere videtur, vobis familiaq; vestrae ornatissimae bene fortunet: vobu diuturnam adhuc vita huiusce mortalu usura largiatur, quo diutius patria vestra, pro laudabilissimo vestro more, atque cofuetudine inseruire atq; prodesse possit: vos deniq; post arumnosam, caducam, fragilemq; hanc vitam caeleftu, aeterna acbeatissima illius vita, quam sua nobu morte peperit, participes reddat. Amen. Tiguri. Kalend. Ianuar. Anno salutis ⸿ ɔ. ɩɔ. XCVIII.
units.tr: Finally, I pray with my whole heart, not to Janus, that two-faced and double-headed figure whom antiquity imagined as the guardian of years and times, but to Christ, [Theanthropos] God-man, who is both the one gate and the doorkeeper of our life and salvation, that he may bless you and your most distinguished family in this new year now beginning. It seems to portend some new evils (which God, in his mercy, turn away) by those three portentous eclipses of the sun and moon. May he grant you a long span of life in this mortal existence, so that your fatherland may serve and profit by you for longer, as is your praiseworthy custom and habit. And at last, after this troubled, fleeting and frail life, may he make you partakers of the heavenly, eternal and most blessed life which he won for us by his own death. Amen. Zurich, 1 January, in the year of salvation 1598.
Your Generous Amplitude's most devoted,
Johann Wilhelm Stucki.
To the Candid and Kindly Reader

units.la: VONIAM, candide & amice Lector, nihil agere, nihil tentare, nihil suscipere debemus, cujus nō aliquam vel probabilem saltem rationem possumus reddere: idcirco mihi quoq; novi hujus mei operis atq; lucubrationis, quæ nunc in lucem prodit, reddenda videtur esse ratio: unde appareat, nihil me fecisse, quod ab officio meo abhorreat. Primùm igitur cùm luo quisq; ducatur & statur studio, & eam, quam quisq; didicit, artem, ut vulgò loquuntur, exercere debeat, fateor equidem, me ab ineunte ætate, miro antiquitatū historiarumq; studio flagrasse, in quo si non tantum profeci, quantum vellem, quantumq; debui, id profecto nō tam meæ negligentiæ, quàm ingenii mei tenuitati estadscribeodum.
units.tr: Since we ought to undertake, attempt or take up nothing for which we cannot give at least some probable reason, a reason for this new work of mine and of my labours, which now comes to light, seems to me also to be owed. From it will appear that I have done nothing unbecoming to my duty. First, then, since each person is led and held by his own zeal, and ought to practise the craft he has learned, as people commonly say, I confess that from my earliest years I burned with a remarkable zeal for antiquities and histories. If in this I have not progressed as far as I wished or as I owed, that must be ascribed not so much to my negligence as to the slenderness of my talent.

units.la: Ad horum autem studiorum meorum rationem suscipiendam & ingrediendā principem mihi fuisse gratā memoriā, mente prædico, & prædicabo, quoad vivam, FRANCISCUM HOTOMANNUM (apud quem Argentorati vixi) clarissimum illud orbis Christiani lumen, qui nunc cœlesti illo lumine fruitur, vitamq; vivit veré vitalem & immortalem, cujus etiam laudabilis gloriōsaq; nominis fama vivit in his terris, in multorum, qui ejus auditores fuerunt atque discipuli, animis, viveteque perpetuò: quam nulla unquam exstinguet ætas, nulla delebit oblivio. Nam præclara quoque ejus monumenta, quæ post se reliquit, quæ multorum quotidie divinis noƗturnis versantur manibus ejus memoriam facilē ab omni plane oblivione vindicabunt.
units.tr: That the revered memory of Francis Hotman was my chief guide in taking up and entering upon these studies, I declare in my mind, and will go on declaring as long as I live. I lived with him at Strasbourg. He was that most famous light of the Christian world, who now enjoys that heavenly light and lives a truly living and immortal life. His praiseworthy and glorious name also lives on in these lands, in the minds of the many who were his hearers and pupils, and it will live on for ever. No age will extinguish it, no oblivion will blot it out. His distinguished writings, which he left behind and which many handle daily, will also easily rescue his memory from all oblivion.

units.la: Accidit etiam divinitus profectò (quod, quoniam in hunc locum incidi, tacitus præterire minimè possum) ut ex eadem illa antiqua nobilitate Hotomannorum familia, legatione nunc (quod felix faustumq̄ue fit) apud nos Helvetios, atque etiam Rhetos, Regis Galliarum & Navarræ numine obeat, ejus & generis & nominis vir ornatissimus & amplissimus, FRANCISCVS HOTOMANNVS, dominus de Morsontaine, &c. Regiæ Majestatis Consiliarius intimus & fidelissimus. Et in hoc ipso honorif centissimę suæ legationis munere (quod ipsum quoq; singulari quodam desi consilio, atque providentia fieri quis dubiter?) eomitem sibi & administrum scivit IoHANNEM HOTOMANNVM de Villiers, agnatum suum, magni illius Hotomanni filium, paternæque virtutis atque doctrinæ imitatorem strenuum.
units.tr: It has also come about, surely by divine arrangement (since I have come to this point, I cannot pass it over in silence), that from that same ancient and noble Hotoman family, there is now among us Swiss, and also the Rhaetians, an embassy, which is happy and fortunate, under the authority of the King of France and Navarre. Its head is Francis Hotoman, a most distinguished and eminent man of that line and name, lord of Morsontaine, etc., intimate and most faithful councillor of His Royal Majesty. In this most honourable office of his embassy (who could doubt that this too was done by a singular plan and providence?) he has as his companion and assistant John Hotoman de Villiers, his kinsman, the son of that great Hotoman and a vigorous imitator of his father's virtue and learning.

units.la: Hic novus autem legatus, etsi & Regis inprimis nomine, qui munus hoc ei imposuit, & ipso jure Gentium, & propter eximias ejus virtutes: tamen hanc quoque ob causam tanto gratior nobis merito esse debet ac jucundior, tantoque meliorem de hac ejus legatione spem habere, & majora nobis bona promittere possumus & debemus, quod ejusdem ferè gentis cognatione nobis est conjunctus, ita ut de benevolo & fideli ejus erga nos voluntate nequaquam nobis fit dubitandū. Majores quamque ejus quasi coloniam ex Germania in Galliam, & quidem Galliæ metropolim, Lutetiam nimirum Parisiorum, civitatem siam amplissimam & celebrem, deduxerunt: ubi & illorum posteriad hodiernum usque diem dignitatibus, honoribus atque opibus florent. Sed in Germania quoque, ut in Silesia, Lusatia, Misnia, Cluia, ejusdem nominis atque familiæ nobilissimæ viri clari & illustres vivunt adhuc atque florent, etiam quondam PHILIPPVS HO-TOMANNVS, clarissimum illud Reipub. Christianæ ornamentum, in quadam suaad Iac. HotoMANNVM, pariter epistola testatus est. Ejusdem quoq; rei testem appellare possumus, IACOBVM Monavium, Vratislaviæ, immò totius gentis Silesiorum decus. Quin ipsum quoque gentilitium nomen Germanicum Hotoman, sive, ut alii scribunt, Hotman (quod interposito p litterā, Hoptman, caput virorū, hoc est, Capitaneuovsonat) gentis hujus & originem, & virtutem bellicam dignitatemq́ue summā quodammodo spirat & significat. Omnino autem constat & Hotomannos Gallos, & Hotomanos Germanos hodie quoque in tanta esse dignitate & honore constitutos, ut maximo & patriæ utriq; & sibi invicem sint decori & ornamento, ac proinde optimo jure de se invicem gloriari possint.
units.tr: This new envoy, however, deserves our gratitude and delight, both on account of the name of the King who laid this charge upon him, and by the law of nations itself, and because of his outstanding virtues. Yet for this additional reason he ought to be all the more welcome and pleasing to us. We can and must hope much better things from this embassy and promise ourselves greater benefits, because he is joined to us by kinship with nearly the same people, so that we need not doubt his kindly and faithful goodwill towards us. Their ancestors led, as it were, a colony from Germany into France, and indeed into Paris, the metropolis of France, a very large and famous city, where their descendants flourish to this day in dignities, honours and wealth. But in Germany too, in Silesia, Lusatia, Meissen and Cleves, men of this same name and most noble family live on, distinguished and illustrious, and still flourish. Philip Hotoman, that most famous ornament of the Christian commonwealth, once bore witness to this in a letter of his to Jacob Hotoman. We may also call as witness to the same thing Jacob Monau of Breslau, indeed the glory of the whole nation of Silesians. Even the very family name, German Hotoman, or as others write Hotman (which, with a p inserted, becomes Hoptman, "head of men," that is, Captain), in some way breathes and signifies both the origin, the warlike virtue and the highest dignity of this people. It is certain that both the Hotomans of France and the Hotomans of Germany are today placed in such dignity and honour that they are a great ornament and credit both to their fatherland and to each other, and so by the best right they may boast of one another.

units.la: Te vero, nobilissi-amicissimq́ueque IOHANNES, communis patriæ id est, Reip. litteraræ nomine rogo & obsecro, ut quemadmodum te fa&tutum promisisti, si chiqua præclara & utilia patris tui beatæ memoriæ opera, quæ adhuc in tua bibliotheca & in tenebris latent, in loecmposa tant dignissima, primo quoque tempore ediac divulgari cures: id quod & Reip. litterarię civilius maxi-mo usui, & tibi totiq̄ue familiæ vestræ ornatissimæ maximo ornamento erit.
units.tr: You, most noble and dearest friend John, I ask and beseech in the name of our common fatherland, that is, of the republic of letters. Just as you promised, if any distinguished and useful works of your father of blessed memory, which still lie hidden in darkness in your library, you will take care to bring to light and publish in a fitting form at the first opportunity. This will be of very great use to the republic of letters, and a very great ornament to you and to your most distinguished family.

units.la: Sed huenefcio quo pacto sum delapsus, candide & amice Lector, quo me præstantissimi illius viri recordatio atque desiderium & incredibile meum grati memorisq̄ue mei ergaipsum, tanquam alterum meum parentem totamque ejus familiam, animi voluntatisq́ue testificandæ studium, quasi æstus quidā, abripuit. Nunc, ut eo, unde digressus sum revertar, cùm superiore anno
units.tr: But by what means I have slipped into this digression, candid and kindly reader, is explained by the remembrance of that most distinguished man and my longing for him. My incredible feeling of gratitude and remembrance towards him, as towards a second father, and towards his whole family, carried me away, like a kind of surge, in my eagerness to show my goodwill. Now, that I may return to where I left off, since last year
John

units.la: SACRORVM SACRIFI- CIORVMQVE GENTI- LIVM DESCRIPTIO.
units.tr: THE DESCRIPTION OF THE SACRED RITES AND SACRIFICES OF THE GENTILES.

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters]EMINEM, qui vel mediocriter in anciquis litterarum monumentis fit versatus, ignorare arbitror, con̄iviorum sacrificiorumq́, maximam semper cum apud Iudaeos, tum apud reliquas gentes, cognationem fuisse et affinitatem. Nullum enim fere sacrificium sine aliquo epulo, et vicissim nullum pene epulum, etiam profanum, publicum praesertim, sine sacris quibusdam ritibus atq́ cerimoniis fuit celebratum. Quin ipsa quoq́ sacrificia quid fuerunt aliud, quam quaedam quasi epulae atq́ con̄vivia, secundum illud Poëtae:
units.tr: No one, I think, who has been even moderately versed in the ancient monuments of literature, is ignorant that there has always been the closest kinship and affinity between feasts and sacrifices, both among the Jews and among the other nations. For almost no sacrifice was offered without some banquet, and conversely almost no banquet, even a secular one, and especially a public one, was held without certain sacred rites and ceremonies. Indeed, what were the sacrifices themselves but a kind of banquets and feasts, according to that saying of the poet:
"To recline at the feasts of the gods?"

units.la: Quamobrem quoniam de Con̄iviis, cum sacris, sum profanis, eorumq́ ritibus sive antiquis, sive recentibus, quaedam pro ingenii mei tenuitate conscripsi et in lucem edidi, opere pretium, nihil, a ratione alteni fallurum me existimavi, si de sacrificiis quoq́ Gentilium quaedam Con̄iviali illi meo operi, quasi appendicis loco subjungerem; in quo non pauca, quae in Con̄iviali illo meo opere fuerunt praetermissa, commode addi possent.
units.tr: Therefore, since I have written and published some things, as far as my modest talent allows, about banquets, both sacred and secular, and their rites, whether ancient or recent, I judged that I would not be acting unreasonably if I added some things about the sacrifices of the Gentiles to that work of mine on banquets, as an appendix. In it, not a few things that were omitted from that banquet book could conveniently be added.

units.la: Sed quae praeterea causae rationesq́ non leves, ut opinor, me ad novum hoc meum Opus conscribendum, atq́ etiam in lucem emittendum impulerint, facis in Praefatione mea supra declaravi. Nunc vero omisis multis paretgis, ἰδρῶτι bocesf., opus ipsum, quod felix faustumq́ sit, agrediamur, Deum precantes, ut illud prosperare, et ad Numinis sui gloriam et Reipublicae litterariae utilitatem dirigere dignetur. Nam, quemadmodum antiquissimus clarissimusq́ ille Ecclesiae primicirius doctor atq́ Martyr Cyprianus pie sapienterq́, dixit: Ut nihil sanctum, nisi Deo sanctificante, nihil potens, nisi ipso corroborante: ita nihil felix, nihil auspicatum, nisi ipso prosperante esse potest.
units.tr: But the other not slight reasons that moved me to write and also to publish this new work of mine, I have explained above in my Preface. Now, however, with many preliminaries omitted, and with sweat [ἱδρῶτι], let us take up the work itself, which may it be happy and fortunate, praying God that he deign to prosper it and direct it to the glory of his divinity and the usefulness of the republic of letters. For, as that most ancient and most famous teacher and martyr of the Church, Cyprian, said piously and wisely: just as nothing is holy unless God sanctifies it, and nothing is powerful unless he strengthens it, so nothing can be fortunate or auspicious unless he prospers it.

units.la: Sed priusquam ad sacrificiorum explicationem accedam, quaedam in genere de religione, sive cultu Deorum, cujus Sacrificia pars fuerunt praecipua, videntur esse praemittenda, exordio duobus anonymibus, quibus religio cultusq́, cum verus, justus et legitimus unius et solius Dei, tum falsus, fucatus et adulterinus fictorum et commentitiorum Deorum in sacris et profanis litteris exprimitur. Nam, ut ille dixit, εἰς τὸ ὁρθὸς διδάσκειν ἀλλὰ φρῶν εξειν τὰ ὀνόματα: quae ut Aristoteles testatur, τῆς θεογονίας τῶν ἐσθὶ μυηνωτα.
units.tr: But before I come to the explanation of the sacrifices, some things must be set forth in general about religion, or the worship of the gods, of which sacrifices were the principal part. This will be done by way of introduction, by which religion and worship are expressed both in sacred and in profane writings, both the true, just and lawful worship of the one and only God, and the false, counterfeit and adulterated worship of fictitious and invented gods. For, as he said, to teach rightly but to have the names [εἰς τὸ ὀρθῶς διδάσκειν ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν τὰ ὀνόματα]; which, as Aristotle attests, belongs to the theogony [τῆς θεογονίας].

units.la: Nomina Latina trica et per vulgata sunt, Religio, Cultus, Pietas, Sanctitas, Cerimonia, Supplicatio, Veneratio, Honos, Adoratio, &c. Religio Ciceroni videtur dicta a relegendo: unde etiam Lex nonnullis videtur dicta. Qui enim, inquit ille de Natura Deorum, omnia, quae ad cultum Deorum pertinent, pertractarent, et tanquam relegerent, sunt dicti religiosi ex relegendo.
units.tr: The Latin names that are common and in general use are: religio, cultus, pietas, sanctitas, caerimonia, supplicatio, veneratio, honos, adoratio, etc. Cicero thinks religio is so called from relegere (to go over again): for those who, as he says in his book On the Nature of the Gods, went over and as it were re-read all the things that pertain to the worship of the gods, were called religiosi from relegendo. Some think the word was also derived from lex (law).

units.la: Alii, ut Lactantius, dictam volunt a religando, quod ea Deo obligati et obstricti simus; vel quod ea hominum mentes atq́ animi quasi vinculo quodam alligentur et obstringantur: unde ille dicendi formulae: Religione implicare, obstringere, obligare, impedire: Religionem expiare, eximere: Religione solvere, exsolvere, liberare. Hinc Aulus Gellius Noctium Atticarum libro 4. cap 9. Religiosus, inquit, is appellabatur, qui nimia et superstitiosa religione se alligaverat, eaq́res vitio assignabatur.
units.tr: Others, as Lactantius, want it to be called from religare (to bind fast), because we are bound and tied to God by these things; or because by them human minds and souls are as if fettered and bound by a certain chain. Hence those expressions: to entangle, bind, oblige or hinder by religion; to expiate or free from religion; to loosen, release or set free from religion. Hence Aulus Gellius, in the fourth book of his Attic Nights, chapter 9: "Religiosus," he says, "was the name for one who had bound himself by excessive and superstitious religion, and this was counted as a fault."

units.la: Nonnulli religionem dictam voluerunt a relinquendo, sefte eodem Gellio, lib. 4. cap 9. Massurius Sabinus in Commentariis, quos de indigenis scripsit, religiosum voluit appellari, quod propter sanctitatem aliquam remotum et sepositum a nobis est. Idem Macrobius affirmat ex Servii Sulpicii sententia. A relinquendo, inquit, religio dicta, ut a carendo cerimonie, &c. Augustinus et alii, religionem voluerunt vocatam ab eligendo, quod Deum, quem diligimus, eligimus. Quid si religio dicta sit a relegando, quod propter eam saepe homines ab hominum consuetudine et frequentia ad loca deserta et solitudines relegentur. Mihi quidem religio falsa, fucata et irreligiosa re-té et a religando, et a relinquendo, et a relegando videtur denominata, propterrea quòd illa hominum mentes mirificè obligatas obstrictasq; tenet, quodq; idcirco, tanquàm animi cor porus, pestis atq; pernicies, merito relinquenda, deferenda, fugienda & ad inferos est ablegan̄da.
units.tr: Some have wanted religio to be named from relinquere (to leave behind), as the same Gellius reports in book 4, chapter 9. Massurius Sabinus, in his Commentaries which he wrote on the native rites, wanted the religiosum to be so called because, on account of some sanctity, it is set apart and removed from us. Macrobius himself affirms the same, on the authority of Servius Sulpicius: "Religion," he says, "is named from relinquere, just as caerimonia is from carere," etc. Augustine and others have wanted religion to be called from eligere (to choose), because we choose the God whom we love. But what if religio was named from relegare (to send away), because on account of it men are often sent away from the company and crowds of other men to deserted places and solitudes? To me indeed false, counterfeit and irreligious religion seems to be named from religare, from relinquere, and from relegare alike, because it holds men's minds wonderfully bound and fettered, and for this reason, like a pest and destruction of body and soul, it is rightly to be left behind, abandoned, fled from, and sent away to the underworld.

units.la: Religionis autem nomen non solùm rem divinam, sed cujusvis etiam muneris functionem & conscientiæ scrupulum & metum seu solicitudinem significat. Hinc Virgilius: Iamnunc religio pavidos terrebat agrestes Dira loci, &c.
units.tr: The word religio, however, signifies not only divine worship, but also the performance of any duty whatever, a scruple of conscience, and fear or anxiety. Hence Virgil: "Already the dread of the place was terrifying the timid farmers," etc.

units.la: Terentius: Dignus cum tua religione isthac odio. Nodum in scirpo quæris. Hinc etiam illa phrases & dicendi forme, quæ passim, præsertim apud Poëtas occurrunt, Religionem offerre, afferre, inferre, inducere, interponere, adhibere, injicere: item, In religionem venire, vertere, trahere: item, Religio mihi est hoc vel illud facere.
units.tr: Terence: "Worthy to be hated with that scruple of yours. You are seeking a knot in a bulrush." Hence also those phrases and forms of speech which occur everywhere, especially among the poets: to offer, bring, inflict, induce, interpose, apply, or inject religion; likewise, to come into religion, to turn, or draw into religion; likewise, it is a religion for me to do this or that.

units.la: In plurali quoq; numero, Religiones, sæpe usurpatur. Cicero pro domo: In religionibus suscipiendis caput est interpretari, quæ voluntas Deorum immortalium esse videatur. Livius, Apud quos juxta divinas religiones humana fides colitur. Quid si religionis nomen ab Hebræo אלהים Elohim, Deum & Deos significante, fit derivatum? Religionem idem Cicero libro de Inventione definit esse, quæ superiori cuidam naturæ, quam divinam vocant, curam cerimoniamq; affert. Idem libro de Natura Deorum, Religionem pio Deorum cultu contineri ait: & libro de Legibus hæc duo conjungit, Cultum Deorum & pium religionem suscipere.
units.tr: In the plural also, religiones is often used. Cicero, in Pro domo: "In taking up religions, the chief thing is to interpret what the will of the immortal gods seems to be." Livy: "Among whom, alongside the divine religions, human good faith is cultivated." But what if the name religio is derived from the Hebrew אלהים [Elohim], which means God and gods? Cicero in his book On Invention defines religion as that which brings care and ceremony to a certain superior nature, which they call divine. The same Cicero, in his book On the Nature of the Gods, says that religion is contained in the pious worship of the gods; and in his book On the Laws he joins these two together: to undertake worship of the gods and pious religion.

units.la: Ab hoc nomine, Religio, religiosus & religiosi, quibus opponitur irreligiosus & irreligiosi, sunt dicti: de quibus vide Gellium eodem libro 4. supra citato, cap. 9. Festus, Religiosi, inquit, dicuntur, qui faciendarum, prætermittendarum, rerum divinarum, secundum morem civitatis delectum habent, nec se superstitionibus implicant. Unde Virgilius, —rivos deducere nulla Religio vetuit. Idest, detergere.
units.tr: From this noun, religio, come religiosus and religiosi, which are opposed to irreligiosus and irreligiosi. On these see Gellius in the same fourth book cited above, chapter 9. Festus: "Religiosi," he says, "are those who, according to the custom of the state, have a choice of doing or omitting divine acts, and do not entangle themselves in superstitions." Hence Virgil: "No religious scruple forbade drawing off streams," that is, to cleanse them out.

units.la: Nam diebus festis rivos veteres fordidatos detergere licebat: Veteres fodere non licebat. Idem Festus, Religiosus est, inquit, uno modo Deorum sanctitatem magni æstimans, sed etiam officiosus ad versus homines. Dies autem religiosi, quibus, nisi quod necesse est, nefas habetur facere, &c. Ita religiosum & sacrum inquit idem, est, ut templa omnia atq; ædes, quæ sacrata dicuntur. Religiosum locum, ut Iurisconsulti affirmant, unusquisq; sua voluntate facere potest, dum mortuum infert in locum suum. Cenotaphium quod, hoc est, sepulchrum, in quo nondum sepulture fit mortuus, quibusdam placuit religiosum dici, quod diri fratres negaverunt. Religiosi etiam dies infames, atq; infausti dicuntur. Cato, Itaq; aliter etiam religiosus nunc dies, aliter in vulgus.
units.tr: For on festival days it was permitted to cleanse out the old, filthy streams; it was not permitted to dig up old ones. The same Festus: "A religiosus," he says, "is one who, valuing the sanctity of the gods greatly in one way, is also dutiful towards men. Religious days, however, are those on which it is considered wrong to do anything except what is necessary," etc. So, he says, religiosum and sacrum are the same, as are all temples and shrines, which are called sacred. A religious place, as the jurists affirm, anyone may make by his own will, provided he carries a dead body into his own place. A cenotaph, that is, a tomb in which the dead man has not yet been buried, some have thought to be called religiosum, which the dire brothers denied. Religious days are also called unlucky and ill-omened. Cato: "Therefore the day is religious in one way now, and in another way for common people."

units.la: Omnino, uti apud Hebræos vox ברך berech & bene & maledicere significat; sic apud Latinos vox Sacri, & vox Religiosi in bonam & malam partem accipiuntur.
