Nam religiosus & locus & dies aliquando accipitur pro sacro seu sacrato, sive sancto: aliquando pro infami, infausto, ominoso sive malo ominoso. Gellius libro 4. cap. 9. Simili modo illa quoq; vocabula ab eadem profectâ religione diversum significare videntur, ut religiosi dies, & religiosa delubra. Religiosi enim dies dicuntur tristi omine, infames, impedientes, in quibus et res divinas facere et rem quampiam nova exordiri temperandum est: quos multitudo imperitorum prave et perperam nefastos appellat. Itaq; Cicero lib. 9. epistolarum ad Atticum, Majores, inquit, nostri funestiores diem esse voluerunt. Allienis pugnæ, quam urbis captæ, quod hoc malum exilio. Itaq; alter religiosus etiam nunc dies, alter in vulgus ignotus. Idem tamen M. Tullius in oratione de accusatore conflictum do religiosa delubra dixit, non ominosa, nec tristia, sed majestatis venerationumq; plena. Atq; hæc de religione: de qua; sicut etiam de pietate, sanctitate, cerimoniis, fide, jurejurando: item quid de templis, delubris, sacrificiis, solemnibus, necnon de auspiciis, quibus præsumus, existimandum sit Cicero copiose agit libris de Natura Deorum.
units.tr: In general, just as among the Hebrews the word ברך [berech] means both to bless and to curse, so among the Latins the words sacer and religiosus are taken in a good and in a bad sense. For religiosus, both of a place and of a day, is sometimes taken for sacred, or consecrated, or holy; and sometimes for infamous, unlucky, ominous, or of bad omen. Gellius, book 4, chapter 9: "In a similar way those words too, which come from the same religio, seem to have different meanings, such as religiosi dies and religiosa delubra. For religious days are said to be of sad omen, infamous, hindering, days on which one must refrain both from performing divine rites and from beginning any new undertaking; which the mass of the unskilled wrongly and improperly call nefasti." Therefore Cicero, in the ninth book of his Letters to Atticus: "Our ancestors," he says, "wanted the day to be more ill-omened: the day of the battle of Allia than the day of the capture of the city, because the latter was the beginning of exile." "So one day is still religious, and another unknown to the common people." Yet the same Marcus Tullius, in his speech on the accuser, called a conflict over religious shrines not ominous nor sad, but full of majesty and veneration. And these are the things about religion; concerning which, as also concerning piety, holiness, ceremonies, faith, and oath, and likewise what should be thought about temples, shrines, sacrifices, solemn festivals, and also about the auspices over which we preside, Cicero treats at length in his books On the Nature of the Gods.

units.la: Cultus sive Cultura Deorum altera vox est, quæ hic consideranda. Augusti. lib. 10. de Civitate Dei, cap. 1. de hoc verbo sic disserit, Cultus Dei varius nominibus appellatur. Si tantummodo cultus ipse dicatur, non soli Deo deberi videtur. Dicimus enim etiam colere homines, quos honorifica vel recordatione vel præsentia frequentamus. Nec solum ea, quibus nos religiosa humilitate subjicimus, sed quadam etiam, quæ subjecta sunt nobis, coli putantur. Nam ex hoc verbo Agricola colæ, Ruricolæ, Coloni, & Incolæ (vel Accolæ) vocantur: & ipsos Deos non ob aliud appellant Cælicolas, nisi quod cælum colant, non utiq; venerando, sed inhabitando, tanquam cæli quosdam colonos. Sed quia & alias rerum dicitur cultus, ideo Latine uno verbo signißcaricultus Deo debitus non poterit. Nam & ipsa religio, quamvis distinctius, non quemlibet, sed Dei cultum significare videtur: unde isto nomine interpretari sunt nostri eam, quæ Græcis θρησκεία dicitur, &c. Hæc Augustinus.
units.tr: Cultus, or cultura, of the gods is the second word to consider here. Augustine, in book 10 of The City of God, chapter 1, discusses this word as follows: "Cultus Dei" is called by various names. If the word cultus is used by itself, it does not seem to be due to God alone. For we also say that men colere (cultivate, honour) those whom we frequent with honour, whether by remembrance or by presence. And it is thought that things are coli (cultivated, honoured) not only when we submit ourselves to them with religious humility, but also when certain things are subject to us. For from this word we get agricola (farmer), ruricola (country dweller), colonus (settler) and incola (or accola, inhabitant). Even the gods are called caelicolae for no other reason than that they colunt (inhabit) heaven, not in the sense of venerating it, but of dwelling in it, as if they were certain colonists of heaven. But since cultus is also used of other things, Latin cannot signify the worship owed to God by one word alone. For religio itself, although in a more distinct sense, seems to signify not just any cult but the worship of God; and for this reason our writers have rendered by this word what the Greeks call threskeia [θρησκεία], and so on. Thus Augustine.

units.la: Facit huc, quod Auctor libri de Inventione pio Deorum cultu contineri Religionē ajt. Colere Deum, sive Deos, metaphora videtur ducta ab agricultura, ad Deos vel homines, ad quæsus res alias, quas cum tractamus, versamus, exercemus, colere dicimur: & sic colimus omnia, quibus inhæremus, incumbimus, studemus: ut colere studium Philosophiæ, litteras, bonas artes, colere virtutes, jus, arma, ludos & similia. Non setus autē atq; agri fertiles inprimis & optimi: sic Dei cultus fructus fert ad vitam æternam uberrimos: qui quidè cultus observantia est, per quam superiores venerantur & colimus. Ouidius, Non bene cœlestes impia dextra colit.
units.tr: To this belongs the statement of the author of the book On Invention that religio is contained in the pious worship of the gods. To colere God or the gods seems to be a metaphor taken from agriculture, and we say that we colere other things, to which we devote ourselves, with which we are busy, and to which we apply ourselves: so we cultivate all those things to which we cling, apply ourselves and devote our zeal, as one colit the study of philosophy, letters, the liberal arts, virtues, law, arms, games and the like. Fertile fields, especially the best ones, bear fruit in the same way, and the worship of God bears most abundant fruit for eternal life. This worship is indeed a reverence by which we venerate and cultivate our superiors. Ovid: "An impious right hand does not worship the heavenly ones well."

units.la: Cicero de Natura Deorum: Deos venerari et colere debemus. Idem: Dii, quos nos colere, precari, venerarig debemus. Idem, Colere templū, delubra, diem natalem, religionem sive religiones, ceremonias sepulchrorum religiose, religiosissimé, magna curā, summa religione, pie, caste, sancte, &c. Quid si colendi verbum ἀπὸ τῆς θεραπείας, ab adulando, sit dictum, so quod plerunq; Dei hominumq; cultus cum adulatione & hypocrisi seu simulatione est conjunctus? Colunturque enim Dii & homines ab hominibus, non tam vere & sincere, quam sicte, simulate et adulatorie.
units.tr: Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods: "We ought to venerate and worship the gods." The same: "The gods, whom we ought to worship, supplicate and venerate." The same: "to worship a temple, shrines, a birthday, religion or religions, funeral rites religiously, most religiously, with great care, with the utmost religion, piously, chastely, holily," and so on. But what if the verb colere was derived from therapeia [ἀπὸ τῆς θεραπείας], that is, from flattering, since the worship of God and men is for the most part joined with flattery and hypocrisy or pretence? For gods and men are worshipped by men not so much truly and sincerely as slyly, feignedly and with flattery.

units.la: Cultus in plurali numero Cicero dixit, Quid est, inquit, quod ullos Diis immortalibus cultus, honores, preces adhibeamus?
units.tr: Cicero used cultus in the plural: "What is it," he says, "that we should offer to the immortal gods in worship, honours and prayers?"

units.la: Tertia vox, qua religionem Latini significant, est Pietas. Hac vere significatur officium, quod præstandum hominibus & quod Numini divino. Pietas, inquit Cicero de Inventione, est, per quam sanguine conjunctis patriæ, bene volis officium & diligens tribuitur cultus. Idem in Partitionibus Oratoris, Pietas est voluntas grata in parentes. Idem in somnio Scipionis, justitia et pietatem, quæ cum sit magna in parentibus & propinquis, tum in patria maxima est. Idem in Partitionibus, Pietas & charitas & bonitas quæ idem valere videntur. Idem, Pietas, qua erga patriam, aut parentes, aut alios sanguine conjunctos officium conservare movemur. Idem de Natura Deorum, Pietas est justitia ad versus Deos. Idem primo de Finibus, Pietas ad versus Deos, &c. Idem pro domo, Nec est ulla erga Deos pietas, nisi honesta de munere eorum & mente opinio. Idem in Oratione antequam iret in exilium, Qua sanctissimi homines pietate erga Deos immortales esse solent, eadem ego erga Populum Romanum semper ero. Ibidem, Illi, quorum animus est religionis pietate defunctus. Idem lib. 1. Officiorum, Deos placatos efficit pietas & sanctitas. Idem de Natura Deorum, Pietas, sanctitas, religio, quæ omnia pure & caste Deorum Numini tribuenda sunt. Ibidem, Pietas, cui conjuncta justitia est, reliquæ virtutes. De hoc eodem Pietatis nomine sit Augustinus lib. 10. de Civitate Dei cap. 1. Pietas quoq; proprie Dei cultus intelligi solet, quam Græci ἐυσέβειαν vocant. Hac tamen & erga parentes officiose haberi dicitur. More autem vulgi hoc nomen etiam in operibus misericordiæ frequentatur: quod ideo arbitror evenisse, quia hæc fieri præcipue Deus mandat, eadem, sibi vel pro sacrificiis vel pro sacrificiis placere sestatur. Ex qua loquendi consuetudine factum est, ut & Deus ipse dicatur pius: quem sane Græci nullo suo sermonis usu ἐυσεβῆ vocant. Hactenus Augustinus.
units.tr: The third word by which the Latins signify religion is pietas. This word properly signifies the duty which is to be rendered to men and to the divine Power. "Piety," says Cicero in On Invention, "is that through which a dutiful and diligent service is paid to those joined by blood, to one's country and to benefactors." The same in The Divisions of Oratory: "Piety is a dutiful disposition towards parents." The same in the Dream of Scipio: justice and piety, which is great towards parents and kin, is greatest towards one's country. The same in The Divisions: "Piety, charity and goodness, which seem to have the same force." The same: "Piety, by which we are moved to preserve our duty towards our country, our parents, or others joined by blood." The same in On the Nature of the Gods: "Piety is justice towards the gods." The same in the first book On Ends: "piety towards the gods," and so on. The same in For His House: "There is no piety towards the gods unless there is an honourable opinion of their gifts and mind." The same in the speech before he went into exile: "With that piety which the most holy men are accustomed to have towards the immortal gods, I shall always be towards the Roman people." In the same place: "those whose mind is free from the piety of religion." The same in the first book of Duties: "Piety and holiness make the gods propitious." The same in On the Nature of the Gods: "Piety, holiness, religion: all these are to be ascribed purely and chastely to the divine power of the gods." In the same place: "Piety, to which justice is joined, is the remaining virtues." Augustine, in book 10 of The City of God, chapter 1, also speaks of this same word pietas. Pietas is also commonly understood properly as the worship of God, which the Greeks call eusebeia [εὐσέβειαν]. Yet it is also said to be shown dutifully towards parents. In common usage this name is also used of works of mercy, which I think has come about because God especially commands these things and declares that they please him, rather than sacrifices. From this manner of speaking it has come about that God himself is called pius, which the Greeks, in no use of their language, call eusebes [εὐσεβῆ]. Thus far Augustine.

units.la: Pietatem porro Veteres voluerunt dictam, quod, quæ in ea sunt, penitus & in penetralibus retinentur. Sed potius a Pio, verbo, quod colere, placare, amare significat. Plautus, Vbi piem, id mon. est, colam, pietatem, si isto more tibi postulem placere? Item, Pio verbum quandoq; capitur pro eo, quod est pie amo. Nemo est, qui suos magis pier liberos. Hinc piens, pientior, pientissimus, pienter, pientis, pientissimé. A Pio fit piaculum, id est, sacrificium cultus. Virgilius, — ea prima piacula junto.
units.tr: Moreover, the ancients thought pietas was so called because the things in it are held deep within and in the innermost parts. But it is rather from the word pius, which signifies to cultivate, to appease, to love. Plautus: "Where I may cherish piety, that is for me, if I should ask you to please me in that manner?" Likewise, pius is sometimes taken for what is loved piously: "There is no one who loves his children more piously." Hence piens, pientior, pientissimus, pienter, pientis, pientissime. From pius comes piaculum, that is, a sacrifice of worship. Virgil: "they join the first expiations."

units.la: Aliquando tamen piacula crimina & flagitia dicuntur. Virgilius, Dislulit in ferarum commissa piacula mortem.
units.tr: Sometimes, however, piacula means crimes and shameful deeds. Virgil: "He deferred death for the crimes committed against the wild beasts."

units.la: Sic apud Hebræos שׁ חטאה Chattā & peccatum & sacrificium, quo expiatur peccatum significat. A Pio item fit expio, quod est purgo, purifico et piatrix sacerdos, quae expiare erat solita, et Piamentum, quo in expiando utebantur, dictum a Poetis Piamen, et porta Piacularis Romae appellata ob quaedam piacula, quae ibi fieri solebant, Festus. Idem, Vel, ut ajt Cloatius, cum per sacrum aliquo piaculo solvitur et alicujus piandi propitiandiq; causa immolatur. Hic piare pro colere, placare, propitiare, sicut et placare pro colere, in illo Horatiano usurpatur,
units.tr: Thus among the Hebrews, chattā [חטאה] means both sin and the sacrifice by which sin is expiated. From pius also comes expio, which means to purge or purify; and the piatrix priest, who was accustomed to make expiation; and the piamentum, which they used in expiating, called piamen by the poets; and the gate in Rome called Piacularis because of certain expiations that were performed there, according to Festus. The same: or, as Cloatius says, when something is released by a sacred expiation and is sacrificed for the sake of atoning and propitiating. Here piare is used for colere, placare, propitiare, just as placare is used for colere in that line of Horace
"They gladly propitiated the earth and Sylvanus."

units.la: Porro piari, veluti proprio verbo, ajt Verrius, dicuntur, qui parum sunt animati, cum mentis suae non sint, et per quaedam verba liberantur incommodo. Piatrix dicebatur sacerdos, quae expiare erat solita, quam quidam fimulatricem; alii sagam; alii expiatricem vocant. Piamenta quod dicebantur, quibus utebantur in expiando. Festus. Piacularia auspicia, teste eodem, appellabant, quae sacrificantibus tristia portendebant: cum aut hostia ab ara profugisset, aut percussa mugitum dedisset, aut in aliam partem corporis, quam oporteret, secidissent. Pius aliquando religiosus dicitur. Virgilius, Du meliora pius: etc.
units.tr: Moreover, those are said to be piari, as if by a proper word, says Verrius, who are little animated, since they are not in their own minds, and are freed from their trouble by certain words. The priestess who was accustomed to make expiation was called piatrix; some call her a simulatrix, others a saga, others an expiatrix. The things they used in expiating were called piamenta. Festus. According to the same writer, they called piacularia auspicia those omens which portended sorrow to those who were sacrificing: when either the victim had fled from the altar, or, having been struck, had bellowed, or the knife had cut into some part of the body other than it should. Pius is sometimes said of the religious. Virgil: "pious, you are better: etc."

units.la: Aliquando, miseritors, benignus. Cicero, Non secus in me pius, quam pater in filios: aliquando Casus Virgilius, Quiq, pii Vates, etc.
units.tr: Sometimes it means merciful, kind. Cicero: "Not otherwise was he dutiful towards me than a father towards his sons." Sometimes it is used of the Virgilian casus: "and you, pious poets," etc.

units.la: Quintilianus, Et pios amores et pudicos. Hinc et piissimus. Ejus contrarium, impietas, im-pius, impie, etc. Cicero de Finibus, Sed nihil est, quod tam miseros facit, quam impietas et fraus.
units.tr: Quintilian: "both pious and chaste loves." Hence also piissimus. Its opposite is impietas, impius, impie, etc. Cicero, On Ends: "But there is nothing that makes men as wretched as impiety and fraud."

units.la: Idem de Legibus, Impius ne audeto placare donis iram Deorum. Idem de Divinat. 2. Est enim periculum, ne aut hic neglectus impia fraude, aut susceptis anili superstitione obligemur. Impia-tus sceleratus, Festus.
units.tr: The same, On the Laws: "Let the impious not dare to appease the anger of the gods with gifts." The same, On Divination, book 2: "For there is a danger that we may be bound either by this neglect with impious fraud, or by the superstition of old women which we have taken up." Impiatus means wicked, according to Festus.

units.la: Sed pietatem ipsam, ut ceteros Deos Romani olim colebant, cui edem ab Acilio consecratam ajunt eo loco, quo quondam mulier habita verit, quae patrem suum inclusum carcere mammis suis clam aluerit, ob quod factum impunitas ei concessa fit.
units.tr: But piety itself, as the Romans of old worshipped the other gods, to which a temple is said to have been consecrated by Acilius in the place where a woman was once held, who secretly nourished her father, shut up in prison, with her breasts; for which deed impunity was granted to her.

units.la: Sanctitas, inquit Cicero libro de Natura Deorum, est scientia colendorum Deorum. Deos placatos, inquit cum post reditum in patriam, pietas efficiet et sanctitas. Idem de Natura Deorum, Pietas, sanctitas, religio, quae omnia pure et caste Deorum Numini tribuenda sunt. In plurali, Sanctitates. Cicero post reditum, Mecum Deorum et hominum sanctitates omnes et religiones adfuerunt.
units.tr: "Holiness," says Cicero in the book On the Nature of the Gods, "is the knowledge of worshipping the gods." "Piety and holiness," he says, "will make the gods propitious" after his return to his country. The same in On the Nature of the Gods: "Piety, holiness, religion: all these are to be ascribed purely and chastely to the divine power of the gods." In the plural, sanctitates. Cicero after his return: "All the holinesses and religions of gods and men were present with me."

units.la: Sanctimonia. Cicero pro Rabirio, Mentes, quae ex hominum vita ad Deorum religionem sanctimoniam demigrarunt. Idem ad Herennium, Omnis sanctimonia hic nuptiarum, uno figno tibiarum, etc.
units.tr: Sanctimony. Cicero, for Rabirius: minds which, from the life of men, have passed over with sanctimony into the religion of the gods. The same, to Herennius: all sanctimony here of marriages, with one signal of the flutes, etc.

units.la: Sanctitudo. Cicero libro quarto de Repub. Eosdem terminos intelligitur hominum cura atque vitae: sic Pontificio jure sanctitudo sepulturae. Sanctus. Cicero, Qui sanctus? Qui religionem colentes; nisi qui meritam Diis immortalibus gratiam honoribus et memori mente persolvunt? Homo sanctus et religiosus. Idem, Qua sanctissimi homines pietate erga Deos esse solent. Idem, Nullum est officium tam sanctum et solenne, quod non avaritia comminuere atque violare foleat. Pro Quint. Vir natura sanctus et religiosus, pro Rosc. Idem pro Archia, Quare suo jure nosser ille Ennius sanctos appellat Poetas; quod quasi Deorum aliquo dono atq, munere commendati nobis esse videantur. Idem post reditum, Numen vestrum aeque mihi gravae et sanctum, ac Deorum immortalium futurum est. Sancte. Pie sancteq; colere Deum. Cicero de Natura Deorum. Idem, Augustè sancteq; consecrare aliquem. Sanctitas igitur, ut etiam sanctimonia et sanctitudo aliquando a Latinis usurpantur pro scientia colendorum Deorum; aliquando generaliter pro integritate et morum vitaq; puritate, vel pro religione, vel pro cassitate. Sancte dicuntur et personae et res. Et cum personae, tum res dicuntur sancta aliquando esse, quod sanctitatis, id est, religionis sunt studiosae et amantes, quod religioni atq; Diis sunt consecratae; aliquando quod ab hominum injuria sunt munitae et immunes, quas violare fit nefas. Sic Tribunipl. apud Romanos dicebantur sancti, item muri civitatis et alia: quemadmodum et leges dicebantur sanctae, quia sanctione quadam subnixae sunt, ut Ulpianus scribit. Sanctum quod propitium. etiam pro propitio Veteres dixerunt.
units.tr: Sanctitude. Cicero, Book 4 of the Republic: the care of men and their life is understood within these same limits; so by Pontifical law the sanctitude of burial. Holy. Cicero: Who is holy? Those who cultivate religion; except those who render to the immortal gods the thanks they deserve with honours and a grateful mind? A holy and religious man. The same: with the piety which the most holy men are wont to show towards the gods. The same: there is no duty so holy and solemn that avarice is not wont to diminish and violate it. For Quinctius: a man holy and religious by nature. For Roscius. The same, for Archias: wherefore, by right, that famous Ennius calls poets holy, because they seem to be commended to us by some gift and favour of the gods. The same, after his return: your divinity will be as weighty and holy to me as that of the immortal gods. Holy: to worship God piously and holily. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods. The same: to consecrate someone august and holy. Therefore sanctity, as also sanctimony and sanctitude, is sometimes used by the Latins for the knowledge of how to worship the gods; sometimes generally for integrity and purity of morals and life, or for religion, or for chastity. Both persons and things are called holy. And not only persons but things are sometimes said to be holy, either because they are devoted to sanctity, that is, are zealous for and fond of religion, and are consecrated to religion and to the gods; or because they are protected and immune from the injury of men, and it is wrong to violate them. Thus among the Romans the tribunes of the plebs were called sacred, and likewise the walls of a city and other things; just as laws too were called holy, because they are upheld by a certain sanction, as Ulpian writes. The ancients also used "sanctum" for "propitious".

units.la: Tibullus de Iunone, At tu sanctafave, etc.
units.tr: Tibullus, on Juno: "But you, holy or..." etc.

units.la: Catullus de Cupidine, Sancte puer, curas hominum qui gaudia miscs.
units.tr: Catullus, on Cupid: "Holy boy, who mix the cares and joys of men..."
The same, on Venus: "Whom holy Venus..." etc.
Tibullus likewise, on the Genius:

units.la: Tunc precor infidos sancto relinque focos.
units.tr: Then I pray that you leave the faithless hearths to the holy one.

units.la: Nomen autem hoc, & unde illud efs deriuacuni, sanciendi verbum nonnulli volunt tractum esse a sanguine, quasi sanguine consecratum, cùm sancire proprie sit aliquid consecrare sub sangui- ne hostiæ: unde etiam sanctio proprie vocatur lex cum terrore pœnæ. Alii verò, qui sanctum pro- priè volunt dici, quod ab hominum iniuria debeat esse commune, nomen hoc volunt deriuatum a sagminibus herbis, quas legati populi Romani ferre solebant, ne quis eos violaret, quemadmodum apud Græcos ea, quæ Cerutia vocantur. Festus Sagmina scribit vocatas fuisse herbas verbenas & puras, quia ex loco sancto arcebantur a consule Prætore ve legati proficiscentibus ad sœdus faciendum, bellumq; indicendum; vel a sanciendo, id est, confirmando. Naevius, Scabot, siue scapos, atq; verbenas sagmina sumpserunc. Item, Lex sacratum Iouis iurandum sagmine.
units.tr: Some hold that this name, and the verb from which it is derived, sancire, comes from blood, as if consecrated with blood, since sancire properly means to consecrate something under the blood of a victim; whence also a law with the threat of punishment is properly called a sanctio. But others, who wish the term "sacred" to be applied properly to what ought to be common and safe from the injury of men, derive this name from the sacred herbs (sagmina) which the envoys of the Roman people were accustomed to carry, so that no one would harm them, just as among the Greeks those things called kerykeia [κηρύκεια] were used. Festus writes that the herbs called verbenae and pure herbs were named sagmina, because they were taken from a holy place by the consul or praetor for envoys setting out to make a treaty or declare war; or from sanciendo, that is, from confirming. Naevius: "They took up the staffs and verbenae, the sagmina." Likewise: "the sacred oath of Jupiter by sagmen."

units.la: Ceremonia, siue, ut alii scribunt per e, loco i, Ceremonie, est sacrorum religio. Religio est, inquit Cicero de Inuentione, quæ Dei curam cerimoniamq; affert. Ibidem, Religionem eam, quæ in metu & cerimonia Deorum fit, appellant. Idem in Verrem, Quorum sacra maximè & occultis- simè cerimoniis continentur. Ibidem, Fecit ludos maxima cum cerimonia. Idem contra Rullum, Domitius, quod per cerimoniam populi fieri nò poterat, ratione assecutus est. Idem pro C. Rabirio, Lucius Flaccus, homo in sacerdocio cerimoniarum, quibus præerat, diligentissimus. Idem pro Cornelio Balbo, Sacra Ceréris summa Majores nostri religione, cerimoniaq; confici voluerunt. Idem pro domo sua, Non alio modo esse constituturus de religione Pontificum, quam cerimoniarum jus coëgerit. Idem de Aruspicum responso, Quod sacrificiorum fit incredibili cerimonia. Ibidem, Sta- tas solennes, cerimonias pontificacu continueri. Ibidem, Omnia solennia librorum omnibus rebus summa cum cerimonia func seruata. Item, Tam e Ponticisicio jure, & cerimoniis sepulcrorum intelligi licet. Cæsar de bello Gallico, Quo more eorum gracissima cerimonia concinetur. Cicero de Legibus. Hoc summam religione cerimoniam, declarat. Ibidem, Cerimonie religionem, in Deos. Pro Domo id ni, Sacre religionis cerimonie. Exhis locis & similibus apparet, cerimonia nomen & singulari & plurali in numero cum pro religione ipsa (unde etiam sœpe cum religionis nomine conjungitur.) tum pro ritibus sacris, siue sacrorum institutis accipi.
units.tr: Ceremonia, or, as others write it with e in place of i, Ceremonie, is the religion of sacred rites. Religion, says Cicero in his On Invention, is that which brings care and ceremony of the gods. In the same place: that which arises from fear and ceremony of the gods they call religion. The same, against Verres: whose sacred rites are contained in the greatest and most secret ceremonies. In the same place: he gave games with the greatest ceremony. The same, against Rullus: Domitius achieved by reason what could not be done by the ceremony of the people. The same, for C. Rabirius: Lucius Flaccus, a man most diligent in the priesthood and in the ceremonies over which he presided. The same, for Cornelius Balbus: our ancestors wished the sacred rites of Ceres to be performed with the greatest religion and ceremony. The same, for his own house: he would not settle the matter of the religion of the Pontiffs in any other way than the law of ceremonies compelled. The same, on the response of the haruspices: which is done with incredible ceremony of sacrifices. In the same place: the set solemn ceremonies are maintained by the pontiffs. In the same place: all the solemnities of the books are observed with the greatest ceremony in all matters. Likewise: it is permitted to understand this also from the Pontifical law and the ceremonies of tombs. Caesar, On the Gallic War: in which manner of theirs the most gracious ceremony is celebrated. Cicero, On the Laws: this declares the highest religious ceremony. In the same place: ceremony, religion towards the gods. In For his House: the ceremonies of holy religion. From these and similar passages it appears that the word ceremonia, in both singular and plural, is taken both for religion itself (whence it is often joined with the word religion) and for sacred rites, or the institutions of sacred things.

units.la: De nominis aucem hujus derivatione & etymologia varie sunt doctorum sententiæ. Cerimoniarum causam, inquit Festus, alii ab oppido Cere distam existimant: alii a caritate distam dicant. Tit. Liuius ab urbe condita lib. 5. de Lucio Albino quoda de plebe Romana sic loquicur, Qui virgines sacrum, Cere plastro vexerit: unde quidam cerimonias distas existimant. Valerius Maximus lib. 1. ejusdem historie meminit, ubi L. Alvancum vocat. Inde, inquit idem, institutum est sacra cerimonias vocari, quod Cerecani ea infratio Reipub. statu perinde ac florence coluerunt. Sabinus apud Aulum Gellium libro 4. cap. 9. a carendo deducit cerimonias, licut religionem a relinquendo. Augustinus lib. Retractationum 1. cap. 37. similicer a carendo vult cerimonias distas, eo quod obseruantes careant in rebus, a quibus abstinent. Verum de urbe Cerite, & situ ejus vide Strabonem lib. 5.
units.tr: The learned have various opinions on the derivation and etymology of this word. Festus says that some think the reason for ceremonies is that they were named after the town of Caere, others that they were named from caritas, dearness. Livy, in his history from the foundation of the city, Book 5, speaks of a certain Lucius Albinus from the Roman plebs in this way: "who carried the virgins' sacred things on a Caerite wagon"; whence some think ceremonies were so named. Valerius Maximus, Book 1 of the same history, mentions it, where he calls him L. Albinus. Hence, says the same writer, it was established that sacred rites be called ceremonies, because the Caerites observed them in the state of the republic as flourishing. Sabinus, in Aulus Gellius, Book 4, chapter 9, derives ceremonies from carendo, to lack, just as religion is derived from relinquendo, to leave behind. Augustine, Retractations, Book 1, chapter 37, similarly wishes ceremonies to be named from carendo, because those who observe them abstain from things which they lack. But on the city of Caere and its site, see Strabo, Book 5.

units.la: Sunt qui cerimonias volunt distas a Græco χαίρειν, quod salutis sint causæ, siue ad salutem spectent: vel quod lætitiæ in in perngendi sit studendum. Thomas Aquinas, Prima 2. quæst. 99. artic. 3. refert, quosdam fuisse, qui cerimonias existimarint distas a Cerere, quasi Cereris munia, siue, ut uno verbo dicam, Ceremunialia: quod Ceres frugum Dea prima seré omnis fuerit culta, & quod sacra illa Cerealia omnis sint antiquissima & sanctissima habita: Unde Cicero pro Cornelio Balbo, sacra Cereris summa dixit religione cerimoniaq; confici suisse soliti. Est ergo elegans paronomasia Cereris in vocabulo Cerimonia. Alii etiā a cereo videtur dista. Verum mihi verisimile videtur dista cerimonia siue cerimonias ab Hebræo חרם Charam, quod de vouere, anathemate ferire, a communi su et consuetudine separare, Deo consecrare significat, siue a חרם Chcrem, quod significat anathema, ré Deo dicatā et côsecratā, ut cerimonia sic quasi cheremonia.
units.tr: Some wish ceremonies to be named from the Greek chairein [χαίρειν], to rejoice, because they serve salvation or look to salvation, or because one must strive to produce joy. Thomas Aquinas, Prima Secundae, question 99, article 3, reports that some have thought ceremonies were named from Ceres, as if they were the duties of Ceres, or, to say it in one word, Ceremonialia: because Ceres, goddess of grain, was the first to cultivate all sowing, and because all those Cerealian rites were held most ancient and most holy. Hence Cicero, for Cornelius Balbus, said that the sacred rites of Ceres were wont to be performed with the highest religion and ceremony. There is therefore an elegant paronomasia of Ceres in the word Cerimonia. Others also think it is named from cereus, waxen. But to me it seems more probable that ceremonia, or ceremonias, is named from the Hebrew חרם [Charam], which means to vow, to strike with an anathema, to separate from common use and custom, to consecrate to God; or from חרם [Cherem], which signifies a thing anathematized, devoted and consecrated to God; so that ceremonia is as it were cheremonia.

units.la: Veneratio Deorum etiam pro culcu sœpe accipicur, quæ re verà suit quasi venatio quedà. Hæc enim sacerdotes & animos & corpora, & forcunat hominii venari conjue verunt. Veneretionem justam, inquit Cicero de Natura Deorum, habet, quicquid excellit. Idem, Deos augusti omnes san Hos veneramur. Idem, Deos venerari & colere debemus. Idem in epistolis, Cùm ignorit omnibus quì multa Deos venerati sunt contra ejus salutem. Idem, Venerari aliquem, aut Deum. Item, Salutare Deos pro venerari. Et pro Plancio, Diis, quos colere, venerari, precarii, solemus. Agataflocles apud Plautum in Pœnulo: Hanc equidem Venerem venerabor ( elegans agnominatio) ut amet posthac propitia. Virgilius, Georg. 1. Inprimis venerare Deos atq; annua magna • Sacra refer Cereri.
units.tr: The veneration of the gods is also often taken for worship, which in truth was, as it were, a kind of hunting; for they were accustomed to hunt men's minds and bodies and fortunes. "Whatever excels," says Cicero in On the Nature of the Gods, "has a just veneration." The same: we venerate all the gods as august and holy. The same: we ought to venerate and worship the gods. The same, in his letters: since all who have worshipped many gods are ignorant of his salvation. The same: to venerate someone or a god. Likewise, to greet the gods means to venerate them. And in For Plancius: to the gods, whom we are accustomed to worship, venerate and pray to. Agorocles in Plautus's Poenulus: "Indeed I will venerate this Venus" (an elegant agnomination), "that she may henceforth favourably love." Virgil, Georgics 1: "Above all, venerate the gods and bring the great annual rites to Ceres."

units.la: Venerari simulachra. Cicero in Verrem, Simulachra ex suis sacris sublata in foro venerabantur. Venerari templa. Cicero de Conf. Forum in urbibus atq; agris augustissima templa venerentur. Venerari autem Pauli videtur verbum compositum ex venia et orando, ut venerari sit quasi venia orare. Vel venerari quasi vereri et revereri, vel orare ut Dii veniant et adsint hominibus vel quasi venari et aucupari Deorum gratiam.
units.tr: To venerate images. Cicero against Verres: "The images, taken from their shrines, were venerated in the forum." To venerate temples. Cicero, on the laws: "Let the forum in the cities and the most sacred temples in the fields be venerated." It seems that venerari is a compound of venia and orando, so that venerari is, as it were, to pray for favour. Or venerari is as if from vereri and revereri, or to pray that the gods may come and be present to men, or as if from venari and aucupari, to hunt for the favour of the gods.

units.la: Cultum praeterea Deorum: Rem divinam vocarunt Ethnici, cum severa illorum res divinae non fuerit res divina, sed potius humana, immo daemoniaca, nimirum ab hominibus vel ipsis potius Daemonibus invenita, excogitata et in mundum introducta. Hinc Plautus: Paucis verbis rem divinam facito. Item in Pœnulo: Cum ab re divina redieris. Sic impias quoq; rerum futurarum praedictiones divinationem et vates suos divinos appellarunt, divinando et praedicendo. In plurali numero, Res divinae. Cicero in Oratione pro Milone, Patera, qua ad res divinas utebatur. Idem, Res illum divinas apud eos Deos in suo sacrario prope quotidie facere vidisti.
units.tr: Besides, the worship of the gods: the Gentiles called it "divine business" (res divina), although their so-called divine business was not divine at all, but human, indeed demonic, devised and invented by men, or rather by the demons themselves, and introduced into the world. Hence Plautus: "Make the divine business brief, in few words." Likewise in the Poenulus: "When you have returned from the divine business." So too they called impious predictions of future events "divination," and their seers "divine," from divining and predicting. In the plural, "divine things" (res divinae). Cicero, in the speech for Milo: "the paten which he used for divine things." Again: "You have seen him perform divine things almost every day in his shrine, before those gods."

units.la: Huc etiam pertinet Adorationis nomen. Adorare apud Antiquos, teste Festo, significabat agere et legati Oratores dicuntur, quia mandata populi agunt. Quidam volunt dictum ab ore, tametsi mente potius, quam ore vera fiat adoratio. Denig. Honos etiam pro cultu accipitur.
units.tr: To this also belongs the name adoration. Among the ancients, as Festus testifies, adorare meant to perform, and envoys are called oratores (speakers) because they carry out the commands of the people. Some hold that it is derived from os (mouth), although true adoration is made in the mind rather than by the mouth. Finally, honour is also taken for worship.

units.la: Lar apud Plautum: Ecquid majorem filius Mihi honorem habueris? Et paulo post: Atq; ille vero minus minusq; impendio Curare, minusq;, me impartire honoribus. Item: Dat mihi cornua, ejus honoris, id est, cultus gratia.
units.tr: Plautus, in the words of the Lar: "Has my son ever shown me greater honour?" And a little later: "But he spends less and less on my care, and less on bestowing honours on me." Likewise: "He gives me horns, for the sake of that honour," that is, for the sake of worship.

units.la: Hactenus de Latinis nominibus, quibus Gentiles suam religionem cultumq;, Deorum insignieruni. Venio ad Graeca nomina. Inter haec primum occurrit verbum σιβειν et σιβασειν, quod Suidas interpretatur ιυλογειν et σιβασιασειν, id est, colere et venerari: quod procul dubio de-rivatum est ab Hebraeo שבח Sabach, id est, sacrificavit, et שבח Sebach, id est, Sacrificium: quae vox et speciatim atq; proprie pro sacrificatione, et generatim pro toto cultu ut purpura-tur: cujus praecipua pars olim fuit sacrificium. Rom. σιβασμος. Euripides in Hippol. σεβειν. Lucianus de Sacrificus, σεβειν. Xenophon. Porro σεβειν interdum aliter colere, observare, venerari etiam de hominibus: interdum pavere vel colere, vel adorari usurpatur. Ab hoc verbo Sabini sunt dicti, ceu a cultura Deorum, quod ea gens Deos praecipue colat. Inde et σεβαζω Poëtae idem est, quod σεβαζεσθαι, et σιβασμαζω. Hinc σιβας, τι (nomen indeclinabile, ut putatur) cum venerationem, cultum divinum, adorationem, tum rem, quam venerantur, et adorantur, tum fluporem ex admiratione significat. Σεβασμος item et σεβασις venerationis dicitur, ac σεβασμα, quod venerantur homines et colunt. Σεβαστος veneratione et admiratione dignus, venerandus, augustus, quod plerunq, Imperio Romano fuit cognomen. Hinc ευσεβης, pius, religiosus, qui probe colit et veneratur Deum. Lucian. de Calum. Ευσεβης probe et religiose Deum colere. Ifocrates in Nicoclem, ευσεβως προς τις θεας. Ευσεβειας dicitur, quod religiose et pie fit. Ευσεβως et contrarie ευσεβως pie, religio-se. Ευσεβεια piu. Ευσεβεια pietas, religio. Ἱερα θεος, cultus Dei, θεος ευσεβειν Deum colere, θεος ευσεβειας, qui Deu sive Deos colit, θεοσεβης, religiose, pie, more eorum, qui Deum colunt. Opposita sunt ασεβεια, impietas, et cotemtus venerationis et cultus divini: ασεβης, impius, irreligiosus, qui contemnit et negligit cultu Deorum: ασεβειν impie agere, impiu et irreligiosum esse. Xenophon ασεβειν εις τα μυσηρα. Athen. ως ασεβουσιν ευ θυοντα κατα τα πατρια κολα-σαντι. Item, ευσεβεια, et ποιητ. ευσεβιση, idem quod ασεβεια, et ευσεβης, idem quod ασεβης.
units.tr: So far concerning the Latin names by which the Gentiles marked their religion and worship of the gods. I turn to the Greek names. Among these the first to occur is the verb sebein [σέβειν] and sebazein [σεβάζειν], which Suidas explains as to praise and to venerate, that is, to worship and venerate. This undoubtedly derives from the Hebrew shabach [שבח], "he sacrificed," and sebach [שבח], "sacrifice," a word used specifically and properly for sacrificing, and generally for the whole worship, of which sacrifice was once the chief part. Romans: sebasmos [σεβασμός]. Euripides in the Hippolytus: sebein. Lucian, On Sacrifices: sebein. Xenophon. Moreover, sebein is sometimes used in another sense: to worship, observe, or venerate, also of men; sometimes it is used for to fear, or to cultivate, or to adore. From this verb the Sabines are named, as if from the cultivation of the gods, because that nation worships the gods above all. Hence sebazo is for the poets the same as sebazesthai and sebasmazo. Hence sebas [σέβας], an indeclinable noun as is thought, signifies both veneration, divine worship and adoration, and also the thing that is venerated and adored, and the awe arising from admiration. Sebasmos likewise is said of veneration, and sebasma of what men venerate and worship. Sebastos [σεβαστός] means worthy of veneration and admiration, venerable, august, and it was mostly a cognomen of the Roman Emperor. Hence eusebes [εὐσεβής]: pious, religious, one who duly worships and venerates God. Lucian, On the Calumny: to worship God duly and religiously. Isocrates to Nicocles: to act piously towards the gods. Eusebeia is said of what is done religiously and piously; eusebos, piously, religiously; eusebeia, piety; eusebeia, piety and religion. Hiera theos: the worship of God; theon eusebein: to worship God; eusebes of one who worships God or gods; theosebes: religious and pious, after the manner of those who worship God. Opposed to these are asebeia [ἀσέβεια], impiety, and contempt of veneration and divine worship; asebes [ἀσεβής], impious, irreligious, one who despises and neglects the worship of the gods; asebein [ἀσεβεῖν], to act impiously, to be impious and irreligious. Xenophon: asebein eis ta musera, to act impiously towards the mysteries. Athenaeus: that they impiously punished him who had sacrificed well according to the ancestral rites. Likewise eusebeia, and poetically eusebiê, is the same as asebeia, and eusebes is the same as asebes.

units.la: Ευσεβειαν Evoȩ́ς ιαν nonnullis voce σίζας volunt deduci, quæ θαῦμα & stupendum quid significat, quod Ευσεβείας in cultu Dei omnia sint θωμασ̃τοί, id est, admiratione digna. Trifmegistus, quem plurimùm & etymon & deo Lactantius & Augustinus ipse sequitur, sυσέβειαν definit Θεοῦ γνῶσιν, & Stoici, auctore Laer-tio lib.7. εὐσέβειαν definierunt δὲ ἐπίςημιν Θεοῦ θρησκείας, id est, scientiam colendi Dei, sive culeus divini. Eandem definitionem adsert Suidas.
units.tr: Some want eusebeia to be derived from thauma [θαῦμα], "wonder," which signifies something stupendous, because in the worship of God all piety is thaumastoi, that is, worthy of admiration. Trismegistus, whom Lactantius and Augustine himself follow closely both in etymology and in God, defines eusebeia as the knowledge of God. The Stoics, according to Laertius, book 7, defined eusebeia as the science of worshipping God, that is, knowledge of divine worship. Suidas gives the same definition.

units.la: Aliud nomen, quo cultus & religio cum vera, tum falsa Ethnicorum a Græcis exprimitur, est Λατρία, nomen λατρείας. Hoc primò quidem in genere quod ῶν servitium profanum, tum divinum si- & varia eȷ̃m gnificat. Idem est λάτρευμα a λατρεύειν, servire, famulari, &c, quod ipsum a λάτρις s κῶν, id est, servus, famulus & serva, famula, deducitur. Significat hoc etiam mercenarium. λάτρης servus μιϭθὼ ἢ ἱ ναύειν, λατρὸν merces. Λαϭδεύς cultor. Apollo etiam & Neptunus λαἵς cognominatur a servitio inomedonti in extruendis murls præstito. Λατρεύειν volunt compositum esse a λα particula intensiva, κῇ τρεὶν, id est, Φοβεῖσθαι, hoc est, tremere, metuere: unde λατρον, id est, tremor. quod servi ad dominorum jussa & imperia vehementer tremere soleant.
units.tr: Another name by which the Greeks express both true and false worship and religion of the Gentiles is latreia [λατρεία]. In general this signifies profane service, and also various kinds of divine service. The same word is latreuma [λάτρευμα], from latreuein [λατρεύειν], to serve, to be a servant, and so on, which itself is derived from latris [λάτρις], that is, a male or female servant. It also signifies hired service: latres [λάτρης], a servant for wages or hire, and latron [λάτρον], wages. Latreus [λάτρευς] is a worshipper. Apollo and Neptune are also surnamed from the service they rendered in building the walls for Laomedon. Some hold that latreuein is compounded of the intensive particle la- and tremein [τρέειν], that is, to fear, to dread, whence latron, trembling, because slaves are wont to tremble greatly at the commands and orders of their masters.

units.la: Etsi vero nomen hoc apud prophanos auctores servitutem, sive servitium prophanum; & Λατρεία quidem mercenarium significat: tamen apud Eccl-siasticos scriptores, ut apud Damascenum & quid apud sacros passim in novo Testamento accipitur cum pro religioso, tum etiam superstitioso cultu, ut Rom.1. scriptores ἰσθίσ̃σιν, ἀ ἱ λάτρευσιν τὴν κτίσεν παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα. Hic cultus eiκονολαϭεία & ειδωλο- λαϭεία vocatur, & εἰδωλολάτρης cultor idolorum & simulacrorum, & εἰδωλολάτρεῖν, idolorum seu simulacrorum cultui studere, vel esse dedituum. Omnino autem τὸ λατρεύειν gentilium suit laterem laṽare, u: est in proverbio.
units.tr: Although this name, among profane authors, signifies servitude or profane service, and latreia in particular means hired service, yet among ecclesiastical writers, as in Damascene, and throughout the sacred books of the New Testament, it is taken both for religious and for superstitious worship, as in Romans 1, where they "served (ἐλάτρευσαν) the creature rather than the Creator" [ἐλάτρευσαν τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα]. This worship is called eidololatria [εἰδωλολατρία], and an eidololatres [εἰδωλολάτρης] is a worshipper of idols and images, and eidololatrein [εἰδωλολατρεῖν] is to be devoted or given over to the worship of idols or images. Indeed, among the Gentiles, latreuein was, as the proverb goes, "to wash a brick."

units.la: Videtur etiam ab hoc verbo λατρύεων derivatum esse Gallicum flatter, cui respondet Germanicum flattieren/ id est, adulari, eo quod servitium sive profanum, sive etiam divinum flattieren a plerunque cum adulatione & hypocrisi est conjunctum: unde etiam adulandi verbum a Græco Λατρεία s' ἀλω, sive ἡ ἀλυεῖν videtur derivatum esse, quod servi ad adulandum valde apti sint atq; pro- derivatum, pensi. Plerung, ὁ ὁ αλυσσ' ἀλίυσιν, ut Græci loquuntur, Fönnen wolaugenbienen/id est sicut a oculus servire.
units.tr: It seems that the French "flatter" is also derived from this Greek verb latreuein, to which corresponds the German flattieren, that is, to flatter, because service, whether profane or even divine, is generally joined with flattery and hypocrisy. Whence also the word for flattering (adulari) seems to be derived from a Greek word, since slaves are very apt for flattering and very ready to serve. Often they serve by the eye, as the Greeks put it, which the Germans express as "to serve for show" (Augendienen), that is, to serve as if with the eyes.

units.la: Perrò ut λατρείας, ita ἀλυλίας quoq; nomen, quæ duo sunt homonyma, cum apud prophanos adulari. quidem auctores pro humano plerunque ser vitio, tum vero apud scriptores Ecclesiasticos, in novo Δουλεία & veteri Testamento partim pro vero unius Dei, partim etiam pro falso & adulterino Deorum cultu usurpatur. De utriusq; autem vocabuli discrimine, quod nonnulli slatuerunt, hæc sunt Au- Discrimen gustini verba lib.10. cap.1. — Latriam nostri, ubicunque scripturarum positum est, interpretari λατρείας sunt servitutem. Sed ea servitus, quæ debetur hominibus, secundum quam præcipit Apostolus ser & Δουλείας vos dominus suus subditos esse debere, alio nomine Græce nuncupari solet. Latria verò secundum ex Augustino. consuetudinem, quæ locuti sunt, qui nobis divina eloquia considerèt, aut semper aut tam frequenter, ut penè semper, sea dicitur servitus, quæ pertinet ad colendum Deum. Proinde si eantummodo cultus ipse dicatur, non soli Deo deberi videtur. Dicimur enim etiam colere homines, quos bonorifica vel recordatione, vel præsentia frequentamus. Hactenus Augustinus, de cujus distinctione ejus Commentator Ludovicus Vives hæc subjicit: λάτρεύεις ἡ Δουλεία, quasi servitio: sed postea Ex Ludoico factum est, ut esset οἰκετεία, teste Suida. Augustinus servitutem hominibus debitam non latriam Vive. appellari vult, sed alio nomine, puta Δουλείαν. Nam ad Ephesios sexto, quem locum citat, sic est Græce: οἱ δοῦλοι ὑπακούετε τοῖς κυρίοις κῇ φόβῳ. Hinc est illa distinctio facta de adoratione, latria, dulia & hyperdulia. Valla docet λατρείαν & Δουλείαν idem esse & utrunque significare Ex Valls. servitutem, quod ex Suida ostedit, qui & ait: λατρείαν ὁ Δουλείαν ἵνα ἢ τῷ μισθῷ, servitutem esse mercenariam. Hucusq; Vives.
units.tr: Moreover, just as latreia, so also douleia [δουλεία] is a name, and these two are homonyms: among profane authors it usually signifies human servitude, but among ecclesiastical writers, in both the New and the Old Testament, it is used partly for the true worship of the one God and partly also for the false and adulterous worship of the gods. Concerning the difference between these two words, which some have laid down, these are the words of Augustine, book 10, chapter 1: "Our writers, wherever it occurs in the Scriptures, render latreia as servitude. But the servitude owed to men, according to which the Apostle bids you servants to be subject to your lords, is usually called by another name in Greek [δουλεία]. Latria, however, according to the custom of those who have expounded the divine oracles to us, is almost always called servitude which pertains to the worship of God. Therefore if it is called only worship, it does not seem to be owed to God alone, for we are also said to worship men whom we frequent with honourable remembrance or presence." So far Augustine. On this distinction his commentator Ludovicus Vives adds: latreia and douleia, as if servitude; but afterwards it became oiketeia, as Suidas testifies. Augustine wants the servitude owed to men to be called not latria but by another name, namely douleia. For in Ephesians 6, which he cites, the Greek reads: "Servants, obey your masters with fear" [οἱ δοῦλοι ὑπακούετε τοῖς κυρίοις μετὰ φόβου]. Hence arose the distinction made about adoration: latria, dulia and hyperdulia. Valla teaches that latreia and douleia are the same, and that both signify servitude, as he shows from Suidas, who also says that latreia is douleia for hire, that is, mercenary servitude. So far Vives.

units.la: Vtrig, autem huic vocumini λατρείας & Δουλείας respondet Hebræum עבדה Abudáh, id est, servitus, & Germanicum Gotteedienst/id est, servitiū sive cultus Dei, & Gottgendienst/ id est, servitium sive cultus, qui præstatur idolis, Dins, alienis.
units.tr: Of these two words, λατρείας and δουλείας, the Hebrew עבדה (Abudah [עבדה]) corresponds, meaning servitude. The German Gotteedienst, that is, the service or worship of God, corresponds to it, and Gottesdienst, that is, the service or worship offered to idols and strange gods, does too.

units.la: Duobus his vocabulis respondet Θεραπεία nomen & verbum θεραπεύειν, quod essi pro- Θεραπεία fanum & servile plerunque servitium significat: tamen ad divinum quoque servitium aliquando accommodatur. Sic Plato dixit θεραπεύειν ἰδέας θεῶν, οἷον οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι τοὺς θεραπόντας θεραμὴ ὠσον, nempe ὑπομνήσει. Sic Suidas ὑσίᾳ εὐχαρίστει definit ἐπισημᾶν θεῶν θρησκείας. id est, sententiam Deo inserviendi, sive ejus colendi. Plutarchus quoq; religionem vocat θεοσέβειαν καὶ ὁσιότητα. & Isocrates μαχίσσῳ θρησκείας dixit, id est, cultum maximum.
units.tr: To these two words corresponds the noun θεραπεία and the verb θεραπεύειν [θεραπεία, θεραπεύειν]. Although they usually mean free service or servile service, they are sometimes applied to the service of God as well. Thus Plato said θεραπεύειν ἰδέας θεῶν [to serve the forms of the gods], and the Jews' servants... θεραπόντας [θεραπόντας]. Thus Suidas defines the word ὁσία [ὁσία], piety, as ἐπιστήμη θεῶν θρησκείας [knowledge of the worship of the gods], that is, the knowledge of how to serve God, or of how to worship him. Plutarch also calls religion θεοσέβεια καὶ ὁσιότης [reverence for God and holiness], and Isocrates spoke of μεγίστη θρησκεία [the greatest worship], that is, the highest cult.

units.la: Sequitur θρησκείας nomen, quod & sacrum & profanum in litteris saepe cum pro vera & legitima, tum pro falsa & fucata religione accipitur. Hoc nomen Suidas a Thracibus vulc fuisse deductum, apud quos Orpheus, Poeta primus ἐπιχολόγος τὴν τῆς ἰδιῶν μυστήρια, id est, initiatus, excogitatus. Graecorum mysteria: quae cum ad alias gentes perlata essent, a Thracibus unde didicerunt, eum cultum θρησκείας appellarunt. Suida verba sunt haec: θρησκεία, λατρεία, θρησκεύειν, id est, θεοσεβεῖν, ὑπηρετεῖν τοῖς θεοῖς. Plutarchus in vita Alexandri. Herod. lib. 3. Dii Thraces, Dii Samothracum, qui, ut est apud Varronem lib. 4. de lingua Lat. habiti sunt sanctissimi.
units.tr: Next comes the noun θρησκεία [thrēskeia], which in literature, both sacred and profane, is often used of true and lawful religion, and also of false and feigned religion. Suidas says this word was derived from the Thracians, among whom Orpheus, the first poet, devised the mysteries of the Greeks, that is, the rites of initiation. When these mysteries were carried to other nations, they called the cult θρησκεία because they had learned it from the Thracians. Suidas's words are: θρησκεία, λατρεία, θρησκεύειν, that is, θεοσεβεῖν, ὑπηρετεῖν τοῖς θεοῖς [worship, service, to worship, that is, to revere God, to serve the gods]. See Plutarch in the Life of Alexander, and Herodotus, book 3. The Thracian gods and the gods of Samothrace were, as Varro says in book 4 of the Latin language, considered most holy.

units.la: Hoc igitur θρησκείας nomen in sacris litteris aliquando bonam in partem accipitur pro vero Dei cultu, ut Act. 27. ubi Paulus dicit, se exactissime secundum sectam suam θρησκείας, id est, religionis sceliceis Pharisaicae vixisse: tamen si potest ibi etiam in malam partem accipi. Iacob. 1. εἴ τις δοκεῖ θρησκὸς εἶναι, μὴ χαλινῶν γλῶσσαν, ἀλλ' ἀπατῶν καρδίαν αὑτοῦ, τούτου μάταιος ἡ θρησκεία. Si quis sibi videtur pius aut religiosus esse, non refrenans suam linguam, sed tor suum decipiens, hujus religio vana est. Et, θρησκεία καθαρὰ καὶ ἀμίαντος ... id est, Religio, pura & immaculata apud Deum & Patrem haec est, in visere orphanos & viduas in afflictione ipsorum, & immaculatum se servare a mundo.
units.tr: In sacred literature this word θρησκεία is sometimes taken in a good sense, for the true worship of God, as in Acts 27, where Paul says that he lived most strictly according to his sect, in the θρησκεία, that is, the religion, of the Pharisees. It can also be taken in a bad sense there. James 1: εἴ τις δοκεῖ θρησκὸς εἶναι... μάταιος ἡ θρησκεία [If anyone thinks himself religious... his religion is vain]: "If anyone seems to himself to be pious or religious, but does not bridle his tongue and deceives his own heart, this man's religion is vain." And: θρησκεία καθαρὰ καὶ ἀμίαντος [pure and undefiled religion]: "Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world."

units.la: In malam partem deinde, pro superstitione videlicet, accipitur fere cum appositione quadam, ut ad Coloss. 2. θρησκεία τῶν ἀγγέλων, superstitio ... Angelorum cultus: & ... dem pro religione ... sive ... ut ... ibidem potius ...
units.tr: Then it is taken in a bad sense, namely for superstition, and this is mostly with some added qualifier, as in Colossians 2: θρησκεία τῶν ἀγγέλων [worship of angels], superstition... the worship of angels. It is also used for religion... or... as in the same place, rather...

units.la: Praeterea ut Sanctitas apud Latinos, ita vox ὅσιον & ὀσιότης & apud Graecos pro religione & cultu divino, sive is verius sit, sive fictus sive commentitius accipitur. Plato in Dialogo, qui Euthyphron Euchyphron inscribitur, sive de Sancto, duo facit τὸ δίκαιον, id est, justi sive justitiae genera: Unum, quod vocant εὐσέβειαν καὶ ὅσιον τὸ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν θεραπείαν, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, as sanctitas is used among the Latins, so among the Greeks the words ὅσιον and ὁσιότης [hosion, hosiotēs] are used for religion and divine worship, whether that worship is true, feigned or invented. In Plato's dialogue called Euthyphro, or On the Holy, Socrates makes two kinds of δίκαιον [the just], that is, of justice: one is what they call εὐσέβεια καὶ ὅσιον, the care of God that is holy and pious, etc.

units.la: Idem omne quidem sanctum, dicit esse justum, sed non omne justum sanctum; non secus atque ubi pudor, ibi est metus: non autem ubi metus, ibi est pudor. Idem omne ὅσιον ... dicit esse ὅσιον, το δὲ μὴ ... id est, omne id, quod Deo gratum est, id dicit esse sanctum: quod Deo non est carum atque gratum, id esse non sanctum seu profanum. Deum enim mensurant atque canonem divini cultus esse optimum. Id probat simili ductu a servo bonis atque probo, qui dominos suos colunt non pro sua, sed ipsorum voluntate. Cultum itaque Dei in obedientia voluntatis divinae maxime consistere. Ibidem ea demum dicit esse ὅσια, id est, sancta, si quae gratae sint Diis, ea norit dicere & facere εὐχέσθαι. Hinc concludit, ὅσιον καὶ ὀσιότητα, id est, sanctum & sanctitatem esse ... Dei ... id est, scientiam sacrificandi & precandi: ὅσιον quidem, id est, sacrificare, esse ... dare, sive largiri Diis, τὸ δὲ ... id est, precari esse petere quid a Diis. Hinc effici ὀσιότητα esse ... sanctus. Iterum ... Cum autem Euthyphron inde vellet concludere, Cultum igitur Dei esse ... θεοῦ ... ἀνθρώποις ... id est, mercaturam negotiationem ... inter Deos & homines, respondet, opinionem hanc ejus refellens, religionem nequaquam mereaturam proprie posse dici, cum ea, quae Dii dant, hominibus omnibus.
units.tr: The same Socrates says that everything holy is just, but not everything just is holy, just as where there is shame there is fear, but where there is fear there is not always shame. He says that everything ὅσιον [hosion] is pleasing to God; whatever is not dear and pleasing to God is not holy, but profane. For they measure God and hold that the rule of divine worship is the best. He proves this by a similar comparison with good and upright slaves, who serve their masters not according to their own will but according to the will of their masters. So the worship of God consists chiefly in obedience to the divine will. In the same dialogue he says that those things are ὅσια, holy, which are pleasing to the gods, and that one who knows how to say and do what is pleasing to them knows how to pray (εὔχεσθαι). From this he concludes that holiness and sanctity are the knowledge of sacrificing and praying: to sacrifice, that is, to give or bestow gifts on the gods, and to pray, that is, to ask something from the gods. From this it follows that holiness is... the holy. Again, when Euthyphro wished to conclude from this that the worship of God is... θεοῦ... ἀνθρώποις [of God... among men], that is, a trade and commerce between gods and men, Socrates replies, refuting this opinion, that religion cannot properly be called a trade, since the things the gods give are given to all men.

units.la: θρησκεία — superstitio in sacris litteris ... omnibus sint nota: cum nihil habeamus boni, quod non ab illis nobis detur. At verò hic, inquit, ἡ ὠφέλεια τοῖς θεοῖς ὅσα ἄνθρ. τὴν ψυχὴν, ἃ παρ' ἡμῶν λαμβάνοντες, hoc est, quid commodi & utilitatis percipiunt Dii ex donis illis atque muneribus, quae a nobis accipiunt? quasi diceret, Nihil. Contra autem, ut in omni contractu: ita in mercatura oportere ut onerum, impensarum atque damnorum: ita utilitatum atque commoditatum esse societatem, atque communionem. Atqui cum nulla in Deum ex religione nostra redundent commoda, non posse dici ἰμπορεύεσθαι. At objiciat non nemo: Deus tamen ab hominibus glorificari & sanctificari: ac bonos atque gloria ejus augeri, propagari & illustrari dicitur. Respondet Socrates, hoc non ita intelligendum quasi aliqua honoris atque gloriae ad Deum fiat accessio, qui cum sit immensus, infinitus, omnibusque numeris perfectus & absolutus, nihil ut essentiae, ita gloriae ejus vel addi, vel demi, aut detrahi potest: sed quia Dei gloria atque honor magis ac magis hominibus patefie ac innotescie. Hoc Solis simulitudine illustrari potest, qui quando longe lateque suos in mundo fulgentes radios, videtur ille ab hominibus illustrari, cum nulla vel minima ad Solem fieri possit splendoris accessio, & non Sol ab hominibus, sed homines potius a Sole illustrentur.
units.tr: θρησκεία [religion] ... superstition ... in sacred literature are well known to all, since we have nothing good that is not given to us by them. But here, he says, ἡ ὠφέλεια τοῖς θεοῖς ὅσα ἄνθρ. τὴν ψυχὴν, ἃ παρ' ἡμῶν λαμβάνοντες [what benefit do the gods receive from the gifts which they receive from us, men, the soul...], that is, what advantage or profit do the gods gain from those gifts and offerings which they receive from us? As if he were saying: nothing. On the contrary, as in every contract, so in trade there ought to be a partnership and fellowship of profits as well as of burdens, expenses and losses. But since no advantage flows to God from our religion, it cannot be called a trade. Yet someone may object: God is nonetheless said to be glorified and sanctified by men, and his good name is said to be increased, spread and made illustrious. Socrates replies that this must not be understood as if some addition of honour and glory came to God. Since he is immense, infinite and perfect and complete in every respect, nothing can be added to or taken from his essence or his glory. Rather, God's glory and honour are more and more revealed and made known to men. This can be illustrated by the likeness of the sun. When the sun sends its rays far and wide through the world, it seems to be illuminated by men, though no light, however small, can be added to the sun; it is not the sun that is illuminated by men, but men who are illuminated by the sun.

units.la: Porrò ἱερὸν, id est, sanctum, nonnulli volunt dici quasi ἁγνὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ ἁγίου, seu ἁγνίζειν, a colendo, seu venerando. Quid si potius ab Hebraeo חסיד, Chasid, sive חסיד, Chaesed, id est, benigno, & misericorde, sive benignitate & misericordia fit derivatum? Ota etiam in plurali numero res sacrae: item justa, parentalia, & exsequiae appellantur, sicut et τὰ ἱερὰ καὶ νόμιμα καὶ νομιζόμενα. Hinc ὅσιον, ἀφοσιοῦν, ἐξοσιοῦν, ἀνοσιοῦν, sanctum & purum scelevis reddere, piare, expiare, sanctificare, consecrare. Inde fit ἀποσίωσις, piaculum, & ἀφοσίωσις expiatio. Opponitur τῷ ὁσίῳ & ὁσιώτῃ, id est, sancto & sanctitati τὸ ἀνόσιον καὶ βέβηλον, id est, impium, nefarium, profanum, καὶ ἀσεβὲς, id est, impietas.
units.tr: Moreover, ἱερὸν [hieron], that is, holy, some want to be said as if it were ἁγνόν [hagnon, pure] from ἅγιος [hagios, holy], or from ἁγνίζειν [to purify], from honouring or revering. But what if it is rather derived from the Hebrew חסיד [chasid], or חסד [chesed], that is, kind and merciful, or from kindness and mercy? Sacred things are also called, in the plural, "the holy things", and likewise justa (funeral rites), parentalia and exsequiae, as are τὰ ἱερὰ καὶ νόμιμα καὶ νομιζόμενα [the sacred and lawful and customary things]. Hence ὅσιον, ἀφοσιοῦν, ἐξοσιοῦν, ἀνοσιοῦν [to make holy, to purify, to expiate, to pollute], meaning to make what is defiled holy and pure, to expiate, to atone, to sanctify, to consecrate. From this comes ἀποσίωσις [atonement], a sacrifice of expiation, and ἀφοσίωσις [dedication], expiation. Opposed to ὅσιον and ὁσιότης, that is, holy and holiness, is τὸ ἀνόσιον καὶ βέβηλον [the unholy and profane], that is, impious, wicked, profane, and ἀσεβές [ungodly], that is, impiety.

units.la: Sed Religio atque cultus divinus etiam τιμή, id est, Honos appellatur: & Deum sive Deos Τιμῆ, τιμᾶν, idem quod colere. Theodoretus, Deos τιμῶν ἐπιστοῖς, id est, annuo epulo, a quo verbo τιμᾶν, Latinum Timendi & Timoris nomen videtur derivatum: quod & ipsum sape pro uniuersfo cultu divino accipitur.
units.tr: But religion and divine worship are also called τιμή [timē], that is, honour; and to honour God or the gods, τιμᾶν [timan], is the same as to worship. Theodoret says that they honour the gods with an annual feast (ἐπισήμῳ ἐπιστοῖς?, "with an annual festival"). From the verb τιμᾶν the Latin words timendi and timoris seem to be derived, and these also are often used for the whole worship of God.

units.la: His adde nomen φόβος καὶ φοβεῖσθαι: quod etiam Timorem & Timere significat. Unde Poëta Φόβος, ille Timorem facit Deorum auctorem: Primus in Orbe Deos Timor fecit.
units.tr: To these add the words φόβος and φοβεῖσθαι [phobos, phobeisthai], which also mean fear and to fear. Hence the poet Φόβος [Phobos] makes fear the author of the gods: "Fear first made gods in the world."

units.la: Es Plutarchus de superstitione, Metus sive timor Deorum qualis? Qui Deos metuit, omnia metuit.
units.tr: Plutarch, in his work On Superstition, asks: what kind of fear or dread of the gods is it? He who fears the gods fears everything.

units.la: Adde postremo hic Θεολογίας nomen. Vetustissimi Graeciae scriptores, ut ajt Lactantius libro de ira Dei cap. 11. Quid de Dius & Deorum cultu agerent, appellari primum sunt θεολόγοι, & eorum scientia θεολογία: non autem ὑπερθέαι. Sed cum Deorum alii Dii tantum: alii Daemones censerentur, jam bipartita coepit esse Ethnicorum Theologia.
units.tr: Finally, add the name of theology (θεολογία). The most ancient Greek writers, as Lactantius says in his book On the Anger of God, chapter 11, were first called theologians (θεολόγοι) because of what they taught about God and the worship of God, and their science was called theology (θεολογία), not "hyperthea" (ὑπερθέαι). But when some of the gods were regarded as gods only and others as demons, pagan theology began to be divided into two parts.

units.la: Alia enim de verò Dius, in quibus Theologiae nomen manet: alia de Daemonibus tractavit. Quae de Dius egit, triplex fuit constituta, ut docet Augustinus ex Varrone lib. 5. de Civie. Deicapite sexto, nempe Mυθικὸν, φυσικὸν, πολιτικὸν, id est, Fabulosa, Physica sen Naturalis, Civilis, seu Politica, Poetica, Philosophica, pro diverso fine, propter quem Deos & eorum gestamentia commemorabant. Quae Daemonum vim explicabat, illa tantum fuit bipartita: quia cum Daemonum alii sint boni & utiles; alii autem mali, noxii & timendi: quae de Daemonibus malis quae triplex, placandis & averruncandis agebat μαγεία & γοντεία est dicta. Quae autem bonos alliciebat & invitabat sacrificiis θυηρία & τελετὴ. Augustinus libro decimo, de Civitate Dei capite nono.
units.tr: One part dealt with the true gods, and it kept the name of theology. The other treated of demons. The part concerning the gods was threefold, as Augustine teaches from Varro, in book 5 of The City of God, chapter 6: mythical (μυθικόν), physical or natural (φυσικόν), and civil or political (πολιτικόν). These are the fabulous, the physical, and the civil, or political, or poetic, or philosophical, according to the different purpose for which they recounted the gods and their deeds. The part that explained the power of demons was only twofold, since some demons are good and useful, while others are evil, harmful and to be feared. The part dealing with the evil demons, which were to be placated and averted, was called magic (μαγεία) and sorcery (γοντεία). The part that attracted and invited the good demons with sacrifices was called thyreia (θυηρία) and teletē (τελετή). Augustine, The City of God, book 10, chapter 9.

units.la: Προσκυνῆσαι etiam & σεβασμὸς adorationem & veneratio nem significat a σέβ- ειν, ἔτοξ τοῦ ἱ.κ. ... alicujus, tanquam sui Domini, honoris & subjectionis causa provolvere: translati vero adorare, ventrari. Aristophanes in Pluto: κῦ φρονοκυνῶ τὰ ἀρχαῖα μὴ τὸν Ἡλιον. Iungitur & cum Dativo in nomo Testamento. Προσκυνητὴς, id est, adorator, voce composita ἀ, σπο & κυνέω, quod idem est, quod κύω, id est, osculor, suavior: (vnde Germanicum nostrum fussen) quod etiam accipitur nonnunquam pro προσκυνεῖν, id est, adorare. Sic προσκυνεῖν apud Æschylum est Deos colere sive honorare.
units.tr: Προσκυνῆσαι and σεβασμὸς also signify adoration and veneration. They come from σέβειν, to throw oneself down before someone, as before one's lord, out of honour and submission; in a transferred sense, they mean to adore or to kiss the hand. Aristophanes in Plutus: "I do not revere the ancient gods, nor the Sun" [κῦ φρονοκυνῶ τὰ ἀρχαῖα μὴ τὸν Ἡλιον]. The verb is also construed with the dative in the New Testament. Προσκυνητής, that is, adorer, is a compound of πρός and κυνέω, which is the same as κύω, that is, to kiss or give a kiss (whence our German "fussen," to kiss the feet). It is sometimes also taken for προσκυνεῖν, to adore. Thus προσκυνεῖν in Aeschylus means to worship or honour the gods.

units.la: Atque hæc de nominibus Latinis & Græcis. Hebræa nomina, quibus cum vera, tum falsa referre ligio designantur, hæc sunt; השתחוה Hischtachauaxh, quod cum affixo legitur 2. Reg. 5. Propter supplicationem in domo Rimnon parcat obsecro Ieboua servo suo. Verbum השתחוה crebro in sacris literis cum proprie civili & politico hominum, tum pro religioso & sacro tum Dei veri, tum Deorum falsorum cultu accipitur. Derivatur autem a שחה, Schachah, id est, inclinavit se, incurvatus & prostratus est: ac proprie significat totius corporis prostrationem ad terram. Rabbi David Kimchi in Psalmum 95. tria hæc recenset vocabula, externum corporis gestum, quo honoris & reverentiæ causa fit, significantia, quæ sic distinguit. Primum est בריך, Bæraxk, προσκυνεῖν Græcis, videlicet genu flexio, Alterum est הבשחווי Hicniah, quod est caput inclinare, tum aliqua corporis incurvatione. Tertium est השתחוה Hischtachauaxh, quod totius corporis prostrationem significat, a שחה Schachah vel שח Schach, quod idem sonat, quod בשח Canah vel שחפאל Schaphal id est, bumiliatus, incurvatus, seu inclinatus est.
units.tr: So much for the Latin and Greek names. The Hebrew names by which both true and false religion are designated are these. First is השתחוה (hishtachawah), which occurs with a suffix in 2 Kings 5: "For the worship in the house of Rimmon, may the LORD, I beg, pardon his servant." The verb השתחוה is frequently used in Holy Scripture both in its proper civil and political sense of men, and in its religious and sacred sense, both of the worship of the true God and of false gods. It is derived from שחה (schachah), that is, he bowed himself, was bent low, and was prostrated; properly it signifies the prostration of the whole body to the ground. Rabbi David Kimchi, on Psalm 95, lists three words that signify the external bodily gesture by which honour and reverence are shown, and he distinguishes them thus. The first is ברך (barach), which the Greeks call προσκυνεῖν, namely the bending of the knee. The second is הכניע (hiknia), which is to bow the head with some bending of the body. The third is השתחוה (hishtachawah), which signifies the prostration of the whole body, from שחה (schachah) or שח (schach), which has the same sound as כנח (kanach) or שפל (shaphal), that is, was humbled, bent, or inclined.

units.la: Nonnulli vertunt supplicationem a supplicando: qua voce absolutè profacrificare, seu, sacra facere, vt suo est Suetonius in Tiberio, his verbis: Post excessum Augusti curiam intravit, quasi pietati simul & religioni satisfacturus, Minor exemplo, thure quidem & vino, sed sine tibicine supplicavit, id est, rem divinam fecit. Græci LXX. aliquando illud expiimunt una voce προσκυνεῖν: aliquando participio προσκυνῶν aut alio aliquo adjecto. Vsurpatur autem hoc verbum sæpe in sacris literis pro honore & cultu civili, sive politico, qui exhibetur hominibus. Aliquando pro cultu religioso, qui vel Deo vero, vel Diis tribuitur: Deo vero, ut 1. Samuel. 15. Et supplicabo Iehoua Deo tuo, &c. Diis alienis, ut Josua 23. Et abeuntes coluerunt Deos alienos & supplicaverunt illis. Eodem sensu legitur 2. Reg. 19. Et factum est, cum ipse adoraret, seu supplicaret in domo Nisroth. Sic Zephan. 1. Et supplicantes super tectis exercitui cœlorum.
units.tr: Some render supplicatio (supplication) from supplicare, a word by which one absolutely "sacrifices," or performs sacred rites, as Suetonius uses it in his Tiberius: "After Augustus's death he entered the senate, as if about to satisfy piety and religion at once. Being the younger, by example he offered worship with incense and wine, but without a flute-player; that is, he performed the sacred rite." The Greek Septuagint sometimes express this with the single word προσκυνεῖν, and sometimes with the participle προσκυνῶν or some other added word. This verb is often used in Scripture for the civil honour and service shown to men, and sometimes for the religious worship given either to the true God or to other gods. To the true God, as in 1 Samuel 15: "And I will worship Jehovah your God," etc. To foreign gods, as in Joshua 23: "And going away they served other gods and worshipped them." In the same sense 2 Kings 19 reads: "And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch." So Zephaniah 1: "And those who worship upon the housetops the host of heaven."

units.la: Aliud nomen est, עבודה Abodah, cultus, servitium: quod ipsum quoque partim civile, partim sacrum & religiosum significat, a עבר, Abád, servivit, seu inservivit: cui respondent supra commemorata & explicata vocabula Græca λατρεία, δουλεία, & θεραπεία; quæ omnia servitutem cum civilem, tum religiosam & superstitiosam significant, quibus cognuit sernaculum nostrum (Gottesdienst, quasi dicas, Dei cultus).
units.tr: Another name is עבודה (avodah), worship, service, which likewise signifies partly civil and partly sacred and religious service. It comes from עבר (avad), to serve or be in service. Corresponding to it are the Greek words λατρεία, δουλεία and θεραπεία, mentioned and explained above. All of these signify servitude, both civil and religious and superstitious, and by this word our own language (Gottesdienst, as one might say, the worship of God) is known.

units.la: Huc etiam referri potest vox שרות vel שרות Scharuth, vel Schareth, quæ item ministerium cum civile & politicum, tum etiam sacrum & religiosum significant.
units.tr: To this may also be referred the word שרות or שרת (scharuth, or schareth), which likewise signifies ministry, both civil and political, and also sacred and religious.

units.la: Chaldaicè cultus divinus מְלַחֲכָה Pulchanah appellatur a פלחן Pulchan, quod a פלח Pelach deduci: ut id est, servivit, coluit, & inde מפלחין Maphlechin, id est, cultores, sive ministri sunt dicti.
units.tr: In Chaldean, divine worship is called פלחן (pulchanah), from פלחן (pulchan), which is derived from פלח (pelach), that is, served, worshipped. Hence מפלחין (maphlechin), that is, worshippers or ministers, were so called.

units.la: Observandum etiam sæpe species sive partes cultus atque religionis sive vera sive falsa, ut, Sacrificare, sive sacrificium, adorare sive adorationem, precari, sive precationem, supplicare, sive supplicationem, in omnibus linguis & sacris ac profanis in literis, synecdochicè pro toto cultu, sive religione usurpari. Hinc de adorandi verbo Virgilius primo Georgicorum: Cunctaque tibi Cererem pubes agrestis adoret.
units.tr: It should also be observed that often the species or parts of worship and religion, whether true or false, such as to sacrifice or sacrifice, to adore or adoration, to pray or prayer, to supplicate or supplication, are used in all languages, both sacred and profane writings, by synecdoche for the whole worship or religion. Hence Virgil, in the first book of the Georgics, on the verb "adore": "And let the rustic youth all adore Ceres."

units.la: Et hæc dicta sint de nominibus.
units.tr: And let these things be said about the names.

units.la: Porro totum cultum sive religionem Ethnicorum, præsertim Romanorum, uno quasi fasciculo Valerius Maximus his verbis complexus est, quæ idcirco ejus epitome, sive compendium appellari possunt. Sic enim libro primo inquit, Majores status solemnes, cerimonias, Pontificum scientia: bene gerundarum rerum auctoritates, Augurum observatione: Apollinis prædictiones, Vatum libros: portentorum depulsa, Hetrusca disciplina explicari voluerunt. Prisco etiam institutorebus divinis opera datur: cum aliquid commendandum est, precatione: cum exposulandi, votorum cùm sol vendum, gratulatione: cùm inquirendum, vel extis, vel fortibus imperio: eùm solennii ritu peragendum, sacrificio: quo etiam ostentorum & fulgurum denunciationes procurantur. His congrua plané & consentanea sunt hæc Ciceronis verba in oratione de Aruspicum responsis: Ego vero, inquit, primùm habeo auctores ac magistros religionùm colendarum Majores nostros: quorum mihi fuisse tanta sapientia videtur, ut satis superq; prudentes sint, qui illorum prudentiam non dicam assequi, sed quanta fuerit, perspicere possint; qui status solennesq; cerimonias, pontificatus: rerum benè gerendarum authoritates, augurio: fatorum veterum prædictiones Apollinis, & vatum librus: portentorum explanationes, Hetruscorum disciplinam contineri putarunt.
units.tr: Valerius Maximus has embraced the whole worship or religion of the Gentiles, especially the Romans, as if in a single bundle, in these words, which can therefore be called his epitome, or compendium. For in book 1 he says: "Our ancestors wished the solemn rites and ceremonies to be explained by the science of the pontiffs; the authority for successful affairs by the observation of the augurs; Apollo's predictions by the books of the prophets; the averting of portents by the Etruscan discipline. Attention is also given to divine matters in the ancient institutions: when something is to be commended, by prayer; when explanations are to be given, by thanksgiving for vows made; when something is to be inquired, either by entrails or by lots, by command; when it is to be accomplished with solemn ritual, by sacrifice; by which also the announcements of omens and lightnings are dealt with." Quite in agreement with these are the words of Cicero in his speech On the Responses of the Haruspices: "Indeed," he says, "first I have our ancestors as the authorities and teachers of the religions to be cultivated. Their wisdom seems to me so great that those who can perceive, if not attain, how great it was, are quite wise enough. They thought that the solemn rites and ceremonies were contained in the pontifical college; the authority for successful affairs in augury; the predictions of the ancient fates in Apollo and the books of the prophets; and the explanations of portents in the Etruscan discipline."

units.la: Religionis autem, (de vera loquor) quæ eandem virtus omnium virtutum regina & domina in medio posita est, duo sunt extrema: Unum extremum est defectus, nempe ἀθεότης, sive ἄθρησκεια, irreligiosicas, Dei, sive Deorum, cultui, divini, sive is reverâ talis sit, sive fucatus, negligentia, contemptio, & irreligiosa tractatio, Atheismus. Alterum extremum est excessus, nempe δεισιδαιμονία, ειδωλολα-τρεία, ἱεροφοβοπρα-κία, ἰδ.λο-φοβον πραξεια, οἱ ἐπὶ ἀμουσία, hoc est, superstitio, quæ est vitium religioni oppositum, secundum excessum. Esi verò omnis Gentilium religio tota, quantacunq; fuit, tota, inquam fuit mera cùm impietas, tum superstitio: tamen ipsi quoque Ethnici duo hæc in religione sua extrema flaturunt.
