Unde Cicero libro primo de Natura Deorum, religioni superstitionem opponit his verbis: Non Philosophi solùm, inquit, verùm etiam Majores nostri superstitionem a religione separa verunt. Et Plutarchus lib. de superstitione: Ut nonnulli, inquit, latronum, aut ferarum infultum, ignémve inconsiderate & imprudenter fugientes, incidunt in locum in via, ubi præcipitia sunt & voragines periculosæ: Sic quidam, superstitionem fugientes, dum transiliunt in medio positum pietatem, in duram pertinatem, incidunt impietatem. Idem impietatis & superstitionis comparationem instituens impietatem dicit esse opinionem falsam: superstitionem vero affectum animi, ex errore natum. Et alibi, superstitionem impietatis esse origines. Cicero libro secundo de Divinatione: Non enim sunt aut scientia, aut arte di vini, sed superstiti vi s Vates impudentes, aut ioli, aut inertes, aut insani, aut quibus egestas imperat, qui sibi fenicam non sapiunt, alios monstrant viam, quibus divinitas pollicentur, ab his drachmam ipsi accipiunt. Item libro eodem secundo de Divinatione: Vis religio prepugnanda est: sic superstitiones sirpes omnes ejiciendæ. Nam primùm quidem inter illos ipsos extiterunt nonnulli, qui vel nullos omnino Deos esse, vel si sint, illos nullam mundi, rerumque creatarum curam habere, ac proinde neque iquam condolesse censuerunt. Nam sublata Deorum providentia omnem religionem eolli Cicero his verbis eleganter docet libro primo de Natura Deorum: Si vera est, inquit, eorum Philosophorum sententia, qui omninò nullam habere censent humanarum rerum procurationem Deos, quæ potest esse pietas? quæ sanctitas? quæ religio? Hæc enim omnia puré & caste Deorum numini sanctè dicata sunt, si animad verteritur ab iis; & si est aliquid a Deis immortalibus hominum generi tributum. Sin autem Dii neque possunt nos juvare, nec volunt, nec curant omnino, nec, quid agamus, animadvertunt, nec est, quod ab his ad hominum vitam pertinare possit, quod ullos Deos immortalibus cultus, honorez preces adhibeamus? Idem libro primo de Natura Deorum: Sanctitate, inquis, & religione sublata, perturbatio vitæ sequitur & magna confusio. Atq; haud scio, an pietate ad versus Deos sublata, fidei etiam & societas humani generis, & una excellentissima virtus justitia collatur.
units.tr: Of religion (I speak of the true religion), which, as the queen and mistress of all virtues, is placed in the middle, there are two extremes. One extreme is a defect, namely atheism (ἀθεότης, ἄθρησκεια), that is, irreligion: negligence, contempt, and irreligious treatment of the worship of God or of the gods, whether that worship be genuine or feigned. The other extreme is an excess, namely superstition (δεισιδαιμονία), idolatry (εἰδωλολατρεία), and the like, which is the vice opposed to religion as its second excess. Yet although the whole religion of the Gentiles, however great it was, was entirely and purely both impiety and superstition, the Gentiles themselves nevertheless recognised these two extremes in their religion. Hence Cicero, in the first book of On the Nature of the Gods, opposes superstition to religion in these words: "Not only the philosophers," he says, "but even our ancestors separated superstition from religion." And Plutarch, in his book On Superstition: "As some people, fleeing thoughtlessly and imprudently from the assault of robbers, wild beasts, or fire, fall into a place on the road where there are precipices and dangerous whirlpools, so some, fleeing superstition, while they leap over piety, which lies in the middle, fall into hard obstinacy and impiety." The same author, drawing a comparison between impiety and superstition, says that impiety is a false opinion, but superstition is an affection of the mind born of error. And elsewhere he says that superstition is the origin of impiety. Cicero, in the second book On Divination: "For these men have neither the knowledge nor the art of divination, but are impudent seers of superstition, or jugglers, or idlers, or madmen, or men whom want compels; they do not know how to make a living for themselves, yet they show others the way, promising them divinity, and from these they themselves receive a drachma." Also in the same second book of On Divination: "Strong religion must be defended; thus all the roots of superstition must be cast out. For at first, indeed, there arose among them some who thought either that there were no gods at all, or, if there were, that they had no care for the world or for created things, and therefore none for humankind." Cicero elegantly shows in the first book of On the Nature of the Gods, in these words, that all religion is undone once the providence of the gods is removed: "If the opinion of those philosophers is true, who hold that the gods have no care at all for human affairs, what can piety be? What holiness? What religion? For all these things are devoted purely and chastely to the divine power, if the gods notice them, and if anything is bestowed by the immortal gods on the human race. But if the gods can neither help us nor wish to, nor care at all, nor notice what we do, and if there is nothing that can reach human life from them, why do we apply any worship, honour or prayers to the immortal gods?" The same author in the first book of On the Nature of the Gods: "Holiness and religion being removed, disorder of life follows, and great confusion. And I do not know whether, with piety towards the gods removed, the faith and fellowship of the human race is not also overthrown, and with it the most excellent virtue, justice."

units.la: Quantum contrà antiquorum Gentilium non solum observande ac conservande, sed etiam augende, propagande & amplificande falsæ illius sue religionis studium fuerit, Valerius Maximus toto libro primo de culcu Deorum, capite primo, de neglecta religione capite secundo, de simulatae religione capite tertio, de auspiciis capite quarto, de ominibus capite quinto, de prodigiis capite sexto, de somniis capite septimo, de miraculis capite octavo, multorum cùm Romanorum, tum Græcorum, atque etiam aliarum nationum illustribus exemplis comprobat atque confirmat.
units.tr: Valerius Maximus, in the whole of his first book, shows and confirms with many illustrious examples, from Romans, Greeks and other nations alike, how keenly the ancient Gentiles strove not only to observe and preserve their false religion, but also to increase, spread and extend it. He does this in chapters on the worship of the gods (chapter 1), on neglected religion (chapter 2), on feigned religion (chapter 3), on auspices (chapter 4), on omens (chapter 5), on portents (chapter 6), on dreams (chapter 7) and on miracles (chapter 8).

units.la: Quanto autem Romani præ cæteris gentibus religionis sue patriæ & antiquæ, seu superstitionis potuit tueri & conservande studio flagrarint Cicero de Aruspicum responsis mulcis ver bu ornate eleganterque exprimit: Cognovi, inquit, multa homines doctissimos sapientissimosque dixisse, &c.
units.tr: How much more than other nations the Romans were burning with zeal to keep and preserve the religion, or superstition, of their country and ancestors, Cicero expresses in many words, elegantly and finely, in his work on the responses of the haruspices: "I have learned," he says, "that many very learned and wise men have said..."

units.la: Alterum extremum, excessu n videlicet, diximus esse superstitionem. De hac sic Plutarchus in libello, quem scripsit de Superstitione, Nullus est animi morbus tam multis erroribus, perturbationibus, scatens, & ex tam inter se dissidentibus & pugnantibus opinionibus refertus, atque superstitio. Idem ibidem, Superstitionis ridicula sunt opera atque effectus, verba, motus, praefigiae, incantationes, circumcursitationes, tympanorum pulsationes, lustrationes impura, sordida castimonia, barbarica & injusta in templis supplicia, quae nonnullos occasione dederunt diceudi peroontumeliam, praestare nullos esse Deos, quam qui talia probent, iisq; deleitentur, adeoq; sint consumeliofi, sordidi & morosi. In superstitione, ait Cicero libro de Inventione, inest timor inanis Deorum, cum scilicet timemus, ubi nullus debet esse timor. Superstitio, ut idem confessus est, fusa est per gentes, oppressit omnium ferè animos, atq; hominum imbecillitatem occupavit. Nec tamen superstitione tollenda, religio tollitur. Idem pro Cluentio, Pietate & religione & justis precibus non contaminata superstitione, nec casis boftius Deos placari dixit. Superstitione qui est imbutus, ut ajt idem de Finibus, quietus esse nunquam potest: tui nulla sunt vel per somnium inducia, ut ait Plutarchus, quia neque vigilans recta ratione utitur, neque ab eo, quod ipsum perturbat, somno liberatur, sed d:rmit ratio, semper vigilat metus, fuga mali aut requies nulla datur. Imbecilli animi facile superstitiosa concipiunt, Idem de Divinatione. Et de Natura Deorum, Ita factum est in superstitioso & religioso; alterum vitii nomen, alterum laudis.
units.tr: We have said that superstition is the other extreme, namely the excess. On this, Plutarch says in his little book On Superstition: "There is no disease of the mind so full of errors and disturbances, and so crammed with opinions that disagree and conflict with one another, as superstition." The same author, in the same place: "The works and effects of superstition are ridiculous: words, gestures, grimaces, incantations, frantic running about, the beating of drums, impure purifications, filthy chastity, and barbarous and unjust punishments in the temples. These have given some occasion for saying, as an insult, that it would be better for there to be no gods at all than for them to approve such things and take pleasure in them, and so be insulting, filthy and peevish." Cicero, in his work On Invention, says: "Superstition involves a groundless fear of the gods, namely when we fear where there ought to be no fear." As the same author admits: "Superstition has spread through the nations, has oppressed almost the minds of all, and has taken hold of human weakness." Yet religion is not abolished by removing superstition. In his speech For Cluentius, Cicero says the gods are not appeased by piety, religion and just prayers unpolluted by superstition, nor by sacrifices. Whoever is steeped in superstition, as the same author says in On Ends, can never be at rest: he has no truce, not even in sleep, as Plutarch says. For he does not use right reason when awake, and he is not freed from what troubles him even in sleep; his reason sleeps while his fear is always awake, and no escape from evil or rest is granted him. Weak minds easily conceive superstitious notions, as Cicero says in On Divination. And in On the Nature of the Gods: "It is so with the superstitious and the religious: the one name is a reproach, the other a praise."

units.la: Superstitiosos M. Tullius, libro secundo de Natura Deorum, volunt dictos qui id totos dies precarentur & immolarent, ut sibi sui filii essent superstites, secundum illud Plauti in Asinaria: Sicut tuum vis uni cum gnatum superesse, id est, superstitem & vitae sospitem esse. Sed vius similiter superstitionem vult dictam a superstite, quae anicularum propria est, quae multam per aetatem superstites sunt, & quae rebus inanibus additae dum volunt videri minimus religiosae, superstitiosae sunt & ita delirant. Hinc superstitio a Cicerone & aliis tributitur mulieribus, & quidem vetulae potißimum, ut quae ad superstitionem inprimis proclivae sunt atque propensae. Hinc superstitio saepe muliebris & amilis appellatur. Idem Cicero de Divinatione, Omnis superstitio, inquit, est imbecilli animi atque amilis. Item de Inventione, Ea superstitiones sunt penè aniles. Item, Et periculum, ne aut neglectis his impietate, aut suscepsis anili superstitione obligemur, de Natura Deorum. Huc fatit illud, Non id dicitur superstitiosè atq; aniliter, sed physica consistentia ratione.
units.tr: Cicero, in the second book of On the Nature of the Gods, holds that the superstitious are so called because they pray and sacrifice all day long that their sons may survive them, in line with Plautus in the Asinaria: "as you wish your son to survive you," that is, to be a survivor and to remain safe and sound. But Varro likewise holds that superstition is named from "superstes" (survivor), which is a peculiarity of old women, who survive for many years, and who, adding empty things to what is real, while they want to seem very religious, become superstitious and so go mad. Hence Cicero and others attribute superstition to women, and especially to old women, as those most prone and inclined to it. Hence superstition is often called womanish and old-wifely. Cicero again, in On Divination: "All superstition," he says, "is of a weak and womanish mind." Likewise, in On Invention: "These things are almost old-wifely superstitions." Again, in On the Nature of the Gods: "There is a danger that we may be bound either by neglecting these things, through impiety, or by taking them up in old-wifely superstition." To this belongs the saying: "This is not said in a superstitious and old-wifely way, but with a reasoning consistent with nature."

units.la: Lactantius verò in Institut. Christi libro secundo, capite vigesimo octavo, exiitimat superstitiosi nem & superstitiosos dici, non eos, qui filios suos superstites optant (Omnes enim optant.) Sed hos, qui superstitiem defunctorum memoriam colunt, aut qui parentibus suis superstites colebant imagines, eorum domi tanquam Deos penates. Nam qui novos sibi ritus affumebant, ut in Deorum vicem mortuos honorarent, quos ex hominibus in coelum receptos putabant, hos superstitiosos vocabant; eos verò, qui publicos & antiquos Deos colerent, religiosos nominabant. Unde Virgilius, Vana superstitio, veterumq; ignara Deorum. Vanam vocat, ceu proprio epitheto superstitionis: unde Sillius Italicus libro quinto. Vana superstitio, Dea sola in pectore virtus.
units.tr: Lactantius, however, in the second book of his Divine Institutes, chapter 28, thinks that superstitious people are not those who wish their sons to survive them (for everyone wishes that). Rather, the superstitious are those who keep up the memory of the dead with superstition, or who, while their parents were still alive, kept their images at home as household gods. For those who adopted new rites to honour the dead as gods in place of gods, supposing that men had been received into heaven, these they called superstitious; but those who worshipped the public and ancient gods they called religious. Hence Virgil: "Empty superstition, ignorant of the ancient gods." He calls it "empty" as if that were a fixed epithet of superstition. Hence Silius Italicus in book five: "Empty superstition; virtue alone is the goddess in the breast."

units.la: Quid si, ut justitia dicta est a jure & sistendo, quid sit virtus, qua jus suum cuiq; sistitur, hoc est, pariter aequabiliter ꝗ tribuitur, & solstitium a sole quasi sistendo; ita superstitio a super & sisten-do dicta sit, quòdea cum Deo, tum Dis alienis sistat, id est, tribuat, quae sunt superstitem, id est, praeter & contra veram rationem seu voluntatem legem divinam. Ita superstitio secundum nominis Latini notationem est nimia & superabundans pietas & religio, secundum illa Ecclesiastici sec-primo capite, Noli esse justus multum, &c. ne impie egeris multum. Tam enim malum judicatur nimium esse justum, id est, superstitiosum, quàm nimium esse sceleratum. Ut enim summum jus, summa est injuria, ita nimia & superfacanea religio, summa est superstitio.
units.tr: What if, as justice (iustitia) is named from law (ius) and standing (sistendo), since justice is the virtue by which each person's right is stood to, that is, is given equally and evenly, and as the solstice is named from the sun standing still, so superstition is named from "super" and "sisto," because it stands over and gives to both God and alien gods what is "superstes," that is, beyond and against the true reason or the will of God's law? So, according to the derivation of the Latin word, superstition is an excessive and superabundant piety and religion, in line with the words of Ecclesiasticus, chapter 7: "Be not righteous over much," and "do not do too much wickedly." For it is judged as great an evil to be excessively just, that is, superstitious, as to be excessively wicked. For just as the highest right is the highest wrong, so excessive and superfluous religion is the highest superstition.

units.la: Graecis superstitio duobus potissimum nominibus insignitur, prout duae superstitionis sunt spe-cies. Una est, qua immediatè in Deum ipsum, qui solus est colendus, peccatur: & hac id est δειςιδαιμονία appellatur, quando in Deum peccatur per idola & simulacra, ut nomen ipsum sonat. Altera species est ἰεροφθαλμία, quae proprie in cultum peccatur. Interdum tamen superstitio appellatur etiam δεισιδαιμονία, id est, Daemonum, Deorumve metus superstitiosus, & δεισιδαίμων, qui meticulosè Dæmonas, seu Deos colit, & dıʼıʼı ... [illegible, ~12 letters] metu Deorum superstitioso teneri seu conscitari. Veré & merito superstitio hoc nomine insignita fuit ab Ethnicis, propterea quòd, ut Cicero ajt libro de Invent. in superstitione timor inanis inanes Deorum. Homines enim superstiti siosi perpetuo Dæmonum metu sive tremore constistantur atq; torquentur. Vnde Cicero de Finibus, Qui superstitione est imbutus, quietus esse nunquam potest: & Plutarchus libro citato, Superstitiosus pallet Coronatus, sacrificans trepidat, tremente voce vota fatit, manubis adolet cirus banibus omninoq; ostedit, nugatum esse Pythagoram, qui dixit optimè nos habero, cum ad Deos accedimus. Tunc enim miserrimè pessumeq; affecti animo sunt. Hæc Plutarchus de superstitione. Ide ibidem superstitiosorū vel superstitiosi exitus dicit esse lethales: cum illi magis impii sint. Nam superstitiosi impias de Diis qui Deos esse negant, habent opiniones. Deorum igitur sunt inimici. Itaque δεισιδαιμονία, id est, superstitio, veré δυσδαιμονία, id est, infortunium, & δεισι δαιμων, id est, superstitiosus veré δυσδαιμων, id est, infelix & infortunatus dici potest. Nos Germani rectè Idololatriam & superstitionem partim Abgötterey, partim Apposteutzle rey & beuchekey appellamus. Abgötterey, quòd a Deo uno animos nostros avocat, atque traducit ad Deos alienos. Apposteutzlerey verò & Heuchelcy ab hypocrisi & simulatione, quia est religio fallax, ficta & simulata. Galli hominem superstitiosum Bigot, & superstitiose Bigotterie appellant voce compositâ ex Bi, vel Bey, quæ vox Germanicè Apud, & Gott, quæ Germanicè Deum sonat: propterea quòd superstitiosi homines simulant, se Deo esse propinquos & proximos, cùm ab eo sint alieniores, longeq; remoti; vel quòd cæco quodam mentis errore Deum, sive Deos sibi propinquos, proximos at præsentissimos esse opinantur. Multa enim sunt, ut hoc obiter dicam, Gallorum & Germanorum communia vocabula, ut etiam Italorum, præsertim militaria, & ea inprimis, quæ a Latina lingua sunt alieniora & remotiora.
units.tr: Among the Greeks superstition is marked chiefly by two names, since there are two main kinds of superstition. One is that by which sin is committed directly against God himself, who alone is to be worshipped; this is called deisidaimonia [δεισιδαιμονία], when sin is committed against God through idols and images, as the name itself indicates. The other kind is hierophthalmia [ἱεροφθαλμία], which sin is committed properly in the cult. Sometimes, however, superstition is also called deisidaimonia, that is, a superstitious fear of demons or gods, and the person who worships demons or gods timidly is called deisidaimon [δεισιδαίμων], and [illegible] to be held or troubled by a superstitious fear of the gods. Superstition was truly and rightly marked by the pagans with this name, because, as Cicero says in On Invention, superstition is an empty fear of the gods. For superstitious people are constantly harassed and tormented by a fear or trembling of demons. Hence Cicero in On Ends: "Whoever is steeped in superstition can never be at rest." And Plutarch in the book cited: "The superstitious man turns pale when crowned, trembles when sacrificing, speaks his vows with a quavering voice, burns incense with a trembling hand, and shows altogether that Pythagoras was joking when he said that we are well off when we approach the gods. For then they are most wretchedly and miserably affected in mind." So Plutarch on superstition. The same author says in the same place that the outcomes of superstitious people, or of superstition, are deadly, since such people are rather impious: for superstitious people hold impious opinions about the gods, since they deny that gods exist, and so are enemies of the gods. Therefore deisidaimonia [δεισιδαιμονία], that is, superstition, may truly be called dusdaimonia [δυσδαιμονία], that is, misfortune, and the deisidaimon [δεισιδαίμων], that is, the superstitious person, may truly be called dusdaimon [δυσδαίμων], that is, unhappy and unfortunate. We Germans rightly call idolatry and superstition partly Abgötterey, partly Apposteutzlerey and Heuchelei. Abgötterey, because it draws our minds away from the one God and turns them to alien gods. Apposteutzlerey and Heuchelei, from hypocrisy and pretence, because it is a deceptive, feigned and pretended religion. The French call a superstitious man a bigot, and superstitious behaviour bigoterie, a word compounded from "Bi" or "Bey," which in German means "by" or "near," and "Gott," which in German means God. This is because superstitious people pretend that they are close and near to God, when they are in fact far more distant and remote from him; or because by a certain blind error of the mind they suppose that God, or the gods, are near, close and most present to them. For there are many words common to the French and Germans, as also to the Italians, especially military terms, and those above all which are more remote and foreign from Latin, to mention this in passing.

units.la: Etsi verò Gentiles, at illorum præsertim ductores, atq; magistri, Philosophi dicti, plurima rationi veritatis, admodum consentanea & de religione & de superstitione memoriæ litteris, prodiderunt: tamen veram religionem a falsa, sive a superstitione discernere nequaquam potuerunt, & veram religionem, ut Iudaeorum antiquam a Deo ipsis præceptam atq; præscriptam appella runt: suas autem vel turpissimas & monstrosissimas superstitiones religiones augusto sanctoq; nomine insignierunt. Nam ut ipse Cicero constetur, superstitio religioni propinqua est, & ut idem testatur, religionem superstitio imitatur, hoc est, religionis vera est imitatrix, æmulatrix, simulatrix quasi quæ simia, quæ speciosam præ se fert religionis speciem. Sit enim, exempli gratia, feré tota illa Gentilium, sive gentium antiquarum religio profecta fuit ex καιροῦλιος, id est, prava, perversa atque præpostera quadam prisca, antique, ac veré divinæ illius religionis, quam Patriarchæ, & illorum posteri, Iudæi, divinitus sibi traditam atq; præscriptam coluerunt, imitatione. Inde certè sumserunt atque mutuati sunt plurimos ritus atque cerimonias. Deus autem ut electum, eximium & peculiarem illum suum populum Hebræum & Iudæum, & Israeliticum distum, a varia, multiplicis, infinita atque monstrosa illa reliquarum gentium superstitione atque idololatria, ab innumeris illarum opinionibus atq; erroribus ab innumerabilium Deorum cultu atque veneratione, ab innumeris, multiplicibus, diversis interque se contrariis eos contrahendi modis atq; formis, ab innumeris illarum templis, delubris, fanis atque lucis, ab innumeris aris & altaribus, ab innumeris idolis, statuis & imaginibus, ab innumeris ludis atque spectaculis, ab innumeris sacris atque sacrificiis, ab innumeris sacerdotibus atque sacerdotiis, ab innumeris ritibus cerimoniis, gestibus seu potius gesticulationibus variis & ridiculis, ab innumeris oraculis, augurijs, auspicijs & observationibus a vocavit atque a vertit: ita se solum & unum verum Deum, ab uno & solo feré illo suo populo, uno in loco, una in regione, uno in tabernaculo atque templo, uno altari, unis festis & solennitatibus, uno modo ab ipsomet præscripto atque tradito, ab unius tribus sacerdotibus atque Levitis, uno animo atque spiritu, absque ullo idolo & simulachro coli & adorari voluit atque præcepit. Ad miser iste populus cùm ipsius Diaboli instinctu atque impulsus, tum authoribus & impossoribus hominibus sepe in impias & impuras Gentilium superstitiones prolapsus est, & idcirco gravissimas, & quidem justissimas poenas luit.
units.tr: Although the Gentiles, and especially their leaders and teachers whom they call philosophers, have handed down in written records many statements about religion and superstition that agree closely with the truth, they were never able to distinguish true religion from false, or from superstition. They called the ancient true religion of the Jews, which God had commanded and prescribed for them, by the name of religion, but they marked their own most base and monstrous superstitions with the august and holy name of religion. For, as Cicero himself admits, superstition is close to religion, and, as he also testifies, superstition imitates religion: it is a kind of ape of true religion, its imitator, rival and counterfeit, which displays a showy likeness of religion. Take, for example, almost the whole religion of the Gentiles, or of the ancient nations: it arose from a perverse, twisted and preposterous imitation [καιροῦλιος] of that ancient and truly divine religion which the Patriarchs and their descendants, the Jews, kept as delivered and prescribed to them by God. Certainly they took and borrowed from it very many rites and ceremonies. But God chose that peculiar and distinguished people, the Hebrew, Jewish and so-called Israelite people, and separated and set them apart from the manifold, varied, endless and monstrous superstition and idolatry of the other nations, from their countless opinions and errors, from the worship and veneration of countless gods, from the countless, many-sided, diverse and mutually contrary ways and forms of worshipping them, from their countless temples, shrines, sanctuaries and groves, from their countless altars and sacrificial hearths, from their countless idols, statues and images, from their countless games and spectacles, from their countless rites and sacrifices, from their countless priests and priesthoods, from their countless ceremonies, and from the various and ridiculous gestures, or rather gesticulations, from their countless oracles, auguries, auspices and observances. He willed and commanded that this people alone should worship and adore the one and only true God, in one place, in one region, in one tabernacle and temple, at one altar, at one set of feasts and solemnities, in one manner prescribed and handed down by himself, through the priests and Levites of one tribe alone, with one mind and spirit, and without any idol or image. Yet this wretched people, driven and impelled partly by the very instigation of the Devil, and partly by the influence of impious men, often fell into the impure and godless superstitions of the Gentiles, and for this they paid the most grievous and most just penalties.

units.la: Porrò de superstitione libellum integrum scripsit Plutarchus, lectu dignissimum, in quo Gen tilium superstitio suis depingitur coloribus.
units.tr: Moreover, Plutarch wrote an entire book on superstition, most worth reading, in which the superstition of the Gentiles is painted in its own colours.

units.la: Deos autem illos suos fictos & commentitios coluerunt partim interne, partim externe. Interne quidem animo atq; mente suâ, vanissimis nimirum suis erroribus, opinionibus & persuasionibus illos amando, omnem salutis atq; felicitatis suae spem in illis collocando, honorificè de illis sentiendo, & illos magnificando. Externè autem eosdem coluerunt variis & multiplicibus ceremoniis, ritibus, gestibus, victu, precibus, templis, altaribus, simulacris, sacrificiis, donariis, anathematis, peregrinationibus, fes-tis, ludis, spectaculis.
units.tr: They worshipped those gods of theirs, which they had made up and invented, partly inwardly and partly outwardly. Inwardly, indeed, with their soul and mind, namely by loving them in their most vain errors, opinions and convictions, by placing in them every hope of their salvation and happiness, by thinking honourably of them and magnifying them. Outwardly they worshipped them with various and manifold ceremonies, rites, gestures, abstinences, prayers, temples, altars, images, sacrifices, offerings, votive gifts, pilgrimages, festivals, games and spectacles.

units.la: Deum autem sive Deos animo potius, spiritu & affectu, & virtutibus quàm externis & corporea rebus, ritibus, caerimoniis, donis atq; muneribus colendos esse atq; placari posse, multi Ethnicorum prodiderunt. Huc illud: Si Deus est animus, nobis ut carmina dicunt, Hic tibi praecipuè fit puramente colendus. Et hoc Ovidii: Non bovè magnato caelestia Numina gaudent, Sed quae praestandae est, vel fine teste, fide.
units.tr: Many of the heathen have taught that God, or the gods, should be worshipped and can be propitiated rather with the mind, spirit and affection, and with virtues, than with external and bodily things, rites, ceremonies, gifts and presents. To this belongs that line: "If God is mind, as the poets say, he is to be worshipped by you above all in purity." And this of Ovid: "The heavenly powers do not delight in a great ox, but in the faith that is to be offered, even without a witness."

units.la: Verùm quicquid fit, tota Gentilium religio nihil fuit aliud, quàm mera superstitio & idololatria: religio, inquam, illorum irreligiosa fuit & superstitiosa: omnis illorum pietas mera fuit impietas: illorum sanctitas profana fuit & pollu-ta: illorum res divina, non res fuit divina, sed potius humana; immò daemoniaca, ab hominibus Daemonum instinctu afflatu, excogitata & in mundum introducta: omnia illorum sacra & vera fuerunt secundum alterum vocabuli hujus significationem sacerrima, hoc est, summopere exsecranda & detestanda atque adeo sacrilega: omnes illorum venerationes Deorum atque cultus omnes veneratio-nis & reverentiae fuit expers. Denique religio seu potius superstitio illorum omnis impietatis & improbitatis, omniumq; scelerum atque flagitiorum mater fuit atque procreatrix, ut ipsorum doctores atque Philosophi met saepe testati sunt atq; confessi.
units.tr: However that may be, the whole religion of the Gentiles was nothing other than sheer superstition and idolatry. Their religion, I say, was irreligious and superstitious; all their piety was mere impiety; their holiness was profane and polluted; their divine worship was not divine but rather human, indeed demonic, devised by men under the prompting and inspiration of demons and introduced into the world. All their sacred things were, in the other sense of this word, most sacred, that is, to be most greatly execrated and detested, and so sacrilegious. All their veneration and worship of the gods lacked every mark of reverence and respect. In short, their religion, or rather superstition, was the mother and producer of every impiety and wickedness, of all crimes and disgraces, as their own teachers and philosophers have often testified and confessed.

units.la: De sacrificiis, parte praecipua religionis Ethnicorum: & primum de nominibus Latinis.
units.tr: On sacrifices, the chief part of the religion of the Gentiles, and first on the Latin names.

units.la: HIS praemissis in genere de religione atq; cultu Deorum gentilitio, nunc ad sacrificiorum nominibus.
units.tr: Having said these things in general about the religion and worship of the Gentile gods, we now turn to the names of sacrifices.

units.la: Sacrificii nomen Latinum aliquando rem, quae sacrificatur sive offertur Deo sive Diis, sicut Hebraeum תבח Tebach, significat: aliquando ipsam sacrificandi actionem, quae sacrificatio proprie appellatur. Est autem vox composita a sacro & facere; ita ut sacrificare fit idem, quod sacrum facere, vel venium petere sacrificatione. Pro sacrificare verò, vel sacrificari Deo, Latini etiam ajunt sacrum, sive sacrificium Deo alicui facere, facilitare, fieri. Plinius libro tertio capite quinto, Diva Angerona est, cui sacrificatur ad diem duodecimum Kalendas Januarii oreobligato, &c. Plautus in Mostellaria, Iovi vivo argento sacrificassem. Idem in Cap. Genio suo quando sacrificat, ad rem divinam, quibus opus est, Samius vasis utitur. Cicero, Cujus Laurentius vos Pontifices ad aram in velabro sacrificium facere soletis. Idem de Aruspicum responsis, qui sacrificia gentilitia illo ipso in sacello, flatuto loco, anniversaria facitarunt. Idem de Sacrificium, quod fiebat pro salute populi.
units.tr: The Latin word sacrificium sometimes denotes the thing sacrificed or offered to God or to the gods, just as the Hebrew zebach [זבח] does. Sometimes it denotes the act of sacrificing itself, which is properly called sacrificatio. The word is compound, from sacer and facere, so that sacrificare is the same as sacrum facere, to make something sacred, or to seek favour by sacrifice. In place of sacrificare or sacrificari Deo, the Latins also say sacrum facere, or sacrificium alicui deo facere, facilitare, fieri. Pliny, book 3, chapter 5: "Angerona is a goddess to whom sacrifice is offered on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, with her mouth bound up, etc." Plautus in Mostellaria: "I would have sacrificed silver to Jupiter while he lived." The same writer, in the Captivi, says that when he sacrifices to his own Genius he uses the Samian vessels that the rite requires. Cicero: "Whose Laurentius, you pontiffs are accustomed to make sacrifice at the altar in the Velabrum." The same, on the responses of the haruspices, who performed the ancestral Gentile sacrifices, held yearly, in that very shrine at a fixed place. The same, on a sacrifice which was made for the safety of the people.

units.la: A sacrificio fit Sacrificus, sive sacrificulus, qui sacrificium, sive sacrum facit. Item, Sacrificum, id quod ad sacra, seu sacrificia pertinet. Item Sacrificati a Cypriano & aliis scriptoribus primitiva Ecclesiae; qui idolis sacrificant: ut thuribficati, qui thura idolis adolerent. Cyprianus, Libellatici, id est, qui libellis conscientiam suam maculaverunt, cum sacrificati non sunt coman-dati.
units.tr: From sacrificium comes sacrificus, or sacrificulus, one who makes a sacrifice or a sacred rite. Likewise sacrificus means that which pertains to sacred rites or sacrifices. Likewise sacrificati is used by Cyprian and other writers of the early Church for those who sacrifice to idols, just as thuribificati are those who burn incense to idols. Cyprian: "Libellatici, that is, those who stained their conscience with certificates, although they had not been compelled to sacrifice."

units.la: Porrò cùm vox sacrificii sit composita, ut dixi, ex sacro & facere, observandum utrumque non modò sacra, sed & sacrificia sacrificatione usurpari. Quoad prius, sacrum & in plurali numero, sacra, saepe pro sacrificio accipitur. Cicero pro Cornelio Balbo: Sed cùm illam, quae Graecum aliud sacrum monstraret & faceret, ex Graecia deligerent: tamen sacra pro civibus ex eorum facere voluerunt. Ibidem, Sacra Cereris per Graecas semper curata sunt sacerdotes. Idem de Legibus, Nec nulla vitiorum sacra obeunte. Idem rem sacram facere saepe dixit. Pertinet huc etiam pro vetribus, luter sacrum & sacra. & saxum. Atq; haec de priori. Quoad posterius; Facere absoluté aliquando idem est, quod facrificare, sive sacrificium facere. Cicero pro Murena, Nolite a sacris patriis lunonis hospitae, cui omnes consules Facere, id est, sacrificare necesse est, domesticum & suum consulem potissmum avellere. Virgilius in Bucolicis: Cum faciam vitulâ pro frugibus ipse venito: Faciam, id est, sacrificabo. Sic Operari idem saepe, quod sacrificare. Virgilius,
units.tr: Moreover, since the word sacrificium is compound, as I have said, from sacrum and facere, we should note that both sacra and sacrificatio are used for sacrifice. As to the first, sacrum, and in the plural sacra, is often taken to mean sacrifice. Cicero, Pro Cornelio Balbo: "But when they chose from Greece that priestess who would point out and perform another Greek sacred rite, they nonetheless wished to make sacred rites for the citizens from them." The same, a little later: "The sacred rites of Ceres were always performed by Greek priests." Cicero, De Legibus: "Nor are there any sacred rites performed for vices." Cicero often said rem sacram facere. To this belong also expressions such as lustrare sacrum and sacra ... Thus far on the first. As to the second: facere used absolutely sometimes means the same as sacrificare, or sacrificium facere. Cicero, Pro Murena: "Do not tear away from the ancestral rites of Juno Hospita, to whom every consul must facere, that is, sacrifice, your own domestic consul above all." Virgil in the Bucolics: "When I faciam with a calf for the crops, come yourself": faciam, that is, sacrificabo, I shall sacrifice. So operari often means the same as sacrificare. Virgil:

units.la: Sacra refer Cereri, laetis operatus in herbis: Operatus, id est, sacrificans. Et Operatio pro sacrificiis. Plautus, Vt isthaec operatio, id est, sacrificatio, crimen expiet. Sic operari sacris, idem est, quod sacra facere, sacris operam dare.
units.tr: "Bring the rites to Ceres, performing them amid the joyful grass": operatus, that is, sacrificing. Also operatio is used for sacrifices. Plautus: "that such an operatio, that is, a sacrifice, may expiate the crime." So operari sacris is the same as sacra facere, to give attention to sacred rites.

units.la: Praeterea Res divina cum generaliter pro tota religione, tum pro sacrificio, seu sacrificatione saepe accipitur. Et in plurali Res divinae. Cicero, Pater, qua ad res divinas, id est, sacrificia, ut bantur. Idem, Res illum divinas apud eos Deos in suo sacrario prope quotidie facere vidisti. Plautus Poenul. Paucis verbis rem divinam facito. Idem Sticho: Iube famulos, rem divinam apparent mihi.
units.tr: Besides, res divina is often taken both generally for the whole of religion and specifically for sacrifice or the performance of a sacrifice. In the plural, res divinae. Cicero: "Father, by which divine things, that is, sacrifices, were performed." The same: "You have seen him perform divine things before the gods in his shrine almost every day." Plautus, Poenulus: "Perform the divine rite in a few words." The same, in the Stichus: "Tell the servants to prepare the divine rite for me."

units.la: Vocantur etiam sacrificia a Latinis victimae & hostiae: quae tamen voces cum generatim pro quovis sacrificio, tum speciatim pro certis generibus sacrificiorum accipiuntur. Ac victimam quidem, tefle Festo, Aelius Stilo voluit esse vitulum, ob ejus vigorem sic dictum: alii inde, quod vincta adducatur ad altare, aut quod hostibus victis immoletur. Quidam sic dictam voluntur, quod ictu percussa concidebat. Sic igitur quadruplex fere hujus vocabuli ratio atq; notatio adfertur. Quid si victima dicta fit a victu, propterea quod sacerdotum & sacrificulorum victus constabat victimis: Victimis enim sacerdotes victitabant, victumq; sibi comparabant: unde Hosteas Prophetae sacerdotes suae aetatis idololatras & superstitiosos dixit peccata populi sui comederefuisse solitos: ubi vox peccatorum pro sacrificiis, ut saepe aliàs in sacris litteris accipitur. Victimam autem speciatim dictam esse eam, quae post victoriam & dextra victrice immolabatur, testantur illa O vidii:
units.tr: The Latins also call sacrifices victimae and hostiae. These words, however, are taken both generally for any sacrifice and specifically for certain kinds of sacrifice. As for victima, Aelius Stilo, according to Festus, held that it was a calf, so named from its vigour. Others derive it from its being led bound to the altar, or from its being slain when enemies are conquered. Some say it was so called because it fell when struck by a blow. So roughly four explanations of this word are offered. What if victima is named from victus, because the livelihood of priests and sacrificers consisted of victims? For priests lived on victims and procured their sustenance from them. Whence the prophet Hosea called the priests of his own age idolatrous and superstitious, who were accustomed to eat the sins of his people, where "sins" means sacrifices, as often elsewhere in Scripture. But that victima was specifically the name of that which was immolated after victory, with the victorious right hand, is attested by these lines of Ovid:

units.la: Victima, quae dextra cecidit victrice vocatur. A victima dicti sunt Victimarii, partim negotiatores, qui victimas emebant & vendebant (Plinius, Vnde victimarii, negotiatores vili mancipio.) partim ministri sacrifici, de quibus infra.
units.tr: "The victim that fell by the victorious right hand is called victima." From victima the victimarii are named, partly merchants who bought and sold victims (Pliny: "whence victimarii, merchants of a cheap trade"), and partly ministers of sacrifice, of whom below.

units.la: Vt autem victimae; ita Hostiae quoq; nomen cum generatim quod vis sacrificium significat, tum speciatim quod victis hostibus immolabatur, secundum idem O vidii, Victima, quae dextra cecidit victrice vocatur: Hostibus a domitus hostia nomen habet.
units.tr: But just as with victimae, the name hostiae also signifies generally any sacrifice, and specifically that which was immolated to conquered enemies, according to the same Ovid: "The victim that fell by the victorious right hand is called victima; hostia has its name from the enemies subdued."

units.la: Sic Christi sacrificium secundum speciale m banc utriusq; vocabuli significationem (si sacra licet miscere profanis) hostia & victima dici potest, quo nimirum omnes eum visibiles, tum invisibiles generis humani hostes, videlicet Diabolus, Mundus, Peccatum, Mors, Infernus, Legis maledictio, domiti, de victi, atq; profligati fuerunt. Hostiam Festus vult dictam ab antiquo verbo Hostire, quod ferire significat, quod hostia hostiebatur, id est, feriebatur, seu caedebatur. Quid si hostia dicta sit vel a Graeco θύω, quasi θύσια, id est, sancta: vel ab Hebraeo חטא Hatta, quod & peccatum est, & hostia pro peccato: vel quòd sit quasi ossium salutis? Inter hostiam autem & victimam speciatim dictam discrimen adferunt, de quo, sicut & de aliis, quae huc faciunt, vide Gyraldum in libris, quos de Diis gentium conscripsit.
units.tr: So Christ's sacrifice, in this special meaning of both words (if sacred things may be mixed with profane), can be called hostia and victima, since all his enemies of the human race, visible and invisible, namely the Devil, the World, Sin, Death, Hell, and the curse of the Law, were subdued, conquered and routed. Festus holds that hostia is named from the old verb hostire, which means to strike, because the hostia was hostiebatur, that is, struck or slain. What if hostia is named either from the Greek θύω, as if θύσια, that is, holy; or from the Hebrew chatta [חטא], which means both sin and sin-offering; or because it is, as it were, a sacrifice of salvation? Between hostia and victima specifically understood, they draw a distinction; on this, as on other matters pertinent here, see Giraldus in the books he wrote on the gods of the Gentiles.

units.la: Porrò Hostiam Antiqui Agoniam vocabant ab agendo: unde Agonium, dies appellabatur, quo Rex hostiam immolabat: quam vis Agonium etiam putabant dici Deum, praesidentem rebus agendis, cujus sessitatem Agonalia vocabant, sive quia agones dicebant montes. Inde Agonia sacrificia sunt, & Agonius ludus. Forsan vel a voce Agone, vel ab agédis pecoribus: unde etiam Agolum dixerunt baculum pastorale, quo pecudes aguntur. Haec Festus.
units.tr: Moreover, the Ancients called the hostia an agonia from agere, to do. Hence the day on which the king immolated the victim was called Agonium, although they also thought that Agonius was the name of a god presiding over things to be done, whose festival they called Agonalia, or because they called mountains agones. Hence agonia are sacrifices, and agonius is a game. Perhaps the word comes either from agon, or from agendis pecoribus, driving the flocks: whence they also called the shepherd's staff, with which the flocks are driven, an agolum. So Festus.

units.la: Sunt praeterea apud Latinos quaedam vocabula, quae tametsi proprie peculiares quosdam ritus significant: tamen in genere pro sacrificio & sacrificatione saepissimè accipiuntur. Hujusmodi sunt libationis, immolationis, mactationis, votorum, initiorum, suppliciorum nomina. Libare igitur proprie nihil aliud erat, quàm res, ad sacrificia destinatas, leviter degustare, & quasi primoribus labris degustare: sepe tamen pro sacrificare ponitur, ut apud Virgilium & Tibullum: Nunc pateras libate Iovi.
units.tr: Moreover, among the Latins there are certain words which, although they properly signify particular rites, are nonetheless very often taken in general for sacrifice and sacrificing. Such are the names libatio, immolatio, mactatio, votum, initia, supplicia. To libare, properly, was nothing other than to taste lightly the things destined for sacrifices, as it were to touch them with the first lips; yet it is often used for sacrificare, as in Virgil and Tibullus: "Now pour libations to Jupiter from the bowls."

units.la: Sic Poma libare pro sacrificare. Sic Immolare proprie erat hostiam mola, id est, farre molito & sale aspergere: treberrime tamen in genere sacrificare significat. Cicero de Natura Deorum, Pythagoras Mulis bovem immolasse dicitur. Sic, Immolari absoluté. Idem de Divinatione, Cum pluribus Diis immolatur, qui tandem evenit, ut alius listetur, alius non luetur? Idem ibidem, Cum Sylla in agro Nolano immolaret, id est, sacrificaret, etc. Inde fit etiam Immolatio, Immolator, de quibus infra.
units.tr: So poma libare means to sacrifice. Likewise immolare properly meant to sprinkle the victim with mola, that is, meal ground with salt; yet very commonly it signifies to sacrifice in general. Cicero, De Natura Deorum: "Pythagoras is said to have sacrificed an ox to the Muses." So also immolari absolutely. Cicero, De Divinatione: "When sacrifice is made to many gods, how does it come about that one is pleased and another is not appeased?" The same, in the same work: "When Sulla was sacrificing in the territory of Nola, etc." Hence also come immolatio and immolator, of which below.

units.la: Idem dicendum de mactandi verbo. Mactare proprie est sacrificare victimis cesis: ut,
units.tr: The same must be said of the verb mactare. Mactare properly means to sacrifice slain victims, as in:

units.la: Et nigram mactabis ovem, lucumq; revises.
units.tr: "And you shall slaughter a black sheep, and return to the grove."

units.la: Hinc apud bonos authores interdum pro interficere ponitur. Interdum etiam significat augere, & tam in bonam, quam malam partem accipitur: in bonam, ut apud Ciceronem, Ferunt laudibus, mactant honoribus: & apud Plautum, Tamen bonefle mactatum reducam domum in malam partem, ut apud eundem Ciceronem in Vatinium, Quo etiam majore malo es mactandus, quod non solum facto tuo, sed etiam exemplo Rempublicam vulneris, neque solum improbus esse, sed etiam alios docere volusti. Sic mactare supplicio, infortunio, damno, malo, re mala, crucie, cruciatu apud Plautum frequenter occurrit. Inde Mactle, vox: ut mactle animi, mactle virtute, vel mactle vir virtute. Sic igitur proprie augeri hostiae ducebantur, quando immolabantur
units.tr: Hence in good authors it is sometimes used for to kill. Sometimes it also means to increase, and is taken in a good as well as a bad sense: in a good sense, as in Cicero, "They praise with words and honour with offices" (mactant honoribus), and in Plautus, "Yet I shall bring you home well honoured." In a bad sense, as in Cicero against Vatinius: "You are to be ruined the more heavily, because you have wounded the Republic not only by your deed but also by your example, and wished not only to be wicked but to teach others." Thus mactare with supplicio, infortunio, damno, malo, re mala, crucie, cruciatu frequently occurs in Plautus. Hence the phrases "honoured in spirit" and "honoured in virtue", or "a man honoured for his virtue". So properly the victims were said to be increased when they were immolated, when meal, wine, and incense poured over them, and similar things, were added, whence the offerings were also called mactae, as if more augmented and heaped up. Thus the victims were immolated.

units.la: adhibita mola, vino, thure etiam fuso, & similibus: unde etiam mactle pellabantur, quasi magis aucte & cumulate. Sed alia quoque significatione augeri hostia dicebantur, quando una hostia non litantes, altera, tertia plures ve adhibebantur, de quo inferius. Hujusmodi autem mactan-
units.tr: with the meal, wine, and incense poured out, and similar things, whence the mactle were also offered, as if more augmented and heaped up. But in another sense victims were also said to be augmented, when one victim did not procure favour, and a second, a third, or several more were added, as I shall discuss below. Now this verb of slaying occurs often,

units.la: di verbum sepe occurrit, praesertim apud Ciceronem: ut mactare victimam. Pro Flacco: Quam potestas P. Lentulo mactare victimam gratiorem? Sic Puerorum extis Deos manes mactare, pro, Dius mactare novo ditendi modo. Cicero in Vatinium, Et quoniam omnium rerum magnarum a Dius immortalibus principia ducuntur, volo ut mihi respondeas tu, qui te Pythagoricum soles dicere, & hominis dolisimi nomen tuus immanibus & barbaris moribus pretendere, quae tanta pravitas te mentis tenuerit, qui tantus furor, ut, cum insaudita & nefaria facta fuerint, cum inferorum animas elicere, cum praesentia eorum extis Deos manes mactare soleas, aupicia, quibus haec urbs condita est, quibus omnis Respublica atque imperium continetur, contempseris, etc. Accius, Autillorum copias fundam iumare, aut navis vestras mactabo, (id est, projiciam, praecipitabo) in mare. Videtur alludere ad morem libandi & exta porriciendi, id est, projiciendi in forum, de quibus infra.
units.tr: especially in Cicero, as in "to sacrifice a victim." In the speech for Flaccus: "What more pleasing victim could the power of P. Lentulus sacrifice?" So too "to sacrifice the infernal gods with the entrails of boys," and "to sacrifice the divinities by a new method of enriching." Cicero against Vatinius: "And since all great affairs take their beginnings from the immortal gods, I want you to answer me, you who are wont to call yourself a Pythagorean and to hide behind the name of a most wicked man under cruel and barbarous manners: what so great perversity has held your mind, what so great madness, that when unheard-of and impious deeds were done, when you were wont to summon the souls of the dead and to sacrifice the gods below with the entrails of boys present, you despised the auspices by which this city was founded and by which the whole commonwealth and empire are maintained," and so on. Accius: "I will either overthrow the forces of the Autillii, or I will smash your ships into the sea" (that is, cast them down and hurl them headlong). He seems to allude to the custom of pouring libations and casting the entrails, that is, throwing them into the forum, which I shall discuss below.

units.la: A mactandi verbo macellum videtur dictum: tamet si alii illud deducunt a macerando, quod petora, dum eo ducuntur, macerentur. Et hoc de verbo mactandi, sacrificiorum proprio.
units.tr: The word macellum seems to be derived from the verb mactandi, though others derive it from macerando, because the cattle, while being led there, are worn down (macerentur). And this is what the verb mactandi properly means, of sacrifices.

units.la: Hic adde pollucendi & litandi verba: quorum primus est proprie sacrificare Herculi: tamen ad aliorum quoque Deorum sacrificia transferitur: posterius, licet a sacrificandi verbo redi-si distinguatur, & proprie, (qui sacrificiorum finis fuit & effectus) Deos placare & veniam ab iis impetrare significet: tamen generaliter sepe pro sacrificare accipi videtur, de quo posteà pluribus.
units.tr: Here add the verbs pollucendi and litandi. The first properly means to sacrifice to Hercules, but it is also transferred to the sacrifices of other gods. The second, though it is distinguished from the verb sacrificandi and properly signifies (as was the aim and effect of sacrifices) to appease the gods and win pardon from them, is nevertheless often taken generally for to sacrifice, of which more later.

units.la: Sic Vota quoq; ut apud Graecos εὐχαὶ, pro sacrificiis aliquando ponuntur. Virgilius 3. Aeneid.
units.tr: Thus vows too, called εὐχαί by the Greeks, are sometimes put for sacrifices. Virgil, Aeneid 3:

units.la: Luftramurq, Iovi, votisq; incendimus aras, id est, sacrificiis, quae voveramus.
units.tr: "We purify ourselves to Jove and kindle the altars with our vows," that is, with the sacrifices which we had vowed.

units.la: Supplicia quoq; Veteres quedam sacrificia supplicando appellabant, scilicet Paulo.
units.tr: The ancients also called certain sacrifices supplications (supplicia), as Paulus says.
Initia are similarly used for sacrifices.

units.la: Maruga, vel, ut alii legunt, absque aspiratione Aruga, hostia est, auctore Donato, ab araz quam alii sic dictam volunt ab hara, in qua includebatur. Haruga, teste Festo, dicebatur hostia, cujus adhaerentia infaciebantur exta.
units.tr: Maruga, or as others read without the aspirate, Aruga, is a victim, according to Donatus, from ara, though others want it so called from hara, in which it was enclosed. Haruga, according to Festus, was the name for a victim whose adhering entrails were offered in sacrifice.

units.la: Offerimenta denique, inquit Festus, dicebantur, qua offerebantur. Hac de nominibus Latinis sacrificiorum. A Graecis sacrificium Dusia appellatur, Vox Dusias propriè sacrificationem,ipsamq; sacrificandi actionem, seu solemnitatem, quæ est in re divina facienda, significat, quam Cicero vertit Rem divinam: Hinc ἁ Dusia Dusiai, Sacra illegitima & polluta, apud Philonem, κῳλλίσυ ποι & κᾳλλίερποι Dusiai, sacrificia bona auspicia, aut rite salta, διαίαπο Dusiai, perpetua Sacra. Ali quando serie, in quibus Sacra fiunt, hac voce denotantur, ut apud Lucianum & Aristotelem libro 8. Ethic.cap.9. Hinc Dusias poiein, sive poiesin dixit Plutarchus, Dusiai Dusiae Plato, Dusiae polein kai thetien Herodotus,id est,sacrificium facere,conficere,curare.Sic enim Herodotus,ὑπὲρ τ βασιλείας Dusias telsas. Porrò Dusias Porphyrius & Grammatici quidam dictam existimant quasi Dusia on, quod primi Mortalium Dusiason,id est,suffitum & evaporationem Dijs offerre & impendere fuerint soliti.
units.tr: Finally, says Festus, the things that were offered were called offerings. This is enough on the Latin names of sacrifices. From the Greeks sacrifice is called Dusia; the word Dusia properly signifies the sacrificing itself, the very act or solemnity of sacrificing which is performed in the divine rite, and which Cicero renders as "the divine thing." Hence the unholy and polluted sacrifices of Philo; good-omened or rightly performed sacrifices; and perpetual sacrifices. Sometimes the places where the sacred rites are performed are denoted by this word, as in Lucian and in Aristotle, Ethics book 8, chapter 9. Hence Plutarch said "to make a sacrifice," Plato "to sacrifice sacrifices," and Herodotus "to make and complete sacrifices," that is, to make, complete, or perform a sacrifice. For Herodotus says, "having performed sacrifices for the kingdom." Porphyry and some grammarians think that Dusia was so called as if from thuein, to offer incense, because the first mortals were wont to offer fumigation and incense to the gods.

units.la: Θύμα vitimam feuholiam significat Luciano de sacrificiis & Plutarcho. Idem est Dusiātia, Athenaeo libro nono,& Iscrates ad Nicoclem. Ejus plurale Θυματα, Galenus apud Hippocratem exponit Θυμιαματα,id est,suffimenta. Alioqui θυματα dicebantur etiā pistorum opus, quod ad animalium formam effectum Diis immolabatur, ut exponit Scholiastes apud Thucydidem libro primo. θυμαλα item παςχαρτα apud Sophoclem in Electra sunt omnu generis fruges, quæ Dijs offerebantur. Inde fit Θυμάπορ,sive Θυμάπορ, par vasa hostia, bestiola, Poetice & apud Suidam.Item, Θυματα, τὸ ᾰςῶ ὴ Dusias μεθαρον Dusiasma,ut exponit Scholiastes Aristoph. sacrificii praeludium,εἰς quæ ante sacrificium offertur,victima praemactata. Idem quod Θεραπείταρ'υμα,libamen sacrificiorum,quod fiebat,antequam hostia feriretur.
units.tr: Thyma signifies a victim, a slaughtered animal, in Lucian's On Sacrifices and in Plutarch. The same is thysiatia in Athenaeus book 9, and in Isocrates to Nicocles. Its plural thymata, Galen explains on Hippocrates as thymiamata, that is, fumigations. Otherwise thymata were also called the work of bakers, which was made in the form of animals and offered to the gods, as the scholiast explains on Thucydides book 1. Thymala likewise, in Sophocles' Electra, are all kinds of fruits offered to the gods. From this come thymaporon (or thymapoion) and similar words for sacrificial vessels, victims, and little animals, a poetic usage also found in Suidas. Likewise thymata is the prelude to a sacrifice, that which is offered before the sacrifice, the victim being slaughtered beforehand, as the scholiast on Aristophanes explains. It is the same as the libation of sacrifices, which was made before the victim was struck.

units.la: Θύω, τὸ θυσ ετιαν Dusiasma significat, hoc est,suffimentum,sive odoramentum, & θυον erat omne illud, quod Deabus sacrificabatur: cujus plurale θυα Hefychius exponit τ μαζα,id & Θυα. est.liba,seu placentulas. Inde fit Θυσιο & θυοσκω, sacrificus,qui Sacra flammis adolet,seu accendit a θύω & χω,id est, καιω Eustathius l.a. oi μαιτε εἰςθυοσκοι ἢ ιερεύς: ubi tradit μαιτ τ ἐςη gentem; θυοσκοι autem ἐ ιερῆς species. At secundum antiquos θυοσκός esse τὰς ἡμ ἐ περιφεροῦσι ἡμαν ἐαυτ, hoc est, ἰμπνεύρ ἡμεραυ ταςπθε ἱερ ἐυ ἀλλο ναμ ἁπο- ιαρ: ιν ἐ ἁμ: ἐ ἱ. ἐ ἀγ ἔχω, αἱ ἱ.
units.tr: Thyo signifies the making of a sacrifice, that is, a fumigation or perfume, and thyon was everything that was sacrificed to the goddesses. Hesychius explains its plural thya as cakes, or small flat loaves. From this come thysios and thyoskos, a sacrificer who burns the sacred offerings in flames, or kindles them, from thyo and kaio (to burn), as Eustathius says. In the ancient view, a thyoskos was one who carried around the fire and the incense, a kind of priest.

units.la: Θυνάλη item & sacrificium, , unde θυνάλη αθυ, sacrificare.) & aruspicis, sive extispicium, ut hoc est,ut Eustathius exponit τῶν ἀξ θυσεῶν ιαυτ εἰ: significat, alio nomine etiam σαιλας- εἰ dicta,hoc est,molis,sacrificiis apta,quæ fiebat ex tenuissima farina:cujusmodi est libum, placenta: ideo etiam pro ἀπαρχῆ posita Il.i. apud Homerum: ὄ ἀ ἔ πυρὶ ἐ ὑλαλᾶ θυνάλη.
units.tr: Thynale too is a sacrifice, whence thynalē, to sacrifice, and extispicy, or the inspection of entrails, as Eustathius explains. It is also called by another name, semidalis, fine meal, that is, meal suited to sacrifices, made from the finest flour. Such is the libum, a cake. Hence it is also used for the first-fruits in Homer, Iliad 1.

units.la: Fi apud Athen. lib.13. ὁ ἴ ἁ ἱ ἐ ὑλαλᾶ ἐ Ἀ κ θυνᾶλᾶ ἐ Ἀ πῶ: ubi videtur significare molas, quæ hostiis inspergun̄tur. Inde fit θυνάλητο ἔ ᾶ ποτ, ut ἡ ἄ ἀ ἱ ἀ ἐ ἀ ἱ ἀ ἀ ἐ θυα ἔ ἐ ἀ ἐ ἐ. ani, quo totus magistratus apparebat, Ϭνῦς ἀξιωσεῖς apud eundem est protransfert sacrificare. Apud Homerum Ϭνεὶ ex Veterum opinione accipi semper pro Ϭυμωτας annotat Eustathius Od. ξ. Ϭυεὶν etiam furere, furibundo & praecipiti furore ferri significat: forsan quia Gentiles iis suis sacrificiis hujusmodi furore ferebantur, seu rapiebantur potius. Quid si Ϭυεὶν & Ϭυσία τὸ τῶ Ϭυ, quasi θεῖον, id est, res divina fit appellata, quod soli Deo fit offerenda? Nec inconsulte etiam ab Hebreo ꞩꞩ, Tabach, id est, macta vit, posse deduci.
units.tr: In Athenaeus book 13 the word seems to mean the meal sprinkled on the victims. Hence the phrase by which the whole magistracy appeared... The verb thyein, to sacrifice, is transferred in the same way. In Homer, according to the opinion of the ancients, thyein is always to be understood as thymoun, to be angry, as Eustathius notes on Odyssey ξ. Thyein also means to rage, to be carried away by a frenzied and headlong fury, perhaps because the Gentiles were carried into such frenzy, or rather seized, by their sacrifices of this kind. What if thyein and thysia were so called from thyos, as if theion, that is, a divine thing, because it is to be offered to God alone? Nor without reason can it be derived from the Hebrew טבח (tabach), that is, to slaughter.

units.la: Ιερὸν item & ιερὰ, numero plurali, ut Sacrum sive Sacra apud Latinos, & sacrificium, sive hostiam seu victimam, & templum sive fanum, & rem divinam significat. Hinc ἱερὰ, sanctā religio, ἱερὰ ἱερὰ, arcana Sacra, τὰ ἐντὸς ἱερὰ incaeta Sacra, ἀβατα καὶ ἀκαλλιερ- τα ἱερὰ, exta triflia: quibus opponuntur τὰ κοινὰ, apud Aeschinem contra Ctesiph. Hinc ille ἀβατα ἱερὰ πολλὰκις κατέσχεν, Sacra haud sacrificata perfeptu comedit: necnon ἀγαπ καὶ σωμα, sancta & veneranda: ut ὑπὸ ἀξίων καὶ σεμνῶν ἱερῶν, ὧν οἱ ψυχοὶ ἐπὶ τὰ ἐψ- καὶ μεγαλοπρεπῶς ἐπιτελέσθη ἀξιον κυ ἀπὸ καπω ἀξιον, Isocrates. Idem; ἐρχομένη τὰ ἱερὰ, Curare Sacra. Πρόσωπον πεῖσθαι μὲν τὰ ἱερὰ, ὡσπερ τοῦ ἱερὰ, Rationem nec facerorum habere, nec festi. Item, ὑπηρετεῖν τοῖς ἱεροῖς, ministrare in sacris, Ϭυεὶν & Ϭυεὶν κα ἱερὰ, Sacra facere, ut μυσαλισμὸς ἐπὶ τὸν ἱερῶν, recipere aliquem in societatem sacrorum, κοινωνεῖν καὶ μετ- ἀλλ' ἐξ τῶν ἱερῶν, nisi eisdem sacris, ἀπελαύειν καὶ ἀπαγόρευσον τὰ ἱερὰ, attingere Sacra & ubis ab limitare, ἐξεχομένη ἐξ ἐξ ἐξ, ἀποκλεῖειν τινὰ τῶν ἱερῶν, excludere aliquem & arcere a Sacris, συλλαβὴ ἐξ συλλαβὴς ἱερὰ, praedari, rapere Sacra. Ab hoc ἱερὸν ἱερὸν ἱερὰ, Sacra vel religionem tradare, & ἱεροὺς, sacrificare, mactare, ut ἱ. ὠρὸς ζῶα, ἐπὶ ὠρα, sacrificare, seu mactare animal in aliquius gratiam, ut Eustathius exponit Odyss. ξ. Et ἱερὰ αἰσθη ad parandum prandium. Inde & ιερεῖον sacrificium, victima hostia, ut ἀπάνευθεν ἱερέων ἀπὸ τὸ βωμὸν, deduci victimam ab ara, ἐν τῷ ἐλλι ιερεῖοι, profferuere victimas, ἐκτὸς ἐξω τὰ ιοῦ, victimas feri- re. Fit inde & ἱερουργία sacrilegium, & ἱεροσυλία, sacrilegium, ἱερὰ ἱεροσυλῶ, sacrilegia, & ἱερηνία, sacrificatio & ἱερω- γείς, sacra operari.
units.tr: Hieron, and hiera in the plural, like Sacrum or Sacra among the Latins, signifies both a sacrifice or victim and a temple or shrine, and also a divine thing. Hence hiera, holy religion; hiera hiera, secret sacred rites; ta entos hiera, the inner sacred things; abata kai akallierēta hiera, ill-omened entrails, which are opposed to ta koina, the profane things, in Aeschines against Ctesiphon. Hence that phrase, he ate the unsacrificed sacred things in secret. Also hagna kai semna, holy and venerable, as in Isocrates: "the sacred and venerable rites, which the souls..." Likewise, to perform sacred rites; to take part in the sacred rites; to minister in sacred things; to exclude someone from the sacred rites and keep him away from them; to plunder and rob sacred things. From this hieruein, to sacrifice, to slaughter, as Eustathius explains on Odyssey ξ: to sacrifice an animal on behalf of someone. Also hiera aisthē, to prepare a meal. Hence hiereion, a sacrifice or sacrificial victim, as in the phrase to lead the victim away from the altar, and to bring forward the victims, and to strike down the victims. From this come hierourgia, sacrilege, and hierosylia, sacrilege, hiera hierosyleō, to commit sacrilege, and hierōsynē, the sacrificing and the performing of sacred rites.

units.la: Ὄργια quoque, ut vult Servius, apud Graecos cum omnia Sacra dicuntur, tum propria Sacra Liberi, vel ἀπὸ ὄργης, id est, a furore, vel ἀπὸ τῆς ὀρ. ὁρᾶν ὀργάς, id est, a monitibus qui d in montium jugis, ut caelo proximis locis (quae Excelsa in sacris licteris appellantur) sacrificare consueverunt. Apollonii Schol. laetis sic vult dicta ποιηθῆν τὸ ἐιχν ἐκ των ἀλλων ἐπὶ ἐκ των, quod a facris profani arceri debeant. Aliquando sanctiora & magis arcana Sacra sic appellantur: idem quod ἱέρειας, sicut exponitur. Inde ὀργιάζειν, Orgia, sive Sacra peragere, vel sine adjectione, vel cum ea, ut ὀργιάζειν τὸν Θεὸν, id est, sacrificare Deum placare apud Platonem: ut apud Lactinos, mactare Deos extis. Item ὀργιάζειν, sacris initiare. Pro ὀργιάζειν dicitur etiam ὀργιάζειν Hesychio. Ὀργιάζεσθαι dicuntur ipsa Sacra, quum peraguntur. Exponitur hoc etiam ἀλἐν, pro, rem divinam facere apud Platonem libro quarto de Legibus.
units.tr: Orgia, as Servius holds, are among the Greeks all sacred rites in general, but the proper sacred rites of Liber (Bacchus) are called orgia, either from orgē [ὀργή], that is, from fury, or from horan orgas [ὁρᾶν ὀργάς], that is, from the mountain ridges, where people were accustomed to sacrifice in high places close to heaven (which in the sacred letters are called high places). The scholiast on Apollonius says that they are so called because the rites must be kept from the profane. Sometimes the holier and more secret rites are called by this name, the same as hiereiai, as it is explained. From this come orgiazein, to celebrate orgia, or sacred rites, either without an addition or with one, as orgiazein ton Theon [ὀργιάζειν τὸν Θεόν], that is, to sacrifice to God, to placate God, in Plato; as the Latins say to slaughter gods with entrails. Orgiazein also means to initiate into the sacred rites. For orgiazein, Hesychius also gives orgiazein. The sacred rites themselves are said to be orgiazesthai when they are performed. This is also explained by the word alein, to perform the divine rite, in Plato's fourth book of the Laws.

units.la: Hinc ὀργιασμὸς, sacrorum peractio, sive operatio, Plutarch. Ὀργιαστὴς eidem, & ὀργιάσAeschylo & Hesychio, sacerdos, qui Orgia, sive Sacra Deorum celebrat, & φιλόργιος, qui Orgia & sacra delectatur.
units.tr: Hence orgiasmos [ὀργιασμός], the performance or celebration of sacred rites, in Plutarch. Orgiastēs [ὀργιαστής] in the same author, and in Aeschylus and Hesychius, is a priest who celebrates the orgia, or sacred rites of the gods; and philorgios [φιλόργιος] is one who delights in orgia and sacred rites.

units.la: Τελετὴ, quasi τελέω, in singulari expiatio est, cerimonia, sacerdotium. In plurali τελετὰι proludi & sacrificia accipiuntur apud Platonem de Republica: quas dicit esse λύσεις καὶ καθαρμοὺς ἀδικημάτων, id est, expiationes & expurgationes iniquitatum. Possunt etiam festa dida esse τελεταὶ ἀπὸ τὸ τελεῖν, quod impendere inter alia significat, quoniam sacrificia, diesque festi maximas impensas requirunt. Aliuqui τελεῖν est & agere, vel celebrare dies festos.
units.tr: Teletē [τελετή], as if from teleō, in the singular means expiation, ceremony, or priesthood. In the plural, teletai [τελεταί] are taken as preliminary rites and sacrifices in Plato's Republic, which he says are releases and purifications from wrongdoings, that is, expiations and purgings of iniquities. Festivals may also be called teletai, from teleein [τελεῖν], which among other things means to spend, since sacrifices and festal days require very great expense. Otherwise teleein also means to perform or celebrate festal days.

units.la: Εἰσιθεῖα quoque Graeci res divinas, sive Sacra sunt dicta, videlicet quae fiebant pro felicitatis principio, quo totus magistratus apparebat: sicut Διαλεγεῖα, sacrificia pro cranfitu & Εὐαγγελία pro re bene gesta. De primo, ἱεροποιὸς εἰσιθεῖα ὑπὲρ πόλεως ὑπερ, rem divinam facere pro felici ingressu dixit Demosthenes. De secundo Plutarchus in Lucullo, ἵσως τοῦ τυχαίαν ἀξιῶς ποιεῖν. De ultimo Isocrates, Εὐαγγελία δὲ ἐν τῷ πόλει, ἐκ εἰς τὴν ἀναστροφὴν ἐπὶ ἐπὶ τῆς πρᾶξεως.
units.tr: The Greeks also call divine rites, or sacred things, eisitheia [εἰσιθεῖα], namely those performed at the beginning of a happy undertaking, when the whole magistracy presented itself; likewise dialegeia, sacrifices for a safe crossing, and euangelia [εὐαγγελία] for a deed well done. Of the first, Demosthenes said that a priest performs the divine rite for the city's happy entry (hieropoios eisitheia hyper poleōs [ἱεροποιὸς εἰσιθεῖα ὑπὲρ πόλεως]), that is, to perform the rite for a happy entrance. Of the second, Plutarch in Lucullus says that it is fitting to do so for a fortunate event. Of the last, Isocrates says that the euangelia are held in the city when something has been well done.

units.la: Musgrave. Mυσηεια etiam Graecis sacra sunt, & quidem generaliter arcana quae vns sacra, siue τα εἰς Μυσηεια τὰς θυὰς. Hinc, ὀργιαζειν, ... violare sacra, idem quod αοσβ ... Violare religionem. Item μυεῖν μυσηεια sacra facere, idem quod ... administrare religiosa sacra, apud Demosthenem. In specie vero significant Sacrificia. Hinc, συναγειν ... congregare aliquos ad sacrificia. Sic autem dicta videntur vel quod ea ... occludere oportet intus, intus custodire, nec cuiquam profano explicare, vel ... ce nry sferia disceder, &c. Asinus mysteria portans.
units.tr: Musgrave. Among the Greeks the mysteria [μυστήρια] are also sacred rites, and in general they are secret things, which are sacred mysteries. Hence orgiazein, to violate sacred rites, the same as to violate religion. Likewise myein mysteria, to perform sacred mysteries, the same as to administer religious sacred rites, in Demosthenes. In particular they signify sacrifices. Hence synagein, to gather some people to sacrifices. They seem to be so named either because they must be kept shut within, kept secret, and not explained to any profane person, or because ... they depart from ... etc. An ass carrying the mysteries.

units.la: Pertinet huc quoq; vox ἀπορρ ..., quam ad χρησθαι ... sive res sacras adhibuerunt: quae libationem, sive libamen significabant. Hinc, ... participem esse libationum & votorum, ... nempe apud Demosthenem: & ... repelli, arceri a libationibus, apud eundem.
units.tr: To this also belongs the word aporrh..., which they used for sacred things (?) that signified a libation, or an offering of drink: hence to be a partaker of libations and vows, namely in Demosthenes; and to be driven back and kept away from libations, in the same author.

units.la: Hebraice sacrificium זבח Zebach, appellatur, a זבח Zabach, sacrificavit: idem quod טבח Tabach, macta vit, & טבח Tebach, mactatio, id est, animalium. Sed טבח Tabach, de mactatione animalium dicitur, quae non sacrificantur: at זבח Zabach, sepisime de mactationc pecorum facta, id est, sacrificatione: ubi notabis saepe sacrificia Israelitarum quae sine vera fide atq; ritu Dei vel Dijs offerebantur, mactationes per contemtum a Spiritu Sanctò appellatas, quoniam eorum Deo nihil erant aliud, quàm profanae animalium mactationes, in quibus etiam solis Israelitarum mentes atq; animi erant defixi, nihil altius, atq; sublimius in iis quaerentes & spectantes. Ab Hebraeo זבח Zebach, vel Sebach, & Graecum σφαγιον, sive σφαγη, σφαγεῖν, sive σφαζεσθαι, & Latinum Sabini & Sabaei (qui religiosissimi olim apud Ethnicos babitaverunt populi) & Sabazius Deus videtur dictus.
units.tr: In Hebrew a sacrifice is called zebach [זבח], from zabach [זבח], he sacrificed, which is the same as tabach [טבח], he slaughtered, and tebach [טבח], slaughter, that is, of animals. But tabach is said of the slaughter of animals that are not sacrificed, whereas zabach is most often used of the slaughter of livestock made into a sacrifice. Here you will note that the sacrifices of the Israelites which were offered without true faith and the rite of God, or to other gods, are by the Holy Spirit called, with contempt, mere slaughterings, since to God they were nothing other than profane slaughterings of animals, in which only the minds and hearts of the Israelites were fixed, seeking and looking for nothing higher or more sublime in them. From the Hebrew zebach [זבח], or sebach, and the Greek sphagion, or sphagē, sphageein, or sphazesthai, and the Latin Sabini and Sabaei (peoples who were once the most religious among the heathen) and the god Sabazius seem to have been named.

units.la: Nomen generaliter est קרבן Korban, quod generaliter significat omne donum, seu munus, quod Deo offertur, tam de pecoribus quam frugibus, aliisq; rebus: unde Oblationis vocabulo Veteres commodissime illud expresserunt. Et reijciendo vox Graeca προσφορά, pro sacrificio sumta, ... offerre: ut προσφέρειν ... Sed nomen hoc προσφορα ... in sacris tantum litteris, non in profanis, quod sciam, proprie sacrificium ponitur. Hujus exemplum habes Leviticì secundo capite, Si obtulerus קרבן Korban, id est, προσφορα, minuneris colucluban, etc. Ubi manifesta notatur differentia inter קרבן Korban, et מנחה Minchah: quod prius sit generalius, posterius specialius & tantum de frugibus terrae dicatur.
units.tr: The general name is korban [קרבן], which generally signifies every gift or offering that is offered to God, whether of livestock or of fruits or other things; hence the ancients most fittingly rendered it by the word oblatio, offering. Rejecting the Greek word prosphora [προσφορά], taken for sacrifice, ... to offer, as prospherein [προσφέρειν]... But this word prosphora, as far as I know, is properly used for sacrifice only in the sacred letters, not in profane ones. You have an example of this in Leviticus chapter two: If he offer a korban [קרבן], that is, prosphora, a meat offering, etc. Here a clear distinction is marked between korban [קרבן] and minchah [מנחה]: the former is more general, the latter more specific and said only of the fruits of the earth.
Difference of the words: Korban and Minchah.

units.la: Hic etiam referri potest verbum הביא Hebi, id est adduxit, attulit, sive obtulit, quod sacrificiis accommodatur Genesis quarto capite. Nam Cainus quidem agricola, הביא Hebi, id est adduxit de frugibus terrae Minchę. Hebel autem, pastor ovium הביא Hebi, id est adduxit, sive obtulit lebove de primogenitis pecudum & adipe earum.
units.tr: Here also can be referred the verb hebi [הביא], that is, he brought, carried, or offered, which is suited to sacrifices in Genesis chapter four. For Cain, a farmer, brought [hebi, הביא] of the fruits of the earth a minchah. Abel, however, a shepherd of sheep, brought [hebi, הביא], that is, offered, from the firstborn of his flock and their fat.

units.la: Porro sacrificiorum origo, ut omittamus Ethnicorum fabulas, secundum sacras litteras tradi potest, a primorum parentum generis humani temporibus. Ac tametsi verisimile est, primos quoque illos nostros parentes Adamum & Evam sacrificia Deo fecisse: tamen eorum nulla in sacris litteris extat mentio, ita ut nihil de illis certi affirmare possimus. Primaque igitur sacrificia, quorum expressa capite quarto Geneseos sit mentio, fuerunt Caini & Hebelis fratrum sacrificia: & haec quidem omnium prima fuisse sacrificia Cyrillus quoq; prodidit libro tertio contra Julianum. Ac Caini quidem Agricolae sacrificium, quod Iehovae obtulit, fuit ex fructibus terrae, vitae nimirum ejus generi ac instituto accommodatum. Hebelis autem, qui opilio seu pastor ovium fuit, sacrificium constitit ex primogenitis ovium sive pecorum & adipe eorum. Eh duo prima sacrificiorum genera; quorum unum fuit Minchà, constans terrae frugibus: alterarum animale, constans ovibus. Deinde unum quidem Deus respexit, hoc est, pro gratio & accepto accepisse dicitur, nempe Hebelis, propter fidem ejus: alterum vero non respexit, sed repudiasse, nempe Caini sacrificium: nonniam illud fide fuit vacuum. Ut igitur Hebelis sacrificium omnis veri & justi sacrificii: ita Caini sacrificium omnium falsorum sacrificiorum typus fuit & origo. Similiter Augustinus toto Libro decimoquinto. de Ciuitate Dei, sed inprimis capite quinto, & decimo septimo ostendit in Caino & Hebele duarum, que in hoc Mundo cernuntur, ciuitatum fundamenta describi & proponi. Vna est terrena, que a Caino fratricida exordium suum habuit, atq; per ejus posteros fuit propagata: Altera est spiritualis & coelestis, que est Ecclesia Dei, cujus primum exemplum fuit Hebel, Matthaei vigesimo tertio.
units.tr: Further, the origin of sacrifices, leaving aside the fables of the heathen, can be traced according to the sacred letters to the times of the first parents of the human race. And although it is likely that those first parents of ours, Adam and Eve, also offered sacrifices to God, yet no mention of them exists in the sacred letters, so that we can affirm nothing certain about them. The first sacrifices, then, whose mention is expressly made in chapter four of Genesis, were the sacrifices of the brothers Cain and Abel; and Cyril also related in the third book against Julian that these were the first of all sacrifices. Cain's sacrifice, which he offered to Jehovah as a farmer, was from the fruits of the earth, clearly suited to his kind of life and occupation. Abel's, who was a herdsman or shepherd of sheep, consisted of the firstborn of the sheep or flock and their fat. These are the two first kinds of sacrifice: one was the minchah, consisting of the fruits of the earth; the other an animal sacrifice, consisting of sheep. Then God regarded the one, that is, it is said that he accepted it with favour, namely Abel's, on account of his faith; but the other he did not regard, but rejected, namely Cain's sacrifice, because it was empty of faith. As Abel's sacrifice was the type and origin of every true and just sacrifice, so Cain's sacrifice was the type and origin of all false sacrifices. Likewise Augustine, throughout the whole fifteenth book of The City of God, and especially in chapters five and seventeen, shows that in Cain and Abel are described and set forth the foundations of the two cities seen in this world. One is earthly, which took its beginning from Cain the fratricide and was propagated through his descendants; the other is spiritual and heavenly, which is the Church of God, whose first example was Abel, Matthew chapter twenty-three.

units.la: Sacrificiorum porro Gentilium varia, multiplicia ac pene innumera fuerunt genera, que numerare omnia difficillimum, operosissimum & δυσεξηγητον plane esse videatur. Verum, ut genere quodam quasi appellat, quae nimirum, ut Labeonis testimonio interpretatur, omnes civese facienti, nec certis familiis erant attributa. Plutarchus hujusmodi sacrificia Θυσίας ὅμως appellat. Privata autem sacra, eodem Festo interprete, dicebantur, quae pro singulis hominibus, familiis, gentibus fiebant, quae etiam gentilitia vocabantur, ut sacra Clodiae gentis apud M. Tullium, & innumera alia. Sacra privata, ut idem ait in libro de Legibus, perpetua manent.
units.tr: The kinds of Gentile sacrifices were varied, manifold, and almost innumerable, so that to enumerate them all would seem most difficult, most laborious, and plainly δυσεξηγητον [hard to explain]. Yet, to speak in a certain general way, they were those which, as Festus explains on the testimony of Labeo, were offered for all citizens and were not assigned to particular families. Plutarch calls sacrifices of this kind public sacrifices. Private sacred rites, by the same Festus' account, were those performed for individual men, families, or clans, which were also called gentilitian, such as the sacred rites of the Clodian clan in Cicero, and countless others. Private sacred rites, as the same author says in his book on the Laws, remain perpetual.

units.la: Et paulo post: De sacris haec pertinent sententia, ut conferventur simper, & deinceps familiis prodantur, ut in Lege posuit, Perpetua sint sacra.
