units.tr: And a little later: "Concerning sacred rites this is the principle: that they should always be preserved and handed down to families in turn, as he laid down in the law, that sacred rites be perpetual."

units.la: Haec privata vero & gentilitia singularum familiarum & gentium sacra videntur, subdividi posse in paterna & adoptiva, secundum illa Ciceronis de Aruspicum responsis: Nec amissis sacris paternis in hac adoptiva venistis. Adhaec sacra privata & hereditaria alludit elegantur parasitus ille apud Plautum in Capt. Sine sacris hereditatem sum aptus (id est, adeptus, ab antiquo verbo apiscor) effertissimam, sive, ut alii legunt, offertissimam, plenissimam, uberrimam, referrissimam. Sine sacris, inquit idem, fine juntu, vitertrimento & oxere, nullo junctu admixto aut adjuncto. Sacra etenim familiaria pecuniam sequebantur, id est, res, ad quos pecunia testatoris pervenerat, puta haedem, bonorum possessorem legatarium, alium vel sic cesserit, si non exflabat haeres. Qui igitur haereditatem praejeci optimam adeptus erit sine sacris, juxta lectarinum praeferit: quia magnum damnum fecisset sine illo interitu. Adhaec illustranda accommodata valde funi illa Ciceronis secundo de Legibus: De sacris autem quo modo patet latius, haec sit una sententia ut conferventur, & deinceps familiis prodantur: & ut in Lege posui, perpetua sint sacra. Hoc posito, haec jura Pontificum ut auctoritate confecta sunt, ut, ne morte patris familias memoria occideret, in ea essent adjuncta, ad quos ejusdem morte pecunia venerit. Quinam autem sacra illa asfringantur, sive ad ligentur, pluribus ibidem Cicero disputat.
units.tr: These private and gentile rites, belonging to individual families and clans, seem capable of being divided into ancestral and adoptive, according to Cicero's words in his On the Responses of the Haruspices: "and you came into this adoptive family without losing your ancestral rites." Likewise the parasite in Plautus's Captivi alludes elegantly to private and hereditary rites: "I am fitted to get an inheritance, very large, without sacred rites" (that is, adeptus, from the old verb apiscor), "very large, or, as others read, offertissimam, most full, most abundant, most rich." "Without sacred rites," he says, "without any burden, without expense, without any added charge, with nothing mixed in or attached." For household rites followed the money, that is, the property went to those to whom the testator's money had come, for example the heir, the possessor of goods, a legatee, or whoever else, if no heir stood forth. So whoever has obtained the best inheritance without sacred rites will, according to the reading, be preferred: because he would have suffered great loss without that money. Cicero's words in the second book On the Laws are also very suitable for illustrating this: "On how sacred rites are to be kept, the matter extends more widely. This is the one principle: that they be preserved and handed down to families in turn, and, as I laid down in the law, that sacred rites be perpetual." Given this, the rulings of the Pontiffs were drawn up with authority so that, lest the memory of the head of the family perish at his death, the sacred rites should be attached to those to whom the money came on his death. Cicero discusses at more length in the same place who are bound to these rites.

units.la: Deinde sacra, sive sacrificia Gentilium divisi, possunt secundum tempus; idque multifariam. Stata sacrificia, inquit Paulus, dicebantur, quae certis diebus fiebant. Cato in ea oratione, quam scripsit de Lucio Vitorio de sacrilegio commisso, cum ei equum ademit: Sueta, inquit, flata, folennia, familia deferuntur. Sic folennia, Festo teste, sacra dicebantur, quae certis temporibus annuatim fieri solebant.
units.tr: Next, the sacrifices or sacred rites of the Gentiles can be divided according to time, and in many ways. Paulus says that "stated sacrifices" were those made on fixed days. Cato, in the speech he wrote about Lucius Vitorius concerning a sacrilege committed when he took away his horse, says: "The customary, stated, solemn rites are carried out by the household." Thus, according to Festus, "solemn rites" were those sacred rites that were customarily performed each year at fixed times.

units.la: Sacra similiter annua & anniversaria sunt dicta, quae omnibus annis fieri solebant. Ser vius in Aeneidos Virgilii, Annua, inquit, quae differre nefas. Anniversaria idem non differuntur, quia nec iterari possunt. Nam Kalendaria, si qua fuerint ratione dilata, possunt repeti, nec piaculum eorum intermissione committitur. Annua sive anniversaria sacra Svsias ὑπομονη a Thucydide appellantur.
units.tr: Likewise sacred rites were called annual and anniversary, those that were performed in every year. Servius, on Virgil's Aeneid: "annual," he says, "those which it is wrong to postpone." Anniversary rites are not postponed, because they cannot be repeated. For calendar rites, if they were put off for some reason, can be repeated, and no offence is committed by their omission. Annual or anniversary sacrifices are called [θυσίαι ἐπομονή] by Thucydides.

units.la: Sic sacrificia quaedam fuerunt diurna; alia nocturna: & diurna quidem vel matutina, vel meridionalia, vel vespertina, sed de his infra pluribus.
units.tr: Thus some sacrifices were by day, others by night; and those by day were either in the morning, at midday, or in the evening, but of these more below.

units.la: Sortita etiam fuerunt Sacra illa sua nomina a certo tempore, ut diebus, mensibus, annis, in quibus illa confici consuevit.
units.tr: Those sacred rites also took their names from the fixed time at which they were usually performed, such as days, months, or years.

units.la: Praeterea sacrificia Gentilium divisa, distincta ac denominata fuerunt secundum Deos, atque Deas, quibus illa fiebant, ut a Cerere Cerealia, a Libero Liberalia, a Baccho Bacchanalia, a Vulcano Vulcanalia, a Vertumno Vertumnalia, a Saturno Saturnalia, a Pale Dea Palilia ut Cerealia etc, sive Parilia, a Termino Terminalia: & sic de reliquis.
units.tr: Moreover, the sacrifices of the Gentiles were divided, distinguished and named according to the gods and goddesses to whom they were offered: from Ceres, the Cerealia; from Liber, the Liberalia; from Bacchus, the Bacchanalia; from Vulcan, the Vulcanalia; from Vertumnus, the Vertumnalia; from Saturn, the Saturnalia; from the goddess Pales, the Palilia, as the Cerealia etc., or Parilia; from Terminus, the Terminalia: and so with the rest.

units.la: Aliquando nomina sua acceperunt a locis, in quibus illa fieri confuerunt: ut Palatuar sacrificium apud Romanos dicebatur, Festo teste, quod fiebat Romæ in Palatino monte. Septimontium, ajt idem, erat dies festus, quod septem in locis faciebant sacrificium, Palatio, Velia, Fagutali, Subura, Cermalo, Celio, Oppio & Cispio.
units.tr: Sometimes they took their names from the places where they were customarily held: thus the sacrifice called the Palatuar among the Romans, according to Festus, was made at Rome on the Palatine hill. The Septimontium, the same writer says, was a festal day, because they offered sacrifice in seven places: the Palatium, Velia, Fagutal, Subura, Cermalus, Caelius, Oppius and Cispius.

units.la: Quinetiam sæpissime sacrificia nuncupata fuerunt a materia, ut Bωδυσία, Hecatombea bo- bus, aut Θεοπρόβυσια ab hominibus, qui immolabantur, ὑςήσια, a suibus, &c.
units.tr: Indeed very often sacrifices were named from the material: as [βουθυσία] (ox-sacrifice), the hecatomb of oxen, or [θεοπρόβυσια] from the men who were sacrificed, [ὑσήσια] from the swine, and so on.

units.la: Distinguebantur etiam & appellabantur a fine: unde alia dicta fuerunt ἱκεσίαι, alia ἱλασμοί, alia μαντικά, Latinæ Consultoria: quæ vel Deo, vel Diis ac Deabus gratias a- gendi, vel eos placandi propitiandive, vel denique eos de rebus futuris consulendi gratia fiebant.
units.tr: They were also distinguished and named from their purpose: hence some were called [ἱκεσίαι] (supplications), others [ἱλασμοί] (propitiations), others [μαντικά] (divinatory), in Latin consultoria (consultative). These were offered either to give thanks to God or to the gods and goddesses, or to placate and propitiate them, or finally to consult them about future events.

units.la: Sacra item sacrificia Gentilium alia erant patria, alia externa & peregrina. Peregrina appellabantur, teste Festo, quæ ab aliis urbibus religionis gratia erant ad vetta: quæ, inquam, aut evocatis Diis in oppugnandis urbibus Romam eraut conlata: aut quæ ob quasdam religiones per pacem erant petita, ut ex Phrygia Matris Magnæ, ex Græcia Cereris, ex Epidauro Æsculapii, quæ colebantur eorum more, a quibus erant acceptæ.
units.tr: Likewise the sacrifices of the Gentiles were some native and others foreign and imported. According to Festus, those were called foreign which were brought from other cities for the sake of religion: either, I say, those which, when the gods had been summoned in the sieges of cities, were transferred to Rome; or those which were sought for certain religious reasons by treaty of peace, such as the Mother of the Great Goddess from Phrygia, Ceres from Greece, and Aesculapius from Epidaurus, which were worshipped after the manner of those from whom they had been received.

units.la: Alia erant tenuia & exigua, Plutarcho dicta μικρά: alia magnifica, eidem λαμπρά καὶ μεγαλοπρεπῆ. Alia fiebant in aperto: alia in operto. Huiusmodi sacrificium in operto fuit sumtuosa. id, quod in Bonæ Deæ honorem fiebat, unde Damium dictum a contrarietate, quod minime efset δημόσιον, id est, publicum. Dea quoque ipsa Damia, & sacerdos ejus Damias appellaba- tur. Hæc Festus.
units.tr: Some were slight and modest, called by Plutarch [μικρά] (small); others magnificent, by the same writer [λαμπρά καὶ μεγαλοπρεπῆ] (splendid and magnificent). Some were performed in the open, others under cover. The sacrifice performed under cover was a costly one, the one made in honour of the Good Goddess, whence it was called Damium by contrast, because it was in no way [δημόσιον], that is, public. The goddess herself was also called Damia, and her priestess Damias. So far Festus.

units.la: Fiebant porro alia pro vivis, alia pro mortuis. Unde idem Festus, Humanum sacrificium, inquit, dicebant, quod mortui causa fiebat. Demq; tametsi omnia Gentilium sacrificia fuerunt impia, fœda, turpia: tamen alia illis erant, seu videbantur potius, pia, alia (cujusmodi reperta erant omnia) impia & scelerata.
units.tr: Moreover some were offered for the living, others for the dead. Hence the same Festus: "A human sacrifice," he says, "was what was made for the sake of the dead." And although all the sacrifices of the Gentiles were impious, foul and base, nevertheless some among them were, or rather seemed, pious, while others (and of this kind all were found) were impious and wicked.

units.la: Atque hæc quidem universe & ut ita loquar, ἐν πάντων de sacrificiorum nominibus atq; generibus prælibare volui. Nunc ad specialem duorum istorum sacrificiorum explicationem redibo: catio sacrificio in quibus ut in omni alio sacrificio, atq; adeo in omni actione hæc: nobis consideranda sunt capita, seu circumstantiæ, nimirum Quando, Quib. Cur, Quo, A quibus, deniq; quo modo, rutu atq; ordine utrunq; hoc sacrificium factum est, peractum fuerit.
units.tr: These things, in general and, so to speak, as a preliminary survey, I have wished to set out concerning the names and kinds of sacrifices. Now I shall return to the detailed explanation of these two sacrifices, in which, as in every other sacrifice and indeed in every action, the following heads, or circumstances, must be considered: namely When, Where, Why, By what means, By whom, and finally in what manner and order each of these sacrifices was made and carried out.

units.la: Est vero mihi animus unum atq; alterum sacrificiorum hujusmodi exemplum, ex antiquis & probatis auctoribus depromtum proponere, & quasi per quandam, hoc est, analysin explicare: Unum quidem ex Homero, quem vere Poetarum Deum possumus appellare: alterum vero ex Apollonio.
units.tr: Indeed I intend to set forth one and another example of such sacrifices, drawn from ancient and approved authors, and to explain them, as it were, by a certain analysis: one indeed from Homer, whom we may truly call the god of poets; the other from Apollonius.

units.la: At apud Homerum quidem nonnulla hujusmodi sacrificiorum exempla illustria exstant: ut Iliad. A. Hecatombei sacrificii fit mentio, quod Rex Agamemnon per Chrysem sacerdotem Apollini pro Danais offerri curavit: necnon epuli, quod sacrificium illud fuit consecutum. Item Iliad. B. Idem Rex Iovi bovem immolavit, ad quod sacrificium atq; epulum Seniorum Græcorum proceres dicitur vocasse. Item Iliad. H. Similiter Iovi bovem idem Rex sacrificavit. Sic Odyss. T. Describitur magnificum sacrificium epulare 81. taurorum, quod Nestor una cum suis Neptuno obtulit: qui idcirco cum ob hoc, sum alia sacrificia, quorum fuit studiosissimus, ἀπὸ Αριστοφάνης in Vesp. dicitur. Odyss. Θ. Iovi etiam bovem sacrificasse dicitur Alcinous: quo peracto sacrificio — ἐξώμισι ἱερὸν ἱλία ἀδώτα Τερπόβυσοι μετὰ ὃ σφιν ἰμέλπο θεῷ Κοιδ ὅς, Id est, summa cum jucunditate atq; cantu suavissimo gloriosum celebrarunt convivium. Odyss. T. Græciumbrosio in luco in Apollinis honorem & sacrificium Hecatombæum et epulum magnificum celebrasse scribuntur.
units.tr: In Homer there are indeed several notable examples of such sacrifices: as in Iliad 1 mention is made of the hecatomb sacrifice which King Agamemnon had offered to Apollo through the priest Chryses on behalf of the Danaans, and also of the feast which followed that sacrifice. Likewise in Iliad 2 the same King sacrificed an ox to Jupiter, and to this sacrifice and feast he is said to have summoned the leaders and elders of the Greeks. Also in Iliad 8 the same King likewise sacrificed an ox to Jupiter. So in Odyssey 3 a magnificent sacrificial feast of 81 bulls is described, which Nestor offered together with his people to Neptune; for this reason, along with his other sacrifices, of which he was most diligent, he is called by Aristophanes in the Wasps ... In Odyssey 8 Alcinous is also said to have sacrificed an ox to Jupiter, and when the sacrifice was finished [they celebrated a banquet with the greatest joy and most sweet song]. In Odyssey 3 the Greeks are written of as having celebrated in a grove of Ambrosia a hecatomb sacrifice in honour of Apollo and a magnificent feast.

units.la: Verum præ ceteris omnibus memorabile inprimis & eximium fuit Nestoris illud & sacrificium & epulum, quod describitur Odyss. T. sub finem: quod paulo fusius & copiosius explicabo, quo melius & facilius Sacrificiorum hujusmodi epularium ratio confuetudoq; intelligatur.
units.tr: But above all others the most memorable and outstanding was Nestor's sacrifice and feast, which is described in Odyssey 3 towards the end. I shall explain it somewhat more fully and copiously, so that the nature and custom of such sacrificial feasts may be understood better and more easily.

units.la: Apud Apollonium vero lib. 11. prolixa admodum & luculenta, Homericæ alli non dissimilis, ex stat sacrificij Argonautarum descriptio, a quo Heroes illi clarissimi celebrem, longam peritulo samq, suum illam nauigationem fuerunt exorsi.
units.tr: In Apollonius, however, in book 2, there exists a very long and brilliant description of the sacrifice of the Argonauts, not unlike Homer's, with which those most famous heroes began their celebrated and long voyage, renowned for their own fame.

units.la: Vtrumq, autem huius sacrificii duæ sunt partes principes, Vna est ipsum Sacrificium: altera & posterior, Epulum, quod ex utrumq; sacrificii reliquiis fuit celebratum. Quod ad priorem, nem-pe Sacrificium, attinet, illius caput primum est, ut antea dixi, Tempus; quando videlicet celebrari suerit solitum. Hoc igitur, quoad Homericum Nestoris sacrificium attinet, suit matutinum. Nam mane, simul atq, aurora illuxit, primò Nestor, deinde illius filii e lectus suis surrexisse, necin multum diem fleritusse (id quod vigilantiæ atque industriæ illorum est argumentum) ac paulò post rem diuinam fecijse dicuntur, id quod religionis est indicium. Idem si nostin vera nostra religione faceremus, diem videlicet a re diuina, hoc est, pretibus, verbi diuini auditione, lectione, meditatione auspicantes, meliùs procul dubio, feliciùs atque innocentiùs totum diem traduceremus. Sic fecisse legimus Dauidem, qui sæpe in suis Psalmis se mane ac summo diluculo Deum adorauisse in vocasse testatur.
units.tr: There are two principal parts of this sacrifice: the sacrifice itself, and the second part, the feast, which was held from the leftovers of the sacrifice. As for the first part, the sacrifice, its first head is, as I said earlier, the time, that is, when it was customarily performed. So, as far as Nestor's sacrifice in Homer goes, it was in the morning. For at dawn, as soon as the sun rose, Nestor first, and then his sons, are said to have risen from their beds, to have not long delayed (which is evidence of their watchfulness and diligence), and shortly afterwards to have performed the sacred rite, which is a sign of their religion. If we Christians did the same, that is, began the day with worship, with prayers, with hearing, reading and meditating on the Word of God, we would undoubtedly spend the whole day better, more happily and more innocently. We read that David did this, who often testifies in his Psalms that he worshipped and called upon God in the morning and at the very break of day.

units.la: Hinc Herculi Romæ in ara Maximæ mane & vesperi sacra fiebant a Pinarijs & Politijs. Hesiodi pulchrum hunc de re extat præceptum, dicentis:
units.tr: Hence, at Rome, sacred rites were performed for Hercules at the Great Altar morning and evening by the Pinarii and the Potitii. There is a fine precept of Hesiod on this matter, where he says:

units.la: Ἀλλοτε δ᾽ ἀσπονδήσεσθ ἔ ἱλάσθαι· Ἡ μὲν ὁ᾽ ἐνώ ... ἀλλ᾽
units.tr: [Ἀλλοτε δ᾽ ἀσπονδήσεσθ ἔ ἱλάσθαι· Ἡ μὲν ὁ᾽ ἐνώ ... ἀλλ᾽]

units.la: Interdum certe libaminibus atq, hostijs placa Deos Et quando cubitum ieris, & quaudo lux sacra venerit.
units.tr: Sometimes, at least, propitiate the gods with libations and victims, both when you go to bed and when the sacred light comes.

units.la: Ac omnino matutinum tempus, quod, teste Hesiodo, ... id est, omne opus promoveret, Antiqui sacrificijs idoneum existimabant: quo quidem Deos assidere templis, & matutinis salutationibus adesse opinabantur. Hinc videtur facere, quod mane, ut Grammaticis volunt, dies clarus dicitur ab omne boni nominis. Manem enim Veteres bonum dicebant, unde forsan Manius quoque, optima corporis humani membra, dicta sunt, & Dij Manes, Dij boni; quos etiam metu mortis supplices venerabantur, ut e contrario Imanes dicimus minimè bonos, sed crudeles. Magi Persarum primo semper diluculo Diis suis laudes hymnos, canere, solemq, Orientem venerari (ut contra alij executari) consueverunt. Indè veró & Gymnosophistæ in meridie, & ubi multum diei processerat, immolare Diis solebant. Meridialem, inquit Festus, veteres hostiam atram appellabant, quam meridie immolabant. Appollonius Tyanæus primo mane cum Dijs esse versandum: procedente mox die de eis loquendum existimauit. Apud Hebræos certè mane & vesperi sacrificabatur: id quod iuge sacrificium dicebatur.
units.tr: And in general the Ancients thought the morning time, which, as Hesiod testifies, ... that is, would advance every work, was suitable for sacrifices; for they believed that the gods sat in their temples and were present at the morning greetings. Hence it seems to agree that the morning, as the grammarians maintain, is called "clear" from every good name. For the Ancients called the morning good (manem), whence perhaps also the Manii were named as the best parts of the human body, and the Di Manes were called the good gods, whom they also worshipped as suppliants out of fear of death; whereas we call the Imanes, on the contrary, not good at all but cruel. The Magi of the Persians customarily sang hymns of praise to their gods at the very first break of day and worshipped the rising sun (as others, on the contrary, worshipped the setting sun). From there the Gymnosophists also used to offer sacrifices to the gods at midday, and when much of the day had passed. Festus says: the ancients called a black victim sacrificed at midday the "meridial" victim. Apollonius of Tyana thought that one should converse with the gods in the early morning, and speak of other matters as the day advanced. Among the Hebrews, certainly, sacrifice was offered morning and evening; this was called the continual sacrifice.

units.la: Quantum veró ad Argonautarum sacrificij tempus attinet, illud quoq, fuisse matutinum, ex circumstantijs nonnullis colligi potest. Hùc accedit, quod Scholiastes ait, moris fuisse vt κατ᾽ ἀρχὸς, id est, defunctus circa Solis octauum: at ἐπίμοι, idest, cælestibus sub aurorem, solusq; ortum sacrificare. Talis autem fuit Apolloni, cui Argonautæ rem diuinam fecerunt.
units.tr: As far as the time of the Argonauts' sacrifice is concerned, it can also be gathered from several circumstances that it too was in the morning. To this is added that the Scholiast says it was the custom to sacrifice [κατ᾽ ἀρχὸς], that is, having just finished, about the eighth hour of the sun; but [ἐπίμοι], that is, to the heavenly ones, at dawn and as the sun rose. Such was the sacrifice to Apollo, at which the Argonauts performed the sacred rite.

units.la: Verum, ut latius aliquanto & plenius de sacrificiorum siue sacrorum tempore & diebus, qui-bus ea ab Ethnicis fieri consueuerunt, dicam, certum omnino est minimè, dubium, tertia tem-pora, certosq, dies singulis sacris siue sacrificijs peragendis destinatos fuisse & dicatos. Hùc pertinet elegans sapiensq, illud Ciceronis dictum, Certos dies, non ut sacrificii, sic consilii exspectari solet. Hi veró dies certi, stati, ac statuti, dies sacri, consecrati, sanctiq, diuini, religiosi, siue habentes religionem, festi, & substantiuè festa: item dies feriati atq, feriæ a Latinis fuerunt appellati.
units.tr: But, to speak somewhat more fully and at greater length about the time and days of sacrifices or sacred rites, on which the heathens customarily performed them, it is entirely certain, and not in doubt, that fixed times and fixed days were set apart and dedicated for the performance of each sacred rite or sacrifice. To this belongs that elegant and wise saying of Cicero: "Fixed days are looked for not only for sacrifice but also for counsel." These fixed, appointed and set days were called sacred, consecrated, holy, divine, religious, or having religion, festive; and substantively, festivals; likewise the Latins called them feriated days and holidays.

units.la: Festi dies dicti sunt, qui, ut Macrobius ait, Dijs erant dicati, in quibus vel sacrificia Dijs offerebantur, vel epulationes celebrabantur, vel ludi in honorem Deorum agebantur, vel serie obseruabantur. Ac festi dies nonnullis videntur dicti a feriis: unde etiam feriati appellantur. Quid si potiùs dicti sint festi, quasi festi, eò quod homines festi, seu defesti ac defatigati reliquorum dierum operibus atq, laboribus, sui refici solerent ac retrerari. Vel festi dicti sunt quasi confesti, quia, ex professo agerentur. Inde & festivus, festiva, festivum, lepidum, amœnum: quoniam dies illi magna cum lætitia, hilaritate & voluptate peragi solebant: & festino verbum, id est, propero: quoniam ad dies festos, propter otium a labore, homines festinant potiùs, quàm ad dies professos, inquibus est laborandum. Hic opponuntur dies profesti, ut sano opponitur profanum: unde ille apud Plautum: Festo die si quid prodegeris, profesto agere liceat, nisi peperteris.
units.tr: Festive days were so called, as Macrobius says, because they were dedicated to the gods, on which either sacrifices were offered to the gods, or feasts were celebrated, or games were held in honour of the gods, or they were observed with rest. Some think festive days were named from the holidays (feriae), whence they are also called feriated. Or perhaps festive days were named as if "fested" (festi), because men, wearied (defessi) and exhausted by the labours and toils of the other days, were accustomed to be refreshed and restored. Or festive days are called as if "all-together-fested" (confesti), because they were held by appointment. Hence also festive (festivus, festiva, festivum) means lively, pleasant, charming, since those days were customarily spent with great joy, cheerfulness and pleasure; and the verb festino, that is, to hurry, because men hurry to festive days, on account of rest from labour, rather than to working days, on which one must labour. Here working days (profesti) are set against festive days, just as the profane (profanum) is set against the sacred; whence that saying in Plautus: "If you have squandered anything on a festive day, may it be lawful for you to make it up on a working day, unless you have paid it back."

units.la: Profesti dies, ajt Festus, dicuntur, qui procul sunt a religione Numinis divini. Item: Praefestum diem dicebant, qui festus non erat. Item: Profestum facere est, tanquam profanum facere, id est, quid eo die, qui dies feriarum non est, facere: vel, ut quidam dixerunt pro eo facere, pro-
units.tr: Working days, says Festus, are those which are far from the religion of the divine power. Likewise: they called the day before a festival a "pre-festal" day, which was not a festival. Likewise: to make a day "profestum" is like making it profane, that is, to do on that day, which is not a holiday, something; or, as some have said, to do in place of that day something, or to do

units.la: cere. luce feriae non sint: aut id facere, quod feriis facere non licebat. Itaq; diem profestum diem sine feriis esse. Macrobius libro primo Saturnalium, capite decimo sexto, quaenam dierum apud Romanos appellatio fuerit atq; ratio perspicue copioseq; explicat. Numam enim ait, cum annum in duodecim mensis distribuisset, eundemq; etiam in certa dietum genera divisisse; ita ut quidam dies essent fasti, quidam profesti, alii intercisi. Fasti dicebantur qui Dies erant dicati. Profesti, qui hominibus ad administrandam rem privatam publicam concessi erant. Intercisi erant Deorum hominum, communes: quibusdam enim illorum horis fas erat, quibusdam non fas erat jus dicere. Nam vel endotercisi cum hostia caedebatur, fari nefas erat: iuter caesaet porrecta fari licebat. (Hoc Varro tempus medium inter hostiam caesam et extra porrecta vocat.) Rursus cum adolebatur, non licebat. Ideoq; intercisi, vel quomodo Veteres pronunciabant, et quomodo etiam Kalendario notantur, Endotercisi vocabantur, aut quod intercederet fas, aut quod interesset fas. Festi porro dies, Divisio festoris inquit idem, dividuntur in sacrificia, epulas, ludos, feriasque. Sic et profesti in Fastos, Comitiales, dierum ex hia Comperendinos, Statos, et Praeliares. Idem, Sacra celebritas est, inquit, vel cum sacrificia Diis offeruntur: vel cum dies divinis epulationibus (quae Caena Deorum appellantur) celebrantur: vel cum ludi in honorem aguntur Deorum: vel cum feriae aguntur. Feriae, inquit Festus, a feriendis Feria unde victimis appellata: unde Germanicum Sevtenid est, feriarum; et Sevtag/id est, feria, seu feria. Alii tamen feriae volunt dictas ab epulis fereudis; quoniam in iis epulae fiebant ex pecorum frugumq; proventibus, unde etiam Feralia dicta sacrificia, quae mortuis fieri solebant, quod tunc Feralia sacrificapulas ferebant ad sepulcrum ejus, cui vellent parentare. Feriae autem Festus a festu sic dictus est. guit: Feriae, inquit, Antiqui fes tas vocabant: et alia erant fine die festo, ut Nundinae: alie cum festo, ut Saturnalia, quibus adjungebantur epulationes ex proventu fructus pecorum frugumq.
units.tr: something, on a day when there are no holidays, or to do what it was not permitted to do on holidays. And so a working day is a day without holidays. Macrobius, in the first book of the Saturnalia, chapter sixteen, clearly and fully explains what was the name and reason of the days among the Romans. For he says that Numa, when he had divided the year into twelve months, also divided these into certain kinds of days, so that some days were lawful (fasti), some working (profesti), and others divided (intercisi). Lawful days were those dedicated to the gods. Working days were those granted to men for the management of private and public affairs. Divided days were common to gods and men; for at certain hours of them it was lawful to pronounce judgment, and at others it was not. For while the victim was being slaughtered it was unlawful to speak; between the slaughter and the placing of the victim outside it was lawful to speak. (Varro calls this interval between the slaughtered victim and the one placed outside the middle time.) Again, while it was being burnt on the altar, it was not allowed. Hence the divided days, or, as the Ancients pronounced it, and as it is also marked in the Calendar, were called endotercisi, either because lawful speech intervened, or because lawful speech was in between. Moreover festive days, says the same author, are divided into sacrifices, feasts, games and holidays. So too working days are divided into lawful, comitial, and of these, the adjourned, the stated, and the praeliares. The same author says: a sacred solemnity is when sacrifices are offered to the gods, or when days are celebrated with divine feasts (which are called the Lord's Supper of the gods), or when games are held in honour of the gods, or when holidays are kept. Festus says: holidays (feriae) are so called from striking (ferire) victims, whence in German Feiertag is the holiday, and Feiertag means holiday or festival. Others, however, want holidays to be named from the bringing of feasts (ferre epulas), since feasts were held in them from the produce of the flocks and crops; whence also the funeral rites (Feralia) were so named, which used to be performed for the dead, because then they carried food to the grave of the one whom they wished to honour with a funeral offering. Festus says that holidays are named from the festival (festus), thus: "Holidays," he says, "the Ancients called festas," and some were without a festival day, like the market days (nundinae), and others were with a festival, like the Saturnalia, to which feasts from the produce of the flocks and crops were added.

units.la: Porro Macrobius feriarum alias ajt esse publicas, alias privatas. Et publicarum quidem Feriae, publica quatuor facit genera. Aut enim erant Stativa, aut Conceptivae, aut Imperativae, aut Nundinae. sunt vel privatae. Et Stativae quidem feria erant uniuersi populi communes, certis et coafitiuiis diebus ac mensibus, et in fastis flatis observationibus annotatae, in quibus praecipue fer vabantur Agonalia, Cat dem: te, et ille quoque Stative, mensalia, Lupercalia. Sic Festus, Statae feriae appellabantur, quod certo flatuto, die observarentur. Conceptivae autem feriae dicebantur, quae quotannis a magistratibus vel sacerdotibus con a Conceptiva, cipiebantur in dies vel certos, vel etiam incertos: ut erant feriae Latinae, Paganalia, Sementina, Compitalia. Imperativae erant, quas Consules, vel Praetores pro arbitrio poterant indicere. 3. Imperative. bant. Nundinae erant Paganorum, id est, rusticorum, quibus convenebant, negociis propriis, 4. Nundinae. vel mercibus proveniunt.
units.tr: Moreover, Macrobius says that some holidays are public and some private. Of public holidays he makes four kinds: for they were either stated (stativae), or appointed (conceptivae), or ordered (imperativae), or market days (nundinae). Private holidays also exist. The stated holidays were common holidays of the whole people, kept on fixed and appointed days and months, and noted in the calendars with set observances; among these were especially the Agonalia, the Carmentalia, and likewise the Mensalia and the Lupercalia. Thus Festus: stated holidays were so called because they were observed on a fixed and appointed day. Appointed holidays (conceptivae), however, were those which were proclaimed every year by the magistrates or priests, on certain or even uncertain days; such were the Latin holidays, the Paganalia, the Sementina and the Compitalia. Ordered holidays were those which the Consuls or Praetors could proclaim at their discretion. Market days (nundinae) were those of the pagans, that is, the country folk, who came together for their own business or to trade goods.

units.la: Privatae feriae dicebantur, quae vel propriae erant familiarum, ut Claudiae familiae, aut Aemiliae, aut Iuliae, aut Corneliae, et si quas feriae propriae quaeq; familia exsu sua domestice celebrita sunt 1. Propria observabat, de quibus loquuntur duodecim Tabulae: Sacra perpetua manento. Vel privatae familiarum. feriae erant singulorum, ut Natalium Fulgurumq; suscepciones, aut Funerii, atq; Expiationum: 2. Singulorum. unde Festus, Privatae feriae, inquit, vocabantur sacrorum proprioram, velut dies natales, operationes, decreteles. Apud Veteres quoq; quicunq; nominabat, ut ajt Macrobius, Semonam, Sejam, Segetiam, Tutilnam, feriasq; observabat. Item, Flaminica (Flaminis uxor) quoties tonitrua audiisset, feriata erat, donec Deos placasset.
units.tr: Private holidays were those belonging to particular families, such as the Claudian, Aemilian, Julian or Cornelian houses, and any holidays that each family celebrated at home at its own expense. The Twelve Tables speak of these when they say: "Let the sacred rites of the family remain perpetual." There were also private holidays of individuals, such as the observances of birthdays, of lightning strikes, of funerals and of expiations. Hence Festus says: "Private holidays were called those of individual rites, such as birthdays, [...] decrees." Among the ancients, whoever named Semonia, Seia, Segetia and Tutilina, as Macrobius says, also observed holidays. Likewise the Flaminica (the wife of the Flamen), whenever she heard thunder, kept a holiday until she had appeased the gods.

units.la: Caeterum ad feriasq; publicas quod attinet, indicebantur illa et proclamabantur singulis men A quibus feriabus a Rege sacrorum et a Praetore. De Rege sacrificulo teste est Varro, libro quinto de lingua publice indici Latina. Rex cum feriasq; menstruas Nonis Februarii edicit, hunc diem Februarium appellat. Et solite: nempe paullo post: Harum rerum vel regia apparent in sacris Nonalibus in arce, quod tunc feriasq; primas menstruas, quae futurae sint eo mense. Rex praedicit. Ex hu verbi satis perspicuum est, Regem sacrificulum singulorum mensium feriasq; proclamasse. Ejus proclamationis hanc formam 1 Rege. Arnobius libro secundo, adversus gentes tradit: Lavatio Deummaerus est, hodie: Iovis epu- Indictionis feriarum forma. lum cras est: Aesculapii geritur celebraturque vindemia: Lestisternum Cereris erit Idibus Feriae publicae proxima: Tellurus natalis est, etc. Praetorem autem etiam ferias, quae Compitalia dicebant, a Praetore. bantur more Majorum, verbis olim solennibus concepisse Agellius libro decimo, Noctium suarum capite 24. & Macrobius libro 1. Saturnaliis capite quarto, auctores sunt. Postquam enim modo die quinti, modo die quinto Veteres dixisse significassent, ad demonstrandam hanc Veterum consuetudinem conferre plurimum, addiderunt hac solennia verba, quibus more Majorum Compitalia Praetor concipere solebat: Die noni post Kalendas Ianuarias: Die quinti Compitalia erunt. Nec vero Compitalitias duntaxat, sed etiam ferias omnes conceptivas & imperativas indicere Praetorem consuevisse, ex eodem Macrobio & ex Suetonio comprobari potest. Suetonius in Claudio scribit: Observavit, seduli, ut quoties terrain urbe movissent, ferias ad vocata concione Praetor in urbe indiceret. Hac de re vide plura apud Iacobum Reardum libro quinto Variorum, capite decimonono.
units.tr: As for public holidays, these were announced and proclaimed for each month by the King of Sacrifices and by the Praetor. Varro is a witness about the King of Sacrifices, in the fifth book of his work on the Latin language: "When the King announces the monthly holidays on the Nones of February, he calls this day February." And a little later: "Of these matters the royal [...] appear in the sacred rites of the Nonae on the citadel, because then the King declares the first monthly holidays which are to fall in that month." From this it is clear enough that the King of Sacrifices proclaimed the holidays of each month. Arnobius, in the second book of his Against the Nations, hands down the form of such a proclamation: "The washing of the gods is today; the feast of Jupiter is tomorrow; the vintage of Aesculapius is being carried out and celebrated; the lectisternium of Ceres will be on the Ides; the public holiday is next; it is the birthday of Tellus," and so on. The Praetor, too, according to the custom of our ancestors, drew up the holidays called Compitalia in solemn words of old; Gellius, in the tenth book of his Attic Nights, chapter 24, and Macrobius, in the first book of his Saturnalia, chapter 4, are authorities for this. For after showing that the ancients had sometimes said "on the fifth day" and sometimes "on the fifth day" (in different forms), they added, to show how much this older custom mattered, the solemn words in which the Praetor used to announce the Compitalia according to ancestral custom: "On the ninth day after the Kalends of January; on the fifth, the Compitalia will be held." It can be shown from the same Macrobius and from Suetonius that the Praetor was accustomed to announce not only the Compitalia but all holidays, whether proclaimed or appointed. Suetonius in Claudius writes: "He took care that whenever they had shaken the city by an earthquake, the Praetor in the city should announce holidays by a summoned assembly." On this matter see more in James Reardon, Variorum, book 5, chapter 19.

units.la: Porro nomina specialiora dies hujusmodi festi, sive festa, & festivitates habuerunt cum a Dis, quibus illi fuerant dicati, ac quorum in honorem erant instituti, tum ab aliis rebus, quas sacras & divinas appellabant, quae in iis peragi solebant: unde etiam metonymice saepe festa pro sacris, & sacra pro festis apud scriptores accipiuntur.
units.tr: Moreover, such days and feasts, and festivities, had more specific names, both from the gods to whom they had been dedicated and in whose honour they had been instituted, and from other things which they called sacred and divine and which were usually performed on them. Hence writers also often use "feasts" metonymically for "sacred rites," and "sacred rites" for "feasts."

units.la: Atq, hi dies festi, sive festa a Graecis iopras & iopsoriot appellantur, ut nonnulli volunt, quod est Erquteoc, id est, appetere, quoniam omnes illos expetunt, ut iopti dicatur quasi iopti. Inde iopti, festum celebrare. Quid si iopti, sive Ionice iopti dicatur, sive opti, ovvioi, id est, in vito, impello, promoveo: vel ab opoxot, unde opoq, impulsus est, & opoq, eo quod diebus festis homines incitantur & impelluntur ad res divinas faciendas & varie movendas.
units.tr: These festive days, or feasts, are called by the Greeks ἑορταί and ἑορτασμοί [heortai, heortasmoi]. Some hold that this comes from a word meaning to desire [ἐρᾶν], since all people desire them, so that the word is derived as if it were a desired thing. Hence ἑορτὴν ἄγειν [heorten agein], to celebrate a feast. Or if the word is derived from the Ionic form, or from ὠθέω [otheo], to push, impel, advance; or from ὁρμή [hormé], impulse, because on feast days men are stirred and impelled to perform divine rites and to be moved in various ways.

units.la: Ab Hebraeis dies festi dicitur Chag, Hebraice festum Chag, appellatur ab animi corporisque voluptate, laetitia & agitatione. Nam Chalal, idem est quod circumagi in gyrum, sive in orbem, & festum celebrare. Appellatur etiam Moed, sive Iom Moed, id est, festum statum, sive statum, quod certo & statu tempore celebratur a Laad, Conveniri, constituit tempus, aut conveniat ad tempus statuum.
units.tr: Among the Hebrews a festival day is called chag [חג], from the Hebrew word for a festival, named from the pleasure, joy and excitement of mind and body. For chalal means to be turned round in a circle, and also to celebrate a feast. It is also called moed, or iom moed, that is, a fixed festival or appointed time, which is celebrated at a set and appointed time, from yaad, to meet, to appoint a time, or to meet at an appointed time.

units.la: Festorum apud Ethnicos infinita prope & innumerabilis fuit copia, atq; multitudo, quae recensere atq; enumerare omnia tam videatur esse impossibile, quam stellas caeli, aut arenas maris.
units.tr: The number of feasts among the Gentiles was almost infinite and countless, and to recount and list them all seems as impossible as to count the stars of heaven or the sands of the sea.

units.la: Ac quo clarius pateat, quanta olim fuerit Ethnicorum superstitio, ac quam longe lateq; patuerit, conflat ex sacris & profanis litteris cum universum tempus, tum singulas ejus partes, mensibus, medias, minimas vel pro Diis ipsis sive Numinibus fuisse habitas atq; cultas, vel certe Diis, eorumque honoribus dicatas & consecratas. Nam tempus primum universum Saturni nomine coluerunt, quem finxerunt filios suos solitum devorare (unde etiam filios suos olim patrentes immolabant) eosdemq; rursus evomere: quo significabatur, tempus per vices cuncta gignere & absumere (unde Tempus edax rerum a Poeta appellatur) & ex se denuo renasci. Hinc xpovos a Graecis, quasi xpovos dictus est.
units.tr: To make clearer how great the superstition of the Gentiles once was, and how widely it spread, it is clear from both sacred and profane writings that the whole of time, and each of its parts (years, months, half-months, and the smallest units), was regarded and worshipped as a god or divine power, or at least dedicated and consecrated to the gods and their honours. For they first worshipped time as a whole under the name of Saturn, whom they imagined used to devour his own sons (whence they also once sacrificed their children by burning them), and then to vomit them up again. By this was signified that time by turns produces and consumes all things (whence the poet calls Time the devourer of things) and is born anew from itself. Hence the Greeks call time χρόνος [chronos], as if so named.

units.la: Annus et anni temporaculta. Sic Annus, quatuor ejus tempora, singuli menses, singulae hebdomadae, singuli dies: adde etiam noctes, singulae deinde horae certis & peculiaribus Diis sive Numinibus fuerunt consecrata. Secundum hanc ipsam vero temporis et singularum ejus partium rationem, dividuntur atque divisionem cum festa ipsa, tum quae in agitari celebrari fuerunt solita, sacra atq; sacrificia dividuntur atq, denominantur. Sic enim festa atq, sacra sive sacrificia alia erant atq, dicebantur annua sive anniversaria, sive solemnia, eaque vel verna sive vernalia, vel aestiva, vel autumnalia, vel hyemalia. Alia dicebantur mensfrua, quae singulis mensibus, & certis mensium diebus peragebantur: de quibus vide Kalendarium Romanum a Paulo Manutio, Sigonio, Huberto, Aria Montano, & aliis antiquitatum scriptoribus conscriptum diligenter & explicatum, in quo inveniues, quae festa, quaeq; sacra singulis mensibus atq; diebus singulis Diis fieri celebrarit, apud Romanos confuerint, quorum enumeratione cum ea longa nimis & prolixa esset futura, & ex auctoribus illis facile depromi possit, sicq; in promtu, mihi hic supersedendum esse exiistimo. Hac omnia diligenter quoq; & accurate collegit ex Antiquitatum scriptoribus vir doctissimus Iohannes Rosinus, Antiquitatum Romanarum libro quarto, capite quarto.
units.tr: Year and the seasons of the year: so the year, its four seasons, each month, each week, each day, and, besides, the nights and then the single hours, were each consecrated to certain and particular gods or divine powers. According to this very scheme of time and its individual parts, both the feasts themselves and the sacred rites and sacrifices customarily celebrated at them are divided and named. Thus feasts and sacred rites or sacrifices were some annual, anniversary or solemn, and these were either spring, summer, autumn or winter. Others were called monthly, which were performed in each month on certain days of the month. On these see the Roman calendar, carefully written and explained by Paulus Manutius, Sigonius, Huber, Arias Montanus and other writers on antiquities, in which you will find which feasts and sacred rites were customarily held among the Romans in each month and on each day, and for which gods. Since listing them here would be overlong and tedious, and can easily be taken from those authors, I think I should pass over them here as readily available. All this has been diligently and accurately collected from writers on antiquities by the most learned John Rosinus, in the fourth book, chapter 4, of his Roman Antiquities.

units.la: Illud tantum addere videtur esse operaepretium de Kalendis, Nonis & Idibus, in quas tres partes parcees singulos menses Romani ex Romuli instituto distribuerunt, quaq; certus sacru atq; sacrificiis fuerunt celebratae.
units.tr: It seems worth adding only this about the Kalends, Nones and Ides, the three parts into which the Romans, following the institution of Romulus, divided each month, and on which fixed festivals and sacrifices were celebrated.

units.la: Ac Kalendas quidem primum cujusq; mensis diem Romani dixerunt a Graeco verbo καλεῖν, id est, vocare: quo etiam prisci Latini frequenter usi sunt. Sic Calatores, ut inquit Festus, dicebantur ser vi χατο τῶ καλεῖν, quod est vocari: quia semper vocari possunt ob necessitatem. Idem judicium est de voce Calonis. Cur autem primum singulorum mensium diem sic vocarint hanc rationem Macrobius affert: Prisci temporibus, inquie, antequam Fasti a Cn. Flavio scripti sunt, patribus, in omnium notitiam proderentur, Pontifici minori hoc provincia delegatum est, ut nova Lunae primum observaret aspectum, visumq; Regi sacrificulo nunciaret: atque tum sacrificio a Rege et minore Pontifice celebraeto, idem Pontifex Kalatā, id est, vocatā, in Capitolium plebe juxta Curiam Calabram, quae casa Romuli proxima erat, quot numero dies a Kalendis ad Nonas superessent, pronunciabat: et quintanas quidem quinquies dicto verbo καλῶ: septimanas vero septies repetito praedicebat. Et hunc diem, qui ex his diebus, qui calarent, primus esset, placuit Kalendas vocari. Ideo autem minor Pontifex numerum dierum, qui ad Nonas superessent, calando prodebat, quod post novam Lunam oportebat Nonarum die populares, qui in agris essent, confluere in urbem, accepturos causas feriarum a Rege sacrorum fciuroisque quid esset eo mense faciendum: unde Nonas volunt esse dictas. Hinc ipsa Curia Calabria, ad quam vocabantur Calabra nuncupata est, et Classis dicta, quod omnes in eam populus vocaretur: unde etiam Classis dicta. Macrobio astipulatur Terentius Varro, qui libro quinto de lingua Latina sic scribit: Primi dies mensium nominantur Kalendae: ab eo, quod iis diebus Kalentur ejus mensis Nonae a Pontificibus, quintanae an septimanae esset futurae, in Capitolio, in Curia Calabra sive Diuc quinque Kalo Iuno Novella. Et, Septem dies te Kalo Iuno Novella. Hic Iosephus Scaliger pro Iuno, non male Ionam quoque (quo nomine Luna a Veteribus sit appellata) et pro Novella, in veteribus Codicibus (quod Turnebus etiam indicat) legie Covella, quod ipse deducit a Covum: quomodo Veteres Caelum appellarunt; ita ut fit Iuno vel Iana Covella: Iuno vel Iana caelestis. Hinc igitur patet Kalendas, id est, primum unusquisque mensis diem fuisse sacrum, Iunoni consectatum in ejus tutela, esse Ovidio primo Fastorum:
units.tr: The Romans called the first day of each month the Kalends, from the Greek verb καλεῖν [kalein], to call, which the early Latins also often used. So calatores, as Festus says, were called servants from καλεῖν, to be called, because they could always be summoned in case of need. The same explanation holds for the word calo. Why they called the first day of each month by this name, Macrobius gives this reason: In early times, he says, before the Fasti were written by Gnaeus Flavius, so that they might be made known to the Fathers and to everyone, it was assigned to the lesser Pontiff to observe the first sight of the new moon and to report it to the King of Sacrifices. Then, once the sacrifice had been performed by the King and the lesser Pontiff, the same Pontiff, calling the people (kalata, that is, vocata) to the Capitol beside the Curia Calabra, which was next to the hut of Romulus, announced how many days remained from the Kalends to the Nones. He announced the fifth day by saying kalo five times, and the seventh by repeating it seven times. And it was decided to call the day which was first among those announced by this calling the Kalends. The lesser Pontiff announced the number of days remaining until the Nones by this calling, because after the new moon the common people who were in the fields had to flock into the city on the Nones, to receive from the King of Sacrifices the reasons for the holidays and what was to be done that month; whence the Nones are said to have been named. Hence the Curia Calabra itself, to which they were called, took the name Calabra, and was also called the Classis, because the whole people were summoned into it; whence also the name classis. Terentius Varro agrees with Macrobius, who in the fifth book of his work on the Latin language writes thus: "The first days of the months are called Kalends, from the fact that on those days the Pontiffs called out (kalentur) the Nones of that month, whether they would fall on the fifth or the seventh day, in the Capitol, in the Curia Calabra." And again, "Five days before... Juno Novella." Here Joseph Scaliger, not unreasonably, reads Iuno as Iona (the name by which the moon was called by the ancients), and, for Novella, reads Covella in the old manuscripts (which Turnebus also points out), deriving it from Covus, the word by which the ancients called the heavens; so that Juno or Iana becomes Covella, the heavenly Juno or Iana. From this it is therefore plain that the Kalends, that is, the first day of each month, was holy and consecrated to Juno, under whose protection it lay, as Ovid says in the first book of the Fasti:
The care of Juno claims the Ausonian Kalends.

units.la: Nota, quod dicit Ausonias Kalendas. Graeci enim Kalendas caruerunt: unde pro verbium, Ad Kalendas Graecas.
units.tr: Note that he says "Ausonian" Kalends. The Greeks had no Kalends, which is why the proverb "at the Greek Kalends" means never.

units.la: Nec vero apud Romanos tantum, sed etiam apud Graecos et Iudaeos ruuvia, id est, novae Lunae erant sacrae, et certus sacrificiis colebantur. Polienus libro octavo auctor est, Argivos Numeria cujusq; mensis; mulieres quidem viribus tunicis et chlamydibus celebrasse, viros autem peplis muliebribus amictos, in memoriam Telesilae potrae, quae Argos oppugnate Cleomene Argivas armatas ad pugnam eduxit: quae armatae in propugnaculis flantes circumcirca muros ruentes Cleomenem repulerunt. His adde, quod Plutarchus in Problematibus Romanorum Antiquitatum docet, apud Veteres Kalendas primum mensem Dies caelestibus habitum sacrum, secundum vero Dies inferis: in quo et lustrationibus quibusdam uti mos erat, et mortuos paren-tabant.
units.tr: Not only among the Romans but also among the Greeks and Jews, the new moons (neomeniae) were sacred and were honoured with fixed sacrifices. Polyaenus, in book eight, reports that the Argives celebrated each month's Numeria: the women wore tunics and cloaks, and the men were dressed in women's robes, in memory of Telesilla the poetess, who led the armed Argive women out to battle when Cleomenes attacked Argos. Standing armed on the battlements, these women drove Cleomenes back from the walls. To this add what Plutarch teaches in his Roman Problems: among the ancients the Kalends, the first day of the month, was held sacred to the heavenly gods, and the second day to the dead. On that day it was customary to perform certain purifications, and they made offerings for the dead.

units.la: Nonae similiter fuerunt sacrae, quas, teste Macrobio, sic dictas existimant, quasi nova observationis initium: vel quod ab eo die ad Idus semper novem dies copulantur. Hucreferri possunt Nundinae, sic dictae, quasi Novendinae. Ter enim in mense, nono quolibet die, ruffici vel mercium, vel negotiorum causa in urbem convenirent ex instituto Servii Tullii. Nundinarum autem feriae Iovi olim sacrae, lege Hortensia inter Fastos erant receptae, ut lites coram Praetore componere possent. Eodem die Trinundino olim propter frequentiam plebis leges etiam promulgabantur, et Candidati in Comitio in colle consistebant, ut ab omnibus conspici possent. Quae tamen postea desierunt, quum etiam internundino die magna plebis esset frequentia, Polydor Virgilio libro sexto, capite septimo, de rerum Inventoribus.
units.tr: The Nones were likewise sacred. According to Macrobius, they were so called as if they were the new beginning of observation, or because nine days always run from that day to the Ides. To this belong the Nundinae, so named as if they were "Novendinae" (ninth-day markets). Three times a month, on every ninth day, country people and traders gathered in the city for the sake of their goods and business, by the institution of Servius Tullius. The holidays of the Nundinae were once sacred to Jupiter, and by the Hortensian law they were received among the festival days, so that disputes could be settled before the praetor. On that same day, the third of the market days, laws were once promulgated because of the large crowd of the common people, and candidates stood on the hill in the Comitium so that they could be seen by everyone. Later these practices ceased, since even on the day between the market days there was a great crowd of the people: Polydore Vergil, book six, chapter seven, On the Inventors of Things.

units.la: Vt autem Kalendae et Nonae: sic Idus quoque apud Romanos dies fuerunt festi et solennes. Nam primum omnes Idus, quae in quo vis mense sunt octo, Iovi fuerunt sacrae: unde etiam Idus, ut dicitur vocabulo Thufco Iris fuit dicta, quod significat Iouis fiduciam. Cum enim Iuppiter sit auctor lu-cis (unde etiam Lucerius & Diespiter: vtam quasi dicitur, hoc est Lucifer dicitur:) hujus autem diei lux non cum solis oceasu finiatur, sed splendorem dei & noctis continuet, Luna illustrante, quod semper in plenilunio, id est, medio mense fieri soleat, ideo merito Iouis fiduciam vocari putant. Alii tamen Idus volunt dictas quasi videus, a videndo, si ne ero ut eid est, quod idem est, nempe videre: vel etiam ἀπὸ τῶ εἶδ εος, id est, species, quod eo die plenam speciem Luna demonstrat: unde quoq; Eidus, per Ei, quidam scribere consueuerunt. Alii putant Hetruscam vocem esse, apud quos Iduare erat diuidere: unde etiam Vidua dicta, quasi a viro diuisa. Ideo autem dies Idus dici, quod mensem diuidant: quia plerunque in medium mensem incidunt. Deinde Ovi a Flamine diali singulis Idibus immolabatur, quae Idulis fuit nuncupata, a qua nonnulli Idus volunt fuisse dictas. Erant etiam praecipue quaedam feriae Idibus dicatae, quas coli obser-uarii, mos erat, quasi negligere erat nefas: de quibus omnibus praeter Macrobium, vide Alexandrum ab Alexandris libro tertio, capite decimosexto. Vide ibidem de Idibus Martiis, quae in honorem Annae Perennae instituta, quo commode annare & perannare liceret, largioribus poculis celebrari solebant: quae tamen infausta & ominosa postea fuisse fuerunt, & Parricidium vocate: quod illa Iulius Cesar Coniunctorum manibus casus occubuisset.
units.tr: As the Kalends and Nones, so also the Ides were festal and solemn days among the Romans. For first, all the Ides, which fall in every month on the eighth day, were sacred to Jupiter. Hence too the Ides, as is said, were named from the Tuscan word meaning Jupiter's trust, since Jupiter is the author of light (whence he is called Lucetius and Diespiter, and he is as it were called Lucifer). The light of this day does not end with the setting of the sun, but continues the brightness of day through the night, the moon shining, which always happens at full moon, that is, in the middle of the month. Therefore they think it is rightly called Jupiter's trust. Others, however, want the Ides to be named as if from videus, from seeing (videre), or from the Greek eidos [ἀπὸ τοῦ εἴδους], that is, appearance, because on that day the moon shows its full appearance; whence some were accustomed to write "Eidus" with an ei. Others think it is an Etruscan word, among whom iduare meant to divide; whence also vidua (widow) is said, as if one divided from her husband. The days are called Ides, they say, because they divide the month, since they mostly fall in the middle of the month. Then, on every Ides, a sheep was sacrificed to Jupiter by the flamen Dialis, and this was called the Idulis, from which some want the Ides to have been named. There were also certain special holidays dedicated to the Ides, which custom required to be observed, since it was thought wrong to neglect them. On all these matters, apart from Macrobius, see Alexander ab Alexandro, book three, chapter sixteen. See there also on the Ides of March, which were instituted in honour of Anna Perenna, so that one might "annare" and "perannare" (have a year and carry it through) pleasantly; they were usually celebrated with rather generous drinking. Yet these days later became unlucky and ominous, and were called "Parricidium" (parricide), because on them Julius Caesar fell, killed by the hands of his associates.

units.la: Obseruandum praeterea, festa apud Ethnicos quaedam fuisse vnius diei, alia plurium diebus. Festa item fuerunt, vt & sacra, propria & peculiaria Ægyptiorum, Græcorum, Lacedæmoniorum, Romanorum, & aliorum, Chaldæorum, Ægyptiorum, Græcorum, Lacedemoniorum, Romanorum, & aliorum.
units.tr: It should further be observed that among the Gentiles some festivals lasted one day, others several days. There were also festivals, as well as sacred rites, proper and peculiar to the Egyptians, Greeks, Lacedaemonians, Romans and others, to the Chaldeans, Egyptians, Greeks, Lacedaemonians, Romans and others.

units.la: Fuerunt praecipua festa, ut etiam sacra & sacrificia, alia propria mulierum, alia virorum: alia propria fuerunt ser vorum, alia liberorum: alia puerorum: alia virorum & senium: alia flultorum: alia bastorum, & sic deinceps: de quibus vide Theatrum. Reuerà autem illos Pauli verbis utar, ἀσάκοντες ἐξ σωφρ ἀπρίαν πνε & ideireo μακρὸν ἐξ εἶ, si ve ἀδέλφ φ: iure potuerunt appellari.
units.tr: There were principal festivals, as also sacred rites and sacrifices: some proper to women, others to men; some were proper to slaves, others to free persons; some to boys, some to men and old men; some to fools, some to the pious, and so on. On these see the Theatrum. Indeed, in Paul's words, one may fittingly say of them that they "observe days and months and times and years" [ἡμέρας καὶ μῆνας καὶ καιροὺς καὶ ἐνιαυτούς] (Gal. 4.10).

units.la: Porro festorum, ut etiam sacrorum, fines fuerunt, Deorum placatio seu propitiatio, gratitudinis erga Deos, bene de se meritos, testificatio, peccatorum deletiorum, expiatio & lustratio, munerum certorum consecratio & inauguratio, denique diuinatio, solemnitatoque & rerum futurarum cupiatio.
units.tr: The ends of festivals, as also of sacred rites, were these: the appeasing or propitiation of the gods; the testifying of gratitude toward the gods who had deserved well of us; the expiation and purification of sins that had been committed; the consecration and inauguration of certain gifts; and finally divination, and the desire to know future things.

units.la: Festa celebrata fuerunt cum sacris rebus, diuinis, rum otio, testatione ab operibus atq; laboribus, laetitia, conuiviis, choreis, tripudiis, ludis, certaminibus, cœdibus, denique omni superstitionis, scelerum flagitiorum genere. Lætitia festa esse celebranda docent illa Ouidii: Du quoq; a cunctis hilari pietate colantur; Tristitiam poni per sua festa iubent.
units.tr: Festivals were celebrated with sacred rites, with divine matters, with leisure, with abstinence from works and labours, with joy, banquets, dances, leaping, games, contests, slaughter, and finally with every kind of superstition and wicked disgrace. That festivals should be celebrated with joy is taught by those lines of Ovid: "Let them also be honoured by all with cheerful piety; they command that sorrow be laid aside on their festival days."

units.la: De modo feriarum celebrandarum, & quibus a rebus in illis sit abstinendum, sic Cicero ex legibus Tabularum disserit libro secundo de Legibus: Feriarum festorum, dierumq; ratio in liberis requietem habet luctum & iurgiorum: in servis operum & laborum: quas compositio anni conferre debet, & perfectionem operum rusticorum.
units.tr: On the manner of keeping holidays and from what things one must abstain on them, Cicero, drawing on the Laws of the Twelve Tables, speaks thus in book two of his On the Laws: "The rule of festivals and holy days has rest for free persons, abstaining from mourning and quarrels; for slaves, from works and labours; these the arrangement of the year ought to bring, and the completion of rural labours."

units.la: Similia hisce vide apud Macrobium libro primo Saturnalium capite decimosexto: Sacerdotes, inquit, affirmabant feriis pollui fi inditis conceptis opus aliquod fieret. Praeterea Regem sacrorum flaminesq; non licebat videre serius opus fieri: & ideo per praeconem denunciabant, ne quid tale ageretur: & praeceperant negligens multabatur. Praeter multam vero affirmabant eum, qui talibus diebus impudens aliquid egisset, porco piaculum dare debere: prudentem expiare non posse Scævola Pontifex asse verebat, & que sequuntur. Huc referri possunt illa Ouidii: Prospera lux oritur, lingua animusq; fauete: Nunc decenda bono sunt bona verba dio. Lite vacent aures, infanaq; protenus absint Iurgia: differ opus lvivida turba ruum. Sal ve festa dies, meliorq; revertere semper, A populo rerum digna potentecoli.
units.tr: Similar things see in Macrobius, book one of the Saturnalia, chapter sixteen: "The priests," he says, "maintained that if any work was done on holidays with a view to a feast, the holiday was polluted. Moreover, the king of sacrifices and the flamens were not allowed to see any work being done, and so by a herald they proclaimed that nothing of the kind should be done; and whoever was negligent was fined. Besides the fine, they maintained that the man who had acted shamelessly on such days ought to give a pig as expiation; the prudent man could not make expiation, as the pontiff Scaevola used to say," and so on. To this belong those lines of Ovid: "A favourable light rises; let tongue and mind be silent. Now good words must be spoken to the good god. Let ears be free from strife, and let quarrels be far away at once. Let the livid crowd put off work. Hail, festal day, and always return better, a day worthy of power among the people."

units.la: Sic Tibullus libro secundo de Agrilustratione, Elegia 1. Luce sacrá requiescat humus : requiescat aruor, Ee grauε suspenso vomere cessét opus. Solvite vincla jugis : nunc ad præsepia debent Plena toronato flare boves capite. Omnia sine optata Deo:non audeat ullus Lanificam pensis imposuisse manum. Vos quoq; abesse protuli jubeo : discedite ab aris Cui tulit hesternâ gaudia nocte Venus. Casta placent superis:purâ tum veste venite, Ee manibus puris sumite fontis aquam.
units.tr: So Tibullus, in book two, On the Lustration of the Fields, elegy 1: "Let the ground rest on this sacred day; let the ploughland rest; let work cease while the plough is held aloft. Loose the yokes from the oxen; now let them stand at the mangers, their heads wreathed, full of fodder. All is done as the god wishes; let no one dare to set a hand to spinning the wool. You too I bid to be away: depart from the altars, you to whom Venus gave joy last night. Chaste things please the gods above; come then in pure garments, and take water from the spring with clean hands."

units.la: Quædam tamen opera diebus festis contesta esse agricolis, scribit Virgilius in Georgicis. Nec verò dies solum integri, sive unus fuerit, sive etiam plures, sed dierum quoq; certæ partes, sive majores, ut mane, meridies, vesper, sed etiam, ut est verisimile, minores, nempe horæ certæ singulis fatis, seu sacrificiis destinata fuerunt & attributæ. Nam cum singulis temporibus civilibus agendis suas Romani attribuerint horas certas, secundum tritum illud Epigramma: Prima salutantes atq; altera continet hora, &c.
units.tr: Yet Virgil, in the Georgics, writes that certain labours were permitted to farmers even on festival days. Nor were only whole days, whether one or several, set apart, but also certain parts of days, whether larger, as morning, midday, evening, or, as is likely, smaller ones; that is, certain hours were assigned and appointed to each rite or sacrifice. For since the Romans assigned fixed hours to each of their civil affairs, according to the well-known epigram: "The first hour holds the greeters, and the second..." etc.

units.la: Cui dubium, quin rebus quoq; sacris & religiosis tractandis & procurandis certæ ab iis fuerint assignatæ horæ ?
units.tr: Who can doubt that fixed hours were likewise assigned to them for handling and carrying out sacred and religious matters?

units.la: Porro temporibus atq; diebus istis sacris & festis, in quibus res divinæ fiebant, opponuntur
units.tr: Moreover, against these sacred and festal times and days, on which divine rites were performed, are set

units.la: De diebus atri, qui fuerunt postridie Kalendas, Nonas, Idus, quos vulgus imperitè nefastos vocat, vide Macrobium libro primo Saturnaliorum, tapite decimosexto & Plutarchum in quæstionib. Rom. quæstione vigesima quinta.
units.tr: On the dark days, which fell the day after the Kalends, Nones and Ides, and which the common people wrongly call unlucky (nefasti), see Macrobius, Saturnalia book 1, chapter 16, and Plutarch, Roman Questions, question 25.

units.la: Sed si verum fateri volumus, ii ipsi Gentilium dies festi, festivi, sacri, sancti, ut eos falsò appellarunt, propter & sacra superstitiosa & impura, & plurima scelera atq; flagitia, quibus in ipsos potissimum operam dederunt, jure non solum profesti, profani, sed etiam diri, atri, infausti, nefarii, Deo hominibusq; infesti, ut funesti potuerunt appellari.
units.tr: But if we are willing to speak the truth, those festal days of the Gentiles, which they falsely called festive, sacred and holy, should rightly be called not only profane but also dire, dark, ill-omened, nefarious and hostile to God and men, because of their superstitious and impure rites and the many crimes and shameful deeds to which they especially devoted themselves. They could fittingly be called baleful.

units.la: Etsi vero plerag; Gentiles sacra certis diebus atq; temporibus fuerunt alligata, tamen nonnunquam pro re nata, & necessitate aliquâ id postulante (quâ, ut vulgo dicitur, non habet legem) & temporum etiam ultra citrâ, illa tempora rebus illis suis divinis operari sunt, quæ sacra extemporanea, sive extemporalia dici possunt. Et hæc dicta sint de sacrorum sive sacrificiorum tempore, quibus Coolophonis loco addere libet quædam de nocturnis sacris, nocturno tempore fieri solitis, de quibus suprá quædam attigimus.
units.tr: Although most Gentiles tied their sacred rites to certain days and seasons, they sometimes performed their rites on the spur of the moment, when the occasion arose and some necessity demanded it (and necessity, as the common saying goes, knows no law). They also performed them at times before or after the proper seasons. These can be called extemporaneous rites. Let this be said about the time of sacred rites and sacrifices. As a conclusion, it pleases me to add some remarks on nocturnal rites, which were customarily performed at night, and of which I have touched on some above.

units.la: At Noctí quidem primum ipsi nocturno tempore sacra fecerunt gallo, ut supra ex Ovidio dictum fuit, & nigro hostias cum lacte; ut ex Statii Papinii libro secundo in Noctis hymno elegan-ter conflat. Hanc Orpheus quoq; & Hesiodus hymnis suis celebrarunt, illam Deorum antiquissimam Chaos filiam, Æthers & Dei, immò Deorum hominumq; matrem, & omnium rerum genesin appellantes. Hæ illorum de Nocte fabulæ atq; commenta forsan profecta fuerunt ex historia illa creationis Mundi: in qua primò omnium הוּ ו בהוּ Thohu, Vabohu, (quod Chaos, rudem & indigestam molem doctissimi quidam interpretantur) & tenebrarum sit mentio, quam consecuta fuit Lucis creatio. Non mirum autem est, Ethnicos, qui in tam profunda, tali-ginosaque errorum atque superstitionum nocte fuerunt demersi, Noctem coluisse, idest, pro Dea habuisse.
units.tr: To Night itself they first performed rites at night, offering a rooster, as was said above from Ovid, and a black victim with milk, as is elegantly set out in Statius Papinius, book 2, in his hymn to Night. Orpheus and Hesiod also celebrated her in their hymns, calling her the most ancient of the gods, daughter of Chaos, of Aether and of God, indeed the mother of gods and men, and the origin of all things. Their fables and inventions about Night perhaps arose from the account of the creation of the world, in which mention is first made of tohu and bohu (which certain learned men interpret as chaos, a rude and undigested mass) and of darkness, which was followed by the creation of light. It is no wonder that the Gentiles, who were plunged into such a deep and murky night of errors and superstitions, worshipped Night, that is, held her to be a goddess.

units.la: Hus referenda Bacchanalia, Cottytia, Aeheneisium sacra (Cotrym sive Coryttum non-nulli volunt esse Proserpinam) & alia inferorum sacra. Hujusmodi autem nocturna festa atque sacra, turpisimarum libidinum, amorum, fluprorum, cædium, aliorumque facinorum occasiones fuerunt atq; causa: unde ipsi Ethnici ea sepe detestati sunt ac sustulerunt. Nam, ut verissimè Poëta ait cecinit, Nox & amor vinumq; nihil moderabile suadent: Illa pudore vacat, vina Venusq; metu.
units.tr: To this category belong the Bacchanalia, the Cottytia, the Aeheneisian rites (some hold that Coryttus or Cotrys is Proserpina), and other rites of the underworld. Such nocturnal feasts and rites were the occasions and causes of the most shameful lusts, loves, debaucheries, murders and other crimes, and for this reason the Gentiles themselves often condemned and abolished them. For, as the poet truly sang: night, love and wine recommend nothing moderate; the one is free of shame, wine and Venus of fear.

units.la: Sed de his vide plura in Antiquitatibus meis Convivialibus.
units.tr: But see more on these in my Convivial Antiquities.

units.la: SECVNDVM membrum in utroq; hoc sacrificio considerandum, ut OBIECTVM, ne pe Numina, quibus Neptor & Argonautæ hac sua sacrificia fecerunt. Ac Neptor quidem immo Minervæ, quam Ethnici ex Iove capite natam, & sapientiæ, prudentiæ, consilii, artium disciplinarumq; matrem ac procreatricem. deniq; belli quoq; præsidem ac moderatricem, finxerunt. Non nisi rum itaque fuit, Neptorem, qui summâ propter vicæ diucurnitatem, ac mutarum rerum experientiam sapientiâ prudentiâq; præditus fuerat, huic potissimum Deæ sacrificare, præsertim cum ei paulo antea vota fecisset, cum ipsi in ventvio quodam apparerent. Neque tanquam voti reus (sic enim antiqui & propriâ sacrorum voce eum appellabant, qui vovet ac suscepto Numinibus obligârat. Virgilius:
units.tr: The SECOND element to be considered in each of these sacrifices is the OBJECT, that is, the deities to whom Neptor and the Argonauts made their sacrifices. Neptor sacrificed to Minerva, whom the Gentiles imagined as born from the head of Jove, and as the mother and begetter of wisdom, prudence, counsel, the arts and the disciplines, and finally the patroness and guide of war. It was therefore not unreasonable that Neptor, who, through his great age and his long experience of changing circumstances, was endowed with wisdom and prudence, should sacrifice especially to this goddess, particularly since he had made a vow to her shortly before, when they appeared to him in a certain wind. He was not, as one bound by a vow (for so the ancients called, in their own sacred language, one who vows and binds himself to the deities by a pledge), Virgil:
Confessing before the altars, making vows, etc.

units.la: Votum illud suum sol vit, quem Damnatum Veteres vocabant, ut testis est Macrobius libro Icundo, Saturnalium capite tertio. At not Christiani a solo Deo, patre luminum, ut D. Iacobus nos docet capite primo, sapienciam suppliciprece petere, & illi soli sacrificare, & piareligio vota facere atq; persolvere debemus.
units.tr: He fulfilled that vow of his, which the ancients called a condemned vow (votum damnatum), as Macrobius bears witness in book 2, chapter 3 of the Saturnalia. But we Christians ought to seek wisdom by humble prayer from God alone, the Father of lights, as St James teaches us in chapter 1, and to offer sacrifice to Him alone, and to make and pay our vows in true piety.

units.la: Argonauta autem longam, difficilem, periculosamq; illam suam navigationem suscepe Apollini prius sacra fecerunt: qui quidem dictus fuit ἀπόλλων, ἀπο ἰὼ ἀ ἀ, teste Scholiaste, propterea quod e littore sol ventibus, & navem ingredientibus is præesse et favere credebatur. Idem Ἀπόλλων a Troezenia fuit propterea cognominatus, teste Gyraldo ex Pausania. Hic referri possunt Dii littorales, qui a Græcis ἀ ἀ ἀ dicti. Catulus:
units.tr: The Argonauts, however, before undertaking their long, difficult and dangerous voyage, first made sacrifices to Apollo. He was called Apollo [ἀπόλλων], as a scholiast attests, because it was believed that from the shore he presided over the winds and favoured those who boarded ships. The same Apollo was surnamed from Troezen, as Gyraldus reports from Pausanias. Here may be placed the gods of the shore, whom the Greeks called by their own name for them. Catullus:

units.la: Neq; nulla vota littoribus Deus sibi esse facta.
units.tr: Nor were vows made to the shores as to a god in vain.

units.la: Sed ut de hoc sacrificiorum Ethnicorum objecto, quod quasi fuit infinitum aliquanto uberius dicam, Deus quidem in Veteri Testamento sibi soli, tanquam uni, soli ac vero Deo, omnium bonorum rerumq; auctori, creatori, conservatori, datori & largitori sacrificari ab hominibus voluit: juxta illud Iacundi Paulipomenon trigesimo quarto capite, Regnino quinto versus, Adoleverunt Dii alienis: ideo effusa manebit effluans in mea in locum hunc & non extinguetur. At homines ductore & impulsore Satanâ, qui Dei honorem atque cultum omnibus modis ad se transferre atq; deniq; vare fuiunt, non soli Iehovæ, sed vero Deo, veatori cœli, terræ atq; maris, sed omnibus creaturis tam visibilibus quam invisibilibus, tum naturalibus quam artificialibus, cum bonis, tum malis, tanquam Dii atq; Numinibus veris sacra fecerunt.
units.tr: But to speak more fully of this object of Gentile sacrifices, which is almost endless: God in the Old Testament wished men to sacrifice to Him alone, as the one, sole and true God, the author, creator, preserver, giver and bestower of all good things. So it is in Paralipomenon, chapter 34, verse 25: "Because they have forsaken me and burned incense to other gods, my wrath shall be poured out upon this place and shall not be quenched." But men, with Satan as their leader and instigator, who tried in every way to transfer God's honour and worship to themselves, sacrificed not only to Jehovah, nor only to the true God, the maker of heaven, earth and sea, but to all creatures, visible and invisible, natural and artificial, good and evil, as if they were true gods and deities.

units.la: Quot itaq; res sunt, sive entia in hac rerum universitate, tot Dii fuerunt Dii atque Numinea, quot finxerunt Deos atq; Numina, tot fuerunt illa sacra atque sacrificia. Nec vero tantum res te vera existentes, quæ existunt in rerum natura: sed etiam res fictas & commentitias, quæ nunquam in rerum natura exitterunt, sacrificium illis fuit atq; sacra colucrunt.
units.tr: So many things or beings there are in this universe, so many gods and deities there were, as many as men imagined as gods and deities; and there were as many rites and sacrifices. Nor did they sacrifice and worship only things that truly exist in nature, but also fictitious and invented things, which never existed in nature.

units.la: Hoc igitur sacrificiorum atque adeo totius cultus sive religionis Ethnicorum objectum in sacris Canonicis litterarum monumentis quatuor ferè modis atque nominibus exprimitur, ne pe nomine Deorum, Creaturarum, Idolorum & Dæmonum, sive Dæmoniorum, quibus Ethni dicuntur sacrificasse. Nam primum quidem sapientiæ in sacris literis cum Ethnici, cum Iudeei Ethnicorum videlicet exemplo & imitatione impiâ Dîis, & quidem Dîis alienis, falsis, adulterinis, dicuntur immolasse. ideoque cum in genere, cum præcipuè huic vel illi Deo alieno, filio, & commentitio. Deinde quoniam falsi & adulterini illi Dii fuerunt creatura, sepe Ethnici creaturas dicuntur coluisse, insque sacra fecisse: unde Paulus i.ad Romanos: ... ut qui Dei veritatem mutarunt in mendacium & coluerint atque ser vierint rebus creatis, præter Creatorem, sive præcerito Creatore, qui est benedictus in sœcula, Amen.
units.tr: This object of sacrifices, and indeed of the whole worship or religion of the Gentiles, is expressed in the canonical writings of Scripture in roughly four ways and names: namely by the names of gods, creatures, idols, and demons or demonic beings, to whom the Gentiles are said to have sacrificed. First, Scripture says that the Gentiles, and the Jews too by the impious example and imitation of the Gentiles, sacrificed to gods, indeed to alien, false and adulterous gods, both in general and to this or that particular alien, fictitious god. Then, since those false and adulterous gods were creatures, the Gentiles are often said to have worshipped creatures and sacrificed to them. Hence Paul, Romans 1: "who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen."

units.la: Præterea quoniam illa Ethnicorum Numina revera fuerunt ειδωλα, id est, simulacra, nomina sunt ac non vera & solida Numina, sed quasi nomina tantum quædam, fictae, falsa, fatilia, vana, ειδωλα. inania, adulterina, dolo fraudis atque fallacie plenissima, & quod illa ipsa falsa & commenticia sua Numina idola, idest, simulacris & imaginibus potissimum coluerunt, denique quod illa ipsa idola atque simulacra inanimata divinis honoribus affecerunt, & tanquam Deos, sive Deos in ipsis coluerunt, idcirco merito Sanctus Spiritus in suo verbo testatur ipsos Idolis sacrificasse, & idolum sacrificia eidolothyta appellantur. Huc pertinent illa Pauli verba 1. Corinth. 8 Etenim si quis viderit te, qui scientia praeditus es, in Idolaeo accumbere, nonne conscientia ipsius, quum infirmus est, aedificabitur, id est, incitabitur & impelletur ad edendum eidolothyta, id est, ea, quae Idolis sunt immolata? Idem ab initio ejusdem capitis, eidolothyta. Deum, pater ille, a quo omnia, ut nos in ipsum, sive in ipso & unus Dominus IESVS CHRISTVS, per quem omnia & nos per ipsum.
units.tr: Moreover, since those Gentile deities were really idols [εἴδωλα], that is, images, they are mere names and not true and solid deities; they are, as it were, only names, feigned, false, fleeting, vain, empty, adulterous idols, full of the deceit and trickery of fraud.
