And because they worshipped those false and invented deities chiefly through idols, that is, images and likenesses, and because they paid divine honours to those lifeless idols and images, treating them as gods or as divine within them, the Holy Spirit rightly testifies in his word that they sacrificed to idols, and sacrifices offered to idols are called eidolothyta [εἰδωλόθυτα]. To this belong Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 8: "For if anyone sees you, who have knowledge, reclining in an idol's temple, will not his conscience, being weak, be built up, that is, be incited and driven to eat eidolothyta, that is, things sacrificed to idols?" Likewise, at the beginning of the same chapter: "...yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we unto him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him."

units.la: Postremò quoniam Satanae ductu & impulsu contra Dei legem & voluntatem Ethnicis imprimis Diabolus sese insinuavit, atque adeo ipsis aperte spiritibus impuris & immundis: quos Daemonas & Genios, Deos mseros, & Manes appellarunt, idcirco merito sacrae litterae testantur, eos Daemonibus sive Daemoniis sacrificasse. Sic enim Leviticii decimo septimo Deus ipse loquitur: Neultra sacrificent sacrificia sua Sejirim, post quos secuti sunt. Hebraei enim Sejirim, sunt Daemones; & quidem in genere vel omnes saedi, immundi, atque fordidi spiritus, vel in specie ill, qui cultoribus suis hirsuti & villosi, instar Hircorum, apparere solebant, quales a Poetis Panes, Faunii, Sylvani, Silani, & voce non abludente ab Hebraeo Satyri, alvi, Diiagreftes deferibuntur; quibus quidem tam sacris & horribilibus specibus Satanae insultabant, persuasit, haec esse Numina, quae ipsis prodeste & obesse possint.
units.tr: Finally, since the Devil, by Satan's guidance and prompting and against God's law and will, insinuated himself especially among the heathen, and indeed through the impure and unclean spirits themselves, whom they called demons, genii, gods of the dead, and Manes, the holy writings rightly testify that they sacrificed to demons or devils. For thus God himself speaks in Leviticus 17: "They shall no more offer their sacrifices to the Seirim, after whom they have gone." For the Hebrews, the Seirim are demons, and indeed either all foul, unclean and filthy spirits in general, or in particular those which used to appear to their worshippers hairy and shaggy, like goats, such as the poets describe as Pans, Fauns, Sylvans, Silenuses, and, by a word not unlike the Hebrew, Satyrs, Dryads and Diagrestes. With these sacred and horrible appearances Satan mocked them, persuading them that these were divinities who could help or harm them.

units.la: Sic Moses Deuteronomii trigesimo secundo cap. 16, decimo, primo versu, in Antico suo Israelitarum defectionem a vero Deo ad Deorum sicitiorum cultum exprobrans, inquit: Sacrificaverunt Lafchedim, Daemonibus, non Deo. Schedim enim Daemones, sive Cacodaemones sunt. Sic dicta Schedim, Schadad, vastando et perdendo: a quo nostri Schaden noxa & nocere sine dubio est deductum. Eorundem sit mentio Psalmo centesimo sexto, versu trigesimo septimo, Sacrificaverunt liberos suos Daemonibus. Sic Psalmo nonagesimo sexto, versu quinto, Dii gentium Daemonia sunt, ut vulgata versio habet: sed in Hebraeo est Elilim, quae vox vanitates & figmenta hominum significat: unde Pagninus vertit Vana. His vero consentanea plane sunt illa Pauli, prima Corinthiorum decimo, Quapropter dilectimei, fugite ab Idolatria. Et paulo post: Nonne qui edunt victimas (idolothyta) participes sunt altaris? Quid ergo dico? Idolum aliquid est, aut eidolothyton, id est, quod Idolis immolatum est, aliquid est? Imo quae immolant gentes, Daemonis immolante, & non Deo. Nolum autem vos participes Daemoniorum esse. Non potestis poculum Domini bibere & poculum Daemoniorum.
units.tr: So Moses, in Deuteronomy 32, rebuking Israel's defection from the true God to the worship of strange gods, says: "They sacrificed to Shedim, to demons, not to God" (Deut. 32:16–17). For the Shedim are demons or cacodaemons. They are called Shedim from Shadad, to lay waste and to destroy, and from this our word Schaden, harm, and "to harm," are without doubt derived. Mention of them is made in Psalm 106:37: "They sacrificed their sons to demons." Likewise Psalm 96:5: "The gods of the nations are demons," as the Vulgate has it; but in the Hebrew it is Elilim, a word meaning vanities and the inventions of men, whence Pagninus translates "vain things." Entirely consistent with these are the words of Paul in 1 Corinthians 10: "Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry." And shortly after: "Do not those who eat the sacrifices [εἰδωλόθυτα] partake of the altar? What then do I say? That an idol is anything, or that what is sacrificed to idols [εἰδωλόθυτον] is anything? Rather, the things which the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I would not have you become partners with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons."

units.la: Etsi vero Gentes non solum Daemonibus & Spiritibus illis malis, sed etiam hominibus, & alium multos creaturis bonis suâ naturâ atque salutaribus sacra fecerunt, & divinos honores culmque tribus detulerunt: idque etiam bona, ut vocant, intentione, sive mente, nonnunquam virtutes denique fecisse: tamen quoniam illa ipsa sacrificia etiam bonas creaturis falsa, repugnarunt divinae vel, voluntati, gloriae, ac majestati, ad ejusdem spectarunt ignominiam atque dedecus, nec Deus ... Diabolorum insinctu & assatu fuerunt facta, idcirco Spiritus Sanctus eos Daemonis sua facisse testatur. Hinc etiam ipsi Ethnici superstitionem (qualis fuit tota illorum relig.) retinent d'eooi auqoviae, id est, Daemonum timorem, qui opponitur Timori Dei, appellarunt.
units.tr: Although the Gentiles offered sacrifices and divine honours not only to demons and those evil spirits, but also to men and to many other creatures good and beneficial by nature, and sometimes even paid such worship to virtues, with what they call a good intention or mind, nevertheless, since those very sacrifices, even when offered to good creatures, were falsely opposed to the divine will, glory and majesty, and aimed at its dishonour and disgrace, and were made at the prompting and instigation of the devils, therefore the Holy Spirit testifies that they sacrificed to demons. Hence the Gentiles themselves called their superstition, which was the whole character of their religion, deisidaimonia [δεισιδαιμονία], that is, fear of demons, which is opposed to the fear of God.

units.la: Porro operaepretium duxi Deorum sive Numinum istorum, quae Ethnici Diaboli infinctu impulsu, coluerunt, generalem quandam brevem descriptionem, ac quasi epitomen & syno- psin hic subjicere; unde partim hominum, qui ista coluerunt, monstrosa vanitas, fluitritia atque infanta, partim Dei, quiex trifli fuatflaque ista Diaboli serviture nos liberavit, inftas atque miserigordia apparebit. quam asidiuus mertio laudibus celebrare debemus.
units.tr: Moreover I have thought it worth while to add here a general, brief description, as it were an epitome and synopsis, of these gods or divinities which the Gentiles worshipped at the instigation and urging of the Devil. From it will appear, on the one hand, the monstrous vanity, foolishness and childishness of the men who worshipped them, and on the other hand the kindness and mercy of God, who has freed us from this slavery to the Devil, and which we ought constantly to celebrate with praise.

units.la: At de Gentilium quidem sive Ethnicorum Dis atque Numinibus, praeter antpteres cum Christianos, ut Tertullianum, Augustinum, Lactantium, Eusebium, Cyrillum, Theodoretum, Arnobium, tum Ethnicos, ut Varronem, Ciceronem, Porphyrium, ... ticum, Theodoretum, Arnobium, tum Ethnicos, ut Varronem, Ciceronem, Porphyrium, nntum & innumeros alios; nostri quidem temporibus copiose elegantereque scripserunt de iis Chartarius Rhegiensis Italicus, Antonius Verderius Dominus Pallas pro sae Latini Chartarii librum in Latinum sermonem transtulit, denique (ut de multis alis Antiquis scriptoribus tateam) Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus Ferrariensis, cujus separatim libri sex magnam ingredi vi dear, breviter tantum atq; summatim, quantum dem insitutii huius se mei ratio postulabit, de iis hic quaedam subjiciam, quae cognitu non inutilia erunt ac inju: unda.
units.tr: Concerning the gods and divinities of the Gentiles, many have written besides those already named: both Christians, such as Tertullian, Augustine, Lactantius, Eusebius, Cyril, Theodoret and Arnobius, and heathens, such as Varro, Cicero, Porphyry, and countless others. In our own times, too, Chartarius of Reggio in Italy has written about them copiously and elegantly, and Antonius Verderius translated Chartarius's book into Latin. Finally (to say nothing of many other ancient writers) Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus of Ferrara wrote, whose six books, taken separately, seem to be a great undertaking. I shall here set out briefly and summarily, as far as the plan of this work requires, some things about them which will be neither useless nor unpleasant to know.

units.la: Observandum autem hic primo omnium, nullam fere rem cum eo ut uni verso hoc mundo, in hac certum unitate atque natura, maximam, mediam, minimam, quam non Deum, Deamve, atque Numen aliquod coluerunt ut ac divinis honoribus affecerunt, tanquam Deum, Deamve, atque Numen aliquod coluerit ut ac divinis honoribus affecerint, tanquam patronum, tutorem, custodem atque praesidem sibi praficitum.
units.tr: It must be observed here, first of all, that there is hardly anything in this whole world, in any kind of nature, the greatest, the middling or the least, which men have not regarded as a god, goddess or some divinity, and honoured with divine honours, as a patron, guardian, protector and president set over them.

units.la: Nec verò res tantum naturales, sive visibiles & corporeas, sive invisibiles & incorporeas, easque cum bonas, utiles ac fulutares, tum etiam malas, pestiferas, exitiosas, detestandas Deorum loco atque numero habuerunt, vel in earum vel ... numam manu atque ope effectas atque elaboratas, hoc est, ut facta a hominum artificium ... rum opera, digitorum humanorum, utrea Lactantius vocat, ludicris atque ludgines, simulacra, statuas, columnas, baculos & alia usui secundi super ... ... flrumenta, ad Deorum honorem conflata, confecta & compara ... ... quaedam, coluerunt.
units.tr: Nor have they regarded as gods only natural things, whether visible and corporeal or invisible and incorporeal, and that both good, useful and wholesome ones and also bad, pestilent, deadly and detestable ones. They also counted among their gods and worshipped things made and wrought by human hand and skill, that is, works of human craftsmanship and of human fingers, as Lactantius calls them: images, statues, columns, staves and other instruments of use, cast, fashioned and prepared for the honour of the gods.

units.la: Duo igitur primarii fuerunt ac principalia Idololatria (superstitionis) ... Ea. Unum naturale, res videlicet a Deo creatae, quas creat ... homines, Deo Creatore derelicto, ea vitios exhibuerunt honore & ... generorum. Alterum artificiale, res nimirum ab hominum ... ... statuae & imagines rerum conditarum: quae tamen, ... ... est, ac cre- tura, naturalibus potest adnumerari.
units.tr: There were therefore two primary and principal kinds of idolatry (superstition). One is natural, namely things created by God, which men, leaving the Creator God, honoured with the worship due to God alone, and so gave to the creatures the honour owed to the Creator. The other is artificial, namely things made by human hands, statues and images of created things; which, insofar as it is a made thing and a creature, can also be counted among the natural.

units.la: Ver. sed, auct hujus obiecti Idololatriae Ethnici, ad ... nprimis luculenta h.: bemus facte esi ... ptura testimonia, quae omnino hic praemittenda minime, praeterea videntur: ex bus factis superis conflatum est Gentium Deos ... lium cum Graecorum, tum Barbarorum Idololatria, seu Idolomania potius cum naturali ... artificiali, hunc in modum differt. ... Ἀπογαλύπτεται γὰρ ὀργὴ θεοῦ ἀπ᾽ οὐρανοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσαν ἀσέβειαν καὶ ἀδικίαν ἀνθρώπων τῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἐν ἀδικίᾳ κατεχόντων. ... ἀλλ᾽ ἐματαιώθησαν ἐν τοῖς διαλογισμοῖς αὐτῶν, καὶ ἐσκοτίσθη ἡ ἀσύνετος αὐτῶν καρδία. Φάσκοντες εἶναι σοφοὶ ἐμωράνθησαν.
units.tr: Now, as to the author of this object of idolatry, the Gentiles' idolatry, both of Greeks and of barbarians, or rather idolomania, we have, first of all, clear testimonies of Scripture, which by no means seem to be omitted here, and which differ in this way from the natural and artificial ones. For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all impiety and injustice of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness [Ἀποκαλύπτεται γὰρ ὀργὴ θεοῦ ἀπ᾽ οὐρανοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσαν ἀσέβειαν καὶ ἀδικίαν ἀνθρώπων τῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἐν ἀδικίᾳ κατεχόντων]. But they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Professing themselves wise, they became fools [ἀλλ᾽ ἐματαιώθησαν ἐν τοῖς διαλογισμοῖς αὐτῶν, καὶ ἐσκοτίσθη ἡ ἀσύνετος αὐτῶν καρδία. Φάσκοντες εἶναι σοφοὶ ἐμωράνθησαν].

units.la: Idest Palam enim est ira Dei de caelo ad versus omnem impietatem & injustitiam hominum, ut qui veritatem injuste detinent, quod de Deo cognosci potest, manifestum est in ipsis: Deus enim eis manifestum fecit. Ipsius enim invisibilia jam inde a condito mundo ex rebus factis intellectu percipiuntur, ... (videlicet) ejus tam potentia, tum divinitas: ad hoc, ut sint inexcusabiles. Propterea quod cum Deum cognoverint, (tamen) ut Deum non glorificaverunt, neq; gratias egerunt: sed vani facti sunt in cogitationibus suis, & obtenebratum est despicieri eorum. Quum se dicerent sapientes, stulti facti sunt. Mutarunt enim gloriam incorruptibilis Dei in effigiem imaginem corruptibilis hominis & volucrum, & quadrupedum, & reptilium. Quamobrem etiam tradidit eos Deus in concupiscentias cordis ipsorum ad immunditiam, ut fiat ad eorum corpora sua inter se: ut qui Deo veritatem in mutabilem transmutarint in falsitatem & coluerunt ac servierunt rebus creatis, praeterito Creatore, qui est benedictus in saecula Amen. Habemus primum testimonium, quo Paulus tum Idololatriae universae causam, originem, vim atque naturam graphice describit, simul quasi colorem prodit: tum rerum partium artificialium, ut imaginum & simulacrorum, eikon & homoiomatum & nominibus, partim naturalium, Xtionoos, id est, creaturae, sive rei conditae nomine, expressam illustremus, mentionemque facit.
units.tr: That is: the wrath of God is indeed revealed from heaven against all the impiety and injustice of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness. For what may be known of God is manifest among them, since God has shown it to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly perceived through the things that are made, namely both his eternal power and his divinity, so that they are without excuse. Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, nor give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Professing themselves wise, they became fools. For they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image resembling corruptible man, and birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things. Therefore God also gave them up, through the lusts of their hearts, to uncleanness, so that their bodies were dishonoured among themselves; they who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen. Here we have the first testimony, in which Paul graphically describes the cause, origin, power and nature of all idolatry, and at the same time sets out its colour. He also mentions the artificial things, images and likenesses, called eikones and homoiomata, and the natural things, called ktisis, that is, creature or created thing, and so illustrates them.

units.la: Alterum testimonium utriusque, Idololatriae, naturalis, ut ita loquar, & artificialis, extat capitulum, qui merito Sapientiae titulo insignitur, propterea quod sapientissima religionis vitae, morum & documentum compleditur. Ac primum quidem mentio fit rerum naturalium, quas Deorum numero (ut ipsi putabant) habuerunt, hae verba, quae sequuntur: Malaeaque iam ...
units.tr: The second testimony, concerning idolatry of both kinds, the natural and, so to speak, the artificial, is a chapter rightly marked with the title of Wisdom, because it is filled with the wisest teaching on the life, morals and doctrine of religion. First, mention is made of natural things, which they (as they themselves thought) counted among the gods, in these words which follow: "...".

units.la: {y} Alterum Sap cap 13. v. 2. 3 4-5. pellant,& Cicero,communem Deorum atq; hominum unitatem,domum, urbem cĩuitatem, templum,tanquam Deum,sive Numen aliquod coluerunt. Mundum, inquit Plinius (lib.2.cap.1. & hoc,quod nomine alto Caelum appellare libuit,cuius circumflexu tegitur cuncta, Numen esse credi par est,aeternum,immensum,neque genitum,neq; inte rum unquam. Strato, Theophrasti audicor,omnem vim diuinam in Natura sitam esse censuit, quae causas gignendi,augendi minuendi ve habeat,sed careat omni sensu & figura. Democritus tum imagines earum, et cuncta in Deorum numero retulit, tum illam naturam, quae imagines fundat ac mittat, tum sientiam, intelligentiam{?}q; nostram, de qua postea. Sic Aristoteles modo Menti tribuit omnem diuinitatem: modo Mundum ipsum dixit esse Deum: modo quendam alium praeiecit Mundo: tum caeli Ardorem dixit Deum esse. Cleanthes, Zenonis auditor,tum ipsum Mundum Deum dixit esse,tum coeli Naturae Menti atq; Animo hoc nomen tribuit, tum ultimum & altissimum atq; undi circumfusum & extremum,omnia cingentem atq; complexum Ardorem,qui Aether nominatur,certissimum Deum iudicavit,Ciceronemque lib.1.de Natura Deorum. Senec idem Xenophanes,qui Mente adiuncta omne praeterea,quod esset infinitum, Deum vocum esse. Vellejus contra Epicureus apud eundem Ciceronem loco citato, portenta & miracula Philosophorum non deterrent, sed somniantium dicit esse, quando vel Mundi opificem & administratorem, ut est apud Platonem in Timaeo, vel θεοσ, sed Providentiam, quam Stoicorum anum fatidicam appellat, vel ipsum denique Mundum animo & sensibus praeditum, rotundum, & de tem volubilem Deum statuunt. Pluribus deinceps hanc de Mundi aeternitate & divinitate Philosophum sententiam refellit.
units.tr: The second [testimony] is Wisdom 13:2-5. ...they considered the rulers of the world to be gods. And Cicero: they worshipped as God, or some divinity, the common unity of gods and men, the home, the city, the state, the temple. Pliny says (book 2, chapter 1): "The world, and this which it has pleased men to call by the lofty name of Heaven, by whose circuit all things are covered, is rightly believed to be a divinity: eternal, immense, neither begotten nor ever to perish." Strato, a hearer of Theophrastus, held that all divine power lies in Nature, which has the causes of generating, increasing and diminishing, but lacks all sense and shape. Democritus referred to the images and all things among the gods, and also that nature which emits and sends forth images, and also the sense and intelligence within us, of which more later. So Aristotle at one time ascribed all divinity to Mind; at another said the world itself is God; at another placed some other being above the world; and then said that the heat of heaven is God. Cleanthes, a hearer of Zeno, said that the world itself is God; then he gave this name to the nature of heaven, to Mind and to Soul; and finally he judged the ultimate and highest, the fiery ether which surrounds the world and encloses and embraces all things, which is called Aether, to be most certainly God (and see Cicero, book 1, On the Nature of the Gods). Xenophanes, who joined Mind to the whole, said that whatever else is infinite is God. Velleius, an Epicurean, against them, in the same Cicero, in the passage cited, says that the portents and miracles of the philosophers do not frighten him, but that they belong to dreamers, since they set up either the maker and administrator of the world, as in Plato's Timaeus, or God... but Providence, which he calls the prophetic old woman of the Stoics, or finally the world itself, endowed with soul and senses, round and rolling, as a god. He then refutes at length this opinion of the philosophers on the eternity and divinity of the world.

units.la: Vnus autem hoc, σαερα a Graecis dictum,sub Panis quoq; nomine coluerunt quem id est nonnulli sic voluerunt fuisse appellatum. Idem coluerunt sub Priapi & Iovis nomine. Iovem etiam illum suum filium & commentitium a Iehova, proprio veri Dei, cond tori Mundi, mente ad summam impietatem traducentes (qui Graeci Zeus, ab emicante & lucente vi a viriditate rerum, quae Hebraeum dicitur, Ziv, est nisi upacius, ummu nisi ve super mum Deorum omnium senserunt, eum tefle Seneca, & Fatum, & Providentiam, & Naturam, & Mundum appellantes, cuius propterea triplex regnum attribuerunt, in Caelo,in Mari,in Inferno, Pulvere in hanc sententiam canit de eo Orpheus: Primus cunctorum est & jupiter ultimus idem. Jupiter & caput & medium est. Sunt ex Iove cuncta. Iupiter & terra basis & stellarum Olympus. Iupiter & mas est, est idem nympha perennis. Spiritus est cunctis, validus, est iupiter ignis. Iupiter est pelagi radix; est Lunae lumen. Cunctorum Rex est, princeps, et orbis auctor: Natus, sinu occultans, dulces in luminis auras Cuncta tulit, sacro versans sub pectore curas.
units.tr: This one, which the Greeks call [σαερα], they also worshipped under the name of Pan, which some think was given to it for this reason. The same they worshipped under the names of Priapus and Jupiter. They also made Jupiter their own son and a fiction, drawing him away from Jehovah, the proper God of truth and Creator of the world, into the greatest impiety. (The Greeks call him Zeus, from the shining and bright power and the greenness of things, which in Hebrew is called Ziv.) They perceived him as the highest and above all the gods, calling him by the names Fate, Providence, Nature and the World; and to him, as witness Seneca, they therefore assigned a threefold kingdom: in heaven, in the sea, in the underworld. Orpheus sings of him in this sense: "Jupiter is first of all, and Jupiter is last. Jupiter is head and middle. All things are from Jove. Jupiter is the earth's foundation and the starry Olympus. Jupiter is male, Jupiter is the everlasting nymph. Jupiter is the breath of all things, strong; Jupiter is fire. Jupiter is the root of the sea; Jupiter is the light of the moon. He is king of all, prince and author of the sphere; born, he hid them in his bosom, and bore all things out into the sweet breezes of light, turning his cares in his sacred breast."

units.la: Phanices,M.Tullio & Macrobio referentibus,Ianum Mundi symbolum sunt arbitrati. Quare Serpente caudam sua vorante,cum επαφεντασα.Mundum enim ipsum alit, & assidue in orbem torquetur: quod rerum omnium motus,interitus, necessitatem atq; instauratione nobis ostendit.
units.tr: The Phoenicians, as Cicero and Macrobius report, took Janus to be the symbol of the world. Hence the serpent biting its own tail [ἐπαφέντασα?], since it feeds the world itself and is constantly turned in a circle; which shows us the motion, the perishing, the necessity and the renewal of all things.

units.la: Nos contra Christiani Mundum hunc unum versum, hanc rerum universi verfeatem,non Deum aliquem,sed Dei Opus. Max.opus seu pisicium, Dei theatrum, speculum atq; speculum esse credimus: in quo Deus suam divinitatem, majestatem atq; potentiam, addit sapientiam, misericordiam atq; justitiam nobis perpetuo spectandam proponit. Vnus versum item hanc Naturam,non Deum, sed Dei ministram atq; familiam, quae sapientissime potentissimeq; ab illo semper regitur ac gubernatur,esse credimus. Idemque ex Aristotelica Mundi definitio libro de Mundo,quae ita habet Κόσμος δ' ἔστι σύνθεσις ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς καὶ τῶν ἐν τούτοις φύσεων, Mundus conflat ex caelo & terra, cuncta, quae in eis continentur, naturis. Appellatur Deus & alterum Mundum, ordinem rerum ordo & administratio, a Deo & per Deum conservari solica. Impurus igitur & immundus fuit hic Mundi ceu Numinis cujusdam cultus, cum Mundus non sit Deus, sed Deo pro-ficium, sex dierum spatio ex Nihilo, hominis causa creatum, a quo etiam ad extremum illum usque diem conservatur, regitur & gubernatur.
units.tr: We Christians, on the contrary, believe that this world, this one universal fabric of things, is not some god, but the work of God, the greatest work, the theatre, mirror and image of God, in which God sets before us to be contemplated without end his divinity, majesty and power, and his wisdom, mercy and justice. Likewise we believe that this Nature is not God, but the servant and household of God, which is always ruled and governed by him most wisely and powerfully. And the definition of the world in Aristotle's book On the World agrees, which reads: "The world is a composition of heaven and earth and the natures contained in them." It is also called another God, the order of things, the arrangement and administration, preserved by God and through God. Impure and unclean, therefore, was this worship of the world as of some divinity, since the world is not God but a creature of God, created out of nothing in the space of six days for the sake of man, and by him preserved, ruled and governed even to that last day.

units.la: Nunc, antequam ad singulas Mundi partes tum maximas, tum minimas, & omnia deniq; quae Mundi sint complexu, continentur, accedamus, de Tempore, cujus eadem fere est cum Mundo origo atq; conditio, prius dicemus: quod ipsum quoq; ceu Numen quoddam, ab Ethnicis fuit cultus, temporis sub Saturni, Ianique, Iovis, & aliorum Deorum nominibus. Ac Saturni quidem nominibus, imaginibus, insignibus variis, quae illi tribuuntur & fabulis, quae de illo traduntur, Tempus (quod Latine a temperando dicitur esse ajt Beda: sive quod unum quodq; tempora spatium temperatum sit, sive quod momentis, horis, diebus, mensibus, annis, feculisq; & aetatibus omnia mortalis vitae curricula temperentur, hoc est, regantur) innui, ac ejus vim, naturam, tommoda & incommoda varia ac multiplicia designari copiose docent illi qui de Ethnicorum Diis scripserunt. Sic enim, ut ex multis pauca delibemus, Saturnum Latine quasi annis saturum, Graece Κρόνον, quasi χρόνον, volunt dictum. Plutarchus in quaestionib. Rom 12. Cur Κρόνο, id est, Saturnum veritatis patrem fecerint Antiqui, hanc rationem reddit, vel quod Tempus est Cronus, ut nonnulli Philosophorum interpretantur. Veritatem autem erunt tempus: Vel, quod cum fabulae Saturni secundum fatiar: justissimum, dubium non sit, quin maximus in illo fuerit veritatis usus. Hinc etiam Saturnum Poëta veteres finxerunt Urani, id est, Coeli fuisse filium, quod tempus nihil aliud esset, nisi quaedam spatium, quod Coelis conversione colligitur: sive mensura motus, qui coelestium orbe conficitur, ad quem motum homines Tempus metiri coeperunt. Eundemque expressisse effigie hominis senis, annosi, operto capite, (cui etiam aperto capite sacrificabatur) falcem manu altera tenentis, liberos (unde etiam liberi et immolabantur) lapides & nescio quae alia de yonav’ν, Quibus significatur, Tempore omnia ad senectutem perduci, aperiri ac patefieri, incidi, confici, consumi ac quasi nia consumuntur. quosenfu Hebraei Tempus ψ, Eth, dixerunt ατ, Auath, id est, consumendo & per vertendo, propterea quod Tempus omnia consumat & perverat, juxta illud Ovidii Metamorphos lib. 15. Tempus edax rerum, tuq; in vidiosa vetustas, Omnia destruitis, vitiataq; dentibus aevi Paulatim lenta consumitis omnia morte.
units.tr: Now, before we come to the individual parts of the world, both the greatest and the smallest, and finally to all the things that the world embraces in its compass, we shall first speak of Time, whose origin and condition is almost the same as that of the world. This too, like some divinity, was worshipped by the heathen under the names of Saturn, Janus, Jupiter and other gods. Indeed, from the names, images, varied emblems which are attributed to Saturn, and from the stories told of him, those who wrote about the gods of the heathen teach at length that Time is signified, and that its power, nature, advantages and disadvantages, many and varied, are represented. To pick a few from many: they say the Latin Saturnus is as if "saturus annis" (full of years), and the Greek Kronos is as if chronos. Plutarch, in his Roman Questions 12, gives the reason why the ancients made Kronos, that is Saturn, the father of Truth: either because Time is Kronos, as some philosophers interpret, and Truth will be Time; or because, since the stories about Saturn are told according to fate, there can be no doubt that the greatest use of truth was in him. Hence the old poets also feigned that Saturn was the son of Uranus, that is of Heaven, because time is nothing else than a certain space, which is measured by the revolution of the heavens, or the measure of the motion which is completed by the circuit of the heavenly bodies, by which motion men began to measure time. The same [Time] they expressed in the figure of an old man, aged, with his head covered (and he was also sacrificed to with his head uncovered), holding a sickle in one hand and his children in the other (whence children also used to be sacrificed), and stones, and I know not what other things, of which the Greek word... By these it is signified that by Time all things are brought to old age, opened and laid bare, cut down, finished and consumed, or as it were consumed. For this reason the Hebrews called Time [עת], Eth, and [אבד?], Auath, that is, from consuming and overturning, because Time consumes and overturns all things, according to the words of Ovid in the Metamorphoses, book 15: "Time, devourer of things, and you, envious old age, you destroy all things, and with gnawing teeth of the years you gradually consume everything in slow death."

units.la: Et Seneca, Tempus non avidum de vorat & chaos.
units.tr: And Seneca: "Time does not greedily devour chaos."

units.la: Huc pertinent, quae Eusebius de Astarte, Coeli filia, Saturni verofrorem & conjuge tradidit, quae rerum quandam ornatum Saturno, fratri & marito suo confecerat, qui quatuor erat oculis praeditus: horum duo ante, duo autem pone erant affixi: hi vicissim circumdebantur atq; patebant, duobus imper vigilantibus: humeris quatuor alas addidit, quarum duae erant expansae, velut anifeli ad volandum parati, duae reductae & complicatae, tanquam stantes. His quoq; Tempus vel atq; natura sunt expressa quod dormitare licet videatur; tamen vigilet: dumque vigilat, sed simul quod dormit: identique stare licet videatur, tamen citissime volat. Unde Tempus mobile, volatile, sive volucre, fugax sive fugitivum, labens, subito, lubricum, a Poëtis appellatur, & nostra lingua Tepus 3CIt; sive 3CI appellantur a Cito, quod cistatissimo cursu labitur, juxta illa Poëtae: —Cito pede labitur aetas.
units.tr: To this belongs what Eusebius relates of Astarte, daughter of Heaven, the sister and wife of Saturn, who made for Saturn, her brother and husband, a certain ornament of things, who had four eyes: two in front and two behind. These in turn were surrounded and then opened, two always watching. To his shoulders she added four wings, two spread out as if ready to fly, and two folded back and held close, as if standing still. By these too Time and its nature are expressed: for although it seems to sleep, it is nevertheless awake; and while it is awake it also sleeps; and although it seems to stand still, it flies most swiftly. Hence Time is called by the poets mobile, volatile or winged, fleeting or fugitive, gliding, sudden, slippery; and in our language it is called [Tempus], or is so named from citus (swift), because it slips away with the swiftest course, as the poet says: "Life slips away on swift feet."

units.la: Nec bona tam sequitur, quam bona prima fuit.
units.tr: Nor does the good that follows match the good that came first.

units.la: Vigitur Mundum, ut a Tempus quoq; pleriq; Veterum Philosophorum aeternum esse existimarunt, quod propterea ψ, Olam, ab Hebraeis dictum fortasse putarunt (a quo Temporis nomen Iaturam Olim, sunt mutuati) eiq; aeternitatem ac divinitatem tribuerunt. Thales & Simonides Tempus appellarunt sapientissimum, quasi ab illo sapientissime efficerentur omnia. Conf. Pythagoricus, sefte Aristotele lib. 4. Physicorum, idem σεφεσιτατον, id est, infinitum, duratione, ut quasi quaedam minimum dixit: quia nimium Temporis sucteffione atque progressu omnia oblivione deleantur & abscondantur. Unde etiam Oblivio sum a Poëta est dictum: Oblivio sum cuncta, sed Tempus vorat.
units.tr: Hence many of the older philosophers also thought Time to be eternal. They perhaps supposed that the Hebrews called it Olam, from which the Latins borrowed the name of Time (Iaturam, Olim), and they ascribed eternity and divinity to it. Thales and Simonides called Time the wisest, as if all things were made most wisely by it. The Pythagorean (according to Aristotle, Physics book 4) called the same thing the most ... (σεφεσιτατον), that is, infinite in duration, as if to say that it is a kind of ... ; because through the endless succession and progress of Time all things are destroyed and hidden by oblivion. Hence the poet also says of Oblivion: "Oblivion devours all things, but Time devours Oblivion."

units.la: Et rectè Saturnus, Temporis Deus, ob hanc causam a נדס Satar, abscondit, deducitur: quem admodum & a latendo Deus Latius sive Latinus est dictus, & Saturnia sedes Latium appellatur.
units.tr: And rightly Saturn, the god of Time, is derived from the Hebrew satar, to hide, for the same reason that the god Latius or Latinus was named from lying hidden, and Saturnia's seat is called Latium.

units.la: Vt autem Tempus ipsum uniuersum: sic singulæ quoque eius partes, ut Annus, Mensis, Stoa mana, Dies, Hora, dicuntur fuerunt consecrata honoribus, hoc est, partim pro Diis culta, partim certis Diis dicata.
units.tr: Just as Time as a whole was consecrated and honoured, so too its individual parts, such as the Year, the Month, the Week, the Day and the Hour, were in part worshipped as gods and in part dedicated to certain gods.

units.la: Annus igitur universus & lovi & Iano fuit consecratus: unde etiam Iani nomine fuit appellatus. Et certè vocis Anni atque Iani magna est affinitas ac similitudo: quæ utraque ab Hebræa רוש Schanáh, Annum significance, videlicet esse derivata: qui quidem hic dictus est a רוש, Schanáh, mutatvic, vicera vic, vel mutacus & iceratus fuit, numerum a mutatione seu revolutione, eo quod annus annum perpetua serie sequatur: unde Annum Latine quasi Annulum, id est, Orbem nonnulli voluerunt esse dictum: alii a Græco ἐνιαυτός. Eos enim Deus fuit anni: qui etiam eundem præcessere videbatur: cuius imaginem exprimebant Phænices similachro Draconis, in orbem redactis, caudamque suam devorantis, ut significarent Mundi & Annum in se resoluti quod in anno varia & temporum & rerum sinc mutationes ac vicissitudines. Hinc Ianum Ethnici finxerunt bifrontem, ad anni principium atque finem, sive tempus præteritum & futurum significandum: & binas ei tribuerunt, unam adolescentem, & alteram iam grandis ætatis: quarum altera tempora mox ad venturi, altera temporis præteriti erat signum. Eidem, canquam Temporum Mundi ianitori, clavem tribuebant, qua & dies & annos laudaret & aperiret. Vere qui demineunte aperires terram, eam ad herbas floresq; producendos movendo, ejusq; ianum faciunt disiunctum patefaciendo: Hyeme autem clauderet, quando ea omnibus suis ornamentis privata constipatur, & nivis atque glaciei rigore constringitur. Plinius libro 34. Naturalis Historiæ, Ianum a Numa Rege dicatum ajs, digitis ita figuratis, ut CCCLXV nota per signi ficationem anni, temporis & æui se Deum judicaret. Tot enim diebus annus constat. Nam apud Antiquos digitorum varia inflexione, quos quasi vellet numeros, facile ostendebat: de qua numerandi ratione exstat adhuc perquam eruditus Bede liber. Suidas scribit, alios Ianum e pugnorem dextera manu tenentem clavem, ut temporum principium, ac anni reclusorem, janumque ita etiam Patulcius & Clusius ab aperiendo & claudendo fuit dictus: alios vero in dextera Ianum finxerunt XX concinentem, ut annum significeat.
units.tr: The whole Year was therefore consecrated both to Jupiter and to Janus, and that is why it was called after Janus. Indeed the words Annus and Ianus are very closely related and alike, and both are derived from the Hebrew shanah, meaning year. This word is itself said to come from shanah, to change or revolve, because the year follows year in a continuous series. Some have held that annus was called in Latin as if annulus, that is, a ring or orb, others that it comes from the Greek eniautos. The Phoenicians expressed the god of the year, which seemed also to be the same as the year itself, by an image of a dragon drawn into a circle and devouring its own tail, to signify that the world and the year return into themselves, since in the year there are varied changes and alternations of seasons and things. Hence the pagans fashioned Janus with two faces, to signify the beginning and end of the year, or past and future time, and gave him two ages: one youthful, the other of advanced years; one face was the sign of the time soon to come, the other of time past. To him, as the doorkeeper of the Times of the world, they gave a key with which he opened and unlocked both days and years. In spring, when he begins to open the earth and stirs it to bring forth herbs and flowers, he opens the divided doorway; in winter he closes it, when the earth, stripped of all its adornments, is bound up with the cold of snow and ice. Pliny, in book 34 of the Natural History, says that Janus was consecrated by King Numa, with his fingers so shaped that they showed the figure 365, to signify that he was the god of the year, of time and of the age; for the year consists of so many days. Among the ancients, by bending their fingers in various ways, they could easily show the numbers they wished; there is still a very learned book by Bede on this method of counting. Suidas writes that others depicted Janus holding a key in his right hand, as the beginning of time and the unlocker of the year; and Janus was also called Patulcius and Clusius from opening and closing. Others again pictured Janus with his right hand holding a counter (or the number 20), to signify the year.

units.la: Nec vero cancum bisipitem & bifrontem, sed etiam quadrifrontem Ianum Etrusci effinxerunt (cujusmodi statua in quodam Etruriæ loco reperta est) ad quatuor anni tempora adiuntur, Ver, Æstas, Autumnus, Hiems: quæ ipsius iter apud Præscos vario aspectu auctoritate habitu designabantur. Eodem arcus Iani quadrifrontes & pertinent, quibus in pompis triumphalibus per urbem Romam ad Iani templum excitabantur.
units.tr: The Etruscans, moreover, fashioned Janus not only two-faced and two-headed but four-faced (a statue of this kind was found in a certain place in Etruria), with faces corresponding to the four seasons of the year: Spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter. These were distinguished among the Sabines by different appearances, dress and habits, marking the course of the year. To the same idea belong the four-faced arches of Janus, under which triumphal processions passed through the city of Rome to the temple of Janus.

units.la: Duodecim simulacer arcu ab Antiquis Ianus positæ, dies sive menses, vel mensium, velocitate signi feri segmentorum, per quæ singulis annis Sol decurrit, ianuarium babebant. Sic Romæ erat templum Iano sacrum, cujus ostium quatuor lumen pilatu fulcentibus, quatuor ianuis vis: in singulis verò loculamenta duodecim, canquam fenestellæ, in quibus flaræ reponuntur. Has quidam exsiliamari mensium, qui in quatuor anni tempora distribuuntur, imaginæ pro sequentes.
units.tr: The ancients set up twelve little images of Janus, which had the days, or the months, or the signs of the zodiac, through which the sun runs each year, as their number of the months. There was at Rome a temple sacred to Janus, whose door was supported by four pillars and had four doors; in each of its walls were twelve small niches, like little windows, in which the lamps were placed. Some have represented these by images of the months, which are distributed among the four seasons of the year, as follows.

units.la: Porrò quatuor Anni tempora, Horæ a Græcis & Latinis appellata, canquam Deæ fuerunt cultæ, quæ Cælum aperire & claudere dicebantur, cesse Eusebio in præparatione Evangelica. Hæ interdum Soli tribuuntur (qui Horus ab Ægypeus fuit dictus) interdum & Cereri, atque ei duos calathos ferunt: alterū florum plenum, quibus Ver tumuitur: alterum siculus, quibus Æstas significatur. Eas Ovidius libro 5. Florae comites facit, sicq; Florum dicencem inducit:
units.tr: Furthermore, the four seasons of the year, called Hours by Greeks and Latins, were worshipped as goddesses, who were said to open and close the sky, as Eusebius says in his Preparation for the Gospel. Sometimes these are attributed to the sun (which the Egyptians called Horus), and sometimes to Ceres, and they bring her two baskets: one full of flowers, with which spring is adorned, the other of ears of grain, by which summer is signified. Ovid, in book 5, makes them companions of Flora, and introduces Flora speaking:

units.la: Ibidem libro 5. Florae comites facit, sicq; Florum dicencem inducit: Conveniunt pluvis incincte vestibus Horæ, Ing leg' calathos muneraque nostra legunt.
units.tr: In the same book 5 Ovid makes them companions of Flora and introduces Flora speaking: "The Hours, dressed in light robes, come together and gather baskets and my gifts."
Description of the Hours.

units.la: Harum Horarū, id est, quatuor Temporū anni, elegantissima hæc exstat apud Ovidiū descriptio: Ver, novum stabat cinctum florente corona. Stabat nuda Æstas et spicea ferta gerebat. Stabat & Autumnus calcatu sordibus uvis, Et glaciali Hyemi, canos hirsuta capillos.
units.tr: Ovid gives an elegant description of these Hours, that is, of the four seasons of the year: "New Spring stood, wreathed with a flowering crown. Summer stood naked and bore ears of grain. Autumn also stood, its feet stained with the juice of trodden grapes, and Winter, shaggy, with its hair grey from the ice."

units.la: Alia item imagine hæc quatuor Anni tempora ostendebantur; sicut Venus pro Vere, pro Æstate Ceres, pro Autumno Bacchus accipiatur. Hiemem parium Vulcanus, ad fornacem ardent. dentem adflans, partim Venti, unâcum eorum Rege Aeolo (Hoc tnim tempore, si unquâ alias, Venti tenipestate iq, excitantur: unde Hiems, Winter/Germans a Wind/ i dest, ventus, dicitur.) repraesentant: de quibus haec pulcherrima exstant Epigrammata,
units.tr: The four seasons of the year were also shown by another image: Venus was taken for Spring, Ceres for Summer, Bacchus for Autumn. Winter was represented partly by Vulcan, blowing at his glowing furnace, and partly by the winds together with their king Aeolus. (For at this time, if ever, the winds are stirred up by storms; hence Hiems, in German Winter, is said to come from Wind, that is, wind.) There are very fine epigrams on these:

units.la: De vere: Cum viridi ridgnt vernantes gramine campi, Et pictis pascunt horti oculos oculus, Alma Venus colitur: Venerem genus omne animantum Sentit: amat blando tempore blanda coli.
units.tr: On Spring: When the fields, blooming with green grass, laugh, and gardens feed the eyes with painted colours, gentle Venus is worshipped: every kind of living creature feels Venus, and in a pleasant season loves to be cherished.

units.la: De Aestate: Aestivari cum Sol premit horrida terga Leonis Virginis & sensim labitur in gremium: Flava Ceres gravibus compensat messibus aestus: Conflans a Superis praemia sudor habet.
units.tr: On Summer: When the Sun, in summer, presses the bristling back of the Lion, and gradually slides into the lap of the Virgin, golden Ceres balances the heat with heavy harvests; the sweat that is poured out has the rewards of the gods above.

units.la: De Autumno: Tertia succedit Bacchi variabilis aetas, Sentit adesse novos rustica turba Deos: Inprimis hilari juvenientem fronte Lyaeum, Est juvenis: juvenes nam facit ille senes.
units.tr: On Autumn: The third age, that of changeable Bacchus, follows; the rustic crowd feels that new gods are present. Above all, Lyaeus, coming with a cheerful brow, is young, for he makes the young old.

units.la: De Hiems: Aeolus ut Boreae laxavit frena furentis Tristibus & speciis tristis oberrat agris: Sic lecis ne luxuriet mens nostra secundis, Admisceat mestis praesicia fata vices.
units.tr: On Winter: As Aeolus loosens the reins of raging Boreas, the sad one wanders over the sorrowful fields with sad appearance; so let our mind not grow wanton with prosperous things, but let foreseen fates mix their changes with sorrows.

units.la: Sic ergo quatuor Anni tempora Horarum nomine aliuq imaginibus fuerunt significata ac admumbrata.
units.tr: Thus the four seasons of the year were signified and shadowed forth under the name of Hours and by other images.

units.la: Iam vero Menses quoq; certus Dijs consecrarunt: omnes quidem Junoni, sexte Plutarcho, ut annum uni versum Iovi & Jano: singulos vero alius arg, alius. Apud Romanos Romulus menses primus: Martium dixit, a Marte, quem voluit esse sum parentem, cui eum consecravit: alii tamen eum Minervae tutela fuisse seruntur. Secundum vocavit Aprilem, a Venere principe sui generis, in cujus tutela hic mensis est, quae Graece a ἀφροδίτη dicitur, ut sic Aprilis, quasi Aphro dilis. Tertium mensem a Jovenibus dixit Majorum, dixit Majum, quem alii a Deo Majo volunt dictum, qui est Jupiter, a magnitudine videlicet & majestate: alii vero a Majestate, Dea magi-stratuum: alii a Maia, Vulcani, vel ut alii volunt, Mercurii uxore. Fuit autem hic mensis in Apollinis tutela. Quaerum a juvenibus junium dixit: quem alii a Junone quasi junonium: alii a Junio Bruto, primo Romanorum Consule, volunt nuncupatum. Hunc peculiariter junoni sacrum fuisse fecit. ut Plutarchus in Quaest. Rom. 86. Cur mense Majo mulieres non ducantur: alii tamen in Mercurii tutela fuisse dicunt. Reliquo denique a numero & ordine nuncupatur. Nam quintum mensem dixit Quintilem: qui postea Julius vocatus est propter Julium Caesarem, postquam is relatus est in numerum Deorum Romanorum. Fuit mensis hic in tutela Jovis. Sextum, quem Ceres tutela fuit, dixit Sextilem, quem Augustum postea dixerunt propter Octavianum Augustum, cui is fuit quoq; dedicatus. Septimum mensem dixit Septembrem: quem Senatus Rom. in Tiberii Augusti honorem Tiberium appellari voluit, quod tamen ne fieret, ipsemet intercessit. Idi Germanicus, Antoninus, Hercules, Tacitus fuit cognominatus, ac in Vulcani tutela fuisse existimatus. Octavum Octobrem; quem Domitianus a suo nomine Domitianum, appellavit, quod eo natus esset mense. Faustinus etiam dictus, in honorem Faustinae uxoris M. Antonini, Imp. ut a Commodo Invictus. Hicin Martis tutela fuit. Nonum Novembrem vocavit, qui a Comodo Imperatorius dictus in Dianae tutela fuit. Decimum deniq; dixit Decembrem: qui ab adulatoribus Commodi Imp. Amazonius appellatur in tutela Vestae fuit. Hic Numa Pompilius duos postea addidit januarium, in honorem Jani, qui vetus fuit cum Saturno Latii rectoe, & Februarium, sic dictum a Februis, id est, inferiis, ac caenis & caeis, quae anni extremo mensis inferebantur sepulchris mortuorum & bustis, ut Umbrae quaeserent ac ne cuiquam molestae esset, ut docet Ovidius in Fastorum libro Fastus, Varro & alii talia sacrorum veterum interpretes. Hunc tamen mensem Macrobius Saturnalium ca. 12. a Februo, Deo lustrationi, vult dictum, cui a Numa fuerit dicatus. Lustrum vero civitatem eo mense necesse fuisse, ut justa Diis Manibus solverentur. V autem januarius in tutela Junonis fuit, sic hic ultimus in Neptuni. Verum de hac vide plura apud Macrobium, Censorinum, Varronem, Ovidium, & apud recentiores, potissimum Gyraldum. Hi autem Dii omnes, qui duodecim mensibus praesse credebantur, uno nomine Consentes, quasi Consentientes fuerunt dicti, qui in consilium Iovis adhiberi putabantur: quorum Augustinus 4. de Civitate Dei, & Seneca lib. 2. Quaestionum naturalium meminit: unde sacra Consentia dicta.
units.tr: Now the months too were consecrated by certain gods: all of them to Juno, as Plutarch says, just as the whole year was to Jupiter and Janus, but each one to a different god. Among the Romans Romulus first named the month Martius, from Mars, whom he claimed as his father, and to whom he dedicated it; yet some say it was under the protection of Minerva. The second he called Aprilis, after Venus, the chief of his own kind, under whose protection this month is, who is called Aphrodite in Greek, so that April is as it were Aphrodilis. The third month he called Maius, from the elders (maiores), and some want it named after the god Maius, who is Jupiter, from his greatness and majesty; others from Majesty, the goddess of magistrates; others from Maia, the wife of Vulcan or, as others say, of Mercury. This month was under the protection of Apollo. He called the fourth Junius, from the young men (iuniores); some want it called from Juno, as if Junonius; others from Junius Brutus, the first consul of the Romans. Plutarch, in Roman Questions 86 (Why women are not married in the month of May), makes this month especially sacred to Juno; yet others say it was under the protection of Mercury. Finally the remaining months are named from their number and order. For the fifth month he called Quintilis, which was later called Julius because of Julius Caesar, after he had been received into the number of the Roman gods; this month was under the protection of Jupiter. The sixth, which was under the protection of Ceres, he called Sextilis, which they later called Augustus because of the emperor Augustus Octavianus, to whom it was also dedicated. The seventh month he called September, which the Roman Senate wished to be called Tiberius in honour of Tiberius Augustus, though he himself prevented this from happening. Thus it was surnamed Germanicus, Antoninus, Hercules, Tacitus, and was thought to be under the protection of Vulcan. The eighth, October, which Domitian called Domitianus after his own name, because he had been born in that month; it was also called Faustinus, in honour of Faustina, the wife of Marcus Antoninus the emperor, and by Commodus Invictus. This was under the protection of Mars. The ninth he called November, which was named Imperatorius by Commodus, and was under the protection of Diana. Finally the tenth he called December, which was called Amazonius by the flatterers of the emperor Commodus, and was under the protection of Vesta. To these, Numa Pompilius afterwards added two: January, in honour of Janus, who was of old, together with Saturn, a ruler of Latium; and February, so called from the Februa, that is, funeral offerings, and the cakes and gifts which were brought at the year's end to the tombs and funeral pyres of the dead, so that the shades might be fed and not troubled anyone. So Ovid teaches in the Fasti, and Varro and other interpreters of the ancient rites say the same. Macrobius (Saturnalia, ch. 12), however, holds that this month was named after Februus, a god of purification, to whom Numa had dedicated it; and that in that month it was necessary for the city to be purified by lustration, so that the due rites might be paid to the Manes. January was under the protection of Juno, and so the last, February, under that of Neptune. On these matters see more in Macrobius, Censorinus, Varro, Ovid, and among recent writers especially Gyraldus. All these gods who were believed to preside over the twelve months were called by one name, the Consentes, as if Consentientes, because they were thought to be called to the council of Jupiter. Augustine (City of God, book 4) and Seneca (Natural Questions, book 2) mention them; hence they were called the Consentian gods.

units.la: Porrò Mensium apud Romanos praecipuae partes erant Kalendae, Nonae, Idus. Kalendae praeerat Iuno. (Sic enim Ovidius:
units.tr: Moreover, among the Romans the chief parts of the month were the Kalends, the Nones and the Ides. The Kalends were presided over by Juno. (For so Ovid says:

units.la: Vendicat Aufonias iunonis cura Kalendas.) itemque Ianus; quia omnium primordiorum Deus putabatur, & idcirco iunonibus fuit dictus, quod omnium mensium ingressum teneret, ut etiam juno, Kalendis, fœneratores pecunias collocare solebant.
units.tr: The care of Juno claims the Ausonian Kalends.) and likewise by Janus, because he was thought to be the god of all beginnings; and for this reason he was called Juno's (Iunones), because he held the entrance of every month, just as Juno did; on the Kalends, moneylenders used to lend out their money.

units.la: Idus omnes jovi sacrae erant; ideoque ipsi ovis inadtabatur, quae ob hoc dicebatur Idulus, Ovidius:
units.tr: All the Ides were sacred to Jupiter. For this reason a ewe was sacrificed to him, and it was called the Idulis. Ovid:

units.la: Idibus alba jovi grandior agna cadit. Festus: Idulis ovis dicebatur, quae omnibus Idibus jovi mactabatur. Idem testatur Macrobius libro 1. Saturnalium.
units.tr: "On the Ides a white lamb, rather large, falls for Jupiter." Festus: the Idulis was a ewe that was slaughtered to Jupiter on every Ides. Macrobius says the same in the first book of his Saturnalia.

units.la: Praeterea, apud Ethnicos, Graecos, Romanos & alios, singulorum mensium dies certos atque festos erant dicati, ut ex Kalendario Romano & multis aliis scriptis liquidis constat.
units.tr: Moreover, among the pagans, Greeks, Romans and others, certain and festal days were dedicated to each month, as is clear from the Roman calendar and many other plain writings.

units.la: Hebdomadum seu septimanarum ratio quoniam solus Hebraeis fuit nota, caeteris autem gentibus incognita: idcirco nihil hic de illis affirmare possumus, quibus nam Dies singula hebdomades fuerint consecratae.
units.tr: Since the reckoning of weeks, or sevens of days, was known only to the Hebrews and unknown to the other nations, we cannot affirm anything here about which days of each week were consecrated to which gods.

units.la: Quantum ad Dies attinet, Dies quidem in genere jovi: Nodes vero junoni erant dicatae. Dies, inquit Festus, dictus, quod diuini sit operis, sive ab jove, ejus, ut putabant, auctore, quem Graece Δία appellant: sive quod aër diurnus debiscat in candorem. Hinc Diespiter dictus jupiter, quasi Dies pater, sicut Dyovis appellatus est, quasi Diem juvant, quod homines die & qualuce juvaret. Unde Lucerium quoque a Veteribus Salius nominatum legimus. Cretenses ψωφο-pov, id est, Luciferum vocarunt. Hinc etiam Idus dicta Iuis, hoc est, jovis fiducia. Vide supra de Idibus.
units.tr: As far as the days are concerned, the days in general were dedicated to Jupiter, and the nights to Juno. Festus says that "dies" (day) is so called because it belongs to divine work, either from Jupiter, its author as they supposed, whom the Greeks call Zeus [Δία], or because the daylight air opens into brightness. Hence Jupiter was called Diespiter, as if "Dies pater" (father Day), and Dyovis, as if helping the day (Diem juvans), because he helped men by day and by light. From this we also read that the morning star was called Lucerius by the ancients, and that the Cretans called Lucifer [φωσφόρον]. Hence also the Ides were called Iuis, that is, the trust of Jupiter. See above on the Ides.

units.la: Nox similiter, quae Dei civilis pars est, ut Dea, ab Ethnicis in suis culta, quam Ararms ἀρχαῖλω, id est, antiquam, & interpres ex Hesiodi sententia Deorum antiquissimam vocat. Hi Hesiodus Chaos filium & Aetherus, atque Dies matrem, Orpheus Deorum hominumque, matrem & genesin omnium vocat: cujus sané sub nomine Tenebrarum, quae dicuntur fuisse ... thohu, vabohu, in sacris litteris in Mundi creatione primo fit mentio. Illius descriptio & hymnus pulcherrimus extat apud Orpheum & Statium Papinium libro 2. Theb. De Noctis nominibus & sacrificiis vide plura apud Gyraldum: quam certe non mirum est Ethnicos, Noctis & Tenebrarum, id est, ignorantiae & erroris filios, ceu matrem suam religiose, seu superstitiose potius coluisse.
units.tr: Night likewise, which is a part of the civil god, was worshipped by the pagans as a goddess. Aratus calls her most ancient [ἀρχαιοτάτην], and an interpreter, following Hesiod's opinion, calls her the most ancient of the gods. Hesiod makes her the offspring of Chaos, and Aether and Day her children; Orpheus calls her the mother and origin of gods and men. Under the name of darkness, which in the sacred letters is said to have been "tohu and bohu" [תֹּהוּ וָבֹהוּ], she is first mentioned at the creation of the world. Her description and a most beautiful hymn to her are found in Orpheus and in Statius Papinius, Thebaid book 2. For more on the names and sacrifices of Night, see Gyraldus. It is no wonder that the pagans, sons of Night and darkness, that is, of ignorance and error, worshipped their mother with religious, or rather superstitious, devotion.

units.la: Jam vero singuli etiam Hebdomadum dies Planetis, quos, ut Deos, colebant, erant dicati, ut Soli, Lunae, Martis, Mercurio, Jovi, Veneri, & Saturno, secundum per vulgatos illos versiculos: Prima dies Phoebi sacrato nomine fulgens Vendicat, & lucens feriam sibi Luna secundam. Inde dies rutilae jam tertia Martis honore. Mercurium quartam splendentem posuisse altam, Quinta Jovi est, de votâ religione dicata. Concordat Veneri magno cum nomine sexta. Emicat alma dies Saturno septima summo.
units.tr: Now each of the days of the week was also dedicated to the planets, which they worshipped as gods: to the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn, according to the common verses: "The first day, shining with the sacred name of Phoebus, claims for itself; and the Moon, shining, claims the second. Then the third day, of ruddy Mars' honour. Mercury has placed the fourth day, bright and high. The fifth belongs to Jupiter, dedicated by a vowed worship. Venus agrees with the sixth, by her great name. The seventh day, kindly, gleams for Saturn, supreme."

units.la: Primus igitur Hebdomadae dies Soli, secundus Lunae, tertius Martis, quartus Mercurii, quintus Jovis, sextus Veneri, septimus Saturno fuit dicatus.
units.tr: Thus the first day of the week was dedicated to the Sun, the second to the Moon, the third to Mars, the fourth to Mercury, the fifth to Jupiter, the sixth to Venus, and the seventh to Saturn.

units.la: Postremo Horas quoque, in quas dies distinguuntur, certis Planetis, tanquam Dies concrarunt, & certis actionibus definarunt, quae Planetariae, Naturales & Inaequales appellantur. Horae principio erant XII; cujus ordinationis haec traditur origo: Hermes Trismegistus, cum esset in Aegypto, sacrum quoddam animal, Serapidicatum, animadvertit in die toto duodecies urinam facere, pari semper interposito tempore: unde per XII Horas diem dividi debere conjecit, & inde Horas nonnulli volunt dictas ΧϏρας του ὑρου, id est, urina, quaß primum dicta sint ὑρας, quae postea sint appellatae ὑρας. Sed & ista X II. Horarum ratio fuit duplicata, & in X X I V. Horarum ratio duplicata. Horas dies divisus. Horam etiam veteres juventutis Deam vocabant: unde Ennius,
units.tr: Finally, they also assigned the hours, into which the days are divided, to certain planets, as if they were days, and defined them by certain activities; these are called planetary, natural and unequal hours. At first there were twelve hours. The origin of this arrangement is said to be this: Hermes Trismegistus, while in Egypt, noticed that a certain sacred animal, consecrated to Serapis, urinated twelve times in the whole day, always at equal intervals. From this he conjectured that the day ought to be divided into twelve hours. Some hold that the hours were so named from urine [οὖρον], as if the hours [ὧραι] were first called "ourai" from it and later called "hōrai." But this reckoning of twelve hours was doubled, and the day was divided into twenty-four hours. The ancients also worshipped Hora as the goddess of youth; hence Ennius: "I venerate you, father Quirinus, and Hora of Quirinus." Some think she is the same as Horta, of whom we shall speak later.

units.la: Te, Quirine pater, veneror, Horamq; Quirini. Hanc nonnulli eandem volunt esse, quae Horta, de qua postea.
units.tr: Te, Quirine pater, veneror, Horamque Quirini. Some hold that this Hora is the same as Horta, about whom more below.

units.la: Et haec de Temporis cum universi, tum singularum ejus partium cultu superstitioso & idolo- Occasio pars latrico: ad quod Occasio quoque referri potest, quam Veteres pro Dea coluerunt. Occasio enim, ut temporis est apud Ciceronem in libro de Inventione, est pars temporis, habens in se aliquae rei idoneam faciendi aut non faciendi opportunitatem. Et, in Occasione ad ipsacum temporis faciendi quaedam opportunitas incelligitur. Item, Tempus actionis opportunum, Graece καιρός, Latine appellatur Occasio. Hanc Poetae filiam Saturni minimam fuisse finxerunt.
units.tr: And these things concern the superstitious and idolatrous worship of time, both of the whole universe and of its individual parts. To this may also be referred Occasion, whom the ancients worshipped as a goddess. For Occasion, as Cicero says in his book On Invention, is a part of time, having in itself a fitting opportunity for doing or not doing something; and in Occasion one understands a certain opportunity for acting at the very moment of time. Likewise, the favourable time for an action, which in Greek is called καιρός [kairos], is called Occasion in Latin. The poets feigned her to be the youngest daughter of Saturn.

units.la: Vt autem illi Tempus superstitiose colueruntur: sic nos Christiani solum Deum, ut Mundi, ita Solus Deus, cum Temporis suae Temporis quoque cum universi, cum singularum ejus partium, vel minimarum, cujusmodi sunt momenta, & creatorem, & confer vitorem, & moderatorem credimus & confitemur esse omnium, dior colendus. pulcherrimum ac sapientissimum. Tempora, ut scripsum est Iob 14. cap. non sunt abscondita ab Omnipotente. Tempora, inquit Christus ipse, & Temporum momenta Pater posuit in sua potestate. Act. 1. cap. Tempora, ut aie Ecclesiasticus cap. 29. immutavit Dei sapientia per motum Solis & Astrorum & dies festos ipsorum: & in illis dies festos celebrare veruic ad horam.
units.tr: Just as they worshipped Time superstitiously, so we Christians believe and confess that the one God alone, the creator, preserver and governor of all things, is to be worshipped as the most excellent and wisest of all. He is the Lord of time as a whole and of each of its parts, even the smallest, such as moments. As it is written in Job 14, "the times are not hidden from the Almighty." Christ himself says, "The Father has put the times and seasons in his own power" (Acts 1). As Ecclesiasticus [cap. 29] says, the wisdom of God has ordered the times by the motion of the sun and stars and their festal days, and it is right to celebrate the festal days in their hours.

units.la: Porro Mundi partes sive membra principalia sunt Caelum, Terra, Maria. Haec quoque & Mundi partes. illorum partes, omniaque quae in iis continentur vel minima, vilissima & abjectissima quaeque, vel Numinum loco fuerunt habita atque culta, vel ceres Numinibus consecrata.
units.tr: The principal parts or members of the world are heaven, earth and seas. These parts, and all that is contained in them, even the smallest, meanest and most abject things, have either been regarded as deities and worshipped in their place, or dedicated to the deities.

units.la: AC COELVM primum ipsum universum (שָּמַים, Schamaim, Hebraeis dictum, quod οὐρανός illic sint aquae; & ὐρανός Graecis, ab altitudine seu lucididate: sive quid dextremus fit Mundi terminus, cultus minus, sive determinatio) Deum appellarunt, et ceu Deum coluerunt, Saturni, idest, Tempora. Caeli. rus patrem fingentes: hujus vero parentes Ae: hera & Diem, ut ceftatur Ci ero de Natura Deorum. Theophrastus modo Menu: divinum tribuit principatum: modo Caelo; tum autem signis fido ribus, caelestibus. Aethiopes, Africae populi, hunc primum Deum apud se regnaffe praedicabant, teste Eusebio, & Diodoro. Persae quoque, teste Strabone, Caelum Deum pucabant, & Iovem appellabant.
units.tr: First of all, heaven itself as a whole, called in Hebrew shamayim [שָּׁמַיִם], because there are waters there, and in Greek ouranos [οὐρανός], from its height or brightness; or because it is the outermost limit of the world. Men worshipped it as God and as a god, feigning Heaven to be the father of Saturn (that is, of Time). Its parents were Aether and Day, as Cicero testifies in On the Nature of the Gods. Theophrastus at one time ascribes the divine principate to Mind, at another to Heaven, and then to the fixed stars and planets. The Ethiopians, peoples of Africa, claimed that this Heaven first reigned among them as god, as Eusebius and Diodorus attest. The Persians too, as Strabo testifies, worshipped Heaven as God and called him Jupiter.

units.la: Hic obser vandum Caelii sive Caelorum nomen in sacris litteris, figurae loquendi, quae a Gram- Caelorum non maticis μετωνυμια, id est, Transnominatio dicitur, pro Deo, sive Domino & possessore Caelorum men pro Deo aliquando ac cepi. Sic quidam inter precandum illa fili perditi & prodigi confessiones verba, Peccavi in Caelum, id est, Deum: ubi per id, quod continet, id quod continet, significatur. Cui & illud addi potest, Baptismus Iohannis de Caelo erat, an ab hominibus? Sic Poeta quidam e veteribus, Caelo gratissimus amnis, dixit, pro Deis, quicunque continentur. Sic Matth. 3. 18. τὸ δί τοὺπνεύτου τὸν εὐρανόν. Eaxiffor tuo οὐρανοὺ σοὺ, ὁν πολλοίς, ὁ ἐ ζαραοις, Non est differentia in conspicuo Caeli sal- var in multis vel in paucis. Rursus Matth. 4. 19. και παραλεγαλεγον. Nunc autem Caelum inclamabimus, utrum misereatur nostri Quibus locis manifesta Deus significatur, sed impropriè, ut dictum. Sed & Rabbini saepenumero ita usurpant, ut cum dicunt, Omnis est in manu Caeli. Item: Sit timor Caeli super nos: & Nomen Caeli frequens in ore ipsius. Sic, Timor hominum sit praevaluerit, excludit, vel ut alii legunt, expellit timorem Caeli. Hac- nus de οὐρανος.
units.tr: Here we must observe that the name "Heaven" or "Heavens" in the sacred letters is a figure of speech which the grammarians call metonymy, or transnomination, and is sometimes taken for God, or the Lord and possessor of the heavens. Thus in the confession of the prodigal son's prayer, "I have sinned against heaven" means against God, where what contains is put for what is contained. To this may be added, "The baptism of John, was it from heaven or from men?" So an ancient poet said "the river most pleasing to heaven," meaning the gods who are contained there. So Matthew 3 [18]: "the heavens" [οὐρανούς]. It makes no difference in the visible heaven whether it saves in many or in few. Again, Matthew 4 [19]: "Now we will call upon heaven, whether it will have mercy on us." In these places God is clearly signified, though improperly, as has been said. The rabbis too very often use the word in this way: as when they say, "All is in the hand of Heaven"; and, "Let the fear of Heaven be upon us"; and the name of Heaven is frequent on their lips. So, "Let the fear of men prevail; it shuts out, or, as others read, drives out the fear of Heaven." Thus far on ouranos [οὐρανός].

units.la: I. Iterum, cum Caeli duae sint partes, nempe Aiθηρ Graece, Latine Aether, & Anp, Latine Aer, uterque illis Numen vel Deus fuit.
units.tr: I. Again, since the heavens have two parts, namely the aether, called Aἰθήρ in Greek and Aether in Latin, and the air, called ἀήρ in Greek and Aer in Latin, each of these was also held to be a deity or god.

units.la: AETHER, Graece sic dicitur est partim ab ardore atque splendore lucidissimo, partim a peren- Aiθρολο- ni perpetuo, cursu, nimirum vel αὐειρ, id est, splendere, vel αὶει, id est, semper currere. Hinc Hesiodus, libro de Natura Deorum, ardorem ultimum, certissimum, undiq; circumfusum, aërem Aetheris. compleitur, in quo astra volvantur, vocat. Idem: Ultimus & a domicilius nostris alicissimus, omnia cinctus & circens Caeli complexus, qui idem Aether vocatur, extrema ora & determinatio Mundi, quam homines Iovem appellant. Atq; hic Aether, ut est apud eundem, Stratoui, Zeno- ni & reliquis fuit. Scaeva videbatur summus Deus mente praeditus, qua omnia reganturi.
units.tr: Aether, as it is called in Greek, takes its name partly from its burning and most bright splendour, and partly from its perpetual, unceasing motion: that is, either from αὐειρ, meaning to shine, or from αἰεὶ, meaning always to run. Hence Hesiod, in his book On the Nature of the Gods, calls the outermost, most certain, all-surrounding fire, which encloses the air of the aether and in which the stars revolve, the aether. He says also: the outermost and most remote from our dwellings, which encircles and embraces all things and the heavens, which is also called aether, is the extreme edge and boundary of the world, which men call Jove. And this aether, as the same writer says, was held to be the highest god, endowed with mind, by which all things are governed, by Strato, Zeno and the rest of the Stoics.

units.la: AETHER autem astra, sidera atque stellas, partim fixas & non errantes, partim errantes, vagas atque mobiles complectitur. Sic enim Cicero: Sidera aethereum locum obtinent. Haec autem stellae uniuersae & singulae, quas exercitum seu multitudinem Caeli sacra scriptura hinc inde vocat, pro Deus ac Deabus ab omnibus fere gentibus habitae fuerunt atque cultae: quod notum est vel ex ipsa sacra scriptura; ubi exprobrat Deus Iudaeis, aliquoties, quod men sam para verint, id est, sacrificaverunt numeris stellarum, more Ethnicorum (sic enim E.5.65.11. quida interpretantur vocem Hebraeam נְכִיוֹר Gad: quam vel alii Martem, alii Iovem; alii Fortunam; alii Saturnum, alii deniq; Mercurium interpretentur.) Sic Amos 5.26. illis exprobrat, quod fidus Dei sui humeris gestaverint, id est, sidera, Deorum more, coluerunt: ubi תְּכוּנָן Cijun (vel, ut alu leguntur כִּיּוּן) Ceuan; unde postea Revan, & Rephan, & tandem Remphan eo Allorum loco, scribi saepe euphoniae gratia) in Iheste Saturnum interpretatur Aben Ezra, & stellam Luciferum Hieroniymus, quem etiam suae dicit a Saracenis cultum fuisse. Idem porro liquidissime constat ex illo loco Sapient. 13. ἀ-στρα, ὡραν, Lumina caeli, a quibus Mundus regitur, Deos putarunt. Et Cicero libro de Natura Deorum id multis probat: ubi inter alios Zenonem, Cretoniatem, Alcmaeum, & Parmenidem inducit: item Ponticum Heraclidem, qui ex Platonis discipulis nam do Mundum: cum Mentem divinam esse putarunt: modo sideribus & errantibus stellis divinatem tribuerunt.
units.tr: The aether, moreover, embraces the stars, the constellations and the planets, some fixed and not wandering, others wandering, roving and mobile. For Cicero says: "The stars occupy the ethereal place." These stars, all together and each one, which Holy Scripture calls the host or multitude of heaven, were held and worshipped as gods and goddesses by almost all nations; this is known even from Holy Scripture, where God often upbraids the Jews because they prepared a table for Gad (or, as some translate the Hebrew word גד, Gad, some Mars, others Jupiter, others Fortune, others Saturn, and finally others Mercury), that is, they sacrificed to the number of the stars, after the manner of the heathen. So in Amos 5:26 he upbraids them because they carried the star of their god on their shoulders, that is, they worshipped the stars after the manner of the gods; there the word כיון, Chiun (or, as others read it, Kiyyun), Kevan, from which later Revan, Rephan and at last Remphan, which in that place of the Septuagint is often written for the sake of euphony, is interpreted by Abenezra as Saturn, and by Jerome as the morning star, which he says was also worshipped by the Saracens. The same is most clearly established by that passage of Wisdom 13: "They thought the stars, the heavens, the lights of heaven, which govern the world, to be gods." And Cicero, in his book On the Nature of the Gods, proves this by many examples, where among others he introduces Zeno, Cleanthes, Alcmaeon and Parmenides, and likewise the Pontic Heraclides, who, among the disciples of Plato, said that the world was a divine mind, and yet attributed divinity to the stars and the wandering planets.

units.la: INTER haec autem Caeli sive Aetheris signa principem locum obtinere constat Solem atque Lunam: quae idcirco pre reliquis astris, a cunctis fere gentibus, praesertim Aegyptiis, omnium mortalium primus, Phoenicibus Graecis, ut papyrum ex omnibus tam sacris, quam prophanis litteratorum monumentis: maxime vero ex Platone, Diodoro Siculo, Plutarcho & aliis liquet) divinis fuerunt assetta honoribus.
units.tr: Among these signs of heaven or aether, it is established that the Sun and the Moon hold the principal place. For this reason, above the other stars, they were honoured with divine honours by almost all nations, especially the Egyptians, Phoenicians and Greeks, as is clear from all the monuments of learned men, both sacred and profane, and above all from Plato, Diodorus Siculus, Plutarch and others.

units.la: Sol, ut inquit M. Tullius, dictus est vel quia solus ex omnibus sideribus est tantus: mirabiliter dine videlicet tanta, quanta astrorum maximo competit; terrae major secundum Ptolemaeum centuet sexagies sexies: sed secundum recentiorem Copernici observationem centies sexagies bis unde maximus Deorum a Persis & Magiis dictus fuit: quem in antiquo quodam venerabantur, teste Lactantio, Statio interprete) vel, quia cum exortus est, obscuratis caeteris lucibus, lumen fulget, dominus diei meus Mundi, cor Caeli, dux & princeps moderator, reliquorum luminum atque temporum, & ut apud Ovidium quarto Metamorphos. de se ait; Ille ego sum, qui longum metior annum, Omnia qui video, per quem videt omnia Mundus, Mundi oculus.——
units.tr: The Sun, as Marcus Tullius says, is so called either because it alone of all the stars is so great, being indeed a wonderfully vast body, as great as the largest of the stars is fitted to be; according to Ptolemy it is larger than the earth one hundred and sixty-six times, but according to the more recent observation of Copernicus two hundred and twenty times... Hence he was called by the Persians and Magi the greatest of the gods, and in some ancient rite he was worshipped, as Lactantius testifies, with Statius as interpreter. Or the Sun is so called because, when it rises, the other lights being obscured, its light shines forth: the lord of the day, the eye of the world, the heart of heaven, the leader and prince who governs the other lights and seasons; and as Ovid says of himself in the fourth book of the Metamorphoses: "It is I who measure out the long year, I who see all things, through whom the world sees all things, the eye of the world."

units.la: Veteribus nomine Iovis, ὁ ὑς ἐξεσσ ἀπολλων. ἀ-τῆς ἀγαθῶν πάντων ... spiritus per omnia comeantes, Phaëtontis, Horus, Serapidis, Osiridis, Mythrae sive Mythras, Beli, Phoebi, Apollinis, Panis, Titanis, aliisq; infinitis (ut Macrobius fuse demonstrat) appellatus: Graecis ἥλιος: Hebraeis & Chaldaeis Chammah, Chaeras, & Schaemasch, partim a talore ... sacrificatione, per excellentiam: partim a ministerio, quod praebet reliquis astris, ex luce submin- istrando.
units.tr: Among the ancients he was called by the name of Jove; Apollo ... the spirit moving through all things, Phaethon, Horus, Serapis, Osiris, Mithras or Mithras, Bel, Phoebus, Apollo, Pan, Titan, and by countless other names (as Macrobius shows at length). The Greeks called him ἥλιος; the Hebrews and Chaldeans called him Chammah, Chaeras and Shemesh, partly from his ... sacrifice, by excellence, and partly from the service he renders to the other stars, by lending them light.

units.la: Nec vero tantum Graeci & aliae gentes Solem illis nominibus appellarunt, sed etiam coluerunt & venerati sunt: quorum quidem Deorum nomina, cognomina, imagines, statuae, & similia, quae fabulae illis affinxerunt innumera, Solis vim, naturam, celeritatem, efficacitatem, pulchritudinem, splendorem admirabilem: (unde in sacris litteris etiam Sponsus, egredienti e talamo, eleganti stimet festite, comparatur) significarunt.
units.tr: Nor did the Greeks and other nations only call the Sun by these names; they also worshipped and revered him. Their names, surnames, images, statues and the like, which the fables attributed to these gods in countless numbers, signify the power, nature, speed, efficacy, beauty and wonderful splendour of the Sun. (Hence in Holy Scripture the bridegroom, going out of his chamber, is compared to him as to a splendid thing.)

units.la: Horum autem Aegyptii appellarunt Solem, voce, ut verisimile est, deducta ab Hebraea ... Or, quae lucem sive lumen significat, quod Sol fons sit luminis, ut dictus. Inde Horae dictae, id est, quatuor anni Tempora; quas Homerus finxit Caeli portae praeesse, Caelum modo claudere, modo aperire, illudque, modo serenum, modo nubilum efficere, & Solis equos curare, quod nimirum Solis currumque sumen furent ac distinguantur: unde Ovidius libro undecimo Metamorph. Iungere equos Titan velocibus imperat Horis: Iussa Deae celeres peragunt.——
units.tr: The Egyptians called the Sun by a word, as is likely, derived from the Hebrew אור, Or, which means light, because the Sun is the fountain of light, as has been said. From him the Hours were named, that is, the four seasons of the year; Homer feigned that they presided over the gates of heaven, now closing and now opening heaven, and making it now serene and now cloudy, and that they tended the horses of the Sun, because indeed they distinguish and divide the Sun's course and chariot. Hence Ovid in the eleventh book of the Metamorphoses: "Titan orders the swift Hours to yoke the horses; the goddess's commands they carry out swiftly."

units.la: Macrobius similiter Horum pro Sole tapi vult, ab eoque Horas, in quat dies est distributus, esse dictas, dicta, lib. 1. Saturnal. Horum idem etiam fuit, qui Osiris, apud Aegyptios, accipitris formā ex- pressus, quae a vi, quia & nocte clarè cernit, & velocissimè volat, Solis clara est imago, ad eius cum splendorem, tum velocitatem exprimendā. Apud quosdam, ut Heliopolitanos, Sol felis erat speciem prae se ferebat, ob eandem rationem. Nam & felis nocte clarissimè cernit, & velocissimus est: unde αἰλουρος fuit dictus. Sic Lycopolitani, quae civitas est Thebaidos Aegypti, pari religione Apollinem, & λύκον, id est, lupum colebat, in utroq; Solem venerantes, quia hoc animal Solis in modum omnia rapit & consumit, & oculorum acutissimā actie praeditū, noctu quoq; videt, tenebrarū, nocturnas vincit: quod notū vel ex proverbio, Lupi vespertinis acutior, Habac. 1. 8. & inde quod λύκος Graecè dictus, ἀπὸ λύκης, id est, a luce videtur dictus. Hic non omittendum videtur, quod Aelianus docet, in historia animalium ita scribens: Οξυόπτατον δ' ἐκ ἴχει ζῶον. ἐ μέτοι & λυκτος & σελήνης ὡς ἕσης οὐ ὄψεως ὄψει ... Quae sic versa sunt in editione Tigurina: Acerrimū (lupus) atq; acutissimus praeditus est oculis. Enim vero intempestiā nocte, vel Luna ipsa silente lucus usum perfruitur, & licet omnib. tenebrae offundantur; non huic tamen lux eripitur.
