Hinc Lycophos id temporis appellatur, cùm lucem is solus naturae munere percepit. Et vero Homerus mihi vocare videtur id tempus, cùm jam nunc cernens lupus se in viam dat, αὐχενικῶς ὑπὸ ἀπάλη. Hactenus Aelianus.
units.tr: Macrobius likewise wishes the Hours to be the same as the Sun, and says that from him the Hours, into which the day is divided, were so named, in the first book of the Saturnalia. The same Horus was also Osiris among the Egyptians, expressed in the form of a hawk, which, because it sees clearly even by night and flies most swiftly, is a clear image of the Sun, to express both its splendour and its speed. Among some, as the Heliopolitans, the Sun was represented in the form of a cat, for the same reason; for the cat also sees most clearly at night and is most swift, and hence it was called ailouros. So the people of Lycopolis, a city of Upper Egypt in the Thebaid, with equal devotion worshipped Apollo under the form of a wolf, lykos, that is, the wolf, honouring the Sun in both animals, because this animal, like the Sun, seizes and consumes all things, has the sharpest power of sight, and sees also by night, overcoming the darkness of night. This is known even from the proverb, "sharper than a wolf at evening" (Habakkuk 1:8), and because the Greek word λύκος is said to derive from λύκη, that is, from light. It seems not to be omitted here what Aelian teaches in his History of Animals, writing thus: "The animal has very keen sight. Indeed, both at an unseasonable night and when the moon itself is silent, the wolf enjoys the use of light, and although darkness is spread over all other creatures, light is not taken from it. Hence at that time it is called lykophos, since it alone receives light by the gift of nature. And indeed Homer seems to me to call that time the time when the wolf, now seeing, sets out upon the road..." Thus far Aelian. The Tigurine edition renders these words thus: the wolf is endowed with the sharpest and most acute eyes; in the dead of night, or when the moon itself is silent, it enjoys the use of light, and although darkness covers all things, light is not taken from it.

units.la: Porrò Beli quoque nomine cultus fuit Sol; quod nomen ratione non tacere scribit Servius: Et quippe Assyriorum lingua Solem significat: unde adspiratione adjectā Graece ἥλιος est vocatus: alii tamen non Assyriorum lingua, sed Phaenicum putant Hel Solem diti; unde Helius ducatur, qui mox & Belus dictus fit. Ab Hel forsan nostrum Germanicum Hell/Id est clarum. Quin & Servius tradit, quod Hal Punicā linguā Deus dicatur: apud Assyrios vero Hel dicebatur quadam sacrorum ratione Sol & Saturnus. Caeterum de Solis fonte, in aquis, in nemorib. 1 Megarenses, Persas, Aegyptios, Elephantinopolitanos, Heliopolitanos & alios vide Gyraldum, Verderium, Chartarium, & eos, qui de hac re fusè scripserunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the Sun was also worshipped under the name of Bel; Servius writes that this name is not to be passed over without reason: for in the language of the Assyrians it signifies the Sun, and from it, with an aspirate added, it was called in Greek ἥλιος. Others, however, think that not the Assyrian but the Phoenician language is meant, in which Hel signifies the Sun, whence Helius is derived, which afterwards became Belus. Perhaps from Hel comes our German Hell, that is, clear. Indeed Servius also relates that Hal in the Punic language means God; but among the Assyrians Hel was used, by a certain sacred usage, for both the Sun and Saturn. For the rest, on the fountain of the Sun, in the waters and in groves, among the Megarians, Persians, Egyptians, Elephantine and Heliopolitans and others, see Gyraldus, Verderius, Chartarius and those who have written at length on this matter.

units.la: SOLI merito subjungenda aurora aurea Titan, id est, Solis nuncia ac praevia. Virgilius: Praevia flammisfiri currus Aurora rubebat. Et: Aurea fulgebat roseis Aurora capillis.
units.tr: Aurora, the golden one, should rightly be joined to the Sun, since she is his herald and forerunner, the Titan's messenger. Virgil: "Aurora was reddening, going before the fiery chariot." And: "Golden Aurora shone with rosy hair."
She too was a goddess of the Gentiles.

units.la: SECUNDUM a Sole inter sidera dignitatis gradum Luna obtinet, a Lucendo dicta; vel potius a לבנה, Lebanah, Hebraeorum voce, qua ab albedine Luna sic dicitur: quemadmodum ex Bathsheba Hebraeis ipsi fecerunt Bathsuam. 1. Chron. 5. 3. Alii tamen sic dictam volunt, quod una, id est, Sola, noctu lucet (unde Noctiluca:) vel quod Sole lucente luceat sola: unde Solis filia, & Luna. Σελήνη, ἡ Σελήνη dicitur Graece ἀπὸ τῆς σελήνης ἐ ἕυ, id est, no' lumine, quod lucem semper habeat nō' vam. In sacris litteris Noctis domina appellatur, & Isidis Dea Aegyptiorum, seu fidus lucidissimum, quod Aegyptio nomine τῶν ... appellatur; item Diana, Junonis, Hecates, Lucina, Veneris, aliuq; nominibus ab Ethnicis fuit insignita & culta. Diana autem dicta est, ab jana, si Macrobio credimus, D littera addita, jana enim Luna est etiam Varronī in libro de re Rustica, forsan ab Hebreo ירח jareach, sic dicta, quod a ירח jarach, propagatur, significante respiratio: propterea quod noctu motu suo respirare facit, refecit & recreat, quae interdiu Solis ardore adusta fuerunt & torrida. Isidis verò nomine appellatam censet Diodorus lib. 1. de sententia quorundam ob antiquitatem: qui sensus est in voce ישא Iasis, quae ἰχαρόςος significat. Verba Graeca sunt, φωνὴ τῆς Ἴσεως ... ὅπερ ... Ἐκεῖνο ... (Greek text).
units.tr: Next after the Sun in rank among the heavenly bodies is the Moon, named from shining, or rather from the Hebrew word for whiteness, לבנה [Lebanah], by which the Moon is so called. In the same way the Hebrews themselves turned Bathsheba into Bathsuam (1 Chron. 5.3). Others want her so named because she alone [una, sola] shines by night, whence Noctiluca, or because she shines alone while the Sun shines, whence she is called the daughter of the Sun, and the Moon. In Greek she is called Selene [Σελήνη], from the light, because she always has light from another source. In Scripture she is called the lady of the night. Among the Egyptians she was the goddess Isis, or the brightest star, which in the Egyptian tongue is called by a name. She was also honoured and worshipped by the Gentiles under the names Diana, Juno, Hecate, Lucina, Venus, and others. Diana, if we believe Macrobius, was so named from Jana, with a D added, for Jana is the Moon, as Varro also says in his book on rustic matters. Perhaps she was named from the Hebrew ירח [yareach], which is derived from ירח [yarach], to breathe, because by her motion at night she makes things breathe again, and refreshes and revives what the Sun's heat has scorched and parched by day. Diodorus in book 1 thinks she was named from Isis, for the sake of antiquity, according to the opinion of some; the sense lies in the Hebrew word ישא [Iasis], which means "very bright." The Greek words are: the voice of Isis ... which ... that ...

units.la: Vt autē Luna Dea: ita & Lunus Deus vocabatur & colebatur (Sic enim plerunq; Dei utriusq; sexus fuerunt exsistimati) ceste Aelio Spartiano de Caracalla Imperatore. Ajt enimipsum Dei Luni templum accessisse, quem Deum miro cultu & veneratione Careni colebant, adeo ut qui Lunam fœmineo genere & nomine pucaret nuncupandā, ut addictus mulierib. semper inservirent: qui vero marem Deum esse crederet, ut dominarentur uxori, neque ullas mulierbres pateretur insidias. Lunam ergo Ethnici & Lunae & Luni in masculeo genere, caeterisq; nominibus colquerunt.
units.tr: Just as the Moon was worshipped as a goddess, so the Moon-god, Lunus, was also called upon and worshipped (for gods of both sexes were thought of in this way). Aelius Spartianus says so of the emperor Caracalla: that he came to the temple of the god Lunus, whom the people of Carrhae worshipped with remarkable devotion and reverence. They so arranged matters that whoever believed the Moon should be named in the feminine gender was to keep women in service, while whoever believed the god was male was to rule over his wife and suffer no female plots against him. So the Gentiles worshipped the Moon as Luna and as Lunus, in the masculine gender, and under other names.

units.la: PORRO' post Astrorum cultū, quæ sunt Cœli ignes, flammæ atq; lumina, de Ignis atq; lucis cultu, sujto ordine, videtur dicendū. Ac Ignis quidē (a quo Soleiam Hebræis dictus est שמש Schæmesch) duplex est: Alius cœlestis; qui, ut inquit Cicero de Natura Deorū, est corporeus, vitalis & salutaris, qui omnia cōservat, alit, auget, sustinet sensuq; affisu. Alius ver restitus; in nostro videlicet foco, quem adhibemus ad vsum vitæ atq; victu Atq; hic noster ignis, ut idem Cicero ait, quē usus vitæ requirit, cosectior est & consumptor omnium, idemq; quacunq; in vadis, vnda dißurbat & dissipat. Verusq; autem Ignis cum maxima sit vtilitas, idcirco Ignem quoq; Ethnici venerati sunt sub Iouis, Vulcani, Vestæ & aliorum Numinum nominibus.
units.tr: After the worship of the stars, which are the fires, flames and lights of heaven, it seems fitting to speak next, in due order, of the worship of fire and light. Fire (from which the Sun is called שמש [Shemesh] by the Hebrews) is of two kinds. One is heavenly, which, as Cicero says in his book On the Nature of the Gods, is bodily, life-giving and wholesome, preserving, nourishing, increasing and sustaining all things, and sustained by its own sense. The other is earthly, namely the fire on our hearth, which we use for the needs of life and for food. And this fire of ours, as the same Cicero says, is needed for the uses of life, is more confined, and consumes everything; and wherever it goes, it stirs up and scatters the water. Since true fire is of the greatest use, the Gentiles also worshipped fire under the names of Jupiter, Vulcan, Vesta and other deities.

units.la: Ac de Thare quidē, patre Abrahami, conflat, eum in Chaldæa coluisse Vr Chaldæorū, id est, Igne, seu focum Ignis: quod Vr deducta ab Hebræo אור, Or, Lux, peperit Latinū Vrere & Vrtica. Eundē postea Persæ sub Vromasda nomine tanquā maximum Deū colebant ac venerabantur. Hinc ꝯ Esch, quod in supreo, id est, Tēplo Ignis, ibi eum colebatur, meminit Triperistia Historia lib.10. cap.30. Ac Magi quidē Ignem tam religiose coluerunt, ut cremare corpora ducerent nefas, ne cada veris contagio Deorum maximū violaret. Alio nomine hic ignis Vrtibasdus.
units.tr: It is agreed that Terah, the father of Abraham, worshipped in Chaldea Ur of the Chaldeans, that is, fire, or the hearth of fire. From the Hebrew אור [Or], light, the word Ur (whence the Latin urere, to burn, and urtica, nettle) is derived. Afterwards the Persians worshipped and venerated him as the greatest god under the name Vromasdes. Hence the Triperistia history, book 10, chapter 30, mentions the Esch, the fire-temple (the supreme temple, where he was worshipped). The Magi indeed worshipped fire so scrupulously that they thought it a crime to cremate bodies, lest the corpse, by contact with the dead, should defile the greatest of gods. This fire was also called by another name, Urtibasdus.

units.la: Ignis Dæmonū, siue faceer a Chaldeis fuit appellatus: quemadmodum Vulcanus, Græce Ἡφαιστος. Ignis inventor, præfectus atq; Deus habitus. Vnde Theodoretus: θεοσεβ, idem, Vulcanū volunt esse τύρ, seu Igne, & sæpe Vulcani nomē pro Igne accipitur. ✓ Ignis Vulcanius dicitur a Statio Lactē novo profusus edet Vulcanus ignis. Serpius Vulcanum quasi Volcanum vult dicū, quod Ignis per aera volet. Varro autem eum a majori vi & violentia ignis nomen hoc vult accepisse. Ejus sanum Romulus propter incendiorum pericula extra urbem vocavit esse, teste Plutarcho in Quæst. Rom. 47.
units.tr: The fire of the demons, or the fire of the hearth, was called Chaldean fire, just as Vulcan, in Greek Hephaistos [Ἡφαιστος], was regarded as the inventor, overseer and god of fire. Hence Theodoret, in the passage on piety: they hold that Vulcan is fire, [πῦρ], and the name Vulcan is often taken for fire. Statius speaks of "Vulcanian fire" in his New ... "the fire of Vulcan will pour forth." Servius wants Vulcan to be called as if Volcan, because fire flies (volet) through the air. Varro, however, holds that he received this name from the great force and violence of fire. Romulus, according to Plutarch in the Roman Questions 47, placed his temple outside the city because of the dangers of fires.

units.la: Ignis Iovis se Iovu quoq; nomine aliquando apud Veteres habitus fuit, sic ut pro Aere juxtā intelligentur: unde etiam Iovis sororem sunt fabulati. Ignis perpetuus, ut in Arcadia in Panis templo, ita Romæ quoque in Vesta templo cultus fuit a Virginibus Vestalibus. Vestalium, Græce ἑστια (quæ voces ambæ a Chaldæa voce אור, Escha, significante Ignem, videntur derivate; eo modo ab ιἑστι Vestis: & inde ejus colendi consuetudo a Chaldeis desuxerit ad Persas, Græcos, Romanos & aliās nationes.) Ignis & focorum præses fuit habita; de hac Cicero lib. 2. de Natura Deorum ita: Vesta, Græce ἱστια; cujus vis ad aras & focos pertinet. Itaq; in ea Dea, quæ est rerū custos intimarum, omnis & precatio & sacrifi:atio extrema est. O vidiue in sexto Fastorum: Nec tu aliam Vestam, quam vivam vtuē geslammam.
units.tr: Fire was also sometimes called by the name of Jove among the ancients, so that the two were understood as the same as air. This is why they also invented a sister of Jove. Perpetual fire was kept burning, as in Arcadia in the temple of Pan, and likewise at Rome in the temple of Vesta, tended by the Vestal Virgins. The name Vesta, in Greek ἑστια [hestia], seems to derive from the Chaldean word אור [Escha], meaning fire, and from vestis (clothing). In that way the custom of worshipping it passed from the Chaldeans to the Persians, Greeks, Romans and other nations. Fire was also regarded as the president of hearths. Cicero speaks of her in the second book of On the Nature of the Gods: "Vesta, in Greek Hestia, whose power pertains to altars and hearths. Therefore, in that goddess, who is the guardian of the innermost things, every prayer and every sacrifice is final." Ovid in the sixth book of the Fasti: "Nor do you know another Vesta than the living flame you see."

units.la: Ac Berosus primum hoc nomen vsurpatum fuisse a Noacho testatur: Primus terram Aretiam, & ignē Estham vocavit. Quin & Delphus mulieres viro carentes in eodem templo custodiernt Ignem, sanquam mamsestum symbolum præsentiæ Dei, atq; hoc nomine ipsum coluerunt.
units.tr: Berosus testifies that this name was first used by Noah: "He first called the earth Aretia, and fire Estha." Moreover, Delphus kept fire in the same temple, tended by women without husbands, as a clear symbol of God's presence, and worshipped it under this name.

units.la: LVCEM quoque Ethnici olim coluerunt ac venerati sunt, seu Ignis effectum, quæ vox, Heb. אור, Or, vel Vr, Latinus sic videtur dicta ἀπὸ Λυκνις, hoc est, prima luce, quæ precedit Solis motum, ἀπὸ τῆς Λυκ, id est, Lupo, qui eam cernens sein vtam dare solet. Lucis autem datorem & largitorem finxerunt Iovem, Lucerium inde dictum. At sacræ litteræ docent Iehovam verum Deum, Lucem primo omnia creasse, quæ postea in Sole, Luna, cæterisq; stellis collecta suit. Cicero similiter in illa sua oratione pro Roscio; Commoda, quibus utimur, lucemq; qua fruimur, spiritumq; quem ducimus, a Deo nobis dari atque imperturi videmus.
units.tr: The Gentiles also long ago worshipped light, or the effect of fire. The Latin word lux seems to be called from the Greek [λύκη?], that is, the first light which comes before the motion of the Sun, and from the wolf [lupus], which, seeing it, is accustomed to give voice. They imagined Jupiter as the giver and bestower of light, and from this he was called Lucerius. But Holy Scripture teaches that Jehovah, the true God, first created light among all things, which afterwards was gathered into the Sun, Moon and the other stars. Cicero says similarly in his speech for Roscius: that the benefits we enjoy, the light we have, and the breath we draw, we see are given and bestowed on us by God.

units.la: ATQVE hęc quidem de Cœlo suprimo, sive Ætherē & quæ in eo continentur. Nunc descendamus ad Cœlum aëreum, sive Aërem, qui in sacris & prophanis litteris sæpe Cœlum appellatur. Aër, nomine Græco, sed recepto usu a Latinis, interjectus inter Cœlum, id est, Ætherem, & Mare, illius quidem tenuitate & calore temperatus, vitalem & salutarem spiritum præbet animantibus (nam spiritu duētus alit & sustentat animantes.) Idem, mari finitimus, frigorum & calorum facit varietates, die & noctē distinguitur: nā, tum susus & extenuatus in sublime fertur, tum concretus in nubes cogitur, humeremq; colligens terram auget imbribus, tum effluens hunc & illuc ventos efficit: ipseque nobiscum videt, nobiscum audit, nobiscum sonat. Nec verisimile tantum, sed etiam verum esse censent, perinde utcunque temperatus fit Aër: ita pueros orientes animari atque formari, ex eo, ingenia, mores, animum, sorpus, actionem vitæ, casus cujusque eventus, fingi. Atque hunc Aërem Veteres, quem masculum & fœminam statuerunt, inter quos Anaximenes & Diogenes Apolloniates apud Ciceronem de Natura Deorum libro primo, Deum statuerunt, eumq; gigni, esseq; immensum & infinitum & semper in motu. Vulgo illum coluerunt sub Diana nomine, quæ idcirco Ἀρτεμὶς, teste Theodoreto, quasi ἀεροτόμος, id est, Aërifeca, quæ per Aërem pergens, eamsecet, est dicta. Præcipuè tamen Aërem junonis nomine (quam ὑπερ Græci vocant, quæ vox cum Græca ἀὴρ magnam affinitatem habet) intellexerunt & coluerunt: quam ideo jonis sororem fabulati sunt, quòd jupiter pro Igne ponereur. Itaque sicut illum Cœli Regem; ita hanc Reginam Cœli vocarunt. Ignis enim atq; Aër in sublimioribus locis degentes majorem vim inves hasi caducas, possidont, quam cæteris duo Elementa. Plato quoq; in Cratylo ὑπορ, id est, Iu-nonem Aërem appellat.
units.tr: So much for the highest heaven, or ether, and what is contained in it. Now let us descend to the airy heaven, or air, which in sacred and profane writings is often called heaven. Air, a Greek name but in common use among the Latins, lies between heaven, that is, ether, and the sea. Tempered by the thinness and warmth of the former, it gives living and wholesome breath to animals (for by breathing it nourishes and sustains living things). Bordering on the sea, it produces the variety of cold and heat, and it is divided into day and night; for sometimes it is thinned and rarefied and carried aloft, sometimes it is condensed into clouds, and gathering moisture it enriches the earth with showers; and sometimes flowing out this way and that it produces winds. It sees with us, hears with us, and sounds with us. And they hold it not merely probable but true that, however the air is tempered, so children are animated and formed at birth, and from this their natures, morals, mind, body, the course of their life, and the outcome of each one's fortunes are shaped. The ancients who regarded this air as male and female, among whom Anaximenes and Diogenes of Apollonia, according to Cicero in book 1 of On the Nature of the Gods, held it to be a god, and that it was begotten, and was immense and infinite and always in motion. Commonly they worshipped it under the name of Diana, who, according to Theodoret, was called Artemis [Ἀρτεμὶς], as if aerotomos, that is, air-cutting, because she goes through the air and cuts it. Yet most of all they understood and worshipped air under the name of Juno (whom the Greeks call hupēr, a word having great affinity with the Greek aēr, air); and they fabled her to be the sister of Jupiter because Jupiter was taken for fire. So just as they called him King of Heaven, so they called her Queen of Heaven. For fire and air, dwelling in the higher places, possess greater power over fragile things than the other two elements. Plato too, in the Cratylus, calls Juno air [ὑπηρ? Juno].

units.la: Ast Aëreni, multorum quidè commodorum, sed multorum etiâ incommodorum caussam, non ut Deis colendâ, pluribus disputat ad versus Gentes Theodoretus in τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἰκκλησιῶν θεραπευτικὰ.
units.tr: But Theodoret, in his Cure of the Hellenic Maladies (τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν παθημάτων θεραπευτικά), argues at length against the Gentiles that the air is the cause of many benefits but also of many harms, and that it should not be worshipped as a god.

units.la: Nec verò tàtum Aërë ipsum venerati sunt, sed etiâ ea, quæ in Aëre cötinentur, ut Aves (de qui bus postea) Meteora et Dæmones sive Genios, quorū sedem Aër sacri et profani austores faciūt.
units.tr: Nor did they venerate the air alone, but also the things contained in the air: the birds (of which more below), the meteors, and the demons or genii, whose seat the sacred and profane writers place in the air.

units.la: QUANTUM ad Meteorum quoq; diuinitatem Ethnicos tribuisse constat. Tempestatem enim ut Deam coluerunt Romani, eiq; ædes a M. Martello extra portâ Capenam ædificata fuit: quam construxit e tempestate liberatus, quam passus erat cum in Corsicam & Sardiniam navigaret; cuju Ouidius meminit hīs versibus: Tequoq; Tempestas meritam delīra fatentur, Cùm pené est Corsis obruta puppis aquis.
units.tr: It is well known that the Gentiles also ascribed divinity to meteors. The Romans worshipped the storm as a goddess, and a temple to her was built by Marcus Marcellus outside the Capene Gate. He built it after he was rescued from a storm that he suffered when he was sailing to Corsica and Sardinia. Ovid recalls this in these verses: "The Storm too confesses that she deserves it, and in her madness, when the ship was almost overwhelmed by the Corsican waters."

units.la: Sed & Ventos Ethnici Deos fecerunt, eosq; hymnis, thuris, templis, altaribus, simulacris, sacri ficiiq; coluerunt, ut Gyraldus & alii multi exemplis atq; testimoniis probant. Hieronymus in λατρείᾳ, Psalmum 103. alex Ventis attributas scribit propter velocitatem, Sic enim inter alia ipse: Neq; illud, inquit, quod de ventis dicitur, Qui ambulat super pennas Ventorum, veré ventos, juxta sa-hulas Poëtarum & pistorum licentiam, pennas habere testatur; sed celerem in cunctâ discursum. Porrò Ventorum profisdem & Deum sinxerunt, Aeolum: vt idem Auctor pluribus docet. Plinius hunc scribit Mitorum rationem in venire: qui quoniam, ut Seruius scribit ex Varronis sententia, & Strabo, ex nebulis consurgentibus, vel, ut alii volunt, ex Igne diligenti observatione, futu ros Ventos tempestates, prædicebat, creditus est arustibus hominibus eas in suo potestate tenere, imperioq; suo premere. Sunt, qui eum volūt Astrologū fuisse, qui tèporanosset, quib. venti flare debent, atq; ideo Ventorū Deum existimatū. Quidā Homeri interpretes Aeolum interpretātur Anum, & ejus duodecim filios, duodecim menses. A Vetis Ninerva Anemotis fuit cognominata. Vt autem Venti omnes Dij fuerunt existimati, ita etiam singulis, tum iis qui Mundi cardines obtinent, tum inde ortus (quorum omnia triginta duos statuunt Nauta nostri temporis) tanquam Dii, Sacra peculiaria fuerunt fatta.
units.tr: The Gentiles also made gods of the winds and worshipped them with hymns, incense, temples, altars, images and sacrifices, as Giraldus and many others prove by examples and testimonies. Jerome, in his Latreia on Psalm 103, writes that the winds were attributed to Aeolus because of their speed. He says among other things: "Nor is that which is said of the winds, 'who walks upon the wings of the winds,' to be taken as if the winds really had wings, in accordance with the poets' and painters' license; rather it means swiftness in every course." Furthermore, the Gentiles also fashioned a god of the winds, Aeolus, as the same author teaches at length. Pliny writes that Aeolus invented the science of predicting the weather. Since, as Servius writes following Varro, and Strabo, the winds arise from gathering clouds, or, as others will have it, from fire, by careful observation he foretold coming winds and storms. Therefore he was believed by ignorant people to hold these in his power and to restrain them by his command. Some want him to have been an astrologer who knew the times at which the winds ought to blow, and for that reason he was thought to be the god of the winds. Some interpreters of Homer explain Aeolus as the year and his twelve sons as the twelve months. Minerva was surnamed Anemotis, from the winds. And just as all the winds were thought to be gods, so each of them, both those that hold the cardinal points of the world and those that rise from them (which sailors of our own time put at thirty-two in all), was given its own sacrifices as a god.

units.la: Hucreferi iinprimis debet Iris, Aërea cognominata, quæ, ut & Mercurius, Deorum cum omnium, tum Iouis & Junonis (unde junonia dicta ab Ovidio) nuncia fuit habita, quam Seruius cultus iridis. vulit dicta quasi ἐιρω, quòd, ut Mercurius pacis (unde eipiωνοῦ & Pacificator dicta) ita hæc litis & contentionis fuerit nuncia. Plato tamē in Cratylo eam ἄρ' ὡς ἐιρω, id est, loquendo vulit dictam, quia sit ἄγγελος, id est, nuncia. A patre Thaumantias & Thaumantea dicta est apud Poëtas, seu potiùs, quod admiratione ob specie suam diversicolorè (unde Multicolor a Virgilio appellatur) & risum moveat. Hæc auctè a Veterib. fuit Dea habita, quam fingebāt habitu muliebris, versicolore veste: nonnunquā & croceo, in obsequiō expedita: alas etiā ei versicolores Virgilius tribuit quarto Aeneidos, cùm eam ad Iunonè missam fingit ad Didonis crimem incidendum: Ergo jris croceis per cœlum roscida pennis Mille trahens varios adverso Solecolores Deuolat.—
units.tr: To this class belongs above all Iris, surnamed "Aerea." Like Mercury, she was held to be the messenger of all the gods, and of Jupiter and Juno in particular (whence she is called Junonia by Ovid). Servius says the worship of Iris is named after her, as if from eirō, because, just as Mercury is the messenger of peace (whence he is called eirēnoun and "Peacemaker"), so she was the messenger of strife and contention. Plato, however, in the Cratylus, derives her name from aro or eirō, that is, from speaking, since she is an angelos, that is, a messenger. Among the poets she is called the daughter of Thaumas, and "Thaumantias" and "Thaumantea," or rather because her appearance, many-coloured (whence Virgil calls her "Multicolor"), causes wonder and laughter. The ancients held her to be a goddess, and they pictured her in a woman's form, in a garment of many colours, sometimes also saffron, and ready for service. Virgil gives her many-coloured wings also in the fourth book of the Aeneid, when he imagines her sent to Juno to bring about Dido's downfall: "Then Iris, dewy through the sky on saffron wings, drawing a thousand varied colours against the sun, flies down."

units.la: Referēda huc sunt reliqua Meteora, & Aëris qualitates, ut Nubes, Pluviæ, Nives, Grandi nes, Nebulæ, Rores, Pruinæ, Fulgura, Fulmina, Tonitrua, atq; id genus alia, quæ a Martiano Capella lib.1. Philologia, sub junonis, quæ Aërūs Dea fuit habita, imagine repræsentantur, quæq; bre vitatu causa hic sponte prætermittemus.
units.tr: Here should be mentioned the remaining meteors and the qualities of the air: clouds, rains, snows, hailstones, mists, dews, frosts, lightnings, thunderbolts, thunders, and other things of this kind. Martianus Capella, in the first book of his Philologia, represents these under the image of Juno, who was regarded as the goddess of the air. For the sake of brevity I will willingly pass them over here.

units.la: PORRO post Astrorum cultū, quæ sunt Cœli ignes, flammæ atq; lumina, de Ignis atq; lucis cultu, justo ordine, videtur dicendū. Ac Ignis quidē (a quo Sol etiam Hebraīs dictus est ‎שמש‎ Schæmesh) duplex est: Alius cœlestis: quā, ut inquit Cicero de Natura Deorū, est corporeus, vitalis & salutaris, qui omnia cōferuat, alit, auget, suslinet sensuq; affixit. Alius terrestris: in nō-stro videlicet foco, quem adhibemus ad usum vitæ atq; victū. Atq; hoc nostri ignis, ut idem Cicero ait, quæ usus vitæ requirit, cōsectōr est & cōsumptor omnū, idem̄, quacunq; in vadit, vntā dis-furbat & dissipat. Vtrius autem Ignis cūm maxima sit utilitas, idcirco Ignem quoq; Ethnici venerati sunt sub Iouis, Vulcani, Vestæ & aliorum Numinum nominibus.
units.tr: NEXT, after the worship of the stars, which are the fires, flames and lights of heaven, it seems proper in due order to speak of the worship of fire and light. Fire is twofold (and the Hebrews called the sun shemesh, שמש, from it). One is heavenly, which, as Cicero says in On the Nature of the Gods, is bodily, life-giving and saving, preserves, nourishes, increases and sustains all things, and is fixed in the senses. The other is earthly, namely the fire of our own hearth, which we use for the needs and sustenance of life. And this fire of ours, as the same Cicero says, is the consumer and devourer of whatever life requires, and wherever it goes it scatters and dissipates whatever it seizes. Since the usefulness of each fire is very great, the Gentiles also worshipped fire under the names of Jupiter, Vulcan, Vesta and other divinities.

units.la: Ac de Thare quidē, patre Abrahami, constat, eum in Chaldæa coluisse Vr Chaldæorū, id est, Ignē, seu focum Ignis: quod Vr dedutū ab Hebræo ‎אור‎, Or, Lux, peperit Latinū Vrere & Vrtica. Eundē postea Persæ sub Vromasde nomine tanquā maximum Deū colebant ac venerabantur. Hinc (qdlt Efeb, quod in ἄνειω, id est, Tēplo Ignis, ab eis colebatur, meminis Tripartita Historia lib.10.cap.30. Ac Magi quidē Ignem tam religiose coluerunt, ut cremare corporaducerēt nefas, ne cada veris contagio Deorum maximū violarēt. ✠ Ilio nomine hic ignis Vrchasdim,
units.tr: It is certain that Terah, the father of Abraham, worshipped in Chaldea the Ur of the Chaldeans, that is, fire or the hearth-fire. Ur, derived from the Hebrew אור, or, light, gave birth to the Latin urere (to burn) and urtica (nettle). Afterwards the Persians worshipped and venerated this same fire under the name of Oromasdes as the greatest god. Hence the temple of fire, which the Persians called Ieb-Eb (Ἀνείω?), where fire was worshipped by them, is mentioned in the Tripartite History, book 10, chapter 30. The Magi indeed worshipped fire so religiously that they thought it wrong to burn bodies, lest they should defile the greatest of their gods by the contagion of a corpse. Under this name this fire was called Urchasdim,

units.la: Ignis Dæmonū, sive sacer a Chaldæis fuit appellatus: quemadmodū Vulcanus, Græcē Ἡφαιστος, Ignis invēntor, prasector atq; Deus habitus. Vnde Theodoretus: ὁ φαιστος, id est, Vulcanū volunt esse πῦρ. seu Ignē, & sepe Vulcani nomē pro Igne accipitur, & Ignis Vulcanius dicitur a Statio: Lalle novo profusus edest Vulcanius ignis. Seruius Vulcanum quasi Volcanum vult dictū, quod Ignis per aera volet. Varro autem eum a majori vi & violentia ignis nomeu hoc vult accepisse. Ejus fanum Romulus propter incendiorum periculas extra urbem voluit esse, teste Plutarcho in Quæst. Rom.47.
units.tr: the fire of the demons, or the sacred fire, by the Chaldeans. In the same way Vulcan, in Greek Hephaestus, was regarded as the inventor, overseer and god of fire. Hence Theodoret: Hephaestus, that is, Vulcan, they want to be fire [πῦρ]. Vulcan's name is often used for fire, and Statius speaks of "the Vulcanian fire": "Flooded by the new flame, it burns with Vulcanian fire." Servius says Vulcan is so called as if Volcanus, because fire flies through the air. Varro, however, holds that he received this name from the greater force and violence of fire. Romulus, according to Plutarch in the Roman Questions 47, wished his shrine to be outside the city because of the danger of fires.

units.la: Ignis Iouis quoq; nomine aliquando apud Veteres habitus fuit, sicut pro Aere Iouē intellexerunt: unde etiam Iouis sororem sunt fabulati. Ignis perpetuus, ut in Arcadia in Panis templo: ita Rome quoque in Vesta templo cultus fuit a virginibus Vestalibus. Vestæ enim, Græcē ἱστία (quæ voces ambæ a Chaldæa voce ‎אשא‎, Escha, significante Ignem, videntur derivata; eo modo ut ab ἱστὸς vestis: & inde ejus colendi consuetudo a Chaldæis desluxit ad Persas, Græcos, Romanos & alias nationes) Ignis & focorum præses fuit habita; de hac Cicero lib. 2. de Natura Deorum ita: Vesta, Græcē ἱστία; cujus vis ad aras & focos persinet. Icaq; in ea Dea, quæ est vera cultos intimarum, omnis & precatio & sacrifi-cio extrema est. Ovidius in sexto Fastorum: Nec tu aliam Vestam, quam vivam intellige flammam.
units.tr: The fire of Jupiter was also sometimes regarded by the ancients under his name, just as they understood Jupiter to be the air; hence they also made him out to have a sister. Perpetual fire was worshipped in the temple of Pan in Arcadia, just as at Rome in the temple of Vesta it was tended by the Vestal virgins. Vesta, in Greek hestia (both words seem to be derived from the Chaldean word esha, אשא, meaning fire, in the way that hestia comes from histos, a web), was regarded as the president of fire and hearths; and from the Chaldeans the custom of worshipping her passed to the Persians, Greeks, Romans and other nations. Cicero, in the second book of On the Nature of the Gods, says of her: "Vesta, in Greek hestia, whose power extends to altars and hearths. Therefore in her, who is the true goddess of the innermost parts, every prayer and every sacrifice ends." Ovid in the sixth book of the Fasti: "Do not understand Vesta as anything else than the living flame."

units.la: Ac Berosus primum hoc nomē usurpatum fuisse a Noacho ssesslatur: Primus terram Aretiam, & ignē Esthām vocavit. Quin & Delphis mulieres viro carentes in eodem templo custodierunt Ignem, stanquam mamsestum symbolum præsentiæ Dei, atq; hoc nomine ipsum coluerunt.
units.tr: Berosus asserts that this name was first used by Noah: "He first called the earth Aretia and fire Esthā." Moreover, at Delphi, women without husbands guarded the fire in the same temple, as a clear symbol of God's presence, and they worshipped it under this very name.

units.la: LVCEM quoque Ethnici olim coluerunt ac venerati sunt, ceu Ignis effectum, quæ vox, Hebræis ‎אור‎, Or, vel Vr, Latinis sic videtur dicta Ἀυκς, hoc est, prima luce, quæ precedit Solis motum, ὅσσ τὸ Αὐχς, id est, Lupo, qui eam cernens se in viam dare solet. Lucis autem dato rem & largitorem sinxerunt Iovem, Lucerium inde dictum. At sacrae litterae docent Iehovam verum Deum, Lucem primo omnium creasse, quæ postea in Sole, Luna, ceterisq; stellis collecta fuit. Cicero similiter in illa sua oratione pro Rofcio; Commoda, quibus utimur, lucemq; qua fruimur, spiritumq; quem ducimus, a Deo nobis datæ atque imperti videmus.
units.tr: The Gentiles also formerly worshipped and venerated light, as an effect of fire. The Hebrew word for it is אור, or, or ur, and for the Latins it seems to have been called Aukē, that is, first light, which goes before the motion of the sun; or it is derived from the Greek word for the wolf, since the wolf, seeing this light, is accustomed to set out on its way. They imagined Jupiter to be the giver and bestower of light, and from this he was called Lucerius. But the sacred writings teach that Jehovah, the true God, first of all created light, which was afterwards gathered into the sun, the moon and the other stars. Cicero likewise, in his speech For Roscius: "We see that the benefits we enjoy, the light by which we live, and the breath we draw, have been given and bestowed upon us by God."

units.la: ATQVE hæc quidem de Cœlo illo supremo, sive Æthere & quæ in eo continentur. Nunc decendamus ad Cœlum æthereum, sive Aërem, qui in sacris & prophanis litteris sepe Cœlum appellatur. Aër, nomine Græco, sed recepto usu a Latinis, interpellatur inter Cœlum, id est, Ætherem; & Mare, illius quidem tenuitate & calore temperatus, vitalem & salutarem spiritum præbet animantibus (nam spiritu dulcius alit & sustentat animantes.) Idem, mari finitimus, frigorum & calorum facit varietates, die & noste distinguitur: nā, tum fusus & extenuatus in sublime fertur, tuū concretus in nubes cogitur, humoremq; colligens terram auget imbribus, tum effluens huc & illuc veutos efficit: ipseque nobiscum videt, nobiscum audit, nobiscum sonat. Nec verisimile tantum, sed etiam verum esse censene, perinde utcunque temperatus sit Aër: ita puerorum orientes animari atque formari, ex eo ingenia, mores, animum, corpus, actionem vitæ, casus cujusque eventusq; fingi. Atque hunc Airem Veterec,quem masculum & fœminam statuerunt,inter quos Anaximenes & Diogenes Apolloniates apud Ciceronem de Natura Deorum libro primo, Deum statuerunt, cumq; gigni,esseq; immensum & infinitum & semper in motu. Vulgo illum coluerunt sub Diane nomine,quæ idcirco Aρτεμις,teste Theodoreto,quasi ἀιερότης,id est, Aerifera,quæ per Aerem pergens,eam secet,est dicta. Præcipuè tamen Aerem Junonis nomine (quam ἠρα Græci vocant, quæ vox cum Græca ἀὴρ magnam affinitatem habet) intellexerunt & coluerunt: quam ideo jovis sororem fabulati sunt,quod supplter pro Igne ponereturę. Itaque sicut illum Cœli Regem; ita hanc Reginam Cœli vocarunt. Ignis enim atq; Aër in sublimioribus locis degentes majorem vim in rebus caducas,possident,quam cætera duo Elementa. Plato quoq; in Cratylo ἠρα,id est, Iu- nonem Aërem appellat.
units.tr: Thus much concerning that highest heaven, or the ether, and the things contained in it. Now let us descend to the ethereal heaven, or the air, which in sacred and profane writings is often called heaven. Air, a Greek word but adopted by the Latins through usage, lies between heaven, that is, the ether, and the sea. Tempered by the ether's thinness and warmth, it supplies living and healthful breath to animals, for it nourishes and sustains them more sweetly than anything else. Lying next to the sea, it also produces the variations of cold and heat and is divided into day and night. For when it is poured out and thinned it is carried upward, and when it condenses it is gathered into clouds, and gathering moisture it enriches the earth with showers; and when it flows hither and thither it makes winds. It sees with us, hears with us, and sounds with us. Nor is it only plausible but even true, you may think, that however the air is tempered, so the children who are born are animated and formed; and from it their talents, manners, mind, body, activity of life, and the fortune and outcome of each person are shaped. The ancients who made this Air male and female, among whom Anaximenes and Diogenes of Apollonia, as Cicero reports in the first book of On the Nature of the Gods, declared it to be God, and to be begotten, and to be immense and infinite and always in motion, held this Air in honour. Commonly they worshipped it under the name of Diana, who, according to Theodoret, was therefore called [Ἄρτεμις], as if [ἀερότης], that is, air-bearing, because she passes through the air and cuts it. Above all, however, they understood and worshipped the Air under the name of Juno (whom the Greeks call [Ἥρα], a word having great affinity with the Greek [ἀήρ]); they feigned her to be Jupiter's sister because she was put in place of fire. Thus as they called him the King of Heaven, so they called her the Queen of Heaven. For fire and air, dwelling in the higher regions, possess greater power over perishable things than the other two elements. Plato too, in the Cratylus, calls [Ἥρα], that is Juno, the air.

units.la: Ast Aërem,multorū quidē commodorū,sed multorum etiā incommodorū caussam,non ut Deū colendū,pluribus disputat advėrsus Gentes Theodoretus in ϊϝ ἑλλιωσὶν ϑεραπεῖα.
units.tr: But Theodoret, in his Therapeutics of the Greek Maladies (against the Gentiles), discusses at length that the air is the cause of many benefits, but also of many harms, and does not argue that it should be worshipped as God.

units.la: Nec vero tātum Aërē ipsum venerati sunt,sed etiā ea,quæ in Aëre cōtinentur,ut Aves (de quibus postea) Meteora et Dæmones sive Genios,quorū sedem Aërē sacri et profani auctorēs faciunt.
units.tr: Nor did they venerate only the air itself, but also those things which are contained in the air: birds (of which later), meteors, and demons or genii, whose seat the sacred and profane authors place in the air.

units.la: Q VANTVM ad Meteora,in quoq; diuinitatem Ethnicos tribuisse constat. Tempestatem enim ut Deam coluerunt Romani,eiq; ædes a M. Marcello extra portā Capenam edificata fuit: quam construxit e tempestate liberatus, quam passus erat cum in Corsicam & Sardiniam navigaret;cuius Ovidius meminit his versibus: Te quoq; Tempestas meritam dellubra satentur, Cum pené est Corsis obruta puppis aquis.
units.tr: As for meteors, it is well known that the Gentiles attributed divinity to them. For the Romans worshipped Tempest as a goddess, and a temple was built to her by Marcus Marcellus outside the Capene Gate. He built it after being rescued from a tempest, which he had suffered while sailing to Corsica and Sardinia. Ovid mentions this in these verses: "You too, Tempest, the temples confess you deserved, when the ship was almost overwhelmed by Corsican waters."

units.la: Sed & Ventos Ethnici Deos secerunt,eosq; hymnis,thure,templis,altaribus,simulacris,sacri Araficusq; coluerunt,ut Gyraldus & alii multis exemplis atq; testimoniis probant. Hieronymus in Ἀαρχία, Psalmum 103.alas Venti attributas scribit propter velocitatem. Sic enim inter alia ipse: Neq; cultus Ventos volud,inquit,quod de ventis dicitur,Qui ambulat super pennas Ventorum,ueré Ventos,juxta sabulas Poëtarum & pistorum licentiam, pennas habere testatur;sed celerem in cunctā discursum. Porrò Ventorum præsidem & Deum sinxerunt,Æolum: ut idem Auctor pluribus docet. Plinius hunc scribit Ventorum rationem in venisse: qui quoniam,ut Seruius scribis ex Varronis sentia, & Strabo,ex nebulis consurgentibus; vel, ut alii volunt,ex Ignis diligenti observatione,futuri Ventos tempestatesq; præducebat,creditus est a rudibus hominibus eas in suo potestate tenere, imperioq; suo premere. Sunt,qui eum volūt Astrologū fuisse,qui tepora nosset,quib. venti slare debent,atq; ideo Ventorū Deum existimati. Quiā Homeri interpretes Æolum interpretātur Anuum,& ejus duodecim filios,duodecim menses. A Vētis Mineruę Anemotis fuit cognominata.
units.tr: But the Gentiles also made the winds gods, and worshipped them with hymns, incense, temples, altars and images, and with sacred rites, as Giraldus and others prove by many examples and testimonies. Jerome, in his [Ἀλληγορία]?? on Psalm 103, writes that wings were attributed to the winds because of their swiftness. For he says among other things: "Nor did the psalm want us to think, when it is said of the winds, 'who walks upon the wings of the winds,' that the winds truly have wings, according to the poets' fables and painters' licence; rather it signifies their swift course over everything." Moreover, they feigned Aeolus as the ruler and god of the winds, as the same author shows at length. Pliny writes that Aeolus invented the reckoning of the winds; since, as Servius writes following Varro's opinion, and Strabo, he foretold winds and storms from rising clouds, or, as others will have it, from careful observation of fire, he was believed by rude people to hold them in his power and to restrain them by his command. Some want him to have been an astrologer who knew the seasons when the winds ought to blow, and therefore he was thought to be the god of the winds. For the interpreters of Homer explain Aeolus as the year, and his twelve sons as the twelve months. Minerva was surnamed Anemotis from the winds.

units.la: Vt autem Venti omnes Dii fuerunt existimati, ita etiam singulis, tum iis qui Mundi tardines obtinent,tum inde ortus (quorum omnia triginta a duos flatuunt Nauta nostri temporis) tanquam Dii,Sacra peculiaria fuerunt sacta.
units.tr: Just as all winds were thought to be gods, so also to each of them, both to those which hold the quarters of the world and to those arising from them (of which our sailors of today count thirty-two), sacred rites of their own were instituted, as to gods.

units.la: Hucreferti inprimis debet Iris,Aërea cognominata,quæ,ut & Mercurius,Deorum cum omnium, tum Iovis & Junonis (unde Junonia dicta ab Ovidio) nuncia suis habita,quam Servius sultus tridi, vult dicta quasi ἰεὶρ,quod ut Mercurius pacis (unde εἰρηνοποιὸς & Pacificator distus) ita hæc luiū & contentionū fuerit nuncia. Plato tamē in Cratylo eam ἴσρα τῦ ἱρεῖρ,id est,loquendo vult dictam,quia sit ἀγγέλος,id est, nuncia. A patre Thaumantiaę & Thaumantea dicta est apud Poëtas,seu potiùs,quod admirationē obspecie suam diuersitoloré (unde Multicolor a Virgilio appellatur) & risum moveat.Hæc autē a Veterib. fuit Dea habita,quam fingebat habitu muliebri,versicolore veste: nonnunquā & croteo, in obsequiū expedita: alas etiā ei versicolores Virgilius tribuit quarto Aeneidos,cum eam ad Junone missam fingit ad Didonis crimen incidendum: Ergo iris croceis per cælum roscida pennis Mille trahens varios aduerso Sole colores De volat.—
units.tr: To this place especially belongs Iris, surnamed Aërea, who, like Mercury, was regarded as the messenger of all the gods, and especially of Jupiter and Juno (whence Ovid calls her Junonia). Servius, in the third book, thinks she was named as if [εἰρήνη], since, as Mercury was the messenger of peace (whence he is called [εἰρηνοποιός] and Pacificator), so she was the messenger of strife and contention. Yet Plato in the Cratylus wants her named from [εἴρειν], that is, from speaking, because she is an [ἄγγελος], that is, a messenger. The poets called her the daughter of Thaumas and Thaumantea, or rather because she moves wonder by her varied appearance and colours (whence Virgil calls her Multicolor) and provokes laughter. The ancients regarded her as a goddess, and used to picture her in female dress with a many-coloured robe, and sometimes with a saffron one, ready for service. Virgil also gives her many-coloured wings in the fourth book of the Aeneid, when he imagines her sent by Juno to cut short Dido's ordeal: "Therefore Iris, dewy with saffron wings, drawing a thousand various colours against the sun, flew down through the sky."

units.la: Referēda hūc sunt reliqua Meteora,& Aërī qualitates,ut Nubes,Pluviæ,Nives,Grandines,Nebulæ,Rores,Pruinæ,Fulgura,Fulmina, Tonitrua, atq; id genus alia, quæ a Martiano Capella lib.1. Philologiæ,sub Junonis,quæ Aëris Dea fuit habita,imagine repræsentantur, quæq; breuitatis causa hic sponte prætermittemus.
units.tr: Here are to be referred the remaining meteors and qualities of the air, such as clouds, rains, snows, hailstones, mists, dews, frosts, lightnings, thunderbolts, thunders, and other things of that kind, which Martianus Capella, in the first book of his Philology, represents under the image of Juno, who was regarded as the goddess of the air. For the sake of brevity we shall willingly pass them over here.

units.la: POSTREMO ad Aërem referëdi omnino videtur esse Dæmones, I. aune Gentiludi, quos nos Angelos vocamus, qui partim boni sunt, partim mali. Plutarchus in Quæst. Ro. 40. Cur jouis flamini nõ liceat sub Dio inungi, inter alia scribit: An, quèadmodū in tepido ant sano nudare sese nefas erat; uta Aërem sub aperto Cœlo et Dio venerari, ut Diu Geniū, referbat? His verbis dno Plutarchus aperte significat, Primum, Ethnicos Aëre venerari fuisse solitos, cen Deū: et quidè sub Dio. Secundo ratione ejus reddit, nempe quod Aëre credebat referri esse Dius atq; Genus.
units.tr: Finally, the demons, that is, the genii of the Gentiles, whom we call angels, who are partly good and partly evil, certainly seem to belong to the air. Plutarch, in Roman Questions 40, why it is not permitted for the flamen of Jupiter to be anointed under the open sky, writes among other things: "Was it, just as it was wrong to bare oneself in warm or healthy weather, so that one should worship the air under the open sky and the sky, as if it were the Dius Genius?" By these words Plutarch clearly indicates two things: first, that the Gentiles were accustomed to worship the air as God, and indeed under the open sky; second, he gives the reason for it, namely that he believed the Dius and Genius to belong to the air.

units.la: Porrò quia a Latinis Genii seu Dii Geniales fuerunt dicti quasi Gentiores, a gignendo, seu generando (vel quòd agant et curent, ut homines gignatur, vel quòd homines genitos suscipiant et tueantur) bi a Græcis dicti sunt Δαίμονες, quod apud Ethnicos nomen fuit commune omnibus spiritibus tam bonis, quàm malis. Unde et Philo testatur, quos Philosophi Δαίμονας vocârint, eos a Mose אלהים, Elohim fuisse appellatos.
units.tr: Moreover, the Latins called the Genii, or Genial gods, as if [gentiores], from begetting or generating (either because they act and care so that men are begotten, or because they take up and protect those who have been begotten). The Greeks called these [δαίμονες], a name common among the Gentiles to all spirits, both good and evil. Hence Philo also testifies that those whom the philosophers called [δαίμονες] were called by Moses [Elohim], that is, אלהים.

units.la: Omnino igitur nomen Δαίμων, ut etiam Genii, in bonam et malam partem accipitur: et alii dicuntur boni Dæmones, quos ὑπ' αἰώνας, καλοὺς αἰωνας et ἀγαθοὺς αἰωνας appellarunt. alii mali; quos ideo καλοὺς αἰωνας vocarunt. Sic Genios quoq; alios vocarunt bonos; alios malos: ut in nostra Religione nobis sunt Angeli alii boni, alii mali. Vox Δαίμονες et Δαιμονιον in sacris literis in malam semper partē accipitur pro impuris illis et immundis spiritibus, qui jusso Dei judicio æternæ sunt damnationi atq; inferoruni cruciatibus addicti, quos Diabolos appellamus.
units.tr: Altogether, therefore, the name [δαίμων], like Genius, is taken in a good and a bad sense; some are called good demons, whom they named [καλοὺς δαίμονας] and [ἀγαθοὺς δαίμονας]; others bad, whom they called [κακοὺς δαίμονας]. So they also called some Genii good and others evil, just as in our religion there are some good angels and some evil. The words [δαίμονες] and [δαιμόνιον] in the sacred writings are always taken in a bad sense, for those unclean and impure spirits who by God's just judgment are condemned to eternal damnation and given over to the torments of hell, whom we call devils.

units.la: Porrò Dæmones illi Ethnicorum sive boni, sive mali, Platoni et aliis Philosophis, suerunt Dii inferiores, quos jovi illi suo, seu Deo supremo, subjecerunt, et tanquam legatos atq; nuncios inter Deum et hominès esse censuerunt. Horum alios fecerunt æthereos, sive cœlestes: alios aëreos, alios æqueos, alios terrestres, alios infernos, id est, subterraneos et circnitores sui vagos. Alii eos aliter divisedere ac distinguere fuerunt soliti. Sed nos (omissis hic variis, multiplicibus, infinitis et perplexis Philosophorū atq; Poëtarum disputationibus de Dæmonum nominibus generibus atq; natura) Dæmonū nomine hic intelligimus secundū sacrarum literarū stilum, impuros et immundos illos Spiritus, qui boni atq; pnritinitio a Deo creati propter superbiam et rebellionē snam veInntarià, cœlestis et suprema illa sede atq; dignitate dejesti fuerunt ac deturbati et in Aëremlum caliginosum, tanquam in carcerē detrusi, nhi ad æternos illos Gebennæ cruci- s refer̈vatur.
units.tr: Moreover, those demons of the Gentiles, whether good or evil, were regarded by Plato and other philosophers as lesser gods, whom they subjected to their Jupiter, or supreme God, and believed to be as legates and messengers between God and men. Of these they made some ethereal, or heavenly; some aerial, some watery, some earthly, some infernal, that is, subterranean, and wandering wardens of their own. Others were accustomed to divide and distinguish them in other ways. But we, leaving aside here the various, manifold, endless and intricate disputations of the philosophers and poets about the names, kinds and nature of demons, understand by the name demons, according to the style of sacred writings, those impure and unclean spirits who, though created good and pure by God, were through pride and their rebellious revolt cast down from that heavenly and supreme seat and dignity, and thrown down and thrust into the dark air as into a prison, where they are reserved for the eternal Gehenna of fire.

units.la: Hi prater alia nomina, Δαίμονες sunt disti quasi δαήμονες, a sciētia et sapiētia, in qua creati sunt, et qua aduc aliqua ex parte sunt prædi, quæ, teste Augustino lib. 9. de Ciuitate Dei, ca. 20. expers est charitatis, et astutia potiùs, atq; malitia, quàm sapiētia dici merentur. Alii tamē vocem hac ab Hebræa voce שדים, Schaddaim, ultima nimirū ejus syllaba, volūt esse dedūtā, Deuc. 32. v. 17. שדים, Schaddaim sive Dæmonia videtur dista, vel a שד, Schad, mamma; a forma nimirum, qua appàrtbant in forma bestiæ mammosæ, ut capreæ, vel vaccæ, vel canis; vel a שדד, Schadad, id est, vastando, quia vastitatis sunt auctores, sive in vastis locis habitant. Non abfurdū videtur, si Δαίμων ab Hebræo אדון, Adon, et hinc vox Latina Dominus, ac Hispanica et Italica Don, Donna, Dontolla et similes deriventur. Aerea enim regioni potissimum dominari impuros istos Spiritus, ibiq; sedeni ac domicilium suum habere et vires suas exserere ex sacrus litteris potest colligi.
units.tr: Besides these other names, demons are called Daimones, as if from daēmones, that is, from knowledge and wisdom, in which they were created and of which they still retain some part. Yet, according to Augustine (De Civitate Dei, bk. 9, ch. 20), they lack charity, and deserve to be called crafty and malicious rather than wise. Others, however, want the word to be derived from the Hebrew שדים, Schaddaim, especially its last syllable, as in Deut. 32:17, where שדים, Schaddaim, that is, demons, seems to be so called either from שד, Schad, a breast, from the form in which they appeared, as beasts with udders, such as a roe, a cow or a dog; or from שדד, Schadad, that is, by laying waste, because they are the authors of desolation or dwell in desolate places. It does not seem absurd that Daimōn is derived from the Hebrew אדון, Adon, and that from this come the Latin dominus and the Spanish and Italian don, donna, donzella and similar words. For it can be gathered from Holy Scripture that these impure spirits rule chiefly over the air, and there have their seat and home and exercise their powers.

units.la: Petrus epistolā 2. cap. 2. testatur Deū Angelis, qui pecçaverāt, non pepercisse, sed in Tartarū eos detrusisse, hoc est, in infimas has regiones, terræ finitimas, nēpe in Aërem. Est enim Tartarus voce intelligitur sæpe locus sub terra positus; ubi puniendi sint animi impiorū, qui locus etiā ἀιδης appellatur: tamē Petrus hoc in loco Aërē, et totū spatium infra Lunā intelligit. Judas ait, Angelos malos suū reliquisse domicilium: et jam sub caligine, judicio magni illius Dei referu̇ari. Unde colligitur eos e Cælo in Aërem hūc caliginosum fuisse præcipitatos. Hinc Steuchus vult spiritus istos malos ab Empedocle vocatos fuisse ὑρίανον τὰς, id est, e cælo motos, sive raptos. Cælius Rho- diginus, antiquarū lectionū lib. 1. cap. 28. ait hoc idē significare voluisse Pythagoram, cū scripsit, Anima fratiū alas e cœlo labi, etc. Paulus 2. cap. ad Ephesios Diabolū vocat ἄρχοντα τῆς ἐξου- σίας τοῦ ἀέρος. principem potestatis Aëris, Idem cap. 6. eos vocat ἀρχὰς, ἐξουσίας, κοσμοκράτορας τῶν σκότους, τῶν αἰῶνος τούτου, πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις, id est, principatus, po- testates, Mūdi reĉtores, tenebrarū, seculi istius, spirituales malitiās in cœlestibus, hoc est, in Aërē: ad versus quos docit nobis esse pugnam.
units.tr: Peter, in his second epistle, chapter 2, testifies that God did not spare the angels who sinned, but cast them down into Tartarus, that is, into these lowest regions bordering on the earth, namely the air. Tartarus is often understood as a place beneath the earth where the souls of the wicked are to be punished, and this place is also called Hades; yet in this passage Peter means the air and the whole space below the moon. Jude says that the evil angels left their dwelling and are kept in darkness until the judgment of the great God. From this it is gathered that they were hurled from heaven into this dark air. Hence Steuchus holds that these evil spirits were called by Empedocles "moved" or "carried off" from heaven. Caelius Rhodiginus (Antiquae lectiones, bk. 1, ch. 28) says that Pythagoras meant the same thing when he wrote, "the souls of the fallen slide from heaven," and so on. Paul, in Ephesians 2, calls the devil "the prince of the power of the air" (ἄρχοντα τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ ἀέρος). In chapter 6 the same Paul calls them "principalities, powers, world-rulers of this darkness, spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places" (ἀρχὰς, ἐξουσίας, κοσμοκράτορας τῶν σκότους, τῶν αἰῶνος τούτου, πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις), that is, in the air, against whom he teaches us we must wage war.

units.la: Sacræ Sacris litteris consentaneé Augustinus quoq; multis in locis Dæmonas siue Dæmonia in Aë-re hoc caliginoso esse, tanquam in carcere,ut sque ad finem Mundi testacur. Tunc inde educendos & destruendos in locum tetriorem & funestiorem: vbi crucientur perpetuo. Idem libro ostavo, de Ciuitate Dei,capite 22. & libro 14. capite 3. & 23. Dæmonas docet e cælo propter peccatum eiectos esse in caliginosum istum Aërem,ubi sint tanquam in carcere,in iudicio extremo pnniendi æterna damnatione cum hominibus. Idem pater ærea quoq,illis corpora tribuis,libro 2. de Ciuit. Dei,cap.10. de quo vide quoq; Celium Rhodiginum lib.1.cap.26.
units.tr: Consistent with the sacred writings, Augustine also, in many places, testifies that demons, or devils, are in this dark air as if in a prison, until the end of the world. Then they are to be led out from there and cast into a more dreadful and deadly place, where they will be tormented forever. In the same work, book 8, chapter 22, and book 14, chapters 3 and 23, he teaches that demons were cast out of heaven on account of sin into this dark air, where they are as in a prison, to be punished with eternal damnation together with men at the last judgment. The same Father also attributes bodies of air to them (De Civitate Dei, bk. 2, ch. 10); on this see also Caelius Rhodiginus, bk. 1, ch. 26.

units.la: Est verò Aër proprius & peculiaris nunc est Dæmonum siue Diabolorum locus,illic prænciipue potentium suam, quatenus illis a Deo est permissa,exercendi: tamen, Dei permissione, ut res ipsa & quotidiana docet experientia, in aquis quoq; & in terra, & subter terram oberrant atque vagantur,hominibus insidiantur,eos tentant,dimexanc, ad mala sollicitant, iis plurima damna inferunt, Dei sunt quasi satellites, lictores, torfores, carnifices, quibus partim ad piorum in hac vita fidem & patientiam exercendam atque probandam, partim ad impiorum impietatem puniendam tritur. Plutarchus quoq; Quæst.Rom.57. (ut Lariius,quos Præslites proprie vocant,præficiatur:ipsi autem caninis vestibus amiciantur )inter alia dicit secundum Chrysippi & sestatoris ejus sententiam, Genios quosdam malos oberrare, quibus alu carnificum loco utantur in puniendo flagitiosis & impiis hominibus: ob quem transcursum per multa loca, pro totius Naturæ Deus habiti ac culti fuerunt.
units.tr: Now the air is the proper and peculiar place of demons or devils, where they chiefly exercise their power, as far as it is permitted them by God. Yet by God's permission, as everyday experience itself teaches, they also wander and roam in the waters, on the earth and under the earth, lie in wait for men, tempt them, deceive them, urge them to evil, and inflict very many harms upon them. They are, as it were, God's attendants, lictors, jailers and executioners, by whom some are trained and tested in the faith and patience of the godly in this life, and others are punished for their impiety. Plutarch also, in Roman Questions 57 (where, as Lerius puts it, certain officers whom the Greeks properly call Prestites are placed in charge, and they themselves are clad in dog-skins), says among other things, according to the opinion of Chrysippus and his follower Sestator, that certain evil genii wander about, whom the executioners use in place of themselves to punish wicked and impious men; because of this roaming through many places they were regarded and worshipped as gods of the whole of Nature.

units.la: Atque hi quidem Spiritus æreri capitales, perennes, atque perpetui Dei hominumq; hostes præcipui sunt, ut omnis peccati, sic Idololatria & superstitionis cum auctores,duces & impulsores,tum obiectum,ut ex sacris constat litteris, quæ idcirco Ethnicos Dæmonibus si ve Dæmonum sacrificasse,hoc est,ea coluisse testantur:unde etiam Idololatria,seu superstitio ingens s eo nd ꝏμὸια ab ipsis Ethnicis passim appellatur: & eodem modo s ἀπομολαγεῖα ,id est, Dæmonum timor atque cultus potest appellari: quem quidem cultum Porphyrius ipse, veritatis ofor & oppugnator irridet, manifestè ostendens, hos neque Deos esse,nec bonos Dæmonas,sed mendacii magistros,omniumq; flagitiorum patres. Dæmones enim,ceu Spiritus mirę subtilitatis, solertiæ, astutiæ, atque callidi tatis, Dei hominumq; implacabili detestandoq; odio flagrantes, quibus vis seferebus cum naturalibus,tum artificialibus, ut simulachris,insinuantes & in quas vis sese species atq; formas transformantes,hominibus apparentes,eos alloquentes, res slupidas efficientes, h̄ mins miris artibus ad se colendos ac divinos honoribus afficiendos pellexerunt. In vidente em Deo suum honorem atq; gloriam,ea omnibus modis ad se transferre sibi, vendicare suos conari: idq; vel immediate,ut quando a Christo se voluit adorari: vel per media,si ve naturalia,sive artificialia.Ipsa quoq; Dei nomina, ipsa sacra, quæ Deus populo suo ad Numinis sui cultum tradiderat atq; præscriptęrat,Dæmones,tanquam Dei simię, mancipiis suis tradiderunt ac prąceperant,multiss fraudulentissimè callidissimeq; vel immutatis, vel additis, vel detractis,ut ex ritibus atq; cerimoniarum Ethnicorum diligenti comparatione cum ritibus Iudaicis diuinitus iustitutis manifestè apparet. Atq; hæc quidem de prima Mundi parte,id est, Cælo, & in, quæ in eo consinentur, sint dicta, quæ innumerabilium Deorum atque Numinum Ethnicorum turbam complectitur. Sequitur pars secunda,nempe Terra.
units.tr: These aerial spirits, then, are the chief, perpetual and everlasting enemies of God and men. As they are the authors, leaders and instigators of all sin, so too of idolatry and superstition, and also their object, as is clear from the sacred writings. These writings therefore testify that the heathen sacrificed to demons, or devils, that is, worshipped them. Hence idolatry, or great superstition, is everywhere called by the heathen themselves "demonolatry" (δαιμονολατρεία), and in the same way the fear and worship of demons may be called "demonophobia" (δαιμονοφοβία). Porphyry himself, an opponent and enemy of the truth, ridicules this worship, plainly showing that these are neither gods nor good demons, but teachers of lies and fathers of every wickedness. For demons, as spirits of wonderful subtlety, skill, cunning and craftiness, burning with implacable and detestable hatred of God and men, insinuated themselves by various natural and artificial means, such as images, and transformed themselves into whatever forms and shapes they wished, appearing to men, speaking to them, and performing amazing deeds, and by wonderful arts they enticed men to worship them and to honour them as gods. Since God's honour and glory are his own, the demons tried in every way to transfer them to themselves, to claim them for themselves and to make them their own, either directly, as when they wished to be worshipped by Christ, or through means, whether natural or artificial. They have also handed over to their servants, as apes of God, the very names of God and the sacred rites that God had given and prescribed to his people for the worship of his divinity, and had enjoined them, changing them, adding to them or taking away from them in many fraudulent and cunning ways; as is plain from a careful comparison of the rites and ceremonies of the heathen with the Jewish rites divinely instituted. And these things have been said about the first part of the world, namely heaven and the things contained in it, which embraces the countless multitude of heathen gods and deities. Now follows the second part, namely the earth.

units.la: PRIMVM igitur uniuersam Terram in Deorum numero Ethnici duxerunt, eique diuinos honores tribuerunt, sub diuersis nominibus, secundum diuersas ejus qualitates. Terra Dea est, ut ita habetur: quæ est enim alia Tellus ? inquit Cicero de Natura Deorum. Sic Terram Deam esse,inquit Plato in Timæo & in Legibus. Eodem libro de Natura Deorum inquit idem: Terram eam esse,quæ Ceres diceretur, disputat Chrysippus. Item, Terram & Cælum refert in Deos Heraclides Ponticus.
units.tr: FIRST, then, the heathen reckoned the whole earth among the gods and gave it divine honours under various names, according to its various qualities. The earth is a goddess, as it is held to be; for what other Tellus is there? says Cicero in On the Nature of the Gods. Plato says in the Timaeus and in the Laws that the earth is a goddess. In the same book of On the Nature of the Gods he says again that Chrysippus argues that the earth is that which is called Ceres. Likewise Heraclides Ponticus refers the earth and the heaven to the gods.

units.la: Nomina autem, sub quibus Terra diuinis honoribus culta fuit, plurima sunt: inter quæ, Tellus & Tellumon, quæ Augustinus libro septimo de Ciuitate Dei,capite 23. ita ex Varro- ne in libro de Diis distinguit,quod Tellus nihil sit aliud,quam vis; & quidem fœminina,quæ semina recipit,aut nubit. Vim autem masculinam,quæ semina producit, Tellumonem dixerunt. Veteres Terram Heram appellarunt (unde Heroas volunt dictos.) Ex Terra enim hominum genus effectum est,teste Martiano, quod idem Græcus Theophrasti,item Iamblichus & vetus interpres Homeri testantur. Hera nomuni respondet Germanicum Ἤρη, quod utroque genere tam masculino, quam feminino coluerunt, Tellurem & Tellumonem Romani dictum, & sciam Græcorum innuentes, vel domus cujusq; præstitem Larem, quem Heert, hoc est, socium dicimus, significantes.
units.tr: There are very many names under which the earth was worshipped with divine honours, among which Tellus and Tellumo, which Augustine distinguishes in this way from Varro's book On the Gods (De Civitate Dei, bk. 7, ch. 23): that Tellus is nothing other than a power, and indeed a feminine one, which receives seed or is married. The masculine power, which produces seeds, they called Tellumo. The ancients called the earth Hera (whence the heroes are said to be named). For the human race was made from the earth, as Martianus testifies, and the Greek Theophrastus, likewise Iamblichus and the old interpreter of Homer, bear witness. The name Hera corresponds to the German Ērē (Ἤρη), which they worshipped in both genders, masculine and feminine, the Romans calling it Tellus and Tellumo; and they indicate either the Greek goddess Hestia or the Lar who presides over each household, which we call Heert, that is, companion.

units.la: Hæc porró Terra dicta est Mater: & quidem Mater magna & alma ; quod plurima pariat, quod cibum gignat, quòd uni versa animalia fructibus suis alat. Plinius libro 2. cap. 63. Hunc nri, inquit, nature partium, eximia propter merita, cognomen indidimus materne venerationis. Sic hominum illa, ut cœlum Dei: quæ nos nascentes excipit, natos alit, femelq; editos sustinet semper, non visibile complexa gremio, jam a reliqua natura abdicatos, tum maxime, ut mater operiens: nullo magn sacramento, quàm quo nos quoq; sacros facit, etiam monimenta ac cultus gerens, nomenq; prorogans nostrum & memoriam extendens contra breuitatem vi. Plura ibidem vide de Terra utilitate: unde Mater ; & quidem Mater magna dicta fuit. Neq; enim homines tantùm aut bellùa, sed etiam ferè alia a terra vitam haurire, ab eaq; ali, mtriri, so vers & confervari videntur.
units.tr: Moreover, this earth is called Mother, and indeed Great and Nourishing Mother, because she bears very many things, because she begets food, because she feeds all living creatures with her fruits. Pliny, book 2, chapter 63: "To this part of nature," he says, "we have given the name of mother, a title of motherly reverence, on account of its remarkable merits. Thus the earth, as heaven is God's, receives us at our birth, nourishes us when born, and always sustains us once brought forth; she embraces us in her lap, which we cannot see, and when we have already been cut off from the rest of nature, she covers us as a mother does, bearing memorials and rites for us, and prolonging our name and extending our memory against the brevity of life." See more in the same place about the usefulness of the earth, whence she is called Mother, and indeed Great Mother. For it seems that not only men and beasts, but also almost all other things draw their life from the earth, and are nourished, raised, increased and preserved by her.

units.la: Dicta est etiam Mater Deûm ab Ethnicis, propterea quod Dii, qui ab iis colebantur, alii quando mortales fuerunt, ac instar mortalium cæterorum, terræ fructibus vixerunt. Ad hoc Cicero quoq; alludit de Legibus: Terra, inquit Plato, ut focus domicilium sacrum omnium Deorum est. Eandem, libro de Universitate, altricem nostrum, diei cœliq; effectricem, cnstodem antiquissimam Deorum eorum, qui intra cœlos signantur, appellat. Qua appellatione Ethnici Deorum suorum nullitatem, snamq; in illis colendis ssinitium atq; dementiam prodiderunt.
units.tr: The pagans also called her the Mother of the gods, because the gods they worshipped were in part once mortals, and, like other mortals, lived on the fruits of the earth. Cicero also alludes to this in his On the Laws: "The earth," says Plato, "is like a hearth, the sacred dwelling of all the gods." In his book On the Universe he calls her our nurse, the creator of day and sky, and the most ancient guardian of those gods who are marked out among the heavens. By this title the pagans revealed the emptiness of their gods and their own folly in worshipping them.

units.la: Hanc eandem non modo Deam, sed etiam Bonam Deam appellarunt, tanquam bonorum plnrimorum parentem & procreatricem. Vnde a Virgilio Omniparens, a Lucano Frugifera, ab Ovidio, Ferax, Fœta, Gravida, aliisq; nominibus insignitur: a Theodoreto vero χαρισιος, καὶ πλουτοδοτείρα, καὶ ὑπνιτρ, καὶ πλοῦτ, καὶ κεινον ἰδαγ, id est, vitæ distributrix, largitrix, parens ac nutrix.
units.tr: They called this same goddess not only Goddess but also Good Goddess, as the parent and bearer of many good things. Hence Virgil names her "All-parent," Lucan "Fruit-bearing," and Ovid "Fertile," "Pregnant," "Heavy with child," and by other names besides. Theodoret calls her [χαρισιος, καὶ πλουτοδοτείρα, καὶ ὑπνιτρ, καὶ πλοῦτ, καὶ κεινον ἰδαγ], that is, the giver of life, the bestower of riches, the bountiful one, parent and nurse.

units.la: Eandem etiam appellarunt & coluerunt Junonis, Opis, Vesta, Rhea, Proserpina, Cybeles, Cereris, Ætergatis & aliis nominibus.
units.tr: They also named and worshipped this same goddess under the names Juno, Ops, Vesta, Rhea, Proserpina, Cybele, Ceres, Atergatis and others.

units.la: Junonis nomine Ethnici nonnunquam Terram intellexerunt, ob rationem, quàm Virgilius in Verbi descriptione adducit, eam Iovis uxorem fingens: Tum Pater Omnipotens fœcundis imbribus Æther, Conjugis in gremium læta descendit, & omnes Magnus alit, magno commissus corpore, sætus.
units.tr: By the name Juno the pagans sometimes meant the earth, for the reason Virgil gives in his description of the storm, where he imagines her as Jupiter's wife: "Then the almighty Father, the Aether, descends with fruitful showers joyfully into his wife's lap, and great, mingled with her great body, he nourishes all things that are conceived."

units.la: Virtus enim quædam feminalis ex superioribus corporibus in terram influit, quà illi vim elargitur ea omnia proferendi, quæ assatim ipsa producit, non secus atque vir genitale mulieri arvum sno semine conspergens, id ad prolem concipiendam suo, temporeeedendam idonenm, reddit. Sic antem Terra dicta est Juno, a juvando: quia mortales maxime juvat. Vnde Iuno credita Dea di vitiarum: id quod Terræ similiter tribuitur.
units.tr: For a certain seminal power flows from the higher bodies into the earth, and by it grants her strength to bring forth all the things she produces in abundance. It is as when a husband sows his seed in his wife's field, making it fit to conceive offspring, which it then brings forth in due time. The earth is called Juno from juvando, helping, because she especially helps mortals. Hence Juno was believed to be the goddess of riches, which is likewise ascribed to the earth.

units.la: Ops deinde nomine Terra fuit culta: quia omnes opes hominum generi Terra tribuit. Vnde & opulenti dicuntur terræ stribus rebus copi- sh, & bostiæ opimæ præcipuè pinguës: & opima magnifica, et ampla. Vnde spoliaquod, teste Festo, quæ dux populi Romani, duci bostis destraxit, opima dicuntur: quanquàm etiam opima quasi optima dici queant. Ab Ope hac (quam fingunt Saturni conjugem, qui ipse nominatus a satu, vel potius a Satana, tenensq; falcem effingitur, quæ est insigne agricolæ) Vernaculum nostrum obo/id est, frutibus, quos superant Terra, & Latinorum Obsionis & obsonare est natum. Macrobius Terram dixit appellatam Opem vel ab Ope, id est, auxilio, quod ejus ope & auxilio vitæ hominum alimenta quærantur: vel ab Opere, per quod fruges fructusq, nascuntur. Vnde etiam Opis Dea Confiverit mentio apud Varronem, quæ nomen habuit a conserendo: quod fit nõ nisi manuu opere et labore. Ejus sesta Opalia quondam dicta fuerunt.
units.tr: Then the earth was worshipped under the name Ops, because the earth gives all wealth (opes) to the human race. Hence also those rich in lands are called opulenti, and sacrificial victims that are fat are called opimae, especially pinguis; and opima means magnificent and ample. Hence the spoils which, according to Festus, a leader of the Roman people took from the leader of the enemy are called opima, though they might also be called optima. From this Ops (whom they make the wife of Saturn, who is named from satus, or rather from Satan, and is depicted holding a sickle, the emblem of the farmer) comes our word for food, the fruits the earth yields; and the Latin obsonium and obsonare arose from it. Macrobius says the earth was called Ops either from ope, that is help, because by her help and aid human food is sought, or from opere, work, through which grain and fruit are born. Hence also Varro mentions the goddess Opis, the Sower, who took her name from conserendo, sowing, which is done only by hand and by labour. Her festival was once called the Opalia.

units.la: Vesta prætera nomine Terra culta fuit, sic dicta, quod viridibus herbis vestiatur. Hinc Cicero eam vestitâ floribus, herbis, arboribus, frugibus, elegantèr appellat lib. de Natura Deorum: Duæ antè fuerunt apud Antiquos Vesta: quarum una Saturni fuit uxor, quæ pro terra posuerunt: alia ejus filia, quæ ignem significabant, id est, vitalè illam caloré, qui per terræ viscera sufus, ominibus, quæ ex ea oriantur, vitam tribuit. Quare nullam ei Antiqui statuam posuerunt. Ovidius 6. sexto Fastorum: Nec tu aliud Vestam, quàm vivam intellige flammam.
units.tr: Vesta was also worshipped under the name of the earth, so called because she is clothed (vestitur) with green herbs. Hence Cicero elegantly calls her clothed with flowers, herbs, trees and fruits, in his On the Nature of the Gods: "Among the ancients there were two Vestas. One of them was Saturn's wife, whom they set for the earth; the other was his daughter, who signified fire, that is, that vital heat which, diffused through the bowels of the earth, gives life to the things that spring from it. Therefore the ancients set up no statue of her." Ovid, Fasti book 6: "Understand Vesta as nothing other than the living flame."

units.la: Vesta templum, teste Ovidio & Festo, rotundum a Numa Pompilio constructum fuit ad Terræ rotunditatem adumbrandam. Porro Vestam idem Ovidius vult dictam a vi sua stando. Ita enim scribit: Stat vi terra sua, vi stando, Vesta vocatur.
units.tr: The temple of Vesta, according to Ovid and Festus, was built round by Numa Pompilius to represent the roundness of the earth. Ovid holds that Vesta is so called from her power of standing: "Vesta is called from her power, from standing, as the earth stands by her strength."

units.la: Cicero a Græco ἐστία vult dictum. Ea enim, inquit, Eσ̄, quæ aliter ista dicitur. Vis autem ejus omnis ad aras & focos pertinet. Theodoretus: Terræ vim principalem, το γηαμονικον, Eστία, id est, Vestam vocarunt.
units.tr: Cicero thinks the name comes from the Greek hestia: "For that is Hestia," he says, "which is otherwise called thus. All its power pertains to altars and hearths." Theodoret says they called the chief power of the earth, the earth-ruling power [το γηαμονικον], Hestia, that is, Vesta.

units.la: Proserpina quoq; nomine fuit Terra culta, sic nuncupata, quod ex ea fruges, metalla & alia exeuntia quasi proserpant. Cicero: Proserpina est, quæ πηροσφερη Græce nominatur, quam frugum semen esse volunt.
units.tr: Proserpina too was worshipped under this name as the earth, so called because grain, metals and other things come forth from her, as if creeping out (proserpant). Cicero: "Proserpina is what in Greek is called perospherē, which they hold to be the seed of grain."

units.la: Rhea quinetiam nomine Terram venerati sunt, teste Phænulo, sic dictam ἀπὸ τῆς ῥοῆς, id est, a fluxu, quod pluviæ ex ea fluant. Sed hoc de quibus vis aquis atque aliis rebus ex ipsa nascentibus & copiosissimè profluentibus dici potest. Non inepte Rhea deduci potest ab Hebræo יְרָה rhaa, sive ירה rha, id est, malo (unde etiam forsan Rhea, Latinè dictus, quem a Re Cicero vult dictum, ut cujus res agatur) quia Terra maledicta fuit a Deo, propter primorum nostrorum parentum apostasiam: vel a רעה raah, id est, pascendo, quod Terra homines atque bestias pascat ac nutriat. Unde Cicero Altricem eam vocat & matrem cibos suppeditantem.
units.tr: They also venerated the earth under the name Rhea, according to Phornutus, who says she was so called from [ῥοή], that is, flowing, because rains flow from her. But this may be said of the waters and other things that arise from her and flow forth abundantly. Rhea may not unfitly be derived from the Hebrew יָרָה rhaa, or ירה rha, that is, evil (whence perhaps the Latin Rhea, which Cicero thinks comes from res, as one whose affairs are being handled), because the earth was cursed by God on account of our first parents' apostasy. Or it may come from the Hebrew רָעָה raah, that is, feeding, because the earth feeds and nourishes men and beasts. Hence Cicero calls her the nurse and the mother who supplies food.

units.la: Præterea Terram adorarunt Cybeles nomine, quam Fejus Pompejus sic vult dictam ἀπὸ τῆς κύβου, id est, Cubo: qua de causa etiam Cubus est fuerit dicatus, ad Terræ stabilitatem monstrandam, cum Cubus, quocunque modo jaciatur, semper flet rectus: vel ita dicebatur, quod magna mater, hoc est, Terra ageret homines in furorem, quem Græci λῆσσα vocant. Rectius Terram Cybelem appellatam dixerimus ab Hebræa voce שׁבֹּלֶת Sibôleth, significante cum spicas, tum ramusculos oliv arum: quod Terra omnis generis fruges atque fructus proferat, ac profundat.
units.tr: Moreover, they worshipped the earth under the name Cybele, whom Festus Pompeius says was so called from [κύβος], that is, a cube. For this reason a cube was also dedicated to her, to show the earth's stability, since a cube, however it is thrown, always falls upright. Or she was so called because the great mother, that is the earth, drives men into madness, which the Greeks call [λῆσσα].
