More correctly we may say that the earth was called Cybele from the Hebrew word שִׁבֹּלֶת Sibboleth, which means both ears of grain and twigs of the olive tree, because the earth brings forth and pours out every kind of grain and fruit.

units.la: In primis autem Cererem nomine Terram coluerunt; quam id circo etiam a gerendis frugibus & spicis appellarunt, quasi Gererem: quonquam Gêres pura puta vox est Hebraica, qua Moses utitur, Ipsicam virentem significans. Aliteum a frendo, quasi Sererem volunt dictam, ea ut quodam prima litera immutata, ut a Græcis. Nam ib illis quoq; Ἀνάπτυγμα, quasi γυναῖκα, id est, Terra Dea nomiyata fuit. Orpheus γῆν, id est, Terram, vocat μητέρα πάντων, Ἀνὰ ἀὸ τὴν ἀρχαῖα, cui consentaneum illud Ovidii: Prima Ceres uno glebam dimovit aratro Prima dedit fruges, alimentaq; mitia terris.
units.tr: Above all they worshipped the earth under the name Ceres, and for this reason they called her by the name of bearing grain and ears, as if she were Gerere. Yet Geres is a pure Hebrew word, used by Moses, signifying "flourishing." Others think she was named from frendo, grinding, as if Serere, with the first letter changed, as the Greeks do. For among them too, [ἀνάπτυγμα], as if [γυναῖκα], that is, the earth was named the goddess. Orpheus calls the earth, that is Earth, [μητέρα πάντων], the mother of all, [ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρχαῖα], from the beginning. Consistent with this is Ovid's line: "First Ceres turned the clod with a single plough; first she gave fruits and gentle food to the lands."

units.la: Unde ab eodem Mumfica dicitur & potens frugum, hæ versiculis: Te Dea munificam gentes ubicunq; loquuntur. Dira potens frugum sylvis erribatur in altis.
units.tr: Hence the same poet calls her munificent and powerful in grain, in these verses: "Goddess, the nations everywhere call you munificent," and "Dire, powerful in grain, she was sought in the deep woods."

units.la: Hu adde Dis nomen, quo eadem fuit culta. Cicero de Natura Deorum: Terrena vis omnium, inquit, atq; natura Diti patri dedicata est: qui Dis, ut est apud Græcos πλούτων, quia recipiant omnia in terras, & oriantur e terris, ut est dictus. Hesiodus Agricolæ præcipit, ut ante aratrionem atq; factionem, ut ferant tenens vota nomine Diti ac Ceres.
units.tr: Add the name Dis, under which the earth was also worshipped. Cicero, in On the Nature of the Gods: "The earthly power and nature of all things," he says, "is dedicated to the father Dis," who is, as among the Greeks, [Πλούτων], "because they receive all things into the earth, and they arise from the earth, as he is named." Hesiod instructs the farmer that before ploughing and sowing he should hold his vows in his hands and pray to Dis and Ceres.

units.la: Postremo Terram etiam Astergatis nomine, quam alii Adarcaten, alii Derceronem vocant, quæ Dea vuit Syriæ sive Assyriæ, coluerunt. Duo autem erant principales Assyriorum Numina; nempe Adad, quod erat nomen summi Dei, & Vnum significat, quem Solem esse Macrobius vult. Adrum, quod est subjungebant, erat Adarcatis, sive Astergatis, quam Terram interpretantur.
units.tr: Finally, they worshipped the earth under the name Atergatis, whom some call Adarcate and others Derceto, a goddess of Syria or Assyria. The Assyrians had two principal deities: Adad, which was the name of the supreme God and means "One," whom Macrobius says is the Sun; and Adrum, which they added, belonged to Adargatis or Atergatis, whom they interpret as the Earth.

units.la: THAEC de Terræ universæ cultu. Iam verò et singulas Terræ partes venerabantur, vel certis consecrabant Diis. Terræ partes sunt montes, colles, valles, campi, nemora, fyl væ, luci. Quantum ad montes, eorum cum altitudinem, tum fœcunditatem et fertilitatem admirantes, vel tunc quoq refert, tanquam Deos colebant, vel Deos eorum fingebant incolas & præsides. Tales montium Diis erant Carmelus & Amanus, qui & certorum montium nomen habebant, ut constat ex historia sacra. Talis erat Iuzatinus Deus, quijugu mentiii præsidebat. Talis Bacchus, idcirco Oreos sive Oreus, id est, monticola dictus. Virg. Bacchus amat colles.—
units.tr: So much on the worship of the earth as a whole. Now they also venerated single parts of the earth, or consecrated them to certain gods. The parts of the earth are mountains, hills, valleys, plains, groves, woods and sacred groves. As for mountains, admiring their height as well as their fruitfulness and fertility, they either worshipped them as gods, or imagined gods as their inhabitants and presiding powers. Such were the mountain gods Carmel and Amanus, which were also the names of certain mountains, as is clear from sacred history. Such was the god Iuzatinus, who presided over the ridge of the mountains. Such was Bacchus, who for this reason was called Oreos or Oreus, that is, mountain-dweller. Virgil: "Bacchus loves the hills."

units.la: Unde & Oreades Nymphæ appellatæ & cultæ, quod in montibus frequenter apparerent.
units.tr: Hence also the Oreades, the nymphs, were so named and worshipped, because they often appeared on the mountains.

units.la: Sic Collium Dea & praeses fingebatur Collina: vallium Vallona sive Valionia: nemorum, lucorum & sylvarum Sylvani, Satyri, Fauni, Sileni, Nemestrinus, Dryades, Faula, Feronia, & Juno (unde Lucina cognominata) camporum, rurum, agrorum item Sylvanus: tui & agrorum colendorum cura fuit tradita: quemadmodum etiam Rufina Dea sive Rurina a rure nomen babuit, quia ipsi rura communi fuerunt: quo pertinent & Terminus, Pan & Priapus. Nam Terminus Deus, inquit Festus, dictus, quod in eius tutela effent agrorum fines. Hic secundum Varronem a T. Tatio consecratus est: secundum alios a Numa Pompilio, & cultus in Capitolio, ubi cum Tarquinius superbus templum amplissimum Jovi Optimo Maximo extruere vellet, & propterea omnium aliorum Deorum aedes exaugurater, Terminus & Juventas et tedere noluerunt, qua de re Livius, Dionysius, Ovidius, Augustinus & alii. Pan deinde, Mercurii filius, Latinè Junus dictus, nomen accepit a pan, Omne: quia non tantum sub ipso universa rerum naturam colebatur, ut dictum est supra, sed quia praerat montibus, sylvis, lucis, agris, pastoribus, ovibus, aliisq; animantibus. Unde Deorum ruricolorum praecipuus fuit habitus, & ex ollo majorum gentium Dius unus: ac propterea Junus dictus, ab eundo pastum cum omnibus animalibus. Ob quam cau-sam etiam simulacrum ejus caprina facie effingebatur, rubro colore, hirtis cornibus, pectore hide-ribus radiante, infima su: parte hispida & caprino pede: altera pede incurvum, quod ejus fimolachrum eleganter interpretatur Macrobius libro primo Saturnalium, capite vigesimo secundo, & ad rerum naturam transfert. Denique rurus & agrorum Deus ac praeses fuit etiam Priapus, Dionysii & Venerit filius, quod ex illo Ovidii fatus loquet:
units.tr: In the same way, the goddess and protectress of the hills was imagined as Collina; of the valleys, Vallona or Valionia; of the groves, thickets and woods, the Sylvani, Satyrs, Fauns, Sileni, Nemestrinus, Dryades, Faula, Feronia, and Juno (whence she was surnamed Lucina); of the plains and countryside, and likewise of the fields, Sylvanus. The care of cultivating the fields was entrusted to him. Rufina, or Rurina, likewise took her name from the countryside (rus), because she presided over the country estates. To this category belong also Terminus, Pan and Priapus. For Terminus, says Festus, was so called because the boundaries of the fields were under his protection. According to Varro he was consecrated by Titus Tatius, according to others by Numa Pompilius, and he was worshipped on the Capitol. When Tarquin the Proud wished to build a very large temple to Jupiter Best and Greatest, and for that reason took the auspices away from the shrines of all the other gods, Terminus and Juventas alone refused to move. Livy, Dionysius, Ovid, Augustine and others tell this story. Next, Pan, the son of Mercury, called Junus in Latin, received his name from pan, "all", because the whole nature of things was worshipped under him, as was said above, and because he presided over mountains, woods, groves, fields, shepherds, sheep and other living creatures. Hence he was regarded as the chief of the rural gods, and one of the great gods of the greater nations, and was called Junus from going (eundo) to pasture with all the animals. For this reason his image was also fashioned with a goat's face, a ruddy colour, shaggy horns, a breast glowing with rays, the lower part of the body hairy, a goat's foot, and the other foot curved. Macrobius, in book 1 of the Saturnalia, chapter 22, explains this image elegantly and refers it to the nature of things. Finally, Priapus, son of Dionysus and Venus, was also a god and protector of fields and gardens, as Ovid's verse shows:
Even the stiff-necked guardian yields to the little ass.

units.la: Ubi Priapum intelligit. Hunc etiam Hortorum Deum et custodem fecerunt, quemadmodum & Alcinoum Regem Phaeacum, quod hortos & pomaria diligentissime curarit. De illo enim pic Vir gilius Ecloga 7. Sinum laetis & haec te liba, Priape, quotannis Exspectare sat est cultos et pauperis horti.
units.tr: There he means Priapus. They also made him the god and guardian of gardens, just as they made Alcinous, king of the Phaeacians, because he tended his gardens and orchards most diligently. For Virgil speaks of him in Eclogue 7: "Priapus, it is enough for you to expect these cakes and this milk each year, you who guard a cultivated and poor garden."

units.la: Fuit is etiam Deus nuptialis dictus Mutinus. de quo alibi. Priapum Theophilus in Ho-sam vult eundem fuisse, quem Hebraei Baalpegor appellarunt, cui myste initiati sacrificabant, qui mares videbantur faemellae fuisse, quae cymbalis utentes, faeminem ululatib. tr: via circuibant.
units.tr: He was also called the god of marriage, Mutinus, of whom I shall speak elsewhere. Theophilus in his Hosea holds that Priapus was the same as the one whom the Hebrews called Baal-peor, to whom the initiates sacrificed, and who were thought to be women among men, who, playing cymbals, went around with women's howling.

units.la: Porro & agriculturae certos Deos ac Deas praefecerunt, utin genere Saturnum: qui a fatu sic dictus, ideo falcem tenens, quae agriculturae esi infigne, effingitur: & in specie farritioni Sarritorem: arationi Cererem & Ofyrin: sationi Satorem & Sejam : occationi Occatorem: Stercoristioni Picumnum (qui & Sterquilinus dictus, & Sterculus: segetibus Segetum sive Segesiam: frumentis germinantibus Proserpinam : geniculis nodisq; culmorum Nodinum sive Nodorum: in volumentis folliculorum Volumnum & Volumnam sive Volutinam: cum folliculi patescunt, ut spica exeat, Patelenam: cum segetes novi aristis aquaneur (quia Veteres aquare Hostire dixerunt) Hostilinam, florentibus frumentis Floram: latte entibus Latturam (Servius in primum Georgic. Latentem Deum esse dicit, qui lacinfundat ... ibus, et eas faciat latefecere) maturescentibus Maturam : cum runcantur, id est, a terra auf runtur, Averruncum & Runcinam, quae & Spinenfis dicta, quae spinas ex agris eradicaret.
units.tr: Moreover, they also appointed particular gods and goddesses over agriculture. In general, Saturn, who is so called from sowing (satus), is depicted holding a sickle, which is the emblem of agriculture. In particular: for weeding, Sarritor; for ploughing, Ceres and Ops; for sowing, Sator and Seia; for harrowing, Occator; for manuring, Picumnus (also called Sterquilinus and Sterculus); for the crops, Segetes or Segesia; for the germinating grain, Proserpina; for the joints and knots of the stalks, Nodinus or Nodotus; for the swelling of the husks, Volumnus and Volumna or Volutina; when the husks open so that the ear comes out, Patelena; when the crops are beginning to ripen into ears, which they called "hostire" (to ripen)... Hostilina; for flowering grain, Flora; for lying hidden, Lactura (Servius on the first Georgic says that Latens is a god who makes things lie hidden and causes them to be concealed); for ripening, Matura; and when the crops are weeded out, that is, uprooted from the ground, Averruncus and Runcina, who was also called Spinensis, because she tore out the thorns from the fields.

units.la: Ut autem & tuto fer varentur frumenta collecta atque recondita certos Deos & Deas illius praefuerunt, qui a tuendo Tutanus & Tutelina, sive Tutelina: ab avertendo rubiginem a segetibus Robigus, & Robigo (cui etiam Robigalia celebrabantur) fuerunt dicti. Pertinet huc Deus Arungus, mala omnis generis a frumentis avertens.
units.tr: So that the grain, once gathered and stored, might be kept safe, they set over it certain gods and goddesses, who were called Tutanus and Tutelina (or Tutelina) from protecting (tuendo), and Robigus and Robigo, from averting rust (robigo) from the crops; the Robigalia were also celebrated in their honour. To this group belongs the god Arungus, who averts every kind of evil from the grain.

units.la: Deniq; et pilendi seu pinsendi frumenti Deum conflituerunt, quem Pilumnum Servius in Sextum Aeneidos vocat, qui Picumni Dei Sterquilini, frater fuit, & praesertim a Pistoribus cuitus: a quo & pilum dictum est. Et quia ante triticum & ejus usum farra fornacibus torrebant, Fornax: Dea fuit excitata: quam hyberno potissimum tempore, rigente frigore, colebant: de qua Ovidius xaxeagxoun & sic loquitur:
units.tr: Finally, they also established a god of pounding or grinding grain, whom Servius in his commentary on the sixth book of the Aeneid calls Pilumnus, the brother of Picumnus Sterquilinus, and who was worshipped especially by bakers; the pestle (pilum) is named after him. And because before wheat and its use, they parched spelt (farra) in ovens, the goddess Fornax was raised up, whom they worshipped chiefly in winter, when the cold was bitter. Ovid speaks of her in the Fasti:

units.la: Falta Dea est Fornax, laeti gaudete coloni. Unde Fornacalia quoq, sacra institutabro 4. de Civitate Dei, capite 11. meminit Dea Fruellefea, quae fructibus praesset; quibus praefuit etiam Saturnus: quemadmodum floribus eorum Flora unde Floralia. Infpecie pomis praefuit
units.tr: Fornax is a goddess; rejoice, happy farmers. Hence also the Fornacalia were instituted. Augustine, in book 4 of The City of God, chapter 11, mentions the goddess Fruticaria, who presided over fruits; Saturn too presided over them, just as Flora presided over flowers, whence the Floralia. Over the kinds of fruit presided

units.la: Dea Pomona (quæ & proprium habebat Flaminem, qui dicebatur Flamen Pomonalis:) icemq; Vertumnus, sive ut alij volunt, Vortumnus, sic dictus quod anni vertentes poma percipiat. Quidam affirmant, Vertumnum fuisse vetustissimum Thuscorum Regem, qui vinearum & pomiferarum arborum serendarum tradiderit rationē, cui Tbuscieillij, qui cum Lucumone in auxilium Romulo venisse dicuntur, Rome templum ædificârint. Hujus signum & templum in vico Thusco ad Opü & Cereris aras constituerunt. Festa ejus, quæ mense Octobri celebrabantur, Vertumnalia appellarunt. Tandem, Agricolæ posteà collectas fruges quiescentes, Deæ Vacunæ sacrificabant.
units.tr: the goddess Pomona (who also had a special flamen, called the Flamen Pomonalis), and Vertumnus, or, as others prefer, Vortumnus, so called because the turning years bring the fruits to maturity. Some affirm that Vertumnus was the most ancient king of the Tuscans, who taught the method of planting vines and fruit trees; the Tuscans who are said to have come with Lucumo to help Romulus built a temple to him at Rome. They set up his statue and temple in the Tuscan quarter, by the altars of Ops and Ceres. They called his festival, celebrated in October, the Vertumnalia. Finally, farmers later sacrificed to the goddess Vacuna when the harvested crops lay at rest.

units.la: Pomo remo quia ars pastoritia & mellificatio quoq; ad agriculturam pertinent: ideo his quoq; Dii ac Deæ pas-ceri Deos ac Deas præfecerunt, sub quibus eas coluerunt. Nam pastorum & pabuli Deum vel florum. Veam fecerunt Mercurium, Pana & Palen; unde Palilia, vel Parilia, festum in ejus honore celebratum. Et bobus præerat Bubona: quorum de furto quia Herculi indicium fecerat Cacus, joror, eaut Dea culta fuit Romæ: unde etiam sacellum meruit, in quo et per virgines ales fiebat res sacra, ut scribit Servius Æneid.8. sic aquis & stabulo Hippona præfuit: quarum meminerunt Augustinus lib 6. de Civitate Dei cap.9. Plutarchus in Parallelis, Apuleius libro 3. de Asino aureo, Tertullianus in Apologetico, & Fulgentius de obscuris vocibus. Mellificationi vero Deus fuit Aristeus, filius Apollinis & Cyneres, filiæ Pemi, qui primus usum mellis invenisse dicitur; Dea vero Mellona, sive Mellonia, cujus meminit inter alios Arnobius. Ac in Peloponneso Melissa Nympha, quæ usum mellis illis dedisse credita est, in sacrorum præfatione adhibebatur. Et de Diis Terræ partiū, quos venerabantur, bateleum: quibus, Co-llarii loco, addi possunt Dii Topici a Græcis & Latinis dicti, qui locorum, regionum, urbium Pugularum, peculiarem curam gerebant: quis interdum Latinè Tutelares, sive Tutani a tutando, & Genii ac custodes appellabantur, quos in dubiis & periculosis rebus invocatos ab ipsis suisse constat.
units.tr: Since the pastoral art and beekeeping also pertain to agriculture, gods and goddesses were likewise set over these, under whom they were worshipped. For they made Mercury the god of shepherds and pasture, and also of flocks, Pan and Pales; whence the Palilia, or Parilia, a festival celebrated in their honour. Bubona presided over oxen. Because Cacus had informed Hercules of the theft of their cattle, the goddess Bubona was worshipped at Rome, and so she earned a little shrine, where a sacred rite was performed by virgins, as Servius writes on the Aeneid, book 8. Likewise Hippona presided over horses and stables; Augustine (book 6 of The City of God, chapter 9), Plutarch in the Parallels, Apuleius in book 3 of The Golden Ass, Tertullian in the Apology, and Fulgentius in De obscuris vocibus, have mentioned them. For the making of honey, the god was Aristaeus, son of Apollo and Cyrene, daughter of Peneus, who is said to have been the first to discover the use of honey; the goddess was Melliona, or Mellonia, whom Arnobius among others mentions. And in the Peloponnese the nymph Melissa, who was believed to have given them the use of honey, was invoked in the preface to the sacred rites. These are enough about the gods of the parts of the earth that they worshipped. To them may be added, as a corollary, the Topic gods, so called by Greeks and Latins, who had particular care of places, regions and cities; these were sometimes called in Latin Tutelares, or Tutani from protecting, and Genii and guardians. It is established that they were invoked in doubtful and dangerous affairs.

units.la: NVNC antequam de iis dicam, quæ in Terra & super Terram continentur, cujusmodi sunt Τριγλίπαι animalia, metalla, quæ vel pro Diis fuerunt habita, atque cultu, vel cercis Diis dicata, aquarū cultus. rius de Aquis cælestibus & terrestribus aquarumq; omnium receptaculo, Mari, nobis est dicendum.
units.tr: Now, before I speak of those things that are contained in the earth and above the earth, such as the animals, the metals, which were either regarded as gods and worshipped, or dedicated to certain gods, we must speak of the worship of waters, of the waters of heaven and earth, and of the sea, the receptacle of all waters.

units.la: Mare igitur ipsum universum, & singulæ ejus partes, fontes, flumina, fluvii, lacus, aquadeнии, & humor universus multos Deorum nominibus consecrata atque culta fuerunt. Aquam ixit initium rerum Thales Milesius; Deum autem eam mentem, quæ ex aqua cunctā fingeret: cuius quidē statim ab initio creationis Mundi fit mentio Genes. 1. Et aquæ erant super Terram, &c V autem Terra; ita Aqua multis Numinibus est ascripta: Lucinæ dicta quasi aqua, quod ficies ejus æqualis sit. Unde & Æquor, qua æqualiter sursum est: vel quasi a qua sint omnia, secundum Thaletem Milesiū sententiam: vel a qua juvamur. Unde aqua & igni interdicti at, a Romanis, quibusdam damnatis, tanquam duabus rebus humanam vitam maxime contentibus, ut inquit Festus Pompeius: Græcis dicitur ὕδωρ, ab humiditate, Ægyptiis & Chaldeis Moi, (unde & Moses, tanquam extractus ex aquis, dictus) Hebræis מים Maim, nisi pro vis litteris a ם lam, id est, Mari, εὐ quod Mare fit quasi mater & πατρόχθιον omnium aquarum.
units.tr: The sea itself, as a whole, and each of its parts, the springs, rivers, streams, lakes, and all moisture, were consecrated under many names of gods and worshipped. Thales of Miletus held that water was the beginning of things, and that the mind which formed everything out of water was God. Of this mind, indeed, mention is made from the very beginning of the creation of the world, Genesis 1: "And the waters were upon the earth," etc. Thus water was ascribed to many deities. The lake (lacus) is so called as if it were "aqua", because its surface is level (aequalis). Hence also the sea (aequor) is so called, because its surface lies level, or because all things come from water, according to the opinion of Thales of Miletus, or because we are helped by it. Hence the Romans forbade water and fire to certain condemned persons, as two things most essential to human life, as Festus Pompeius says. The Greeks call it water [ὕδωρ], from its moisture; the Egyptians and Chaldeans call it mou (whence Moses too was named, as one drawn out of the waters); the Hebrews call it [מים] maim, unless it is derived from the letter mem [ם], that is, from mare (sea), since the sea is, as it were, the mother and source of all waters.

units.la: Hæ autem Mare universum & has aquas omnes coluerunt sub Neptuni nomine. Huic enim inter fratres, secundum Ethnicorum fabulas, qui illum Opu & Saturni filium finxerunt, sub Neptuni no-me patrem Iovis ac Plutonis, maritimū, Amphitridis, administratio Maris & aquarum fuit comm: unde dictus ab Ovidio, Æquoreus, Cæruleus, rector Maris & Deus: a Plauto Salsiposen: Hesiodo parens aquarum.
units.tr: Men worshipped the whole sea and all these waters under the name of Neptune. According to the fables of the heathen, who made him a son of Ops and Saturn, Neptune was the brother of the others and the father of Jupiter and Pluto. He was the sea god, the husband of Amphitrite, and the rule of the sea and the waters was his. Hence Ovid called him the sea-born, the blue-green ruler of the sea and god. Plautus called him the salt-drinker, and Hesiod the parent of the waters.

units.la: Porro quia Mare terras obnubit, ut nubes cælum, Neptunus est dictus: quamvis alii eum quasi nubes ∼ nantem appellent. Inde Neptunalia, hujus Dei marini feriæ posteæ dictæ, & celebrata.
units.tr: Because the sea hides the lands as clouds hide the sky, he was called Neptunus, though others derive the name from his swimming, as if he were "nubes-nantem." From him the Neptunalia, the festival days of this sea god, were named and celebrated.

units.la: Præter hunc, alii Dii ac Deæ marinæ fuerunt, ut: Nereus pater, Nereides filiæ, Proteus, Aquæ culta ea-ronnus, Tethys, Doris, Pollux, Castor, Glaucus, Vertumnus, Amphitrite, Sirenes, Naiades tiam alias sub Numinibus. fan a מים Maim, Hebreo nomine, per conversionem litteræ liquidæ Man N.) Tritones, qui figura partim hominem, partim piscem referebant, Melicertem filium & Leucothoe matrem, quae prius Ino fuit dicta, & Matuta Dea, cuius memimit Ovidius his verbis: Leucothoë Grajus, Matuta vocabere nostris.
units.tr: Besides him there were other sea gods and goddesses: Nereus the father, the Nereids his daughters, Proteus, Aquaeus (called Aquarius), Tethys, Doris, Pollux, Castor, Glaucus, Vertumnus, Amphitrite, the Sirens, the Naiads, and many others worshipped as divinities. [Naiads are linked to the Hebrew word for water, מים Maim, by the change of the liquid letter, m to n.] There were also the Tritons, who were partly men and partly fish; Melicertes the son and Leucothoe the mother, who was earlier called Ino; and the goddess Matuta, whom Ovid mentions in these words: "Leucothoe to the Greeks, but to us you will be called Matuta."

units.la: Ee Propertius: Quaeq; tibi excepit tum Dea Leucothoë.
units.tr: And Propertius: "And the goddess Leucothoe, who then received you."

units.la: Huc referenda est Dea Salacia, a Salo cognomen, seu concitando dicta, cujus meminit Varro lib. 4. de lingua Latina, & Festus in Fragmentis ita scribens: Salacia dicta est, quod salum cieat. Antiquos autem, ajunt, eo vocabulo Poetas pro aqua ipsa usos esse. Pacuvius: Hinc se vittam Salaciae fugimus, laeti, munere vestimur Ceres. Et Ovidius: Nymphae, falacet.
units.tr: To this group belongs the goddess Salacia, named either from the sea (salum) as her epithet or from stirring it up. Varro mentions her in the fourth book of his On the Latin Language, and Festus in his Fragments writes: "Salacia is so called because she stirs the sea (salum cieat)." They say the ancient poets used this word for water itself. Pacuvius: "Hence we flee, glad, from the ribbon of Salacia, we are clothed with the gift of Ceres." And Ovid: "Nymphs, ..."

units.la: Pertinet huc portuum marinorum Deus, ab ipsis cultus, quem putabant esse eum, qui Palaemonem a Graecis, & Portumnus Latinis dicitur, seu nauta reducere suis navigationibus sacrificaret, seu comiti Neptuni. Hic & alii Dii littorales ἀλιεῖς, id est, τοῖς ἐν τῇ ἀκτῇ τιμώμενοις, quo tpitheto etiam Apollinem insignat Apollonius, id est, in littore colitur.
units.tr: To this group belongs also the god of the sea harbours, whom the heathen worshipped on the shore. They believed he was the one called Palaemon by the Greeks and Portunus by the Latins, and that he brought sailors home safely on their voyages, or else that he was the companion of Neptune. He and other shore gods are called "those honoured on the shore [τοῖς ἐν τῇ ἀκτῇ τιμώμενοις]," which is the epithet Apollonius also gives Apollo, meaning that he is worshipped on the shore.

units.la: Vt autem Mare ipsum & portus ejus divinis fuerunt honoribus culti: sic fonte, quoque de Fontinalia, feria certa: quibus & in fontes coronas jacie-bant, & puteos coronabant. Vt & Romae Fontinalis porta. Plautus:
units.tr: Just as the sea itself and its harbours were honoured with divine worship, so too were springs, and there was a set festival, the Fontinalia, at which they threw garlands into the springs and crowned the wells. There was also a Fontinal Gate at Rome. Plautus: "Do you prefer to take command from Fontinalis or from Liber?"

units.la: Vtrum Fontinali an Libero Imperium te mbibere mavis?
units.tr: "Do you prefer to take command from Fontinalis or from Liber?"

units.la: Sic fluminibus, flagnus, lacubusve cum unis persis, cum singulis divinitas & venerantio fuit tributa, eas simulachra, statuas, aras, vota & sacrificia facta & instituta: quorum simulacra tum quaedam humana facie, quaedam bulla effingebantur. Pertinent huc Archeloë, Nilus, Tiberis, Nymphae sive lymphae: quibus statuae, aras & sacella, praecipue a Romanis, porta, ius vota facta & preces pro amoliendo malo. Has enim Antiquitas sentendas divulgas credebat, si ob culpam Sacrorum demulcerentur. Super flitionem illam: ipse quoq; Cicero videtur subridere his verbis Earum, inquit, Deorum templum inflammari: quarum ope etiam alius templi subvenit Nymphae hinc salutifere dictae: de quo epithelo Saxopolis in Dacia, in templo bujusmodi Nymopharum monumentum extat: NYMPHIS SALVTIFERIS SACRVM M. LVCILIVS LVCILIANVS AVG COS. PRO SALVTE SVA. ET L. ANTISTI. SIMI AVG. CONS.
units.tr: In the same way, divinity and veneration were given to rivers, pools, and lakes, and each had its own; images, statues, altars, vows, and sacrifices were made and established for them. Their images were fashioned partly with human faces and partly as bulls. To this group belong Achelous, the Nile, the Tiber, and the Nymphs or Lymphs, to whom statues, altars, and small shrines were set up, especially by the Romans, and to whom vows and prayers were made to avert evil. For antiquity believed that these divinities would be provoked against men if they were not appeased by sacred rites. Cicero himself seems to smile at this superstition, with the words: "The temples of those gods, he says, are set on fire, by whose help the temple of another god is also rescued." Hence the Nymphs were called salutary (Salutiferae). An inscription on this epithet survives at Sarmizegetusa in Dacia, in a temple of this kind of Nymphs: "To the Salutiferous Nymphs, sacred. Marcus Lucilius Lucilianus, Augustan consul, for his own safety, and L. Antistius, Augustan consul." [The inscription is garbled in the Latin.]

units.la: Hae autem eadem Numina, Dii a quae Dea Marii Fontium, Fluminum, Stagnorum Lacuum; Pollux, qui in celebris illa navigatione... nomine Dioscuri, quos Antiqui... (apparent autem signa, Hecie... apud Graecos (inquit Cicero) Natura Deorum) multos modis nominantur. Proserpinae... Ebulus, Dionysus. ... Neptunus. Numinum aquarum ... omnium rerum ... que ripis cinxit ac circumdedit: tanquam terminus, limitibus & oflius, ne in terram erumpant. Iob. 38. Proverb. 8.
units.tr: These same powers, the gods of fountains, rivers, pools and lakes, are called by many names: Pollux, in that famous voyage, under the name of the Dioscuri, whom the ancients ... (the signs appear, as Cicero says, among the Greeks in On the Nature of the Gods); Proserpina ... Ebulus, Dionysus ... Neptune. The waters of the deep ... all things ... which he encircled and surrounded with banks, as a boundary, with limits and doors, so that they do not burst out onto the land. Job 38; Proverbs 8.

units.la: VENIAMVS nunc ad animalium, plantarum & metallorum, quae cum in terris, tum in aquis sunt, cultum. Quantum ad animalia rationis experta, sive bestias, illas partim Deorum numero fuisse ab Ethnicis cultas: partim certis Diis consectatas et dicatas, passim sacris et prophanis temporibus. Quot igitur fuerunt bestiarum genera, tot tis fuerunt Numina. quod Idololatriæ genus apud Gentiles, Ægyptios præsertim, qui Deos maximè monstrosos & portentosos coluerunt, familiare fuit: apud quos nullum fere brutorum genus repertum, quod non coluerint. Hoc aperte divinus Paulus indicat in epistola ad Romanos, capite primo; ubi docet, Gentes gloriam Deiimmortalis commutasse in figurum atque imaginem non solum hominum corruptibilis, sed etiam Volucrium, Quadrupedum & Reptilium.
units.tr: Let us now come to the worship of animals, plants, and metals, which exist both on land and in water. As for animals endowed with reason, or beasts, the heathen worshipped some of them among their gods, and dedicated others to particular gods, here and there, on both sacred and profane occasions. So there were as many deities as there were kinds of beasts. This kind of idolatry was common among the Gentiles, especially the Egyptians, who worshipped the most monstrous and prodigious gods; among them there was almost no kind of beast they did not worship. The divine Paul points this out plainly in his Epistle to the Romans, chapter one, where he teaches that the Gentiles exchanged the glory of the immortal God for an image and likeness not only of corruptible men, but also of birds, four-footed beasts and creeping things.

units.la: Vt autem animalium rationis expertium alia sunt simplicis vitæ: alia amphibia: ficutriusque generis animalia singula coluerunt aut ea certis Dijs consecrârunt. Aërea quidem Volucres, ut aves. Nam Syri columbas coluerunc & adoraverunt · Ægyptii gryphones, aquilas, vulturesque, quibus ad auspitia maximè sunt usi, vespertiliones, sibes & accipitres, capite primo; sub quarum symbolo Osirim, qui apud eos Sol est, intelligebant. Hinc apud eos pileum rubrum unâ cum accipitre ut ales[?] rerum sacrarum scriptores gestare fuerunt soliti. Coluerunt porro & adoraverunt recigallos: Theffali ciconias, quas occidere apud eos erat nefas: Latini picos, quibus uniuersi magnopere abstinebant: Romani anseres (unde Plutarchus in Quæstionibus Romanis quæstione nonagesima octava, in hunc modum loquitur: Censoribus magistratus ineuntibus nihil prius erat locatione alimentorum pro sacris anseribus.)
units.tr: Some animals with reason are simple, others amphibious, and the heathen worshipped each kind of animal singly or dedicated them to particular gods. Of the air-dwellers, the birds: the Syrians worshipped and adored doves; the Egyptians revered griffins, eagles, and vultures, which they especially used for augury, and also bats, owls, and hawks. Under the symbol of the hawk they understood Osiris, who among them is the sun; hence the writers of sacred things were accustomed to wear a red cap with a hawk's feathers as birds do. They also worshipped cocks; the Thessalians, storks, which it was forbidden to kill among them; the Latins, woodpeckers, from which everyone strictly abstained; the Romans, geese. Plutarch, in his Roman Questions, question ninety-eight, speaks thus: "When the censors took office, nothing came before the contracting of the food supply for the sacred geese."

units.la: Has verò atq; alias aues Ethnici etiam certis Dijs ac Numinibus consecrarunt. Nam Veneri & Apollini Ycnus sacer erat; & illi quidem etiam ardeâ: huic verò columba, gallus (qui & Æsculapio & Mineruæ) coruus (qui & Marti ob rapinas) & accipiter, ob vilius præstantiam atiem, quanquam columbæ candidæ etiam Veneri fuerint dicatæ, a quibus currus ejus veheretur. Aquila sovi fuit sacra: turtur propter silentium Harpocrati: fulica (Græcè λάρος, a vs rapax, a cujus rapacitatte Comici sepenumero homines furaces appellant Laros, & Galli larrons, id est, fures) Herculi & Mercurio: noctua Minervæ: phœnix Solis: pavo, ciconia (quæ etiam Concordiæ Deæ) anser & vultur Iunoni: (unde pavonis penna apud Ægyptios non tantum Ifidis simulacrum coronari solitum, sed domorum nobilitatem & antiquitatem, secundum Alexandri Neapolitani sententiam, ostendendam: cujus quidem nobilitatis & pavonis el anti ma apud Bocatum exstat comparatio) picus Martis: grus Cereri (utin libro de abstinentia ab animantibus testatur Porphyrius:) Ibis Mercurio, cuius cordis omnisque rationis præsidi & moderatori. Vnde cor volentes indicare Æ-gyptii, ibin pingebant, quia Ibis per seipsa, magna ex parte, cordi consimilis est. Hinc Cicero libro primo de Natura Deorum, Ægyptii, inquit, nullum beluam, nisi ob aliquam utilitatem, quam ex ea caperent, conseruerunt. Ibes maximam vim serpentium conficiunt, cum sint aves exacruribus rigidis, corneo proceroque rostro: avertunt pellem ab Ægypto, cum volucres, tum angues, ex vastitate Lybiæ vento Africo in vettas, interficiunt atque consumunt: ex quo fit, ut ille nec morsu virus noceanc, nec odore mortuæ. Hallenas ille.
units.tr: The heathen also dedicated these and other birds to particular gods. The ibis was sacred to Venus and Apollo, the heron to them too; the dove to Venus, the cock (which was also sacred to Aesculapius and Minerva), the raven (also to Mars for its plundering) and the hawk, for its swiftness and swooping flight, though white doves were also dedicated to Venus, by whom her chariot was drawn. The eagle was sacred to Jove; the turtle-dove to Harpocrates for its silence; the coot (in Greek laros [λάρος], from laro, meaning greedy, whose rapacity comics often used to call thieving men laros, and the French larron, that is, thief) to Hercules and Mercury; the owl to Minerva; the phoenix to the sun; the peacock, the stork (which was also sacred to Concord), the goose and the vulture to Juno. Hence among the Egyptians the peacock's feather was customarily used to crown not only the image of Isis but also to show the nobility and antiquity of families, according to the opinion of Alexander of Naples, and a comparison of this nobility and the peacock's soul survives in Boccatus. The woodpecker was sacred to Mars, the crane to Ceres (as Porphyry attests in his book On Abstinence from Animals), and the ibis to Mercury, the guardian and governor of the heart and of all reason. Hence the Egyptians, wishing to indicate the heart, painted an ibis, because the ibis in large part resembles the heart. Hence Cicero, in the first book On the Nature of the Gods: "The Egyptians, he says, have worshipped no beast except for some usefulness they derived from it. The ibises destroy a great number of snakes; they are birds with stiff legs and a long horned beak. They drive away from Egypt both birds and serpents, which the south wind brings from the wastes of Libya into the settled lands, and they kill and devour them. As a result, those creatures do no harm either with their bite or their smell in death." So far Cicero.

units.la: Co luerunt deinde & animalia aërea gradientia; eaq; Quadrupedia, ut feles, hircos, boves, aries, canes, sues, mures, Ægyptii. (Hircum quidem, quod falacissimum sit animal: quem etiam Mendesii eximiis venerabantur honoribus, teste Theodoreto.) Memphiæ taurum: Theobantimus, Ielam: Lycopolitæ & Delphici lupum, quod sacrum aurum in templo expilatum & deorum fodisset: Samii ouem, quod aurum ibidem sure-ptum e templo indicasset: Leontopoli-te Leonem (quem Ægypti Solis, ut & bouem dedicarunt) & leonam in Ambracia, cen-tindicem bertatis, quod tyrannuni interemisset: Cynopolitani canem & cynocephalum, quod animal nutrunc ιο ανο ταγόις; partim quod animalis ιτι ab esu piscium abhorret, partim quod cuncti sum gignitur, quam circumcisionem sacerdoces curare & peragere fuerunt soliti.
units.tr: Next the Egyptians also worshipped land animals that walk on foot, and four-footed beasts such as cats, goats, oxen, rams, dogs, pigs and mice. (They honoured the goat especially, since it is a very lustful animal, and the people of Mendes venerated it with special honours, as Theodoret testifies.) At Memphis they worshipped the bull; the Theobantimi, the ... ; the Lycopolitans and the Delphians, the wolf, because it had dug up and stolen the sacred gold from the temple; the Samians, the sheep, because it had revealed the gold stolen from the temple there; the Leontopolitans, the lion (which the Egyptians dedicated to the sun, as also the ox) and the lioness, in Ambracia, the avenger of liberty, because it had killed a tyrant; the Cynopolitans, the dog and the dog-headed ape, because they nourish ... partly because that animal shrinks from eating fish, and partly because it is born circumcised, a rite the priests were accustomed to carry out and perform.

units.la: Hæc verò tantum etiam hæc animalia coluerunt & adoraverunt Gentiles: sed certis quibusdam Numinibus ea dedicarunt atque consecrarunt: ut, incer alia quidem, equum & lupum Martis, ex quibus lupum etiam Apollini dedicarunt: lyncem & tigrum Baccho: cervam Dianæ: leonem Cybelæ: bovem Lunæ, Soli, & Apollini (cui etiam caper æneus sacer fuit) capram Diti: canem Hecaten & Anubim: cynocephalum Mercurio: asinum Priapo (cujus vilissima asininum caput) & Baccho.
units.tr: These animals were not only worshipped and adored by the Gentiles. They also dedicated and consecrated them to certain gods. Among others, they gave the horse and the wolf to Mars, and of these they also dedicated the wolf to Apollo; the lynx and the tiger to Bacchus; the hind to Diana; the lion to Cybele; the ox to the Moon, the Sun and Apollo (to whom the bronze goat was also sacred); the she-goat to Dis; the dog to Hecate and Anubis; the cynocephalus to Mercury; and the ass to Priapus (whose most worthless part is the ass's head) and to Bacchus.

units.la: Tertio exius, quæ sunt simplicis vitæ, & quidem aërea bumi reptantia, potissimum coluerunt Serpentem, animal reptile, terreæ ac frigidæ naturæ, corpore toto tereti, ut uno tramite a culum.
units.tr: In the third place, among creatures of simple life, and especially those that crawl upon the earth and in the air, they worshipped above all the serpent, a reptile of earthy and cold nature, its whole body round and stretching in a single line from head to tail.

units.la: E capite ad tauda extrenum porrectlo,brachius,pedibus, & alis carens,praeter Indicos quosdam & Africanos:tujusmodi in Africa primo bello Punico ab Attilio Regulo repertum,dicq; oppugnatum,centum amplius pedes longum fuisse scribit Agellius.
units.tr: It has no arms, feet or wings, except for certain Indians and Africans. A serpent of this kind was found in Africa in the First Punic War by Attilius Regulus, who attacked it; Gellius writes that it was more than a hundred feet long.

units.la: Coluerunt hoc animal,ipsum divinae cujusdam naturae exiflimantes,Romani,Graeci,Phoenices & Aegyptii. Ad Romanos quod attinet , nota est Aesculapii fabula,ex Epidauro Romam serpentis subimagine translati, ac in insula Tiberina sedem sibi eligentis, cujus ope pestilentia gravissima urbis fit sublata: quae Historia in monumentis Romanis passim est obvia. Hinc in nummis antiquis pictura serpentis est hieroglyphica pro salute & bona fortuna.
units.tr: The Romans, Greeks, Phoenicians and Egyptians worshipped this animal, thinking it of some divine nature. As for the Romans, the story of Aesculapius is well known: he was brought from Epidaurus to Rome in the form of a serpent and chose for himself a seat on the Tiber island, and by his help a most grievous plague of the city was lifted. This history is found everywhere in Roman monuments. Hence on ancient coins the picture of a serpent serves as a hieroglyph for health and good fortune.

units.la: Nec vero tantum a Romanis, sed & Graecis & Aegyptiis serpentes ( sub quo nomine draconas, angues, aspides, basiliscos, & consimiles species, quae omnes in Aesculapii tutela fuerunt, intelliguntur ) cultus fuit & sacro sanctus habitus , ac tanquam salutis indicium atq; symbolum nummis antiquis incusus : ut in Gordiani numis videre licet. Ita hodie quoque apud Samogitios, Sarmatiae populos, serpentes pro Laribus tutelaribus in aedibus alii feruntur.
units.tr: Nor was the serpent worshipped and held sacred only by the Romans, but also by the Greeks and Egyptians. Under this name are understood dragons, snakes, asps, basilisks and similar kinds, all of which were under the protection of Aesculapius. They were stamped on ancient coins as a sign and symbol of safety, as can be seen on the coins of Gordian. So today too among the Samogitians, a Sarmatian people, serpents are kept in houses and regarded as guardian household gods.

units.la: Hujus autem idololatriae & superstitionis serpentinae haec prumium affirri potest ratio,quod Sarmatas, serpentes sive draconis antiquum,ea praecipue in imagine se gentibus patefecit, falsitatem illa mentiens. At in ipso quidem Paradiso primis noxtris parentibus per serpentem illusit fumum, fecit,eos in laudem capitalem impellens. Deinde nota est illa serpentis aeneis in Defectu Historia, qui Israelitas morbus serpentium venenatorum iclus, salutifuit : qui quidem Christi Servatoris & salutis nostrae unica typus illustris fuit, Christo ipso teste & interprete, Iohannis tertio, versu decimo quinto. Unde miruni non sunt, hunc quoque ob causam serpentem salutis atque sanitatis apud Ethnicos fuisse symbolum. Sed naturalis quoque ratio adferri potest, cur serpens salutis & valetudinis nota fuerit. Ea enim suam Asclepiadis exuens, ex lenti la squa-lore abster so,quotannis juvenescit : & eum mihi sibi affiate recondat : totantum tamen, quantum-vis longum, hyemem jejuna ac incolumis transfigit.
units.tr: The main reason for this serpent idolatry and superstition can be stated thus: the serpent, that ancient dragon, revealed himself to the nations especially in this image, lying with that falsehood. For in Paradise itself he deceived our first parents through the serpent, driving them into capital sin. Then there is the well-known history in the wilderness of the bronze serpent, which healed the Israelites bitten by poisonous serpents. This was a distinguished type of Christ our Saviour and of our salvation, Christ himself being the witness and interpreter, John 3:15. It is no wonder, then, that for this reason too the serpent became a symbol of salvation and health among the heathen. But a natural reason can also be given why the serpent was a mark of health and well-being. Casting off its old skin, it sheds the filthy scale and renews itself every year. And it hides itself in a secret place, and though it passes the winter without food, it comes through unharmed, however long the winter lasts.

units.la: Nec vero tantum etiam ipse per se fuit cultus & sacer habitus serpens, sed nominibus terrestribus Delim, ac Dearum dicatus & consectatus, ut Aesculapio, in cujus tutela fuit : ut Cereri : ut Minervae : de qua re vide Verderium. Sic tortuosus ille serpens atque draco tartareus, ut statim in ipso Paradiso : ita postea serpentis forma & imaginae fuit in hominum gratiam insinua vit: & ut primi nostri parentes, ita posteri quoque illorum Saturnum sub serpentis, animalis callidi, fimi (ideo Hebraeus dicti נחש Nachash, aturisofa obser ratione & infidus ) specie atque forma coluerunt.
units.tr: Nor was the serpent worshipped and held sacred in itself alone. It was also dedicated and consecrated to earthly gods and goddesses: to Aesculapius, in whose protection it was; to Ceres; to Minerva (on this matter see Verderius). Thus that twisting serpent, the Tartarean dragon, as in Paradise itself, so afterwards insinuated the form and image of the serpent for the favour of men. And as our first parents did, so their descendants worshipped Saturn under the form and shape of a serpent, an animal cunning, filthy, and crafty in its watchful observation, which is why the Hebrews call it [נחש] nachash.

units.la: Porro aquea quoque animalia simplicis vitae coluerunt,& adoraverunt,ut Piscres: eos, vel in genere omnes,vel certas species ; Omnes quidem,ut Aegyptii & infulae Pharii incolae, ac cervitatis Syenes , quae civitas est Thebaidis . item, intola Neotidos paludis. Praecipue tamen piscibus honores cultumq, divinum exhibuerunt Syrii, qui inde & Deum suum principem ac tutelarem Dagon appellarunt, quem alii piscem interpretantur : alii volunt frumenti Deum fuisse. Nam בג Dag, Hebraice piscem significat : & fortasse Dagon erat Neptunus. Unde Cicero, Dag maximum fuisse Deum dixit, sive Neptunus, sive altus quispiam fuerit: de quo idolo Hebraeorum traditum, illud ab umbilico sursum uersus humana forma fuisse: deorsum vero ut piscem desinere. Dagon ipsum, ut ex etymo colat fuit Deus aliquis marinus: quales fuerunt apud Gentiles multi, de quibus postea. Infpecie idem Aegyptii angulium coluerunt & Delphines, quos Neptuno voverunt, teste Tertulliano:& Larum piscem incolae urbis Latonis : cui certa sacra, festa, templa, sacrificia, epulas, & post mortem sepulchra sumptuosa instituerunt & celebrarunt.
units.tr: Further, they also worshipped and adored aquatic animals of simple life, such as fishes, either all of them in general or certain species. All of them, indeed, were worshipped by the Egyptians, the inhabitants of the island of Pharos, and the people of Syene, a city of the Thebaid, and likewise on the island in the Neotic marsh. The Syrians, however, paid especially great honour and divine worship to fishes. From this they called their chief and tutelary god Dagon, which some interpret as "fish" and others think was the god of grain. For [דג] dag in Hebrew means fish, and perhaps Dagon was Neptune. Hence Cicero said that Dagon was the greatest god, whether Neptune or some other high power. Concerning this idol the Hebrews have handed down that it was human in form from the navel upward, but ended below like a fish. Dagon, as his name suggests, was some sea god; there were many such among the Gentiles, of whom more later. In the same way the Egyptians worshipped eels and dolphins, which they vowed to Neptune, as Tertullian witnesses. The inhabitants of the city of Latona worshipped the lates fish, to which they established fixed rites, festivals, temples, sacrifices and feasts, and after its death they built sumptuous tombs.

units.la: Coluerunt praeterea etiam amphibia animalia,bos est, ea, quae inter aërem & aqueum animantes sunt naturae, eaq; partim quadrupedia, ut ranas & crocodilos, partim reptilia, ut natrices : partim volucria, ut mergos & anates,cui superstitioni Aegyptii, potissimum fuerunt devoti : prae aliis tamen maxime Crocodylum, quem Aesculapio attribuerunt, colentes, ob ejus folertiam: de cujus pictura quarum rerum symbolum fit, vide Hieroglyphica Pierii. Hic adde, quod Troglodytae testudines,quas Veneri confecrarunt,coluerunt & adoraverunt,teste Plinio in lib ris de Naturali historia. Denique infecta quoque,quod est animalium genus, incisuris corpus distinctum habens, sine ἔντομο καρνε (unde Exsanguia sunt dicta) in Deorum numero repositi sunt. Nam ab Aegyptiis ara- λάφεια, nec, cantharí, qui praecipue scarabeos maximi fecerunt, scilicet Eusebio, scorpiones & scarabei, quos infectoricul. Mercurio & Apollini dicabant, colebantur; quem admodum ab Acaronitis, vel Ecromitis mu- tua, sce, vespae & similes culte fuerunt: quarum Deum nominarunt Baal-Zebubum, id est, Sminthium, Myagrum, sive Myiothem Deum, ut legendum est apud Plinium libro 29. nat. bift. cap. 6. quo significatur muscarum Deus, vel muscas abigens. Hunc vero muscae figuram habuisse testu est Nazianzenus ὑηλιτόπικος β. contra Iulianum. Is Deus alio nomine etiam Abaddon dici- tur, de quo vide Verderium. Atque haec de Ζωολατρεία; a quam merito omnes Christiani abhorrere debent, ut quae cum blasphemia nefanda est conjuncta nominis divini, secundum illa secundi praecepti verba: Ne facito tibi sculptile, aut ullam imaginem eorum, quae sunt in coelis superius aut quae in terra infra: aut quae in aquis infra terram. Ne incurvans te, honorem exhibeto eis, neque colito ea, &c.
units.tr: They also worshipped amphibious animals, which are of a nature between air and water: some quadrupeds, such as frogs and crocodiles; some reptiles, such as water snakes; some winged creatures, such as cormorants and ducks. The Egyptians were especially devoted to this superstition, and above all they worshipped the crocodile, which they attributed to Aesculapius because of its cunning. For the picture of this, as a symbol of such things, see the Hieroglyphics of Pierius. Add to this that the Troglodytes worshipped and adored the tortoises, which they consecrated to Venus, as Pliny witnesses in his Natural History. Finally, insects also, a kind of animal with a body divided by notches, without blood (whence they are called exsanguious), have been placed among the gods. For by the Egyptians, spiders and beetles, which they especially honoured, scorpions and scarabs (which, according to Eusebius, were dedicated to Mercury and Apollo) were worshipped. In the same way, by the people of Akkaron or Ekron, flies, wasps and similar creatures were honoured. They called their god Baal-Zebub, that is, the Smintheus, the Myagrus, or the Myiothes god, as should be read in Pliny, book 29, chapter 6, which means the god of flies, or the one who drives flies away. Indeed, Gregory Nazianzen, in his fourth oration against Julian, testifies that this god had the figure of a fly. This god is also called Abaddon by another name, on which see Verderius. So much for zoolatry, which all Christians ought rightly to abhor, since it is joined with the unspeakable blasphemy of the divine name. Thus the second commandment says: "You shall not make for yourself a graven image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the waters under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or worship them," and so on.

units.la: NEC VERO animalia tantum rationis expertia, sed etiam plantas, stirpes & arbores omnis generis totam, adeo vim quinque, quam Dionysium vocarunt, teste Theodoreto, coluerunt, τρεία, plantāNam, ut nihil dicam de Aegyptiis (qui etsi omnium fere populorum habiti fuerunt sapientissimi & reli- giosissimi: unde reliquae gentes suam baufferunt sapientiam & religionem, tamen eo stolididitatis & insaniae devenerunt, ut allium, cepas, & alias plantas pro Diis colerent) etiam caeterae gentes plantas et similia, vel coluerunt (ut inter alias Celtae Germani quercum excelsam) vel certis Numinibus consecrarunt: ut stirpes in genere Neptuno: earum putationes Putae Deae: Cu- pressum Plutoni: Acer Stuperi, scilicet Seruio: Laurum Apollini: Oliuam Aristaeo, Apollinus fi- lio: Pinum Pani & Cybele: Liliam candidam Iunoni. Oleam Minervae: Quercum & Aesculum Iovi: Myrtum Veneri: Populum Herculi: Narcissum florem & Adiantum, sive Cincinnalem Pluroni: Papaver Lunae, quod quidem fertilitatis symbolum erat apud Aegyptios. Idem iudicium est de reliquis: quo referri possunt etiam Vitis, Hedera & Ferula: quas Baccho consecrarunt, quia ferendae vitis auctor creditus.
units.tr: Nor did they worship only irrational animals, but also plants, stems and trees of every kind, and indeed the whole power of nature, which they called Dionysus, as Theodoret testifies. To say nothing of the Egyptians (who, though they were considered the wisest and most religious of nearly all peoples, from whom the other nations drew their wisdom and religion, yet fell into such stupidity and madness that they worshipped garlic, onions and other plants as gods), the other nations too either worshipped plants and similar things (as, among others, the Celts and Germans worshipped the tall oak) or consecrated them to certain deities. Thus they assigned plants in general to Neptune; the groves to the goddess Pota; the cypress to Pluto; the maple to Stupor, that is, Servius; the laurel to Apollo; the olive to Aristaeus, son of Apollo; the pine to Pan and Cybele; the white lily to Juno; the olive tree to Minerva; the oak and the ash to Jupiter; the myrtle to Venus; the poplar to Hercules; the narcissus flower and the maidenhair fern, or the Cincinnalis, to Pluto; and the poppy to the Moon, which was indeed a symbol of fertility among the Egyptians. The same judgment applies to the rest, to which may also be referred the vine, ivy and fennel, which they consecrated to Bacchus because the vine was believed to be the author of bearing grapes.

units.la: METALLA item & lapides coluerunt, ut Aurum, Argentum, Aes, Ferrum, Plumbum, Stan- num, & similia, in genere sub Diis, Plutonis et aliorum Deorum nominibus. Singula vero certis Diis consecrarunt, tanquam eorum in ventoribus & artificibus, ut Aurum Iovi, vel Soli, Argentum Lunae, Argentum vivum Mercurio, Plumbum Saturno, Stannum Veneri. Sic inter lapides, prae aliis quadratos pro Diis coluerunt, quorum acervi circa Mercurii statuam congregebantur. Haec de Metallorum culta.
units.tr: They also worshipped metals and stones, such as gold, silver, bronze, iron, lead, tin, and the like, in general under the gods, under the names of Pluto and the other deities. Individually, however, they consecrated each to particular gods, as to their patrons and craftsmen: gold to Jupiter or the Sun, silver to the Moon, quicksilver to Mercury, lead to Saturn, tin to Venus. Among stones, they worshipped the square ones above the rest as gods, and heaps of them were gathered about the statue of Mercury. So much on the worship of metals.

units.la: Atque haec quidem sint dicta de Mundi & ejus membrorum cultu divino. VENIO nunc ad HOMINEM, tanquam ad μικροκόσμον, id est, Mundum parvum, sicuti a Veteribus fuit appellatus, propter quem magnus hic Mundus cum omni sua suppellectile a Deo Omnipotente Hominum culo fuit conditus & conservatus. Hujus itaque Mundi magni, homo et finis, et pars, et incola, et culto atque colonus, & spectator denique atque contemplator dici potest.
units.tr: So much may be said about the divine worship of the world and its parts. I come now to MAN, as to a microcosm, that is, a little world, as the ancients called him, for whose sake this great world, with all its furnishings, was created and preserved by Almighty God. Man may therefore be called both the end and the part of this great world, its inhabitant, its worshipper and cultivator, and finally its spectator and contemplator.

units.la: Vt autem in magno illo Mundo, de quo adhuc dictum: ita in parvo hoc Mundo, hoc est, Homo idololatra Homine, cumulus sese Deorum falsorum offert ingens. Atque adeo ut universae Idololatriae causa jeⁱ sa quidem atque auctor primarius est Diabolus: ita causa atque auctor ejusdem secundarius est cundaria. Homo. Is enim cum in Mundo & per Mundum hunc universum, tanquam per speculum clarissimum, sue ipsius praesertim utilitatis atque salutis causa creatum, Deum ejus Conditorem cognoscere atque colere venerari, debuisset: ipse pro vitio, prava per versa, sua natura, Diaboli afflatu impulsus, non Deum Creatorem, sed Mundum universum singulas, ejus partes, etiam minimas ac vilissimas potius colendas venerandasq; suscepit. Quemadmodum autem mundus & magistro Diabolo, creaturas atque naturas reliquas omnes sive visibiles, sive invisibiles, sive corporeas, sive incorporeas, sive animatas, sive inanimes, tam bonas quam malas, partim in Deorum numero repositi atque coluit, partim certis Numinibus, tanquam custodibus attribuit & consecravit: sic ejusdem Diaboli suasu & bortatu multo magis justioreque quasi de causa seipsum, suam naturam, suum animum, suum corpus, omnes animi corporisque sui vires, & facultates, omnem suam vitam a principio usq; ad finem, omnes vitae suae actiones, virrutes, vitia, casus, eventus secundos & adversos, omnia denique quibus vita haec nostra est exposita, bona atque mala vel pro Dis sibi colenda, vel certis Dis conseruandi docuit: ut ex singulorum enumeratione postea melius patebit. Ac Aegyptii quidem, ut Theodoretus ex Porphyrio probat, Hominem primum in genere coluerunt pro Deo, cui super aram sacrificarunt, & certo tempore proprium conveniensque epulum obtulerunt: unde postea innumerabiles alienorum & falsorum Deorum turba atque multitudo promanavit. Deinde in specie coluerunt Pythagorae discipulum: quam antiquam quidem, sed paucam & exsecrandam consuetudinem secuti Lycaonie incole, quorum fit mentio in Actis Apostolicis capite decimoquarto, discipulos Christi, Paulo & Barnabae divinos honores exhibere voluerunt, quos illi repudiarunt: quod ipsum & de Petro, cum Cornelius Centurio divinam ei adorationem tribuere vellet, legimus: utque de Angelo in Apocalypsi, qui αὐθεντικὸς λατρεία hanc, sive προσκύνησιν ei ferre proberet.
units.tr: But just as in that great world of which we have spoken, so in this little world, that is, man, a vast heap of false gods presents itself, for man is an idolater. Just as the Devil is the primary cause and author of all idolatry, so man is its secondary cause and author. For man, who ought to have known and worshipped God his Creator in and through this whole world, as through a most clear mirror, created for his own particular use and salvation, through the perversity of his nature, impelled by the breath of the Devil, undertook instead to worship and venerate not the Creator but the parts of the universe, even the smallest and vilest of them. Just as, with the Devil as his teacher, man placed among the gods and worshipped all other creatures and natures, visible or invisible, corporeal or incorporeal, animate or inanimate, good as well as evil, and assigned some of them to particular deities as guardians, so, at the Devil's persuasion and urging, and with even greater and more plausible pretext, he has taught himself to honour as gods, or to commit to certain gods for preservation, himself, his nature, his soul, his body, all the powers and faculties of soul and body, his whole life from beginning to end, all his actions, virtues, vices, chances, and successes and adversities, in short everything to which this life of ours is exposed, both good and bad. This will become clearer later from the enumeration of each. The Egyptians, as Theodoret shows from Porphyry, first worshipped man in general as a god, sacrificing to him on an altar and offering him a proper and fitting feast at a set time; from this there afterwards sprang an innumerable crowd and multitude of foreign and false gods. Then they worshipped in particular a disciple of Pythagoras. Following this ancient but rare and accursed custom, the inhabitants of Lycaonia, mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter fourteen, wished to pay divine honours to the disciples of Christ, Paul and Barnabas, which they refused. We read the same of Peter, when Cornelius the centurion wished to offer him divine adoration; and of the angel in the Apocalypse, who, to show that this worship was owed to God alone, refused to receive the adoration [προσκύνησις] offered him.

units.la: Nam primum constat, vel Ethnicorum ipsorum testimonio, maximam, & quidem praecipuorum, quos ipsi coluerunt, Deorum commentitiorum partem, homines fuisse mortales, qui quidem propter eximias animi corporisque vires atque dotes, propter egregias virtutes atque actiones, propter praeclara ergo genus humanum merita atque beneficia, propter verum & artium utilissimarum et praestantissimarum inventionem, vel adhuc vivi, divinis fuerunt affecti honoribus, vel certe mortui in Deorum numerum relati, religiosissime culti. Cicero libro primo de Natura Deorum: Suscepit, inquit, vita hominum consuetudoque communis, ut beneficiis excellentes viros in caelum fama ac voluntas tulerit. Hinc Hercules: hinc Castor & Pollux: hinc Aesculapius: hinc Liber, etc. Idem: Perseus, Zenonus auditor, eos dixit habitos esse Deos, a quibus magna utilitas ad vitae cultum effet inventa, ipsaque res utiles & salutares Deorum esse vocabulis nuncupatas. De more, bene meritos de genere humano referendi inter Deos, scribit etiam Plinius libro secundo de Historia, capite septimo, in hanc sententiam: Deus est mortali juvare mortalem (unde ille apud Plautum, Deus est homo hominem, ant lupus) & hac ad aeternam gloriam via. Hac vere Romani: hac nunc caelesti passu cum liberis suis vadit maximus omnis e vi relictor Vespasianus Augustus, sed in rebus subversis. Hic est vetustissimus referendi gratiam bene merentibus mos, ut tales Numinibus adscribantur. Quippe & omnium aliorum Deorum nomina, & quae supra sidera retulit, ea hominum nata sunt meritis. Iovem quidem aut Mercurium, alterve aliis inter se vocari, & esse caelestis nomenclaturae, qui non interpretatione naturae fateatur? Cicero libro tertio de Natura Deorum: Iam vero in Graecia multos habens ex hominibus Deos, Alabandum Alabandi, Tenedi Tenem, Leucothean, quae fuit Ino, etc.
units.tr: For first, it is established, even by the testimony of the heathen themselves, that the greatest part, and indeed the chief part, of the fictitious gods whom they worshipped were mortal men. On account of their outstanding gifts and endowments of mind and body, their eminent virtues and deeds, their remarkable merits and benefits toward the human race, and their discovery of the truth and of the most useful and excellent arts, these men were either honoured with divine honours while still alive, or, when dead, were numbered among the gods and worshipped with the utmost devotion. Cicero, in the first book of On the Nature of the Gods: "Human life and common custom," he says, "have held that fame and goodwill have raised men of outstanding services to heaven. Hence Hercules, hence Castor and Pollux, hence Aesculapius, hence Liber, and so on." The same author: "Perseus, a pupil of Zeno, said that those were held to be gods by whom great usefulness for the cultivation of life had been discovered, and that useful and salutary things themselves were named by the names of gods." Pliny also writes, in the second book of his Natural History, chapter seven, to this effect: that it is a custom to number among the gods those who have deserved well of mankind. "To help a mortal is to be a god to a mortal" (whence that saying in Plautus, "man is a god to man, or a wolf"), "and this is the way to eternal glory. By this way the Romans went; by this way now, with heavenly step, goes the greatest of all who have left us, Vespasian Augustus, with his children, though amid the ruins of the state." This is the most ancient custom of repaying gratitude to those who deserve well: such men are ascribed to the divinities. Indeed the names of all the other gods, and those which he set above the stars, arose from the merits of men. Who, except one who gives a natural explanation, would admit that Jupiter or Mercury, or others, are called by one another's names and belong to a heavenly nomenclature? Cicero, in the third book of On the Nature of the Gods: "Now indeed in Greece there are many gods from among men: Alabandus of Alabanda, Tenes of Tenedos, Leucothea, who was Ino, and so on."

units.la: His consentanee Theodoretus de hac Σνοποῦα κρίσει disserit Sermone tertio, ad Graecos infideles de Angelis, Diis, Daemonibus: Postea, inquit, homines virtutibus rebusque gestis illustres, artium utilium in ventores, post obitum eorum, ισονομα es, ideo in Deorum numerum retulerunt, ut Saturnum, Rheam, Iovem, Iunonem, Herculem, Aesculapium, Castorem & Pollucem, Bacchum, etc. Idem eodem Sermone tertio ad Graecos: Etiam Herculem ὅς ἡμῖν ἀνθρώπου τοιαῦτα, ut generosum fortemque hominem.
units.tr: Theodoret agrees with this and discusses this kind of judgement, of things that share a name [ἰσώνυμα], in the third sermon, To the Unbelieving Greeks, concerning Angels, Gods and Demons: "Afterwards," he says, "men who were illustrious for their virtues and deeds, and inventors of useful arts, after their death were numbered among the gods, as Saturn, Rhea, Jupiter, Juno, Hercules, Aesculapius, Castor and Pollux, Bacchus, and so on." The same writer, in the same third sermon to the Greeks: "Hercules too, who for us was a man of such a kind," that is, a noble and brave man.
They made them gods.

units.la: Nec vero tantum bene meritos de genere humano, Ethnici olim, praesertim Graeci, Deos sibi fecerunt, sed Tyrannos etiam, qui genus humanum horrendum in modum portentosa sua immanitate afflixerunt: ut ex ipsorum Ethnicorum historiis poterit colligi. Hinc Plutarchus de Superstitione: Tyrannos, inquit, quoque coli & salutari videmus, ut aureas statuas poni ab iis, qui tacite eos oderunt & exsecrantur: quo referenda fuisse Alexandri Magni & Caligulae exempla. In hanc prorsus sententiam etiam Theodoretus: Hanc consuetudinem (Graecorum videlicet) Romani secuti suos Imperatores non solum iustos, sed etiam iniustos & tyrannos, ut Neronem, Domitianum, Commodum, post eorum mortem σνοποῦα ἐδιώσαν, id est, divinitate dignos censuerunt.
units.tr: Nor did the heathen of old, especially the Greeks, make gods only of those who deserved well of the human race, but also of tyrants, who afflicted mankind in a dreadful manner by their monstrous savagery. This can be gathered from the heathen histories themselves. Hence Plutarch, in his book On Superstition: "We see tyrants too," he says, "honoured and hailed, and golden statues set up to them by men who secretly hate and curse them." To this category belong the examples of Alexander the Great and Caligula. Theodoret too says exactly this: "The Romans, following this Greek custom, deified their emperors, not only the just ones but also the unjust and tyrants, such as Nero, Domitian and Commodus. After their death they judged them worthy of divinity" [θεότητος].

units.la: Sed quid dicam, quod plerique iflorum Numinum apud Ethnicos homines fuerunt lasciv ifimi, scortatores, meretrices, aliisque nefandis & detestandis sceleribus atque flagitiis infames! Unde idem Theodoretus in hec verba: Non solum bene de genere humano merito s, sed lasciuissimos etiam,tum uiros,tum mulieres,Graeci Deos fecerunt. Hinc conflat,Larentiam & Floram meretrices, monstra impudicitiae horrenda, eos pro Dijs coluisse: quod ipsum quoque admiratus est Plutarchus in Quaestionibus Romanis, quaestione trigesima quinta: Quid vero causse est, inquit, quod Larentiam tanto afficiunt honore, cum fuerit meretrix?
units.tr: But what shall I say, that most of these heathen divinities were most lascivious men, whoremongers, harlots, and infamous for other unspeakable and detestable crimes and disgraces! Hence the same Theodoret, in these words: "The Greeks made gods not only of those who deserved well of the human race, but also of the most lascivious men and women." Hence it is clear that they worshipped as gods Larentia and Flora, harlots, dreadful monsters of impurity. Plutarch himself marvelled at this, in his Roman Questions, question thirty-five: "What is the reason," he asks, "that they pay Larentia such great honour, when she was a harlot?"

units.la: Porro quemadmodum & ex Angelis illis caelestibus plurimi, & postea primi illi nostri parentes Angelorum seu Diabolorum illorum afflatu serpentino,teterrimo, exemplo & incitatiovivi. ne incitati,non contenti illa Dei imagine,ad quam sicti & formati fuerunt, illa, dignitate sublemi,in qua fuerant collocati, ad superiorem, & quidem parem plane & aequalem divinae majes-tatis dignitatem aspirarunt (quae utrimq; ruinae perpetuaeque miseriae caussae extitit) sic ab illo tempore omnibus seculis plurimi exititerunt inter homines superbi & arrogantes, qui partim vi, partim dolis, fraudibus atque blanditiis divinos honores cultusq; ambierunt, eosq; sibi adhuc vivis deferri curarunt. Sic Persarum Reges divino honore affici, et ceu Dii colioberviarij, voluerunt. Sic Alexander Magnus Persico more adorari voluit. Unde Polypercon, cum unum ex venerantibus mento contingentem humum per ludibrium tepisse hortari, ut id vehementius ad terram quateret, Alexander indignabundus, Tu,inquit,non veneraberis me? Detractumq; Polyperconta e leto praecipitavit in terram, & cum is pronus corruisset: Vide sine, inquit, idem te faciffe, quod in alio ante ridebas? Sic Aulus Vitellius, teste Suetonio, Cajum Caligulam Caesarem adorari ut Deum instituit, cum reversus ex Syria,non aliter adire ausus esset, quam capite velato (more scilicet & habitu eorum, qui Deos venerabantur) circumvertens se, deinde procumbens: Ritu nimirum priscorum, qui in adorandis Diis corpus circumagebant, deinde procumbentes sedebant, Numa instituto, vel Persarum more, qui procumbentes humi & mento humum contingentes Regem suum colebant, quod ϑεοπροπειν vocant. Exempla plura arrogantiae atque superbiae ipsius plusquam Luciferianae, ut Herodis Agrippae Regis Iudae, Diocletiani Imperatoris Romani, Menenatus Medici praestantissimi Macedonia, vide in Academia Gallica Petri Domini de la Primaudaye, & in aliis antiquis historiis. Hic commodus dicendi locus esset de more & consuetudine,ritibus atq; ceremoniis exhibitis in Snomoiia defunctorum Regum & Imperatorum, aut , etiam aliorum illustrium hominum : sed quoniam de hac re fuse alii scripserunt: ideo nos ea sponte praetermittemus.
units.tr: Moreover, just as many of the heavenly angels, and afterwards our first parents, were incited by the serpentine, most foul example and inspiration of those angels or devils, so too, not content with that image of God in which they had been made and formed, they aspired, from the lofty dignity in which they had been placed, to a higher dignity, indeed one plainly equal to the majesty of God; and this was the cause of ruin and perpetual misery on both sides. So from that time onward, in every age, there have been many proud and arrogant men among mankind, who, partly by force, partly by deceit, fraud and flattery, sought divine honours and worship, and took care to have them paid to themselves while still alive. Thus the kings of Persia wished to be honoured with divine honour and to be worshipped like gods. Thus Alexander the Great wished to be adored in the Persian manner. Whence Polyperchon, when one of those who venerated Alexander, touching the ground with his chin, was mocked by someone who urged him to strike the earth even more vigorously, Alexander, indignant, said: "Will you not worship me?" and, dragging Polyperchon from his couch, flung him to the ground; and when he lay prone, said: "See, is it not you who are doing the very thing you laughed at in another a moment ago?" Thus Aulus Vitellius, according to Suetonius, arranged that Gaius Caligula Caesar be adored as a god: returning from Syria, he dared not approach him except with head veiled (in the manner and dress of those who worshipped gods), turning himself round and then prostrating himself. This was the rite of the ancients, who turned the body round in adoring the gods and then prostrated themselves, following the institution of Numa; or the Persian custom, whereby men prostrated themselves on the ground and touched the earth with their chin in worshipping their king, which they call theoproponein [θεοπροπεῖν]. Further examples of his arrogance and pride, more than Luciferian, may be seen in Herod Agrippa, king of Judea, in Diocletian, Roman emperor, and in Menenatus, the most excellent physician of Macedonia; see Pierre de la Primaudaye's French Academy and other ancient histories. This would be a fitting place to speak of the custom, usage, rites and ceremonies displayed at the apotheosis of dead kings and emperors, or of other illustrious men. But since others have written about this at length, we will willingly pass it over.

units.la: Ut autem Homines,Reges praesertim & Imperatores, aliique viri illustres, tum ipsi sibi vivis divinos arrogarunt honores, tum ab aliis, tanquam Dii coli & adorari voluerunt: ita post mortem etiam eorum,ipsis honoribus fuerunt affecti:id quod cum ex supra citatis testimoniis Theodoreti satis superq; constat, tum exempla modo posita clarissime ostendunt. Haec de ⁠ ⁠ ⁠ ⁠ ⁠ ⁠ hominis in genere.
units.tr: Just as men, especially kings, emperors and other illustrious men, both claimed divine honours for themselves while alive and wanted others to worship them as gods, so after their death they too were honoured in the same way. This is clear both from the testimonies of Theodoret cited above and from the examples just given. So much for man in general.

units.la: NEC VERO tantum Homo ipse totus, sive vivus, sive mortuus pro Deo Ethnicus habitus fuit: sed singulae quoque ejus partes, ex quibus compositus est, atque conflatus,nempe Anima & Corpus, & singulatum harum partium principalium partes minores, qualitates item & accidentia, sive bona sive mala,cuncta denique, quae ad humanarum rerum naturam atque ritam pertinent bona atque mala,commoda & incommoda,tum interna, quae animi & corporis,tum externa,quae bona & mala fortuita, sive Fortunae vulgo appellantur, in Deorum numero abijsdem fuerunt repositi,vel certis Diis adscripta & consecrata.
units.tr: Nor was man himself, whether living or dead, the only thing the heathen regarded as a god. Each of the parts of which he is composed and made up was also deified: soul and body, the lesser parts of these principal parts, and likewise qualities and accidents, whether good or bad. Finally, all the things that pertain to the nature and life of human affairs, good and bad, advantages and disadvantages, both internal ones of mind and body and external ones commonly called good and bad fortune or Fortune, were placed among the number of the gods or were assigned and consecrated to particular gods.

units.la: Primum igitur ut Mundus hic magnus duabus constat partibus primarijs, Coeli nimirumatque Terra: ita Mundus hic parvus,id est, Homo ex duabus similiter conflatus est partibus, Anima,quae cor-Anima nimirum & corpore : quarum illa quidem Coelo, haec Terrae respondet. Et ut Coeli duae lo,& corpus, sunt partes principales, Aether & Aer: sic animi similiter sunt duae quasi partes principales, Menssive Intellectus, & Cor, sive affectus: quarum illa Aetheri, haec vero Aeri affinis est atquesimiles.
units.tr: Just as this great world consists of two principal parts, heaven and earth, so this little world, man, is likewise made up of two parts, soul and body. The former corresponds to heaven, the latter to earth. And just as the two principal parts of heaven are ether and air, so the soul has two principal parts, as it were: mind or intellect, and heart or affections. The former is akin and similar to ether, the latter to air.

units.la: Trigitur de Animo primo dicamus, is cum totus, tum singulae ejus partes, potentiae, fa-cultates, habitus, affectus boni & mali divinae fuerunt consecrati honoribus. Mens a Roma-ni, ut Livius & Cicero tradunt, fuit consecrata, ut mentem ea bonam concederet; quod & S. Augustinus non semel affernit, & ante cum Lactantius. Ovidius in Fastis:
units.tr: Let us speak first of the soul. Its parts, powers, faculties, habits and good and bad affections, both as a whole and singly, were consecrated with divine honours. The Romans consecrated Mind (Mens), as Livy and Cicero relate, so that it would grant a good mind. St Augustine affirms this more than once, and Lactantius did so before him. Ovid, in the Fasti:

units.la: Mens quoq; Numen habet, Mensq; deluhra videmus Vota, metu belli, perfide Pœne, tui.
units.tr: Mind too has divine power, and we see shrines dedicated to you, Mind, by those who in fear of war made vows to you, faithless Carthaginian.
Propertius:

units.la: Mens bona si qua Dea es, tua me sacraria dono Exciderant surdo tot mea vota Iovi.
units.tr: Good Mind, if you are any goddess, your shrines were granted to me as a gift, since so many of my vows fell on deaf Jove.

units.la: Philosophi quoq; pleriq;, vouῶ, hoc est, mentem Deam fecerunt, sed non eodem modo. Cicero de Legib. lib. 2. Aɩ̈ illa, propter quæ datur hominiafentsus in Cœlum, Mentem, Virtutem, Pietatem, Fidem, earumq; laudum delubra sunto; nec ulla vitiorum sacra solennia obeunto. Et paulo post: Bene vero; quod Mens, Pietas, Virtus, Fides consecratur mana: quarum omnium Romæ dedicata publicè tem.pla sunt: ut illa qui habeant (habent autem omnes boni) Deos ipsos in animis suis collocatos putent. Idem: Resipsa, in qua vis inest, major aliqua, sic appellatur, ut ea ipsa nominetur Deus, ut Fides sunt, ut Mens, quasi in Capitolio dedicatas videmus proxime a Marco Aurelio Statuto. Ante autem ab Attilio Calatino eras Fides consecrata. Vides virtutem templum. vides Honoris, a M. Marcello renovatum.
units.tr: Many philosophers also made Mind (νοῦς) a goddess, though not in the same way. Cicero, De Legibus, book 2: "Those things on account of which a place in heaven is given to men, Mind, Virtue, Piety and Faith, let them have shrines of their praises, and let no one perform the solemn rites of vices." And a little later: "Well indeed is it that Mind, Piety, Virtue and Faith are consecrated as goddesses. Temples to all of these have been dedicated publicly at Rome, so that those who have them (and all good men do) may think that the gods themselves are placed in their minds." Again: "That in which some greater power is present is so called, so that it itself is named a god, as Faith is, as Mind is. We see them, as it were, dedicated on the Capitol, recently set up by Marcus Aurelius. Earlier, Faith was consecrated by Attilius Calatinus. You see the temple of Virtue; you see that of Honour, restored by Marcus Marcellus."

units.la: Porro ut Mentis duæ sunt partes: ita ambas quoq; voluerunt, & adoraruni, nempe Intellectum & Voluntatem. Et intellectus quidem tum operationes, tum effectus: quæ dao a Græcis νοήσεις & δόξαις appellantur, inter alia sub se continentia artes, disciplinas atque scientias, quæ liberales & ingenuæ appellantur: quarum quidem ut in ventrices, ita Deas coluerunt Musas. Plutarchus in ton τιν vis: Musæ omnino indigenantur, si putemus ipsarum opus esse citharam & fistulam: non morum institutionem, & affectuum moderationem, quæ consequuntur, quæ cantilenis & concentibus utuntur. His adnumerari poêtæ etiam artes ille, quæ manuum labore atque opera constant, vulgo artes mechanicæ sive manuariæ dicta, quæ in manui us & reliquis corporis membris tractentur, atq; extrceanitur: tamen a mente, ingenio & cogitatione fuerunt profecta, & mente etiam atq; animo potissimum excoluntur.
units.tr: Since Mind has two parts, both were worshipped and adored: Intellect and Will.
