Intellect, in its operations and its products, which the Greeks call noēseis and doxai, includes under it the arts, disciplines and sciences that are called liberal and free-born. Of these, as their inventors, they worshipped the Muses as goddesses. Plutarch, in his work on the Muses, says that the Muses would be quite pointless if we thought their business were only the lyre and the flute, and not the training of morals and the moderation of the affections that follow from those who use songs and harmonies. To these are added the arts that consist in the labour and work of the hands, commonly called mechanical or manual arts, which are carried out with the hands and the other members of the body. Yet these too proceeded from mind, intellect and thought, and are chiefly cultivated by mind and spirit.

units.la: Quarum vis igitur artium unlium & fructuosarum humano generi in ventores pro Diis fuerunt culti. Ac generales quidem omnium fere artium ut in ventores, ita Dei ac Deæ vitæ fuerunt Apollo, Minerva (unde τοὺς τέχνας, artes, ὠξ φάσις, id est, Vulcanum appellarunt, quia ignis admiraculo plurag, artes ut untur) Mercurius & Hercules: quorum duo illum etiam Gymnasiorum, Academiarum & Scholarum præsides fuerunt, atque antistites. Hinc Mercurii statuæ, Herme dictæ, quadratæ tum in Academiis & Gymnasiis, tum etiam ante domorum privatarum ostia positæ solitæ. Idem propterea quoq; Sermonis, qui Mentis est instrumentum, Deus fuit habitus, idcirco Cyllenius dictus, quem admodum & lingua ob hanc tanquam illi fuit dicata & consecrata. Æsgyptii quoq; omnium bonarum artium, ut legum, litterarum, Musicæ, Geometriæ, interventorem Mercurium fecerunt, quem Thoir, vel Theut nominaverunt, teste Platone, Iamblicho, & Cicerone libro tertio de Natura Deorum. Galenus similiter in oratione Isaforia Mercurium & orationis parentem & artium omnium auctorem fecit. Sic Apollo, Pythius vocatur ius, qui dissicere incipiunt & percunctantur: Delius & Phanius ius, quibus iam aperitur & elucescit veritatis aliquid: Ifmenius scientibus. Lescheopt Ais, qui iam ut untur ac fruuntur scientia, ac inter se disputant & philosophantur.
units.tr: So the divine powers of the useful and fruitful arts were worshipped as their inventors and as gods. The general inventors of almost all the arts were, as gods and goddesses of life, Apollo, Minerva, Vulcan (so called because fire, by which many arts are practised, is wonderful), Mercury and Hercules. Two of these, Mercury and Hercules, were also the presiding patrons and overseers of gymnasia, academies and schools. Hence statues of Mercury, called Hermae, square in shape, were customarily set up both in academies and gymnasia and before the doors of private houses. For the same reason Mercury was also regarded as the god of speech, which is the instrument of the mind, and was therefore called Cyllenius, just as the tongue was dedicated and consecrated to him. The Egyptians too made Mercury, whom they called Thoth or Theut, the inventor of all good arts, such as laws, letters, music and geometry, as Plato, Iamblichus and Cicero (Book 3 of De Natura Deorum) attest. Galen likewise, in his oration, made Mercury the parent of eloquence and the author of all the arts. So Apollo is called Pythius for those who begin to inquire and ask questions; Delius and Phanaeus for those in whom some truth is now revealed and shines forth; Ismenius for those who know; and Lescheus for those who now make use of and enjoy knowledge and debate and philosophise among themselves.

units.la: Inspecie deinde præfuerunt Medicinæ Æsculapius, & ejus filia Hygia, sive Sanitas, & Apollo: quibus ideo multa monumenta fuerunt posita. Paean idco Apollinem quidam vocaverunt, quod remedians morbus finem faceret talis gratuitatis quandam alii sic vocarunt, quod fugitarum illo eum nocere putabant. Eʃ enim πεᾶιν, ferire: unde fuerunt pa rite Latinum profertre, inquit Festus. Iurisprudentia deinde præfuit Themis, quæ & Carmenta Dea fuit dicta & Fatorum, Evandri mater: alio nomine Nicostrata, Carmenta appellata a carminibus, quibus oraculi tauebat: vel ut alii volunt, quasi carens mente, ob insinitus nimirum dinos, quibus ad fatiloquia fundenda carmina impellebatur. Sunt, qui Carmentam putaruntesse Parcam. Fluc matrone templum Romæ dedicarunt eamq; coluerunt. Plut. teste Quest. Rom 56. Sic numerandi arti praefuit Dea Numeria, aliiq; Dii. Ac Numerum quidem ipsum ceu Deu, colebant. Hinc par numerus Diis inferis olim consecratus; impar in nuptiis adhibitus: quo & Coelestes inprimis gaudere putabant. Huc referenda ἀριθμωπεία, & λογαριθμωπεία, id est, Numeratio in numero: de qua vide Peucerum.
units.tr: In particular, Medicine was presided over by Aesculapius, his daughter Hygia or Health, and Apollo, to whom therefore many monuments were erected. Some called Apollo Paean because a remedy brings the disease to an end. Others called him so because they thought that these illnesses harmed him; for paiein means to strike, as Festus says, whence the Latin verb for striking. Jurisprudence was presided over by Themis, who was also called the goddess Carmenta and of the Fates, the mother of Evander. Under another name she was Nicostrata, and was called Carmenta from the carmina (verses) by which she uttered oracles. Or, as others hold, she was so called as if carens mente (lacking mind), on account of the frenzied impulse by which she was driven to pour out prophecies in verse. Some have thought Carmenta to be the Parca. The Romans dedicated a temple at Rome to this matron and worshipped her (Plutarch, Roman Questions 56). So too the art of numbering was presided over by the goddess Numeria and other gods. They worshipped Number itself as a god. Hence the even number was once consecrated to the gods below, while the odd number was used at weddings, since the heavenly gods were thought to delight especially in it. To this belong arithmancy and logarithmancy, that is, numbering by number; see Peucer on this.

units.la: Sic Agriculturae, & rei rusticae ac pastoritiae artis Dii ac Deae plurimae fuerunt (de quibus su-pra) praecipue autem maxime Pales; quae ideo Dea rustica ab Ovidio lib.4. Fastorum dicitur: Rustica praecipuè est hoc Dea laetatur. Serviit ajt eam fuisse Deam pastorum & pabuli: cui sacrificarint pro felici pro ventu pabuli & pecorum: unde pastorum domina ab Ovidio appellatur: Pastorum domine grandia liba Pali.
units.tr: Agriculture, rural life and the art of herding had many gods and goddesses (of whom we spoke above), but above all Pales. Ovid calls her the rustic goddess in Fasti book 4: "Above all, it is the rustic goddess who delights in this." Servius writes that she was goddess of shepherds and of fodder, and that sacrifices were offered to her for a prosperous yield of fodder and of flocks. Hence Ovid calls her mistress of shepherds: "Mistress of shepherds, great cakes to Pales."

units.la: Fuisse Pales dicebatur Dea pastorum. Serviens scribit, alio pascere eam Veslam esse, alios magnum Deum. Feltum, quodin ejus honorem instituitur fuit; e dixi: aprid, Palilia sive Parilia fuit natalis videlicet urbis Romae, a pastoribus condita. Propertius lib.4.
units.tr: Pales was said to be the goddess of shepherds. Servius writes that some hold her to be Vesta, others a great god. The festival instituted in her honour was the Palilia or Parilia, the birthday of the city of Rome, which shepherds founded. Propertius, book 4:

units.la: Urbi feliz erat, dixere Palilia Patres: Hic primus capit maeribus esse dies.
units.tr: The Fathers said the Palilia was a happy day for the city; this was the first day to belong to the city's walls.

units.la: Notat Servius, Palem a Virgilio genere foeminino dici: ab aliis masculino. Sed pare illius dixerant, apud alios quoq; scriptores genere foeminino reperitur: apud quos frequens ejus sit meutio, ut non tantum apud Virgilium, Ovidium & Propertium, sed Tibullum, Varronem & alios. Haec de Pale.
units.tr: Servius notes that Virgil uses Pales in the feminine gender, while others use the masculine. But although they disagreed on her gender, other writers also use the feminine, and her name occurs often in them: not only Virgil, Ovid and Propertius, but also Tibullus, Varro and others. So much for Pales.

units.la: Porro Mercaturae, negotiationis, mercium & negotiatorum Deus fuit Mercurius, ipsefprop-terea vendiitor & negotiatur dictus, ab Hebraea voce מכר, Macar, vendidit, emendum tradidit: unde מכר, Maccar, merx, res venalis, & מכרות, Maccaroth vendiitiones, commutationes. Quid si Graeca vox μαχωμοθ, ab Hebraea מכר Macar derivetur; quod ob divitias & opulentiam, quae emptionibus & venditionibus comparantur, homines felices & beati sint habendi. Eun dem Lucae & paleae at in ventorem, ita Deum constituerunt, cujus Horatius in hymno in eum meminit. Inde Philostratus Palestram Mercurii filium finxit eiq, sedentis oleae ramus in sinu positus erat, quoniam luctatores oleo se inungebant.
units.tr: Mercury was the god of commerce, trade, merchandise and merchants. He is called the seller and trader for this reason, from the Hebrew verb מכר [makar], he sold or handed over for purchase, whence מכר [mekhar], merchandise or saleable goods, and מכרות [makharoth], sales and exchanges. Or if the Greek word μακαρωμός is derived from the Hebrew מכר [makar], it would mean that people are to be considered happy and blessed because of the riches and abundance gained through buying and selling. They made Mercury the god of gain and of the palaestra in the same way, and Horace mentions him in this role in his hymn. Philostratus then made Palaestra a son of Mercury, and gave her a sprig of olive placed in her bosom, because wrestlers anointed themselves with oil.

units.la: Arti vero canendi & instrumentis Musicis Iudendi fuerunt Musae, Pan, Apollo: quorum potremus etiam jaculandi & sagittandi artis fuit Deus, dictus ideo a Latinis Sagittarius & jaculatrix a Graecis Poetis, ἰχνοβολῶν. Euclio apud Plautum: Apollo quaeso subveni mihi atq; adjuva, Confige sagittis fures thesaurarios.
units.tr: The arts of singing and playing musical instruments belonged to the Muses, Pan and Apollo. Of these, Apollo was also the god of the art of hurling and shooting arrows. For this reason the Latins called him Sagittarius, and the Greek poets called him the archer [ἰχνοβολῶν]. In Plautus, Euclio says: "Apollo, I pray you, come to my aid and help me; pierce with your arrows the thieves who guard my treasure."

units.la: Atq; hujusmodi fuit cultus primae partis, mentis nempe intellectus. Coluerunt etiam alterampartem, videlicet Voluntatem, cujus Numina fuerunt Voluminus, & Volumna, a volendo dicta. inde & ejus Ut autem Voluntas ad supremum intellectus decretum libera propensione fertur; ad bonum di vine benignitate; ita Virtutes, coluerunt; & ad malum, ex praeve nimirum naturae inclinatione omnis generis Vitia.
units.tr: This was the worship of the first part of man, namely his intellect. They also worshipped the other part, the will, whose deities were Volumnus and Volumna, named from volo, to will. From this also came ... [the will is carried freely by its inclination to the highest decision of the intellect toward good, by divine kindness; so they worshipped the virtues, and toward evil, from the inclination of corrupt nature, they worshipped every kind of vice.]

units.la: Quod igitur attinet ad Virtutes, ex quibus actiones honestae & liberales proficiscuntur, primoVirtutem ipsam Deam finxerunt. Juvenalis: Vt colitur Pax atq; Fides, Concordia, Virtus.
units.tr: So as far as the virtues are concerned, from which honourable and noble actions proceed, they first made Virtue itself a goddess. Juvenal: "as Peace and Faith, Concord and Virtue are worshipped."

units.la: Huc etiam Romae delubrum fuit positum. Cur autem ante Honoris templum id factum; rationem reddit Verlerius, quem vide.
units.tr: A shrine to her was also set up at Rome. Verlerius gives the reason why this was done before the temple of Honour; see him.

units.la: Pietas & Virtutis species coluerunt & variissimaginibus expresserunt, tam Ethicas, siveMonetas, quae ἐκ σωφρόνων ἀγαθῶν versantur, quam intellectuales sive Dianoeticas, quae ἐκ Σωφρονικῆς occupantur. Ethicas quidem: ut Fortitudinem: Temperantiam: Liberalitatem; Magnificentiam circa pecuniā in magnis: Magnanimitatem circa honores in magnis: Majestatem: Honorem, unde & Honorium Deum, cui Romae fanum fuit positum: Clementiam & Misericordiam: Annicitiā, Veritatem: Fidem, unde & Deus Fidius, de quo Plautus; Per Deum Fidium curato mihi. Pudicitiā, & Pudorem, quae Athenienses praecipuè coluerunt; et cui sacellum Romae in Vico longo erat positum, item, in foro boario: Concordiam & Pacem: Spem (de qua Cicero lib.2. de Legib. Quoniam est pacificatione rerum bonarū erigitur animus, rectè etiam Spes a Calatino confecrata est) justitiam,alio nomine Nemesin dictam: uel Dicem & Dicaeosynen, quae Dea & praeses judiciorum fuit,lites & contentiones dirimens:cuius ministri vocabantur Dicaftae,quasi litium dirementes.Deniq; & Pietatē:quam,ut Deos caeteros colebant Romani:cui edem ab Acilio constectam ait Festus,eo loco, quo quondam mulier quaedam habita verit, quae patrem suum,includendum carceri mammis suis clam aleret, ob quod factum impunitas et consessa.
units.tr: They worshipped the forms of piety and virtue and expressed them in many images, both the ethical or moral virtues, which concern the good of conduct, and the intellectual or dianoetic virtues, which concern the good of thought. Among the ethical virtues they worshipped: Fortitude; Temperance; Liberality; Magnificence, concerning large expenditure of money; Magnanimity, concerning great honours; Majesty; Honour, whence also the god Honorius, to whom a shrine was set up at Rome; Clemency and Mercy; Friendship; Truth; Faith, whence also the god Fidius, of whom Plautus says: "By the god Fidius, see to it for me." Chastity and Modesty, which the Athenians especially worshipped, and to which a little shrine was set up at Rome in the Vicus Longus, and likewise in the Forum Boarium; Concord and Peace; Hope (of which Cicero says in book 2 of On the Laws: "Since the mind is raised up by the pacifying of good things," and rightly Hope was also consecrated by Calatinus); Justice, otherwise called Nemesis, or Dice and Dikaiosyne, who was the goddess and patroness of judgments, settling lawsuits and disputes; her ministers were called dicastae, as if they were settlers of lawsuits. Finally also Piety, which the Romans worshipped as they worshipped other gods. Festus says a temple to her was built by Acilius in the place where a certain woman was once held, who secretly fed her father, shut up in prison, with her breasts, and for this deed was pardoned and the place was consecrated.

units.la: Ad Dianoeticas vero virtutes,vulgo ἰδέαι ἀνθρώπων dictas, quod attinet, similiter eas in Dearum numero refuerunt. Hinc Dea Sapientia:Dea Prudentia:Dea Providentia (quarum Numen fuit Minerva:) Deus Catius,homines callidos, id est, acutos reddens: Deus Confusio, consiliorum Deus (unde Consualia:) Deus Sententiae,sensus largitor,ut Virtutum,vitae.
units.tr: As for the dianoetic virtues, commonly called ideas of men, they likewise placed them among the goddesses. Hence there was the goddess Wisdom, the goddess Prudence, the goddess Providence (whose deity was Minerva); the god Catius, who makes men clever, that is, sharp; the god Confusio, god of counsels (whence the Consualia); the god Sententia, bestower of sense, as of virtues and of life.

units.la: Atq; hoc modo coluerunt Voluntatem; quatenus fertur ad bonum,ut Virtutes. Eandem colebant luerunt quoq; quatenus ad malum fertur, ut Vitia,cupiditates & affectus pravos: qui cultus quam absurdus fit, & abomnis ratione alienus,docet Theodoretus,inquiens: Graeci gentiles,Philosophi χαρίτων ὑμνῶντες εἰς τὸ ἱμέρῳ πεφιλαμμένον, sumum fugientes in ignem inciderunt. Sic enim primum ipsa Voluptas Voluptae Deae nomine culta est, & amor impurus,ac libido nefaria nominibus Veneris & Priapi: Veneris quidem; quod ea libidinem,laficiuiam,cogitationes hominum ad motus injiceret,quas etiam ad opus deducendas curaret. Itaq; eam Amoris matrem finxerunt, quod scilicet nunquam fere mas cum famina conjungatur,nisi amore intercedente. Theodoretus:Venerem, inquit, ἀκολασίας διδάσκαλον χαλασμοῦ ἐν τάξει libidinis magistram, prostitutae corporis meretricem coluerunt,ceu Deam. Eandem etiam Veteres,sicut & Hymenaeum ac Junonem nuptiis praeposuerunt:eam namq; contrahuntur,ut per concubitum prolem consequantur. Hinc Cupido refertur Venerem filium: uti gemina Venus; ita geminus Cupido. Hic adde Veneris comites fiue filias, quae Gratiae fuerunt & Horae: item Mutinum Deum & Floram: inprimis autem Deam Libentinam,fiue Libentiniam,a libidine, (unde & nuffrum litbe) sic dictam.Hanc una cum Bumo Arnobius libidinum tutelis praefuisse dixit.
units.tr: In this way they worshipped the will insofar as it tends to good, as with the virtues. They also worshipped the same will insofar as it tends to evil, as with vices, lusts and wicked affections. How absurd this worship is, and how far from all reason, Theodoret teaches, saying: the Greek pagan philosophers, singing the praises of the Graces, [and of what is charmingly loved] [χαρίτων ὑμνῶντες], fleeing smoke, fell into fire. For first Pleasure herself was worshipped under the name of the goddess Voluptas, and impure love and wicked lust under the names of Venus and Priapus. Venus, because she stirred up lust, wantonness and thoughts of men into movement, and took care to lead them on to action. Hence they made her the mother of Love, because almost no male is joined to a female except with love intervening. Theodoret says: they worshipped Venus, the teacher of licentiousness [ἀκολασίας διδάσκαλον], the mistress of lust, the harlot of the prostituted body, as a goddess. The ancients also set her before marriage, as they did Hymenaeus and Juno, for people marry in order to obtain offspring through intercourse. Hence Cupid is said to be the son of Venus; as there is a twin Venus, so there is a twin Cupid. Here add Venus's companions or daughters, who were the Graces and the Hours; likewise the god Mutinus and Flora; and above all the goddess Libentina, or Libentinia, so called from libido (whence also the word libitina). Arnobius said that she presided over the protection of lusts together with Bumus.

units.la: Porro quia laetita juvenilis cum Amore & libidine conjuncta est, hanc quoq; pro Dea venenati sunt,nomine Vitulae Deae. (Nam Veteres Vitulari docebant pro gaudere; quemadmodum & Risum Deum fecerunt,ac coluerunt sub Ridiculi fiue Rideculi Dei nomine; cuius etiam portam Capenam fanum construxerunt Romani,& templa Lacedaemonii dicarunt teste Plutarcho.
units.tr: Moreover, since youthful joy is joined with love and lust, they also worshipped this as a goddess, under the name of the goddess Vitula. (For the ancients used vitulari for to rejoice.) In the same way they made Laughter a god and worshipped him under the name of the god Ridiculus or Rideculus. The Romans built a shrine to him at the Porta Capena, and the Lacedaemonians dedicated temples to him, as Plutarch attests.

units.la: Praeterea conviviorum seu comissationum intemperiatum, atque Gulae Deos constituerunt Comum & Saturnum: sicut ebrietatis, temulentiae & crapulae Bacchum,fiue Lacchum, qui etiam Dionysium,Lenaeum,Lyaeum,ab Aegyptiis Ofiris,et Liber pater,quod vino nimio usi omnia libere loquantur fuit appellatus.
units.tr: Besides, they set up Comus and Saturn as gods of the intemperance of banquets and revelries and of gluttony; likewise Bacchus, or Lacchus, for drunkenness, intoxication and surfeit. He was also called Dionysus, Lenaeus, Lyaeus, by the Egyptians Osiris, and Liber Pater, because men who have used too much wine speak freely about everything.

units.la: Avaritiae, hoc est, cupiditatis divitiarum inordinate & inhonestae, ipfarumq; divitiarum & lucri fiue quaestus Dii habiti fuerunt Plutus, Pluto, Dus, Mercurius: quibus addi potest furtum & furtorum Dea Furina,unde Furinalia: (quae tamen fecundum Etruscos Dea fortium fuit,ad dirimendas videlicet lites) & Laverna,sic dicta vel a latendo vel a lavando. Namfures Lavatores fiue Laverniones olim dicebantur. Horatius lib.1.epift. Pulchra Lavans da mibifallere,da sanctum jusjurandum, videri. Aegeus tamen eos ἀ ἐκ τῷ δολῷ ἐν ὁ ἐν ἐμῷ dictos.
units.tr: The gods of avarice, that is, of an immoderate and dishonourable desire for riches, and of riches themselves and of gain or profit, were Plutus, Pluto, Dis and Mercury. To these may be added theft, and the goddess of thieves, Furina, whence the Furinalia (though according to the Etruscans she was the goddess of the brave, namely for settling quarrels). And Laverna, so called either from lying hidden or from washing, for thieves were formerly called lavatores or laverniones. Horace, Epistles book 1: "Give me to seem fair, give me to seem holy, though I wash [the lie away]." Aegeus, however, called them by a Greek name derived from cunning [ἀπὸ τοῦ δόλου].

units.la: Con vicis, maledicentiae ac reprehensionis Deus fuit Momus: Nofis at Somnifilius; ac Calumniae, &, quae ipsam comitatur Fraudi & Impudentiae aras confecrarunt Athenienses: inter quas Calumniae effigies etiam ab Apelle depicta. Cicero lib.2. de Legib. Nam illud vitiosum Athenis, quod Cylenio, fcelereexpiato, Epimenide Cretae suadente, fe eorunt Contumeliae fanum & Impudentiae: Virtutes enim non vitia consecrare decet. Et paulo ante: Necnulla viriorum sacra solemnia obeunto. Pertinet huc Fama Dea; unde diminutivum Famella,a fando dicta,ut apud Graecos ἐμμανῆς φάσματος, Festo teste.
units.tr: The god of mockery, slander and reproach was Momus; Nox also had a son, Somnus. The Athenians set up altars to Calumny, and to Fraud and Impudence, who accompany her. A picture of Calumny was also painted by Apelles. Cicero, book 2 of On the Laws: "For it was a fault at Athens that, after a crime was expiated by Cylenius, at the urging of Epimenides of Crete, they dedicated a shrine to Insult and to Impudence; for it is fitting to consecrate virtues, not vices." And a little before: "Nor let them perform any solemn rites of men's vices." To this belongs the goddess Fama, whose diminutive is Famella, named from fari (to speak), as the Greeks say ἐμμανῆς φάσματος [mad apparition], according to Festus.

units.la: Sic Invidiam,Proterviam,Discordiam,Veteres coluerunt. Hinc fabulae de Discordia, caelo pulsa: & Discordiam pomum in medium Deorum jecisse,de quibus vide Verderum. Cicero lib.1. de Natura Deorum: Parmenides bellum, discordiam, cupiditatem, caeteraq; generis ejusdem ad Deum revocant. Hi admunerant possunt Murcea, fiue Murcia, Dea Desidiae, quae homines murcidos reddebat:item Dea Furina (unde Furinalia) Furor Deus,quem Graeci θυμόν id est, vim incitabilem, & ἄρεα, id est, Martem appellant,aliud innumerabiles. VENIO ad alteram hominis partem, nempe Corpus. Hoc non tantum integrum coluerunt: sed singulas quoque eius partes sive membra certis quibusdam Diis adscripserunt, sub quorum illa esse ere curã ac tutela. Sic enim, exempli gratia, in genere quidem omnibus vitalibus partibus humani corporis praeesse credebant Carneam, vel potius Carnam Deam, sic dictam, vel a cardinibus corporis, vel carne: a qua tamen potissimum petebant, ut jecinora & corda, quaeque sunt intrinsecus viscera, salva conservarent: cui templum, pulso Tarquinio, junius Brutus in Celio monte constituit, Kalendis, Junii sacrum Vestireum fecit: quod quidem pulte fabacea & lardo fieri solebat: unde & Kalendae ipsae Junii Fabaceae dictae. In specie deinde caput Iovi deferebant: linguam Mercurio, quod in eloquentia Deus esset: oculos Cupidini, Veneris filio, in quibus excubet, tenspeculâ quadam: aures Memoriae: frontem Genio (unde Deum venerantes, frontem tangimus, inquit Servius) supercilia Junoni, quod iis protegantur oculi, per quos luce fruimur, quam ajunone tribui (ideo Lunae & Lucinae dicta) putabant. Eidem tribuebant brachia: unde Hermes, qui unicuique Deo pulcherrimum aliquod membrum tribuit, a quo eum cognominet, Iunonem Ἀδκωλλαον appellat. Locum vero retro dextrum Nemesi asscribebant: quo referenda illa Plinii; Tacto ore ptoximum a minimo digitum veniam sermonis a Dis ibi recordantes. Dextra Fidei sacra fuit. Nam in fide ea porrigitur. Dorsum & posticae partes Plutoni: sicut renes, inguina, pudenda Veneri & Priapo: pedes Mercurio: genua Miserlcordiae: tali plantae vel pedum Thetidi & digiti Minervae fuerunt consecrati.
units.tr: So the ancients worshipped Envy, Shamelessness and Discord. Hence the fables of Discord, driven from heaven, and of Discord throwing an apple into the midst of the gods; see Verderius on these. Cicero, book 1 of On the Nature of the Gods: "Parmenides calls War, Discord, Desire and other things of the same kind back to God." To these may be added Murcea, or Murcia, goddess of sloth, who made men sluggish; likewise the goddess Furina (whence the Furinalia), and the god Fury, whom the Greeks call θυμόν [thymos], that is, unrestrained force, and ἄρεα [Ares], that is, Mars; and countless others. VENIO to the other part of man, namely the body. They worshipped not only the whole body, but also assigned each of its parts or members to certain gods, under whose care and protection those parts were. For example, in general they believed that Carnea, or rather the goddess Carna, presided over all the vital parts of the human body, so named either from the hinges (cardines) of the body or from flesh. From her in particular they sought that the liver and heart, and whatever viscera lie within, be kept safe. Junius Brutus, after Tarquin was expelled, set up a temple to her on the Caelian hill, and on the Kalends of June made a sacrifice of beans; this was usually made with bean porridge and lard, whence the Kalends of June themselves were called the Kalends of Beans. Next, in particular, they assigned the head to Jupiter, the tongue to Mercury, because he was the god of eloquence; the eyes to Cupid, son of Venus, in whom they keep watch as from a lookout; the ears to Memory; the forehead to the Genius (whence, Servius says, we touch the forehead when we worship the god); the eyebrows to Juno, because the eyes, through which we enjoy the light, are protected by them, and this light they thought belonged to Juno (therefore she was called Luna and Lucina). They also assigned the arms to her; hence Hermes, who gives to each god some most beautiful member and is named after it, calls Juno "Ankylloglossus" (having bent arms). But they ascribed the right side of the back to Nemesis, to which belongs that saying of Pliny: "Touching the mouth, and the little finger nearest to it, they remember there the pardon of speech from the gods." The right hand was sacred to Faith, for in pledging faith it is extended. The back and hinder parts were given to Pluto; likewise the kidneys, groin and private parts to Venus and Priapus; the feet to Mercury; the knees to Mercy; the ankle or sole of the foot to Thetis, and the fingers to Minerva.

units.la: Nec vero tantum integrum hominem, ejusque partes, animam & corpus, horumque membra singuli divini affecerunt honoribus: sed corporis etiam cum bona, tum mala sunt venerati; Bona quidem, ut Sanitatis praecipue, quam vel ipsam pro Dea habuerunt, vel certis aliis Diis ac Deabus consecrarunt: ut Aesculapio, qui Medicinae Deus praecipuus fuit existimatus; & ejus filiae Hygiae, a Graeca voce ὑγίεια, sanitatem significantes, sic dictae, quam etiam Salutem appellabat: uem Apollini, & Medicinae, Deae medicamentorum, a medendo nuncupatae, cujus sacra dicebantur Meditrinalia, quibus, teste Festo Pompeio, mos erat Latini populis, quo die quisque primum gustaret mustum, diceretominus gratia: Vetus novum vinum bibo, veteri novo morbo medeor. Plinius quidam loco non tantum Hygiani Aesculapii filium facit, sed & Aeglen, Panaceam, sive Panaciam & Iasonem. Idem lib.25. cap.4. Panaces genera (quo nomine omnium morborum remedia promittuntur) enumerans, unum Asclepios dicit cognominari, quoniam is filia Panaciam appellari: a qua voce forsan Panaceae istius Ammyaldine in montis Helvetiae origo esse potest. Deinde & mala corporis, ut morbos, omnesque, sanitati contrarios affectus sunt venerati, iisque certos Deos ac Deas praefecerunt; ut Febrim, Timorem sive Pavorem, Pallorem & similes. De Febri Dea ita scribit Valerius Maximus: Febrim ad minus nocendum templum colebane, quorum unum adhuc in palatio, alterum in arce Marianorum, tertium in summa parte vici Longi, in eaq; remedia, quae corporibus aegrotorum innexa fuerant, deferebantur. Meminit eidem hujus Deae aliquotes etiam Cicero, & inter alia, lib.3. de Natura Deorum, hac ejus verba fun:: Qui tantus error fuit, ut perniciosis etiam rebus non modo nomen Deorum tribuerent, sed etiam sacra conflituerunt. Febris enim fanum in palatio, & edem Larum, & etiamala Fortunae Equilis condecrata videmus. Omnis igitur talis a Philosophia pellatur error, ut, cum de Diis immortalibus disputemus, dicamus digna Diis immortalibus. Idem lib.2. de Legibus: Araq; vetus stat in palatio Febris & altera Equilis male Fortunae. Porro Timorem sive Pavorem sub Pane nomine, unde Panicus dictus, tanquam a Pane immissi solitus coluerunt. Vulnerum quinetiam ratione habita, eorum obligationi primogenitum Aesculapii filium, qui eam in venisse credebatur, praefecerunt: quemadmodum ut vi purgationi et dentium e vulsioni filii illius tertiogenitum. Tres enim Aesculapius filios habuisse, antiquitus credebatur. Sic Angeronae Deae sacra a Romanis instituta sunt, in gratiam hominum & animalium brutorum, quae angina laborarent & consumerentur: cujus festa Angeronalia sunt dicta; de quibus Varro: Angeronalia ab Angerona, cui sacrificium sit in curia. Pertinet huc Mena Dea, quae fluxibus menstruis mulierum praeesse credebatur, ut Augustinus docet lib.7. de Civitate Dei. Iovis filia haec, ut Luna, credita est, quippe Graeci Lunam μλωνν dicitur, quam ideo Iunonis privignam dicit idem Augustinus.
units.tr: Nor did they honour only the whole human being and its parts, soul and body, and each of the body's members, with divine honours. They also worshipped the good and the bad things of the body. The good things they worshipped especially in Health, whom they either regarded as a goddess herself or dedicated to certain other gods and goddesses. Thus Aesculapius, who was thought to be the chief god of medicine, and his daughter Hygieia, named from the Greek word ὑγίεια [hygieia], meaning health, whom they also called Salus (Safety). Thus too Apollo, and Medicina, goddess of medicines, named from healing, whose rites were called the Meditrinalia. Festus Pompeius reports that the Latin peoples had a custom that on that day each person first tasted the new must, and said by way of thanks: "I drink the old new wine; I cure the old new sickness with the old." One passage of Pliny makes Hygiea not only the daughter of Aesculapius but also Aegle, Panacea (or Panacia) and Iason. In the same book, chapter 4, listing the kinds of panacea (a name under which the remedies for all diseases are promised), he says that one of them is called Asclepios, because he was the son of Panacia. From this word perhaps the origin of that Ammyaldine panacea of the Helvetian mountains may come. Then they also worshipped the evils of the body, such as diseases and all the conditions contrary to health, and set over them particular gods and goddesses: Fever, Fear or Dread, Pallor, and the like. Valerius Maximus writes thus about the goddess Fever: "They worshipped Fever in a temple, to do the least harm; one of these temples still stands on the Palatine, another on the citadel of the Mariani, a third at the top of the Vicus Longus, and into it were carried the remedies that had been bound to the bodies of the sick." Cicero also mentions this goddess several times, and among other places in the third book of On the Nature of the Gods, he says these words: "What a great error there was, that they gave the name of gods not only to hurtful things but even established rites for them. For we see a shrine of Fever on the Palatine, a temple of the Lares, and an altar of Bad Fortune on the Esquiline, consecrated. Therefore let every such error be driven away from philosophy, so that when we discuss the immortal gods we may say only what is worthy of the immortal gods." And in the second book of On the Laws: "There stands an ancient altar of Fever on the Palatine, and another of Bad Fortune on the Esquiline." Further, Fear or Dread they worshipped under the name of Pan, whence he was called Panic, as if sent by Pan. Also, with regard to wounds, they set over their binding the firstborn son of Aesculapius, who was believed to have invented it; and in the same way, for the cleansing of wounds and the extraction of teeth, they set over it that son's third-born. For it was once believed that Aesculapius had three sons. So the rites of the goddess Angerona were instituted by the Romans for the sake of men and of brute animals that suffered from quinsy and were wasting away; her festival was called the Angeronalia, of which Varro says: "The Angeronalia are named after Angerona, to whom a sacrifice is offered in the curia." To this belongs the goddess Mena, who was believed to preside over women's monthly flows, as Augustine teaches in the seventh book of The City of God. She was believed to be a daughter of Jupiter, like the Moon, since the Greeks call the moon μήνη [mene]; and Augustine says for this reason she is the stepdaughter of Juno.

units.la: Porro ut animi corporisq; humani bona atq; mala, ita Fortunae quoq; cum bona tum mala (quae etiam externa & fortuita appellantur) pro Diis fuerunt existimata. Ac primum quidem ipsa Fortuna sive bona sive mala, Τύχη Graece dicta, a cunctis fere gentibus Dea, Primigenia & omnium rerum humanarum non tantum regina, atq; domina, sed etiam principium fuisse habita, serum dum illa Iuvenalis:
units.tr: Further, just as the good and evil of the human soul and body were worshipped, so also the good and evil of fortune (which are also called external and chance things) were regarded as gods. And first of all Fortune herself, whether good or bad, called Τύχη [tyche] in Greek, was regarded by almost all nations as a goddess, the first-born, and not only the queen and mistress of all human affairs but also their origin; hence that line of Juvenal:

units.la: Nullum Numen abest, si sit prudentia. Sed te Nos facimus, Fortuna, Deam, caelo locamus.
units.tr: "No divinity is absent, if there is wisdom. But we, Fortune, make you a goddess and place you in heaven."

units.la: Plinius lib.2.cap.7. Toto quippe Mundo, inquit, & locis omnibus omnibusq; borsi, omniu vocibus Fortuna solain vocatur, & una nominatur: una accusatur: una agitur rea: una cogitatur; sola laudatur: sola arguitur & cum convicus colicur: volubilis, a plerisq; vero & caeca existimata, vaga, inconstans, incerta, varia, indignorum fautrix. Huic omnia expensa, huic omnia ferum tur accepta; & in tota ratione mortalium sola uiramq; paginam facit. Hanc Aegyptii coluerunt Ifidis nomine.
units.tr: Pliny, book 2, chapter 7: "Indeed, throughout the whole world, in all places, in all mouths, Fortune alone is called upon and named; she alone is blamed, she alone is brought to trial, she alone is thought of; she alone is praised and she alone is reproached, and she is worshipped with abuse. She is fickle, and by most people thought blind, wandering, inconstant, uncertain, changeable, a patroness of the unworthy. To her all our losses are charged, to her all our gains are credited; and in the whole reckoning of mortals she alone fills both pages." The Egyptians worshipped her under the name of Isis.

units.la: His addi debet Fors, Sors, (quae sunt Fortunae nomina) & Sortes; quarū Deam & moderatricem Ethnici cum Fortunam ipsam, cum Tenitas quasdam Deas, a tenendo sic dictas, Feftefle,finxerunt. Cicero: Sortes bodie Fortunae monitu tollunter. Item: Quid igitur in his fortibus poteit certi, quae fortune monitu, pueri manu misencur atq; ducuntur?
units.tr: To these should be added Chance and Lot (which are also names of Fortune), and the Lots; the heathens made a goddess of these, and of Fortune herself, and certain goddesses called Tenitae (Guardians), named so from holding (tenendo), and Festae. Cicero: "Today lots are drawn at the prompting of Fortune." Again: "What certainty, then, can there be in those lots which are drawn and shaken by boys' hands at the prompting of Fortune?"

units.la: Duas autē Fortunas finxerūt: Bona unam: alteram Malā, quam & breve ac parvam vocant. Huic ad versa omnia; illi prosperis adscriptsū. Bona candido vultu; mala alio erat praedita.
units.tr: They also imagined two Fortunes: one Good, and the other Bad, which they also called Brief and Small. To the Bad they ascribed all adversities; to the Good, prosperities. The Good had a bright countenance; the Bad had a different one.

units.la: Bona Fortuna Felicitas qu: que poeti appellari, & bonus evenitus, sive fallum: qua & ipsa, Graece τύχη αυτοῦ dicta, pro Dīs fuerunt culta. Hinc Fortunae reduci ara ponebatur ob felicem reditum. Eam Dion lib.54. de Augusto loquens τύχην ἐπαρᾶσθαι vocat his verbis: ΤΩΝΑ τὰ ... Multa & varia illi decreta sunt a Pop. Romano, quorum ille nihil accepit, praecerquā Fortunae reduci ara consecrari passus est.
units.tr: Good Fortune is also called Felicitas by the poets, and a good outcome, or success; this too, called in Greek τύχη αὐτοῦ [tyche autou], was worshipped as a god. Hence an altar of the Fortune of Return was set up for a happy return. Dio, speaking of Augustus in book 54, calls it, in these words, the Fortune of the return. "Many and various honours were decreed to him by the Roman people, of which he accepted nothing, except that he allowed an altar of the Fortune of Return to be consecrated."

units.la: Ex advetso Mala quoq; Fortunae religio fe culca fuerunt: quibus Cicero de Natura Deor. aram Esquilus consecratam fuisse dicit. Pertinec huc Dea ατη, sive Ate, quae noxas mortalibus immittit, Hesiodo ab ἀτω, id est ... sic dicta.
units.tr: On the other side, the worship of Bad Fortune too was cultivated: Cicero in On the Nature of the Gods says that an altar to her was consecrated on the Esquiline. To this belongs the goddess Ate, or Atē, who sends harms upon mortals, called so by Hesiod from ἄτη [ate], that is, harm.

units.la: Vt autem & ipsa Fortuna in genere, & cum Bona, tum Mala: Fortuna fuit Dea habita: sic Fortunae utrius; effectus cum boni, sum etiam mali fuerunt consecuti. Sic, exempli gratia, Occasionem (quam nonnulli eandem cum Fortuna esse voluerunt,) Latinus Deam, Graeci ut Deum (Καιρὸς enim in masculino genere Graecis idem, quod Occasio Latinis) coluerunt. Sic ut Deas ac Deos coluerunt Salutem, Honorem, Amiciciam, Concordiā, Pacem, Securicatem, Quietem, (cuius aedes extra portam Collinam fuit in via Labicana, Livio tefe: unde & Orcus Quietalis dictus) Libertatem, Favorem, Divitias, Famam, Beneficium ac Premium, Marteam, Deam heredum, quam accepta hereditate coluerunt, Spem, Pecuniam, Monetam; Vnde Cicero de Natura Deorum: Ergo etiam Spes Dea est, & Moneta, omniaq; quae cogitatione nobis metipsis finigere possumus. His adde e contrario Pauperitatem, & Pœnam; quoru posterius Democriti Numen fuit, sicut & Beneficium: item Discordiam & Bellum; quorum Numina fuerunt Pelloniā Dea, ut hostes depellerentur, Achilles, quin Epiro cultus, Hercules, Bellona, Castor, Pollux, Victoria, Exesxeiα induciarum praeses (cujus simulachrum in Olympia quondam exstabat) Minerva, alio nomine Pallas dicta a ΠΑΛΛΩ, Palas, agitandi, & versandi verbo, quod in bello arma agitaret & verteret: idem etiam armata fingi & pingi solita; quo significabatur, prudentiam & sapientiam in bellis gerendis Martis esse administram, sine qua nemo felicer regnare potest. Ob eandem causam Oleaginem coronā mimitrus triumphantiū usos fuit et teltus est Feltus. Quid Minerva, praeterquā quod Olea in vetrix esset, & belli Dea esse putabatur. Praecipuus belli Deus & armorū fuit Mars, sive Mavors, apud Thraces natus, Bellonae frater, cujus minifiri fingebantur Impetus, Discordia, Ira, Furor: quem quidem Furorem furiosissimi Ethnici coluerunt Furiarum nomine, quas Plutonis administrat finxerunc, & Furina Deae nomine; cujus miminie Cicero lib.3. de Natura Deorum, quam idem vult esse Furias. Hinc Furnalia, sive, ut alii legunt, Furinalia sacra Furinae, quam Deam dicebant, teste Festo.
units.tr: Now just as Fortune herself, in general, and both good and bad Fortune, was regarded as a goddess, so too the effects of each Fortune, both good and bad, were worshipped. Thus, for example, Occasion (whom some wished to be the same as Fortune) the Latins worshipped as a goddess, but the Greeks as a god (for Καιρός [kairos] in Greek, masculine, is the same as Occasio in Latin). So they worshipped as goddesses and gods Safety, Honour, Friendship, Concord, Peace, Security, Quiet (whose temple stood outside the Collline Gate on the Labican Way, as Livy witnesses; hence also Orcus was called Quietalis), Liberty, Favour, Riches, Fame, Benefit and Reward, the goddess Martea, whom they worshipped when an inheritance was received, Hope, Money, and Moneta. Hence Cicero in On the Nature of the Gods: "Therefore Hope is also a goddess, and Moneta, and all those things which we can imagine for ourselves in thought." To these add, on the contrary, Poverty and Punishment; of which the latter was a divinity of Democritus, as was also Benefit; likewise Discord and War, whose divinities were the goddess Pellonia, who drives away enemies; Achilles, who was even worshipped in Epirus; Hercules; Bellona; Castor; Pollux; Victory; Eirene [εἰρήνη], the guardian of truces (whose statue once stood at Olympia); and Minerva, otherwise called Pallas, named from the Greek ΠΑΛΛΩ [pallō], to shake or turn, because in war she shook and turned arms; she was also commonly imagined and painted armed, signifying that prudence and wisdom are the handmaids of Mars in waging wars, without which no one can reign happily. For the same reason the triumphant generals were accustomed to use a crown of olive, as Festus reports. Why Minerva, except that the olive was her emblem, was also thought to be the goddess of war? The chief god of war and arms was Mars, or Mavors, born among the Thracians, brother of Bellona, whose ministers were imagined to be Onset, Discord, Anger, and Fury. This Fury the most frenzied heathens worshipped under the name of the Furies, whom they imagined to be the attendants of Pluto, and under the name of the goddess Furina, whom Cicero in the third book of On the Nature of the Gods mentions and whom he wishes to be the same as the Furies. Hence the Furnalia, or, as others read, Furinalia, the rites of Furina, whom they called a goddess, according to Festus.

units.la: Fortuna opponitur Fatum. Hoc igitur quod pro Deo; & quidem loveponisimum, coluerunt. quod Fortunam vincere existimarunt. Referenda huc videntur Dea Necessitas, Dea Violentia, Dea Providentia & similes.
units.tr: Fortune is opposed to Fate. So they worshipped as a god the power which they thought could overcome Fortune, and indeed they honoured it most of all. To this class seem to belong the goddess Necessity, the goddess Violence, the goddess Providence and others like them.

units.la: Iam vero si totius vitæ humanæ & principium & medium & finem considerare voluerimus, rursus unde existec quasi innumerabilis Deorum falsorum numerus atq; copia. Varronem legimus a bonceptione hominis Deos narrare cœpisse ad decrepiti usque hominis mortem. Potest, meo judicio, omnis vitæ humanæ, quæ est quasi Tragico-Comedia quedam in quinq; partes, seu actus quosdam diuidi. Is sunt primò Conceptio & Nativitas. Deinde Nutritio & Educatio. Tertio Munus seu officium, & quæ ad munus sive officium quod vis efficiendum ac exsequendum requiruntur, Actio & Oratio. Quarto Matrimonium. Denique Mors & Funus, sive Exsequiæ. Singulis his vitæ humanæ partibus plurimi ab Ethnicis præpositi fuerunt Dii atq; Dea.
units.tr: Indeed, if we want to consider the beginning, middle and end of the whole human life, we find again an almost countless number and variety of false gods. We read that Varro began to tell of gods from the conception of a human being down to the death of the decrepit man. In my judgement the whole of human life, which is like a tragicomedy, can be divided into five parts or acts. The first is conception and birth. Next come nurture and education. Third come one's office or duty, and the actions and speech required to carry out whatever office or duty one must perform. Fourth is marriage. Last are death and burial, or funeral rites. The pagans set over each of these parts of human life very many gods and goddesses.
On Conception and Birth

units.la: Quorum igitur ad primam partem sive actum principium numirum sive exordium vi humanæ attinet, quod est CONCEPTIO & NATIVITAS seu hominis in hanc lucem adtio, Junonem primo Ethnici finxerunt Fluoniam, quam mulieres colebant, quod eam sanguis ius fluminis in conceptu retinere putabant. Deinde & partus & parturientium eadem fuit Dea; juno quidem dicta a juvene scendo, & Lucina quasi Lucida, quam mulieres, uscibi adesset in partubus invocabant, sicut & Lunam: Unde Glycerium apud Terentium, cum partus dolores experiretur, exclamans ait: juno Lucina for opem, serva me obsecro. Et hoc: Per tæruleum astrorum polum Partus celerantem, Lunam.
units.tr: Accordingly, for the first part or act of human life, which is conception and birth, that is, the bringing of a human being into this light, the pagans first imagined Juno Fluonia, whom women worshipped, because they thought she held back the flow of blood in the womb. Then the same goddess presided over both the birth and the women in labour; she was called Juno from "young" [iuvenis] and Lucina, as if "the bright one" [Lucida], and women invoked her when she was present at childbirth, just as they invoked the moon. Hence Glycerium in Terence, when she was experiencing the pains of labour, cries out: "Juno Lucina, bring help, save me, I beg you." And again: "By the azure pole of the stars, the moon, who hastens birth."

units.la: (Facilius enim mulieres sub plenilunium videntur prolem eniti.) Cicero: Apud nostros Iunonem Deas, quos Ζωγόνος Græci, Latini Vitumnum & Sentinum sive Sentiam & Sentam tus præsset: Nascio sive Nacio: (de qua Cicero lib.3. de Natura Deorum: Nascio quoque putanda est, cui, cum sana circumus in agro Ardeatis, rem divinam facere solemus: quæ est parturndo dicti: Prosa vel Prorsa, & Post versa sive Postvorta, ob pariendi disserimina. Prosa enim præsse illa existimabatur quæ statum & legitimum partum ederent; Post versa vero, agris & infirmis, et cum præpositere partus ederbatur.) Egeria, quæ mulieribus opiculari crebitur, partum egerendo, ut ait Festus: Genius, Iuppiter Lucetius, qui lucis causa esset, Nundina Dea (anono dienascentium nuncupata, qui Lustricus appellabatur, quo scilicet infantes lustrabantur, & nomen eis impone-batur:) Alena menstruorum Dea, & Mana Geneta ortus ac partus præses a manuum dicta. Porro mulieri fæce etiam post partum Deos custodes adhibebant, ne Sylvanus Deus per noctem ingressus eas vexaret. Horum auxeri custodum significandotussa cres homines circumire limina domus singebant, quorum primus Intercido dicitur, li-mina secum ferrebat: alter, Pilumnus, pilo: certa, Dea Deverra, scopis de verrebat: quibus Dii custodes contra vim Dei Sylvani sacta conservabatur. Hæc Varro.
units.tr: (For women are thought to bring forth offspring more easily around the full moon.) Cicero: among our people, Juno was the goddess whom the Greeks call Zōgonos ("life-giver"), and whom the Latins called Vitumnus and Sentinus or Sentia and Senta, who presided over life and feeling. Nascio or Nacio (of whom Cicero, in book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods: "Nascio too must be thought of, to whom we are accustomed to perform sacred rites when we go round the fields of Ardea; she is named from being born"). Prosa or Prorsa, and Postvorta or Postversa, named for the perils of childbirth. For Prosa was thought to preside over those births which came forth in the proper and normal way, while Postvorta presided over those which came out feet first and with difficulty. Egeria, who is invoked for women, to carry the birth out, as Festus says. Genius, Jupiter Lucetius, who was the cause of light; the goddess Nundina, named from the ninth day after birth [nona die], when the child was called Lustricus, that is, when infants were purified and given their names. Alemona, goddess of the menses; and Mana Genita, the goddess presiding over birth, named from the hands [manus]. Moreover, after childbirth they also assigned guardian gods to the woman in childbed, lest the god Silvanus should enter by night and harass them. To signify the power of these guardians, they imagined three men going round the threshold of the house: the first, called Intercidona, carried the threshold with him; the second, Pilumnus, a pestle; the third, the goddess Deverra, swept with a broom. By these guardian gods the woman was protected against the violence of the god Silvanus. So Varro.
On Nurture and Education

units.la: SEQUIDVS actus vitæ humanæ est NVTRITIO & EDVCATIO. Habuit simi liter hæc quoq; suos Deos ac Deas. Ac infantibus quidem, jam in lucem editis, hos Deos, ceu cu-stodes ssoe prafecerunt: Vagicanum, & Fabulinum, cum vagire & fari infantes incipiunt: Cunina, cuius existunt: Fafinum, cum fassia involvuntur: Ossilaginem, cum ossa eorum solidari incipiunt, Dea solidacrix dicta: Levanam, cum e terra levantur: Statilinum, ut statim legunt, Statinum & Statanum, cum jam possunt stare: Ruminam vel Rumiam, cum lactent & alunter (a Roma dicitur, id est, mamma: unde Ruminales ficus; ad quam Lupa Romulo mammam præbuit: & Germanicum nostrum Naumen vel Numen, lactentium cibus.) Edufam & Potiuam, cum edere & potare possunt: deniq, Paventiam, quæ pavores ab eis arcere, undeetiam ap-pellata, teste Augustino.
units.tr: The second act of human life is nurture and education. This too had its own gods and goddesses. For newly born infants they set over them, as it were, guardian gods: Vagitanus and Fabulinus, when infants begin to cry and to speak; Cunina, who protects the cradle; Fascinus, when they are wrapped in swaddling bands; Ossilago, when their bones begin to harden, and she was called the goddess who makes firm; Levana, when they are lifted up from the ground; Statilinus, or as others read, Statinus and Statanus, when they can now stand; Rumina or Rumia, when they suckle and are fed (she is named from the Roman word for the breast, that is, mamma; hence the Ruminal fig, under which the she-wolf offered her teat to Romulus; and our German Naumen or Numen, the food of sucklings). Edusa and Potina, when they can eat and drink; finally Paventina, who keeps fears away from them, and she is named for that reason, as Augustine testifies.

units.la: TERTIVS vitæ humanæ actus est OFFICIVM sive MVNVS, vitæ genus & instituin. Secundū igitur diversa vitæ genera & institutæ, officia atq; munera plurimi ac diversi- fuerunt apud Ethnicos Dii, quos coluerunt, quosq; omnes enumerare difficillimum fuerit.
units.tr: The third act of human life is one's office or duty, the kind of life and occupation a person follows. Therefore, according to the diverse kinds of life and occupations, the pagans had very many and various gods of office and duty, whom they worshipped; it would be most difficult to list them all.

units.la: Sic exempli gratia Philosophi, & quarum vis sive liberalium, & ingenuarum, sive etiam illiberalium, mechanicarum & manuariarum artium magistri, aut professores, item Reipublicæ præfides, religionis antistites & cultores, opifices, artifices & fabri singuli, mercatores & negotiatores, milites, agricolæ, pastores, nautæ, & piratæ: artium quin etiam turpium cultores, ut meretrices, lenones, fures, & similes, tertos & peculiares habebant Deos, quos colere & in vocare solebant, quoniam, sibi vel prodesse, vel obesse posse existimabant.
units.tr: Thus, for example, the pagans had their own special gods and goddesses, whom they were accustomed to worship and call upon, because they thought these could either help or harm them: for philosophers, and for the teachers or professors of the liberal and noble arts, and likewise of the illiberal, mechanical and manual arts; also for the rulers of the commonwealth, the high priests and worshippers of religion, craftsmen, artificers and each kind of smith, merchants and traders, soldiers, farmers, shepherds, sailors and pirates; and even for the practitioners of shameful arts, such as prostitutes, pimps, thieves and the like.

units.la: Ad munus & officium referebatur Oratio & Actio. Orationis sermonis atque eloquentiæ, cuius symbolum fuit Pan, Dii atq; Dea fuerunt primò Mercurius Græcè Ἑρμῆς: sermonis; & quidem veri, Deus, parens atq; præses. Dictus autem fuit Ἑρμῆς, cem interpres, quod sermo sit interpres atq; nuncius mentis: unde sermo ipse, præcipio a fronte S. a Græco Ἑρμῆς fuit appellatus. Porro Mercurii nomen obtinuit, teste Arnobio, quasi medius currens, quòd sermo medius inter homines sit. Eadem de causa mercibus præesse putabatur, a quibus Festus Pompejus, Ifidorus et alii eum vo-
units.tr: Speech and action belong to one's office and duty. The god of speech, of discourse and of eloquence, whose emblem was Pan, was first Mercury, in Greek Hermes [Ἑρμῆς]. He was the god, indeed the true god, and parent and president of speech. He was called Hermes, as it were "interpreter" [hermeneus], because speech is the interpreter and messenger of the mind; hence speech itself, with the initial H prefixed, was called by the Greek name Hermes. Moreover, he received the name Mercury, according to Arnobius, as if "running in the middle", because speech is in the middle between human beings.

units.la: lunt dictum, quòd interementes & vendentes sermo sit medius. Quod alas ei in capite & pedibus affigi vere Antiqui, id significare volucrunt, volucrem per aerem ferri sermonem: unde Ἑρμῆς ei data, ut verus sermo innuerentur, qui semper consistit, nec cuiquam eum oppugnanti cedit: sicut a quodam, ut nonnulli volunt, Arcadiæ monte, ubi fit natus. Sed Festus eum ita vult appellatum, quod omnem rem sermone, sine manibus conficiat, quibus partibus corporis qui carent, κυλλοὶ το
units.tr: For the same reason he was thought to preside over merchandise, and Festus Pompeius, Isidore and others want him to be named from this, because speech is the middle term between those who buy and those who sell. That the ancients gave him wings on his head and feet, they meant to signify that speech is carried through the air like a bird; hence he was given the name Hermes, to indicate true speech, which always stands and never gives way to anyone who attacks it. Some think it was from a mountain of Arcadia where he was born. But Festus wants him named thus because he accomplishes everything by speech without hands, and those who lack these parts of the body are called cripples [κυλλοί].

units.la: cantur. Eandem hanc ob causam Veteres linguam Mercurio consecrarunt; & mos fuit, cum cubitum irent, aut vinum libarent, & victimarum linguas ei sacrificarent. Mercurius etsi Barba tus nonnunquam & Pileatus fuit pileus; plerunq, tamen Imberbis describitur: quo significabatur: sermonem nunquam sevescere. Et quoniam per sermonem omnia enunciantur: ideo etiam Nuncius dictus Mercurius, ut auctor est Augustinus lib.7. de Civitate Dei. Plato in Cratylo, & eum exponens Proclus, Ἑρμῆν dictum vult ab eo, quod est ἰρεὺν & μείσπω θύω quia loqui ex-
units.tr: For this same reason the ancients consecrated the tongue to Mercury; and it was the custom, when they went to bed, or poured a libation of wine, to sacrifice to him the tongues of victims. Although Mercury was sometimes bearded and wearing a cap [pileus], he is usually described as beardless, to signify that speech never grows old. And because all things are declared through speech, Mercury was also called the messenger, as Augustine states in book 7 of The City of God. Plato in the Cratylus, and Proclus in his exposition of it, want Hermes to be named from the fact that he devised speech [eirein, to speak, and mēstōr, a contriver], because he devised and contrived to speak.

units.la: cogitare verit et machinatus sit, ut et iris dictus, quòd Nuncia sit. Διάκτορος quinetiam, id est internuncius Mercurius dictus, quod sermo sit interpres, nuncius et internuncius mentis nostræ. Dictus, ajit Phurnutus, Ἑρμῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑρμηνεύειν τὰ νοήματα ἡμῶν εἰς τὰς τῶν ἀλλοτρίων ψυχὰς, id est, quod sensa nostra referat in eorum animos, qui prope sunt, & ut Iohannes Grammaticus in Commentariis in Hesiodum ait, quod explicet τὰ ἐν ψυχῇ νοήματα τῶν ἐν θυμῷ, id est, animæ mentis, cogitationes. Atq; hac de Mercurio præcipuo sermonis Deo.
units.tr: Mercury was also called Iris, because he is a messenger. Moreover, he was called Diaktoros, that is, the go-between Mercury, because speech is the interpreter, messenger and go-between of our mind. Phurnutus says: "Hermes is named from interpreting our thoughts [hermēneuein ta noēmata hēmōn] to the souls of others", that is, because he conveys our feelings to the minds of those who are near. And John the Grammarian, in his Commentaries on Hesiod, says that he explains "the thoughts within the soul to those in the heart", that is, the thoughts of the mind of the soul. So much for Mercury, the chief god of speech.

units.la: Sermonis deinde atq; linguæ & aëris Dea habita etiam fuit Echo, a Pane adamata, & Ajus Locutivus, a loquendo nomen habens, quod locutus fuerit, & præmonuerit Romanos de adventu Gallorum; de quo ita Livius lib.5. M. Cedtius de plebe nuncia vit Tribunis, sein nova via, ubinunc facellu est, supra adem Vesta, voce nocturna silentio audivisse, clariorem humanâ, quæ Magistratibus dici juberet, Gallos adventare; id, ut fit, propter auctoris humilitatem spretum. Et paul post Camillo expiande etiam vocis nocturnæ, quæ nuncia cladis ante bellum Gallicum au dita neglectæ, effet mentio illata, insumd, et templum in nova via Ajo Locutio fieri. Eandem histomam recitat Cicero lib.1. de Divinatione: quem Plutarchus in libro de Fortitudine Ro mana φωνὴν καὶ ἀκοὴν vocat, propter vocem divinitus editam: quæ Romanos de subito illo & occulto Gallorum adventu admonuerat. Budæus lib.4. de Asse: Nempe, inquit, quod Ajus ille Locutius arcanum nihil esse finit eorum, quæ in aula geruntur. Ædes hujus Dea a P. Victore ponitur in IIX. Urbs regione: a Cicerone tamen & Marco Terentio Varrone non ædes, sed ara tantum ei constructa esse scribit.
units.tr: Then, as goddess of speech, language and the air, there was also Echo, loved by Pan; and Aius Locutius, whose name comes from speaking, because he spoke and forewarned the Romans of the coming of the Gauls. Livy, book 5, tells of this thus: "Marcus Caedicius, a plebeian, reported to the tribunes that in the new road, where the little shrine now stands above the temple of Vesta, he had heard in the night silence a voice clearer than a human voice, which bade the magistrates be told that the Gauls were coming. As happens, this was scorned because of the humble status of the one who reported it." And a little after, when Camillus was making expiation, mention was made also of the nocturnal voice, which had been heard before the Gallic war as a messenger of disaster and had been neglected; a temple was built to Aius Locutius in the new road. Cicero, book 1 of On Divination, recounts the same story; Plutarch, in his book on Roman courage, calls it a voice and a hearing [phōnēn kai akoēn], because of the voice divinely uttered, which had warned the Romans of that sudden and secret coming of the Gauls. Budaeus, book 4 On the As: "Indeed," he says, "that Aius Locutius was nothing secret of those things which are done in the court." P. Victor places the shrine of this goddess in the eighth region of the city; but Cicero and Marcus Terentius Varro write that only an altar was built to her, not a temple.

units.la: Eloquentiæ, ut & prudentiæ, Deum Herculem quoq; flaturunt: cujus quidem vim inter alia Galli simulacbro adumbrarunt.
units.tr: They also ascribed eloquence, as well as prudence, to the god Hercules; and the Gauls, among other things, represented his power by an image.

units.la: Hinc referri potest persuadendi Dea, a Græcis πειθὼ, ab Hebræo ןתפ Patach quod suade persuadere, latitare, seducere significat, a Latinis Suada & Suadela dicta (unde nostrum Ἄνθρωπον & Ἀπάτην) Quidam Leporem dixere; cujus Dea sacellum fuit apud Si cyonios, teste Pausania. Hinc Pytho Dea in Periclis labris habitare dicebatur; & Ceibegut
units.tr: From this one may refer the goddess of persuasion, called by the Greeks Peitho [πειθώ], by the Hebrews Patach [פתח], which means to persuade, to lie hidden, to seduce, and by the Latins Suada and Suadela. Some called her Lepus. She had a shrine among the Sicyonians, as Pausanias testifies. Hence Pytho was said to dwell on the lips of Pericles, and [Ceibegut, unclear].

units.la: Suadæ medulla ab Eunio vocatus, propter insignem utriusq; eloquentiam, & quid vis alijs persuadendi vim & facultatem. Huc pertinet per vulgatum illud Gratorum, ὑκ ἐξι πειθὼς ἰιρὸν ἀλλὰ πολλὼ λόγω, None est aliud Suadelæ sacrum, præter orationem. Sed & Diana ἐπιθῶ fuit cognominata. Observandum etiā Veteres Pytho collocasse inter Gratas Veneris comites, (ut etiam cum Mercurio Venerem comjungere solebant) & Suadelam cum Venere coluisse: quo significabant Amorem, sive bonum, sive etiā malum, sermone & eloquentia maximè conciliari.
units.tr: Ennius called her "the marrow of Suada," on account of her outstanding eloquence and whatever power and skill in persuading others. To this belongs the common saying of the Greeks, "There is no shrine of Peitho except much speech" [οὐκ ἔστι Πειθοῦς ἱερὸν ἀλλὰ πολλὰ λόγος]. Diana too was surnamed [epitho]. We should also note that the ancients placed Peitho among the Graces, the companions of Venus (just as they habitually joined Mercury with Venus), and worshipped Suadela together with Venus. By this they signified that love, whether good or even bad, is won chiefly by speech and eloquence.

units.la: Huc addi potest Dea consolandi, quam cum Pytho saltam fuisse a Praxitele Pausanias testatur. Dea ⟨ἀφολαυδὶ⟩ statur, quæ παραμύρῳ, id est, consolatrix dicta & in Attica posita fuerit.
units.tr: To these may be added the goddess of consolation, whom Pausanias testifies Praxiteles made standing beside Peitho. The goddess [Paramythia] is named the consoler [paramythion], and was set up in Attica.

units.la: Porro ut dicendi, loquendi, persuadendi & consolandi suis silendi atq; tacendi Deos atq; Deas Dii silentii finxerint, Harpocratem videlicet & Angeroniam sive Angeronam (unde Angeronalia) Mutam: apud Ethnicos. tam & Tacitam. Harpocratus Apulejus, Martianus lib. 1. & 7. (ubi puerum piceum appellat) Tertullianus in Apologetico, Varro in libro de lingua Latina, Catullus, Artemidorus oniro criticus, Plinius & Cassiodorus meminerunt. Non desunt inter scriptores, qui hunc Deum Sigaleona vocari existimant ab Aufonio illo versu: Aut tua Sigaleon Aegyptius oscula signet.
units.tr: Further, that the gods and goddesses of speaking, talking, persuading and consoling, and likewise of keeping silence and being quiet, were imagined by the gods of silence: namely Harpocrates, Angeronia or Angerona (whence the Angeronalia), Muta among the Gentiles, and also Tacita. Apuleius, Martianus in books 1 and 7 (where he calls the boy "pitch-black"), Tertullian in the Apologeticus, Varro in his book On the Latin Language, Catullus, Artemidorus in the Oneirocritica, Pliny and Cassiodorus all mention Harpocrates. Not a few writers think this god is called Sigaleon, from that line of Ausonius: "Or let the Egyptian Sigaleon seal your kisses."

units.la: & a Lucano hoc versu: Vestiraq; Sigaleon Aegyptius ora resignet:
units.tr: and from this line of Lucan: "And the Egyptian Sigaleon unseal the mouth:"

units.la: Fuit enim Aegyptiorum Deus, ex Ifide & Ofiride natus, cujus simalachrum fingebatur digito labris admoto: ταῦτα πόσα ὁ Ἀσκὸς, a fileudo & populo dictus, quod scilicet populus silentium indicat.
units.tr: For he was a god of the Egyptians, born of Isis and Osiris, whose statue was fashioned with a finger raised to the lips, [these things how the Ask(?)]. He was named from keeping silence and from the people, because, of course, the people signify silence.

units.la: De reliquis silentii Deabus ac Numinibus nempe Angeronia sive Angerona, Tacita & Muta, vide Gyraldum & Verderium.
units.tr: Concerning the other goddesses and deities of silence, namely Angeronia or Angerona, Tacita and Muta, see Giraldi and Verderius.

units.la: Not veró Christiani, ut bene dicendi; ita bene silendi atq; tacendi, quæ non minor est virtus, Deum verus sic magistrum optimum ac solum agnoscimus Deum. Tempus est tacendi & loquendi, inquit Ecclesiastes cap. 3. Tacebit vir prudens, inquit Ben Syrach. Linguam & os hominis Propheta Dei Deus moderatur. Exod. 4. Linguam eruditam dedit mihi Dominus, ut sciam sustentare eum, qui lassus est verbo. Iesa. 50. Linguas gubernare Domini est, inquit Solomon in Proverbiis: quas proinde non Mercurio, ut etiam reliquas corporis nostri partes, sed soli Deo consecrare debemus, eumq; precari, ut eas cum reprimendi, coercendi & refrænandi, sum sit bene ac recte utendi facultatem largiatur.
units.tr: But we Christians, as we value speaking well, so too value keeping silence and being quiet well, which is no less a virtue; and we acknowledge the true God as the best and only teacher of this. "There is a time to keep silence and a time to speak," says Ecclesiastes ch. 3. "A wise man will keep silence," says Ben Sirach. "God moderates the mouth and tongue of man, the prophet of God" (Exod. 4.). "The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain him who is weary with a word" (Isa. 50.). "The government of the tongue is of the Lord," says Solomon in the Proverbs. Therefore we ought to consecrate our tongues not to Mercury, as also the other parts of our body, but to God alone, and to pray that he would grant us the power to restrain, check and bridle them, and to use them well and rightly.

units.la: Ut autem orationis; ita actionum quoq; in genere quarumvis, certa quædam Numina finxerunt Ethnici, quæ nimirum hominet ad bene genuiter, feliciter, agendum excitarent atq; follicitarent: sive rebus agendis præessent. Hujusmodi Dii ac Deæ generales quidem fuerunt Genius, Agenius Deus, & Agenoria Dea, ab agendo sic dicti: unde Agonalia festa, quod hominet ad agendum instigarent. Talis fuit & Dea Horta, quasi similiter, ut Antiftius Labes tradidit, ab hortando dicta, ad bonestas actiones exhortabatur & incitabat (unde forsan vernaculum nostrum hurtig/id est, agilis, a lacer, promptus, est deductum.) Hac etiam Stimula fuit appellata, ut-tramodum adagendum flimulant: itemq; Horaæ ⟨ὥρα⟩ tu ὄραν, id est, a videndo, ut Deam provi-dentem, seu res inspicientem significet. Plutarchus in quæstionibus Romanis, quæstione quadragesima quinta, An Horta ea sit, quam nunc Horam dicunt, quæ observet omnia, & sollicita sit de omnibus, nunquam ab ea ret humanat negligi tradit: unde nec ejus edem clandi solitam; ea scilicet de tau-stâ, quod homines semper ad præclari aliquid agendum hortarentur & acceffando dehortaretur. Hanc Romuli uxorem fuisse, cum viveret, & Herfiliam dictam volunt, ut testatur idem Plutarchus.
units.tr: Just as the Gentiles imagined gods for speech, so too, in general, for actions of every kind they devised certain divinities, who would stir up and urge men to act well, happily and successfully, or who presided over doing things. Such general gods and goddesses were Genius, the god Agenius, and the goddess Agenoria, named from agere (whence the Agonalia festivals, because they urged men on to act). Such too was the goddess Horta, as Antistius Labeo related, named from hortari (to exhort), who exhorted and incited to honourable actions (whence perhaps our vernacular "hurtig," that is, agile, quick, is derived from alacer, prompt). She was also called Stimula, as it were stimulating men to act. Likewise [Hora, from ὥρα] and [horan, ὁρᾶν], that is, from seeing, so as to signify a goddess who looks ahead, or who oversees things. Plutarch, in the Roman Questions, question 45, asks whether Horta is the one they now call Hora, who observes all things and is anxious about all, and never lets human affairs go neglected. Hence, he says, her temple was not customarily closed; namely because by its very nature she always urged men to something noble and turned them back from the opposite by her approach. They wish that she was the wife of Romulus when he was alive, and was called Hersilia, as Plutarch also testifies.

units.la: Talis agendarum rerum Dea ac præses fuit Murea, cujus sacra apud Romanos in usu fuerunt; & Strenua, sive Strenia, sicodicibus antiquis credendi est; & præsertim Varroni, de lingua Latina sic scribenti: Hinc oritur caput sacræ viæ, ab Streniæ sacello. Porro à strenuè agendo sic denominabatur, seste Augustino in libris de Civitate.
units.tr: Such a goddess and president of doing things was Murcea, whose rites were in use among the Romans; and Strenua, or Strenia, as ancient books are to be believed, and especially Varro, who writes thus in On the Latin Language: "Hence arises the head of the Sacred Way, from the shrine of Strenia." Moreover, she was so named from acting vigorously (strenue), as Augustine testifies in the books On the City of God.

units.la: Singularum deinde actionum quoq; Dii certi ac Deæ fuerunt: ut rerum petendarum Peta Dea: rerum disputandarum Dea Dice: professionum, peregrinationum, viarum & itinerum Meriu rius (ideo Ερμῆς dictus sive Hermes ab Hebræa voce רמם Ramás, celta vit, iter fecit:) Hecate: Sanctius. Lares viales: Fessonia Dea, quòd fessos ex itinere recrearet (sicut contrà Sylvanus vulgo quiescentes inviadere ac pondere suo pressos gravare credebatur:) Eunus, ab eundo: Panda Dea, a pandenda seu aperienda via: Abeona & Adeona ut abeundi facultatem praestarent: Viblia, quòd ab erroribus viarū liberarct; cujus meminit Aruobius lib.4. Atq; hi quidem actionum Dii ac Deę fuerant praecipuę.
units.tr: Then there were also certain gods and goddesses of individual actions: the goddess Peta, of things to be sought; the goddess Dice, of things to be disputed; Mercury, of professions, journeys, roads and itineraries (hence he was called Hermes, from the Hebrew word [רמם, Ramas], "he trod, he made a journey"); Hecate; Sanctius; the Lares viales; the goddess Fessonia, because she refreshed the weary after a journey (just as, conversely, Sylvanus was commonly believed to attack those who were resting and to weigh them down with his weight); Eunus, from eundo (going); the goddess Panda, from pandere, to open or clear the way; Abeona and Adeona, who granted the power of departing and returning; Viblia, because she freed travellers from wandering off the road, of whom Arnobius speaks in book 4. These were the chief gods and goddesses of actions.

units.la: Cōmodebus videntur subjungi posse, ceu altioribus diametro repugnātes, Dii ac Dea, Deus Somnus, Dea Quies, Dea Murcea, sive Murcia, quòd homines murcidos, languidos & ignavos faceret, Dea Vacuna, a vacando dicta, quæ otiosis & vacantibus praeesset.
units.tr: Perhaps there may be added, as directly opposed to those higher ones, the gods and goddesses Somnus (Sleep), Quies (Rest), Murcea or Murcia, because she made men sluggish, languid and idle, and Vacuna, named from vacare (to be free), who presided over the idle and unoccupied.

units.la: SEQVITVR nunc quartus vitæ humanæ actus, nempe NVPTIAE, & MATRIMO- NIVM. Horum igitur quoq; plurimi apud Ethnicos fuerunt Dii ac Deæ: inter quas praecipua fuit Juno; quæ idcirco Gaunīa, sive Nupcialis a nuptiis, juga a subjugando, Interduca & Domiduca, a domum novam nuptam ducendo, Cinxia, quòd nuticio cinxinque cingulum solveret, Socia gena, quòd nubentes associaret & copularet, Populonia vel Populone, quòd ex nuptiis populi procrearentur, aliisq; nominibus fuit appellata.
units.tr: Now follows the fourth act of human life, namely the NUPTIALS and MARRIAGE. Of these too there were very many gods and goddesses among the Gentiles, of whom the chief was Juno. For this reason she was called Gamelia, or Nuptial, from nuptiae; Juga, from subjugating; Interduca and Domiduca, from leading the new wife into a new home; Cinxia, because she loosened the girdle of the bride; Socigena, because she joined and coupled those who married; Populonia or Populona, because peoples were produced from marriages; and she had other names besides.

units.la: Talia Numina fuerūt Venus, ceu anterus virorum ac mulierum, ut Plutarchus scribit, matuae effectrix, ob voluptatem, corporibus simul commiscens ac colliquefaciens animos: Cupido, ejus filius: Hymeneus: Thalasius, sive Thalasius: Virginensis Dea, quae adhibebatur, cum virgini sponsa Zona solveretur: Razenna Dea ab Etruscis culta in Nuptialibus: Tellumon: Rufona: Subigus Deus pater, qui adhibebatur, ut virgo a viro subigeretur: Prema Tea quae cul- sa, ne subacta viro, cum premeretur, se commoveret: jugatinus Deus, qui cultus, cum nias & fa.mina conjungebantur; vel quod ipse conjuges conjungeret: Domitius Deus, ut in domo esset nova nupta: Manturna Dea, ut illa cum viro maneret, nec abeo a vellerctur.
units.tr: Such deities were Venus, as Plutarch writes, the author of the union of men and women, the producer of marriage, on account of pleasure, mixing and melting bodies together with souls; Cupid, her son; Hymenaeus; Thalasius, or Talasius; the goddess Virginensis, who was invoked when the bride's virgin girdle was loosened; the goddess Razenna, worshipped by the Etruscans at nuptials; Tellumo; Rufona; the god Subigus, the father, who was invoked so that the virgin might be subdued by her husband; the goddess Prema, who was worshipped lest the bride, subdued by her husband, should stir herself when she was pressed down; the god Jugatinus, who was worshipped when husband and wife were joined, or because he himself joined spouses; the god Domitius, so that the new bride might be in the house; the goddess Manturna, so that she might remain with her husband and not be torn away from him.

units.la: His adde Deam Lydorum Anaicin; cujus ministerio dedicabant praestantes nobilitate puellas, quæ corporis pudicitiā, in vulgus data, velut augustiores factae, mox viris nubebant. Adde & Deam Viriplacam, viris placandis praepositam, quaundo odio a maleribus dissiderent. Nam, ut Valerius Maximus lib.2.cap.1. scribit, Quoties inter virum & uxorem al:quid jurgij intercesserat, su sacellum Deæ Viriplacæ, quod erat in palatio, veniebāt; ubi in vicem locuti, quæ ve- luerant, contentione animorum depositā, concordes se vertebantur. Dignissimum sanè conjugio sacrum institutum. Adde deniq; & Picumnum, Pilumnum, Volumnum ac Volumnam, a volendo sic appellatos, qui praesiabant, ut conjuges bona vellent & bene ac feliciter conjungerentur: quibus omnibus Dii ac Deabus nuptialibus & matrimonialibus non incommodè addideris Anorem; quem Cicero lib.3. de Natura Deorum, Erebo & Nocte natum, Æthereis ac Dieiferatrem fuisse scribit: quicum vinculum est matrimonii: unde a PontanoSocialis & Facundo: ab OviOvidio Socius: a Valerio Maximo Concors: a Castello Zelotypus, id est, forma vel alieni amo- ris æmulus, quod frequentissimum est in matrimonio vitium: a Campano Geniālis ac Dionæus, ab epithero Veneris Dionea, quæ matrimonii præcipua Dea est habita, fuit appellatus. Libet vero huic loco annectere elegantissimam Georgii Buchanani descriptionem Amoris, quæ in Epigrammatis illius exstat: Quis puer ales? Amor. Genitor quis? Blandus ocelli Ardor. Quo natus tempore? Vere novo. Quis locum excepit? Generosi pectoris aula. Quae nutrix? Primo flore juventa deceus. Quo nutrit victu? Illecebris, pulsuq; modestio. Qui comites? Levitas, otia, luxus, opes. Cur puero belli semper furiosa cupido? Impellunt a vide spes, crepidiq; metus. Nonmetuit mortem? Non. Quare? Sape renasci, Sape mori decies hunc bretus hora videt.
units.tr: To these add the Lydian goddess Anaïtis, by whose ministry they dedicated girls of outstanding nobility, who, having given the chastity of their bodies to the public, as if thereby made more honourable, soon married husbands. Add also the goddess Viriplaca, set over placating husbands when they were at odds with their wives through hatred. For, as Valerius Maximus writes in book 2, chapter 1, whenever some quarrel had arisen between husband and wife, they came to the shrine of the goddess Viriplaca, which was in the palace; there, speaking in turn, they laid aside the strife of their minds, and turned back to one another in agreement. A most worthy sacred institution for marriage. Finally, add Picumnus, Pilumnus, Volumnus and Volumna, so called from volo (to wish), who presided so that spouses would wish each other well and be joined well and happily. To all these nuptial and matrimonial gods and goddesses you may not unfittingly add Amor (Love), whom Cicero, in book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods, writes was born of Erebus and Night, and was brother of Aether and Day, and with whom there is the bond of marriage. Hence Pontanus calls him Socialis and Facundus; Ovid calls him Socius; Valerius Maximus, Concors; Castellus, Zelotypus, that is, the jealous rival of another's love, which is the most frequent vice in marriage; Campanus, Genialis and Dionaeus, named from Dione, an epithet of Venus, who is regarded as the chief goddess of marriage. It is pleasing to add here the most elegant description of Love by George Buchanan, which exists among his Epigrams: "What winged boy? Love. Who is his father? The blandishing fire of the eyes. At what time was he born? In new spring. Who received him? The hall of the noble breast. Who was his nurse? Youth, the grace of the first bloom. On what food was he nourished? On allurements and [pulsu? modest?]. Who are his companions? Levity, idleness, luxury, wealth. Why is the boy always a furious desire for war? Hopes and fears drive him on. Does he not fear death? No. Why? Often he is reborn, often he dies; ten times in one brief hour this boy sees."

units.la: Postremò & Lariibus familiaribus pro salutis nuptiis supplicare solitum, docet ille Plauti En- clio in Aulularia; Nunc tusculum emi, & haec coronas floreas;
units.tr: Lastly, Euclio in Plautus's Aulularia shows that people were also accustomed to pray to the household Lares for a prosperous marriage: "Now I have bought a little farm, and these garlands of flowers."

units.la: Hæc Hec imponentur in foco nostro Lari
units.tr: Let these be placed on our hearth for the household Lar,
So that he may make the marriage of my son a fortunate one.

units.la: Quoniam autem nuptiarum & matrimonii effectus est partus, naturali ordine hoc quoq; loco de parturientium & infantium Dijs esse dicendum. Sed quoniam supra de iis in actu vite bumanæ primo & secundo, nempe Natiuitatis & Nutritionis fuit dictum, nolumus hic dedita opera eorum catalogum repetere.
units.tr: Since the outcome of marriage and wedlock is childbirth, it is fitting in the natural order to speak here also of the gods of women in labour and of infants. But since we have already spoken of them above, under the first and second acts of human life, namely birth and nurture, we do not wish to repeat their catalogue here on purpose.

units.la: Porro ad Matrimonium sive conjugium referri quoq; possunt Dii domestici & familiares, ut Mania Dea, quæ horum omnium mater fuit, Genii, Penates, Lares, & singularum partium domus custodes.
