De Penatibus, quos dictos dicit Ifidorus ideo, quod essent in penetralibus, id est, in secretis, exflat illud Comici Poeta: —Dii Penates, Vobis mando meum parentem, rem bene ut tuemini.
units.tr: The household and family gods may also be referred to marriage or wedlock, such as the goddess Mania, who was the mother of all of them, the Genii, the Penates, the Lares, and the guardians of the individual parts of the house. Concerning the Penates, whom Isidore says were so called because they were in the penetralia, that is, the inner recesses, there is that line of the comic poet: "Penates, I entrust to you my father; see that you keep his property well."

units.la: Hinc Tutelares & Parrii sunt dicti. Virgilius: Quem secum patrios ajunt portare Penates, Ac Dijs connubialibus adaumerantur in illo Pontani: Pax colitur, colitur, thorus, castia, Penates.
units.tr: From this they were also called Tutelares and Patrii. Virgil: "whom they say they carry with them as their ancestral Penates." And among the marriage gods, in that line of Pontanus: "Peace is worshipped, worshipped are the marriage bed, chastity, and the Penates."

units.la: Idem judicium est de Laribus quos etiam domi tutari credebant: unde & Tutelares & Præstises fuerunt appellati, ob quam causam & canina pellibus amicti, et canis iis præpositus fuit, quia iflud animal domus magnum curam gerat. Hoftilii ideo etiam dicti sunt, quod a domo hostes eos arcere credebantur. De Laribus edium custodibus qui pluru defiderat; videat Lambinum in prologuni Aulularia Plauti, ubi Lar familiaris sic loquens introducitur: Ne quis miretur qui sim, paucis eloquar. Ego Lar sum familiaris, ex hac familia: Vnde exeuntem me aspexisti, hanc domum Iam multos annos est cum posside & colo.
units.tr: The same judgement holds for the Lares, whom they also believed protected the home; hence they were called both Tutelares and Praestites, and for this reason they were clothed in dog-skins, and a dog was set over them, because that animal takes great care of the house. They were also called Hostilii, because they were believed to keep enemies away from the house. Whoever wants more about the Lares, guardians of buildings, let him see Lambinus in the prologue to Plautus's Aulularia, where a household Lar is introduced speaking thus: "So that no one may wonder who I am, I will say it briefly. I am the household Lar of this family. Whence you saw me going out, I have now for many years possessed and tended this house."

units.la: Festus: Lauee effigies compitalibus nofiu dabantur: quod Lares, quorum ii erat dies festus, animam putabantur esse hominum, redactum in numerum Deorum. De Laribus Vialibus, qui peregrinantes tuebantur, dictum est supra. De his ille apud Plautum sic loquitur: —Invoco Vos Lares Viales, ut me bene ja vetis.
units.tr: Festus: "Little waxen images were given to the Lares of the crossroads, because the Lares, whose festival day this was, were thought to be the souls of men, raised to the number of the gods." Concerning the Lares Viales, who protected travellers, it was said above. Of them that man speaks thus in Plautus: "I call upon you, Lares Viales, that you may help me well on my way."

units.la: Quod attinet ad domos, vel edes ipsas; iis quidem in genere præfuit Aediculus Deus: quod vero ad singulas earum partes, liminibus primum præfecerunt Deum Limentinum, ut eam custodiret: Deinde Porta Portulum, ne ipsis dormientibus eas quisquam auferret: foribus Forulum, sive Forculum: cardinibus Cardeam vel Cardineam sive Carnum Deam, quæ, ut canis Ovidio lib.6. Fastorum, ab jano compressa, priusquam nunciupata, clausa aperiret, aperta clauderet: (quo pertinet Empanda Dea, quæ patentibus foribus præerat) & fornacibus, Fornacem Deam (unde Fornacalia, feria instituta farris torrendi gratia: quidad ad fornacem, quæ in pistrinis erat, sacrificium fieri solebat) focus Lateranum Deum, a lateribus, e quibus foci construbantur: arcus & tapfis Arculum Deum, qui tutelam gererent arcanum: scopas, ut domus possent verrere Deverrere Deam. His addi possunt Dii & Dee Ancillarum, quæ scopas minuntur, dicti Anculi & Anculæ, ab antiquo verbo Anculare, quod est servire & ministrare. Hactenus de quarto actu.
units.tr: As for houses, or the buildings themselves, Aediculus was set over them in general; but for their individual parts they appointed, first, the god Limentinus over the threshold, to guard it; then Portunus over the door, so that no one could carry it off while the inhabitants slept; Forculus, or Forculus, over the doors; Cardea, or Cardinea, or the goddess Carna, over the hinges, who, as Ovid says in book 6 of the Fasti, was seduced by Janus, and was given the power to open what was closed and to close what was open (to which belongs the goddess Empanda, who presided over doors standing open); over the ovens, the goddess Fornax (whence the Fornacalia, a festival established for the sake of roasting grain, since a sacrifice was customarily made at the oven, which was in the bakeries); over the hearth, the god Lateranus, named from the bricks (lateres) from which hearths were built; over the vaults and the hearth-stones, the god Arculus, who had charge of the secret chests; over the brooms, the goddess Deverra, so that they might sweep the house. To these may be added the gods and goddesses of the maidservants, who are called by the brooms, the Anculi and Anculae, from the old word anculare, which means to serve and to minister. So far on the fourth act.

units.la: VLTIMVS & postremus vite humane actus, ejus clausula atque terminus est mors: Huius Numen & Dea fuit Morta; culta quidem olim a Lacedæmoniis & Hispanis: apud quos utrosq; templa illi dicata atque consecrata fuerunt: potissimum vero in urbe Gadera Hispanorum: cui addi possunt Parcæ, quasi minime parcentes, alio nomine Fata dicta: unde Dee fatales, quarum officia a Poetis vulgo sic distinguuntur, ut velint, unam esse, quæ vitam hominis ordinatur, aliam quæ contexat, tertiam quæ filum rumpat, ac finiat. Hæi igitur quoq; und cum Morte ceu Deas coluerunt & venerati sunt Erbnici.
units.tr: The last and final act of human life, its close and end, is death. Its divinity and goddess was Morta, worshipped formerly by the Lacedaemonians and the Spaniards, among whom temples were dedicated and consecrated to her, especially in the city of Gades in Spain. To her may be added the Parcae, as if they spared no one, also called by another name the Fates, whence the goddesses of destiny, whose functions the poets commonly distinguish thus: that they wish one to be the one who ordains the life of a man, another who spins it out, a third who breaks the thread and ends it. These, then, the heathen also worshipped and venerated as goddesses together with Death.

units.la: His addendum Funus & Exsequie, quibus certa quoq; Numina præposuerunt: ut Deam Libitinam, Epicymbiam, Neniam; cujus sacellum extra portam Viminalem fuit dedicatum. Hinc Nenia, teste Festo, est carmen, quod in funere laudandi gratia cantatur ad tibiam; quam quidem ideo volunt dictam, quod verisimiliter querimonia fluentium fit.
units.tr: To these must be added Funus and Exsequiae, over which they also placed certain divinities: such as the goddess Libitina, Epicymbia, and Nenia, whose shrine was dedicated outside the Viminal gate. Hence nenia, according to Festus, is a song sung to the flute in praise of the dead at a funeral; which they think was so called because it is probably made of the lamenting of those who weep.

units.la: Porro & post mortem coluerunt homines sub certis Numinibus: item animas & cadaveris F 2 ta illorū: De quo multu hominū jam mortuorum Citero lib.2.de Natura Deorum sic scribit: Quid absurdius, inquit,quàm aut res sordidas aut deformes, Deorū honore afficere: aut homines, jam morte deletos,reponere in Deos,quorum omnis cultus esset futurus in luctu ?
units.tr: Moreover, men also worshipped many of the dead after death under certain divinities, as well as their souls and corpses. Concerning this, Cicero writes thus in book 2 of On the Nature of the Gods: "What could be more absurd," he says, "than to honour with divine worship either base or deformed things, or to place among the gods men already destroyed by death, whose whole worship would be mourning?"

units.la: Pertinens huc Dii inferi,ut Manes,Sumanus, qui & Orcus & Plutus sive Pluto, Cerberus, Cocytus, Phlegeton, Charon, Acheron, Minos, Aeacus, Rhadamantus, Damones, Eudemones, Cacodemones, Lemures, Incubi, Succubi & alii: item Dea infera, Styx, Furie, Eumenides, Hesperides, Proserpina, Megara, Chimera, Tisiphone, Cotho, Lachesis, Atropos aliaq; immortales; quas divinis honoribus affecerunt & coluerunt, de quibus Cicero lib.3. de Natura Deorum: Illos,qui fluere apud Inferos dicuntur, Acheronteh, Cocytum, Stygem, Phlegetontem, Deos putarunt. Et alibi: Charon, Cerberus, Orcus Dii fuerunt habiti. Item eodem tertio libro de Natura Deorum: Aetherii & Dii fratres agentaloqui antiqui sic nominati sunt, amor, dolor, metus, labor, in videntia, fatum, fenestra, morbus, tenebrae, miseria, querela, gratia, fraus, pertinacia, Parce, Hesperides, somnia, quos omnes Erebo & Nocte natos ferunt. Ac de Manibus quidem Dii ita Festus: Manes Dii, inquit, ab auguribus vocabantur, quod eos per omnia manere credebant, eosq; superos atq; inferos dicebant. Idem: Manes pro bonis accipiuntur a supplicitur veneratoribus propter metum mortis. Isidorus: Manes dicunt Deos mortuorum, quorum potestatem inter lunam & terram afferunt: a quibus & mane dictum existimant, quos putant ab aëre, qui manent, id est, rarus est, Manes dicti: sive quia late manant per aurai: sive quia mites sunt in manibus, contraria nomine hoc appellantur. Apuleius autem ait eorum & in Θεοῖς dici Manes, hos est, mites ac modestos, cum sint terribiles & immanes: ut Parcas, ut Eumenides, etc.
units.tr: Pertaining here are the infernal gods, such as the Manes, Summanus, who is also Orcus and Plutus or Pluto, Cerberus, Cocytus, Phlegethon, Charon, Acheron, Minos, Aeacus, Rhadamanthus, the Daemones, Eudaemones, Cacodaemones, Lemures, Incubi, Succubi, and others; likewise the infernal goddesses, Styx, the Furies, the Eumenides, the Hesperides, Proserpina, Megaera, Chimaera, Tisiphone, Cotho, Lachesis, Atropos, and other immortals, whom they honoured with divine worship and cultivated. Of these Cicero says in book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods: "They thought that those who are said to flow among the dead, Acheron, Cocytus, Styx, and Phlegethon, were gods." And elsewhere: "Charon, Cerberus, and Orcus were regarded as gods." Also in the same third book of On the Nature of the Gods: "The ancient writers named the children of Aether and the gods ... Love, Grief, Fear, Labour, Envy, Fate, Fraud, Obstinacy, Disease, Darkness, Misery, Complaint, Favour, Fraud, the Parcae, the Hesperides, Dreams, whom they all say were born of Erebus and Night." And concerning the Manes, Festus says: "The Manes were called gods by the augurs, because they believed that they remained through all things, and they called them above and below." Again: "Manes is taken to mean the good by those who worship them with supplication, out of fear of death." Isidore: "They call the gods of the dead Manes, whose power they place between the moon and the earth; and they think the word mane is derived from the air, which remains, that is, is thin, so they were called Manes; or because they spread widely through the air; or because they are gentle towards the dead (in manibus); a name opposite to the thing." Apuleius, however, says that in Greek they are called the Manes of the gods, that is, gentle and mild, although they are terrible and savage, like the Parcae and the Eumenides.

units.la: Summanum vero dixerunt, quasi summum Manium, omnia rapientem ac devorantem; quippe sub cujus potestate consistat omnis Aëris a Lunā diffusio, שמש Rakia Hebraeis. Inde verbū Summanare finxit Plautus, pro auferre et rapere. Hinc Curculio, parasitus apud Plautum, Summanum se ab omnibus, vocari dicit, quòd ad exemplum Summani Dei, omnia, quae incidant, rapiat. Similiferè notatione Hebraei שאול, Schcol, vel שאול Scheolāh, Orcum sive infernum dixerunt a שאל postulavit, petiit, tanquam infernus semper petat: juxta illud Prov.30. Tria sunt insatiabilia: sepulchrum vel infernus, vulva occlusa, et terra quae non satiatur aquis; cujus nominis etymon etiam Lactantius reddidit, videlicet hoc verlu: Inferus insatiabiliter ca va gur iuna pandit.
units.tr: They called Summanus, as if it were the highest of the Manes, the one who snatches and devours everything; for under his power is all the diffusion of air from the moon, which the Hebrews call rakia [רקיע]. From this Plautus coined the verb summanare, meaning to carry off and snatch away. Hence Curculio, the parasite in Plautus, says that he is called Summanus by everyone, because, after the example of the god Summanus, he snatches away everything that falls in his way. The Hebrews by a similar derivation called sheol [שאול], or sheolah [שאולה], the underworld or hell, from sha'al, to ask, seek, as if hell always seeks; according to that passage in Proverbs 30: "Three things are insatiable: the grave, or hell; the closed womb; and the earth, which is not satisfied with water." Lactantius also gave the etymology of this name, namely in this verse: "Hell opens its hollow jaws insatiably."

units.la: Ortum porrò ab urgendo mortem dixerunt (Antiquissimè enim pro G frequenter ponebant C.) Ifidoa rus vero eum quasi receptorem mortium vocat: unde & Orca nuncupatur vas, quod recipit aquas. Et quia mortem, cujus Nomen fuit Orcus, quies sequitur, Orcus Quietalis, sive Quietalis fuit nuncupatus. Notationes reliquorum Deorum ac Dearum hujus classis qui scire volet, videat Gyraldum, Verderium & alios, qui de his ex professo scripserunt.
units.tr: They said that Orcus derives from "urging" death (for in very ancient times they frequently put C for G). Isidore, however, calls him as it were the receiver of the dead; whence also a vessel that receives water is called orca. And because rest follows death, whose name was Orcus, he was called Quietalis, or Quietalis Orcus. Whoever wishes to know the derivations of the remaining gods and goddesses of this class, let him see Giraldus, Verderius, and others who have written on these matters expressly.

units.la: Ata, ita ac libus vitae humanae cunctis certa Numina, Deos ac Deas praeferunt olim Gentiles. Referendae huc sunt aetates, Senectus et juventa; quae cum ipsae pro Deabus habitae fuerunt, tum sub certis Numinibus cultae. Senectuti quondam templa dicabant et consecrabant Lacedaemonii et Hispani, in Gadera urbe: juventa vero alio nomine Hebe, dicta, sive juventas, quod Ludovico Vivi & Carolo Sigonio magis placet, inquit Augustinus libro quarto de Civitate, ca-
units.tr: Likewise, the Gentiles of old set up certain divinities, gods and goddesses, over every stage of human life. Old age and youth belong here. Both were regarded as goddesses and worshipped under particular deities. The Lacedaemonians and the Spaniards, in the city of Gades, once dedicated and consecrated temples to Old Age. Youth, also called Hebe, or Juventas (the name that Ludovico Vives and Carlo Sigonio prefer), is, as Augustine says in the fourth book of De Civitate Dei, chapter eleven, and elsewhere, a goddess who receives a person after the boyhood robe is put aside and takes up the beginnings of youth.

units.la: pite undecimo, & alibi, Dea est, quae post pretextam excipit juventutis aetatis exordia. Hanc Romani a Servio Tullio ufq; in Capitolio coluerunt. Quare cum Tarquinius Priscus templum Jovi Capitolino extruere vellet, & propterea omnium aliorum Deorum, qui in Capitolio colebantur, templa exaugurarat, Terminus & juventas tedere noluerunt, quod Romani in omen traxerunt, fore ut nunquam termini vires moverentur, nec unquam juventutis vigor deesset. Dionysius Halicarnassaeus lib.5. Augustinus de Civitate Dei,lib.6.cap.1. Juventas Dea cum Termino Jovi voluit concedere in Capitolio coudendo, Livius lib.5.extremo. Ludos etiā hujus adhe dedicandae causa factos; & quidem cum majore religione, quod nomen cum Antiocho bellum cum inflaretur, author est idem Livius.
units.tr: The Romans worshipped her from the time of Servius Tullius, and on the Capitol. When Tarquinius Priscus wished to build a temple to Jupiter Capitolinus, he had already taken the auspices away from all the other gods who were worshipped on the Capitol. Yet Terminus and Juventas would not give way. The Romans took this as an omen: the boundaries would never be moved, and the vigour of youth would never fail. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 5; Augustine, De Civitate Dei, book 6, chapter 1. Juventas, along with Terminus, was willing to yield to Jupiter when the Capitol was being built. Livy, book 5, near the end. Games were also held in her honour when she was dedicated, and with greater religious observance, because this happened when the war with Antiochus was being stirred up; Livy is again the authority.

units.la: Atq; haec quidem fins dicta de Diis & Numinibus Gentilium naturalibus, quae nihil sunt aliud, quàm res naturales, a Deo create atque condita, quas Mortales Dei Creatoris loco habuerunt atq; coluerunt; qui cultus non inepro, meo judicio, ratione subjecti, idololatria seu superstitio naturales dici poterit.
units.tr: So much, then, has been said about the natural gods and divinities of the Gentiles, which are nothing other than natural things, created and founded by God, and which mortals have treated as the Creator God and worshipped. In my judgment, this worship, given its subject matter, may not inappropriately be called natural idolatry or superstition.

units.la: Horum autem omnium Deorum naturalium descriptio atq; cultus, cum generalis, tum specialis singulorum, bis fere constat loci, qui quidem singuli diligenter accurateq; considerati totidem sunt argumenta, quae cum ad Deorū illorum vitas, id est, nullitatem, seu futilitatem, sunt ad eorum, qui illos coluerunt, stultitiam atq; dementiam demonstrandam pertinent.
units.tr: The description and worship of all these natural gods, both general and particular to each one, consists roughly of certain heads. Each of these, considered carefully and precisely, provides as many arguments. They serve to show the vanity or futility of those gods, and the folly and madness of those who worshipped them.

units.la: Primus locus sunt nomina, cognomina, agnomina, tituli, epitheta, elogia, eaq; duplicia: primi ge sive Numina: Graeca θεός, θεοί; item varia & multiplices nominum flexiones. Hebraea אלוהים, Aelohim, בעל, Baal, & בעלים Baalim: Germanica Gott / Götter/Abgott/ Götz/Götzen. Nomina specialia singulorum Deorum, quae ex affectibus, opinionibus & ratio-nibus hominum fuerunt profecta: ubi observandum, eos nomina & attributa, soli vero Deo conve-nientia & propria, ad fictos suos Deos exprimendum esse mutuatos, seu potius suffuratos. Sic, ut ex innumeris, nunc tantum exemplum proferam. Iehova, veri Dei nomen proprissimum & essentiale, ad filium illum suum Deum, Deorum principem, qui Iovem vocant, transtulerunt. Nomi-nibus vero ipsis, Deorum suorum naturalium vim, naturam, vires, actiones, munera & officia alia atq; alia, quae ius affinxerunt, exprimere fuerunt conati. Ex Gentilibus tamen quidā Deos abfq; nominibus coluerunt, quos Deos ἀνωνύμους & ἀγνώστους, ignotos seu incognitos vocarūt, ut apud Atheniensis, quorū Paulus meminit Actorum 17. & Pelasgos. De his Cicero lib. 1. de Natura Deorum: Chrysippus inquit, magnam turbam congregavit ignorantium Deorum, atq; ita ignororum, ut nos ne conjectura quidem informari possimus, cum mens nostra quid vis videatur posse depingere. Econtra alii Deos multos, variis ac multiplicibus nominibus coluerunt, qui ᾿Αναύνυμοι, ditebantur: quos ὀνόματα, & ἀνωνύμους & ἀναυνύμους Theodoretus vocat ἀλλοδαύμους, tanquam indignos Dei vero nomine, quibus nomina divina magnifica & angusta, quae illis tribubantur, nequaquam convenientur. Nam quod Latinis Deorum fuerit princeps Iupiter a Iuvando, quasi iuvans, pater a Graecis Zεὺς a Zῆν, seu viventem, ab Assyriis, & Chaldaeis בעל, Baal, id est, dominus, patronus ac marites, aliaq; nominibus fuit appellatus, ut Βάαλ, ὁμόνυμος, Opitulus, Opitulator, Servator, Conservator, haec omnia nomina non Dis illis fictis, sed soli vero Deo sunt propria.
units.tr: The first head is names: names, surnames, additional names, titles, epithets, and eulogies. These are twofold. First come the general names of the deities, or divinities: the Greek θεός, θεοί [theos, theoi]; likewise the various and manifold inflections of the nouns. The Hebrew אלוהים [Elohim], בעל [Baal], and בעלים [Baalim]; the German Gott, Götter, Abgott, Götz, Götzen. Then come the special names of individual gods, which arose from people's feelings, opinions and reasoning. Here it should be noted that the Gentiles borrowed, or rather stole, names and attributes that belong to God alone and are proper to him, and applied them to their fictitious gods. To give just one example among countless others: Jehovah, the most proper and essential name of the true God, they transferred to their son, the chief of their gods, whom they call Jupiter. By the names themselves they tried to express the power, nature, strength, actions, functions and various offices which they had invented for their natural gods. Some Gentiles, however, worshipped gods without names, whom they called anonymous and unknown, ἀνωνύμους and ἀγνώστους [anonymous and agnostous], as the Athenians did, of whom Paul speaks in Acts 17, and the Pelasgians. On these Cicero, in book 1 of De Natura Deorum, says: "Chrysippus gathered a great crowd of ignorant gods, and so unknown that we cannot even form a conjecture about them, since our mind cannot seem to depict anything at all." On the other hand, others worshipped many gods under various and manifold names. These were called ἀναύνυμοι [anaunymoi], and Theodoret calls them ἀλλοδαύμους [allodaumous], as though unworthy of the true name of God, since the grand and narrow divine names given to them do not in any way fit them. For example, Jupiter was the chief of the Latin gods, named from iuvando, helping, as if "the helper"; among the Greeks, Zeus, from Zῆν [Zen], living; among the Assyrians and Chaldeans, בעל [Baal], that is, lord, patron and husband; and he was called by other names too, such as Βάαλ [Baal], ὁμόνυμος [homonymos], Opitulus, Opitulator, Servator, Conservator. All these names belong not to those fictitious gods but to the one true God alone.

units.la: Secundus locus est Numerus, nisi rursus duplex: Primo universalis omnium Deorum, qui fuit innumerabilis pene ac infinitus, qualis arenarum maris, pulverisve terrae, ac stellarum coeli. Hic tamen observandum, quosdam nullum omnino volui esse Deum aut Numen esse, inter quos fuerunt quidam Philosophi clari & celebres; de quo genere hominum Theodoretus: Non athei solum, inquit, qui Deum esse negat, sed etiam Homerus, Hesiodus, Philosophi, qui multos Deorum ordines fabulati sunt: ex quibus triginta millia Deorum numerat Hesiodus; de quo quidem numero quidam varie & monstrose fuerint hominum opiniones. Plinius copiose enumerat libro sua historia secundo, capite septimo. Qui vero praeter unum Deum plures statuerunt Deos, eorum nonnulli tertium fixerunt Deorum numerum: alii vero, & quidem plurimi, Deos finxerunt innumeros. Iam vero singulorum quoq; Deorum numerus varius fuit & multiplex. Sit trecentos Iovez seu Iupiterros & Marco Varrone enumeratos esse testatur Tertullianus: Cicero tamen non nisi tres enumerat, sicut & tandem Dioscuros, novem Musas, plures Vulcanos, Apollines, Dionysios, Minervas, Veneres, Iunones, Mercurios, Bacchos, Aesculapios, & alios.
units.tr: The second head is number, which again is twofold. First, the general number of all the gods, which was almost innumerable and unlimited, like the sand of the sea, the dust of the earth, or the stars of heaven. Here, however, it should be observed that some have wanted there to be no god or divinity at all. Among these were certain famous and renowned philosophers. Concerning this sort of people Theodoret says: "Not only the atheist, who denies that there is a God, but also Homer and Hesiod and the philosophers, who invented many orders of gods." Of these, Hesiod counts thirty thousand gods. Concerning this number, opinions among people have varied and been monstrous. Pliny lists them at length in book 2, chapter 7, of his Natural History. Those who posited several gods besides the one God, some fixed a third number of gods, while others, and indeed most, invented innumerable gods. Next, the number of each particular god also varied and was manifold. Tertullian testifies that Marcus Varro counted three hundred Jupiters. Cicero, however, lists only three. Likewise there are two Dioscuri, nine Muses, many Vulcans, Apollos, Dionysii, Minervas, Venuses, Junos, Mercuries, Bacchuses, Aesculapiuses, and others.

units.la: Tertius locus est Sexus. Deorum alios finxerunt masculos, sive mares: alios feminas. Quinimmo in plerisq; sexus fuit anceps, masculus simul & foeminea, ut Lunus, Luna, Tellumon, Tel-lus & alii.
units.tr: The third head is sex. Some of the gods they imagined as male, others as female. Indeed, in many the sex was ambiguous, both male and female at once, such as Lunus and Luna, Tellumo and Tellus, and others.

units.la: Quartus locus hujus profopographiae Deorum, est illorum Ortus, sive Nativitas. Quo referendi parentes, genus, familia, patria, sive locus natalis, tempus, modus. Deorum enim quidā babuerunt tantum patrem, ut Minervā, ex capite Iovis nata: quidā tantum matrem, ut Vulcanus ex Iunone procreatus, sine patre. Quorundam plures parentes fuerunt, ut Iovem primum & secundum natos in Arcadia finxerunt; alterum quidem patre Aethere, ex quo etiam Proserpinam natam fernunt & Liberum; alterum vero patre Coelo, qui genuisse Minervam dicitur, quam principem & in ventricem belli ferunt; tertium Cretenfem Saturni filium, cujus in illa iussula sepulcrum ostenditur. Idem autem judicium esto de patria.
units.tr: The fourth head of this prosopography of the gods is their origin or birth. To this belong their parents, lineage, family, homeland or place of birth, time and manner. Some gods had only a father, such as Minerva, born from the head of Jupiter; some had only a mother, such as Vulcan, born of Juno without a father. Some had several parents. For example, they imagined a first and a second Jupiter, born in Arcadia: one, indeed, by the father Aether, from whom they also say Proserpina and Liber were born; the other by the father Caelus, who is said to have begotten Minerva, whom they call the leader and inventress of war; a third, the son of Saturn, a Cretan, whose tomb is shown on that island. The same judgment should be made about their homeland.

units.la: Quintus locus est Aetas. Plinius lib.2.cap.7. Matrimonia quidem, inquit, inter Deos credi, tanto& ævo ex his neminem nasci & alios esse grandaevos, semperq; eosdem; alios juvenes atq; puerosque, atri colorem, aligeros, claudos, ovo editos, & alterum diebus ventos morientes, puerilium prope deliramentorum est. Cicero lib.3. de Natura Deorum: Gelo, Chartaginensium tyrannus, Aesculapii Epidaurii barbam aureum demississe; neq; enim convenire barbatum esse filium, cum in omnibus fanis pateris nber hu esset. Lactantius postquam longa oratione multa argumentus priscorum Deos homines fuisse, qui post mortem in Divos essent relati, probavenit, subjungit eos ideo diverse fuisse aetatis, alios nempe pueros, alios adolescentes, alios senes, alium demum aliam, eam propriam, statuam positam, ut aetas habuisset, referretur, in quibus morientes sunt reperti.
units.tr: The fifth head is age. Pliny, book 2, chapter 7: "To believe that there are marriages among the gods, and that none of them is born from these, and that some are very old and always the same, while others are youths and boys, black in colour, winged, lame, hatched from an egg, and others dying on alternate days, is nearly the stuff of childish ravings." Cicero, book 3 of De Natura Deorum: "Gelo, tyrant of the Carthaginians, had the golden beard of Aesculapius of Epidaurus removed, since it was not fitting for the son to be bearded when in all the temples the father was beardless." Lactantius, after a long speech in which he proved by many arguments that the ancient gods had been men who, after death, were raised to the rank of divinities, adds that they were therefore of different ages: some were boys, some youths, some old men. Finally, each was given a statue of the age he had had, and they are found in the same condition in which they died.

units.la: Sextus locus est Educatio sive Nutritio singulorum Deorum, de qua similiter multe exstant fabellae aniles ac monstrose; quas hic enumerare non est necesse. Summa enim est tantum singulorum capita perstringere animus est.
units.tr: The sixth head is the education or nurture of each god. Similarly, there exist many old wives' tales and monstrous stories about this, which it is not necessary to list here. My intention is only to touch briefly on the main points of each.

units.la: Septimus locus est Matrimonium vel Caelibatus. Deorum enim suorum Ethnici alios finxerunt caelibes ac virgines, alios matrimonio junctos. Matrimonia quidem, inquit Plinius libro supra citato, secundo, capite septimo, credi inter Deos, tanto, ævo ex his neminem nasci puerilium prope delirament. Hucrefereude Deorum libidines, adulteria, nmores; quos singulis certos attribuerunt. Hinc tot amasij, amasiæ, & liberi illorum. Hinc pulli Iovis, de quibus fabulæ exstant, aliaq; id genus propè infinita. Plinius ibidem: Sed super omuem impudentiam, inquit, adulteria inter ipsos fingi, mox jurgia atq; odia, atq; etiam furtorum esse scelerum Numina. Cicero lib.1. de Natura Deorum: Poëta & ira inflammatos & libidine furentes induxerunt Deos, fecerunt, ut eorum bella, pugnas, praelia, ortus, pulueris s. ....... odia praeterea discordias, ortus, interitus, querelas, lamentationes effusas, in omni interpreantia libidines, adulteria, vincula, cum humano genere concubitus, mortalesq; ex immortali procreatos. Pertinent huc Deæ meretrices, Flora, & aliæ plurimæ.
units.tr: The seventh head is marriage or celibacy. The Gentiles imagined some of their gods as unmarried and virgins, others as joined in marriage. Pliny, in the book cited above, book 2, chapter 7, says: "To believe that there are marriages among the gods, and that none is born from these, is nearly the stuff of childish ravings." To this belong the lusts, adulteries and manners of the gods, which they assigned to particular gods. Hence so many lovers, mistresses and their children. Hence the "young of Jupiter," about whom stories exist, and almost endless things of this kind. Pliny in the same place: "But beyond all shamelessness, they imagined adulteries among them, then quarrels and hatreds, and even that there were divinities of thefts and crimes." Cicero, book 1 of De Natura Deorum: "The poets introduced gods inflamed with anger and raging with lust. They made their wars, battles, fights, births, ... hatreds, discords, deaths, complaints and lamentations, and everywhere all kinds of lusts, adulteries, bonds, intercourse with the human race, and mortals born of immortals." To this belong goddesses who were prostitutes, Flora and many others.

units.la: Octavus locus est Sedes atq; Domicilium. Singulos enim Diis certas affinxerunt sedes, domicilia atq; habitationes. Hinc alios finxerunt superos, alios inferos, alios aethereos, alios aereos, alios terrestres, alios maritimos, alios subterraneos & infernos.
units.tr: The eighth place is Seat and Dwelling. For they assigned to each god certain seats, homes and habitations. Hence they imagined some gods above, some below, some heavenly, some aerial, some terrestrial, some marine, and some subterranean and infernal.

units.la: Nonus locus est, Munus, Officium, Imperium, Domuatus, Potestas, seu Tyrannis potius, varia & multiplex. Singulos enim Diis certa assignarunt officia, munera sive munia, imperia, potestates. Item uni Deo atq; Deæ multa attribuerunt munera, de quibus sufficientum esset dicere. Sic enim, exempli gratia, Minervam & belli & artium disciplinarum, omnium secerunt Deam, Junonem suxerunt Deam Aeris, Terra, parturientium, etc. Hinc secundum diversa illa munia diversis illis imposuerunt nomina atq; coguomina.
units.tr: The ninth place is Office, Duty, Command, Rule, Power, or rather tyranny, varied and manifold. For they assigned to each god certain offices, functions, duties, commands and powers. Likewise they attributed many functions to one god or goddess, too many to list. For example, they made Minerva the goddess of both war and the liberal arts, and Juno the goddess of the air, of the earth, and of women in labour. Accordingly, they gave these deities different names and surnames to match their different functions.

units.la: Decimus locus sunt Actiones, res gestae cum bone & laudabiles, tum etiam male, impie & improbae, nempe vitia, scelera atq; flagitia plurima, quae Diis atq; Numinibus illis suis commentitiis tribuerunt. Observandum igitur nos solum propter virtutes & actiones laudabiles, verum etiam propter vitia & malefacta, homines inter Divos retulisse sua Numina, ut passim ex illorum historiis atq; fabulis colligi potest.
units.tr: The tenth place is Actions: deeds both good and praiseworthy, and also bad, impious and wicked, namely the many vices, crimes and shameful acts which they ascribed to their gods and fictitious divinities. We must note that men placed their divinities among the gods not only for virtues and praiseworthy actions, but also for vices and misdeeds, as can be gathered everywhere from their histories and fables.

units.la: Undecimus locus sunt plurimi Deorum istorum commentitiorum Casus, cum prosperi, & secundi, tum infelices & adversi, de quibus utrisque similiter legi possunt Ethnicorum historiae atque fabulae.
units.tr: The eleventh place is the many fortunes of these fictitious gods, both prosperous and successful, and unhappy and adverse. Of both kinds one may read in the histories and fables of the heathen.

units.la: Duodecimus locus est Mors, sepultura, monumenta atq; sepulchra: de quibus quàm diversi & monstrose fuerint opiniones & errores, colligere promptum est ex Ethnicorum mes scriptis.
units.tr: The twelfth place is Death, burial, monuments and tombs. How diverse and monstrous their opinions and errors about these were is easy to gather from the writings of the heathen.

units.la: Decimus tertius locus, qui ad cultum Deorum potissimum spestat, sicut & reliqui sequentes quinque continet Idola, simulacra, imagines, effigies, statuas, quæ etiam ligna appellantur: quæ quidem sæpissime pro Diis ipsis, quorum fuerunt sepulcra & simulacra, tanquam ipsi offent, Dii, vel certè Dii in illis essent praesentes, habita fuerunt atque culta. In his ipsis autem simulacris consideranda eorum effectus, seu fabricator, materia, forma, finis. Materia simula-
units.tr: The thirteenth place, which pertains chiefly to the worship of the gods, like the five that follow, contains idols, images, likenesses, effigies and statues, which are also called wooden things. These were very often held and worshipped as the gods themselves, whose tombs and images they were, as if the gods themselves were present in them. In these images one must consider their maker, material, form and purpose. The material of images

units.la: cromwan trorum antiquissima, maximaque communis fuit lignum: de quo quidem deinceps; cum de Diis artificialibus agemus. Forma Deorum ipsorum varia fuit & multiplex, vel humana, vel bellua, vel mixta, & composita ex homine & bellua: ut, exempli gratia, Panis imago conflabat ex capro & homine. Ad formam pertinent Cornua diversa; ut Bacchi taurina, Iovis arietina, &c. Corona diversa; ut querne Iovis, oleagine Minervae, &c. Animalia varia singulis Diis dicata, ut turtur Harpocrati, fulica Mercurio, &c. Plantae & arbores certae, singulis Diis dicatae; ut Myrtus Veneri, quercus Iovi, &c. Iusfugia & instrumenta, ut arma, hasta, virga, baculi, sceptra, &c. Vestes vel viles, vel pretiosae, vel feminae vel masculae. Currus & quadrigae varia, in quibus considerantur animalia, a quibus fingebantur vehi, ut Dracones, a quibus Saturnus: aquila, a quibus Iupiter: equi, a quibus Mars & Sol: corvi, a quibus Mercurius: turtur, a quibus Venus: homines, a quibus Luna vehebatur.
units.tr: was in the most ancient times, and most commonly, wood, of which we shall speak later when we treat of artificial gods. The form of the gods themselves was varied and manifold: either human, or beastlike, or mixed and compounded of man and beast, as for example the image of Pan was made of a goat and a man. To the form belong the different horns, such as the horns of Bacchus, which were those of a bull, and of Jupiter, which were those of a ram; different crowns, such as the oak crown of Jupiter and the olive crown of Minerva; various animals dedicated to particular gods, such as the turtledove to Harpocrates and the coot to Mercury; certain plants and trees dedicated to particular gods, such as the myrtle to Venus and the oak to Jupiter; emblems and implements, such as arms, spears, rods, staffs and sceptres; garments, either coarse or costly, either female or male. There are various chariots and four-horse teams, in which are considered the animals by which the gods were imagined to be carried: dragons, by which Saturn was carried; eagles, by which Jupiter; horses, by which Mars and the Sun; ravens, by which Mercury; turtledoves, by which Venus; men, by which the Moon was carried.

units.la: Decimus quartus locus fuit, Aedes, Templa, Fana, Delubra, Sacella.
units.tr: The fourteenth place is temples, shrines, sanctuaries, chapels and small shrines.

units.la: Decimus quintus fuit Ara & Altaria, quae in Deorum horum fictorum cultum fuerunt constituta.
units.tr: The fifteenth place is the altar and altars, which were set up for the worship of these fictitious gods.

units.la: Decimus sextus fuit sacrificia, libationes, anathemata, donaria, thus, suffitus & similia, quae illis faciebant.
units.tr: The sixteenth place is sacrifices, libations, offerings, gifts, incense, fumigations and the like, which they made to them.
The seventeenth is games.

units.la: Decimus octavus, Dies festi, festivitates, & solemnitates. Haec in genere de idololatria seu superstitione naturali.
units.tr: The eighteenth is feast days, festivals and solemnities. These are the general points about idolatry, or natural superstition.

units.la: SEQUVNTVR nunc Dii atque Numina artificialia, quae nimirum hominum manu, artefacta atque opere constant: tametsi eorum materia est naturalis. Haec sunt idola, simulacra, statuae, imagines, effigies, et aliaë generis, quae ab Hebraeis אלילים Elilim, id est, אלים al Elim, non Dii, id est, creaturae & vanitates: a Graecis χειροποίητα & χειρόκμητα, passim vero sacris in litteris Opera manuum humanarum: a Lactantio, qui acerrimus eiusmodi χ... id est, imaginum & idolorum oppugnator fuit, digitorum mortalium ludibria & fragilia fragmenta, appellantur, hoc est, manibus humanis effecta & elaborata. Unde idem libro secundo, capite secundo: Quid igitur potestatum inquit, habere possunt simulacra, quae fuerunt in hominibus potestate, vel ut aliud fierent, vel ut omnino non fierent. Horum autem cultus & veneratio proprie idololatria appellatur, voce composita ab εἴδωλον, id est, simulachrum, species, figura & λατρεία, id est, cultus sive veneratio: quam quidem idololatriam artificialem, sive manuariam, reffe Etiu scilicet subiecti, licet appellare.
units.tr: Now follow the gods and divinities made by art, which clearly consist of artefacts and works made by human hands, although their material is natural. These are idols, likenesses, statues, images, effigies and others of that kind. The Hebrews call them אלילים Elilim, that is, אל אלים al Elim, "not gods", that is, creatures and vanities. The Greeks call them χειροποίητα and χειρόκμητα, and in the sacred writings generally, "works of human hands". Lactantius, the fiercest opponent of such images and idols, calls them "the playthings of mortal fingers and fragile fragments", that is, things made and fashioned by human hands. Hence in book two, chapter two, he says: "What power, then, can images have, which were in men's power, either to be made otherwise or not to be made at all?" The worship and veneration of these is properly called idolatry, a compound word from εἴδωλον, that is, image, appearance, figure, and λατρεία, that is, worship or veneration. This artificial, or handmade, idolatry may rightly also be named from its subject matter.

units.la: Prior idololatriae species primo Decalogi praecepto: altera secundo prohibetur; & in libro Sapientiae capite decimo tertio, priori primo fit mentio: posteriori secundo loco: acibidem posteriorem docet magis esse ἀ ποσ... Alogos, id est, absurdam & a ratione alienam. In prompta ratio est; quia nimirum a ratione magis abhorrent opera humana, ut sunt idola atque simulacra, quam opera divina, sive opera digitorum & manuum divinarum: cuiusmodi sunt, omnes res naturales Deorum loco habere ac divinis afficere honoribus. Res enim naturales, quae quidem sexu atque motu, ac suprimis ratione et intelligentia sunt praeditae, longe propius ad Dei simulitudinem et imaginem accedunt, et clariores illustriores, longe sunt imagines et simulacra, quam res quae vel artificiosissimae, quae exquisitissimo opere, summo artificio summaque arte sunt perfectae; cum illa inanimata sint atque muta, omnique non solum ratione atque intelligentia, sed etiam sensu motuque careant.
units.tr: The former kind of idolatry is forbidden in the first commandment of the Decalogue, the latter in the second. In the book of Wisdom, chapter thirteen, the former is mentioned first, the latter second, and there it teaches that the latter is more absurd [ἄλογος], that is, foolish and foreign to reason. The reason is plain: human works, such as idols and images, are more repugnant to reason than the works of God, or the works of the divine fingers and hands. Of this kind are all natural things, which are to be held as gods and given divine honours. For natural things, which are endowed with sex and motion, and above all with reason and understanding, come much nearer to the likeness and image of God, and are far more clear and illustrious images and likenesses, than things which are most skilfully made, perfected with the finest workmanship, the highest craft and the greatest art; since those are lifeless and mute, and lack not only reason and understanding but also sense and motion.

units.la: De his ipsis autem Gentilium imaginibus atque simulacris duo extant libri: Unus Vincentii Chartarii, Italicus: alter Autoris Verderii, qui eum Latine reddidit, Latinae; tam elegantur & tam accurate, ut nihil fere eis addi posse videatur, ad quorum lectionem quosvis ejus rei studiosos remitto. Sed tamen, ne omnino nihil hac in parte, quae coti huic meo institutio est accommodata, egisse videar, breviter & summatim quaedam, quae fuse copiose, in sacris litteris continentur & explicantur, hic proponere & cum iis, quae apud profanos scriptores exstant, quantum fieri potest, conferre est animus.
units.tr: Two books exist on these very images and likenesses of the heathen: one by Vincenzo Cartari, an Italian, and the other by Antoine Verdier, its author, who translated it into Latin, and so elegantly and accurately that little seems to be able to be added. I refer anyone interested in this subject to their reading. But so that I may not seem to have done nothing at all in this part, which is suited to my present plan, I intend here to set out briefly and summarily some things which are set forth and explained fully and copiously in the sacred writings, and to compare them, as far as possible, with what exists in the profane writers.

units.la: Etsi vero passim in sacris, veteris praesertim, Testamenti libris idolorum, imaginum, simulacrorum mentio occurrit, tamen duae imprimis luculentae copiose eorum descriptiones sunt, egregie.
units.tr: Although idols, images and likenesses are mentioned everywhere in the sacred books, especially those of the Old Testament, there are two outstanding and full descriptions of them, admirable above all.

units.la: F. ✚ prionesextant; Vna quidem capite decimo tertio & decimo quarto libri qui inscribitur Sapien‑tia Salomonis ; cuius supra quoque meminimus: Altera sexto capite Baruchi, quae vocatur Epi‑stola Ieremiae, scripta & missa ad Iudaeos, in seruitutem Babylonium abducendos, quae illos gra‑uissime ab idolorum simulachrorum, Gentilium cultu dehortatur.
units.tr: There are two of these: one in chapters thirteen and fourteen of the book entitled the Wisdom of Solomon, which we also mentioned above; the other in chapter six of Baruch, which is called the Epistle of Jeremiah, written and sent to the Jews who were to be led away into Babylonian slavery, and which very earnestly dissuades them from the worship of idols and the heathen images.

units.la: Ad duo autem capita praecipua cum ille allegata, tum alia , quae exstant in sacris litteris, idolorum simulachrorum, descriptiones possunt referri. Vnum sunt ipsa idola sive simulachra: Alterum est eorum cultus & veneratio : unde Idololatria suum habet nomen , utrunque simul complectens.
units.tr: To these two chief chapters, both those cited and others which occur in the sacred writings, the descriptions of idols and likenesses may be referred. One part concerns the idols or likenesses themselves; the other is their worship and veneration, from which idolatry takes its name, embracing both together.

units.la: Porro idolorum simulachrorum, Gentilium vanitatem demonstrant sacrae litterae , seu ipsae potius Spiritus Sanctus,illarum auctor , hu fere argumentis ; quorum alia dulta sunt a nomine bus eorum, notatione : alia a causis: alia ab effectibus.
units.tr: Moreover, the sacred writings, or rather the Holy Spirit himself, their author, demonstrate the vanity of heathen idols and likenesses by roughly these arguments; of which some are drawn from the names of them, some from their causes, and some from their effects.

units.la: Quautum ad eorum attinet nomina , & quidem Hebraea ; in sacris litteris vocantur , ut su‑pra dictum, ​Elilim, sive Elilim, id est, Aelohim non Deus, per transpositionem litterae Aleph: quo sensu primo praecepto Decalogi Aelohim Aelohim acherim, Dii alieni, id est, falsi, fucati, fictitii, commentitii & adulterini: sive Dii Goiim, sive gentium alibi, & a David Demonia appellantur. Pulchre huc alludit Spiritus Sanctus Ha‑bac. 2. verba faciens de Idolis. Et non Deus ipse; quod Chaldaeus Paraphrastes reddidit: Et artifex fecit illum Deum, in quo nulla est utilitas. Et LXX. ἡ ἐκ ἡμέρα τὸ ἕτεράν θεοῦ ... Sicenim distinguitur Deus verus a factis fictitiis, illis Dus: qui recte appellantur Alie‑ni; quia alieni sunt a Dei natura, nihil, habent divinitatis, & nomine tantum sunt Dii (ut Rex pictus nihil habet praeter colores Regis) in quibus non modo nullum est Numen, sed ne sen‑sus quidem, aut motus, aut vs ulla, aut efficacia. Deinde quia indigni sunt, qui colantur, alieni sunt a verapietate, ac bonis moribus, Exod.20. Deuteron.30.2. Reg 17. Sic Aelohe hannecar, Dii peregrini, & alienigenae eandem ob causam dicuntur Gen. 35. 2. Iacob removeri iubet & ad se in Sichem allatos defodit sub quercu. Dicet autem ipse Spiritus Sanctus ab surdum & ab omni ratione esse alienum opus manuum humanarum, animae, sensu motuque carens Deum appellare, eiq; illud ἀκακρίζων Dei nomen tribuere: ut legimus capite supra cap. tato 14. Sapientia Salomonis.
units.tr: As for their names, and first the Hebrew ones: in Holy Scripture they are called, as said above, Elilim or Elilim, that is, Aelohim, "not God," with the letter Aleph transposed. In this sense the first commandment of the Decalogue speaks of Aelohim acherim, "other gods," that is, false, counterfeit, fictitious, invented and spurious gods. Elsewhere they are called gods of the Goiim, or of the nations, and David calls them demons. The Holy Spirit alludes to this aptly in Habakkuk 2, speaking of idols: "not God himself," which the Chaldee paraphrast rendered, "and the craftsman made that god in which there is no profit." The Septuagint has [οὐ θεός], "not God." Thus the true God is distinguished from made-up fictions, which are rightly called "other" or "strange," because they are alien to the nature of God, have nothing of divinity, and are gods only in name, as a painted king has nothing but the king's colours. In them there is not only no divine power but not even sense, motion, voice or efficacy. Further, because they are unworthy of worship, they are alien to true piety and good morals (Exod. 20; Deut. 30:2; 2 Kings 17). For the same reason "Elohe hannecar," foreign and strange gods, are so called in Genesis 35:2, where Jacob orders them removed and buries those brought to him at Shechem under an oak. The Holy Spirit also calls a work of human hands, which is senseless, alien to all reason, and lacking soul, sense and motion, a god, and gives it that name, as we read in Wisdom 14.

units.la: Idem docent alia nomina Hebraea, quibus sacris in litteris appellantur; cuiusmodi ab illorum vel formas, ​specie: vel vanitate atq; effectu perniciosis sumuntur. Huiusmodi est Pesel, id est, sculptile, idolum deiolatum ex ligno vel lapide Exod. 20.4. Lev. 26. ​Pafal, dedolavit, exsculpsit: vel a Pefil, quod est falsum, profanum, veritati con‑trarium: cuiusmodi sunt idola, res vanae, inanes, falsae & mendaces.
units.tr: Other Hebrew names by which they are called in the sacred books teach the same thing. They are taken from their form and appearance, or from their vanity and pernicious effect. Such is Pesel, that is, a carved image, an idol hewn from wood or stone (Exod. 20:4; Lev. 26), from pasal, to hew or carve out; or from pesil, which is false, profane and contrary to truth. Such are idols, vain, empty, false and lying things.

units.la: Talis vox, idolorum vanitatem & idolatriam, sive nullitatem arguens, est Nasach, significans idolum, quod ex auro, argento, aut aliis metallis est conflatum a Nasach, con‑flavit, fudit. Significat etiam imaginem lapideam, aut ligneam, auro et argento ornatam. Nam vox Nasach, etiam auri vel argenti laminam, quales vi fuisse in idolis, significat. Hinc Rabbi David Kimchi Ornamenta idolorum vertit eo loco Esaie 44.
units.tr: A term that shows the vanity, or nothingness, of idols and their idolatry is Nasach, meaning an idol cast from gold, silver or other metals, from nasach, to cast or pour out. It also means a stone or wooden image adorned with gold and silver, for the word nasach also means a plate of gold or silver, such as were apparently in idols. Hence Rabbi David Kimchi renders "ornaments of idols" at that place in Isaiah 44.

units.la: Similiter vox est Iezar, figmentum ; a Iezar, figuram rebus induxit: quod ver‑bum & angustiam significans, docet , idola hominibus maximas angustias, anxietates & mole‑stias creare.
units.tr: Similarly, Iezar means a figment, from yatsar, to shape a figure. This word also signifies distress, and it teaches that idols create the greatest distress, anxieties and troubles for men.

units.la: Huc pertinet vox Thoar, forma, seu figura , eodem Esaie loco, tam de sculptis, quam de pictis, atq; etiam de animi idolo, quae solo affectu, sine externa imagine concipiuntur, & ufur‑pantur : item vox Tiphcareth, effigies ab ornatu & decore fictitia : item vox Demuth, similitudo,rem aliam repraesentans : idem quod Themunah, forma videli‑cet & figura alterius rei : qualis est & vox Mazzebah, statua, lapis erectus in monu‑mentum,a stando sive statuendo, sic dictus, quemadmodum etiam ipsum Latinum Statua, quam Graeci illo loco Levit.26. Et statuam non fingetis, vertunt ἀλιδούσ... Praeterea a vanitate sua, idola sive simulacra, appellantur Schekeer: quae vox merda cium & vanitatis vanissimam significat: cuiusmodi voces sunt vox Hebel, & Aven: unde Bethel sepe Beth-Aven, id est, domus vanitatis dicitur ob idololatriam, illic fieri solitam.
units.tr: Here belongs the word Thoar, form or figure, used in the same passage of Isaiah both of carved and painted things and of an idol of the mind, which is conceived and used by feeling alone, without any external image. Likewise Tiphcareth means an effigy that is fictitious because of its ornament and decoration. Likewise Demuth means a likeness representing another thing, the same as Themunah, namely the form and figure of something else. So too is Mazzebah, a statue, an upright stone set up as a monument, from standing or setting up, so called just as the Latin statua itself is. The Greeks render it in Leviticus 26, "and you shall not make a statue," by a word meaning [ἀλιδούσ]... Besides, idols or images are called Schekeer from their vanity; this word signifies a lying and utter vanity. Of this kind are the words Hebel and Aven, whence Bethel is often called Beth-Aven, that is, house of vanity, because of the idolatry commonly practised there.

units.la: Appellantur idola etiam רוחות Ruchoth, Venti, a flatu, quia cito evanescit: & Paulus רוחות idolum dicit esse Nihil, id est, rem nihili faciendam. Hinc Isaie 41. foc legimus: Ecce vos estis מעא Meain, de nihilo, et opus vestrum est מפעא Meapha, id est, de nihilo: ubi idoאין la & opera illorum dicuntur אין Ain, vel En, id est, res, non existentes in rerum natura. Hinc Sapientiæ 13. capite, homines ipsi propter idolorum simulachrorum, cultum μεγαλαυ, id est, vana, ni appellantur. Mάταιοι autem, id est, vanum, dici videtur quasi ua, sive un ὄν, non existens. Reite igitur & veri idola a vanitate et nihilo suum nomen habent, propterea quod & nihili sunt atque vana, & vanitatis sunt caussæ, & ad nihilum tandem redigunter.
units.tr: Idols are also called Ruchoth, winds, from their breath, because they quickly vanish. And Paul calls an idol "nothing," that is, a thing to be reduced to nothing. Hence we read in Isaiah 41: "Behold, you are of nothing (Meain), and your work is of nothing (Meapha)," where idols and their works are called Ain or En, that is, things not existing in the nature of things. Hence in Wisdom 13 men themselves, on account of their worship of idol images, are called vain (mataioi). Mataioi, vain, seems to be so called as if from ua or un on, not existing. Rightly, then, idols have their name from vanity and nothingness, because they are both nothing and vain, are causes of vanity, and are in the end reduced to nothing.

units.la: Sed, ut adhuc magis intelligatur, idola atque simulacra Gentium non modo fuisse & esse גללים rei vanas, inanes, mendaces, fallaces, fatiles & inutiles, verum etiam abominandas, exsecrandat, sedas, turpes, noxias & perniciosas, illa etiam גללים Gelalim, id est, stercora & ex-cremtenta, 2. Reg. 17. & שקוצים Schikuzim, id est, abominationes appellantur, 1. Reg. 11. שקוצים propterea quod res erant turpes, foedæ & exsecrabiles in consp. ctu Dei, hominesq. quiea colebant, reddebant Deo exosos, in vitos & exsecrabiles.
units.tr: But, so that this may be understood even more clearly, the idols and images of the Gentiles have been and are not only vain, empty, lying, deceptive, fleeting and useless things, but also abominable, accursed, filthy, shameful, harmful and pernicious. They are also called Gelalim, that is, dung and excrements (2 Kings 17), and Schikuzim, that is, abominations (1 Kings 11), because they were shameful, foul and detestable in the sight of God, and the men who worshipped them made themselves hateful to God, vile and abominable.

units.la: Hic adde vocem עצבים Azzabim, quæ in sacris litteris trita valde est & usitata, præfertim Psal. 106. & 135. Idola gentium aurum & argentum, &c. Sic dicta a עצב Azab, fantia nit, contristavit, dolore affecit: eo quod maximos laboribus atque doloribus idolorum cultores conficiuntur & excruciantur: quod, in & animi & corporis, & cum temporales, tum æternos dolores atque cruciatus conciliant. Quid si etiam dicta sint a עץ Ez, id est, ligno, propterea quod antiquissima maximè, communia Gentium idola atque simulachra ex ligno fuerunt: de quo postea pluribus.
units.tr: Add the word Azzabim, which is very common and usual in the sacred books, especially in Psalms 106 and 135: "The idols of the nations are gold and silver," etc. It is so called from Azab, to grieve, to afflict with pain, because the worshippers of idols are worn out and tormented with very great labours and pains, which bring upon them, in both soul and body, both temporal and eternal pains and torments. Or perhaps it is so called from Ez, that is, wood, because the most ancient and most common idols and images of the Gentiles were made of wood, of which more later.

units.la: Adde bis postremò vocem תרפים Theraphim, quorum Genes. 13. 1. Samuel. 19. Iud. 17. & תרפים & 18. 2. Reg. 23. & Hos. 13. sic mentio: quæ vox in plurali numero vel in genere quæ vis simulacra; vel certum simulacrorum genus denotat: cujus varia notationes afferuntur. Quidam sic volant dici a רפא Rápha, dimisit, remisit; id, vel quod in loco, ubi posita sunt, sive domi, sive in templo, dimittantur, nec alio facile transferantur: vel, quod, qui ea consulebant, secundum illorum responsa vel quid continuabant, vel omittebant. Quid si potius ita dicta sunt, quod illa essent dimittenda, rejicienda & missa facienda: vel, quod suos cultores rebus in ardua atque periculis dimittebant seu deferebant, omni ope auxiliaque suo destitutos: vel denique, quod cultores suos reddebant remissos, languidos et pigros? Quid si etiam Theraphim dicti, qua si Seraphim: quod nomen est, Angelorum? Inde forsan vox Græca ὑπηρέτης, monstrum, prodigium, est derivata.
units.tr: Add lastly the word Theraphim, which is mentioned in Genesis 13, 1 Samuel 19, Judges 17 and 18, 2 Kings 23 and Hosea 13. This word, in the plural, denotes either images in general or a certain kind of image; various explanations of it are given. Some think it is so called from rapha, he dismissed or let go, either because the images are left in the place where they are set, whether at home or in the temple, and are not easily moved elsewhere, or because those who consulted them followed or omitted things according to their replies. Or perhaps they were so named because they were to be dismissed, rejected and sent away; or because they let down and deserted their worshippers in difficulties and dangers, leaving them destitute of all help; or finally because they made their worshippers slack, languid and lazy. Or perhaps Theraphim was so called as if it were Seraphim, which is the name of angels? From this perhaps the Greek word for a monster or prodigy is derived.

units.la: Alii Theraphim sic volunt dicta idola a רפא Rápha, fanavit, medicinam adhibuit, forsan quia morborum aliorumque malorum remedia ab ipsis petere, sperare & exspectare homines solebant. LXX. vocant Theraphim Χαρπιος quos Chaldæus Paraphrastes simulacrorum cultores reddit. Aben-Ezra vult statuas & simulacra fuisse magica, sive instrumenta astrologica & divinatoria, ita fatis, ut astrorum observatione responsa & oracula reddere possent. Et hæc de nominibus idolorum Gentilium Hebræis, quibus ipsorum vana, futilia, inania, fœda, turpia, noxia & perniciosa, exsecranda denique & abominanda natura demon-stratur.
units.tr: Others hold that idols are called Theraphim from rapha, he healed, applied medicine, perhaps because men used to seek from them, and hope and wait for, remedies for diseases and other evils. The Seventy render Theraphim by a Greek word, and the Chaldee paraphrast renders them worshippers of images. Aben Ezra holds that the statues and images were magical, or astrological and divinatory instruments, so that by observing the stars they could give responses and oracles. And these things concerning the Hebrew names of the Gentile idols show that their nature is vain, trifling, empty, foul, shameful, harmful and pernicious, and finally accursed and abominable.

units.la: Nomina Græca secundum & linguæ ipsius copiam, & Gentii Græca flagrantissimum olim superstitionis studium, sunt immumera; maximè tamen trita & communia hæc sunt:
units.tr: The Greek names, both because of the richness of the language itself and because the Greeks were once extremely zealous in superstition, are countless; yet these are the most common and widely used:

units.la: Εἴδωλον, si Tertulliano in libro de Idololatria de hac voce differenti credimus, diminuti-vum est, & dicitur παρὰ τὸ εἶδος, quæ formam speciemque rei vivantis vel mortuæ, verè vel falsa significat. Nihil enim refert. Nam ipsa rei repræsentatio significatur hoc verbo: non veritas aut vita. Ex voce etymologia, etiam ipso Cicerone auctore & interprete libri primo de finibus bonorum & malorum, εἴδωλον est imago. Εἴδωλα vocantur nonnunquam imagines & phantasmata, in cœlo apparentia, ac flatim e consessu evanescentia, tanquam inflabilia parumque firma. Latinè Idolum paßim pro simulacro usurpatur. Sic Idolum Ceres, Plinius vocat simulacrum libro trigesimo quarto, capite quarto, Et Viatru- ius itidem Dianæ Idolum vocat simulacrum, libro secundo, capite undecimo. Et ista
units.tr: Εἴδωλον [eidōlon], if we believe Tertullian in his book On Idolatry about this differing word, is a diminutive, and is said to derive from εἶδος [eidos], which signifies the form and appearance of a thing, whether living or dead, true or false. For it makes no difference: this word signifies the representation of the thing itself, not its truth or life. From the etymology of the word, as Cicero himself attests and explains in the first book of On the Ends of Good and Evil, εἴδωλον is an image. Eidōla are sometimes called images and phantoms that appear in the sky and vanish at once from the gathering, as if they were windy and scarcely firm. In Latin, idolum is commonly used for a likeness. Thus Pliny, in book thirty-four, chapter four, calls the idol of Ceres a simulacrum; and Vitruvius likewise calls the idol of Diana a simulacrum, in book two, chapter eleven. And these
The Greek names of idols.

units.la: Lactantius Firmianus omnia gentilia Idola vocat simulacra a simulando dicta. Hieronymus in Isaia Prophetæ caput undecimum ait, Idola imagines esse morientium. Et in sacris litteris, ubi Græci habent εἴδωλα, Latinus interpres habet simulacra. Εἰδωλον etiam pro effigie accipitur: & Εἰδωλεῖον pro templo, sive fano, in quo profanum Idolum est positum & colitur. Εἰδωλολάτρης illud, quod Idolis immolatur. Εἰδωλολάτρης, ut qui Idola seu simulacra colit, & Εἰδωλολατρεία Idolorum, seu simulacrorum cultus.
units.tr: Lactantius Firmianus calls all pagan idols simulacra, named from simulating. Jerome, on the eleventh chapter of the prophet Isaiah, says that idols are images of the dead. And in Holy Scripture, where the Greeks have eidōla, the Latin translator has simulacra. Eidōlon is also taken for an effigy, and eidōleion for a temple or shrine in which a profane idol is placed and worshipped. Eidōlothuton is that which is sacrificed to idols. Eidōlolatrēs is one who worships idols or likenesses, and eidōlolatreia is the worship of idols or likenesses.

units.la: Εἰκόνες, εἰκασμα, & ἀπεικάσματα similiter appellantur imagines & simulacra. Item Ξόανα, ἀγάλματα, ἴδλ. Εδν Ἀγῶν Βαγίως pro ἀγάλματα, id est, figura vel sigilla Deorum interpretatur. Edos etiam sedem, pavimentum, solum & templum significat: forsan sic & templa & simulacra Gentilium dicta ab edendo. (Nam ædoc, accentu in ultima, voracem significat) quod in templis & Idolorum suorum cultu gule indulgebant.
units.tr: Eikones, eikasma and apeikasmata are likewise called images and likenesses. Also xoana, agalmata, and so on. Agōn Bagios [Hesychius?] interprets agalmata as figures or little images of the gods. Edos also means a seat, a floor, a base or a temple; perhaps for this reason temples and the likenesses of the pagans were called from eating (edein), for edos with the accent on the last syllable means a glutton, because in their temples and in the worship of their idols they indulged their gullet.

units.la: Βρίτας etiam simulacrum Græce dicitur ξόανον ἀπὸ ξοανοῦ, quod Mortalium speciem habent, teste Suida. Ξοανον, εἴδωλον & ἀνδριάντα Ammenius sic distinguit, quod ξοανον proprie est signum, sive flatua, quæ Heroibus erigitur: εἴδωλα, quæ Diis: ἀ- ἀρικὰς, quæ Regibus, tanquam maxime viris. Quicquid sit ξοανον ἀπὸ τοῦ ξέειν, id est, a polyendo, & sculpendo sive scalpendo videtur derivari: unde proprie est simulacrum sculptile. Ἀγάλματα, id est, flatuæ, imagines sive simulachra Græce videntur dici ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀγαλλεῖν, καὶ χαίρειν, propterea quod homines illos valde lætantur & delectantur, ea iactant, ut gloriantur & exultant. Hoc enim significat verbum ἀγαλλεῖν, quasi ἀγα-αλλεῖν, id est, nimis, pra lætitia exilire & exultare, auffpzingen von frewde: quale est Hebræorum גד אל vel גד, Gad, Gal vel Gail, a quo Græcum illud sine dubio est ortum, & Germanum gcilen/lasciuire prægaudio, & gcil/lafcirus.
units.tr: Brítas is also called in Greek a simulacrum, xoanon, from xoanos, which have the likeness of mortals, according to Suidas. Ammonius distinguishes xoanon, eidōlon and andrias thus: xoanon properly means a sign or statue erected to heroes; eidōla are those for the gods; andriantes are those for kings, as being most of all men. Whatever the case, xoanon seems to be derived from xeein, that is, from smoothing and carving or scraping; hence it properly means a carved likeness. Agalmata, that is, statues, images or likenesses, are seemingly so called in Greek from agallein and chairein, because men greatly rejoice and delight in them and boast of them, exulting and glorying. For the verb agallein signifies, as it were agan-allein, that is, to leap and exult excessively for joy, "to jump for joy" (auffspringen von frewde). This is like the Hebrew gad, Gal or Gail, from which that Greek word is without doubt derived, and the German gcilen/lasciuire (to be wanton) for great joy, and gcil/lafcirus (wanton).

units.la: Latina vocabula, quibus artificialia & manuaria ista Gentium Numina exprimuntur, sunt Idolum (quæ vox licet sit Græca, tamen pro Latina etiam sufurpatur) quæ non inepte ac per jocum dixerimus, Idola sic dicta, quod doli sint, atque dolores plenissima.
units.tr: The Latin words by which these man-made and handmade divinities of the Gentiles are expressed are idolum (although this word is Greek, it is nevertheless also used as Latin), which, not inaptly and in jest, we may say are called idola because they are full of deceit (doli) and of sorrows (dolores).

units.la: Simulacra dicta sunt a simulando, sive simulatione, quæ vox deceptionem sive circumvencionem significat. Cicero ad Lentulum libro primo. A quibus tuendus fuerat, derelictus, idque non solum fronte atque vultu, quibus simulatio facillime sustinetur. Idem in 3. Verrinis: Nullæ sunt occultiores insidiæ, quam hæ, quæ latent in simulatione officii, aut in aliqua necessitudinis nomine. Vel dicta sunt a similitudine. Ac recte fani vel a simulitudine, & a simulatione, vel etiam, si vis, a simulatate sunt dicta, propterea quod non vera sunt, sed ficta, simulata atque fucata: unde Lactantius libro secundo, capite secundo. Cum simulacrum a similitudine homeu habeat, non possunt simulata, quæ nihil feuriunt, nec moveantur, Deo similia ducari. A simulatate etiam ea possumus derivare, eo quod simulatem & inimicitiam inter Deum & homines gignunt. Hucillud Pauli secunda Corinthiorum sexto, versu decimo quinto: Quod enim consortium justitiæ cum iniquitate? Et quæ commune Luci cum tenebris? Et quæ concordia Christo cum Belial? Aut quæ portio fideli cum infideli? Et quæ consensio templo Dei cum simulacris?
units.tr: Simulacra are so called from simulare, or simulatio, a word that signifies deception or circumvention. Cicero, in the first book To Lentulus: "He had been left by those whom he ought to have protected, and that not only by their face and expression, by which pretence is most easily maintained." The same, in the third Verrine: "There are no more hidden snares than those which lie concealed under the pretence of duty, or under the name of some close relation." Or they are so called from similitudo (likeness). And rightly so are they called fani, from likeness and from pretence; or even, if you wish, from simulata (pretended), because they are not true but feigned, pretended and painted over. Hence Lactantius, in book two, chapter two: "Since the simulacrum has the likeness of a man, things that are pretended, which feel nothing and do not move, cannot be considered like God." We may also derive them from simulatas (pretences), because they produce pretence and enmity between God and men. To this belongs Paul's saying in 2 Corinthians 6:15–16: "For what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness? And what communion has light with darkness? And what concord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion has the believer with the unbeliever? And what agreement has the temple of God with idols?"

units.la: Porro imaginis quoque nomine insigniuntur: quæ vox vel ab imitatione, ut Festo videtur, quia imago est rei alicujus imitatio, vel a voce Græca μίμημα, & est dicta.
units.tr: Furthermore, they are also marked by the name imago (image): a word which is derived either from imitation, as Festus thinks, because an image is an imitation of some thing, or from the Greek mimēma.

units.la: Effigies quinetiam dicitur, vel effigia. (Utrumque enim dicitur, & effigies & effigia, ut Nonius Marcellus aunotat ex Afranio Vopisco) ab effingendo: sicut signa & sigilla a significando. Ergo ut Hebræa, ita Græca & Latina nomina Idolorum sive simulacrorum, vanitatis, simulationis, mendacii sunt symbola.
units.tr: They are even called effigies or effigia (for both are used, effigies and effigia, as Nonius Marcellus notes from Afranius Vopiscus), from effingere (to form), just as signa and sigilla are from significare (to signify). Therefore, as the Hebrew names of idols or likenesses, so the Greek and Latin names are emblems of vanity, pretence and lying.

units.la: Germani duo habent præcipua nomina, quibus idola & simulacra exprimuntur. Vnum est Gött, quod in malam semper partem accipitur, derivatum a Gott/Deo, quasi dicas, Dei imago sive simulacrum, sive Deaster, Deus fictus & imaginarius: quod vocabulum & probomine stupido atq; stolido qui nimirum similis idolo sive simulacro inanimato, omnes sensus rationesque experti, & ölgöt/ pro homine insigniter stultitiæ stupiditatisque accipitur, qui etiam truncus, stipes, lapis (unde antiquitus simulacra maxima ex parte fiebant) metaphoricè nuncupatur. Alterum nomen est bild & bildnuß,quod bonam et malam in partem accipitur, & imi Bild & Bildginem significat. Hoc non inepte quis deduceret a Belo,quod primum simulacrum fuisse,et a Ni-nuß. no patre positum : unde simulacrorum origo fuerit,antiqui scriptores testantur : nisi quis ab Idolo,per metathesin litterarum.præposita litera B.malit derivare. Hæc de nominibus Idolorum & simulacrorum.
units.tr: The Germans have two principal names by which idols and likenesses are expressed. One is Gött, which is always taken in a bad sense, derived from Gott (God), as if you were to say the image or likeness of God, or Deaster, a fictitious and imaginary god; and this word is also used of a stupid and dull man, who indeed is like an idol or a lifeless likeness, having experienced all senses and reasons, and is used proverbially (ölgöt) of a man notable for foolishness and stupidity; it is also used metaphorically of a stump, a log, or a stone (from which in ancient times most likenesses were made). The other name is bild and bildnuß, which is taken in a good and a bad sense, and signifies an image and a likeness. Someone might not unfittingly derive this from Belus, because he was the first image and was set up by Nimrod his father, whence the origin of images, as the ancient writers attest; unless one prefers to derive it from idolum by metathesis of letters, with the letter B prefixed. These things concerning the names of idols and likenesses.

units.la: Deinde idolorum simulacrorumque Gentilium vanitas a sancto spiritu demonstratur,argu- mentu dullis ab illorum causis : Ac primo quidam ab illorum origine,in ventione , causis efficientibus,cum primaris,tum secundariis.
units.tr: Next, the vanity of pagan idols and likenesses is shown by the Holy Spirit, by an argument taken from their causes: and first from their origin, invention, and efficient causes, both primary and secondary.

units.la: Quantum ad originem & inventores primos idolorum simulacrorumque attinet ; variæ de ijs fuerunt Ethnicorum opiniones. Alii enim ad Prometheum inventum hoc retulerunt : alii ad Hercules : Latini ad Ianum,qui primus in Italia templa, altaria, simulacra,sacrorumque rumritus instituerit. Græci ad Pelasgos : Hi ad Thesum ,idolorum & idololatriæ originem referunt. Quidam Telchines apud Rhodum Deorum statuas primum fecisse voluntnonnulli Hebrusos , seu Tyrrhenos prædicant. Alii Cadmo , Agenoris filio apud Græcos id tribuerunt. Sunt , qui Armodio & Aristogitoni primas statuas positas prodant , quod Athenas tyrannidis jugo liberassent. Alii Ægyptios idolorum simulachrorumque primos inventores atque cultores faciunt. Plerique tamen scriptorum Ethnicorum in hoc videntur consentire , idola eorumque cultum uniuersum , qui idololatria appellatur , una cum Philosophia & artibus atque dis-ciplinis liberalibus , ab Ægyptiis ad Græcos : a Græcis ad Romanos : a Romanis denique ad reliquas gentes omnes promanasse. Vnde quidam omnivo,quæ quatuor illarum Monarchiarum fine Imperiorum Mundi generalium : eadem Idololatriæ videtur fuisse successio & propagatio, ita ut ab Assyriis & Chaldæis,ad Medos & Persas : ab his ad Græcos : a Græcis ad Romanos; & inde ad omnes reliquas gentes atque nationes profluxerit.
units.tr: As far as the origin and first inventors of idols and likenesses are concerned, the opinions of the heathen have been various. For some have referred this invention to Prometheus, others to Hercules; the Latins to Janus, who first, they say, instituted temples, altars, likenesses and the rites of sacrifices in Italy. The Greeks refer it to the Pelasgians; these to Theseus, as the origin of idols and idolatry. Some have said that the Telchines at Rhodes first made statues of the gods; some proclaim the Hebrusians or Tyrrhenians. Others have attributed it among the Greeks to Cadmus, son of Agenor. There are those who report that the first statues were set up to Harmodius and Aristogiton, because they had freed Athens from the yoke of tyranny. Others make the Egyptians the first inventors and worshippers of idols and likenesses. Yet most of the heathen writers seem to agree on this: that idols and their whole worship, which is called idolatry, together with philosophy and the liberal arts and sciences, flowed from the Egyptians to the Greeks, from the Greeks to the Romans, and at last from the Romans to all the remaining peoples. Whence some observe that, as there were four monarchies or general empires of the world, so the succession and propagation of idolatry seems to have been the same, so that it flowed from the Assyrians and Chaldeans to the Medes and Persians, from these to the Greeks, from the Greeks to the Romans, and thence to all the remaining peoples and nations.

units.la: Primigeniam vero illam sanctorum Patriarcharum Ecclesiam ante & post Diluuium, prim: Patriarc. idolorum simulachrorumque usu cultuque caruisse vel inde constat, quod nulla illorum in sacris ch: Ecclesiæ litteris plane fit mentio ; nisi uno tantum in loco Geneseos trigesimo primo capite : ubi Rachel caruerunt ido-Deos patris sui Labani, qui Syrus fuit, clam, infisio & ignorante Iacobo subfurata fuisse dici-ut. tur. Isigitur , ut eo libro, trigesimo quinto capite scriptum est, profecturus in Bethel, familiæ suæ pracepit, ut omnes Deos peregrinos, idolo atque simulacra Deorum alienorum, sibi adferrent , quos statim in Sichem terra obruit. Ex hoc ipso igitur loco constat , Iacobum ab idolis simulacrisque ipsis , ex Syria furtim a Rachele (ut semper mulieres inprimis ad idololatriam sunt propensæ) allatis,abhorruisse, & idcirco , tanquam pium religiosumque patrem familiæ illa non humo solum , sed etiam perperua obliuione voluisse obruta esse atque sepulta.
units.tr: The primeval Church of the holy patriarchs, both before and after the Flood, was free of the use and worship of idols and images. This is clear from the fact that the sacred letters of the Church make no plain mention of them, except in one place only, Genesis chapter 31, where Rachel is said to have secretly stolen the gods of her father Laban, a Syrian, without Jacob's knowledge. Then, as is written in chapter 35 of that book, Jacob, about to set out for Bethel, ordered his household to hand over to him all the foreign gods, the idols and images of alien gods, and he straightway buried them under the earth at Shechem. From this very passage it is clear that Jacob abhorred the idols and images themselves, which Rachel had secretly brought from Syria (women, as always, being especially prone to idolatry). Therefore, as a pious and religious father of his household, he wished them to be buried and sunk not only in the ground but in perpetual oblivion.

units.la: Postquam vero sanctissimorum illorum Patriarcharum filiorum atque propago , hoc est, Patriarchæ et Hebræi sive Iudæi ex ductura funestaque illa servitute Ægyptiaca in libertatem a Deo fuerunt vindicati,ab eodem illis omni idolorum simulacrorumque usu cultuque , lege illa in monte Sinai lata ac promulgata , diserte fuit interdictum : qui tamen et statim & postea divinam illam liberationem in ipso deserto, ut sacræ testantur historiæ , & postquam in terram illam promistam fuerunt introducti, sepissime sese idolorum simulacrorumque Gentilium cultu, contra expressam Dei legem,ejusque interpretes atque doctores , sacerdotes nimirum atque Prophetas, polluerunt atque contaminarunt ; & idcirco crebras graves que pænas justo Dei judicio luerunt, ut ex sacris litteris satis superque constat.
units.tr: After the descendants and offspring of those most holy patriarchs, namely the Hebrews or Jews, had been rescued by God from that harsh and deadly Egyptian servitude into liberty, God expressly forbade them, by the law given and promulgated on Mount Sinai, all use and worship of idols and images. Yet they nonetheless, both immediately and afterwards, as the sacred histories attest, both in the wilderness itself after that divine deliverance and after they had been led into the promised land, very often defiled and contaminated themselves with the worship of Gentile idols and images, against the express law of God. Even its interpreters and teachers, namely the priests and prophets, took part in this pollution. Therefore they paid for it with frequent and grievous punishments by the just judgment of God, as is sufficiently and more than sufficiently clear from the sacred letters.

units.la: Non igitur ab antiquissima & primigenia illa Ecclesia populoque Dei , sed a reliquis gentibus atque nationibus , a quibus Deus populum illum suum peculiarem semper voluit esse separatum & separatum , idola ista atque simulacra profecta sunt : & idcirco paßim in sacris litteris Du alieni,peregrini, gentium , aliusque nominibus appellantur , a quibus Deus semper voluit populum suum esse alienum.
units.tr: Therefore these idols and images did not proceed from that most ancient and original Church and people of God, but from the other peoples and nations, from whom God always wished his peculiar people to be separated and set apart.
