For this reason they are everywhere in the sacred writings called by the names "strange," "foreign," "of the Gentiles," and others, since God always wished his people to be estranged from them.

units.la: Sapiens ille in illo suo Sapientiæ libro capite decimo tertio,Idololatriæ originem pariter & Idololatriæ om incrementum; satis perspicuè tradit. Ac ab initio quidem illius capitis,mentione facta & naturalis ris & artificialis idololatriæ, utrinque, causam generalem docet esse hominum vanitatem , veriDeiignorationem , quæ ipsis a natura fit insita. Sic enim exorditur : Μάταιοι μὲν ... ignoratio. αἰθέρι πῶσι φύσει, οἷς πᾶσιν ἀγνωσία, hoc est, Vanietenim sunt naturâ omnes homines: quibus inest Dei ignoratio. Hanc igitur ille primam & generalem omnis idololatriæ, qua res naturales, sive quâ artificiales, id est, idola & simulacra coluntur, affirmavit esse.
units.tr: The wise man, in the thirteenth chapter of his book of Wisdom, sets out quite clearly both the origin and the growth of idolatry. At the beginning of that chapter, having mentioned both natural and artificial idolatry, he teaches that the general cause of both is the vanity of men and their ignorance of the true God, which is implanted in them by nature. For he begins thus: [Μάταιοι μὲν γὰρ πάντες ἄνθρωποι φύσει, οἷς πᾶσιν ἀγνωσία θεοῦ], that is, "For all men are by nature vain, in whom there is ignorance of God." He therefore affirmed that this is the first and general cause of all idolatry, by which natural things or artificial things, that is, idols and images, are worshipped.

units.la: Deinde verò capite decimo quarto, versu decimo quinto specialem idolorum sive imaginum caussam refert ad nimium & inordinatum hominum affectum, amorem ac desiderium erga defunctos. Sic enim loquitur: Ἀοῤῥω ... μυσηρίας. Ἐπὶ ... ἀγάπη ... Intempestivo enim luctu nexatus pater, cito rapti filii imaginem faciens, tunc mortuum hominem, nunc ut Deum coluit, & tradidit subditis mysteria & sacrificia. Deinde in tempore quæ unvaluerat impia consuetudo, tanquam lex custodita est, & Regum imperiis colebantur sculpta.
units.tr: Then, in the fourteenth chapter, at the fifteenth verse, he traces the particular cause of idols or images to the excessive and disordered affection and love and longing of men for the dead. For he speaks thus: [Ἀορὰ πατὴρ ... μυστήρια ... ἀγάπη]. "For a father, consumed by untimely grief, made an image of his son who had been suddenly taken away, and then began to honour as a god the man who was now dead, and handed down to his subjects mysteries and sacrifices. Then, in time, this impious custom grew strong and was kept as a law, and carved images were worshipped by the commands of kings."

units.la: His consentanee Diophantes Lacedæmonius, qui Antiquitatum libros quatuordecim scripsit, Syrophanem ajit Ægyptium, hominem locupletissimum, filio superstite, ejus desiderio simulacrum domi flatuisse, ad quod familiares, si quando in Domini iram & offensionem inciderent, confugerent, illuda, floribus, coronis, ferteis, ornantes, sic Domini iram placarent & ve-
units.tr: In agreement with this, Diophantes the Lacedaemonian, who wrote fourteen books of Antiquities, says that Syrophanes the Egyptian, a very wealthy man, after his son had died, set up in his house an image of him to satisfy his longing. To this image his household, whenever they fell into the anger and displeasure of the lord, would flee, adorning it with flowers, garlands and offerings, and in this way would appease the lord's anger and obtain pardon.

units.la: niam consequerentur. Sic Adrianus Imperator suum Antinoum defunctum sculpi jussit, & divinis ornari honoribus. Sic Semiramis quoque illa Assyriorum Regina Belum, maritum suum mortuum, erecta ejus flatuâ, lugeri & pro Deo coli voluit. Hanc quoque scriptores profani tradunt pro insana sua ambitione admontem Mediæ, Bagislbenem nomine, suam in petra effigiem decem & septem stadiorum insculpi jussisse: quam Centum viri, tanquam sacerdotes, donis muneribus atque sacris nonnullis assiduè venerantur.
units.tr: So the emperor Hadrian ordered his dead Antinous to be sculpted and honoured with divine honours. So too that queen of the Assyrians, Semiramis, wished her dead husband Belus to be mourned and worshipped as a god, after erecting a statue of him. Profane writers also relate that Bagistanes, in the mountain of Media, out of his insane ambition, had his own likeness carved into the rock, seventeen stadia high, which a hundred men, as priests, constantly venerate with gifts and offerings and certain sacrifices.

units.la: Addit porro Sapiens ad Idololatriæ istius progressum incrementum, significandum, morem hunc atque consuetudinem simulacra fabricandi atque colendi temporis progressu ita invaluisse, ut legus sum obtinuerit. Sic enim dixit: ἐὰν ... Deinde auctâ corroboratâ, illâ impietate consuetudo tanquam lex fuit observata. Accesserunt porrò & tyrannorum de idolis faciendis colendisque, edicta atque mandata: accessit sulpi & imperitæ multitudinis adulatio, qui Reges & Principes suos, longo locorum interval-lo a se disjunctos, cum coràm colere non possent, coluerunt eos absentes, tanquam αὐθαίρετον, id est, Numen quoddam, per imagines nimirum & simulachra, quæ ipsis fieri curarunt. Sic passim in Romano imperio erecta statuæ & imagines apro vincialibus tum metu supplicii, tum studio adulandi.
units.tr: The wise man further adds, to show the progress and growth of this idolatry, that this custom and practice of making and worshipping images, as time went on, grew so strong that it obtained the force of law. For he said: [ἐὰν ...]. "Then, as that impiety increased and was strengthened, the custom was observed as law." Moreover, there were added the edicts and commands of tyrants concerning the making and worship of idols; there was added the flattery of the common and ignorant multitude, who, since they could not worship their kings and princes, who were separated from them by a long distance, worshipped them in their absence, as [αὐθαίρετον], that is, as a certain divinity, namely through the images and statues which they had made for them. Thus, throughout the Roman empire, statues and images were set up everywhere in the provinces, partly from fear of punishment and partly from a desire to flatter.

units.la: Huc postremò accessit ipsorum artificum (adde his sacerdotes) φιλοπλία, id est, ambitio: immo & φιλαργυρία, id est, argenti questus, cupiditas: quæ Idololatriam istam valde auxerunt & amplificârunt. Hæc Sapiens hic, sive ut fuerit Salomon, sive quis alius, sapientissimè sane literæ memoriæ prodidit, de idolorum, simulacrorum & imaginum, atque adeo Idololatriæ origine, progressu, incrementis atque caussis: quæ sunt, ut paucis eas compleAar, naturalis hominis vanitas, Dei ignoratio, per versus inordinatisque erga defunctos & absentes affectus atque desiderium, mos & consuetudo diuturna, tyrannorum leges & edicta, vulgi adulatio.
units.tr: Lastly, to these was added the ambition (add to these the priests) of the craftsmen themselves, [φιλοτιμία], that is, ambition; and indeed also [φιλαργυρία], that is, the desire for profit from silver. These greatly increased and magnified that idolatry. This the wise man, whether he was Solomon or someone else, most wisely handed down in writing concerning the origin, progress, growth and causes of idols, images and indeed of idolatry. These causes are, to sum them up briefly: the natural vanity of man, ignorance of God, disordered affections and longing for the dead and absent, long-standing custom, the laws and edicts of tyrants, the flattery of the common people, and the ambition and avarice of the craftsmen.

units.la: Latio, artificum ambitio atque avaritia. His adde, quod eodem in libro idola κυρτοθξία, id est, vana hominum opinione in Mundum dicit fuisse introdućta: non fuisse ab initio: non esse annequa; & sinem habitura tristem ac funestum.
units.tr: To these add that in the same book he says that idols were introduced into the world by [κενοδοξία], that is, by the vain opinion of men; that they did not exist from the beginning, that they will not last, and that they will have a sad and deadly end.

units.la: Primaria igitur idolorum simulacrorumque Gentilium caussæ sunt cum Homo, unde Inventa hominum appellantur: sum Satan; cujus instinctu afflatique homines illa & fabricarunt et coluerunt. Sic Scholastici Theologi hominem Idololatriæ caussam Dispositivam; Diabolum verò Completivam vocant. Ac Diabolus quidem slatim ab initio per serpentem, animal callidissimum, tanquam per imaginem & simulacrum quoddam, se se in primorum nostrorum parentum gratiam insinuavit, iis sucum fecit atque imposuit, itaut inde quoque idolorum simulacrorum, origo repetenda esse videatur. Unde Theodoretus Sermone septimo de sacrificiis, Scom. septimo ad Græcos infideles: Simulacra, inquit, Satan curavit fieri in usum eorum, qui litterarum sunt expertes, ut in ad superstitionem incitarentur.
units.tr: The primary causes of idols and Gentile images are therefore both man, from whose inventions they are called "the inventions of men," and Satan, at whose instigation and inspiration men both made and worshipped them. So the Scholastic theologians call man the disposing cause of idolatry, and the Devil the completing cause. Indeed the Devil, right from the beginning, through the serpent, the most crafty of animals, as though through a kind of image or likeness, insinuated himself into the favour of our first parents, deceived them and imposed upon them, so that the origin of idol images also seems to be traced back to this. Hence Theodoret, in his seventh sermon on sacrifices, and in his seventh discourse to the unbelieving Greeks, says: "Satan took care that images should be made for the use of those who lack letters, so that they might be stirred up to superstition."

units.la: Et certé gravis ac nefaria fuit illa primorum nostrorum parentum idololatria, qui serpentemillum astutissimum,arborem illam speciiosissimam, ejusque fructum, denique ipsius Diaboli, qui per serpentem illum, tanquam per os organumq́ suum locutus est, blanditissima mendacissi-maque verba,tanquam idola,simulacra Deosq́ alienos,ipsi Deo vero,cæli terræq́ creatori , patri ac domino suo beneficentissimo ejusque præceptis atque mandatis verissimis ac saluberrimis longé anteposuerunt ; atque ita, ut Paulus loquitur,creaturam, præterito negleẗoque Creatore, coluerunt atque venerati sunt.
units.tr: Certainly that idolatry of our first parents was grave and wicked, for they preferred that most crafty serpent, that most beautiful tree and its fruit, and finally the Devil himself, who spoke through that serpent as through his mouth and instrument, and his most flattering and most deceitful words, as though they were idols, images and strange gods, far above the true God himself, the creator of heaven and earth, their most bountiful Father and Lord, and his most true and most wholesome precepts and commands. And so, as Paul says, they worshipped and venerated the creature, neglecting and passing over the Creator.

units.la: Sepenumero præterea Sanctus Spiritus in sacris litteris , argumento dulco ab idolorum fimulacrorumque fabris,lignariis , ferrariis , aliisque artificibus,illorum vanitatem , hominum-que ea colentium dementiam arguit : cùm illa artificibus suis, qui homines sunt mortales,æqualia sint atque adeò longé inferiora ; & ipsi cùm artifices atque fabri , tum cultores idolis sint simites,ut ex Isaia capitibus 40.44.& 46. item ex Psal.115.Ieremiæ 6.Habacuci 6.& alias ex locis constat. Cùm igitur idolorum simulacrorumqʒ fabri & artifices homines sint nihili , mortales & caduci,& qui tandem confundentur,ut in locis paullò antè citatis scribitur,inde constat ipsa quoque idola & simulacra res esse nihili,vanas, futiles, fragiles & caducas.
units.tr: Moreover, the Holy Spirit often exposes in Holy Scripture the emptiness of idols and images, and the madness of the men who worship them, by mocking the makers of idols and images: the carpenters, woodcarvers, metalworkers and other craftsmen. These idols are equal to, and indeed far inferior to, the men who make them, who are mortal. The craftsmen and smiths are themselves idolaters, as is clear from Isaiah chapters 40, 44 and 46, and likewise from Psalm 115, Jeremiah 6, Habakkuk 6 and other passages. Since the makers and craftsmen of idols and images are worthless, mortal and frail men, who in the end will be put to shame, as is written in the passages just cited, it follows that the idols and images themselves are also worthless, empty, trifling, fragile and perishable things.

units.la: Hanc verò idolorum simulacrorumq́ vanitatem Lactantius eodem hoc argumento demonstrat,his verbis : Quæ igitur amentia est, aut ea fingere,quæ ipsi postmodum timeant, aut timere,quæ finxerint ? Et paullo post : Nec intelligunt homines ineptissimi,si sentire simulacra & moveri possent,ultró adoraturas fuissent homines,a quibus sunt expolita , quæ essent aut incultus, aut horridus lapis : aut materia informis & rudis , nisi fuissent ab hominibus formata. Homo igitur illorum quasiparens putandus est, per cujus manus nata sunt,per quem specuem,figuram, pulchritudinem habere cœperunt. Etiam melior,qui fecit,quàm illa , quæ fatta sunt. Et tamen factorem ipsum nemo suspicit,aut veretur. Quæ fecit , timet , tanquam plus possit esse in spere, quàm in opifice. Rectè igitur Seneca in libris moralibus : Simulacra , inquit,Deorum venerantur,genuposito illa adorant,illis per totum assident diem, aut assiant , illis stipem jaciunt,vitisimas cædunt : & cùm hæc tantopere suspiciant, fabros , qui illa fecerunt,contemnunt. Quid inter se tam contrarium , quàm slatuarum despicere factorem,slatuam adorare , & eumne in convitium quidem admittere,qui sibi Deos faciat ? Quam ergo vim , quam potetslatem habere possunt,cùm ipse , qui fecit , illam non habeat: sed ne hæc quidem dare his poterat,quæ habebat, videre,audire,loqui,moveri ? Quisquam ne igitur tam ineptus est, ut putet aliquid esse in simulacro Dei,in quo ut hominus quidem quicquam est,præter umbram?
units.tr: Lactantius demonstrates this emptiness of idols and images by the same argument, in these words: "What madness is it, then, to make things that afterwards they themselves fear, or to fear things that they have made themselves?" And a little later: "Those most foolish men do not understand that, if images could feel and move, men would have worshipped them first, the men by whom they were fashioned out of what was either an uncut or a rough stone, or shapeless and crude matter, unless it had been formed by human hands. Man, then, must be thought of as the parent of these things, through whose hands they came into being, and through whom they began to have shape, figure and beauty. The maker is even better than the things that were made. Yet nobody reveres or fears the maker himself. They fear what they have made, as if there could be more power in the image than in the craftsman." Seneca rightly says in his Moral Letters: "People worship the images of the gods; they kneel before them, sit or stand beside them the whole day, throw them coins, and offer them the most humble prayers. Yet while they revere these things so greatly, they despise the craftsmen who made them. What is so contrary as to despise the maker of a statue while worshipping the statue, and to tolerate in contempt the man who makes gods for himself? What power, what strength can those things have, when the one who made them does not have it? Indeed, they could not even give to these things what they themselves possessed: sight, hearing, speech, movement. Is anyone so foolish as to think there is anything in an image of God in which there is, as a man, nothing at all except a shadow?"

units.la: Idem libro secundo,capitibus secundo,tertio,quarto,&c.citans illud Persianum: O curvæ in terras animæ,&c.
units.tr: In the second book, in chapters two, three, four and so on, he quotes the line of Persius: "O souls bent down to the earth," etc.

units.la: Plurimum exagitat extremam hominum dementiam, qui erectí & vultu & corpore ad contemplationem rerum cœlestium a Deo conditi,se incurvant & abjiciunt ad terram,id est simulacra terrena,& lutea,quasi doleant , se non quadrupedes natos.
units.tr: He strongly rebukes the utter madness of men who, though made by God upright in both face and body for the contemplation of heavenly things, bend and cast themselves down to the earth, that is, to earthly and clay images, as if they were grieved that they were not born four-footed beasts.

units.la: Refutat idem eodem capite communem & usitatam idololatarum obiestionem & excusatio-nam : Non ipsa,inquiunt,timemus , sed eos , ad quorum imaginem silla , & quorum nominibus consecrata sunt (Consecratio hæc,ut obiter hoc addam, siebat unstione olei.Vnde Arnobius:Quò pinguior,sò religiosior est lapis) Respondet Lactantius : Aut in cœlis sunt vestri Dii , aut non. Si non essent in cœlis , eos non coleretis. Quod si sunt in cœlis , cur non in cœlos oculos tollitis,& ad vocatis eorum nominibus , in apertosacrificium celebratis ? Cur ad parietes , & ligna , & lapides potissimum , quam illo spectatis , ubi eos esse credatis ? Deinde simulacra , inquit, aut mortuorum,aut absentium sunt monumenta. Nam omnium fingendarum similitudinum ratio idcirco ab hominibus invenita est,ut posset eorum memoria retineri,qui vel morte sublati, vel absentiâ fuerunt separati. Ergo Dii vestri aut mortui sunt , cur ergo eos colitis ? Aut sunt vivi. Ergo supervacua sunt hæc mortuorum monumenta. Item Dii vestri aut sunt absentes , aut sunt præsentes. Si sunt absentes. Ergo non sunt colendi. Si nec vident , quæ facimus , nec audiunt , quæ precamur. Si sunt ubique præsentes. Ergo supervacua sunt simulacra. Sed de his vide plura apud ipsum Lactantium. Et hæc de causis idolorum simulacrorumque effi-ciendibus.
units.tr: In the same chapter he refutes the common and familiar excuse of the idolaters: "We do not fear the images themselves," they say, "but those whose likeness they bear and in whose names they were consecrated." (This consecration, as I add in passing, was done by anointing with oil. Hence Arnobius: "The fatter the stone, the more sacred it is.") Lactantius replies: "Either your gods are in heaven or they are not. If they are not in heaven, you should not worship them. But if they are in heaven, why do you not lift your eyes to heaven, call them by their names, and celebrate sacrifice openly? Why do you look chiefly to walls, wood and stones, where you believe they are, instead of looking to heaven? Next, images," he says, "are monuments either of the dead or of the absent. For the reason why men invented the making of all likenesses was that the memory of those might be kept who had been taken away by death or separated by absence. Therefore, either your gods are dead, and then why do you worship them? Or they are alive, and then these monuments of the dead are superfluous. Likewise, your gods are either absent or present. If they are absent, they are not to be worshipped. If they neither see what we do nor hear what we pray, they are not gods. If they are present everywhere, then images are superfluous." But see more on this in Lactantius himself. These are the reasons concerning the makers of idols and images.
G

units.la: Sed tamen quoque eorum materialis crebra mentione, Spiritus Sanctus ipsorum vanitatem comprobat. Materia autem eorum semper varia fuit & multiplex. Antiquissima maximeque communis materia eorum fuit lignum atq; lapis, quae idcirco in sacris literis saepe conjunguntur; ut Habac. secundo: Va illi, qui dicit ligno, Expergiscere; & Surge, lapidi tacenti. Sic Ieremiae tertio capite scriptum legimus: Machata est cum lapide & ligno. Ligni trebertrima in sacris literis fit mentio, ut Isaiae quadragesimo quarto, Hierem. decimo, Baruch. sexto & psalm in omnibus fere illis sacra scriptura locis, in quibus Idololatria taxatur. Sic et Plato ex ligno voluit esse Deorum simulacra. Paufanias similiter scribit, primus illis temporibus lignea fuisse apud Graecos simulacra; illa praesertim, quae Aegyptii confecisset. Apud Romanos quoque lignea erant idola: unde signi ligneis per vetusti meminit Cicero Verrina sexta, quod fuit Bona Fortuna. Et
units.tr: Yet the Holy Spirit also confirms their emptiness by frequent mention of the material of which they were made. Their material was always varied and manifold. The most ancient and most common material of images was wood and stone, which for this reason are often joined together in Holy Scripture, as in Habakkuk 2: "Woe to him who says to wood, 'Awake,' and to a silent stone, 'Arise.'" So too we read in Jeremiah 3: "She has committed adultery with stone and tree." Mention of wood is made in Holy Scripture in Isaiah 44, Jeremiah 10, Baruch 6, and in almost all the passages of Scripture in which idolatry is condemned. Plato also held that images of the gods should be made of wood. Pausanias likewise writes that in earlier times the images among the Greeks were wooden, especially those which the Egyptians had made. Among the Romans too the idols were of wood; hence Cicero, in the sixth Verrine, mentions a wooden statue of Good Fortune, which was of wood. And

units.la: Tibullus Deos Penates alloquens sic libro primo Eleg. decimo canit: Neu pudeat prisco vos esse stipite factos: Sic veteris sedes incoluisse avi. Tunc melius soluere fidem, cum pauper cultu Stabat in exigua ligneus aede Deus. Et pacatus erat, si quis lubi verat unum; Seu dederat sanctae pica ferca coma. Atque aliquis voti compos liba ipse ferebat. Postque comes purum filia parva fuit.
units.tr: Tibullus, addressing the household gods, sings thus in the tenth elegy of the first book: "Nor be ashamed that you were made of ancient wood; so did you dwell in the seats of our old forefathers. Then men paid their vows more faithfully, when a poor god of wood stood in a small shrine, simply worshipped. And he was content if someone gave him a single offering, or hung a little pig's tail upon his sacred hair. And one who had obtained his prayer would himself bring the cakes, and afterwards the little daughter would be his pure companion."

units.la: Sic Propertius de sua statua ita loquentem Pertumnum inducit: Stipes acer nus eram, properanti falce dolatus, Ante Numam grata pauper in urbe Deus.
units.tr: So Propertius, introducing Pomona's statue speaking of itself, says: "I was a sharp maple stump, shaped with the hurrying axe; before Numa's time I was a poor god, pleasing in the city."

units.la: Plinius naturalis historiae libro tricesimo quarto, capite septimo: Mirum mihi videtur, in- quit, cum statuarum in Italia tam vetus origo sit, potius lignea aut fictilia Deorum simulacra mdelubris dicata usque ad devictam Asiam: unde irrepsit & luxuria, &c.
units.tr: Pliny, in the thirty-fourth book of his Natural History, chapter seven: "It seems strange to me," he says, "that, although statues have such an ancient origin in Italy, wooden or earthenware images of the gods were dedicated in shrines until Asia was conquered; and from that time luxury crept in, and so on."

units.la: Vide ibidem plura de antiquis statuariis, signis, statuis & colossis etiam, pretiis ignorum immodicis.
units.tr: See there more about the ancient statuaries, figures, statues and even colossi, and their immoderate prices.

units.la: Hinc Spiritus Sanctus merito irridet fabros lignarios, sive materiarios; peritos licet suae artis & ingeniosos, qui casa aliquas arbores ex uno eodemque ligno & vas aliquod sive instrumentum ad vice humanae usum conficiunt, & ex reliqua ejus parte, quae fit nodosa, cortuosa, incurva & inutilis Deum, ideo idolum, sive simulatrum sculpunt, quod vel hominis vel bestiae ali- cujus speciem referat, eique rubrica aliave materia colores addunt, omnesque ejus maculas ab- stergunt. Denique ejusdem ligni ξυλοβλαστου, sive refegminibus cibos coquunt.
units.tr: Hence the Holy Spirit rightly mocks the woodcarvers, or carpenters, who, though skilled and clever in their craft, cut some trees out of one and the same piece of wood and make some vessel or tool for common human use; and from the rest of the same wood, which is knotty, gnarled, bent and useless, they carve a god, that is, an idol or image, which represents the form of a man or of some beast, and they add colours to it with red ochre or other material, and wipe off all its stains. Finally, from the same wood, what is called xylcoblastos [ξυλοβλάστου], or from its scraps, they cook their food.

units.la: Simili fere iarta fimo Horatius cum fabrorum lignariorum, tum idololatrarum fulitiam deridet, ubi Priapum, id est, ejus idolum per profopopeiam his verbis loquentis introducit: Olim truncus eram ficulnus, inutile lignum, Cum faber, incertus stamnum facere ne Priapum, Maluit esse Deum, Deus inde ego furum avium que Maxima formido, &c.
units.tr: Horace, in a similar vein, mocks both the foolishness of the woodcarvers and of the idolaters, where, personifying it, he introduces Priapus, that is, his image, speaking thus: "Once I was a fig-tree trunk, a useless piece of wood, when a carpenter, uncertain whether to make a stool or a Priapus, preferred to make me a god. So I became a god, the great terror of thieves and birds," etc.

units.la: Plutarchus quoque antiquissima apud Graecos & Romanos Deorum simulacra tefatur fuisse lignea. Hinc simulacrum ligneum Delubrum etiam fuit dictum. Delubrū, inquit Festus, dicebant ipsum delibratum, hoc est, decorticatum, quem venerabantur pro Deo.
units.tr: Plutarch also testifies that the most ancient images of the gods among the Greeks and Romans were of wood. Hence a wooden image was also called a delubrum. Festus says: "They called delubrum the thing that had been stripped of its bark, that is, peeled, which they worshipped as a god."

units.la: Nec tamen ex quovis ligno simulacra illa confecerunt, sed singulis Dii certa ligna erant destinata, secundum tritum illud dictum: Non quovis ex ligno fingitur Mercurius. Sit enim, exempli gratia, Venus ex myrto, Hercules ex populo, Iupiter ex quercu, Minerva ex olea, Mercurius ex buxo, Priapus ex ficulno fiebat. Plinius libro decimo quarto, capite secundo: Iovis, inquit, simulacrum in urbe Populonia ex una confecimus vite, sed & vis incorruptum. Item Masfilia pateram. Mecaponti templum Iunonis virigines columnis stetit. Etiamnum scalis teatu Ephesiae Dianae scandetur vice una Cypria, ut ferunt, quoniam ibi ad praecipuam altitudinem ex- eunt. Nec est ligno ulli aeternior natura. Porro ex vitice (ut Paufanias refert) id est, fraxice in fluminum ripis at torrentum alveis nascente, et assurgente in arborem, quadam Latoniae urbe, flatua Aesculapii fuit effigia: unde is Agnitet, a Graca vitis voce ἀγνὸν, fuit cognominatus, cen ex vitice confectus. Idem auctor ajt, se animad vertisse, has fere tantum arbores ad idola atq; simulacra conficienda fuisse adhibitas, nempe ebenum, cupressum, cedrum, quercum, similatem, buxum. His oliue raditem in minoribus simulacris addit Theophrastus in libris de plantis. Mera curiositate non ex quovis ligno, ut est in proverbio, fieret: praecipue tamen ex Thya, quam Troiagem vocavit Homerus, fieri solebat. Epidaunii ut est apud Herodotum, duas statuas, secundum Apollinis Delphici oraculum atq; responsum; unam Damiae; alteram Auxesiae, quae erant Deae illorum tutelaret, ex oleo non sylvestri posuerunt. In primo Iunonis templo, quod erat Argis simulacrum ex trunco pyri erat dedicatum. Romae ubi Regina vocitabatur, duae ejus erant ex cupresso effigies, quae solemni pompa gestabatur in illius sacrum, quae tunc primum fuerunt instituta, sicut Livius refert, quando Annibal Italiam devastabat. Plinius libro 13. capite 1. de Syria arboribus verba faciens, Cedri majoris, inquit, materia est aeternitas. Itaq; & simulacra Deorum exea factaverunt. Isaias 44. Cedri, ilicis & quercus mentionem facit Propheta, ex quibus nimirum Deorum signa conficiebantur solita.
units.tr: Nor did they make those images of any kind of wood, but each god had a fixed wood assigned to him, according to the common saying: "Mercury is not made of just any wood." Thus, for example, Venus was made of myrtle, Hercules of poplar, Jupiter of oak, Minerva of olive, Mercury of box, and Priapus was made of fig. Pliny, in the fourteenth book, chapter two: "We have made," he says, "an image of Jupiter in the city of Populonia out of a single vine, and it is still uncorrupted. Likewise at Massilia a bowl. At Mecaponte the temple of Juno stood on columns of virgin wood. Even now, by a single Cyprian beam, as they say, people climb by ladders to the very high image of Ephesian Diana, because there the wood is exceptionally tall. Nor is any wood of more enduring nature." Further, according to Pausanias, out of the willow (as he reports), that is the ash, which grows on river banks and in the beds of torrents and rises into a tree, in a certain city of Latona, was the figure of Aesculapius; hence he was surnamed Agnites from the Greek word for willow, agnon [ἀγνὸν], since he was made from willow. The same author says that he had observed that only a few such trees were used for making idols and images, namely ebony, cypress, cedar, oak, plane and box. Theophrastus, in his books on plants, adds olive wood for smaller images. Out of mere curiosity they did not make them of any wood, as the proverb has it, but especially of the thuya, which Homer called Trojan wood, was it usually made. The Epidaurians, as is told by Herodotus, set up two statues, of Damia and of Auxesia, who were their protecting goddesses, made of wild olive, according to the oracle and answer of Delphic Apollo. In the first temple of Juno, which was at Argos, an image was dedicated made from a pear trunk. At Rome, where she was called Queen, there were two of her images made of cypress, which were carried in solemn procession in her honour, and these were first established, as Livy relates, when Hannibal was ravaging Italy. Pliny, in the thirteenth book, chapter one, speaking of the trees of Syria: "The timber of the greater cedar," he says, "is eternal. Therefore they also made images of the gods from it." The prophet Isaiah, in chapter 44, mentions cedar, holm oak and oak, from which, no doubt, the usual images of the gods were made.

units.la: Iam vero & lapideorum Deorum, id est, simulacrorum, passim apud sacrorum & profanorum autorum floret fit mentio, quae tum ex vulgaribus et vilibus, tum ex pretiosis lapidibus fiebant. Nonnulli ex atro lapillo Deumes fingebant: quo significabant eum ab oculorum acie penitus esse remotum. His adde, quod Pausanias in Achaja describitione refert, in quadam ejus regionis parte triginta quadratos lapides extitisse; in quorum singulis lapidum Deorum nomen: abeq; tamen eorum effigie effet inscriptum, qui maxima cum religione ab incolis custodirentur. Antiquum enim Graecorum erat institutum, hujusmodi lapidibus parem cultum, atq; Deorum simulacris impertire.
units.tr: Now indeed mention is made everywhere, in sacred and profane authors alike, of stone gods, that is, images, which were made both of common and cheap stones and of precious ones. Some fashioned their god from a black pebble, by which they signified that he was utterly removed from the sight of the eyes. To these add what Pausanias, in his description of Achaia, reports: that in a certain part of that region there stood thirty square stones, each bearing the name of a god, though without any figure of him, and these were guarded with the greatest reverence by the inhabitants. For it was an ancient custom of the Greeks to give such stones the same worship as the images of the gods.

units.la: Marmoreorum quoq; simulachrorum saepius apud auctores veteres fit mentio. Cicero pro domo sua: Ejus simulacrum e marmore in sepulcro positum fuit. Idem ad Atticum: Ennius in sepulchro Scipionum putatur esse constitutus e marmore. Idem sexta Verrinae: Chrysas, inquit, est amnis, qui per Affirmorum agros fluit: is apud illos habetur Deus, et religione maxime colitur. Fanum ejus est in agro, propter ipsam viam, quae Assiro itur Enaam. In eo est simulacrum, praeclare factum ex marmore. In eadem oratione meminit & Cupidinis signis marmoreis, id est, ex marmore facti. Sed plura marmoreorum hujusmodi simulacrorum exempla retenfer Plinius libro Historiae suae naturalis tripartito sexto, capite quinto.
units.tr: Mention is also often made by ancient authors of marble images. Cicero, in his speech for his house: "A statue of him in marble was placed in the tomb." The same, to Atticus: "Ennius is thought to have been set up in the tomb of the Scipios, made of marble." The same, in the sixth Verrine: "The Chrysas," he says, "is a river that flows through the fields of the Assorini. It is regarded by them as a god and is worshipped with the greatest devotion. Its shrine is in the field, beside the very road which goes from Assorus to Aenna. In it is a statue, finely made of marble." In the same speech he also mentions marble statues of Cupid, that is, made of marble. But Pliny, in the sixth book, chapter five, of the third part of his Natural History, records more examples of such marble images.

units.la: His adde signa ate, simulacra Deorum ebur-nea, quae & ipsa olim magno frequentia fuerunt usu. Plinius lib.8. cap.10. Dentibus (elephantorum) ingens pretium, inquit, & Deorum simulacra laudantissima ex ea materia. Et paullo post: Magnitudo dentium in templis quidem videtur praecipua. Idem libro 12. capite 1. Ex arbore & simulacra Numinum fuere, nondum pretio excogitato belluarum tada verum, ante quam ut a Phiis nato jure luxuria, eodem ebore Numinum ure peltarentur & mensarum pedes. Plato tamen in libris de Legibus, ebur, tanquam ex animalium mortuo sumtum, non dignum esse putat; ex quo Deorum statuae conficiantur.
units.tr: To these add ivory images of the gods, which likewise were once in very frequent use. Pliny, book 8, chapter 10: "Elephants' tusks," he says, "have a great price, and the most celebrated images of the gods are made of that material." And a little later: "The size of the tusks seems especially prominent in temples." The same, book 12, chapter 1: "Images of the deities were also made of wood, before the price of the beasts' tusks had been devised, and before luxury, born of the Phrygians, had also used ivory to adorn the legs of couches and tables." Plato, however, in the books on the Laws, thinks that ivory, as taken from the dead bodies of animals, is not fit to be used for the statues of the gods.

units.la: Iam vero ex argilla quoque & creta Deorum simulacra fingi fuisse solita, passim scribentes antiquis testantur.
units.tr: Indeed, writers of antiquity testify everywhere that images of the gods were also commonly fashioned from clay and chalk.

units.la: Postremo ex omni metallorum genere, ut auro, argento, aere, ferro, chalybe, plumbo, stanno, idola Deorum fingi atque sculpi confuisse, cum sacra, tum profana litterarum monumenta referunt, quorum pauca tantum quaedam exempla atque testimonia proferam.
units.tr: Lastly, both sacred and profane records report that idols of the gods were cast and carved from every kind of metal, such as gold, silver, bronze, iron, steel, lead and tin; of these I will offer only a few examples and testimonies.

units.la: Aureorum & argenteorum simulacrorum passim sacrae & profanae literae meminerunt; quae metalla principem inter metalla locum obtinent. In sacris literis notissimum est quibusvis, qui vel primoribus labris est degustarunt, aureum ille deserti vitulum, a Iudaeis ingratis & perfidis factum positum exitum ex Aegypto, absente Moyse, perversa praepostera Aaronis indulgentia, ad Apis nimirum illius Aegyptii imitationem, cypum & figuram fabricatus. Notissimi quin etiam sunt duo illi vituli aurei, a Ieroboamo, Rege Israel, conflati, quorum unum in Bethel, alterum in Dan, oppidis celeberrimis & famosissimis, ad cultum fuerunt collocati, plus nimirum quam vitulina Iudeorum stupiditas, lascivia atque petulantia testificandae gratia. Sic David Propheta Psalmo 115. simulacra gentium argentea & aurea, opera manuum hominum, appellat.
units.tr: Sacred and profane letters everywhere mention images of gold and silver; these metals hold the first place among metals. In the sacred letters it is most familiar to everyone who has tasted them even with the lips that the golden calf, made by the ungrateful and faithless Jews in the desert after the exodus from Egypt while Moses was absent, was fashioned by Aaron's perverse and misguided indulgence, in plain imitation of that Egyptian Apis, in its form and shape. Indeed, the two golden calves cast by Jeroboam, king of Israel, are also very well known; one of them was set up for worship in Bethel and the other in Dan, most famous and renowned towns, plainly to attest the calf-like stupidity, wantonness and wilfulness of the Jews. So the prophet David, in Psalm 115, calls the images of the nations silver and gold, the work of men's hands.

units.la: Erant autem illa Gentilium sacra vel plané aurea & argentea, ex solido auro & argento: vel inargentata & inaurata, ut ex sacris & profanis litteris colligi potest. Plato etiam in libris ante citatis de Legibus, etiam aurum & argentum remoueri, ut quae a varitie potius & ostentationis superbæ, quàm religionis sint argumenta & inuitamenta. Aureum statuam & solidam primus hominum, teste Plinio libro trigesimo tertio, capite quarto, fuit posuit Georgius Leontinus, Delphis in templo, Olympiade septuagesima.
units.tr: Now those sacred objects of the Gentiles were either wholly of gold and silver, made of solid gold and silver, or gilded and silvered, as can be gathered from sacred and profane letters. Plato also, in the aforementioned books on the Laws, would remove gold and silver as being rather tokens and incitements of vanity and proud display than of religion. The first of men to set up a solid gold statue, as Pliny testifies in book thirty-three, chapter four, was Georgias of Leontini, at Delphi in the temple, in the seventieth Olympiad.

units.la: Æreorum similiter siue æneorum idolorum usum olim apud Gentiles fuisse frequentem passim sacræ & profanæ historiæ testantur. Herculis simulacrum inquit Cicero in sexta Verrina, ex ære in Herculis templo sanctè & religiosè colebatur apud Agrigentinos. Idem ibidem: Æneæ duo signa non maxima, verum eximia venustate, virginali habitu atque vestitu, quæ manibus sublatis sacra quædam, more Atheniensium virginum repositæ in capitibus sustinebant: Canephoræ ipsæ vocabantur, Polycleti artificis opus. Idem ibidem: Simulacrum Dianæ ex ære apud Segestanos, tum summâ atque antiquissimâ præditum religione, tum singulari opere artificioque perfectum, quod Verres sustulit. Item eadem oratione: Matris magnæ famum apud Enguinos fuit, in quo loricæ galeæque æneæ, cælatæ opere Corinthio, hydriaeque grandes simili in genere, atque eadem arte perfectæ, &c. Et primum Romæ simulacrum ex ære Cereris factum reperto, inquit Plinius libro trigesimo quarto, capite quarto, ex peculio Sp. Cassii, quem regnum affectantem pater ipsius interemerat. Transit & ab Diis ad hominum statuas atque imagines multis modis. Antiqui pingebant eas bitumine; quo magis mirum est, plurimusque auro integere. De statuarum origine, honore, generibus & figuris vide ibidem plura. Proxima, ut idem auctor testatur libro trigesimo quarto, capite primo, dicantur ærea metalla, & in usu proximum est pretium: immo verò ante argentum, ac pene etiam ante aurum Corinthium. Idem capue secundo, Antiquissima, inquit, ærea gloria Deliaca fuit, mercatus in Delo concelebrante toto Orbe; & ideo cura officinis triclinioru pedibus fulcrisque. Ibi prima nobilitas eius. Pervenit deinde ad Dei m simulacra effigiem, hominum & aliorum animalium, &c.
units.tr: Likewise, sacred and profane history everywhere attests that the use of bronze, or brass, idols was once frequent among the Gentiles. "The image of Hercules," says Cicero in the sixth Verrine, "was devoutly and religiously worshipped among the Agrigentines in the temple of Hercules, being of bronze." The same, in the same place: "Two statues of Aeneas, not very large but of rare beauty, in the dress and habit of maidens, which with their hands raised held up certain sacred vessels on their heads, after the manner of the Athenian virgins; they were called Canephorae themselves, the work of the artist Polyclitus." The same, in the same place: "The image of Diana of bronze among the Segestans, endowed both with the highest and most ancient religion and perfected with singular workmanship and skill, which Verres carried off." Likewise, in the same speech: "There was a shrine of the Great Mother among the Enguinians, in which were bronze breastplates and helmets, engraved in Corinthian work, and large water-jars of similar kind and made with the same art, etc." And Pliny, book thirty-four, chapter four, reports that the first bronze statue of Ceres was made at Rome, from the property of Sp. Cassius, whom his father had slain when he aspired to kingship. It passes from gods also to statues and images of men in many ways. The ancients painted these with bitumen, and it is the more remarkable that they covered many with gold. For the origin, honour, kinds and forms of statues, see more in the same place. Next, as the same author attests in book thirty-four, chapter one, bronze is mentioned, and in use it is next in value; indeed, Corinthian bronze was valued even before silver and almost before gold. The same, chapter two: "The most ancient bronze glory was the Delian, traded in Delos when the whole world gathered there; and so it was used for the feet and supports of dining couches. There was its first fame. It then came to the form of images of gods, of men and of other animals, etc."

units.la: Sed & simulacrorum ex ferro passim in antiquis monumentis occurrit mentio. Plinius libro eodem trigesimo quarto, capite decimo quarto scribit, Dinocratem architectum Alexandriæ Achinois templum ex magnete lapide concamerare inchoasse, ut in eo simulacrum ejusdem ferro pendere in aëre videretur. Intercessit mors & ipsius & Ptolemæi, quæ id sororem fuisset fieri. De ferro, ferreis metallis, ferrique differentiis vide ibidem plura. Ferrum quoque Plato neutiquam putavit Deorum simulacris conuenire, cùm id belli sit seruitio aptum instrumentum.
units.tr: But mention of images of iron also occurs everywhere in ancient monuments. Pliny, in the same book thirty-four, chapter fourteen, writes that Dinocrates, the architect of Alexandria, began to vault a temple to Arsinoe with magnetic stone, so that an image of her made of iron might seem to hang in the air. His death and that of Ptolemy intervened, which had caused it to be done for his sister. On iron, iron metals and the differences of iron, see more in the same place. Plato also thought that iron was by no means suitable for images of the gods, since it is an instrument fit for the service of war.

units.la: De plumbeis & stanneis simulacris, quæ videntur fuisse rarior, non opus est multa vera ba facere: de quo utroque metallo vide eundem Plinium, libro trigesimo quarto, capite decimo sexto & septimo.
units.tr: There is no need to say much about images of lead and tin, which seem to have been rarer; on these two metals see the same Pliny, book thirty-four, chapters sixteen and seventeen.

units.la: Omnem autem ferè hanc idolorum simulacrorumque materiam & Baruchi liber capite sexto, & Historia illa Danielis capite quinto completitur: Bibebant autem, inquit, & laudabant Deos suos aureos, & argenteos, & æneos, & ferreos, & ligneos, & lapideos. Item illo Baruchi capite: Lapidibus de montibus similes sunt Diis illorum, idest, Babyloniorum, & ligneis, & lapidei, & aurei, & argentei.
units.tr: Almost all this material of idols and images is also summed up in the book of Baruch, chapter six, and in that history of Daniel, chapter five: "They drank," it says, "and praised their gods of gold, and of silver, and of bronze, and of iron, and of wood, and of stone." Likewise in that chapter of Baruch: "They are like stones from the mountains, their gods, that is, the gods of the Babylonians, both wooden and stony, and of gold and of silver."

units.la: Observandum autem Gentilium simulacra aliquando ex unâ tantùm materiâ fuisse facta; aliquando, & quidem plerumque ex multiplici materiâ; qualis fuit illa statua, quæ divinitus Danieli in somno apparuit, quæque quatuor universalium Mundi Imperiorum sive Monarchiarum typus fuit & figura. Hæc ipsa autem simulacrorum imaginumque Gentilium materia, sive vili, sive etiam pretiosissima, quæ quidem omnes perpetuæ mutationibus atque periculis, corruptioni denique & interitui est subjecta, Sanctus Spiritus probat, & Deos ifloς Gentilium artificiosos, id est, idola atque simulacra mutabilia esse ac corruptibilia, &, quod est consequens, homines desipere plane ac insanire, qui aliquid divinitatis illis inesse putant, ac vel boni quid ab illa sperantes, vel etiam mali quid ab isdem metuentes, tanto studio ea colunt atque venerantur.
units.tr: It must be observed that the images of the Gentiles were sometimes made of one material alone, and sometimes, and indeed most often, of many materials; such was that statue which appeared to Daniel divinely in a dream, and which was a type and figure of the four universal monarchies of the world. The Holy Spirit proves that this very material of Gentile images and likenesses, whether cheap or even most precious, which is all subject to perpetual changes and dangers, and finally to corruption and destruction, shows that the artificial gods of the Gentiles, that is, the idols and images, are changeable and corruptible, and, as a consequence, that men who think some divinity is in them, and who worship and venerate them with such zeal, hoping for some good from them or fearing some evil from them, are plainly foolish and mad.

units.la: Porrò de idolorum, simulacrorumque iflorum varijs, & quidem ridiculis plerisque, monstrofis, periculosis, turpissimis, sædissimisque figuris atque formis, legat, qui volet, vel ad satietatem usque Chartarij & Verderij libros, qui omnes Deorum iflorum idolorumque imagines, a vertice usque ad plantam pedis suis, ut ita loquar, depinxerunt coloribus.
units.tr: Further, on the various kinds of these idols and images, most of them ridiculous, monstrous, dangerous, and foul and filthy in their shapes and forms, let whoever wishes read the books of Chartarius and Verderius until he is sick of them. They have painted all the images of those gods and idols, from head to foot, so to speak, in their colours.

units.la: Ex his autem omnibus apparet, quàm ridicula, quàm turpis, quàm monstrosa fuerit Gentilium, idola venerantium, impietas. Quoniam autem nihil est tam extremè malum, cui non boni quid insit, & ex quo non aliquid boni posse elici, observandum est, ex illis ipsis, tam variis picturis, figuris, imaginibus atque simulacris Gentilium, multa partim Physica præcepta, ad rerum Physicarum seu naturalium vim atque naturam cognoscendam utilia, partim vitæ morumque documenta petì posse, ut doctorum litteratorumque hominum allegoriæ, & cum Physicæ, ium Ethicæ, tum etiam Metaphysicæ interpretationes & expositiones abundè satis docent. Idem de Gentilium quoque fictis fabulis, quas de Dijs illis suis Poetæ prodiderunt, dici potest. Atque ficex stercoribus, ut vulgo dicitur, legendum est aurum.
units.tr: From all this it is plain how ridiculous, how shameful, and how monstrous was the impiety of the Gentiles who worshipped idols. Yet since nothing is so utterly evil that some good does not lie in it, and since nothing good can be drawn from it, we should observe that from those very varied pictures, figures, images and statues of the Gentiles, many lessons can be sought: partly physical precepts useful for knowing the power and nature of physical or natural things, and partly teachings for life and morals. The allegories of learned and literate men, and their physical, ethical and also metaphysical interpretations and expositions, abundantly show this. The same can be said of the fabulous tales which their poets handed down about those gods. As the common saying goes, gold must be gathered from dung.

units.la: Postremò quod de idolorum simulacrorumque iflorum & causis efficientibus, & materiâ, & formâ dictum, idem de finibus quoque, qui illorum fabris pariter atque cultoribus fuerunt propositi, dici potest, illos videlicet, non vanos modo fuisse atque futiles, sed etiam funestos. Sperabant miseri, se hoc pacto soliditorum suorum Numinum & iram placare & gratiam sibi conciliare & memoriam retinere posse: at illi contra in veri Dei gratiam vilissimam iram atque furorem incurrerunt, omnemque fere ejus memoriam amiserunt. Deinde pro dignitatibus & honoribus, pro divitijs & opibus, pro voluptatibus terrenis ac caducis, quas in illa idolorum & simulacrorum fabricatione ac veneratione spectârunt, se cœlesti & æternâ illâ gloria, divitiis ac voluptatibus privârunt, contraque perpetuam sibi ignominiam, dedecus, inopiam atque miseriam pepererunt.
units.tr: Lastly, what has been said of the efficient causes, the matter and the form of these idols and images, the same can be said of the purposes which those who made them and those who worshipped them alike had in view. Those purposes were, namely, not only empty and futile but also deadly. Wretched people hoped that by this means they could appease the anger of their solid gods, win their favour and keep their memory alive. But on the contrary they incurred the most foul anger and wrath of the true God, and almost lost all memory of him. Then, in exchange for dignities and honours, for riches and wealth, and for earthly and fleeting pleasures, which they looked to in making and venerating those idols and images, they deprived themselves of that heavenly and eternal glory, of riches and of true pleasures, and they brought upon themselves perpetual shame, disgrace, poverty and misery.

units.la: Quantum ad effectâ denique idolorum, cultusque eorum attinet, illa passim in sacris litteris nobis, ad arguendum eorum vanitatem, proponuntur & inculcantur: quæ sunt omnino dupli- cia; nempe Malacula pe, id est, omnis generis peccata, scelera atque flagitia: & Malapa-ne, sive panalia, id est, omnis generis miseria, & temporales & æternæ. Unde Sapientia libro, capite decimo tertio ficscripturn legimus: Ηὶ ἀ ἀ ὀ ἀ ὡ ὡ ὡ ὀ ὀ ὀ ὀ ἀ. Idolorum simulacrorumque venerationi omnis mali & initium & causa & finis est. Ibidem, Idola & simulacra, ex creaturis Dei fabricata, vocat βδελύγματα, σκανδαλα και ποιήματα, id est, abominationes, hominumque scandala & laqueos, sive tendicula. Addit: ἀρχή γὰρ πορνείας ἐπίνοια εἰδώλων, ἐυρεσις ὧν ἀ ὀ ὀ ὀ ὀ ὀ, id est, Initium enim fornicationis idolorum excogitatio, eorumque inventio est corruptela vitæ. Et, ut Paulus ad Romanos capite primo; ita Sapiens in hoc suo Sapientiæ libro longum catalogum texit recensimorum quorumque scelerum atque flagitiorum, quæ ex idolis atque idololatria promanârunt, inter quæ primo loco recensetur ταλάς ταβοφόνος, κρυφία μυήσεις, θεμισαλ ἐ κῶμος, id est, sacrificia liberorum, mysteria clandestina, immanes & infames epulas, sive commissationes, &c.
units.tr: Finally, as for the effects of idols and of their worship, Scripture everywhere sets these before us and impresses them on us to refute their vanity. These effects are of two kinds: namely, malacula pe, that is, every kind of sin, crime and wickedness; and malapane, or panalia, that is, every kind of misery, both temporal and eternal. Hence in the book of Wisdom, chapter thirteen, we read that the idolatry of images and idols is the beginning, the cause and the end of all evil. In the same place, Wisdom calls idols and images, which are made from God's creatures, abominations, stumbling-blocks and snares for men, that is, abominationes, scandala et laqueos. It adds: "For the beginning of fornication is the invention of idols, and their discovery is the corruption of life." And as Paul does in Romans chapter one, so the Wise Man in this book of Wisdom weaves a long catalogue of the countless crimes and shameful deeds which sprang from idols and idolatry. Among these, the first to be listed is the sacrifice of children, secret mysteries, and monstrous and infamous feasts or revels, and so on.

units.la: Denique hunc referendum idolorum & idololatrarum exitium & interitus: Nam quod de vitulino illo idolo dicitur in sacra scriptura, illud in frusta, seu segmenta, sive fragmenta, ut quidam scindi-llas interpretantur) scindendum esse, id de omnibus idolis seu simulacris eorumque cultoribus est intelligendum. Videlicet totum cultum sive superstitionem idolorum aboleri, affatim confringi, & quasi in cineres tandem redigi: de quo plurima extant Prophetarum vaticinia, quæ Christi adventu in carnem, & Apostolorum temporibus potissimum suum exitum fuerunt sortita. Unde Sanctus Augustinus libro vigesimo de Civitate Dei capite decimo quarto: Agamus igitur, inquit, nos Christiani Domino Deo nostro gratias: non Cœlo: non Terræ: sicut illi disputant, sed ei, qui fecit Cœlum & Terram, quod per altissimam Christi humilitatem, per Apostolorum prædicationem, per fidem Martyrum, pro veritate morientium & cum veritate vivéntium, non solum in cordibus religiosis, verùm etiam in ædibus superstitiosis, liberâ suorum servitute, simulacra subverterit.
units.tr: Finally, the destruction and ruin of idols and idolaters should be understood in this light. What Scripture says of the calf idol, that it was to be cut into pieces, or segments and fragments (as some translate it, "to be torn apart"), that must be understood of all idols and images and of their worshippers. That is, the whole worship or superstition of idols is to be abolished, utterly broken and at last reduced, as it were, to ashes. Many prophecies of the prophets concern this, and these found their fulfilment chiefly at the coming of Christ in the flesh and in the times of the apostles. Hence St Augustine, in book twenty of The City of God, chapter fourteen: "Let us Christians, then," he says, "give thanks to the Lord our God: not to heaven, not to earth, as those philosophers argue, but to him who made heaven and earth; because through the most high humility of Christ, through the preaching of the apostles, through the faith of the martyrs who die for the truth and live with the truth, he has overthrown the images, not only in religious hearts but also in superstitious temples, by freeing his people from their service."

units.la: VENIO nunc ad Deorum iflorum artificialium, hoc est, idolorum simulacrorumque ἀνάψυχων, seu inanimatorum cultum, qui uno nomine idololatria a Graecis appellatur. Hic quàm fuerit non solim impius, & exsecrandus, sed etiam ridiculus, absurdus & ab omni cum divina, tum humana ratione alienissimus, praeter mnumera alia sacrae scripturae testimonia, ille ipse Sapientiae liber, & illa Hieremiae epistola, quae Baruchi capite sexto continetur, id locupletissime testantur. Fuit autem varia omnino ac multiplex ista apud Gentiles, idolorum simulacrorumque cultura: de qua amplissima sanè copiosissimaque, sese hic offerret scribendi materia: sed brevitati, quoad dejus fieri potest, studebimus, nos intra illorum ipsorum scriptorum, quae jam aliquoties allegavimus, quasi terminos atque cancellos continentes, eaque in illis de simulacrorum cultu disputantur, ad certa capita revocantes & exemplis quibusdam atque testimoniis illustrantes.
units.tr: I come now to the worship of those artificial gods, that is, of idols and images, the anapsycha, or inanimate things, which is called by the single Greek name idololatria. How impious and accursed this was, and how not only impious but also ridiculous, absurd, and most alien to all reason, both divine and human, the book of Wisdom itself and that epistle of Jeremiah contained in Baruch chapter six most fully attest, besides countless other testimonies of Scripture. This worship of idols and images among the Gentiles was various and manifold. It would offer a very ample and copious matter for writing; but we shall aim at brevity, as far as possible, keeping within the limits, as it were, of those very writers whom we have already cited several times, in which the worship of images is discussed. We shall reduce it to certain headings and illustrate it with some examples and testimonies.

units.la: Primum igitur cultus ipsius incultissimi, ut ita loquar, & inconsultissimi caput fuit ipsa idolorum simulacrorumque fabricatio, in qua Gentiles nullis fere pepercerunt vel laboribus, vel sumtibus & impensis. Dederunt enim operam, ut pretiosissima effet illorum materia & artificiosissima elegantissimaque, illorum forma atque figura, quo nimirum illa plus auctoritatis haberent apud vulgus. Unde τέχνης ἰματαλήψις vocatur Idolum Sapientia decimo tertio. Ipsius autem uberrimus cum in ipsos artifices, atque fabros, tum in sacerdotes redundabat fructus atque qualis. In ipsius quoque, cum materia, tum formae deletu curiosa, ut supra dixi, superstitiosaque, habita fuit ratio atque cura, ut nimirum singulis Deus atque Numinibus seu Daemonibus potius, quorum illa fuerunt organa, apta essent & accommodata.
units.tr: First, then, the first head of that worship, most unlearned and most ill-advised, so to speak, was the very making of the idols and images. In this the Gentiles spared almost no labour, expense or outlay. For they took pains that the material of these should be most precious and the workmanship most skilful and elegant, and that their form and shape should be such that they would carry more authority with the common people. Hence Wisdom chapter thirteen calls an idol the deceit of art. The fruit of this, abundant and of a kind, flowed both to the craftsmen and makers themselves and to the priests. Care and attention were given to the choice both of material and of form, which, as I said above, was curious and superstitious, so that each image should be suited and fitted to the particular god or divinities, or rather demons, of whom it was the instrument.

units.la: Secundum cultus ipsius caput est ὀνομαςοθεσία, id est, nominis impositio. Idola enim ista atque simulacra sua inanimata velut ipsius Dei nomine insignire non dubitarunt, Deoque appellarunt, eo quod Deorum essent symbola atque monumenta, divinitatem multum habere viderentur: de quo supra quoq; dictum est.
units.tr: The second head of this worship is onomatothesia, that is, the giving of a name. For they did not hesitate to mark these lifeless idols and images with the very name of God itself, and to call them gods, because they were symbols and monuments of the gods and seemed to have much of the divine. This too was said above.

units.la: Tertium cultus ipsius insani caput fuit illorum initiatio, seu consecratio & inauguratio. Nam ut templa, ita idola & simulacra Dius illae suis filiis, & commentitiis, certis quoque ritibus, ceremoniis, gestibus ipsisque ritualibus, & historicis praeceptis vel carminibus dedicare, conservare atque inaugurare solebant. De hac magnam apud Gentes consecratione & dedicatione ita scribit Augustinus Epistola quadragesima nona: Imagines, inquit, a Gentibus, sanctis sedibus, honorabili sublimitate, locate, ut a precantibus atque immolantibus attendantur. Talibus simulacris divinum cum timore cultum exhibent, eaque niventibus similia venerantes adorantesque, contuentur, isque velut praesentibus preces alligant, victimas immolant, vota persolvunt.
units.tr: The third head of this mad worship was the initiation, or consecration and inauguration, of these idols. For, just as with temples, so the gods used to dedicate, keep and inaugurate their idols and images for their sons and their fictitious devotees, with certain rites, ceremonies, gestures, ritual actions, and historical precepts or songs. On this great consecration and dedication among the Gentiles Augustine writes thus in letter forty-nine: "Images," he says, "are placed by the Gentiles in holy seats, in honourable elevation, so that they may be attended to by those who pray and sacrifice. Before such images they render divine worship with fear, and worshipping and adoring them as though they were nodding, they gaze at them, and, as though they were present, they bind their prayers to them, slaughter victims and pay their vows."

units.la: Quartum caput est eorundem in certis locis atque sedibus collocatio. Illa enim, in locis maxime sacris & religiosis, quaelibet ipsis esse videbantur, ut in templis atque delubris suis collocarent, & parietibus illorum confuderunt, tamen loca quoque profana, tum in urbibus, tum in agris idolorum simulacrorumque ipsorum eorum, florum erant plenissima.
units.tr: The fourth head is the placing of the same in certain places and seats. For they seemed to them to be fittest in the most sacred and religious places, and so they set them up in their temples and shrines and crowded them against the walls. Yet profane places as well, both in cities and in the countryside, were completely full of the images and idols of these gods.

units.la: Quintum caput cultus ipsius ridiculi & absurdi fuit vestitus eorum & amictus, sive induenta ornamenta varia & multiplicia cum totius corporis, tum singularum partium sive membrorum. Illa enim puerorum & puellarum, puppas suas vestientium & ornantium ritu atque more, certis diebus festis vestire atque ornare solent. Unde Hieremias in illa sua epistola ad Judaeos merito irridet Babylonios, qui idola sua purpurea veste induebant, abstergentes pulverem, qua facies illorum propter populi turbam reoblebatur. Ibidem: Vestimenta, inquit, (idolorum) auferunt sacerdotes, quibus uxores & filios suos vestiunt. Sic eodem in loco docet, sacerdotes coronas aureas, quibus capita illorum erant ornata, ius detraxisse, & in privatum usum, atque adeo etiam in meretrices suas erogasse. Deinde cum aurum illud & argentum a meretriciis suis recepissent, id rursus ad idolorum, ceu amasiorum suorum, cultum ornatumque consulisse. Dionysius, ille tyrannus Syracusanus, cum ad Peloponnesum classem appulisset, & in fanum Veneris Iovis Olympii, aureum et detraxit amiculum grandi pondere: quo Iovem ornaret ex manubriis Carthaginensium tyrannus Gelo. Atque in eo etiam cavillatus est, Aestate gravem esse amiculum aureum, hyeme frigidum: eiq; laneum pallium injecit, cum id esse apeum ad omne anni tempus diceret.
units.tr: The fifth feature of their ridiculous and absurd worship was the clothing and dress they put on their images, that is, the various and manifold ornaments put on the whole body and on each of its parts. They dressed and adorned them on certain feast days, in the manner and custom of boys and girls who dress and adorn their dolls. Hence Jeremiah rightly mocks in his letter to the Jews the Babylonians, who clothed their idols in purple robes and wiped off the dust with which their faces were smeared by the crowd of the people. In the same place he says: "The priests take away the garments (of the idols) with which they clothe their wives and sons." In that same place he also teaches that the priests took from the idols the golden crowns with which their heads were adorned, and turned them to private use, and even spent them on their prostitutes. Then, when they had received the gold and silver back from their harlots, they again devoted it to the worship and adornment of the idols, as though they were their lovers. Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse, when he had landed his fleet at Peloponnesus, and had gone into the temple of Venus and of Jupiter Olympius, took away a golden cloak of great weight, with which the tyrant Gelo had adorned Jupiter from the spoils of the Carthaginians. He also mocked it, saying that the golden cloak was heavy in summer and cold in winter; and he threw a woollen cloak over it, saying that this was suitable for every season of the year.

units.la: Hus adde, quòd idem Aesculapii Epidauri barbam auream demi jussit: neq; enim convenire, barbatum esse filium, cum omnibus in fanis pater (Apollo) imberbus esset: Cicero libro tertio de
units.tr: Add to this that the same Dionysius ordered the golden beard of Aesculapius of Epidaurus to be removed; for it was not fitting that the son should be bearded when the father (Apollo) was beardless in all the temples. Cicero, book three, On the Nature of the Gods.

units.la: Natura Deorum. Suetonius de Caligula: In templo simulachrum, inquit, stabat aureum iconium. (Iconium simulacrum Tranquillus appellat, in quo erat expressa membrorum ipsius similitudo atq; oris lineamenta) amiciebatur, quo si die veste, quali ipse uteretur. Hinc qui fungebantur officio simulacra vestiendi, vestitores Deorum appellabantur. Firmicus Maternus quarto Matheoseos libro tradit, Mercurii cum Venere in tertio ab Horoscopo loco facere vestitores Deorū.
units.tr: Suetonius, on Caligula: "In the temple there stood a golden statue (which Suetonius calls an iconium, a statue in which the likeness of his limbs and the features of his face were expressed), and he dressed it each day in the same clothes that he himself wore." Hence those who performed the office of dressing the images were called dressers of the gods. Firmicus Maternus, in the fourth book of the Mathesis, teaches that Mercury with Venus in the third place from the Horoscope makes dressers of the gods.

units.la: Hucreferri debet, quod Hieremias in eadem epistola mentionem facit sceptri, gladii, securis, quam idola maxibus suis tenebant: Sceptrum, inquit, idolum habet ut homo, sicut judex regionis, quinifpeccantem non interficit. Tenet etiam manu sua gladium: se tamen a bello & latronibus liberare non potest. Huc pertinet Plutarchi quaestio Graeca quadragesima quinta: Cur Zabradensis in Curia simulacrum non sceptrum aut sulmen, sed securim elatam teneat.
units.tr: To this belongs what Jeremiah mentions in the same letter about the sceptre, sword and axe which the idols held in their hands: "The idol holds a sceptre like a man, like a judge of the region, yet it does not kill the one who sins. It also holds a sword in its hand, yet it cannot free itself from war and robbers." To this also belongs Plutarch's Greek question forty-five: why the Zabradensian statue in the Curia holds not a sceptre or thunderbolt but a raised axe.

units.la: Ac innumerae quidem res commemorantur in imaginum & simulacrorum Gentilium descriptione, quas manibus suis tenebant, cuiusmodi fuerunt sceptrum, gladius, securis, arcus, sagitta, clypeus, tridens, pomum, herba, cornucopiae, falx, animal aliquod, patera, corona, tympanum, sistrum, sulmen & similia, quae in antiquis numis cernuntur. Cicero lib. 3. de Natura Deorū de Dionysio tyranno: Victoriales, inquit, aureas, & pateras coronasq; quae simulacrorum porrectis manibus sustinebantur, sine dubio tollebat, eaq; se accipere, non auferre diceba t esse eni n stultitiaa quibus bona precarentur, ab iis porrigentibus & dantibus nolle sumere.
units.tr: Indeed innumerable things are mentioned in the description of Gentile images and statues which they held in their hands: such as the sceptre, sword, axe, bow, arrow, shield, trident, apple, herb, cornucopia, sickle, some animal, bowl, crown, drum, sistrum, thunderbolt and similar things, which are seen on ancient coins. Cicero, book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods, says of the tyrant Dionysius: "He undoubtedly took the golden Victories, and the bowls and crowns which were held out in the outstretched hands of the statues; and he said that he was receiving them, not taking them away. For it was folly, he said, not to be willing to accept good things from those who offer and give them, when they pray for blessings."

units.la: Sextum caput atq; modus culturae simulacrorum suis gestatio sive circumgestatio; ad quae morem Gentilium similiter alludit, eumq; irridet Hieremias, cum inquit: Sine pedibus, in humeris portantur, sostentantes ignobilitatem suam hominibus. Certis igitur temporibus idola illa sua honoris & religionis ergo huc & illuc ferre atq; circumferre solebant.
units.tr: The sixth feature and mode of worshipping images was their carrying about or procession, to which the custom of the Gentiles is likewise alluded to, and which Jeremiah mocks when he says: "Without feet, they are carried on shoulders, bearing their own baseness to men." At set times, therefore, they used to carry their idols here and there, to and fro, for the sake of honour and religion.

units.la: Septimum cultus istius idolorum caput fuerunt peregrinationes crebrae; & quidem longinquae, sumtuosae, difficiles, & periculosae, quas ad haec vel illa idola atq; simulacra, ea colendi, venerandi, atq; de rebus privatis & publicis consulendi gratia suscipiebant: quarū similiter in sacris & profanis litteris crebra fit mentio. Hujusmodi, ut ex innumeris unum proferam, erant illae Israelitarum peregrinationes in Bethel, in Dan, in Gilgal, & alia in loca ad vitulos illos aureos, & ad alta idola, a quibus sepe Prophetae eos debortabant.
units.tr: The seventh feature of this worship of idols was frequent pilgrimages; and indeed long, costly, difficult and dangerous ones, which they undertook to these or those idols and images, for the sake of worshipping and venerating them and of consulting them about private and public affairs. Mention of these, too, is frequent in sacred and profane letters. Of this kind, to give one out of countless examples, were those pilgrimages of the Israelites to Bethel, to Dan, to Gilgal and to other places, to the golden calves and high places, from which the prophets often called them back.

units.la: Octavum caput atq; modus fuerit vota, preces atq; supplicationes, quas ad idola & simulacra illa sua faciebat. Harum mentio sit eodē Sapientiæ lib. cap. 14. ubi significatur, quātas ista sit, non solum sultitia, sed etiā demētia hominū, qui idola alloquuntur, & ea pro fortuna possessionib. nuptiis, atq; liberis suis precatur: ab iis & vitā petūt, quae animae vitaeq; omnis plane sunt expertia, quae ne sibi quidē ipsis, suedi alia possut opitulari. & ster atq; profestione feliꝯ, quae gressu, incessu, motuq; omni caret: et vsu pulerum, operis cujus vis efficiēdi facultate, quae manib. suis nihil efficere possū.
units.tr: The eighth feature and mode was the vows, prayers and supplications which they made to those idols and images. Mention of these occurs in the same book of Wisdom, chapter 14, where it is shown how great is not only the folly but the madness of men who address idols and ask them for fortune, possessions, marriage and children. From them they seek life, though they are utterly devoid of soul and life; they ask for help from those who are without experience; for a journey from one who cannot walk; for gain, work and success from one whose hands can accomplish nothing.

units.la: His adde Osculationē, amplexū, genuflexione, corporis prostrationē, capitis aperitionē, et alios id generis gestus seu gesticulationes potius, quas in precib. illis suis adhibere, quibusq; idola illa sua atq; simulachra colere atq; honorare cosueverūt. Sic osculationis aureorū illorū vitulorū metio sis manifesta. Hosea 13. Sic Cicero in Verrinis narrat, aeneū quoddā Herculis simulacrū os meutiq; habuisse attritū, propter illa ofculantiū frequentiā. Omnib. tamē, ut aras, sic signa et simulacra nō faserat attingi. Sic enim exspligratia Cicero: Pudicitiae signū inquit, quod erat Romae in foro boario nō fas ent attingi, nisi ab ea, quae semel nupsisset. Festus idem affirmat de signo Fortunae mulierbri, quod erat in via Latia. Quod attinet ad amplexum eorum, constat, sit aras & templa, sic simulachra ab sla homiū fuisse, ad quae in periculis confugiebant & ea amplectebantur.
units.tr: To these add kissing, embracing, genuflection, prostration of the body, uncovering of the head, and other gestures of this kind, or rather gesticulations, which they were accustomed to use in those prayers, and by which they were accustomed to worship and honour their idols and images. Thus the kissing of those golden calves is clearly mentioned in Hosea 13. Thus Cicero in his Verrines tells that a bronze statue of Hercules had its mouth and chin worn down by the frequent kissing of worshippers. Yet, as with altars, so statues were not permitted to be touched by everyone. For Cicero explains this: "The statue of Modesty (Pudicitia), which was in Rome in the cattle market, was not lawful to touch except by a woman who had been married only once." Festus says the same of the statue of Fortune of Women, which stood on the Latin Way. As for embracing them, it is clear that, as with altars and temples, so the images too were embraced by men, and that they fled to them in dangers and clung to them.

units.la: Nonum caput atq; modus venerationis idolorum fuerunt omnis generis odores, cerei atq; lumina, cornua, quaeidolis illis accenderunt, tum denique omnis generis hostiae, sacrificia & anathemata, quae idolis simulacris, illis suis, omni sensu motū, carentibus, obstulerunt, & suspenderunt: de quibus ipsis iam dicta sunt quedam, partim plura dicentur. Lucernarum fit mentio Baruchi sextoin illa Hieremie epistola, quas contra omnem rationē testatur, idolis simulacris, illis caecis, omniq; plane sensu vacuis accendi fuisse solitas. Sic Cicero lib. 3. officiorum: Sta: uis cerei & suffitus apponuntur: sub quibus odores, thymiamata, sacrificia, hostiae, hostiarum, instrumenta, aræ nimirū atque altaria, omnis generis anathemata atque donaria & his similia comprehenduntur: de quibus partim jam quoque dicta quedam fuerunt: partim plura adhuc dicentur.
units.tr: The ninth feature and mode of venerating idols was every kind of incense, wax candles and lights, which they lit before those idols; then every kind of victim, sacrifice and offering, which they presented and hung up before the idols and images, which lack all sense and motion. Some of these things have already been discussed, and more will be said. Mention of lamps is made in Baruch, chapter six, in that letter of Jeremiah, where he testifies that they were customarily lit before idols, which are blind and utterly devoid of all sense, although this was contrary to all reason. Thus Cicero, book 3 of On Duties: "Statues, wax, and incense are offered; under which are comprehended odours, incense, sacrifices, victims, the instruments of sacrifice, altars and the like, every kind of offering and gift, and such things." Some of these things have already been mentioned, and more will be said later.

units.la: Hus ipsis ritibus Moabitæ suum Baal coluerunt; de quo Numerorum libro, capite vigesimo fecundo: & Baalpehor; de quo eodem libro, capite vigesimo quinto, & Psalmo centesimo quinto: & Chamos; de quo libro illo Numerorum capite primo & vigesimo primo, Iudicum decimoter
units.tr: With these same rites the Moabites worshipped their Baal, concerning whom in Numbers, chapter twenty-two; and Baal-peor, concerning whom in the same book, chapter twenty-five, and in Psalm 105; and Chemosh, concerning whom in that book of Numbers, chapters one and twenty-one, and in Judges, chapter ten

units.la: tio primo Regum undecimo; & fecundo libro, vigesimo tertio capite, ac Hieremiæ quadragesimo octavo. Quibus item Madianitæ suum Baal berith; de quo Iudicum octavo & nono: Et Syri Deum Rimmon; de quo fecundo Regum quinto. Et Ammonitæ idolum Moloch, primo Regum decimoquinto: Et Sidonii Astbaroth, de quo Iudicum libro, capite fecundo, & pruno Regum undecimo, ac fecundo, vigesimo tertio: Et Philistini suum Dagon, de quo Iudicum decimo sexto, & primo Samuelis decimo quinto: Et Ammonitæ suum Baalzebub, de quo fecundo Regum primo: Et Babylonii fuû Belem, ac Statuâ, Ieremiæ quadragesimo & Danielis tertio & decimoquarto.
units.tr: and 1 Kings 11, and 2 Kings 23, and Jeremiah 48. By the same means the Midianites worshipped their Baal-berith, concerning whom in Judges 8 and 9; and the Syrians the god Rimmon, 2 Kings 5. The Ammonites worshipped the idol Molech, 1 Kings 15; the Sidonians Ashtoreth, concerning whom in Judges 2, 1 Kings 11 and 2 Kings 23; the Philistines their Dagon, concerning whom in Judges 16 and 1 Samuel 15; the Ammonites also their Baal-zebub, 2 Kings 1; and the Babylonians their Bel and Statue, Jeremiah 40, Daniel 3 and 14.

units.la: Hanc ipsam autem Gentilium idololatriam artificialem vel ipsi humanæ naturæ contrariam & in micâ non sacræ folium litteræ & omnes primitiuæ Ecclesiæ doctores atq; patres, sed ex ipsis quoq; Gentilibus multi, quiinter ipsos sapientiores sunt habiti, duce & magistra natura culpārunt, damnârunt, irriserunt, ac contemperunt, quorum quædam testimonia hic libet addere:
units.tr: Not only the Holy Scriptures and all the early Fathers and teachers of the Church, but also many of the Gentiles themselves, those held wisest among them, guided by nature as their teacher, have blamed, condemned, mocked and despised this idolatry of the Gentiles, which is artificial and contrary to human nature itself. I will add some of their testimonies here.

units.la: Varro,teste Augustino, libro quarto de Civitate Dei, capite trigesimo primo, scripsit, Romanos plusquam centum & septuaginta annos Deos sine simulacro coluisse. Quod si adhuc, inquit, mansisset, castius Dii observarentur. Cujus addit Augustinus, sententiæ suæ testem adhibet ineeer cætera etiam gentem Iudæam:nec dubitat eum locum ita concludere,ut dicat,qui primi simulachra Deorum populis posuerunt, eos civitatibus suis & metum demphsse, & errorem addidisse (hanc Varronis sententiam etiam capite nono ejusdem libri allegat) prudenter existimās,Deos facile posse in simulacrorum stoliditate contemni.
units.tr: Varro, according to Augustine in the fourth book of The City of God, chapter 31, wrote that the Romans worshipped their gods without images for more than 170 years. "If this had continued," he says, "the gods would be worshipped more purely." Augustine adds that Varro calls in other witnesses for this opinion, including the Jewish people. Augustine does not hesitate to conclude the passage by saying that those who first set up images of the gods among the peoples took away the fear of the gods from their cities and added error. (He cites this opinion of Varro again in chapter 9 of the same book, judging wisely that the gods can easily be despised in the stupidity of their images.)

units.la: Dionysius Halicarnasseus testatur, Lucium Tarquinium Priscum, primum, vanitate & stultitiâ Græcarum religionum imbutum, simulacrorum statuarumq; usum in Romanam Rem publicam invexisse. Tertullianus striliter scribens, Romæ religionis ritum,a Numa,non splendidis cerimoniis & absq; simulacris institutum Tarquinium Priscum, tanquam Græca & Hetruscæ religionis adprimè peritum, testatur primum statuarū simulacrorumq; cultū introduxisse.
units.tr: Dionysius of Halicarnassus testifies that Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, the first to be steeped in the vanity and folly of Greek religions, introduced the use of images and statues into the Roman commonwealth. Tertullian, writing sharply, says that the Roman religious rite was established by Numa without splendid ceremonies and without images, and that Tarquinius Priscus, thoroughly versed in Greek and Etruscan religion, was the first to introduce the worship of statues and images.

units.la: Plutarchus quoq; testatur, Numam Pompilium nesas duxisse imaginem aut effigiem aliquâ Deo tribuere.
units.tr: Plutarch also testifies that Numa Pompilius thought it unlawful to attribute any image or likeness to God.

units.la: Plinius libro secundo,capite secundo, effigiem Dei,inquit,formamq; quærere imbecillitatis humanæ reor.
units.tr: Pliny, in the second book, chapter 2, says: "I think that to seek an image or form of God is a sign of human weakness."
