units.la: Hermes,distus Trismegistus,asserebat,eos videri Deos non credere in cælo esse, qui eorum statuas sibi ante oculos sisti volunt,aut certè diffidere, sua vota ac preces illacusq; pervenire posse. Atq; ex hac per versa animi inductione Deorû simulacra prodiisse,atq; Numina cæpisse appellari.
units.tr: Hermes, called Trismegistus, asserted that those who want their statues set before their eyes do not seem to believe that the gods are in heaven, or at least doubt that their vows and prayers can reach them there. And from this perverted movement of mind, he said, the images of the gods came forth and began to be called divinities.

units.la: Lycurgus, Lacedemoniorû legislator, dicitur legibus suis probibuisse, ne Dii hominū aut ulli bestiarum similes fierent,& idcirco statuas & simulacra e Republica sua exterminavit.
units.tr: Lycurgus, the lawgiver of the Lacedaemonians, is said to have forbidden by his laws that the gods be made like men or any beasts, and therefore banished statues and images from his commonwealth.

units.la: Lactantius Firmianus scriptum reliquit,Ægyptios elumenta, sed absque imaginibus,divinis effecijse bonoribus.
units.tr: Lactantius Firmianus left it in writing that the Egyptians paid divine honours to animals, but without images.

units.la: Apud Persas & Lybes primis temporibus nullas neq; statuas, neq; semplas, neq; altaria fuisse multi Historici testantur.
units.tr: Many historians testify that in earliest times the Persians and Libyans had neither statues, nor temples, nor altars.

units.la: Scythæ,ut refert Herodotus,etsi Vestam,Iovem, Apollinem,Martem, & multos alios Deorum loco habuerunt atque coluerunt; nulli tamen, præterquam Marti,templum statuerunt, aut aram dedicarunt,& chuisis uno eodemq; risu sacrificarunt.
units.tr: The Scythians, as Herodotus relates, although they held and worshipped Vesta, Jupiter, Apollo, Mars and many other gods, nevertheless set up a temple or dedicated an altar to none of them, except Mars, and they sacrificed to them all with one and the same laughter.

units.la: Effedones quoque, Scythapum populus,eodem teste, nullum aliud simulacrū, nisi hominis calvarium venerabantur:cujus descriptionem vide apud eundem,nec non Pomponium Molam, Solinum & alios.
units.tr: The Essedones too, a people of the Scythians, according to the same witness, worshipped no image except a man's skull. For its description see the same author, and also Pomponius Mela, Solinus and others.

units.la: Theodoretus,Cyrensis Episcopus, Sermone ad Græcos infideles tertio,de Angelis,Diis,De monibus; Xenophanis Colophonii & aliorum Gentilium testimonia contra istum simulacrorum usum atq; cultum profert.
units.tr: Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, in the third sermon To the Unbelieving Greeks, On Angels, Gods and Demons, brings forward the testimonies of Xenophanes of Colophon and other Gentiles against this use and worship of images.

units.la: Zeno Citiensis,ut idem testatur, in eo,quem de Republica librum edidit, Deorū & templa & simulacra fieri prohibuit:quandoquidem utrumq; Deo esset indignum.
units.tr: Zeno of Citium, as the same author testifies, in the book on the commonwealth which he published, forbade that temples and images of the gods be made, since both were unworthy of God.

units.la: Plato,ut idem scribit,haud penitus hæc confici vetuit,timens videlicet, ne Atheniensium gratia benitia benivolentia, exciderent, ne ve ei, sicuti olim Socrati, venenū porrigeretur: cum tamē ipse quoque Deorum statuas & simulacra plurimum carpat. Citat locum quendam ex Platone, quo Plato docet, simulacra, neq; aurea, neq; argentea, neq; eburnea, neque ferrea esse debere, sed lignea tantum atq; lapidea. Ex hoc ipso loco colligit Theodoretus, Platonem simulachra in contemptum volusse adducere, dum ea non ex pretiosa, sed vili tantum materia fieri praecepit.
units.tr: Plato, as the same writer says, did not entirely forbid these things to be made, fearing, no doubt, that he would lose the favour and goodwill of the Athenians, or that a cup of poison would be handed to him as once to Socrates. Yet he himself greatly criticises the statues and images of the gods. Theodoret cites a passage from Plato in which Plato teaches that images should be made neither of gold, nor silver, nor ivory, nor iron, but only of wood and stone. From this very passage Theodoret infers that Plato wished to lead people to contempt for images, since he ordered them made not of precious but only of cheap material.

units.la: Illustre quoq; est illud Sophoclis, antiquissimi & celeberrimi Poeta testimonium, quod justi-nus Martyr citat in sua Admonitione ad Graecos: Εἷς ταῦ ἀλήθειαυτν, εἷς ὅξι Θεός Ο ὑρανὸν ἐτὸ χω, γῆν γαῖαν μακραν, Πόντυτι χαρῶν οἰδ' ὑμφ, ἀνέμων βίας Θνητοί δ' πολλοί κρῶδια πλασσόμενοι Ιδρυσαμεδα πημάτων πωρὰ ξυγλὼ Θεὸν ἀγάλματ' ἐκ λίθων τε καὶ ξύλων Η Χρυσοτυκτων, ἡ ἐλεφαντίνων τυπως Θυσίας τύπους ἐκ λας παντυρεις Τεύχοντες, ἄτιμος ἐυσεβεῖν νομίζουσι.
units.tr: That saying of Sophocles, the most ancient and most famous poet, is also famous, which Justin Martyr cites in his Exhortation to the Greeks: "For truly there is one God, who made the heaven and the wide earth, the bright waves of the sea and the force of the winds. But mortals, fashioning foolish hearts by pitiful art, have set up as gods images of stone and wood, or of gold or ivory, and, thinking they are doing their pious duty, offer sacrifices to them and celebrate festivals." [Εἷς γὰρ ἀληθῶς ἔστιν εἷς ὅδε θεός, ὃς οὐρανὸν ἔτευξε καὶ γαῖαν μακράν, πόντου τε χαροπὸν κῦμα, ἀνέμων βίας· θνητοὶ δὲ πολλοὶ κραδίας πλασσόμενοι ἱδρυσάμενοι πήμασιν πρὸς ξυγκλῶ θεῶν ἀγάλματ' ἐκ λίθων τε καὶ ξύλων ἢ χρυσοτύπων ἢ ἐλεφαντίνων τύπους θυσίας τύπους ἑκάστοτε τεύχοντες ἀτίμως εὐσεβεῖν νομίζουσι.]

units.la: His verbis quid non modo clarius & illustrius, sed etiam verius & sacris litteris religionique non sit convenientius dici posset, quibus ille primum quidem unum: unumquam, revera testatur esse Deum, coeli, terrae, maris, ventorumq; conditorem? Deinde Mortales reprehendit, qui caeco quodam mentis errore Deorum simulacra ligned, lapidea, aurea & argentea fabricantes, iisq; sacra facientes, diesq; festos celebrantes, pulchre sibi pietatis officio fungi videntur.
units.tr: What could be said more clearly and more brilliantly than these words, or more truly, or more fittingly for sacred letters and religion? In them he first testifies that there is one God, indeed the only one, the maker of heaven, earth, sea and winds. Then he rebukes mortals who, by a certain blind error of mind, make images of the gods out of wood, stone, gold and silver, and who, performing sacred rites to them and celebrating festivals, seem to themselves to be discharging their duty of piety beautifully.

units.la: His addam quae Tacitus libro trigesimo Annalium de Iudaeis scripsit: Aegyptii, inquit, pleraq; animalia effigies, compositas venerantur. Iudei mente sola, unumq; Numen intelligunt: profana eos, qui Deum imagines mortalibus materiis in species hominum effingunt (alii legunt, effigiant) summum illud, & aeternum, neq; mutabile, neq; interiturum. Igitur nulla simulacra urbibus suis, nedum templis sunt. Non Regibus haec adoratio: non Caesaribus honos.
units.tr: To these I will add what Tacitus wrote about the Jews in the thirtieth book of his Annals: "The Egyptians," he says, "worship many animals and composite figures. The Jews understand God by the mind alone, and as one. They count profane those who fashion God in images from perishable materials into the likeness of men (others read, 'fashion into images'). That supreme and eternal being is neither changeable nor subject to decay. Therefore they have no images of him in their cities, much less in their temples. Such worship is not given to kings, nor such honour to the Caesars."

units.la: Huc silentio non possum praetermittere, quod Aelius Lampridius in Alexandri Severi vita prodidit: Alexander Severus, inquit, Christo templum facere voluit, eumq; inter Deos recipere. Quod & Adrianus cogitasse fertur, quia ipla in omnibus civitatibus sine simulacris juserat fieri, quae bodie idcirco, quia non habent Numina, dicatur Adriani, quia ille ad hoc parasse dicebatur, sed prohibitus est ab his, qui consulentes Sacra reprererant omnes Christianos futuros, si id optato venisset & reliqua templa deferenda. Haec ille. Ex quibus colligimus, priscorum illorū Christianorum templa simulacris caruisse, quemadmodum & Romanorum priscorū fana, Varrone teste, ut supra dictum, centum se praeginta circiter annis imaginum atq; simulacrorū fuerunt experta: Numa Pompilii nimirum instituto, qui Pythagorae, summi ac nobilissimi illius Philosophi discipulus fuit, ac proinde secundum illius documenta ne fas ducebat, primum illud omnium rerū principiū, omnis sensus ac perturbationis expers, caduci alicujus hominis atq; animalis imagine exprimere: hujus rei testes est Plutarchus in vita Numa Pompilii.
units.tr: Here I cannot pass over in silence what Aelius Lampridius reported in the life of Alexander Severus: "Alexander Severus," he says, "wished to build a temple to Christ and to receive him among the gods." Hadrian too is said to have intended the same, because he had ordered that in all cities temples be built without images, which today are called temples of Hadrian for that reason, although they have no divinity; he was said to have prepared this, but he was prevented by those who, consulting the sacred books, discovered that all Christians would become such if this were done in the way they wished, and that the other temples would be abandoned. So far Lampridius. From these things we gather that the temples of those early Christians lacked images, just as the ancient shrines of the Romans, as Varro testifies, as said above, were without images and statues for about 170 years. This was certainly the institution of Numa Pompilius, who was a disciple of Pythagoras, that most noble and eminent philosopher; and so, following his teaching, he thought it wrong to express the first principle of all things, free from all sense and passion, by the image of any perishable man or animal. Plutarch in the life of Numa Pompilius is a witness to this fact.

units.la: In eandem sententiā Strabo lib.16. de Mose verba facit, quae quia magni videtur esse momenti, subjicere volui: Iudaeorum, inquit, progenitores esse Aegyptios vulgo fama obtinet. Nam Moses unus ex Aegyptiis sacerdotibus, cum partem quandam regionis illius possiderest, eorumq; institutae molestie ferret, inde Hierosolymam commigravit, cui sese multi comites atq; socii adiunxerunt, quia bus divina cordi erant. Docebat enim ille neq; Aegyptios recte sentire, qui ferarū ac pecorum imagines Deo tribuerent, nec Graecos, qui Deos hominis figuris insigniurent. Id solum Deum esse, quod nos contineret, terrum ac mare, quod coelum & mundū & rerum omnium naturā appellamus. Hu jus sanè imaginē nemo sana mente, nostrae similē audeat effingere, ac proinde relicta omni simulacrorum effigie, templo, quod eo dignum sit, excitato, sine omni forma colendum esse. Haec ille.
units.tr: To the same effect Strabo, in the sixteenth book, speaks of Moses, and since his words seem to be of great importance, I wished to add them: "It is commonly held," he says, "that the ancestors of the Jews were Egyptians. For Moses, one of the Egyptian priests, when he possessed a certain part of that region and bore with ill grace the institutions there, migrated from there to Jerusalem, and many companions and associates joined him, those whose hearts were set on divine things. For he taught that neither the Egyptians were right to attribute images of wild beasts and cattle to God, nor the Greeks, who adorn gods with human shapes. He taught that the only God is that which encloses us, the land and the sea, which we call heaven, the world and the nature of all things. No one in sound mind would dare to shape an image of him like anything we know; therefore, leaving aside all the form of images and raising a temple worthy of him, God should be worshipped without any form." So far Strabo.

units.la: Eandem quoque summi cuiusdam Philosophi, Cheremonis nomine (cujus Plutō in lib. de Lapidibus facit mentionem) sententiam fuisse Eusebius lib.3. cap.3. Praeparationis suae Evangelicae testatur. Mortales homines eos existimavit fuisse, quibus imagines ac simulacra a Veteribus fuerint tributa. Denique verum nullum ex ligno, vel quavis alia materia verum posse esse simulacrum. Quiem enim, dicebat ille, adeo stultus erit, ut ligneum simulacrum atque effigiem Dei Cretorum omnium similitudinem habere arbitretur? Natura enim divina omnem materiam, & omnia, quæ percipimus, excedit, mentè solummodo, ac sanctis animis comprehensa. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Eusebius, in the third book, third chapter, of his Preparation for the Gospel, testifies that the same opinion was held by a certain most eminent philosopher named Chaeremon (whom Plutarch mentions in his book On Stones). He thought that those men were mortals to whom images and statues had been given by the ancients. In short, he said, no true image can be made of wood or any other material. "For who," he said, "would be so foolish as to think that a wooden statue and image of God has the likeness of all things? For the divine nature exceeds all matter and all that we perceive, and is grasped only by the mind and by holy souls." So far Chaeremon.

units.la: ET HAEC de secundo membro sacrificiorum veterum Gentilium, in specie simul & in genere: nempe Objectio, cui videlicet illa olim facta & oblata fuerint. In specie quidem Neptor sacrificiis suum Minervæ fecit; Argonautæ vero Apollini. In genere deinde quibusvis Dijs, creaturis, idolis & Dæmonibus Ethnici quondam sacrificarunt.
units.tr: These things are said about the second part of the ancient Gentile sacrifices, both in particular and in general: namely, the object, to whom they were once made and offered. In particular, Neptune made his sacrifice to Minerva, and the Argonauts to Apollo. In general, the Gentiles at various times sacrificed to all sorts of gods, creatures, idols and demons.

units.la: SEQVITVR nunc membrum tertium in ucro, hoc sacrificio confiderandū, MATERIA videlicet, sive QVID sacrificarint Neptor & Argonautæ. Ac utrique quidem boves immolasse dicuntur, ab Homero & Apollonio. Neptor unum; Argonautæ vero binos, pro felicia navigatione. Binos quidem; ut vult interpres, propter duo Apollinis cognomina, quæ fuerunt ἱππιος & ἀμφι. Apollinem autem tauro inprimis placari solitum testantur illa Virgilii:
units.tr: Now follows the third part to be considered in this sacrifice, namely the MATTER, or what Neptune and the Argonauts sacrificed. Both are said, on the authority of Homer and Apollonius, to have sacrificed oxen: Neptune one, the Argonauts two, for a safe voyage. Two, indeed, as the commentator says, on account of two surnames of Apollo, which were Hippios and Amphi. That Apollo was commonly placated with a bull is attested by these lines of Virgil:

units.la: Taurum Neptuno: taurum tibi, pulcher Apollo.
units.tr: A bull for Neptune; a bull for you, fair Apollo.

units.la: Sic apud Ægyptios in Osyridis, veluti frugum ac fructuum repertoris memoriam apud posrot immortalem, boves rufas, quoniam viderentur colore similes Typhoni, qui Osyrideni necavit, immolari fuit permissum. Ludis quoq; Apollinaribus a Romanis, ex carminum Sibyllinorum religione, bove aurato & capris duabus albis aureis XVIII. Augusti placabatur; & Latona Jamina bove aurata. Aliæ tamen aliis aliq, alijs animalibus placari fuisse solitas, passim hillo ria testantur.
units.tr: So among the Egyptians, in memory of Osiris, the discoverer of grains and fruits, which they kept immortal among posterity, it was permitted to sacrifice red oxen, since they seemed similar in colour to Typhon, who killed Osiris. Also at the Roman Apollinarian games, by the religion of the Sibylline books, Apollo was placated on the eighteenth of August with a gilded bull and two white goats with gilded horns; and Latona with a gilded cow. Yet other writers testify everywhere that different gods were placated by different things and different animals.

units.la: Sed ut de hoc quoq; membro, quid fere ipsum etiam infinitum est, uberius aliquanto & copiosius dicamus, sciendum est, Veteres sacrificia vel animalia, inter quæ sunt boves illi, quorum auctores citati in sacrificiis Neptor & Argonautarum meminerunt, velinanimata vel, mixta, quæ partim animalibus, partim plantis omnis generis frugibus atq, fructibus constabant. Dijs ac Numinibus suis obtulisse.
units.tr: But so that we may speak somewhat more fully and copiously about this part too, which is almost endless, it must be understood that the ancients offered to their gods and deities sacrifices either of animals (among which are those oxen whose authors cited mention in the sacrifices of Neptune and the Argonauts) or of inanimate things, or of mixed things, which consisted partly of animals and partly of plants, of every kind of grain and fruit.

units.la: Hæc igitur sacrificiorum atq; adeo totius cultus sive religionis Ethnicorum materia fuit triplex: Prima animata, ut animalium: altera inanimia, ut plantarum; herbarum frugum & fructuum. Tertia, mixta, ex animalibus videlicet, vel plantis.
units.tr: Therefore this matter of sacrifices, and indeed of the whole worship or religion of the Gentiles, was threefold: the first animate, as of animals; the second inanimate, as of plants, herbs, grains and fruits; the third mixed, namely of animals or plants.

units.la: Porro animata materia sacrificiorum, est duplex: Animalium nimirum ratione utentium, ut hominum; & rationis expertium, ut bestiarum. Humana enim cum seu potius inhumana, immanis, horrenda & plane diabolica hujusmodi sacrificia cum antiquissima tum omnibus pene gentibus, tam Judæis, quam Ethnicis, in toto terrarum orbe communia & ultissima fuisse fatur, prophanus litterarum historiarumq, monumentis satis superq; constat. Unde in sacris litteris Levitici libro, capite decimo octavo & vigesimo: item Deuteronomii capite duodecimo & aliis in locis gravissima capitalia, pœna prohibentur.
units.tr: Further, the animate matter of sacrifices is twofold: of animals that use reason, such as humans, and of those that lack reason, such as beasts. For human (or rather inhuman) sacrifices of this kind, monstrous, dreadful and plainly diabolical, were both very ancient and, as profane records of letters and history abundantly attest, common to nearly all peoples, Jews as well as Gentiles, throughout the whole world, and most cruel. Hence Sacred Scripture forbids them under the gravest capital penalty in Leviticus chapters 18 and 20, and likewise in Deuteronomy chapter 12 and elsewhere.

units.la: Observandum autem eos, hominem primo integrum & solidum Diis suis offerre fuisse solitos; deinde certat ejus partes sive membra. Prioris generis est hoc, quod Arnobius scribit libro octavo ad versus Gentiles, Infantes innocentes Aphrica partibus Saturno fuisse immolatos. Item Iovem Latiarem homicidio coli fuisse solium. Quo pertinet id, quod Tertullianus scribit in Apologetico capite nono, Saturnum inprimis humana victima delectarum fuisse, quidque circo tumultu filiorum fuit appellatus. Scribit de hoc etiam Plinius libro septimo capite secundo; & inter alias terræ partes, in Sicilia ac Italia usitatissima fuisse hanc hominum integrorum sacrificia significat. Et libro trigesimo sexto, capite quinto, Pœnos ad Herculis simulacrum omnibus annis humanam victimam sacrificare fuisse solitos. Sic Cicero in Oratione pro Fonteio, Gallos humanos hostiis Deus placare confueville testatur. Quis ignorat, inquis ibidem, eos (Gallos) usq; ad hanc diem retinere illam immanem ac barbaram consuetudinem hominum immolandorum? Porphyrius inter alia sacrificiorum humanorum exempla hæc profert: Apud Rhodios in honorem Saturni mactabatur XVI Kalend. Novemb. homo; quod cum perditus fervatu fuisset, in consuetudinem abiit. Quendam enim ex viris, qui publica sententia damnati essent, ad capitale supplicium usq; Saturnalia virum asservabat. Idem testatur, in Safamine insula hominem mactari solitum Aglaula, Cecropis filia. Hominem ito erat apud Argyptiam Heliopolin singulis diebus mactabantur. Quin etiam Lacedæmonii hominem Marti immolabant; & Græci cum ad bella progrederentur, ab humana cade sui runt auspicati. Hac Theodoretus ex Porphyrio. Philo etiam Historicus scribit, Aristomenem Messenium trecentos olim homines Iovi Ithemio immolasse. Sic Tauri Scythæ pro hostiis Diænæ advenas immolabant, præsertim, quos, ut inquit Athanasius, pro vidientia eriipuerat, host ipsi jugulabant. Alii, postquam e bello redierant, captivos per centurias dividebant, et ex singulis unum sumentes, tot Martiɩ jugulabant, quot ex unaquaque centuria delegissent. Scribit Procopius, apud Thulitas, idem, Thule insulæ habitatores, Iuo tempore, hoc est, Iustiniani Imperatoris, victimarum potissimam suisse, virum quempiam, quem primum in prælio cepissent, Martis sacrificasse, ut quem Deorum maximum ducerent. Sedea, inquit, est apud hos immolandi consuetudo, ut non solum hostiam mastant, sed in arbore vivam hanc prius suspendant, indeque inter senticeta et vepres projeciam, sic variis ac miseris modis excruciando consiciant. Legimus item paucis ante annis ab Hispani nautis, orbem lustrantibus, insulam repertam, quam ipsi a Caroli, suo Rege, Carolinam dixere, in qua frequentes visebantur statuæ æneæ suorum Numinum, quæ intrinsecus cavæ, manibus juncti passiui, fuerant, in quibus infantes et puerulos, quos Deis suis immolabant, includere solebant et crudelissimè incendebant, in cavea statuarū et simulacrorum igne accenso, et are calorem concipiētē. In Asia Laodicaei Miuerve virginem mastabant, Arcades Iovi Lycæo puerum: plerique juxta Boristhenem, recordati animo homines victimas dare et in Deorum sacrificiis humanis ossibus adolere solebant. Blemyæ, Cymbri, Galli, Druidæ et Germani, flatis diebus humanos hostiis litare et captivorum cruore adolere aras consueverunt. Fuit quoq; apud Phœnices et Carthaginenses usus diu observatus, ut infantes, qui principum filii essent, forte dučtos, regio ornatu Saturno immolarent hostias: et quem Sors morti destinarat, subtrahere mortiuo licebat. Quare multorum civium largis fletibus deplorata fuere su nera. Hinc Imilce, Annibalis uxor, cum Asdrubal ejus esset mastandus filius, apud Siliumin calce quarti libri Punicorum dolens ait: Quæ porrò hæc pietas, delubra aspergere tabo? Heu prima scelerum caussa mortalibus ægris, Naturam nescire Deum: justa ite precari Thure pio, sædisq; feros avertite ritus: Mite et cognatum est homini Deus: hastenus ora Sit satis ante aras cæsos vidisse juvencos. Aut si velle nefas Superos sixum, sedetq. Me me, quæ genui, vestru absumite votu, Curspolitare juvat Libycas hac iudole terras?
units.tr: It should be observed that they were accustomed first to offer a man whole and entire to their gods, and afterwards his parts or limbs. Of the first kind is what Arnobius writes in book eight Against the Gentiles: that innocent infants were sacrificed to Saturn in Africa. Likewise, that Jupiter Latiaris was worshipped with murder. To this belongs what Tertullian writes in his Apology, chapter nine: that Saturn above all delighted in human victims, and that for this reason he was called the god of the circus of the sons. Pliny also writes of this in book seven, chapter two, and, among other parts of the earth, indicates that this sacrifice of whole men was most common in Sicily and Italy. And in book thirty-six, chapter five, that the Carthaginians used to sacrifice a human victim every year at the statue of Hercules. So Cicero, in his speech for Fonteius, testifies that the Gauls were accustomed to placate their god with human victims. "Who is ignorant," he says there, "that they (the Gauls) have kept that savage and barbarous custom of immolating men down to this day?" Porphyry, among other examples of human sacrifice, offers this: among the Rhodians, a man was slaughtered in honour of Saturn on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November; and when this was abolished because of a wicked act, it passed into custom. For they kept a man from among those condemned by public sentence until the Saturnalia, and then put him to death. The same writer testifies that on the island of Salamis a man used to be slaughtered for Aglaurus, daughter of Cecrops. There was also a custom at Heliopolis in Egypt that men were slaughtered every day. Indeed the Lacedaemonians immolated a man to Mars, and the Greeks, when they set out to war, took omens from human slaughter. So Theodoret, from Porphyry. The historian Philo also writes that Aristomenes of Messene once sacrificed three hundred men to Jupiter Ithomatas. So the Scythians of the Tauri used to slaughter strangers as victims for Diana, especially those whom, as Athanasius says, they had snatched from the sea, and whom they themselves cut the throat of. Others, after returning from war, divided their captives into hundreds, and taking one from each, slaughtered as many to Mars as they had chosen from each hundred. Procopius writes that among the Thulites, the inhabitants of the island of Thule, in his time, that is, the time of the Emperor Justinian, the most excellent victim was a man whom they had first captured in battle, and that they sacrificed him to Mars, whom they regarded as the greatest of the gods. Indeed, he says, it is the custom among them in sacrificing not only to slaughter the victim, but first to hang him alive on a tree, and then to throw him among the brambles and thorns, tormenting him in various wretched ways until he dies. We read also that a few years ago the Spanish sailors, sailing round the world, discovered an island which they named Carolina after their king Charles. In it were frequently seen bronze statues of their gods, which were hollow inside, with their hands joined and their arms extended. Into these they used to put infants and little boys whom they sacrificed to their gods, and they burned them most cruelly, with a fire lit in the hollow of the statues and images, which conveyed the heat to the hollow. In Asia, the people of Laodicea slaughtered a virgin for Minerva, and the Arcadians a boy for Jupiter Lycaeus. Many near the Borysthenes, mindful that men must give themselves as victims, used to burn human bones in the sacrifices of their gods. The Blemyes, the Cimbri, the Gauls, the Druids and the Germans, on set days, have been accustomed to sacrifice humans as victims and to sprinkle altars with the blood of captives. There was also among the Phoenicians and Carthaginians a custom long observed: that infants who happened to be the sons of princes, chosen by lot, were sacrificed to Saturn as victims in royal ornaments; and whoever Fate had destined for death, it was permitted to substitute someone else for the one to be killed. Hence the funerals of many citizens were mourned with great weeping. Hence Imilce, the wife of Hannibal, when her son Hasdrubal was to be slaughtered, says in grief in the last book of Silius's Punica, near the end of the fourth book: What, then, is this piety, to sprinkle the shrines with gore? Alas, the first cause of wicked deeds for sick mortals is not to know God. Pray with a righteous, pious incense, and turn the savage rites away from the foul: God is gentle and akin to man. Hitherto let it be enough to have seen the young bulls slain before the altars. Or if it is a sin to wish that the gods above should be fixed, and it is Me, Me whom I bore, take your fill of my vows: does it please you to wander through Libyan lands with such a character?

units.la: Abistu vero sacris cum desissent, postea victi ab Agathocle, Deos propterea subiratos arbitrantur, ut Numen placarent, ducentos Nobilium filios mastasse feruntur ad aras. Id quod etiam a Cretensibus fastitatum comperimus, ut hominem epulis graviatum ac pueros impuberes, festis diebus, Saturno et ipsi mastarent. In Chio et Salamine, cujus supra mentio factæ, mos per multa secula viguit, ut Diomedi et Dionysio homines discerptos jugularent. Ejusdemq; Dionysii templum in Arcadia fuit, in quo puelle ad aram disflagellabantur ad nec em, sicut et Sparta in arce Orthiæ Dianæ pueri. Quinetiam alii ingenti simulacro, vimintibus intexto et vivis hominibus oppleto, ac igne succenso, ipsis sædum in modum examinatis, maximum holocaustoma Diis suis offerre putaverunt. Galatæ et Massagetæ non aliter Deos suos riti consuli arbitrabantur, quam jugulato homine apud aras Deorum: ex cujus casu, tam ex membrorum laniatu, et sanguinis fluxu, futura divinabant. Cymbri noxios homines servatos, sudibus affixos, Diis pro hostiis dabant. Galli, præter Hesum et Theutatem, quos Deos humano cruore placabant, gravioribus morbus aut periculis affectis, ad placandas Deorū iras, aut homines immolabat, aut se immolaturos vovebant: ad cujus aram etiā grandeꝰ ætate, victimarū loco prosecabat. Thraces Zamolxin, quē maximū suum Deū putabant, nō alia ratione sibi propitium fieri arbitrabatur, quam si ad ara facili lanceariū stu homo conciderat, tam optimā et Dius gratissimam victimā opinati. Germani quoq; ritu barbarico, Mercurio humano cruore litare religiosissimū putabat. Idem etiā Senones tradi tur, qui caso publice homine, infanda sacra statis diebus celebrabāt, his portiū expiari delista credebant. Persis etiā, ad habēdas suis Diis gratias, vivētes juvenes eosq; adhuc spi rantes, sub terra defodere, assuetum fuit: quem etiam morem Græcis inoleuisse accepimus, ut in anniuersaria celebritate Bacchi viuos homines sacrificarent: quod ita fuisset immolatus, maximam inter suos probitatis, ac religionis laudem ferebat. Porro Leucadius hoc commune fuisse quidam tradunt, ut in Apollinis Leucadii sacro ad a verticem Deorum iram, hominé de montis specula deiicerent, & in mare precipitem deuoluerent. Fuit & idem moris Albanis, ut homines sacris initiatum, qui sanctitate polleret, diu asseruatum & opiparé saginatum, apud aras sisteret eumq; furiali carmine excantatum, de votumq; additus quibusdam precationibus, cum alius nitti mis immolarent. Quin & Britanni longo tempore morem fuisse accepimus, ut conjuges & nurus nudas, & quodam herbarum succo delibutas, ad templa ducerent, & ita supplicarent, capti vorum sanguine Diis litarét. At vero Corinthii, supra mille prostitutas in templo Veneris assiduè degisse, et inflammata libidine quæstui meretricio operam dedisse, velut sacrorum ministras Deæ samilari solitas, memoriæ esse prodictum. Hic tibi mitto sacratas Lydias & Cyprias libidines. Pigeat vero pudescá, referre, Romanos rerum dominos, quibus sœdera, leges & sacra exteris date nationibus imperium fuisse: quanto in errore, & quàm tetra caligine versatus fuerit victor ille gentium populus, & totius dominator orbis, omni superstitioni obnoxius: sascinos & mutinos nedum funones & Genios quotidie sibi asciscendo, & obscœna numina adoptando: quæ etiam extra ordinaria sacra, ex fatalibus libris facere coactus, Græcè & Græcá, toridemq; Gallos in foro boario ad placandas Deorum iras, sub terras viuos defodere veritus non fuerit. Licuit si illi diu in sacris hominem interimere, & Diis immolare, adeò ut Saturnum & ipse, & Latialem Iovem, humana placaret hostia. Cuius simulachrum dum sacrificaret, humano sanguine proluebant: donec Cn. Cornelio Lentulo, P. Licinio Crasso Coss. Senatu Consulto cautum fuit, ne novam inducere religionem, neve hominem immolare, aut humano sanguine litare liceret.
units.tr: And when, after they had ceased their sacred rites, they were afterwards defeated by Agathocles, they supposed that the gods were angered at them for this reason; so, to placate the divinity, they are said to have slaughtered two hundred sons of nobles at the altars. We have learned that the Cretans also did this, slaughtering for Saturn on festival days a man laden with feasting and immature boys. Among the Chians and at Salamis, of which mention was made above, the custom flourished for many ages of slaughtering men torn to pieces for Diomedes and Dionysus. There was also a temple of this same Dionysus in Arcadia, in which girls were flogged at the altar until blood flowed, just as at Sparta boys were flogged at the citadel of Artemis Orthia. Moreover, others thought they offered their gods a great holocaust by filling a huge image woven of wicker with living men, and setting fire to it, so that the men were burned in a horrible manner. The Galatians and Massagetae believed that their gods could be placated in no other way than by killing a man at the altars of the gods; and from the manner of his death, both from the tearing of his limbs and the flow of his blood, they foretold the future. The Cimbri gave harmful men, impaled on stakes, to their gods as victims. The Gauls, besides Hesus and Teutates, whom they placated with human blood, when afflicted by more serious illnesses or dangers, either sacrificed men or vowed that they would sacrifice them, in order to appease the anger of the gods; and at this altar even those advanced in age were cut up in place of victims. The Thracians thought that Zalmoxis, whom they believed to be their greatest god, could be made propitious to them in no other way than if a man was struck down at the altar by the thrust of a lance, thinking him the best and most pleasing victim to Zalmoxis. The Germans too, with barbarian rite, held it most religious to make an offering to Mercury with human blood. The same is handed down of the Senones, who, when a man had been publicly slain, celebrated unspeakable rites on set days, believing that their city was purified of its crimes by these. It was also customary among the Persians, to give thanks to their gods, to bury young men alive, still breathing, under the earth; and we have heard that this custom also grew up among the Greeks, that at the annual festival of Bacchus they sacrificed living men; and whoever had been sacrificed in this way bore the greatest praise among his own people for uprightness and piety. Further, some write that it was a common custom at Leucas that, in the sacred rite of Apollo Leucadius, to avert the anger of the gods, a man was thrown from a mountain lookout and hurled headlong into the sea. The Alban people also had the custom that a man initiated into the sacred rites, who excelled in holiness, was kept for a long time and fattened richly, then brought before the altars and cursed with a furious chant; and, with some prayers added, when they had been made, others sacrificed with stones. Indeed, we have learned that the Britons for a long time had the custom that wives and daughters-in-law, naked and smeared with a certain juice of herbs, were led to the temples, and in this way they besought the gods, and sought to appease the deities with the blood of captives. But it is recorded in memory that the Corinthians kept more than a thousand prostitutes constantly in the temple of Venus, and, their lust being inflamed, they devoted themselves to harlotry for gain, as if they were customarily taken as servants of the sacred rites of the goddess. Here I send you the consecrated lusts of the Lydians and Cyprians. It shames me and makes me blush to relate that the Romans, lords of affairs, to whom empire was given over foreign nations, along with treaties, laws and sacred rites, how deep in error and how dark the mist in which that victorious people of the nations, and ruler of the whole world, was immersed, subject to every superstition: daily taking to themselves the sorcerer's charms and the mutterers, to say nothing of the funones and Genii, and adopting obscene deities. Being compelled to perform extraordinary sacred rites from the fatal books, they did not hesitate to bury alive in the cattle market, under the earth, both a Greek man and a Greek woman, and likewise two Gauls, to placate the anger of the gods. It was once permitted for them to kill a man in sacred rites for a long time, and to sacrifice him to the gods, so much so that Saturn and Jupiter Latiaris were placated by a human victim. While they were sacrificing before his statue, they used to bathe it in human blood, until, in the consulship of Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus and Publius Licinius Crassus, by a decree of the Senate it was provided that no new religion should be introduced, and that no one should be permitted to immolate a man or to sacrifice with human blood.

units.la: Ex quibus exemplis satis superq́; constat, Ethnicos & Barbaros, hostias rationales, id est homines, integros & solidos, eosq́; secundum ætatem, sexum & conditionem distinctos, Diis suis offerre confuuerisse. Idem etiam hominis partes singulas siue membra Numinibus suis obtulerent, atq́; sacrificarunt. Constat enim ex eodem Arnobio, libro ante citato, Diti & Saturno olim humanis capitibus fuisse supplicatum: & Bojos ac Celtas hostis cal-varium auro celare, & in eo posolentium libare religiosissimum duxisse: item Lusitanos veterem morem fuisse, ex hominis incęstinis exta prospicere, atq; inde omina & varicinia captare, abscissaq; capti vorū dextras pronare Diis offerre. Adde quòd apud Lacedæmonios sanguine hominis aras imbuta fuit: & in Arcadia, Dionysii templo, sacrificii loco, puellæ ad aram flagellabatur ad necem: item quod Bellon̄ sacerdotes non animali hostia, nec victima, sed suo cruore sacrificant. Gladiosenim districtos utráq; manu tenentes, humeros sibi & lacertos, tanquam fanatici, dissecant, hoc sanguine lica & crimina expiari putantes. Sic prodicum memoriæ est, Romulum, nunquam vino in sacris, sed lacte libasse. Ac dedicabant virgines Romane, mature viro, compositiū capillum Palladi. Trazene verò puellæ Hippolyto crinem consecrabant. In Sicyonia quoq; Sanitatis simulacrum fuit, cui virgines crines resecare, & capillos dicare solebant. Athenienses, cùm ex ephœbis excessissent primitias crinium Delphos deferebant: & cùm antiquiores comam circa tempora, aut posterio-rem crinem Apollini & fluminibus tonderent, ævo succedente Theseus τὰ α̈ꝛ̈ꝑ, hoc est, anterioré capillum Delphis dedicavit. Vnde Thesei tonsura prodita est, cujus exemplo juvenes, cùm primùm ex ephebis excessissent, anteriorem comam Phoebo, & Æsculapio, aut Libero obtulere primitias. Postea Romani adolescentes magnæ indolis, primæ lanuginis barbam, Diis consecrari ufurparunt. Hæc Alexander ab Alexandro. Longum vero biscesset exsequi, qui Taurorum populorum mores fuerint, ut apud aram hominem sisterent, qui post solemnes quasdam preces hominis, caput ejus claua feriebant, crucí, illud affigebant; tuncum porro corpus ex ingeni rupe in præceps dabant. Quantaetiam Gentilium hæc insipientia & libido fuerit in hoc sacriciorum genere, dum in templis coiré, & nefandis libidinibus immisceri, ac pudendis genitalibus sacra facere, quid procreationis seminaria essent, nefas non putarent, abunde ex Veneris sacri& Priapi colligere promtum est. Linguam deniq, Mercurio sacrificarunt, de quo supra.
units.tr: From these examples it is quite clear that Gentiles and barbarians were accustomed to offer to their gods rational victims, that is, whole and unblemished human beings, distinguished according to age, sex and condition. They also offered and sacrificed single parts or members of the human body to their deities. For it is established from the same Arnobius, cited above, that long ago Dis and Saturn were propitiated with human heads; that the Boii and Celts thought it most religious to hide an enemy's skull in gold and to drink from it at feasts; and that the Lusitanians had the ancient custom of inspecting the entrails of a human being, seeking omens and predictions from them, and of offering the severed right hands of captives to the gods. Add that among the Lacedaemonians an altar was soaked with human blood; and in Arcadia, at the temple of Dionysus, a girl was flogged at the altar until she died, as a sacrifice; also that the priests of Bellona sacrifice not an animal or a victim but their own blood. For holding drawn swords in both hands, they cut their shoulders and arms like fanatics, believing that crimes are expiated by this blood. Thus it is recorded that Romulus never made libations in sacred rites with wine, but with milk. Roman virgins, when they were married, dedicated their combed hair to Pallas. At Troezen girls consecrated their hair to Hippolytus. In Sicyon too there was an image of Health, to which virgins were accustomed to cut off their locks and dedicate their hair. The Athenians, when they had left the ephebi, carried the first fruits of their hair to Delphi; and when the older men cut their hair at the temples or at the back for Apollo and the rivers, in a later age Theseus dedicated the front hair [τὰ ἔμπροσθεν] to Delphi. Hence the tonsure of Theseus came to be known, and following his example young men, once they had left the ephebi, offered the front hair as first fruits to Phoebus, Aesculapius or Liber. Later the Roman youths of great promise took up the custom of consecrating to the gods the beard of their first down. These things are reported by Alexander ab Alexandro. It would be long to go through all the customs of the Tauri peoples, who would set a man before the altar and, after certain solemn prayers, strike his head with a club, fix his body to a cross, and then cast the body down headlong from a rock. How great the folly and lust of the Gentiles was in this kind of sacrifice, when they did not think it wrong to gather in temples and mingle in unspeakable lusts, and to perform rites upon the private parts as if they were seedbeds of procreation, can easily be gathered from the rites of Venus and Priapus. Finally, they sacrificed the tongue to Mercury, as mentioned above.

units.la: Hujusmodi autem humanas, seu potius inhumanas, & merè diabolicas hostias dubium non est, quin pleræq; Gentes, cùm Deorum suorum, id est Dæmonum oraculà, suasu & hortatu prę cipue. tipuè, tum Abrahami Patriarchæ, qui filium suum Deo, pro singulari sua fide mactare atq; immolare voluerat, exemplo, seu potiùs κατοχηλιαν, tum denique vaticinium illis de futura Christi victima, de qua aliquid audire potuerunt, expiatrice peccatorum totius Mundi, & reconciliatrice Dei, irati Mundo ob illa peccata, adduɛti & impulsi, fecerint atq; celebrarint.
units.tr: There is no doubt that most nations offered such human, or rather inhuman, purely diabolical victims, at the urging and especially at the instigation of the oracles of their gods, that is, of demons, and by the example of the patriarch Abraham, who had wished to slaughter and sacrifice his son to God on account of his singular faith, or rather by a counterfeit of it; and finally by the prophecy, of which they could have heard something, concerning the future sacrifice of Christ, the expiator of the sins of the whole world and the reconciler of God, who was angry with the world for those sins. Driven and impelled by these things, they performed and celebrated such sacrifices.

units.la: De hís ipsis autem sacrificiis: præsertim autem de feelefta & nefaria Heliogabali, Hadriani, Valeriani, Iuliani Apostatæ ἀνθρωποθυσίας, ἀνθρωπομαντείας, id est, hominum immolatione sceleri hac & divinatione ex matlatorum hominü viscceribus, vide Camerarii meditationum historicarum ἀνθρωποcaput quinquagesimum nonum: ubi & de sacrificiis apud Hetruscos, Gallos & aliost populos; ho- Θυσιας dus verò apud Indos Orientales & Occidentales, & nouis illis insulis, fieri solitus, multa scribit ferè ipsè letu dignissima. De Massilienfibus memoria proditum est: Quoties pestilentia laborabat, unus expauperibus sese offerebat alendum, anno integro, publicis precioforibus cibis. Hic posteà vestibus ornatus, & sacris vestibus indutus per totam urbem ducebatur cum exsecrationibus, ut in ipsum omnia civitatis mala reciderent: & sic Dijs immolabatur. Ab hac consuetudine Gallorum traxum videtur verbum Sacrum, pro exsecrando & celesto. Virgilius: ——quid non mortalia pectora cogis Auri sacra fames?
units.tr: Concerning these very sacrifices, and especially the wicked and unspeakable human sacrifices [ἀνθρωποθυσίας] and divinations from human entrails [ἀνθρωπομαντείας] of Heliogabalus, Hadrian, Valerian and Julian the Apostate, that is, the immolation of men and divination from the entrails of slaughtered men, see Camerarius's Meditationes historicae, chapter 59, where he also treats of the sacrifices among the Etruscans, the Gauls and other peoples. He writes many things, nearly all well worth reading, about the sacrifices customary among the Indians of the East and West and on those new islands. The following record concerns the Massilians: whenever the city was afflicted by pestilence, one of the poor offered himself to be maintained at public expense for a whole year on choice foods. Afterwards he was dressed in garments and sacred vestments and led through the whole city with curses, so that all the city's evils would fall upon him; and so he was sacrificed to the gods. The word "sacer," used for accursed and devoted, seems to have been derived from this custom of the Gauls. Virgil: "To what do you not drive mortal hearts, accursed hunger for gold?" Plautus: "Of all men, the most accursed to man is as much of mankind as the earth can bear."

units.la: Plautus: Homini quantum hominum terra suffinet sacerrimo. De his legeetiam Plutarchum de oraculorum defectu: Cælium Rhodiginum libro decimo tertio, capite vigesimo tertio: Alexandrum ab Alexandro libro sexto, capite sexto, & Lactantium Firmianum de Religione libro primo, capite vigesimo primo, & libro quinto, capite decimo: item Theodoretus sermone septimo ad versus Græcos infideles, sub finem. Meminerunt abominandorum illorum sacrificiorum etiam Eusebius & Augustinus, atq; insuper ex Historiis Q. Curtius libro quarto, Iustinus libro decimo octavo, Orosius libro quarto capite sexto, nec non Plato in Minore: clarissimus item Ζ uingerus in Theatro, apud quem, præter superiora, plurima alia exstant exempla eorum, qui homines mactarunt atq; sacrificarunt. Quomodo autem id fieret, & quàm crudelissimè, narrat Diodorus libro vigesimo Bibliothec. & Vivet in Commentariis in caput decimum nonum, libri septimi de Civitate.
units.tr: On these matters read also Plutarch on the decline of oracles; Caelius Rhodiginus, book 13, chapter 23; Alexander ab Alexandro, book 6, chapter 6; Lactantius Firmianus, On Religion, book 1, chapter 21, and book 5, chapter 10; likewise Theodoret, sermon 7 against the Greek unbelievers, near the end. Eusebius and Augustine also mention those abominable sacrifices; and from the histories, Quintus Curtius, book 4; Justin, book 18; Orosius, book 4, chapter 6; and Plato in the Minos. The most distinguished Zwinger in his Theatrum also, besides what has been said above, gives very many other examples of those who slaughtered men and sacrificed them. How it was done, and how cruelly, is related by Diodorus in book 20 of his Bibliotheca, and by Vives in his commentary on chapter 19 of book 7 of The City of God.

units.la: Nec verò tantùm apud gentes profanas & barbaras sed etiam apud ipsum populum Dei, Iudaeos nimirum & Israelitas, exsecranda illa hominum, immolandorum consuetudo inualuit atq; viguit: id quod vel hinc manifestum est, quod liberos suos immolare Iudæi vsitata olim prohibentur Leuitici capite vigesimo, versu secundo, & quod in honorem Molechi, idoli Hammonitarum parentet igne filios suos transfmittere dicuntur secundo Regum, vigesimo tertio, versu decimo tertio.
units.tr: Not only among profane and barbarous nations, but also among God's own people, the Jews and Israelites, that accursed custom of immolating human beings took hold and flourished. This is clear from the fact that the Jews were forbidden long ago to offer their children, as stated in Leviticus, chapter 20, verse 2; and from the fact that, in honour of Molech, the idol of the Ammonites, they are said to have made their sons pass through fire, in 2 Kings, chapter 23, verse 13.

units.la: Nobis quidem Christianis victima humana primaria est victima Christi, qua sola Deus no- sic scribit: Παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοί... παραστῆσαι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν θυσίαν ζῶσαν, ἁγίαν, εὐάρεστον τῷ Θεῷ... Hortor igitur vos fratres, per misericordiam Dei, ut sistatis corpora vestra hostiam viventem, sanctam, acceptam Deo, rationalem illum cultum vestrum. Et ne vos configuratæ seculo isti, sed transformatæ vos per renovationem mentis vestræ, ad hoc, ut probetis quæ sit voluntas Dei, bona illa, accepta & perfecta. Hæc de ἀνθρωποθυσία, si ve immolatione animalium rationalium, quam ipse quoq; Pythagoras summopere, licet Ethnicus, improbavit, censent, cædenon litandum: animalia Dei non mactanda: altaria nullius cede & sanguine imbuenda.
units.tr: For us Christians the chief human victim is the victim of Christ, with which alone God is pleased. Thus Paul writes: "I beseech you, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service [Παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοί... παραστῆσαι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν θυσίαν ζῶσαν, ἁγίαν, εὐάρεστον τῷ Θεῷ]. And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the will of God, good, acceptable and perfect." Concerning human sacrifice, or the immolation of rational animals, which even Pythagoras, though a Gentile, greatly disapproved, these things are held: that blood is not to be offered; that the animals of God are not to be slaughtered; and that altars are not to be soaked with anyone's blood.

units.la: Quantum ad Animalia rationis experientia atq; bruta attinet, cöstat omnis generis animantia, pecora atq; bestias a Gentibus Diis fuisse immolatas, ut terrestres veluti Quadrupedia, & Reptilia: aereas, sive cœlestes, cujusmodi sunt aves aquatiles item & ancipites: licet quasdam gentes a bestiarum vel occisione & immolatione, vel etiam manducatione; idq; vel omnino omnium, vel ocium nonnullarum abhorruisse legamus.
units.tr: As for rational and irrational animals, it is established that the Gentiles sacrificed to their gods animals of every kind, cattle and beasts: terrestrial ones such as quadrupeds and reptiles, aerial or heavenly ones such as birds, and aquatic and amphibious ones as well. Yet we read that some nations abhorred killing, sacrificing or even eating beasts, either all of them or some of them.

units.la: Omnium autem anciquissima apud Echnicos animalium quadrupedum sacrificia, (de quibus idcirco primo loco scribemus) judicarunt esse porcorum atq; suum sacrificia; de quo animali tradunt, id præcipuè Circensibus sacrum fuisse, quod Ioven infantem a Rhea matre, ne a Sacurno parente devoraretur, absconditum in Creta, lactaverit: & ne pueri vagitus a patre audiretur, grunnitu suo obsticeret.
units.tr: Among the Gentiles, the most ancient sacrifices of quadruped animals (which is why we shall write about them first) were judged to be those of swine and sows. They say this animal was especially sacred at the Circensian games, because Rhea, his mother, hid the infant Jupiter in Crete and nursed him, so that he would not be devoured by his father Saturn; and that, so that the baby's cries would not be heard by his father, the sow stifled them with her grunting.

units.la: Sus porrò, inquit Marcus Varro, Græce dicitur ὗς, olim δὸς, a verbo θύειν, quod est, immolare: quoniam a Sullo genere pecoris immolandi initium sumptum videcur: cujus vestigia; quòd initiis Cereri porci immolatur; & quòd initiis pacis fœdus cum feritur, porcum occiditur; & quòd nuptiarum initio antiqui Reges ac sublimes viri in Hecruria, in conjunctione nupciali no- va nupta & novos maricus, primum porcu immolanc. Prisci quoq; Latini & etiam Græci idè factis- tasse videntur. Nam & Romanæ mulieres, maximè nutrices, naturam, quaseminæ sunt, in viginibus appellanc porcum, & Græcè χοῖρον significantes esse dignum insigni nuptiarum. Ob id etiam Hippocrates & Galenus a verbo ἱσπὸν, sacrifico, suem ἱερὸν, idest, victimam passim vocanc; ac præcipuè Galenus in Methodo & de Temperatura. Ac Murecus lib. 3. variarum lectionum cap.7. In Cereris mysterijs, inquit, sa fuit consuetudo, ut quisq; pro se Cereri porco fa- ceret: scu, quòd animal illud infestum Cereri crederetur: scu quòd a suillo rostro arandæ & in vercende cerræ ratio primùm accepta esset. Illud ecia observabatur, ut ec præpinguis essec, & nulla sui parte manceret ac mutilus, quod etiam uri verse in toco victimarum genere servabat. Ergo porcos mysticos seu mystericos vocabanc, qui pinguissimi & incegerrimi essenc. Plautus sinceros sacres vocac. Quare Megarensis ille Aristophanes, qui filius sa as pro porcis vendere cuperec, jubes ejs, ut sacrum ingresse ica grunnirent, ut porci mystici esse videancur. Eadè scribic Erasmus in Adagiis, cujus verba juvat addere: Iniciandi, inquic, cossue veruncimmolare porcum. Suidas ex Aristophane cicac:
units.tr: "The sus," says Marcus Varro, "is called in Greek hys, formerly dos, from the verb thyein, which means to sacrifice, since the pig seems to have been the first kind of animal used for sacrifice. Traces of this remain: a pig is sacrificed at the rites of Ceres; when a treaty of peace is struck, a pig is killed; and at the beginning of marriages the ancient kings and noblemen of Etruria, at the nuptial ceremony, first sacrificed a pig for the new bride and the new groom." The early Latins and the Greeks seem to have done the same. For Roman women, especially nurses, in their girls' talk call the female private parts a pig, which in Greek is [χοῖρον], as if it were worthy of the emblem of marriage. For this reason Hippocrates and Galen commonly call the pig [ἱερὸν], that is, a victim, from the verb meaning to sacrifice; especially Galen, in his Method and On Temperament. Murecus, in book 3, chapter 7 of his Variae lectiones, says: "In the mysteries of Ceres there was a custom that each person sacrificed a pig to Ceres, either because that animal was believed to be hateful to Ceres, or because the method of ploughing and harrowing was first learned from the pig's snout. It was also observed that the victim should be very fat and without any blemish, unmaimed, which is kept in every case as the rule for all victims." Therefore they called the pigs mystic or mysterious, those which were the fattest and most unblemished. Plautus calls them sincere sacred pigs. Hence that Megarian Aristophanes, who wanted to sell his sons as pigs, tells them to go into the sacred precinct and grunt, so that they would appear to be mystic pigs. Erasmus writes the same in his Adages, and his words are worth adding: "At initiations, he says, it was the custom to sacrifice a pig with a spit." Suidas quotes from Aristophanes:

units.la: Εἰς ποιὸν ἰδρύμενον ὧ πάρπαν ἐπὶ τὰ ὀρχημένα·
units.tr: Into whatever place, you fool, for the dances [Εἰς ποιὸν ἰδρύμενον ὧ πάρπαν ἐπὶ τὰ ὀρχημένα]

units.la: Δεῖ γὰρ μυήθῆναι μὲ, ὥσπερ τεθυκέναι. id est,
units.tr: For I must be initiated, just as one who has sacrificed a pig [Δεῖ γὰρ μυήθῆναι μὲ, ὥσπερ τεθυκέναι]. That is:

units.la: Qui portum eman mihi mutua nunc cres drachmas:
units.tr: Will you now lend me three drachmas,

units.la: Initiandus sum prius, ac morcem oppetiam.
units.tr: Before I am initiated and get my pig [Initiandus sum prius, ac morcem oppetiam]?

units.la: Item Plautus in Menæchmis, porcum fincerū & sacrem immolare jubet eum, què mente captum significat. Adolescens, quibus hic precis pore veneum sacres, sinceri, nummi unum en a me accipe: lube te piari de mea pecunia. Naēgo cuidem infastum esse ce cereū scio. Opinor, quod vecerum usu, qui cujussiam nati Nun inis in cem perus agereteur, hoc præculo se folerent purgare.
units.tr: Likewise Plautus, in the Menaechmi, bids a man sacrifice a sincere pig, which signifies a man out of his mind. "Young man, since you are sacred and sincere, take a coin from me and have yourself purified with my money." I certainly know that it is unlucky to be out of one's mind. I suppose that by the ancient custom, those who were to be purified in the course of some family's funeral used to cleanse themselves in this way.

units.la: Est & Græcis proverbium, Ἀσε ἀνὴρ τὶ ἰσχυεῖν, Veneri suem sacrificavit: ubi quis offerit id munus, quod minimè grate sit. Invisite quippe Veneri sus propter Adonus necem. Hinc ὑσηκέα, ceste Athenæo, sacrificii illius celebritas atq; festum ab Argivis, quo suem Veneri sacrificare consueverunc, suc di ctum. Ec in mense Majo mercacores Maiæ, Mercurii parenci, porcam impregnatam immolabant.
units.tr: The Greeks also have a proverb, "He sacrificed a pig to Venus" [Ἀσε ἀνὴρ τὶ ἰσχυεῖν], said when someone offers a gift that is not at all welcome. For the pig was hateful to Venus on account of the death of Adonis. Hence, as Athenaeus says, the celebration and festival of that sacrifice among the Argives, at which they used to sacrifice a sow to Venus, was called the hysēkea [ὑσηκέα]. And in the month of May the merchants used to sacrifice a pregnant sow to Maia, the mother of Mercury.

units.la: Quæ vero familiæ purgandæ causa Cereri immolabatur, porca præcidanea, ut ajc Veranius, est dicta: quòd pars quædam ejus sacrificii sic in conspectu morchi ejus, cujus sunus instituitur. Ac porcam vel agnum regina sacrorum, id est, Regis sacrorum uxor, inquic Festus, in omnibus Kalendis Junoni immolabat. Meminit idem & porci propudiani, sic dicti, ut aji Capito Ateius, qui in sacrificio gentis Claudiæ, veluc piamentum & exsolucio omnis costrieæ religionis est. Fœdus, eodem teste, appellatū ab eo; quòd in paciscendo scederet bostia, præcipuè porca, necaretur. Virg.
units.tr: The sow that was sacrificed to Ceres for the purpose of purifying a household was called the porca praecidanea, as Verrius says, because a part of that sacrifice is performed in the sight of the dead man whose funeral is being arranged. Festus says that the queen of the sacred rites, that is, the wife of the King of the Sacred Rites, used to sacrifice a sow or a lamb to Juno on every Kalends. The same writer also mentions the porci propudiani, so called, as Ateius Capito says, because in the sacrifice of the Claudian clan, it is an expiation and a release from all scrupulous religion. The word foedus (covenant), according to the same witness, was named from this, because in making a treaty the victim, especially a sow, was killed.

units.la: Et cessá jungebant fœdera porcá: vel quia in fœdere inccerponatur.
units.tr: Virgil: "And they joined their covenants by slaying a sow," or because it was interposed in the covenant.
Ovid, Fasti, book 1.

units.la: Prima Ceres a vide gavisa est sanguine porca.
units.tr: "First Ceres rejoiced in the blood of a sow."

units.la: Porco Tellurem placari olim solicam, custacur Horacius, secunda epistola:
units.tr: Horace, in the second Epistle, records that the Earth was once customarily appeased with a pig:
"They appeased the Earth with a pig, and Silvanus with milk."

units.la: quo in loco Porphyrius vult porcum pro porca positum. Arnobius libro primo, Telluri, inquit, sua tri Scropha ingens immolacur fœta, &c.
units.tr: In this place Porphyry holds that "porcus" is put for "porca" (sow). Arnobius, book 1: "To Tellus a huge pregnant sow is sacrificed," and so on.

units.la: Quòd autem Cereri, Telluri & Bonæ Deæ, Macri Dei & Magnæ matri, quæ Deæterram significabant, sues, & quidem prægnances, olim offerebantur, duæ asseri possunt rationes; Vna, quod conuenieus gratuitó ei esset hoc sacrificium. Sus enim humi semper volutatur, juxta illud Horatianum: amica luto sus.
units.tr: As for why sows, and indeed pregnant ones, were once offered to Ceres, Tellus, the Good Goddess, and the Mother of the Gods (Magna Mater), who all signified the goddess Earth, two reasons can be given. First, because this sacrifice was fitting and suitable, since the sow always wallows on the ground, in accordance with the Horatian line: "a sow, friend of the mud."

units.la: Et ut plurimum est niger; sicut & Terra suapte natura nigra est & opaca. Praeterea hae bellua terrae fecunditatem egregie adumbrat. Itaq; interdum Cereri porca praegnans caedebatur. Nam ea legitur ad viginti foetus uno partu edidisse. Triginta ea porca pepererat, quae Aeneae in Tiberi ripa, prodigii loco, visa est, quemadmodum Virgilius refert.
units.tr: And it is generally black, just as the earth itself is black and dark by nature. Besides, this beast vividly represents the fertility of the earth. So sometimes a pregnant sow was slaughtered for Ceres. For she is read to have brought forth about twenty young at one birth. A sow had given birth to thirty, which was seen by Aeneas on the bank of the Tiber as a portent, as Virgil reports.

units.la: Aliem ratio est a contrario. Ratio enim, cur alue victimae aliis Dijs maclarentur, juxta Servium, non tantum ad consensum referenda est, quem bellua cum Deo aliquo habet, sed etiá quod quaedam inter eos inimicitia exsistit. Haec, de causa sunt, qui in Cereris sacrificijs suem volunt fuisse adhibitam, quód scilicet Deae isti gratum id esse spectaculum, si inimica ejus, adipsius pedes mortua jaceret, quae non solum segetes vastaret, sed & feminaipsa, terrae mandata, devoraret. Eadem quoq; ratione Baccho caper immolabatur, tanquam bestia, vitibus maximè adversa.
units.tr: The other reason is from the opposite. For the reason why other victims were slaughtered for other gods, according to Servius, must be referred not only to the affinity which the beast has with some god, but also to the fact that some enmity exists between them. These are the grounds of those who say that a sow was used in the sacrifices of Ceres: namely, that this spectacle would be pleasing to the goddess if her enemy lay dead at her feet, an enemy that not only laid waste the crops but also devoured the very woman committed to the earth. By the same reasoning a goat was sacrificed to Bacchus, as an animal especially hostile to vines.

units.la: Etsi vero Sylvanus latte, ut supra ex Horatio est dictum, fuit culeus: tamen eundem porco quoq; interdum placari fuisse solitum, testantur illa Juvenalis:
units.tr: Although Silvanus was, as said above from Horace, appeased with milk, nevertheless it is attested that he too was sometimes appeased with a pig, as the words of Juvenal testify:
"To give a pig to Silvanus, and to wash for a farthing."
And in the second Satire:
"And they appease him with the tender belly of a sow."

units.la: Termino quoq; etsi Numa Pompilius flaturerat, neex re animata res sacra fieret: agnam tamen & porcam illi immolari solitam prodidit Ovidius lib.2. Fastorum; & Horatius:
units.tr: Although Numa Pompilius had forbidden that any sacred rite be performed with a living thing, Ovid, in book 2 of the Fasti, reports that a lamb and a sow were customarily sacrificed to Terminus; and Horace says:
"And lambs slain at the Terminalia."

units.la: ubi Acron, Terminaliorum inquit diem institutum, ut per epularum festivitatem caesis agnis finis servari faceret; de quibus plura Festus & Macrobius.
units.tr: Where Acron says that the day of the Terminalia was instituted so that, by the festivity of the feast, the boundaries might be kept by slaughtering lambs. Festus and Macrobius say more about these matters.

units.la: Aliae tamen gentes a fusilli pecoris & esu & immolatione abhorruerunt. Namapud Phaenicces ut in canis, sic in sacrificiis a suibus abstinere praecipiebatur: & in Mysia Abretani Iovis templum erat, in quo suem comesse aut mactasse piacul erat, teste Alexandro ab Alexandris lib.3,cap.12. Sed de hoc suillo sacrificio vide, si vis, plura apud Gyraldum, fyutagmate 17 Hiforiae Deorum.
units.tr: Other nations, however, shrank from eating and sacrificing domestic animals. For among the Phoenicians, as with dogs, abstaining from swine was prescribed in their sacrifices. In Mysia there was a temple of Jupiter Abretanus, in which eating or slaughtering a pig was an expiation, according to Alexander ab Alexandro, book 3, chapter 12. But on this swine sacrifice, see, if you wish, more in Giraldus, Syntagma 17 of the History of the Gods.

units.la: Adde huic Sueovetaurilia, sacrificium ex sue, ove & tauro, toties fieri solitum, quoties milites retenfebantur, & exercitus lustratio fiebat, ut docet Livius lib.7. Hujusmodi sacrificii exemplum, & simago exstat in Columna illa marmorea Trajani, Romae in medio foro erecta, nunc etiam exstante, quae gentinae ejus Imperatoris in Dacos expeditionis rerumq; gestarum infigne est monumentum. Ex illo ipso autem monumento liquet, maesculà fuisse ea animalia; quandoquidem illic videre licet arietem & verrem.
units.tr: Add to this the suovetaurilia, a sacrifice of pig, sheep and bull, which was often performed whenever soldiers were mustered and the army was purified, as Livy teaches in book 7. An example and image of this sacrifice survives on that marble column of Trajan, erected in the middle of the Forum at Rome, still standing today, which is a famous monument to the Emperor's expedition against the Dacians and to his deeds. From that same monument it is clear that these animals were male, since there one can see a ram and a boar.

units.la: Hoc ipso vero, ut hoc quoq; colophonis loco addam, impuri immundi, animalis sacrificio (a cujus & esu & immolatione Deus populum suum sacrosanctum abstinere atq; adeò animus suis pe nunc abhorrere voluit) cui magnam Deos suos placandi, res quasi vis & personas iniciandi, purgandi atq; lustrandi vim tribuebant, satus superq; suam eum natura, vitae atq; morum, tum religuorum sacrificiorum superstitionum, suarum impuritatem atq; furciti prodiderunt ac demonstrarunt. Ipsi, inquá, Ethnici, tanquam sues, sive porci lutulenti & immundi Dij, seu Daemonib. portuis suis, ceu suibus atq; porcis feedu impuris & immundis, sues mersto atq; porcos immolarunt.
units.tr: Indeed, to add this too by way of a colophon: the impure and unclean animal (from whose eating and sacrificing God wished his holy people to abstain, and indeed to make their minds shrink from it) was attributed by the Gentiles with great power to appease their gods, as if to bind and atone for persons and things, to purify and lustrate. These very Gentiles, by their own nature, life and morals, and by their other superstitions, have shown and demonstrated their own impurity and filthiness. They themselves, I say, like pigs, or muddy and unclean gods, or like swine and hogs, foul, impure and unclean, sacrificed sows and pigs to demons, their companions.

units.la: Denique, de jurandi ritu & exsecrationibus superpoream, quasi in fœderibus Romani concipiebant, praesentibus facialibus vide Verderum. Haëtenus de ioSvoia, sive immolatione suum.
units.tr: Finally, concerning the ritual of swearing and curses, which the Romans used in treaties in the presence of the fetials, see Verderus. Thus far on the sacrifice of swine.

units.la: Aggrediamur nunc immolationem boum (sub quibus juvenci, tauri, vaccae, vitulí atque vitulae comprehenduntur) quam a Graecâ βυσιας voce Latini, eodè nomine retento, Buthysiam appellant, ut, praeter alios, Suetonius in Nerone. Unde & verbum βυσιεύειν, quod duo significat. Primò bovem immolare: deinde, quoniam bovem immolare non erat nisi divitum atq; Regum, in genere quod vis magnum, splendidum & sumtuosum sacrificium facere significat (cujusmodi erat Hecatombe) quo verbo Aristophanes in Pluto & Arrianus usus est; quod Grammatici a Bü, particulae, quae intendendi vim habet, derivant, ut βούλιμον, βυσινεω, βυσιναν dicunt, cum magnam famem, sicum, & sitim significare volunt.
units.tr: Let us now take up the sacrifice of oxen (under which heifers, bulls, cows, calves and young cows are included), which the Latins, keeping the same name from the Greek word βυσία, call buthysia, as Suetonius does, among others, in Nero. Hence also the verb βυσιεύειν, which has two meanings. First, to sacrifice an ox. Then, since sacrificing an ox was only for the rich and kings, it signifies in general to make any great, splendid and costly sacrifice (of which kind was the hecatomb). Aristophanes in Plutus and Arrian used this word. Grammarians derive it from βού, a particle having the force of intensifying, whence they say βούλιμον, βυσινάω, βυσίναν, when they wish to signify great hunger, thirst and dryness.

units.la: De hac porrò spetie animalis, nempe bovis, nō tantum in utraq; hac re divina; Neftoris quidem apud Homerum; Argonautarum vero apud Apollonium, sed etiam apud Ethnicos fere omnes crebra frequentia, falsa est immolatio, de qua Plinius libro octavo, capite quadragesimo quinto dicit opimas esse victimas, & lautissimam Deorum placationem.
units.tr: Concerning this kind of animal, namely the ox, sacrifice of oxen is frequent and common not only in those divine rites of Nestor in Homer and of the Argonauts in Apollonius, but also among almost all the Gentiles. Pliny, in book 8, chapter 45, says that such victims are rich and the most sumptuous appeasement of the gods.

units.la: Primum igitur hoc loco legimus Minervae Nestoris, & Apollini Argonautas boves immolasse: & Minervae quidem bovem luteum, id est, juvencam; quia Euphathius etymologice, sive hoc loco interpretatur, idest, unius tantum anni: item, ad μίτλων, ad ἀρήσσον, hoc est, interpretetur ipsfo Homero, ἀν ἐπω ἐν ἐργάω ἀπ' ἀπὸ χαλκὸς δυ ἡ πόρ, indomitam, quondam jugo subtatum: cuiusmodi boves Latini Injuges vocant, & Virgilius intactas cervice juvencas: Homerus vero ἡχίζω ἀκέρα τῶς, quae nondum flumulum experta sunt. Paulanias boves ἡχίζω vocat, eodem tefle, ἀρχαδὰς, ἀ ἄλ ὠμιδὸς ἀ, ὁ ἐμά ὅ ἀ ἀ, Con venichat autem bujusmodi boves, ut inquit Euphathius, Minervae ἀ ἀ ἐ ἀ ἀ, id est, semper juvenescentia atque conjugii experti. Testatur idem Arnobius, inquiens: Telluri matrisferoa ingens immolatur fata: Minervae virgini virgo caditur vitula, nullis unquam simulis, nullius operis excitata conatu. Alias, ut hoc quoque addam, bos jam jugo subactus non purus habebatur. Agamemnon Iovi sacrificavit ... Iliad. B.id est, quinquennalem: quae insignis victima ducebatur.
units.tr: First, then, in this place we read that Nestor sacrificed oxen to Minerva, and the Argonauts to Apollo: to Minerva a yellow ox, that is, a heifer, because Eustathius interprets it in his commentary as meaning one of only one year old. Likewise, as Homer himself describes it, an ox "unbroken, never yet subjected to the yoke" (such oxen the Latins call injugae, and Virgil "heifers untouched in the neck"), which has never yet experienced the plough. Pausanias, by the same witness, calls such oxen Arcadian. Such oxen suited Minerva, as Eustathius says, being always young and never having experienced marriage. The same Arnobius testifies, saying: "A huge pregnant mother-sow is sacrificed to Tellus; to the virgin Minerva a virgin heifer is slain, never yoked to any labour or drawn to any work." Otherwise, to add this too, an ox already broken to the yoke was not considered pure. Agamemnon sacrificed to Jupiter (Iliad B), that is, a five-year-old ox, which was regarded as a distinguished victim.

units.la: Argonautae vero boves immolarunt Apollini simul & Neptuno. Est enim, ut Euphathius in quit, bos, sive taurus oixeiov ... Sacrificios Minervae victima mari familiaris: id quod Herodotus quoque docet his verbis: ... Mari mattari soliti tauri.
units.tr: The Argonauts sacrificed oxen to Apollo and Neptune together. For, as Eustathius says, the ox or bull is [οἰκεῖον] ... The victim for sacrifices to Minerva is one familiar to the sea, as Herodotus also teaches in these words: ... bulls accustomed to the sea.

units.la: Porro et alias gentes, ... personas. (Nam de hac quoque immolatione latius aliquato videtur esse dicendum) hoc genere sacrificiis usus esse passim apud autores cum sacros, tum profanos legimus: id quod de Agamemnone praecipue & Alcinoo de Homero testatur, eos vimirum Iovi bove immolasse: et de Pythagora Cicero, qui bove immolanti Musis. Sic Plutar. tradit Aegyptios Typhoni boves rufas mactasse. Eede Lacedaemonius traditur, eos Marti bovem immolasse, quando victoriam potitisse ... Sic bove aurato XVIII. Aug. placabatur: et Herculi mactabatur in ara apud eosdem maxima juvencus in quo sacrificio Praefi aut Perifex, qui rem divinam facit, folia lauro, nec alia fronde coronabatur: cui mulierib. adesse sacris & rem divinam facere omnis. Fere liceat; huic tamen sacrificio adesse, vel exta tagere, aut vestiri, aut solennia etiam videre, religio non permittebat. De hoc sacrificio & variis ejus cerimoniis legendus Alexandrus ab Alexandro lib.2. cap.14. Idem testis est, Iovi a Flamine dialiomnib. Idib. bove cantidum & ex agro Falisco, vel Mevania immolatum: qui & Hordalii dierum festorum meminit, in quib. hordeo hoc est, pregnates immolabatur boves, etiam in dieb. atris & nefastis, in quibus aliis nullum sacrificium ritè fieri poterat. Sic Telluri, terrae Deae, mense Aprili Romani bovem forda, id est, gravidam mactabat, vaccas, pregnates: ex quib. vitulos, aminiferis enectos, maxima virgo crematur. Hinc Fordicidia ... in quib. boflus, quae uterus ferax immolare solebat; quorum meminit ... Alexandrus ab Alexandris. Mercurio quoq; Phlefio ... Arrianus cum sus fos ... Trapezuntis, antequam vastimaris Euxini navigatione periculosa immolasse, ho ... Fuit aut hic veterum mos, ut quoties grave aliquod, longue periculosum, iter esset suscepturi, primo Diis sacra facerent, vel bove, vel alia belua immolata: quae idcirco ab illis ἑκάτης appellabatur. Eiusmodi non tantum Arriani hujus, sed & Xenophontis olim ara Cyri, et Argonautarum, quorum supra meminimus, ante quam navigationem suam maris inirent, sacrificium fuerit. De hoc sacrificio lex etiam opimorum ploriorum in libris Pontificum loquitur: Cujus auspicio classe procinita opimaplolia capiuntur, Iovi Feretrio darier oporteat, & bovem caedito, qui cepit eam ducenta. Secunda pyhlia in Martis aram in campo, Solitaurilia utra volueris, cedito. Tertia pyhlia Iano Quirino agnum marem caedito centum, qui ceperis ex aere dato. Festus.
units.tr: Other nations too, ... persons. (For this kind of immolation also seems to require a fuller discussion.) We read in both sacred and profane authors that this kind of sacrifice was used everywhere. This is attested especially of Agamemnon, and of Alcinous in Homer, that they sacrificed an ox to Jupiter; and Cicero says of Pythagoras that he sacrificed an ox to the Muses. Thus Plutarch relates that the Egyptians slaughtered red oxen for Typhon. It is also recorded that the Lacedaemonians sacrificed an ox to Mars when they had won a victory ... Thus Augustine's account has a gilded ox placating (XVIII. Aug.). At the altar of Hercules among the same people a great young bull was slain. In this sacrifice the Praefect or Perifex, who performs the holy rite, was crowned with bay leaves and no other foliage; women were generally allowed to be present at sacred rites and to perform them, but to be present at this sacrifice, to touch the entrails, to be dressed for it, or even merely to watch its solemnities, was forbidden by religious law. Alexander ab Alexandro, book 2, chapter 14, should be read on this sacrifice and its various ceremonies. The same witness says that a white ox, castrated and taken from the Falerian or Mevanian land, was sacrificed to Jupiter by the Flamen Dialis on all the Ides. He also mentions the Hordicalia, the festival days on which pregnant oxen were sacrificed with barley, even on dark and unlucky days, when no other sacrifice could properly be made. Thus the Romans sacrificed a pregnant cow, a forda, to Tellus, the goddess of the earth, in April, and the Vestal virgin burned the calves taken from those cows. Hence the Fordicidia, at which the people used to sacrifice a fruitful pregnant cow; Alexander ab Alexandro also mentions these. Arrian, too, relates that Phlesian Mercury ... and that a sow ... was sacrificed at Trapezus before the dangerous voyage across the Euxine Sea. It was indeed the custom of the ancients that whenever they were about to undertake any grave and very dangerous journey, they first performed sacred rites to the gods, with an ox or another beast sacrificed; and for this reason such a victim was called [ἑκάτη]. Such a sacrifice was made not only by this Arrian, but also long ago by Xenophon at the altar of Cyrus, and by the Argonauts, whom we mentioned above, before they entered upon their voyage on the sea. The law of the rich spoils in the books of the Pontiffs also speaks of this sacrifice: "By whose auspices the fleet is prepared and rich spoils are taken, an ox shall be given to Jupiter Feretrius and slaughtered, which he who captured it shall lead." Second, "in the Campus Martius at the altar of Mars, choose whichever of the solitaurilia you wish, and slaughter it." Third, "for Janus Quirinus, slaughter a hundred male lambs, which he who captured them shall give from the money." Festus.

units.la: Pertinet huc, quod Lunae taurus quilibet: cujus quidem cornua similia videntur tauro: & lunoni taurus albus olim caedebatur: e contrà, quod vitulis nec quis Dianae immolet, lex erat: & quod ixaruliciis yilulcem, centenum & millenum mactatorum boum sacrificium inde natum etiá de cuius quidam centenarii numeri sacri praefatio vide epistolam Iuliani ad Sarapionem. Legimus tamen etiam Minervae taurum album immolatum fuisse Romae: & Veneri Cornuta apud Tuffas gentem Aegyptiam, vaccam quamvis; (apud alios tamen Aegyptios vaccam immolare erat nefas.) Proserpina vero vaccam sterilem. Testatur hoc Virgilius in sexto Aeneidos: Sterilemq; tibi Proserpina vaccam.
units.tr: To this belongs the fact that any bull is sacred to the moon, whose horns seem similar to a bull's; and that a white bull was once sacrificed to the moon. On the contrary, it was law that no one sacrifice a calf to Diana. And from the hecatomb, the sacrifice of a hundred or a thousand slaughtered oxen, a custom arose, as to which, for the sacred meaning of certain numbers of hundreds, see Julian's letter to Sarapion. We nevertheless read that a white bull was also sacrificed to Minerva at Rome, and to Venus Cornuta among the Tuffas, an Egyptian people, a cow, though among other Egyptians it was forbidden to sacrifice a cow. Proserpina, however, received a barren cow. Virgil bears witness to this in the sixth book of the Aeneid: "and a barren cow for you, Proserpina."

units.la: Et Aur. Prudentius in primo contra Symmachum: Rapta ad Tartarei thalamum Proserpina Regis, Placatur vacca sterilis cervice resecta.
units.tr: And Aurelius Prudentius in the first book against Symmachus: "Proserpina, carried off to the bedchamber of the King of Tartarus, is appeased by a barren cow with its neck cut."

units.la: Seneca quoq; teste est, principes victores tanrorū & vitulorū ingentē numerū Diis suis immolasse.
units.tr: Seneca also testifies that victorious leaders sacrificed huge numbers of bulls and calves to their gods.

units.la: Nec vero tantum immolatio hæc bonm, tanrorum, vitulorum, & vitularum apud Gentiles in usu fuit: sed etiam Israelitas hanc Deus exprobrat apud Hoseam Prophetam, inquiens capitis duodecimo, ver.su duodecimo: In Gilgale boves sacrificant, sciliect Dijs suis alienis: quasi dicas, nullus est locus non impuritissimus sacrificiis illis & altaribus Ethnicorum profanatus.
units.tr: Nor was this immolation of oxen, bulls, calves and heifers used only among the Gentiles; God also rebukes the Israelites for it through the prophet Hosea, saying in chapter 12, verse 12: "In Gilgal they sacrifice oxen" to their strange gods. As if to say, there is no place that was not polluted by those sacrifices and altars of the heathen.

units.la: Hallenus dictum est etiam de Bucolia, sive immolatione boum, & reliquarū ejus speciarum: quod sacrificium, etsi a pleriq; gentibus magnifico, splendido, apparatu & frequenter, robus pretertium in arduis & magni momenti, fuit celebratum, & factum: tamen apud nonnullas ipsum illicium atque nefarium exilitimabatur. Solonis quidem lege de bove nulli Deo sacrificare licebat, quia animal putaretur innocuum, colonū, laboris humani socium.
