Tantæ enim veneratio ut Veteribus quibusdam fuit, ut æque capitale censerent bovem, ac cīvem macasse. Sic Aegyptii bovem, Apin dictum, summa veneratione coluerunt, ut teste est Plinius libro octavo. Homerus cecinit, Apollinem, sive Solem, Hyperionis focus graviter succensuisse, quod illi bovem, animal τροφὸς εἰς πόλιν occiderint, de quo Caelius Rhodiginus libro duodecimo, capite primo. Postea tamen, boves sacrificia crebro admodum frequentata & celebrata fuisse legimus, ut ex indutione inperiorum exemplorum splendidissime elucet: quibus addit, colophonus loco, Bovem primo a Prometheo occisum fuisse, secundum nonnullos: quidam Erechteum, Atheus imperantem primum omninum in Iovis Polei ara bovem immolasse ajunt: unde Bucoea, vetus fettis fit profectum; de quo Gyraldus Syntagmate decimoseptimo Historiæ Deorum sic disserit: Bucoea festivitas quedam fuit apud Athenienses, quæ in Dei Polei, id est, Iovis Polei honore agebatur: in bos bos mactaba-tur ab eo, qui ex re Bucoeo, id est, bovicida dicebatur. Festa ipsum ab vetustatem desitum nomen tantummodo retinuit: siquidem cum prius bos caderetur, mox papanon pro bove offerebant: papanon ipsum, id est, placentæ nuncupantes bove, ut ex Hesychio cōstat. De Buphoniis vero meminit in Nebulis Aristophanes, ἐν νάξει, Bupovion, Et Cecida, inquit, & Buphoniorū. Hæc illa.
units.tr: So much has been said about the Bucolia, or slaughter of oxen, and its other kinds. Although this sacrifice was performed by many nations with magnificent, splendid and frequent preparation, and in matters of great difficulty and importance, yet among some it was considered unlawful and wicked. By the law of Solon, no one was allowed to sacrifice an ox to any god, because it was thought to be an innocent animal, the farmer's companion in human labour. Some of the ancients held the ox in such reverence that they judged slaying an ox to be as capital a crime as slaying a citizen. Thus the Egyptians worshipped with the greatest veneration the ox called Apis, as Pliny attests in book eight. Homer sang that Apollo, or the Sun, the son of Hyperion, was deeply angered because they had killed the oxen, [τροφὸς εἰς πόλιν], the city's nurturers; Caelius Rhodiginus discusses this in book twelve, chapter one. Afterwards, however, we read that ox sacrifices were very often frequented and celebrated, as is most splendidly clear from the citation of the above examples. To these he adds, by way of conclusion: the ox was first killed by Prometheus, according to some; others say that Erechtheus, reigning at Athens, first sacrificed an ox at the altar of Jupiter Polieus; whence the Bucoea, an ancient festival, took its origin. Gyraldus treats this in book seventeen of his Historia Deorum as follows: "The Bucoea was a festival among the Athenians, celebrated in honour of the god Polieus, that is, Jupiter Polieus. An ox was slaughtered in it by one who was called the Bucophonus, that is, the ox-slayer. The festival, after the custom of antiquity, retained only the name; for although formerly an ox was killed, they afterwards offered cakes in place of the ox, calling the cakes papanon, that is, placentae, as is clear from Hesychius." Concerning the Buphonia, Aristophanes makes mention in the Clouds: "in the Naxian (?) ... Bupovion, and Cecida, and of the Buphonia." So far Gyraldus.

units.la: SEQVITVR nunc Ιππωνπίς, sive equorum immolatio. Hæc immolatio non minus frequens & usitata olim Ethnicis fuit, quam illa boum, sive taurorum. Hinc Romæ Idibus Decembribus, a ludis Circensibus, dexter equus, qui vicerat, sacer Martii immolabatur, preciṡamq; caudam quisquis ad Reginam appellatam portabat, aramq; sanguine cōspergebat. De capite quidam a Sacra via, alii a Suburra descendentes depugnabant. Virum, ut ajunt nonnulli, quod equo captam arbitrentur Trojam, equum multant, ut qui Troja mixta essent fobolesprælara Latinis:
units.tr: NEXT comes the Hippōpolis, or sacrifice of horses [Ἱππονπίς]. This immolation was in ancient times no less frequent and customary among the heathen than that of oxen or bulls. Hence at Rome, on the Ides of December, after the Circus games, the right-hand horse that had won was sacrificed to Mars. Whoever carried its tail to the place called the Regia sprinkled the altar with its blood. Men from the Sacred Way and from the Suburra came down and fought over the head. Some say that because they thought Troy had been captured by a horse, they punished the horse, since the Trojans who had been mixed in with the Latins were the offspring of ...

units.la: An quod ferox, bellax, & martialis equus fit, gratissima & maximè Diis immolant? Immolatur victor, quod victoria auctor hic sit Deus: vel potius, quod stabilitatis opifex Martii sit: ac faperunt, qui locum tenent in acie, illos qui deserūs locum & fugam capiunt: punissurū ut timiditatis occasio pernicitas, discunt, per ænigma eam fugientibus non esse salutarem. Hæc Plutarchus in quæstionibus Romanis.
units.tr: Or is it because the horse is fierce, warlike and martial, that they sacrifice it to the gods, who most like it? The victor is sacrificed because this god is the author of victory; or rather, because Mars is the maker of steadfastness. And those who hold their place in battle teach that those who desert their post and take to flight, as if to punish the cowardice of the swift, learn by this riddle that flight is no safe refuge. So Plutarch in his Roman Questions.

units.la: Ab hac consuetudine immolandi equos, October equus, Festo testæ, appellabatur, qui in capo Martio, mense Octobri, Martii quotannis immolabatur, de cujus capite maxima erat contentio inter Subnrianos & Sacravienses; ut hi in regiæ pariete: illi ad turrim Mamiliam id figerent: cujus cauda ut ex ea sanguis in focum distillaret, participandæ rei divinæ gratia, magna celeritate perferebatur in regiam. Ejunm autem hostiæ loco quidam Martii bellico Deo sacrari dicebant, non ut vulgus putabat, quia velut supplicii de eo sumeretur, quod Romani Ilios fuit orinn-di, & Trojani ista effigie fuit capti.
units.tr: From this custom of sacrificing horses the October Horse was named (Festus), which was sacrificed every year in the Campus Martius in October to Mars. Over its head there was great contention between the men of the Suburra and the men of the Sacra Via: the former fixed it on the wall of the Regia, the latter at the Mamilian tower. Its tail was carried swiftly to the Regia, so that the blood dripping from it onto the hearth could be shared in the divine rite. Some said that a horse of Mars was consecrated to the warlike god in place of a victim, not, as the common people thought, as a punishment exacted from it because by that effigy the Romans were ... of Troy, and the Trojans were captured.

units.la: Paulus præterea testatur, Romanos solitos fuisse equi ipsius Idibus Octobris, in campo Martio, immolati caput panibus redimisse, quia sacrificium fiebat ob frugum evectum, & equum potui, quam bovem fuisse immolatum: quod hic bos frugibus pariendis esset aptus.
units.tr: Paulus further testifies that the Romans used to wreathe with loaves the head of a horse sacrificed on the Ides of October in the Campus Martius. The sacrifice was made for the sake of the harvest, and a horse was offered rather than an ox, because the ox is suited to producing crops.

units.la: Nec vero tantum Romanis, sed multis etiam aliis gentibus equum hostiarum numero habitus fuisse testimonio sunt, ut inquit Festus, Lacedemonii, qui in monte Taygeto equis Ventis immolabant, ibidemque adolebant, uteorum flatu cinis ejus perfinis quam latissime deferretur: Et Salus, apud quos Menzanae Iovi dicatus Ἱππιος conjiciebatur in igne: Et Rhodii, qui quotannis quadrigas Soli consecratas in mare jaciebant, quod ut talis vehiculo Mundi feratur circumvehi. Sic Persae equo placare fuerunt solitis, teste Ovidio in Fastis:
units.tr: Horses were counted among the victims not only by the Romans but by many other nations as well. Festus is a witness: the Lacedaemonians, who on Mount Taygetus sacrificed horses to the winds and burned them there, so that the ash might be carried as widely as possible on the breath of the winds; and the Salii, among whom a horse dedicated to Jupiter [Menzanae] was thrown into the fire [Ἱππιος]. Also the Rhodians, who each year cast into the sea four-horse chariots consecrated to the Sun, because the Sun is carried around the world by such a vehicle. So the Persians used to propitiate the Sun with a horse.

units.la: Placat equo Persis, radius hyperiona cinctum.
units.tr: The Persians propitiate with a horse the Sun, Hyperion, girt with rays.

units.la: Et Strabo libro undecimo equum a Massagetis Soli victimam mactari scripsit. Idem Herodotus a Scythis fieri tradit. Philostratus in Heroicis refert, Palamedes Graecis praecepisse, ut orienti Soli equum candidum mactarent. Parrhasii tamen in Arcadia Apollini Epicurio, id est, auxiliari aprum sacrificabant, de quo postea. Myfi quoq; non nisi immolato prius equo et litato ex eius depasftu vota conceperunt. Sic Gothos, testatur Iohannes Magnus libro primo capite decimo tertio, procedeferos in praelium, equos ad aras immolare fuisse solites: quorum abscisa capita continuo excepta, subjectis fiipitibus distentos faucium ritus ante acies praeferebant.
units.tr: Strabo, in book eleven, wrote that the Massagetae slaughtered a horse as a victim for the Sun, and Herodotus reports the same of the Scythians. Philostratus, in the Heroica, relates that Palamedes instructed the Greeks to sacrifice a white horse to the rising Sun. The Parrhasians in Arcadia, however, sacrificed a boar to Apollo Epicurius, that is, the Helper, of which more later. The Mysians too never made vows without first sacrificing a horse and obtaining favourable omens from its grazing. John Magnus, in book one, chapter thirteen, testifies that the Goths, when they went out fiercely to battle, were accustomed to sacrifice horses at the altars. Their heads, cut off at once, were held up before the battle lines on stakes placed beneath them, with the distended jaws.

units.la: Ad hunc morem equos immolandi alludit etiam Arrentinus lib. 1. Annalii Bojorum, sic scribens: Vnus ducis Maforum, qui per Marcii Crassum vicit fnnt ante aciem postulato filio: Quos vos, inquit, estis? Respondunt inVice, Romani rerum domini. Et illi, Ita, inquiunt, fiet, si nos vicerit: et flatim ante acie immolato equo, cuccpere vota, ut ceferi ducis extis et litarct et vsfcerentur.
units.tr: Arrentinus, in book one of his Annals of the Boii, also alludes to this custom of sacrificing horses, writing thus: One of the chiefs of the Boii, who was defeated by Marcus Crassus, asked his son's ... before the battle line. "Who are you?" he said. They answered in turn, "Romans, masters of the world." "So it will be," they said, "if he defeats us." At once, before the battle line, a horse was sacrificed, and they began their vows, so that the leader and the rest might both obtain omens from the entrails and eat of them.

units.la: Nam etiam hoc animal legimus apud Gentiles certis Diis ac Numinibus fuisse consecratum. Hinc quia et a Carmanis Mars colebatur: huic ante meque ovi immolare Veteres solebant, quibus quidem illi carent; ideo asinos, quibus in bello uterentur, illi sacrificabant, ut Strabo in xv. scribit. Scytharum quinetiam bofias fuisse asinos testatur Arnobius. Priapi quoq; bofias fuit asinus, propter membri virilis magnitudinem: cujus fabulam vide apud Lactantium Firmianum, et Ovidium in Fastis, quincer alia sic canit:
units.tr: We read also that among the Gentiles this animal was consecrated to certain gods and divinities. Since Mars was worshipped by the Carmanians, the ancients used to sacrifice horses to him before battle, but the Carmanians lack horses. Therefore they sacrificed asses, which they used in war, as Strabo writes in book fifteen. Arnobius testifies that asses were also the victims of the Scythians. The ass was also the victim of Priapus, on account of the size of his male member. For his story see Lactantius Firmianus and Ovid in the Fasti, who sings elsewhere: "A little donkey is also sacrificed to the stiff guardian of the field."

units.la: Ceditur et rigido custodi ruris asellus: Vbiper custodem ruris Priapum intelligit, de quo officio ejus dictum est supra, cum de Dijs agriculturae ageremus.
units.tr: By "the guardian of the field" he means Priapus, whose office was spoken of above, when we treated of the gods of agriculture.

units.la: Ac alia quidem fuerunt propria et ordinaria huic vel illi Deo offerri solita: alia extraordinaria pro re, loco atq; tempore. Ut, exempli gratia, Priapi bofia propria fuit asinus, ut paullo antea dictum est: Eidem tamen sacrum hebac et vitulā et hircō birfuto, et saginato agno: quae impropria et extraordinaria sacra illi fuerunt habita. Sic in Priapeis:
units.tr: Some offerings were proper and customary for this or that god; others were extraordinary, according to the matter, place and time. For example, the ass was Priapus' proper victim, as was said a little before. Yet the kid, the heifer, the shaggy he-goat and the fattened lamb were also sacred to him, and these were regarded as improper and extraordinary sacrifices to him. So in the Priapea:
"The boy of the master's blooming lamb"

units.la: Poma Priapo offert, etc. Lectumetiam in hifloria est, ab Hyperboreis Apollini asinum immolari: cui sententiae affipulatur Cullimachus.
units.tr: "offers apples to Priapus," and so on. It is also read in history that the Hyperboreans sacrifice an ass to Apollo, and Callimachus supports this opinion.

units.la: Τέρπνοι λιναμφει φοῖβος οἱ ἰδοφορο, id est, pingues Apollinem obleftant asinorum jugulationes. Sed et de Hyperboreis Pindarus in Pythiis:
units.tr: "Delightful ... Phoebus ... the fat ones": that is, the fat ones appease Apollo with the slaughter of asses [Τέρπνοι λιναμφει φοῖβος οἱ ἰδοφορο]. But Pindar also speaks of the Hyperboreans in his Pythian odes:

units.la: Παρ' οἷς ποτὶ πρoσόμεις ἰὸ αὐτῶν λαζίτας Βῶμον λαθλθέ πλείας ὅτι ιχθύων.
units.tr: "Among whom, approaching the ... altar of ... they ... many ... of the fish" [Παρ' οἷς ποτὶ πρoσόμεις ἰὸ αὐτῶν λαζίτας Βῶμον λαθλθέ πλείας ὅτι ιχθύων].

units.la: Vide Caelium Rhodiginnm libro trigesimo capite vigesimo primo antiquarum lectionum.
units.tr: See Caelius Rhodiginus, Antiquarum lectionum book 30, chapter 21.

units.la: Fnit autem hoc quoq; sacrificii genus Gentilibus valde consueuit: quos non mirum est sacrificia sua fupiditate asinos Dijs suis, qui et ipsi asini fuerunt, sacrificasse. Hinc adde mulos et camelos: e quibus Romani in Confnalibus mulum suo sacrificio immolabant, quod hoc genus quadrupedum primum vehiculo junctum fuisse dicetur: Camelos autem, prae fertim pingues, Arabes sacrificant in ara Ignoti Dei, sicut nuptura virginibus camelii. Heroi bus vero tauro, capro et arieti litant.
units.tr: This kind of sacrifice was also very common among the Gentiles. It is no wonder that they, who were themselves asses in their superstition, sacrificed asses to their gods, who were asses too. Add mules and camels. Of these, the Romans at the Consualia sacrificed a mule, because this kind of quadruped is said to have been the first to be yoked to a vehicle. The Arabs sacrifice camels, especially fat ones, on the altar of the Unknown God, as maidens about to marry sacrifice to ... To heroes they make offerings of a bull, a goat and a ram.

units.la: Atq, hoc quidem modo majora, quae vocant, pecora, nt boves, equos, asinos, mulos et camelos, veteres Gentiles Diis suis sacrificarunt atq, immolarunt.
units.tr: In this way the ancient Gentiles sacrificed and slaughtered to their gods the animals called larger: oxen, horses, asses, mules and camels.

units.la: Idem etiam sacrificarunt minora, ut sues (de quorum sacrificio, quia omnium primum et animantium perhibetur, primo est dictu) ovesque, agnos vel agnas, hircos, capros vel capras, verres, arietes et similes. Ac ovesquidem Iovi et Dianae immolabatur: Iovi, Idibus unius cujusq; mensis: unde et ovis Idulis, lingua Hetrusca est dicta, et Idus ipsas nonnulli volunt dictas. Dianae vero immolabatur ớves a Persis,quæ ideo Perfia,vel Persica seu Perfea est nuncupata; de quo sic Dio-dorus: Colitur,inquit,& a Persis plurimum Diana,cui mysteria instituerunt Barbari; quæ, ut ajt,ad suum usu,tempus Persea dicebantur. Sed enim Dea hæc trans Euphratem colebatur sum-ma religione & cultu, cui sacræ pascebantur ovES, nullo custode. Quin & Ælianus scribit,quod cum Samius aurũ furto sublatũ ovis in venisse, Mandrabulus Samius sunoni ovem confecrarit.
units.tr: They also sacrificed smaller animals: swine (of whose sacrifice, because it is said to be the first of all animals, we shall speak first), sheep, lambs (male or female), he-goats, she-goats, boars, rams and the like. Sheep were offered to Jupiter and Diana. To Jupiter they were offered on the Ides of each month, whence the Etruscan name for the Ides' ewe, and some think the Ides themselves were named from it. To Diana the Persians offered sheep, and for this reason the month was called Persia, Persica or Persea. Diodorus says of it: "Diana is also worshipped most of all by the Persians, for whom the barbarians instituted mysteries; these, as he says, they called Persea at the time of their use. This goddess was worshipped beyond the Euphrates with the greatest devotion and cult, and sacred sheep were pastured there with no guardian." Ælian also writes that when a Samian's gold had been stolen and a sheep was found to have it, Mandrabulus the Samian consecrated a sheep to Juno.

units.la: Præcipuè autem agnos vel agnas olim sacrificarunt: eo quòd sit hostia pura & immolationi apta. Vnde agnus a Græco ἀγνὸς, pium,purũ & castum significat: quam ob vim alii ex Græco ἁμάδς deducant; quod nomen apud majores communis fuisse generis, sicut & lupus fuit,quod venit ex Græco λύκῳ, testatur Festus. Isidorus tamen,ut hoc quoque addam, Latinos hoc nomen habere putat,eo quod pra caeteris animantibus matrem agnoscat,adeò ut ,etiamsi in magno grege erra-verit, statim balatu recognoscat vocem parentis. Caeterum Iovi & Mineruæ de agna res divi-na siebat; Iovi quidem de agna bima: Mineruæ veró Tubilastrio die, quo turbæ lustrabantur. Iuvenalis de hoc sacrificio: —Ni reàm regina ducimus agnam Par vellus dabicur pugnanti Gorgone Mauri: Id est,
units.tr: Lambs and ewe-lambs were especially sacrificed of old, because they are pure victims fit for sacrifice. Hence the Greek hagnos, meaning pious, pure and chaste, from which some derive the Latin agnus; for this reason, as Festus attests, the word was of common gender among the ancients, as lupus was, which comes from the Greek lykos [ἁμάδς]. Isidore, to add this too, thinks the Latins have this name because the lamb recognizes its mother above all other animals, so that even if it has strayed in a large flock, it at once recognizes its parent's voice by its bleating. Moreover, the divine rite was performed with a ewe-lamb for Jupiter and Minerva: for Jupiter with a two-year-old ewe, and for Minerva on the Tubilustrium, the day on which the crowds were purified. Juvenal, on this sacrifice: "Unless we lead the queen lamb, a like fleece will be given to Pallas fighting the Moorish Gorgon." That is,

units.la: Palladi,quæ Mauritana Gorgone, capite Medusæ usa a Poëtis fingitur. Athenienses quoque annua solennia tauro & agno celebrare solebant,ut ait Alexander.
units.tr: Pallas, who by the poets is imagined with the Mauretanian Gorgon, that is, the head of Medusa. The Athenians too used to celebrate their annual festivals with a bull and a lamb, as Alexander says.

units.la: Ad hircos deinde seu capros quod attinet,constat Lusitanos in sacrificiis,quæ Tεγzοῦοῖα Martifecerunt usos. Sic hircum coloatus Pani sacrificabatur, qui ad specus agebatur, in quo immolatio hirci Pan ipse diversari putabatur,ut docet Lucianus. Quin etiam Dionysio, seu Baccho hircum vel cornum, &c. caprum mastabant,quòd hoc animalis genus maxime vites rodat; unde illud est: Vitè caper morsà Bacchi mastacus ad aras Ducitur ultorus, &c.
units.tr: As for he-goats or goats, it is established that the Lusitanians used them in the sacrifices which they made to Mars [Tεγzοῦοῖα]. Thus a goat was sacrificed to Pan, led to a cave in which Pan himself was thought to dwell during the offering of the goat, as Lucian teaches. Indeed, to Dionysius or Bacchus they slaughtered a he-goat or a goat, because this animal gnaws the vines most. Hence the verse: "The goat, which bit the vine, the shaggy avenger of Bacchus, is led to the altars, etc."

units.la: Virgilius in Georg.secundo: —Baccho caper omnibus aris Cæditur, & veteres ineunc proscennialudi, Et mox idem: Ergo ruè suum Baccho dicemus honorem Carminibus patrijs,lancesq, & liba feremus, Et dustus cornu slabit sacer hircus ad aram, Pinguiaque in verubus torrebimus exta columnis.
units.tr: Virgil in the Georgics, book two: "To Bacchus the goat is slaughtered at all the altars, and the ancients in turn held the games of the stage." And soon after: "Therefore we shall duly pay our own honour to Bacchus with ancestral songs, and bear dishes and cakes; and the sacred goat, led by its horn, stands at the altar, and we shall roast the fat entrails on spits."

units.la: Hinc etiam Prudentius contra Symmachum: His nunc pro meritis Baccho caper omnibus aris Cæditur & virides discindunt ore chelydros.
units.tr: Hence also Prudentius, against Symmachus: "For these things, as they deserve, the goat is slaughtered for Bacchus at all the altars, and they tear green serpents with their mouths."

units.la: Ovidius in Fastis: Rodè caper vites:tamen binc cum slabit ad aras, In tua quod sparsi cornua posse erit.
units.tr: Ovid in the Fasti: "The goat gnawed the vines; yet now when it stands at the altars, it will be in your horns that ..."

units.la: Meminit hujus vitium, Baccho offerri solitæ, etiam beatus Cyprianus de duplici Martyrio, laquens: Non levius crimen Christianorum est, cogere ad ebrietatem, quàm bircum Baccho immolare. Pertinet huc quod Fauno res sacra siebat de hædo & vino,nonas Decembribus: unde celebritas hæc Faunalia dicebatur, ut Acron Porphyrionque consentiunt. Horatius libro tertio Carminum ad Faunum ipsum sic canit: Si tener pleno cadit hædus anno, Larga nec desunt Veneris sodali Vina craterę, vetus aramulto Fumat odore.
units.tr: The blessed Cyprian, in On the Twofold Martyrdom, also recalls this vice of offerings made to Bacchus, saying: "The crime of Christians is no lighter for compelling men to drunkenness than for sacrificing a goat to Bacchus." To this belongs that a sacred rite was performed for Faunus with a kid and wine on the Nones of December, whence this festival was called the Faunalia, as Acron and Porphyrion agree. Horace, in book three of the Odes, sings thus to Faunus himself: "If a tender kid falls in its full year, and the wine of Venus's companion is not lacking in the wide bowl, the old altar smokes with much incense."

units.la: Et mox: Cum tibi nonæ redeunt Decembres,
units.tr: And soon after: "When the Decembers' Nones return for you,"

units.la: Aliitamen etiam agno eidem sacra fasta volunt.
units.tr: Others, however, hold that sacred rites are also due to that same god with a lamb.

units.la: Capras praeterea frequenter Dijs suis atque Numinibus mastarunt & obtulerunt: id quod Aιγοθυ-ειã cum ex Alexandri testimonio manifestum est, rum ex Pausania & aliis. Alexander libro immolatio tae quarco,capite duodecimo testatur,in Pedasia,regione Carię,cum Iovi Lycæo statà die sacrifica-prarum. tur,caprum e Pegaso sua sponte ad sacrificii locum venire & se immolandum sistere. Et Pausa-nias. Ħ 4.
units.tr: Moreover, they often sacrificed and offered goats to their gods and divinities. This practice of goat-sacrifice [αἰγοθυσία] is clear both from the testimony of Alexander and from Pausanias and others. Alexander, in book four on sacrifices, chapter twelve, testifies that in Pedasia, a region of Caria, when sacrifices are offered to Zeus Lykaios on the appointed day, a goat comes of its own accord from Pegasus to the place of sacrifice and presents itself to be slain. And Pausanias, in book four.

units.la: {¶} Et mox idem: mas in Laconicis refert, solos Graecis omnibus Lacedaemonios solenne habere Iunonem colere, quam Aegophagam nominant, sidemq; capras immolare. Herculem quidè produnt, primum templum dedicasse, & Deæ caprum mactasse. Id illum fecisse, quod contra Hippocoontem filios pugnanti nihil Inno ad versi objecerit, cùm perinde atq; in alios certaminibus contra pugnaturum pu taffet: caprum verò fecisse, quod alie victime non fupperent. Idem testatur in Boeticis, Potnius, urbe Boeotiæ, fuisse olim Liberi patris ædes, cognomine Ægoboli, id est, caprum cædentes. Ita enim aliquando accidit, ut, dnm sacrificarent per temulentiam, eo necordiæ processerint, ut ipsum Liberi patris sacerdotem occiderint. Quod piaculum cùm atrox pestilentia consecuta effet, ex Delphici Apollinis responso, puerum Liberò jam pubescentem mactandum acceperunt. Sed non multo post annus Deum ipsum capellam pro puero supposuisse.
units.tr: {¶} And soon after, the same writer: in his Laconica he reports that the Lacedaemonians alone among all the Greeks made it a solemn custom to worship Juno, whom they call Aegophagus, and to sacrifice goats to her. They relate that Hercules was the first to dedicate a temple and slay a goat to the goddess. He did this because Juno, when he fought against the sons of Hippocoon, raised no objection to him, though she seemed to be going to oppose him in his other contests; and he sacrificed a goat because other victims were not sufficient. The same writer testifies that in his Boeotica, at Potniae, a city of Boeotia, there was once a temple of Father Liber, with the surname Aegobolus, that is, "goat-slayers." For it once happened that, while they were sacrificing in drunkenness, they went so far in their madness as to kill the very priest of Father Liber. When a dreadful pestilence followed this atrocity, they received from the Delphic Apollo's oracle the command to sacrifice a boy who had already reached puberty to Liber. But not long after, they say, the god himself substituted a she-goat in place of the boy.

units.la: Æfculapio verò de capra res divina inprimis fiebat, quoniam capra nunquam sine febre esse dicitur. Saluti autem Deus Æfculapius. Sed & Iovi unâ, sicut Apollini duæ albæ capræ aureæ cum bove XVIII. Augustii immolabantur.
units.tr: Sacred rites with a goat were especially performed for Aesculapius, since a goat is said never to be without fever. Aesculapius is the god of health. Also, to Jupiter one, and to Apollo two white she-goats of gold were sacrificed along with an ox on the eighteenth of August.

units.la: Porrò etiam arietis & verris immolandi consuetudo apud Ethnicos, Ægyptios præsertim, frequentata & celebrata fuit: quibus adde Gallos Cisalpinos, qui Marti verrem immolarunt. Ac Aries vel ἀρὴν τῷ ἀρηΐ, id est, a Marte vocatus est, eo quòd Marti potissimum hoc pecus immolatum est: sive quòd apud Latinos in gregibus masculi mares dicuntur: vel etiam quòd hoc pecus a Gentilibus non tantùm in Martis honorem, sed etiam aliorum Deorum fictitiorum primum aris est immolatum. Aries, quòd aris imponeretur. Unde est illud: — Aries mactatur ad aram.
units.tr: Furthermore, the custom of sacrificing rams and boars was frequent and widespread among the Gentiles, especially the Egyptians. To these add the Cisalpine Gauls, who sacrificed a boar to Mars. The ram [aries] is also called ἀρήν for τῷ Ἄρει, that is, named after Mars, because this animal was chiefly sacrificed to Mars; or because among the Latins the males in a flock are called "rams"; or because this animal was first sacrificed on altars by the Gentiles not only in honour of Mars but also of other fictitious gods. Aries is so called because it was placed on the altar [aris imponeretur]. Hence the line: "The ram is slain at the altar."

units.la: Minoribus pecudibus adde canes; quorum immolatio non minus frequens & usitata olim fuit apud Ethnicos & Gentiles, quàm reliquorum pecudum minorum. Plutarchus testis est, in Quæstionibus Romanis, Lacedaemonios Neptuno immolasse canem, & Boetios, cane in duas partes dissecto per medium, iræ expiationem fuisse. Idem & Caribus: ut exta Dius offerrein usu haberent. Inde proverbium, Carica victima. Sic Gynaeciæ Romani pro bis, qui domi nascuntur, canem immolabant. Est autem Gynecia, quam Romani Bonam Deam vocant, quæ ex corruptibilibus generationes fatit. Cui cùm res divina fit, optant neminem bonum fieri, qui domi nascatur. Idem Romanorum in Lupercalibus canem Pani immolare fuerunt soliti, mense Februario; quia Lupo canus infensus est, & in expiationibus cane litatum legimus apud Plutarchum. Inde fortè quòd Lupercos allatrarent & interpellarent canes per urbem discurrentes, aut etiam quia Pani, cui sacrificium boe celebrabatur, acceptus esset ob caprarum greges canis. Idem porro Romani ad placandum Canicula fidus, frugibus inimicum, maltabant canes: quas fi russæ non sunt, puras non putarunt: quod sacrum Canarum augurium nuncuparunt. Festus: Rutila canes, id est, non procul a rubro colore immolabantur, ut ajt Atejus Capito, canario sacrificio pro frugibus deprecandæ sævitiæ canisidera canicula. Pro frugibus quoque & pecoribus, ut rubigo a vertatur, latiente catulo sacrum fieri consuenerat: ideo Robigalibus per Quirinalem flaminem sacrum extra urbem fieri: in quo super exta canis chus & merum infundere mos erat. Tales quoque catulos, recens editos, tam in adjicialibus, quam Deorum caenis eos sepe adhibuisse testatur Alexander libro tertio, eapite duodecimo. Idem Manæ Geneta canem immolabant, votumque faciebant, ne quos dominatorum bonus esset, id est, mortuus. Nam eo loco Plutarchus in Quæstionibus Romanis, quæstione quinquagesima secunda, aliisque in locis Bonus ponitur pro mortuo.
units.tr: To the lesser animals add dogs. Their sacrifice was once no less frequent and customary among the heathen and Gentiles than that of the other lesser animals. Plutarch witnesses in his Roman Questions that the Lacedaemonians sacrificed a dog to Neptune, and that the Boeotians, cutting a dog in two through the middle, used this as a means of atoning for anger. The Carians too, so that they might have the entrails offered to Zeus, kept this custom; hence the proverb "a Carian victim." So too the Roman women, for Gynaecia, sacrificed a dog for those who were born at home. Gynaecia, whom the Romans call the Good Goddess, is the one who produces generations out of corruptible things. When sacred rites are performed to her, they pray that no one born at home may become good. Likewise the Romans, in the Lupercalia in February, were accustomed to sacrifice a dog to Pan, because the dog is hostile to the wolf; and we read in Plutarch that a dog was used in purifications. Perhaps this was because the dogs that ran through the city barked at and harassed the Luperci; or perhaps because the dog was acceptable to Pan, to whom the sacrifice was made, on account of the goat-herds. Moreover, the Romans, to appease the Dog Star, the enemy of the crops, used to sacrifice dogs; and if they were not reddish, they did not think them pure. They called this the sacred augury of the dogs. Festus: "Reddish dogs, that is, dogs not far from red colour, were sacrificed, as Ateius Capito says, in a dog-sacrifice to avert the fury of the Dog Star for the sake of the crops." For the sake of crops and herds, too, that rust might be turned away, it was customary to make a sacrifice while the puppy lay hidden; hence at the Robigalia a sacrifice was made outside the city through the Quirinal flamen, at which it was the custom to pour wine over the entrails of a dog. Alexander, in book three, chapter twelve, also testifies that the Gentiles often used such newly born puppies both in their public rites and in the feasts of the gods. The same people sacrificed a dog to the Manes Geneta and made a vow that none of their masters might be good, that is, dead. For in that passage Plutarch, in his Roman Questions, question fifty-two, and in other places, uses "good" for "dead."

units.la: Pertinet hnc Panegyris canum, a Romanis mense Augusto celebrari solita, quia ἀνάλαξις, id est, fine latratu egerant, cùm Capitolium a Gallis occupatum esset, anseribus ampliter sono reo, clamantibus. Tunc ergo vivas canes cruci fabbucinæ affigebant, atque inter ædes Iuvenatu tutus & Sumani singulis annis Romæ, ansere insidente, defirebantur.
units.tr: To this belongs the festival of dogs, which the Romans were accustomed to celebrate in August, because, when the Capitol had been seized by the Gauls, the dogs had kept silence [ἀνάλαξις] and had not barked, while the geese, which were sacred, cried out loudly. Then, therefore, they fastened live dogs to crosses, and every year at Rome they were carried through the houses of Juventas and Summanus, with a goose sitting upon them.

units.la: Nec verò tantùm Romani canino boc sacrificio plurimum nsi & deleftati fuerunt, sed etiam Græci, qui Hecatæ Chthoniæ canem pro domi nascentibus immolabant (sicut Romani, ut supra dictum, Manæ Geneta:) licet diversimodè quidem. Nonnulli enim Proserpinam exifimantes, si de cane sacra fatiebantur, seu Deæ inferæ. Nam ut Plutarchus quodam loco in quæstionibus infert, Veteres hoc animal impurum omnino esse putaverunt. Unde cælestium Deorum nulli prorsus canis consecratus sit. Argivos etiam Socrates ajt Lucinæ rem sacrum cane fecisse ob pariendi facilitatem. Quin cane Græcio omnibus ferè piaculis usi fuerunt pro piacularibus hostiis. Catuli Hecatæ inter alia purgamentis offerebantur expiandosque catulis tangebant, quam februationem, id est, purgationem, seu lustrationem, Græcè καθαρμόν, id est, circumcatulatione vocârunt, quod ex catulis sacrum fieret, ut Plutarchus scribit.
units.tr: Nor did only the Romans take great pleasure in this canine sacrifice, but also the Greeks, who sacrificed a dog to Hecate Chthonia on behalf of those born at home (just as the Romans did for the Manes Geneta, as said above), though in different ways. For some, thinking that she was Proserpina, or some other goddess of the underworld, performed sacred rites with a dog. For, as Plutarch states in one place in his Questions, the ancients considered this animal wholly unclean; hence no dog was consecrated to any of the heavenly gods. Socrates says that the Argives also performed a sacred rite with a dog for Lucina, for the ease of childbirth. Indeed, the Greeks used the dog as a sacrificial victim for nearly all their expiations. Among other things, puppies were offered to Hecate, and people were purified by touching the puppies. They called this februation, that is, purification or lustration, in Greek καθαρμός, that is, "circling with puppies," because the sacrifice was made from puppies, as Plutarch writes.

units.la: Canem porrò Marti Enyalio mactabant Lacedæmonii, ut ajt Pausanias in Laconicis. Scribit enim ephebos Lacones, cùm pugnam essent inter se initurì, Marti canis catulum immolasse, Deo scilicet validissimo, victimam validissimam, & cicurem se dicare arbitrantes. Subdit idem, catulos non sacrificari a Græcis, Colophoniis exceptis, qui catellam nigram noctürno tempore immolabant Triviæ. Sed de canibus apud Græcos & alios secus, quàm Pausanias tradit, sacrificatum fuisse, ostendunt cùm superiora exempla, tum Sabaorum & Thracum; de quibus Ovidius sic canit: Exta canum Triviæ vidi libare Sabæos Et quicunque tuas accolit Æmenivues.
units.tr: Moreover, the Lacedaemonians sacrificed a dog to Mars Enyalius, as Pausanias says in his Laconica. For he writes that the Lacedaemonian youths, when they were about to join battle with one another, sacrificed a puppy to Mars, the most powerful god, thinking that they dedicated a most powerful victim, and one that was tame. The same writer adds that the Greeks did not sacrifice puppies, except the Colophonians, who sacrificed a black puppy to Trivia at night. But the earlier examples, as well as those of the Sabaeans and Thracians, show that dogs were sacrificed among the Greeks and others in a manner different from what Pausanias relates. Ovid sings of them thus: "I have seen the Sabaeans pour out the entrails of dogs to Trivia, and whoever dwells on your Aemenian shores."

units.la: Sic igitur, ut hoc quoque addam, Gentiles canina impudentia atque rabie, canina sacrificiis fuerunt delectati.
units.tr: So then, to add this too: the Gentiles, with canine shamelessness and fury, took delight in dog sacrifices.

units.la: Nec vero domesticà tantum & mansueta animalia, sed etiam feras Diis suis immolarunt. Sic enim, exempli gratia, aprum Parrhafii in Arcadia Apollini Epicurio, id est, auxiliari: cervam Dianæ. (Hæc enim ei victima pro Iphigenia data fuisse creditur:) lupum, ut etiam picum Latini, Marti dicabant atq; sacrificabant.
units.tr: Nor did they sacrifice only domestic and tame animals to their gods, but also wild beasts. Thus, for example, the Parrhasians in Arcadia sacrificed a boar to Apollo Epicurius, that is, the helper; a hind to Diana (for this animal is believed to have been given as a victim in place of Iphigenia); and the Latins dedicated and sacrificed a wolf, and also the woodpecker, to Mars.

units.la: Atque hæc quidem de τῶν ἀπούσιον hoc est, in immolatione animalium Quadrupedum fatis: sed, quitur ut nunc secundo loco agamus de ὀπτοσθυσίας, hoc est, avium immolatione: quarum quidam omnes generis Gentiles Diis suis offerre fuerunt soliti: inter quas celebre valde & usitatum apud eos fuit sacrificium galli gallinacei, qui partim Noctì Deæ sacrificabatur & nocturno tempore, juxta illud Ovidii in Fastis: Noctè Deæ Noctis cristatus cæditur ales Quod tepidum vigili provocat ore diem.
units.tr: These are enough about the sacrifice of four-footed animals, which the Greeks call ἀπουσιοθυσία... that is, the sacrifice of animals. But now, in the second place, we are to deal with ornithothysia [ὀρνιθοθυσία], that is, the sacrifice of birds. Some of the Gentiles were accustomed to offer every kind of bird to their gods. Among these, the sacrifice of the cock was especially famous and customary among them, which was offered partly to the goddess Night and at night-time, according to the line of Ovid in the Fasti: "To the goddess Night the crested bird of Night is slain, which with its wakeful mouth calls forth the warm day."

units.la: Partim verò a Lacedæmoniis Marti: quando aperto Marte vicerant; quando verò strategemate, bovem immolabant: id quod ab eis non sine ratione fiebat, quòd pluris æstimabant incruentam victoriam, quàm cruentam. Idem, & quidem albus, Æsculapii quoque fuit victima. Sed & Gallinæ: & hæc quidem rostro nigro, nigrisque pedibus & digitis imparibus. Si enim luteo essent rostro vel pedibus, impura putabantur ab aruspicibus. Verum & Iovi & Cybeli & Menstrnæ verdum dicatus fuit. Est & apud Plutarchum in libro Ifidis & Osiridis, ubi de Anubi agit & Hermanubi: Ad hunc, inquit, inferiora sicut ad illum superiora pertinent. Quapropter illi candidum gallum; huic croceum immolant. Sed Pyrrhus quoque rex, cùm splendè laborantibus medeteatur, albo gallo sacrum peragebat. Porrò non modo Aristophanes in Pluto, quomodo sacra fierent & sanarentur ægrotì in templo Æsculapii docet, sed & Philostratus in vita Apollonii Tyanei, & alii plerique.
units.tr: Partly, however, the Lacedaemonians sacrificed an ox to Mars: when they had conquered in open battle; but when they had won by stratagem, they sacrificed a cock. They did this not without reason, because they valued a bloodless victory more than a bloody one. The same, and indeed a white one, was also the victim of Aesculapius. Hens too were sacrificed, with black beaks, black feet and uneven toes; for if they had yellow beaks or feet, the diviners considered them unclean. Indeed, the hen was dedicated to Jupiter, to Cybele and to Mens. Plutarch also has it in his book On Isis and Osiris, where he treats of Anubis and Hermanubis: "To this one," he says, "the lower things belong, as to that one the higher. For this reason they sacrifice a white cock to the one and a saffron-coloured cock to the other." But King Pyrrhus also, when he cured those labouring under a severe illness, performed a sacred rite with a white cock. Moreover, not only does Aristophanes in the Plutus show how sacrifices were made and sick people healed in the temple of Aesculapius, but so also does Philostratus in the Life of Apollonius of Tyana, and many others.

units.la: Hu adde, quòd Pythagoras quandoque Iovi gallum albis plumis immolasse dicitur, licet ejus symbolum hoc quoque fuisse constet, Gallum enutrias, sed ne sacrificet. Legimus item apud Pausaniam, Troezenios, gallo albis alarum pennis discerpto, Africum ventum e sinu Saronico agrum & vineas perflantem, novo sque pampinos acriter torrentem, placare. Sic Socrates Mercurio gallum gallinaceum immolari jussit: sospan per contemptum, cùm idem affirmarit Deum nequaquam victimis indigere.
units.tr: To this add that Pythagoras is said to have sometimes sacrificed a white-feathered cock to Jupiter, although it is well established that this too was one of his symbols: "Keep a cock, but do not sacrifice it." We also read in Pausanias that the Troezenians, by tearing a white cock by the wing feathers, placated the south-west wind that blew from the Saronic Gulf over their fields and vineyards and scorched the new shoots. So Socrates ordered a cock to be sacrificed to Mercury, as a jest, although he himself affirmed that God has no need of victims at all.

units.la: Anseres quinetiam, ad placandos Deos, sacrificiis adhibiti fuerunt, quòd vigilantiæ symbolum hæc sint in fuerit. Is autem Ifidi, Deæ Ægyptiorum, quæ & Lunæ putabatur, ab aliquibus Ceres, maSabatur, securo, illi apponebatur, ut Herodotus & Ovidius testantur: tametsi Macrobius alii, nonnulla asserant, Ægyptios thure & precibus Deos placasse.
units.tr: Geese too were used in sacrifices to appease the gods, because they are a symbol of vigilance. One was offered to Isis, the goddess of the Egyptians, who was also thought to be the Moon and was called Ceres by some, as Herodotus and Ovid attest. Yet Macrobius and others maintain that the Egyptians placated their gods with incense and prayers.

units.la: Pertinent huc tetraones, quos Plinius decimo libro inter genera anserum recenset; cujus verba hæc sunt: Decet et tetraones suus nitor, absolutaq; nigritia: in supercilius cocci rubor. Tamen seri omnes Plinianì codices non Tetraonas habent. Sed Erythrotaonas.
units.tr: To this belong the tetraones, which Pliny in his tenth book counts among the kinds of geese. His words are these: "The tetraones have their own gloss and deep blackness, and on the eyebrows a scarlet redness." However, all the manuscripts of Pliny do not read "Tetraones" but "Erythrotaones."

units.la: Præter hunc bostiam e tetraonibus, Caligulam sibi generatim per singulos dies immolari soluisse etiam phœnicopteros, pavones, numidicas, meleagrides, phasianas, Suetonius cessatur in ejus vita: ubi per phœnicopterum, avem incelligit, cujus linguam optimi esse saporis Apicius docuit, nepotum, ut Plinius ait, altissimus gurges. De phœnicopero Martialis libro decimo tertio.
units.tr: Besides this sacrifice of tetraones, Suetonius, in his life of Caligula, records that Caligula had flamingos, peacocks, guinea fowl, meleagrides and pheasants immolated to him every day. By "phoenicopterus" he means the flamingo, whose tongue Apicius taught was of the finest flavour; it was, as Pliny says, the deepest whirlpool of spendthrifts. Martial speaks of the flamingo in his thirteenth book:

units.la: Dat mihi penna rubens nomen: sed lingua gulosisNostra sapit, quid si garrula lingua foret?
units.tr: "A red feather gives me my name; but my tongue, if it were a chattering tongue, would taste of our gluttony."

units.la: Juvenalis: Et Scychicæ volucres, & phœnicopteris ingens.
units.tr: Juvenal: "And Scythian birds, and huge flamingos."

units.la: Per Numidicas veró gallinas Africanas intelligit, quæ aleriùs, Numidicæ dicuntur, quæ que, ut docet Columella, nonè eædem sunt, sed Meleagridibus similes, nisi quòd rutilam cristam ca pice gerunt, quæ sunt utraque in Meleagride cærulea. Varro autem in tertio de re rustica, Galli nas Africanas Meleagrides esse tradit. De Meleagridibus hæc Plinius in decimo, supra citato: Similis modo pugnant Meleagrides in Bæotia Africæ: hoc est, gallinarum genus gibberum, variis sparsum plumis, quæ non vissime sunt peregrinarum avium in mensas recepta propter ingratum virus: verum Meleagri cumulus nobiles eas fecit: ubi Tranquillus, Jentiens cum Colu mella separat Meleagridas à Numidicis. Nam jejunium potius, quam conjunctim singula hæc legi debent. De Numidica hæc ait Peeronius arbiter:
units.tr: By "Numidicae" he means African hens, which are elsewhere called Numidicae. As Columella teaches, these are not the same as the meleagrides, but resemble them, except that they have a reddish crest where the meleagrides have a blue one. Varro, in the third book of his work on agriculture, says that the African hens are meleagrides. On the meleagrides Pliny says, in the tenth book cited above: "The meleagrides of Boeotia are like those of Africa; that is, a kind of hunched hen, spotted with varied feathers, which were not admitted to tables from abroad, for their unpleasant flavour; but the cargo of Meleager made them famous." Here Suetonius, along with Columella, separates the meleagrides from the Numidicae; these words should be read separately rather than together. Of the Numidica Petronius the arbiter says:

units.la: Gallina tibi Numidica: cibi gallus spado.
units.tr: "A Numidian hen for you, and for food a gelded cock."

units.la: Sed & phasianas immolari debuisse Caligulæ Suetonius tradit; quas constat à Phasi flu vio Colchorum phasianas nominatas, unde primum transportatam se phasiana testatur apud Epi grammatislam. Adrianus, ut hoc quoque addam, tecraphármaco, vel poculis pentaphármaco usus est, quod cibi regii genus est, constans ex rebus quinque, hoc est, sumine, phasiano, pavone, cru sulato & aprugna. Obiter etiam hoc libet addere: Antonius Geca habebat issam confuetudi nem, ut prandia pararijuberet, per singulas litteras, veluti per f. uc ita edulia omnia, quæ inciperent ab ea litera, apponerentur, ut fasianus, sarraca, ficus, ficedula: & modo per a, u: anser, a nas, &c. modo per p. ut pullus, perdix, p, porcellus, &c. Alexander Romanus Imper. diebus tantum festis phasianum adhibuit in mensa.
units.tr: Suetonius also tells us that pheasants were to be immolated to Caligula. They are named after the river Phasis of the Colchians, from which, as the pheasant itself declares in an epigram, they were first brought. Hadrian, to add this too, used the tetrapharmacum, or the pentapharmacum, a dish of five ingredients, which is a kind of royal food: sow's udder, pheasant, peacock, crustulum and boar's ham. Here I should also add that Antonius Geta had the habit of ordering dinners by a single letter: all the dishes beginning with that letter were set before him, such as pheasant, sparrow, fig, and fig-pecker; and at another time with A or U: goose, duck, and so on; or with P, such as chicken, partridge, piglet, and so on. The Emperor Alexander Severus served pheasant at table only on festival days.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad epulum sacrum, nempe sacrificium. Ad hoc præter gallos, gallinas, anseres & reliquas aves, de quibus modo distum, adhibita etiam fuerunt albæ columbæ, coturnices & alia. Albas columnas Veneri dicabant & consecrabant. Et ideo Æneas apud Poëtam macernas appellat aves. De coturnice Achenæus scribit libro nono, Herculem lo'in & Asterie filium in Libyam proficiscentem, a Typhone fuisse interemium: re vocatum aucen: in vitam odore coturnici, illi ab Iolao admoca: & ob eam caussam Phœnices Herculi coturnice sacrificare.
units.tr: But let us return to the sacred feast, that is, the sacrifice. For this purpose, besides cocks, hens, geese and the other birds just mentioned, white doves, quails and others were also used. They dedicated and consecrated white doves to Venus, and so the poet has Aeneas call them "macernae" birds. On the quail Athenaeus writes in his ninth book: Hercules, son of Alcmene and Asterie, setting out for Libya, was killed by Typhon; he was revived by Iolaus, who held a quail to his nose and restored him to life with its smell. For this reason the Phoenicians sacrificed quail to Hercules.

units.la: Hæc de ὀφιοθυσία, hoc est, immolacione avium: Superest Aquatilium immolatio, & in sestorum omnis generis. Ad Aquatilia quod attinet, inter ea potissimum anguillas Copaïdas, & lacu sic votatas, à Bæotiis, hostiarum in morem coronacas nolaq, perfusas, Diis sacrificari pro bat Achenæus, opinione Syllæ cuiusdam in Symposiacis Plutarchi, ἰχθύων θυσία· ὕδε, ἐκ ἱεροσιῶς, validis argumentis quasi ex professo labefactans. Idem scribit & piscatores ex sbynnu, quem maximum cepissent, Neptuno immolare solitos, & sacra ea Thynna appellasse. Mnaseas etiam Aergatidis Deæ sacra piscibus fieri prodidit, cùm veris & costis, tum simu lacis ex auro & argento. Phaselicæ quoq, in Lycia piscium salsamenta quotannis patrio ritu Diis suis, & præsertim Marci, offerre solebant: idque sacrum insticutum, quod Lacius Argivus a pastore Cylabra campum emisse ad ædificandam urbem piscium salsamentis fertur potuit quàm farina vel melle. Quinetiam & aruspicinam Lycios exercuisse Athenæus ex Polycharmo prodit ex piscibus, & sucura prædixisse. Porró & mullum piscem, id est, trigilam, Proserpinæ, ac item Dianæ sacrificari unt antiqui, & citharon Apollini, Mercurio bocas, Libero patri catte lum, apuam Veneri, Neptuno pompilum, quem & sacrum piscem quidam vocavere, ut pluribus Athenæus exposuit & Aelianus. Porró & hoc observatum est, mullum barbatulum non attingi a sacrificantibus sacerdotibus, nec a fœmina Argolica Iunonis sacerdote. Ab Ægyptiis certè in sacris pisces interdici testatur Brod.in primo Epigrammatum.
units.tr: This is what I have to say about sacrifice of birds [ὀφιοθυσία]. What remains is the immolation of aquatic animals, and of fish of every kind. As for aquatic creatures, Athenaeus holds that the eels of Copais and Lake Copais, which the Boeotians used to crown and sprinkle with wine and bring as victims, were offered to the gods; here he follows the opinion of a certain Sulla in Plutarch's Symposiacs, who refutes it with strong arguments, as if on purpose, calling it "fish sacrifice" [ἰχθύων θυσία], which is not holy [ὅσιος]. The same Athenaeus writes that fishermen used to immolate to Neptune the largest tuna they had caught, and called these sacred rites "thynna." Mnaseas also reported that sacred rites of the goddess Atargatis were performed with fish, both real ones and ones made of gold and silver. Likewise the Phaselitae in Lycia used to offer salted fish every year to their gods, according to their ancestral custom, and especially to Mars; and this custom was instituted because Lacius of Argos is said to have bought from a shepherd Cylabras the field on which to build his city, and paid for it with salted fish rather than with flour or honey. Athenaeus, citing Polycharmus, also reports that the Lycians practised divination from fish and foretold the future from them. Moreover, the ancients sacrificed the mullet, that is, the trigla, to Proserpina, and likewise to Diana; the cithara to Apollo; the boce to Mercury; the catteium to Father Liber; the apua to Venus; and the pompilus to Neptune, which some have even called a sacred fish. Athenaeus and Aelian have explained this at length. It has also been observed that the bearded mullet was not touched by the priests while sacrificing, nor by the Argive woman who was priestess of Juno. Certainly the Egyptians forbade fish in their sacred rites, as Brodaeus attests in the first book of his Epigrams.

units.la: Quid dicam quòd ne parvula quidem,— quæ exemplo est magni formica laboris:
units.tr: What shall I say of that tiny creature, the ant, which is an example of great labour:
Myrmecoleon: the immolation of ants.

units.la: Vt de ea Horatius canit, ab hac immolatione fuic immunis: quam similiter Diis offerri solitam fuisse legimus; & quidem in Isthmo Nepcuno & Soli.
units.tr: As Horace sings of it, this sacrifice was exempt from that practice, which we read was likewise customarily offered to the gods, and indeed at the Isthmus to Neptune and to the Sun.

units.la: Hujusmodi autem esse etiam animalium brutorum, seu ratione carentium Sorta, sive immo latio: quae per inde ut animalia ratione utentia, non tantum integra & solida, sed etiam illorum partes, excrementa, atq; fætus sive fructus Diis offerebantur: quæ partes Screbula in plurali nu mero Umbrorum linguâ fuerunt appellatae, ccfte Pompejo. Utque sanguis humanus e partibus hu manus potissimum fuit immolatus: ita & pecudum. Idem judicium esto de reliquis, quae illic inter partes sacrificacas victimæ humanæ fuerunt a nobis posita.
units.tr: Sacrifice or immolation of brute animals, that is, creatures without reason, was of this kind too. Just as animals that use reason were offered to the gods, so were not only their whole and solid bodies but also their parts, excrements, and offspring or fruits. Among the Umbrians, these parts were called "screbula" in the plural in their language, as Pompey tells us. And just as human blood was mainly offered from human parts, so also was that of cattle. The same judgment holds for the rest, which we have already listed among the parts of the victims offered in human sacrifice.

units.la: Excrementa quinetiam & stercora jumentorum & pecorum quidam immolarunt. Hinc de Kyrgesiis Tartaros, qui cater ratim in campis degunt, Guagninus in descriptione Tartariae li teris memoriaq; prodidit, eos ritum gentilem hujusmodi habere. Sacrificiis ipsorum quo tempore tem divinam peragit, tunc sanguinem, lac & fimum jumentorum terramq; sumit, commixtioneq; simul facta, in vas quoddam infundit, & una cum hoc arborem ascendit, ad populumq; circumstantem concionatur. Concione peracta in flulcam plebeculam prædictam commixtionem spargit: populus vero in terram pronus provoluitur, aspersunculamq; hanc pro Deo colit, firmeq; credit nihil esse perinde salutare humano generi, ac terrain, pecus, armentaq.
units.tr: Some even offered the excrement and dung of beasts of burden and of flocks. Hence Guagninus, in his description of Tartary, has recorded in writing and memory concerning the Kyrgesii, the Tartars who live scattered in the fields, that they have this sort of pagan rite. When they perform their divine service, they take the blood, milk and dung of their beasts of burden, together with earth, and once these are mixed they pour the mixture into a certain vessel. Carrying this, the priest climbs a tree and preaches to the people standing around. When the sermon is finished, he sprinkles the mixture on the common folk. The people fall prostrate on the ground and worship this sprinkling as a god, firmly believing that nothing is as beneficial to the human race as the earth, cattle and herds.

units.la: Ad fœcus sive fructus quod attinet, constat animalium eorum ova, tum lac, tum mel, tanquam expiationibus quoque aptas, immolari & sacrificari fuisse solita. De ovorum immola- tione sic Iuvenalis: nisi se centum lustraverit ovis.
units.tr: As for eggs or fruits, it is established that the eggs of these animals, as well as milk and honey, were customarily immolated and sacrificed as being also suitable for expiations. Juvenal speaks thus of the immolation of eggs: "Unless he has purified himself with a hundred eggs."

units.la: Et Tertullianus de spectaculis: Honori Caesarum adscribunt (Gentiles) quibus illos ovo editos credendo de Cygno Iove non nerubescunt.
units.tr: And Tertullian, in his work On the Spectacles: "The Gentiles ascribe to the honour of the Caesars that they were hatched from an egg, and they do not blush to believe that Jupiter was a swan."

units.la: Quancum deinde ad lac attinet, constat ejus quoque usum olim in sacrificiis fuisse frequen- sissimum. Hinc Plinius in prolog. 1. Verum & Diis, inquit lactè rusticî multæque gentes supplicanc, & mola tantum salsa litant, qui non habent thus. Idem libro decimo quarto, capite decimo, Romulum ajt, lacte, non vino libasse, cujus rei indicio sunt sacra ab eo instituta. Cur Ruminæ Deæ sacrificantes mulierces lac, non vinum victimæ in vergere, sive infundere fuerint solitæ, rationem reddit Plutarchus in quæstionibus Romanis: idque fieri puta erit propter ficum uminalem, sub qua Romulus Rumam, id est, mammam sixit: vel quod vinum infantibus mimis con venire existimabatur. Sic Mercurio quoque lacte, non vino supplicabatur Romæ in vico, qui idcirco Sobrius dictus: alii tamen sic dictum putant, quod in eo caberna nulla fuerit.
units.tr: As for milk, it is clear that its use in sacrifices was once very frequent. Hence Pliny, in the prologue to book 1: "But rustic people and many nations also pray to the gods with milk, and offer only salted meal, who have no incense." The same author, in book 14, chapter 10, says that Romulus offered libations with milk, not wine, and that the rites he instituted are evidence of this. Plutarch, in his Roman Questions, gives the reason why women sacrificing to the goddess Rumina were accustomed to pour milk, not wine, over the victim. This was done, he suggests, either because of the wild fig tree under which Romulus suckled Rumis, that is, the breast, or because wine was thought unsuitable for infants. So too Mercury was propitiated at Rome with milk, not wine, in a district called Sobrius for this reason. Others, however, think it was so named because there was no tavern in it.

units.la: Sed in Nolis quoque & Fortunæ sacris lac legimus fuisse adhibitum. Forcunæ quidem virilis; mensæ Aprili imitati cum thure, melle & papavere: quod sacrum & Ceræri commune fuit, Lacte similiter Syl vanum placabant, Horatio teste: Tellurem porco, Sylvanum lacte piabant.
units.tr: But we also read that milk was used in the rites of Fortuna Virilis, and at the April table, along with incense, honey and poppy seed. This rite was common also to Ceres. Likewise they appeased Silvanus with milk, as Horace bears witness: "They propitiated Tellus with a pig and Silvanus with milk."

units.la: Sed & Plutoni, idest, Diti patri, vino, melle, lacte, sanguine & sterilibus pecudibus sacra fieri fuerunt solita. De more lactata utendi potione in Oscillorum festo testatur Festus.
units.tr: Moreover, sacrifices to Pluto, that is, Dis Pater, were customarily made with wine, honey, milk, blood and barren cattle. Festus attests to the custom of drinking milk at the festival of the Oscilla.

units.la: Pales quoque pastorum pabulique Dea, cujus festa dicta Palilia, vel, ut alii volunt, Parilia, lacte fuit culta. Tibullus: Et placidam niveo spargere lacte Palem.
units.tr: Pales, too, goddess of shepherds and fodder, whose festivals were called Palilia, or, as others prefer, Parilia, was honored with milk. Tibullus: "And to sprinkle gentle Pales with snowy milk."
Ovid: "And to propitiate Pales with fresh milk."

units.la: Huic & pro partu pecorum sacra fiebant lacte. Hanc Palen Varro scribit ab aliis Vestam; ab aliis matrem Deûm nominari; item, genere feminineo appellari; ab aliis masculino, de quo supra.
units.tr: For her, sacrifices were also made with milk for the increase of flocks. Varro writes that this Pales is called Vesta by some, and the Mother of the Gods by others; she is also called by a feminine name, and by others a masculine one, as noted above.

units.la: Vt autem lactis, sic mellis quoq; (cujus Deam finxerunt Mellonam, sive Mellonitam: Deum autem Aristæum, Athenien sem) non parvus in sacris apud Gentiles usus fuit. De Mellis mulsiquè natura & viribus vide Plinium libro vigesimo secundo, capite decimo quarto, ubi incer alia: Multi, inquit, senectam longam multi tantum nutritu tolerare, neque ullo alio cibo, celebri Pollionis Romuli exemplo, quem centesimum annum excedentem cum Divus Augustus hostes interrogasset, Quanam ratione maximè vigorem illum animi corporisque custodisset ille respondit: Intus mulso, foris ove.
units.tr: Just as with milk, so too honey had no small place in the rites of the Gentiles (they imagined a goddess Mellona, or Mellonita, and a god Aristaeus of Athens). On the nature and powers of honey and mead, see Pliny, book 22, chapter 14, where, among other things, he says: "Many have borne long old age on a diet of mead alone, and no other food, as in the famous example of Pollio's Romulus. When the divine Augustus asked him, as he was past his hundredth year, by what method he had especially kept his vigour of mind and body, he replied: 'Mead within, oil without.'"

units.la: Præcipuè autem Athenienses Mnemosynae, Aurorae, Soli, Lunae, Vraniæ & Nymphis, non vino, sed aquâ, melle dilutâ sacrificearunt. Sic in Asopo, in Eumenidum ede, non nisi mulso libare, & prò coronis floribus uti permissum erat, teste Alexandro ab Alexandro, libro tertio, capite duodecimo. Sic Areslæ & Hygiæ nomina erant mellituræ, quæ in sacrificiis deguslandæ præbebantur. Huc illud Apulei libro tertio, Melle montano libat.
units.tr: The Athenians in particular sacrificed to Mnemosyne, Aurora, the Sun, the Moon, Urania and the Nymphs, not with wine but with water diluted with honey. So at Asopus, at the shrine of the Eumenides, it was permitted to pour only mead, and to use flowers for garlands, as Alexander ab Alexandro testifies in book 3, chapter 12. Thus Aresla and Hygia had names meaning "honeyed," and honeyed offerings were provided in sacrifices to be tasted. To this belongs the line of Apuleius, book 3: "He pours a libation of mountain honey."

units.la: Diti patri, idest, Plutoni melle, vino, lacte, sanguine & sterilibus pecudibus sacra fieri fuisse solita, & Fortunæ melle, lacte & papavere; supra dictum fuit: & tamen Plutarchus quæstione quinta Symposiacôn, cur mel sacrificiis non fuerit adhibitum, hanc rationem affert, quòd ejus admixtione vinum corrumpi videatur, eoque libabatur, & ebrietas parabatur, antequam vinum exiisset. Et certè melius usus in sacrificiis Iudaicis fuit prohibitus. Nam Levitici, capite secundo hæc verba legimus: Nec quicquam mellis, aut fermenti adolebis in sacrificio: quæ præcepto allegoricè, sive tropologicè, mellis quidem nomine adulatio, assentatio, voluptas & delicia; fermenti verò nomine cum hypocrisis & fucus, tum malitia & obstrepatio intelliguntur, a quibus in sacrificiis, cultuque Dei prorsus est abstinendum.
units.tr: We have said above that sacrifices to Dis Pater, that is, Pluto, were customarily made with honey, wine, milk, blood and barren cattle, and to Fortuna with honey, milk and poppy. Yet Plutarch, in Symposiaca, question 5, asks why honey was not used in sacrifices, and gives this reason: because when mixed in, it seems to spoil the wine, from which libations were made, and drunkenness was produced before the wine had run out. And surely it was rightly forbidden in Jewish sacrifices. For in Leviticus, chapter 2, we read these words: "You shall not burn any honey or leaven in the sacrifice." Allegorically, or in terms of morals, by the name of honey are understood flattery, fawning, pleasure and delights; by the name of leaven, both hypocrisy and deceit, and also malice and contention. From these things one must wholly abstain in sacrifices and in the worship of God.

units.la: Et hæc de materia sacrificiorum atque adeo totius cultus, sive superstitionis potius, Ethnicorum animatâ, nempe omnis generis animalium, tam rationalium, quam brutorum, tam ciuium, quam ferarum, tam minorum, quam majorum, satis finè dicta, quantum quidem propositi nostri ratio postulabat.
units.tr: Enough has now been said about the matter of animal sacrifices, and indeed of the whole animate worship, or rather superstition, of the Gentiles, namely of every kind of animal, rational as well as brute, domestic as well as wild, small as well as large, as far as the plan of our purpose required.

units.la: VENIAMVS ad materiam inanimatam, nempe plantas omnis generis, frugesque atque fructus, quæ Dijs suis ac Numinibus obtulerunt Gentiles: quarum quidem sacrificia antiquissima habita fuerunt, antiquiora longè illis, quæ ex animalibus constabant. Id testatur Plato libro sexto de Legibus, docens homines primos, non solum cibis, sed etiam sacrificiis cruentis abstinuisse, omnibusque rebus ἐμψύχοις, id est, animatis: sola verò ἄψυχα, id est, inanimata, ejus arbitrio & sacrificasse. Et hunc quidem primum hominum tum victum, cum sacrificia fuisse testantur omnes ferè Poëtæ & scriptores antiqui, ut ex illorum monumentis satis constat. Quæ de re videntur potes etiam Danei libellum de prima Mundi ætate.
units.tr: Let us now come to inanimate matter, namely plants of every kind, grains and fruits, which the Gentiles offered to their gods and divinities. Sacrifices of these were held to be the most ancient, far older than those made of animals. Plato testifies to this in book 6 of the Laws, teaching that the first men abstained not only from flesh-foods but also from bloody sacrifices, and from all things animate [ἐμψύχοις], that is, living; they offered at their discretion only things inanimate [ἄψυχα]. Almost all the ancient poets and writers testify that this was the first diet of men, and that sacrifices then existed, as is sufficiently clear from their records. On this subject you may also see the little book of Daneus on the first age of the world.

units.la: Duo autem antiquissima in sacris literis legimus illa fuisse Caini & Abelis sacrificia duorum fratrum germanorum, filiorum Adami & Evæ, quorum ille quidem primogenitus, tanquam agricola, ex terra frugibus; hic verò tanquam opilio ex primogenitis pecudum suarum & de adipe illarum Deo sacrificasse legitur.
units.tr: The two most ancient sacrifices we read of in Holy Scripture are those of Cain and Abel, the two brothers, sons of Adam and Eve. The firstborn, Cain, as a farmer, offered fruits of the earth; Abel, as a shepherd, is read to have offered to God the firstborn of his flocks and their fat.

units.la: Porrò Gentilium sacrificia, quæ constant ex iis, quæ terra producit, varia fuerunt & multiplicia secundum diversa eorum, quæ ex terra nascuntur, genera, ut sunt omnis generis herbæ, olera, flores, poma, Cerealia, frumentacea, legumina, fruges atque fructus. Hæc ipsa verò sacrificia inanimata vel etiam simplicia & cruda, vel composita fuerunt atque cocta.
units.tr: Furthermore, the sacrifices of the Gentiles which consisted of what the earth produces were various and manifold, according to the different kinds of things that grow from the earth: all kinds of herbs, vegetables, flowers, apples, cereals, grains, pulses, crops and fruits. These sacrifices were either inanimate, simple and raw, or compounded and cooked.

units.la: Exordiamur autem ab farre & hordeo: quæ quidem omnium prima Ethnici exifimârunt esse sacrificia. At Ægyptii certè, teste Diodoro Siculo, in asiate spicas Isidi offerebant, invocantes et implorantes Deam, ut fruges prosperaret. Illa enim tritici & hordei in ventrix fuisse credebatur. Eandem ob causam Græci & Romani quoque Cereri Deæ frugum (quam eandem nonnulli volunt fuisse cum Iside illa Ægypta) spicas, & ex eis coronas frugumque primitias offerebant.
units.tr: Let us begin with spelt and barley, which the Gentiles thought to be the very first of sacrifices. The Egyptians, at any rate, according to Diodorus Siculus, offered ears of grain to Isis, invoking and imploring the goddess to make the crops prosper, for it was believed that she was the inventor of wheat and barley. For the same reason the Greeks and Romans also offered ears of grain to Ceres, goddess of the crops (whom some hold to be the same as that Egyptian Isis), and garlands made from them, and first-fruits of the harvest.

units.la: Numa Pompilius, ut inquit Plinius libro decimo octavo, capite secundo, Deos fruge coli, & mola falsa supplicari instituit: quam molam ex farre, sale & aqua compositam, sine qua nullum sacrificium ratum fieri censuit. Atque id far nisi tostum esset, ad rem divinam non esse purum flatuit; quoniam tostum cibo salubrius esset. Farris autem torrendi causa Fornacalia instituit, certas videlicet ferias; de quibus sic Festus: Fornacalia feria instituta, funs farris torrendi gratia, quòd ad Fornacem, quæ in pistrino erat, sacrificium fieri solet. Item, Fornacalia erant sacra, cùm far in fornaculis torrebant. Idem Plinius, Far primum Anciquis in Latio cibum fuisse testatur, & Adoreum à Veteribus dictum, à cujus honore gloriam ipsam Adoreum appellabant. Festus, Adoreum inquit, gloriam dicebant, quia gloriosum eum putabant esse, qui farris copia abundaret: unde ab ץ Aeder, Hebraorum voce, gloriam significante Zachariæ undecimo, Kimchi interpreté, videtur deducta.
units.tr: Numa Pompilius, as Pliny says in book 18, chapter 2, established that the gods were to be worshipped with grain and propitiated with salted meal. This meal was made of spelt, salt and water, and without it he judged no sacrifice to be valid. He also decreed that spelt, unless it was toasted, was not pure for divine worship, since toasted grain was more wholesome. For the sake of toasting spelt he instituted the Fornacalia, a set festival. On this Festus says: "The Fornacalia was a festival instituted for the sake of toasting spelt, because a sacrifice is usually made at the oven which was in the mill. Likewise the Fornacalia were rites when they toasted spelt in little ovens." The same Pliny testifies that spelt was the first food of the ancients in Latium, and that the ancients called it adoreum, and from its honour they called glory itself adoreum. Festus: "They called glory adoreum, because they thought him glorious who had an abundance of spelt." Whence it seems to be derived from the Hebrew word [אדר], meaning glory, as in Zechariah 11, according to the interpretation of Kimchi.

units.la: Quin & in sacris, inquit idem Plinius, libro decimo octavo, capite tertio, nihil religiosius Confarreatione. confarreationis vinculo erat, quoniam nuptae farreum praeferebant. De Confarreatione autem ista sic scribit Dionysius Halicarnassaeus in Romulo: Sacras nuptias ait Farratia esse dicta, quod eodem farre conjuges vescerentur: quo etiam victimas respergerent. Itaq; Ulpianus Tit. 11. Institutionum: Farre, inquit, conveniunt in manum certis verbis & testibus decem praesentibus & solenni sacrificio facto, in quo panis quoque farreus adhibetur. Tacitus libro tertio Annalium, Confarreandi consuetudinem aut omissam, aut inter paucos retentam fuisse docet. Boëtius tribus modis, inquit, uxor habebatur, usu, farre, coemptione: sed Confarreatio solus Pontificibus conveniebat: id sic interpretatur Ra-vardus, eamper solos Pontifices peractam fuisse. Farreum porro, cujus eodem illo loco Plinius meminit, aliquando locum, ubi far reponitur atque reconditur, ut horreum granarium; aliquando libum ex farre confectum significat. Festus: Farreum genus libi ex farre factum. Et alibi: Horreum Antiqui dicebant farreum a farre. Meminit & Diffarreationis Festus, quae genus erat sacrificii, quod inter virum & mulierem fiebat dissolutio: Diffarreatio dicta. Diffarreatio, quia fiebat farreo libo adhibito.
units.tr: Moreover, in sacred rites, says the same Pliny in book 18, chapter 3, nothing was more sacred than the bond of confarreation, since brides carried spelt cake. On this confarreation Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in his Romulus, writes: "He says that sacred marriages were called farratia, because the spouses ate the same spelt with which they also sprinkled the victims." Thus Ulpian, Institutes, title 11: "They come into manus by spelt, with certain words, ten witnesses being present, and a solemn sacrifice performed, in which spelt bread is also used." Tacitus, in book 3 of the Annals, shows that the custom of confarreation was either abandoned or kept among a few. Boethius says: "A wife was regarded in three ways: by use, by spelt, by coemption; but confarreation belonged to the Pontiffs alone." Ravardus interprets this as meaning that it was performed by the Pontiffs alone. Farreum, which Pliny also mentions in the same place, sometimes denotes the place where spelt is stored and kept, like a granary; sometimes a cake made from spelt. Festus: "Farreum is a kind of cake made from spelt." And elsewhere: "The ancients called a granary farreum, from far." Festus also mentions diffarreation, a kind of sacrifice by which the union of husband and wife was dissolved: "It was called diffarreation because it was done with the spelt cake being used."

units.la: Mola igitur salsa ex farre & sale confiebat, unde immolatio dicta, quae erat hostia quasi consecratio, nibilque proprie erat aliud, quam mola in caput victimae infusio, sive collocatio. Ab hac sacerdos sacrum incheabat, fruges nimirum aut molam salsam, in caput victimae deponendo, addito thure masculo, ut tessatur Plinius libro tertio, capite septimo. Huc pertinet illud pro-verbium, unde θύειν ἀπὸ ἀλφίτων. Ne sacrifices sine farina, quae a farre dicta. Item hoc: Ador far-reus genus edor quondam appellatum ab edendo, vel quod aduratur, ut fiat tostum: unde in sacri-ficio mola salsa efficitur: Festus. Vitellium Imperatorem Suetonius scribit, hominem adeo uon profunde modo, sed iuterpellavit quoque & sollicitam gula fuisse, ut ne in sacrificio quidem muuquam aut utinere ullo temperarit, quin inter altaria ibidem flatum visceus, id est, carnes holocaustorum & farra pone tapta foco manderet.
units.tr: Salted meal was therefore made from spelt and salt, and from this the immolation (immolatio) took its name. The immolation was a kind of hallowing of the victim, and properly it was nothing other than pouring or placing the meal on the victim's head. From this the priest began the sacred rite, namely by laying the grain or salted meal on the victim's head, with male frankincense added, as Pliny says in book 3, chapter 7. To this belongs the proverb "to sacrifice from barley-meal" [θύειν ἀπὸ ἀλφίτων], and "do not sacrifice without meal," which is so called from spelt. Likewise this from Festus: "Ador is a kind of spelt, once called edor from eating, or because it is parched so that it becomes toasted; hence salted meal is made for sacrifice." Suetonius writes of the Emperor Vitellius that he was a man so given not only to lavish living but also to gluttony that, even at sacrifices, he never restrained himself, in any place or at any time, from eating, right there among the altars, the entrails of the burnt offerings and the spelt cakes placed on the hearth.

units.la: Ut autem Romani far, sic Gracorum plerique non far, sed hordei primitias libumque & placentas ex hordeo Dis offerebant, hordeumque sale inspersum inprimis infundi satius duxere, fine quo sal ya religione nullum sacrum fieri poterat. Illum qui primitias ejusmodi colligebat Critbologum dixere, teste Plutarcho in Quaestionibus Graecis, quaestione sexta, & Alexandro ab Alexand. libro tertio, eapite duodecimo. Graeci igitur has molas salsas ἀλοχύτα, sive ἀλφιτταῖς suae lingua appellabant, voce composita ex ἁλς, id est, ordeum molitum & χύτοις, id est, infusione. (Apud Homerum saepe ἀλοχύτας ἀφεσβόλους, id est, molas porriciebant.) Hujus vero cerimonia Eustathius ἀλκ̄ ... hanc rationem reddit: Veteres, inquit, in suis sacris ἀλοχύτας, sive ἀλοχύτας, ordeum hoc, sive hordeum, sale συγχέ-ραμον, commixtum semper praemittebant: ut hoc ipso Deorum erga homines bynignitatem in frugum inventione (inter quas ordeum primum fuisse traditur: quam ob causam ἀρχή Graecus dictum est ἀπὸ τὰ ἀλφεῖται, quoniam manfuetiore vitâ homines usi, a belluina quoque natura sensim segregati fuere) & Respublica conflitutione (cujus symbolum est sal; quoniam sicuti ex varus guttulis una falis mica solida, victus quotidiani condimentum, nascitur: ita etiam ex multis civibus, quos manfuetior vita cultus in unam, frugum inventarum beneficio, reduxit, una civitas & Respublica oritur) ob oculos ponerent, & suam quoque gratitudinem testarentur, atq; ita cum beneficiorum recordatione, tum gratiarum actione Deorum benevolentiam porro sibi comparaient. Pramifsis bisce molis preces subjungebant & sacrificia peragebant. Hactenus Eustathius. Megaris verò dum ad Terei-fepulcrum sacrum fiebat, pro hordeo calculis utebantur, teste eodem Alexandro libro quarto, capite decimo septimo. Ac Dianae Propylee Eleusiniae mulierem nullam, nisi ex ibinato hordeo molam confecere fuit, Virgines porró Vestales, teste Alexandro libro quinto, capite duodecimo, molâ casta & sale tuso in ollam fictilem misso, mox in aquam injecto Vestae sacra faciebant, cultibusque fictilibus, quos Culullos ditebant, Vesta & Dius lib abant. Eidem Dea frugum primitia sacrum fiebat, pro hordeo calculis utebantur, teste eodem Alexandro libro quarto, capite decimo septimo. Erat autem casta mola sacrificii genere proprium virginum Vestalium, ut Festus tessatur. Pertinet huc Pecunia, sive pecunia, sacrificium, ut Paullus testatur, quod fieri dicebatur, cum fruges frugibusque offerebantur, quia ex his rebus omnis res familiaris conflat, quam nunc Pecuniam dicimus. Hac de Cerealibus.
units.tr: But as the Romans offered spelt, so most of the Greeks offered to the gods not spelt but the first fruits of barley, along with cakes and flatbreads made of barley; and they thought it better to pour the barley first, sprinkled with salt, since no sacred rite could be performed in religion without salt. The one who gathered such first fruits they called the Critheologus, as Plutarch testifies in his Greek Questions, question 6, and Alexander ab Alexandro book 3, chapter 12. The Greeks therefore called these salted meals in their own tongue "alochyta," or "alphita," a compound word from "hals" (salt), meaning barley ground up, and "chytos," meaning pouring. (In Homer they often threw down "aloschytas" [ἀλοχύτας], that is, meal cakes.) Eustathius gives this account of the ceremony of these rites: "The ancients," he says, "in their sacred rites always first offered barley (or the barley-meal) mixed with salt, so that by this very act they might set before their eyes the goodness of the gods towards men in the discovery of crops (of which barley is said to have been the first), for which reason the Greek word for barley was derived from 'alphe-ein' [ἀρχή?], because men, living a gentler life, were gradually separated also from a brutish nature; and the constitution of the commonwealth (whose symbol is salt, since just as one grain of salt is formed from many drops, the daily seasoning of food, so also from many citizens, whom a gentler way of life, by the benefit of discovered crops, has brought together into one, one city and commonwealth arises). They set these things before their eyes, and also bore witness to their own gratitude, and so, with the remembrance of benefits and the giving of thanks, they further gained for themselves the goodwill of the gods." After these meals were offered, they added prayers and performed the sacrifices. So far Eustathius. At Megara, indeed, when the sacrifice was made at the tomb of Tereus, they used pebbles in place of barley, as the same Alexander testifies, book 4, chapter 17. And at the Eleusinian Propylaea of Diana no woman was allowed to make the meal except from barley-meal kneaded in water. The Vestal Virgins, moreover, as Alexander testifies in book 5, chapter 12, performed the sacred rites of Vesta with chaste meal and crushed salt put into an earthen pot, then thrown into water, and with earthen vessels which they called "cululi," they offered to Vesta and to Jupiter. To the same goddess the first fruits of the crops were offered as a sacred rite. Chaste meal was a kind of sacrifice peculiar to the Vestal Virgins, as Festus says.
