To this pertains the "pecunia" (or "pecunia") sacrifice, as Paulus testifies, which was said to be made when crops were offered with crops, because from these things every household property is formed, which we now call "pecunia" (money). So much on cereals.

units.la: Leguminum quoque in sacris maximus olim usus fuit. Hinc aras dedicaturi aut simulatura ...
units.tr: Pulses also once had a very great use in sacred rites. Hence, those about to dedicate altars or to imitate ...

units.la: Ολυμπιονίκας oblatio legumi-num. Dei alicujus, legumina elixa pro primitiis offerebant dedicatis, ob memoriam gratiæ animi, mo vitiu. Aristophanes in Danaïs: Testor, inquit, Iovis Herceollas, cum quibus ara dedicatur est olim. Sic Mercuriales statuas pro foribus, & alia sigilla dedicantes, quo felicior esset erestio ollas polentæ adhibebant, ut testatur Suidas in voce χύτροι ιερ᾽ύτια, Ollis pax sancienda.
units.tr: Oblation of pulses [Ολυμπιονίκας]. For some god they offered boiled pulses as first fruits to those being dedicated, in memory of grateful feeling. Aristophanes in the Danaids: "I call to witness," he says, "Zeus Herkeios, with whom the altar was once dedicated." So too, when dedicating Mercurial statues before doors and other small images, they used pots of pottage so that the dedication might be more fortunate, as Suidas testifies in the word "chytroi" [χύτροι]. "Peace is to be ratified with pots."

units.la: Suffimenta ex faba mistoque aspersa mulso Diis offerri absque vitulina; quo tempore calente prelo premuntur, testatur Alexander ab Alexandro libro secundo, capite vigesimo secundo.
units.tr: Fumigations of beans mixed with sprinkled mead were offered to the gods without veal, at the time when they are pressed while still warm, as Alexander ab Alexandro testifies, book 2, chapter 22.

units.la: Porrò fabæ ipsæ, teste Festo, & in Lemuribus iaciebantur larvis, & in parentalibus sacrificiis adhibebantur, Manes placandi gratia, in quarum flore lucius litteræ apparere videntur: unde pallens a Martiale videtur dici; & Manes idcirco sese vulgo dicebantur in fabis abdere. Hanc ipsam autem ob causam impure habebantur, quas ideo, ut Festus indicat, Dialis flamini, nec tangere, nec nominare licebat, quod numinum putabantur ad mortuos pertinere. De isdem Alexander ab Alexandro libro tertio, capite duodecimo sic scribit: In Lemuralibus sabam noctu iacere sosurpatum est, Lemures se ex domo exire clamantes. Eam nigrum esse conuenit: ipsamque lotus manibus & pedes modo per ora versare, & post terga rejicere, arisque tinctum facere: ut Lemures sabas redemti, domo abirent, noctu vices orare: idque Majo mense strebus noctibus fieri, donec solutis religione animis, Manes expiatos ducerent. In Parentalibus assumere sabas sus obtinuit: sicut in per vigilius citer: ac semles cænas lentesque & offas ad sepulcra illorum ferre, quibus parentaræ ius erat (quæ etiam Fermia aferendis epulis dicta sunt) & in defunctorum sepulchris super nudam filicem apponere.
units.tr: Moreover, according to Festus, beans themselves were thrown at the Lemures, the ghosts, and were used in parental sacrifices to appease the Manes, and on their flower certain letters seem to appear; whence "pallens" (pale) is said by Martial to be derived; and it was commonly said that the Manes hid themselves in beans. For this very reason beans were regarded as impure, so that, as Festus points out, the Flamen Dialis was not allowed either to touch them or to name them, because they were thought to pertain to the spirits of the dead. On the same matter Alexander ab Alexandro, book 3, chapter 12, writes thus: "In the Lemuralia it was customary to throw beans at night, while crying out that the Lemures were leaving the house. The bean had to be black; and having washed hands and feet, one was to turn it in the mouth, and throw it over the back, and make it stained with blood, so that the Lemures, redeemed by the bean, would leave the house; and this they did, with the nine nights in turn, in the month of May, until, with minds freed from superstition, they should consider the Manes expiated. In the Parentalia it was the custom to take beans, as on the vigils of the dead; and to carry simple dinners, lentils and cakes to the tombs of those to whom the right of parental rites belonged (which are also called 'Fermia' from bringing the feast), and to place them on the bare fern upon the graves of the dead."

units.la: His adde, quod ab hoc usu sacro sabæ, ea Refriva dicta est; de quo cognomine sic Festus: Refriva faba dicitur, ut ait Cincius quoque, quæ ad sacrificium referri soler domam ex segete auspicium caussa quasi re vocent fruges, ut domum datantes te virtuo ad rem diuinam faciendam. Ælius dubitat, an ea sit, quæ prolata in segetem, domum refrictur; ex qua refrigatur, quod est correatur: sed opinionem Cincii adjicit, quod in sacrificiis publicis, eum puls fabata Diis dantur, nominatur refriva.
units.tr: Add to this that from this sacred use the bean was called "refriva." Festus speaks thus about this surname: "A bean is called 'refriva,' as Cincius also says, which is customarily carried back to the sacrifice from the crop, as a means of auspices, as it were, calling back the fruits, the bean-harvesters bringing them home to perform the divine rite. Aelius doubts whether it is the bean which, carried out into the field, is brought back home, from which it is 'refrigatur' (cooled), that is, is brought back; but he adds the opinion of Cincius, that in public sacrifices, when a bean porridge is given to the gods, it is called 'refriva.'"

units.la: Alliorum præterea & papaverum capitibus Romani Manie, quæ mater Larium fuit, in Compitalibus sacrificia fecerunt, pro incolumitate videlicet familiæ: pro qua antea illi pueros mactabant. Testis hujus rei est idem Alexander.
units.tr: Moreover, the Romans offered sacrifices at the Compitalia to Mania, who was the mother of the Lares, with heads of garlic and poppies, for the safety of the household, namely, for which safety they had formerly sacrificed boys. Witness to this fact is the same Alexander.

units.la: Arborum quinetiam ramos ac palmites cum suis racemis olim Ethnici Diis suis consecrabant atque immolarunt. Id præcipue memoriæ proditum est de pueris ingenuis pubescentibus apud Athenienses, qui in templum Minervæ Seriados arborum ramos & palmites cum racemis ferebant, eique offerebant quod festum sive celebritas ideo Oschophoria fuit appellata ὀσχοφόρια, id est, ramis: cuius apud auctores, inprimis Plutarchum crebra fit mentio.
units.tr: Indeed, the pagans once also consecrated and sacrificed to their gods the branches of trees together with their vine shoots and clusters. This is especially recorded of freeborn youths at puberty among the Athenians, who carried branches of trees and vine shoots with clusters into the temple of Minerva Seriados and offered them there. The festival or celebration was therefore called "Oschophoria" [ὀσχοφόρια], that is, bearing of branches; and it is frequently mentioned by authors, above all by Plutarch.

units.la: Frumentorum, leguminum & arborum quoque flores ac fructus obtulerunt: unde Dea Flora nomen obtinuit, & ab hac Floralia. Scribit Plutarchus, simulacrum Florae in ede Capitolii & Pollucis, Praxiteles summa industria formatum, multis coloribus, tunica indutum fuisse, in cujus Dea decora flores fabarum & ciceris fuerint. In his floribus tradit Porphyrion Ædiles cicer & faba popido spargere solitos. Versicolor autem color ideo Florae attributus, quia nullus color est, qui in floribus non reperiatur. Sane Chloris, quam Ovidius Floram ajit, meminit & Catullus, & ante hos Homerus in Odyss.
units.tr: They also offered the flowers and fruits of grain, pulses and trees: whence the goddess Flora obtained her name, and from her the Floralia. Plutarch writes that the statue of Flora in the temple of the Capitol and of Pollux, formed with the greatest skill by Praxiteles, was clothed in a tunic of many colours, and on the goddess's garments there were flowers of beans and chickpeas. Porphyrion records that the aediles were accustomed to scatter chickpeas and beans among the people as these flowers. The varied colour is attributed to Flora for this reason, that there is no colour which is not found in flowers. Indeed Chloris, whom Ovid calls Flora, is mentioned by Catullus too, and before them by Homer in the Odyssey.

units.la: Ex fructibus vero arborum olim ficus & poma in sacris adhiberi & offerri solita constat: Poma quidem Priapo potissimum. Sic enim in Priapeis: —Puer domini florentis agelli Poma Priapo offert: &c.
units.tr: From the fruits of trees it is known that figs and apples were formerly used and offered in sacred rites, apples especially to Priapus. For so it runs in the Priapea: "A boy, master of a flowering little field, offers apples to Priapus," etc.

units.la: Et forsan etiam Pomonæ, Pomorum Deæ ac patronæ.
units.tr: And perhaps also to Pomona, goddess and patroness of fruit.

units.la: Denique nimis operosum esset ac pene infinitum, panum, placentarum, liborum, eduliorum que variorum, que ex frumento, farre & leguminibus confecta & composita fuerunt, genera Diis offerri solita, enumerare. Proprii quibusdam Diis panes erant dicati, de quo sum nonnullis
units.tr: Finally, it would be too laborious and almost endless to list all the kinds of loaves, cakes, pastries and various sweet confections, made from wheat, spelt and pulses, that were customarily offered to the gods. Some loaves were dedicated to particular gods, and of these...

units.la: Athenæus & Pollux libro sexto scribunt : cujusmodi præ aliis erant Obeliophori, in Bacchi celebritatibus : Pelani verò omnibus Diis erant communes. Placentæ nomen erat & hoc cornuta, Apollini, Dianæ, Hecatæ & Lunæ attributa.
units.tr: Athenaeus and Pollux write in their sixth book. Among these, the Obeliophoroi were especially used in the festivals of Bacchus, while the Pelanoi were common to all the gods. "Placenta" was also the name of a horned cake, attributed to Apollo, Diana, Hecate and the Moon.

units.la: Huc pertinent Prothymata, in sacris potissimum Æsculapii, ut est apud Aristophanem, adhibita : item Melitutæ, Arista & Hygiea molestiae : item Ἀθάνας, Attice Ἀθάρη, panis caeus, sive excavatus, fine farina, quam in sacris suis comedebant, ut idem multis testatur, gravissimus autor, Aristophanes : cujusmodi buccea panis excavata est & μυξίλη, qua pulmentum aut jus hauriretur.
units.tr: To this class belong the prothymata, used especially in the sacrifices of Aesculapius, as Aristophanes mentions; likewise the melitutae, aristae and hygieiae. Also the Attic athare, which the Greeks called athanas [ἀθάνας], a hollow bread without flour, which they ate in their sacrifices, as Aristophanes, a most weighty authority, attests in many places. Of this kind is the hollow bread called buccea, and the myxile [μυξίλη], by which broth or soup was scooped up.

units.la: Pertinent huc etiam πόπανα, placentulæ tenues rotundæ, sacrificiis aptæ : item πόλαγοι, Popana. miles feré placentulæ, in sacrificiis usitatæ, de quibus vide Aristophanem & ejus Scholiastem. Sic Pastillum, auctore Festo, genus erat libi rotundi, quod Dijs offerebatur : Et Pa-Pastilla, illus, teste Paulo, forma panis parvi. Utrunque & Pastillum, & Pastillus diminutivum a pane.
units.tr: To this class also belong the popana [πόπανα], thin round little cakes suited to sacrifices; likewise the polagoi [πόλαγοι], almost the same little cakes used in sacrifices, on which see Aristophanes and his scholiast. So too the pastillum, according to Festus, was a kind of round cake offered to the gods; and the pastilla, according to Paulus, was the shape of a small loaf. Both pastillum and pastillus are diminutives of panis.

units.la: Placentæ porro, quæ ex farre & melle constabant ; & Deorum sacrificiis potissimum erant Liba. destinata, Liba vocarunt Latini, quæ nos Germani Ieib dicimus, ut Libum panis, Ieib biote : de quibus Virgilius : Et adorea liba per herbam Subjicunt epulis, &c.
units.tr: Cakes made of spelt and honey, in particular, were destined for the sacrifices of the gods. The Latins called these liba, which we Germans call Ieib, as libum panis is Ieib biote. Of these Virgil writes: "And they set honeyed cakes (adorea liba) on the grass beneath the feast," etc.

units.la: Et Ovidius : Cui cum Cereale sacerdos Imponit libum.
units.tr: And Ovid: "To whom the priestess of Ceres lays a libum."

units.la: Vocat Cereale, tanquam confectum Cerere, id est pane. Cererem enim pro pane frequenter usurari notius est, quam ut quenquam fugiat. Obeandem causam dicebatur etiam farreum, tanem ex farre confectum. Hoc, inter alia, fiebat diffarreatio, de qua supra, quæ genus erat ficii, quo fiebat inter virum & mulierem dissolutio macrimonii scilicet, per confarreationem contractis. Libum autem, teste Varrone, fuit dictum, quod libaretur primum quam esset, ut ei coiluni. A voce hac libi ipse Bacchus nonnullis visus est Liber dictus, cum quod ea exhibuit, Liber. ut tradit Plutarchus Quaestione Romana centesima quarta, tum quod liba & mella, mense Martio, offerri fuerunt solita. Tibullus 1. Sic venias hodierne: tibi nam thuris honores Libaque Mopsopio dulcia mella feram.
units.tr: He calls it "Cereale," as if made of Ceres, that is, of bread; for it is well known that Ceres is often used for bread. For the same reason it was also called farreum, as made of spelt. Among other things, this was used in the diffarreatio mentioned above, a kind of rite by which the marriage between husband and wife, contracted by confarreatio, was dissolved. Libum, according to Varro, was so named because it was offered first (libare) before it was eaten. From this word libi, some thought that Bacchus himself was called Liber, both because he gave these things and because libum and honey were customarily offered in March, as Plutarch relates in Roman Question 104. Tibullus, book 1: "So may you come today; for I shall bring you the honours of incense and sweet honey-cakes of Mopsopia."

units.la: Hinc forsan & Liberalia sunt dicta, ceu Liberi a libis appellati, festa, quae apud Græcos dicun-Liberalia, tur Διονυσια ; unde si Nævius a libera lingua ea denominet, inquiens : Libera lingua loquemur ludis libertilibus.
units.tr: Hence perhaps the Liberalia also took their name, as festivals of Liber, who was named from the libi; the Greeks call them Dionysia. Whence, if Naevius derives it from "free tongue," saying: "We shall speak with a free tongue at the games of liberty."

units.la: Ad libi genera pertinet Ianual, genus libi, Festo auctore, quod Iano tantummodo libabatur: Ianuel. & Punicum, quod translatum a Pœnis, etiam genus libi erat, dictum alio nomine Probum, quia Punicum. erat præ ceteris suavissimum. At Moretum genus erat edulii rusticani, Rhea Dea offerri solitum. Moretum. Ejusdem descriptionem vide apud Virgilium; & confectionem apud Columellam libro de re rustica ultimo. Sic Cocetum genus erat edulii ex melle & papaveris factum, auctore Festo. Fer-Cocetum. tum item sive Feretum libi genus erat, quod crebriùs ad sacra ferebatur; nec sine Strue, altero genere libi, quod qui adferebant Strufertarii, sive Struisfertarii, sive etiam Strusertarii sunt dicti, voce composita a Strue & ferro : Festus. Strusifertarii sive Strusfertarii, ut idem testatur Struisfertarii fuerunt dicti, qui quædam sacrificia ad arbores fulguritas faciebant, a Ferto scilicet, quodam qui. facrifi-nere : quod ipsum Isidorus vocat oblationem, quae alteri offertur, & sacrificatur a Pontificibus, a quo Offertorium nominatur, quasi propter fertum. Strues porro genera liborum sunt, digitorum conjunctorum non dissimilia, quae superjecta paniculo in transferfum continentur. Arculata quinetiam certa genera liborum erant, circuli videlicet, quiex farina in Arculata. sacrificiis fiebant. Sic Africia, Gratilla, Catumeum, Confboleum, Cubulum, erant certa liborum Africia, &c. sacrorum nomina atque genera, quorum Arnobius meminit. De vitlu autem antiquissimo, de pulte, pulmento, pulmentario, tritico, farre, libo, tessuaceo, placenta vide Varronem libro quarto de lingua Latina. Acpulte quidem vel offa, non pane, longo tempore vixisse Romanos manesfestum est, quoniam inde & pulmentaria hodie quoque dicuntur. Et Ennius ant-quisimus Vates obliditionis famem exprimens, offam eripuisse plorantibus liberis patres commemorat. Et hodie sacra prisca atque Natalium pulte fritilla eosuiciuntur, inquit Plinius libro decimooctauo, capite octauo. Puls, inquit Festus, potissimum dabatur pultes in auspiciis, quia ex eanecesse erat aliquid decidere, quod tripudium faceret, id est, terripauium. Pa-vireenim ferire est, ut Jupiter quoque aquam ex eodem Festo.
units.tr: To the kinds of libum belongs the ianual, a kind of libum, according to Festus, which was offered to Janus alone. The Punicum, carried over from the Carthaginians, was also a kind of libum, called by another name probus, because it was the sweetest of all. Moretum was a kind of rustic food offered to the goddess Rhea; see its description in Virgil, and its preparation in Columella's last book On Agriculture. So too cocetum was a food made of honey and poppy seed, according to Festus. Likewise the fertum, or feretum, was a kind of libum, which was more often carried to sacred rites, and not without the struem, another kind of libum. Those who brought these were called struferarii, or struisferarii, or struserarii, a compound word from struem and ferre (Festus). Struisferarii, as the same Festus attests, were so called from those who performed certain sacrifices at trees struck by lightning, from ferire, to strike. Isidore calls this an offering that is made to another and sacrificed by the pontiffs, and from it the offertorium takes its name, as if from fertum. The strues are kinds of libum, not unlike fingers joined together, which, laid across a platter, are held together. Arculata too were certain kinds of libum, namely round cakes made of flour in sacrifices. So the Africia, Gratilla, Catumeum, Conboleum and Cubulum were certain names and kinds of sacred cakes, of which Arnobius makes mention. About the most ancient food, and about pulse, pulmentum, pulmentarium, wheat, spelt, libum, tessuaceum and placenta, see Varro, book four of On the Latin Language. That the Romans lived for a long time on pulse or a morsel, and not on bread, is clear, since even today pulmentaria are so named from it. And Ennius, the most ancient of poets, describing famine under siege, records that the fathers snatched a morsel from their weeping children. And Pliny, book eighteen, chapter eight, says that even today sacred rites and birthdays are celebrated with pulse of spelt and fritilla. Festus says: puls was given especially in the auspices, because from it something had of necessity to fall, which made the tripudium, that is, a striking of the ground (terripavium). For pavire means to strike, as also Jupiter with the water, from the same Festus.

units.la: Denique, ad libri genera pertinet etiam placenta, ex farina & casio melle confecta: sic dista nonnullis quod vel offerentibus ipsa placeat, vel Diis, quibus offertur, atque ita ea soleret Deos placare: sed potius a Græca voce πλακοῦς, πλακοῦντος, contracta a πλακοῦς, υ τ ῷ, placentam significante deriuatur. Athenæus libro tertio: πλακοῦς ὑπ γαλακτοῦ ἐξίωντες, ἡ ὁ ῥυμάτιον λίβον ἐν ἀλούσι, quam Romani libum vocant.
units.tr: Finally, the placenta, made of flour and fresh honey, also belongs to the kinds of libum. Some say it is so called because it pleases either those who offer it or the gods to whom it is offered, and that in this way it would appease the gods. But it is rather derived from the Greek word plakous, plakountos, meaning a flat cake, contracted from plakous [πλακοῦς]. Athenaeus, book three, says: "a plakous made with milk, or ... which the Romans call libum" [πλακοῦς ὑπὸ γαλακτοῦ ...].

units.la: Huc referri debent Fitilla & Frumen, quæ interpretē Arnobio, similiter fuerunt pultium nomina, sed genere & qualitate diuersa. Arnobius alia quoque pultium seu pulmentorum, & borum, quorum dicit esse mille species, nomina enumerat: qua, ut idem ait, Ethnici fecerunt obscuriora, ut augustiora vulgo offent.
units.tr: Here should be referred the fitilla and frumen, which, according to Arnobius, were likewise names of pulses, though different in kind and quality. Arnobius also lists other names of pulses or dishes and of libum; he says there are a thousand kinds, which, as he observes, the heathen made more obscure so that they would seem more august to the common people.

units.la: Libet hic subjicere eiusdem Arnobii verba, quibus Ethnicorum insanam istam idololatriam mirificè exagitat: In hoc enim, inquit, diuitius loco huic caussæ vel maxime necessario immoramur, insistimus, in haremus, cupientes addiscere, quid cum pultibus Deo fit, quid cum libis, quid diversis cum fratribus confectionis iure multiplici, atque impensarum varietate conditis? Opiparis Numina cænis afficiuntur, aut prandiis, ut innumeras conveniat excoquare hu dapes? a ve: lionibus slomachoriu laborant? & ad expellendas fastidia saporii varietas quæritur, ut modo his assa, modo cruda ponantur, semicocta modo & semicrudæ quod si omnes has partes, quas præsiciat ductus, accipere Dii amant, suntque illis gratiæ, vel voluptates aliquæ, vel dulcedinis sensu, quid interceditc, quid prohibet, ut non semel hæc omnia totis cum animantibus inferatur? Quæ caussa, quæ ratio est, ut caro strebula separatim, ruma cauda & plascea separatim, ibi silicet olum, omentum solum, augmentorum adjicitur in cansam? Pulmentorum varietatibus assi: iuntur Dii calites, ut sieri mos est, post cænarum ditium & loculptum saginas, frissilia hæc parpula pro suassibus maceolus sumuntur, non quibus fanem sedent, sed ut palatus admoveant ocium, seque ipsos plena appetitu voraciuntur instigent? O Deorum magnitudo mirabilis? O nullis hominum comprehensa, nullis intellesta naturis? siquidem, ut prosint, cessiculus pecudum redimuntur & runus, neque prius iras atque animos ponunt, nisi sibi adoleri paratas conspexerint nanias, offasque penitas.
units.tr: It is worth adding here Arnobius's own words, with which he vigorously lashes the mad idolatry of the heathen: "For in this matter, he says, we linger longest and most necessarily dwell, we insist and cling, wishing to learn what is done for the gods with pulses, what with libum, and with the various confections prepared under a manifold rule of cookery and varied expense. Are the gods gratified with sumptuous dinners or luncheons, so that countless delicacies must be cooked for them? Do they labour under weak stomachs, so that a variety of flavours is sought to drive off their distaste, so that now these things are offered roasted, now raw, now half-cooked and half-raw? If the gods love to receive all these parts which the process of preparation supplies, and if they take pleasure in them, or some delight from the sense of sweetness, what hinders or prevents all these things being offered at once, with the whole animal? What cause, what reason is there that the flesh of the shin, the tail and the entrails are added separately, and the fat alone, the omentum alone, as if for their own sake? The heavenly gods are regaled with varieties of broth, as is the custom, after the rich dinners and the gorging of the feast; these little dishes of fried things are taken up to tempt the palate, not that they may satisfy hunger, but so that, with their appetites full, they may spur themselves on to greed. O marvellous greatness of the gods! O greatness comprehended by no man and understood by no nature! For, that they may be favourable, the flocks of cattle are bought up and the flocks of sheep, and they do not lay aside their anger and their moods until they see the entrails and the cakes prepared to be burned for them."

units.la: Hactenus Arnobius: quibus quidem verbis insanam, ut dixi, perstringit idololatriam Gentilium: ubi simul hæc quoque notanda, in gentium sacris usitata. Per strebulam carnem, vel ut Poeta tonitrum strebulam per carostribulam (quam vocema ψαῖτεν deducit Varro, a loci, id est, coxendiculi nerusura) partes carnium sacrificata: ut appellari Imbrorum lingu, qua & Strebula in plurali dicuntur, neutro genere. Deinde a versionem slomachi hanc affectionem esse, quam Galenus ollauo de compositione medicamentorum capite tertio ἀπορίαν vocat. Præsicias verò quæ præsesta vel præsesta projiciuntur, unde Turnebus suis in Varronem commentariis legit prosiciat, addueius Varronis authoritate, qui quarto de lingua Latina Insitia deri-vatur ab eo, quod insesta taro, & quod in extis dicitur nunc prosestum. Ouidius: Cujus ut imposuit prosesta ealentibus aris.
units.tr: Thus far Arnobius. In these words, as I said, he exposes the mad idolatry of the Gentiles. Several other points here are also worth noting, concerning practices in use in the rites of the Gentiles. The "strebula" was flesh, or as the poet has it, "tonitrum strebulam," through the "carostribula" (which Varro derives from the Greek word for the hip joint, that is, the sinew of the hip). It meant the pieces of meat offered in sacrifice, and this is why in the plural "strebula" is said in the neuter gender, as the word of the Imbri. Next, this is a disorder of the stomach, which Galen, in the third chapter of his book on the compounding of medicines, calls aporia. The "praesectae" or "prosectae," which are cut forward and thrown on the altar, are read by Turnebus in his commentaries on Varro as "prosiciat," citing Varro's authority. In the fourth book of his On the Latin Language Varro says that "insitia" derives from the fact that the entrails were cut, and that what is now called "prosectum" in the entrails. Ovid: "When he laid the prosecta on the warm altars."

units.la: Nam prosecari exta dicebantur. Tranquillus in Augusto: Semicruda nipta foco exposeita. Prosicium etiam ait Festus, quod prosestum projicitur, ατ τῷ ζωμῷ ἀπαρχαῖς, ut inquit Scialiger. Horum prosestorum quidam etiam Poetarum memiuerunt. Lucanus: —Si pectora pleno Sæpe dedi, la-ni talido prosesta terebro.
units.tr: For the entrails were said to be "prosecari," cut forward. Suetonius in Augustus: "He placed semi-raw entrails on the hearth." Festus also says that "prosicium" is what is thrown forward as the prosectum, along with the broth as first-fruits, as Scaliger says. Some of the poets also mention these prosecta. Lucan: "If I have often given full breasts... with the sharp drill, the prosecta..."

units.la: Statius: Vbi ad verso dederat prosesta tonantis.
units.tr: Statius: "Where he had given the prosecta to the thundering god."

units.la: Nonius vero ait: Prosesta exta, quæ aræ dabantur, ex fibris pecudum dissesta,
units.tr: Nonius says: "Prosecta are the entrails that were given to the altars, cut from the fibres of the animals."

units.la: Licinius Macer in Ornithogonia: — Vulgari tosta vapore,
units.tr: Licinius Macer in Ornithogonia: "Roasted over a common heat,"
"they bring forth with rods the prosecta."
Valerius Flaccus, book three of the Argonautica:

units.la: Tunc pirtee mactantur oves, profestaq; partim.
units.tr: "Then sheep are slaughtered on the spot, and partly the prosecta."

units.la: Pectora per medios, partim geris ob vius Idmon.
units.tr: "The breasts through the middle, partly the entrails, Idmon offers."

units.la: Praeterea Rumam partem esse colli, qua esca devoratur, unde irruminare & ruminare: Festus. Mateolas autem (sive, ut Adrianus Turnebus iisdem commentariis in quartum Varronis de lingua Latina putat, Mateolis diminutivè legendum, a nomine Mattia, vel matta) pretiosa esse edulia, quorum Suetonius meminit in Caligula, his verbis: Et multis venenatas mattas misit. Quo in loco multi legunt Mattyas, alias Matteas, item Mattya: quae, ut differt Athenaeus libro decimo quinto, capite ultimo, Omne scitamentum, & omnis cupedia, jucundumque & pretiosum edulium vocatur: cum tamen proprie initio esset, tanquam quaedam maza. Idemque utrumque eadem est origo. Male autem legi videtur Mate, ab eo, quod GraeciΜαττύω κτλ. Porrò mazam, inquit Caelius libro nono, capite duodecimo, putant ex farina, oleo & aqua confici solitam. Suidas etiam ex latte: unde mox paullo nata est & mattya, dictaque eo nomine pretiosa edulia.
units.tr: Festus also says that the "ruma" is the part of the neck through which food is swallowed, whence "irruminare" and "ruminare." The "mateolae" (or, as Adrianus Turnebus thinks in the same commentaries on Varro's On the Latin Language, book four, it should be read as a diminutive from the name Mattia or matta) were costly delicacies. Suetonius mentions them in Caligula: "He sent poisoned mattae to many." Some read "Mattyas" here, others "Matteas" or "Mattya." As Athenaeus says in book fifteen, last chapter, every dainty, every confection and every pleasing and costly food is called by this name, though originally it was properly a kind of "maza." Both words have the same origin. It seems wrong to read "Mate," from the Greek verb meaning to knead. Caelius, book nine, chapter twelve, says that the maza was usually made from flour, oil and water. Suidas says it was made from milk, whence shortly afterwards the "mattya" arose, and dainty foods were named by that name.

units.la: Martialis libro decimo: Dives & ex omni posita est instructa macello Cœna tibi, sed te mattya sola juvat.
units.tr: Martial, book ten: "A rich dinner, furnished from the whole market, is set before you, but only the mattya pleases you."

units.la: Hallenus etiam de placentis, libis & similibus: quae e Cerealibus & leguminibus confecta dicuntur, in sacris sacrificiis, Gentilium fuerunt usitata.
units.tr: Thus far also concerning cakes, libae and the like, which are said to be made from grains and pulses, were in use among the Gentiles in their sacred sacrifices.

units.la: AGAMYS nunc paucis de vino, quo & ipso, praeclaro quidem & eximio Dei dono, ut ad luxuriam; sic ad idololatriam atque superstitionem nefarie olim abusi fuerunt Gentiles. Nam in plerisque illorum sacrificiis vinum fuit adhibitum: immo antiquissimâ fere & simplicissima dorum sacrificia vino atque thure (unde haec duo saepe conjunguntur) conflabant. Suetonius in vita Augusti scribit, Imperatorem illum instituisse, ut patres Curiam ingressi, prius quam sedent, thure & mero apud aram ejus Dei, in cujus templum coiretur, sacrificarent. Hinc, eodem auctore, Tyberius Caesar, ex quo primum die post excessum Augusti Curiam intravit, quasi pietati simul & religioni satisfacturus, Minois exemplo, thure quidem ac vino, verum fine tibicine (qui nimirum omnibus in sacrificiis adhiberi consueverat) supplicavit. Ovidius: Mox ego cur quamvis aliorum Numina placens Iane, tibi primum thura merumq; fero.
units.tr: Now briefly concerning wine. This too is a remarkable and excellent gift of God, yet the Gentiles wickedly abused it, both for luxury and for idolatry and superstition. For wine was used in most of their sacrifices; indeed, the most ancient and simplest sacrifices of the gods were almost always made with wine and incense, which is why these two are often joined. Suetonius in the life of Augustus writes that that emperor instituted that the senators, on entering the Senate, should sacrifice with incense and undiluted wine at the altar of the god in whose temple they were meeting, before they sat down. Hence, on the same authority, Tiberius Caesar, when he first entered the Senate on the day after Augustus's death, as if to satisfy both piety and religion, offered worship in the manner of Minos, with incense and wine, but without a flute-player, who was of course customarily employed in all sacrifices. Ovid: "Now why, though I please the gods of others, do I bring incense and undiluted wine first to you, Janus?"

units.la: Lucius Papyrius dimicaturus advertus Samnites votum fecit, si vicisset, Iovi pocillum vini.
units.tr: Lucius Papirius, about to fight against the Samnites, made a vow that if he won he would give Jupiter a little cup of wine.

units.la: Etsi vero vinum, ut dixi, in pleriisque sacrificiis fuit adhibitum: tamen erant quorundam Deorum sacra, in quibus illud adhibere nefas erat. Inde duo sacrificiorum genera fuerunt apud Veteres: Alia; & quidem pleraque, in quibus vinum adhibebatur, quae idcirco a Graecis Συσίαι οἴνο-σπονδία fuerunt appellata. Alia vero, quae vino carebant, dicta ἀάτος & νηφάλια, id est, vino carentia; & sobria, ut docet Iulius Pollux. Unde & νηφαλίωσις, hoc est, ejusmodi sacrum uti.
units.tr: Although, as I said, wine was used in most sacrifices, there were nevertheless rites of certain gods in which it was wrong to use it. Hence the ancients had two kinds of sacrifice: the first, and indeed most of them, in which wine was used, and which for that reason the Greeks called spondai or libations with wine; and the second, which lacked wine, called aoina and nephalia, that is, without wine, and sober, as Julius Pollux teaches. Whence also the word nephaliosis, that is, to celebrate such a sacrifice.

units.la: Suidas ajit, apud Athenienses Nephalia, sive sobria exhibita fuisse Mnemosyna, Eurorae, Soli, Lunae, Veneri, Vrania & Nymphis. In hoc autem sacrificio non vinum, sed aquam mulsam libabant. Pausanias tamen ait, Eleos thure cum tritico, melle subacto, additis olea- quaeque, & quod ramis, aras suffire solitos & uti vino: Solis autem Nymphis, ἀπὸ ταῖς ἀκροσὶ ἀεὶ ἔστιν, id est, non fumida.
units.tr: Suidas says that among the Athenians the Nephalia, or sober offerings, were presented to Mnemosyne, Eurora, the Sun, the Moon, Venus, Urania and the Nymphs. In this sacrifice, however, they did not pour out wine but honeyed water. Pausanias nevertheless says that they used to fumigate the altars with incense, with wheat kneaded with honey, adding olive oil and boughs, and they used wine; but to the Sun and the Nymphs they offered things that were never smoky.

units.la: Sic Soli sacrificantes, ut autor est Phylarchus libro Historiarum duodecimo, mellibant, vinum non inferunt altaribus: quia aquum esse arbitrantur, ut Deum ipsum, qui omnia tonat, omnibus dominatur, semperque Mundum circumeat, ab ebrietate prorsus alienum esse credant.
units.tr: So too those who sacrificed to the Sun, as Phylarchus writes in the twelfth book of his Histories, offered honey and did not pour wine on the altars, because they thought it right and believed that God himself, who thunders over all things, rules all, and always goes round the world, must be wholly free from drunkenness.

units.la: Sic Vesta non vino, sed de Numicio flumine Romani libant, quibus diebus mense Iunio molæ frumentariæ & asini fertis & pane coronabantur: ad cujus templum juxta forum nisi nudo pede accedere non convenit: sicut in Aede Dianæ apud Cretenses, quam Britomartum nominant: Teste est Alexander ab Alexand. libro eodem tertio, supra aliquoties citato, capite duodecimo.
units.tr: So too the Romans offer water, not wine, to Vesta from the river Numicius, on which days in June the grain mills and the asses were garlanded with flowers and bread. It was not fitting to approach her temple beside the forum except barefoot, as also in the temple of Diana among the Cretans, whom they call Britomartis. Alexander ab Alexandro, in the same third book cited above several times, chapter twelve, is the witness.

units.la: Ac Seleucus apud Athenæum libro secundo, negat apud Veteres fuisse morem, ut vini copia, aut aliud quidlibet deliciarum inferretur in sacrificia. Quum enim sacrificia Deorum gratiâ peragerentur (unde & Σοῖνας, & Σωλίας, ac μάθας appellabant. Σοῖνας; quod Deorum gratiâ vino uterentur: Σωλίας; quod Deorum gratiâ vesciterentur, convenirentque: μὴ Σως verò; quod: ut indicavit Aristoteles, ματὰ τὸ θύειν, id est, postquam sacrificium vino uterentur) non conveniebat illic ventris negotium agere.
units.tr: And Seleucus, in Athenaeus, book two, denies that it was the custom among the ancients to bring in a quantity of wine or any other delicacy for sacrifices. For when sacrifices were performed for the sake of the gods (whence they also called them soinas, solias and mathas: soinas, because they drank wine for the sake of the gods; solias, because they feasted and gathered for the sake of the gods; and mathas, which, as Aristotle showed, is from sacrificing, that is, after the sacrifice they drank wine), it was not fitting to attend to the business of the belly there.

units.la: Hujusmodi fuerunt Rumine Deæ sacra, in quibus ipsius Romuli antiquissimo instituto mactres non vino, sed lacte tantum uti fas erat, quod bellis invergi, sive inspergi solitum fuerat, ut Plutarchus in Quæstionibus suis Romanis tessitur, eamque rationem reddit quæstione sexagesima octava, de quo supra.
units.tr: Such were the rites of the goddess Rumina, in which, by the very ancient institution of Romulus himself, the sacrificers were permitted to use not wine but only milk, which was customarily poured out at the altars, as Plutarch explains in his Roman Questions, and he gives this reason in question sixty-eight, mentioned above.

units.la: Sic in sacris Bonæ Deæ, quam & Floram nuncupant, cum vinum libabant, lac esse dicebant, teste Alexandro libro tertio, capite duodecimo.
units.tr: So too in the rites of the Good Goddess, whom they also call Flora, when they offered wine they said it was milk, as Alexander reports in book three, chapter twelve.

units.la: Sic Cererîs sacra, quæ Ceres atque etiam Orci nuptiæ fuerunt appellata, sine vino celebrabantur. Hinc Plautus in Aulularia: Sta. Cererîn', Strobile, has facturi nuptias? Strob. Qui? Sta. Quia temeti nihil allatum intelligo. Macrobius hunc locum citat libro tertio Saturnalium, capite decimo tertio. Contrà tamen Cato libro de re rustica, capite trigesimo quarto: Postea, inquit, Cereti exta & vinum dato. Hunc nodum Lambinus in Plautum confitetur sibi esse inexplicabilem; nisi alium dicamus in hac re fuisse Græcorum ritum, quám Romanorum. Nam Σνοιμοφοείοις, id est, Cerealibus, seu festis diebus (quæ etiam Ἀνωμία sunt dicta) Ceres, vini usu interdictum erat, neque vinum libabatur, neque vinum in sacris adhibebatur, ex quo Σιούας ὑπὸ λοι sunt dicta, de quibus supra. Tum mulieres ea sacra tractabant atque administrabant, quæ perpetuò apud Romanos temeto carebant: apud Græcos verò salternis diebus sese a vino abstinebant. Nonnulli sic solvunt, ut dicant, Cererem eandem esse atque Vestam, seu potius Terram. Apud Plutarchum libro de tuenda valetudine hæc verba legimus: Nam ipsi quoque Bacchonephalia sacra frequenter exhibemus, a jobe are sic appellata, quòd in his vinum bibere nefas erat: retinè nosmet ipsos assuefacientes, ne semper merum requiramus.
units.tr: So too the rites of Ceres, which were also called the nuptials of Ceres and of Orcus, were celebrated without wine. Hence Plautus in the Aulularia: "Stasimus: Are you, Strobilus, about to hold these nuptials of Ceres? Strobilus: Why? Stasimus: Because I understand nothing has been brought of wine." Macrobius cites this passage in book three of the Saturnalia, chapter thirteen. Cato, on the other hand, in On Agriculture, chapter thirty-four, says: "Afterwards, he says, give entrails and wine to Ceres." Lambinus, in his commentary on Plautus, confesses that he finds this knot inexplicable, unless we say that the Greek custom in this matter differed from the Roman. For at the Thesmophoria, that is, the Cerealia or festival days (which are also called Anodia), wine was forbidden to Ceres; neither was wine poured out nor used in the sacrifices, whence those rites were called aoina, as mentioned above. Then women handled and administered those rites, which among the Romans were always kept free from wine, while among the Greeks they abstained from wine for certain days. Some resolve the matter by saying that Ceres is the same as Vesta, or rather the Earth. In Plutarch's book On the Preservation of Health we read these words: "For we ourselves also often celebrate the Bacchic-Nephalian rites, so called from sobriety, because it was wrong to drink wine in them, restraining ourselves and accustoming ourselves not always to seek undiluted wine."

units.la: Servius Grammaticus in illa Virgiliana Georgicorum primo: In primis venerare Deos, atque annua magna Sacra refer Cereri, lætis operatus in herbis, Extremæ sub cafuhyemis, jam Vere sereno: Tunc agni pingues & tunc mollissima vina, &c.
units.tr: Servius the grammarian, on the first book of Virgil's Georgics, "First of all worship the gods, and bring the yearly great sacrifices to Ceres, working in the joyful grass at the end of the wintry season, now in clear spring: then the fat lambs, and then the softest wines," etc.

units.la: ostendit, aliud esse Ceres sacrificium; aliud Orci nuptias. Inhoc enim vinum non inferri soliitum; in illo utique.
units.tr: He shows that the sacrifice to Ceres is one thing, and the nuptials of Orcus another. For wine was not customarily brought in at the latter, but certainly was at the former.

units.la: Huc pertinet illud, Vinum rogo ne respergito. Plinius libro decimo quarto, capite duodecimo, dicit Romulum, inquit, lacte, non vino libasse, indicio sunt sacra ab eo instituta, quæ bodie custodiunt morem. Numæ Regis posthumia lex est: Vino rogum ne respergito: quod sanxisse illum propter inopiam rei nemo dubitat. Festus tamen, Respersum, inquit, vinum dixerunt, quia vino sepulcro pergebatur. Et hæc de sacrificiis tam ἀποάρ ὁρδοις, quàm αἰτιος, id est, cum vino celebrari solitis & absque vino.
units.tr: To this belongs the line, "Pour no wine on the pyre, I beg you." Pliny, in book fourteen, chapter twelve, says: "Romulus, he says, made libations with milk, not wine; the sacred rites he instituted, which even today keep that custom, are the evidence. The law of King Numa is posthumous: 'Pour no wine on the pyre.' No one doubts that he decreed this on account of scarcity." Festus, however, says: "They called the wine 'sprinkled' (respersum) because people went to the grave with wine." And so much for sacrifices, both those customarily celebrated with wine and those celebrated without it.

units.la: Porrò vinum non quod ut in sacris fuit adhibitum. Plinius libro decimo quarto, capite duodecimo: Lege Numæ Regis ex imputata vite libari vina Dii nefas statuit, mutione exeo-gitatâ, ut putare cogerentur, aliàs aratores & pigri circa arbusti pericula. Idem capite decimo nono: Et quoniam religione vita conflat, prolubare Dius nefasque habetur vino, præter impunitate vitis, fulmine tactæ, quamque juxta hominis mors laqueo penderit, aut vulneratus pedibus calcata, & quod circumcisis vinaceis profluxerit. aut superne decidus immundiore lapsu aliquo politum. Item Graeca; quoniam aquam habeat. Idem libro eodem decimo quarto capite deci mo*Sauo : Apud eosdem ( Thafios ) vitis Theriace vocatur, cujus & vinum & uva contra serpentium ictus medetur : Libaneos thuris odore, ex qua Dijs prolibant. E diverso Asprendios damnata arii.
units.tr: Moreover, wine was not used in sacred rites in the way it was used elsewhere. Pliny, book fourteen, chapter twelve: "By the law of King Numa, the gods were declared not to be offered wine from an unpruned vine. The rule was devised as a sort of trick, so that men would be forced to think about it; otherwise ploughmen and the idle would be careless about the dangers to the vines." The same author, chapter nineteen: "And since religion is bound up with the vine, it is considered impious to pour libations to the gods from wine taken from a vine struck by lightning, or from one on which a man hanged himself with a noose, or from one trodden underfoot, or from wine that has flowed from grapes with the seeds removed, or from wine that has fallen from above in some dirtier way." Likewise the Greek... since it contains water. The same author, book fourteen, chapter ten: "Among the same Thasians the vine is called Theriace; both its wine and its grape cure the bites of serpents. The Libyans (?) burn incense, from which they pour libations to the gods. On the contrary, the Asprendians rejected it (?)."

units.la: Sic Festus : Spurcum vinum est, quod sacris adhiberi non licet, ut ait Labeo Antistius libro decimo Commentarii Iuris Pontificii, cui aqua admixta est, defrutum ve aut igne tactum est, cum. muslum ve, antequam defervescat.
units.tr: Festus: "Spurcum wine is that which may not be used in sacred rites, as Labeo Antistius says in book ten of his Commentary on Pontifical Law. It is wine to which water has been added, or defrutum, or wine that has been touched by fire, or must before it has finished fermenting."

units.la: Idem: Sacrima appellabant muslum, quod Libero sacrificabant pro vinetis & vasis, & ipso vino confer vando, sicut praemeffum, sive praemetium, de spicis, quas primum messuissent, sacrificabant Cereri.
units.tr: The same: "They called must sacrima, which they sacrificed to Liber for the vines and the vessels, and for the wine itself when it was being conveyed. Likewise, the praemessum or praemetium, of the ears of grain that they had first reaped, they sacrificed to Ceres."

units.la: Calpar, ut idem testatur, vinum dicitur novum, quod ex dolio demitur sacrificii causa, ante quam gustetur; Iovi enim prius sua vina libabant, quae appellabantur festa vinalia. Calpar erat genus vasis fictilis. Idem: Vinalia diem festum habebat, quo die vinum novum Iovi libabant. Hinc adiegrare olim erat vinum in sacrificiis augere. Integrare enim & adtegrare erat minus fatum in statuum redigere, eodem Festo interprete.
units.tr: Calpar, as the same author attests, is the name for new wine drawn from the cask for sacrifice before it is tasted; for they first offered their wines to Jupiter, and these were called the Vinalia festivals. Calpar was a kind of earthenware vessel. The same: "The Vinalia had a festal day on which they poured new wine to Jupiter." Hence "adiegrare" was once to increase wine in sacrifices. For integrare and adtegrare meant to bring what was less than whole back to completeness, according to the same Festus as interpreter.

units.la: Porro potionis quodda genus ex vino & sanguine temperatum Assiratum (sive Asparatum) apud aliquos dicebatur, quod Latini prisci sanguinem Assir vocarent.
units.tr: Moreover, a kind of drink tempered from wine and blood was called assiratum (or asparatum) among some, because the early Latins called blood assir.

units.la: De ritu vinum infundendi victimis vide Angelum Politianum Centuriis primae, capite vi- gesimo sexto. Modum item libationum bujusmodi, & dicendi formam, qua in actione illa ute- bantur, Arnobius his verbis describit. Merum, inquit, thurus est socium, quod explanari con- similiter poscimus, cur ei super infundatur incensioni. Si enim ratio, cur fiat, non offendetur, nec habebit expositam sui causam, non jam iustad errori obiiciendum est ludicro, sed, ut dita- tur expressius, infanie, dementie, caecitati. Vt enim jam saepius dictum est, debet omne, quod geritur, canfiam sui habere perspicuam, nec caliginis alicuius obscuritate contectam. Si ergo fidi- is facto, aperite, monstrate, liquor ille cur detur, id est, vinum superinfundatur alteribus ? Nunquid enim Numinum corpora sitim sentiunt aridam, & eorum necesse est siccitates humore aliquo temperari ? Nunquid nobis, ut mortalibus mos est, caenis intermiscere potiones, ari etiam more poste solitos victus liborum & pultium, hostiarumque caesarum, quo putrefiat facilius & percoquatur tibus, frequentissimo irrigant accipiuntque se vino ? Date quaeso im- mortalibus Dijs bibant, scyphos, brias, pateras, lympiniaque depromite; & quoniam taurus pin- guibusque se dapibus atque opimis interficiunt eosdem ; ne quod in flomachi tramite male irant voratum substiterit viscus : juccurrite, properate, Iovi Optimo Maximo meram, ne praefocetur, date, cupit erutari, nec potus est : ac ni illa labatur & dissolvatur obstructio, periculum maximum est, ne oblisus interrumpatur spiritus, & viduatum remaneat fine suis ad- miniftratoribus caelum. Sed frustra, inquit, inequitas nobis : nos enim Superis ob eas profundimus merum causas, tanquam illos existimemus aut sitire, aut bibere, aut sua- vitatis ejus affectu laetari. Honoris ejus ergo datur, quo fiat illorum elator, ampliot, au- gustiorque sublimitas, altaria super ipsa libamus, & venerabiles cinissas ( xtiare est n tis missias aidoius, ruine seu pinguedinis accense fumus, Eustathio interprete ) carbonibus excitamus extinctis. Et quae gravior infligi contumelia Dius potest, quam si eos cre- das accepto mero propitios fieri : aut honorem existimes habitum his magnum, si modo vi- ni exiguantur super vividam jecoris atque infilla veris prunam ? Non nobis est fermo cum hominibus rationis expertibus, neque quibus non fit communis intelligentia veri- tas ineste & vobis sapientia ineste sensus, verumque nos dicere apud vos, ipsi interiore judicio sciti. Sed quid facere possumus, considerare nolentibus penitus rei ipsas, secumque ipsos loqui ? Facitis enim, quod fieri cernitis, non quod fieri oportere confidites : nimirum quia apud vos plus valet nullam habens confutando rationem, quam rerum insitella natura veritatis examinatione ponderata. Quid est enim Deo cum vino, aut in ejus natura vis qualis aut quanta est, quod cum effusum fuerit, sublimitas ejus augescat & bonoa vata existimetur auctoritas ? Quid, inquam, Deo cum vino est Venereis reproxima, nervos omnium deletitatis virtutum, verecundiae, pudoris & caititatis inimica ? quod in infa- l & nias & furores mentes sepius praecipitavit exitias,ipsosq; illos Deos maledictis cōpulit ex aulo nare dementibus, Itáne iflud non nefas, & pleunm sacrilegii crimen est, honori hoc dare, quod su a vidiis sumpseris,quid facias,nescias: quid loquaris, ignores:ad extremum temulenti, luxuriosi & perditi,corrivitium infamiamq; metuerit? Operaepretium est, etiam verbi ipsa deprome re,quibus, cùm vinum datur,uti, ac supplicare consuetudo. Mactus hoc vino inferio ejlo. Infe rio,mquit Trebatius,verbum ea causa est additum,eaq; ratione profertur: ne vinum omne omnino, quod in cellis atq; apotheca est conditum, ex quibus illud, quod effunditur, promtum est, esse sacrum incipiat,& ex usibus eripiatur humanis. Addito ergo hoc verbo, solum erit,quod in ferretur, sacrum, nec religione obligabitur. Caeterum qualis ergo hic bonor est, in quo imponitur quasi lex Deo,ne plus quaerat,quàm datum est? aut cujus ipse est, a viditatis Deus, qui nisi ver bi fuerit praescriptione submotus,cupiditate suam protendat ulterius, & apotheca suis supplicem privet? Mactus hoc vino inferio ejlo: injuria est, ista:non bonor, quid enim divus amplius hoc vocet, neq; erit contentus illatoī nonne infigniter dicendum est, Ledi, qui honorem atcipere cum conditione cogatur? Nam si exceptione non addita, sacrum necesse est fieri omne omnino, quod in cellis est vinum,manifestum est & Deo contumeliam fieri,cui modus constituatur in vito:& vos ipsos in re sacra cerimoniarum officia violare, qui non tantum tributis vini, quantū Deum videtus sibi velle praestari. Mactus hoc vino inferio esto: quid est aliud, quam dicere tantum esto mactus,quantum volo:tantum amplificatus,quantum jubeo: tantum bonoris assumito,quantum te habere decerno,& verborum circumscriptione definio. O Deorum sublimitas praepotens, quā venerari, quam colere officium omnibus cerimoniis libus debeas! cui lege venerator imponit, quam cum pastionibus adorat & formulis: quae per unius formidinem verbi ab immodicus vini cupiditatibus arcetur. Sed sit,ut vulcis, honor in vino, sit in thure, immolatione, & cedibus hostiarum ire Numinum offensionem placeniur.
units.tr: On the rite of pouring wine on victims, see Angelo Poliziano, Centuria I, chapter 26. Arnobius also describes the manner of such libations and the form of words used in that action, in these words: "Wine," he says, "is the companion of incense, and we ask why it is poured over it when it is burned. If the reason for doing it gives no offence and has no obvious cause, then it must not be thrown at us as a childish thing, but, as is said more plainly, as folly, madness and blindness. For, as has often been said already, everything that is done ought to have a clear reason, and not be covered by any obscurity of darkness. So if you faithful, tell us, show us, why that liquid is given, that is, why wine is poured over the others? Do the bodies of the gods feel dry thirst, and must their dryness be moistened by some liquid? Do we, as mortals are accustomed to do, mix drinks with our dinners, and do you, as is also customary, drench the food of livers and porridge, and the slain sacrificial victims, very often with wine, so that they rot more easily and are cooked through? Come, bring cups, bowls, dishes and flagons for the immortal gods to drink; and since they slaughter bulls and kill them with rich and abundant feasts, hurry, run, give Jupiter Best and Greatest neat wine, lest, if some food swallowed down the channel of the stomach sticks there, he be choked; he longs to be refreshed, and he has no drink. Unless that blockage slips away and is dissolved, there is the greatest danger that the breath will be interrupted by the obstruction and heaven will be left bereft of its administrators." But, he says, it is in vain that we make this attempt; for we pour neat wine out to the gods for these reasons, as though we thought they were thirsty, or drinking, or delighted by the enjoyment of its sweetness. So it is given in their honour, so that their loftiness may be exalted, enlarged and made more majestic; we pour libations over the altars themselves and stir up the venerable ashes, with the coals extinguished, (the smoke of burnt offerings, in the interpretation of Eustathius, is a kind of fat or rich smoke). What greater insult can be inflicted on the gods than to believe that they are made favourable by the receipt of neat wine, or to think that great honour is paid to them if a little wine is poured over the living liver and the hot coal of the sacrifice? We are not speaking with men lacking reason, nor with those to whom the common understanding of truth is not given. You have wisdom within you, and senses within you, and we are speaking truly to you, you who are skilled in inner judgement. But what can we do, when you are unwilling to consider the matter itself thoroughly and to talk with yourselves? For you do what you see is done, not what you are confident ought to be done; clearly because among you what counts for more is an argument that has no refutation, rather than the truth weighed by the examination of the nature of things. For what has the god to do with wine, or what power or what quantity is there in its nature, that when it is poured out his majesty should grow and his authority be thought more honoured? What, I say, has God to do with wine, which is close to sexual pleasure, the sinews of all the virtues of the soul, the enemy of modesty, shame and chastity; which has often cast minds down into destructive abysses of stupor and madness, and has driven even those gods themselves into insults, the gods who are mad from wine? Is it not then unlawful, and a crime of the greatest sacrilege, to give to a god as honour what you have taken up from drunkenness, not knowing what you are doing, not knowing what you say; in the end, drunk, debauched and ruined, fearing reproach and infamy? It is worth while also to bring out the very words with which, when wine is given, it is customary to pray and to use them. 'Mactus hoc vino inferio esto.' Trebatius says that the word 'inferio' has been added for this reason, and is spoken with this intention: so that all the wine at all that is stored in the cellars and storerooms, from which what is poured out is taken, should not begin to be sacred and be snatched away from human use. So by adding this word, only what is poured out will be sacred, and it will not be bound by religious obligation. But what sort of honour is this, in which a kind of law is imposed on the god, so that he may not ask for more than has been given? Or whose is it, that God of the wine-cellars, who, unless he is held back by the wording of the formula, would stretch his desire further and deprive the storerooms of their suppliants? 'Mactus hoc vino inferio esto': this is an injury, not an honour. For what more could the god say, and will he not be content with what is offered? Should it not be said plainly, 'Be gone,' to one who is compelled to accept an honour on conditions? For if without this exception it would necessarily follow that everything at all that is wine in the cellars became sacred, it is clear that an insult is done to God, to whom a limit is set in the wine; and that you yourselves violate the duties of ceremony in sacred matters, since you do not offer as much wine as you think he wishes to be given. 'Mactus hoc vino inferio esto': what is this other than to say, 'Let him be honoured as much as I wish; let him be magnified as much as I order; let him take as much honour as I decree he should have,' and to define it by the wording of the formula? O sublime and mighty majesty of the gods, how great the duty you owe to venerate and worship in all sacred rites! The one whom your law imposes on worshippers, whom they adore with fixed formulas and words, is held back from the excessive desires for wine by the fear of a single word. But let it be, as you say, that the honour lies in the wine; let it lie in the incense, in the sacrifice, and in the slaughter of victims: yet by these you will placate the anger of the gods."

units.la: Hu verbis Arnobius libationum: statum modum, formam, materiam, finem simulq; vanitātem clarifi mé expressit; de quo nunc parcius scribo,cum in libris Antiquitatum mearum Covivialium prolixè admodum copiose, de iis scripserim.
units.tr: In these words Arnobius set out very clearly the state, manner, form, matter, purpose and vanity of libations. I write about them more briefly here, since I have treated them at great length and in full detail in my books on the Antiquities of Banquets.

units.la: Porrò & certa vasa ... nibus adhibebantur, ut Calpar, de quo suprá, Coturnium qua in sacrificiis vinum fundebatur. Armillum item vas erat vinarium in sacris, dictum, quod ar mo,id est, humum ... Adde Brias, Pateras, Simpinia,quorum Arnobius suprá mentio nem fecit, & Sympulum,quod vas erat par vum,non dissimile cyatho; quo vinum in sacrificiis le babatur:unde & mulieres rebus divinis dedite Sympulatrices dicebantur. Varro Sympula ai fuisse calices fictiles,& vasc̈ula,quibus utebantur in sacrificiis, a fumendo dicta, quod his vinum sumebant minutatim. juvenalis:
units.tr: Certain vessels were also used for these rites, such as the Calpar, mentioned above, and the Coturnium, from which wine was poured in sacrifices. The armillum was likewise a wine vessel used in sacred rites, named from the arm (armus, that is, the shoulder), since it was carried on the shoulder. Add the brias, the patera and the simpinium, which Arnobius mentioned above, and the sympulum, a small vessel, not unlike a cyathus, from which wine was poured in sacrifices. That is why women devoted to sacred rites were called sympulatrices. Varro says the sympula were earthenware cups and little vessels used in sacrifices, named from taking (sumendo), because with them they took wine in small measures. Juvenal:
Numa laughing at the little sympulum, and so on.

units.la: Plinius libro trigesimo quinto,capite duodecimo: In sacris,inquit, non niurrinā, criftallinis ve, sed fictilibus sympulis prolibabatur innocentiis.
units.tr: Pliny, book thirty-five, chapter twelve: "In sacrifices," he says, "libation was made not from murrhine or crystal vessels, but from earthenware sympula, in simple innocence."

units.la: Et haec de vino ejusq; usu in sacrificiis: Sequitur,ut de thure,quod vini socium appellat Arno bius,ejusq; usu quoq; agamus. Thuris antiquissimus sané ac frequentissimus olim in Sacra Gen tilium usus fuit:unde nonnulli ipsum,probabilis sané ratione, ⁂ ⁂, id est,sacrificando tulunt fuisse dictum,propterea quod antiquitas solo thure fuerit sacrificatum, praesertim a pauperi bus. Unde posteā illud in omnibus sacrificiis fuit adhibitū. Germani weyhrauch/id est, fumus sacrū sive consecratum appellant,wote composita a weyh/quod idem est,quod geweyht/id est, sacrum sive consecratum,& rauch/id est,fumus. Nam,ut boc obiter addam,weiden Ger manus & cedere loco & conficerare significat,eo quod ea res,quae conficrantur,quasi cedunt usui pro pano,hoc est,ab illo recedunt,& fiunt sacrae. Sic Aqua lustralis weyhwasser/id est, aqua sacra, sive consecrata dicitur: & aspergillum,virga sive instrumentum,quo aqua: illa rebus & per sonis aspergitur,weyhwadel/id est,sacrum flabellum vocatur. Sic nox simul arg, dies Dominī natalitius weyhnacht/id est, sacra nox appellatur, Gallicé Noel: forsan, vel quasi Nox El,id est, Dei,vel quasi Noster El,id est,Deus, seu Deus nobiscum: prop:erea quod Christus, verus Deus,illo tempore nobis natus est,secundum carnem,factus Immanuel,id est, Deus nobiscum. Sic dicimus Eircheyhl/id est, Encaenia,templorum dedicationem seu consecrationem, ... uoce [?] iuniter compositá a Tirch idest, templo, quod ipsum a Graeca voce ναος, ut est deductum, tanquam domus Domini, & weyb/idest, dedicatio, seu consecratio. Sed haec obiter.
units.tr: So much for wine and its use in sacrifices. Next, we must treat of incense, which Arnobius calls the companion of wine, and of its use. Incense was certainly very ancient and very frequent in the sacred rites of the Gentiles, so that some have reasonably supposed that the word itself (thus) comes from the Greek verb thuein, that is, to sacrifice, because in antiquity sacrifice was made with incense alone, especially by the poor. Afterwards it was used in all sacrifices. The Germans call it Weyhrauch, that is, sacred or consecrated smoke, a compound of weyh, which means the same as geweyht, that is, sacred or consecrated, and rauch, that is, smoke. For I may add in passing that the German weihen means both to yield to a place and to consecrate, because the things that are consecrated, as it were, yield to common use, that is, withdraw from it and become sacred. So holy water is called Weyhwasser, that is, sacred or consecrated water, and the aspergillum, the rod or instrument with which that water is sprinkled on things and persons, is called Weyhwedel, that is, a sacred fan. Likewise the night of the Lord's birth is called Weyhnacht, that is, the holy night, in French Noël; perhaps either as Nox El, that is, the night of God, or as Noster El, that is, our God, or God with us, because Christ, the true God, was born for us in that season according to the flesh, made Immanuel, that is, God with us. So we say Eircheyhl, that is, Encaenia, the dedication or consecration of churches, compounded from Tirch, that is, church, which is derived from the Greek naos, as if it were the house of the Lord, and weyh, that is, dedication or consecration. But these are incidental remarks.

units.la: Tus tamen alii scribentes per S. Simplex, sine aspiratione, volunt dictum a tundendo, quod glebe tundantur, cum quibus diciur fluens cum arboribus concrescere. Ab Hebraeo נבה, Lebonah, quia candidam, est dictum: quod nomen etiam apud Graecos retinuit: unde & Libanus, mons, ab arboribus thuriferis, quae λιβανοφόροι a Graecis appellantur, fuit nuncupatus.
units.tr: Other writers, however, write tus with a simple s, without aspiration, and hold that it is named from tundere (to beat), because the lumps are beaten, and because the liquid that flows from the trees hardens with them. From the Hebrew לבונה [lebonah] it is called so because it is white; the Greeks also kept this name, and from the frankincense trees, which the Greeks call libanophoroi, the mountain Lebanon was named.

units.la: Aufonius: Florum spirat odor, Libani seu montis honor thus.
units.tr: Ausonius: The scent of flowers breathes, and the honour of Lebanon or of the mountain, incense.

units.la: Hincnata videtur illa de Libano puero fabula, qui sacrificiis majorem in modum deditus, & invidia interemptus, in plantam, ei cognomen, Deorum miseratione dicitur fuisse mutatus: quam fabulam copiosius explicat in Geoponico Heron sive Constantinus.
units.tr: Hence seems to have arisen the fable of the boy Libanus, who, devoted to sacrifices beyond measure and destroyed by envy, is said to have been changed by the pity of the gods into a plant, which bears his name. Heron, or Constantinus, in the Geoponica, explains this fable more fully.

units.la: Arabia in primis thuris olim fuit abundantissima: unde Plinius libro duodecimo, capite decimo quarto: Thura, inquit, praeter Arabiam, nullis; ac ne Arabiae quidem universae. Idem capite precedente: Principalia in Arabia Foeli & beata fuerunt thus & myrrha. Sabei, inquit idem libro duodecimo, capite decimo septimo, eibos thuris ligno coquunt. Hinc fallum, ut metonymicos Arabiae vocabulum saepe apud autores pro odoribus, si ve thymiamatis usurpetur. Sic Arabicè dare pro coquere odores, vel accendere Veteres dicebant. S. ve Tertullianus de Corona militis: Arabiae, inquit, aliquid accendunt, id est, thuris. Plautus in Panulo: Arabius murrhinus, omnia odor complebat. Arabius odor, id est, ex thure Arabio, si ve Arabico. Et in Milite gloriosò: Inde ignem in aram, ut Ephesiae Dianae laudes letas, Gratesh, agam, sed, ut Arab co fumificem odore amene Quae me in locum Neptunis, tenuplique turbulentus Servavit saevus fluctibus, ubi sum affliatus multum.
units.tr: Arabia was in former times especially rich in incense. Hence Pliny, book twelve, chapter fourteen: "Incense," he says, "grows nowhere except Arabia, and not in the whole of Arabia." In the preceding chapter he says: "The principal places in Arabia were Felix and the Blessed, which had incense and myrrh." The Sabaeans, says the same Pliny in book twelve, chapter seventeen, cook their frankincense with wood. Hence the name of Arabia was often used by authors, by metonymy, for perfumes or incense generally. So the ancients said to "give Arabia" for to cook perfumes, or to kindle them. Tertullian, in De Corona militis: "They kindle something of Arabia," he says, that is, of incense. Plautus in Pseudolus: "Arabian myrrh; the whole place was filled with scent." An Arabian scent, that is, from Arabian or Arabic incense. And in the Miles gloriosus: Then I would put fire on the altar and give thanks, as to Ephesian Diana, with joyful praise, so that I might fumigate with a sweet Arabian scent, she who saved me from the place of Neptune and from the savage, turbulent waves of the thin sea, when I was much tossed about.

units.la: Ut Arabico fumificem odore, id est, fumum faciam, hoc est, suffitum, seu suffimentum faciam odore Arabico, id est, thure Arabico incenso, seu thuris odore incenso. Festus: Arabiae olet, id est, odoribus Arabicis.
units.tr: That I may fumigate with Arabian scent, that is, make smoke, that is, make a fumigation or suffumigation with Arabian scent, that is, with Arabian incense burned, or with the scent of incense burned. Festus: "It smells of Arabia," that is, of Arabian perfumes.

units.la: Hinc thura dicta Panchaia. Virgilius in Culice: Ille colit luco sibi Panchaia thura.
units.tr: Hence incense was called Panchaean. Virgil in the Culex: "He worships in his grove with Panchaean incense."

units.la: Et Aeneidos secundo: Totaque thuriferis Panchaia pinguis arenis.
units.tr: And in Aeneid book two: "And Panchaea, rich in incense-bearing sands."
Panchaea is a region of Arabia.

units.la: Huc facit, quod Plinius scribit libro duodecimo, capite decimoquarto, de Alexandro Magno. Is enim cum magnam thuris vim, sine parsimonia ausi inferret, Leonides paedagogus ei dixit, ut de vidis gentibus thuriferis hoc modo Dis supplicaret. At ille Arabia potitus thure onustam navem eimisit, simulillum cohortatur, ut large Deos adoraret.
units.tr: To this belongs what Pliny writes in book twelve, chapter fourteen, about Alexander the Great. When he rashly poured out a great quantity of incense without restraint, his tutor Leonides told him that he should supplicate the gods in this way only when he had won the incense-bearing lands. But Alexander, having gained possession of Arabia, sent a ship loaded with incense, and at the same time urged his tutor to worship the gods lavishly.

units.la: Nec vero universa Arabia, ut supra ex Plinio dictum, sed Sabaeorum duntaxat regio fuit thurifera: quam gentem Agatarchides ὑπὸ ... vocant appellat, id est, gentem Arabiae maximam, & omnis felicitatis compotem. Dionysius Alexandrinus eosdem αρωματ., id est, divites appellat. Idem Strabo libro decimo sexto, Theophrastus libro nono Historiae plantarum, & Herodotus libro tertio testantur.
units.tr: Nor, as said above from Pliny, was the whole of Arabia incense-bearing, but only the region of the Sabaeans, a people whom Agatharchides calls the greatest nation of Arabia, and sharers in all prosperity. Dionysius of Alexandria calls the same people aromatic, that is, rich [ἀρωματ.]. Strabo in book sixteen, Theophrastus in book nine of the History of Plants, and Herodotus in book three bear witness to the same.

units.la: Praeter alias autem illorum divitias, cujusmodi fuerunt aurum, ebur, gemmae, & plantae pretiosae; ut myrrha, cinnamomum, cassium & balsamum, thura quoq; commemorantur. Unde Virg. —molles sua thura Sabaei. —solis est thuréa virga Sabaeis.
units.tr: Besides their other riches, such as gold, ivory, gems and precious plants like myrrh, cinnamon, cassia and balsam, frankincense is also mentioned. Hence Virgil: "soft Sabaeans with their incense"; "the golden rod belongs to the Sabaeans."

units.la: Hinc & thus ipsum dictum Sabaeum. Virgilius: —centum, Sabaeo Thure calent arae.
units.tr: Hence the incense itself was called Sabaean. Virgil: "A hundred altars glow with Sabaean incense."

units.la: Plinius libro duodecimo, capite decimoquarto: Sabaeorum, inquit, regio thurifera Saba appellatur: quod significare Graeci mysterium dicunt, spessans ortus Solis assirii, undiq; rupibus in via, & a dextris maris scopulus in attessa. Haec ille.
units.tr: Pliny, book twelve, chapter fourteen: "The region of the Sabaeans, rich in incense, is called Saba, which the Greeks say signifies a mystery, because of the rising of the Assyrian sun; on the road there are rocks on every side, and on the right a reef jutting into the sea." So he.

units.la: Sabam itaq; Graecè ... putant dictum, quod mitteret thus, quo in sacrificiis utun-tur. Nam ut in hac verba adnotat Lambinus, neq; Genio, neq; Laribus quidquam animi tum immolabatur: Genio, quia Deo rerum gignendarum nefas esse putabant Veteres, quidquam, cui vitam ademissent, immolare; & quo die lucem intuleri & animam ducere coepissent, eo die (die autem isto Genio sacrificabant) aliquod animal anima privare: Laribus, vel quia eo dem Deos Lares vita Genios existimabant: vel quia, si dissimiles erant Lares, vitæ patrus familiaris, & matrisfamilias, & familiarum custodes habebantur. Diis autem vitæ custodibus sacrificantes, manus suas sanguine cruentare & animalis vitam adimere nefas arbitrabantur. Laribus autem supplicare solebant Kalendis, Idibus, Nonis, cum festus dies erat. Caro de re rustica, capite centesimo quadragesimo tertio: Villica focum purum, circum versum quottidie, prius quam cubitum eat, habeat. Kalendis, Idibus, Nonis, festus dies cum erit, coronam in focum indat, per eos, dies Lari familiari pro copia supplicet. Perfius Satyra secunda:
units.tr: Saba is therefore thought to be named in Greek from sending incense (thus), which is used in sacrifices. For, as Lambinus notes on these words, nothing was sacrificed at that time either to the Genius or to the Lares. Not to the Genius, because the ancients thought it wrong to sacrifice to the god of generation anything whose life had been taken; and on the day on which they had first seen the light and begun to draw breath (and it was on that day that they sacrificed to the Genius) they deprived some animal of its life. Not to the Lares, either because the Lares were thought to be the same gods as the Genii, or because, if the Lares were different, they were regarded as the guardians of the life of the father of the household, the mother of the household and the household itself. Sacrificing to the gods who guard life, they thought it wrong to stain their hands with blood and to take away the life of an animal. But they used to supplicate the Lares on the Kalends, Ides and Nones, when it was a festal day. Cato, On Agriculture, chapter 143: "The housewife should keep the hearth clean, swept every day before she goes to bed. On the Kalends, Ides and Nones, when it is a festal day, she should put a garland on the hearth and, on those days, pray to the household Lar according to her means." Persius, Satire two:
Pour wine for the Genius.

units.la: Caeterum quia thurris magnus olim apud Gentiles in sacris usus fuit: idcirco Pium est dictum. Ovidius:
units.tr: Moreover, since incense was of great use in former times in the sacred rites of the Gentiles, it was therefore called pious. Ovid:
He bore pious incense to the gods above.

units.la: Item Votivum: unde idem Ovidius tertia Elegia:
units.tr: Likewise votive: whence the same Ovid in the third Elegy:

units.la: Afflicit ara preces, votiva que thura piorum.
units.tr: The altar receives prayers and the votive incense of the pious.
Hence it is also called sacred. Crinitus:
With sacred incense, I beg you, look upon us.

units.la: De hoc usu sacro thuris scribit preter alios etiam Macrobius, reflatarq; Aegyptios quoq; thure & precibus Deos suos placasse. Unde Niliacum, id est, Aegyptium Statius ipsum vocat quare to Syll.
units.tr: Among others, Macrobius also writes about this sacred use of incense, and he reports that the Egyptians too propitiated their gods with incense and prayers. For this reason Statius himself calls the Egyptian incense Niliacum.
Or they keep Nilean incense or pepper.

units.la: A thure porro dicti fuerunt in primitiva Ecclesia Thurificati, qui thus Idolis adolebant; de bus Cyprianus de duplici martyrio: Horret, inquit, abominandum Thurificati, aut Libellati nomen, ipse forte thurificatis ac libellatis deterior.
units.tr: In the early Church, those who burned incense to idols were called Thurificati, from thus (incense). Cyprian, in his book On the Twofold Martyrdom, says: "I shudder at the abominable name of the Thurificati or the Libellati, and I myself am perhaps worse than the thurificati and libellati."

units.la: Arnobius libro septimo ad versus Gentiles, multis differens contra istam Gentilium Λιβανο-tia, primum quidem scribit, rem esse novellam; cum temporibus heroicis, quid nam thus esset, contrarium, ipsa superstitionis genitrix & mater ejus opinionem aut famam non veritur, ac ne ipse dem Romulus, aut in religionibus comminiscendis artifex Numa, aut esse, aut nasci non verit, pium sar monstra: quo peragi mos fuit sacrificiorum solennium munia. Hinc igitur sic concludit: Si sine thure religionis officium claudi tur necessarium, vis ejus est, qua propitios faciat, mi-nus hominibus celites: peccatum fuisse ab Antiquis: quin imo placulas plenam fuisse omnem illorum vitam: qui quod maxime conveniens Deorum fuerit voluptati pax incursam ueglexerint libertatem. Sin autem temporibus prisci neq; homines, neque Dii hujus thuris expetivere materiam, nunc comprobari, & hodie frustra illud inaniter præstari. Quod neq; Antiquitas necessarium credidit, & sine ullo novitas rationibus appetivit. Deinde significat, cui quidquid fit, ab hominibus oporteat suas habere caussas, nullam afferri posse rationem aut caussam, cùr ante ipsa Numinum thura injiciantur altaribus, & ex eorum incendio familiaria exstimentur fieri & mista. Quid si objiciunt, si hu honorare, respondet, In cultu & religione non hominum, sed Numinum seu sum ac voluntatem requiri. Addit, thus illud vi scum esse, ex torticibus profluens, ita ut ex amygdalo, cera solacrymabili deflillatione coalescens. Alienum itaque a ratione esse existimare, Deos honorari aut placari posse hujusmodi Panchaicis, id est, Arabicus, resinalis, ignis odore sive fumo, ex arboris resina confectio. Quod si, addit, contenduns, Deos odorum atque nidorum hujusmodi sua vitate capi, ac delectari, inde colligi potest ipsos esse corporeos & mortalium similes. Sin autem, ut a Sapientibus (præterquam a Stoicis, qui Deum finxerunt οσωματουσ, corpore esse præditum teste Theodoreto) creditur, Iant incorporales, neque odore aliquo afficiuntur; manus apud hos odoresq; nec sensibiliter cumverit aura eos potes est nidoris aliquim: non si millè pondera masculi thuris incendas, cælumi, hoc totum redundantium vaporum nebulositate claulatur. Hæc Arnobius.
units.tr: Arnobius, in book seven of his work Against the Gentiles, disputes at length against this Gentile frankincense-worship [Λιβανωτια]. First he writes that the practice is a novelty: in the heroic times no one knew what incense was. Superstition, the mother of such things, does not fear to say that its origin and reputation are unknown, and that neither Romulus himself nor Numa, the craftsman who invented religious rites, either existed or was born, while the pious ministers were carrying out the duties of the solemn sacrifices. From this he therefore concludes: "If the service of religion is held to be impossible without incense, its power is such as to make the gods favourable, but less so to men. The ancients would have been guilty of sin, or rather their whole life would have been full of guilt, since they neglected a liberty that would have been most pleasing to the gods. But if neither men nor gods in ancient times desired the material of this incense, why is it now approved, and why is it offered today in vain? Antiquity did not think it necessary, and novelty has demanded it without any reason. Moreover, whatever is done, men must have their reasons for it. No reason or cause can be given why incense is thrown on the altars before the very images of the divinities, and why it is thought to be pleasing to them from its burning and smoke. If they object that this is done to honour them, he answers that worship and religion require not the will and pleasure of men, but of the divinities. He adds that this incense is a kind of resin flowing from the trees, formed like the tears that trickle from the almond. It is therefore unreasonable to think that gods can be honoured or appeased by such Panchaean (that is, Arabian) resinous things, by the scent or smoke of a substance made from tree resin. But if, he adds, you contend that the gods are taken and delighted by the sweet odours and vapours of this kind, it can be inferred from this that they are corporeal and like mortals. But if, as the wise believe (except the Stoics, who imagined God to be corporeal, as Theodoret testifies), they are incorporeal and are affected by no odour, then the smell of any incense is not perceived by them at all; even if you burn a thousand pounds of male frankincense, the whole heaven is clouded over with this mass of rising vapour." These are the words of Arnobius.

units.la: Sed & instrumenta certa thuri sacro destinata erant, ut Thuribula & Acerræ. Acerra Pompejus Festus, vocat arculam thurariam, scilicet ubi thus reponebant: quam alii aram interpretantur, quae ante mortuum poni solebat, in qua odores incendebantur, teste eodem Festo. Suetonius in vita Sergii Galbae: Quum, inquit, exterritus (Galba) hoc primum, ad expiandum somnium, praemissis qui rem divinam apparrent Tusculum, excucurrisset, nihil invenit praeter tepidam in ara favillam, atratumque juxta senem in catino vitreo tus tenentem, et in calice filtili merum. Ex hoc quoq; loco primum apparet, tus et merum adhiberi solita sacrificiis: Deinde Catinum vitreum turis quidem; Calicem vero filtilem meri fuisse instrumenta et vasa. Alioqui Catinus, Varrone tolle de re rustica libro primo, vas erat promendi frumenti, quod curculiones exesse incipiunt.
