Id enim cum promptum esset, in Soleponere oportere aquae catinos, quod eo convenunt, ut ipsi se necent.
units.tr: Certain instruments were also assigned to sacred incense, such as the thuribula and the acerrae. Pompeius Festus calls the acerra a little incense-box, that is, the place where they kept the incense; others interpret it as the altar that was customarily placed before the dead, on which the odours were burned, as the same Festus testifies. Suetonius, in the life of Servius Galba: "When Galba, terrified, first ran to Tusculum to expiate the dream, having sent ahead men to prepare the sacrifice, he found nothing but warm ashes on the altar, and beside it an old man, dressed in black, holding incense in a glass dish and wine in a clay cup." From this passage it appears, first, that incense and wine were customarily used in sacrifices. Second, a glass dish was the vessel for incense and a clay cup the vessel for wine. Otherwise, as Varro says in the first book of On Agriculture, the catinus was a vessel for taking out grain, which weevils begin to gnaw; for when it was taken out, it was necessary to put dishes of water in the sun, so that they would drown themselves there.

units.la: Apuleius in Apologetico praeter Catinum, etiā Sympulum in Asaos vīcia atq; adeo omnibus sacrificiis adhiberi fuisse solutum, testatur his verbis: Pauperas Populo Romano imperii a primordio fundavit, prog; eo in hodiernum Dius immortalibus Sympulo et catino fictili sacrificat. Pro Sympulo alii legunt Simpuvium, vel Sympullum, vel etiā Simpunium, ut legit Arnobius. De Simpunio ita scribit Varro: Simpuvium est modus matulae ... Non vides ipsos Deos, si quando volunt gustare vinum, deripere ad hominum fana, et tamen tum ipsi illi libero simpuvio vinitari? Sed de hoc quoq; supra adlatum est, cum alia vasa vinaria a nobis essent posita; quorum in sacrificiis erant usus: cujusmodi praeter illa, vas vinariū grandius erat Sinum, ab sinu; quod sinum majorem cavationem, quam pocula habebat: et Depesta, Graece Ἀποπόσια, quae in duobus sacris, Sabinus vasa vinaria in Deorum mensa ponebantur: et Guttum, quae vinum dabant, at minutatim funderet, a guttis appellatū. Haec de oblatione thuris: quod ipsum tamen Porphyrius, Theophrastus testimonio, Veteres solitos offerre negat, sed pauxillum decerpti fami, tanquam genitalis rei partem, manibus in altum sublatum, flammis imponere cōsuevisse, atq; ita demum apparentes celestes Deos excepisse: Theodoretus sermone septimo ad versus Graecos Gentiles.
units.tr: Apuleius, in his Apology, besides the catinus, testifies that a sympulum was also used in the sacrifices of Asia and indeed in all sacrifices, in these words: "He founded the Roman people's empire from its beginnings, and up to the present day he sacrifices to the immortal gods with a sympulum and an earthen dish." Some read simpuvium, or sympullum, or even simpunium for sympulum, as Arnobius reads it. Varro writes about the simpunium thus: "The simpuvium is a measure of a small cup… Do you not see that the gods themselves, when they wish to taste wine, go down to the temples of men, and yet the free simpuvium is then poured out for them?" But this has also been mentioned above, when we set out the other wine vessels, which were used in sacrifices. Besides those, the larger wine vessel was the sinus, named from its sinus (hollow), which had a larger hollow than cups; also the depesta, in Greek apoposia (ἀποπόσια), which Sabinus says were wine vessels placed on the tables of the gods at two kinds of sacred rites; and the guttus, which gave out wine, so that it poured it out drop by drop, named from the drops (guttae). These matters concern the offering of incense. Porphyry, however, relying on the testimony of Theophrastus, denies that the ancients offered it in this way. Rather, they used to take a little piece from the first fruits, as if it were a part of the seed, lift it up in their hands, and place it on the flames; and only then did the heavenly gods, appearing, receive it. So Theodoret in the seventh discourse against the Greek Gentiles.

units.la: Fuit porro etiā Olei usus in Gentilium sacris et religionibus varius et multiplex. Ingenere autem usus ipse est duplex: Alius quidem prophanus sive corporeus: alius sacer, sanctus, religiosus, sive etiam superstitiosus. Vterq; parabola illa Iudicum nono comprehendi videtur: ubi oleae pinguedinem sive oleo et Dii et Homines dicuntur honorari: sicut vinum Dis hominesq; laetificari et exhilarari dicuntur. Hi enim duo liquores, ut Plinius inquit, libro decimoquarto, capite nigrante fecundo, humanis corporibus gratissimi, intus vini, foris olei, arborum genere ambo praecipui, sed olei necessarius.
units.tr: The use of oil in the sacred rites and religions of the Gentiles was also varied and manifold. In general, the use itself is twofold: one is profane or bodily; the other is sacred, holy, religious, or even superstitious. Both seem to be contained in that parable in Judges chapter nine, where it is said that gods and men are honoured with the fatness of the olive, that is, with oil, just as wine is said to gladden and cheer gods and men. For these two liquids, as Pliny says in book fourteen, chapter two, are most pleasing to the human body: wine within, oil without; both are outstanding products of trees, but oil is the more necessary.

units.la: Quoad priorem itaq; olei usum, prophanum nimirum et vulgarem; is apud Orientales potissimum populos frequentissimus sane celeberrimusq; fuit: idemq; duplex: vel quatenus corporibus humanis applicatur, quibus liquor ille, teste Plinio, est gratissimus: vel quatenus in pecorum corporibus, aliusq; rebus inanimatis adhibetur. Dicitur porro corporibus humanis duplici modo prodest, vel quatenus ejus extrinsecus adhibetur: hoc est, corpora, vel sola, vel quadam ejus partes atq; membra eo vel illinuntur, vel etiam perfunduntur; idq; vel necessitatis et medicinae, vel voluptatis et jucunditatis gratia: vel quatenus potatur, sive intra corpus sumitur. Nam licet Plinius oleum foris, ut vinum intus, dicat corporibus humanis esse gratissimum: tamen ejus quoq; ... eet id varius, intra corpus sumti, non levius saepe est usus.
units.tr: Concerning the former use of oil, namely the profane and common one, this was certainly most frequent and most celebrated among the peoples of the East; and it was twofold: either as it is applied to the human body, to which that liquid is most pleasing, according to Pliny, or as it is used on the bodies of animals and on other inanimate things. Furthermore, oil benefits the human body in two ways: either as it is applied externally, that is, when the bodies, or only some parts and limbs of them, are anointed or even drenched with it, and this either for the sake of necessity and medicine or for the sake of pleasure and delight; or as it is drunk, that is, taken into the body. For although Pliny says that oil outwardly, as wine inwardly, is most pleasing to the human body, nevertheless its use taken into the body, though varied, has often been no less frequent.

units.la: Ac apud Iudaeos quidem potissimum (oleum regio oleorum nobilissimorum fuit abundans, fi ... ) ... continus morem fuisse totum corpus, praecipue autem caput, inungi, sive perfundi, multa sacra scriptura loca abunde fatis testantur; ut Ecclesiastici nono: Omni tempore sint vestimenta tua candida, et oleum super caput tuum ne deficiat. Item Psalmo vigesimo tertio Olei imagine, in Lexte et opiparo convivio fundi solito summam beatitudinem sive felicitatem depingit: Caput, inquis, meum oleo impinguasti: alludens nimirum ad unguenta in lautis convivis usurpari solita, ut dixi. Ab eodem more ducta similitudine fraterna concordiae felicitas a David expressa: Psalmo centesimo trigesimo tertio. Sicut oleum optimum in capite defluens ad barbam. Eodem spectat Christi sermo Matthaei sexto: Tu autem cum jejunas, unge caput tuum. Et Lucae septimo, Oleo caput hospitum ungendum esse praecipitur. Hinc illa mulier in Evangelio unguento capit. caput totum, corpus Christi perfudisse dicitur, Matthei vigesimo sexto. Et Marci decimo quarto dicitur effudisse unguentum illud super caput, fratio alabastro. Nam teste Plinio libro decimo tertio, capite secundo, Vngventa optima servantur in alabastris, odores in oleo. Item Lucae septimo, Christus ad mulierem, quae pedes quoq; ejus irrigarat lacrymis: capillis deinde exficcarat, & unguento iunxerat, iuquit: Oleo caput meum non unxisti: haec autem unguento inunxit pedes meos. Hic obiter notandum, plus fuisse pedes oleo iuuugere, quam caput; id quod crebro fuit in usu. Plinius libro decimo tertio, capite tertio, ubi docet, Vnguenta materia luxus esse, e cuntis maximè su per vacuu, quippe cum margaritae gemmae, ad heredem tamen traufeaut, vestes prolongentur pes: at unguenta illico exspirent, & suis moriantur horis, iuter alia inquit: Sed quos dam crasitu do maxime delectat, id ipsum approbantes: linia, jam, non solum perfundi unguentis gaudent. Vidimus etiam vestigia pedu tiugi, quod M. Osthouem mouftrasse Neroni principi ferebant. Que four sentiretur juvariab ea parte corporis? Hac Plinius.
units.tr: Among the Jews especially (Judea was rich in the most excellent olive oil), it was the custom to anoint or drench the whole body, and especially the head, as many passages of Holy Scripture abundantly testify. Thus in Ecclesiasticus chapter nine: "At all times let your garments be white, and let oil not fail upon your head." Likewise in Psalm twenty-three, the image of oil, which was customarily poured out at a sumptuous and lavish feast, portrays the highest blessedness or felicity: "You have anointed my head with oil," alluding, of course, to the ointments customarily used at lavish banquets, as I have said. From the same custom David expressed the felicity of brotherly concord, in Psalm one hundred and thirty-three: "It is like the precious oil running down upon the head, down upon the beard." To this also refers the saying of Christ in Matthew chapter six: "But when you fast, anoint your head." And in Luke chapter seven, it is commanded that the head of guests be anointed with oil. Hence that woman in the Gospel is said to have poured ointment on Christ's head, and indeed on his whole body, in Matthew chapter twenty-six. And in Mark chapter fourteen it is said that she poured that ointment over his head, having broken the alabaster flask; for, as Pliny says in book thirteen, chapter two, the best ointments are kept in alabaster flasks, and their scents in oil. Likewise in Luke chapter seven, Christ, speaking to the woman who had also wet his feet with tears, then dried them with her hair and anointed them with ointment, says: "You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment." Here it should be noted in passing that it was more common to anoint the feet with oil than the head, which was frequent in use. Pliny, in book thirteen, chapter three, where he teaches that ointments are a matter of luxury and are the most superfluous of all things, since pearls and gems pass down to heirs, garments are lengthened, but ointments immediately evaporate and die within their own hours, says among other things: "But some people take special delight in being thick with them, approving the very thing; they are not content merely to have their bodies drenched with ointments. We have even seen footprints, which they say M. Otho showed to the emperor Nero. What sensation could be felt from that part of the body?" So Pliny.

units.la: Sed ratio videtur reddeda, cur oleo cum uni versum corpus, tum vero atq; inprimis caput per fundi olim confuerit. Constat certe oleum maximam habere vim penetrandi, quia tenuissimum est & humidissimum. Vnde vestem aqua madefactam videmus mox reficcari: olei autem macula non facile elui possunt: quaudo & vinum quoq; dilutum Aristoteles ait difficilius elui e vesti bus, quod magis tenue factum in meatus subeat.
units.tr: But a reason ought to be given for why it was once customary to anoint with oil not only the whole body but especially the head. It is certain that oil has a very great power of penetrating, because it is the thinnest and most fluid of substances. Hence we see that a garment wetted with water dries out soon, but oil stains cannot easily be washed out. Aristotle also says that even wine, when diluted, is harder to wash out of garments, because, having been made thinner, it passes into the pores.

units.la: Porro de oleiusu & effectu in genere libet pulcherrima & elegantissima illa Plinii & aliorum addere, antequam de oleiusu sacro apud Gentiles dicamus. Sic iguur Plinius lib.15.cap.4..diffe- rit de oleinatura, viribus & utilitate: Oleo natura tepefacere corpus, & contra algores munire. Eidem fervores capitis refrigerare. Vsum ejus ad luxuriam vertere Graeci, vitiorum omniu geutorcs, iugymasiis publicando. Quintilianoiu erpreta, Palaestricos damnat & luctatores, quibus pars vitae in oleo, pars in viuo consumitur, qui corporum curâ mentc obruerunt. Seneca quoq; in epistolis moralibus, huc alludeus, ajt: Luctatores & totam oleo & luto conflautem scientiam (Palaestricam) expello. Ideui Plinius: Omni oleo mollitur corpus, vigorem & robur accipit. Et alibi, Oleum laftitudinum perfrictioumq, est refectio, vulneribus utile, sanitatis, agilitatis, roboris caussa, corpora calefacit, discutit sudores. Quin & cutis, oleo imbuta, venena respuit, adeo fi quis cutem admotis cauteriis erodente medicamento exulcerare pergat, illa oleo puugat, frustra titur, operamq, luserit. Non enim adhaerescunt, quae applicantur, nec penetrant.
units.tr: Furthermore, before we speak of the sacred use of oil among the Gentiles, I should like to add in general those very fine and elegant remarks of Pliny and others on the use and effect of oil. Pliny, in book 15, chapter 4, thus discourses on the nature, powers and usefulness of oil: "By its nature oil warms the body and guards it against chills. The same oil cools the heat of the head. The Greeks turned its use to luxury, the source of all vices, by making it public in their gymnasiums." Quintilian, interpreting this, condemns the wrestling-masters and athletes, for whom part of life is spent in oil and part in wine, and who have overwhelmed the care of the body upon the mind. Seneca too, alluding to this in his Moral Letters, says: "I reject the wrestlers and that whole science (of the wrestling-school) made up of oil and dust." Pliny again: "The body is softened by all oil, and gains vigour and strength." And elsewhere: "Oil is the refreshment of weariness and chilling, useful for wounds, and for health, nimbleness and strength; it warms the body and drives out sweat. Indeed the skin, soaked in oil, even rejects poisons, so that if someone, having applied cauteries, should keep trying to ulcerate the skin with an eroding medicine, the oil protects it; he labours in vain and wastes his effort. For what is applied does not adhere or penetrate."

units.la: Hac & alia Plinius: quibus adde illa Plutarchi in vita Alexandri: Πόνων ἀροματικ ἔλαιον Plutarchus. (Plato.) Plato.
units.tr: Pliny says these and other things, to which add that remark of Plutarch in the life of Alexander: "Oil is the sweat of toils" [Πόνων ἱδρὼς ἔλαιον]. Plutarch. (Plato.) Plato.
These things are from Eusebius, Pliny, Plutarch and Plato.

units.la: Hinc consentanee scribit etiam Eusebius lib.4. demonstrationis Evangelicae in hunc modum: Eusebius.
units.tr: Eusebius also writes to the same effect, in book 4 of the Demonstration of the Gospel, in this way:

units.la: Hanc enim, lumen auges, a laboribus reficit, ab operibus liberat, pulchros efficit eos, qui eo illinuntur, oleum) lumen auges, a laboribus reficit, ab operibus liberat, pulchros efficit eos, qui eo illinuntur, splendere facit visum in morem coruscationum, ica ut eo utentibus pellucentem & illustrem, præbeat visum. Hac de suo olei prophano, si ve corporo.
units.tr: For oil "increases light, restores from labours, frees from works, makes beautiful those who are anointed with it, makes the sight shine like flashes of light, so that it gives a clear and bright vision to those who use it." These things are said about the profane oil of the body.

units.la: Vt autem Olei usum Græcos, quos omnium viciorum genitores vocat Plinius, dixit vere ille ad luxuriam: sic Gentiles, quos similiter omnia superstitionum genitores merito dixerimus, oleo (quod non Minerva, aut Aristeius, sed Dei donum est) ad superstitionem & idololatriam multifariam fuerunt abusi. Hinc cum ipsos sacerdotes, eu simulacra et omnes generis instrumenta, ad sacra sacrificia adhiberi solita oleo inungi pasim apud prophanos autores legimus. Ac de sacerdocio quaedam Iovis, sub Dio inungi solitum, exstat illustre testimonium Plutarchi in Quaest. Ro. Ide de simulacris, ad quae inungenda oleo usi fuerunt, mane festum est. Sic enim Saturni simulacra Romæ intue oleo fuit repleti: quod factum illud est, partim simulacra sua consecrandi & carie vindicandi gratia.
units.tr: Just as that wise man rightly said that the Greeks, whom Pliny calls the originators of all vices, abused oil for luxury, so we may rightly call the Gentiles the originators of all superstitions, and they abused oil, which is a gift of God and not of Minerva or Aristaeus, for superstition and idolatry in many ways. Hence we read everywhere in profane authors that the priests themselves, their images and all kinds of instruments used in sacred rites were customarily anointed with oil. And there is a notable testimony of Plutarch in the Roman Questions about a certain priesthood of Jupiter, in which it was customary to anoint under the open sky. Likewise it is well known that they used oil to anoint images. For thus the statues of Saturn at Rome were once filled with oil; this was done partly to consecrate their statues and partly to protect them from decay.

units.la: Olei quoq, usus superstitiosissimus fuit in lucernis, luminibus & ignibus illis sacris fovedes; de quo ipso superstitiosissimo lucernarum atq, luminum in templis usu sic disserit Lactantius lib.6.c.4. Iustit. Deo, inquit, accendit lumina, veluti in tenebris agenti. Ita: Non indiget lucernis eorum, qui in ipsum hominum tam eandem luce dedit. Ita: Non igitur mentis sue corpus putandus est, qui authori & datori luminis candelarum ac cereorum offert pro munere. Aliud vero ille lumen a nobis exigit, nō fumidū, sed, ut Poëta ait, liquidū & clarū, mentis sc. Illorū Dis, quæ terrenis, indigēt lumināb.
units.tr: The use of oil was also most superstitious in the lamps, lights and sacred fires that were fed in temples. Lactantius discourses on this most superstitious use of lamps and lights in temples in book 6, chapter 4 of the Institutes: "Does God," he says, "kindle lights, as if he were acting in darkness? ... He who gave the same light to all men does not need their lamps." And again: "Therefore he is to be thought out of his mind who offers candles and wax tapers as a gift to the author and giver of light. He demands from us another light, not smoky but, as the poet says, clear and bright, namely of the mind. Those gods who need earthly lights..."

units.la: Præterea in Regū inaugurationibus & initiationibus usitatum fuisse oleum & unguenta legimus hinc inde. Plinius lib.13.cap.2. Ergo regale, sinquic, unguentum appellatū, quod Parthorum Regibus ita temperatur, cōstat myrobalano, costo, amomo, cinnamomo, com.ro, cardamomo, nardi spica, myrrha, casia, stracle, ladano, opobalsamo, calamo, juncoq, Syrio, xenanthe, malabathro, senchato, cypero, aspalatho, panace, croco, cypro, amaraco, colato melle & vino. Idem auctor c.3. Vnguenta, ajt, & in castra penetrasse. Aquilas ac signa pulverulenta illa & custodius horridas se fiu diebus inungi fuisse solita. Id quoq, verisimile est superstitionis ergo factum.
units.tr: Moreover, we read here and there that oil and unguents were used at the inaugurations and anointings of kings. Pliny, book 13, chapter 2: "Therefore the unguent called royal, which is so mixed for the kings of the Parthians, consists of myrobalanum, costus, amomum, cinnamon, comum, cardamom, spikenard, myrrh, cassia, storax, ladanum, opobalsam, calamus, Syrian rush, xenanthes, malabathrum, sesame, cyperus, aspalathus, panax, saffron, Cyprian oil, amaracus, with curdled honey and wine." The same author, chapter 3: "Unguents," he says, "even penetrated into the camp. Eagles and those dusty and rough standards were customarily anointed on certain days." This too is probably done for the sake of superstition.

units.la: Deniq, ipsis sacris & sacrificiis oleum & unguenta adhibita fuisse legimus: sicut deinceps, ubi de cerimoniis sacrificiorum agetur, copiosius audiemus.
units.tr: Finally, we read that oil and unguents were used in the sacred rites and sacrifices themselves, as we shall hear more fully later, when the ceremonies of the sacrifices are discussed.
On Salt.

units.la: Nunc, quoniam etiam Salis usus frequens admodū in sacris sacrificiis, olim fuit, ideo de hoc quoq, nonnulla addemus. Ac de eo quidē in genere multa similiter disserit Plinius lib. 31. cap. 7. Vita, inquit, humana fine Sale nequit degere; adeoq, necessarium elementum est, ut transferit in telletius ad voluptates animi quoq. Nam ita sales appellantur: omnisq, vitae lepos, & summa laritas, laborumq, requies non alio magis vocabulo constat. Honorium etiam militiaq, interpositur salarium inde dictus, magna apud antiquos auctoritate, sicut apparet ex nomine Salaria Via, quoniam illa Salin Sabinos portari confuerat. Aucus Martius Rex salis media sex millia ia congiario dedit populo, & salinas primus instituit. Varro etiam pulmentarii nec usus Veteres auctor est. Efita visse enim salem cum pane & cafeo; ut Proverbio apparet. Maximum tamen in sacris intelligitur auctoritas, quando conficiuntur fine mola salsa. Hac Plinius.
units.tr: Since salt was also in frequent use in holy rites and sacrifices in former times, I will add a few remarks on it as well. Pliny discusses salt in general at length in Book 31, chapter 7: "Human life cannot be lived without salt, and it is so necessary an element that it extends even to the pleasures of the mind. Hence the word 'sales' is used for every charm of life, for wit and urbanity, and for the relief of toil. Salary, too, takes its name from salt and is an honour among the men of war; the Salarian Way is so called because salt was commonly carried along it from the Sabines. King Ancus Martius gave the people six thousand measures of salt at a public distribution and was the first to establish salt-pits. Varro also tells us that the ancients used no relish but salt, having only bread and cheese, as the proverb shows. Yet its greatest authority is seen in sacred rites, since sacrifices are not performed without salted meal." So Pliny.

units.la: Plutarchus similiter Sympos. lib.5. quæst.10. multa de Salis utilitate disseruit. Ac primum est Aristophanis Gramatici testimonio, probat pro verbio, ad sale et cuminū amicos dici, qui ita sint familiares, ut etiā sale & cumino solis propositis unā comenī. Deinde quaestione movet, cur & Homerus salem divinū appellet Iliad.1. Divino sale conspersit: & Platonis Timaeo lege hominis corpus Dis dicat esse carisimū, cum Aegyptiorum sacerdotes, castisimū eum sint, sale in unum versum abstinēas, edeo ut pane quoq, insulso vescantur. Cur igitur, querat aliquis, sacerdotes salem sunt abominati, cum ut divinus sit, & Dis gratus? Ac divinū quidē salem vult ab Homero dictū, propter magnā & multiplicē ejus in vita humana utilitate, propter quam alius quoq, rebus divinitatis & Dei nomē tribuitur; Salubus autē abstinuisse sacerdotes, qui castitati se destinū rat, quod ui ob talorē ad rem Venereum incitēt: id quod explus nonnullis probat: & hac quoq, ob causam salem posse dici divinū, cum omne id, quod generādi vim habet divinū esse videatur: cum quidē Deus genicor fit atq, principium rerum omnium. Sed præter has rationes, quas Plutarchus affert, hac quoq, videtur esse non minima, quod salis olim in sacris maximus usus fuit.
units.tr: Plutarch, in the fifth book of the Table-Talk, question 10, likewise discussed the usefulness of salt at length. First, on the testimony of the grammarian Aristophanes, he proves the proverb that people who are so close that they share even salt and cumin at a meal are "friends of salt and cumin." Then he raises the question why Homer calls salt "divine" in the first book of the Iliad ("he sprinkled it with divine salt"), and why Plato in the Timaeus says that the human body is most dear to the gods, while the priests of Egypt are most chaste and abstain from salt entirely, eating even their bread unsalted. Why, someone may ask, did the priests shun salt, if it is divine and pleasing to the gods? Plutarch holds that Homer called salt divine on account of its great and manifold usefulness in human life, for which reason other things too are given the name of divinity and of God. The priests abstained from salt because they had dedicated themselves to chastity, since salt is thought to stir up desire for sexual union, as some instances prove. For this reason too salt may be called divine, since everything that has the power of generating seems to be divine, God being the Father and beginning of all things. But beyond these reasons which Plutarch gives, this one also seems not least: salt was of old in very great use in sacred rites.

units.la: Acapud Iudaeos quidem omnia sacrificia oportebat condisale consecrato, qui sal fæderis ni cabatur, eo, accedi igne, qui in tabernaculo Domini asservabatur & sovebatur, quod ex igne sui tus immisso sacrificiis a Mose & Aarone suscepit fuisse quidā conjiciūt. Sic Ethnici nunc quadam ignem similiter in sacrificiis suis adhibuerunt. Cur sal ayrvns ϰῷ θεὸς ab Homero fit dictus, vide pulchra multa apud Eustathium Iliad. 1. & Antiquitates meas con-viviales.
units.tr: Among the Jews, indeed, every sacrifice had to be salted with consecrated salt, which was called the salt of the covenant. Some conjecture that, with fire, which was kept and tended in the tabernacle of the Lord, it was taken from the fire that Moses and Aaron received, when fire was put upon the sacrifices. Thus the Gentiles too in their sacrifices likewise used a certain fire. As for why salt was called divine [θεῖος ἅλς] by Homer, see the many fine things in Eustathius on the first book of the Iliad, and my own Convivial Antiquities.

units.la: Salinum in mensa pro aqnali solitum esse ponit Varro, cum patella; quia nihil aliud fit sal, quàm aqua: Festus. Salinum cum sale in mensa ponere figulis cur religioni olim fuerit habitum, vide Festum.
units.tr: Varro says that a salt-cellar was customarily set on the table in place of a water-vessel, along with a dish, because salt is nothing but water. So Festus. As for why setting a salt-cellar with salt on the table was once regarded as a matter of religious scruple for potters, see Festus.

units.la: Muries, eodem auctore, dicebatur sal, in pila tunsum, & in ollam fictilem conjectum, & in furno percoctum: quo debinc in aquam misso Vestales virgines utebantur in sacrificio. Idem: Muries est quemadmodum Veranius docet, ea, quae fit ex sale sordido, in pila pinsato, & in ollam fictilem conjecto, ibique operto gypsato, & in furno percocto, sui Virgines Vestales ferra ferrea se&longs;to, & in seriam conjecto, quae est intus in aede Vestae, in penu exteriore, aquam jugem, vel quamlibet, praeterquam quae per fistulas venit, adduxit, atque ea demum in sacrificiis utuntur.
units.tr: According to the same authority, "muries" was the name for salt pounded in a mortar, put into an earthen pot, and baked in an oven, which was then dissolved in water and used by the Vestal Virgins in sacrifice. Festus again: "Muries," as Veranius teaches, is that which is made from crude salt, pounded in a mortar, put into an earthen pot, covered with a plaster lid and baked in an oven. The Vestal Virgins carried water in an iron vessel, from a perpetual spring or any source other than that which comes through pipes, and poured it into a cistern inside the temple of Vesta, in the outer storeroom; and only then did they use it in sacrifices.

units.la: His adde, quod idem ait, Murrata potione antiquos usos indicio est, quod etiam nunc Aedi-lis per supplicationes Diis addunt ad pulvinaria, & quod duodecim tabulas caveatur, Ne mortuo adurtur, ut ait Varro in antiquitatum libro.
units.tr: Add to this what the same author says: that the ancients used a drink of salt and wine, as is shown by the fact that even now the aediles add it to the couches of the gods at public supplications, and by the provision of the Twelve Tables that it not be applied to the dead, as Varro says in his book on antiquities.

units.la: Sic explicatum est etiam tertium membrum, quod in hoc sacrificio Nestoris & Argonautarum, atque adeo in omni sacrificio, observandum a diximus, semper Materia, seu, Quid sacrificare olim Veteres cognoverunt. Unde sane constat magna hanc fuisse Ethnicorum amentiam, quod partim omnis generis fruges atque fructus, partim animalia, quibus vescuntur, Deos esse crediderunt: in quam sententiam pul-bre sic Cicero libro tertio de Natura Deorum: Etquem, inquit, tam amentem putas esse, qui illud, quo vescatur, Deum credat esse?
units.tr: In this way the third point also has been explained, which we said must be observed in this sacrifice of Nestor and the Argonauts, and indeed in every sacrifice: the matter, or what the ancients offered in sacrifice. From this it is clear that the Gentiles were in great madness, since they believed that some kinds of grain and fruit, and some of the animals they eat, were gods. Cicero expresses this view finely in the third book On the Nature of the Gods: "And whom do you think so mad as to believe that the thing he eats is a god?"

units.la: SEQVITVR nunc quartum membrum, nempe LOCVS: in quo videliect illud a Nestore & Argonautis sacrificium fuit factum. Is, quoad Nestorem quidem, ab Homero non exprimitur. Probabile tamen est, vel in templo, vel alio loco sacro & religioso fuisse. At locus, in quo Argonautae sacrificium fecisse Apollonius testatur, Lictus fuit: in quo ara primum extructa est, quia ideo &ἀχ& & ἰταχν, id est, littoralis hic appellatur, sicut ipse Apollo, cui victima haec fuit oblata ἰταχν & ἰμπαχν, propterea appellatur de quo supra.
units.tr: Now follows the fourth point, namely the PLACE, where that sacrifice by Nestor and the Argonauts was made. As for Nestor, Homer does not say where. It is nonetheless probable that it was in a temple or some other holy and sacred place. The place where Apollonius testifies that the Argonauts made their sacrifice was the shore, and there the altar was first built. Therefore Apollo is called "of the shore" [ἀκταῖος] and "of the landing" [ἐπακταῖος], the god to whom this victim was offered, as was said above.

units.la: Vt autem ibidem de temporibus sacrificiorum, in genere quidem omnium, ita nunc de eorundem locis, in quibus ista fieri fuerunt solita, quaedam dicamus. Nam ut temporis, ita loci quoq, qui busquis in actionibus, fuerunt communes & opportunitas. De his autem magna repetere licet in sacris & profanis litteris opinionum & consuetudinum varietatem atq, diversitatem. Nam primum quidem plerique Gentilium Deos in et sub tectis atq, aedificiis colendos esse arbitrabantur: & idcirco in illorum honorem templa atq, aedes magnis laboribus atq, sumtibus extruebant. Alij vero, a templorum aedificatione, usu culusq, abhorrentes, cum nefas putarent esse Deos tectis atq, aedificiis, quasi carceribus quibusdam atq, ergastulis, quodammodo includere, Deos sub dio, in lucis, memoribus, campis atq, vallibus, extra aedificia venerandos existimabant. Fuerunt etiam non nulli, qui quosdam Deos in aedificiis, alios extra aedificia sub dio putabant colendos.
units.tr: Just as we spoke above about the times of sacrifices in general, so now we will say something about the places where these rites were customarily performed. For as with time, so too with place, there was in these actions a common and convenient usage. Yet in sacred and profane writings one may find a great variety and diversity of opinions and customs concerning them. For, first, most of the Gentiles thought the gods were to be worshipped under roofs and in buildings, and so for their honour they raised temples and shrines at great labour and expense. Others, however, shunning the building of temples, thought it wrong to shut up the gods under roofs and buildings as if in prisons or workhouses, and held that they should be venerated under the open sky, in groves, woods, fields and valleys, outside buildings. There were also some who thought that certain gods should be worshipped in buildings, and others outside, under the open sky.

units.la: Deinde quoniam alios Deos maritimis: alios in terrestribus: alios locis editis & excelsis, sed coelibus atq, montibus: alios loeis planis, ut vallibus: alios defertis, & vastis: alios frequentibus & celebribus: alios campis & agris patentibus: alios sylvis atq, lucis delectari, atq, illos incolere putabant; ita his vel illis in locis hos vel illos Deos sacris illis suis atq, cerimoniis usitatis colebat.
units.tr: Further, since they believed that some gods delight in the sea, others on land, others in high and lofty places, but in the heavens and on mountains; others in level places such as valleys; others in deserted and waste places, others in crowded and frequented places, others in open plains and fields, others in woods and groves, and that they dwell there, so they worshipped these or those gods in these or those places with their own rites and customary ceremonies.

units.la: Ac in genere quidem, Loens captus, ut inquit Festus, dicebatur ad sacrificandum locus, ubi ime constitutum. Quoniam autem plerique Ethnicorum templis & aedibus sive aedificiis sacris, & in illis Deos adorandos esse existimabant, idcirco de illis nobis primo loco dicendum: & quidem de eorum nominibus Latinis, Graecis & Hebraeis primum, tum de illorum primis in ventoribus aliisq, in templis sen aedibus sacris, observatu rebus dignis.
units.tr: In general, as Festus says, a place "taken" (captus) was called a place set aside for sacrificing, where it was established. Since most of the Gentiles believed that the gods were to be adored in temples and houses, or sacred buildings, and in them, we must speak of these first. And first of their names in Latin, Greek and Hebrew, and then of their chief parts and fittings in temples or sacred houses, which are worth noting.

units.la: A Latinis aedificia hujusmodi, Templa, Delubra, Fana, Aedes, Sacra, Sacella, & Sacraria, generalibus quidem nominibus fuerunt appellata. Templum dici vult Varro a templando vel tuendo, id est, conspiciendo; & triplicem habere significationem. Primum significare coelum: deinde certa loca inaere, vel in terra, qua Augures captandorum auguriorum causa definire solebant, quae Templa dicebantur, quod ex omni parte, vel quod ex iis omnis pars cospicii possit: tertio vero significare loca sub terra. De prima & tertia significatione hic non agimus: sed dunc axat de secunda. cunda. Ab eo vero templo, quod ab Auguribus definiebatur, quia id oporteret septum esse, nec plus quàm nnum introitum habere, sacellum est, ut non solùm aedes sacra, sed etiâ alia loca septa, & nnû tantùm introitum habentia. Templa appellantur, etiâ si sacra non essent ut Curia Hostilia, quae templum non erat, licet sacra non essent. Ita Festus: Templum significat & aedificium Deo sacratum, & tignû, quod in aedificio transversum ponitur. Cicero in epistolis familiaribus: Venit Servilius, lo'vi ipsi iniquus, cujus in templo res agebatur. Idem in Verrem: Herculis templi sanè sanctum apud Agrigentinos, & religiosum fuit. Idem pro Domo sua: Curia est sedes ac templum publicicon cilii. Idem pro Milone: Curia est templi sanctitate, amplitudine, mentis, concilio publici, caput urbis, ara sociorum, portus omnium gentium. Idem de Somnio Scipionis: Cujus Deo hoc templum est omne, quod consecratur.
units.tr: Among the Latins, buildings of this kind were called by general names: templa, delubra, fana, aedes, sacra, sacella and sacraria. Varro holds that "templum" is so called from "templare" or "tueri," that is, to observe, and that it has a threefold meaning. First, it signifies the heavens; second, certain places in the air or on the earth, which the augurs used to mark out for taking omens, and which were called templa, because from every part, or from them, every part could be seen; third, it signifies places under the earth. Of the first and third meaning we are not speaking here, but only of the second. Only of the second. From the temple which was marked out by the augurs, since it had to be enclosed and have no more than one entrance, comes the sacellum, so that not only sacred houses but also other enclosed places with only one entrance are called sacella. Things are called templa even if they are not sacred, as the Curia Hostilia, which was not a temple though it was not sacred. So Festus: templum signifies both a building consecrated to a god and a beam laid transversely in a building. Cicero in his Letters to Friends: Servilius has come, unfriendly to Jupiter himself, in whose temple the business was being conducted. The same in the Verrines: the temple of Hercules among the Agrigentines was indeed holy and sacred. The same in For his House: the Curia is the seat and temple of the public council. The same in For Milo: the Curia is by the sanctity, size and dignity of the temple, the council of the public, the head of the city, the altar of allies, the harbour of all nations. The same in the Dream of Scipio: the whole of that which is consecrated is the temple of that god.

units.la: Porrò templum & sepulcrum dici potest Veteri auctoritate, inquit Nonius Marcellus. Unde Virgilius Aeneidos quarto: Praeterea fuit in tectis de marmore templum Conjugis antiqui.
units.tr: Moreover, "templum" and "sepulcrum" can both be called by the authority of the ancients, says Nonius Marcellus. Hence Virgil in the fourth book of the Aeneid: "Moreover, there was in the halls a temple of marble to her ancient husband."

units.la: Monimenta etiâ templa dici posse auctor est Marcus Tullius in Verrem Actione secunda: Ab fine esse in aede Castoris celeberrimo, clarissimo, monimento, &c.
units.tr: Marcus Tullius, in the second action against Verres, is the authority that monuments too can be called temples: "Then, in the most famous and most renowned temple of Castor, a monument," etc.

units.la: Alterum nomen, quo aedificia sacra a Latinis infinituntur, est Delubrum: locus videlicet, in quo Dei simulacrum dedicatum est: vel, ut Macrobius ex Varrone citat, in quo praecer eidem fit area assumtâ, cujus quidem nominis derivatio a Grammaticis multiplex traditur. Dictum vult Servius, quòd nno tecto plura complectatur Numina: utest Capitolium, in quo est Minerva, Jupiter, Juno. Alii dictum volunt a diluendo. Religio enim sacrificii apud antiquos exigebat, ut ante sacrum sacrisiculus manus abluerent. Festus scribit, Delubrum dictum fuisse delibratum, hoc est, decorticatum, quae veneratur pro Deo: in quâ sententiâ, ligneum simulacrum Delubri decimus, inquit alicubi Servius, a libro, hoc est, a ralo ligno factum, quod Graecè ξόανον dicunt. Cicero in Verrem: Verres Delubra sanctissimus religionibus consecrata depeculatus est. Ibid: Simulacra sanctissima Deorum ex Delubris religiosissimis instinxit. Idem pro Archia Poëta: Smyrnaei Delubrum Homerotis oppido dedicaverunt. Ibidem: Delubra Musarum coluere etiam praeantisimi Imperatores. Idem pro Domo sua: Novum Delubrum in urbis clarissimo loco inchoaverunt. Idem de Natura Deorum: Menfasargenteas de omnibus. Delubrusjustiauferri. Ibid, Aras Delubra, Hecates in Graecia videmus. Ibidem: Pugnare pro Templis, atque Delubris. Idem de Legibus: Consuetudo a patrib. Delubra habentur.
units.tr: The second name by which the Latins designate sacred buildings is "delubrum": that is, the place in which the image of a god is dedicated, or, as Macrobius cites from Varro, the place in which the rite is performed at an altar set up for the same god. Grammarians give many accounts of the derivation of this word. Servius holds that it is so called because it encloses several deities under one roof, as the Capitol contains Minerva, Jupiter and Juno. Others want it derived from "diluere" (to wash), since the religion of sacrifice required the sacrificing priests to wash their hands before the sacrifice. Festus writes that "delubrum" was so called from "delibratum", that is, stripped of its bark, the wood being worshipped as a god. In this sense Servius says somewhere that a wooden image is called a "delubrum", being made from a rough log, which the Greeks call xoanon [ξόανον]. Cicero against Verres: Verres plundered the most holy shrines consecrated with religious rites. Ibid.: he stripped the most sacred images of the gods from the most reverenced shrines. Idem for the poet Archias: the Smyrnaeans dedicated a shrine to Homer in their town. Ibid.: even the most distinguished generals cultivated shrines of the Muses. Idem for his own house: they began a new shrine in the most famous place in the city. Idem, On the Nature of the Gods: silver statues of all kinds; a shrine rightly carried off. Ibid.: we see altars and shrines of Hecate in Greece. Ibid.: to fight for temples and shrines. Idem, On the Laws: it is customary for shrines to be held by the fathers.

units.la: Tertium nomen, quo aedificia sacra designantur a Latinis, est Fanum: idè nimirum quod delbrum vel templum, sic dictum vel a Fannis, Latinorum Deus, qui iudormientibus responsa dare solebant, ut ait Martianus Capella: vel a Fano, qui, autore Probo Grammatico, primus oraculi conditor fuit. Festus, Fanum a Fano, vel a fando, deducit; quod Pontifex in dedicatione templi certa verba praefari solebat. Varro ait, Fana nominata, quod Pontifex in sacrando fatis finisfinem. Sunt tamen, qui hoc nomen per ph scribunt, ὅτι τὸ φωτ ὅ, quod significat manifestum, quòd ephano aperta responsa dabantur. Cicero in epistolis familiaribus: Ut pecunia in fano poneretur, Idè pro Cajo Rabirio: Pro fanu atq; delubris propugnandū est. Idem de Inventione: Crotoniatae fanum Junonis religiosissimè colebant. Idè de Finibus: Plurima in sua patria sacrificia, & fana non contemnebat. Idem de Legibus: Athenienses Contumeliae & Impudentiae fanum fecerunt.
units.tr: The third name by which the Latins designate sacred buildings is "fanum". This is so named either from the "delubrum" or temple, or from Fanus, a god of the Latins who used to give answers to those sleeping, as Martianus Capella says; or from Fanus, who, according to the grammarian Probus, was the first founder of an oracle. Festus derives "fanum" from "Fanus" or from "fari" (to speak), because the pontiff used to pronounce certain set words when dedicating a temple. Varro says that fana are so named because the pontiff, in consecrating, fixes the boundary by fixed words. Some, however, write the word with "ph", because of φῶς [phōs], which means manifest, since open answers were given in the fanum. Cicero in his Letters to Friends: that the money be placed in the fanum. For Gaius Rabirius: one must fight for the fana and shrines. In On Invention: the Crotoniates worshipped the fanum of Juno most religiously. In On Ends: he did not despise the many sacrifices and fana in his own country. In On the Laws: the Athenians made a fanum of Insolence and Shamelessness.

units.la: Ab hoc nomine adjectivum deducitur Profanus: idè, quod nihil habens religionis, a religione remotus, sacra non iniciacus: qui fanum intrare non poterat: vel quod ex religioso, aut sacrorum hominum usus conversum est, quasi porrò, id est, procul a fano. Barbari Latinum vocant, quasi populares, quem tur ecsum Latinos profanum appellabat. Varro profanum interpretatur quod est ante fanum, vel fano conjunctum. Sed in hoc significato positum hoc nomen nec legere ut memini. Vsitationis igitur significationis cantum hac exempla sunto. Cicero in Verrem Actione sexta: Hastabulas Marcus Marcellus, cum omnia illa victoria sua profana fecisset, tamen religio ne impeditus non attigit. Idem pro Domo sua: Si ista consecratio legitima est, quid est, quod profanum in tuis bonis esse possit? Idem de Aruspicum responsis. Loca sacra & religiosa profana habebat. Idem de Natura Deorum: Limina profanarum ad imum contaminari nihil refert. Virgilius Aeneidos sexto: —Procul hinc procul esse profani. Idem: Faune precor miserere, tuq; optima ferrum Terra tene, colui vestros si semper honores, Quos contra Aeneadae bello fecere profanos.
units.tr: From this noun is derived the adjective "profanus": either because it has nothing of religion, is remote from religion, and is not admitted to sacred things, since it could not enter the fanum; or because it has been turned from religious or sacred use to common use, as if "pro-fanum", that is, far from the fanum. The barbarians call the Latin tongue ... as if common; and those whom the Greeks called profane. Varro explains "profanum" as that which lies before the fanum, or is joined to the fanum. But I do not remember this word being read in that sense. Therefore only these examples of the usual meaning are given. Cicero, Verrine Action 6: when Marcus Marcellus had made all those spoils of his victory profane, he nevertheless, hindered by scruple, did not touch them. Idem for his own house: if that consecration is lawful, what can be profane among your goods? Idem, On the Responses of the Haruspices: he regarded sacred and religious places as profane. Idem, On the Nature of the Gods: it makes no difference that the thresholds of the profane are defiled to the bottom. Virgil, Aeneid book 6: "Hence, hence, be far away, you profane!" Idem: "Faunus, I pray, have pity; and you, best earth, hold fast the sword, since I have always kept your honours, which the sons of Aeneas made profane in war against us."
Horace:
"I hate the profane crowd and keep it at a distance."

units.la: Inde etiam sit verbum Profanare, ideo, profanum facere, vel facere ex sacro promiscuum usibus humanis. Titus Livius ab Vrbe Condita libro tertio: Ita profanatis omnibus rebus fine religione vixit. Idem de Bello Macedonico, libro primo: Sacra sacerdotes, quae ipsius Majorumve ejus honoris causa institutae essent, omnia profanarent.
units.tr: From this comes also the verb "profanare", that is, to make profane, or to turn what is sacred into a common thing for human use. Livy, in the third book of the History from the Founding of the City: "So, with all things profaned, he lived without any religion." Idem, in the first book on the Macedonian War: the priests profaned all the sacred rites which had been instituted for his honour or that of his ancestors.

units.la: Hinc deductum verbale Profanatio. Plinius libro decimo, capite quarto: Postquam civilium bellorum profanatione meritum coepit videri, civem non occidere, &c.
units.tr: From this is derived the verbal noun "profanatio" (profanation). Pliny, book 10, chapter 4: "After the profanation of civil wars the killing of a citizen began to seem a merit," etc.

units.la: Quartum nomen, quo aedificium sacrum denotant, ideo Aedis, vel Aedes quod essent quasi aedes Deorum, sicuti caelum etiam, quod domicilium Deorum esse, Templum dictum fuisse, paulló ante est indicatum. De hac voce Servius in secundum Aeneidos ita scribit: Aedem in numero singulari de templo tantum dicimus: plurali & de domibus, & de templis. Haec ille. At Valla eandem sententiam fuisse tractat, ita scribens: Aedes in plurali accipitur, pro domo; nec unquam aliter. Caeterum sic dici Aedem vel Aedes idem Servius scribit ab Edo, quod in ea sacrificantes edere confuev- erint. Nam quaedam sunt nomina, inquit, quae initio diphthongum recipiunt, quanquam a verbo monophthongo derivantur, ut Aedes, Aesculus, &c. Varro libro quarto de lingua Latina ab aditu fieri putat, quod scilicet plano pede eam adibant: unde etiam prima syllaba diphthongum accepit. Ejus: Aedes, quid in edito ponsi solerent. Alii Aedem dici existimant, quod inea avum degatur, quod Graece αὐλὴν vocatur. Sed & hujus vocis plurima apud probatos authores exstant exempla; & quoad primam quidem ejus significationem, qua pro templo in singulari atq; adeo in plurali accipitur, haec illustria sunt apud Ciceronem. In Philipp. Ex eo die, quo in eadem Telluris convocatii sumus in quo templo, quantum in me fuit, jeci fundamenta pacis. In quo templo, id est, in qua aede Telluris. Sed hac in re differt a templo, quod semper in utroque numero habet adjectionem: ut in aede Iovis, Mercurii, in aede Concordiae, Telluris, Honoris, Virtutis, &c. in aede sacra: & in plurali, sacras aedes, aedes Deorum, aedes Nympharum, &c. Nam cum ait Lucretius, de Iove loquens: Ipse suas aedes disturbat, &c.
units.tr: The fourth name by which they designate a sacred building is "aedis" or "aedes", because they were as it were the houses of the gods, just as heaven too, which is the dwelling of the gods, was called "templum", as was indicated a little above. Servius writes on this word in his commentary on the second book of the Aeneid: "We use 'aedem' in the singular only of a temple; in the plural both of houses and of temples." So he. But Valla treats the same opinion, writing: "'Aedes' in the plural is taken for a house, and never otherwise." Besides, Servius writes that "aedes" or "aedem" is so called from "edo" (to eat), because the sacrificers used to eat in it. For, he says, there are some nouns which take a diphthong at the beginning, although they are derived from a monophthong verb, such as "aedes", "aesculus", etc. Varro, in the fourth book On the Latin Language, thinks it comes from "aditus" (approach), because they approached it on level foot; whence the first syllable also took a diphthong. Hence: "aedes" (what they used to eat in the sacred place). Others think "aedes" is so called because in it the hearth [aulē, αὐλὴ] is kept, which is called in Greek αὐλήν. But there are very many examples of this word in approved authors; and as to its first meaning, by which it is taken for a temple in the singular and still more in the plural, these are clear instances in Cicero. In the Philippics: "On that day on which we were called together into the temple of Tellus, in which, as far as I was able, I laid the foundations of peace." In which temple, that is, in which shrine of Tellus. But in this matter "aedes" differs from "templum", in that it always has an addition in either number: as in the shrine of Jupiter, of Mercury, in the shrine of Concord, of Tellus, of Honour, of Virtue, etc.; in the sacred shrine; and in the plural, sacred shrines, shrines of the gods, shrines of the nymphs, etc. For when Lucretius, speaking of Jupiter, says: "He himself throws down his own shrines," etc.

units.la: Perinde est, ac si dixisset, Iovis aedes. Igitur pro templo dicemus, duas, tres, quatuor Deorum aedes, duas aedei sacras. Pro domo vero binas, ternas, quaternas, privatas aedes. Haec Valla, libro tertio: quibus addi possunt haec etiam exempla. Cicero: Vidi epistolam; in qua de aede Telluris me admonet. Ibidem: In aede Apollinis senatus consultum factum est. Idem in Verrem: Aedium sacrarum publicorum, operum depopulatio ea misera fuit. Idem pro Domo sua: Consecrabantur aedes, non privatorum domitiliae. Idem pro Flacco: Pecuniam in aedem sacram reficiendum persuadere.
units.tr: It is the same as if he had said "Jovis aedes" (the shrines of Jupiter). Therefore, for a temple we shall say two, three, four shrines of the gods, two sacred shrines. But for a house we say two, three, four private houses. Thus Valla, book 3; to which may be added these examples too. Cicero: "I have seen a letter in which he reminds me about the shrine of Tellus." Ibid.: "In the shrine of Apollo a decree of the senate was made." Idem against Verres: "That plundering of sacred public shrines and works was a wretched thing." Idem for his house: "Shrines were consecrated, not the homes of private persons." Idem for Flaccus: "to persuade them to contribute money for repairing the sacred shrine."

units.la: Porro ab Aede fis Aedicula, ut ab Apis, Apicula: unde non Aedes in recto singulari. (Tum enim Aedecula, ut a vulpes vulpecula diceretur) esse dicendum evinit. Ponitur autem pro aede parva, id est sacello. Cicero pro Domo sua: Eam aram & aediculam & pulvinar sub saxo sacro dedicavit. Titus Livius: Iisdem diebus aedicula in Victoriae prope aedem Cocordiae M. Porcius dedicavit. Deducitur hinc & Aedituus, sacrae aedis tuitor, id est, curam gerens.
units.tr: Further, from "aedes" comes "aedicula", as from "apis" comes "apicula"; whence it is shown that the nominative singular is not "aedes" (for then it would be "aedecula", as "vulpes" becomes "vulpecula"). It is used for a small shrine, that is, a chapel. Cicero for his house: "He consecrated that altar, and the little shrine and the couch beneath the sacred rock." Titus Livy: "On the same days Marcus Porcius dedicated a little shrine near the shrine of Victory, close to the shrine of Concord." From this is also derived "aedituus", the guardian of a sacred shrine, that is, one who takes care of it.

units.la: Quintum nomen est Sacrum, & ejus diminutivum Sacellum. Ac Sacrum quidem, quando est subfantivum, pro templo accipitur, ut Graece ἱερὸν, & ejus plurale ἱερὰ. Paulus Iureconsultus: Sunt autem Sacrilegi, inquit, qui publica sacra compilarunt; at qui privata sacra, vel aediculas incuslodias tenta verint, amplius quam fures, minus quam sacrilegi merentur. Sacellum deinde locum significat parvum, Deo sacratum cum ara. Cicero de Lege Agraria: Sunt enim loca publica urbis, sunt sacella, &c. Idem de Divinatione: Cum vellet sororis suae filiam in matrimonium collocare, exiit in quoddam sacellum ominis capiendi causa: quod fieri more Veterum solebat. Trebatius Iureconsultus scribit, Sacellum compositum esse verbum, quasi sacra cella. Sed hoc neque verum videtur, neq; verisimile. Nam diminutivum esse sacri, ex ipso etiam Festo & Varrone liquet. Festus: Sacra, inquit, dicuntur loca Dis sacrata, sine tecto. Varro: In aliquot sacreis & sacelleis scriptum habemus: Ne quid scorteum (ex corio & pellibus factum) inde, ne morticinum quid adsit.
units.tr: The fifth name is Sacrum, and its diminutive is Sacellum. When Sacrum is used as a noun, it means a temple, as the Greek ἱερὸν [hieron] and its plural ἱερὰ [hiera] do. The jurist Paulus says: "Those are sacrilegious who have plundered public sacred things; but those who have broken into private shrines or small chapels are punished more severely than thieves, though less severely than sacrilegious persons." Sacellum then means a small place consecrated to God, with an altar. Cicero, in On the Agrarian Law, says: "There are public places in the city, there are shrines, etc." The same Cicero, in On Divination, writes: "When he wanted to marry off his sister's daughter, he went into a certain shrine to take an omen, as was customary in the manner of the ancients." The jurist Trebatius writes that Sacellum is a compound word, as if it were a "sacred cell." But this seems neither true nor probable. For it is clear, from Festus and Varro, that it is a diminutive of sacri. Festus says: "Sacra are places dedicated to the gods, without a roof." Varro says: "We have it written in some sacra and sacella: let nothing made of leather (from hide or skins) be brought in there, nor any carrion."

units.la: Sexto, nomine quoq; Sacrarii Veteres Latini pro templo, sive aedificio sacro olim sunt usi. Festus: Sacerdotulam sacrario Marciali fecit oletum, id est in templo. Sacrarium tamen, secundum nonnullos, est locus sacer in templo, in quo sacra reponuntur, Graecis ιεροφυλάκειον, ἀδυτον. Unde a Cicerone Sacrarium bonae Deae nominatur. Seneca libro quinto Quaestionum: Arcana illa rerum naturae sacra non promisfcuè & omnibus patent redulta, & in interiori sunt clausa sacrario. Aegesippus libro quinto scribit, Sacrarium cempli Hierofolymitani fuisse & profanatum a gentibus, quo solus semel in anno princeps sacerdotum solebat intrare, non sine sanguine. Quid intersit inter sacrarium locum & sacrarium, ostendit Ulpianus inquiens: Sacer locus est consecratus: Sacrarium, in quo sacra reponuntur. Suetonius tamen de Augusto, non tam pro sacrorum repositorio, quàm pro sacello loco, sacrato sumpsit. Nacus est, inquit, Augustus ad capita bubula, ubi nunc sacrarium habet, aliquanto pòst, quàm excessisset, constituitur. Ponitur & sacrarium pro Lararium in aedibus privatus. Cicero ad Memmium libro decimoquarto: Cajo Arvano Evandro, qui habitatin tuo sacrario, & ipso multum utor, & patrono ejus, &c. Idèm in Verrem Actione sexta: Erat apud Hejum sacrarium magna cum dignitate in aedibus a Majoribus craditum perantiquum. Echae quidem cemplorum generalia nomina fuerunc.
units.tr: Sixthly, the ancient Latins also used the name Sacrarium for a temple or sacred building. Festus: "She made the little priestess' ... in the Sacrarium of Mars," that is, in the temple. Yet according to some, a sacrarium is a sacred place within a temple in which sacred objects are stored; the Greeks call it ιεροφυλάκειον [hierophylakeion] or ἄδυτον [adyton]. Hence Cicero calls the shrine of the Good Goddess a Sacrarium. Seneca, in the fifth book of the Quaestiones naturales: "Those secret sacred things of nature are not thrown open promiscuously to all, but are shut away in the inner sanctuary." Hegesippus, in the fifth book, writes that the Sacrarium of the temple at Jerusalem was profaned by the Gentiles; into it the high priest alone used to enter once a year, and not without blood. Ulpian shows what difference there is between a sacred place and a sacrarium, saying: "A sacred place is consecrated; a sacrarium is that in which sacred objects are stored." Suetonius, however, in his life of Augustus, used the word less for a store of sacred objects and more for a consecrated chapel: "Augustus was born at Capita Bubula, where a shrine now stands, set up some time after he had departed this life." Sacrarium is also used for the household Lararium in private houses. Cicero, in the fourteenth book To Memmius: "To Gaius Arvanus Evander, who lives in your sacrarium, and I myself use it a great deal, and to his patron, etc." The same Cicero, in the sixth action against Verres: "At Heius's house there was a very ancient sacrarium, held in great honour, handed down in the house from our ancestors." These, then, were the general names for temples.

units.la: A diversis deinde Diis quoq;, & boftiis atq; partibus, quarum aliae alii s inceriores & sacrarium res habebantur, specialia quoq; nomina apud Latinos templa sunt sortita. Hinc quoddà dicebatur Fagantal, facellii videlicet loous, in quo fuit Fagus arbor, quae lovi sacra habebatur. Quoddam dicebatur Bidental, quod in eo bidentibus bostiis sacrificaretur. Bidentes autem sunt ovės, duos dentes longiores ceteris habences. Quoddà dicebatur Vaniffa, locus in quo erat agna inclusa circa templa. Sunt autem, qui putant, fanissas esse in capitolio cellis cisternis, similes, ubi reponi eranc solita ea, quae in templo vetustate erant falsa inutilia.
units.tr: Next, since different gods, sacrifices, and districts were held in different and more or less sacred regard, the Latins also gave special names to temples. Hence one place was called Fagutal, that is, the little place where there was a beech tree, which was held sacred to Jupiter. One was called Bidental, because victims called bidentes were sacrificed there. Bidentes are sheep that have two teeth longer than the rest. One was called Vanissa, a place in which a lamb was enclosed near the temples. Some think that the fanissae were in the Capitol, like cisterns or cells, where things that had become old and useless in the temple were usually stored.

units.la: Hu adde Tesqua sive Tesca, per c. simplex, quasi tuesca, a tuendis sacris: quae Varro interpretatur loca agresti, Deo cupiani consecrata, Accii tesimonio idipsum confirmans ex Tragaedia, cui Philoctetes nomen est, in hunc modum citato: Quis cu es morcalis, qui in deserta & tesca te apportes loca?
units.tr: To these add the Tesqua or Tesca, spelled with a simple c, as if from tuesca, from guarding sacred things. Varro explains these as rural places consecrated to a god, confirming this with the testimony of Accius, quoted from a tragedy whose title is Philoctetes: "Who are you, mortal, who bring yourself into deserted and tesca places?"

units.la: Quid autem tescorum nomine ibidè intelligere debeamus, explicat idem Accius, paullò post subjungens: Celsa Cabyrum delubra cenes myfleriaq; priflina Cafteis, concepta sacra.
units.tr: What we should understand by the name tesca there, the same Accius explains, adding shortly after: "The lofty shrines of the Cabyri, and the ancient mysteries of the Casteis, sacred things conceived."

units.la: Inprimis huc pertinent Penus, Penetralium, Penetralis, & Cellae nomina. Penus quidem vocabatur, inquit Festus, locus in aede Vestae intimus. Is saepius certis diebus circa Vestalia aperiebatur, qui dies religiosi habebantur.
units.tr: Chiefly relevant here are the names Penus, Penetralia, Penetralis, and Cella. Penus, says Festus, was the innermost place in the temple of Vesta. It was opened fairly often on certain days around the Vestalia, which were regarded as holy days.

units.la: Penetralia vero dicebantur Penatium Deorum sacra: quae & Lararia sunt dicta a Laribus, inquit idem Festus.
units.tr: The Penetralia were the sacred rites of the household gods, the Penates, which are also called Lararia from the Lares, says the same Festus.

units.la: Penetrale eodem auctore, sacrificium fuit dictum, quod interiore parte sacrarii (unde & sacrarium ipsum hoc nomine insignitum) conficiebatur. Hinc & penetralia cujusq; dicuntur, & penes nos, quod in Vestae loco nostra est.
units.tr: According to the same author, a penetrale was the name of a sacrifice performed in the inner part of a sacrarium (whence the sacrarium itself was also marked with this name). Hence things belonging to each person are called penetralia, and among us penes, because it is ours in the place of Vesta.

units.la: Cella quoq; significatio aliquando huic loco convenit, cum accipitur pro parte templi sacrario, in quam ingredi fas non erat. Cicero in Philippicis: Armatos in cella Concordiae inclusit. Ibidem: In hac cella Concordiae cum gladius homines collocati erant. Ticus Livius: In cella Iovis exsul habicabar.
units.tr: The word cella also sometimes fits this place, when it is taken for the part of a temple within the sacrarium, into which it was not lawful to enter. Cicero, in the Philippics: "He shut armed men into the cell of Concord." Again: "In this cell of Concord men were placed with swords." Livy: "I lived as an exile in the cell of Jupiter."
These are the Latin names of temples.

units.la: Graeci deinde templum appellarunt ἱερὸν, id est sacrum, sive sacrarium. Hinc ἱερὸν ἀδυτον τοῖς πολλοῖς, templum, in quod aditus non patet improbis: & ἱερὸν ἀμώμητον, ἀρχαιότατον, ἁπλῶς μόνον ἢ ἀνθρωπικὸν, ἀνθρωπελὰς, κοινὸν, religiosissimum, antiquissimum, publicum aut municipale, populare aut solenne, commune templum probaci autores dixerunc. Item καθίσταται, οἰκοδομῆσαι ἱερὸν, aedificare, extruere templum: & κοσμεῖν τὰ ἀγάλματα, ornare fana, &c. Idem templum vocarunt etiam ναὸν, σηκὸν, & Atticé νεώς, a verbo: αἰνω, id est, habito, 2. Naòs, εἰς τὸ ςυνάιεσθαι ἐν αὐτῷ τὰς Θεὰς, quòd Dii in ius credantur habitare. Eustathius vult ναὸν de- ναῶ & ναὸς ducit ἀπὸ τῶ ναὶ, quod est συμέινω, accumulo, quod ad illa loca donaria colligerentur a diversis: νεὼς. vel forsan propter molem aedificii sic sunt dicta, quòd ναὸς fit quasi σωρὸς, id est cumulus materiæ.
units.tr: The Greeks then called a temple hieron [ἱερόν], that is, sacred, or sanctuary. Hence hieron adyton [ἱερὸν ἄδυτον], a temple into which the wicked have no open entrance; and hieron amometon [ἱερὸν ἀμώμητον], the most ancient, the simple or human, the common, the most religious, the public or municipal, the popular or solemn common temple, as approved authors have called it. Likewise they used kathistasthai and oikodomēsai hieron [οἰκοδομῆσαι ἱερόν], to build or erect a temple, and kosmein ta agalmata [κοσμεῖν τὰ ἀγάλματα], to adorn shrines, and so on. They also called a temple naos [ναός], sekos [σηκός], and in Attic neōs [νεώς], from the verb naiō, that is, to dwell, because the gods are believed to dwell in it. Eustathius wants naos to be derived from naō, and naos from nai, which is the same as synainō, to accumulate, because gifts were gathered at those places from various people; or perhaps the name neōs was given for the bulk of the building, since a naos is, as it were, a heap [sōros] of material.

units.la: Hæc tamen vox ταὼς videtur Aëtorum decimo nono pro simulacris sive idolis accipi: ubi Naòs etiam Demetrius aurifex, tumultus illius Ephesini auctor, dicitur fabricasse ναὸς ἀργυρᾶς ἀρτέμι- templi idolum δ&, simulacra & effigies Dianæ argenteas. Interpres vertit, Aedes argenteas. Sed & forsan significat. ξυβαέιν innuit: quod nomen pro sacris vasis usurpatur, quorum mentionem facit Athenæus libro undecimo; quæ sic appellata apparent a forma, similis fabæ Ægyptiæ. Hanc enim & ξυβάεων & κολαχάτιον dixere. Inde vero & Νεωκόρῳ, id est, Ædituus vel Ædituma dicta est civitas Ephesiorum, seu Dianæ tuleris peculiaris, a νεὼς videlicet & κορέω, quod idem est, quod κοσμέω, id est, ornare, instruere: unde & Νεωκόροι & Ζακόροι, Ædituii dicti, quia sacra & aedes sacras curent. Pertinent huc per vulgata illa Ιδρύσεις νεὼς καὶ β ωμὸς θεῶν, Collocare templa & altaria Deorum, iuxta ἀφανίζω νεὼς, intendere templa, & apud Plutarchum, ἡφανισεν αὐτὸν εἰς τὸν νεὼν, in templum recondidit sese.
units.tr: Yet the word naos seems in Acts 19 to mean images or idols, where Demetrius the silversmith, the author of that Ephesian uproar, is said to have made silver naoi of Artemis, that is, silver images and effigies of Diana. The translator renders this "silver temples." But perhaps it also means the vessels called xybaeon [ξυβαέων], which Athenaeus mentions in his eleventh book; these seem to be so named from their shape, like an Egyptian bean. They called them xybaeon and kolachation. From this comes neōkoros [νεωκόρος], that is, temple-keeper, the name of the city of the Ephesians, or of Diana's special temple, from neōs and koreō, which is the same as kosmeō, to adorn or furnish. Hence neōkoroi and zakoroi [Ζακόροι] were called temple-keepers, because they look after the sacred things and the holy buildings. Relevant here too are the common phrases idrysis neōs kai bōmos theōn [ἱδρύσεις νεὼς καὶ βωμὸς θεῶν], to set up temples and altars of the gods; aphanizō neōs [ἀφανίζω νεώς], to destroy temples; and in Plutarch ephanisen heauton eis ton neōn [ἡφάνισεν ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὸν νεών], he hid himself in the temple.

units.la: Vocarunt porrò Græci templa τὰ ἱερὰ θεῶν ἱδρύματα, Deorum diversoria, sedes & delubra. 3. Τὰ ἱερὰ θεῶν Istrates: εξωμερατίεσθαι ἐς τὰ ἱερὰ θεῶν τολμῆσαι τὰς, aut: violare templa Deorum. Idem: Συ- ἀν τὸ ἱερὰ, λέγειν & κλέαιειν ἐν πόλει ἐστὶν τὰ ἱερὰ θεῶν, plo- luare & incendere non dubitarunt Deorum fana.
units.tr: The Greeks also called temples ta hiera theōn hidrymata [τὰ ἱερὰ θεῶν ἱδρύματα], dwelling places, seats and shrines of the gods. Isocrates: "to dare to violate the temples of the gods," or "to plunder the temples of the gods." The same author: "to plunder and burn the shrines of the gods" was, in the city, something they did not hesitate to do.

units.la: Σηκὸς quinetiam & τέμενος: & templum Græcus significat; Et τηκὸς quidem non tantum 4. Σηκὸς templum uni versum in genere: sed specialiter templi partem interiorem, alio nomine ἀδυτὸν, sive adytum dictam: quam vis proprie significat ovium vel caprarum mandram, caulam, stabulum ve, in quo seorsum agni lactentes claudantur. Fit inde nomen σηκοφόρος, vel ὀνκακόρος, ædituus, ædiuni sacrarum custos, & curator. Τέμενος & verò est proprie est nemus: tamen synec- 5. Τέμενος dochicé delubrum quodcunque Dus dicatum & consecratum, seu locum quem ves separatum in honorem Dei alicujus aut heroïs significat. Aristophanes in Pluto: ἔσοὶ τὸ θεῖον ὧν τῷ Θεῷ, in delubrum Dei ivimus. Ejus derivatum est τεμενάζω, ædituus, loci sacri custos.
units.tr: Sekos [σηκός] and temenos [τέμενος] also mean a temple in Greek. Sekos signifies a temple in general, but specifically the inner part of the temple, otherwise called adyton; properly, however, it means a fold or pen for sheep or goats, a stall in which suckling lambs are shut up apart. From this comes sekophoros or onkakoros, a temple-keeper, guardian and curator of the sacred things. Temenos properly means a grove; yet by synecdoche it signifies any shrine dedicated and consecrated to a god, or a place set apart in honour of some god or hero. Aristophanes in Plutus: "we went into the shrine of the god." Its derivative is temenazō, to be temple-keeper, guardian of a sacred place.

units.la: Denique templum idololatricum, cujusfoidi fuerunt omnia veterum Gentilium, eidωλεῖον 6. Εἰδωλεῖον nuncupatur a Græcis, id est, Idoli domus, ab εἶδωλον, voce, ut supra dictum est, idolum seu simulacrum significante.
units.tr: Finally, an idolatrous temple, of which the ancient Gentiles had very many, is called by the Greeks eidōleion [εἰδωλεῖον], that is, the house of an idol, from eidōlon [εἴδωλον], which, as said above, means an idol or image.

units.la: Sed & plerunque templa ab ipsis Deorum nominibus appellata in venimus, ut ab Iunone ἡρεῖον, a Diana ἀρτεμίσιον, a Venere, ἀφροδίσιον a Marte ἀρείον, ab Heroibus ἡρῷον, & ejusmodi alia.
units.tr: Moreover, we often find temples named after the gods themselves: from Juno hēreion [ἡρεῖον], from Diana artemision [ἀρτεμίσιον], from Venus aphrodision [ἀφροδίσιον], from Mars areion [ἀρεῖον], from heroes hērōon [ἡρῷον], and other such.

units.la: Fiat de Græcis nominibus templorum. Hebræis templum idololatricum dicitur in genere Nomina Hebræorum (בית הכלא Hecal, id est palatium sive regia, in qua Dii habitant (cui respondet Basilicæ bræa templos nomen) & בית אלהים Beth-aven, domus idoli & iniquitatis, ειν Θεῶν Θαυς. In specie ve- rum. ro בית דגון Beth dagon, certi cujusdam idoli domus, sive templum. Sic Hosea & alii Pro- בית אל phetæ locum & oppidum Bethel, quod antiquitus prisca & vera religione multis miraculis divinis insigne erat (unde Domus Dei dictum) per contemptum propter vitulum aureum, qui in eo colebatur בית און Beth-aven, id est, domum idoli frequenter appellant, quasi dicant: nidt ein Gotthaus, sonder ein Götzenhaus. Hujusmodi fuerunt templorum nomina etiam Hebræa.
units.tr: So much for the Greek names of temples. Among the Hebrews an idolatrous temple is named in general bēt hēkal, that is, a palace or royal house in which the gods dwell (to which the Latin basilica corresponds), and bēt elohim, bēt aven, the house of an idol and of iniquity. In particular, beth dagon, the house of a certain idol, or its temple. So Hosea and the other prophets, by way of contempt, call the place and town of Bethel, which in ancient times was distinguished by true religion and many divine miracles (whence it was called the House of God), because of the golden calf worshipped there, beth-aven, that is, the house of an idol, frequently. As if they were saying: not a house of God, but an idol-house. Such were also the Hebrew names of temples.

units.la: HIS PRAEMISSIS, ditamus nunc quaedam de hujusmodi sacrorum aedificiorum origine: seu primis in venerationis; de quibus quidem varie sunt apud auctores prophanos sententiae. Latini ferè omnes ad Ianum originem hanc referunt, cujus idcirco nomen in sacrificiis veteri instituto perpetuò prefari solebant: alii ad Faunum, a quo fana appellata Probus scribit: alii ad Iovem, Cretensium Regem, unde inter Deos primum ipse locum fuerit sortitus: alii ad Vulconem, apud Phænices: alii ad Phoronem aut Meropem, aut Aeacum Iovis filium: alii ad Dionysium, cum ludos debellasset: alii ad Cecropem in Attica: alii ad Arcades: alii ad Aegyptios: alii ad Chaldæos: alii ad Thracos: alii ad Cyprios. Græci Epimenidem Circensem: alii Pykium architectum, qui apud Prienenses templum Minervæ primus posuerit: alii denique alios atque alios primos templorum auctores atque conditores fuisse.
units.tr: Having premised these things, we now touch on some matters concerning the origin of such sacred buildings, or the first places of worship. Opinions about them among the profane authors vary. Almost all Latin writers refer this origin to Janus, whose name they therefore always used to say first in sacrifices, by ancient custom. Others refer it to Faunus, from whom Probus writes that shrines (fana) took their name. Others to Jupiter, king of the Cretans, from whom he himself first obtained a place among the gods by lot. Others to Vulcan among the Phoenicians; others to Phoroneus or Merops, or Aeacus the son of Jupiter; others to Dionysus, after he had subdued the games; others to Cecrops in Attica; others to the Arcadians; others to the Egyptians; others to the Chaldeans; others to the Thracians; others to the Cyprians. The Greeks name Epimenides the Cretan; others Pyxius the architect, who first set up a temple of Minerva at Priene; others, finally, various others as the first authors and founders of temples.

units.la: Porrò plerique ex sepulcris initium templa sumsisse arbitrati sunt: quam originem ædium sacrarum diligentissimi quoque scriptores tradunt Eusebius & Lactantius. Quadere & Clemens Alexandrinus in Protreptico sic scriptum reliquit: Superstitio, inquit, templa condere persuasit. Quæ enim prius hominum sepulcra fuerunt, magnificentius condita, templorum appellatione vocata sunt. Nam apud Larissæam civitatem in arce, in templo Palladis, Acrisii sepulcrum fuit, quod nunc sacrarium loco celebratur: in arce quoque Athenieńsi, ut est ab Antiocho in nono Historiarum scriptum, Cereris sepulcrum fuit: in templo vero Palladis, quam Poliada Græci appellant, jacet Erichthonius. Ijmarus autem Eumolpi atque Daira filius in Eleusine una cum Celei natabus sepultus. Hæc Clemens.
units.tr: Moreover, most have thought that temples took their beginning from sepulchres. The most diligent writers, Eusebius and Lactantius, also hand down this origin of sacred buildings. Clement of Alexandria too left this written in his Protrepticus: "Superstition," he says, "persuaded men to build temples. For what were formerly men's tombs, more magnificently built, were called by the name of temples. For at the city of Larissa, in the citadel, in the temple of Pallas, was the tomb of Acrisius, which is now celebrated as a sanctuary. In the citadel of Athens too, as Antiochus wrote in the ninth book of his Histories, was the tomb of Ceres; and in the temple of Pallas, whom the Greeks call Polias, lies Erichthonius. Ismarus, son of Eumolpus and Daira, was buried at Eleusis together with the sons of Celeus." So Clement.

units.la: Nos autem hanc omissis sacrarum litterarum testimonio atque auctoritate edoceri scimus, verorum quidem templorum primum auctoreni eundem esse, qui hujus amplissimi pulcherrimique templi, id est, Mundi creator est, nempe Deum Optimum Maximum. Ac prisca illa planeque aurea sanctissimorum Patriarcharum atas externis quidem manufactis templis caruit: qui quidem partim in privatis atque domesticis suis ædibus, partim nomadum instar, vagam vitam perseguentes, passim hinc inde variis in locis, in quibus Deus illis apparuerat, & aliqua sua præsentiæ signa dederat, erectis aris sive altaribus Deum invocarunt, sacrificia ut obtulerunt, denique familiam suam in vero Dei cultu atque religione pie fideliterque instituerunt: cujus rei vel unicum illud Iacobi exemplum; de quo Genes. vigesimo octavo, illustre est testimonium, qui in sancto illo atque augusto loco, in quo Deus ei mirabilis modo apparuerat (quam ob causam eum Portam seu Domum Dei appellat) erecto altari una cum familia sua, repurgata prius ab omnibus idolis, sacrum cultum, orationes nimirum & sacrificia Deo exhibuit.
units.tr: But we, setting aside these, know from the testimony and authority of Sacred Scripture that the first author of true temples is the same one who is the creator of this most vast and most beautiful temple, that is, the world: namely, God, the Best and Greatest. That ancient and truly golden age of the most holy Patriarchs lacked externally built temples. They, partly in their private and domestic houses, partly living a wandering life like nomads, here and there in various places where God had appeared to them and given some sign of his presence, erected altars, invoked God and offered sacrifices. Finally, they piously and faithfully instructed their families in the true worship and religion of God. One illustrious testimony to this is the example of Jacob, from Genesis 28, who in that holy and august place where God had appeared to him in a wonderful manner (for which reason he calls it the Gate or House of God), after an altar had been erected and his household was present, having first purged everything of idols, offered sacred worship to God, namely prayers and sacrifices.

units.la: Horum deinde & posteros in miserabili illa Ægyptiaca servitute nulla templa habuisse legimus, apud quos procul dubio omnis veri Dei cultus, divini memoria plane obliterata fuerat. Unde certe colligimus, hujusmodi sacra ædificia, licet ad cultum sacrum peragendum atque celebrandum sint utilia: non tamen ita esse necessaria, ut non fine iis quoque, sicut res atque necessitas postulet, Deus etiam sub dio, locis quibusvis patentibus rectè vitæ, ut coli possit.
units.tr: Moreover, we read that their descendants in that wretched Egyptian servitude had no temples at all, and among them undoubtedly all true worship of God had been utterly forgotten. From this we surely gather that such sacred buildings, although they are useful for performing and celebrating the sacred worship, are not so necessary that God cannot be worshipped without them, when need and circumstance require it, under the open sky and in any open place whatever.

units.la: Postea exitum vero Israelitarum ex Ægypto Deus in deserto, ut constat Exod. vigesimo quinto, certum quoddam admodum operosum atque splendidum, sed portabile, quod facile hue illuc transferri posset, tanquam illorum vagu peregrinationibus accommodatum, extrui jussit ædificium, quod quidem אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד Ohel mohed, id est, Tabernaculum testimonii, sive conventionis aut contubernium appellatur. Hoc tabernaculum cum diu fuisset in Silo, etiam temporibus Eli & Samuelis, tandem ab illo loco in Sionem montem fuit translatum, ibique collocatum. Simile tabernaculum ad Templi formam extructum, in bellicis expeditionibus Consultantium circumvexisse, in eoque conventus egisse festus est Sozomenus libro 1. capite 8.
units.tr: Afterwards, when the Israelites had left Egypt, God ordered them, in the wilderness, as is clear from Exodus 25, to build a certain structure, very elaborate and splendid but portable, which could easily be carried from place to place, suited to their wandering journeys. This is called Ohel mohed [אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד], that is, the Tabernacle of Testimony, or of meeting or assembly. This tabernacle remained for a long time at Shiloh, even in the times of Eli and Samuel, and at last was moved from that place to Mount Zion and set up there. Sozomen, in book 1, chapter 8, reports that a similar tabernacle, constructed in the form of the Temple, was carried about by the consultants during their military expeditions, and that they held assemblies in it.

units.la: Post annorum autem, ab hac prima tabernacula divini conflationis CCCCLXXX.
