(qui fuerunt inter Mosem & Salomonem) a Salomone in monte Moriah, ubi Isaac patre Abrahamo immolandus erat, templum magnificentissimum illud & splendidissimum simul, totius ferè Mundi miraculum, Dei jussu atque mandato, Davidis ejus ædificandi facultate adempta, ædificatum fuit, eo consilio, ut populus, ab idololatria abstractus, in legitimo Dei cultu retineretur. Fuit enim templum illud, ceu unica totius gentis paratia, ad quam tribus solennioribus festis cultus externi in eo exercendi gratia populus Dei præcepto atque mandato confluebat.
units.tr: Then, four hundred and eighty years after this first tabernacle of divine construction (the years between Moses and Solomon), the magnificent and at the same time most splendid temple, almost the wonder of the whole world, was built by Solomon on Mount Moriah, where Abraham had been about to sacrifice Isaac his son. It was built by God's command and order, David being deprived of the right to build it, with this purpose: that the people, drawn away from idolatry, might be kept in the lawful worship of God. For that temple was, as it were, the single place of assembly for the whole nation, to which the tribes came together by God's precept and command at the more solemn feasts, to perform the external worship there.

units.la: Hoc templum cum fletiffet annis M. CCCCXLII. tandem ob peccata populi gravissima, justissimo Dei judicio a Nabuchodonosore, Rege Babyloniorum, juxta Prophetarum plurima luculentissimaq; vaticinia una cum urbe solo aquatum est & concrematum.
units.tr: This temple stood for 1,442 years, and at last, because of the people's most grievous sins, by the most just judgement of God, it was razed to the ground and burned along with the city by Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, in accordance with very many and most clear prophecies of the prophets.

units.la: Idem post captivitatem illam Babyloniam Dei jussu a Zorobabele rursus ædificatum, ab Herode Antipatre magnificentissime auctum & amplificatum tandem anno secundo Vespasiani Imperatoris. XL. circiter annis post Christi ascensum in cœlos, juxta ejus vaticinium, Titus dux, una cum urbe funditus deletum atque extinctum fuit. Id aliquot annis post Judæi, Julian Apostate permissu, frustra restaurare sunt conati: conatum hunc illorum Deo magno quodam miraculo impediente.
units.tr: After the Babylonian captivity the same temple was rebuilt by Zerubbabel at God's command, and was enlarged and extended most magnificently by Herod the son of Antipater. Finally, in the second year of the emperor Vespasian, about forty years after Christ's ascension into heaven, in accordance with his prophecy, it was utterly destroyed and wiped out, together with the city, by the general Titus. Some years afterwards the Jews tried in vain to restore it under the permission of Julian the Apostate; their attempt was prevented by God through a certain great miracle.

units.la: Hujus autem tam splendidi, tam augusti & sancti templi, in toto orbe terrarum celeberrimi cujus veris Dei autor & architectus fuit, ædificatione, adductos quadam κατοχὴν ἀλλά seu prava imitatione Ethnicos Dii suis filiis & commentitiis, quorum hinc inde fit mentio, templa, delubra, fana, ædes sacras, & similia ædificia extruere voluisse, verisimile est, illit adulterinum & idololatricum suum cultum exerendi causâ.
units.tr: Now it is probable that the Gentiles, drawn on by a certain katochē alla [κατοχὴν ἀλλά], that is, by a perverse imitation of this so splendid, so majestic and holy temple, famous throughout the whole world, whose author and architect was the true God, wished to erect temples, shrines, sanctuaries, sacred houses and similar buildings to their gods, the sons of their own invention, of whom mention is made here and there, in order to practise their own counterfeit and idolatrous worship there.

units.la: Tametsi, ut hoc quoq; addam, quod certè silentio non est prætermittendum, extiterunt quiLam Philosophi, atque etiam Gentes, quæ nulla templa Diis ædificanda, nec templis, vel in templis Deos colendos esse arbitrabantur, atq; ita omnem templorum usum respuerunt, ceu alienum a divina majestate. Sit enim Persæ, ab omni templorum usu abhorrentes ex Magorum suorum sententia, impiè eos facere existimarunt, qui Deos adium ac parietum septis includerent, quibus omnia deberent esse patentia, & libera, quorumque hic Mundus omnis templum esset ac domus, atq; idcirco, Magis autoribus, non modò nulla Diis suis templa extruebant, sed etiam passim Græcorum & aliarum nationum templa demoliri, destruere, concremare, & solo æquare consuserunt, ut passim ex bistoriis patet: inprimis autem Xerxes hac de causa inflammasse templa Græciæ dicitur. Sit montis Carmeli incolæ nullum Dei sui templum, sed aras tantummodo inmonte habuerunt: nec non Germani illi profci, teste Tacito, pro templis lucos & nemora, Deorum suorum nominibus appellata, habuerunt & coluerunt: quod ipsum tamen nec veteres tantum Germanos, sed ante eos Ethnicos plurimi & alii factitârunt. Nam Massilienses, qui Galliam Narbonensem inhabitant, in lucis, in quibus nulla erat effigies, sacra faciebant, interdumque arborum truncos venerabantur, tanquam aliquid divinitatis eis inesset. Hinc Servius no-tat, Manes & Heroum animas, qui Lares vitales dicerentur, lucos tenere: quos & ideo fit diΙtos arbitrantur nonnulli, quod ibi lumina fierent religionis causâ: quanquam alii per contrariam; quod minimè luceant propter arborum umbras opacas. Inde & Virgilius in sexto: Nulli certa domus, lucis habitamus opacis.
units.tr: And yet, so that I may add this also, which certainly must not be passed over in silence, there were some philosophers and also peoples who thought that no temples should be built for the gods, and that gods should be worshipped neither in temples nor within temples, and so they rejected all use of temples as foreign to the divine majesty. Thus the Persians, abhorring all use of temples according to the teaching of their Magi, thought it impious of those who enclosed the gods within the walls and roofs of buildings, since everything ought to be open and free, and this whole world is the temple and house of God. For this reason, following the authority of the Magi, they not only built no temples for their gods, but also were accustomed to tear down, destroy, burn and level to the ground the temples of the Greeks and of other nations wherever they found them, as is clear from the histories everywhere; and Xerxes in particular is said to have set fire to the temples of Greece for this reason. Thus the inhabitants of Mount Carmel had no temple for their god, but only altars on the mountain. Likewise those Germans of old, according to Tacitus, had and worshipped groves and woods, named after their gods, in place of temples; yet not only the ancient Germans but very many other Gentiles before them did the same. For the people of Massilia, who inhabit Narbonese Gaul, performed their sacred rites in groves in which there was no image, and sometimes they venerated the trunks of trees, as if some divinity dwelt in them. Hence Servius notes that the spirits of the dead and the souls of heroes, who were called household gods of life, dwelt in groves; and some think they were so called because lights were kindled there for the sake of religion, although others take the opposite view, that they do not shine at all because of the dark shade of the trees. Hence also Virgil in book 6: "No fixed home have we; we dwell in the dark groves."

units.la: Et primo: Lucus in urbe fuit media, lætissima umbra.
units.tr: And in the first book: "There was a grove in the middle of the city, most pleasant in its shade."

units.la: Vbi Servius: Vbicunque Virgilius lucum ponit, sequitur etiam consecratio, ut: Lucorum forte parentis Pilumni Turnus sacrata valle sedebat.
units.tr: Where Servius says: Wherever Virgil places a grove, consecration also follows, as in: "Turnus was sitting in a consecrated valley of the grove of Pilumnus, his ancestor."

units.la: Et octavo: Hinc lucum, quem Romulus acer asylum.
units.tr: And in book 8: "Hence the grove which fierce Romulus made an asylum."

units.la: Vbi obiter nota, Asylum etiam templi quoddam genus fuisse, ex quo nullus posset extrahi; dicum a Servio quasi Asyrum: quod tamen non fuit in omnibus templis, nisi quibus consecratio-nis lege concessum esset. Ejusmodi Asylum fuisse templum Apollinis Delii scribit Livius. Sed enim & Valla scribit de Luco libro quarto in hunc modum: Lucus nequaquam cædunus est, quin p otiiis manu consitus, religiosusque, atque vel alicui Deo, vel alicujus hominis cineribus consecratus: ideoque aut cirta delubra hominum, aut circa sepulcra est positum. Cicero pro Milone: Vos enim Albani tumuli atque luci, vos, inquam, implore atque obtestor.
units.tr: Here note in passing that an asylum was also a kind of temple, from which no one could be dragged out; Servius derives the word as if it were asyrum. This, however, was not the case in all temples, but only in those which had been granted this by the law of consecration. Livy writes that the temple of Apollo at Delos was such an asylum. Valla also writes about groves in book 4 in this way: "A grove is by no means cut down, but planted by hand, sacred and dedicated either to some god or to the ashes of some man; and therefore it is placed either around temples of men or around sepulchres." Cicero, in the speech for Milo: "For you, the hills and groves of Alba, you, I say, I implore and call upon."

units.la: Ovidius secundo Fastorum: multis incidunt arvis, Junonis magne nomine lucus erat.
units.tr: Ovid, in book 2 of the Fasti: "They fell upon many fields; there was a grove under the great name of Juno."

units.la: Statius libro tertio Syll. Festaque pallentes bilarent altaria lucos.
units.tr: Statius, in book 3 of the Silvae: "And altars, glad with feast-days, gladdened the pale groves."

units.la: Flaccus libro quinto: Visa parens tristis Hecates excedere lucis.
units.tr: Flaccus, in book 5: "The sad mother was seen leaving the grove of Hecate."

units.la: Sic lucus Martis dictus, in quo Mars Iliam, Vestalem virginem, compressit, ut esset apud Iustinum & Plutarchum. Fuit & Martis lucus apud Colchos, in quo Poëtæ finxerunt aurum Phryxi, nei ariete vellus a pervigili dracone asservari: cujus luci aliquoties Valerius ille Flaccus in Argonauticis meminit, & Juvenalis Satyrâ primâ: Nulli nota magis domus est sua, quàm mihi Martis Lucus, &c.
units.tr: Thus the grove was called the grove of Mars, in which Mars lay with Ilia, the Vestal virgin, as in Justin and Plutarch. There was also a grove of Mars among the Colchians, in which the poets feigned that the golden fleece of Phrixus, carried by the ram, was guarded by a sleepless dragon. Valerius Flaccus often mentions this grove in his Argonautica, and Juvenal in his first satire: "No house is more known to anyone than my house by the grove of Mars," and so on.

units.la: Cornelius Front.de differentiis vocabulorum lucum dicit esse locum,templum, sacellum, delu- brum. Hujusmodi lucos Plutarchus quaestione Rom.oftogesima septima,multos ajt circa urbem Romae Diis fuisse consecratos, quorum reditus in spectaculo insumebantur: unde pecunia , qua spectaculo impendebatur, Lucar olim fuerie dicta. Sic Festus: Lucar appellatur es, quod ex lucis captatur, sive capitur: & Lucaris pecunia , quae in luco erat data. Hinc etiam dicta Lucaria , festae , quae in luco colebant Romani , qui permagnus inter viam Salariam & Tiberim fuit: pro eo, quod vicii a Gallis fugientes e praeliosi sese occultaverunt. Hinc etiam Oblucinasse, sive Oblucaniasse dicebant Antiqui mente erraste, quasi in luco Deorum alicui occurrisse: Festus.
units.tr: Cornelius Front(o), in his work on the differences of words, says that a lucus is a place, a temple, a shrine, a sanctuary. Plutarch, in Roman Question 87, says that many such groves were consecrated to the gods around the city of Rome, and that their revenues were spent on public shows; hence the money that was spent on the show was once called lucar. So Festus: "Lucar is so called because it is taken or seized from the grove," and lucaris pecunia is the money that was given in the grove. Hence also the Lucaria were named, festivals which the Romans celebrated in the grove, which was very large between the Salarian Way and the Tiber, because the Gauls, fleeing from the Vicii, hid themselves there after the battle. Hence also the ancients said oblucinasse, or oblucaniasse, meaning to err in mind, as if one had met someone of the gods in a grove: Festus.

units.la: Lucorum bujusmodi idololatricorum in sacris etiam litteris crebra fit mentio: ut lucorum ad eras Baalis , quarto Regum decimo tertio: & lucorum in Samaria,Esaie sexagesimo quinto & alibi:quos quidem loftas,Rex religiofiffimus,dicitur excidisse ex Iudaea, secundo Paralipomenon trigesimo quarto.
units.tr: Mention of such idolatrous groves is frequent also in the sacred letters: for example, the groves at the altars of Baal, in 4 Kings 13; and the groves in Samaria, Isaiah 65 and elsewhere. Those groves King Asa, the most religious of kings, is said to have cut down out of Judea, in 2 Chronicles 34.

units.la: Meminit lucorum siflorum,ut hoc colophonis loco addam,Lucianus quoque de sacrificiis inquiens: Primum lucos Diis attribuerunt,tum & montes dicarunt: praeterea aves consecrarunt deinde suam cuique arborem assignarunt. Postea per regiones illos distribuerunt coluntque, ut luc in civitatem suam recipiunt, nempe Apollinem Delphii Delium, Minervam Athenien- sem, Argivi Iunonem, Migdonii Rheam, Venerem Paphii, Cretenses Iovem. Postremo fanus innorem illorum erectis,ne tectis videlicet aut Penatibus careant,formas illorum exprimunt,adhibito ad id vel Praxitele, vel Polycleto, vel Phidio.
units.tr: Lucian also mentions sacred groves, which I will add here as a kind of coda, in his work on sacrifices: "First they assigned groves to the gods, and afterwards dedicated mountains to them. Besides this, they consecrated birds, and then assigned to each god a tree of its own. Later they distributed these across the regions and worshipped them, and each people took its god into its own city: the Delphians Apollo, the Delians Diana, the Athenians Minerva, the Argives Juno, the Migdonians Rhea, the Paphians Venus, the Cretans Jupiter. Finally, having erected temples for these gods, lest they lack a roof and household gods, they fashioned their images, employing for this purpose Praxiteles, or Polyclitus, or Phidias."

units.la: Porro & Zenonis, principis sectae Stoicorum , qui vixit Olympiade septuagesima, vel obgefime circiter,quo tempore Xerxes,de quo supra, Graeciam vastavit,& Romani , ejectis Regibus consules creari coeperunt, vixit , hoc celebre dogma fuit , ἱερὰ Θεῶν ἀπὸ οἰκοδομίης, Templa Deorum non aedificanda. Eadem quoque in sententia & Diagoras , qui temporibus etiam Xerxis docebat in Graecia, & Theodorus Epicurus,athei dicti , fuisse perhibentur. Nec enim Diis templa ponebant,quos omnino non esse credebant; ac si Dii essent, eos templis non indigere, sed haec in illorum cedere ignominiam.
units.tr: Moreover, Zeno, the founder of the Stoic sect, who lived around the seventieth Olympiad, about the time when Xerxes, mentioned above, laid waste Greece, and when the Romans, after the kings were expelled, began to elect consuls, held this famous doctrine: "Temples of the gods are not to be built" [ἱερὰ Θεῶν ἀπὸ οἰκοδομίης]. Diagoras, who also taught in Greece in the time of Xerxes, and Theodorus, the Epicurean, both called atheists, are likewise said to have held the same opinion. For they did not set up temples for gods whom they utterly did not believe to exist; and, if gods there were, they held that such beings had no need of temples, and that such buildings would rather be a disgrace to them.

units.la: Duo itaque hominum genera videntur fuisse eorum , qui Diis negant templa esse ponenda. Unum quidem eorum; qui Deos sive Deas prorsus negant , ac proinde nec templa aedificanda esse, cujusmodi fuerunt duo illi athei,tanquam communi sensu,ipsisque naturae principiis refragantes. Alterum vero eorum,qui licet Deos esse crederent, iis tamen templa litruere nefas putabant, probabilibus, uti videtur, rationibus adductis, quoniam nimirum Deus minime, ut cibopotu, vesse, ita aedificiis quoque ad caloris frigorisque vim depellendam indigeat , eundemque longe lateque per omnia diffusum parietum claufris comprehendere atque coercere , non modo natione, verum etiam a pietate alienum videatur.
units.tr: There seem, therefore, to have been two kinds of people who held that no temples ought to be built for the gods. The first kind were those who utterly denied that there are gods, male or female, and who therefore thought that no temples should be built; of this sort were those two atheists, who were, as it were, opposed to common sense and to the very first principles of nature. The second kind were those who, although they believed that gods exist, nevertheless thought it wrong to erect temples to them, for reasons which seem plausible: namely, that God does not need buildings to ward off the force of heat and cold, just as he does not need food and drink; and that to enclose within walls of masonry one who is spread far and wide through all things seems not only unnatural but also foreign to piety.

units.la: Adde quod illorum sententia simul & sententiae duplex haec ratio,modo commemorata, ipsarum sacrarum litterarum , seu potius Spiritus Sancti, earundem auctoris, testimonio authoritateque niti videatur. Sic enim Deus per Prophetam exclamat: Coelum sedes mea,& terra scabellum pedum meorum. Ubi igitur erit domus , quam aedificabitis mihi ? Et ubi erit locus meae quietus? Omnia nanque ista fecit manus mea,quae fata sunt, inquit Dominus. Sic Salomon in templi illius magnificentissimi dedicatione inquit : Caeli caelorum, hoc est, extremi,te non capiunt. Sic Paulus ad Athenienses: Deus,inquit,qui fecit Mundum & omnia,quae in eo sunt,quum sit caeli et terrae Dominus,in manufactis templis non habitat.
units.tr: Add to this that their opinion, together with this twofold reason just mentioned, seems to rest upon the testimony and authority of the sacred writings, or rather of the Holy Spirit, the author of those writings. For thus God cries out through the prophet: "Heaven is my throne, and earth is my footstool. Where then will the house be that you will build for me? And where will be the place of my rest? For my hand has made all these things, says the Lord." So Solomon, at the dedication of that most magnificent temple, says: "The heaven of heavens, that is, the highest heavens, cannot contain you" (1 Kings 8). So Paul to the Athenians: "God," he says, "who made the world and all things in it, since he is Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made with hands" (Acts 17).

units.la: Sed haec & alia hujusmodi sacrae scripturae loca, quae Deum non incolere templa manufacta, ita non comprehendi,ea denique nolle, illis Naomachis minime profecto patrocinantur. Ita enim Spiritus sanctus, sibi semper constans, non simpliciter sacra aedificia,quae ipsemet fieri masdavit,& in quibus se praesentem fore promisit,atque adeo reipsa & exitu magnus miraculos suos sepe in iisdem singularem quandam gratiam exercuit , vetat & prohibet : sed potius fallam ati, per versam hominum opinionem ex illorum animis tollere , atq; extirpare conatur,quae nimirum templis & uni verso culcui externo nimium tribuebant, posthabito veri Dei cultu vero & spirituali, Deum iis quasi includebant & alligabant , eumque minime rectè ristque coli sine in exiflimabant: fiinabant: denique totam religionis ac per consequens salutis proram & puppim in externorum templorum magnifica structura, assidua frequentatione, negligeto virtutum rectoq; factorum fluodio collocabant. Non ergo, ut summatim dicam, ipsa templa, sed eorum potius abusum, per verba aut opera de templis & de ipso Deo opinionem damnat.
units.tr: But these and other similar passages of Scripture, which teach that God does not dwell in temples made by hands, and that he does not wish them to be so, certainly do not in any way lend support to those sophistries. For the Holy Spirit, ever consistent with himself, does not simply forbid and prohibit sacred buildings, which he himself commanded to be made, and in which he promised that he would be present, and indeed, by the very outcome, he often exercised a singular grace in them through his great miracles. Rather, he seeks to remove and root out of men's minds the false opinion which granted too much to temples and to all outward worship, setting aside the true and spiritual worship of the true God; which enclosed and bound God, as it were, within them, and believed that he could not be rightly worshipped without them; and, in short, which placed the whole helm and stern of religion, and consequently of salvation, in the magnificent construction and constant frequenting of external temples, while neglecting the pursuit of virtue and of right conduct. Therefore, to put it briefly, it is not the temples themselves that Scripture condemns, by its words or deeds, but rather their abuse, and the false opinion about temples and about God himself that goes with it.

units.la: Hactenus de templorum origine, seu primis inventoribus, quibus hec quoque Arnobii libet addere, tanquam huic loco accommodatissima: Quorum (templorum) inquit, si quaeris audire quis prior fuerit fabricator, aut Phoronem Aegyptius, aut Merops tibi fuisse monstrabitur: ut terra structa, laqueariibus aut remedeant aureis, splendeant hic gemmae, & sidereos evomant variata intertione fulgores: terra sunt haec omnia, et si res ea pretiis carioribus penditis, delectari credendum est hos Deos; nec recusare, nec sperare, quo minus se sepiant, & eorum objectionibus coerceantur inclusi. Templi, inquit, hoc Martis est, hoc Iunonis & Veneris: Apollo hic habitat, in hoc manet Hercules, illo Summanus. Ista non prima & maxima contumelia est, habitationibus Deos habere dislrictos? cuiusmodi hic dare conclavia & cellulas fabricari, & eis existimari necessarias resse, quae hominibus, felibus, quae sunt formiculi, et lacertae, quae fugacibus, parvidis atque exiguis muribus. Sed non (inquit) idcirco attribuimus Deis templa, tanquam humidos ab his imbres, ventos, pluvias arceamus, aut soles: sed ut eos possimus coram & comminus contueri, affari de proximo, & cum praesentibus quodammodo veneratione colloquia miscere. Sub axe enim nudo, & sub aethereo tegmine invocati si fuerint, nihil audiunt: & nisi de proximo admoveantur his preces, tanquam nihil diccatur, obstrictis, atq; immobiles stabunt. Atquin nos arbitramur omnem Deum omnino (si modo nominis huius vi pollet) ex quacunq; mundi parte, quod quisq; conceperit sub objectu & tacita sensibus cognitione antitipata praesumere: atq; ut astra, sol, luna, cum supra terras meant, omnibus omnino cernentibus sta tum sunt & ubiq; praesentes: ita quoq; convenit audientiam Numinum nullis esse clausam linguae semper, esse praesentem: quanvis ad eam voces regionibus ex distantibus confluant. Hoc est enim proprium Deorum, complere omnia vi sua, non partiliter ubiam, sed ubiq; esse totos: non adesse, non abesse, non cenatum ad Aethiopas pergere, & post dies bissenos privatum ad domicilium redire. Quodsi ita non erit, tollitur omnis spes opis, & erit in dubio audiamur a Diis, uecne: si quando res sacras cerimoniarum conscientiis debitas. Constituamus enim cognoscenda rei causa, templum Numinis alicujus esse apud Canarias insulas, ejusdem apud ulcimam Thy lem: eiusdem apud Seras esse, apud furvos Garamantas, & si qui sunt alii, quot ab sui notitia maria, montes, sylvae, & quadrini disterminant cardines. Si omnes uno in tempore rebus diuinis factis, quod sua quoq; necessitas cogitare compellit poscant de Numine, referendi beneficii, quaenam omnibus esse erit, si non undique ad se missam vocem Deus exaudiret, & erit ulla longinquitas, quo penetrare non possit auxilium poscentis oratio? aut enim nullis in partibus erit praesens, si uspiam poterit aliquando non esse, aut aderit unis tantum, quoniam praebere coma muniser suum non potest atque indiserentis auditum.
units.tr: So far concerning the origin of temples, or their first inventors. To these I am pleased to add the words of Arnobius, as most fitting to this place: "If you ask," he says, "who was the first builder of these temples, you will be shown either Phoroneus the Egyptian or Merops. Those gods are supposed to take delight in these things, which are built of earth, and whose ceilings are of gold, where precious stones shine and send forth sparkling lights in varied arrangement, all of them earthly things, and things of great price. Nor do they refuse or hope to be fenced in and confined, shut up by these enclosures. 'This is the temple of Mars,' they say, 'this of Juno and Venus; Apollo lives here, Hercules remains in that one, Summanus in another.' Is it not a first and greatest insult to have gods confined in dwellings, and to build rooms and little cells for them, and to think them in need of these, when even men, cats, ants, lizards, and the fleeting, timid, small and tiny mice have their own holes? But," he says, "we do not assign temples to the gods as if we were keeping off rains, winds, or sun from them, but so that we may be able to look upon them face to face, speak with them at close range, and mingle conversations with them, as it were, with the reverence due to those present. For if they are invoked under the open sky and under an ethereal canopy, they hear nothing; and unless prayers are brought close to them, they will stand, as it were, bound and immovable, as if nothing had been said. Yet we believe that every god, from whatever part of the world, can be assumed, by a sort of anticipated conception, to be present under the object conceived and by tacit knowledge of the senses (if indeed the name of god has any force in it); and just as the stars, the sun, and the moon, while they move above the lands, are visible to all who look and are everywhere present, so too it is fitting that the hearing of the divinities is never closed to any tongue; that it is always present, although voices flow to it from distant regions. For this is the property of the gods: to fill all things by their power, to be whole everywhere not in parts at one place, not to be present or absent, not to go off to the Ethiopians for dinner and return home after twelve days. But if it were not so, all hope of help would be taken away, and it would be doubtful whether we are heard by the gods at all, when we perform the holy rites due to their sacred ceremonies. For let us suppose that for the sake of argument there is a temple of some divinity in the Canary Islands, another of the same in the farthest Thule, another among the Seres, another among the dark Garamantes, and as many others as seas, mountains, forests, and quarters of the sky separate from our knowledge. If all of them, at one time, performing their divine rites, as their own need also compels them to think, should ask something of the divinity, what good could it do them, if God did not hear the voice sent to him from every side? And would there be any distance to which the help sought by the prayer of the suppliant could not penetrate? For either he would be present in no part, if he could ever be absent anywhere; or he would be present to only a few, since he could not provide his care and attention to all, nor give ear to all alike.'"

units.la: At ista perficitur, ut aut nullus Deus opitulelur omnino, si occupatus re aliqua ad audiendas voces non qui verit advolare: aut ex audiri tantummodo uni abeant solis, nihil egerint caeteri. Quid quod nullae ex his templa, quae tholus sunt aureis, & sublimibus elata fastigiis, auctorum conscriptionibus comprobatur contegere cineres atque ossa, & functorum esse corporum sepulcuras? Nonne patet, & prompium ei, aut pro Diis immortalibus mortuos vos colere, aut inexplicabilem fieri Numinibus contumeliam, quorum delubra & templa mortuorum superlata sunt buslin? In historiaru Antiochus nono, Athenis in Minervio memorat Cecropem esse mandatum terre in templo rursus ejusdem, quod in arce Lariffae est, cüditus scribitur atq; indicatur Acrisius. Erichthonius Poladus in sano, Dairas & Immanarchus fratres in Eleusinis confecto, quod civi ciatus sub culte est. Quid Colei virgines? non in Cereris Eleusina bumatae habere perhibentur officia? non in Dianae delubro, quod in Apollinis confliciturn est Delii, Hyperocha, Laodicea, quas ad vestas illuc esse finibus ex byperboreis indicatur, in Didymaeo Milesio Chrochi dicit babuisse supremaLeandrus funeris Leucophrinae monumentu insano apud Magnesia Dianae esse, Mynn dius profitetur at memorat Zeno, sub Apollinis arula, quæ Telmessi apud oppidum visitur, Telmessumesse conditum vatem, non scriptus constantibus indicatur Agesarchi? Ptolemaeus Phi- lopator quem edidit primo, Cinyram regi Paphi cum familia omni sua, immo cum omni profanis in Veneris templo sitam esse, litterarum auctoritate declarat. Hadlenus Arnobius: qui reste sane templa Gentilium sepulchra hominum mortuorum appellat, unde Busta per contumeliam a Christianis antiquitus fuerunt appellata. Ac re vera illa nihil aliud fuerunt, quam sepulcra quaedam cadaverum foedissima & putidissima: licet auro, argento, marmore, ebore, & aliis rebus preciosis refulgerent. Plura de origine templorum ex sepulcris vide apud Gyraldum, & Plutarchum, qui inter alia Lycurgum narrat permisisse, ut mortui in urbe sepelirentur, & monumenta essent templis vicina.
units.tr: But this is so, that either no god gives help at all, if, occupied with some matter, he cannot fly swiftly to hear voices; or else he is heard only by a few, and the rest accomplish nothing. What of the fact that, according to the writings of authors, some of these temples, which are domed with gold and raised on lofty gables, cover ashes and bones and are the sepulchres of dead bodies? Is it not clear that either you worship the dead as immortal gods, or else an incredible insult is done to the divinities, whose shrines and temples are heaped over with the tombs of the dead? In the ninth book of his Histories, Antiochus records that Cecrops was buried in the temple of Minerva at Athens; and it is written and reported that Acrisius was buried again in the temple which is on the citadel of Larissa. Erichthonius of Pallas, and the brothers Dairas and Immarados, were buried in a temple in Eleusis, which is situated under the citadel. What of the Coan virgins? Are they not said to have carried out funeral duties in the temple of Ceres at Eleusis? Hyperoche and Laodice, whom the Hyperboreans are said to have sent there as offerings, are buried in the shrine of Diana, which stands in the precinct of Apollo at Delos. Chrochi says that Leander kept the highest... ; Leucophryne's funerary monument is in the temple of Diana at Magnesia; Mynnius professes it, and Zeno mentions that under the little altar of Apollo, which is seen at the town of Telmessus, the seer Agesarchus is recorded as buried at Telmessus in an inscription of reliable witnesses. The Ptolemy Philopator, whom he published first, declares on the authority of letters that Cinyras, king of Paphos, lies with his whole household, indeed with all his possessions, in the temple of Venus. Arnobius rightly calls the temples of the Gentiles the sepulchres of dead men, whence in ancient times they were called, by way of insult, tombs (busta) by the Christians. And in truth those were nothing other than sepulchres of corpses, most foul and most stinking, although they gleamed with gold, silver, marble, ivory, and other precious things. For more on the origin of temples from tombs, see Gyraldus and Plutarch, who, among other things, relates that Lycurgus permitted the dead to be buried within the city, and that the monuments should be close to the temples.

units.la: TEMPLA porro illa, ab hominibus extructa, solebant propter certas causas votoveri, consulens rei multae exempla passim in historiis reperiuntur. Quando voto erant, & id, propter quod vota erant, profiteri successerat, tum definiebantur, vel certi illius templi fines constituebantur: id quod dicebatur Effari templa, teste Varrone, vel Sistere fana. Sic enim Festus: Sistere fanum, cum in Urbe condenda dicitur, significat loca in oppido futurorum fanorum constituere. Id vero ab Auguribus fieri solitum docet Varro. Ibi ita definita essent, tum condebantur: condita dedicabantur ab iis, qui ea votiissent: tandem ab Auguribus inaugurabantur, id est, suis augurius sanctiora reddebantur. Hoc enim nisi fieret, templa esse non poterant, teste apud Agellium Varrone: sed aedes tantum dicebantur; unde discrimen inter templa & aedes sacras facile intelligitur.
units.tr: Temples built by human hands were commonly vowed for certain reasons, and many examples of this practice are found throughout the histories. When the vow had been made, and the purpose for which it was made had been declared, the temple was then marked out, or its precise boundaries were fixed. This was called effari templa (to pronounce temples), according to Varro, or sistere fana (to set up shrines). Festus explains sistere fanum: when it is said of founding a city, it means to mark out the places in the town where shrines are to be. Varro teaches that the augurs usually did this. Once the sites had been so defined, the temples were built. When built, they were dedicated by those who had made the vow. Finally, they were consecrated by the augurs, that is, made more sacred by the augural rite. Unless this was done, they could not be temples, according to Varro as reported by Aulus Gellius; they were called only aedes, shrines. From this the difference between templa and aedes sacrae is easily understood.

units.la: Verum & in hujusmodi templorum votione, definitione, & edificatione, dedicatione, inauguratione, vel etiam exauguratione, quando minimum profana reddebantur, hae obser vari consueverant, solitae circumstantiae, nempe quibus, a quibus, quo modo, quibus verbis, gestibus, ritibus atque ceremoniis ea fierent.
units.tr: Moreover, in the vowing, marking out, building, dedication, and consecration of such temples, or even in their deconsecration, when they were reduced to profane use, certain customary circumstances were observed: namely, by whom, by what means, in what words, with what gestures, rites, and ceremonies each act was performed.

units.la: Ac Romani quidem, qui, ut Prudentius contra Symmachum testatur, tot templa Deorum habuerunt, quot in urbe sepulcra Heroum numerare licuit, in bellis atque praelius plerumque cum alia, tum in primis Dius suis templa vovere solebant: id quod primum Romulum fecisse Dionysius Halicarnassensis libro primo testatur: alii Numam: Tertullianus camen in Apologetico adversus gentes, tapite vigesimo quinto post Numam demum & simulacrorum & templorum usum in Republicam illam introducturum fuisse voluit. Sic enim inquit: Nam etsi a Numa concepta est curiositas superstitiosa: nondum tamen aut simulacrum, nec templus res divina apud Romanos constabat: frugi religio, & pauperes ritus, & nulla capitolia certantia caelo, sed ceraemeraria de cespite altaria, & vasa adhuc Samia, & nidor ex illis, & Deus ipse nusquam. Non enim tunc ingenuia Graecorum atque Tuscorum fingendis simulacris inundaverant. Haec Tertullianus. Quicquid sit, illud quidem conflatum, templa esse apud Romanos primo tenuia atque parva, tamen progressu temporis suis illos votionibus, definitionibus, aliisque ceremoniis atque ritibus magnificentiora fuisse facta, innumerabilique fere numero aut a. Votionis hujus illustre exemplum extat apud Livium Decade prima libro decimo, ubi Appius Consul & Imperator bis jusmodi precationis formam Bellonae templum vovet: Bellona, si hodie nobis victoriam dus: si ego templum tibi voveo.
units.tr: The Romans, who (as Prudentius testifies against Symmachus) had as many temples of gods as the city could show tombs of heroes, used to vow temples to Dis, especially in wars and battles, along with other gods. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in book one, testifies that Romulus first did this; others say Numa. Yet Tertullian, in his Apology against the Heathen, chapter twenty-five, maintains that the use of images and temples was only introduced into that commonwealth after Numa. He says: "For although a superstitious curiosity had been conceived by Numa, nevertheless there was as yet neither image nor temple in the worship of the gods among the Romans. Their religion was simple, their rites poor, there were no Capitols vying with heaven, but hastily made altars of turf, vessels still of Samian ware, and the savour of offerings from them, and God himself nowhere. For the clever Greeks and Tuscans had not yet flooded them with the making of images." So Tertullian. Whatever the truth, it is clear that temples among the Romans were at first small and modest, but that in the course of time they were made more magnificent by vows, definitions, and other ceremonies and rites, and came to almost countless numbers. A famous example of such a vow is found in Livy, Decade one, book ten, where the consul and commander Appius vows a temple to Bellona with this form of prayer: "Bellona, if you give us victory today, I vow a temple to you."

units.la: Fuit autem hic Diis et templum vovendi mos, non in bellis tantum, sed etiam domi cum ob publicas causas, hoc est, calamitates vel praesentes, vel imminentes, tum pii vatas, ut ambitionem & alias, frequentissimus & creberrimus. Sic enim Caligula, teste Suetonio, quoniam divinus sibi vendicabat honores, ut Deus coli voluit, confitens saepe inter fratres Deos medius, ut sedatum adeuntibus exhiberet, & templum etiam Numini suo proprium, & sacerdoces, & exoquitatissimas hostias instituit. In illo templo, quod sibi voveri, & extrui curarat, simulacrum sua bat aureum iconium: amiciebaturque quotidie vestis, quali ipse uteretur: magistrum sacerdotum ditissimus quisque & ambitione & licitatione maxima victibus comparabant. Hostia enim Phoenicopteri: & quae sequuntur.
units.tr: Among the gods, the custom of vowing temples was very frequent and common, not only in wars but also at home, both for public causes, that is, present or threatened calamities, and for private ones, such as ambition and other things. Thus Caligula, according to Suetonius, since he claimed divine honours for himself and wished to be worshipped as a god, often placed himself between the statues of the gods, so that he might display himself to those approaching; and he also established a temple for his own divinity, with priests and the most exquisite victims. In that temple, which he had arranged to be vowed and built for himself, a golden image of him stood, and every day a garment such as he himself wore was put upon it. The richest men, through ambition and very great bidding, bought the office of chief priest. The victims were flamingos, and what follows.

units.la: Idem templa magna etiam religione, seu superstitione potius extruere & aedificare sunt soliti: ubi locus, situs, materia, forma religiose observabatur. Namque ad locum attinet, non omnibus omnibus Diis promiscuè omni loco ædificari templa solebant. Alias enim intra urbem quæ urbana fuerunt dicta; alias extra eam; alias in montibus; alias in foro; alias alibi, templa constituebantur. Sic, exempli gratia, Vulcani templum Romulus extra urbem condiderat, & Veneris ad portum erat conditum: Mercurii in foro: Isidis & Serapidis in emporio: Apollinis, patrisq; Liberi secundum theatrum: Herculis, in quibus civitatibus non sunt gymnasia, neq; amphitheatra, ad circum. Æsculapii quoque fanum & Cereris & Bellonæ apud Romanos fuit extra urbem; cuius quidem rationem reddit Plutarchus in quæstionibus Romanis, quæst. 47. quem vide. Plato libro 10. de Legibus, hanc legem fert de loco constituendi templa vel sacella: Ιερὰ μυλῶν ἐς ἐν οἰκίας οἰκίας ἐκ τῶν... Sacella nemo in privatis ædibus habeto. Quum alicujus animum sacrificandi studium incesserit, ad publica sacrificatarus accedito. Idem lib. 6. de Legibus, ubi de ædificiorum condendorum ratione verba facit, de loco fanorum constituendorum, sic loquitur: ... Templa circa forum struantur. Inxta hæc, Magistratuum palatia, & Curiæ, juri dicendo attributa, in quibus, velut angustissimus sanctissimus locus, jura dentur & accipiantur: partim ipsis judicibus, veluti de rebus sacris judicaturis; partim vero veluti in ipsis Curiis Deorum sint sedes & delubra. Hac de loco.
units.tr: The same people also used to erect and build temples with great religion, or rather superstition, observing carefully the place, situation, material, and form. As to place, temples were not built for all gods in every location. Some were built within the city and were called urban; others outside it; others on the hills; others in the forum; others elsewhere. So, for example, Romulus founded a temple of Vulcan outside the city; that of Venus was founded at the harbour; that of Mercury in the forum; those of Isis and Serapis in the market; those of Apollo and Father Liber beside the theatre; those of Hercules in cities which had no gymnasia or amphitheatres, near the circus. The shrines of Aesculapius, Ceres, and Bellona among the Romans were also outside the city. Plutarch gives the reason for this in his Roman Questions, question 47, which may be consulted. Plato, in book ten of the Laws, sets down this law concerning the place for establishing temples or chapels: [ἱερὰ ἐν οἰκίαις μηδενί] "Let no one have shrines in private houses. When the zeal for sacrifice has taken hold of someone, let him go to the public sacrifices." The same author, in book six of the Laws, where he speaks about the plan for building, and about the site where shrines are to be set up, says: "Let temples be built around the forum. Next to these, let the palaces of the magistrates and the courts assigned to pronouncing law be placed, in which, as in the most narrow and sacred place, judgments are given and received; partly for the judges themselves, as they are to judge matters sacred; partly so that in the courts themselves there may be seats and shrines of the gods." So much concerning place.

units.la: Quod ad situm attinet; ut plurimum templa ad Orientem solem constitui solita scribit Lucianus. Vitruvius item de templorum & sacrarum ædium situ... sed multa egregia, hanc loco convenientissima scribit lib. 1. & 3. & 4. cujus inter alia hæc sunt verba: Iovi Fulguri, & Cælo, & Soli, & Lunæ, ædificia sub divo, hypæthra, constituntur. Horum enim Deorum & specierum, & affectus in aperto Mundo atque lucenti præsentes videmus.
units.tr: As to situation, Lucian writes that temples were usually set up facing the rising sun. Vitruvius likewise writes about the position of temples and sacred buildings, and many excellent things most suited to this place, in books one, three, and four; among these are the words: "For Jupiter the Thunderer, for Heaven, Sun, and Moon, buildings are erected under the open sky, hypaethra. For we see these gods and their powers and influences present in the open and bright world."

units.la: Materia porrò templorum partim fuit lapidea, partim lignea, partim mixta. Seneca: Thalines, inquit, lapis (quondam rerum in aliquo spectaculum templo) pi-cinas nostras circundat.
units.tr: The material of temples was partly stone, partly wood, partly mixed. Seneca says: "Thaline stone, once a spectacle in a certain temple, surrounds our fish-ponds."

units.la: Formas præterea varias etiam templorū ab Antiquis descriptas reperimus. Nam Solis quidē ædem, Liberi, patris rotundā Veteres probarunt: Iovis vero templ. quod omnium rerum femina Deus pateface credebatur, tecto esse oportere ajebat Varro perforato. Aedes Vestæ, quā cum terra eandem pt abat, rotundā, ad pilæ similitudinē formabant. Cælestibus et Superis alis, a terra templa extare volebant: Inferis Deis sub terra: chthoniis et ... ribus media ponebant sepiis.
units.tr: Moreover, we find that various forms of temples were described by the ancients. The Ancients approved a round temple for the sun and for Father Liber. Varro said that the temple of Jupiter, who was believed to be the female principle of all things, ought to have an open roof. The temple of Vesta, which they regarded as the same as the earth, they shaped round, in the likeness of a ball. For the heavenly and celestial gods they wished temples to stand above the earth; for the gods below, under the earth; and for the chthonic gods they placed them in the middle, on the level ground.

units.la: Sed & de variis formis templorum & sacrarum ædium idem Vitruvius scribit loco supra citato; cujus hæc inter cætera sunt verba: Minervæ & Martis, & Herculis ædes Doricæ fient. His enim Diis propter tenerit. fine delicijs ædificia constituit docet. Veneri, Floræ, Proserpinæ, Fontium Nymphis, Corinthio genere constituta aptas videbuntur habere proprietates, quod his Diis propter teneritatem graciliora & florida, foliuq; & volutis ornata opera facta, augere videbuntur justum decorē. Innoni, Dianæ, Liberò patri cæterisq; Diis, qui eadem sunt similitudine, si ædes Ionicæ constituentur, habit a erit ratio mediocritatis, quod ab severo more Doritorū, & a teneritate Corinthiorum temperabitur earum proprietatis instituto. Hæc Vitruvius, ex quo conjici, formas templorum fuisse Doricas, Ionicas, Corinthias, aliosque genere constituas.
units.tr: But Vitruvius, in the passage cited above, also writes about the various forms of temples and sacred buildings. Among other things he says: "Temples of Minerva, Mars, and Hercules shall be built in the Doric style, for he teaches that these gods, being of a severe character, should have buildings without delicate ornament. For Venus, Flora, Proserpina, and the nymphs of the fountains, temples built in the Corinthian order will seem suitable, since for these gods, because of their tenderness, works made more slender, flowery, and adorned with leaves and volutes will seem to increase the proper grace. For Juno, Diana, Father Liber, and the other gods of similar character, if temples are built in the Ionic style, there will be a due measure, since it will be tempered by the severe manner of the Dorians and the tenderness of the Corinthians, in the arrangement of its proportions." So Vitruvius. From this it may be inferred that the forms of temples were Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and others of this kind.

units.la: Quo pertinet: quod Franciscus Polletus lib. 1. Histor. Rom. cap. 3. adnotat templa Veterum non fuisse absimilia. Constabant enim, ajit, cella sanctiore, nos Chorū vocamus, quæ cella sive formis templorum & porticibus distinguebatur Plinteo, & quasi altero pronao, nos non mali Pulpitum vocamus, quod in more pulpiti, aut tabulati erectus sit: quidā ex vulgo Threnum vocant, forte quod illic threni Ieremiæ prophetæ recitentur, & aliæ Homiliæ sacræ. Basilica vero, quam nos Navem, aut Carinā vocamus, deambulationes, quæ utrinq; sunt vestitum, quæ sunt veluti fori in Carina. Cella sanctior solū rebus sacris destinabatur. Basilica vero & porticus & pronaon ferē usibus prophanis exponebantur. Illic n. & nundinæ mercium et proxenetica contractus, prologi nnpisarū, colloquia transactionum et bodie apud nos, nimis impie, exercebantur. Hactenus Polletus: quibus adde, & certas templorum partes dum extruerentur, fuisse tom Partes templi fuisse: quarum sinistra ab Oriente, dextra ab Occidente, antica ad Meridiem, postica ad Septrionem.
units.tr: To this belongs what Francesco Pollet notes in book one of his Roman History, chapter three, that the temples of the ancients were not very unlike ours. For, he says, they consisted of a more sacred cell, which we call the choir, and this cell, or the part of the temple, was separated by a screen and a sort of second forecourt, which we call the pulpit, because it was raised like a pulpit or platform; some of the common people call it the threnus, perhaps because the Lamentations of the prophet Jeremiah and other sacred homilies were read there. The basilica, which we call the nave or keel, consisted of the walks on either side, which were like market-places along the keel. The more sacred cell was set apart for sacred things alone. But the basilica, the porticoes, and the forecourt were generally given over to profane uses. For there markets for goods, bargaining, and business dealings, the speeches of lawyers, and conversations about agreements were carried on, and even today, all too impiously, among us. So far Pollet; to these may be added that when temples were built, certain parts were also distinguished: the left side toward the east, the right toward the west, the front toward the south, and the back toward the north.

units.la: L. nem distebantur. Publius tamen Victor, sum ajt in libello de XIV. Urbis regionibus, ante Cel- lam, partem nimirum templi sacrationem, esse prodomon; post templum opisodomon, templum in tres duntaxat partes divisit, mediamque, ubi Dei esse cella, quam hodie Chorum dicunt, vocat: quae antecedit ᾱρχηδόμοι; quae sequitur ὀπισθόδομον. Vide Hadrianum Turnebum libro vigesimo secundo, capite decimo septimo.
units.tr: ...were distinguished. Publius Victor, however, in his little book on the fourteen regions of the city, says that the part of the temple before the cella, which is the consecrated area, is the prodomos; the part after the temple is the opisthodomos. He divided the temple into only three parts, and he calls the middle part, where the cella of God is, which today they call the choir, the part that precedes [ἀρχηδόμοι] and the part that follows [ὀπισθόδομον]. See Hadrianus Turnebus, book 22, chapter 17.

units.la: Vt autem in extruendis & edificandis, ita in reflaurandis & reficiendis templis summam cu- ram, magnani teligionem, varias cerimonias, atq; ritus, adhibuerunt; quos quidem uno quasi fa- miculo Cornelius Tacitus complexus est, in lustratione area templi Iovis, quod a Vespasiano tum restitutum fuerat: Vespasianus, inquit, curam restituendi Capitolii in L. Vestimum confert, equestris ordinis virum, sed auctoritate famaq; inter proceres. Abeo contracti Haruspices momuere, ut reliquiae priores delubri in paludes averterentur, templum iisdem vestigiis fulleretur, nolle Deos mutari veterem formam. Vndecimo Kalend. Iulias, serena luce, spatium omne, quod templo dicabatur, e vinculo vittis coronisq; ingressi similes, quibus fausta nomina, felicibus ramis, deinde virgines Vestales cum pueris puellisq; pastrimis matrimusq; aqua rivus & fontibus amnibusq; hausta, perluere. Tum Helvidius Priscus Praetor, praeunte Planto Eliano Pontifice, lustrata Suo vetauritibus area, & super ceptum rebus extis, Iovem, Iunonem, Minervam, Pri- dieis, Imperii Deos precatus, uti coepta prosperarent, fedesq; suas pietate hominum inchoatas, divina ope attollerent, & vittas quibus ligatus lapus, innexiq; funes erant, tonsigit. Simul ceteri Magistratus & Senatus, & Equet, & magna pars populi, studio laetitiaq; connixi, saxum ingens traxere: pasimq; injectae fundamentis argenti, auri, stipes, & metallorum primitiae nullis formacibus vitae sed ut gignuntur, Praedixere Haruspices, ne temerarentur opus saxo auro ve in aliud destinatio, &c. Hallenus Tacitus. Hu adde Horatiana illa. Horatius de re Delicta Majorum immeritus lues Dies te minorem quod geris imperat. instauratione Romane: donec templa refeceris Huc omne principum, huc reffer exitum. templorum. Aedesque labentes Deorum, & Dii multa neglecti dederunt Foeda nigro simulacra fumo Hesperiae mala luctuosa.
units.tr: In building and constructing temples, the ancients showed the same great care and deep reverence, and used various ceremonies and rites in restoring and repairing them. Cornelius Tacitus gathers these, as it were, into one bundle, in his account of the purification of the area of the temple of Jupiter, which Vespasian had then restored. "Vespasian," he says, "entrusted the task of rebuilding the Capitol to Lutatius Vestinus, a man of the equestrian order, but one who stood among the nobles in authority and reputation. Then the haruspices, who had been summoned, advised that the former remains of the shrine be carried away into the marshes, that the temple be built on the same foundations, and that the gods did not want the old form changed. On the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in clear light, the whole space that was to be dedicated to the temple was entered by men wearing fillets and garlands, like those who bore lucky names on fortunate branches. Then the Vestal virgins, with boys and girls whose fathers and mothers were still living, sprinkled it with water drawn from springs, rivers and streams. Then Helvidius Priscus, the praetor, with Plautius Aelianus, the pontiff, going before him, purified the area with the sacrificial victims, and, having offered the entrails over the work begun, he prayed to Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, the Penates and the gods of the empire, that they would make the undertakings prosper and, with divine help, raise the foundations begun by human piety. He also cut the fillets with which the stone was bound and the ropes that were tied to it. At the same time the other magistrates, the senate, the knights and a great part of the people, eager and joyful, strained together and dragged a huge stone. Gold and silver, and first-fruits of metals, not melted down but as they are found in nature, were thrown into the foundations. The haruspices had declared in advance that the work must not be defiled by changing the destination of the stone, gold or silver," and so on. So far Tacitus. Add to this the Horatian lines on the restoration of the temples: "Because of the neglect of the temples and the ruined shrines of the gods, you suffer punishment, Rome, and bear the evils of this age, though you are less than your ancestors. Until you restore the temples, all the misfortunes of the princes will return upon you." Also: "The gods, neglected, have given Hesperia its dire evils, and their images are foul with black smoke."

units.la: Tanta apud Gentiles fuit templorum reneratio, ut eorum ruinas quoq; atque rudera coluerint, ut ex his Seneca verbis apparet: Non magis contemnitur Papiens, cum jacuit, quam cum sacrarum edium ruinae calcantur, quas religio fique at flantes adorant.
units.tr: Among the Gentiles, the restoration of temples was held in such high regard that they even honoured their ruins and rubble. Seneca's words show this: "Pavia is not held in less contempt when it lies in ruins than when the ruins of sacred buildings are trampled, which people revere and worship with religious feeling."

units.la: Haec de aedificatione & reflauratione templorum. Audiamus illorum porro dedicationem fine consecrationem & inauguratoriam. Hanc praesertim apud Romanos magno in pretio fuisse, colligitur non tantum ex eo, quod templi primum Romae Iovi Feretrio, a Romulo, urbis regni conditore, dedicatum teste est Livius Decade prima, libro primo: sed etiam ex illa M. Horatii Pulvilli atque Valerii Publicolae Coss. historia id confitat, de quaecum Livius lib. 2. Dec. 1. Non- dum dedicata erat in Capitolio Iovis aedis. Valerius Horatiusq; Coss. sortiti, uter dedicaret, Horatio forte evenit. Publicola ad Veientinum bellum profectus. Aegrius quam dignum erat, tulere Valerii necessarii, dedicationem tam incleci templi Horatio dari: id omnibus modis impedire conati, postquam alia frustra tentata erant, postiam jam tenenti Coss. focum inter precationem Deum nuncium incutiunt; mortuum ejus filii esse, funestaq; familiā dicare eum templum non posse. Non trediderit factum, an tamen roborus fuerit, nec traditur certum, sed interpre- tatio facilis est: nihil aliud ad eum nuntium a proposito a verfius, quam ut cada ver offerri juberet, teneret postem, precationem peragaret, & templum dedicaret. Hec Livius: sibi inter alia mentionem facit postis, quem is, qui dederat, manu tenebat, de quo & Cicero pro Domo sua: Po- rit, inquit, cui postem tenenti, & Capitolium dedicanti mors filii nuntiata est, quam ille exaudi- se dissimulans & solennia Pontificalis tarminis verba (Nota, quia certe verbis a Pontifice dedicari solebant fana, inde videntur a fando dicta, sese Festo) concepit gemitu non interrumpente precationem, & ad filii sui nomen Iovi propriato, putaret ejus luctus aliquem finem esse debere, cujus primus dies primus impetus ab altaribus publicis et fausta nuncupatione nō abduxit patri; dignus me hercule memorabili dedicatione, dignus amplissi sacerdotio, qui colere deos, ne irritas qui dem defluxit. Idem tamen ut rediit domi, implevit oculos, et aliquas voces flebiles emisit, & peraltis, que moseratpraestare defunctis, ad Capitolium hilari redit vultu. De hoc Horatio Pul-villo videtiam Dionysium Halicarnasseum, & Valerium lib.5.cap.10.
units.tr: So much for the building and restoration of temples. Let us now consider their dedication, or consecration, and the rite of inauguration. That this was held in great esteem among the Romans is shown not only by the fact that the first temple at Rome, to Jupiter Feretrius, was dedicated by Romulus, the founder of the city and kingdom, as Livy witnesses in the first book of the first decade. It is also confirmed by the story of the consuls Marcus Horatius Pulvillus and Valerius Publicola, which Livy tells in book 2 of the first decade: "The temple of Jupiter on the Capitol had not yet been dedicated. The consuls Valerius and Horatius cast lots to see which of them should dedicate it, and the lot fell to Horatius. Publicola had set out for the war against Veii. The relatives of the Valerii took it badly, and more bitterly than was right, that the dedication of so famous a temple should be given to Horatius. They tried to prevent it by every means, and when other attempts had failed, they broke in on the consul, who was holding the doorpost while praying, with a messenger who announced that his son was dead, and that a house in mourning could not dedicate the temple. Whether the thing was reported falsely or whether it was true is not recorded, but the interpretation is easy: the message had no effect on his plan, except that he ordered the corpse to be carried out, kept his hand on the doorpost, finished the prayer, and dedicated the temple." So Livy. He mentions the doorpost, which the man who was dedicating held with his hand; Cicero also speaks of it in his speech For His House: "Horatius, he says, when the death of his son was announced to him while he was holding the doorpost and dedicating the Capitol, pretended not to hear it, and, with the solemn words of the pontifical formula (note that temples were regularly dedicated by the pontiff's words, whence they are thought to be named from fari, to speak, as Festus says), he continued without interrupting the prayer, and, addressing Jupiter by his son's name, he showed that his grief must have some limit, since its first day did not draw him away from the public altars or from the lucky proclamation of the name. He was worthy, by Hercules, of a memorable dedication and of the highest priesthood, since he did not lose his prayers even in the moment of grief. Yet when he returned home he filled his eyes with tears, uttered some mournful words, and performed the funeral rites that custom requires for the dead, and then returned to the Capitol with a cheerful face." On this Horatius Pulvillus, see also Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and Valerius Maximus, book 5, chapter 10.

units.la: Sic, ut idem Liuius scribit Decade primâ, libro quarto, cùm Cn.Iulius Consul eàdem Apollinis, absente collega sine fede dedicasset, aegré id passus Quintius, cùm dimisso exercitu in urbem redisset, nequicquam in senatu est conquestus.
units.tr: So too, as Livy writes in the first decade, book 4, when Gnaeus Julius the consul dedicated a temple of Apollo in the absence of his colleague, without the authority of the senate, Quinctius took it badly. When he had disbanded his army and returned to the city, he complained about it in the senate, but to no effect.

units.la: Non licebat autem cuiuis antiquitus templa dedicare, sed Consulibus tantùm & Imperatoribus: item Decemuiris, & Censoribus, & aliis hujusmodi: cuius rei testis est illa Historia Cn. Flacci, quam idem Liuius Decade primâ libro nono enumerat. Is enim scribat, patre libertino, humilifortuna ortus, & aedilis curulis aedem Concordiae in area Vulcani summâ in uidià Nobilium dedicauit, coactus, consensu Populi Cornelius Pontifex mox verba praire, cùmmore Majorum negaret, nisi Cons. aut Imperatorem posse templum dedicare. Itaque ex auctoritate Senatus latum ad Populum est, Ne quis templum aràmve injussu Senatus, aut Trib. plebis partes majores dedicaret. Illa Lex lata fuit a Q.Papirio, Trib.pl. quae idcirco Papyria fuit appellata. Ejus fit mentio apud Ciceronem, in oratione pro Domo sua: Video enim, inquit, eam legem veterem Tribunicia, quae veteri injussu plebis aedes, terram, aramve consecrare: neq; tum hoc ille Q. Papirius, qui hanc legem rogavit, sensit, &c. Et paullo post: Lex Papyria vetat, aedes injussu plebis consecrari. Idem pro Domo sua: Cùm Licinia, inquit, virgo Vestalis, summo loco nata, sanctissimo sacerdotio prædita, T. Flaminio, Q. Metello Cons. aram, & ædiculam & pulvinar sub saxo saero dedicasset, non eam rem ex auctoritate Senatus, ad hoc collegium Sextus Iulius Praetor retulit. Tum P. Scaevola, Pontifex Maximus, pro Collegio respondit, quid in loco publico Licinia C. F. injussu Populi dedicasset, sacrum non videri.
units.tr: In ancient times it was not permitted to anyone at all to dedicate temples, but only to consuls and commanders, and likewise to the decemvirs, censors and others of this kind. The story of Gnaeus Flavius, which Livy lists in the first decade, book 9, bears witness to this. He was the son of a freedman, of low fortune, and as curule aedile he dedicated the temple of Concord in the area of Vulcan, against the highest wishes of the nobles. Compelled by the consent of the people, Cornelius the pontiff then began to recite the words, though he complained that according to the custom of their ancestors only a consul or commander could dedicate a temple. Therefore, by the authority of the senate, a proposal was brought before the people that no one should dedicate a temple or altar without the order of the senate or of the tribunes of the plebs, the greater tribunes. This law was proposed by Quintus Papirius, tribune of the plebs, and for that reason it was called the Papirian law. Cicero mentions it in his speech For His House: "For I see," he says, "that the old law of the tribunes, which forbids anyone to consecrate a house, land or altar without the order of the people, is ancient; yet Quintus Papirius, who proposed this law, did not perceive this, etc." And a little later: "The Papirian law forbids a house to be consecrated without the order of the people." Also in the same speech: "When the Vestal virgin Licinia, born of the highest rank and endowed with the most holy priesthood, dedicated an altar, a little shrine and a couch under a sacred rock in the time of the consuls Titus Flaminius and Quintus Metellus, the praetor Sextus Julius did not refer the matter to this college on the authority of the senate. Then Publius Scaevola, the chief pontiff, replied on behalf of the college that a sacred rite was not seen to have been performed when Licinia, daughter of Gaius, dedicated something in a public place without the order of the people."

units.la: Praeterea ille, qui dedicare volebat, prius ad sacerdotem publicorum atq; Pontificum colle-gium referre id cogebatur. Sic enim Cicero pro Domo sua inquit, Classum censorem de signo Con-cordiae dedicando ad Pontificum collegium retulìsse, eiq; M. Emilium Pontificem Maximum pro collegio respondisse, nsi eam Populus Romanus nominatim praefecisset, atq; ejus jussu faceret, non videri, si ea rite posse dedicari. Idem: Atq; ille tamen C. Quintius Martius Censor ad collegium retulit: cu ad quem retulìsti? Si quid deliberares, si quid tibi aut piandum, aut instituendum fuisse religione domestica, tamen instituo caeterorum ad Pontificem deducisses: Novum debrum cum in urbis clarissimo loco, nesando quodam atq; inaudito instituto inchoares, referendum ad sacerdotes publicos non putasti? Ec si collegium Pontificum adhibendum non vide-bar, nonne horum tibi idoneus vĭsus est, qui etate, honore, auctoritate, antecellunt, ut cum eo dedicationem communicares? Hinc ergo colligimus, non licuisse injussu Populi & inscio sacerdotum collegio, cuiquam templum aut aram, aut quid vis aliud dedicare.
units.tr: Moreover, the man who wished to dedicate a temple was first compelled to refer the matter to the public priests and the college of pontiffs. Cicero says so in For His House: "The censor Crassus had referred the dedication of the statue of Concord to the college of pontiffs, and Marcus Aemilius, the chief pontiff, replied on behalf of the college that it could not be properly dedicated unless the Roman people had named him expressly and he acted by their order." And again: "Yet Gaius Quinctius Martius, the censor, referred it to the college. To whom did you refer it? If you were in doubt about something, or if something had to be atoned for or established by domestic religion, you would still have consulted the pontiff. When you began a new shrine in the most famous place in the city, by a strange and unheard-of plan, did you not think it should be referred to the public priests? And if you thought the college of pontiffs need not be called in, was it not fitting for you to take as partners in the dedication those who excel in age, honour and authority?" From this we conclude that it was not permitted for anyone to dedicate a temple, an altar, or anything else at all without the order of the people and without the knowledge of the college of priests.

units.la: Is porrò, qui dedicare volebat vel totum collegium ad Pontifices, vel unum aut alterum Pontificum adesse jubebat, qui ei verba praeirent: cujus quidem ad vocationis Cicero pro Domo sua hujusmodi formam praescribit: Ades, ades, Luculle, Servili, dum dedico domum Ciceronis, ut mihi praeatis, postemq; vocaris.
units.tr: Moreover, whoever wished to dedicate a building either summoned the whole college of Pontiffs, or ordered one or two of the Pontiffs to attend and dictate the words to him. For this summons Cicero, in his speech On His House, gives the following form: "Come, come, Lucullus, Servilius, while I dedicate Cicero's house, so that you may go before me and be called upon."

units.la: Dedicationis autem hujusmodi forma bisce feré ritibus atque cerimoniis constabat: Omne spatium, quod erat templo dicatum, coronis atq; vittis vinciebatur: idem cùm a populo felicibus ramis, tum a virginibus Vestalibus aqua perluebatur. Is, qui dedicabat, postem tempii, quì, ut inquit Cicero, ibi est, ubi aditus templi, & velvae ambulationi sunt, manu sua tenebat, certa quaedam atque solennia verba, sive precationem, praeunte aliquo Pontifice, effabatur (unde idem de Legibus, Templa liberata & effata habento:) Area item certis sacrificiis lustrabatur, exta super cessuem reddebantur, vittae, quibus ligatur lapis, inuexique funes erant, a dedicante contingebantur: populus etiam uniuersus saxum primum tangebat, fundamenta certas res, ut auri & argenti stipes injiciebant, simulacrum Dii aut Deae illius, cui templum dedicabatur, saepe quoque alunde translatum, ut de Iunonis simulacro Veiis, Romam advecto, Liuius scribit Decade primâ, libro quinto: in templo ipsum quoque prius unctione dedicatum, unâ cum ara & pulvinari collocabatur. Haec ex Liuio, Cicerone, Cornelio Tacito, & aliis colligere licet, quos quidem ritus omnes atque cerimonias videre licet in Capitolii restauratione apud Tacitum eo loco, quem supra citavi.
units.tr: The form of dedication consisted of the following rites and ceremonies. The whole space given to the temple was wreathed with garlands and fillets. It was sprinkled with water, first by the people with branches of good omen and then by the Vestal Virgins. The one dedicating held in his hand the doorpost of the temple, which, as Cicero says, is where the entrance of the temple and the passage to the vestibule are, and he spoke certain set and solemn words, or a prayer, with a Pontiff leading the words (whence the same writer in On the Laws says, "Let temples be freed and consecrated"). Likewise the site was purified with certain sacrifices, the entrails were offered over the pyre, and the fillets with which the stone was bound and the ropes that had been drawn up were touched by the dedicator. The whole people first touched the stone, and they threw into the foundations certain valuable things, such as contributions of gold and silver. An image of that god or goddess to whom the temple was dedicated was often also brought in from elsewhere, as Livy writes in the fifth book of the first Decade about the statue of Juno brought to Rome from Veii. In the temple, the image, first anointed and dedicated, was placed together with the altar and the couch. These matters may be gathered from Livy, Cicero, Cornelius Tacitus and others, and all these rites and ceremonies may be seen in Tacitus' account of the restoration of the Capitol, in the passage I cited above.

units.la: {a} Inauguratio tē plorum non cuiuslibet olim coa-cessa.
units.tr: {a} The inauguration of temples was formerly not granted to just anyone.

units.la: Præter hanc dedicationem, consecrationem, nuncupationem, initiationem, & inauurationem templorum Liuius meminit etiam exauurationes, quas Veteres templa sua suis augurijs prosana reddere consueuerunt. Sic enim libro primo ab Vrbe condita scribit: Et ut libera a cæteris religionibus area esset tota Iouis templumque ejus, quod incœpt dificaretur, exauguraræ fana, sacellaque statuit, quæ atque ibi a Tatio Rege ꝑ sumum in ipso dis crimine ad versus Romulum pugnæ vota, consecrata, inauguratáque posset fuerant, inter principia condendi bujus operis monuisse Numina ad indicandum tanti impetu molem traditur Deos. Nam cum omnium sacellorum exaugurationes admitterentur a Vestalibus Terni fano non addixerunt.
units.tr: Besides this dedication, consecration, nuncupation, initiation and inauguration of temples, Livy also mentions exauguration, by which the ancients customarily made their temples profane through their augury. For he writes thus in the first book from the founding of the city: "And so that the whole area of Jupiter and his temple, which was being begun, might be free from other cults, he decreed that the shrines and chapels which Tatius the king had vowed, consecrated and inaugurated there in the battle against Romulus should be exauguried." It is said that, at the very beginning of this work, the gods warned that such a great structure would be started under a sign of the highest omen. For although exauguration of all the shrines was permitted by the Vestals, the shrine of Terminus would not yield.

units.la: Sed & ut templa magni religione suis superstitione, extrui & edificari, dedicari & inaugurari: ita ornari, cultodiri, sarta, tecta, pura atque munda conseruari, pollutaq; denique expiari consueuerunt. Ornamentorum, monimentorum & eorum, quæ in templis Diis dicata taponi, ex thoris, aut parietibus, aut etiam columnis affigi, & suspendi solebant, varia ac multiplicia fuerunt: quæ Græci ἀναθήματα, & ἀναθέματα. Latini donaria, aliisque nominibus appellarunt. Hinc illæ apud Demosthenem loquendi formæ: κατασκευάζειν καλλιστα ἱερὰ ... ꝑ parare ornamenta templorum: ἀναθῆναι ... consecrare donaria: πολυτελῶν τῶν ἀνα-θήματων, bellum inferre religioni. Macrobius: Ornamenta verò sunt, unquitè, clypei, corona & buiusmodi donaria: quæ vox tamen nonnunquam pro loco ponitur, in quo dona reponuntur, & pro ipso etiam templo, sicut supra de Sacrario dictum fuit. Hinc Virgilius lib.3. Georgicorum: Tem-pore non alio dictus regionibus illis Quæsitas ad sacra boves Iunonis & uris Imaribus dutos alta ad donaria currus.
units.tr: But just as they built, constructed, dedicated and inaugurated temples with religious scruple and superstition, so they also customarily adorned them, guarded them, and kept them intact, roofed, pure and clean, and finally purified them when they were polluted. The ornaments and memorials dedicated to the gods in temples, which were hung or fixed on the doors, walls or even the columns, were many and varied. The Greeks called them anathemata and anathemata, the Latins donaria, and they had other names as well. Hence those expressions in Demosthenes: to furnish the temples most beautifully [κατασκευάζειν καλλιστα ἱερὰ], to dedicate offerings [ἀναθῆναι], and of costly offerings [πολυτελῶν τῶν ἀναθημάτων]; that is, to make war on religion. Macrobius says: "Ornaments, to speak strictly, are shields, crowns and such offerings; yet this word is sometimes used for the place where the gifts are set, and even for the temple itself, as was said above of the sanctuary." Hence Virgil in the third book of the Georgics: "At no other time were oxen sought for sacred rites in those regions, and the cars drawn by bulls were brought to the high offering-places of Juno."

units.la: Gellius libro secundo, cap. 1. decimo: Vt repom solerem signa vetera, quæ ex eo templo collassent, & alia quædam religiosa Donaris consecrata. Apuleius: Ibi donarium Dea pero-pulentum, plurima aurea & argentea ratio in lanctibus, sphœculis, poculis, & buiusmodi utensilibus.
units.tr: Gellius, in the second book, chapter 10: "When I was accustomed to restore the old statues which had fallen from that temple, and certain other sacred things consecrated as offerings..." Apuleius: "There the goddess had a treasury very rich, with very many golden and silver vessels, in the form of lamps, mirrors, cups and such utensils."

units.la: Inter hæc autem ornamenta & monimenta (Livius quoque annalis reponitur, qui, te-ste Flo, figebatur in parietibus sacrorum ædium per annos singulos, ut per eos numerus colligere-tur annorum. Eodem pertinent cerui iun cornua, quæ in Diana templo solebant affigere: ut Plutarchus in quæstionibus Romanis quæstione quarta quæritur, cur in ejusdem Dea templo, quo-niam Aventino, non ferrorum, sed suum cornu affixerint. Ad eadem vero Iovis Feretrii, ma spolia poni solebant, testimonio sunt libri Pontificales, inquit Festus: quanquam in templa ex ferri non vult Plato arma, bellis capta a crtibus ejus, quam instituit, civitatis. Sic enim ille in de Legibus: Οὐ ... ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀνάθηματα ... Nec verò arma in templa transferemus, ea Deo dedicaturi præsertim Græcorum arma, si nul modo cure est beni volentiá colere cum cæteris Græcis maximè verò formidabimus, nec scelus inexpiabile proprio et domestico usu ad res sacras transferre bujusmodi res: nisi quid deme aliquid ediderit. Aedilis deinde hoc erat apud Romanos munus atque officium commune, ut templa sarta, tecta, pura atque munda conservarent, quæ Aedituri vocabantur, Græcè Νεωκόροι, ... est ac nostrum, ornare, instruere, addere specie pulchritudinis. Eius: Aedituus, mittit ditus est magistratus, qui ædui non tantum sacrarum, sed etiam privatarum curam rebat. Aedituus, sacræ ædis tuitor, sive tutor, id est, curam gerens, & Ædituus ædis intus.
units.tr: Among these ornaments and memorials was also placed the Annales of the Pontiff Livy, which, according to Florus, was fixed to the walls of the sacred buildings year by year, so that the number of years might be gathered from them. To the same category belong the horns of stags, which they used to fix in the temple of Diana. Plutarch, in his Roman Questions, question four, asks why, in the temple of this goddess on the Aventine, they fixed not the horns of wild beasts but those of tame cattle. To the same purpose, the spoils that used to be placed in the temple of Jupiter Feretrius are attested by the Pontifical books, says Festus. Yet Plato does not wish arms captured from enemies to be placed in temples in the state he founded. For he says in the Laws: "[But] the offerings ... Nor shall we carry arms into temples, especially Greek arms, if we are at all concerned to worship well together with the other Greeks; and we shall greatly fear to transfer to sacred use, for private and domestic purposes, things of this kind, an unexpiable crime, unless some god should clearly indicate otherwise." Next, it was a common office and duty among the Romans of the aedile that they should keep the temples intact, roofed, pure and clean. Those who did this were called aedituri, in Greek neokoroi ... and, as with us, to adorn, equip and add beauty. From Eius: the aedituus is a magistrate who had charge not only of sacred but also of private buildings. Aedituus is the guardian or keeper of a sacred building, that is, one who takes care of it, and the aedituus is the one within the building.

units.la: Deniq; templa quoq; vel claudendi vel aperiendi certa ob ser vabatur ratio. Hinc Ianus templorum illo sedebat. Ille Belli portæ dicebantur, quas Virgilius in 7. Æneid. ita describit: Sunt geminæ belli portæ (sic nomine dicunt) Religione sacræ & sævi formidine Martis.
units.tr: Finally, there was a fixed rule for closing or opening temples. Hence Janus was seated in the temples. Those gates were called the gates of war, which Virgil in the seventh book of the Aeneid describes thus: "There are twin gates of war (so they are named), sacred through religion and the dread of cruel Mars."

units.la: Dum igitur bellum durabat, portæ aperiuntur patebant: quo confestò statim clauderentur. Hoc Numa instituit a posteris sancte religioseque semper servatum fuit, quemadmodum Plutarchus refert. Quare Ianus pacem bellumque in manibus habere dictus est, ut de sejo apud O-ma. dium primo Fastorum praedicat. Et hæc de vuluarum aperiendarum atque laudendarum ritu, quia in templo Iani observabatur. Hinc Ianus Patulejus atque Clusius ab aperiendis claudendique portis vel pacis, vel belli tempore dictus. Cur vero Horta templum semper manseritiapertum, rationem reddit Plutarchus in quaestionibus Romanis, quaestione quadragesima sexta. Certum porro diebus aperiebatur Pennis, locus in ade Vestae intimus: quiquidem dies religiosi habebantur, festo Festo. Templorum item aditus et accessus quibusdam patebat: alius non. Unde apud Rhodios cur in Geridionis sacellum non ingrediebatur praeco, rationem reddit Plutarchus in quaestionibus Graecis, quaestione vigesima septima.
units.tr: So while war lasted, the gates stood open; as soon as it ended, they were immediately closed. Numa instituted this, and it was always observed by posterity with reverence and religion, as Plutarch reports. Hence Janus is said to hold peace and war in his hands, as Ovid declares in the first book of the Fasti. And so much for the rite of opening and closing the doors, which was observed in the temple of Janus. Hence Janus was called Patulcius and Clusius from opening and closing the gates in time of peace or war. Why the temple of Hora always stood open, Plutarch gives the reason in his Roman Questions, question forty-six. Certainly, on certain days the innermost place in the temple of Vesta was opened, and these days were held to be religious, a festival. Likewise, access to and entry into some temples was open, but not to others. Hence, among the Rhodians, why the herald did not enter the shrine of Geridion, Plutarch gives the reason in his Greek Questions, question twenty-seven.

units.la: Hac de templis: quae ab usu sanctâ, sacra, sacrosanctâ, sacrata, augusta, religiosa, impollura, tui Templorum ta, mystica, votiva, opima, pinguia, venerabilia: a vetustate antiqua, vetusta: a quantitate grandia, immania, excelsa, alta, sublimia, spaciosa, ardua, ampla: a pretio magnifica, operosa, laquearia, marmorea, eburnea, aurata, lucida, fulgentia, pretiosa, conspicua, aliisque nominibus fuerunt suncupata.
