Plinius, ut hoc colophonus loco addam, arbores scribit fuisse olim Numinum templa, et harum quidem genera sis dicata fuerunt. Verbailliius haec sunt libro duodecimo, capite primo: Arbores fuere Numinum templa, prisocque ritu ut simplicia rura, etiam nunc Deo praecellentem arborem dicant. Nec magis auro fulgentia atque ebore simulacra, quam lucos et in eis silentia ipsa adoramus. Arborum genera Numinibus suis dicata perpetuo servantur, ut Iovi aesculus, Apollini laurus, Minervae olea, Veneri myrtus, Herculi populus. Quin et Sylvanos Faunosque, et Deorum genera sylvis, ac sua Numina, tanquam e caelo attributa, credimus. Hactenus Plinius.
units.tr: Concerning temples so far. They have been called by many names: from use, holy, sacred, sacrosanct, consecrated, august, religious, unpolluted, mystical, votive, opulent, fat, venerable; from age, ancient, old; from size, great, huge, lofty, high, sublime, spacious, steep, ample; from value, magnificent, elaborate, panelled, of marble, of ivory, gilded, bright, gleaming, precious, conspicuous, and by other names. Pliny, to add this as a kind of supplement at this point, writes that trees were formerly the temples of the gods, and that certain kinds of trees were dedicated to them. His words in the twelfth book, first chapter, are these: "Trees were once the temples of the gods, and in the ancient manner, like simple country folk, people still call a tree that stands before a god sacred. We adore groves, and the very silence within them, no less than statues shining with gold and ivory. Kinds of trees dedicated to their gods are kept forever: the oak to Jupiter, the laurel to Apollo, the olive to Minerva, the myrtle to Venus, the poplar to Hercules. Indeed we also believe that Silvanus and the Fauns, and the kinds of divinities in the woods, with their own powers, are assigned as it were from heaven." So far Pliny.

units.la: POST TEMPLA videtur de aris, sive altaribus scribendum, quae quidem templorum De Aris vel fuerunt ornamenta, sacrificiorumque loca magis propria, atque adeo Satrorum praetipua fere altaribus. instrumenta. Exordiemur autem, pro more nostro, ab eorum nominibus.
units.tr: After the temples, it seems one should write about altars, which were indeed ornaments of temples and the places most proper to sacrifice, and in fact the chief instruments of sacrifice. I shall begin, as is my custom, with their names.

units.la: ARA, Hebraice dicta est מזבח Mizbach et זבח Zabách, sacrificandi, nimirum ab usu ejus primario: cui respondet vox Graeca θυσιαστήριον, quasi dicas in Hebraea et sacrificatorium, hoc est, instrumentum sacrificiale, sive locus, in quo sacrificatur: Chaldaicè dicitur אגר Agar, ab אגר Agar, necessitate conduxit, collegit, congregavit: quae vox etiam Chaldaea, aedificium validum et cumulum significat. Sic forsan dicta, quod inde sacerdotes mercem suam colligebant, tanquam mercenarii: vel quod erant aedificia altè extructa et bene communita atque munita.
units.tr: The altar (ARA) is called in Hebrew מזבח Mizbach and זבח Zabách, for sacrificing, plainly from its chief use. To this corresponds the Greek word θυσιαστήριον, as if you were to say a place of sacrifice, that is, a sacrificial instrument, or the place where sacrifice is made. In Chaldee it is called אגר Agar, from אגר Agar, meaning he hired, gathered, or assembled by necessity. This word in Chaldee also means a strong building and a heap. It may perhaps be so called because the priests gathered their wages from it, like hired workers, or because the altars were lofty structures, well fortified and secured.

units.la: Graeci multa habent nomina, quibus Aram exprimunt; inter quae duo sunt maxime communia, nempe θυσιαστήριον, sive Poëticè θυτήριον apud Aratum, et βωμός. Θυσιαστήριον, altare, dicunt a θυσία ἕστι, sacrificando, sive sacrificii, uti supra dictum est, ab usu nimirum: cui respondet vox Hebraica מזבח Mizbeach, unde etiam θυμίαμα dicitur, ἀπὸ τὸ θύειν quia vox sacrificium significat, ad sacrificium adhiberi solitam. Graeca. Arum nomina
units.tr: The Greeks have many names by which they express the altar. Among them two are most common: θυσιαστήριον, or poetically θυτήριον in Aratus, and βωμός. They call θυσιαστήριον, altar, from θυσία, sacrifice, that is, from sacrificing, as said above, plainly from its use. To this corresponds the Hebrew word מזבח Mizbeach, whence it is also called θυμίαμα, from θύειν, because the word means sacrifice, and it was commonly used for sacrifice. Greek names of altars

units.la: Alterum nomen est βωμὸς, quod βαίνω etiam significat et locum, ubi currus reponuntur. 2. Βωμὸς, Homerus: Ἀρμα ἐπὶ ἂν ὅ τ’ ἔτ’ ἔτ’ ἐμπίσει τιθέι, ἑτ. Sic autem dicitur à βῶ, quod pascere et vadere significat; vel quod inde vitilitarent atque pascerentur, quod et in ... Unde Suidas Βωμός: ἐκ τοῦ ἀναβαίνειν... ἐπ’ ἀλλήλ ἑστίνει, delubrum, sive nemus sacrum, et locus ascensum habens, ad dicendum aptus, ut inde quis facile exaudiri possit.
units.tr: The other name is βωμὸς, which also signifies βαίνω, and a place where chariots are put away. (2) βωμὸς, in Homer: a chariot upon which... The word is derived from βῶ, which means to feed and to go; or because from it victims were fed and fattened, which also in ... Whence Suidas, Βωμός: from ascending... one upon another; it signifies a shrine or sacred grove, and a place with an ascent, fit for speaking, so that one may be easily heard from it.

units.la: Sed mihi potius vox Graeca βωμὸς videtur derivata ab Hebraea et Chaldaea בית Bamàh, vel במה Bamathà, quae vox Excelsa, et Altaria edita excelsa, in locis extructa significat, et in sacris literis frequenter occurrit. Unde Rabbi David Kimchi in tertiu Regum, caput tertium, scribit Moysem altare aeneum in Excelsis aedificasse, in quo sacrificia Deo sint facta, antequam templum esset extructum. Hinc Gentes κωρολίκια quadam similiter fana atque altaria Diis suis in omni colle, et sub quovis ligno frondosò caepisse erigere. Aliquando etiam vox במה Bamoth, fumiter pro columnis et gradibus quibusdam, in quibus lex recitabatur: et במה Bimàh, suggestum, tribunal (unde Graecum βῆμα) quod editio in loco constitui solet: et במוס Bimus, idem quod lapis incisus, id est, altare, idolo in Excelsis dedicatum significat.
units.tr: But to me the Greek βωμὸς seems rather derived from the Hebrew and Chaldee בית Bamàh, or במה Bamathà, a word which means high places, and lofty altars set up on heights, and it occurs frequently in the sacred letters. Hence Rabbi David Kimchi, on 1 Kings chapter 3, writes that Moses built a bronze altar on the high places, on which sacrifices were made to God before the temple was built. Hence the Gentiles similarly began to set up shrines and altars to their gods on every hill and under every leafy tree. Sometimes also the word במה Bamoth is taken for pillars and certain steps on which the law was read; and במה Bimàh means a platform or tribunal (whence the Greek βῆμα), which is usually set up in a place of assembly; and במוס Bimus, the same as a hewn stone, that is, an altar dedicated to an idol on high places.

units.la: Hinc igitur vox Graeca βωμὸς est deducta: quae ab usu suo θυσίας ab Hesiodo dicta, à sacris βωμὸς θυσὶς
units.tr: From this, then, the Greek word βωμὸς is derived. From its use in sacrifices it is called by Hesiod... from the sacred rites, βωμὸς θυσίς.

units.la: L. 3 videlicet, quae in altari fierent, vel suffimentis, quae in eo adolerentur: Latini sacrificium, fumi- dam & fumosum simili loquendi genere aram appellarunt. Eandem ob causam Hesychius μὸς appellavit θυοδόχες, id est, τὰ θυμιώμενα ἀγγεῖα, suffimentorum receptrices. Hinc Demosthenes: Βωμοὶ καὶ πύρ, ἐπὶ πανταχοῦ τοῖς θεοῖς ... Deorum in omnibus urbibus. Item: ... ab eodem dicuntur. Item: ... propositae. Sic ἀγεῖν, ἀπὸ βωμοῦ ... & ... ferre ab ara, idem dixit: quemadmodum Isocrates ... χάριτες, excruere aram gratiae.
units.tr: That is, the things done on the altar, or the incense burned upon it; the Latins called the altar by a similar figure of speech, "smoking" and "smoky." For the same reason Hesychius called the altar θυοδόχος, that is, the vessels for burning incense, the receptacles of incense. Hence Demosthenes: altars and fire, everywhere for the gods... of the gods in all cities. Likewise: ... are named from the same. Likewise: ... set forth. So also ἀγεῖν, from the altar... and ... to bring from the altar, he said the same thing; just as Isocrates... the Graces, to raise an altar of grace.

units.la: Ἀπὸ τοῦ βωμοῦ, id est, ab ara, dictum, diminutivum, apud Herodotum: & Ἐωμάς, locus aut conterratio aræ: ... aras sacra peragit: item Ἐωμεῖς, altareus, ad altare pertinens. Hinc ab Euripide Ἐωμοποιΐα ... Ἐωμοποίος ... ara accipitur. & Ἐωμολόγια, sive Ἐωμολογία, conjicium: & Ἐωμολογεῖσθαι conjiciari: forsan, quia plerumque ... Ἐωμοζεῖν, ad aras sacrificare, & ἐωμοξεῖν ... cui ara cum alio communis est.
units.tr: Named from τοῦ βωμοῦ, that is, from the altar, as a diminutive in Herodotus; and Ἐωμάς, a place or sprinkling of the altar: ... performs the sacred rites at the altar; likewise Ἐωμεῖς, of the altar, belonging to the altar. Hence in Euripides Ἐωμοποιΐα... Ἐωμοποίος... the altar is understood. And Ἐωμολόγια, or Ἐωμολογία, a conjecture; and Ἐωμολογεῖσθαι, to be conjectured; perhaps because for the most part... Ἐωμοζεῖν, to sacrifice at altars, and ἐωμοξεῖν... with which the altar is shared with another.

units.la: Porro Ἐωμοῖ, ... Porphyrio Philosopho sic distinguuntur: Ἐωμοί, id est, aras, inquit, & templa statuebant Diis caelestibus: Chthonius autem, id est, cerrestribus & Heroibus ... videtur dictum: & Hypochthonius, hoc est, subterraneis Diis fossas et scrobes, quae a Graecis ... Mundo & Nymphis, caeterisque, hujusmodi aris dicantur: unde antri Nympharum apud Homerum decimo tertio Οὐδʼ... fit mentio.
units.tr: Further, Ἐωμοί... are distinguished thus by the philosopher Porphyry: Ἐωμοί, that is, altars, he says, and temples they set up for the heavenly gods; but Chthonius, that is, for the earthly gods and heroes... seems to be so called; and Hypochthonius, that is, for the subterranean gods, trenches and pits, which by the Greeks... are dedicated to Mundus and the Nymphs and others of this kind of altar; whence mention is made of the cave of the Nymphs in Homer, book thirteen.

units.la: His fere similia Festus prodidit: Superis, ma vis Diis, aris a terra exaltatis: terrestribus in terra ... in antris et cavernis ... Soli vero in sublimi.
units.tr: Festus handed down things nearly similar to these: for the celestial gods, altars raised up from the earth; for the earthly gods, on the earth... in caves and caverns... but for the sun, on high.

units.la: Quentum ad L. ... vocabula attinet, ea sunt Ara & Altare; Ara quidem varie affertur ... Servius ... inquit, aras & Diis esse superis & infernis consectatas: Alcarii vero esse superorum ... ceterorum, quae ab altitudine constat esse nominata. Idem in secundo Aeneidos ... Macrobius libro tertio Saturnalium capite undecimo: Multifariam legitur, quod litare sit ... Hinc Varro libro de Divinatione quinto ... Aras autem... Virgilius ... Varro de lingua Latina ... ara ... Ara ... Propter hoc ... Ara ... Festus ... Nisi potius ab ardore ... Hinc Arnobius arulas petorū sanguine delibrat dixit, & Prudentius lib. 2 contra Symmachum: Omnibus ante pedes posita est sua cuique vetusta Arula, &c.
units.tr: As to the Latin words, they are Ara and Altare. Ara is brought forward in various ways... Servius says that altars were dedicated to both the gods above and the gods below; but altars belong to the gods above... of the rest, which is named from height. The same in the second book of the Aeneid... Macrobius, in the third book of the Saturnalia, chapter eleven: it is read in many ways, that to sacrifice is... Hence Varro in the fifth book on Divination... but altars... Virgil... Varro on the Latin language... ara... ara... on this account... ara... Festus... unless perhaps from ardor... Hence Arnobius said he sprinkled little altars with the blood of... and Prudentius, book 2 against Symmachus: Before everyone's feet is placed each one's ancient little altar, etc.
Altars

units.la: Altaria deinde sunt, ut Festus ait, in quibus ignis adolentur: altaria quidem ab altitudine dicta, quasi ara altae: quae vox Altus, alta, &c. ab Hebraeo הלע Alàh, ascendit, videcur deinde quia ad alta opus ascensu. Quae de causa etiam Graeci dicti, quod Antiqui Dii super inaedificia, a terra exaltatis, sacra faciebant: Diis terrestribus in terra: Diis infernalibus essossa terra. Sic Lactantius Grammaticus Thebaidos septimo, tria fuisse in sacrificiis lota ait, per quæ expiationem facerunt, scroiculo factio inferis; aris terrestribus; cœlestibus socis: Unde denominaci eciam sunt altaria, ad quæ,cum sacrificabant,manus in alcum porrigebant.
units.tr: Next are the altars, on which, as Festus says, fires are burned. Altars are indeed named from their height, as if they were "high altars." The word altus, alta, and so on, comes from the Hebrew alah [עלה], to ascend, and seems to be so called because they are raised high, so that one must climb to them. For this reason the Greeks too gave them their name, since the ancient gods received sacrifices on buildings raised high above the earth: to the earthly gods on the ground, and to the gods of the underworld in earth that had been dug out. So Lactantius the Grammarian, in his seventh book on the Thebaid, says that three things were used in sacrifices by which they made expiation: a pit dug for the dead, altars for the earthly gods, and heavenly altars for the heavenly gods. Altars are also named from the fact that, when they sacrificed, they stretched their hands upward toward them.

units.la: Alcarium porro,ut etiam templorum,originem,scriptores antiqui ad Ægyptios referunt, in- ser.quos Herodotus libro duodecimo. Ante Dei num satrificiorum quidem,ut Abelis & Caini, goad Aegy- ptios reserenda sed altarium nulla,quod sciam,sit mentio in sacris literis. An igitur in solo ipso ac parvimento, sed an vero,quod videtur esse verisimilius, in altari aliquo ad sacrificium erecto, illi prisci sanctihomines siverò Deo,si ve etiam alienis Diis sacrificarint, incertum est. Nonnunquam certè Græcos sine ara, in nudo solo & parvimento sacra peregisse compertum est. Eumeus apud Homerum super ἑρκείου, id est, focum vitiatum fuit. Arabes arulus, super aram cøstituebant, Solis inilla immolare & chura adolere consueverunt. Post diluvium primum altare, cujus in sacris sicteris fit mentio,sint illud, quod Noachus exstruxit Genesseos capite octavo. Patriarchas deinde passim hinc inde altaria Deo exstruxisse & in iis sacrificasse legimus.
units.tr: Ancient writers trace the origin of altars, as of temples, to the Egyptians, as Herodotus does in the second book. Before the Law, we indeed read of sacrifices, as of Abel and Cain, but, so far as I know, there is no mention of altars in the sacred letters. It is uncertain whether those early holy men offered sacrifices on the bare ground and open space, or, as seems more likely, on some altar erected for the sacrifice, whether to the true God or to foreign gods. It is certain that the Greeks sometimes performed sacred rites without an altar, on the bare ground in the open. In Homer, Eumaeus made his offering at the hearth-enclosure [ἑρκείου], that is, at the hearth. The Arabs set up small altars upon which they sacrificed to the sun and burned incense. The first altar after the Flood that is mentioned in the sacred writings is the one Noah built, in Genesis chapter eight. We read that the patriarchs afterward built altars to God here and there and offered sacrifices on them.

units.la: Porrò ut templa & altaria sibi soli Deus extrui & ædificari s, consecrari s, voluit: sic Ethnici quoq;, lumine naturæ,non usi sint, qui Dii essent aeq; Numina, templa atque altaria erigi facesse ni nisi Diis puteabant. Hinc Augustinus semo decimo,sermone sexto: Nam illi (Ethnici) quod Numen habeant,& pro Numine atcipiantissam flagicam,ara testatur. Quid illæc faciant ara,si illud non habetur pro Numine? Nemo mihi dicas, Non est Deus. Iam dixi. Vtinam ipsi sic norint hoc,quomodo no vimus omnes nos. Sed quid habeant,pro quæ re habeant,quid ibi faciant,ara illa testa- tur. Hactenus Augustinus.
units.tr: Just as God willed that temples and altars be built and consecrated to himself alone, so the Gentiles too, by the light of nature, who thought that gods were divine powers, did not erect temples and altars except to the gods. Hence Augustine, in sermon ten, sermon six: "For those Gentiles, that they have a divinity and regard as divine that shameful lust, the altar bears witness. What do these altars do, if that is not regarded as divine? Let no one say to me, 'It is not God.' I have already said so. Would that they knew this as well as we all do. But what they hold, for what reason they hold it, and what they do there, that altar bears witness." So far Augustine.

units.la: Quoniam igitur olim Reges, Principes, Imperatores & Tyranni inter Ethnicos a subdi- tis, & vivi & mortui pro Diis fuerunt culti, & ipsi pro insana sua ambitione atq; superbia divi- nos honores sibi arrogarunt,ac pro Diis colivoluerunt, idcirco passum legimus in historiis templa & alcaria ipso fuisse ædificata & consecrata,atque adeo illos sibi hæc erigi atque exerui curasse. Ejus rei testes sunt aræ illæ, ab Alexandro Magno ad Tunas fontes excitatæ, ad quas aras Cicero scribit in epistolis familiaribus,se castra po vilsse. Adrianus Imperator,ut Antoninus Spartianus in ejus vita cestatur, Athenis eadem loci Olympio,sibi ; aram posuit, & per Asiam uster facierent, passim templa sui nominis fieri consecrari, cura vit. Ηut enim, ut omnes historici testantur,mirum in modum ambitiosus.
units.tr: Since, then, in former times kings, princes, emperors, and tyrants among the Gentiles were worshipped as gods by their subjects, both while alive and after death, and they themselves, out of insane ambition and pride, claimed divine honours for themselves and wanted to be worshipped as gods, for this reason we read in histories that temples and altars were built and consecrated to them, and that they themselves took care to have these erected. Witnesses to this are those altars which Alexander the Great set up at the springs of the Tanais, at which Cicero writes in his letters to friends that he had pitched his camp. The Emperor Hadrian, as Spartianus says in his life, set up an altar to himself at Athens in the temple of Olympian Zeus, and throughout Asia he took care that temples bearing his name were built and consecrated everywhere. For he was, as all historians attest, wonderfully ambitious.

units.la: Aliquando autem singulis Diis atq; Numinibus templa atque altaria ædificarunt: aliquan- do vero duobus aut pluribus Diis unum templum atq; altare, tanquam illis commune erexerunt. singulis Diis, sic enim, exempli gratia, Apollinus, & Mercurii communem in Græcia aram fuisse Pausanias statur,quod Mercurium Lyræ, Apollinem Cytharæ invencorem fuisse Græciputarent. Sic Cicero Vérrinā sextā: Aristeus,inquit,qui,ut Græci ferunt, Liberi filius, inventor oleitesse dicitur, ana cum Libero patre apud Syracusanos eodem erat in templo cösecratus. Sic Arriauus in Periplo Ponti Euxini, Philisium & Mercurium voluit ejusdem templi & altaris societate conjungi, quod Græce eleganter vocat ἑπιφώνιον, ἑφιλοῦς ἑρμεύς sieri. Cur communis fuerit ara Herculis & Musarum Plucarchum vide in Quæstionibus Romanis,quæstione quinquagesima nona.
units.tr: Sometimes temples and altars were built for single gods and divine powers, and sometimes one temple and altar was erected for two or more gods, as if common to them. For instance, Pausanias reports that there was a common altar of Apollo and Mercury in Greece, because they thought Mercury was the inventor of the lyre and Apollo of the cithara. So Cicero in the sixth Verrine speech: "Aristaeus," he says, "who, as the Greeks report, is said to be the son of Liber and the inventor of the olive, was consecrated together with Father Liber in the same temple among the Syracusans." So Arrian, in his Periplus of the Euxine Sea, wished Philesius and Mercury to be joined in the fellowship of one and the same temple and altar, which he elegantly calls by the Greek word [ἐπιφώνιον]. For why the altar of Hercules and the Muses was common, see Plutarch's Roman Questions, question fifty-nine.

units.la: Sed & in ædificatione Altarium religiose observabatur materia. Hæc varia fuit & multiplex. Arrianus in Periplo Ponti Euxini,juxta Trapezuntem,si vicatem in mari sitam, scribit rium. se vidisse aras erectas ex aspero & imposito lapide,addita, se slatuisse,ibi arat albo lapide dedicare, & epigrammata perspicuis & illustribus notis insculpere. Sic Angelus Polit tianus Apollinis Delo aram corneam exstructam fuisse cessacur, quam βωμον κεράτινον votatam dicit. Sic Deus in veteri Testamento aram vel ex Cespitibus terræ, vel ex rudi & impoliro lapide sibi se staricari, voluit. Ac ara aurea Babyloniorum meminit Athenæus:in qua nullum animal, ni se edens immolatum Herodoti testimonio probat. Ex marmore item candido aras olim fieri s s es solitas innumeri scriptores testantur. Hinc illud Poetæ: Marmoreas stanc sulua canum simulatra per aras, Et Ovidius de ara Dianæ Orchilocha verba faciens monet: Decolor a sulo tincta cruore rubet.
units.tr: In constructing altars, the material too was carefully observed. It was varied and manifold. Arrian, in his Periplus of the Euxine Sea, writes that near Trapezus, on a rock situated in the sea, he saw altars erected of rough, unhewn stone, and he resolved to dedicate an altar there of white stone and to carve epigrams in clear and conspicuous letters. So Angelus Politianus reports that at Delos there was an altar of Apollo built of horns, which he calls a horned altar [βωμὸν κεράτινον]. So God in the Old Testament willed that an altar be made for himself either of earth's turf or of rough and unpolished stone. Athenaeus mentions a golden altar of the Babylonians, on which, as Herodotus attests, no animal except a sucking infant was sacrificed. Countless writers also testify that altars were once customarily made of white marble. Hence the poet's line: "Here, in the bloody shrines, stand marble images of dogs." And Ovid, speaking of Diana's altar, when he treats of the words of Archilochus, says: "The colourless marble, stained with blood, turns red."

units.la: Huc Martialis etiam libro nono alludit; Liberitur tibi candidas ad aras,
units.tr: Martial also alludes to this in his ninth book: "Let there be a free passage for you to the white altars."

units.la: Forma quoq; altarium vel fuit quadrata, ut templorum, vel rotunda. Super aras ver ó tam quadratas, quam rotundas teipsum quidem ex ordinie, sive verbenas (quae omnibus fere in sacris, seu faustis, fuerunt adhibita, quas etiam sacro ex loco decerpere oportebat) apponere consueverunt.
units.tr: The form of altars too was either square, like temples, or round. Upon both square and round altars they were accustomed to lay sacred cakes in order, and also verbenae (which were used in almost all rites, whether of ill or good omen, and which had to be plucked from the holy place itself).

units.la: At singulorum quidem Deorum aras, ut etiam victimas, & seipsos, iis frondibus coronare, ornare soliti fuerunt, quae singulis Diis fuerunt consecrata: ut Iovi aram, aesculo, Apol. inis lauro, Minervae oleâ, Veneris myrto, Herculis populo, Bacchi hederâ (sed & pampinis interdum, ramusq; ficulneis plerunq;.) Panu pino, Sylvani & Dius cupressu, aliorumq; aliis frondibus, atq; arboribus coronarunt. Hinc quia aras frondibus, graminibus, herbis floribusq; ornari solebant, a Poetis Frondentes, Gramineae, Herbosae, Virides, Coronatae, sunt dicta. Valerius Flaccus lib. 3. tertio: —Et summas frondentibus insulit aras, Libantesque dapes, &c,
units.tr: Moreover, they were accustomed to crown and adorn the altars of individual gods, as well as the victims and themselves, with those leaves which were consecrated to each god: to Jupiter with oak, to Apollo with laurel, to Minerva with olive, to Venus with myrtle, to Hercules with poplar, to Bacchus with ivy (and sometimes too with vine tendrils and fig branches), to Pan with pine, to Silvanus and Diana with cypress, and with other leaves and trees for others. Hence, because the altars were usually adorned with leaves, grasses, herbs, and flowers, the poets called them leafy, grassy, herby, green, and crowned. Valerius Flaccus, in book three: "And he leaps upon the high altars, leafy with foliage, and offers feasts, etc."

units.la: Syllius libro quarto: Gramineas undis straevit socialibus aras.
units.tr: Silius, in book four: "He strewed the grassy altars with social waves."

units.la: Ovidius decimoquinto Metamorphoseos: Placat odoratis herbosas ignibus aras.
units.tr: Ovid, in the fifteenth book of the Metamorphoses: "He appeases the herby altars with fragrant fires."

units.la: Martialis libro duodecimo: Si terrure coli, vitides, pigebit ad aras.
units.tr: Martial, in book twelve: "If you are ashamed to worship at the altars with garlands..."

units.la: Propertius libro tertio: Inde coronatas ubi thure piaverit aras.
units.tr: Propertius, in book three: "Then where the crowned altars have been appeased with incense."

units.la: Ut autem Deorum & Sanctorum, & templorum; sic altarium quoque apud Gentiles & apud Iudaeos, Gentilium exemplo (de quo Deus sapientissime per Prophetas suos tonquerunt) numerus fuit maximus: quem altarum multipli actionem Hosea Propheta vocat, capite duodecimo, cum, Israelitas exprobrat: Altaria in ipsis eorum, tanquam aterni lapidum super sulcos agri, ut hi passim omnibus in locis altaria exstruunt.
units.tr: Just as there was a great number of gods, saints, and temples, so too the number of altars, both among the Gentiles and among the Jews, was very large, following the Gentile example, which God most wisely condemned through his prophets. The prophet Hosea calls this multiplication of altars, in chapter twelve, when he rebukes the Israelites: "Their altars shall be like heaps of stones on the furrows of the field," since they set up altars everywhere in every place.

units.la: Porro & dedicari ata, consecrari aras & altaria olim certa forma magna, religione solebat, ut ad eum, seu praesipuum fere membrum, hic esse confideraudum. Dedicationis autem hujus illustre exemplum est dedicatio Arae, Augusto posita apud Narbonenses, cuius hac inscriptio est:
units.tr: Moreover, the dedication and consecration of altars were once accompanied by a certain established form and great reverence, so that this should be considered here as a nearly principal part of the matter. An illustrious example of this dedication is the dedication of the altar set up at Narbo in honour of Augustus, whose inscription reads:

units.la: L. CASSIO LONGINO COSs. x. KAL. OCTOBR.
units.tr: In the consulship of L. Cassius Longinus, on the tenth day before the Kalends of October

units.la: NVMINI AVGVSTI VOTUM SVSCEPTVM A PLEBE NARBONENSIVM IN PERPETVVM.
units.tr: THE VOW MADE TO THE DIVINITY OF AUGUSTUS BY THE PLEBS OF NARBO, TO LAST FOREVER.

units.la: QVOD BONVM, FAVSTVM, FELIXQVE SIT IMP. CAESARI DIVI F. AVGUSTO P.P. PONTIFICI MAXIMO TRIB. POTESTAT. XXXIIII. CONIVGI, LIBERIS, GENTIQVE EIVS, SENATVI, POPVLOQVE ROMANO, ET COLONIS, INCOLISQVE C.I.P.N.M. QVI SE NVMINI EIVS IN PERPETVVM OBLIGAVERVNT, PLEBS NARBON. ARAM NARBONE IN FORO POSVIT AD QVAM QVOTANNIS VIIII. KAL. OCTOB. QVA DIE EVM CVLI FELICITAS ORBI TERRARVM RECTOREM EDIDIT, TRES EQVITES ROMANI, A PLEBE, ET TRES LIBERTINI HOSTIAS INVLAS IMOLENT, ET COLONIS ET INCOLIS AD SVPPLICANDVM NVMINI EIVS THVS ET VINVM DE SVO EA DIE PRAESTENT. ET VIII. KAL. OCTOB. THVS, VINVM, COLONIS ET INCOLIS ITEM PRAESTENT. KAL. QVOQVE IANVAR. THVS ET VINVM COLONIS ET INCOLIS PRAESTENT, VII. QVOQVE
units.tr: For the good fortune, prosperity and happiness of Imperator Caesar, son of the divine one, Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the thirty-fourth time, and for his wife, his children and his family, for the Senate and the Roman people, and for the colonists and residents (who have bound themselves to his divinity forever), the plebs of Narbo set up an altar in the forum at Narbo. Each year, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, the day on which the good fortune of the world gave birth to him who is ruler of the lands, three Roman knights and three freedmen chosen by the plebs shall sacrifice victims, and on that day shall provide incense and wine from their own resources for the colonists and residents to offer in supplication to his divinity. Likewise on the eighth day before the Kalends of October they shall provide incense and wine for the colonists and residents. Also on the Kalends of January they shall provide incense and wine for the colonists and residents, and on the seventh day before

units.la: IDVS IANVAR. QVA DIE PRIMVM IMPERIVM ORBIS TERRARVM AVSPICATVS EST, THVRE, VINO SVPPLICENT. ET HOSTIAS SINGVL. IMMOLENT. ET COLONIS INCOLISQVE THVS, VINVM EA DIE PRAESTENT.
units.tr: the Ides of January, the day on which he first undertook the rule of the lands of the world, they shall offer incense and wine in supplication, and each shall sacrifice a victim, and on that day they shall provide incense and wine for the colonists and residents.

units.la: ET PRIDIE KAL. IVNIAS, QVOD EA DIE T. STATILIO TAVRO, M. AEMILIO LEPIDO COSS. IVDICIA PLEBIS DECVRIONIBVS CONIVNXIT, HOSTIAS SINGVLAS IMMOLENT, ET THVS, ET VINVM AD SVPPLICANDVM NVMINI EIVS COLONIS ET INCOLIS PRAESTENT.
units.tr: And on the day before the Kalends of June, because on that day, in the consulship of Titus Statilius Taurus and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, he joined the judgments of the plebs to the decurions, they shall each sacrifice a victim, and provide incense and wine for the colonists and residents to offer in supplication to his divinity.

units.la: EXQVE IIS TRIBVS EQVITIBVS ROMA LIBERTINIS VNV Reliqua deficiunt.
units.tr: And from these three Roman knights and three freedmen, one ... [The rest is missing.]

units.la: Qui plura dedicationis hujus exempla cupit, inspiciat clarissimi & antiquitatis peritissimi viri Dn. Adolphi Occonis, amicismei singularis, Numismata antiqua, & Antiquitatum Romanarum a Johanne Rosino collectarum librum fecundum.
units.tr: Whoever desires more examples of this dedication should consult the Ancient Coins of the most distinguished and most learned man in antiquity, Dr. Adolph Occo, my special friend, and the second book of the Roman Antiquities collected by Johannes Rosinus.

units.la: Dicamus nunc de altarium apud Gentiles usu. Primus & praecipuus altarium usus fuit, quod sacrificia omnis generis cum animata, tum inanimata in iis fiebant: unde etiam בְּמוֹת, Mizzebechoth Hebraice, & Συνεστίας Graece fuerunt appellata, de quo usu sacrificiali satis superque constat. Propter hunc ipsum usum ara varia & elegantibus epithetis a Poetis insigniuntur, ut quod festae, sacrae, sacratae, sacrosanctae, divinae, tuste, sacrificae, fumantes, fumidae, fumosae, pinguës, odoratae, flagrantes, thuritremae, thurifere, lucentes, ardentes, calentes, aliusq; id generis nominibus appellantur. Statius etiam vaporatum vocat Altare, & thureum ab hoc usu sacrificandi.
units.tr: Let us now speak of the use of altars among the Gentiles. The first and chief use of altars was that all kinds of sacrifices, both of living and of inanimate things, were made on them. Hence they were called in Hebrew bamoth [בָּמוֹת] and in Greek synestiai [συνεστίαι], as is quite well established regarding this sacrificial use. Because of this very use, poets adorn the altar with various and elegant epithets: it is called festal, sacred, consecrated, most sacred, divine, sacrificial, smoking, fuming, smoky, rich in fat, fragrant, blazing, incense-bearing, incense-yielding, shining, burning, glowing, and by other names of this kind. Statius also calls the altar "vaporous" and "incense-bearing," from this sacrificial use.

units.la: Deinde, ad sive, ante altaria fiebant preces, vota ac juramenta: cujus usus exempla passim occurrunt. Macrobius libro tertio Saturnaliorum, capite secundo: Multifariam legimus, inquit, quod a. Ad aliquid litare sola non posset oratio, nisi is, qui Deos precatur, etiam aras manibus apprehendat. Hinc aras precesfiebant nonnulli ab ἀφοσιώσει, id est, oro, vel ἀπὸ τῆς ἀξίας, ut supra quoque dixi, id est, a precibus volunt & juramenta dictas, & ansas Varro voluit antiquitus appellatas, quod eas, a sacrificantibus, adde precantibus, necessarium esse teneri. Virgilius septimo Aeneidos:
units.tr: Next, prayers, vows and oaths were made before altars, and examples of this custom occur everywhere. Macrobius, in book three of the Saturnalia, chapter two: "We read in many places," he says, "that prayer alone cannot make an offering to anything unless the one who prays also grasps the altars with his hands." Hence some hold that altars were named from aphosiosis [ἀφοσίωσις], that is, from praying, or from apo tēs axias [ἀπὸ τῆς ἀξίας], as I said above as well, that is, from prayers; and Varro held that they were anciently called ansae, because those who sacrifice, or rather pray, must necessarily hold them. Virgil, in the seventh book of the Aeneid:
Thus praying with such words, and holding the altars,
The Almighty heard, etc.

units.la: Sic Delifuit ara Apollinis ἡμιτροφ, id est, Genitoris, quia nullum animal sacrificabatur, quam Pythagoram velut in violatam adorarivisse ferunt. Nutrix hac omnia faciebat in verbenis ac verbis sive hostiis, ut Deliad Apollinis Genitorem.
units.tr: Thus the altar of Apollo at Delos was called hemitrophos [ἡμιτρόφος], that is, of the Begetter, because no living creature was sacrificed on it; this altar, they say, Pythagoras worshipped as inviolate. The nurse did all these things with sacred herbs and words or victims, as at the Delian altar of Apollo Genitor.

units.la: Sic jurantes quoq; manu aram tangebant. Virgilius:
units.tr: So those swearing also touched the altar with their hand. Virgil:

units.la: Tango aras, medios ignes, ac Numina testor.
units.tr: I touch the altars, the middle fires, and call the gods to witness.

units.la: Cicero pro Flacco: Is si aram tenens juraret, crederet nemo. Celebratur hinc nobilis illa Periclis sententia, Ad aram usq; amicum me esse oportet: qua significatur, Neminè amici causa aut pejerare, aut quippiam inhonestum facere oportere. Adde etia per vulgatum illud Aristophanis verbum ὁ ἀγορεύοντος, οἱ ὄντες ... id est, Quem nec ara, nec fides, nec ulla Deorum fides durant. De vehementer perfidis. Dilium est, in Spartanos, quorum perfidiam tanquam Aristophanes.
units.tr: Cicero, in defence of Flaccus: "If he swore while holding the altar, no one would believe him." Hence the famous saying of Pericles is celebrated: "It is right for me to be a friend even to the altar," by which is meant that no one ought to commit perjury or do anything dishonourable for the sake of a friend. Add also the well-known word of Aristophanes, that neither altar nor faith nor any reverence for the gods holds such men, which is said of those who are most treacherously faithless, such as the Spartans, whose faithlessness Aristophanes mocks.

units.la: Arae praeterea erant asyla atq; perfugia hominum sacrosancta. Unde: Confugere in aram. Cicero post reditum: Qui nisi in aram tribunatus confugisset, dum Praetoris effugere non potuisset, pro Roscio: Sicut in aram, confugit in ejus domum. Idem in quaestionibus Tusculanis: Tanquam in aram orbatum, cum in aram confugisset, boftilis manus interemit. Ab ara itaq; non licebat supplices abstrahere. Hujusmodi ara erat; ara Concordiae, cujus meminit Hieronymus, adquam si quis confugisset, tanquam ad Caesaris statuam, a velut eum inde nefas habebatur. Plautus in Rudente:
units.tr: Altars were moreover sacred places of refuge and asylum for men. Hence the phrase "to flee to the altar." Cicero, after his return: "Who, unless he had fled to the altar of the tribunate while he could not escape the praetor..." In defence of Roscius: "As to an altar, he fled into his house." The same, in the Tusculan Disputations: "As an orphan takes refuge at an altar, a hostile hand slew him when he had fled to the altar." Therefore it was not lawful to drag suppliants away from an altar. There was such an altar, the altar of Concord, which Jerome mentions; if anyone fled to it, it was regarded as a sacrilege to touch him there, just as at the statue of Caesar. Plautus in the Rudens:

units.la: Sed quid ego cessò fugere in fanum at dicere hac
units.tr: But why do I hesitate? Let us flee to the temple rather than say this:
Let us first flee to the altar of the wrestling-ground,

units.la: Quain hunc scelestus leno ventus, meq, hic opprimat?
units.tr: Lest this wicked pimp seize me here and crush me!
The same, in the Mostellaria:

units.la: Tranio ser‑vus: Ego interim banc aram occupabo.
units.tr: Tranio the slave: "Meanwhile I shall take hold of this altar."

units.la: Servi enim, sibi male conscii, & poenam suorum malefactorum ac peccatorum metuentes, deprecatorem parabant, & aram aliquam, a qua nefas erat eos a vellere, occupabant.
units.tr: For slaves, conscious of their own wrongdoing and fearing punishment for their misdeeds and sins, sought an intercessor and seized some altar, from which it was unlawful to drag them.
Terence in the Heautontimorumenos:

units.la: Nemo accusat, Sire, nec eu aram tibi, neq; precato rem parnbó.
units.tr: "No one accuses you, sir, nor does anyone pray for you at the altar, nor does he plead for the matter."

units.la: Cicero de aruspicum responsis: Sacerdotem abiphs aris & pulvinaribus detraxisse. Idem libro tertio de Orat. Quod cum facere non potestis, tanquam in aram confugicis ad Deum. Idem: Magistratuum autem vestrorum injurias ista multas tulerunt, ut nunquam antehac ad aram legem praesidium, vestrum publico consilio confugerint. Ovidius quarto Tristium:
units.tr: Cicero, on the responses of the haruspices: "He had dragged the priest away from the altars and the couches of the gods." The same, in the third book of On the Orator: "Since you cannot do this, you flee to God as to an altar." The same: "Yet the wrongs of your magistrates have brought many such things that never before have the laws sought refuge at the altar, by public counsel of you all." Ovid, in the fourth book of the Tristia:

units.la: Unica fortune cu ara reperta mea, idest, asylum. perfugium, portus. Hinc Plutarchus de superstitione aram vocat Εωμόν, a quam confugimus.
units.tr: My only hope was found at the altar, that is, asylum, refuge, harbour. Hence Plutarch, in On Superstition, calls the altar the hestia [ἑστία] to which we flee.
Why the holy altar is so called.

units.la: Ob quam caussam Cicero eam quoque sanctam, hoc est, inviolatam vocat: cujus quidem etiam hoc argumento est, quod idem in oratione pro Cornelio Balbo ostendere volens Lucium Marcum primi pilicenturianem foedus, quod fecerat, semper inviolate pietatis, fervaffe, hoc proverbio utitur: Ara sanctior. Sic idem: Qui & vetierem illam speciem foederis Marciani, semper omni sanctiorem ara duxerunt.
units.tr: For this reason Cicero also calls it sacred, that is, inviolable. This is shown by the following passage. In his speech for Cornelius Balbus, wishing to show that Lucius Marcius, centurion of the first rank, had always kept inviolate the covenant he had made, he uses the proverb: "more sacred than an altar." Likewise the same author writes: "Those who thought that old form of the Marcian covenant more sacred than any altar."

units.la: Ac quoniam ara & foci praecipua erant cultus religionis, instrumenta, quae idcirco saepe me-tonymice pro ipsa religione cupiuncur, unde promanavit provertbialis illa locutio: Pro aris & foris pugnare, sive certare, cum cotis viribus certamus, tanquam nihil nobis prius, aut carius esse dixeat sacrorum defensione. Cicero de Natura Deorum libro ter. in: Quoniam ad vesperascit, dabis diem nobis aliquem, ut contra ista dicamus. Est enim mihi pro aris & focis certandum, & pro Deorum templis atque delubris. Seneca tamen ait: Aras, quae vertunt, injuriam Diis non faciunt.
units.tr: Since altar and hearth were the chief instruments of religious worship, they are often put metonymically for religion itself. Hence the proverbial phrase "to fight for altars and hearths," that is, to contend with all our strength, as if nothing were dearer to us than the defence of sacred things. Cicero, in book three of On the Nature of the Gods: "Since evening is coming on, give us some day so that we may argue against those views. For I must fight for altars and hearths, and for the temples and shrines of the gods." Seneca nevertheless says: "Altars which are overturned do no injury to the gods."

units.la: Hic, quae de aris, & altaribus baftenus dicta fuerunt, adde quod ab ara Aruga dicta est, sive, ut alii legunt, Haruga cum aspiratione ab hara, in qua includebatur hostia. Ducebatur autem teste Festo, cum adhaerentia infpicebatur exta. Inde & Aruf ex, sive Harufex, ara inspector, fuit appellatus: quas cerce Gentilium aras vere dixerimus haras, super quas antiquius sues porcimum, aliaq; immunda animalia maclabantur; quae quidem suum sacrificia Gentiles fcipcores tuent prima & antiquissimi fuit, sacrificia, de quo supra.
units.tr: To what has been said so far about altars, add this: the altar was called "aruga," or, as some read it, "haruga" with an aspirate, from "hara," in which the victim was enclosed. According to Festus, the entrails were inspected while still attached to it. From this also the "harufex" or "aruspex," the inspector of the altar, took his name. These altars of the Gentiles we may rightly call "haras," on which in older times sows, pigs and other unclean animals were slaughtered. Indeed the Gentile priests were the first and most ancient to make such sacrifices, as noted above.

units.la: Alcatibus atq. focus merito annumerande atque subjungenda sunt mensae, quarum in templis sacrusq. Gentilium ut magnus fuit usus, ita saepe fit mentio. Mensae, inquit ! eftus, in aedibus aram sacrum obtinebant. Hinc Cicero aras, focos & mensas conjungit in oratione de Aruspicum responsis: Dei-rum, inquit, ignes, solennes mensae, abdiri & penetrales foci.
units.tr: Hearths and altars should rightly be joined by tables, whose use in the temples and rites of the Gentiles was as great as the frequency with which they are mentioned. "Tables," says Festus, "in houses held the place of altars." Hence Cicero joins altars, hearths and tables in his speech on the responses of the haruspices: "The fires of the gods, the solemn tables, the hidden and inner hearths."

units.la: Ac mensae quidem in genere omnes sacrae habebantur, & Dijs, amicitiae hospitii, patronus erant consecratae, ut Plucarchus in convivio suo testatur. Mensam autem mimsterius divinam Fuflus tradit Anclabrin fuisse distam, ut vasa quoque aenea, quibus sacerdotes in re divina utebantur, Anclabria fuerunt appellata, nimirum ab antiquo verbo Anclare sive auclare, quod a Graeco ἀνάλω def endens haurire significat, sive ab anculare antiquo verbo, quod dicebant Antiqui pro ministrare, ex quo & Ancillas volunt dictas, hoc est, ministras, & Ancillas, Anculas Deos ac Deas, quae olim fuerunt culcae.
units.tr: Indeed all tables were regarded as sacred in general, and were consecrated to the gods of friendship and hospitality, as Plutarch attests in his Symposium. Festus tells that the table used in divine service was called "anclabris," just as the bronze vessels which priests used in sacred rites were called "anclabria." This is no doubt from the old verb "anclare" or "auclare," which means to draw up or drink, from the Greek ἀνάλω, or from the old verb "anculare," which the ancients used for "to minister." From this too they say "ancillae," that is, maidservants, and that the gods and goddesses, which were formerly called "culcae," were called "anculae."
The curial table.

units.la: Curiales porro etiam cercae mensae fuerunt dictae, in quibus iunoni immolabatur, quae Curia fuit appellata. Idem quadratas Afcarias, rotundas, Cinles, Ajsidelas olim fuisse dictas testatur.
units.tr: Moreover, tables were also called "curiales," on which sacrifice was made to Juno, who was called Curia. The same author records that square tables were formerly called "ascariae," round ones "cinles," and others "asidelae."
Sacred tables were once made of wood.

units.la: Ac ligneas quidem antiquitus fuisse apud Romanos sacras atque sacrificas has mensas Dio-nyfius Halicarnaffeus his verbis prodidit: Ἐγὼ γὰρ ἐν ἰδρυσαμένῳ ἐν ἱεροῖς οἰκίαις ... μάζας, καὶ ποτήρια ... ἀρχαίων ... Ilis quidem verbis aperte ligneas mensas in templis ufitatas fuisse docet.
units.tr: That in ancient times the sacred and sacrificial tables among the Romans were of wood, Dionysius of Halicarnassus declared in these words: "For I [...] in the sacred houses [...] cakes, and cups [...] of the ancients" [Ἐγὼ γὰρ ἐν ἰδρυσαμένῳ ἐν ἱεροῖς οἰκίαις ... μάζας, καὶ ποτήρια ... ἀρχαίων]. By these words he clearly shows that wooden tables were in use in the temples.

units.la: Mensarum autem aurearum & argenteatum usum in templis atque sacris biftoria fasse arguunt. Unde Dionysium Syracusanum Valerius Maximus libro primo, capite duodecimo, de neglecta.
units.tr: That tables of gold and silver were used in temples and sacred rites, the histories prove. Hence Valerius Maximus, in book one, chapter twelve, on neglected religion, writes that Dionysius of Syracuse took golden and silver tables from the temple of Apollo.

units.la: neplectà religione scribit mensas aureas & argenteas ex Apollinis templo sustulisse. Et Cicero libro tertio de Natura Deorum: Iam mensas,inquit,argenteas de omnibus delubris jussit auferri: in quibus quod more veterum Graecia inscriptum esset BONORVM DEORVM, uti se illorum bonitate dicebat.Idem Verrem mensas Delphicas e marmore, cráteras ex ere pulcherrimas, vim maximam vasorum Corinthiorum ex omnibus aedibus sacris abstulisse,dixit.
units.tr: Cicero, in book three of On the Nature of the Gods: "He then ordered silver tables to be removed from all the shrines, on which, as was the custom of the ancients, was inscribed 'OF THE GOOD GODS,' as he said, so that they might be seen to be good by their goodness." The same author says that Verres took from all the sacred buildings the Delphic tables of marble, the most beautiful bronze craters, and a great quantity of Corinthian vessels.

units.la: Hactenus etiam de aris sive altaribus & mensis.
units.tr: So far concerning altars and tables.

units.la: Sequitur QVINTVM membrum, sive circumstantia, videlicet Personae, quae, ut in hoc sic in omni sacrificio, atq; adeò in omni actione diligenter sunt considerandae. Sunt autem personae hic, homines per quos, sive a quibus sacrificia offerebantur: quorum differentia est triplex. Alii enim sunt, qui sacrificiis praesunt, sive praesidentes, ut sunt sacerdotes & sacrifici sive sacrificuli, quorum munere hic Nestor & Argonautae funguntur; alii sunt ministri: alii denique qui iis communicant, quia ad sacrificia sunt vitati.
units.tr: Next comes the FIFTH member, or circumstance, namely the persons, who, in this as in every sacrifice and indeed in every action, must be carefully considered. The persons here are the men through whom, or by whom, sacrifices were offered, and they are of three kinds. Some preside over the sacrifices, as priests and sacrificers or lesser sacrificers, whose office Nestor and the Argonauts here discharge. Others are ministers. Others, finally, share in the sacrifices, because they are invited to them.

units.la: Personae primariae & principes sunt Nestor,& Argonautae,qui quidem sacrificiorum munera potissima in Buthysia isla seu immolatione boum, cujus Homerus & Apollonius meminerunt, obiisse perhibentur. Vbi notandum, Reges quoque & principes apud Ethnicos sacrificare suisse solitos: id quod lege divina scimus fuisse prohibitum. Sic Nestor hic,qui Rex fuit,cùm manus lavandi, & molae vitimus inspergendi initium fecit: tum preces ad Minervam fudisse primùm, deindeetiam crura igni injecisse atque concremisse dicitur. Idem colligitur ex illo Virgilij Aeneid.3.
units.tr: The chief and principal persons are Nestor and the Argonauts, who are said to have performed the principal offices of the sacrifices in the Buthysia, that is, the slaughter of oxen, which Homer and Apollonius mention. Here it should be noted that kings and princes among the heathen were also accustomed to sacrifice, which we know was forbidden by divine law. Thus Nestor here, who was a king, began the washing of hands and the sprinkling of the meal; then he first poured out prayers to Minerva, and then is said to have cast the thighs into the fire and burned them. The same is gathered from that line of Virgil, Aeneid 3.

units.la: Rex Anius,rex idem hominum Phoebi,sacerdos: in quod Servius,Majorum,inquit,hac erat consuetudo, ut Rex esset etiam sacerdos & pontifex. Vnde hodie quoque Imperatores Pontifices dicimus.
units.tr: "King Anius, king of men and priest of Phoebus." On this Servius says: "It was the custom of our ancestors that the king should also be priest and pontiff. Hence even today we call the emperors pontiffs."

units.la: Ministri deinde sacrificantes in sacrificio quidem Nestoris, sunt cùm Laerces aurifaber, qui strantes qua formaarum cornua bovis inaurat:tum bubulcus,qui juberet bovem ex agro in urbem adducere:tum ancilla, quarum munus fuit ligna & aquam afferre comitumq; adornare: tum denique filii Nestoris,qui principem in hoc ministerio locum obtinent: Horum enim ministerio & opera utitur cùm in πα- ραγκλιυ sive Δητρικόν,hoc est,apparatu sacrificii,tum in ipsa actione. Nam quoad παραγκελ- λόμνοι illorum, alium jubet celeriter se in agrum conferre & bubulco jubere, ut sine mora bovem in urbem adducat: alium jubet Telemachi socios accersere: alium jubet vocare aurifabrum ad boves strnua deaurandum: alii denique mandat, ut per ancillas curent lignum & aquam comportari, coenamq; adornari: id quod ancillarum in hujusmodi sacrificiorum apparatu munus fuisse Eustathius docet.
units.tr: Then the ministers who sacrificed in Nestor's sacrifice were: Laerces the goldsmith, who gilds the horns of the ox after shaping them; then the herdsman, who was to bring the ox from the field into the city; then the maidservants, whose task was to bring wood and water and to attend to the company; and finally the sons of Nestor, who hold the chief place in this ministry. For he uses their service and labour both in the preparation, the paraskeuē or "dētrikon," that is, the equipment of the sacrifice, and in the rite itself. For in giving his orders, he bids one go quickly into the field and tell the herdsman to bring the ox into the city without delay; another he bids summon the companions of Telemachus; another he bids call the goldsmith to gild the horns carefully; and finally he charges another to see that wood and water are brought in by the maidservants and that dinner is prepared. Eustathius teaches that this was the maidservants' office in the preparation of such sacrifices.

units.la: Notanda vero hic bene morata & constitutae rei familiaris, sive oeconomiae ratio. Nestor enim, ceu paterfam. bene & prudenter suis domesticis imperat,singulis certa sua munera,quae efficere & exsequi debeant,diligenter praescribit.Liberi autem atq; famuli summa industria & celeritate patris & domini sui jussa atque mandata exsequuntur. Id docet Homerus verbo illo sibiτουεν,ιδ εἴ ξ, ἐπὶ ὑνῶν, (nam a τόν πιτ sit τοῦ νοῦ per reduplicationem & interpositionem sofa) sum- mopere elaborabant, nimirum Nestoris mandata coscere: id quod, ut inquit Eustathius, ἀπ ὑπ ὑπ ὑπ ὑπνικ ὑπο ὑπ, servilis studii atque industriae est indicium. Hanc quoque industriam celeritatem, in exsequendis jussis & mandatis Nestoris idem ruls exprimi ipsa dicendi forma, qua Homerus utitur, quae Gorgo dicitur. Idem deinde filii,ut dicetur, gnavam & industriam suam operum patri suo in ipso sacrificio navant.
units.tr: Here we should note the well-ordered conduct and the good management of a settled household. For Nestor, like a good and prudent father of a family, commands his household and carefully prescribes to each his own duties, which they must perform and carry out. Children and servants carry out their father's and master's orders with the greatest diligence and speed. Homer teaches this by the word "sibiton" (for it comes from ... by reduplication and insertion), "they laboured very hard," namely to carry out Nestor's commands. As Eustathius says, this is a sign of servile zeal and diligence. The very form of expression that Homer uses, which is called the "gorgo" (the quick style), also expresses this same diligence and speed in carrying out Nestor's orders. Then the sons, as will be said, show their eagerness and diligence in serving their father in the sacrifice itself [αὐτοδιακόνοι].

units.la: Quod autem filiorum potius,quàm servorum operâ Nestor in hoc sacrificio utitur, id, Eustathius non honoris modo atque reverentiae erga Deos gratia factum fuisse testatur, verùm ætiam ex communi seru Herorum more & consuetudine, qui in multis αὐτουργεῖν sive αὐτοδρομο ἔ, sunt soliti:unde αὐτοδιακόνοιαι Homero sunt dicti Iliad.7. Addit idem,beatam fuisse domum Nestoris domum,cui non tam mancipia, quàm ipsi liberi inservierint. Eandem insententiam Achilleus quoquehujusce sacrificii mentionem faciens disserit,cùm inquit:Nestor,cùm esset Rex & utiliis imperaret: tamen amicissimus & φιλουνσιμος suis liberis pocißimum ministris in illo sacrificio atque conviviò est usus. Addit,sοιωτότη ἔ αὖτη ἐ ὑσία ἔ ἐξ ὑσί ἐ ὑ ἔ ἁ ἐσ ἐ ἕ ἐ ἐ ἡ ἐ ἡ ἐ ἡ ἐ ἑ ἐ, ἡ ὁ ἡ ὁ οἰκίαν ἡ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἑ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ, sanctissimum enim,diuq; gratissimum est. illud sacrificium, quod per illos fit, quibus mutua familiaritate beni volentia, fiunt conjunctâ. Eodem modo (sic ea, quæ verè sacra sunt, licet cum his superstitiosis conferre) multo veruis & justius nos Christiani affirmare possumus, sacrosanctum illud convivium dominicum tanto gratius Deo & acceptius esse, quanto major & ardentior est illorum, qui communicant, beni volentia mutua atq; charitas.
units.tr: As to why Nestor uses the work of his sons rather than of his servants in this sacrifice, Eustathius testifies that this was done not only out of honour and reverence towards the gods, but also from the common custom and practice of the heroes, who in many things were accustomed to do the work themselves. Hence Homer calls them "self-servers" [αὐτοδιακόνοι], Iliad 7. The same writer adds that the house of Nestor was blessed, in which his children rather than slaves did the serving. To the same effect Achilles, mentioning this sacrifice, argues when he says: Nestor, though he was a king and gave orders, nevertheless, most friendly and kind to his children, used his sons as his chief ministers in that sacrifice and feast. He adds that that sacrifice is most holy and most pleasing to God which is made by those who are joined by mutual familiarity and goodwill, for it is most sacred and most welcome. In the same way (since those things which are truly sacred may be compared with these superstitious rites), we Christians can affirm much more truly and justly that the holy Lord's Supper is so much the more pleasing and acceptable to God as the mutual goodwill and love of those who take part in it is greater and warmer.

units.la: Illi porrò, qui sacrificio huic atq; epulo communicarunt, fuerunt cum uxor, & filiæ; tum Timothëus & illius socii, qui fuerunt in vita, nam hic fuit mos Ethnicorum, ut sacrificia Dijs saltari, suos vicinos, cognatos, amicos & familiares ad illa invitarent: utex Antiquitatibus meis Convivialibus satu superâ apparet.
units.tr: Those who took part in this sacrifice and feast were the wife and daughters, and then Timotheus and his companions who were still alive. For it was the custom of the heathens to invite their neighbours, kinsfolk, friends and household to the sacrifices that were offered to the gods with dancing, as is clear from my Convivial Antiquities above.

units.la: Porrò quoad personas sacrificiorum, principes quidem nempe sacerdotes; quorum manus his ferè verbis definitur. Plato in Politico: Sacerdotum genus, inquit, quod est legitimum, docet partim, quo pallo donaria & sacra Dijs sint offerenda, quæ ipsis sint grata: partim quæ vota sint faciendi, quidve boni a Dijs sit petendum; de his, inquam similiter, ut de templis & genere quedam dicamus; & primum de nominibus quæ sunt vel generalia, vel specialia.
units.tr: As to the persons who offer sacrifices, the chief are of course the priests, whose office Plato defines in roughly these words in the Politicus: "The legitimate kind of priests," he says, "teaches partly in what manner gifts and sacred offerings are to be made to the gods so that they may be pleasing to them, and partly what vows are to be made, or what good thing is to be asked of the gods. Of these I say we shall speak in the same way, as about temples and kinds. And first about the names, which are either general or special."

units.la: Apud Hebræos duo sunt sacerdotum nomina generalia, nempe כהן Cohanim, & כמרים, Cemarim. Vox prior cum de veris, tum etiam de falsis & idololatricis sacerdotibus usurpatur: כהן Cihen, id est, sacrasive rem divinam facere sacerdotio fungi, quod LXX ιεράτευειν vertunt. Voci huic affinis est כוהן Coach, id est, vires, potentia, propterea quod cum verorum, tum etiam falsorum & idololatricorum sacerdotum maxima semper fuit dignitas, auctoritas & potestas.
units.tr: Among the Hebrews there are two general names for priests: כהן Cohanim and כמרים Cemarim. The former word is used both of true priests and of false and idolatrous priests. כהן Cihen means to perform sacred rites or to exercise the priesthood, which the LXX render as ιεράτευειν [hierateuein]. Akin to this word is כוהן Coach, that is, strength or power, because the priesthood, both of true priests and of false and idolatrous ones, has always had the greatest dignity, authority and power.

units.la: Vox deinde כמרים, Cemarim, semper pro sacerdotibus falsis & idololatricis accipitur. Quidam volunt eam vocem (unde forsan vox Latina Camillorum, de qua infra) proprie significare sacerdotum minis tros, ut dictos vel a thuris incensione & precibus ardentibus, quas pro populo faciebant: vel ab atro vesti u, quo erant amicti. Alii sic volunt dictos ab incenso & inflammato sacrorum studio. Quidam a flagmatibus, quæ facie illorum, vel etiam reliquo corpori erant infusa. Nam כמר Camar, (unde forsan vaiaus, id est, Caminus dictus) accendi, exardescere, aduri significat. Hæc de nominibus Hebraicis.
units.tr: The word כמרים Cemarim is always taken for false and idolatrous priests. Some hold that this word (whence perhaps the Latin Camilli, discussed below) properly signifies ministers of the priests, named either from the burning of incense and the fervent prayers they offered for the people, or from the black clothing in which they were dressed. Others hold that they are named from the burning and inflamed zeal for sacred things, and some from the soot that was smeared on their faces or other parts of the body. For כמר Camar (whence perhaps caminus, that is, furnace, is named) means to be kindled, to blaze up, to be burned. So much for the Hebrew names.

units.la: Græcè sacerdos dicitur ιερεὺς, ιερεία sacrificula, & ιερωπόλος: ιεροποιὸς vir cui sacrorum semper est memor, & ἱεράρχων αρχηπεχ. Nec verò solum veri sacerdotes, sed etiam adulterini & fucati volu erunt ἱερεῖς appellari a τῷ ἱερὰν, a sacris, quæ tractarent, sum non modo sed ut ἡγεμών id est, accipiatur potius dici mererentur, quod accipiatur & aliarum ἀνδρῶν munera atque dona accipiendi cupiditate, id est, avaritia flagrarent.
units.tr: In Greek the priest is called ιερεὺς [hiereus], and a female priest ιερεία [hiereia], and ιερωπόλος [hieropolos], and ιεροποιὸς [hieropoios], a man always mindful of sacred things, and ἱεράρχης [hierarches], the high priest. Not only true priests but also counterfeit and pretended ones wished to be called ἱερεῖς [hiereis], from τὰ ἱερά [ta hiera], the sacred things they handled. And they deserved to be called not so much that as rather ἡγεμών [hegemon], since they burned with the desire of receiving the gifts and offerings of other men, that is, they were gripped by avarice.

units.la: Nomina præterea alia sacerdotum apud Græcos fuerunt multa, quæ Julius Pollux in Onomastico libro primo & octavo recenset. Ea sunt ἱερεὺς, ἱερόφαντης, ἱερομνήμων, ἱεροποιὸς, ἱερόμανις, ἱερεταῖς, καθαρτὴς, ἱερηκ, & quo nomine Poëtæ ut sunt, ἀπόλλων. Sunt item, quæ in vaticiniis & Deorum ornatu reddendis illis impositæ fuere, ut ἀγαλματοφόρος, ἡγεμών, ἱερηκ, & quæ de ἱεροποιοῦ ἱερεῖς, mystagogus, ἱεροφάντης, σπονδοφόρος. Sunt præterea hæc quoq, κύριος, ἀλλαῖς ἐπιμελητής, ἡ ἱερομανὴς, ἡ ἱερόμαντις, ἡ ἱεροποιὸς, ἡ ἱερὸς, curator rerum mysteriorum, & ἱερεὺς ἐκ ἱερῶν ἱερῶν ἐπιμελητῆς, id est, præfectus rerum divinarum apud Demosthenem. Mυσταγωγὸς, mystagogus, Syracusani vocabant eos, qui bospites ad fana simulacra, & ornamenta vinenda ducere, & unumquodq; ostendere solebant. Ægyptii homines rebus sacris & cerimoniis addictum vocabant μυσταγωγὸν ἐκ τελεστοῦ, eumq; cicada imaginem primebant, quæ non ore, sed tergo resonans pulcherrimum edit, dulcissimumq; concentum.
units.tr: The Greeks also had many other names for priests, which Julius Pollux lists in his Onomasticon, books one and eight. They are ἱερεὺς [hiereus], ἱερόφαντης [hierophantes], ἱερομνήμων [hieromnemon], ἱεροποιὸς [hieropoios], ἱερόμανις [hieromanis], ἱερεταῖς [hieretais], καθαρτὴς [kathartes], and that name by which the poets call Apollo. There are also those who were appointed to give oracles and to dress the gods' images: ἀγαλματοφόρος [agalmatophoros], ἡγεμών [hegemon], and the mystagogue, the hierophant, the spondophoros. Besides these there are also κύριος [kyrios], ἐπιμελητής [epimeletes], the curator of the mysteries, and the prefect of divine things, as Demosthenes calls him. The Syracusans called mystagogues those who led strangers to the shrines and images and used to point out and explain each thing. The Egyptians called the man devoted to sacred rites and ceremonies μυσταγωγὸς [mystagogos], and they made an image of him as a cicada, which sings not with its mouth but resounding from its back, with a most beautiful and sweetest tune.
Such were the Greek names.

units.la: Apud Latinos voces maximè generales sunt Sacerdos, Sacrificus & Sacrificulus. His nominibus non tantum veri sacerdotes, qui Deo dicati sunt ad sacra faciendo, quos Tertullianus etiam sacrificatores & adoratores, Græce ὀθύσεις, ἱερουργοὶ vocat, & Isidorus Originum libro septimo quasi sacra dantes, sed falsi quoque & superstitiosi sacerdotes insigniri solebant, ut qui sacris idololatricis essent dediti, sacra Dijs fictis facerent & tractarent. Sed sacerdos falsus & idololatricus recte sic videatur dictus voce composita a ὀφειλ, id est, ἡ ἱερὸς, saccus, & ὠρισὸς, id est, ... crum, sive quæstus, propterea quòd ille sit quasi saccus quidam lucri, qui nunquam expleri facile potest. Vel etiam sacerdotes illi Gentilium χἱρωνος potius, quàm sacerdotes dici potuerint; quo nomine Græcè appellantur φιλοχρήματοι, id est, homines lucri cupidi, qui unde lucrum capere possunt, quos Latini Lucriones appellant: Vel etiam non tam sacerdotes, quàm Cerdones dici merebantur; quod nomen eos significat, qui artes illiberales & sordidas lucri quæstuique gratia exercent (ἀπὸ τῶν κερδῶν) at quibus lucri odor, quaˇ vis ex re vel turpissima, suæ vilissimus est & turpissimus: Vel deniq; illi Gentilium sacerdotes sic veré dicti fuerunt ea significatione, qua vox Sacri in malam sæpe partem pro impio & exsecrabili usurpatur: qua significatione Virgilius dixit, Auri sacra fames, &c. Sic Sacer, teste Festo, dictus etiam fuit, quem populus judicavit ob maleficium: neq; fas est eum immolari; sed qui occidit, parricidii non damnatur. Nam lege tribunitia prima cavetur, Si quis eum, qui eo plebeiscito sacer sit, occideris, parricidas ne fit: ex quo quivis homo malus atq; improbus sacer appellari solet. Secundum hunc igitur sensum & significationem sacerdotes ibi impii, sacerrimi, hoc est, exsecrabiles, mali atque improbi, ut leno quidam apud Plautum vocatur, dici poterant. Erant deniq; illi sacerdotes, tanquam Epicuri de grege porci, & idcirco sacres sues dici poterant; quos tamen Festus interpretatur sacros puros, qui Lares bus offerri solebant.
units.tr: Among the Latins the most general words are Sacerdos, Sacrificus and Sacrificulus. By these names are designated not only true priests, dedicated to God for performing sacred rites, whom Tertullian also calls sacrificers and worshippers (in Greek θυσιασταί [thysiastai] and ἱερουργοί [hierourgoi]), and whom Isidore in the seventh book of the Origins calls "those who give sacred things." They also designated false and superstitious priests, who were devoted to idolatrous rites and performed and handled sacred things for fictitious gods. But a false and idolatrous priest may rightly be thought to be named by a compound word, from sacer and saccus, a bag, and from lucre or gain, because he is like a kind of money-bag of gain, which can never easily be filled. Or those priests of the Gentiles could be called chrematistae rather than priests, a name in Greek for lovers of money, men who take gain wherever they can, whom the Latins call lucriones. Or they deserved to be called not so much priests as cerdones, a name for those who practise base and sordid crafts for the sake of gain and profit (from κέρδη [kerde], gains), since to men who love gain, any gain at all, however shameful, is most cheap and most disgraceful. Or finally those priests of the Gentiles were truly called sacri in that sense in which the word sacer is often used in a bad sense for the impious and accursed. In this sense Virgil said "accursed hunger for gold." So too, according to Festus, one was called sacer whom the people judged guilty of wrongdoing; it is not lawful to sacrifice him, but whoever kills him is not condemned for parricide. For the first tribunician law provides: "If anyone kills a man who is made sacer by that plebiscite, he shall not be guilty of parricide." From this, any wicked and dishonest man is commonly called sacer. In accordance with this sense and meaning, the impious priests there could be called sacerrimi, that is, accursed, wicked and dishonest, as a certain pimp is called in Plautus. Finally, those priests were like Epicurus's herd of pigs, and so could be called sacred pigs, which Festus explains as holy pure ones offered to the Lares.

units.la: Dicti sunt etiam Antistites sacrorum & fanorum: ac Præsitem quoq; teste Festo, olim in eadem significatione dicebant Antiqui, quem nunc dicimus Antistitem.
units.tr: They were also called antistites of sacred things and temples. And the ancients, as Festus also attests, used to call by the same meaning the praesul what we now call the antistes.

units.la: Prophetas, ut ait Festus, in Adrasto Julius nominat Antistites fanorum oraculorumq; interpretes. Cùm capita viridi lauro inquit, velare imperant Prophetæ, sancta ita tacte qui putant sacra.
units.tr: As Festus says, Julius in his Adrastus names the prophets as antistites of temples and interpreters of oracles. "When the prophets command that their heads be veiled with green laurel, they regard these things as sacred, so to speak, and untouchable."

units.la: Nomina deinde specialia sacerdotum dicta sunt, vel a Diis, quorù sunt sacerdotes; vel a certis sacris, cerimoniis, officiis atq; muniis; vel a corporis cultu atq; habitu. A Diis quidem, sive Numinibus; ut Vestales a Vesta: Furnales a Furina: Vulcanales a Vulcano: Ifiaci ab Ifide: Canephora virgines, quæ Junonis sacra administrabant: Palatualis Flamen, qui ad sacrificandum ei Dea constituta erat, sin cujus tutela Palatium esse putabant.
units.tr: The special names of priests were then taken either from the gods whose priests they were, or from certain sacred rites, ceremonies, offices and duties, or from their bodily dress and appearance. From the gods, or divinities: as the Vestals from Vesta; the Furnales from Furina; the Vulcanales from Vulcan; the Isiaci from Isis; the Canephorae, virgins who administered the rites of Juno; and the Flamen Palatualis, who was appointed to sacrifice to the goddess believed to guard the Palatine.

units.la: Kisbologi verò dicti sunt apud Opuntios ab illo ritu seu munere, quod Græcorum plerique in sacrificiis hordeo uterentur, ejusq; primitias offerrent. Hi autem primitias istas colligebant. Ceteroqui duos habuisse sacerdotes Opuntios Plutarchus testatur in quæstionibus Græcis: Unum, qui Deorum; alterum qui Geniorum sacra administrabat. Sic Hypocausti ram Solenses appellabant Minervæ antistitam, quòd averruncandorum malorum gratia certis quibusdam sacris operarentur. Sic etiam Arvales, qui arvorù sacerdotes erant: Augures sab auguriis sunt dicti, & Fociales a foro, sive ferio, quòd penes eos belli pacisve ferendæ seu faciendæ, fœderisq; feriendi jus ac potestas esset: Inter Fociales autem Pater patratus principem locum obtinebat dignitatis. Is, teste Plutarcho in Quæstionibus Romanis, quæstione sexagesima secunda erat, qui habebat liberos vivo & superstite adhuc ejus patre: dictusq; est patratus, id est, perfectus & absolutus, Is erat juris jurandi & panis præses, quem, ut ait Homerus, oportet prorsum & retrorsum videre. Ejus fides atq; custodia committebat Prætor liberos, qui propter formam & florem ætatis custodia videbantur indigere.
units.tr: The Kisbologi were so called among the Opuntians from the rite or office which most Greeks observed in their sacrifices with barley, offering its firstfruits; these men gathered those firstfruits. Otherwise Plutarch testifies in his Greek Questions that the Opuntians had two priests: one who administered the rites of the gods, and another who administered the rites of the Genii. So the Solenses called the priestess of Minerva the Hypocaustra, because she performed certain rites to avert evils. So too the Arval Brothers, who were priests of the fields; augurs are named from auguries; and the Fetiales from the forum, or from ferio, because the power and right of bearing or making war or peace, and of striking a treaty, rested with them. Among the Fetiales the Pater patratus held the chief place of dignity. He, according to Plutarch in the Roman Questions, question sixty-two, was one who had children while his father was still living and surviving; and he was called patratus, that is, perfected and complete. He presided over the oath and the sworn agreement, and, as Homer says, one must look at him forwards and backwards. The praetor committed to his faith and custody those children who, on account of their beauty and the flower of their age, seemed to need guarding.

units.la: A corporis porrò habitu atq; cultu dicti fuerunt apud Romanos Flamines, quasi Filamines, quòd, cùm in capite pilum haberent, in quo bre vis erat virga desuper, habens lanæ aliquid: id autem pro aestu ferre non possent, filo tantùm capita religare tæperunt. Nam nudis eos penitus capitibus incedere nefas erat. Verùm tamen festis diebus filo deposito, pileum imponebant, pro sacerdotii eminentia. Hac Isidorus. Sic ςεφανηφόροι Herculis sacerdotes, apud Græcos fuerunt appellati, quibus ferre coronam, & comam promissam proprium erat.
units.tr: The Romans also named the Flamines from their bodily dress and appearance, as if they were "Filamines," because they wore on the head a small staff (virga) with a little wool on top, a cap (pilum) that they could not bear in the heat, so they bound their heads only with a thread (filum). For it was forbidden for them to go with bare heads at all. On festival days, however, they put down the thread and put on a cap (pileum), as a mark of the eminence of their priesthood. So Isidore. Thus among the Greeks the priests of Hercules were called stephanephoroi [στεφανηφόροι], for it was proper to them to wear a crown and to let their hair grow long.

units.la: Erant etiam apud singulos populos certa sacerdotù nomina. Sic Indorum sacerdotes Brachmanes, Gallorum Druidæ, aliorum alii nominibus fuerunt appellati. Et hæc de sacerdotum nominibus.
units.tr: Each nation also had particular names for its priests. Thus the priests of the Indians were called Brachmanes, the Gallic priests Druids, and others were called by other names. So much on the names of priests.

units.la: Nunc de eorum electione, nominatione, creatione, inauguratione & initiatione quadam dicamus. Munus ipsùm Græcè ἱεροποιῶν, in genere appellatur. Inde καταδιαλέγουσι, ἱεροποιεῖν, ἱεροποιῶν. præficere aliquem, sive sacerdotem creare: & ἀληθῶς ἱερασωνῆς, ὁ ἱερὸς ὡς, ἐορτίρι sacerdotium: & ἀρχιερεὺς ἱερασωνῶν, suscipere sacerdotium: & ἐχει id ἰᾶς ἱεροσωνίν, privatum bahere sacerdotium: & μετάχειν μυςμῶν ἱεροσωνῶν, nullius sacerdotii adipiscendi jus habere; sive esse capacem, apud Demosthenem. Item apud eundem αἱρεῖσθαι ἱερωσύνην, eligere sacerdotem, & ἀρχῶν ἱερέως, electus sacerdos.
units.tr: Now let us say something about their election, nomination, creation, inauguration and initiation. The office itself is called in Greek hieropoiōn [ἱεροποιῶν] in general. From this come the verbs meaning to set someone over the sacred rites, or to create a priest [ἱεροποιεῖν]; to be a true priest, and to hold the priesthood [ἱερασύνη]; to undertake the priesthood; to have the priesthood privately; and to have no right to obtain any priesthood, that is, to be incapable of it, in Demosthenes. Likewise in the same author, to choose a priesthood [αἱρεῖσθαι ἱερωσύνην], to elect a priest, and "a priest who has been elected" [ἱερεὺς αἱρεθείς].

units.la: Apud Latinos deinde hoc munus in genere dicitur Sacerdotium: quod tamen aliquando est dignitas: unde dicimus, Sacerdotium habere, & sacerdotio præditum esse; aliquando vero, proventus sacerdotii, quæ vulgo Beneficia appellantur. Ad hoc autem munus peculiariter pertinet Nominandi verbum, ut patere ex illis Plinii verbis in epistolis: Sic illo die, quo solent sacerdotes nominare, quos sacerdotio dignissimos nominant, me semper nominabant. Hinc dicta Nominatio. Suetonius: Claudius Cæsar, ineunte, in cooptandis per collegia sacerdotibus, neminem nisi juratus nominavit.
units.tr: Among the Latins this office is called in general the sacerdotium, which sometimes means a dignity, whence we say "to hold a priesthood" and "to be endowed with a priesthood." Sometimes, however, it means the revenues of a priesthood, which are commonly called benefices. The word nominate pertains particularly to this office, as is clear from Pliny's words in his letters: "So on that day, when priests are accustomed to nominate, they always nominated me, as the most worthy of the priesthood." Hence the term nomination. Suetonius: "Claudius Caesar, at his entry into office, when priests were being co-opted through the colleges, nominated no one except under oath."

units.la: Cooptandi quoq; verbum electioni erat accommodatum. Cicero: Cooptatum me ab eo in collegium recordabar. Plinius: Me pene adhuc puerum patronum cooptavit. Sacerdotium dari mandari dicitur. Itaq; Iovi illud sacerdotium amplissimum Theomnesto datur. Cicero in Verrem: Populus per religionem sacerdotia mandare non poterat. Idem contra Rullum: Eligere viros amplissimos ad sacerdotia. Idem: Erit causa, quia consilium majorum in eligendis ad sacerdotia viris amplissimis jure ac merito laudare possimus. Idem pro Domo sua: In sacerdotium venire, minos dicimus, an cin ampt Fommen. Inire sacerdotium, idem Cicero: an sein Priesterlich ampt trecten. Hinc & sacerdotium habere idem Cicero dixit: Cujus nomen exisset, haberet sacerdotium, id est, in face: dos esset. Sorte enim nonnunquam sacerdotes fiebant. Hinc sacerdotio præditus, qui habet sacerdotium. Cicero: Licinia virgo Vestalis sanctissimo sacerdotio prædita. Et albi: Amplissimo sacerdotio præditus. Et præesse sacerdotio. Qui & sacra publica tenuerunt, & publicis sacerdotiis præfuerunt. Idem de Senectute: Metellus, Pontifex Maximus, viginti & duos annos sacerdotio præfuit. Idem pro C. Rabirio: Lucius Flaccus homo in sacerdotio terimoniusq;, quibus præerat, diligentissimus.
units.tr: The word co-opt was also suited to election. Cicero: "I remembered that I had been co-opted into the college by him." Pliny: "He co-opted me as advocate when I was still almost a boy." The priesthood is said to be given or entrusted. Thus that most distinguished priesthood of Jupiter is given to Theomnestus. Cicero against Verres: "The people, because of religious scruple, could not entrust priesthoods." The same, against Rullus: "to elect the most distinguished men to priesthoods." The same: "There will be a reason why we may justly and rightly praise the judgment of our ancestors in choosing the most distinguished men for priesthoods." The same, in his speech for his house: we say "to come into a priesthood" [in sacerdotium venire], or in German "ein Priesterlich ampt antreten." Hence Cicero also said "to have a priesthood": whoever's name came out would have the priesthood, that is, would be the heir. For sometimes priests were made by lot. Hence "endowed with a priesthood" means one who holds a priesthood. Cicero: "Licinia, a virgin Vestal, endowed with the most sacred priesthood." And elsewhere: "endowed with the most distinguished priesthood." And "to preside over a priesthood," said of those who held public sacred rites and presided over public priesthoods. The same, in his On Old Age: "Metellus, the Pontifex Maximus, presided over the priesthood for twenty-two years." The same, in his speech for Gaius Rabirius: "Lucius Flaccus, a man most diligent in the priesthood and in the ceremonies over which he presided."

units.la: Capiendi quoq; verbum sacerdotum electioni erat accommodatum. Tranquillus in Augusto: Sacerdotium, in qua et numerum & dignitatem, sed & commoda auxit; præcipuè Vestalium virginum. Quum, in demortuæ locum alium capi oporteret, ambirent q; multi, ne filia in sortem darent, adjuravit si cujusquam neptium suarum competeret ætas, oblaturum se fuisse eam. Capitigitur dicebatur virgo Vestalis, quando ad id sacerdotium legebatur: propterea quod Pontifex Maximus hæc verba dicebat, cum virginem tapiebat: AMATA TE CAPIO. Ideo autem Amata inter capiendum a Pontifice Maximo appellabatur, quoniam eam, quæ prima capta fuit, hoc fuisse nomine, tradit Gellius in primo Noctium Atticarum. Sic Flamines quoque Diales; item Augures & Pontifices capi dicebantur. De Flamine capto exemplum est apud Livium libro vigesimoseptimo ab Urbe condita. Flaccus Flamen captus, P. Licinio Pontifice Maximo.
units.tr: The word take (capere) was also suited to the election of priests. Suetonius in his Life of Augustus: "He increased the number and dignity of the priesthoods, and their privileges too, especially those of the Vestal virgins." When another had to be taken in place of one who had died, and many were ambitious, lest they give their daughters into the lot, he swore that if the age of any of his granddaughters fitted, he would offer her himself. A Vestal virgin was therefore said to be "taken" (captus) when she was chosen for that priesthood, because the Pontifex Maximus said these words when he took the girl by the hand: "I take you, Amata." Amata was called by the Pontifex Maximus during the taking, because Gellius, in the first book of his Attic Nights, relates that the first one taken bore this name. So also the Flamen Dialis, and likewise augurs and pontiffs, were said to be "taken."
