An example of a taken Flamen is in Livy, book twenty-seven from the founding of the City: "Flaccus, Flamen, was taken, while Publius Licinius was Pontifex Maximus."

units.la: Quod autem Sortis fit mentio in electione Vestalium, scribit Gellius Papiam legem se in venisse, quacavebatur, ut Pontifices Maximi arbitratu virgines e populo viginti legerentur, fortitioque in tonsione ex eo numero fieret: quanquam huic legi Popilia sit postea lege abrogatum, ita ut unitusque liceret, modo ætas competeret, filiam ad id sacerdotium ultrò offerre. Aristoteles libro quarto Politicorum: Ut de magistratibus, inquit, queritur, e quibus eos deceat creari, & a quibus, & quomodo: ita de sacerdotibus, qui & quales sint creandi. Idem: Ut magistratus, sic sacerdotes alios dicit esse αἱρετούς; alios κληρωτούς, & alios esse perpetuos, alios diuturnos, alios vero neutros horum. Ibidem focerdotes sive αἱρετούς, sive κληρωτούς, sive suffragiis sint electi, sive forte ducti velit non esse in magistratibus numerandos.
units.tr: As for the mention of the lot in the election of Vestals, Gellius writes that he found the Papian law, by which it was provided that twenty maidens from the people should be chosen at the discretion of the Pontifices Maximi, and that by lot, at the shearing, one should be made from that number. Yet this law was afterwards repealed by the Popilian law, so that any girl whose age fitted might offer herself voluntarily for that priesthood. Aristotle, in book four of the Politics: "As he asks about magistrates, from whom they should be created, and how, so he asks about priests: which and what kind should be created." The same: "Just as with magistrates, so he says some priests are elected (airetoi), some chosen by lot (klērōtoi), and some are for life, some for a long time, and some neither of these. In the same place he says that priests, whether elected (airetoi) or chosen by lot (klērōtoi), or whether appointed by votes or led by chance, should not be counted among the magistrates."

units.la: Donis vero & muneribus sæpe viam sibi muniebant adista sacerdotia: eaq; erant venalia, ut etiam profana munem. Tranquillus de Caligula: Magistreria, inquit, sacerdotii ditissimus quis, & ambi-
units.tr: Indeed they often paved their way to these priesthoods with gifts and bribes, and these were for sale, as even profane offices were. Suetonius on Caligula: "Among the priesthoods, he says, there was one of the richest, and by ambition ..."

units.la: Sacerdotium Latinè. & ambitione & licitatione maximè vicibus comparabat, hoc est, Vnus quisque ex diuriori bus immen̄o pretio & ambitu emebat sacerdotium illud,dicatum ipsius Numini, ut scilicet efset magister & quasi ὀρχιερεὺς, id est, princeps temporarius sacerdotum.
units.tr: "Priesthood" in Latin. It was obtained above all by ambition and by bidding at auction, that is, each of the richer men bought that priesthood, dedicated to the god himself, at an immense price and by canvassing, so that he might be the master and, as it were, the high priest (archiereus), that is, the temporary prince of the priests.

units.la: Obseruandum autem alios fuisse sacerdotes generales omnium Deorum,qui quorum vis Deorum sacris præerant: alios verò fuisse certorum Deus erant destinati: unde etiam nomina sua habuerunt, de quibus supra. Ad hoc alludens Cicero de Legibus: Divis alis,inquit,alii sacerdotes,omnibus Pontifices,singulis Flamines sunto.
units.tr: It must be observed that there were some general priests of all the gods, who presided over the sacred rites of all the gods, and others who were appointed to particular gods; whence they also had their own names, of which we spoke above. Alluding to this, Cicero in his On the Laws says: "Let there be other priests for the divine beings, pontiffs for all, and flamines for each one."

units.la: In omnibus autem hisce generalibus omnium Deorum, sive particularibus cæterorum singulorum, Deorum sacerdotibus hac feré quæ sequuntur antiquitus, præsertim in eorum creatione, atq; electiû obseruari solebant: nempe Animus, Corpus, Vestitus, Sexus, Ætas, Conjugium sive Cælibatus, Natio, Vitæ genus ac institutum, Honosæ Dignitas, Potestas, Gradus, Merces, Lucrum atq; Prouentus, Pœnæ atq; Supplicia, Numerus denig;, & Victus,jejunia item & abstinentia a certis diebus vel etiam aliis rebus.
units.tr: In all these priests, whether general for all the gods or particular for each of the other gods, the following were customarily observed in ancient times, especially in their creation and election: namely, mind, body, dress, sex, age, marriage or celibacy, nation, manner and rule of life, honour, dignity, power, rank, pay, gain and income, penalties and punishments, number finally, and diet, also fasts and abstinence from certain days or even from certain things.

units.la: Primùm igitur ipse Animus, ejusq; habitus, nempe scientia, cum aliarum artium ac disciplìnarum,tum verò atque inprimis eorum sacrorum, quibus erant præpositi, quæq; illos erant curanda, requirebatur. Vnde Cicero: Arrogans de religione,de rebus diuinis cerimoniis, sacris Pontificibus docere conati. Deinde virtutes quoque animi, ut castitatem, sobrietatem, temperantiam, vigilantiam & diligentiam in administrandis sacris requirebant. Inde Seneca: Pro pudicitia vota facienda sunt, profitutæ mandabitis? Et Vestalium virginum si qua incestì contrà efset,anteorn ciuium mæsto silentio offerebatur, νύαξ, circa Collinam portam in subterraneum stecum dimissa, terrâq; slatim superinjecta necabatur: Gellius. Erant tamen plerique ipsorum sacerdotes cum magicis artibus, tum omni vitiorum, scelerum, flagitiorumq; genere (quorum parens & procreatrix est idololatria) dediti & addicti.
units.tr: First, then, the mind itself and its disposition were required, namely knowledge, both of other arts and disciplines, and above all of those sacred rites over which they were set and which they were to attend to. Hence Cicero: "Arrogant men have tried to teach the pontiffs about religion and the divine ceremonies and sacred rites." Then the virtues of the mind were also required in administering the sacred rites, such as chastity, sobriety, temperance, watchfulness and diligence. Hence Seneca: "Vows must be made for chastity; will you hand them over to a prostitute?" And if any Vestal virgin was found to have committed incest, she was brought before the people with sorrowful silence, lowered alive into an underground chamber near the Colline Gate, and earth was at once thrown over her and she was killed, so Gellius. Yet most of these priests were devoted and addicted both to magic arts and to every kind of vice, crime and shameful deed (of which idolatry is the parent and producer).

units.la: Secundò ut animi, ita corporn quoque certam dispositionem in sacerdotibus suis requirebant. Ac illos quidem corpore volebant esse sano & integro: eos autem, qui insigni aliquo corporis vitio laborabant,membrosque aliquo captierant ac mutili,eos nequaquam ad rem diuinam trabtan dam existimabant aptos esse & idoneos, sed admittere nefas putabant. Ad utrumque referenda est lex illa antiqua de sacerdotibus: Sacerdos sit integer, de qua hæc leguntur apud Senecam: Metellus Pontifex,cùm arderet, Vestæ templum, dum Palladium raptu, oculos perdit, sacerdotum illi negatur. Et postea: Lex integrum ad animum refert,non ad corpus, Lex æstimari hoc voluit tunc,cùm quis peteret,non cùm haberet sacerdotium. Idem: Ambitiosa lex est ad sacerdotium, notas non sanctitatis tantùm, sed felicitatis admittit, inquirit in mores, in corpus, in vitam. Vide tu quem admodum tam morosæ legi fatus facias. Idem: Fas sacerdoti non esse,ancillam tibi similem habere,fieri ne sacerdotem fas erit? Et post: Non potest & in ea sperari sacerdos,in qua sperari meretrix potest: alii oculis leno vitam æstimat,alii Pontifex. Idem: Absint ex hoc foro lenones, absint meretrices, ne quid parum sanctum occurrat, dum sacerdos legitur. Et post: Quo mihi sacerdotem,cujus precaria est castitas, si mater tua profitiisset tibi noceret. Idem: Pro libertate vota facienda sunt,captivæ mandabitis? Idem : Ancillæ ex lupanaribus sacerdoti non emuntur. Coram sacerdote obscœni homines absistinent. Non sine causa sacerdoti licitor apparet. Occurrenti tibi meretricem submovisset? Idem: Castigationem ex Pontificis Mariani arbitrio meruerat sacerdos si te e lupanari redemisset. Idem : Sacerdos non integri corporis,quasi mali ominis res vitanda est. Hoc in victimis notatur, quanto magis in sacerdotibus? Potest sacerdotium magis observanda est nobilitas. Non enim sine ira Deorum debilitatur sacerdos. Apparet non propitios esse sacerdoti Deos, quem ne sanati quidem servant. Hactenus Seneca de personis & minustris sacrorum : ut ne sacerdos nisi integer adsumatur & qui integer sit habendus.
units.tr: Secondly, just as they required a certain disposition of mind, so too they required a certain disposition of body in their priests. They wanted them to be sound and whole in body. Those who suffered from some notable bodily defect, or who were maimed or mutilated in some limb, they thought in no way fit or suitable to be admitted to the sacred service, but considered it wrong to admit them. To both of these refers that ancient law concerning priests: "let the priest be whole," of which Seneca writes as follows: "When the temple of Vesta was burning, Metellus the Pontifex, while snatching the Palladium, lost his eyes, and the priesthood was denied him." And afterwards: "The law refers 'whole' to the mind, not to the body. The law wished the man to be assessed at the time when he sought the priesthood, not when he held it." The same: "The law for the priesthood is ambitious; it admits marks not only of holiness but of good fortune; it inquires into morals, body and life. See how you may satisfy so fussy a law." The same: "It is not right for a priest to have a maidservant like you; will it be right to make you a priest?" And later: "A priest cannot be hoped for in a woman in whom a prostitute can be hoped for; some judge life by the eyes of a pimp, others by the eyes of a pontiff." The same: "Let pimps and prostitutes be absent from this forum, lest anything unseemly meet the eye while a priest is being chosen." And later: "Why do I want a priest whose chastity is precarious? If your mother had professed it, it would have harmed you." The same: "Vows must be made for liberty; will you hand them over to a captive?" The same: "Maidservants are not bought from brothels for a priest. Obscene men keep away from a priest. Not without reason does a lictor appear before a priest. Would he not have driven away a prostitute meeting you?" The same: "A priest who had redeemed you from a brothel would have earned a rebuke at the discretion of the Pontifex Marianus." The same: "A priest who is not of whole body is to be avoided as a thing of ill omen. This is noted of victims; how much more of priests? Nobility must be observed more carefully in the priesthood, for a priest is not weakened without the anger of the gods. It is clear that the gods are not favourable to a priest whom they do not even preserve when he is healed." So far Seneca on the persons and ministers of the sacred rites, namely that a priest should be taken only if whole, and that one who is whole must be kept.

units.la: Extat de hac etiam re quæstio apud Plutarchum in quæstionibus Romanis, Cur interdictum fuerit Auguri, Si ulcus haberet, aves observare. Idem ibidem, Vt vitiatam, inquit, aut avem ulcerofamreisacræ faciunde gratia usurpare nefas erat: si camino ab omnibus molestiis & quasi ulceribus ac morbibus vacuo, sincero, puro & integro tractari oportet. Et quæstione quadragesima Romanarum, apud Charonenses coronatum esse, comam alere, ferro armatum Phocen- <bl>M</bl> 2 fium fines non ingredi,propria fuisse sacerdotis munia ceßtatur idem. Sic apud Magos qui essent lentiginosi, tanquam Dijs in visi,ab aris summo vebantur: item qui elati reuerenter, quibusque viventibus exsequiæ factæ essent, veluti profani a sacris propellebantur, teste Herodoto. Sic apud Hebræos menstruatis factis posset quadraginta dies, & qui impetigine deformes essent, eemplí aditus erat interclusus.
units.tr: This matter is also discussed by Plutarch in his Roman Questions, under the question why it was forbidden for an augur to observe birds if he had a sore. The same author says in that place that it was unlawful to use a bird that was blemished or ulcerous for performing sacred rites; the bird had to be handled in a pure, sound, whole and unblemished state, free of all troubles and, as it were, of sores and diseases. In the fortieth of his Roman Questions the same author states that the priest's proper duties were these: to be crowned, to let his hair grow, and not to enter the territory of the Phocians armed with iron, among the Charonenses. <bl>M</bl> 2 So among the Magi, those who were scabby were carried down from the altars as if they were hateful to the gods; likewise those who had been reverently buried, or for whom funeral rites had been performed while they were still alive, were driven away from the sacred rites as profane, according to Herodotus. Likewise among the Hebrews, a woman who had menstruated was kept from the sacred rites for forty days, and those who were disfigured by scabs or eruptions were shut out from access to the altar.

units.la: Præterea ut animorum,ita corporum quoque puritatem judicabant suis sacerdotibus esse necessariam. Volebant, inquam, eos & animis & corporibus esse puros ac mundos. Nam corpore impuro & sordido sacra tractare, nefas ducebant: qui quidem corporis cultus atque habitus fuit vel naturalis, vel artificialis, vel affectitius: alii erant capite raso; alii comati; alii barbati; alii imberbes: alius erat barbæ breves; alius promissa. Sic, exempli gratia, Isiaci, id est, Isidis sacerdotes apud Ægyptios erant raso capite: contra Stephanophoros, Herculis sacerdotibus, apud Græcos, ferre coronam & comam promissam proprium erat, teste Alexandro ab Alexandro libro sexto, capite duodecimo, & libro secundo, capite octavo. Ita Cybelis sacerdotes variis fucatos coloribus, & facies pigmento delitos, oculosque obunctos, cum mitella & crocoto, lineo calcamento, ante simulacrum Deæ incedere solitos & cum tinnita Cymbalorum & sonitu tympanorum sacrum facium fecisse legimus apud eundem Alexandrum libro secundo, capite eodem octavo. Sic Britannorum conjuges nuriuque glasto toto corpore oblitas quibusdam in sacris nudas incestuisse, Æthiopum colorem imitantes, scribit Plinius libro vigesimo secundo, capite primo. Pertinet huc symbolum Pythagoræ, Penes sacrificium nefas cæsis unguibus: quod unguium quoque habitam fuisse rationem indicio esse poterit. Referendæ præterea huc, illa aquæ lustrales, quibus vel totum corpus, vel aliquot ejus partes, ut caput, manus, atque pedes abluebant.
units.tr: Besides this, they judged that purity of body, as well as of soul, was necessary for their priests. They wanted them, I say, to be pure and clean both in mind and in body. For they considered it sinful to handle sacred things with an impure and filthy body. The care and appearance of the body was either natural, or artificial, or assumed: some had their heads shaved, some wore their hair long, some were bearded, some were beardless; some kept short beards, others long. Thus, for example, the Isiac priests, that is, the priests of Isis among the Egyptians, had shaven heads; whereas among the Greeks it was the particular custom of the Stephanophori, the priests of Hercules, to wear a crown and long hair, as Alexander ab Alexandro testifies in book six, chapter twelve, and book two, chapter eight. So too we read that the priests of Cybele, painted with various colours, their faces smeared with paint, their eyes anointed, with a mitre and saffron and linen shoes, used to walk before the image of the goddess and perform their sacred rite with the clashing of cymbals and the sound of drums, as the same Alexander reports in book two, chapter eight. Pliny, in book twenty-two, chapter one, writes that the wives and daughters of the Britons, smeared with woad over their whole bodies, went naked in certain sacred rites, imitating the colour of the Ethiopians. To this belongs the saying of Pythagoras, that it is unlawful to perform sacrifice with the nails cut; this may show that care was also taken of the nails. Here too belong those lustral waters with which they washed either the whole body or some of its parts, such as the head, hands and feet.

units.la: Tertio, quod attinet ad vestitu & amictum sacerdotii sive eorum, qui sacris procurandis præerant, ejus curiosa valde superstitio atque habita fuit in sacris ratio. Hinc, Pura Vestimenta, inquit Paullus, sacerdotes ad sacrificium habebant, id est, non obscura, non fulgurita, non fusca, non maculatam habentia. Pure lavatum, ut est apud eundem, erat idem, quod pura aqua lavatum. Nam ut corpora; ita vestimenta quoque sacerdotum, ut etiam aliorum, ante quam ad sacra accederent ablui, sive lavarentur solita. Plato: Nam, inquit, in sacrificiis & celebritatibus pulchra vestæ aureæ, corona sacerdotes rem divinam facit. Sacerdos autem, qui victimam ciebat pura in vestis & candidæ plerunque intextilis flola, nec majoris operæ quam menstruæ nunquam in purpura & auro.
units.tr: Thirdly, as regards the clothing and dress of the priesthood, or of those who presided over the sacred rites, there was a very scrupulous superstition and a set practice in worship. Hence Paul says: "The priests had pure vestments for the sacrifice," that is, vestments that were not dark, not dyed, not dusky, and had no stain. To be washed purely, as the same author has it, meant the same as to be washed with pure water. For just as bodies, so also the vestments of the priests, and of others too, were customarily washed or cleansed before they approached the sacred rites. Plato: "For," he says, "in sacrifices and solemn celebrations the priest performs the divine rite in a beautiful vest, golden, with a crown." The priest who offered the victim wore a pure and white vest, generally of linen, and never anything of greater labour than a woollen one, nor anything in purple and gold.

units.la: Fuit autem univerus hic sacerdotum vestitus omnino varius ac diversus, secundum vel corporis partes, vel materiam, vel colorem, vel formam, vel sexum, vel quantitatem, vel ejus rem cum brevitatem, tum longitudinem. Ut vero corporis duæ potissimæ partes sunt extremæ, caput nimirum atque pedes: ita hæ certo modo ac certis vestibus indui atque ornari potissimum solebant.
units.tr: This whole vesture of the priests was, however, altogether varied and diverse, according to the parts of the body, the material, the colour, the form, the sex, the quantity, and the length or shortness of the garment. Now the two chief extreme parts of the body are the head and the feet; accordingly these were especially wont to be covered and adorned in a fixed manner and with fixed garments.

units.la: Quantum ad caput attinet alii aperto erant capite, alii operto atque tecto: & quidem alio tempore capita sua aperire, alio tegere atque velare confuerunt: Observandum tamen perpauca fuisse sacra, quæ aperto nudo, capite erant celebranda. Nam plerique sacerdotes acommes ii, qui sacra faciebant, isque interesse operto ac velato; non autem aperto & nudo capite fuerint. Plautus in Curculione: Quis hic est, qui operto capite Æsculapium Salutat, id est, adorat ac veneratur?
units.tr: As regards the head, some priests went with the head uncovered, others with it covered and wrapped; and indeed at one time they were accustomed to uncover their heads, at another to cover and veil them. It should be observed, however, that there were very few rites that had to be celebrated with the head bare and uncovered. For most priests, and those who performed the sacred rites and took part in them, were covered and veiled, not bare-headed. Plautus, in the Curculio: "Who is this who, with his head covered, greets, that is, adores and reveres, Aesculapius?"

units.la: Suetonius de Aulo Vitellio: Idem miri, inquit, in adulando ingenii, primus Cajum Cæsarem adorari, ut Deum, instituit, quum reversus ex Syria non aliter adire ausus esset, quam capite velato, circumvertensque, deinde procumbens. Vitellius igitur, cum Caligulam adorare, ut Deum, vellet, capite velato eum salutavit, qui mos erat eorum, qui Deos venerabantur. Sic Romani sacerdotes cum adorarent, rem divinam factturi, capita velabant vittis, mitris, coronis: cum Græci aperto essent capite. Plutarchus testis est in quæstionibus, virot inter gentes, et inprimis quidem eos, qui Romanorum legibus vivebant, solitos fuisse velatis capitibus Deos adorare & inter sacra vestem ad auresque attollere: partim quidem id eo gestu & habitu humiliores se reddere: partim vero inter precandum trifle quid aut ignominiosum alicunde occurreret, quo animi attentio religiosa turbaretur. Meminit hujus ritus Virgilius, qui Helenum Aeneae sic dicentem introducit: Purpureo velare comas adoperta amictu, Ne qua inter sanctos ignes in honore Deorum Hostilis facies occurrat, & omnia turbet. Hunc, socii, morem sacrorum, hunc ipse teneto. Haec casu maneant in religione nepotes.
units.tr: Suetonius, on Aulus Vitellius: "He, a man of wondrous talent in flattery, was the first to institute the worship of Gaius Caesar as a god, since, when he returned from Syria, he did not dare to approach him otherwise than with his head veiled, turning round and then prostrating himself." So Vitellius, wishing to adore Caligula as a god, greeted him with his head veiled, which was the custom of those who worshipped the gods. Thus the Roman priests, when they prayed and were about to perform the divine rite, covered their heads with fillets, mitres and crowns; the Greeks, however, were bare-headed. Plutarch is a witness in his Questions that many peoples, and especially those who lived under Roman laws, were accustomed to adore the gods with veiled heads and to raise their clothing to their ears during the sacred rites: partly to make themselves more humble by this gesture and posture, and partly so that, if anything sad or ill-omened happened to come upon them while they prayed, the religious attention of their mind might not be disturbed. Virgil also mentions this rite, introducing Helenus speaking thus to Aeneas: "Covering your hair with a purple mantle, lest among the holy fires, in the honour of the gods, some hostile sight should meet you and upset everything. Companions, keep this custom of the sacred rites, hold it yourselves; let your descendants preserve it in religion."

units.la: Exhis ipsis igitur versibus liquet, sacrificantes Diis omnibus caput velare solitos, ideo ne inter litigionem vagis aliquid offerrent obturbitur.
units.tr: From these very verses, therefore, it is clear that those who sacrificed to all the gods were accustomed to veil their heads, so that nothing ill-omened should disturb them in the midst of the rite.

units.la: At vero Saturno Romani capite aperto rem divinam faciebant, propterea quod Veritas occultari obscurarive non potest, cujus parentem ac Deum Romani Saturnum habebant. Hinc Lucem facere Saturno sacrificantes dicebantur, inquit Festus: quod ipsum factum est more Graeco. Unde Plutarchus. Ritu peregrino & capite aperto, conjungit. Caussas hujus rei multas affert idem, sic scribens: Quid est, inquit, quod Saturno capite aperto immolant? An quod velandi capitis ritum Aeneas tradidit? Saturni vero sacrificium pervetustum est? An illud potius quoniam Dii caelestibus immolantes velantur? Saturnum vero terrestrem & chthonium esse arbitrantur? An quod veritas oculi obscuratur, non potest? Veritatis autem parentem ac Deum Romani habent? Haec Plutarchus. Exillis autem ratione, quam inter alias affert, An, quoniam Diis caelestibus immolatur, velantur? Saturnum vero terrestrem & chthonium esse arbitrantur, videtur posse colligi, illos Dis tectos sumus velato; terrestribus autem aperto capite sacra fecisse. Festus, Saturnii, inquit, dicebantur qui capitum in clivo Capitolino incolebant, ubi ara dicata ei Deo ante bellum Trojanum fuerat: quia ante eam supplicant apertis capitibus. Macrobius in 2. Saturno ex Balbi sententia apud arum Maximam, in qua Hercules Bos sacrificabatur, observatum ait, ne lestisternium fieret; ubi etiam aperto capite omnes sacra fecisse tribus: quod fiebat, ne quis Dei habitum imitaretur. Nam ibi ipse operi caput erat. Varro ait, sacrorum hunc fuisse morem, ut sicut Graeco ritu sacrificari tur in ara Maxima. Hoc et ammonuit addit Bassus, idcirco hoc factum fuisse, quia ara Maxima ante adventum Aeneae in Italia constituta est, quibus hunc ritum capitis velandi in vexit.
units.tr: But the Romans performed the divine rite to Saturn with the head uncovered, because truth cannot be hidden or obscured, and the Romans regarded Saturn as the parent and god of Truth. Hence, says Festus, those sacrificing to Saturn were said "to make light," which itself was done after the Greek manner. Whence Plutarch: "with a foreign rite and with the head uncovered" he joins the two. The same author gives many reasons for this, writing thus: "Why is it that they sacrifice to Saturn with the head uncovered? Is it because Aeneas handed down the custom of veiling the head? Or is the sacrifice to Saturn very ancient? Or is it rather because the gods are veiled when they sacrifice to the heavenly gods? Or do they think that Saturn is earthly and chthonic? Or is it because the truth of the eye is obscured, and cannot be? Or do the Romans hold that Truth has Saturn as her parent and god?" These are Plutarch's words. From his reason among the others, "Or is it because they are veiled when sacrifice is made to the heavenly gods, while they think Saturn is earthly and chthonic?", it seems one may gather that the Romans performed sacred rites with the head veiled for the heavenly gods, but with the head bare for the earthly ones. Festus: "The Saturnii," he says, "were called those who dwelt in the Capitoline slope, where an altar had been dedicated to that god before the Trojan War, because they prayed before it with uncovered heads." Macrobius, in book two, says that according to the opinion of Balbus, at the Ara Maxima, in which the Hercules ox was sacrificed, it was observed concerning Saturn that there was to be no lectisternium; there too all the three tribes performed the sacred rite with the head uncovered, which was done so that no one should imitate the dress of the god; for there the god himself had his head uncovered. Varro says that this custom of sacred rites was observed, namely that sacrifice was offered at the Ara Maxima in the Greek manner. Bassus adds that this too was reminded of, and that this was done because the Ara Maxima was set up in Italy before the arrival of Aeneas, who brought in this rite of veiling the head.

units.la: Praeterea Honori quoque Deo, aperto capite, rem divinam faciebat, quia splendidum quidem et illustre & apertum latet, patens sit gloria. Nobiliores vero & potentiores viros capite aperto venerabantur, ut in vidicam illis detrahierent, ne pares Dius immortalibus honorent ere, nec ea eodem cultu delectari viderentur. Testis idem Plutarchus, quaestione decima quinta. Amen Marcus Varro capi: caperiri affectum magistratuum, non venerationis causa, sed veletudinis prodidit, ut sententia asserti Plinius libro vigesimo octavo. Cur parentes obstant & filii velatis capitibus, filiae nudis capitibus pudenda, crimibus, & mulieres tectae; mares autem nudis capitibus in publicum prodire fuerint soliti, vide Plutarchum quaestione decima quarta Romanas um quaestionum.
units.tr: Furthermore, the divine rite was also performed to the god Honos with the head uncovered, because what is splendid, illustrious and open lies exposed, and glory ought to be manifest. Men of higher rank and greater power, however, were worshipped with the head uncovered, so that they might be stripped of the crowning honours lest they seem to honour mortals equally with the immortal gods and to delight in the same worship. The same Plutarch is a witness, in question fifteen. Marcus Varro reported that the covering of the head by magistrates was done not for the sake of reverence but for the sake of health, as Pliny asserts in book twenty-eight. On why fathers and sons were veiled, daughters with bare heads was shameful, women were covered, while men were accustomed to go out in public with bare heads, see Plutarch's fourteenth question of the Roman Questions.

units.la: Pileorum capitis integumenta varia fuerunt & multiplicia. De Pileorum quidem usu apud Romanos, & de capitis aperiendi vel operiendi more atque ritu vide plura apud Iustum Lipsium de Amphitheatro. Hujusmodi autem, inter alia integumenta capitis, illud fuit quod Varro vocat; de quo sic scribit: Capital dictum a capite, quod sacerdotale in capite e. iamnum habere solent. Idem de Rica, alio genere integumenti: Rica dicta a ritu, quod Romano ritu facium fuisse feminae cum faciunt, capita velant. Festus: Rica erat velamen quadratum, fimbriatum, purpureum, quo Flaminicae pro palliolo utebantur. Alii dicunt, quodex lana fiat fuccalba, quod confiscant Virgines ingenuae patrimae, matrimae civis, et inficiatur cerevio colore. Idem: Rica & Ricula vocantur par vaiictura, ut palliola, ad usum capitis facta. Gramius quidem ajt esse muliebre cingulum capitis, quo pro viet a laminica redimiatur.
units.tr: Coverings for the head were varied and many. On the use of caps among the Romans, and on the custom and ritual of uncovering or covering the head, see more in Justus Lipsius, On the Amphitheatre. Among the other head coverings of this kind was the one Varro calls the capital, and on it he writes thus: "The capital is so called from the head (caput), because priests are accustomed to wear it on their heads even now." Of another kind of covering, the rica, he says: "The rica is so named from the rite, because Roman women, when they perform sacred rites, cover their heads with it." Festus says: "The rica was a square veil, fringed and purple, which the Flaminica used in place of a little cloak." Others say it is made of wool, white, which freeborn girls whose fathers and mothers are citizens wear, and that it is dyed with saffron. Again: "The rica and the ricula are named as a kind of wrap, like little cloaks, made for use on the head." Gramius indeed says it is a woman's headband, by which the hair is bound up in front of the forehead band.

units.la: Sic Tutulum dicebant Flaminicarum capitis ornamentum, quod fiat vitta purpurea, inv ea crinibus, & extrállum in altitudinem. Quidam pilcum lanarum, formæ tali figuratum, quæ Flamines ac Pontifices utebantur. Ennius: Filiorcs, Argeos & tutulatos.
units.tr: So also the tutulus was the ornament of the Flaminicae's head, which was made of a purple ribbon, with the hair bound up in it and raised to a height. Some say it was a cap of wool, shaped in such a form, which the Flamens and Pontiffs used. Ennius: "Of sons, Argei and wearers of the tutulus."

units.la: Albogalerus, eodem teste, a galea nominatur pileum capitis, quo Diales Flamines id est, sacerdotes jovis utebantur. Fiebant enim ex hostia alba, lovi caesa: cui affigebatur apex virgæ oleaginæ.
units.tr: The albogalerus, by the same authority, takes its name from galea (helmet): it is the cap of the head which the Dialis Flamens, that is, the priests of Jupiter, used. For it was made from a white victim sacrificed to Jupiter, and to it was fastened a point (apex) of olive wood.

units.la: Apex, ut idem Festus ait, sacerdotum erat infigne, dictus ab eo, quod comprehendere Antiqui vinculo, apere dicebant. Unde apinus id, qui conveniente alicui iunctus est. Hinc Apiculum, ut idem ait, filum, quo Flamines velatum apicem gerunt.
units.tr: The apex, as the same Festus says, was the badge of priests, and it was named from the fact that the ancients used to call binding with a cord apere. Hence apinus is the word for one who is joined to someone in a suitable bond. From this comes the apiculum, as the same writer says: the thread by which Flamens wear the veiled apex.

units.la: Calyptra item genus erat integumenti, quo capita aperiebant sacerdotes, sacra sua administrantes.
units.tr: The calyptra was likewise a kind of covering with which priests veiled their heads while performing their sacred rites.

units.la: Arculum appellabant circulum, quem capiti imponebant ad sustinenda commodius vasa, quae ad sacra publica capite portabantur.
units.tr: They called the arculum a circle which they placed on the head to support more conveniently the vessels that were carried on the head at public sacrifices.

units.la: Hic referende mitræ, diademata, infulæ, ferta, corona & alia capitis ornamenta, vel ex aro, argento, margaritis, gemmis, vel ex herbis, floribusque variis confecta. Pileî Pontificalis meminit etiam Plutarchus, in quæstionibus Romanis quæstione quadragesima sic scribens: Pontifices apud Romanos proprium hoc erat, ut capite velato, neque distinctis, ab urbe abesset, neque pileum (apicem ipsi vocabant: unde Flaminis nomen) unquam deponeret.
units.tr: Here belong the mitres, diadems, fillets, garlands, crowns, and other head ornaments, made either of gold, silver, pearls, and gems, or of various herbs and flowers. Plutarch also mentions the Pontifical cap, in the Roman Questions, question forty, writing thus: "It was a peculiar custom of the Roman Pontiffs that, with head veiled, they were not absent from the city without being distinguished, and that they never put off the cap (which they themselves called the apex, whence the name Flamen)."

units.la: Dixi de capite: Veniamus ad pedes. Aliquando igitur pedibus nudis: aliquando calceatis sacrificabant. De priorit ritu sic scribit Plato: Triumphales viri, & qui amplissimos honores adempti fuissent, in triumphi ornatu, uni in praetexta lotis manibus & fronde coronati, sanctis & venerabiles nudis pedibus & tonsa coma ad rem divinam accedebant; idque jam a Pythagora ritum Lacedæmonii observarunt, qui nudis pedibus adorandum sacrificandumque censuerunt. Hinc Nudipedalia sacra. Ac notum est illud symbolum Pythagoricum: Discalceatus sacrifica & adora. Ex ad verso quod ad posteriorem attinet ritum, calceatos Ægyptiorum sacerdotes sacrificasse scribit Herodotus, & papyraceos quidem calceos gestasse. Alexander ab Alexandro Cybelis sacerdotis lineo calceamento ante simulacrum Deæ incedere solitos fuisse.
units.tr: I have spoken of the head; let us come to the feet. Sometimes, then, they sacrificed with bare feet, sometimes shod. On the former rite Plato writes thus: "Men who had celebrated triumphs, and those who had been deprived of the highest honours, came to the divine rite in triumphal dress, crowned with a wreath and wearing the praetexta, with washed hands, holy and venerable, barefoot and with shorn hair; and the Lacedaemonians observed this rite from the time of Pythagoras, who judged that one should worship and sacrifice barefoot." Hence the sacred Nudipedalia. And that Pythagorean saying is well known: "Sacrifice and worship unshod." On the other hand, as to the later rite, Herodotus writes that the priests of Egypt sacrificed shod, and wore sandals of papyrus. Alexander ab Alexandro writes that the priests of Cybele used to walk before the image of the goddess in linen shoes.

units.la: Manibus etiam suis tenere atque gestare fuerunt foliis quædam munera sui insignia & instrumenta, ut baculos, virgas & alia generis. Hinc Iiaci apud Ægyptios manibus sistrum tenebant, aut ramum abjuntibus marinis, vel nuces pineas; de quo vide Theophr.
units.tr: They also held and carried in their hands certain gifts, their insignia and instruments, such as staffs, rods, and other things of that kind. Hence among the Egyptians the priests of Isis held a sistrum in their hands, or a branch, or pine nuts; on this see Theophrastus.
Linen-bearers.

units.la: Materia quoque vestium sacerdotalium & sacrificantium fuit varia & multiplex. erat lana, linum, purpura. Ægyptiorum quidam sacerdotum vestes erant ex lino: unde nigeri fuerunt dicti Iisdis, Dea Ægyptiorum, sacerdotes: sicut ipsa quoque Isis Linigera dicitur. Ovidius: Vidi ergo linigera numen violasse fatentur. Isis, &c.
units.tr: The material of priestly and sacrificing vestments was also varied and manifold: there was wool, linen, and purple. Some of the priests of Egypt wore garments of linen; whence the priests of Isis, the goddess of the Egyptians, were called linigeri, just as Isis herself is called Linigera. Ovid: "They confess that they saw the god of the linen-bearing one violated, Isis, etc."

units.la: Juvenalis de sacerdotibus ejus: Cum grege linigero circumdatus & grege calvo.
units.tr: Juvenal, of her priests: "Surrounded by the linen-bearing crowd and the bald crowd."

units.la: Martialis: Linigeri fugiunt calvi, fistratăq; turba.
units.tr: Martial: "The bald linen-bearers flee, and the crowd of sistrum-players."

units.la: De religiosis Ægyptiorum vestibus sic scribit Herodotus: Sacerdotes linea ferunt vestimenta, semper recens ablua, huic rei semper vacantes. Idem calceos papyraceos gestant, aliam vestem aut alios calceos induere ejus fas non est. Genitalia circumcidunt ritu Iudaeorum. Plinius libro decimo nono, capite primo scribit, frutice gigni in Ægypto, quem Gossypion vocat, plurima xylon: & ideo lina inde fa&a xylina: ex quibus sacerdotibus Ægyptiis gnarissime fiunt. Quin etiam Apuleius cesimonias Ægyptiorum luculenter explicans sic ait: Influunt turba sacrorum. mistiata viri, fœminæque omnis dignitatis, lineæ vestis candore puro lumis. Tranquillus Suetonius Tiberio Cæsare: Externas cerimonias, anguis, Ægyptios Iudaicosque ritus compescuit, colentes qui superstitione ea tenebantur, religiosas vestes cum instrumento omni comburere. Iudeorum vestes religiosæ quales fuerint Hieronymus in epistola ad Fabiolam de vestibus sacerdotalis & Iosephus libro tertio Antiquitatum & libro sexto belli Iudaici copiose describunt.
units.tr: Herodotus writes thus about the sacred garments of the Egyptians: "The priests wear linen garments, always freshly washed, being always devoted to this business. The same priests wear sandals of papyrus; it is not lawful for them to put on any other clothing or other sandals. They circumcise their genitals after the manner of the Jews." Pliny, in book nineteen, chapter one, writes that a shrub called gossypion grows in Egypt, which yields much xylon, and that linens made from it are called xylina; and from these the Egyptian priests are very skilfully made. Moreover, Apuleius, explaining the ceremonies of the Egyptians with brilliance, says: "A crowd of sacred persons flows in, men and women of every rank, clothed in linen of pure, shining whiteness." Suetonius, in the life of Tiberius Caesar: "He suppressed foreign ceremonies, Egyptian and Jewish rites, and compelled those who were held in that superstition to burn their sacred vestments with all their equipment." What the sacred vestments of the Jews were like, Jerome in his letter to Fabiola, On the Priestly Garments, and Josephus in book three of the Antiquities and book six of the Jewish War, describe at length.

units.la: Quantum ad colorem vestium sacerdotalium attinet; alii nigris; alii, & quidem plerique alibi seu candidis vestibus erant amicti: Sic enim exempli gratia, Ægyptiorum sacerdotes ex lino puro & candido vestes habebant. Sic Romanos albatos fuisse dicebus festis, testatur in Eleftra Lipsius. Sic Ianoni vestes candida sacrificabatur: i temà, Cereri, mense Aprili cum lampadibus, & rodis accensis, quando porcam illi mactarent. Vestæ, vel Dees, si quando Vestales virgines sacra libarent, eo cultu ornatæ, ut erant, & vittata penegebant. Album tamen præterea vestimentum, quod subfibulum vocabatur, oblongum, & præextextum, & quadrangulum in capite sumebant, fibulaque subnectebant. Tertullianus libro de Pallio & cultu docet, Cereris Eleusiniæ sacerdotes candido, Saturni rubro, Bellonæ nigro habitu fuisse, Æsculapii pallium cum cupidis gestabat. Verba ejus hæc sunt: Cur illos non spectas vel illos item habitus, qui no vitare vestitus religionem mentiantur, cum obcultum omnia candidatum & ob velum vittæ & privilegium galeri Ceres initiantur: cum ob dei versam affectionem tenebricæ vestes, & tetrici super caput vellers in Bellonæ monetes fugantur: cum lactoris purpuræ ambitio & galatici rubor insuperbia Saturnum commendat: cum ipsum hoc pallium morosis ordinatum, & crepidæ Græcatæ gracatum Æsculapio adulentur. Et cur in lucta mulieres albas gesserint vestes, albataque vittas, Plutarchus rationem reddit in quæstionibus Romanis, quæstione vigesima sexta.
units.tr: As for the colour of priestly garments, some were clothed in black, others, and indeed most, in white or other bright garments. Thus, for example, the priests of Egypt had garments of pure white linen. That the Romans were clothed in white on festival days is attested by Lipsius in his Electa. So white garments were offered to Juno, and to Ceres in the month of April, with torches and burning pine, when they sacrificed a sow to her. When the Vestal virgins offered sacred rites to Vesta or to the gods, they were adorned with that dress just as they were, and carried the fillets. Besides this, they also took up a white garment, which was called the subfibulum, long, bordered with purple, and square, and fastened it on the head with a clasp. Tertullian, in his book On the Pallium and Dress, teaches that the priests of Eleusinian Ceres wore white, those of Saturn red, and those of Bellona black; and the priest of Aesculapius wore a cloak with a hood. His words are these: "Why do you not look at those other garbs too, which pretend to avoid the religion of clothing, when all things are hidden, and Ceres is initiated with a veil of ribbon and a cap's privilege; when, because of the goddess's altered disposition, dark garments and gloomy veils are put over the head in the mysteries of Bellona; when the splendour of the purple toga and the flush of the Gallic cloak commend Saturn for pride; when this very pallium, arranged for the fastidious, and the Greek sandal, are flattered as Greek for Aesculapius." And why women wore white garments and white fillets in the rites of Luna, Plutarch gives the reason in the Roman Questions, question twenty-six.

units.la: Secundum sexum quoque aliæ quidem erant marium, aliæ fœminarum vestes. Et tamen viri muliebri veste, & mulieres viriles Veneri sacra fecerunt, est Pholochoro. Hos adde, quod Plutarchus scribit quæstione quinquagesima quinta quæstionum Romanarum, tibicines Idibus Ianuarii vestimentis muliebrem, urbem circum fuisse solitos. Idem rationem reddit quæstione quinquagesima octava, quæstionum Græcarum, cur apud Choos Herculis Sacerdos in Antimachia muliebri veste indutus capite vittato sacrificium fecerit.
units.tr: Also, according to sex, some garments were those of men and others of women. And yet men in women's dress, and women in men's dress, have performed sacred rites for Venus, according to Pholochorus. Add to these what Plutarch writes in question fifty-five of the Roman Questions: that the flute-players were accustomed to go about the city in women's garments on the Ides of January. The same writer gives the reason, in question fifty-eight of the Greek Questions, why at Cos the priest of Hercules, dressed in a woman's garment, with his head bound with a fillet, performed the sacrifice in the Antimachia.

units.la: Secundum quantitatem vestes aliorum sacerdotum erant ample: aliæ strictæ & angustæ: aliæ item breves & curtæ: alii vero longæ ac promissæ, ad talos usque demissæ. Nam in fanum aut templo nudare se nefas erat apud quosdam, teste Plutarcho, quæstione quadragesima, quæstionum Romanarum. Apud plerosque tamen facta agitabantur a nudis, & quidem a nudis vel toto corpore, vel aliqua corporis parte denudatis. Sic glaziolo Britannorum conjuges nurus, toto corpore oblitas quibusdam in sacris nudas incedere, supra ex Plinio audivimus.
units.tr: According to size, the garments of other priests were ample; others were close and narrow; others again were short and brief; but some were long and flowing, reaching down to the ankles. For among some peoples it was a sacrilege to strip oneself in a shrine or temple, as Plutarch says in question forty of the Roman Questions. Among most peoples, however, rites were carried out by naked persons, and indeed by those stripped either over the whole body or in some part of it. Thus, as we heard above from Pliny, the wives of the Britons, smeared with woad over the whole body, went naked to certain sacred rites.

units.la: Etsi præterea sacerdotes plerunque erant inermes in sacris: sacrificia tamen quædam ab armatis fieri solita testatur Antiquitas.
units.tr: Moreover, although the priests were generally unarmed in their rites, antiquity attests that certain sacrifices were customarily performed by armed men.

units.la: Et hæc quidem de vestitu sacerdotum illorum prisorum Gentilium, quibus colophonius loco addam verba Baruchi sive Ieremiæ, quibus sacerdotum Babyloniorum vestitum habitumque corporis perstringit ac reprehendit. Sedent, inquit (ubi notandum, eos in sacris sedere solitos) Babyloniorum sacerdotes in idolorum ædibus (quæ ἀλλάσσει Græce uno nomine appellantur) habentes tunicas scissas (sic enim sacerdotes Baalitici & alii pro insana sua superstitione vestes suas dilacerant) & capita et barbam rasam: quorum capita ἀπαλλάσ ... nuda sunt. Hinc apparet sacerdotes Babylonios barbam & capita habuisse rasa, eaque fuisse nuda & aperta, cum orum sacerdotes operto & velato fuerint in sacris suis curandis capite. Addit deinde: Rugiunt autem clamantes ante Deos suos ὡς τὸ ἀλλὰ ... sicut mortui. Alludit ad illorum preces, clamosas et insanas, quas ad idola Deosque suos fundere fuerunt soliti; quas quidem ruginio et ipsos simul leonibus rugientibus per contemtum comparat.
units.tr: So much for the dress of those ancient Gentile priests. To this I will add, as a kind of appendix, the words of Baruch, or Jeremiah, in which he censures and ridicules the dress and bodily appearance of the Babylonian priests. "They sit," he says (note here that they were accustomed to sit during their rites), "the priests of the Babylonians in the temples of their idols (which are called by one name in Greek), having torn tunics (for the Baalite priests and others tear their garments in their mad superstition), and with their heads and beards shaven; their heads are bare." From this it is clear that the Babylonian priests had their beards and heads shaven, and that these were bare and uncovered, whereas the priests of the others were covered and veiled about the head while performing their sacred duties. He then adds: "They howl, crying out before their gods as men do for the dead." He alludes to their prayers, which were loud and frenzied and which they were accustomed to pour out to their idols and gods; and he compares this howling, with contempt, to the roaring of lions.

units.la: Porro secundum sexum sacerdotum alii fuerunt mares, alii fœminæ; & aliorum quidem Deorum ... ra non nisi a sexu fœmineo: aliorum non nisi a sexu virili fieri fas erat: & ad sacra quosdam non nisi virum: ad alia non nisi fœminas, ad alia utrumque patebat aditus. Sic fœmius aditus ad sacrificia Herculis erat incorclusus atq; prohibitus, cum reliquis sacris fere omnium Deorum iis liceret adesse, vel extra tangere, aut vesti, atque manus adhibere, aut solennia videre, teste Plutarcho, qui & causam hujusce rei recenset. Sic contra viris ad sacra Bonae Deae accedere in ea affiitere nefas erat: quicquid erat masculum, domo exigebatur, quando sacrum illud hebat. Cicero de Aruspicum responsis: Occulta & maribus non in visa solum, sed etiam inaudita sacra inexpiabilis scelere pertentit. Sic ad Martii Sylvani reni diximus mulieri accedere non licuisse Cato de re rustica testatus est. De Ceteris item sacro, quod non nisi per mulieres ac virgines confici poterat, egregiae locus exstat apud Ciceronem Verrin. secundo, quem hic omnino subjiciendum puto: Sacrarium, inquit, Cereris est, apud Catinenses, eadem religione, quae Romae, quae in caeteris locis, quae prope in eodem orbe terrarum. In eo sacrario intimo fuit signum Cereris per antiquum: quod vis inon modo cujusmodi esset, sed ne esse quidem sciebant: aditus enim in id sacrarium non est viris: sacris per mulieres ac virgines confici solent: hoc signum nostu clam sitius fervi ex illo religiosissimo atque antiquissimo fano sublatum est. Posteriore sacerdotes Cereris ac quae illius fani antistitae, majores natu, probatae ac nobiles mulieres, rem ad magistratus suos detulerunt. Haec Cicero.
units.tr: Furthermore, among the priests some were men and others women, and for some gods the sacred office could be undertaken only by women, for others only by men; for some rites only a man could be admitted, for others only women, and for still others access was open to both. Thus access to the sacrifices of Hercules was closed and forbidden to women, although women were allowed to attend nearly all the other rites of the gods, to stand at a distance, to touch the sacred objects and lay hands on them, or to watch the solemn ceremonies, as Plutarch testifies, and he also gives the reason for this. Conversely, it was a crime for men to approach or attend the rites of the Good Goddess; whatever was male was driven out of the house when that rite was being performed. Cicero, in his work on the responses of the haruspices: "Secret rites, not only seen but even unheard of, were polluted by men with an inexpiable crime." Likewise, we have said that it was not permitted for a woman to approach the rites of Silvanus Martius, as Cato testifies in his work on farming. Concerning another rite, which could be performed only by women and virgins, there is a remarkable passage in Cicero's second Verrine, which I think should be quoted here in full: "There is a shrine of Ceres at Catana," he says, "held in the same reverence as at Rome and in other places, indeed almost throughout the whole world. In the innermost part of that shrine stood an ancient image of Ceres, which no one, however, knew what it looked like, or even whether it existed at all; for access to that shrine is not allowed to men, and the rites are customarily performed by women and virgins. Recently this image was secretly stolen by a Greek slave from that most sacred and ancient temple. Afterwards the priests of Ceres and the priestess of that shrine, elderly, esteemed and noble women, reported the matter to their magistrates." So Cicero.
V. The age of priests.

units.la: Aetatis quoque in sacerdotibus legendis habita fuit ratio. Sic, exempli gratia, qui de Virginibus nec Vestalis capiendis scripserunt, minorem, quam annos sex, maiorem, quam annos decem natam negaverunt capi fas esse. Item quae non parima, aut matrima, hoc est, quae nec patrem, nec matrem haberet. Suetonius de Augusto: Quinque in demortuae (virginis Vestalis) locum capi aliam oporteret, ambirentque multi, ne filias in sorcem darent, adjuratio, si cujusquam neptum sacrum competeret aetas, oblacturam se fuisse eam. Antiliuis Labeo eam (ut quem Vestalem, quae expiando esset) minorem sex annos natam esse oportere negavit, majorem annos decem. Cicero pro Domo sua: Quae magis consumelia est, quam venire in sacerdotium mulierum adolescentulum?
units.tr: Age also was taken into account in choosing priests. Thus, for example, those who wrote about choosing virgins for the office of Vestal denied that it was lawful to take a girl younger than six or older than ten years. Likewise one who had no father or mother, that is, was neither patrimus nor matrimus. Suetonius, on Augustus: when another had to be chosen in place of a deceased Vestal virgin, and many were canvassing, lest they give their daughters by lot, he swore that if the age of any of his granddaughters fitted the sacred office, he would have offered her. Antistius Labeo held that the girl (as the one who was to be a Vestal, who was to perform the expiations) ought to be not younger than six years nor older than ten. Cicero, in his speech for his house: "What greater insult is there than to be given into the priesthood of women as a young girl?"
VI. The marriage of priests.

units.la: Praeterea si consanguinitas, ut sacerdotum necessario alii erant caelibes, virgines, eunuchi & castrati: alii necessario conjugati. Hinc Flamen Dialis uxore, quae Flaminica dicebatur, moriuntur, Flamen, hoc est, sacerdotali hac sua dignitate se abdicare cogebatur apud Romanos, ut Censorum uno mortuo ejus collega similiter alteri censuram cogebatur deponere. Vide de hac re Plutarchum, quae sitione quadragesima nona quaestionum Romanarum. Idem quaestione quinquagesima Sacerdotum uxores saepe iis in sacris rerum obeundis adfuisse, neque iis absentibus esse peragi poterat. Hinc, ut supra dictum, Flamen Dialis uxore mortua Flaminio decedebat, propterea quod plerisque in sacris obeundis uxoris opera utebatur, ita ut ea absente ea peragere non posset. Caeterum, uxore mortua aliam confestim ducere neque facile est, neque tamen humanum.
units.tr: Further, as for consanguinity, so for marriage: some priests were necessarily celibate, virgins, eunuchs and castrated men, while others were necessarily married. Hence, among the Romans, when the Flamen Dialis lost his wife, who was called the Flaminica, he was compelled to give up the flaminate, that is, to renounce his priestly dignity; and just as when one of two censors died his colleague was likewise compelled to lay down the censorship. On this matter see Plutarch, in his forty-ninth question of the Roman Questions. In the fiftieth question he also says that the wives of priests often assisted them in performing their sacred duties, and that these could not be carried out without them. Hence, as said above, when the wife of the Flamen Dialis died, he gave up the flaminate, because in many of his sacred duties he used his wife's help, so that without her he could not complete them. Yet to take another wife immediately after the death of one is neither easy nor, indeed, humane.

units.la: Sic apud Romanos illae Vestae cultrices perpetuique ignis custodes erant virgines: Vestales inde dictae, quarum officium in tria tempora erat distributum: Unum; quo discebant: Alterum, quae praecepta sua peragebant; Tertium, ut alias deinde docerent. Idem penè fuit in virginibus Dianae Ephesiae. Iuniores enim sacerdotes μελλιηρας, deinde iegos, postremo τεχνης esse opera tebat.
units.tr: So among the Romans the cultivators of Vesta and the guardians of the perpetual fire were virgins, called Vestals from that name. Their duty was divided into three periods: the first, in which they learned; the second, in which they performed the precepts they had learned; the third, in which they then taught others. It was almost the same with the virgins of Diana of Ephesus. For the younger priestesses were called melissae (bees), then hiereiai (priestesses), and finally they were employed in the craft [τέχνης].

units.la: Matris vero Deum, sive magnae matris, sive Cybeles, sacerdotes erant castrati, Galli dicti a Gallo fluvio, Phrygiae flumine, cujus aquam potantes in insaniam verterentur. Carmenta porro templum matronas & antiquitus dedicasse & Deam illam primum colere eique sacrificare solitas, testes est Plutarchus quaestione quinquagesima sexta Romanarum quaestionum.
units.tr: Now the priests of the Mother of the Gods, whether called the Great Mother or Cybele, were castrated men, called Galli from the river Gallus in Phrygia, whose water, if drunk, turned men into madness. Plutarch, in the fifty-sixth question of the Roman Questions, is a witness that matrons in ancient times also dedicated a temple to Carmenta, and that they were accustomed first to worship that goddess and to sacrifice to her.
The Nationality of Priests

units.la: Secundum Nationem quoque Sacerdotes olim considerabantur. Erant enim alii paerit, alii peregrini: Sacra carmen pleraque per civites atque indigenas celebrari solebant: quamvis quaedam ut peregrina & advenitia per peregrinos administrari atque tractari oportebat. Hinc Cicero Graecorum sacrorum & sacerdotum meminit. Sic enim pro Cornelio Balbo: Sacerdos illa, inquit, quae Graecum illud sacrum (Cereris) monstraret & faceret. Idem pro Caelio: Sacra Cereris per Graecas semper curata sunt sacerdotes. Fejus: Graeca sacra fella Cereris ex Graecia translata, quæ ob in ventionem Proserpinæ matronæ colebant: quod sacrum, dum non essent matronæ, quæ facerent, propter cladem Cannensem & frequentiam lugentium inflitutum est, ne amplius cum eum diebus lugeretur.
units.tr: Priests were also formerly distinguished by nationality. Some were native and others foreign. Most rites were usually celebrated by citizens and natives, though certain rites that were foreign and imported had to be administered and handled by foreigners. Hence Cicero mentions Greek rites and priests. In his speech for Cornelius Balbus he says: "That priestess," he says, "who showed and performed that Greek rite of Ceres..." The same author, in his speech for Caelius: "The rites of Ceres were always managed by Greek priests." Festus: "The Greek rites of Ceres, brought over from Greece, which matrons used to observe because of the abduction of Proserpina. This rite, since there were no matrons to perform it on account of the disaster at Cannae and the great number of mourners, was instituted so that mourning would no longer be kept for so many days."

units.la: Quancum ad vitæ conditionem, genus & instituum sacerdotum attinet, obseruandum apud Romanos & Græcos, Reges quoque sacerdotum suscipere atque obire fuisse solitos: cuius muleain historiis prophanis exempla occurrunt. De hoc Plutarchus in quæstionibus Romanis sic scribit: Olim Reges pleraque & præcipua sacra faciebant, ac rebus diuinis ipsi cum sacerdotibus operabantur. Ut vero in solescere cœperunt, arrogantesque & duri esse, plerique Græci decrato ejs imperio solum sacra faciendi Diis faculatè reliquere. De Regibus Spartanorum scribit idem Alexander ab Alexandro libro secundo, capite octavo. Verba ejus hæc sunt: Reges Spartanorum, quum primum in eam assumci sunt dignieacem, privilegio honoris præcipui Ioues cœlestis & Lacedemonii sacerdotio funguntur: quibus ex omni Scrophatum sœtu porcus debebatur, ut si Diis immolare vellent, nunquam victima deesset. Sic ex Cæsaribus C. Iulius Cæsar Augustum simul & Pontificacum: Galba autem triplex sacerdotium gessisse dicitur. De hoc more scribit etiam Guanguinus in Prussia, cuius verba addere libet: Anno Domini DIII. Prucenis, tmquiè, sive Vmigavis Rex quidam, Bruteno dictus, imperavit: qui cum iustos annos ætatis consecutus esset, quiecami vicam ducere instituens, fractem Verdenutum successorem sibi in regno fecie: ipsi summus sacerdos effectus est, nomenque ei dignicatis indicum fuit Kirie Kirieyto, quasi dicas, Proximus nostrer Dominus. Huic Pontifici suo Pruceni præclaram adem sub quercu quadam erexerunt, locoque Romanæ a Roma nomen indiderunt. Hæc Gnaguinus.
units.tr: As for the condition of life, the kind and the institution of priests, it should be noted that among the Romans and Greeks kings also used to undertake and perform priesthoods. Examples of this are found in profane histories. Plutarch writes about this in his Roman Questions as follows: "Formerly kings performed most and the chief sacred rites, and they themselves worked at divine matters together with the priests. But when they began to grow proud and harsh, most of the Greeks, having deprived them of their power, left the performance of sacred rites to the gods alone." Alexander ab Alexandro, in book 2, chapter 8, writes about the kings of the Spartans. His words are these: "When the kings of the Spartans are first admitted to that dignity, they perform the priesthood of heavenly Jupiter and of the Lacedaemonians as a privilege of their chief honour. From every litter of pigs a pig was owed to them, so that if they wished to sacrifice to the gods, a victim would never be lacking." Among the Caesars, in the same way, Gaius Julius Caesar held the augurate and the pontificate together, and Galba is said to have held a threefold priesthood. Guagninus also writes about this custom in his account of Prussia, and I am pleased to add his words: "In the year of the Lord DIII, a certain king of the Prussians, or Vmigavis, called Bruteno, ruled. When he had reached a full age of years, resolving to lead a quiet life, he made his brother Verdenutus his successor in the kingdom. He himself was made chief priest, and the title of his dignity was Kirie Kirieyto, as if you were to say 'our neighbour lord.' For this high priest the Prussians erected a splendid temple under a certain oak and gave the place the name Romuva." Thus Guagninus.

units.la: Pertinent hucea, quæ L. Fenestella de Regè sacrorum scribit capite undecimo in sacerdotiis Romanis: Rex sacrorum, inquit, qui & sacrificulus dicitur, creari cœpus est Iunio Bruto, & M. Valerio primus consulibus. Ejus creandi occasionem dedit, quid quum nuper exactis regibus pleræq; sacra a solis Regibus obiri consueta, Regum exactione vacare viderentur; idque molestè admodum populus ferrec, utpote, quod cultui divino Regum exactione videretur derogatum, sacerdotem creari placuit: quem quo minus eidem authoritatis inesset (alii legunt deesse) regio nomine decorarunt, sacrorum Regem appellantes. Subjecerunt tamen Pontifici Maximo, ne simulius dicti (alii legunt, Ne si nullius dictionis alias) sciset supponerunt, jam exactis Reges, reductis Reges esse viderentur, vel crederentur. Qua vero huic partes injunctæ essent, nunc tempora minimè reperiuntur. Hæc Fenestella.
units.tr: What Fenestella writes about the king of sacred rites in chapter 11 on Roman priesthoods pertains here: "The king of sacred rites, who is also called the little sacrificer, was first created in the consulship of Junius Brutus and Marcus Valerius. The occasion for creating him was this: since, after the kings had recently been driven out, most sacred rites that were customarily performed by kings alone seemed to be left unperformed through the expulsion of the kings, and the people took this very badly, as if the worship of God had been diminished by the expulsion of the kings, it was decided to create a priest. So that he should not have the same authority (other editions read 'should lack it'), they adorned him with the royal name, calling him king of sacred rites. Nevertheless, they made him subordinate to the Chief Pontiff, so that he should not seem, or be believed, to be a king again, now that the kings had been expelled and had been brought back. But what parts were assigned to this office is nowhere found in our times." Thus Fenestella.

units.la: Meminit Regis sacrificuli etiam Pomponius Lætus, cuius hæc verba: Postquam Romani, inquit, jam liberi, extincto regio nomine, necubi desiderium Regis esset propter quædam sacra publica, quo Reges faciebant, Regem sacrificulum constituerunt, & e Patribus elegerunt, C. Manlium Papyrium, & id sacerdotium Pontificis subjecere, ne novæ libertati addirus nomini honos officeret. Is Papyrius quieau studiosissimus fuit. Hactenus Pomponius.
units.tr: Pomponius Laetus also mentions the king of sacrifices, and his words are these: "After the Romans, now free, had abolished the royal name, lest anywhere there should be a longing for a king because of certain public sacred rites that kings used to perform, they appointed a king of sacrifices and chose him from among the Fathers, Gaius Manlius Papyrius, and they subordinated this priesthood to the Pontiff, so that the honour of the old name should not be a hindrance to the new liberty. This Papyrius was very devoted to his duties." Thus Pomponius.

units.la: Ob eandem hanc causam, quod nimirum Rex esset sacerdos & pontifex, Romani Imperato res Pontifices appellabantur. Hinc Iuvenalis Satyra quarta de Domitiano: Deflinat hoc monstrum Cymbæ, linique magister Pontifici summo, &c.
units.tr: For this same reason, namely that the king was both priest and pontiff, the Roman emperors were called pontiffs. Hence Juvenal, in Satire 4, about Domitian: "He destines this monster for Cybele, and a master of anointing for the chief pontiff, etc."

units.la: Plato in Politico docet, Sacerdotes & Vates magnanimitate, intelligentia & claritate florere ob earum rerum, in quibus versantur, amplitudinem & dignitatem: & idcirco addit, Apud Ægyptios non licuum fuisse Regem absque sacerdotio imperio: quin immo si ex alio genere quispiam per vim regnum nsurpasse, coactum fuisse tandem ἀποτελεῖσθαι, id est, sacris iuniuaria: Prætereà in plurimis Græcorum civitatibus, & apud Athenienses præsertim, præcipua a magistratibus summis insitui fuisse solea: & creati Regis fidei augustissima sacra, maximeque pia civis antiquissimarum religionum ritus fuisse demandatos. Idem alibi regio muneri sacerdotium vult esse proximum & vicinum. Cicero: Itaq; Populus Romanus breui tempore neque Regem sacrorum, neque Flamines, neque Salios habebit.
units.tr: Plato in the Statesman teaches that priests and seers flourish in magnanimity, intelligence and renown because of the greatness and dignity of the matters in which they are engaged. And for this reason he adds that among the Egyptians it was not permitted for a king to rule without the priesthood; indeed, if someone from another class had seized the kingdom by force, he was eventually compelled to be purified [ἀποτελεῖσθαι], that is, to be initiated into the sacred rites. Moreover, in most Greek states, and especially among the Athenians, the chief sacred duties were usually instituted by the highest magistrates, and the most august sacred rites of the faith, and the most devout rites of the most ancient religions, were entrusted to the king who had been appointed. Elsewhere he holds that the priesthood should be close and neighbouring to the royal office. Cicero: "So the Roman people will before long have neither a king of sacred rites, nor flamens, nor Salii."

units.la: Aliquando tamen & apud nonnullos non erat licitum munus profanum cum sacro conjungere. Hinc Aristoteles Politicorum libro quarto, Sacerdotes, sive illi sint αἰρετοὶ sive ἀληγοὶ, non permisimus.
units.tr: Sometimes, however, among some peoples it was not lawful to combine a secular office with a sacred one. Hence Aristotle, in book 4 of the Politics: "We did not allow priests, whether they are elected [αἰρετοὶ] or chosen by lot [κληρωτοί]."

units.la: Liber ut tibi candidas ad aras,
units.tr: Liber ut tibi candidas ad aras,

units.la: Forma quoq; altarium vel sint quadrata, ut templorum, vel rotunda. Super aras vero iam quadratas, quam rotundas cepisse quidem ex ordine, sine verbenas (quae omnibus fere in sacris, seu sacrificatum fuerunt adhibita, quasi etiam sacro ex loco decerpere oportebat) apponere consueverunt.
units.tr: Altars too were of one shape or another: square, like those of temples, or round. Upon altars, though now square rather than round, they were accustomed to lay sprigs of verbena, which were used in almost all sacred rites and sacrifices, since it was thought necessary to pluck them from a holy place.

units.la: At singulorum quidem Deorum aras, ut etiam vittas, & frondibus coronari, ornare solitas fuerunt, quae singulis Diis fuerunt consecrate: ut Iovi arum acliculo, Apollini laureo, Minervae oleo, Veneri myrto, Herculi populo, Bacchi hederae (sed & pampinis interdum, ramusq; ficulneis plerunque.) Pani pino, Sylvano & Diis cupresso, aliorum, alias frondibus, arboribus coronarunt. Hinc quia ara frondibus, graminibus, herbis floribusq; ornari solebant, a Poetis Frondentes, Gramineae, Herbosae, Virides, Coronatae sunt dicta. Valerius Flaccus lib. 3 tertio:
units.tr: The altars of individual gods, like their fillets, were customarily crowned and decorated with garlands, each being consecrated to a particular god: for Jupiter with oak, Apollo with laurel, Minerva with olive, Venus with myrtle, Hercules with poplar, and Bacchus with ivy (sometimes also with vine tendrils, and for the most part with fig branches). Pan was crowned with pine, Silvanus and the gods with cypress, and others with other leaves or trees. Hence, because altars were customarily adorned with leaves, grasses, herbs and flowers, the poets called them leafy, grassy, herbaceous, green and crowned. Valerius Flaccus, book three:
And he brought to the leafy altars the highest...
and poured libations and feasts, etc.
Silius, book four:
He strewed the grassy altars with sociable waves.
Ovid, book fifteen of the Metamorphoses:
He appeases the herb-covered altars with fragrant fires.
Martial, book twelve:

units.la: Si terrure coli, viridesq; pigebit ad aras.
units.tr: If you are ashamed to worship at the green altars...
Propertius, book three:

units.la: Inde coronatas ubi thure pia verus aras.
units.tr: Thence, where the devout woman crowns the altars with incense...

units.la: Vt autem Deorum & Sacrorum, & templorum; sic altarium quoque apud Gentiles & apud Iudaeos, Gentilium exemplo (de quo Deus sepius per Prophetas suos conquerit ur) numerus maximus: quem alterum multiplicationem Hosea Propheta vocat, capite duodecimo, & Israelitas exprobrat: Altaria in quit, eorum, tanquam acervi lapidum super sulcos agri, sed pro omnibus in locis altaria exstruunt.
units.tr: Just as there were many gods, sacred rites and temples, so among the Gentiles and among the Jews there was a very great number of altars, following the Gentile example, about which God often complains through his prophets. Hosea the prophet calls this a multiplication, in chapter twelve, and reproaches the Israelites: "Their altars," he says, "are like heaps of stones upon the furrows of the field, but they build altars in all places."

units.la: Porro & dedicari atq; consectari aras & altaria olim certa forma magnaque religione solebant, seu praecipuam ferre membrum, hic exfluit. Dedicationis autem huius illustre exemplum dedicat Ara, Augusto posita apud Narbonenses, sumbac infer pronte:
units.tr: Moreover, altars were once dedicated and consecrated with a set form and great religious solemnity; whether this deserves a separate treatment, I will not discuss here. An illustrious example of such a dedication is the altar set up to Augustus among the people of Narbonne, with the following inscription:

units.la: L. CASSIO LONGINO COSS. X. KAL. OCTOBR.
units.tr: In the consulship of Lucius Cassius Longinus, ten days before the Kalends of October

units.la: NVMINI AVGVSTI VOTVM SVSCEPTVM A' PLEBE NARBONENSIVM IN PERPETVVM.
units.tr: A vow undertaken by the commons of Narbonne in perpetuity to the divinity of Augustus

units.la: QVOD BONVM, FAVSTVM, FELIXQVE SIT IMP. CAESARI DIVI F. AVGVSTO P.P. PONTIFICI MAXIMO TRIB. POTESTATIS XXXIIII. CONIVGI, LIBERIS, GENTIQVE EIVS, SENATVI, POPVLOQVE ROMANO, ET COLONIS, INCOLISQVE C.I.P.N. QVI SE NVMINI EIVS IN PERPETVVM COLENDO OBLIGAVERUNT, PLEBS NARBON. ARAM NARBONE IN FORO POSVIT AD QVAM QVOTANNIS VIIII KAL. OCTOB. QVA DIE EVM SVLCI FELICITAS ORBI TERRARVM RECTOREM EDIDIT, TRES EQVITES ROMANI, A PLEBE, ET TRES LIBERTINI HOSTIAS SINGVLAS IMOLENT, ET COLONIS ET INCOLIS AD SVPPLICANDVM NVMINI EIVS THVS ET VINVM DE SVO EA DIE PRAESTENT. ET VIII. KAL. OCTOB. THVS, VINVM, COLONIS ET INCOLIS ITEM PRAESTENT. KAL. QVOQVE IANVAR. THVS ET VINVM COLONIS ET INCOLIS PRAESTENT, VII. QVOQVE
units.tr: That this may be good, prosperous and happy for the Emperor Caesar, son of the divine Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power for the thirty-fourth time; for his wife, his children and his family; for the Senate, the Roman people, and the colonists and residents, who have bound themselves to worship his divinity forever: the commons of Narbonne set up this altar in the forum at Narbonne. Every year, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, the day on which the good fortune of the world gave birth to him, the ruler of the lands of the earth, three Roman knights chosen by the commons and three freedmen are each to sacrifice victims, and on that day the colonists and residents are to provide incense and wine from their own means for supplicating his divinity. Likewise on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, incense and wine are to be provided for the colonists and residents. Also on the Kalends of January, incense and wine are to be provided for the colonists and residents, and on the seventh day before the Ides of January

units.la: IDVS IANVAR. QVA DIE PRIMVM IMPERIVM ORBIS TERRARVM AVSPICATVS EST, THVRE, VINO SVPPLICENT. ET HOSTIAS SINGVL. IMMOLENT. ET COLONIS INCOLISQVE THVS, VINVM EA DIE PRAESTENT.
units.tr: On the Ides of January, the day on which he first took up the rule of the world, they are to supplicate with incense and wine, each sacrifice victims, and on that day the colonists and residents are to provide incense and wine.

units.la: ET PRIDIE KAL. IVNIAS, QVOD EA DIE T. STATILIO TAVRO, M. AEMILIO LEPIDO COSS. IVDICIA PLEBIS DECVRIONIBVS CONIVNXIT, HOSTIAS SINGVLAS IMMOLENT, ET THVS, ET VINVM AD SVPPLICANDVM NVMINI EIVS COLONIS ET INCOLIS PRAESTENT.
units.tr: And on the day before the Kalends of June, because on that day, in the consulship of T. Statilius Taurus and M. Aemilius Lepidus, he joined the judicial power of the commons to the decurions, they are each to sacrifice victims, and to provide incense and wine to the colonists and residents for supplicating his divinity.

units.la: EXQVE IIS TRIBVS EQVITIBVS ROMA LIBERTINIS VNV Reliqua deficiunt.
units.tr: And from these three tribes, the knights, Rome, and the freedmen, one ... The rest is lacking.

units.la: Qui plura dedicationis bujus exempla cupit, inspiciat clarissimi & antiquitatu peritissimi vi-n, Dn. Adolphi Occonis, amicimei singularis, Namifmata antiqua, & Antiquitatum Romano ficebatur. rum a Iohanne Rofino colleclarum librum fecundum.
units.tr: Whoever desires more examples of this dedication should consult the most distinguished man and most learned in antiquities, Mr. Adolf Occo, my particular friend, in his ancient coins, and the Roman antiquities collected by Johann Rosinus, book two.

units.la: Dicamus nunc de altarium apud Gentiles usu. Primus & praecipuus altarium usus fuit, quid sacrificia omnis generis cum animata,tum inanimata in iis fiebant: unde etiam ארבות, Mizbechoth Hebraice, & Svoiacrneia Graece fuerunt appellata, de quo usu facrificiali fatis fuperf, conflat. Propter hunc ipsum usum ara varus & elegantibus epithetis a Poëtis insigniuntur, ut quod feste, sacra, sacrate, sacrosancte, divinae, c.iflae, sacrifica, fumantes, fumide, fumose, pingues, odorate, flagrantes, thuricreme, thurifere, lucentes, ardentes, calentes, aliusq; id generis nominibus appellantur. Statim etiā vaporatum vocat Altare, & thureum ab hocipfo sacrificandi.
units.tr: Let us now speak of the use of altars among the Gentiles. The first and chief use of altars was that sacrifices of every kind, both of animate and of inanimate things, were made upon them; whence they were also called Mizbechoth [מזבחות] in Hebrew and thysiasteria [θυσιαστήρια] in Greek, as is sufficiently clear from what has been said above about their sacrificial use. Because of this very use, poets adorn the altar with many elegant epithets: it is called holy, sacred, consecrated, most holy, divine, sacrificial, smoking, smoky, fat, fragrant, blazing, incense-bearing, shining, burning, glowing, and by other names of this kind. Likewise Statius calls it the steaming altar, and the incense altar, from this very sacrificing.

units.la: Deinde, ad, si ve, ante altaria fiebant preces, vota ac juramēta: cuius usus exempla passim occurrunt. Macrobius libro tertio Saturnalii, capite fecundo: Multifariam legimus, inquit, quod litare sola non possit oratio, nisi is, qui Deos precatur, etiā aras manibus apprehendat. Hinc aras precesfiebant nonnulli ab ἀγορά, idest, oro, vel ἀπο τῷ ἀγῶν, ut supra quoque dixi, id est, a precibus volunc & juramenta dictas, & ansas Varro volunt antiquitus appellatas, qu d eas a sacrificantibus, adde precantibus, necessarium esset teneri. Virgilius septimo Aeneidos: Talibus orantem dictis, arasq; tenentem Audiit Omnipotens, &c.
units.tr: Next, prayers, vows and oaths were made at or before altars; examples of this custom occur everywhere. Macrobius, in book three of the Saturnalia, chapter two: "We read in many places," he says, "that prayer alone cannot make an offering acceptable unless the one who prays also grasps the altars with his hands." Hence some derive ara from ἀγορά, that is, "I pray" (oro), or from ἀπὸ τῶν ἀρῶν, as I said above, that is, from prayers. Varro holds that they were formerly called ansae, because they had to be held by those sacrificing, that is, praying. Virgil, Aeneid book seven: "While he spoke such words and held the altars, the Almighty heard..."

units.la: Sic Delifiuit ara Apollinis ψυχοποῦ, idest, Genitoris, quam Pythagoram veluti in violatam adorasse tradunt. Cujus Nutrix haconinia faciebat in arbenis ac verbis five hostius, ut Deli ad Apollinis Genitoris ara.
units.tr: So the altar of Apollo at Delos, called the Begetter's altar, that is, of the Genitor, is said to have been worshipped by Pythagoras as if it were inviolable. Its keeper performed the rites in silence, with words and by signs, at the altar of Apollo the Begetter at Delos.

units.la: Sic iurantes quoq; manu aram tangebant. Virgilius: Tango aras, medios ignes, ac Numina testor.
units.tr: So too those swearing touched the altar with their hand. Virgil: "I touch the altars, the middle fires, and call the divinities to witness."

units.la: Cicero pro Flacco: Isti aram tenens iurarct, crederet nemo. Celebratur hinc nobilis illa Periclis sententia, Ad aram ufq; amicum ne esse oportet: quae significatur Neminē amici cau sa aut pestare, aut quippiam inhonestum facere oportere. Adde etia per vulgatum illud Aristophanis s. s. s. s. s. s. s., Quos nec ara, nec si-des, nec ulla durant sedera. De vehementer perfidis. Distum est in Spartanos, quorū perfidiam taxavit Aristophanes.
units.tr: Cicero, Pro Flacco: "If he had sworn while holding the altar, no one would have believed him." Hence comes that famous saying of Pericles: "One must not be a friend up to the altar," which means that one ought not to perjure oneself or do anything dishonourable for a friend's sake. Add also the well-known verse of Aristophanes, "whom neither altar, nor faith, nor any oath holds fast," said of the very treacherous; it was said of the Spartans, whose perfidy Aristophanes censured.

units.la: Arapraeterea erant asyla atg, perfugia hominum sacrosanētā. Vnde: Confugere in aram. Cicero post redit um: Qui nisi in aram tribunatus confugisset, cum Praetoris effugere non potuisset. Idem pro Roscio: Sicut in aram, confugit in ejus domum. Idē in questionibus Tusculanis: Tantus genie orbatum, cum in aram confugisset, hostilis manus interemit. Ab ara itaq; non licebat supplices abstrahere. Hujusmodi ara erat; ara Concordiae, cujus meminit Hieronymus, ad quam si quis confugisset, tanquam ad Cefaris statuam, a vellēm inde nesas habebatur. Plautus in Rudente: Sed quid ego cesso fugere in fanum ac dicere hac Palestra in aram uti confugiamus prius, Quam huc scelefus leno venit, meq; hic opprimat? Idem in Mostellaria: Tranio ferv{s}: Ego interim hanc aram occupabo.
units.tr: Besides, there were asylums and places of refuge for men, which were sacrosanct. Hence the phrase "to flee to the altar." Cicero, after his return: "who, unless he had fled to the altar of the tribunate, could not have escaped the praetor." The same in Pro Roscio: "as to an altar, he fled into his house." The same in the Tusculan Questions: "a man bereaved of his sons, when he had fled to the altar, was slain by a hostile hand." Therefore it was not lawful to drag suppliants away from the altar.
