There was such an altar, the altar of Concord, mentioned by Jerome, to which if anyone fled, as to the statue of Caesar, it was considered wicked to drag him away from it. Plautus in the Rudens: "But why do I delay? Let us flee into the temple and say, in this wrestling-ground, let us first take refuge at the altar, before the wicked pimp comes here and catches me." The same in the Mostellaria, Tranio: "Meanwhile I will occupy this altar."

units.la: Seruienim, sibi malè conscii, & poenam suorum malefactorum ac peccatorum metuentes, deprecatorem parabant, & aram aliquam, a quanefas erat eos avellere, occupabant.
units.tr: For slaves, conscious of their own guilt and fearing the punishment of their wrongdoing and sins, used to prepare an intercessor and seize some altar, from which it was unlawful to tear them away.
Terence in the Heautontimorumenos:

units.la: Nemo accusat, Sire, nec tu aram tibi, neq; precatorem parabit.
units.tr: "No one is accusing you, Syrus; nor will you need to find an altar or an intercessor for yourself."

units.la: Cicero de aruspicum responsis: Sacerdotem abiphis aris & pulvinaribus detraxisse. Idem libro tertio de Orat. Quod cum facere non poteflis, eanquam in aram confugitis ad Deum, Idem: Magistratuum autem vestrorum injurias ita multas tulerunt, ut nunquam antehac ad aram legem praesidium, vestrum publico confugerint. Ovidius quarto Tristium:
units.tr: Cicero, on the responses of the haruspices: "He had dragged the priest from the very altars and couches." The same, book three of On the Orator: "Since you cannot do this, you flee to God as to an altar." The same: "Your magistrates have inflicted so many wrongs that never before have the laws and public protection fled to the altar." Ovid, Tristia book four:

units.la: Unica fortuna tu ara reperta mea, idest, Asylum perfugium, portus. Hinc Plutarchus de superstitione aram vocat ςωμὸν φυγῶν, ad quam confugimus.
units.tr: "You alone, altar, were found as my fortune," that is, asylum, refuge, harbour. Hence Plutarch, in his treatise on superstition, calls the altar the altar of refuge, to which we flee.

units.la: Ob quam eauffam Cicero eam quoque sanctam, boc est, inviolatam vocat: cujus quidem etiam boc argumento est, quod idem in oratione pro Cornelio Balbo offendere volens Lucium Marcum primi pili centurionem fedus, quod fecerat, semper turpiolate piè, fervasse, boc proverbio utitur: Ara sanctior. Sic idem: Qui & vetere illam speciem faederis Marciani, semper omni sanctiorem ara duxerunt.
units.tr: For this reason Cicero also calls it sacred, that is, inviolable. This too is shown by the following: in the speech for Cornelius Balbus, wishing to censure Lucius Marcius, centurion of the first rank, who had always kept the covenant he had made shamefully, he uses this proverb: "more sacred than an altar." Likewise: "they always regarded that old form of the Marcian covenant as more sacred than any altar."

units.la: Ac quoniam ara & foci praecipua erant cultus religionis, instrumenta, quae idcirco saepe metonymice pro ipsa religione capiuntur, inde promanavit proverbialis illa locutio: Pro aris & focis pugnare, sive certare, cum totis viribus cereamus, tanquam nihil nobis prius, aut carius esse debeat sacrorum defensione. Cicero de Natura Deorum libro ter 10: Quoniam ad vesperascit, dabis dium nobis aliquam, ut contra ista dicamus. Est enim mibi pro aris & focis cereandum, & pro Deorum templis atque delubris. Seneca eamen air: Aras, quae vertunt, injuriam Diis non faciunt.
units.tr: And since altar and hearth were the chief instruments of religious worship, and these instruments are for this reason often taken by metonymy for religion itself, the proverbial expression arose: "to fight for altars and hearths," or "to contend" with all our strength, as though nothing ought to be dearer to us than the defence of sacred things. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods, book three: "Since evening is coming on, you will give me some time so that I may speak against those things. For I must fight for altars and hearths, and for the temples and shrines of the gods." Seneca, however, says: "Altars that are overturned do no injury to the gods."

units.la: Altaribus atq; focis merito annumerandae atque subjungenda sunt mensae, quarum in eempla facrusq; Gentilium ut magnus fuit usus, ita saepe fit mentio. Mensa, inquit Ifleus, in aedibus aravum vicem obtinebant. Hinc Cicero aras, focos & mensas conjungit in oratione de Arispicum responsis: Deorum, inquit, signes, folennes mensae, abdici & penetrales foci.
units.tr: Tables are rightly to be counted with altars and hearths and joined to them. Examples of these in Gentile rites are as numerous as their use was great, and mention of them is frequent. "The table," says Isaeus, "in houses took the place of altars." Hence Cicero joins altars, hearths and tables together in the speech on the responses of the haruspices: "the signs of the gods, the solemn tables, the hidden and inner hearths."

units.la: Ac mensae quidem in genere omnes sacrae habebantur, & Dius, amicitiae hospitii, paeronis erant consecratae, ut Plutarchus in conviviis suo testatur. Mensam autem minisferis divinis aptam Foslus tradit Anclabrin fuisse dictam, ut vasa quoque aenea, quibus sacerdotes in re divina utebantur, Anclabria fuerunt appellata, numerum ab antiquo verbo Anclare sive anclare, quod a Graeco ἀντλᾶν def endens haurire significat, sive ab anculare antiquo verbo, quod dicebant Antiqui pro minifrare, ex quo & Ancillas vocant, ancillas, quae dictae sunt, Ancilas Deos ac Deas, quae olim fuerunt cultae.
units.tr: All tables in general were regarded as sacred, and those of Zeus, of friendship, of hospitality and of patronage were consecrated, as Plutarch attests in his Table-Talk. Festus relates that the table fit for sacred ministries was called anclabris, and that the bronze vessels which priests used in sacred rites were called anclabria, the name derived from the old verb anclare or anclare, meaning to draw out, from the Greek ἀντλᾶν; or from the old verb anculare, which the ancients used for "to minister," from which they also call the ancillae, the handmaids, who were so named as serving the gods and goddesses who were formerly worshipped.

units.la: Curiales porro etiam certae mensae fuerunt dictae, in quibus iunoni immolabatur, quae Curia fuit appellata. Idem quadratae Aficarias, rotundas, Civiles, Assidelas olim fuisse dictas testatur.
units.tr: Tables used for sacrifice to Juno were also called "curial" tables, which were named Curia. The same author records that square tables were once called Aficarias, round ones Civiles, and Assidelae.

units.la: Ac ligneas quidem antiquitus fuisse apud Romanos sacras atque sacrificas has mensas Dionysius Halicarnasseus hoc verbis prodidit: Εχω γὰρ ἰδίαν ισοτομίαν ἐν ἱεροῖς αἰ ἐν κλεῖσι ἐμοι ὅσα ἀπὸ τῶν ἐπιγῆς ἀπαλλαγέντος φύσεως. Hiis quidem verbis aperte ligneas mensas in templis usitatas fuisse docet.
units.tr: That such sacred and sacrificial tables were once made of wood among the Romans, Dionysius of Halicarnassus reports in these words: "For I have my own ... in the sacred places, in the closets, of all that has been removed from the earth's nature" [Εχω γὰρ ἰδίαν ισοτομίαν ἐν ἱεροῖς αἰ ἐν κλεῖσι ἐμοι ὅσα ἀπὸ τῶν ἐπιγῆς ἀπαλλαγέντος φύσεως]. In these words he shows clearly that wooden tables were in use in the temples.

units.la: Mensarum autem aurearum & argenteatum usum in templis atque sacris biftoriae fatis aruguntur. Unde Dionysium Syracusanum Valerius Maximus libro primo, capite duodecimo, de neglecta. ut epletta religione scribit mensas aureas & argenteas ex Apollinis templo sustulisse. Et Cicero libro tertio de Natura Deorum: Iam mensas,inquit,argenteas de omnibus delubris iussit auferri, quibus quod more veteris Graeciae scriptum esset BONORVM DEORVM, uri feilorum bonitate dicebat.Idem Verrem mensas Delphicas e marmore, crateras ex ere pulcherrimas, vim maximam vasorum Corinthiorum ex omnibus aedibus sacris abstulisse,dixit.
units.tr: Histories also record the use of golden and silver tables in temples and sacred places. Valerius Maximus, in book 1, chapter 12, "On neglected religion," writes that Dionysius of Syracuse removed the golden and silver tables from the temple of Apollo. Cicero, in book 3 of On the Nature of the Gods, says: "Now he ordered the silver tables to be taken away from all the shrines, and said that they were to be melted down, since the inscription on them, written in the old Greek manner, showed they belonged to the good gods." The same author says that Verres carried off from all the sacred buildings the Delphic tables of marble, the most beautiful bronze mixing bowls, and a great quantity of Corinthian vessels.

units.la: Hactenus etiam de aris sive altaribus & mensis.
units.tr: So much on altars and tables.

units.la: Sequitur Q. VINTVM membrum, sive circumstantia, videlicet Personae, quae, ut in hoc sic in omni sacrificio, atque adeo in omni actione diligenter sunt considerandae. Sunt autem personae hae, homines per quos, sive a quibus sacrificia offerebantur: quorum differentia est triplex. Alii enim sunt, qui sacrificiis praesunt, sive praesidunt, ut sunt sacerdotes & sacrifici sive sacrificuli, quorum munere hic Nestor & Argonautae funguntur: alii sunt ministri: alii denique qui ius communicant, quia ad sacrificia sunt in vitati.
units.tr: Next comes the fifth element, or circumstance, namely the persons, who must be carefully considered in this sacrifice and indeed in every action. These persons are the men through whom, or by whom, sacrifices were offered, and they are of three kinds. Some preside over the sacrifices, such as priests and sacrificers or minor sacrificers, whose office here is performed by Nestor and the Argonauts. Others are attendants. Finally, others take part in the rite, since they are invited to the sacrifice.

units.la: Personae principes & principes sunt Nestor, & Argonautae, qui quidem sacrificiorum munera potissima in Buthysia ista seu immolatione boum, cuius Homerus & Apollonius meminerunt, obiisse perhibentur. Vbi notandum, Reges quoque & principes apud Ethnicos sacrificare fuisse solitos: id quod lege divina scimus fuisse prohibitum. Sic Nestor hic, qui Rex fuit, cum manus lavandi, & molae vitimus inspergendi initium fecisse: cum preces ad Minervam fudisse primum, deinde etiam crura igni injecisse atque concremasse dicitur. Idem colligitur ex illo Virgilij Aeneid.3.
units.tr: The chief persons and leaders are Nestor and the Argonauts, who are said to have performed the principal parts of the sacrificial office in that sacrifice of oxen, the Buthysia, which Homer and Apollonius mention. Here it should be noted that among the heathen kings and princes were accustomed to sacrifice, which we know was forbidden by divine law. So Nestor, who was a king, is said to have begun the rite by washing his hands and sprinkling the first of the sacrificial meal, then to have poured out prayers to Minerva, and finally to have laid the thighbones on the fire and burned them. The same custom is inferred from that line of Virgil's Aeneid 3: "King Anius, at once king of men and priest of Phoebus."

units.la: Rex Animi, rex idem hominum Phoebi, sacerdos: in quod Servius, Majorum, inquit, hoc erat consuetudo, ut Rex esset etiam sacerdos & pontifex. Unde hodie quoque Imperatores Pontifices dicimus.
units.tr: On this line Servius comments: "It was the custom of our ancestors that the king should also be priest and pontiff. Hence even today we call the emperors pontiffs."

units.la: Ministri deinde sacrificantes in sacrificio quidem Nestoris, sunt cum Laerces aurifaber, qui vornua boves in aurarium bubulcus, qui jubetur boves ex agro in urbem adducere: cum ancille, quarum munus fuit ligna & aquam afferre comitium, adornare: cum denique filii Nestoris, qui principem in bocministerio locum obtinent: Horum enim ministeria & opera utitur cum in ...
units.tr: The ministers who assisted in Nestor's sacrifice were: Laerceus the goldsmith, who was to gild the horns of the oxen; the cowherd, who was ordered to bring the oxen from the field into the city; the maidservants, whose task was to bring wood and water and to prepare the place; and finally the sons of Nestor, who hold the chief place in this ministry. For he uses their service and labour in ...

units.la: Notanda vero hic bene morate & constitute rei familiaris, sive oeconomiae ratio. Nestor suum, ceu paterfam. bene & prudenter suis domesticis imperat, singulis certa sua munera, quae efficere & exsequi debeant, diligenter praescribit. Liberi autem atque famuli summa industria & celeritate patris & domini sui jussa atque mandata exsequuntur. Id docet Homerus verbo illo ...
units.tr: Here we should note the well-ordered management of household affairs. Nestor, like a good and prudent father of a family, commands his household and carefully assigns to each person a particular duty which they must perform and carry out. The children and servants carry out their father's and master's orders and commands with the greatest diligence and speed. Homer teaches this by that phrase ...

units.la: Quod autem filiorum potius, quam servorum opera Nestor in hoc sacrificio utitur, id, Eustathius non honoris modo atque reverentiae erga Deos gratia factum fuisse testatur, verum etiam ex communi sere Heroum more & consuetudine, qui in multis avrnpyeiv sive avrovpyeiv sunt soliti: unde avrodiaxovoi ab Homero sunt dicti Iliad.7. Addit idem, beatam fuisse hanc Nestoris domum, cui non tam mancipia, quam ipsi liberi inservirent. Eandem in sententiam Athenaeus quoque hujusce sacrificii mentionem faciens disserit, cum inquit: Nestor, cum esset Rex & multis imperaret: tamen amicissimus & suavissimus suis liberis potissimum ministrat in illo sacrificio atque conviviis est usus. Addit, ... illud sacrificium, quod per illos fit, qui mutua familiaritate beni volentiaq; sunt conjuncti. Eodem modo (si ea, quae vere sacra sunt, licet cum his superstitiosis conferre) multo verius & justius nos Christiani affirmare possumus, sacrosanctum illud convivium dominicum tanto gratius Deo & acceptius esse, quanto major & ardentior est illorum, qui communicant, beni volentia mutua atq; charitas.
units.tr: As to why Nestor uses the work of his sons rather than of his servants in this sacrifice, Eustathius testifies that this was done not only out of honour and reverence towards the gods, but also from the common custom and practice of the heroes, who were accustomed to do many things with their own hands. Hence Homer calls them autopdiakonoi, self-servers, in Iliad 7. The same writer adds that Nestor's house was blessed, since not so much slaves as his own children served him. Athenaeus also mentions this sacrifice to the same effect, saying: "Nestor, though he was a king and ruled many, was most friendly and kind, and he served chiefly through his own sons at that sacrifice and at his feasts." He adds that this is a sacrifice performed by those who are joined together by mutual familiarity, goodwill and friendship. In the same way (if it is permitted to compare these superstitious rites with what is truly sacred) we Christians can affirm much more truly and justly that the holy Lord's Supper is so much more pleasing and acceptable to God as the mutual goodwill and love of those who communicate is greater and warmer.

units.la: Illi porro, qui sacrificio huic atq; epulo communicarunt, fuerunt cum uxor, & filia; tum Temlemiches & illius socii, qui fuerunt in vitati. Nam hic fuit mos Ethnicorum, ut sacrificia Dii facturi, suos vicinos, cognatos, amicos & familiares ad illa invitarent: ut ex Antiquitatibus mens Convivialibus satis superq; apparet.
units.tr: Those who took part in this sacrifice and feast were Nestor's wife and daughter, then Temlemiches and his companions, who were invited. For it was the custom of the heathen, when they were about to sacrifice to the gods, to invite their neighbours, kinsmen, friends and household to those rites, as is sufficiently clear from the ancient accounts of banquets.

units.la: Porro quoad personas sacrificiorum, principes quidem nempe sacerdotes; quorum munus bis fere verbis describit Plato in Politico: Sacerdotum genus, inquit, quod est legitimum, docet partim, quo pacto donaria & sacra Diis sint offerenda, quae ipsis sint grata: partim quae vota sint faciena, quid de boni a Diis sit petendum; de his, inquam, similiter, ut de templis in genere quaedam dicamus; & primum de nominibus quae sunt vel generalia, vel specialia.
units.tr: Regarding the persons of sacrifices, the principal ones are of course the priests, whose office Plato describes in roughly these words in the Statesman: "The lawful class of priests," he says, "teaches partly how gifts and sacred offerings are to be made to the gods so that they may be pleasing to them, and partly what vows are to be made and what good things are to be asked from the gods. Of these matters, I say, we shall speak in the same way as we say something about temples in general; and first about the names, which are either general or special."

units.la: Apud Hebraeos duo sunt sacerdotum nomina generalia, nempe כהן Cohanim, & כמרים Cemarim. Vox prior cum de veris, tum etiam de falsis & idololatricis sacerdotibus usurpatur: כהן Cihch, id est, sacra, sive rem divinam facere sacerdotio fungi, quod LXX inpuepyein vertunt. Vocabulum Coach, id est, vires, potentia, propterea quod cum verorum, tum etiam falsorum & idololatricorum sacerdotum maxima semper fuit dignitas, authoritas & potestas.
units.tr: Among the Hebrews there are two general names for priests, namely kohanim [כהן] and kemarim [כמרים]. The former word is used both of true priests and also of false and idolatrous priests. Kihen [כהן] means to perform sacred rites, to serve in the priesthood, which the Seventy render hierateuein [ἱερατεύειν]. The word koach [כח], meaning strength or power, is related to it, because the dignity, authority and power of both true priests and false and idolatrous priests has always been very great.

units.la: Vox deinde כמרים Cemarim, semper pro sacerdotibus falsis & idololatricis accipitur. Quidam volunt eam vocem (unde forsan vox Latina Camillorum, de qua infra) proprie significare sacerdotum minixtros, sive d: illos vel sacras vel sburn incensione & precibus ardentibus, quas pro populo faciebant: vel ab arro vesti u, quo erant amicti. Alii sic volunt dictos ab incensio & inflammatio sacrorum studio. Quidam a stigmatibus, quae faciei illorum vel etiam reliquo corpori erant inusta. Nam כמר Camar (unde forsan vox Camara, id est, Caminus dictus) accendi, excandescere, aduri significat. Haec de nominibus Hebraicis.
units.tr: The word kemarim [כמרים] is always taken for false and idolatrous priests. Some hold that this word (whence perhaps the Latin word camilli, discussed below) properly means the ministers of the sacred things, either from the burning and fervent prayers which they offered for the people, or from the black garment with which they were clothed. Others hold that they were so called from the zeal of burning and inflaming the sacred things. Some derive it from the marks which were branded on their faces or on the rest of their bodies. For kamar [כמר] (whence perhaps the word camara, that is, the so-called caminus) means to be kindled, to grow hot, to be burned. So much on the Hebrew names.

units.la: Graeci sacerdos dicitur ιερεύς, ιερεια sacrificiala, & ιεροποιος: ιεροποιησις item quasi qui sacrorum semper est memor, & ιεραρχος aruspex. Nec verò solum veri sacerdotes, sed etiam adulterini & fucati voluerunt ipsos appellari a ιερων, a sacris, quae tractarent, cum non hi, sed iegarus, id est, accipitres potius dici merentur, qui accipitrum & aliarum avium similes, inexplebilis insatiabilis munera atque dona accipiendi cupiditate, id est, a vaga flagrarunt.
units.tr: The Greek word for priest is hiereus [ιερεύς], and for priestess hiereia [ιέρεια], sacrificer [ιεροποιός], and likewise hieropoiesis [ιεροποιησις], as one who is always mindful of the sacred rites, and hierarches [ιεράρχος], high priest. Not only true priests but also counterfeit and pretended ones have wished to be called after the sacred things (hiera) which they handled; but these men deserve rather to be called hierakes [ἱέρακες], hawks, who, like hawks and other birds, burned with an insatiable and unending desire to receive gifts and presents.

units.la: Nomina praeterea alia sacerdotum apud Graecos fuerunt multa, quae Julius Pollux in Onomastico libro primo & octavo recensent. Ea sunt ιεροπόροι, θύται, τηλεσκοι, ισοπρόπολοι, καθάρται, σπονδοφόροι, quae nomine Pontifices ... Sunt item, quae in vaticiniis & Deorum ornatu reddendis, illis impostia fuere, ut ... Mystagogos, mystagogos, Syracusani vocabant eos, qui bosphites ad fanum, simulacra, & ornamenta misenda ducere, & unumquodq; offendere folebant.
units.tr: Among the Greeks there were many other names for priests, which Julius Pollux lists in the first and eighth books of his Onomasticon. These are hieroporoi, thytai, teleskoi, isoprophoroi [ἱεροπόροι, θύται, τηλεσκοι, ισοπρόπολοι], katharatai [καθάρται], and spondophoroi [σπονδοφόροι], which are called pontiffs ... There are also those who were employed in giving oracles and in dressing the gods, as ... The Syracusans called those who led the people to the temple and were accustomed to show the images and ornaments and to explain each thing mystagogoi [μυσταγωγοί], mystagogues.
These were the Greek names of this kind.

units.la: Apud Latinos voces maxime generales sunt Sacerdos, Sacrificus & Sacrificulus. His nominibus non tantum veri sacerdotes, qui Deo dicati sunt ad sacra facienda, quos Tertullianus etiam sacrificatores & adoratores, Graeci Sutes, x, Sutes vocat, & Isidorus Originum libro septimo quasi sacra dantes, sed falsi quoque & superstitiosi sacerdotes insigniri solebant, ut qui sacris idololatricis essent dediti; sacra Diis fictis facerent & tractarent. Sed sacerdos falsus & idololatricus ratio sic videatur dictum voce composita a caixo, id est, saccus, & xipa id est, ... cruent. crum, sive quæflus, propterea quòd ille fit quasi saccus quidam lucri, qui nunquam expleri satiari potest. Vel etiam sacerdotes illi Gentilium ιεροποιοὶ potius, quàm sacerdotes dici potuerūt; quo nomine Græcè appellantur φιλοχρημάτοι, id est, homines lucri cupidi, qui unde lucrum capcanc, quos Latini Lucriones appellant: Vel etiam non sam sacerdotes, quàm Cerdones dici metrebantur; quod nomen eos significat, qui artes illiberales & sordidas lucri quæstus gratia exercent (ἀπὸ τῶν ἱεροῦς) ac quibus lucri odor, quaevis ex re vel curpissima, sua visissimus est & turpissimus: Vel denique illi Gentilium sacerdotes sic vere dicti fuerunt ea significatione, qua vox Sacri in malam saepe partem pro impio & exsecrabili usurpatur; qua significatione Virgilius dixit, Auri sacra fames, &c. Sic Sacer, teste Festo, dictus etiam fuit, quem populus judicavit ob maleficium: neq; fas est eum immolari; sed qui occidit, parricidii non damnatur. Nam lege cribuniția prima cavetur, Si quis eum, qui eo plebeiscito sacer sit, occideric; parricida ne sit: ex quo quivis homo malus acq; improbus sacer appellari solet. Secundum hunc igicur sensum & significationem sacerdotes ibi impii, facerrimi, boccè, exsecrabiles, mali atque improbi, ut leno quidam apud Plautum vocatur, dici poterant. Erant denique illi sacerdotes, canquam Epicuri de grege porci, & idcirco sacres sues dici poterant; quos tamen Festus interpretatur sacros puros, qui Lares ibus offerri solebant.
units.tr: Among the Latins the most general words are Sacerdos, Sacrificus and Sacrificulus. These names were applied not only to true priests, dedicated to God for performing sacred rites, whom Tertullian also calls sacrificers and worshippers, whom the Greeks call [Sutes], and whom Isidore in his Origins, book seven, calls "those who give sacred things" (quasi sacra dantes). They were also applied to false and superstitious priests, namely those devoted to idolatrous rites, who performed and handled sacred rites for fictitious gods. The reason why a false and idolatrous priest is called sacerdos may be seen in a word compounded from saccus, a sack, and a Greek word for gain, that is, quaestus, because such a man is like a sack of gain that can never be filled or satisfied. Or those priests of the Gentiles could be called idol-makers [ἱεροποιοί] rather than priests. In Greek they are called [φιλοχρήματοι], that is, men greedy for money, who take profit wherever they can, and whom the Latins call Lucriones. Or they could be called not so much priests as cerdones, a name for those who practise base and sordid arts for the sake of gain, and to whom the smell of profit is most pleasing, from whatever source, however filthy. Or finally those priests of the Gentiles were truly called sacri in that sense in which the word sacer is often used in a bad sense, for impious and detestable. Virgil used it this way when he wrote of "the accursed hunger for gold". So Sacer, according to Festus, was also the name for a man whom the people had judged for a crime. It is not lawful to sacrifice him, but whoever kills him is not condemned for parricide. For the first law of the tribunes provides that if anyone kills the man who is made sacred by that plebiscite, he shall not be a parricide. From this, any wicked and wretched man is commonly called sacer. According to this sense and meaning, impious, most wicked, detestable, evil and base priests could be so called, as a certain pimp is called in Plautus. Finally, there were those priests who were like a pig from Epicurus' herd, and so could be called sacred pigs. Festus, however, interprets these as "sacred pure ones", who were accustomed to be offered to the Lares.

units.la: Dicti sunt etiam Antistites sacrorum & fanorum: ac Præsticem quoq; teste Festo, olim in eadem significatione dicebanc Antiqui, quem nunc dicimus Ancistitem.
units.tr: They were also called antistites of sacred rites and temples. Festus also says that the ancients used to call the praestices in the same sense, which we now call antistites.

units.la: Prophetas, ut ait Festus, in Adrasto jultus nominae Antistites fanorum oraculorum, interpreces. Cùm capita viridi lauro inquit, velare imperant Prophetæ, sancta ita casse qui putanc sacra.
units.tr: As Festus says, in Adrastus prophets were called antistites of oracular shrines, that is, interpreters. "When the prophets order the heads to be veiled with green laurel, they say that those who hold sacred things are thus made holy."

units.la: Nomina deinde specialia sacerdotum ducta func, vel a Diis, quorum sunt sacerdotes; vel a certis sacris, cerimoniis, officiis acq; muniis; vel a corporis culcu atq; habitu. A Diis quidem, sive Numinibus; ut Vestales a Vesta: Furnales a Furina: Vulcanales a Vulcano: Iliaci ab Ilside: Canephoræ virgines, quæ Iunonis sacra administrabant: Palatualis Flamen, qui ad sacrificandum ei Dea consultatus erat, in cujus tutela Palacium esse putabant.
units.tr: The special names of priests are derived either from the gods whose priests they are, or from certain rites, ceremonies, offices and duties, or from bodily appearance and dress. From the gods or divinities: thus Vestals from Vesta; Furnales from Furina; Vulcanales from Vulcan; Iliaci from Isis; Canephorae, virgins who administered the rites of Juno; the Palatual Flamen, who was consulted by the goddess for sacrificing, and in whose protection they thought the Palatine was.

units.la: Kichologi vero dicti sunt apud Opuntios ab illo ritu seu munere, quòd Græcorum plerique in sacrificiis hordeo ucerencur, ejusq; primitias offerrent. Hi autem primitias istas collighebant. Ceteroqui duos habuisse sacerdotes Opuntios Plutarchus cesserat in quæstionibus Græcis: Unum, qui Deorum; alterum qui Geniorum sacra administrabat. Sic Hypocaustriam Solenses appellabant Minervæ ancistitam, quòd averruncandorum malorum gratia cercis quibusdam sacris operaretur. Sic etiam Arvales, qui arvorû sacerdotes erant: Augures ab augurijs sunc dicti, & Fociales a foro, sive ferio, quòd penes eos belli pacisve ferendæ seu faciendæ, fœderisq; feriendi jus ac potestas esset: Inter Fociales autem Pacer pacratus principem locum obtinebat dignatu. Is, teste Plutarcho in Quæstionibus Romanis, quæstione sexagesima secunda orat, qui habebacliberos vivo & superstite adhuc ejus patre: dictusq; est patratus, id est, perfectus & absolutus, Is erat juris jurandi & panis præses, quem, ut ait Homerus, oportet prorsum et retrorsum videre. Ejus fides acq; custodiæ commicebat Prætor liberos, qui propter formam & florem ætatis custodiæ videbantur indigere.
units.tr: The Kichologi were so called among the Opuntians from that rite or office, because most Greeks in their sacrifices were crowned with barley and offered its firstfruits. These men gathered those firstfruits. Plutarch in his Greek Questions also wrote that the Opuntians had two priests: one who administered the rites of the gods, and another who administered the rites of the Genii. So the Solenses called the ancistita of Minerva Hypocaustria, because she worked with certain rites to avert evils. So also the Arvales, who were priests of the fields. Augurs were named from augury, and Fetials from the forum, or from ferire, because the right and power of bearing or making war and peace, and of striking a treaty, lay with them. Among the Fetials, the patratus pater held the chief place in dignity. He, according to Plutarch in the Roman Questions, question sixty-two, was one who had children while his father was still alive and surviving. He was called patratus, that is, perfected and completed. He was president of the oath and of the bread, "whom, as Homer says, one must look at forward and backward". The praetor entrusted to his faith and custody the children who seemed to need guardianship on account of their beauty and the bloom of their age.

units.la: A corporis porrò habitu atq; cultu dicti fuerunt apud Romanos Flamines, quasi Filamines, quòd, cùm in capite pileum haberent, in quo bre vis erat virga desuper, habens lanæ aliquid: id autem pro æstu ferre non possent, filo cantum capica religare cæperunt. Namnudis eos penicus capitibus incedere nefas erat. Verum camen festis diebus filo de pofico, pileum imponebanc, pro sacerdotû eminentia. Hæc Isidorus. Sic Herculis sacerdotes, apud Græcos fuerunt appellati, quibus ferre coronam, & comam promissam proprium erat.
units.tr: The Romans called the flamines from their bodily appearance and dress, as if they were Filamines, because they wore on the head a cap with a small rod on top, having some wool. But since they could not bear this in the heat, they began to bind the head only with a thread. For it was unlawful for them to walk about with bare heads. Yet on festival days they put on the cap with a woollen thread, as a mark of priestly distinction. So Isidore. So among the Greeks the priests of Hercules were called, and it was proper for them to wear a crown and long hair.

units.la: Erant etiam apud singulos populos certa sacerdotû nomina. Sic Indorum sacerdotes Brachmanes, Gallorum Druidæ, aliorum alii nominibus fuerunt appellati. Et hæc de sacerdotum nominibus.
units.tr: Among individual peoples there were also certain names for priests. So the priests of the Indians were called Brahmans, those of the Gauls Druids, and others were called by other names. And these are the things about the names of priests.

units.la: Nunc de eorum electione, nominatione, creatione, inauguratione & iniciatione quædam dicamus. Munus ipsū Græcè ἱεροποιία, in genere appellatur. Inde καθιέρωσις ἀνὰς ἔπι ἱεροποιίας, ἱεροποιῶν.
units.tr: Now let us say something about their election, nomination, creation, inauguration and initiation. The office itself is called in Greek [ἱεροποιία] in general. Hence the verbs [καθιέρωσις] and [ἱεροποιῶν] are derived.

units.la: M præficere aliquem, sive sacerdotem creare: & κληρῶσθαι ἱεροσυνῆς, ὁ ἱεροσύνῶν, sortiri sacerdotium: & λαμβάνειν ἱεροσυνῆν, suscipere sacerdotium: & ἔχειν id iam ἱεροσυνῆν, privatum habere sacerdotium: & μετάγειν μηδεμίας ἱεροσυνῆς, nullius sacerdotii adipiscendi jus habere, sive esse capacem, apud Demosthenem. Item apud eundem αἱρετὸς ἱεροσύνη, ἱεροσυνῆ, aliquem ἱερός, hoc ἐμβαλλειν ἱεροῦ, eligere sacerdotem, & ἀγχοῦ ἱερεύς, electus sacerdos.
units.tr: To appoint someone, or to create a priest: [κληροῦσθαι ἱεροσύνης], to obtain a priesthood by lot; [λαμβάνειν ἱεροσύνην], to take up a priesthood; [ἔχειν τὴν ἱεροσύνην], to hold a priesthood privately; and [μετέχειν μηδεμιᾶς ἱεροσύνης], to have no right to obtain any priesthood, or to be incapable of one, in Demosthenes. Likewise in the same author, [αἱρετὸς ἱεροσύνης], one chosen for priesthood; [ἱερεὺς αἱρετός] and [ἐμβάλλειν ἱερέα], to choose a priest; and [ἄγχου ἱερεύς], a priest who has been elected.

units.la: Apud Latinos deinde hoc munus in genere dicitur Sacerdotium: quod tamen aliquando est dignitas: unde dicimus, Sacerdotium habere, & sacerdotio prædictum esse; aliquando vero, prouentus sacerdotum, quæ vulgo Beneficia appellantur. Ad hoc autem munus peculiariter pertinet Nominandi verbum, ut peter ex illis Plinii verbis in epistolis: Sic illo die, quo solent sacerdotes nominare, quos sacerdotio dignissimos nominant, nec semper nominabant. Hinc dicta Nominatio. Suetonius: Claudius Cæsar, inquit, in cooptandis per collegia sacerdotibus, nemine nisi iuratus nominavit.
units.tr: Among the Latins this office in general is called sacerdotium, which sometimes means a dignity, whence we say to have a priesthood, or to be endowed with a priesthood. Sometimes it means the income of priests, which are commonly called benefices. The word nominare pertains especially to this office, as can be seen from these words of Pliny in his letters: "So on that day, on which priests are accustomed to nominate, they nominate those most worthy of the priesthood, though they did not always do so." Hence nominatio. Suetonius: Claudius Caesar, he says, in co-opting priests through the colleges, nominated no one except one who had been sworn.

units.la: Cooptandi quoq; verbum electioni erat accommodatum. Cicero: Cooptatum me ab eo in collegium recordabar. Plinius: Me pene adhuc puerum patronum cooptavit. Sacerdotium dari mandari dicitur. Itaq; Iovis illud sacerdotium amplissimum Theomnesto datur. Cicero in Verrem: Populus per religionem sacerdotia mandare non poterat. Idem contra Rullum: Eligere ut ut amplissimos ad sacerdotia. Idem: Erit causa, qua consilium majorum in eligendis ad sacerdotia viris amplissimis iure ac merito laudare possimus. Idem pro Domo sua: In sacerdotium venire, ut nos dicimus, an cum ampt Fomnen. Inire sacerdotium, idem Cicero: an sem Pricfterlich amptrecten. Hinc & sacerdotium habere idem Cicero dixit: Cuius nomen exisset, haberet sacerdotium, id est, in sacerdos esse. Sorte enim nonnunquam sacerdotes siebant. Hinc facerdotio prædicus, qui habet sacerdotium. Cicero: Licinia virgo Vestalis sanctissimo sacerdotio prædita. Et alibi: Amplissimo sacerdotio præditus. Et præesse sacerdotio. Qui & sacra publica coluerunt, & publicis sacerdotiis præfuerunt. Idem de Senectute: Metellus, Pontifex Maximus, viginti & duos annos ei sacerdotio præfuit. Idem pro C. Rabirio: Lucius Flaccus homo in sacerdotio cerimoniis, quibus præerat, diligentissimus.
units.tr: The verb cooptandi was also suited to election. Cicero: I recalled that I had been co-opted by him into the college. Pliny: he co-opted me as an advocate when I was still almost a boy. Priesthood is said to be given or entrusted, so that great priesthood of Jupiter is given to Theomnestus. Cicero against Verres: the people could not entrust priesthoods because of religious scruples. The same against Rullus: to choose the most distinguished men for priesthoods. The same: there will be a case in which we can rightly and deservedly praise the counsel of our ancestors in choosing men of the highest rank for priesthoods. The same in his speech for his house: to enter upon the priesthood, as we say, or with the German phrase, to take up the priestly office. Hence Cicero also said "to have the priesthood": whose name had come out would have the priesthood, that is, would be a priest, for sometimes priests were made by lot. Hence sacerdotio praeditus, one who has a priesthood. Cicero: Licinia, a virgin Vestal endowed with the most holy priesthood. And elsewhere: endowed with the most distinguished priesthood. And to preside over the priesthood: those who both kept the public sacred rites and presided over public priesthoods. Cicero in De Senectute: Metellus, Pontifex Maximus, presided over that priesthood for twenty-two years. The same in the speech for C. Rabirius: Lucius Flaccus, a man most diligent in the ceremonies over which he presided.

units.la: Capiendi quoq; verbum sacerdotum electioni erat accommodatum. Tranquillus in Augusto: Sacerdotium, inquit, & numerum & dignitatem, sed & commoda auxit; præcipue Vestalium virginum. Quum, in demortua locum alium capi oporteret, ambirenti, multi, ne filias in sortem darent, adjurare vit si cujusquam neptium suarum competeret etas, oblaturum se fuisse eam. Capitolium... Capiendi Vestalis, quando ad id sacerdotium legebatur: propterea quod Pontificis manu prebensa ab eo parente, in cujus potestate erat, veluti bello captam, abducebatur. Pontifex Maximus hac verba dicebat, cum virginem capiebat: AMATA TE CAPIO. Ideo autem Amata inter capiendum a Pontifice Maximo appellabatur, quoniam eam, quæ prima capta fuit, hoc fuisse nomine, tradit Gellius in primo Noctium Atticarum. Sic Flamines quoque Diales; item Augures & Pontifices capi dicebantur. De Flamine capto exemplum est apud Livium libro vigesimoseptimo ab Urbe condita. Flaccus Flamen captus, P. Licinio Pontifice Maximo.
units.tr: The verb capiendi too was suited to the election of priests. Suetonius in Augustus: he increased the priesthoods, he says, in number and dignity, and also in their privileges, especially those of the Vestal virgins. When another had to be taken in place of one who had died, many people, while he was seeking it, swore that if the age of any of their granddaughters fitted, they would offer her, so that they would not have to give their daughters by lot. Capitolium... Capiendi Vestalis, when she was chosen for that priesthood: because she was led away by the hand of the Pontifex from that parent in whose power she was, as if taken in war. The Pontifex Maximus spoke these words when he took the virgin: "AMATA, I TAKE YOU." Amata was called by the Pontifex Maximus during the taking because, Gellius tells us in the first book of his Attic Nights, the first captured virgin had that name. Thus the Diales flamines were also "taken", and augurs and pontiffs were likewise said to be taken. An example of a captured flamen is found in Livy, book twenty-seven, from the founding of the City: Flaccus, flamen, was taken while P. Licinius was Pontifex Maximus.

units.la: Quod autem Sortis fit mentio in electione Vestalium, scribit Gellius Papiam legem se in ea esse, qua ca'vebatur, ut Pontificis Maximi arbitratu virgines e populo viginti legerentur, fortitioque in concione exeo numero fieret: quanquam huic legi Popilia fit posita lege abrogatum, ita ut unicuique liceret, modo etas competeret, filiam ad id sacerdotium ultro offerre. Aristoteles libro quarto Politicorum: Ut de magistratibus, inquit, quaeritur, e quibus eos deesse creari, & a quibus, & quomodo: ita de sacerdotibus, qui & quales sint creandi. Idem: Ut magistratus, sic sacerdotes alios dicit esse αἱρετούς; alios κληρωτοὺς, & alios esse perpetuos, alios diuturnos, alios vero neutros horum. Ibidem sacerdotes sive αἱρετοὺς, sive κληρωτοὺς, sive suffragii sint olim sive forte ducti vult non esse in magistratibus numerandos.
units.tr: As for the mention of the lot in the choosing of the Vestals, Gellius writes that he has the Papian law, which provided that twenty maidens should be picked from the people at the discretion of the Pontifex Maximus, and that from that number a choice should be made by lot in an assembly. Yet this law, he adds, was repealed by the Popilian law, so that anyone might freely offer his own daughter for that priesthood, provided she was of a suitable age. Aristotle, in book four of the Politics: "As we inquire about magistrates, from which classes they should be appointed, by whom, and how, so we must inquire about priests, who and what kind should be appointed." The same author: "As with magistrates, so he says some priests are elected [αἱρετούς], others chosen by lot [κληρωτούς], and some hold office for life, others for long terms, and others neither of these." In the same place he holds that priests, whether elected [αἱρετούς], chosen by lot [κληρωτούς], or formerly appointed by vote or drawn by chance, are not to be counted among the magistrates.

units.la: Donis vero & muneribus saepe viam sibi muniebant ad ista sacerdotia; ea, erant venalia, ut etiam profana munera. Tranquillus de Caligula: Magistratia, inquit, sacerdotii distinguisset quis & ambi& ambitione & licitatione maxima vitibus comparabat, hoc est, Vnus quisque ex diuitiI bus immenso pretio & ambitu emebat sacerdotium illud, dicatum ipsius Numini, ut stilicet esfes magister & quasi principes temporarius sacerdotum.
units.tr: Gifts and bribes often paved the way for men to these priesthoods; they were for sale, even as profane offices were. Suetonius, on Caligula: "He had distinguished the offices of priesthood and magistracy, and he obtained them by canvassing and by the greatest bidding, that is, each rich man bought that priesthood, dedicated to the godhead itself, at an enormous price and by bribery, so that he might be, as it were, its master and temporary prince of the priests."

units.la: Observandum autem alios fuisse sacerdotes generales omnium Deorum, qui quorum vis Deorum sacris praerant: alios vero fuisse certorum Deorum ministros, qui certis Diis erant destinati: unde etiam nomina sua habuerunt, de quibus supra. Ad hoc alludens Cicero de Legibus: Diuos alios, inquit, alii sacerdotes, omnibus Pontifices singulis Flamines junco.
units.tr: It should be observed that there were general priests of all the gods, who presided over the rites of all the gods, and others who were ministers of particular gods, appointed to certain deities. Hence they also had their own names, of which we have spoken above. Cicero alludes to this in his book On the Laws: "Some priests, he says, are for the gods, others for all; the Pontiffs for all, the Flamens for single gods."

units.la: In omnibus autem hisce generalibus omnium Deorum, sive particularibus ceterorum singulorum, Deorum sacerdotibus haec fere quae sequuntur antiquitus, praesertim in eorum creatione, atque deletu observari solebant: nempe Animus, Corpus, Vestitus, Sexus, Aetas, Conjugium sive Caelibatus, Natio, Vitae genus ac institutum, Honos ac Dignitas, Potestas, Gradus, Merces, Lucrum atque Provencus, Poena atque Supplicia, Numerus demique, & Victus, jejunia item & abstinentia a certis diebus vel etiam aliis rebus.
units.tr: In all these priests, whether general for all gods or particular for each of the other gods, the following things were customarily observed, especially in their creation and selection: namely, mind, body, dress, sex, age, marriage or celibacy, nation, manner and form of life, honour and dignity, power, rank, pay, gain and profit, penalties and punishments, number, and finally food, likewise fasts and abstinence from certain days or even other things.

units.la: Primum igitur ipse Animus, ejusque habitus, nempe scientia, cum aliarum artium ac disciplinarum, tum vero atque inprimis eorum sacrorum, quibus erant praepositi, quaeque illis erant curanda, requirebatur. Unde Cicero: Arrogans de religione, de rebus divinis cerimoniisque sacris Pontificibus docere conati. Deinde virtutes quoque animi, ut castitatem, sobrietatem, temperantiam, vigilantiam & diligentiam in administrandis sacris requirebant. Inde Seneca: Propudicitia vota facienda sunt, proflituta mandabitis? Et Vestalium virginum si qua incesti convicta esset, ante ora civium maesto silentio offerebatur, vivas, circa Collinam portam in subterraneum specum dimissa, terraque flatim superiniecta necabatur: Gellius. Erant tamen pleriq; ipsorum sacerdotes tum magicis artibus, tum omni vitiorum, scelerum, flagitiorumque genere (quorum partes et procreatrix est idololatria) dediti & addicti.
units.tr: First, therefore, the mind itself and its disposition were required, namely knowledge, both of the other arts and disciplines and, above all, of those sacred rites to which they were set over and of what was to be cared for in them. Hence Cicero: "Arrogant men who tried to teach the Pontiffs about religion and divine affairs and sacred ceremonies." Then they also required virtues of the mind, such as chastity, sobriety, temperance, watchfulness and diligence in administering the sacred rites. Hence Seneca: "Are vows to be made for chastity, and will you hand over prostitutes?" And if any of the Vestal virgins was convicted of incest, she was carried before the eyes of the citizens with sad silence, put alive into an underground pit near the Colline Gate, and buried at once under earth: Gellius. Yet most of these priests were given over and addicted both to magic arts and to every kind of vice, crime and shameful deed, of which idolatry is both the part and the parent.

units.la: Secundo ut animi, ita corporis quoque certam dispositionem in sacerdotibus sui requirebant. Ac illos quidem corpore volebant esse sano & integro: eos autem, qui insigni aliquo corporis vitio laborabant, membroque aliquo capti erant ac mutili; eos nequaquam ad rem divinam tractandam existimabant aptos esse & idoneos, sed admittere nefas putabant. Ad utrunque referenda est lex illa antiqua de sacerdotibus: Sacerdos sit integer, de quibus haec leguntur apud Senecam: Metellus Pontifex, cum arderet, Vestae templum, dum Palladium rapit, oculos perdit, sacerdotium illi negatur. Et posse: Lex integrum ad animum refert, non ad corpus. Lex aestimari hoc voluit tunc, cum quis peteret, non cum haberet sacerdotium. Idem: Ambitio fa lex est ad sacerdotium, non sacris non sanctitatis tantum, sed felicitatis admittit, inquiris in mores, incorpus, in vitam. Vide tu quemadmodum tam morosa legi satis faciasa. Idem: Fas sacerdoti non esset, ancillam tibi similem habere, fieri ne sacerdotem fas erit? Et posse: Non potes ciniam sperari sacerdos, in qua sperari meretrix potest: alias oculis leno vitam effumat, alius Pontifex. Idem: Absint ex hoc foro lenones, absint meretrices, ne quid parum sanctum occurrat, dum sacerdos legitur. Et posse: Quo mihi sacerdotem, cujus precaria est castitas, si mater tua profiteretur tibi nonne. Idem: Pro libertate vota facienda sunt, captive mandabitis? Idem: Ancilla ex lupanaribus sacerdoti non emuntur. Coram sacerdote obscoeni homines abfinent. Nonfine causa sacerdoti litor apparet. Occurrenti tibi meretricem submovisse? Idem: Castigationem ex Pontificis Maximi arbitrio meruerat sacerdos si te e lupanari redemisset. Idem: Sacerdos non integricorporis, quasi mali ominis res vincanda est. Hoc in victimis notatur, quanto magis in sacerdotibus? Pot sacerdotium magis observandae est nobilitas. Non enim sine ira Deorum debilitatur sacerdos. Apparet non propitios esse sacerdoti Deos, quem ne sanati quidem servant. Hallenus Seneca de personis et minus sacrorum: ut ne sacerdos nisi integer adsumatur et quis integer sit habendus.
units.tr: Secondly, just as they required a certain disposition of mind, so they also required a certain disposition of body in priests. They wanted them to be healthy and whole in body; but those who suffered from some notable bodily defect, or who were maimed or mutilated in some limb, they judged in no way fit and suitable for handling sacred things, but thought it wrong to admit them. To both points belongs that ancient law about priests: "Let the priest be whole," of which these things are read in Seneca: "When Metellus the Pontifex, as the temple of Vesta was burning, was snatching the Palladium, he lost his eyes, and the priesthood was denied him." And elsewhere: "The law refers wholeness to the mind, not to the body. The law wished this to be assessed when someone sought the priesthood, not when he already held it." The same: "Ambition is a fault for the priesthood; it admits not only holiness for sacred things but also good fortune; you inquire into morals, into body, into life. See how you may satisfy so fastidious a law." The same: "It would not be lawful for a priest to have a maidservant like you; will it be lawful to make you a priest?" And elsewhere: "You cannot hope for a chaste priest from whom a prostitute can be hoped for; in other cases a pimp breathes out his life with his eyes, another as Pontiff." The same: "Let pimps be kept away from this forum, let prostitutes be kept away, lest anything less than holy meet us while the priest is being chosen." And elsewhere: "What do I want with a priest whose chastity is precarious, if your mother would profess it to you, would she not...?" The same: "Are vows to be made for liberty, will you hand over captives?" The same: "Maidservants are not bought from brothels for a priest. Obscene men keep away from the presence of a priest. Not without cause does the priest's lictor appear. Did you remove a prostitute from meeting you?" The same: "A priest would have earned punishment at the discretion of the Pontifex Maximus if he had redeemed you from a brothel." The same: "A priest is not to be whole in body, as if it were a thing of ill omen to be avoided. This is noted in victims; how much more in priests? For the priesthood ought rather to be observed for its nobility. For the priest is not weakened without the anger of the gods. It is clear that the gods are not favourable to a priest whom they do not even keep sound." Thus Seneca, on persons and the less important sacred matters: that no priest should be taken unless he is whole, and who is to be regarded as whole.

units.la: Exiat de hac etiam re quaestio apud Plutarchum in quaestionibus Romanis, Cur interdictum fuerit Augurii, Si ulcus haberet, a vest observare. Idem ibidem, Vt villimam, inquit, aut avem ulcerosam reli sacrae faciunde gratia usurpare nefas erat: sic animo ab omnibus molestiis et quasi ulceribus ac morbis vacuo, sincero, puro et integro tractari oportet. Et quaestione quadragesima Romanorum, apud Charonenses coronatum esse, tomam altare, ferro armatum Phocensis fiuni fines non ingredi, propria fuisse sacerdotes munia testaturi idem. Sic apud Magos qui essent lentiginosi, tanquam Dijs in visi, ab aris summo vebantur: item qui elati reuixerunt, quibusque viventibus exsequiae factae essent, veluti profani a sacris propellebantur, teste Herodoto. Sic apud Hebraeos menstruatis fatis posteq; quadraginta dies, & qui impetigine deformes essent, cemplis aditus erat interclusus.
units.tr: This question is also raised in Plutarch's Roman Questions: why it was forbidden for an augur to observe if he had an ulcer. The same author there: "As it was unlawful to use a victim or a bird with an ulcer for making sacred offerings, so the mind must be handled empty of all troubles, and, as it were, of ulcers and diseases, sincere, pure and whole." And in Roman question forty, he indicates that among the Charonians the priests' proper duties were to be crowned, to have the altar, and to be armed with iron; the Phocians did not enter the borders [of the sanctuary]. So among the Magi, those who were freckled were thrust down from the altars as if they were displeasing to the gods; likewise those who had been carried out for dead and came back to life, and those for whom funeral rites had been performed while they were still living, were driven away from the sacred rites as profane, according to Herodotus. So among the Hebrews, women who were menstruating were excluded from the temple for forty days after, and those who were disfigured by a skin disease had their access to the temples cut off.

units.la: Praeterea ut animorum, ita corporum quoque puritatem judicabant suis sacerdotibus esse necessariam. Volebant, inquam, eos et animi & corporibus esse purosque ac mundos. Nam corpore impuro & sordido sacra tractare, nefas ducebant: qui quidem corporis cultus atque habitus fuit vel naturalis, vel artificialis & asciticius: alii erant capite raso; alii comati; alii erant barbati; alii imberbes: aliis erat barbae brevis; alios promissa. Sic exempli gratia, Iisaci, id est, Isidis sacerdotes apud Aegyptios erant rasso capite: econtra Stephanophoros, Herculis sacerdotibus, apud Graecos, ferre coronam & comam promissam proprium erat, teste Alexandro ab Alexandro lib. sexto, capite duodecimo, & libro secundo, capite octavo. Ita Cybelis sacerdotes variis flucatos coloribus, & facies pigmento delitos, oculosque obuntos, cum nitella & crocoto, lineo calceamento, ante simulacrum Deae incedere solitos & cum tinnitu Cymbalorum & sonitu tympanorum sacrum fecisse elegimus apud eundem Alexandrum libro secundo, capite eodem octavo. Sic Britannorum conjuges miruq; glasto toto corpore oblitas quibusdam in sacris nudas incessisse, Aethiopum colorem imitantes, scribit Plinius libro vigesimo secundo, capite primo. Pertinet huc symbolum Pythagorae, Penes sacrificium ne fis caelis unguibus: quod unguium quoque bitam fuisse rationem indicio esse potest. Referende praeterea huc, illa aquae lustrales, quibus vel totum corpus, vel aliquot ejus partes, ut caput, manus, atque pedes abluebant.
units.tr: Besides, just as they judged purity of mind, so they judged purity of body also to be necessary for their priests. They wanted them, I say, to be pure and clean both in mind and in body. For they thought it wrong to handle sacred things with an impure and filthy body. This bodily care and dress was either natural or artificial and adopted: some had their heads shaved, others wore long hair, some were bearded, others beardless; some had short beards, others let them grow long. Thus, for example, the priests of Isis, that is the Isiacs, among the Egyptians had shaved heads; on the contrary, to bear a crown and to wear long hair was peculiar to the Stephanophoroi, the priests of Hercules among the Greeks, according to Alexander ab Alexandro, book six, chapter twelve, and book two, chapter eight. So too the priests of Cybele, painted with various colours, their faces smeared with pigment and their eyes daubed with stibium and saffron, in linen shoes, used to march before the image of the goddess, and, with the clashing of cymbals and the sound of drums, performed the sacred rites, as we learn from the same Alexander, book two, the same chapter eight. Likewise the wives of the Britons, smeared over their whole bodies with woad, are written by Pliny, book twenty-two, chapter one, to have walked naked at certain sacred rites, imitating the colour of the Ethiopians. To this belongs the saying of Pythagoras, "Do not cut your nails at a sacrifice," which can be an indication that the nails too had their own regulation. Also to be referred here are those lustral waters, in which they washed either the whole body or some parts of it, such as the head, hands and feet.
III. The vestments of the priests.

units.la: Tertio, quod attinet ad vestitu & amictum sacerdotii sive eorum, qui sacris procurandis praerant, ejus curiosa valde superstitio suisque habita fuit in sacris ratio. Hinc, Pura Vestimenta, inquit Paullus, sacerdotes ad sacrificium habebant, id est, non oblita, non fulgurita, non funesta, non maculam habentia. Puri lauum, ut est apud eundem, erat idem, quod pura aqua lantum. Nam ut corpora; ita vestimenta quoque sacerdotum, ut etiam aliorum, antequam ad sacra accederent ablui, sive lavari erant solita. Plato: Nam, inquit, in sacrificiis & celebritatibus pulchra vestae aureusq; coronaque sacerdos rem divinam facit. Sacerdos autem, qui victimam sciebat pura in veste & candida pierunque intexit: illa flora, nec majoris operae quam minstruae nunquam in purpura & auro.
units.tr: Third, as regards the clothing and dress of the priesthood, that is, of those who presided over the sacred rites, their practice was very scrupulous and carefully observed in worship. Hence Paul says: "The priests had pure garments for the sacrifice," that is, garments not stained, not scorched by lightning, not dirty with mourning, and not bearing any spot. In the same author, to be "pure" (lauum) meant the same as being washed only with clean water. For as the bodies of the priests, so also their garments, like those of others, were customarily washed or cleansed before they approached the sacred rites. Plato says: "For in sacrifices and festivals the priest performs the divine rite in a fine robe, golden, and with a crown." The priest who knew how to handle the victim wore a pure and white garment, woven mostly of flax, not of greater labour than a woollen one, and never in purple and gold.

units.la: Fuit autem uniuersus bic vestitus omnino variis ac diversus, secundum vel corporis partes, vel materiam, vel colorem, vel formam, vel sexum, vel quantitatem; ejus autem cum brevitatem, tum longitudinem. Ut vero corporis duae positissimae partes sunt extrema caput nimirum atque pedes: ita hae certo modo ac certis vestibus indui atque ornari potissime solebant.
units.tr: This whole clothing was indeed of many kinds and varied, according to the parts of the body, the material, the colour, the shape, the sex, or the size; and according to its length and its shortness. Since the two most prominent extremes of the body are, of course, the head and the feet, so these were usually dressed and adorned in a certain manner and with certain garments.

units.la: Quantum ad caput attinet alii aperto erant capite, alii operto atque tecto: & quidem alio tempore capita sua aperire, alio tegere atque velare consuevere: Observandum tamen perpauca fuisse sacra, quae aperto nudoq; capite erant celebranda. Nam pleriq; sacerdotes ac omnes ii, qui sacra faciebant, usq; intererant operto ac velato; non autem aperto & nudo capite fuerunt. Plautus in Curculione: Quis hic est, qui operto capite Aesculapium Salutat, id est, adorat ac veneratur?
units.tr: As for the head, some went with it uncovered, others covered and wrapped, and at different times they were accustomed to uncover their heads and at other times to cover and veil them. It should be noted, however, that there were very few rites which had to be celebrated with the head bare and uncovered. For most priests, and all those who performed the sacred rites, stood there with the head covered and veiled, and not with it bare and uncovered. Plautus in the Curculio: "Who is this who, with his head covered, greets Aesculapius," that is, adores and venerates him?

units.la: Suetonius de Aulo Vitellio: Idem miri, inquit, in adulando ingenii, primus Cajum Caesarem adorari, ut Deum, instituit, quum reversus ex Syria non aliter adire ausus esset, quam capite velato, circumvertensque, deinde procumbens. Vitellius igitur, cum Caligulam adorare, ut Deum, vellet, capite velato eum saluta vit, qui mos erat eorum, qui Deos venerabantur. Sic Romani sacerdotes cum adoraret, rem divinam factur, capita velabant vittis, mitris, coronis: cum Graeci aperto essent capite. Plutarchus teste est in questionibus, virost inter gentes, et inprimis quidem eos, qui Romanorum legibus vivebant, solitos fuisse velatis capitibus Deos adorare & miter sacra vestem ad aurea usq; attollere: partim quidem ut eo gestu & habitu humiliores se redderent: partim vero ne inter precandu triste quid aut ignominiosum aliunde occurreret, quo animi attentio religiosa turbaretur. Memmit hujus ritus Virgilius, qui Helenum Aeneae sic dicentem introducit: Purpureo velare comas adoperta amictu, Ne qua inter sanctos ignes in honore Deorum Hostilis facies occurrat, & omnia turbet. Hunc, socii, morem sacrorum, hunc ipse teneto. Hac casti maneant in religione nepotes.
units.tr: Suetonius, on Aulus Vitellius: "The same man, he says, had a remarkable talent for flattery; he was the first to establish that Gaius Caesar be adored as a god, since, on returning from Syria, he dared not approach him in any other way than with his head veiled, turning round and then prostrating himself." Vitellius, therefore, when he wished to adore Caligula as a god, greeted him with his head veiled, which was the custom of those who worshipped the gods. So the Roman priests, when they prayed and performed the sacred rite, covered their heads with fillets, caps and garlands, while the Greeks had their heads bare. Plutarch bears witness in his Questions that the nations generally, and especially those who lived under Roman law, were accustomed to adore the gods with veiled heads and to raise their hands in sacred worship up to their ears: partly so that by this posture and bearing they would make themselves more humble, and partly so that nothing sad or ill-omened might meet them from elsewhere during prayer and disturb the religious attention of their minds. Virgil also recalls this rite, introducing Helenus speaking to Aeneas: "Cover your hair with a purple cloak, lest in honour of the gods, amid the holy fires, any hostile sight should meet you and disturb everything. Comrades, keep this custom of the rites; let my own descendants keep this pure religion."

units.la: Ex his ipsis igitur versibus liquet, sacrificantes Diis omnibus caput velare solitos, ideo ne inter religionem vagus aliquid offerrent obtutibus.
units.tr: From these very verses, then, it is clear that those sacrificing to all the gods were accustomed to cover their heads, so that nothing wandering should present itself to their eyes during worship.

units.la: At vero Saturno Romam capite aperto rem divinam faciebant, propterea quod Veritas ortuleari observari ve non potest, cujus parentem ac Deum Romani Saturnum habebant. Hinc te aperto fa-I.ucem facere Saturno sacrificantes dicebantur, unde Festus quod ipsum factum est more Gra-co. Unde Plutarchus. Run peregrino & capite aperto, conjungit. Caussas hujus rei multas affert idem, sic scribens: Quid est ergo? quid Saturno capite aperto immolant? An quid velandi capitis ritum Aeneas tradidit? Saturni vero sacrificium per vetustum est? An illud potius, quoniam Diis coelestibus immolantes velantur? Saturnum vero terrestrem & chthonium esse arbitrantur? An quod veritas oculi observari, non potest? Veritatis autem parentem ac Deum Romani habent? Haec Plutarchus. Ex illa autem ratione, quam inter alias affert, An, quoniam Diis coelestibus immolatur, velantur? Saturnum vero terrestrem & chthonium esse arbitrantur, videtur posse colligi, illos Diis coelestibus velato; terrestribus autem aperto capite sacrificare. Festus, Saturnis, inquit, dicebantur qui capitum in clivo Capitolino incolebant, ubi ara dicata ei Deo ante bellum Trojanum videtur; quia ante eam supplicant aperto capitibus. Macrobius in 3. Saturno ex Ballo ente apud Arum Maximam, in qua Herculis Bos sacrificabatur, observatum ajt, ne lethifernum fieret; ubi etiam aperto capite omnes sacra faciebant: quod fiebat, ne quis Dei habitum imitaretur. Nam ibi ipse operi tocapite erat. Varro ajt, sacrorum hunc fuisse morem, ut scilicet Graeco ritu sacrificaretur in ara Maxima. Hoc etam-addit Bassus, idcirco hoc factum fuisse, quia ara Maxima ante ad venum Aeneae in Itaconsistitur ei, qui hunc ritum capitis velandi invexit.
units.tr: Yet at Rome they performed the sacred rite to Saturn with the head uncovered, because Truth, as they say, cannot be observed or grasped, and the Romans held Saturn to be her parent and god. Hence those sacrificing to Saturn were said to do so with the head bare, and Festus joins the rite to be done "in the Greek manner" with the head uncovered. Plutarch also says so. Plutarch gives many reasons for this, writing thus: "What then is the reason that they sacrifice to Saturn with the head uncovered? Or did Aeneas hand down the custom of veiling the head? Or is the sacrifice to Saturn an ancient one? Or is it rather because they veil themselves when sacrificing to the heavenly gods, and they consider Saturn to be earthly and of the underworld? Or because the truth of the eye cannot be observed? Or because the Romans hold Truth to be the parent and god?" So Plutarch. From that reason, which he gives among others, namely whether it is because they veil themselves when sacrificing to the heavenly gods, and because they consider Saturn to be earthly and of the underworld, it seems possible to conclude that they sacrificed to the heavenly gods with veiled heads, but to the earthly gods with heads uncovered. Festus says: "Saturnii were called those who lived on the Capitoline hill, where an altar dedicated to that god seems to have existed before the Trojan War, because they pray before it with uncovered heads." Macrobius, in the third book, notes that Saturn was observed at the Ara Maxima, where Hercules' ox was sacrificed, so that it should not become deadly; there too everyone performed the sacred rites with uncovered head, which was done so that no one would imitate the appearance of the god. For there the priest himself was bareheaded. Varro says that this was the custom of the rites, namely that the sacrifice at the Ara Maxima was performed in the Greek manner. Bassus adds that this was done for this reason: the Ara Maxima had stood there from earlier times, when Aeneas came to Italy, in honour of the man who introduced this custom of veiling the head.

units.la: Praeterea Honori quoque Deo, aperto capite, rem divinam faciebant, quia splendidum quid& illustre & apertum latet, patens fit gloria. Nobilores vero & potentiores viros capite aperto idcirco venerabantur, ut in vidiam illis detraherent, ne partes Dius immortalibus honores fere, nisi eodem velut delectari viderentur: Testis idem Plutarchus, quaestione decima quinta. Tamen Marcus Varro capitis aperti asfellum magistratuum, non venerationis causa, sed velatudinis prodidit, ni sententiae asfiplari videtur Plinius libro vigesimo octavo. Cur parentes ojiant & filii velatis capitibus, filiae nudis capitibus passieri, crinibus, & mulieres tectis; mo-res autem nudis capitibus in publicum prodire fuerint soliti, vide Plutarchum quaestione decima quarta Romanarum quaestionum.
units.tr: Moreover, they also performed the sacred rite to the god Honos with uncovered head, because whatever is splendid, illustrious and open lies exposed, and glory becomes manifest. Indeed, they honoured more noble and powerful men with uncovered heads, so that they might take away from them the envy that would otherwise attach to them, lest they seem to take pleasure in honours that belong to the immortal gods. Plutarch is again the witness, in his fifteenth question. Nevertheless, Marcus Varro reported that the bared head of magistrates was not a sign of reverence but of health, unless Pliny in book twenty-eight seems to agree with him in this opinion. As to why parents and sons go with veiled heads, while daughters go about with uncovered heads, letting their hair hang loose, and women with covered heads, while men were accustomed to appear in public with uncovered heads, see Plutarch's fourteenth question of the Roman questions.

units.la: Por capitis integumenta varia fuerunt & multiplicia. De Pileorum quidem usu apud Romanos & de capitis aperiendi vel operiendi more atque ritu vide plura apud Juslum Lipium de Amphitheatro. Hujusmodi autem, inter alia integumenta capitis, illud fuit quod Varro vocat; de quo sic scribit: Capital dictum a capite, quod facerdotulae in capite exiamnum habere solent. Idem de Rica, alio genere integumenti: Rica, dicta a ritu, quod Romano ritu velicium foeminae cum faciunt, capita velant. Festus: Rica erat vestimentum quadratum, fimbriatum, purpureum, quo Flaminicae pro palliolo utebantur. Alii dicunt, quod ex lana fiat succida alba, quod consciunt Virgines ingenuae patrimi, matrimi civeis, & inficiatur celeo colore. Idem: Rica & Ricula vocantur parva ricinia, ut palliola, ad usum capitis facta. Grantius quidem aji esse muliebre cingulum capitis, quo pro vitta Flaminica redimiatur.
units.tr: The coverings for the head were various and many. On the use of caps among the Romans, and on the custom and rite of uncovering or covering the head, see more in Justus Lipsius, On the Amphitheatre. Among the other head coverings of this kind was that which Varro calls the capital; of it he writes thus: "Capital is so named from the head, because the little priestesses are accustomed to have it on the head even now." Of another kind of covering, the rica, he writes: "Rica is named from the rite, because women, when they perform the Roman rite of veiling, cover their heads with it." Festus says: "The rica was a square garment, fringed and purple, which the Flaminica used in place of a little cloak." Others say that it is made from white woollen fabric, which free-born virgins, whose fathers and mothers are living, weave and dye with a deep colour. Festus again: "Rica and ricula are the names for small veils, like little cloaks, made for use on the head." Granius, indeed, says that it is a woman's band for the head, with which the Flaminica binds her hair in place of a fillet.

units.la: Sic Tutulum dicebant Flaminicarum capitis ornamentum, quod fiat vitta purpurea, cui crinibus, & extra stlum in altitudinem. Quidam pileum lanatum, formae talis figuratum, Flamines at Pontifices utebantur. Ennius: Fictores, Argeos & tutulatos.
units.tr: So they called the tutulus the ornament of the head of the Flaminicae, which is made of a purple fillet, to which the hair is bound, and which rises high from the top of the head. Some say that the Flamines and the Pontiffs used a woollen cap of such a shape. Ennius: "Carpenters, Argei, and those wearing the tutulus."

units.la: Albogalerus, eodem teste, a galea nominatur pileum capitis, quo Diales Flamines, id est cerdotes JOVIS utebantur. Fiebant enim ex boftia alba, lovi caesa: cui affigebatur apex virgula oleagina.
units.tr: The albogalerus, according to the same witness, is named from galea (helmet): it is a cap for the head, which the Diales Flamines, that is, the priests of Jupiter, used. For they were made of white leather, killed for Jupiter, and to it was attached a apex, a little rod of olive wood.

units.la: Apex, ut idem Festus ait, sacerdotum erat infigne, dictus ab eo, quod tomprehendere Antiqui vinculo, apere dicebant. Unde aptus is, qui convenienter alicui junctus est. Hinc Apiculum, ut idem ait, filum, quo Flamines velatum apicem gerunt.
units.tr: The apex, as the same Festus says, was a distinguishing mark of priests, and was so called from the fact that the ancients used to say apere for binding together with a tie. Hence aptus is one who is fittingly joined to something. Hence, as the same author says, the apiculum is the thread by which the Flamines wear the apex veiled.

units.la: Calyptra item genus erat integumenti, quo capita aperiebant sacerdotes, facrn sua administrantes.
units.tr: A calyptra was also a kind of covering with which the priests covered their heads while performing their sacred rites.

units.la: Arculam appellabant circulum, quem capiti imponebant adfustinenda commodius vasa, quae ad sacra publica capite portabantur.
units.tr: They called the arcula a ring, which they placed on the head so that the vessels carried on the head at public sacrifices could be supported more conveniently.

units.la: Hucreferendae mitrae, diademata, infulae, serta, corona & alia capitus ornamenta, vel exauro, argento, margaritis, gemmis, vel ex herbis, floribusque varius confecta. Pilei Pontificales meminit etiam Plutarchus, in quaestionibus Romanus quaestione quadragesima sic scribens: Pontifices apud Romanos proprium hoc erat, ut capite non veherentur, neque diutius trinoctium ab urbe abessent, neque pileum (apicem ipsi vocabant: unde Flaminis nomen) unquam deponeret.
units.tr: To this class belong mitres, diadems, fillets, garlands, crowns, and other head ornaments, made of gold, silver, pearls, or gems, or variously woven from herbs and flowers. Plutarch also mentions the Pontifical caps, in Roman Questions, question forty, where he writes: "It was a peculiar custom of the Roman pontiffs not to be carried in a litter, not to be away from the city for more than three nights, and never to lay aside the pileus (which they called the apex, whence the name of the Flamen)."

units.la: Dixi de capite: Veniamus ad pedes. Aliquando igitur pedibus nudis: aliquando calceatae sacrificiabant. De priori ritu sic scribit Plato: Triumphales viri, & qui ampli honoris ademptis fuissent, in triumpho ornatu, ami in praetexta lotis manibus & fronde corona, sancti & venerabiles nudis pedibus & tonsa coma ad tem divinam accedebant: idque jam a Pythagora tradi tum Lacedaemonii observarunt, qui nudis pedibus adorandum sacrificandumque censuerunt. Hinc Nudipedalia sacra. At notum est illud symbolum Pythagoricum: Discalceatus sacrisica & adora. Ex ad verso quod ad posteriorem attinet ritum, calceatos Aegyptiorum sacerdotes sacrificasse Herodotus, & papyraceos quidem calceos gestasse. Alexander Alexandro Cybeles sacerdotes lineo calceamento ante simulacrum Dea incedere solitos tradit.
units.tr: I have spoken of the head; let us now come to the feet. Sometimes the priests offered sacrifice barefoot, and sometimes shod. Concerning the former rite Plato writes thus: "Men who had celebrated triumphs, and those who had been deprived of high honour, in triumphal dress, and in the praetexta, with washed hands and a crown of leaves, approached the divine rite as holy and venerable men, with bare feet and shorn hair." The Lacedaemonians also observed this custom, which had already been handed down from Pythagoras, since they judged that worship and sacrifice should be performed barefoot. Hence the sacred rites of the Nudipedalia. Yet the Pythagorean motto is well known: "Sacrifice and worship without shoes." On the other hand, as regards the later rite, Herodotus says that the priests of the Egyptians sacrificed shod, and wore sandals of papyrus. Alexander ab Alexandro reports that the priests of Cybele were accustomed to walk before the image of the goddess in linen shoes.

units.la: Manibus etiam funi tenere atque gestare fuerunt soliti quaedam munera fui instrumenta, ut baculos, virgas & alia id genus. Hinc Ifiaci apud Aegyptios manibus sistrum tenebant, aut ramum absinthii marini, vel nuces pineas; de quo vide Theatrum Zuingeri.
units.tr: The priests also used to hold and carry in their hands certain objects proper to their functions, such as staves, rods, and things of that kind. Hence the priests of Isis among the Egyptians held a sistrum in their hands, or a branch of sea wormwood, or pine nuts; on this see Zwinger's Theatrum.

units.la: Materia quoque vestium sacerdotalium & sacrificantium fuit varia & multiplex erat lana, linum, purpura. Aegyptiorum quidam sacerdotum vestes erant ex lino: unde nigeri fuerunt dicti Ifidis, Dea Aegyptiorum, sacerdotes: sicut ipsa quoque Isis Linigera dicitur. Ovidius: Vidi ergo linigeras numen violasse fatentur. Isis, &c.
units.tr: The material of priestly and sacrificing garments was also varied and manifold: wool, linen, and purple. Some of the priests of the Egyptians wore garments of linen; hence the priests of Isis, the goddess of the Egyptians, were called "linen-wearers" (nigeri), just as Isis herself is called Linigera. Ovid: "I saw therefore the linen-bearers, who confess that the deity has been violated by Isis, etc."
Juvenal on her priests:

units.la: Cum grege linigero circumdatus & grege calyo. Martialis: Linigeri fugiunt calvi, fistrata, turba.
units.tr: "Surrounded by a crowd of linen-wearers and bald priests." Martial: "The linen-wearers, the bald ones, and the crowd of the sistrum-bearers flee."

units.la: De religiosis Aegyptiorum vestibus sic scribit Herodotus: Sacerdotes linea serunt vestimenta semper recens abluta, sed rei semper vatantes. Idem talaeos papyraceos gestant, aliam vestem aut alios taleos induere ojs fas non est. Gemitalia circumcidunt ritu Iudaeorum. Plinius libro decimo nono, capite primo scribit, frutice gigni in Aegypto, quem Gossypion vocat, plurimum xylon: & ideo lina inde fatta xylina: ex quibus sacerdotibus Aegyptiis gmnisfime fiunt. Quin etiam Apuleius terminus Aegyptiorum luculenter explicans scribit: Influunt turba sacris ... mittata viri, fœminaque omnis dignitatis, lineæ vestis candore purpurumve fi. Tranquillus Suetonius.
units.tr: Herodotus writes thus about the religious garments of the Egyptians: "The priests wear linen clothing, always freshly washed, but they are always careful about their cleanliness. The same priests wear sandals of papyrus; it is not lawful for them to put on any other clothing or other sandals. They circumcise their genitals after the manner of the Jews." Pliny, in book nineteen, chapter one, writes that in Egypt there grows a shrub, which he calls gossypion, yielding a great deal of xylon; and therefore linens made from it are called xylina, and out of these are almost all the garments of the Egyptian priests made. Indeed Apuleius, clearly describing the Egyptian rites, writes: "The crowds flow into the sacred rites... men and women of every rank, in the whiteness of linen clothing..." Suetonius, too, in the life of Tiberius, writes: "He suppressed foreign ceremonies, he said, and the Egyptian and Jewish rites, compelling those who were devoted to such superstition to burn their religious garments together with all the equipment."

units.la: Tiberio Cæsare: Externas cerimonias, sinquit, Ægyptios Iudaicosque ritus compescuit, eosdem qui superstitione ea tenebantur, religiosas vestes cum instrumento omni combrerere. Iudeorum vestes religiosæ quales fuerint Hieronymus in epistola ad Fabiolam de veste sacerdotali et libro tertio Antiquitatum et libro sexto belli Iudaici copiose perscribitur.
units.tr: What the religious garments of the Jews were is set out fully by Jerome in his letter to Fabiola, on the priestly garment, and in the third book of the Antiquities and the sixth book of the Jewish War.

units.la: Quantum ad colorem vestium sacerdotalium attinet; alii nigris, alii, et quidem plerique albis seu candidis vestibus erant amicti: Sic enim exempli gratia, Ægyptiorum sacerdotes ex linteo puro et candido vestibus habebant. Sic Romanos albatos fuisse diebus festis, vestiatur in Electis. Lupus. Sic Iunoni vestie candida sacrificabatur: item Cereri mense Aprili cum lampadibus, et tædis accensis, quando porcam illi mactarent. Vestæ, vel Deis, si quando Vestales virgines sacra libarent, eo cultu ornatu, ut erant, et vittate peragebant. Album tamen præterea velamentum, quod suffibulum vocabatur, oblongum, et præextextum, et quadrangulum in capite sumebant, fibulaq; subnectebant. Tertullianus libro de Pallio et cultu docet, Cererı Eleusinia sacerdotes candida, Saturni rubro, Bellonæ nigro habitu fuisse, Æsculapii pallium cum crepidis gestasse. Verba ejus hæc sunt: Cur ipsos non speciat vel illos item habitus, qui novitate vestitus religionem mentirentur, cum ob cultum omnia candidatum et ob velum vittæ et privilegium galeri Cereri imitantur: cum ob diversam affectionem tenebricæ vestis, et tetrici super caput vellerum in Bellonæ montes fugantur: cum latioris purpuræ ambitio et galaticı ruboris superjectio Saturnum commendat: cum ipsum hoc pallium morosi ordinatum, et crepidæ Græcaeque gracatum Æsculapio adulentur. Et cum in lullu mulieres albas gesserint vestes, albataque vittas, Plutarchus ratiouem reddit in quæstionibus Romanis, quæstione vigesima sexta.
