units.tr: As regards the colour of priestly garments, some were clothed in black, others, and indeed most, in white or bright garments. For example, the priests of the Egyptians wore vestments of pure, white linen. It is said in the Electa of Lupus that the Romans were dressed in white on festival days. White victims were offered to Juno; likewise to Ceres in April, with torches and lighted pine-brands, when they slaughtered a sow for her. When the Vestal virgins offered sacrifices to Vesta or to the gods, they performed the rite in the dress and adornment they wore, with fillets. Moreover they took up on their heads another white covering, called the suffibulum, oblong, bordered with purple, and square, and fastened it with a clasp. Tertullian, in his book On the Pallium and Dress, teaches that the priests of Ceres at Eleusis were in white, those of Saturn in red, those of Bellona in black, and that the priests of Aesculapius wore a cloak with sandals. His words are these: "Why does he not regard those also who, in the novelty of their dress, feign religion, when they imitate Ceres in all things being white, in the veil and the fillets and the privilege of the cap; when they are dressed in dark garments and in the shaggy fleece on the head, as those who flee to the mountains of Bellona; when the broad-bordered purple and the sprinkling of red on the cap commend Saturn; when they flatter Aesculapius with this very cloak, arranged as for a fastidious man, and with Greek sandals?" And since women in the Lupercalia wore white garments and white fillets, Plutarch gives the reason in the Roman Questions, question twenty-six.

units.la: Secundum sexum quoque alias quidem erant marium, aliæ fœminarum vestes. Et tamen vi-ri muliebri veste, et mulieres virili Veneri sacra fecerunt, sejje Philochoro. Hiis adde, quod Plutarchus scribit quæstione quinquagesima quinta quæstionum Romanarum, tibicines Iudibus Ianuaris vestem indutos mulieb em, urbem circuire fuisse solitos. Idem rationem reddit quæstione quinquagesima octava, quæstionum Græcarum, cur apud Choos Herculis Sacerdos in Antimachia mulebri veste indutus capite vittato sacrificium fecerit.
units.tr: Clothing also differed according to sex: some garments were for men, others for women. Yet men performed sacred rites in women's dress, and women in men's dress, for Venus, as Philochorus says. Add to these what Plutarch writes in question fifty-five of the Roman Questions: that the flute-players used to go round the city in women's dress at the Januarian festival. He gives the reason also in question fifty-eight of the Greek Questions, why among the people of Cos the priest of Hercules, dressed in a woman's garment in the Antimachia, with a fillet on his head, performed the sacrifice.

units.la: Secundum quantitatem vestes aliorum fuerant amplæ: aliæ strictæ et angustæ: aliorum vero longæ ac promissæ, ad talos usque demissæ. Nam in sacerdotum templo nudare se nefas erat apud quosdam, vestes Plutarchus quæstione quadragesima quinta: Romanorum. Apud plerosque tamen sacra agitabantur a nudis, vel quidem a nudis vel corpore, vel aliqua corporis parte denudatis. Sic glasto Britannorum conjuges nuruvq, toto corpore oblitas quibusdam in sacris nudas incedere, supra ex Plinio audivimus.
units.tr: According to size, the garments of some were ample, of others close and narrow, and of others long and flowing, reaching down to the ankles. For among some peoples it was a sin to be naked in the temple of the priests, as Plutarch says in question forty-five of the Roman Questions. Yet among most, sacred rites were performed by naked persons, or by persons naked in body or in some part of the body. Thus, as we heard above from Pliny, the wives and daughters of the Britons, smeared all over with woad, went naked in certain sacred rites.

units.la: Essi præterea sacerdotes plerunque erant inermes in sacris: sacrificia tamen quædam ab aratoribus fieri solita vestitur Antiquitas.
units.tr: Moreover, the priests were generally unarmed in the sacred rites; yet antiquity records that certain sacrifices were customarily performed by ploughmen.

units.la: Et hæc quidem de vestitu sacerdotum illorum priscorum Gentilium, quibus colophonis loco addam verba Baruchi sive Ieremiæ, quibus sacerdotum Babyloniorum vestitum habitumque corporis perstringit ac reprehendit. Sedent, inquit (ubi notandum, eos in sacris sedere solitos) Babyloniorum sacerdotes in idolorum ædibus (quæ ἐνδυκοῦ Græce uno nomine appellantur) habentes tunicas scissas (sic enim sacerdotes Bualitici et aln pio mfana jua perstitione vestes suas dividere solebant) et capita et barbam rasam: quorum capita δικαυνδ nuda sunt. Hinc apparet sacerdotes Babylonios barbam et capita habuisse rasa, eaque fuisse nuda et aperta, cum Romanorum sacerdotes operto et velato fuerint in sacris suis curandis capite. Addit deinde: Regiunt autem clamantes ante Deos suos ut rō ἀ Ἀλ πo sicut mortui. Alludit ad illorum praesumptionem et insanas, quas ad idola Deosque suos fundere fuerunt soliti, quasquidem imitati lebuntur, et ipsos simul leonibus rugientibus per contemptum comparat.
units.tr: These are the points concerning the dress of those ancient Gentile priests. To these, as a conclusion, I will add the words of Baruch, or Jeremiah, in which he censures and condemns the dress and bodily appearance of the priests of Babylon. "They sit," he says (where it should be noted that they used to sit during their rites), "the priests of Babylon in the temples of the idols (which are called by the single Greek name [ἐνδυκοῦ]), having their tunics torn (for thus the priests of Baal and of the idols, in their superstition, were accustomed to tear their garments), and their heads and beards shaved, their heads bare [ἀκάλυπτοι]." From this it appears that the priests of Babylon had their beards and heads shaved, and these were bare and uncovered, whereas the priests of the Romans were covered and veiled on the head when attending to their sacred duties. He adds: "They howl, crying out before their gods, as [ὡς νεκροί] the dead." He alludes to their presumption and mad shouting, which they were accustomed to pour out before their idols and gods, which indeed they imitate even now, and he compares them, with contempt, to roaring lions.

units.la: Secundum sexum sacerdotum alii fuerant mares, alii fœminæ; et aliorum quidem Deorum ara non nisi a sexu fœmineo: aliorum non nisi a sexu virili fieri fas erat: et ad sacra quædam non nisi virus: ad alia nonnisi fœminas: ad alia utrumque patebat aditus. Sic fœminam adiquæ ob in ventionem Proserpinæ matronæ colebant: quod sacrum, dum non essent matronæ, quæ sacerent, propter cladem Cannensem & frequentiam lugentium institutum est, ne amplius cum diebus lugeretur.
units.tr: Among the priests, according to sex, some were men and others women; and for some gods the altar might be tended only by women, for others only by men; and for certain rites only men, for others only women, while for others both had access. Thus certain women worshipped Proserpina as matrons, because of her return; this rite was instituted, since there were no matrons to perform it, on account of the Cannae disaster and the number of mourners, so that there should be no more mourning with the days.

units.la: Quantum ad vitæ conditionem, genus & institutum sacerdotum attinet, obfernandum apud Romanos & Græcos, Reges quoque sacerdotium suscipere atque obire fuisse solitos: cuius multa in historiis prophanis exempla occurrunt. De hoc Plutarchus in quæstionibus Romanis scribit: Olim Reges pleraque & præcipua sacra faciebant, ac rebus divinis ipsi cum sacerdotibus operabantur. Verò iusolescere cœperunt, arrogantesque & duri esse, plerique Græci detracto eis imperio solum sacra faciendi Dis facultatem reliquere. De Regibus Spartanorum scribitidem Alexander ab Alexandro libro secundo, capite octavo. Verba eius hæc sunt: Reges Spartanorum, quum primum in eam assumti sunt dignitatem, privilegio honoris præcipui Iovis cælestis & Lacedemonii sacerdotio funguntur: quibus ex omni Scrophatum fœtu porcus debebatur, ut si Dii immolare vellent, nunquam victima deesset. Sic ex Cæsaribus C. Iulius Cæsar Augurատum simul & Pontificatum: Galba autem triplex sacerdotium gessisse dicitur. De hoc more scribit etiam Guauguinus in Prussia, cuius verba addere libet: Anno Domini DIII. Prutenis, inquit, sive Vlmiga vis Rex quidam, Brutenoditius, imperavit: qui cum iustos annos ætatis coufecturus esset, quietam vitam ducere instituens, fratrem Verdenutum succedentem sibi in regno fecit: ipsumque summus sacerdos effectus est, nomenque ei dignitatis indicum fuit Kirie Kirieyto, quasi dicas, Proximus nostrer Dominus. Huic Ponsiti suo Pruteni præclaram eidem sub quercu quadam erexerunt, locoque Romanæ a Romæ nomen indiderunt. Hæc Gnaguinus.
units.tr: As regards the condition of life, the class and institution of the priests, it should be observed that among the Romans and Greeks kings also used to take up and discharge the priesthood; many examples of this occur in profane histories. Plutarch writes about this in the Roman Questions: "Formerly the kings performed most and the chief sacred rites, and themselves took part in divine services together with the priests. But when they began to grow proud, arrogant and harsh, most of the Greeks took away their power and left them only the right to perform sacred rites for the gods." Alexander ab Alexandro also writes about the kings of the Spartans, in book two, chapter eight. His words are these: "The kings of the Spartans, as soon as they are raised to that dignity, perform the priesthood with the special privilege of honour of heavenly Jupiter and of the Lacedaemonians; to them, from every litter of pigs, a pig was owed, so that if the gods wished to be sacrificed to, a victim should never be lacking." Thus among the Caesars, Gaius Julius Caesar held the augurate and the pontificate at the same time, and Galba is said to have held a threefold priesthood. Gaguinus also writes of this custom in Prussia, whose words I am pleased to add: "In the year of the Lord 1003, a certain king of the Prussians, or Vulmigas, named Brutenoditius, ruled; who, when he was about to complete the full years of his life, resolved to lead a quiet life, and made his brother Verdenutus, who succeeded him, king; and he himself was made chief priest, and the title of his dignity was Kirie Kirieyto, as if you were to say 'our nearest lord.' To this man the Prussians erected a famous image beneath a certain oak, and gave the place the name of Romove, from Rome." Thus Gaguinus.

units.la: Pertinent huc ea, quæ L. Fenestella de Rege sacrorum scribit capite undecimo in sacerdotiis Romanis: Rex sacrorum, usquit, qui & sacrificulus dicitur, creari captus est Iunio Bruto, & M. Valerio primus consulibus. Ejus creandi occasionem dedit, quod quum nuper exactus regibus pleraque, sacra a solis Regibus obiri consueta, Regum exactione vacare viderentur; idque modo, ut admodum populus ferret, utpote, quod cultui divino Regum exactione videretur derogatum, sacerdotem creari placuit: quem quo minus eidem authoritatis inesset (alii legunt deesse) regio nomine decorarunt, sacrorum Regem appellantes. Subiecerunt tamen Pontifici Maximo, ut finilius dicti (alii legunt, Nec si nullius ditionis alias) fuisset suppositus, jam exactis Regibus reducti Reges esse viderentur, vel crederentur. Quæ vero huic partes injunctæ essent, nunc tempora minime reperiuntur. Hæc Feneslella.
units.tr: Here belongs what Fenestella writes about the King of the sacred rites in chapter eleven of his work on Roman priesthoods: "The King of the sacred rites, who is also called the little sacrificer, was created in the consulship of Junius Brutus and M. Valerius, the first consuls. The occasion for creating him was this: since the kings had recently been expelled and many sacred rites, which were usually performed by the kings alone, seemed to lie neglected without them, and the people took this very badly, as if worship of the gods had been diminished by the removal of the kings, it was decided to create a priest. To make sure he would not have too much authority (others read 'lest he should have any authority'), they gave him the title of king and called him King of the sacred rites. Yet they placed him under the Chief Pontiff, so that, if he had been placed under no one's control at all, the kings would seem, or be believed, to have been restored even though they had been driven out. What duties were assigned to this office, however, cannot be found in any record. So far Fenestella."

units.la: Meminit Regis sacrificuli etiam Pomponius Lætus, cuius hæc verba: Postquam Romani, inquit, jam liberi, extincto regio nomine, necubi desiderium Regis esset propter quædam sacra publica, quo Reges faciebant, Regem sacrificulum constituerunt, & e Patribus elegerunt, C. Manlium Papyrium, & id sacerdotium Pontificii subiecere, ut novæ libertati additus nomini honos officeret. Is Papyrius quietus studiosissimus fuit. Hadrianus Pomponius.
units.tr: Pomponius Laetus also mentions the little sacrificer, and his words are these: "After the Romans were free, with the royal title abolished, lest anywhere there be a longing for a king because of certain public sacred rites that the kings used to perform, they appointed a King of the sacred rites and chose him from the Fathers, namely Gaius Manlius Papyrius, and they placed this priesthood under the Pontiffs, so that the honour of the name, added to their new freedom, would do no harm. This Papyrius was a most diligent and quiet man." So far Pomponius Laetus.

units.la: Ob eandem hanc causam, quod nimirum Rex esset sacerdos & pontifex, Romani Imperato res Pontifices appellabantur. Hinc Iuvenalis Satyra quarta de Domitiano: Deslinat hoc monstrum Cymbe, liuique magisler Pontifici summo, &c.
units.tr: For this same reason, namely that the king was both priest and pontiff, the Roman emperors were called Pontiffs. Hence Juvenal in the fourth satire, about Domitian: "Cybele designates this monster, and the master of the ... for the chief pontiff," etc.

units.la: Plato in Politico docet, Sacerdotes & Vates magnanimitate, intelligentia & claritate florere ob earum rerum, in quibus versantur, amplitudinem & dignitatem: & idcirco addit, Apud Ægyptios non licitum fuisse Regem ab que sacerdotio imperio: quin immo si ex alio genere quispiam per vim regnum usurpasset, coactum fuisse tandem ὑπ' ἱερέων, id est, sacris initiari. Prætereaque plurimis Græcorum civitatibus, & apud Athenienses præferein, præcipua ac pratibus summis institui fuisse solita: & creati Regis fidei augustissima sacra, maximeq; pa tros antiquissimarum religionum ritus fuisse demandatos. Idem alibi regio muneri sacerdotium vult esse proximum & vicium. Cicero: Itaq; Populus Romanus bre vi tempore neque Regem sacrorum, neque Flaminès, neque Salios habebit.
units.tr: Plato in the Statesman teaches that priests and seers flourish in greatness of spirit, understanding and renown because of the importance and dignity of the affairs they handle. He therefore adds that among the Egyptians it was not lawful for anyone to hold the kingship without the priesthood; indeed, if a man from another class had seized the kingdom by force, he was in the end compelled to be initiated into the sacred rites [ὑπ' ἱερέων, by priests]. Moreover, in most Greek cities, and especially among the Athenians, the more important and highest offices were customarily given to priests, and the most august sacred rites of the state, and especially the rites of the most ancient religions, were entrusted to those who had been appointed King. Plato elsewhere holds that the priesthood is next to and a neighbour of the royal office. Cicero: "And so the Roman people will before long have neither a King of the sacred rites, nor Flamens, nor Salii."

units.la: Aliquando tamen & apud nonnullos non erat licitum munus profanum cum sacro conjungere. Hinc Aristoteles Politicorum libro quarto, Sacerdotes, sive illi sint αἱρετοί sive κληρωτοί, non permissum. id est, sine suffragiis electii, sine sorte ducti, vult non esse in magistratibus numerandos, ... genus hominum aliud a civilibus magistratibus seiunctum. Sic Flaminibus Dialibus permissum non erat, ut magistratum susciperent, aut ambirent: quod cur factum sit Plutarchus ratione reddit, quaestione tentatissima decima tertia, in Romanis, quem vide. Haec de vitae genere sacerdotum.
units.tr: Yet at times, and among some peoples, it was not permitted to combine a secular office with a sacred one. Hence Aristotle in the fourth book of the Politics holds that priests, whether they are chosen by election [αἱρετοί] or by lot [κληρωτοί], should not be counted among the magistrates, but should form a class of men separate from the civil magistrates. So the Flamen Dialis was not allowed to take up or seek a magistracy; Plutarch gives the reason for this in his Roman Questions, question thirteen, which you may consult. This is enough on the manner of life of priests.

units.la: IX. Fuit apud Ethnicos sacerdotum quoque maxima dignitas, honos, auctoritas et potestas, id quod cum ex supra citato loco Platonis in Politicis colligitur, scribentis, sacerdotes et vates magnanimitate, intelligentia, et claritate floruisse: tum hinc constat, quod praesertim virgines Vestales maximo in pretio et honore fuerunt apud Romanos. Unde Ovidius: locum date sacra ferenti Non mihi, sed magno poscitur ille Deo. Sit Demones ille senex apud Plautum: Qui homo est, tanta confidentia Qui sacerdotum violare audeat: At magno cum malo suo? etc.
units.tr: IX. Among the heathens the priests also had the greatest dignity, honour, authority and power. This is gathered from the passage of Plato's Politics cited above, where he writes that priests and seers flourished in greatness of spirit, understanding and renown; and it is clear also from the fact that the Vestal Virgins in particular were held in the highest esteem and honour among the Romans. Hence Ovid: "Make room for one who carries the sacred things; he is not called for me, but for the great god." Plautus has the old man Demones say: "What man is so bold in his confidence as to dare to violate priests, and to do so at such great cost to himself?" etc.

units.la: X. Ordo quoque sacerdotum et gradus, in iis creandis et iam creatis, quoad illorum honorem et dignitatem religiosè observabatur; de quo ita Festus: Maximus videbatur Rex, quia potentissimus huic Martialis; quod Mars Conditor Urbis parens. Quarto loco Quirinalis, socio imperii Romani Curibasito Quirino. Quinto Pontifex Maximus; quod Iudex et arbiter haberetur rerum divinarum humanarumque. Itaque in conviviis solus Rex supra omnes accubabat. Sed Dialis supra Martialem et Quirinalem: Martialis supra proximum: omnes deinde supra Pontifices. Haec etiam Festus.
units.tr: X. The order and the ranks of the priests, both in appointing them and in those already appointed, were also scrupulously observed with regard to their honour and dignity. Festus speaks of this as follows: "The King seemed the greatest, because he was the most powerful. Next the Martial priest, since Mars was the founder and parent of the City. Fourth place to the Quirinal priest, companion of the Roman empire, along with Quirinus of Cures. Fifth the Chief Pontiff, because he was regarded as the judge and arbiter of divine and human affairs. Therefore at banquets the King alone reclined above all others. But the Dialis was above the Martial priest and the Quirinal; the Martial priest above the next; and then all were above the Pontiffs." So Festus.

units.la: In quanta item gratia et honore fuerint apud Romanos illi, qui coluerunt diligenter Deos, inter alia exempla testatur Numae Pompilii exemplum, qui ab Romano Rege habitus fuit, eam tantummodo ob tauffam, quod rei divinae faciendae studiosissimus fuit. Nec certe olim alii principes Romani tam amabantur et honorabantur, quod victoriis ergo hostes clari et celebres efficerent, quam quod diligenter et studiose Deos coluissent. Id quod de Tarquinio Prisco etiam constat, eum cum ob alia beneficia in Populum Romanum, tum ob singulare studium in religionem maximo honore fuisse affectum. Testantur enim historiae eum, praeterquam quod religiosissimus Deos ventrabatur, templa frequenter adibat, illud quoque famosissimum templum Iovis in Patrio Capitolio extruendum curasse. Idem judicium de aliis, qui de religione, seu superstitione pietatis Ethnicorum bene meriti erant.
units.tr: Among other examples, the Roman authors bear witness to how much favour and honour were shown among the Romans to those who diligently worshipped the gods. The example of Numa Pompilius is one: he was regarded as the Roman king solely on account of his piety, because he was most zealous in performing the divine rites. Indeed, the earlier leading men of Rome were not so loved and honoured for making enemies famous and celebrated by victories as they were for worshipping the gods diligently and devotedly. This is also established for Tarquinius Priscus: although he had merited well of the Roman people in many ways, he was held in the greatest honour for his singular zeal for religion. For the histories relate that, besides being most devout in worshipping the gods, he frequently visited the temples, and that he took care to have built that most famous temple of Jupiter on the Capitol. The same judgment holds for others who deserved well of the religion, or rather the superstition, of the heathen piety.

units.la: XI. Sequitur merces sive salarium sacerdotum, hoc est, reditus, proventus et vectigalia eorum, quae cum in genere ipsius nominibus appellabantur, tum peculiariter ob certa quaedam munia atque officia alis atque alia. Tale erat Curiouium; de quo ita Festus: Curionium, inquit, est dicebatur, quod dabatur Curioni ad sacerdotum Curionatus. Pertinet huc totum nomen caput, de quo antea dixi. Nam honoris dignitatis, gradus sacerdotum, nihil erat aliud, quam merces, praemiumque eorum, qui sacra studiose ac diligenter obirent. De hoc praemio pulchre et copiose Alexander ab Alexandro libro secundo capite octavo sic scribit: In tantum honoris culmen Pontificatus, et eo excellentiae crevit, ut Cn. Cornelio praetori, quod M. Aemilio lepido, Pontifici Maximo, convictum fecisset, multa dicta fuerit: ipsumque regia dignitate proximum crederent. Nam et lictor apparebat, et curulis regia sella ac lectica insignis erat, quam ante vestibulum constitutam afferunt: ad cujus fores pro splendore dignitatis viridis laurus affixa videbatur. Cumque ceteri, honoribus functi, rationem administrati muneris reddere cogerentur, Pontifex tamen Maximus pro majestate, gesti honoris rationem dare minime cogi poterat: ipse pro imperio et potestate, quoque plus dignitatis ferret, cum galero esse et carpento, ut reliquis sacerdotibus ingredi licebat. Quippe Pontifici proprium infigne erat galerus, sicut litus Auguribus, paludamentum Imperatoribus, diadema Regibus. Et cum in Capitolium nulli fas foret carpento vehi, solus Pontificibus sacerdotibus, Tarpejum asscendere carpento licuit: ad eumque fuisse confugissent, ea die a poena immunes erant. Hactenus Alexander: quibus adde ea, quae Plutarchus in Numa & Gellius scribunt: Stipendium Numa Vestalibus de publico statuit, & eas perpetua virginitate aliisq; cerimoniis venerabiles fecit, Carpento vehebantur, magistratus, illis assurgebant: si cui forte occurrisset ad supplicium rapto, si mortis poena eximebatur. Iusjurandum autem exigebatur a virgine, fortuitum fuisse et inconsultum nec praemeditatum occurrisse. Idem Gellius libro sexto, capite septimo: Caja Tarratiae, sive Suffetiae Vestali, quia campum Tiberinum sive Martium Pop. Rom. donaverat, virtutem tamen Horatiae lege amplissimi honores decreti; ut una omnium foeminarum testabilis esset, hoc est, ius testimonii dicendi haberet. Praeterea si quadraginta annos nata, sacerdotio abire ac nubere voluisset, id salva religione posset. Haec de praemio.
units.tr: XI. Next comes the reward or salary of the priests, that is, their revenues, incomes and dues. Some of these were named under a general term, and others were called by particular names for certain specific duties and offices, as with the others. Such was the curionium, of which Festus says: "The curionium," he says, "was so called because it was given to the curio for the office of curio." The whole matter of which I spoke earlier belongs here. For the honours, dignities and ranks of the priests were nothing other than the pay and reward of those who performed the sacred rites zealously and diligently. Alexander ab Alexandro writes of this reward, beautifully and at length, in book two, chapter eight, as follows: "The pontificate rose to such a height of honour and excellence that the praetor Gnaeus Cornelius was fined for having convicted Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, the Chief Pontiff, and men believed the pontiff to rank next to royal dignity. For a lictor attended him, and his curule chair, the royal seat and litter, was distinguished, which they carried and set down before the vestibule; and at its doors, for the splendour of the dignity, a green laurel was seen fixed up. While the others who had held office were compelled to render an account of how they had administered it, the Chief Pontiff, by reason of his majesty, could not be compelled to give an account of the honour he had held. For the sake of his authority and power, and that he might have more dignity, he was allowed to enter with the cap and the carriage, as the other priests were. Indeed, the cap was the peculiar badge of the Pontiff, just as the lituus was of the augurs, the cloak of generals, and the diadem of kings. And since no one was allowed to ride in a carriage on the Capitol, only the Pontiffs were permitted to ascend the Tarpeian rock in a carriage; and if anyone had fled to them, on that day he was exempt from punishment." So far Alexander. To this add what Plutarch in his Life of Numa and Gellius write: Numa established a stipend for the Vestals from the public treasury, and made them venerable through perpetual virginity and other ceremonies. They rode in carriages, and magistrates rose to make way for them. If by chance someone was being led to execution and met them, he was released from the penalty of death. An oath was required of the virgin that she had met the man by chance, unexpectedly and without premeditation. Gellius says in book six, chapter seven: Caja Tarratia, or Suffetia, a Vestal, because she had given the Campus Tiberinus or Martius to the Roman people, was granted the most ample honours by the Horatian law, so that she alone of all women could bear witness, that is, had the right to give testimony. Moreover, if she had wished, having reached the age of forty, to leave the priesthood and marry, she could have done so without violating her religious duty. So much for the reward.

units.la: E contra qui munus officium, suum violassent sacerdotes non modo praemium atq; mercedem nullam consequebantur, sed gravissime afficiebantur poenis & supplicijs. Hinc Festus: Lex erat, probrum virginis Vestalis ut capite puniretur: vir qui eam incestavisset, verberibus necabatur. Et Gellius: Vestales ignem perpetuum servabant, qui, si per incuriam extinctus esset, flagro a Pontifice Maximo cui iuberant, caedebatur. Si qua incesti convicta esset ante oratium moesto silentio efferebatur, vivaq; circa Collinam portam in subterraneum specum demissa, cerraque flatum superinjecta necabatur.
units.tr: On the other hand, priests who had violated their office and duty not only received no reward or recompense, but were severely punished with penalties and torments. Hence Festus: there was a law that a Vestal virgin who disgraced herself should be punished by death, and the man who had defiled her was beaten to death. And Gellius: the Vestals kept the perpetual fire, and if it went out through negligence, they were beaten with a whip by the Pontifex Maximus, to whom they were subject. If a Vestal was convicted of incest, she was carried out in mournful silence, lowered alive into an underground vault near the Colline Gate, and killed by having a covering of earth heaped over her breath.

units.la: Numerus praeterea, primo in genere ut Deorum & sacrificiorum; ita Sacerdotum quasi i- nnumerabilis fuit.
units.tr: Moreover, the number of priests was, in general, as countless as that of the gods and sacrifices.

units.la: Deinde in specie sacerdotum particularium certus fuit ac definitus. Cicero de Oratore: Pontifices veteres propter multitudinem sacrificiorum tres viros Epulones esse voluerunt. Praeter Epulones fuerunt Pontifices, Reges sacrorum, Salii, Flamines, Augures, Feciales, Arvales, Vestales, ut Geganiae, Varenia (unde Canuleja, sive Camilla & Tarpeja) Caja Terraria sive Suffetia, Teretia, Claudia, Tuctia, Fonteia, Fabia, Licinia, Vidia, aliique, Indorum, Aegyptiorum, Graecorum, Romanorum, sacerdotes innumerabiles.
units.tr: Next, among the particular priests there was a fixed and defined number. Cicero, in De Oratore: "The ancient Pontiffs wished that, because of the multitude of sacrifices, there should be three Epulones." Besides the Epulones there were the Pontiffs, the Kings of the sacred rites, the Salii, the Flamens, the Augurs, the Fetiales, the Arval Brothers, the Vestal Virgins, and, as they are called, the Geganiae, the Varenia (whence the Canuleia, or Camilla, and the Tarpeia), Caja Terraria or Suffetia, the Teretia, Claudia, Tuctia, Fonteia, Fabia, Licinia, Vidia, and others; and among the Indians, Egyptians, Greeks and Romans there were countless priests.

units.la: Denig, & victum sacerdotum ac jejunia, seu abstinentiam super pistiofam a certis cibis, atque etiam certarum rerum contactu atque visu, in nominatione eorum considerabant. Sic Aegyptii sacerdotes olim a piscium esu in sacris abhorrebant eumque exsecrabantur, cum pisces omnes animal sit κτενοποιοσ, μυσ, ἀλλαςοφαρ, exhauriens quae vis, & in suum ipse genus saeviens. Unde Aegyptii abstinebant & abominandam significare volentes Piscem pingebant. Idem a pelicani esu abstinebant, item ab ave Oryge, sola inter volucres signata, quod Lunae Deae & Soli Deo videbatur infesta. Sic Flaminis Diali non licebat apud Romanos farinam aut fermentatum tangere, teste Plutarcho quaestione centesima nona quaestionum Romanorum. Festus item Flamini Diali, inquit, sabam nec tangere, nec nominare licebat. De abstinentia a leguminibus castitatis causa vide Plutarchum in eodem quaestionibus. Sed & omnis carnis crudae contactum interdictum Flamini Diali erat, sicut ederam quoq; ei non licebat tangere. Sic non poterat idem salva religione opus facientes videre, vel classem procinctam, id est, paratam ad bellum, & multitudinem militum. Multo minus eidem jurare, & dira alia precari per leges licuisse testatur Plutarchus, quemadmodum nec per viam transire; penes quam vitium propagines in sublimi erant collocatae: quo significabant, nefas esse sacerdotem ebrietati esse deditum.
units.tr: Finally, they also took account of the diet of priests and their fasts, or abstinence from certain foods, and even of contact with and sight of certain things. Thus the Egyptian priests once shrank from eating fish in their sacred rites and held it in abhorrence, since every fish is a killer, a mouse-like creature [κτενοποιὸς, μυς], a devourer that drains whatever strength it can and rages against its own kind. Hence the Egyptians abstained from fish, and, wishing to signify something abominable, they painted a fish. They likewise abstained from eating the pelican, and also from the bird oryx, which alone among birds was marked out because it seemed hostile to the goddess Moon and the god Sun. So too among the Romans the Flamen Dialis was not permitted to touch flour or anything leavened, as Plutarch witnesses in question 109 of the Roman Questions. Festus likewise says that the Flamen Dialis might neither touch nor name the bean. On abstinence from pulses for the sake of chastity, see Plutarch in the same work of questions. Moreover, contact with any raw flesh was forbidden to the Flamen Dialis, just as he was not allowed to touch ivy. Likewise he could not, consistently with his religious duty, see men at work, or a fleet made ready for battle, that is, prepared for war, or a multitude of soldiers. Much less, Plutarch testifies, was it lawful for him to swear or to utter dire imprecations; just as he might not pass along a road where vines had been trained on high, by which they signified that it was wrong for a priest to be given to drunkenness.

units.la: Et haec quidem de principibus personis sacrificiorum dicta sint satis.
units.tr: Let these things suffice for the principal persons of the sacrifices.

units.la: DICAMVS nunc quaedam de sacrorum sacrificiorum, ministrorum: quorum multi fuerunt in Gentilium sacrificiis. Horum descriptionem pulcherrimam videre licet in antiquissima & celeberrima illa Trajani Caesaris columna marmorea, quae Romae in medio Trajani foro erecta, folia ferè inter alias vetustatis reliquias est superstes & integra, quae geminae Imperatoris illius in Dacos expeditionis res praeclare feliciterq; gestas, ac uniuersi illius belli historiam pulcherrimis simulacris exsculptam complectitur. In hac igitur praeter plurima alia antiquitatum monumenta (quorum columna illa quasi epitome quaedam veritissime dici potest) ministrorum bujusmodi; nec tantum ministrorum, sed sacrificiorum, victimarum, libationum, altarium, sacerdotum, rituum denique, cerimoniarum, sacrificalium, pictura atq; imagines clare & illustres visuntur: quam quidem Alphonsus Ciaconus Hispanus, vir doctissimus, breviibus quidem, sed doctis accuratuq; commentariuncul is quasi vivus coloribus expressit & illustravit. {y} Note on the column: Pontifices, Flamines and Vestales described.
units.tr: Now let us say something about the ministers of the sacred rites and sacrifices, of whom there were many in the sacrifices of the Gentiles. A most beautiful depiction of them can be seen on that very ancient and celebrated marble column of Trajan Caesar, erected in the middle of Trajan's forum at Rome, which is almost the only one of the ancient relics that survives intact. It portrays in most beautiful carvings the two glorious and successful campaigns of that emperor against the Dacians and the whole history of that war. On this column, then, besides very many other monuments of antiquity (of which the column may truly be called a kind of epitome), pictures and images of such ministers are clearly and vividly to be seen, and not only of ministers but of sacrifices, victims, libations, altars, priests and, finally, of rites and sacred ceremonies. Alphonsus Ciaconus, a Spaniard and a most learned man, has expressed and illustrated these as if they were alive, in short but learned and carefully written little commentaries. {y} Note on the column: Pontiffs, Flamens and Vestals described.

units.la: Postquam igitur Imperator ille, pugnæ semper sacrificium præmittens, proponitur, idq; secundum tritam & pervulgatam Romanorum consuetudinem, quà non licebat Imperatori cum hostibus congredi, nisi prius Dijs esset sacrificatum, illic Tibicinum quoq; & Camillorum ac Popæarum Vißimariorum, descriptio exprimitur; qui omnes sacrificio solenni adsistunt, laureati, ritu Gabino accincti. Erat autem cinctus Gabinus vestimenti genus, quo sacerdotes sive præsides sive ministri cujusq; Dei, ritus & templi pariter utebantur: quale est camisinum lineum candidum, quo hodie sacerdotes nmntur, ab Italis Cotta, ab Hispanis Alva, ab albedine nimirum vocatum. Id cum esset latum, adeoque oblongum, ut discinctum per solum traheretur, postea cinctum pendentem, supra cingulum faciebat undique sinum. Ritus vero Gabinus fuit dictus, a Gabinis pri-mum, deinde Romanis nsurpatus, ut Livius libro quinto & Virgilius testantur: Virgil.
units.tr: After that emperor, who always sent a sacrifice ahead of a battle, is shown, and this according to the common and well-known custom of the Romans, by which an emperor might not engage the enemy unless sacrifice had first been made to the gods, there is also depicted there a description of the trumpeters and of the Camilli and the Popae Vissimarii. All of them attend the solemn sacrifice, crowned with laurel and girded in the Gabine manner. The Gabine belt was a kind of garment which the priests, whether presiding priests or ministers, of any god, of any rite and of any temple, equally wore: like the white linen camisa which today priests put on, called cotta by the Italians and alva by the Spanish, named from its whiteness. Since it was wide, and so long that, if left unbelted, it trailed along the ground, when it was belted and hung down it made a fold all round above the girdle. The Gabine rite was so named, first from the Gabines, and then it was adopted by the Romans, as Livy in book five and Virgil bear witness:
The consul himself, in his Quirinal robe with Gabine belt,
Conspicuous, shall unbar the creaking gates.

units.la: Vide de hac re & Blondum libro primo Romæ triumphantis.
units.tr: See also Blondus on this matter, book one of Rome Triumphant.

units.la: Porrò tibicines, tubicines & liticines erant ministri sacrorum, tibiis, tubis & litui inter sacrificandum insonantes, quorum non tantum imagines videre licet in hac Trajani columna, sed eorum paßim in omnibus sacrificiis fit mentio. Hi igitur interim dum sacrificium peragebatur, tibiis, tubis atque lituis canebant, lauro redimiti. Tibia instrumentum vocabatur musicum, oblongum, teres & foraminosum, quod inflatum & digitis modo addnctis, modo reductis tempe-rum non injucundam reddit symphoniam, Græcis αὐλὸς dictum. Hanc primum ex gruum tibiis confectam existimant; & inde nomen accepisse. Horatius de Arte:
units.tr: Furthermore, the tibicines, tubicines and liticines were ministers of the sacred rites, sounding their flutes, trumpets and litui during the sacrifice. Their images can be seen not only on this column of Trajan, but mention of them is made everywhere in all sacrifices. These, then, while the sacrifice was being performed, played on flutes, trumpets and litui, crowned with laurel. The tibia was a musical instrument, long, cylindrical and perforated, which, when blown and with the fingers now closed, now opened, makes a not unpleasing harmony; the Greeks called it aulos. They think it was first made from the leg-bones of cranes, and that it took its name from this. Horace, in the Art of Poetry:

units.la: Tibia non ut nunc orichalco vincta, tubaeque
units.tr: The flute was not then bound with brass, and rival to the trumpet,
But slender and simple, with few holes.
Ovid, Tristia book five, elegy one:
That flute suits my funerals.
Virgil, Eclogue eight:
Begin, my pipe, with me the Maenalian verses.

units.la: Cicero primo Tusculanarum: Non intelligo quid mutuat, quum tam bonos septenarios fundat ad tibiam. Idem de claris Oratoribus: Si tibia inflata non ferat sonum, abjiciendas sibi tibicen putet.
units.tr: Cicero, Tusculan Disputations book one: I do not understand what he is borrowing, when he pours out such fine septenarii to the flute. The same, in On Famous Orators: if the inflated flute does not give out a sound, the player should think he must be thrown away.

units.la: Tuba verò instrumentum erat incur-vum ex ære argento vel, cujus sonitus non tantum sacrifi-cantes excitabantur, sed milites equique ad prælium inflammantur: a tubi, hoc est, canalis ca-vitate nomen habens. Hujus inventionem Pifeo Tyrrheno tribuit Plinius libro sexto capite quinquagesimo sexto. Cicero in Catilinam: Quum tubas & signa militaria scirem esse prælia.
units.tr: The trumpet was a curved instrument of bronze or silver, and by its sound not only were those sacrificing roused, but soldiers and horses were fired up for battle; it has its name from the hollowness of the tube (tubus). Pliny, in book seven, chapter fifty-six, attributes its invention to Tyrrhenus, the son of Telephus. Cicero, against Catiline: since I knew that trumpets and military standards signal battles.
Virgil, book two of the Aeneid:
There rises a shout of men and a clangour of trumpets.

units.la: Author ad Herennium libro quarto: In concione de virtute loqueris, in prælio per ignaviam tube sonitum perferre non potes. Lucanus libro primo:
units.tr: The author of the Ad Herennium, book four: you speak about virtue in an assembly, but in battle, through cowardice, you cannot bear the sound of the trumpet. Lucan, book one:
The Vangiones and the Batavians, and the fierce men whom the curved bronze
Trumpets, screaming, have goaded on, etc.

units.la: Tacitus libro secundo: Tum Sentius occanere cornua tubasq; & peti aggerem, origi scalæ jußit, ac promptißimum quemq; succedere.
units.tr: Tacitus, book two: Then Sentius ordered the horns and trumpets to sound, the rampart to be attacked, the ladders to be raised, and each man most ready to advance to the front.

units.la: Ad litnos, quibus sacrificiorum administri intebantur, quod attinet, eorum Plutarchus hæc descriptionem prodidit: Ἔςι, inquit, Ἐύλον ιαυτικὸν ἔδιαχαυτὸν: ἐκθαυτὸν ἀγαῖ ἐξ ἀπ τὸν ἀρχαῖον ἀ ἐλάσι ἐξω ἐμβ: Baculus est incurvus, quo sedentes Augures avibus templa designabant. Gellius libro quinto capite octavo: Litunus est virga brevis, in parte, qua robustior est, incurva. Primus litunus insus a Romulo manasse creditur, qui, dum urbem conderet, hujusmodi baculo regiones de-rexit: quod clarissimum est, ipsum asserit Cicero libro primo de Divinatione: Quid, inquit, litunus iste vester (quod clarißimum est infigue Augnratus) unde nobis est traditus? Nempe eo. Romulus regines direxit tum, cùm urbem condidit. Qui quidem Romuli litunus, id est, incurvum & leviter e summo inflexum bacillum (quod ab ejus litui, quo canitur, similitudine nomen invenit) cùm sutus esset in Curia Saliorum, quæ est in palatio, eamque deflagrasset, in ventus est integer. Ea-dem fert dem fere de hoc luso scribit Plutarchus in vita Romuli: Lituus, inquit consecratus est in Palatio, ille usque ad Gallorum tempora, a quibus captâ urbe incensa fuit. Sed postea expulsis a Camillo hostibus inter altissimas favillas illaesus, quum ignis omnia consumpsisset, inventus est. Festus de lituo inter alia sic scribit: Lituus est buccinae genus incurvum, gracilem edens sonum, quo in bello utebantur: quo qui canebat, Liticen dicebatur. Virgilius libro sexto Æneidos.
units.tr: As for the lituus, which was used by the attendants of the sacrifices, Plutarch gives this description of them: "It is," he says, "a crooked staff [ἔστι ... βακτηρία καμπύλη], with which augurs sitting marked out the temples for the birds." Gellius, book five, chapter eight: the lituus is a short staff, curved at the end where it is stouter. The first lituus is believed to have come from Romulus, who, while founding the city, marked out the regions with such a staff; Cicero, in book one of On Divination, clearly asserts this: "What," he says, "is that lituus of yours (a most famous sign of the augur)? Whence was it handed down to us? Surely from him. Romulus marked out the regions when he founded the city." This lituus of Romulus, that is, the curved staff bent slightly at the top (which takes its name from the resemblance to the lituus by which the call is sounded), when it had been placed in the Chamber of the Salii, which is on the Palatine, and that chamber had been burned, was found unharmed. Plutarch writes much the same about this in his Life of Romulus: "The lituus," he says, "was kept consecrated on the Palatine, until the time of the Gauls, by whom the city was taken and burned. But afterwards, when the enemy had been driven out by Camillus, it was found unharmed amid the highest ashes, when the fire had consumed everything." Festus, writing among other things about the lituus, says: the lituus is a kind of curved trumpet, giving a thin sound, which they used in war; the one who sounded it was called a liticen. Virgil, book six of the Aeneid:

units.la: Et lituo pugnas insignis obibat & hastla.
units.tr: And he went into battle, marked out by the lituus and the spear.
Lucan, book 1:
The screech of the lituus and the clangour of trumpets.
Ovid, Fasti, book 3:

units.la: Iam litui pugnae signa daturus erat.
units.tr: He was about to give the signal for battle with the lituus.
Statius, Thebaid, book 6:
And the ears are struck on every side by the shrill lituus.

units.la: Sed & Camillos & Camillas Antiqui vocabant ministros & ministras sacris inservientes.
units.tr: The ancients also called the attendants and female attendants who served the sacred rites Camilli and Camillae.

units.la: Quoad popas; illi quidem sacrorum ministri erant, ut in Trajani Columna videre licet, sed popae minudi & succinctii, lauroque redimiti, victimas qui venales habebant, easque aris alligabant & cultro feriebant: unde & cultrarii dicti. Propertius libro quarto:
units.tr: As for the popae: they were indeed ministers of the sacrifices, as can be seen on Trajan's Column, but the popae were the lesser attendants, girded up and crowned with laurel. Those who kept victims for sale tied them to the altars and struck them with a knife, whence they were also called cultrarii (knife-men). Propertius, book 4:

units.la: Succinctiisque calent ad nova sacra popae.
units.tr: And the girded popae glow for the new rites.

units.la: Spartianus in vita Getae: Percussit bostiam popa, nomine Antonius. Suetonius in vita Caligulae: Admota altaribus victima, succinctus popa ut habitu, elato alte malleo cultrarium malla vit. Hi autem victimas confecturi utebantur certo vestis genere, quae Linus fuit dicta. Erat vestis Linus vestis genus ab umbilico ad medias usque tibias descendens, ad illorum pudenda tegendum, habens in extremo sui purpureum limum, ad efl, flexuosum: unde & nomen accepit. Nam Limum obliquum dicimus. Hujus vestis meminit Virgilius duodecimo Æneidos:
units.tr: Spartianus, in the Life of Geta: "A popa named Antonius struck the victim." Suetonius, in the Life of Caligula: "The victim having been brought to the altars, a girded popa, his arm raised high, struck the knife-man with a hammer." Those who were to despatch the victims used a particular kind of garment, which was called the linus. The linus was a type of garment that hung from the navel to the middle of the shins, to cover their private parts. At its lower edge it had a purple stripe, slanting and wavy, and it took its name from this, since we call a slanting line limus. Virgil mentions this garment in book 12 of the Aeneid:
Veiled in the linus, their temples bound with verbena.

units.la: In alterius porro sacrificii simulacro, quod est in Trajani columnia, Popa dextra tenet cortnua tauri mactandi, sinistra securim, qua bostiam feriat. In alio item ejusdem columnae sacrificio taurum, in victimam mactandam, popa succinctus & lauro coronatus deducit, clavam longo manubrio gestans, qua taurum conficiat.
units.tr: Moreover, in the representation of another sacrifice on Trajan's Column, the popa holds in his right hand the horns of the bull to be slain, and in his left the axe with which he will strike the victim. Likewise, in another sacrifice on the same column, a girded popa crowned with laurel leads a bull to be slaughtered as a victim, carrying a club with a long handle with which he will kill the bull.

units.la: Victimarii sacerdotum ministri erant, qui victimas adducebant & ligabant, quaque culcrum; victimarii itemaquam, molam & reliquà, quae sacris erant necessaria parabant. Valerius Maximus libro i. cap. primo: Libros Petilius Praetor urbanus ex auctoritate Senatus, per victimarios fallo igne, in conspectu populi cremavit. Livius libro decimo de bello Macedonico: Libri in Comitio, igne a victimariis falso in conspectu populi cremati sunt. Victimariorum hujusmodi pictura in eadem Trajani Columna exstat: ubi verré unus, et alter arietem ad sacrificium deducentes pinguntur: Solebat autem Victimarius paratus esse succinctus. Unde Ovidius:
units.tr: The victimarii were ministers of the priests; they brought the victims and tied them, and also the slaughter-knife; the victimarii likewise prepared the wine, the salted meal and the other things necessary for the rites. Valerius Maximus, book 1, chapter 1: "Petilius, the urban praetor, by authority of the Senate, had the books burned in the sight of the people with a false fire by the victimarii." Livy, book 10, on the Macedonian war: "The books were burned in the Comitium, in the sight of the people, with a false fire by the victimarii." A picture of such victimarii is also found on the same Trajan's Column, where one of them is shown turning a spit, and another leading a ram to the sacrifice. The victimarius was commonly girded up, ready for his task. Hence Ovid:

units.la: Nominis esse potest succinctus caussa minister
units.tr: The reason for the name may be that the minister is girded,
By whose striking the victim falls to the heavenly gods.

units.la: Adde hu Praecones, qui praeter alia munera & officia silentium in celebratione sacrificiorum Praecones imponebant: & Lictores; quos constat non tantum Consulum, Proconsulum & similium ministros Lictores: fuisse, sed etiam Pontificum Maximorum, & eorum qui sacra facere & sacrificia fuerunt soliti. Hinc enim Festus: Exestoy extra esto ... enim Filistor in quibusdam sacri ... clamitat ... STIS, VINCTVS, MVLIER, VIRGO exesso, scilicet interesse prohibebantur. Et hac quidem etiam de ministris sacrorum & sacrificiorum.
units.tr: Add to these the praecones, who, besides their other duties and offices, imposed silence during the celebration of sacrifices; and the lictors, who are known to have served not only consuls, proconsuls and the like, but also the chief pontiffs and those who were accustomed to perform sacred rites and sacrifices. For Festus says: "Exesto, let him be outside..." ... "clamitat" ... "STIS, VINCTVS, MVLIER, VIRGO," that is, they were forbidden to be present. And this is what I have to say about the ministers of sacred rites and sacrifices.

units.la: HIS POSTREMO subjungam sacerdotum Gentilium,tum eorum qui sacra præsum ministrantium,at idolorum simulachrorumq; quorum sacerdotes præcipui fuerunt cultores que mancipia, comparationem quandam, quæ ad clariorem utrorumq; explicationem per Nam reverâ secundum illam Dauidis, seu ipsius potius Spiritus sanctiderum imprecationi qui ea (idola) colunt,ipsis fiant similes,nõ modo vulgus et tndis imperitaq; multitudo,verum ipsi inprimis sacerdotes,idololatriæ coryphæi atque ducei,magnam licet sapientiæ, scientiæ tatisq; speciem præseferant : tamen illis ipsis idolis & simulacris suis,quorum cultus præcipue dictis erant & manciapati: & unde etiam maximum uberrimumq; quæstum capiebant, runt simillimi,idq; iusto Dei judicio, ut Dauid cecinit. Inde apud Zacharam Prophetam tenundecimo passer,id est, sacerdot sal us & s s(Acelil, hoc est idolum) crum appellatur, ob magnam nimirum idolâtriæ & affinitatem. Acelil autem,idolum,Hebræo dictum a vanitate siue stu idolum res sit vanissima & stultissima. Unde u,qui ea colut,summæ merito vanitatis stu nomine sint accusandi.
units.tr: Last of all I shall add a comparison between the priests of the Gentiles, namely those who ministered at the sacred rites, and the idols and images, of which the priests were the chief worshippers and also the slaves. This comparison is for a clearer explanation of both. For truly, according to David's words, or rather those of the Holy Spirit himself, those who make and worship idols become like them, not only the common people, the unlearned and ignorant multitude, but above all the priests themselves, the leaders and chiefs of idolatry. Although they display a great show of wisdom, knowledge and holiness, they are very like the idols and images themselves, whose worship they especially directed and whose servants they were, and from which they also drew their greatest and richest profit, and this by the just judgment of God, as David sang. Hence in the prophet Zechariah the worthless shepherd is called, in the Hebrew, Acelil [אֱלִיל], that is, an idol, by reason of their great likeness and kinship in idolatry. Acelil, an idol, is so called in Hebrew from vanity or folly, because an idol is a most vain and foolish thing. Therefore those who worship it are rightly to be accused of the highest vanity and folly.

units.la: Videtur etiam hoc nomine Acelil, id est, idoli, ad nomen El, et Ae him,quæ nomina sunt veri Dei,alladi,ut hac pranomasia stue agnominatione significetur, lum habere quidem Numinis diuini speciem & similitudinem quandam, sed diuinitatis n ut dicatur Acelil,quasi Al,El,non Deus: cui assens videtur vox nostra vernacula Θεὸς idolum, a Gott/ dest, Deo, derivata,quasi dica, non Deus,sed Deasser.
units.tr: By this name Acelil, that is, of an idol, there seems also to be an allusion to the names El and Elohim, which are the names of the true God, so that by this paronomasia or play on words it is signified that an idol has indeed a certain appearance and likeness of divine majesty, but not divinity itself. It is called Acelil, as if Al, El, not God. Our vernacular word for an idol, Θεὸς [theos] in Greek, which is derived from Gott (God), seems to agree with this, as if one were to say: not God, but a god-thing.

units.la: Primùm igitur,ut ad hanc nostram compa-rationem veniamus, & ab ipso capite capiamus exor um,quemadmodum Gentilium idola atque simulacra habuerunt quidem sua capita cum humanis ruon etiam belluina,& eorum uadam non unum tantum,sed etiam bina,trina, quaterna, vel ei ti im pluri;ut tamen omnes sensus,motus rationiq; fuerunt experti: sic illorum quoque sacer dotes habuerunt capita, vera quidem ,sed sensu, ratione,atque intelligentia vacua, quippe o m nonm rrorum,de rriorum ,s lenissima. Fuerunt igitur illi Gentilium sacerdotes, uod de tu go s vere,quasi beluæ πολυκεφαλοι,id est multorum capitum, aut quos illorum su s fuerunt sensus,sententiæ,opiniones,errores s aly. supi mi & ab omni non si ... ... etiam humana ratione alieni ...
units.tr: First, then, to come to this comparison of ours, and to begin from the very head: just as the idols and images of the Gentiles had heads, human indeed, but some also beastly, and some of them not one only but two, three, four or even more, yet all of them were lacking in sense, motion and reason; so too the priests of the Gentiles had heads, true indeed, but empty of sense, reason and understanding, being in truth most dull and most foolish. Those Gentile priests were therefore like beasts with many heads, polycephalous, that is, of many heads, or whatever their senses, opinions and errors were, utterly remote from the highest and from all, even human, reason...

units.la: Inde ut idolorum mulacrorum, Gentilium capita parium fuerunt nuda & aperta, par tim tecta & operta variis integumentis,& ferris quoq; atque coronis omnis generis ornata: quæ redimita: sic sacerdotum quoque capita plerunque, in sacrorum præsertim administratio opertæ fuerunt atque tecta & ferris atque coronis ornata.
units.tr: Again, just as the heads of the idols and images of the Gentiles were in some cases bare and open, in others covered and hidden under various coverings, and adorned with fillets and crowns of every kind, so too the heads of the priests were for the most part covered and hidden, especially in the performance of the sacred rites, and adorned with fillets and crowns.

units.la: Item ut idolorum simulacrorum,ill rum capita alia fuerunt rasa; alia capillata,atque co mata; sic sacerdotum quoque alii super slitione fuerunt capite raso,alii capite comato.
units.tr: Likewise, as the heads of the idols and images were some shaved and some hairy and long-haired, so too some of the priests had shaven heads and others wore their hair long.

units.la: Præterea quemadmodum Gentilium idola atque simulacra habuerunt suos oculos (tametsi Iouis simulacrum apud Cretenses,Plutarcho teste,& oculos & auribus carnit: & similiter Fortunæ,Pluti,atque Fauors idola fuerunt cæca) & quædam eorum non binos tantum, sed etiam curius (ut Iouis statua apud Argiuos) & quaternos, (ut Saturni statua) atque etiam pluri ocu le suerunt prædita: & horum alii suerunt torti, trisles, truces atque minaces, alii amabi let,hilares atq; sereni; cum tamen,ut Dauid cecinit,cæca fuerint omnique videndi facul fitatem s fuerunt sic sacerdotes quoque Gentilium idololatræ,etsi in rebus terrenis & humanis ad se latriam & superstitionem pertinentibus,oculati ualde fuerunt atque perspicaces. tamen in his diuinis atque cœlestibus,ad religionem veram stiuam,æternam pertinentibus uel ipsis n stuis aut talpis cæciores fuerunt.
units.tr: Moreover, just as the idols and images of the Gentiles had their eyes (although the image of Jupiter among the Cretans, according to Plutarch, had both eyes and ears; and the idols of Fortune, Wealth and Favour were blind), and some of them had not only two eyes but even one (like the statue of Jupiter among the Argives), or four (like the statue of Saturn), or even more eyes, and some of these eyes were twisted, sad, fierce and threatening, others lovely, cheerful and serene; yet, as David sang, they were blind and lacked all power of seeing; so too the idolatrous priests of the Gentiles, although they were very sharp-eyed and perceptive in earthly and human matters pertaining to their idolatry and superstition, were in these divine and heavenly matters, which pertain to true and eternal religion, more blind than moles or the very worms.

units.la: Spartanoi (tametsi Iouis simulacrum apud Cretenses auribus caruit) cum tamen surda plac omnique audiendi sensu fuerint destituta: ita sacerdotum quoque Gentilium aures auritæ, u dam, ut dem, ut ita loquar, & attentæ fuerunt ad idololatriam atque superstitionem, ad ea, quæ ad ipsorum sperabant lucrum atque quæstum: sed quantum ad res diuinas & cælestes & ad veritatem attinet, surditate, ut ita loquar, ipsa furdiores & obtusiores exstiterunt.
units.tr: The Spartans (although the image of Jupiter among the Cretans lacked ears) were deaf and lacked all sense of hearing; so too the ears of the priests of the Gentiles were, so to speak, given ears and attentive to idolatry and superstition, to those things which they hoped would bring them gain and profit; but as far as divine and heavenly matters and the truth are concerned, they were, so to speak, more deaf and dull than deafness itself.

units.la: Præterea quemadmodum Gentilium idola atque simulacra pictos quidem fictosque habuere runt nasos atque nares, quibus etiam odores, suffitus atque unidores bene & male olentes fuerunt actenti, cum tamen nullum penitus habuerint olfaciendi odorandi ve sensum: sit eorundem sacerdotes idololatrici nafutissimi quidem & sagacissimi fuerunt in iis omnibus, quæ ad idololatriam atque superstitionem, & ad iporum commoda atque ad sperabant: at vero ea, quæ pietatem religionemque verám redolebant, nequaquam odorari atque sentire potuerunt: quin immo illis odoris inflar fuerunt tetri atque mortiferi.
units.tr: Moreover, just as the idols and images of the Gentiles had noses and nostrils, painted and fashioned, with which they were attentive to scents, incense and perfumes, pleasant and foul, yet had no sense of smell or scent at all; so the idolatrous priests of the Gentiles were indeed most keen-scented and shrewd in all those things which pertained to idolatry and superstition and to their own advantage and profit, but in what smelled of true piety and religion they could in no way perceive or sense the odour; nay, to them such things were rather a foul and deadly stench.

units.la: Item non secus atque Gentilium idola, atque simulacra sua quidem habuerunt ora, labia, linguas, dentes, palatum & alia loquendi instrumenta; cum tamen ne mutire, ut nullum vel minimum sonum aut vocem edere potuerint, muta omnino fuerint atque elinguia: sit illorum sacerdotes om quidem linguasque habuerunt ad quæ vis nugas, mendacia, blasphemiaseffutiendas ac blaterandas gravilas valde & loquaces: at in iis, quæ ad veritatem pietatemque pertinent, muti penitus fuerunt atque elinguet.
units.tr: Likewise, just as the idols and images of the Gentiles had mouths, lips, tongues, teeth, palates and other organs of speech, yet could not make the faintest sound or utter any voice at all, and were altogether mute and tongueless, so their priests had tongues and mouths, and were very ready and talkative in babbling out trifles, lies and blasphemies, but in what pertains to truth and godliness they were wholly dumb and tongue-tied.

units.la: Et ut Gentilium idola atque simulacra habuerunt quidem illa paullo ante commemorata, ut loquendi, ita edendi bibendiq; instrumenta: quibus etiam epulæ dedicatæ atq; dapes opiparæ ab hominibus superstitiosis fuerunt appositæ: cum tamen nihil quisquam cibi potusque sumere potuerit: sit fuerunt idolatrici gulosi quidem & ebriosi fuerunt, dapesque illas idolis suis appositas summâ cum avidate, voluptate & devorarunt: at cibos animi salutares omnes fastidierunt plane & aspernati sunt.
units.tr: And just as the idols and images of the Gentiles had, as mentioned a little earlier, organs for eating and drinking as well as for speaking, and feasts were consecrated to them and sumptuous dishes set before them by superstitious people, yet no one could take any food or drink, so their priests were idolatrous gluttons and drunkards, and devoured those dishes set before their idols with the greatest eagerness and pleasure; but they utterly loathed and rejected all the foods that are healthful to the soul.

units.la: Item ut Gentilium simulacra & idola, alia fuerunt barbata; alia imberbia; & alia quidem barbam habuerunt promissam; alia curtam: sic sacerdotum quoque ipsorum alii quidem superstitionis ergo barbam nutriunt & imberbes fuerunt alii vero barbam aluerunt & fuerunt barbati.
units.tr: Likewise, just as some of the idols and images of the Gentiles were bearded, some beardless, and some had long beards while others had short ones, so too among their priests some grew beards for the sake of superstition and were beardless, while others cultivated beards and were bearded.

units.la: Præterea ut Gentilium idola atque simulacra habuerunt quidem brachia atque manus, nec binas tantum, sed etiam quaternas: (sic enim Apollinis statua apud Spartanos quattuor auribus, & totidem manibus fuit prædita) cum tamen omni tangendi vi atque facultate carueriunt: sic eorundem sacerdotes manus quidem ad accipienda dona atque munera habuerunt semper aperitas & porrectas: at nihil eorum, quæ ad verum Dei cultum pertinent, attingere mentis suæ mavunt atque percipere valuerunt.
units.tr: Moreover, just as the idols and images of the Gentiles had arms and hands, not merely two but even four (for the statue of Apollo among the Spartans was furnished with four ears and as many hands), yet had no power or faculty of touching at all, so their priests kept their hands always open and outstretched to receive gifts and offerings, but they were never willing or able to take hold of or perceive anything that pertains to the true worship of God.

units.la: Et ut Gentilium idola atque simulacra pingebantur manibus illis suis gestantia omnis generis res, ut animalia, plantas, vestes, organa ac instrumenta, sacra & profana, belli atque pacis, ut pateram, poculum, scyphum, urnam, torquesque, fibulas, gemmas, malas, punica, flammeum, cistam, circulum, fistulam, tympanum, lyram, pedum incurvum, virgam, baculum, falcem, faces, fulmina, clavem, parmam, clypeum, securim, gladium, lanceam, haslam, arcum, sagittas, & alia id genus: sicuti in antiquorum numismatum & veterum parte videre licet: sic sacerdotes idololatricos in sacris præsertim suis obeundis baculos, virgas, scipiones, lituos & alia hujusmodi munera sua organa atque insignia gestare fuerunt soliti. His adde Commentacula, Fasto testæ, quæ virgæ erant, quas Flaminas portabant, pergentes ad sacrificium, ut a le homines amoverent.
units.tr: And just as the idols and images of the Gentiles were painted holding in their hands all kinds of things: animals, plants, garments, instruments and implements, sacred and profane, of war and of peace, such as a dish, a cup, a bowl, an urn, necklaces, clasps, gems, apples, pomegranates, a veil, a chest, a hoop, a pipe, a drum, a lyre, a curved staff, a rod, a stick, a sickle, torches, thunderbolts, a key, a small shield, a shield, an axe, a sword, a lance, a spear, a bow, arrows and other things of that kind, as may be seen in the ancient coins and monuments, so the idolatrous priests, especially when performing their sacred rites, were accustomed to carry staves, rods, sceptres, crooked staffs and other such emblems and insignia of their office. To these add the Commentacula and the Fasto-tesserae, which were rods that the Flamens carried as they went to sacrifice, to drive people away from themselves.

units.la: Vt porro Gentilium idola & simulacra habuerunt quidem suos pedes, eosque vel nudos vel calceatos, otreisque item vel fortes nonnunquam indutos, quibus etiam tertas quasdam res calcabant, cum tamen ne latum quidem unguem ingredi atque intedere possent, effentque plane immota. sic sacerdotum illorum pedes; agiles quidem erant atque celeres ad quaevis superstitiones exterendas, & ad quævis fictæ atque flagitia perpetranda: at ad opera bona, sancta & pia peragendum claudi erant, manci atque mutili.
units.tr: Again, just as the idols and images of the Gentiles had their feet, either bare or shod, and sometimes also wore sandals or boots, with which they trod on certain things, yet could not take even a broad step or move forward, but stood wholly motionless, so the feet of those priests were nimble and quick to tread down every superstition and to perpetrate every deceit and crime; but for doing good, holy and pious works they were lame, crippled and maimed.

units.la: Et ut Gentilium idola atque simulacra fingebantur, modo stantia; modo sedentia, ac insidentia folio, currubus, equis, leonibus, aquilis & aliis animantibus; modo currentia; modo salcantia; modo natantia; modo volantia: sic sacerdotum ipsorum, in sacris præsertim suis obeundis & procurandis variis, multiplices; & quidem ridiculi erant gestus, seu potius gesticulationes.
units.tr: And just as the idols and images of the Gentiles were fashioned, some standing, some sitting on thrones, chariots, horses, lions, eagles and other animals, some running, some leaping, some swimming, some flying, so their priests, especially in performing and managing their various sacred rites, made many gestures, and indeed they were ridiculous gestures, or rather grimaces.

units.la: Praeterea ut Gentilium simulacra & idola alia fuerunt nuda; eaque vel toto corpore, vel certis ejus partibus; alia fuerunt vestita, quae simulacr vestitus vel fuit splendidus & nitidus, vel horridus, qualitates & incultae; vel mulierebres, vel virilis, vel virginales, vel coniugales: sic sacerdotes quoque ipsorum, in sacris praesertim, aliquando nudi erant, vel toto corpore, vel certis corporis membris: sed plerunque habitu culto corporis utebantur vario, multiplici & monstrosso nonnunquam atque ridiculo.
units.tr: Furthermore, just as some of the idols and images of the Gentiles were naked, either over the whole body or in certain parts, and others were clothed, and the dress of the images was either splendid and shining or rough and unkempt, and they were either womanly, or manly, or maidenly, or matronly, so their priests too, especially in sacred rites, were sometimes naked, either all over or in certain parts of the body; but for the most part they used a decorated bodily attire, varied, manifold and sometimes monstrous and ridiculous.

units.la: Item ut Gentium idola atque simulacra & secundum sexum erant vel virilia, vel mulieribria, vel virginalia, vel maritalia: & secundum etatem alia forma atque specie erant, vel puerili, vel juvenili, vel virili, vel senili, vel etiam decrepita: ita illorum quoq; sacerdotes super- stitiones ergo & secundum sexum oportebat esse vel viros, vel mulieres, vel virgines, vel conjugatos, & secundum etatem vel juvenes, vel senes: unde, ut supra dixi, & sexus & etatis certa habebatur ratio.
units.tr: Likewise, just as the idols and images of the Gentiles were, according to sex, either male, female, maidenly or matronly, and according to age were of different form and appearance, either childlike, youthful, manly, aged or even decrepit, so their priests too, for superstition's sake, had to be, according to sex, either men, women, virgins or married, and according to age either young or old; whence, as I said above, a fixed regard was had both to sex and to age.

units.la: Hu adde, quod ut Gentilium idola atque simulacra certis precibus, unguentis aliisque ceremoniis munita, & initiata fuerunt atque consecrata: sic ipsi fere modis illorum quoque sacerdotes initiari, consecrari & inaugurari solebant.
units.tr: Add to this that just as the idols and images of the Gentiles were fortified and consecrated and initiated with certain prayers, ointments and other ceremonies, so their priests were also usually initiated, consecrated and installed in almost the same ways.

units.la: Postremo ut Gentilium idola atque simulacra maximo fuerunt in pretio & honore: immo sacrosancta inviolataque habita, multis modis atque cerimoniis, ut vestibus, ceres, luminibus, odoribus, sacrificiis, officiis, amplexibus, votis precibus, festis, circumgestationibus, peregrinationibus & aliis fuerunt culta: sic sacerdotum quoque ipsorum magna fuit dignitas, authoritas, potestas, magnusque, atque adeo fere divinus honoribus fuerunt affecti.
units.tr: Lastly, just as the idols and images of the Gentiles were held in the greatest esteem and honour, indeed regarded as sacrosanct and inviolable, and were worshipped with many rites and ceremonies, such as with garments, candles, lights, incense, sacrifices, services, embraces, vows, prayers, festivals, processions, pilgrimages and others, so their priests too had great dignity, authority and power, and were honoured almost with divine honours.

units.la: Sed ut idolorum simulacrorumque Gentilium, sic sacerdotum quoque ipsorum tandem tristes funestiqueque fuerunt, justo Dei judicio, exitus atque interitus.
units.tr: But just as the idols and images of the Gentiles at last had sad and dismal ends and ruin, by the just judgement of God, so did their priests.

units.la: Et hæc de idolorum atque sacerdotum cognatione atque collatione, uti etiam de primo eorum, qui sacris & sacrificiis Gentilium inter fuerunt genere in unum verbum, nempe hominibus, quae fuerunt vel praesides, vel administri factorum & sacrificiorum.
units.tr: And this is what I have to say about the kinship and comparison of the idols and the priests, as also about the first kind of those persons who were among the Gentiles' rites and sacrifices, namely men, who were either the presiders or the ministers of the acts and sacrifices.

units.la: SEQVITVR nunc alterum genus personarum illarum. Ea sunt Dii sive Dea, quibus sa- crificia facta sunt, quosque vel quas adesse sive interesse crediderunt: ut hoc loco Minerva, cur hæc sacra facta sunt, dicitur illis obviam esse facta, sacrificii interfuisse, ΗΛθε ΑΘΗΝΗ Ιεῶν ἀνίωσα, &c. Pallas venit obvia sacris.
units.tr: NOW follows the second kind of those persons: these are the gods or goddesses to whom the sacrifices were offered, and whom they believed to be present or to take part; as in this passage, where it is said that Minerva came to meet them when these rites were performed and took part in the sacrifice: "Pallas Athene came to meet the sacred rites" [ἦλθε Ἀθηνῆ ἱερῶν ἀνίωσα].

units.la: In hæc verba sic egregie commentatur Eustathius ex Achenaeo libro 8. Antiqui, inquit, quo hominum cupiditate quam animad vertebant incitatam, ut a precipitem ferri ad voluptates, fucipsos, Deos adesse existimabant, id est, humana specie atque forma præditos ad primitias atq; libamina venire finxerunt, quo nimirum hominas illorum praesentia moti tantomagis sibi ab intemperantia atq; lasciviâ temperarent, magna cum modestia, verecundia atq; sobrietate illas sacrorum atq; con- vivorum festivitates obirent. Nam si vel in hominis alicujus fenis atque honesti praesentia illos pudet inhonesti quippiam dicere aut facere, (secundum illud Epicharmi: ... ) Multo majoris momenti ipsam Deorum praesentiam existit mabat. Hæc Eustathius.
units.tr: Eustathius comments excellently on these words, drawing on Athenaeus, book 8: "The ancients," he says, "when they saw that men's desire was stirred and that they were carried headlong into pleasures, imagined that the gods were present, that is, they feigned that they, endowed with human form and appearance, came to the first-fruits and libations, so that men, moved by their presence, might all the more restrain themselves from intemperance and wantonness, and conduct those festivals of sacrifices and banquets with great modesty, shame and sobriety. For if men are ashamed to say or do anything dishonourable in the presence of some respectable and honourable man (according to the saying of Epicharmus: ...), much more did they think that the very presence of the gods was of great weight." Thus Eustathius.

units.la: Extant deinde praesentia bujusce Deorum vel Dearum apud Homerum nonnulla alia exempla: ut de eodem Minerva & Neptuno: Odys. α. —ΗΛΘε δ' ΑΘΗνη ιφῶν αὐτὴ σοθ ῥὶ ο ποσειδὼν, id est, Pallas venit obvia sacris,
units.tr: There are then several other examples of this presence of gods or goddesses in Homer, as of the same Minerva and Neptune in the Odyssey, book 1: "Pallas Athene came to meet the sacred rites, and Poseidon" [ἦλθε δ' Ἀθήνη ἱερῶν ... Ποσειδῶν], that is, "Pallas came to meet the sacred rites."
And Neptune, etc.

units.la: Et alio in loco Ia. α. Αἰθιοπας μετὰ δὲ ταύτην τιλοῦ ἱόντας Ἀρνόων τας, ἐψῳ ἀρχεῖον ἱκανοῦβας. Æthiopas ad longinquos venit, assuetus ille
units.tr: And in another place, Iliad book 1: "Going to the Ethiopians, far away, he came, having been feasted by them" [Αἰθιοπῆας μετὰ δαῖτα ... ]: "He went to the distant Ethiopians, accustomed to their rites."
Of the slaughtered [victims]...

units.la: Mallatis agnis ac tauris forsè sacratis. —χρῆ ὁ ζεὺς Ζηνὸς ἴσῃ μητὶ ἀλλᾶξ, ἀρὰ ἀλλὰ ἀμα πάντες ἐπονται: Et Iuppiter Ivit ad hesperna conviviæ lauta, secuti Pone Dei simul omnes.
units.tr: "Of the slaughtered lambs and perhaps consecrated bulls" [Ζεὺς γὰρ ἐς Ὠκεανὸν μετ' ἀμύμονας Αἰθιοπῆας ... ἅμα πάντες ἐπονται]: "For Zeus went to Ocean, among the blameless Ethiopians, to a sumptuous feast, and all the gods followed him together."

units.la: Antiquitus itaque cum putarent, Deos sibi esse præsentes, sestivitates suas decore & temperanter celebrabant: unde neq; decumbere apud antiquos morem fuit, sed sedentes epulabantur, neq; ad ebrietatem, sed quantum sat erat bibentes, libatione peracta, domum se recipiebant. At verò qui nunc se Diis sacrificare simulant, vocatis ad sacrificium amicis & familiarissimis, posteà (ubi ui-nitum sese immoderato vini potu ingurgitarint) & liberes suos exsecrantur, & uxores conviciis atq; maledictis proscindunt, & servos atq; familiares verberibus caedunt, & denique ob vini quicquid dira quaedam comminantur; tantum non Homericum illud usurpantes Iliad. 8.
units.tr: Since the ancients believed that the gods were present with them, they celebrated their festivals with decorum and moderation. For this reason it was not the custom among the ancients to recline at meals. They ate sitting up, drank only as much as was enough, and once the libation was finished they went home. But those who now pretend to sacrifice to the gods invite friends and close intimates to the sacrifice, and afterwards, when they have gorged themselves on wine, they curse their children, tear their wives apart with abuse and insults, beat and slaughter their servants and household members, and finally threaten all manner of dreadful things because of the wine. They scarcely fail to use that line of Homer from Iliad 8:

units.la: Nuν δ' ἰρχειθαι δὲ ἀλέντον, ἱνα ξωάγομεν ὅρνε, Quod superesse læti, gestis bene corpora rebus Procurate viri & pugnam sperate parati.
units.tr: "Now, since the day is left, let us prepare: that, rejoicing, you may attend to your bodies with good things, men, and be ready to hope for battle."

units.la: Hisce ergo verbis Eustathius et Athenaeus docent, epularia hæc sacrificia, antiquitus summa cum modestia, verecundia atq; temperantia celebrari solita, tandem in luxum, luxuriam atque lasciviam degenerasse. Hic autem uostrorum seftorum atq; conviviorum, quae in iis agitantur, clarifsimam imaginem videre licet, in quibus homines, ut quotidiana docet experientia, exutâ ferè omnî humanitate bestiarum; imò furiarum infernalium iustar, nou modo in alienos & extraneos, sed etiam in amicos, familiares & domesticos suos, atq; adeò in fidissimas suas tori conjortes, in charissimâ sua pignora atq; vitscera & verbis & factis immanissime sæviunt. Verùm ut ad propositum redeam, quemadmodum Ethnici finxerunt falsos illos Deos suis sacrificiis præsentes esse: ita Deus Opt. Max. suam sæpe præsentiam in populi sui sacrificiis manifestis signis declarà vit. Atque hæc quidem satis sint dicta de personis.
units.tr: By these words Eustathius and Athenaeus teach that these feast sacrifices, which were once customarily celebrated with the greatest modesty, reverence and temperance, at last degenerated into luxury, extravagance and lasciviousness. In our own sacrifices and feasts, and in what goes on at them, one can see a very clear picture of the same thing. As daily experience shows, men there, having put off almost all human feeling, like beasts, or rather like infernal furies, rage most savagely, not only against strangers and outsiders but even against their friends, household and domestic companions, and indeed against their most faithful partners in marriage, and against their dearest pledges and their very bowels, both in words and in deeds. But to return to my purpose: just as the heathen imagined that their false gods were present at their sacrifices, so the Lord God Most High often declared his presence in the sacrifices of his people by clear signs. Let this be enough said about the persons.

units.la: SVPEREST ultimum & fere præcipuum Caput, in sacris sacrificiis, considerandum, ipsa forma, modus, ordo, & quasi processus ac methodus sacrificiorum: quæ licet multiplex do, & ordine fuerit atq; varia apud alios atque alios populos, & alias atque alias temporibus: tamen hæc, quam sacrificiorum ratio : cui respondet illa apud Apollonium sacrificii Argonautici descriptio.
units.tr: There remains the last and almost the principal head to be considered in the holy sacrifices: the very form, manner, order, and, as it were, the course and method of the sacrifices. Although these differed in multiplicity, order and variety among different peoples and at different times, nevertheless this is the method of sacrifices to which Apollonius's description of the Argonauts' sacrifice corresponds.
On the form and manners

units.la: Porrò in utriusq; sacrificii descriptione ipsa primum παρασκευὴ ἢ ἀλλαχαῖη ἀλλὰ ἀπ' Ευ-περοντος ἀνατflatio quodam in loco appellatur, hoc est, præparatio sacrificialis, occurrit, uempe & hostiarum, hic consideratur & personarum, & aliarum rerum, quae in sacrificiis adhiberi fuerunt solitae. Hæc verò omnia, quæ sacrificiis præmittebant, eorumq; erant quasi primordia sive præludia, παρὰ λεια uno nomine & παρίω-μα Græce fuerunt appellata. Qua igitur sertæ atque ordine sugula in utroq; sa-crificio narrantur, eodem, ut adhuc fecimus, singula persequemur. Nam qui duorum iflorum sacrificiorum speciatim ; idem cunctorum ferè aliorum sacrificiorum ordo fuit, ritus atque modus.
units.tr: In the description of each sacrifice, first comes the preparation, which in one place is called by the Greek term paraskeuē, that is, sacrificial preparation.
