Here both the victims and the persons and the other things customarily used in sacrifices are considered. All those things which they placed before the sacrifices, and which were as it were their beginnings or preludes, the Greeks called by one name, and so, in the same way as we have done so far, we shall go through each item in order, as they are narrated in each of the two sacrifices. For the order and rite of the other sacrifices was almost the same as that of these two taken individually.

units.la: Primùm omnium apud Apollonium electionis victimarum mentio fit luculenta hic verbis; quibus Iason pastores suos assatus iis mandat, ut boves ex grege selectos adducant: —ὅρες δ'ἴωσιν Δμοῖτε ἰμοὶ ςα βων σαμάνδαρ, οἳ μίμνηλαν Δηὸς βόας ἀγάλλων ἰνεχαν αρτις ἰλάσα. —Vt autem eant Vt boves huc ex grege electos adducant.
units.tr: First of all, in Apollonius there is a clear mention of the choice of victims, in these words, by which Jason, having summoned his shepherds, bids them bring oxen chosen from the herd: "And let them go and bring hither oxen chosen from the herd, which they kept for the god."
The choice of victims

units.la: Vbi verbo ἰνεχειν utitur, quod valde est emphaticum, quo delectus hostiarum diligens exprimitur: non ait, ἰνεχειναι, sed ἰνεχειναται, quod est ἐμφαντικὰ, & figuificat, hostias eligere, illas non temerè, sed bene, magnâ, cum ratione atq; judicio ex toto illo pecorum grege, tanquam egregias, eximias, ad sacrificia aptas. Deoq; gratas & decoras à bubulcis fuisse selectas & segregatas. Hoc enim sibi vult verbum ιναλεις, quod non simpliciter secernere, excernere, seligere, sed bene secernere & eligere significat: ut Odyss. ξ. τὸ ἀείσον ἐπιλλιπίζε ἀπόντ. ----
units.tr: Here he uses a verb which is very emphatic and expresses a careful selection of victims. He does not say simply "chosen," but "chosen out well," which is emphatic and signifies that the victims were picked not carelessly but well, with great reason and judgment, from the whole flock, as outstanding and excellent, fit for sacrifice, and pleasing and becoming to the god, and selected and separated by the herdsmen. For the word means not merely to separate, pick out or choose, but to separate and choose well, as in Odyssey 1 [...] the verb is used of the things that are selected.

units.la: Ab ἐκλέγειν fit ἐκλεκτός, delectus, qui exemptus est e numero, eximius, egregius, ut ἐκλεκτὸν ἀπὸ Platonem de Legib. Summa igitur cura, ratio, atque iudicium in deligendis ad sacrificia bestiis adhibebantur, ut nimirum illæ essent integræ, sincerę, purę, omnis carentes labe atque macula, non mancæ, mutilæ, claudæ, cæcæ, morbidæ, maculentæ, aut insigni aliquo notio laborantes. Hinc Seneca: Sacerdos, inquit, non integri corporis quasi mali ominis res vitæ est. Hoc in victimis notatur, quanto magis in sacerdotibus?
units.tr: From eklegein comes eklektos, meaning chosen, taken out from the number, distinguished, excellent, as in Plato's Laws. Therefore the greatest care, reason and judgment were used in choosing beasts for sacrifice, so that they would be whole, sound, pure, free from every stain and blemish, not maimed, mutilated, lame, blind, diseased, spotted, or suffering from any conspicuous defect. Hence Seneca: "A priest," he says, "whose body is not whole is, as it were, a thing of ill omen for life." This is noted in victims; how much more in priests?

units.la: Deinde peculiaris quoque speciatim singulis Diis certæ peculiaresque offerri solitæ bestiæ, habita ratione generis, ætatis, sexus, numeri, coloris. Quod ad genus attinet, omnis generis, cum aliis tum tælistes, ut gallos gallinaceos, anseres & similes: tum terrestres, ut oves, sues, capras, boves & alias: tum aquatiles: tum ancipites; tum etiam infectas legimus Ethnicos falso illis sive Diis obtulisse: licet quasdam gentes a bestiarum vel occisione vel immolatione, vel etiam manducatione, id, vel omnino omnium, vel etiam nonnullarum abhorruisse legamus.
units.tr: Next, particular animals were customarily offered to each particular god, with regard to kind, age, sex, number and colour. As to kind, we read that the heathen offered to their false gods every kind of animal: birds, such as cocks, geese and the like; land animals, such as sheep, pigs, goats, oxen and others; water creatures; amphibious creatures; and even insects. Yet we read that some nations abhorred killing, sacrificing, or even eating these animals, either all of them or some of them.

units.la: Sic Ætatis quoque habebatur ratio: ut hanc Minervæ hostiam hic legimus frufle ἀλλά, juvencam, id est ἑτέρως, sive ἐξ ... μάγον ... Eustathio interprete, id est, unius tantum anni.
units.tr: Age was likewise taken into account. Thus here we read that a heifer was the victim for Minerva, that is, one of only one year, according to the interpretation of Eustathius.

units.la: Adhæc Sexus quoque observatus fuit. Nam, ut supra ex Cicerone dictum est, alii Diis maribus, alii fœminis sacrificabatur victimis. Sic hostia hæc Minervæ feminei fuit generis: sicut Agamemnon contra Iovi βοῦν ἀρτεῖα, id est, bovem masculum immolavit. Ita dos H & B.
units.tr: Sex was also observed. For, as was said above from Cicero, some victims were sacrificed to male gods and others to female gods. Thus this victim for Minerva was of the female kind, just as Agamemnon sacrificed to Jupiter a bull, that is, a male ox [βοῦν ἄρσενα]. So also the rest.

units.la: Ita Numeri habita fuit ratio. Nam vel una, vel duæ, vel tres, plures sive hostiæ uni Deo immolabantur: ut hic Minervæ tantum una offertur bestia a Nestore loco ante citato: & Argonautæ duos tauros Neptuno immolasse legunter. Fuerunt quoque apud Veteres, ut Eusebius docet, Hecatombæ & Chiliombæ, cum centum, vel etiam mille animalia immolarentur in epinicis maxime usitatæ. Hujusmodi Hecatomba fuit illa, quam Agamemnon Iliad. α. & Achinus Odyss. ν. Apollini, quæ κλύθι sive vsqe, id est, inclyta & sacra dicitur, obtinuerunt. Huc facit, quod superis impari: inferis autem pari numero sacrificandum erat. Denique quoque colorem capram album quidam Pani Lycæo voluit in Lupercalibus offerri fuisse solitam: nonnulli hircum; ex cujus corio Luperci sacerdotes coria confecissent, undique per urbem fœminas feriebant. Sic taurum sive juvencum candidum Iovi Capitolino offerebant triumphantes: seu alii taurum nigrum Neptuno. Idem judicium esse de aliis, de quibus supra dictum est. Ita de Cicero de Legibus: Quæ quoque Divo decora gratæ, sunt hostiæ providento. Et paullo post lcgis hujus explicatione: Illud ex inflituto Pontificum & hæruspicum non mutandum est, quibus hostiis immolandum cuique Deo, cui majoribus, cui lactentibus, cui maribus, cui fœminis.
units.tr: Number was likewise taken into account. One, two, three or more victims were sacrificed to a single god; thus here only one animal is offered to Minerva, as Nestor has it in the place cited above, and the Argonauts are said to have sacrificed two bulls to Neptune. There were also among the ancients, as Eusebius teaches, hecatombs and chiliombs, when a hundred or even a thousand animals were slaughtered, most commonly at victory celebrations. Of this kind was that hecatomb which Agamemnon in Iliad 1 and Achilles in Odyssey ν offered to Apollo, which is called klythi, that is, illustrious and sacred. This fits with the rule that odd numbers were offered to the gods above and even numbers to the gods below. Lastly, some have held that a white she-goat was customarily offered to Pan Lycaeus at the Lupercalia, others a he-goat, from whose hide the Luperci priests made thongs, with which they struck women everywhere through the city. Likewise triumphant generals offered a white bull or steer to Capitoline Jupiter, while others offered a black bull to Neptune. The same judgment applies to the others mentioned above. So Cicero says in his De Legibus: "Those victims which are pleasing to each god are to be provided." And a little later, in explaining this law: "That rule of the pontiffs and haruspices is not to be changed, by which victims are to be offered to each god: to some the older, to some the younger, to some males, to some females."

units.la: Atque hujusmodi quidem hostiæ ex reliquo grege exitu atque eligi solitæ, quæ cuique Deo apte essent & decoræ. Eximiæ fuerunt dictæ & egregiæ. Egregiæ, inquit Festus, id est, e grege electæ. Unde Apollonius: ἀγὴ ἀλλοὶ ... ἐκκρίτος, id est, egregi bene eligentes. Et, Eximium, ut idem Festus ait, inde dictum, quod in sacrificiis optimum pecus eximebatur, vel quod primum erat natum.
units.tr: So such victims were customarily chosen from the rest of the flock, namely those which were suitable and becoming for each god. They were called eximiae and egregiae. "Egregiae," says Festus, that is, chosen from the herd. Hence Apollonius: "choosing out, distinguished," that is, choosing well and picking out the best. And "eximium," as Festus says as well, is so called because the best of the flock was taken out for sacrifice, or because it was the first born.

units.la: Ut autem hostiæ eligendi, sita electæ ad templa arasque, sive focos, ubi mactandæ et immolandæ erant, agendi, ducendi, seu adducendi, diligens apud Gentiles habita fuit ratio, ut ex duobus locis mulus aliis facile potest colligi. Apud Homerum quidem Nestor dans singulis suis certa mandata ad rem divinam, quam parabant, pertinentia, ajit:
units.tr: But the careful arrangement made by the Gentiles for choosing the victims, for bringing them to the temples and altars or hearths, where they were to be slaughtered and offered, and for driving or leading them there, can easily be gathered from two places of Homer. In the one, Nestor, giving each of his men certain orders relating to the divine service they were preparing, says:

units.la: Sed alius quidem rus caussa bovis est, ut celerrimè veniat (cum tamen ut est in provincia, bos lenti proceedat) adducat autem eum bubulcus vir.
units.tr: But the one thing that matters for the ox is that it comes quickly (though in the country an ox moves slowly), and that a man, the herdsman, leads it in.

units.la: Et paullo post: ἦλθον ... βοῦς. Venit quidem bos ex agro, &c. ac posllea duo Nestoris filii Stratius & Echephron bovem cornibus adducunt, scilicet ad aram. Sic enim Homerus:
units.tr: And a little later: "They came... the ox." The ox indeed comes from the field, etc., and then the two sons of Nestor, Stratius and Echephron, bring the ox by its horns, namely to the altar. For so Homer says:

units.la: Bουῶ δ' ἀγίτην καρᾶων Στρέπτ.ῶ ἡ Διὸς ἱχίφορον,Bovem adducebant cornibus Stratius & divinæ Echephron.
units.tr: Stratius and divine Echephron were leading the ox by the horns. [βοῦν δ' ἀγέτην κεράων Στράτιός τε Ἐχέφρων]

units.la: Morn enim fuit, ut Lucianus inquit de sacrificiis, victimam ad aram adducere, ut eam in oculos Des jugularenc. Hujus ritus meminit etiam alibi Homerus, ut λ. α. —τοῖ δ' (ἀχαιοὶ) ἀνα Ζεὺ (Απόλλωνι) ἀλεπτὸν ἱκατόμυεν Εξείνε ἱσπονο τοῦ μπλον (εὐδούλλα sive ἱυκιραϙον) ἀξὶ βωμον.
units.tr: For it was the custom, as Lucian says in his work on sacrifices, to bring the victim to the altar so that it might be slaughtered before the god's eyes. Homer also mentions this rite elsewhere, in book 1. "And they (the Achaeans) to Zeus (Apollo) offered a sacred hecatomb... and [...] the altar." [οἳ δ' ἀνὰ Ζεὺς ... ἱερὴν ἑκατόμβην ... βωμόν]

units.la: Apud Apollonium similiter, Bubulci duos illos boves, quos Argonautæ Apollini immolarunt ex grege in urbem adduxisse dicuntur; id quod ex his verbis colligitur: Τοίως δ' αὐτ' ἀγίλην δή ωσ inkas ἄγοντες Βυκόλοι αἰσσιδυο δ' ἐω βόι. τῆς δ' ἰρύσαιτο. Κυρότεσι ἱταιέγον βωμῶ χιδὼν:
units.tr: Similarly in Apollonius, the herdsmen are said to have brought the two oxen, which the Argonauts sacrificed to Apollo, into the city from the herd; this is gathered from these words: "Then the herdsmen, driving the cattle from the herd, brought the two oxen of the son of Aeson; and the younger men [...] to the altar." [Τοῖος δ' αὖ ἀγέλην ... ἄγοντες βουκόλοι ... βοῦς ... βωμόν]

units.la: Tunc postquam ex grege præmiserunt adducentes Bubulci Æsonidis duos boves: illos vero admonerunt iuniores ex foeis are, &c.
units.tr: Then, after the herdsmen had sent them out of the herd, bringing the two oxen of the son of Aeson, the younger men, who had been warned, [led them] from the field to the altar, etc.

units.la: Ut igitur apud Homerum, sic apud Apollonium, bubulci ex agro quidem boves adduxerunt: sed apud Homerum duo Nestoris filii: apud Apollonium autem Argonautica narrationes sequi, qui inter illos erant iuniores, eosdem boves ad aram adduxerunt: non autem bubulci. Scholiastes in hunc locum κυρόλεγει, inquit, ὁ Σωιας Ἠδῶν juniores boe sacrificium peragunt, propterea quod Deus Apollo semper singatur esse juvenis.
units.tr: So, as in Homer, so in Apollonius: the herdsmen indeed brought the oxen from the field; but in Homer it was the two sons of Nestor, while in Apollonius the younger men who were among them, following the Argonautic narratives, brought the same oxen to the altar, and not the herdsmen. The scholiast on this passage says: "The younger men perform the sacrifice of the ox, because the god Apollo is always pictured as a youth."

units.la: Ac omnino non fine singulari cerimonia atq. religiose hostias ad altaria, non tanquam ad affligum, sed ad præsentissimam mortem agi atq. duci fuisse solium, cum ex his ipsis locis, tum ex plurimis aliis litterarum monumentis patet. Verba quibus Homerus & Apollonius hunc ipsum actum exprimunt, sunt ἀγλ, ἱλὼν sive ἐλεύλ & ἱρυλ. quæ agere, ducere, adducere, admovere, figere. Apud Latinos duo sunt verba maxime communia, quibus actus hic designatur, nempe Ducere & Agere. Priori usus est Virgilius hoc versu: —hanc etiam via Tityre duco.
units.tr: It is clear, both from these very passages and from many other written monuments, that victims were led and brought to the altars, not as to slaughter, but to immediate death, and that this was done not without a particular ceremony and religious care. The Greek verbs by which Homer and Apollonius describe this very act are ἄγειν, ἄγεσθαι (or ἐλαύνειν) and εἰρύειν, meaning to drive, to lead, to bring, to move up, to fix. Among the Latins two verbs are most commonly used for this act, namely ducere and agere. Virgil used the first in this line: "This way too, Tityrus, I lead [the goats]."

units.la: Posterius, a Græco ἀγλν deductum, cum in re pastoritia, tum in sacris valde fuit usitatum. Apud Græcos Grex pecorum ἀγίλην dictus est, nimirum ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀγὲ, & ἱλά-, id est, ab agendo, ut ducendo & impellendo, propterea quod pecori ductu atque ductoribus (quod pastorum præcipuum est officium) maxime indigent, ad quam etymologiam Apollonius loco ante citato videtur alludere, cum dixit ἀγίλαν ἱστ ἀγοντες, id est ex grege agentes, si ve dux entes, scilicet bubulci. Agere porro, inquit Festus, modo significat ante se pellere, id est, minare (unde sine dubio verbum Gallicum mener, id est, ducere.) Virgilius: Et potum pastas age Tityre, &c.
units.tr: The second, derived from the Greek ἄγειν, was very much in use both in pastoral matters and in sacred ones. Among the Greeks a flock of animals was called ἀγέλη, namely from ἄγειν and ἐλαύνειν, that is, from driving and pushing, because cattle need guidance and guides (which is the chief duty of shepherds). Apollonius seems to allude to this etymology in the line cited above, when he said "driving from the herd," that is, the herdsmen who drive or lead from the flock. Moreover, as Festus says, agere now means to drive before oneself, that is, to threaten (whence without doubt the French verb mener, to lead). Virgil: "And, Tityrus, drive the flocks to pasture and water, etc."

units.la: Et Varro: Agitur pecus pastum, qua ἡ agi poresi. Hinc Agolum pastorale baculum (quod etiam pedum appellant) quo pecudes aguntur, ut Festus testatur. Agonium, ut idem ait, dies appellatur, quo Rex hostiam immolabat, quam hostiam Anci ii Agonem vocabant. Hinc Agonalia, de qua Festus, & dies Agonalis, de quo Ov dius: Pars, quia non veniant pecudes, sed aguntur ab aëtu, Nomen Agonalem eredit habere diem.
units.tr: And Varro: "The cattle are driven to pasture where they can be driven." Hence agolum, the shepherd's staff (which they also call pedum), with which the herds are driven, as Festus testifies. Agonium, as the same writer says, is the name of the day on which the king sacrificed a victim, which victim the people of Ancus called the agon. Hence the Agonalia, which Festus discusses, and the Agonal day, about which Ovid says: "Some think the day has the name Agonal because the animals are not brought but driven (agitur) by the priest."

units.la: Et Varro dies Agonales vult dictos, per quos Rex in regis arietes immolabat dictos ab Agone: eo quod interrogabatur a principe civitatis, & princeps gregis immolabatur. Sed de hac voce interrogationi Agone, formulaq dicendi, Hoc age, qua silentium & attentio imperabatur, postea pluribus. Adde & Agonias hostias ab agendo dictas.
units.tr: Varro also holds that the Agonal days were so named because on them the king sacrificed rams, named from agon, since he was questioned (interrogabatur) by the chief of the state, and the chief of the flock was sacrificed. But I shall say more later about this word agon, the form of question, and the phrase Hoc age, by which silence and attention were commanded. Add also that the Agonian victims were so called from agere.

units.la: Porro bestiæ & a certis personis ad id delectus, & cum pompa quadam ad aram usq. duci eonsuerunt, quod ex duobus his locis facile est conjicere. Cicero de Divinatione: Cum Censor popalum lustravit, bonus omnibus, qui hostias ducerent, eligebantur. Plinius libro vigesimo octavo, capite secundo: Cur publicis lustris etiam nomina victimasducentium prospere eligimus? Communi aliis more & consuetudine hostiæ a popis & victimarius, a quib. deinde jugulari, atq. mactari consueverant, ad aras adducebantur. Præcedebant etiam nonnunquam, pi efertim in majoribus sacris ficiis, ut Hetacombis, tubulnes, tibicines, & tibicines, vel tubis, vel tibus vel litus canentes.
units.tr: Moreover, beasts were chosen for this purpose by certain persons, and were customarily led to the altar with a certain ceremony; this is easy to infer from these two passages. Cicero, On Divination: "When the censor purified the people, all those who were to lead the victims were chosen as good men." Pliny, book twenty-eight, chapter two: "Why do we choose, at the public purifications, the names of those who lead the victims for good luck?" By the common custom of other peoples, the victims were led to the altars by the priests and the attendants, by whom they were afterwards struck and slaughtered. Sometimes, especially in the greater sacrifices such as hecatombs, trumpeters, pipers and flute-players, playing either trumpets or pipes or flutes, went before them.

units.la: Etsi vero illi, qui hostias ad sacrificia praebebant, omnem dabant operam, ut illae essent pura, integra ac perfecta, & sacrificiis apta, summamq; in illarum delectu cautionem adhibebant: cameque sacerdotes quoq;, & illorum ministri, ut popa & victimarii ea isdem a planta pedis usq; ad caput diligentissime explorabant, nunquid illis messet virii, ita ut nullum vel minimum vitium in iis latere posset, quo nimirum illi, qui hostias illas ad sacrificandum praebuerant, extra omnem essent culpam. Nam ut apud Hebraeos, sic apud Ethnicos nefas ducebatur, bestiam aliquam mutilam, mancam, claudam, morbidam, aliquaue labe vitiove infectam immolare. Isaq; nisi pure integraq; fuissent & lecta ad rem divinam, minus proficere putabant. Eligebantur ergo hostiae, & ex grege secernebantur, quae ideo & lectae & eximiae dicebantur, unde Legere verbum proprium est [?] Factorum. Servius lib.4. Aeneid. in illa verba, —Maflant lectas de more bidentes, notat vocari, Lectas. Moris enim fuerat, ut ad sacrificia eligeretur oves, quibus nihil deesset: ut in Iexto, Aeneidos Nunc grege de intacto septem mactare iuvencas. Veracius in Pontificalibus quaestionibus ducet, eximias dictas hostias, quae ad sacrificium destinatae eximerentur e grege: vel quod eximia specie quasi offerrendae Numinibus eligantur. Hinc Virgilius: Quatuor eximios praestati corpore tauros: ubi quod eximuntur, eximios; quod eligatur, praestanti corpore monstrauit. Et tamen Tertullianus in Apologetico cap.14. Ethnicus suis temporis objicit, quod suis Dijs tabidosa & scabiosa quaeq; mactarent. Et cap.30. Cum hostiae probantur penes vos a vitiosissimis sacerdotibus, cur praecordia potius victimarum quam ipsorum sacrificiorum examinantur. Lucianus quoq; de sacrificiis: jam vero, inquit, cum immolant, primum fertis coronant pecudem, multoq; ance explorant, num legitima sit & idonea sacris, ne quid forte mactans ex hus, quae religio repudiat: quae quidem exploratio varius modis fiebat. Nam Graecitauros farinae capros cinerubus, capras aquae frigida explorabat, teste Pe[?]ucero. Plutarchus de eodem delectu sic scribit, ... Victimam enim sacris aptam oportet & animo & corpore puram, integram, incontaminatam esse.
units.tr: Although those who supplied the victims for sacrifices took every care that they should be pure, whole and perfect, and fit for sacrifice, and used the greatest caution in choosing them, the priests too, and their assistants, the attendants and the victim-bearers, examined them most carefully from the sole of the foot to the head, lest any blemish should be found on them, so that no fault, however small, could lie hidden in them, and so that those who had supplied the victims for sacrifice should be free of all blame. For just as among the Hebrews, so among the heathens it was thought impermissible to sacrifice an animal that was mutilated, maimed, lame, diseased, or infected with any stain or defect. They also thought that if the victims were not pure and whole and chosen for the sacred rite, they would be of little avail. Victims were therefore selected and separated from the flock; they were called both chosen and select (lectae and eximiae), whence legere is the proper word for choosing. Servius, on book 4 of the Aeneid, on the words "They sacrifice chosen two-year-old sheep according to custom," notes that they were called lectae. For it was the custom to choose for sacrifice sheep that lacked nothing, as in the text of the Aeneid: "Now from the untouched flock to slay seven heifers." Veranius, in his Pontifical Questions, says that victims were called eximiae (select) because they were taken out (eximerentur) from the flock and set apart for sacrifice, or because they were chosen for their outstanding appearance, as if to be offered to the divinities. Hence Virgil: "Four bulls of outstanding body"; where they are called eximii because they are taken out, and praestanti corpore because they are chosen. Yet Tertullian, in the Apology, chapter 14, reproaches the heathens of his time for slaughtering to their gods whatever was diseased and scabby. And chapter 30: "When victims are approved among you by the most faulty priests, why are the entrails of the victims examined rather than the sacrifices themselves?" Lucian too, in his work on sacrifices: "Indeed, when they sacrifice, first they crown the beast and, long before, examine whether it is lawful and fit for sacred use, lest by chance they slaughter any of those things which religion rejects." This examination was done in various ways. For, as Pelusius reports, the Greeks tested bulls with flour, goats with ashes, and she-goats with cold water. Plutarch writes about this same choice as follows: "For a victim fit for sacred rites must be pure in both soul and body, whole and undefiled."

units.la: Adducebant deinde victimas ad aram nonnunquam ligatas: nonnunquam solutas. Hinc Servius in illa Virgilii Aeneidos tertio: Ecce flauam ante aras aurata fronte iuvencam; notat hostias minores ante aras nullo vinculo ligatas, fuit solitas esse, cum in sacris nihil vinctum esse deberet. Verum contra Iuvenalis ita scribit: Sed procul extensum peculans quatit hostia funem, Tarpejo servata iovi, fronte temq; corusca: Quippe ferox vitulus templi maturus & aram Spargendusq; mero, etc.
units.tr: Then they brought the victims to the altar, sometimes bound, sometimes loose. Hence Servius, on that line of Virgil's Aeneid book 3, "Behold, before the altars, a yellow heifer with gilded brow," notes that smaller victims were customarily brought before the altars with no binding at all, since nothing bound ought to be used in sacred rites. But Juvenal writes otherwise: "But the victim, pulling far off on its stretched rope, shakes the cord, kept for Tarpeian Jove, with its forehead gleaming; for the bold calf, grown fit for the temple, is to be sprinkled with wine, etc."

units.la: Ex quo loco constat, victimas solitas fuisse funibus duci, quae si geflaretur humeris, non litabant. Idem obser vat Plinius lib.8. cap.46. scribens, vitulos ad aram humeris hominum allatos nec fere litare: sicut nec claudicantem: nec aliena hostia Deos placari. Unde mali ominis ipsis erat, si victima non sponte sequeretur, sed vi trabenda esset, vel si ex ducentium manu se propriupisset, vel profugisset: quem admodum etiam; si percussa mugitum dedisset, aut in aliam partem corporis, quam par erat, concidisset: quippe piacularia inde faciebant auspicia, quae, ut inquit Festus sacrificantibus hostia praetendebat.
units.tr: From this passage it is clear that victims were customarily led by ropes. If one was carried on men's shoulders, the sacrifice did not give a favourable omen (non litabant). Pliny makes the same observation in book 8, chapter 46, writing that calves brought to the altar on men's shoulders hardly ever gave a favourable sign, nor did a lame one, and that gods were not appeased by a foreign victim. Hence it was a bad omen if the victim did not follow of its own accord but had to be dragged by force, or if it broke free from the hands of those leading it or ran away. It was the same if, when struck, it bellowed, or fell onto a part of its body other than the proper one. From such things they drew inauspicious omens, which, as Festus says, the victim gave to those sacrificing.

units.la: Isidorus quoq; victimam vocatam tellatur, quod vincta ad operas ducebatur: sed hoc alii ad ferociam victimae, dum duceretur: alii ad tempus ance sacrificium referunt: quo ligatae fuerunt. Scribit enim Servius in ratione sacrorum, quod par est & animae et corporis causa. Nam pleruque, quae non possunt circa animam, fiunt circa corpus, ut est ligare & solvere: cum non possit anima per se, ex cognatione potest. Festus similiter vult dictam, quod vincta ad altare adduceretur.
units.tr: Isidore also says that the victim (victima) is so called because it was led bound (vincta) to the rites. Others refer this to the ferocity of the victim while it was being led, and others to the time before the sacrifice, when the victims were bound. For Servius writes in his Ratio sacrorum that this is fitting for both soul and body. For most things that cannot be done to the soul are done to the body, such as binding and loosing, since the soul cannot do them by itself but can through its kinship with the body. Festus likewise holds that it was so called because it was led bound to the altar.

units.la: Siue autem ligatas siue solutas Victimas adducerent ad aram, eas certis ritibus atq; certimo- nijs ernare atq; coronare solent foliis: cuius quidem ornatus, cultus, atque habitus apud Homerum sit mentio luculenta. Nestor enim inter alia mandata, quae dedit filijs suis, accersiri jubet χρυσοχοον, aurificem. Inquit enim: —ἔρεξα βοῦς χρυσον κέρασιν ἀμφιέλισσαν,
units.tr: Whether the victims were brought to the altar bound or unbound, they were usually adorned and crowned with leaves according to fixed rites and ceremonies. A clear mention of this adornment, care and dress is found in Homer. Nestor, among other instructions he gave to his sons, orders that the goldsmith (χρυσοχόος, chrysochoos) be summoned. He says: "I sacrificed an ox, gilding its horns [ἔρεξα βοῦς χρυσὸν κέρασιν ἀμφιέλισσαν]."

units.la: idest, Bovis cornibus ut aurum circumfundat. Ac paullò post, Faber ille, quem χαλκέα vocat, forcipe, malleo, aliisq; instrumentis instructus fabrilibus dicitur advenisse, qui aurum, a Nestore acceptum, —βοῦς κέρασιν ἀμφιελίσσαν Αστικόσας, ἐν χαλκῷ δυοι εχορῶ χρυσον, idest, —Bovi cornibus circumfudit.
units.tr: That is, to spread gold around the ox's horns. And a little after, that smith, whom he calls the coppersmith (χαλκεύς, chalkeus), is said to have arrived equipped with tongs, hammer and other smith's tools. He took the gold received from Nestor and "gilded the horns of the ox, which he had shaped [Βοῦς κέρασιν ἀμφιελίσσας ... χρυσὸν ἐχεύω]," that is, "poured gold around the ox's horns."

units.la: Aptans, ut simulacrum Dea gauderet videns.
units.tr: Fitting it so that the goddess might rejoice at the sight.

units.la: Ex hoc loco, ut etiam alij conflat, hunc morem bellatarum frontem atque cornua inaurandi fuisse per antiquum: unde βοῦς χρυσοκέρως, id est, bos inauratis cornibus praeditus saepe ab Homero & aliis appellatur. Et hic quidem majorum bostiarum fuit ornatus, dependentibus ab utraque parte cornuum vittis sive falsis nonnullis. Plato quoq; in Alcibiade mores hujus mentionem facit, ubi ait Lacedaemoniorum vota precari, Diis gratiores esse, quam Graecorum βοῦς χρυσοκέρως, boves aurata cornua gerentes; & quae vis illorum vel magnificentissima sacrificia. Hunc morem a Graecis ad Romanos fuisse translatum conflat. Exflat Senatus consultum de ludis Apollinaribus primum facien dis, quod Macrobius primo Saturnal. recitat, in quo Decem viri praeceperi fuit, ut Graecorum bostia sacrum facerent, Apollini bovem aurato, & caprae duabus albis auratis, Latone bovem faemina aurata: Vide Ovidium: —Induitaque cornibus auro Victima votà facit, &c.
units.tr: From this passage, as others also show, the custom of gilding the forehead and horns of cattle was ancient. Hence the ox with gilded horns (βοῦς χρυσοκέρως, bous chrysokeros) is often called by Homer and others. This was the adornment of the larger victims, with ribbons or some kind of hanging fillets from each side of the horns. Plato in the Alcibiades also mentions this custom, where he says that the prayers of the Lacedaemonians are more pleasing to the gods than those of the Greeks, with their oxen with gilded horns (βοῦς χρυσοκέρως) and their most magnificent sacrifices. It is clear that this custom passed from the Greeks to the Romans. There survives a senatus consultum on establishing the Apollinarian games, which Macrobius quotes in book 1 of the Saturnalia. In it the decemvirs were ordered to make the sacrifice in the Greek manner: an ox with gilded horns for Apollo, and for Latona a heifer with gilded horns. See Ovid: "Having decked the victim with gold on its horns, she makes her vow," etc.

units.la: Eylalibi: —Blando induta cornibus auro Concederant illae niveae tervice juvencae.
units.tr: Elsewhere: "Decked with gold on its pleasing horns, those snow-white heifers had gone forth."

units.la: Juvenalis: —Frontemq; coruscat, scilicet propter cornua aurata,
units.tr: Juvenal: "...and it glitters on its forehead," namely because of its gilded horns.

units.la: Stfeanius apud Virgilium decimo Aeneidos: Et statuam ante aras aurata fronte juvencum Candentem pariterq; caput cum macte ferentem.
units.tr: Statius, in the tenth book of Virgil's Aeneid: "And a bullock with gilded forehead, gleaming white, set before the altars, carrying its head high in its sacred dignity."

units.la: Vitur flatuendi verbo cui respondet illud Homericum in fulli factificii descriptionem Τν μὰλα πίονα πιν ταῖτηρ ἐν ιχώον ἐπ' ἱερῷ
units.tr: The verb "to set up" (statuere) corresponds to that Homeric line describing the sacrifice of a fat swine, which [Greek verse in Homer's description of the sacrifice].

units.la: Suem valde pinguem, quinquennem flatuerunt in foco sive ante focum.
units.tr: They set up a very fat swine, five years old, on the hearth or before the hearth.

units.la: Ejusdem moris Plinius quoq; meminit libro tricesimo tertio. Idem, ut hoc quoq; obiter addam, libro decimo sexto, capite quadragesimo tertio, de luxuria suorum temporum differens: Caepere tingi, in quit, animalium cornua, dentes secari, lignumq; ebore distingui.
units.tr: Pliny also mentions this custom in book 33. The same author, to add this in passing too, in book 16, chapter 43, discussing the luxury of his own times, says: "They began to dye the horns of animals, to saw their teeth, and to inlay wood with ivory."

units.la: Minores autem bestiae coronari fuerunt solitae ramis illius arboris, quae Deo illi, cui res di vina sicbat sacra erat. Erant praeterea redimitae infulis laneis, ex quibus duae dependebant facie, quas Graeci taenias, Latini vittas appellant. Huc pertinet locus Luciani, quem supra citavi; iam vero cum immolant, primum fertis coronant, &c.
units.tr: Smaller beasts were usually crowned with branches of the tree sacred to the god to whom the sacrifice was offered. They were also decked with woollen fillets, from which two hung down in front, which the Greeks call taeniae and the Latins vittae. Here belongs the passage of Lucian I cited above: "Now when they sacrifice, they first crown the victims with garlands," etc.

units.la: Illud quoq; moris erat, ut Victimarii atq; minis fri omni suo fludio atq; opera hostias cicurarent ac manfuefacerent, ne quid sinistri & inauspicati accideret, quo irritari possent fieri sacrificia. Idcirco etiam mansueta plerunq; animalia, quae se facile duci atq; regi patiebantur, ut ovest, boves, atq; prae, in sacrificiis adhibebantur.
units.tr: There was also this custom: the attendants and ministers, with all their zeal and effort, tamed and gentled the victims, so that nothing inauspicious would happen by which the sacrifices might be spoiled. For this reason, gentle animals that allowed themselves to be easily led and guided, such as sheep, oxen and calves, were commonly used in sacrifices.

units.la: Nam etiam fuit, ut victima, quae aufugerat ab altari, eo ipso in loco mactaretur, sin quo retenta fuerat. Ett vero inauspicatum censebatur, quando victima relictabatur: sicut nec vitulos ad aras humeris hominis allatos non fere litare, nec clauderetur, nec aliena hostia Deos placari, Plinius ripsit, libro octavo capite quadragesimo quinto: tamen Julius Caesar, ut testis est Tranquillus, prae tasfla religione, relictante licet victima, quae erat immolanda, feliciter cum hostibus pugnavit. Ethes de bestiis ducendis sive ad aram adducendi, probandi, ornandi deniq; & coronandi rutibus atque cerimoniis sint dicta, quae uno quasi fasciculo complectitur illa in Columna Trajani sacrificii descriptio, qd exercitus lustrandi causa factu fuit, et a materia dicta Sueotetaurilia, quod sue, ariete & tauro constabat. In illo taurum quidam popa succinctus & lauro coronatus deducit, tamoq; constrictum regit, clavam longo manubrio gestans, qua taurus erat maMandus. Villimarii autem verrem maMandum dorsualis ornatum feriteo & arietem agunt. Precedunt liticines & tibicines lituus & tibiis insonantes, Laurenti tunsi redimiti.
units.tr: It was also the rule that a victim which ran away from the altar was slaughtered in the very place where it had been held. It was regarded as inauspicious when a victim was left behind, just as Pliny wrote that calves brought to the altars on men's shoulders hardly ever gave a favourable sign, nor a lame one, nor did gods accept a foreign victim (book 8, chapter 45). Yet Julius Caesar, as Suetonius testifies, out of excessive scruple, fought successfully against the enemy even though the victim that was to be sacrificed had been left behind. And the rites concerning the leading of cattle to the altar, examining them, adorning them and finally crowning them, are the ones which the sacrifice depicted on Trajan's Column gathers together in a single bundle. It was made for purifying the army, and from its materials it was called suovetaurilia, because it consisted of a pig, a ram and a bull. In it a priest, girt and crowned with laurel, leads the bull, which is bound, and holds it with a club on a long handle with which the bull was to be struck. The attendants drive the boar to be struck, adorned with ribbons, and the ram. Trumpeters and flute-players go before, sounding the curved trumpet and the flutes, and all are wearing laurel crowns.

units.la: Porro adduša ad aram hostia, ab Homero & Apollonio commemorantur, quae in omnibus fere sacris fieri fuerunt solita: quaeq; percussionem & mactationem procedebant. Ea erant Ablutio, sive Lavatio, Preteatio, Immolatio & Libatio.
units.tr: Further, the victims brought to the altar are mentioned by Homer and Apollonius. These steps were customary in almost all sacred rites and came before the striking and slaughter. They were washing (ablutio), or lavation; the preliminary formula (praefatio); immolation; and libation.

units.la: Quantum ad primum attinet, apud Homerum quidem Aretus Nestoris filius dicitur γούσεται (alias χεσρονιται), aquam ad lavandas manus attulisse ... (illud est, Euphathio interprete, χρισιον) ... paulo post Nestor inquit,
units.tr: As far as the first is concerned, in Homer Aretus, son of Nestor, is said to have brought water for washing the hands, the word being γούσεται (in other texts χεσρονιται) ... (that is, according to Eustathius, χρισιον) ... shortly afterward Nestor says,

units.la: Hujus autem ablutionis manuum, quae facta sunt ante sacrificium, trebra fit mentio apud Homerum & alios auctores. Vt ilia, ... id est, manus lavantur, sive abluerunt ante sacrificium. Sic enim Eustathius exponit ... Eodem verbo Lysias quoq; usus est ... inquit, ... Anonymus quidam apud Suidam inquit ... ubi a metaphora ... dicitur ... tanquam purgatricem. Idem Homerus etiam ... in sacrificiis cuiusdam, quod fuerat interpositum, de scriptione, meminit hujus ritus inquiens:
units.tr: Frequent mention of this washing of the hands, which was done before sacrifice, is made in Homer and other authors, as in the passage ... that is, the hands are washed, or were washed, before sacrifice. For Eustathius explains it so ... Lysias too used the same word ... An anonymous writer quoted by Suidas says ... where by metaphor ... it is called as if it were purifying. Homer also, in the sacrifice of a certain man, which had been interposed in the narrative, mentions this rite, saying:

units.la: Ac super Regum manus aquas fundebant:
units.tr: "And they poured water over the hands of the kings."

units.la: ubi Eustathius Regum manibus, inquit, infundebant aquas, ... id est, tanquam sacrificaturis. Ibidem Agamemnonis Regis inprimis sacrificantes fit mentio. Quoniam autem apud Antiquos sacrificii ratio postulabat, ut ante sacrum sacrificaturi manus abluerent, idcirco ipsa Delubra nonnulli volunt a diluendo fuisse dicta. Pertinet huc, quod Lu. ianus alibi de sacrificiis scribens, addit: Quin & in frontispicio posita erat scriptura, ne quis intra vasa pura cum fiat, qui manibus sit impuris. Similiter Apollonius lib. 2. de Argonautarum sacrificio hujus ablutionis mentionem facit:
units.tr: Where Eustathius says that water was poured on the hands of the kings, ... that is, as for those about to sacrifice. In the same place mention is made of King Agamemnon as especially sacrificing. Since among the ancients the rite of sacrifice required that those about to sacrifice wash their hands beforehand, some therefore think the temples (delubra) were so named from washing away (diluere). To this belongs what Lucian adds, writing elsewhere about sacrifices: indeed an inscription was placed on the frontispiece, that no one with unclean hands should enter within the pure precincts. Similarly Apollonius, in book 2, on the sacrifice of the Argonauts, mentions this ablution: [Greek verse on washing the hands].
[Greek verse of Apollonius, Argonautica book 2, on washing the hands.]

units.la: Certam autem fuisse aquam, non quamvis, sed huc usum destinatam ex illis Thucydides vero... apparet lib. 4. ... id est, Aquam etiam, quam nefas esset ipsis tangere, nisi ad abluendas in sacrificiis manus, in aliis usus haurire. Item ex his verbis Dionysii Halicarnassei libro septimo ... Et pura aqua lustrantes sacra. His adde, quod sacerdotes, legum maxime observantes, lustrandi sui causa aquam inde petebant, unde Ibis, avis quaedam ... biffet, quod aquam infectam, aut insalubrem nullam avis hac tangat, ut reflatur Plutarchus de Iside, & in libro de folertia animalium. Et quia Aegyptii ... ideo lustrandi expiandi sum, aquae & ignis elementis ineste putabant, idcirco ... puritatem captatemq; non tantes ignem & aquam pingebant; ... Hierapolon. in suis Hieroglyphicis.
units.tr: That the water was kept apart, not for any use whatever, but for this purpose, is clear from those passages of Thucydides in book 4: water which it would be unlawful for them to touch, except for washing their hands in sacrifices, they drew for other uses. Likewise from these words of Dionysius of Halicarnassus in book 7: "and purifying the sacred rites with pure water." To these add that the priests, most observant of the laws, drew water from there for their own purification, whence the ibis, a certain bird ... drinks, because this bird never touches water that is tainted or unwholesome, as Plutarch reports in his book On Isis and in the book on the intelligence of animals. And because the Egyptians thought that the elements of water and fire were inherent in purification and expiation, therefore ... to signify purity and cleansing they painted not only fire and water ..., as Horapollo says in his Hieroglyphics.

units.la: Aqua porro sacrificantes aspergi, lustrari, & purgari: non tantum manibus, sed reliquis corporis partibus solebant: quae purgatio tamen etiam taeda & sulphure fiebat, at audiemus. Purgantur autem et personae sacrificantes, & aliae personae atque rei. Itaq; ... nupta in nuptiis facem praeferebat, inquit Festus, in honorem Cereris, et aqua aspergebatur, sive ut casta pura ad ...
units.tr: Moreover, those offering sacrifices were used to being sprinkled with water and purified and cleansed, not only on their hands but on the other parts of the body. This purification, however, was also done with torch and sulphur, as we shall hear. Persons offering sacrifices are purified, and other persons and things as well. Thus ... the bride carried a torch at her wedding, says Festus, in honour of Ceres, and was sprinkled with water, either so that she might be pure and chaste, or ...

units.la: {y} Ablutio manuum: quae aqua fieri solita. Hic v. ut ipsum aquae. ret: si ve ai aquam & ignem cum viro communicaret. Sic funus prosecuti redeuntes aum supergrediebantur aqua aspersi. quod purgationu genus vocabant suffitionem.
units.tr: Washing of the hands, which was customarily done with water ... if he should share water and fire with a man. Thus those who had followed a funeral, on returning, stepped over fire and were sprinkled with water. This kind of purification they called suffitio.

units.la: adde ijlos Virgilu versus. Tu genitor cape sacra manu patriosq; Penates, Me bello e tanto digressum, & cede recenti Attrectare nefas, donec me flamine purgo Abluero, &c.
units.tr: Add those verses of Virgil: "Do you, father, take the sacred things and the ancestral Penates in your hand, for I have come away from so great a war, and it is wrong for me, still stained with fresh slaughter, to touch them, until I cleanse myself in running water," and so on.

units.la: Hujus moris indicio sunt etiam bi versus Homeri Ilia. Λειγεῖ, ἐκ Ιαυ Ἐνάλ, Ἐν Εἴσι ἕλιδας ἀφῆσθ, Οἷ δ' ἀπελυμαινοντο, ἐς ἑσ ἁλς λυμαντ Ἱ ἔλλοῦ Populos autem Atrides lustrari jussit.
units.tr: Evidence of this custom are also these verses of Homer in the Iliad: "[They purified themselves and cast the defilements into the sea]." And Atreus' son ordered the people to be purified.

units.la: Illi autem lustrabantur & in mare sordes jaciebant.
units.tr: Those, however, were purified and cast their filth into the sea.

units.la: Quae verba Iohannes Spondanus, vir eximiae eruditionis, sic scribit: Novit etiam hoc illa priata blasphemias ab impuris hominibus sacrificia minime Diis accepta esse, adeo ut non solum eorum piacula Diis non exaudirentur, sed etiam magis eorum iram in se concitarent. Fiebant ergo lustrationes variis modis: sed ea erat praecipua, qua manus lavare ad aras accedentes hominibus erat in usu. Iamen, cum aras ipsorum Deorum precantes essent apprehensuri, ut diligenter ob-servarent Natalis Myrobolo libro primo, capite decimo & decimoquarto. Itaq; Asterium fulmine ... dam manibus impuris aram Iovis attingisset, vetulae Timarchidas in libro de Coro-nis hac sunt carmina ab eodem Natalis recitata: Χαρεὶ ἀπὸ πλοῦτον ἀξιος Διὸς ἡλιος βωμῷ Τὸ ἱματ πυρὸς πατρ κατ' ἡλὶ ξέ κρεμ'ς. ἐκ γ' αυ σαυ χὴ θυπὸν θεῶ σιδ εἰ.
units.tr: John Spondanus, a man of exceptional learning, writes these words: "It is also known that sacrifices offered by impure men were in no way acceptable to the gods, so that not only were their expiations not heard by the gods, but they even stirred up their anger against themselves. Lustrations were therefore performed in various ways, but the principal one, which men used in common, was washing the hands before approaching the altars. Yet when they were about to lay hold of the altars of the gods while praying, they took care to observe this diligently," as Natalis notes in book 1 of his Myrobolon, chapters 10 and 14. Thus when Asterius had touched the altar of Jupiter with impure hands, Timarchides, in his book On Garlands, has these verses, recited by the same Natalis: "Rejoice, you who are worthy of the riches of Zeus, hanging ... at the altar of the sun ..." (the verses are corrupt in the text).

units.la: Dicitur autem lustrationes pro ratione Deorum, quibus sacrificia destinabantur. Nam [?] Superis ... ificatur sexet, toti lavabantur, a fieri poterat: sin autem, falcem manu: at Inferos litaturi, tenui aqua tantum irrorabantur. Hac Spondanus: quibus adde, Aluia, cujus Homerus meminit, purgamentum. Si ve sordes, dici quasi Αὐλὴ, ὅπερ ἐν τοῖς Λυσιάν ἀπέδαλλετο, quod Eustathius, a λούω derivans: ut λουτὰ proprie sint sordes, quae ex ablutione corporum nascentur. Hinc lᾰ.ξ. Λύματα παύτα καθαίρει,
units.tr: The lustrations, however, are said to vary according to the gods to whom the sacrifices were dedicated. For to the Superi they were wholly bathed, if it could be done; otherwise they washed the hand with a sickle; but those about to sacrifice to the Inferi were merely sprinkled with a little water. So Spondanus. To these add the aula, which Homer mentions, as a purgation. Or sordes, called as if from αὐλή, which in Lysias was thrown away, which Eustathius derives from λούω, so that λουτά properly means the filth that arises from washing bodies. Hence [Λύματα πάντα καθαίρει]: "He purifies all filth."
He expiates all filth.

units.la: Quando λύματα dicuntur etiam ventris purgamenta apud Suidam, item piacula, in malam partem, quales erant homines, qui propejiste expiandi aliove morbo immolabantur, quod, καθαρμα & ἀφ' ἀδ dicta.
units.tr: The word λύματα is also used, according to Suidas, for the purgings of the belly; likewise for expiatory offerings in a bad sense, such as those men who were sacrificed to expiate a plague or other disease, and were called [καθάρματα].

units.la: Sunt autem in usu λύματα sive sordes istas projecerint, Euflathius rationem reddit: Quia, qui naturales sordibus abluendis est apius nata. Unde Euripides in Iphigenia: Θάλασσα κλύζει παντ' ἀνθρώπων κακά, Mare eluit cuncta hominum mala.
units.tr: Eustathius gives the reason why λύματα, or sordes, are cast into the sea: because the sea is naturally suited to washing away filth. Whence Euripides in the Iphigenia: "The sea washes away all the evils of men" [Θάλασσα κλύζει πάντ' ἀνθρώπων κακά], that is, the sea cleanses all the evils of men.

units.la: Quod dixisse ea de causa dicit Laertius in vita Platonis, quod m Aegypto, cum morbo com-plexi, a sacerdotibus marina curatione fuisset absolutus. Quod autem abluendi vires habeat aqua dulcis mare habeat, sine dubio illud propter illius salsuginem fit. Salis autem usum esse καθαρτικὸν docet Oribasius in Medic. Collect. libro decimoquinto & de Vi-um medicamentorum libro secundo. Itaque in sacrificiis, quae aliquis sui purgandi causa eadem aut commissum sceleris inflituebat, mos erat in salem aquam conjicere, & pater terrorare, post quam sulphuris accensi fumo eum lustrare vissent, ut indicavit Theo ... —καθαρὸς ἦ πυρὸς πατ ἐ ἀ ατα Ἰ ... ἅ Πέρτον, ἐ ἀπὸ ἀλλὰ ἀ μένειν ὅς τὸ πᾶσ Ὀλὸ ἢ ἐ ἐ ἴ ... δι ἔ ... ἀ ... ἡ.
units.tr: Laertius says this in the Life of Plato, adding that in Egypt, when he was seized by a disease, he was cured by the priests with sea treatment. That sea water has greater power to cleanse than fresh water is undoubtedly due to its saltiness. Oribasius teaches in the Medical Collections, book 15, and in On the Powers of Medicines, book 2, that salt is cathartic. Thus in sacrifices, which anyone performed for purging himself or for a crime he had committed, it was the custom to throw salt into water and sprinkle the person, and afterwards to cleanse him with the smoke of burning sulphur, as Theo... indicated.

units.la: Hoc loco purgamenta suarum lustrationum in mare projiciunt, quae tamen in alias aquas dulces projici solebant, prout vicinitas aquarum ferebat. Quibus enim mare vicinum erat, illi commode sordes illas in mare poterant ejcere; qui vero fluvium, illi quoq; commode in fluvios. Sic Damon apud Virgilium: Fer cineres, Amarylli, foras rivoq; fluenti Transq; caput jace: ne respexeris, &c.
units.tr: Here they cast the purgings of their lustrations into the sea, though in other cases they were usually cast into fresh waters, as the nearness of the waters allowed. For those whose homes were near the sea could conveniently throw those filths into the sea; those near a river could conveniently throw them into rivers. So Damon in Virgil: "Carry out the ashes, Amaryllis, and cast them into the flowing stream, and throw them over your head; do not look back," and so on.

units.la: Vbi notandus etiam mos projiciendi a tergo, ne sordes viderentur: unde putabant vitium etiam aliquod & immunditiem contrahi, quod forsan etiam Graeci observarunt.
units.tr: Here the custom of casting them behind the back should also be noted, so that they might not be seen. Hence they believed that some fault or defilement was also contracted by this, which perhaps the Greeks also observed.

units.la: Haec de usu aquae in luftratione & purgatione. Aquae quoq; usus fuit in libatione, ut videret ea liberatur; Et quidem Inferi Inferum potissimum. Unde Arferiam aquam Festus vulgo ferendo, quae Inferi libabatur, five, ut alii volunt fuit vas vini, quod sacris adhibebatur. Aqua ergo in sacris adhibita usus varius fuit & multiplex. Nam partim homines ut abluebantur & ftrabantur: partim vitium iis abluebantur & coquebantur: partim iis libabatur, unde facrificia quaedam dicta, quae nonnisi aquis peragebantur: de quibus supra.
units.tr: These are the uses of water in lustration and purgation. Water was also used in libation, and indeed especially to the Inferi. Hence Festus, in his common usage, speaks of the arferia aqua, which was poured out to the Inferi, or, as others wish, was a vessel of wine used in sacred rites. The use of water in sacred rites was therefore varied and manifold. For partly men were washed and sprinkled with it; partly vessels were washed and cleansed with it; partly libation was made with it, whence certain sacrifices were so called, which were performed with water alone, concerning which see above.

units.la: Infi umentorum quoq; quibus Eelunici usi in aqua aspergenda fuerunt, habita fuit ratio. Nam enim quae vis, sed peculiaria ac certa eo in ritu adhibebantur: ut inter alia ramus lauri aut oliuae. Romani usi sunt instrumento, quod Aspergillum vocarunt; cujus pictura vide apud Gruterum. Du Choul in libro Gallico de Religione Romana, Apud eundem eodem libro vide etiam piluram vasis antiqui marmorei, quod erat fixum in lumine templi, in quo aqua lustralis cinebatur, & minoris vasis, quod erat portatile: cujusmodi vas sua lingua Beneftior appellabat, vasis aquae lustralis nostrae aetatis simile. Meminit Festus etiam Favisse ad luftrationem aqu fieri solitam, adhibita ea: quae locus erat, in quo aqua inclusa circa templa continebatur.
units.tr: Account was also taken of the instruments the Gentiles used for sprinkling water. For there were various ones, but peculiar and fixed ones were used in that rite, such as, among others, a branch of laurel or olive. The Romans used an instrument they called the aspergillum, of which see the picture in Gruter. Du Choul, in his French book on the Roman religion, in the same book also shows a picture of an ancient marble vessel, which was fixed at the entrance of the temple and held the lustral water, and of a smaller vessel, which was portable. Such a vessel their language calls a benitier, similar to the vessels of lustral water of our own age. Festus also mentions the favissa, which was used for lustration with water, a place where water was enclosed around the temples.

units.la: Porro atque aqua, ita taeda quoq; & sulphur antiquitus in Gentilium quarundam rerum luftrationem fuerunt adhibita. De aqua diximus esse, nunc addamus nonnulla de taeda & sulphure. Tuin quidem meminit Plinius libro decimo sexto, capite decimo, inquiens: Taeda sacrorum lumini ea. Est autem proprie arbor ex earum genere, quae resinam ferunt, abundantiorque succo, quam ea quae similis generis: parcior tamen liquidiorq;, quam picea. Improprie tamen taedas appellant ea picea fatis ne partes imas, tum alia quoq; ligna, quae vel naturali pinguedine, vel oleo picæ veluti.
units.tr: As with water, so also torch and sulphur were used of old in the lustration of certain Gentile things. We have spoken of water; now let us add some things about torch and sulphur. Pliny indeed mentions the torch in book 16, chapter 10, saying: "The torch is for the light of sacred rites. It is properly a tree of those kinds that bear resin, and richer in sap than the similar kind; yet it is sparer and more liquid than the pitch-pine. Improperly, however, they call pitch-pine torches the lower parts ... and other woods which, by their natural fatness or oil of pitch, ..."

units.la: facula modo lucent. Hinc quia taedas dicitur inflammaffe Ceres, cum investigare vellet filiam Proferpinam, a Plutone abreptam, Poeta eam taedifera vocans, inter quos Ovidius Fastorum: Quos cum taedifera nunc habet ille Dea.
units.tr: ... shine only like torches. Hence, because Ceres is said to have kindled torches when she wished to search for her daughter Proserpina, carried off by Pluto, the poets call her "torch-bearing," among them Ovid in the Fasti: "Which the torch-bearing goddess now holds..."

units.la: Item epiftol. 2. Et per taedifera mystica sacra Dea.
units.tr: Likewise, in Epistle 2: "and the torch-bearing goddess with mystic rites."

units.la: Taeda etiam accipitur pro nuptiis, five pro ipso conjugio. Moftenim Antiquorum erat, ut in ptiis, inquit Varro, faces & taedae semper praerent, quod olim nonnisi per noctem nubentes ducebantur aflenfis. Virgilius quarto Aeneidos: Si non pertaesum thalami taedaeq; fuisset. Haec de taeda.
units.tr: Torch is also taken for marriage, or for marriage itself. For it was the custom of the ancients, says Varro, that at weddings torches and faces always went before, because formerly brides were led only at night, with torches lit. Virgil in the fourth book of the Aeneid: "If he had not been weary of the marriage bed and the torch." So much on the torch.

units.la: Quantum ad sulphuris, Proclus testatur sacerdotes eo usos fuisse in luftrationibus cum adsta, to, bitumine & aqua marina: quod quidem non fine caussa iis sacris & ad luftrationes fuit adhibitum, etiam ejus maxime sint vires ad versus corruptionis genus, propter illam vim, quem urendo emittit, facredinem. Unde ab Homero Od. χ. eleganter admodum αναειν αχω. Fulphur remedium appellatur: cujus sufficit Vyfius edes, procorum caedeconcaminatas, fuerat gataē. Sic autem ille: Οἱσι θίειον ἡνὶ καζῶν ἀ<Ϙ>, οἱοι δὲ μὴ πῦρ Οὓς θεῖ ὡσπερ μίσοςον, idest, Porta sulphur, anne, malorum me delam, porta mihi ignem Vt fumigem domum, &c.
units.tr: As for sulphur, Proclus testifies that priests used it in lustrations, together with alum, bitumen and sea water. This was used in those rites and for lustrations not without reason, since its power is especially against kinds of corruption, on account of the force it gives off when burned, namely its sacred quality. Whence Homer, in Od. χ., quite elegantly calls sulphur the "averter of evils": [θεῖον μὲν φέρε, γρηῦ, κακῶν ἀλεξίμορον, φέρε δέ μοι πῦρ, ὄφρα θειώσω δῶμα]: "Bring sulphur, nurse, the averter of evils; bring me fire, that I may fumigate the house," and so on. Vyfius, ...
And a little after:

units.la: Ηνίχα δ' ἀμα πῦρ ἔχῃ θύειν αὐτῷ Ὀδυσεύς
units.tr: When Odysseus is about to burn sacrifice with fire [ἠνίκα δ' ἀμφὶ πυρὶ θείου ἔχῃ θύειν αὐτῷ Ὀδυσεύς]

units.la: Ευ Διὸς ἱωσιν μάγαςῃ, ἔ δῶρα, ἢ αὐλὼ
units.tr: Well through the fragrant hall, the gifts, or the hall [εὖ διὰ μέγαρα θυήεντα, ἢ δῶρα, ἢ αὐλήν]

units.la: Porta vit igitur ignem & sulphur: at Vlyffes
units.tr: Porta therefore brought fire and sulphur, and Ulysses

units.la: Bene adole vit domum amplam & domum & aulam.
units.tr: Duly fumigated the house, the ample house and the hall.

units.la: Plinius item de sulphuris usu & viribus multa disserit: inter alia autem libro trigesimo quinto, capite decimoquinto: Habet, inquit, & in religionibus locum ad expiandas suffitu domos. Tingi etiam solitæ ex eo & illini statuæ.
units.tr: Pliny likewise discusses at length the use and powers of sulphur. Among other things, in book thirty-five, chapter fifteen, he says: "It has also a place in religious rites, for purifying houses by fumigation. Statues too were customarily stained and smeared with it."

units.la: Hæc de lustratione cum rerum, tum personarum in specie.
units.tr: So much for purification, both of things and of persons in particular.

units.la: In genere vero personarum, quæ ad sacra facienda erant accessuræ, præparatio apud Gentiles omnino erat duplex, nimirum alia animi, alia corporis: quæ quidem Latine purgatio, purificatio, sanctificatio, lustratio, expiatio, consecratio inauguratio, initiatio, a Græcis καθαρμὸς, ὁσιασμὸς, ἀγνισμὸς, τελείωσις, ἐξοδοσιασμὸς, sive καθαρμὸς ἱερουργιασμὸς, & alius id generis nominibus sunt appellata.
units.tr: In general, among the Gentiles there was a twofold preparation of the persons who were about to take part in sacred rites: one of the mind, the other of the body. In Latin these are called purgatio, purificatio, sanctificatio, lustratio, expiatio, consecratio, inauguratio, initiatio; among the Greeks they are called καθαρμός, ὁσιασμός, ἁγνισμός, τελείωσις, ἐξοδοσιασμός, or καθαρμὸς ἱερουργιασμός, and by other names of this kind.

units.la: Accorporis quidem præparatio, ut de illa prius dicamus, quam etiam illi plurisplerunque, faciebant, quàm præparationem animi, in hıs ferè consistebat, quæ sequuntur: PRIMO in varia & multiplici ablutione corporis cum totius, cum singularum ejus partium: manuum inprimis atq; pedum, de qua modo dictum est. Huic adde vestimentorum quoq; ablutionem.
units.tr: Let us speak first of the preparation of the body, which most of them also performed before the preparation of the mind. It consisted mainly of the following. FIRST, in various and repeated washing of the body, both as a whole and of its individual parts, especially the hands and feet, of which we have just spoken. To this add the washing of the garments as well.

units.la: SECVNDO posita erat præparatio illa in certo corporis cum totius, tum singulorum ejus membrorum, capitis præcipue atq; pedum vestitu, habitu, cultu atq; ornatu: vel etiam nonnunquam in corporis cum totius, cum singularum ejus partium in sacris quibusdam denudatione: de quibus partim supra egimus in loco de perfunctis sacrificantibus, partim nunc agendum videtur, quoad delicet cultum & ornatum capitis, ex coronis, sive corollis & sertis fieri solitum.
units.tr: SECOND, this preparation consisted in a fixed form of dress, bearing, care and adornment of the body, both as a whole and of each of its members, especially the head and feet; or sometimes also in the baring of the body, both as a whole and of its separate parts, in certain sacred rites. Some of these we have treated above, in the place on those who perform sacrifices, and some must now be discussed, namely the care and adornment of the head, which was customarily done with crowns, or garlands and wreaths.

units.la: In præparatione igitur corporis ad sacrificia & sacra Gentilium usus coronarum atq; sertorum fuit frequentissimus: & ut ferè quadruplex. Nam primum quidè ac principaliter in ornari conviviis, ubi ...
units.tr: In preparing the body for sacrifices and for the sacred rites of the Gentiles, the use of crowns and garlands was very frequent, and in roughly four ways. For first and chiefly, they were used to adorn banquets, where ...

units.la: Coronas floreas vocat coronas ex floribus, quas Tibullus dixit serta florea, Elegia prima lib.1. Nam veneror seu stipes habet desertus in agris, Seu vetus in trivio florea serta lapis.
units.tr: He calls them "floral crowns," crowns made of flowers, which Tibullus called "flowery wreaths," in the first elegy of book one: "For I worship it, whether a stump lies neglected in the fields, or an old stone at the crossroads wreathed with flowers."
In the same poet's second elegy:

units.la: Te meminisse decet, quæ plurima voce peregi Supplice, cum pestis florea serta darem.
units.tr: "You should remember how many prayers I offered in a suppliant voice, when I hung up flowery wreaths against the plague."

units.la: Demore sacerdotes & eos, qui sacris intererant: item victimas, simulachra & aras variis coronarum generibus coronandi & ornandi vide Tranquillum etiam, & Lucianum, & ex recentioribus Gyraldum. Tranquillus in vita Octavii Augusti, de eo sic scribit: Compitales Lares (quibus compita dicata sunt, & quorum in honorem fiebant ludi Compitalitii) ornare bis in anno instituit vernis floribus & festivis: ubi per vernos flores intelligit heliochrysson, hyacinthum, rosam & violam album, quæ prima florum est. Ver nuntiantiu: quam Columella Græca dictione λειρίοιον vocat, quasi dicas album violam: Per festivos verò flores, eos qui vernum succedunt, cujusmodi sunt Lychnis, Iouis flos, amaracus, iris & quoddam genus lilii. Nam lilium quedam sunt verna, quædam estiva, quædam autumnalia.
units.tr: As for the priests, and those who took part in the sacred rites, and likewise for how victims, images and altars were to be crowned and adorned with various kinds of garlands, see also Suetonius, Lucian, and among more recent writers Giraldus. Suetonius, in the life of Augustus, writes of him thus: he ordered the Compitalian Lares (to whom the crossroads were dedicated, and in whose honour the Compitalitian games were held) to be adorned twice a year with spring and festive flowers. By spring flowers he means heliochrysum, hyacinth, rose and white violet, which is the first of the flowers that announce spring; Columella calls it in Greek leirion, as if you were to say the white violet. By festive flowers he means those which follow spring, such as lychnis, Jupiter's flower, marjoram, iris and a certain kind of lily; for there are spring lilies, summer lilies and autumn lilies.

units.la: o Lucianus deinde ejusdem meminit his verbis: jam vero cum immolaut, prius fertā coronā atq; petudē. Sic Gyraldus fyntagmate decumo septimo copiosē de hoc more scribit, cujus verba addere noui libet, ne allum agere videamur. Pleraque autem hujusmodi corona atq; ferta (paucis exceptis, quae ex lapidibus pretiosis, gemmis, unionibus et metallis, ut auro et similibus hebanc; quorum quidem alicubi memini Plato hos verbis: In sacrificiis, inquit, et celebritatibus pulchra vestis, anreus, coronis ornatus sacerdos rem divinam facit ex plantis floribus, herbis, graminibus, arborumq; ramis atq; frondibus fuerunt confectae (uno nomine Pancarpia corona dicta, de ift, ex vario genere florum:) ex plantis quidem et arboribus maxime ex lauro, atq; olea, vel iis arborum bus, quae cuiq; Deo, cui sacra fiebant, erat dicata; de qno supra pluribus. Quibus addi hoc loco potest, sunt Verbenae, cercis genus herbae, in omnibus fere sacris fauste habitae, et fumece de loco sacro Capitolii, qua coronabantur faciales, et pater patratus sedera salluri, vel bella indicturi. Sanecessario tamen etiā verbenas vocam omnes frodes sacratas ut est, laurus, oliva vel myrtus. Tertio. Ex aris binc verbenas fume. Nam myrtum fuisse Menander testatur, de quo id translulit Tertutiens. Donatus vero verbenas aie esse omnes herbas et frondes sectas, ad aras coronandas, ex aliquo loco puro decerptas, dictasq; autumas esse quasi herbenas. Plinius vero libas nomine sagminum et verbenarum significatas prodidit gramen ex arce cū sua terra evulsum. Verbena semper et legati, tum ad hostes clarigatum mittebantur, ut id est, res raptas clare repetentur: unde uiiq; verbenarius vocabatur. Idem 25. Verbenacam peculiariter vocat herbam, quam Graeci ποδοτρίχλον, quasi sacram herbam dicunt. Aliqui αἰσχρὸν α, quasi columbaria. Hec est, inquit, quam legatos ferre ad hostes indicavimus. Magi circa hanc insanuisse, adjuntq; si aqua sparguntur triclinium, quā madueri, lectiores convivia fieri. Livius libro decimo secundi belli Punici, ide quod Plinius, figuas, videlicet verbenas et sagmina idem significare. Esse autem genus herbae arce sumtum. Pl obiter declarandum privas verbenas, et privos filices a Lūvio dici fingunt quia veteres priva dixerunt, quae nos singula dicimus; quo verbo Lucilius usus est: Abdomina thynia priva dabo, cephaleamq; Carnē. Festus quoq; sagminū et Verbenarū munit. Sagmina dicebat, inquit, herbas verbenas quia ex loco sancto arcebantur legatis proficiscentibus ad fadus faciendum, bellumq; indicendum: vel a sanciendo, id est, confirmando. Nevius: Sacrabos atq; verbenas sagmina fumpsertit, Idem: Capita Deorū appellabantur safituli fata de verbenis; qui etiam Struppi dicti, eodem tepste. Struppi vero vocabantur in pulvinaribus fasciculi de verbenis fatti, qui pro Deorum capitibus ponebantur. Ec hac quidem de coronis, in sacrificiis ulto vestitu atq; ornatu potissimum adbiberi foliis, quae vel ex me: allis, vel floribus, vel plantis plebantur: eamet is, ut hoc quoq; addam, plantae quae in nonnullis sacris adhibitae, in aliis prohibitae fuerint: id quod de Hedera inprimis conflat, et Olympiis sacris arceri solitā, et neq, Athenis in Iunonis, neq; Thebis in Veneris sairus ullum locum fuisse, quamvetiam Flamen Dialis ueone tangere, neque nominare audebat: et tamen ipsam Baccbanalibus fuisse adhibitam, teste Plutarcho in quaestionibus Romanis quaestione 11. Hos commode subjungi poceft praeparatio, quae certa vestle, quā n puram religio fam vel sacram vocabant, fieri et inflitui solebat: cujus usus non minus frequens olim fuit, quam reliquorum rerum ac cerimoniarum. Hinc legimus eosdem Indorum Magos, qui ad Solis sacerdotii promos erant, lineis velatos sub divo vitam egisse. Et Plato sacerdotem, qui victimam faciebat, purā in vestle, et candida, plerunq, intexcili tela, nec majoris operis, quam menstruae indutum tesatur. Vnde Tibullus libro secundo: —pura cum veste venite. Et Ovidius tertio Amorum: More Patrum sancta velate vestibus albis Tradita suppolito vertice sacra ferunt. Pura autem et religiosa vel sacra vestis dicebatur, ut Festus ait et Servius, quarem divinam salluri festo vestlo habebatur. Ea quidem erat soluca omni vinculo, nullis maculis, nec aliquo fquallore obsita, nec funesta, aut fulgurita. Caper et Hyginus in illos Virgiliit —fontemque ignemque ferebant Velati lino, et verbena tempora vinxti. Quo loco non,lino,sed,limo,legendum ajunt. Limū enim vestem fuisse dicunt,in extremo sui purpurum limam,id est, flexuosam habens: unde nomen accepit. Aliqui tamen malunt,Limbum,legere potiust,quam Limum vel Linum. Sanè Ægyptii lanceas vestes in Deorum templa non inferebant. Hinc & Linigeri diāi. Et Flaminica,junonis antistita,mense Maio,jubeātur esse tonstrica,laVacroque & ornatu abstinere: testis Plutarchus quaestione octogesima sexta, quaest. Romanarum. Hæc de vestitu.
units.tr: Lucian then mentions the same custom in these words: "Now indeed, when they sacrifice, first with a garland and a fillet..." Giraldus, in his Syntagma seventeen, writes fully about this custom, and I am happy to add his words, lest we seem to be doing the work twice. Most such crowns and garlands were made of plants, flowers, herbs, grasses, and branches and leaves of trees (apart from a few made of precious stones, gems, pearls and metals, such as gold and similar materials; Plato, I recall somewhere, speaks of these in these words: "In sacrifices and festivals, a priest in a fine robe, golden, adorned with garlands, performs the rite"). Such garlands, called by one name a pancarpian crown from the varied kind of flowers, were made especially of plants and trees, above all of laurel and olive, or of those trees which were dedicated to whichever god the sacrifice was made; on this we have said more above. To these may be added here the verbenae, a kind of herb, held almost everywhere to be auspicious in sacred rites; and the turf from the sacred place of the Capitol, with which the fetials were crowned, and the father patratus when about to make a treaty or declare war. Yet of necessity verbenae are also called all sacred leaves, such as laurel, olive or myrtle. Third: from the altars then, verbenae... Menander testifies that myrtle was used, which Tertullian has also translated. Donatus says that verbenae are all herbs and leaves cut for crowning altars, gathered from some pure place, and that they were so named as if they were herbenae. Pliny, under the names sagmina and verbenae, reports grass pulled up from the citadel together with its earth. The verbena was always carried by heralds when they went to the enemy to demand back the seized goods, which is "clarigatio"; hence the herald was called verbenarius. In book twenty-five Pliny specially calls verbena the herb which the Greeks call a sacred herb. Some call it columbaria, the dovecote plant. "This is," he says, "the herb which we showed heralds carry to enemies. The Magi went mad about it, and added that if a dining room is sprinkled with water in which it has been soaked, the banquets become more select." Livy, in book ten of the Second Punic War, says the same as Pliny: that sagmina and verbenae mean the same thing, and that they are a kind of herb taken from the citadel. It should also be explained in passing that some pretend that privae verbenae and privi filices are so called by Livy because the ancients used priva for what we call single; Lucilius used the word: "I will give privae of thyme and the head of a cow." Festus too explains sagmina and verbenae: "They called herbs verbenae sagmina, he says, because they were carried from a sacred place by heralds setting out to make a treaty or declare war; or from sanciendo, that is, confirming." Naevius: "They took up the sagmina and the sacred verbenae." Festus again: "The heads of the gods were called sasituli made of verbenae, which were also called struppi on the same occasion. Struppi were bundles made of verbenae that were placed on the couches of the gods in place of their heads." These remarks on garlands must suffice. In sacrifices, beyond clothing and adornment, leaves were chiefly used, which were plaited either from branches, flowers, or plants. And that plants which were admitted in some rites were forbidden in others, I shall add this too: this is established above all for ivy, which was customarily kept away from the Olympian rites; nor was there any place for it in Athens in the temple of Juno, nor in Thebes in that of Venus; yet the Flamen Dialis did not dare even to touch or name it. And yet it was used in the Bacchanalia, as Plutarch attests in his Roman Questions, question eleven. It is fitting to add here the preparation which was customarily made by a certain garment, which they called pure, religious or sacred; its use was formerly no less frequent than that of the other rites and ceremonies. Hence we read that the same Magi of the Indians, who were the priests of the Sun, lived under the open sky wrapped in linen. And Plato says that the priest who performed the sacrifice wore a pure and white garment, usually of linen cloth, and clothed in nothing of greater work than a menstrual garment. Hence Tibullus in book two: "Come in a pure garment." And Ovid in the third book of the Amores: "In the manner of the fathers, veiled in white garments, they bear the sacred things handed over with a crown placed on the head." A pure and religious or sacred garment was so called, as Festus and Servius say, because it was held to be the proper dress for the divine rites. It was free from every knot, without any stains, and not covered with any filth, nor funereal, nor mourning. Caper and Hyginus, on the lines of Virgil, "They carried fire and water, veiled in linen, and their temples bound with verbena," say that here one should read not linum but limum. For they say limus was a garment having at its edge a purple border, that is, a winding one, and from this it took its name. Some, however, prefer to read limbus rather than limus or linum. Indeed the Egyptians did not bring woollen garments into the temples of the gods; hence also the Linigeri. And the Flaminica, the priestess of Juno, was ordered in the month of May to be shorn, and to abstain from wine and ornament; Plutarch attests this in Roman Question eighty-six. So much for clothing.

units.la: TERTIO posita erat ista præparatio corporis in jejunio & abstinentia a carnibus,a vino & certis aliis cibis ac potionibus; idq; vel omnino ac semper, vel ad certum aliquod tempus unde Dea nanæ cerimoniæ alie fuerunt dicte, alie Tricenarie, quibus sacra adituris decem continuis,vel trignta certus quibusdam rebus carendum erat: quo nomine cerimonias ipsas nonnulli volunt distinui,quasi carimonias,a carendo,quod religionis caussa certus rebus fit carendū. Hinc & Festus: Purimenstrio esse dicuntur,qui sacrorū caussa toto mense in cerimoniis sunt,id est, puri sint certis rebus carendis. Sic igitur legimus Numam Pompilium,cum pro frugibus facerēt,su carnium abstinuisse, & julianum Cæsarem,& si Procopio credimus, Iustinianum oleribus leguminibusq; contentum sæpe cænitasse,ob religionem: eos item, qui initiandi essent Isidis, sacris dies decem per cere carnibus & vino. Quin & Ægyptios festis quibusdam diebus jejunia serūasse: id quod & Hebræos adhuc observare animadvertimus. Sic Gymnosophistas legimus adeo abstinentiæ stu-diosos fuisse,ut pomis solum,oryza & farina alerētur. In Creta quoq;,ut Eurypides testatur,quos vocabāt Iovis Prophetas,non modo carnibus,sed ne cœtis quidem,vesci solitos fuisse: & Indorū magos prodium esse,qui ad Solis sacerdotum promoti fuerant carnibus abstinuisse.
units.tr: Third, this bodily preparation consisted in fasting and abstinence from meat, wine and certain other foods and drinks, either entirely and always or for some fixed period. For this reason the goddess's rites were called some "nonary" and others "tricenary," since those about to take part in the sacred rites had to go without certain things for ten days in a row or for thirty. Some hold that the ceremonies themselves take their name from this, as if they were "carimoniae" from carere (to lack), because for the sake of religion one goes without certain things. Hence also Festus: those are called "purimenstrual" who spend the whole month in the ceremonies for the sake of the sacred rites, that is, who are pure by abstaining from certain things. Thus we read that Numa Pompilius, when he made offerings for the crops, abstained from meat, and that Julius Caesar did so too, and, if we believe Procopius, that Justinian often dined on vegetables and pulses alone, out of religious scruple. Likewise those who were to be initiated into the rites of Isis kept ten days of sacred observance, abstaining from meat and wine. Moreover, the Egyptians kept fasts on certain festival days, a custom we notice the Hebrews still observe. Thus we read that the Gymnosophists were so devoted to abstinence that they lived only on fruit, rice and flour. In Crete too, as Euripides attests, those whom they called Prophets of Jove were accustomed to abstain not only from meat but even from cheese; and it is reported that the magi of the Indians, who had been promoted to the priesthood of the Sun, abstained from meat.

units.la: QVARTO consistebat præparatio illa corporis in abstinentia quoq;, a consuetudine conjugali,omniq; coitu; idq; vel semper & perpetuo: vel ad tempus aliquod. Hinc Æneas ex ritu Deos precaturus,cum ab aliis rebus,tum a Venere abstinuisse perhibetur, ut ad sacra celebranda latus ac mundus accederet. Idem legimus Numam Pompilium fecisse,p eterquā quod suum carnium abstinuit,ut supra dictum. Quin & Ægyptii aquæ quidem aspersione labeni colli & castimoniam præslari putabant,præterq; Mysos & Lieos,aliosq;,qui ob religionem coitu abstinebāt,cœlibem vitam agebant illi,qui Abii et Nymphi diēti sunt. Costat præterea sacerdotes Martis Deūm Samia testa sibi virilia amputasse,atq; illos, qui maxima sacra obscurat,ut in casta religione manerent, & procul a mulierum contagio vitam agerent,herbis quibusdam evirati, & virilitatem amittere: utque nulla nisi sacrorum maneret cura,nudiq; (unde Nudipedalia) & vacui religioni ac pietati intendērent,cunctarum se rerum dominiis abdicare; quod jure Pontificio veterica veri quidam putant illis verbis: AD DIVOS ADEUNTO CASTE: PIETATEM ADHIBENTO: OPES AMOVENTO, qui secus saxit,Dens ipse Vindex erit. Quam castimoniam apud exteros observatam hic notamus. Quippe in Tesmophoriis (erant sacra Cereris & Anuirzia,sive Cerealia dicta) matronæ Atheniēnses, ut Venerem cohiberent,folios viticis cubilia substerneb ant. Nonnulligaro ex pisciculus,qui squamam non habent (quod incendia libidinum reprimere feruntur, & irritos facere conatus venereos) in sacris usi suere: quid Ægesilaus putabat Deos non tam religiosos operibus, quam sacrificiis castis delectari. Legimus preteria Hierophantas Atheniensium, postquam in sacerdotium cooptati erant,ut castē sanctē, sacrū sacerent, cicutē sorbitione se castrauisse: Ægyptios vero sacerdotes,negotiis omissis, mulieribus aliquando indulsisse. Faciunt huc illa Poetæ: Vos quoq, abesse procul jubeo, discedite ab aris Cui tulit hesterna gaudia nocte Venus. Casta placent Superis, pura cum mente venite, Et manibus puris sumite fontis aquam.
units.tr: Fourth, this bodily preparation also consisted in abstinence from marital intercourse and from every sexual union, either always and perpetually or for some period. Hence Aeneas, when he was about to pray to the gods according to the rite, is said to have abstained from other things and from Venus in particular, so that he might approach and celebrate the sacred rites with a clean and pure body. We read that Numa Pompilius did the same, besides abstaining from meat, as mentioned above. Indeed the Egyptians thought that purity was secured by sprinkling with water. Apart from the Mysians and Lydians, and others who abstained from intercourse for religion's sake, those called Abians and Nymphians lived a celibate life.
