It is further recorded that the priests of Mars in Samos cut off their own genitals with a potsherd; and that those who performed the greatest rites, in order to remain in chaste religion and to live far from contact with women, were rendered eunuchs by certain herbs and lost their virility. So that nothing but care of the sacred things might remain, and so that, naked (whence the Nudipedalia) and free of all else, they might devote themselves to religion and piety, they renounced ownership of all things. Some think this is rightly stated in the Pontifical law by those words: "Let them approach the gods chastely, let them bring piety, let them put wealth aside; whoever acts otherwise, God himself will be the avenger." Here we note this chastity observed among foreigners. Indeed at the Thesmophoria (rites of Ceres, also called the Anthesteria or Cerealia) the matrons of Athens, to restrain Venus, spread beds of willow leaves. Some used in their rites small fish that lack scales (which are said to quench the fires of lust and make venereal attempts fruitless). Agesilaus thought the gods delighted less in works than in chaste sacrifices. We read further that the Hierophants of the Athenians, once they had been co-opted into the priesthood, so that they might sacrifice chastely and holily, castrated themselves by drinking hemlock; whereas the Egyptian priests, setting business aside, sometimes gave themselves up to women. The poets also bear on this: "You too I bid to stay far off, depart from the altars, you to whom Venus gave last night's pleasures. Chaste souls please the gods; come with a pure mind, and take water from the spring with clean hands."
Juvenal, Satire 6:

units.la: Ille petit veniam quoties non abstinet uxor Concubitu,sacris observandiq; diebus.
units.tr: He seeks pardon whenever his wife does not abstain from intercourse on the days set apart for the sacred rites.

units.la: QVINTO præparatio illa posita erat in abstinentia a contactu, atq; etiam aspectu sestarum rerum,Hinc si opus facientē inter sacra videre sacerdoté cōsisset, ts temerari & pollui putabatur.Iedo Praefia si ve præclamitatores præmitteb ātur, qui denunciarent opisciōibus,ut manus ab-stiuerēt vis eorum,s veri si. flinerent ab opere, nesi vidisset sacerdos facientem opus sacra polluerentur. Idem antem iudicium de reliquis.
units.tr: Fifth, this preparation was laid down as abstinence from contact, and even from the sight, of unclean things. Hence if a priest saw someone working while the sacred rites were being performed, the rites were thought to be profaned and polluted. Heralds, or public criers, were sent ahead to warn the workmen to keep their hands off and to stop working, lest the sacred rites be defiled if the priest saw someone at work. The same judgment applied to the rest.

units.la: SEXTO, quirem divinam rite factur-us esset, etiá confessione culpae & reatus sui se praeparabat, hoc est, se uprimis reum dicere solebat, & noxae poenituisse, & admissa fateri, multisque submittebat, ad omnem se modestiam fingeus. Hujus quidem, & omnium singulorum exempla atque testimonia passim occurrunt apud profanos authores, de quibus vide Alexandrum ab Alexandro, Gyraldum syntagmate decimo septimo Historiae Deorum, & Guilielmum de Choul, libro de antiqua religione.
units.tr: Sixth, one who was about to perform the divine rite properly also prepared himself by confessing his guilt and his liability. That is, he was accustomed first to call himself a sinner, to declare that he repented of the offence, to confess what he had committed, and to humble himself before many, feigning all modesty. Examples and testimonies of this, and of each of these practices, occur everywhere in profane authors. On these see Alexander ab Alexandro, Giraldus in the seventeenth Syntagma of his History of the Gods, and Guillaume du Choul in his book on ancient religion.

units.la: PRAEPARATIO deinde ANIMI posita erat cum in abstinentia a profanis & cogitationibus et sermonibus: tum e contra in silentio et attenta sacrorum, quae peragenda erant, meditatione: ad quam haec sacerdotis vel praeconis publici, ad sacra praecedentis vox erat usitata: HOC AGE; qua voce populum excitabat, virgaque turba summovebat, quae Commentaculum dicebatur, de qua supra: & silentium indicebat, ne mala aliqua vox obstreperet, ut ne quid triste audiretur: hoc modo sacra favere & accentos eos esse jubens.
units.tr: Next, the preparation of the mind consisted partly in abstaining from profane thoughts and talk, and partly, on the contrary, in silence and attentive meditation on the sacred rites that were to be performed. To this the usual call of the priest, or of the public herald who went before the sacred rites, was "Attend to this" (HOC AGE). With this cry he roused the people and drove off the crowd with a rod, which was called the commentaculum, mentioned above. He also enjoined silence, so that no ill-omened voice might interrupt and nothing inauspicious be heard. In this way he ordered them to keep the sacred rites in silence (favere) and to attend to them.

units.la: Ad mentis castitatem et puritatem quod attinet, idem illud Ciceronis de Legibus testimonium huc referri debet, quod supra citavi: Ad Divos caste adeunto, piecatem adhibento. Et alibi: Casté jubet lex adire ad Deos, ut mo videlicet, in quo sunt omnia: nec tollit castimoniam corporis; sed hoc oportet intelligi, cum multum animus corpori praeest, observeturque ut capta corpora adhibeantur, multo esse in animis id servandum magis. Nam incestum vel asperssione aquae, vel dierum numero tollitur: animi labes nec diuturnitate vanescere, nec manibus ullis eluipotest. Quod autem pietatem adhiberi, opes amoveri jubet: significat probitatem gratiam esse Deo, sumptum esse removendum. Et paullo post: Meliús Graeci, atque nostri, qui ut augerent piecatem in Deos, easdem illos urbes, quas nos incolere volnerunt. Affert enim hac opinio religionem utilem civitatibus: siquidem & illud bene dictum est a Pythagora, doctissimo viro, tum maxime & pietatem & religionem versari in animo, cum rebus divinis operam daremus: & quos Thales, quos sapientissimos in septem fuisse, homines existimare oportere, Omnis quae cernerent Deorum esse plena. Fore enim omnes castiores. (Hic similiter castificatam animi requiri docet, seu praecipuam in sacris virtutem) veluti, in fanis essent, maxime religiosos. Hac cuiusquibus adde illa Socrate: In victimis, licet opimae sint, auroque praefulgeant, non est Deorum honos, sed in pia ac recta voluntate venerantium. Itaq; boni etiam farre ac fictilis religiosi fuisse, inalsque rursus non effugiunt impietatem, quam vis aras sanguine multo cruenta verint. Idem: Colitur Deus, inquit, non tam, rum opimis corporum consecratis, non auro, non argento, non in thesauros lupe infusa: sed pia & recta voluntate.
units.tr: As for chastity and purity of mind, that same testimony of Cicero's On the Laws, which I cited above, should be applied here: "Let them approach the gods chastely, let them bring piety." And elsewhere: "The law commands us to approach the gods chastely, meaning chastely in mind, in which all things lie. It does not remove chastity of body; but this must be understood: since the mind ought to rule the body greatly, and care is taken that pure bodies be brought, this must be kept all the more in souls. For impurity is removed either by sprinkling with water or by the passing of days, but the stain of the soul can fade neither with time nor be washed away by any hands." That he orders piety to be brought and wealth to be removed signifies that uprightness is pleasing to God and that expense must be put aside. And a little after: "The Greeks and our own people did better, who wished the same cities that we live in to increase piety towards the gods. For this opinion makes religion useful to states. Indeed what Pythagoras, a most learned man, rightly said is also true, that piety and religion dwell most of all in the mind when we are engaged in divine matters; and those whom Thales and the others, the wisest of the seven, were, men must think, who held that all things they saw were full of gods. For all would be more chaste (here too he teaches that a chastened mind is required, or chiefly virtue in sacred things), as if they were in temples, most religious." To this add that saying of Socrates: "In victims, however fat they are and gleaming with gold, there is no honour of the gods; it lies in the pious and upright will of those who worship." Thus good men were religious even with spelt and earthen vessels, while the wicked do not escape impiety, though they stain the altars with much blood. Again: "God is worshipped, he says, not so much with fat consecrated bodies, not with gold, not with silver poured into treasuries, but with a pious and upright will."

units.la: Silentium deinde et taciturnitas, etsi in communi & profano vice usu atq; confuerudine decerpere solebant, &c. Idem Pythagoreorum: plerunq; est & utilis: tamen eam Gentiles in sacris maxime requirebant, secundum illud Virgilii: — Fida silentia sacris.
units.tr: Silence and taciturnity, although people were accustomed to practise them in ordinary and profane life and custom, are generally useful; nevertheless the Gentiles especially required them in sacred rites, following that line of Virgil: "faithful silences for the sacred rites."

units.la: In sacrificiis, inquit Festus, praecones clamantes populum sacrificiis favere, id est, bona fari iubebant. Nam Favere est bona fari, at veteres Poëtae pro Silere ubi favere tua bouam ominationem significat. Idem: Pa-facto linguam, in sacrificiis dicebatur, id est, coercetur, continetur, tacere. Cicero lib. 1 de Divinatione: Neq, solum, inquit, Deorum voces Pythagorei observaverunt, sed etiam hominum, quae vocant omina, quae Majores nostri, quia vilerent cessabant, idcirco omnibus rebus agendis, quod bonum, fautum, felix fortunatumq; esset precabantur, rebusq; divinis, quae publice fierent, ut favere ut linguis imperabantur, inq; ferris imperandis, utilitas et jurgia se abstinerent. Ergo favere sacris, favere linguis, pascere linguam propriam & tacere in sacris erunt dicendi formulae, quibus silentiū imperabatur, ut ad sacrorum observationem tanto essent attentiores, nec strepitu et murmure sacer cultus intercurbaretur. Ad id significandum Harpocratem, tanquam silentii Deum (quem Graeci Σιγαλίωνα vocarunt.) Aegyptii sacrum ... adhibuerunt, de quo vide Polisianum Centuria prima, capite octogesimo tertio. Sic Plinium libro tertio scribit, Angeronam Deani silentii ore obligato atq, signato in ara Volupiae collocatam, ut intelligeremus religionis arcana (quae idcirco ab ore occludendo, idest, ψ̓ το̃ ἀ̓πόῤῤτ̓ο̃ mystica: item occluse sacra, & opertanta sacra, seu ἀπόρρητα sunt dicta) non evulganda: id quod
units.tr: In sacrifices, says Festus, the heralds, calling out, ordered the people to favour the sacrifices, that is, to speak words of good omen. For favere means to speak well, and the old poets used favere for silere (to be silent), where "favere" with the tongue signifies a good omen. Likewise, "to pacify the tongue" in sacrifices was said, that is, to be restrained, held in check, to keep quiet. Cicero, in the first book of On Divination: "The Pythagoreans observed not only the voices of the gods but also those of men, which they call omens. Our ancestors, because they wished to be silent, therefore in every undertaking prayed for what was good, favourable, happy and fortunate; and in the divine rites performed publicly they were ordered to favour with their tongues, and when holidays were proclaimed they were ordered to abstain from quarrels and lawsuits." Therefore "to favour the sacred rites," "to favour with the tongue," "to feed one's own tongue," and "to be silent in sacred rites" will be the forms of speech by which silence was commanded, so that the worshippers might be the more attentive to the observance of the sacred rites, and the holy worship not be interrupted by noise and murmuring. To signify this, the Egyptians employed Harpocrates as the god of silence (whom the Greeks called Sigalion [Σιγαλίων]), of whom see Politian, Centuria I, chapter 83. Pliny, in book three, writes that Angerona, goddess of silence, with her mouth bound and sealed, was placed on the altar of Volupia, so that we might understand that the secrets of religion (which for that reason, from closing the mouth [μύειν], are called mystica, and likewise closed and hidden rites, or apporrheta) should not be divulged; which

units.la: Numa Pompilius instituit, quando aliam quandam silentii Deam, Tacitam, inde dictam, colendam proposuit, cum ros di vinas cacere nos oporteat. Hinc Apuleius & Martianus libro primo rec: mitum puerum fingunt, ad os compresso digito, salutari, quasi silentii homines admonentem. Hinc etiam Appium Caecum ob Herculaneum sacrum ser vitis in vulgatum captum tradiit oculis. Et Numentius noxa contraxit, quod Eleusinia sacra retexisset, cui Deae in somnis se prostitutas quaedam sunt. Hut pertinent etiam illa Matrobii: Intercisorum dierum quibusdam horas fas erat: quibusdam fas non erat fari. Nam quando hostia caedebatur, fari nefas erat: inter caesa & porrecta fari licebat.
units.tr: Numa Pompilius established, when he proposed that another goddess of silence, Tacita, named after that quality, should be worshipped, since we ought to keep silent about divine matters. Hence Apuleius and Martianus, in the first book, depict a boy with a finger pressed to his mouth, as if warning people to silence. Hence too it is related that Appius Caecus was deprived of his sight because he divulged the Herculean sacred rite to the slaves. Numentius also incurred harm because he revealed the Eleusinian rites, and certain women are said to have been exposed to that goddess in dreams. To this belong also those words of Macrobius: on certain days, when sacrifices were interrupted, it was lawful for some people to speak for certain hours, and for others it was not lawful to speak. For while the victim was being slain, speaking was forbidden; between the slaughter and the setting out of the offering, speaking was permitted.

units.la: Ad silentium hoc in sacris alludit quoq; Ovidius libro tertio Amorum: Ore tacent populi tunc, cum venit aurea pompa Ipsa saterdotes subsequiturq; suas.
units.tr: Ovid also alludes to this silence in the sacred rites in the third book of the Amores: "Then the people fall silent, when the golden procession comes, and the priests themselves follow their own images."

units.la: Et Horatius libro tertio Carminum: —Favete linguis Carmina non prius audita Musarum, sacerdos, Virginibus puerisq; tanto.
units.tr: And Horace in the third book of the Odes: "Favour with your tongues: I, a priest of the Muses, sing songs not heard before for maidens and boys."

units.la: Porròditendi bi fe ogi got occasio de more & consuetudine Gentilium artendi quosdam ac summonendi a suis sacris, tanquam iis indignos, cuius crebra admodum apud auctores profanos fit mentio, Hi autem in genere a Graecis dicti fuerunt βεβηλοι ἀευν, ἀτελέστοι, μυσταῖ ... ἄθεοι, a Latinis profani, non centes, &c. Ob quem morem excommunicandi, festa, quibus excommunicatio fiebat, ὄργια τὰ μυστήρια putant dicta παρὰ τὸ ἐργον τοῖς ἀμυήτοις, ab arcendo profanos abiis. Lictor, inquit Festus, in quibusdam sacris clamitabat, HOSTIS, VINCTVS, MVLIER, VIRGO EXESTO, id est, extra esto, scilicet interesse prohibebatur. Ad hanc consuetudinem Commentatulo utebantur, eodem Festo teste, quod erat virgulae genus, quas Flamines portabant, perventes ad sacrificium, ut a se homines amoverent. Sic apud Graecos ad sacrificium accedurus hoc primum praefatus est τις πόδι, hoc est, Quis hic? Illi, qui sacris interesse, respondebant: πολλοὶ καὶ ἀγαθοί, id est, multi & boni. Supra cita vitellimonium Tibulli, ex quo constat, quibus & quae dicendi forma certus hominibus, crimine nimirum aliquo pollutis, sacris fuerit interdictum. Hic nunc alia quaedam subjungam: Pythagoras Σύμβολα ἐξ ἀπὸ ... fores occludere profanis jubet: & Livius: Et cum omnia praefatio sacrorum, inquit, aos, quibus non sunt pura manus, sacris arceat, nos penetralia nefasta contaminari, cruento latronis cruere tinctus. Callimachus in hymnis: ἐκὰς, inquit, ἐκὰς, ὅσοι ἀλιτρῷ, procul proculom ius profanus: quod & similiter Virgilius ut supra, Aeneidos sexto, cum ait: —Procul, o procul este profani, Conclamat vates, totoq; abstinete luco.
units.tr: Moreover, there is now an occasion to speak of the custom of the Gentiles, by which certain people were kept off and warned away from their rites, as unworthy of them. Frequent mention of this is made among the profane authors. These people were called in Greek βέβηλοι [profane], ἄθυτοι [unsacrificed], ἀτελέστοι [uninitiated], μύσται [...], ἄθεοι [godless]; by the Latins, profani [profane], non initiati [uninitiated], and so on. Because of this custom of excluding people, the festivals at which such exclusion took place are thought to have been called ὄργια τὰ μυστήρια [the mysteries], from the fact that they were kept from the uninitiated, that is, from warding off the profane from them. Festus says that the lictor, in certain rites, used to cry out: "HOSTIS, VINCTVS, MVLIER, VIRGO EXESTO", that is, let the enemy, the bound man, the woman, the maiden be outside, namely, let them be forbidden to be present. For this custom they used the commentaculum, as Festus also testifies, a kind of rod which the Flamens carried, and with which, as they approached the sacrifice, they kept men away from themselves. So among the Greeks, the one about to approach the sacrifice first asked, "τίς ὅδε;" [Who is here?], and those who were permitted to take part in the rites answered: "πολλοὶ καὶ ἀγαθοί" [many and good]. Above I cited the testimony of Tibullus, from which it is clear what formula was fixed for people polluted by some crime, to forbid them from the sacred rites. Now I will add some others. Pythagoras bids that the doors be shut against the profane. And Livy says: "When the priest of the rites keeps away from the sacred rites all whose hands are not pure, so that we may not defile the unlawful sanctuaries with blood-stained hands." Callimachus, in his Hymns, says: "Far, far away, all who are sinners, be off, profane ones." Virgil, as above, in the sixth book of the Aeneid, when he says: "Far, O far off, be the profane; the prophetess cries out, keep away from the whole grove."

units.la: Claudianus libro secundo de raptu Proserpinae: —Gressus removeste profani, id est, procul a Deorum fanis templisq; arcendi.
units.tr: Claudian, in the second book of the Rape of Proserpina: "Step back, you profane ones", that is, keep far away from the shrines and temples of the gods.

units.la: Hinc simile est illud Ovidianum: Innocui veniant: procul hinc, procul impius esto Frater, & in partus macer acerba suos: Cui pater est Ψιμαχ: qui matris digerit annos: Quae premit in visam sacrum iniqua narum. Tantalidae fratres absint, & Iasonis uxor, Et quae ruricolis femina tosta dedit, Et Eorum, & Progne, Tereu\u0304 duabus, iniquus, Et quicung; suas per scelus auget opes.
units.tr: Similar to this is that Ovidian passage: "Let the innocent come; away from here, away with the impious one, the brother and the wretch bitter to his own children, whose father is Psimachus, who counts the years of his mother, who presses an unjust hand upon the sacred eye. Let the Tantalids keep away, and Jason's wife, and the woman who served her country-dwelling guests roasted meat, and Progne, and Tereus, and whoever increases his riches by crime."

units.la: Idem hoc apistola septima: Pone Deos & quae tangendo sacra profana, Non bene caelestes impia dextra colit.
units.tr: The same in the seventh epistle: "Set aside the gods, and the things profane to touch; the impure right hand does not worship the heavenly ones well."

units.la: In eandem sententiam Silius Italicus libro decimoseptimo sacerdotem introducit interdicentem polluenti sacrorum contactu, ubi verbis: Tum puppe e media magno clamore sacerdos: Parcite pollutis contingere vincula palmis: Et procul hinc moneo, procul hinc quecunque profana Ferte gradus: nec vos sacro misicete labori, Dum facis est momissse Dee: quod si qua pudica Mente valet: si qua illa sibi corporis adstat Conscia, vel solis subeat pia manera dextra
units.tr: To the same effect Silius Italicus, in the seventeenth book, introduces a priest forbidding those who would pollute the sacred rites by touch. His words are: "Then from the middle of the ship the priest cried out loudly: 'Spare touching the bonds with polluted hands; and I warn you, far from here, whatever is profane, turn your steps away; do not join the sacred labour while the goddess's rites are being performed. But if any woman with a chaste mind is strong enough, if any is conscious of her body being pure, let her approach with a pious right hand.'"

units.la: Hic adde, quae Statius quoque in hanc sententiam prodidit libro tertio Sylvarum: —Adeste Diiq; homines, sacris procul hinc, procul ite nocentes, Si cui corde nefas taciturn, fusique fenestus Longa patris: si quis pulsate conscius unquam Matris, & infernâ rigidum timet Aeacon urnâ. Insontes castosq; voco, &c.
units.tr: Add also what Statius too set forth to the same effect in the third book of the Silvae: "Be present, gods and men; far from the rites, far away go, you guilty ones, if anyone has wickedness in his heart, and has hidden a lengthy outpouring of his father's blood; if anyone has ever been conscious of striking his mother, and fears rigid Aeacus in the infernal urn. I call the innocent and the chaste..."

units.la: Ubi obiter declarandum, vocem, Procul, usitatam in hujusmodi interdictione a sacris, videri dicam, quasi porro, id est, longe, ab oculis.
units.tr: Here it must be explained in passing that the word "Procul" [far off], customary in this kind of prohibition from sacred rites, seems to be said as if it meant "porro", that is, far, far from the eyes.

units.la: Ac omnino apud Graecos hic mos excommunicandi, hoc est, interdicendi ab externo cultu, ceteris aliorum hominum, Deos colentium, usitatissimum fuit. Hinc apud eos legimus sacra quaedam ἀξιεσθαι nuncupata, in quibus interesse profanis haud fas fuerat: uti βιθλου, ad quae etiam praefari admitterentur. In numero autem profanorum istorum repossuerunt homicidio pollutos, humano infectos sanguine, ceterosque ejusmodi: item mulieres innuptas, aut servitio pressos, vel ere coemptos, quos in sacrorum apparatu altiorem arcere solere supra dixi. Sic & in Cherone e servus et servus inter profanos numerabantur. Namillic sacerdos, lorum tenens, pro edibus sacris Matute, ide est, Leucothee, clamitabat: Servum non ingredi, non servam, non Aetolum, non Aetolam. Iis enim sacrificio adesse eo loci non licebat. Apud Magos, qui essent lentiginosi, tam quam profani et Dii infames, ab arus summo vebantur. Item, qui elative vixerant, de quibus pro. Germanos vi, qui scuta amisissent in acie, sacris interesse haud licebat, et apud Aetolos. In acie, in solemnibus libere non potestant: reliqui initiati interesse sacris non possunt.
units.tr: Indeed, among the Greeks this custom of excommunicating, that is, forbidding people from external worship, was very common, against all other men who worshipped gods. Hence we read that among them certain rites were called [ἀξιεσθαι], at which it was not lawful for the profane to be present, such as [βιβλου], to which even those who were to pronounce the formula were admitted. Among these profane people they counted men polluted by homicide, stained with human blood, and others of that kind; likewise unmarried women, or those held in servitude, or bought with money, whom, as I said above, they used to keep at a greater distance from the preparations for the rites. Thus also in Chaeronea a slave and a servant were numbered among the profane. For there the priest, holding a whip, cried out before the sacred house to Matuta, that is, Leucothea: "Let no slave enter, no female slave, no Aetolian man, no Aetolian woman." For it was not lawful for them to be present at the sacrifice in that place. Among the Magi, those who were leprous were cast down from the top of the [...] as profane and as gods' enemies. Likewise, those who had lived in disgrace, about whom I spoke earlier. Among the Germans, those who had lost their shields in battle were not allowed to be present at the sacred rites, and so among the Aetolians. In battle, and at solemn rites, they could not freely [...]; the rest, who were initiated, could not be present at the rites.

units.la: Hic vis hac funestah habita fuit poena, qua ii, quibus sacris erat interdictum, dirs et exsecrationibus publicis fertebantur, et Dis Manibus atque Inferis, tanquam cruciatibus, poscebantur. Pollux: τοις ... Qui ablutionibus et purgationibus ... Romanarum: Καπιθος, inquit, ... Plutarchus ... Sacerdotes tamen mares, quam feminae, una cum legum custodibus, quum aliquem a sacris arcere id pie, et sanctè, et ex legis formula agant. Is vero cui sacris interdictum est, nisi lubens moriatur.
units.tr: Here this dreadful penalty was in force: those from whom the sacred rites were forbidden were carried off with public curses and execrations, and were consigned to the Manes and the gods below, as to torments. Pollux: [...] who by ablutions and purifications [...] Roman [...]. Plutarch says: "Priests, both male and female, together with the guardians of the laws, when they keep anyone from the sacred rites, do so piously, holily, and according to the form of the law. But he from whom the rites are forbidden, unless he dies willingly..."

units.la: Pro hujusmodi autem execrationibus et diris expiandis aqua niebantur lustrali et ablutionibus ut supra dictum, et sacrificiis, secundum illud Virgilii.
units.tr: To expiate such curses and execrations, they used lustral water and ablutions, as said above, and sacrifices, according to that verse of Virgil.

units.la: Lustrantur. Lustramur, sive, votis, accendimus aras: Votis, id est, sacrificijs, quae voveramus: quas lustrationes, ut ait Plato, libro secundo de Republica, τελεταὶ vocabant, nimirum quod ἐν τῷ τελεῖ, id est, in morte ea sacrificia fierent Diis Manibus, ne ipsi defuncti ullos paterentur Manes & poenas. Quisquis a diris & exsecrationibus sive de votionibus ipsius et sacrorum interdictione erant expiari atque liberati καθαρσεῖς, id est, puri dicebantur. Inde καθαιρεῖν, ἰδεμ quod λυμαίνειν, expiare, rejectare, purgare, expurgare, purificare. Exsecrationis, sive excommunicationis inter Ethnicos usurpatae, simul & Refecrationes seu expiationes & absolutionis exemplum illustre exstat apud Æmilium Probum in vita Alcibiadis. Nam sacerdotes Eumolpidae, ut Alcibiadem, a populo coactum, dirum devoverunt & exsecratum fuerunt: ita eundem posse resecrare fuerunt coacti. Exsecrarigitur est qui sic eos vel a sacris excludere, & Resecrare, sacris restituere.
units.tr: "Lustrantur. Lustramur, sive, votis, accendimus aras": "Lustramur" [we are purified], that is, by sacrifices which we had vowed; these lustrations, as Plato says in the second book of the Republic, they called τελεταί [rites of initiation], because they were performed ἐν τῷ τελεῖ [at the end], that is, at death, as sacrifices to the Manes, lest the dead themselves suffer any punishments from the Manes. Whoever was to be freed from curses and execrations, or from the forbidding of sacred rites, was called καθαρσεῖς [purified], that is, pure. Hence καθαιρεῖν [to cleanse], which is the same as λυμαίνειν [to defile], meaning to expiate, cleanse, purge, purify. A notable example of the execration of excommunication used among the Gentiles, and likewise of resecration, that is, expiation and absolution, is found in Aemilius Probus in the life of Alcibiades. For the priests, the Eumolpidae, cursed Alcibiades as accursed and execrated him when the people compelled them; and they were then compelled to resecrate him. To execrate, therefore, is to exclude someone from the sacred rites, and to resecrate is to restore them to the sacred rites.

units.la: Hic, colophonius loco, subjungam Ovidii versus libro Fastorum, quibus irridetur Homicidia, ac hae Ethnicorum opinio, qui sibi persuadebant homicidia, aliaq; scelera & flagitia aquis lustrari & expiari posse. Sunt hujusmodi: Omne nefas, omnemq; malum purgamine caussam Credebant nostri tollere posse senes. Gracia principium morus dedit, illa nocentes Impia lustratos ponere facta putat. Aliorum Peleus, ipsam quoq; Pelea Phoci Cade per Æmonias sol vit Acastus aquas Vellum franatis per viane draconibus Ægeu· Credidus immeritâ Phasida fore ope. Amphiaraides Nampacteo Acheloo Sol ve nefas dixit: Sol vit & ille nefas. Ah nimium facites, qui tristia crimina cede Flumineâ tolli posse putatis aquâ
units.tr: Here, as a kind of colophon, I will add Ovid's verses from the Fasti, in which the opinion of the Gentiles is mocked, for they persuaded themselves that homicides and other crimes and disgraceful deeds could be cleansed and expiated by water. They are of this kind: "Our forefathers believed that every wrong and every evil could be removed by the cleansing of the old men. Greece gave the beginning of the custom; she thinks that impious deeds are laid aside by purified persons. Peleus, and Acastus, who freed Phocus's own Peleus through the Aemonian waters, believed that Phasis, though innocent, would be freed by the same help. Amphiaraus said that a wrong was loosed in the Acheloüs at Pactolus, and he too was loosed of it. Ah, you do too much, you who think that sad crimes can be removed by river water."

units.la: Atque haec quidem de Ablutione, & in genere de personarum praeparatione ad sacra, earundemq; excommunicatione, id est interdictione a sacris, apud Ethnicos usitata, sint dicta.
units.tr: So much, then, concerning ablution and, more generally, the preparation of persons for sacred rites, and their exclusion, that is, their prohibition from sacred rites, as practised among the Gentiles.

units.la: SEQVITVR nunc caput secundum τῷ σφαγῳ ... (quae etiam σφέρτιλεια dicta) hoc eorum, quae ante sacrificium fieri consueverunt, Precatio nimirum & Vota. Horum, ut hoc loco, sic etiam alibi, crebra admodum ab Homero fit mentio. Hic quidem, in his verbis: —πολλὰ δ' Αθδὶν Εὔχετ' ἀπαχόμενος, id est, —Multis autem Minervae Supplicavit, initia faciens, &c.
units.tr: NOW follows the second chapter on the slaughter [τῷ σφαγῷ] (which is also called sphertileia), that is, of the things customarily done before the sacrifice: namely prayer and vows. Homer often mentions these, both in this passage and elsewhere. Here, in these words: "But he prayed much to Athena, making a beginning" [πολλὰ δ' Ἀθηναίην εὔχετ' ἀπαχόμενος], that is, "But he prayed much to Minerva, beginning, etc."

units.la: Alibi vero: ut Ιλιαδ. α. Καλῦβι ἰσὺν ἀρχυεσῶς δὲ χρύσεω ἀμφιβαίνας Κίλλαν τε ζαθέων, τενέδοιο, ἠδὲ σὺ ἰσατεῖς Σμινθεῦ, εἴποτί σ' ἰχαρεῖστ' ἐδὲ νηὸς ἱρὸν, Ηεί ἡ ποτί τι κατὰ πίονα μηρί' ἔκηα Ταῦρον ἡ δ' αἰγῶν, τόδ' μοι κρήνων ἐλδωρ. Audi me, argenteum arcum habens, qui Chrysam tueris, Cillamq; valde divinam, Tenedoq, fortiter imperas, Sminthe u. si quando tibi gratum templum coronavi, Vel si quando tibi pinguès coxas cremavi Taurorum & caprarum, hoc mihi perfice desiderium.
units.tr: Elsewhere, in Iliad 1: "Hear me, you who bear the silver bow, who protect Chryse and holy Cilla, and who rule Tenedos mightily, Smintheus. If ever I have built a graceful temple for you, or if ever I have burned for you the fat thighs of bulls and goats, fulfil this desire of mine" [Κλῦθί μευ, ἀργυρότοξ' ... τὸ δή τέλος ἐκ' ἐμὸν ἔλδωρ].

units.la: Et paulo post: Ως ἰφαρ' ἰυχόμενος, τὸ δ' ἐκλυε φοῖβος Απόλλων.
units.tr: And a little later: "So he prayed, and Phoebus Apollo heard him" [ὣς ἔφατ' εὐχόμενος, τοῦ δ' ἔκλυε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων].

units.la: Sic dixit orans: hunc autem exaudivit Phoebus Apollo.
units.tr: Thus he spoke in prayer; and Phoebus Apollo heard him.

units.la: Ic apud Apollonium hujus precationis, ante sacrificium fieri solita, sit mentio. Illic enim Iason inquit: Εὔχετο κακλόμενος πατρῷον Απόλλωνα,
units.tr: Here, in Apollonius, there is mention of this prayer, which was customarily made before the sacrifice. For there Jason says: "He prayed, calling upon his ancestral Apollo" [εὔχετο κικλήσκων πατρῷον Ἀπόλλωνα].
ρ +

units.la: Supplica vit in vocans patrium Apollinem: ubi & formulam precationis adhibet, jungit ——Καὶ ὦ ἀνάξ, &c. Audi Rex.—
units.tr: He prayed, invoking his ancestral Apollo. Here he also uses the form of prayer, adding: "And, O lord, hear, etc." [Καὶ ὦ ἄναξ], "Hear, O King."

units.la: Et paullo post: Καὶ οὐ' ἰυχωλὴ ἀεσ̔ ὑ̔ζας βάλλει, Et simul cum voto molam, sive hordea infudit, scilicet in aurem victimae.
units.tr: And a little later: "And he threw barley-groats" [οὐλοχύτας βάλλει], that is, he poured in the meal or barley together with the vow, namely upon the ear of the victim.

units.la: Ante sacrificia ergo fiebant preces & vota, quae fundebant ad illos Deos, quibus sacrificabant: unde sacrifice preces dictae a Seneca: & Diodorus Siculus usitatam, apud Aegyptios pro premittiolim solita. fertur, in sacrificiis fuisse familiam precationem & Regis laudationem, victimas ad aram adducis, testatur: quippe precatio, ut inquit Iamblichus, libro quinto, capite vigesimo primo non minima fuit pars sacrificiorum: imo fere praecipua, quae sacra potissimum impleri, absolvi, consummari, atque inde vim roburque suum accipere videbantur. Hanc sacrificiorum principium medium ac finem esse affirmat idem his verbis: Ipsa, inquit, interdum praemittitur, ut precatio quasi vestibulum ante sacrificium faciem praeparans atque muniens. Rursus, tanquam mediator intercedit aliquando in sacrificiis. Interdum etiam finem sacrificiorum explet. Addit: Sic omnino flatuendum, sacrum opus in sacro cultu rite & auspicato fieri absque supplicationibus & precibus. Subjungit inde multa de precum supplicationumque usu, vi, virtute, atque efficacia, de quis postea plura. Plato quoque in Alcibiade, sacrificia vel sumtuosa & magnificentissima tractatur non Dius esse grata, quam supplicationem & animum pium. Idem in Euthyphrone definit ... paullo post: ... sacrificare est nam offerre Deo: precari autem Deo invocare, sive dona ab illis petere. Quae omnia egregie conveniunt cum illo Psalmi: Sacrifica Deo laudem & redde Excelso vota tua. Tertullianus: Qui ei offert optimam & majorem hostiam, quam ipse mandavit, orationem decam pudicam, de anima innocente, de spiritu sancto profectam. Caeterum & Plutarchus harum cationum meminit in Dione inquiens, ... Euthyphron idem verbum & καυχᾶσθαι & λιτανεύειν & εὐχεσθαι significat testatur. Idem Iamblichus definit ...: sic forsan dictum velut euxyλων, propterea quod is, qui precatur, id facit ... Poeta Homerus, inquit idem in Iamblicho, ... id est, nullam precationem jussam facit, casum & irritam. Magnaque tribuerunt precibus.
units.tr: Before sacrifices, therefore, prayers and vows were made, which they poured out to those gods to whom they sacrificed. Whence Seneca calls sacrifices "prayers". And Diodorus Siculus reports that among the Egyptians a family prayer and praise of the king were customarily offered when the victims were led to the altar, as a prelude. For prayer, as Iamblichus says in the fifth book, chapter twenty-one, was no small part of sacrifices; indeed it was almost the chief part, by which sacred rites seemed principally to be fulfilled, completed and consummated, and from which they received their force and strength. The same writer affirms that this is the beginning, middle and end of sacrifices, in these words: "Sometimes it is sent ahead, so that prayer, like a vestibule, prepares and fortifies the way before the sacrifice. Again, it sometimes intervenes as a mediator in sacrifices. Sometimes it even completes the end of sacrifices." He adds: "This must be laid down entirely: that a sacred work is rightly and auspiciously performed in sacred worship only with supplications and prayers." He then goes on at length about the use, power, virtue and efficacy of prayers and supplications, of which more later. Plato also, in the Alcibiades, holds that sacrifices, however sumptuous and magnificent, are not pleasing to God so much as supplication and a pious mind. In the Euthyphro he likewise says ... a little later: "To sacrifice is to offer to God; but to pray is to call upon God, or to ask gifts from him." All of this agrees admirably with the psalm: "Offer to God praise, and pay your vows to the Most High." Tertullian: "He who offers to him the best and greatest victim, which he himself has commanded, offers a chaste prayer, proceeding from an innocent soul and from the Holy Spirit." Moreover Plutarch also mentions these prayers in Dion, saying ... Euthyphro testifies that the same word signifies both to boast, to supplicate and to pray. The same Iamblichus defines ... so perhaps it was called as if "euxylon", because he who prays does so ... The poet Homer, says the same writer in Iamblichus, ... that is, he makes a prayer that was not commanded, void and vain. And they ascribed great things to prayers.

units.la: Haec cum ita se habeant, latius aliquanto & copiosius de Gentilium precibus & votis in genere animum dicere, exordio ducto ab harum quoq; nominibus, quae precum supplicationumq; naturam declarant.
units.tr: Since these things stand thus, I shall speak somewhat more broadly and fully of the prayers and vows of the Gentiles in general, beginning with the names of these practices, which declare the nature of prayers and supplications.

units.la: LATINI, ut ab illis incipiam, hanc actionem multes nominibus exprimunt, cujus quodvis Orare, quod duplicem significationem habet: unam in precibus positam: alteram in suffrarum actione. Quoad priorem significationem; Cicero Verrina sexta orandi causa fanum adire dicit. Unde hoc verbum aliquoties conjungit cum verbis rogandi, obsecrandi, obtestandi, supplicandi & similibus. Quoad posteriorem significationem; idem in Bruto inquit: Quo nemiem unquam meliois ullam orationem capitis causam, cum ipse defenderet, loculis autor scripsit Thucydides. Hinc Festus: Orare, antiquos dixisse pro, agere, testimonio sunt, quod & Oratores, & nunc quidem legati, sunt vero oratores, quod Reipublicae mandatas partes agebant. Et Paulus: Orare antiqui dixerunt pro agere. Unde & Oratores causarum actores, & oratores, qui nuncupantur, quod Reipublicae mandata peragerent. Idem: Oratores ex Graeco ὀρᾶτορες dicti, quod mandatis ad Reges nationes, Deos solerent ἀφ' ὧν ... ut est, legati. Himodo appellantur legati.
units.tr: THE LATINS, to begin with them, express this action by many names. Of these, "orare" has a double meaning: one, in prayer; the other, in the act of pleading. As to the first meaning, Cicero in the Verrines says that he went to the temple "orandi causa", for the purpose of praying. Hence he often joins this verb with words of asking, beseeching, entreating, supplicating and the like. As to the second meaning, the same Cicero in the Brutus says: "No one ever wrote a finer speech for the defence of a man's life than Thucydides, when he himself was defending himself." Hence Festus: that the ancients used "orare" for "agere" (to act, to plead) is attested by the fact that both "oratores" and, now indeed, "legati" are called "oratores", because they carried out the duties entrusted to them by the Commonwealth. And Paulus: the ancients used "orare" for "agere". Whence both the pleaders of causes are called "oratores", and those who are called "oratores" because they carried out the commissions of the Commonwealth. Again: "oratores" is derived from the Greek ὀρᾶτορες, because they were commonly sent with commissions to kings, nations and gods ... just as "legati" (envoys) are. In this way envoys are called.

units.la: Ab Orare deducitur & Oratio, vox similiter duo illa significans, nempe precationem causarum actionem: dicta ab ore; sicut & omen Festus vult dictum quasi oramen. Quod si oratio vel orationis vox ... Hinc & Adorare, quod similiter, teste Festo, apud antiquos significabat agere, & Ador, farris genus, edor quandam appellatum, ab edendo: vel quod aduratur, ut fiat tostum: unde in sacrificio mola salsa efficitur. SimiSimile verbum, quo precandi actio exprimitur, est ipsum Precari: quod est precibus petere, pretes adhibere, supplicare, obtestari: quod tam in malam, quàm bonam partem accipi solet. Mala enim & bona alicui precari possumus. Cicero ad Quintum fratrem: Haec utinam non experiare; quod precarer Deos, nisi meas preces audire defisient. Verum tamen precor, sit his infinitis nostris malis contenti sint. Idem in Verrem: Verres in iudicium venit, ubi ne precari quidem Deos atq; ab eis auxilium petere possit. Idem in Catilinam: Deos immortales precari, venerari atq; implorare debetis, ut urbem defendant. Idem pro Rabirio: A Iove Opt. Max. caeterisq; Deis, Deabus immortalibus pacem & veniam peto, precorq; ut, &c. Idem pro Cornelio Balbo: Ut Deos immortales peregrina, meuste domestica precaremur. Idem in Pisonem: Verum tamen optabilius putas, sic exire a patria, ut omnes sui civis salutem, incolumitate, redeuntem precentur, quod mihi accidit: an quod tibi proficisceris venit, ut omnes exsecrarentur, male precarentur, unam tibi illam viam & perpetuam esse vellent? Idem de Natura Deorum: Stultitia est, a quibus bona precamur ab iis dantibus nolle sumere. Idem in Pisonem: Nec ego si unquam vobis mala precer, quod saepe feci, in quo Dii immortales meas preces audierunt, morbum, aut mortem, aut crucem precarer. Ibidem: Haec ego semper de vobis expetivi, haec optavi, haec precatus sum: Et pro Seftio: Quibus utinam eventissent ea, quae tum homines precabantur.
units.tr: From "orare" is derived also "oratio", a word likewise signifying both those two things, namely prayer and the pleading of causes; it is called from the mouth (ore). Festus also thinks "omen" was named as if "oramen". If oratio or the word orationis ... Hence also "adorare", which, as Festus attests, among the ancients similarly signified "agere"; and "ador", a kind of spelt, called "edor" from eating, or because it is roasted (aduratur) so as to become toasted; whence in sacrifice salted meal is made. A similar verb, by which the act of praying is expressed, is "precari" itself: to seek by prayers, to use entreaties, to supplicate, to implore; which is commonly taken in a bad sense as well as a good one. For we can pray evil things upon someone as well as good. Cicero to his brother Quintus: "Would that you did not experience this; for I would pray to the gods, unless they had ceased to hear my prayers. Yet I pray that they may be content with these infinite evils of ours." The same in the Verrines: "Verres came to trial, where he could not even pray to the gods nor seek help from them." The same in the Catiline: "You ought to pray to, worship and implore the immortal gods that they defend the city." The same in the Pro Rabirio: "I seek peace and pardon from Jupiter Best and Greatest and the other gods and goddesses immortal, and I pray that, etc." The same in the Pro Cornelio Balbo: "That we should pray to the immortal gods for foreign and domestic affairs." The same against Piso: "But do you think it more desirable to leave the fatherland in such a way that all its citizens pray for your safety and wellbeing on your return, as happened to me; or to depart in such a way that everyone curses you, wishes you ill, and wishes that this single road were perpetually yours?" The same in On the Nature of the Gods: "It is foolish to refuse to accept from those who give what we pray for good things." The same against Piso: "Nor, if I ever prayed evil upon you, as I often did, would the immortal gods have heard my prayers so as to ask for disease, death, or the cross." Likewise: "These things I have always sought for you, these I have wished, these I have prayed for." And in the Pro Sestio: "Would that those things had come to pass which men were then praying for."

units.la: Porro ab hoc Precari descendunt precator, precatio, preces, precarius, precario, deprecari, deprecator, deprecatio, imprecari: quorum singulorum & explicationem & exemplum unum aut alterum addere libet, quandoquidem hunc de precibus locum copiosius explicare instituimus. Precator igitur est is, qui precatur pro re aliqua, sive id faciat pro se, sive pro alio. Terentius in Heautont. Nec accusat, Syre te: nec tu eam tibi, neq; precatorem parnis. Ibidem: Miror, non iusssisse me arripi. Ad Menedemum hinc pergam, eum precatorem mihi paro: sed non nostro fide inhibiti habeo.
units.tr: Further from this "precari" are derived precator, precatio, preces, precarius, precario, deprecari, deprecator, deprecatio, imprecari. It is worth adding an explanation and one or two examples of each of these, since we have undertaken to explain this topic of prayers more fully. A precator, therefore, is one who prays for something, whether he does so for himself or for another. Terence in the Heautontimorumenos: "Nor does he accuse you, Syrus, nor do you keep her for yourself, nor do you make yourself a suppliant." Likewise: "I am surprised he did not order me to be seized. I shall go from here to Menedemus; I am getting him as my intercessor; but I have him held by no trust of mine."

units.la: Precatio deinde significat rogationem vel obsecrationem. Cicero pro Murena: Si illa solennis Comitiorum precatio Consularibus auspiciis consecrata, tantam habet vim, quanta, &c. Idem de Natura Deorum: Iu ea Dea, quae est rerum custos intimarum, omnis precatio & sacrificatio extrema est. Ibidem: In Augurum precatione plurimum nomina videmus.
units.tr: Precatio then means a request or an entreaty. Cicero, Pro Murena: "If that solemn prayer of the Comitia, consecrated under the consular auspices, has so much force, as..." The same author, De Natura Deorum: "To that goddess who is the guardian of inner things, every prayer and sacrifice is the last resort." Ibidem: "In the prayer of the augurs we see very many names."

units.la: Preces similiter pro rogatione usurpantur, utemq; obtestatione, ubi obiter notandum, nomen hoc per rectum pluralem hic & alis locis ponit, quod singulares usitatum non habeat. Vix enim dicitur prax. Reliqui tamen casus singulares crebro admodum & frequenti in usu sunt. Cicero ad Quintum fratrem: Quod precarer Deos, nisi meas preces audire desisient. Idem ad Atticum: Nihil tuli gravius, quam me non posse matris tuae precibus cedere. Idem pro Cluentio. Nocturna illius sacrificia scelerata, preces, & vota cognoscimus. Idem ad Herennium: Nec prece, nec pretio nec simulare a recta via deduci oportet. Idem in Verrem: In precibus & gratulationibus non solum id simulacrum venerari, sed etiam officiali solent.
units.tr: Preces is likewise used for a request, and obtestatio as well. Here it should be noted in passing that this noun is used in the plural nominative in this and other places, because the singular is not in common use, for the form prex is hardly ever said. The other singular cases, however, are very frequent in use. Cicero to his brother Quintus: "Because I would pray to the gods, unless they had stopped hearing my prayers." The same, to Atticus: "I have borne nothing more grievously than that I could not yield to your mother's prayers." The same, Pro Cluentio: "We know of her nocturnal sacrifices, wicked prayers and vows." The same, to Herennius: "One ought not to be turned from the straight path by prayer, by bribe, or by pretence." The same, In Verrem: "In prayers and thanksgivings they not only venerate that image but are also accustomed to perform their services to it."

units.la: Precarium est, quod precibus petenti utendum concediur tandiu, quandiu is, qui concessit, pateatur. Cicero ad Oltaviam: Cuius a vus fuit argentarius, astipulator pater, uterq; vero precarii fuerunt quasi quoddam. Brutus Ciceroni: Quod tibi cum Antonio privatum odium? Nempe quia postulabat hoc, salutem a se peti precariam, nos incolumitate habere, a quibus ipse libertate accepisset.
units.tr: A precarium is something given for use to one who asks by prayer, for as long as the one who granted it permits. Cicero to Octavia: "Whose grandfather was a banker, and whose father a surety; both were, as it were, a kind of precarious holders." Brutus to Cicero: "What private hatred do you have with Antony? Surely because he demanded that salvation be sought from him as a favour, that we should hold our safety by his grace, we from whom he himself had received his liberty."

units.la: Precario est prece vel precibus. Et precario habere aliquid dicitur, qui possessionem corporis vel juris adeptus est ex hac solum causa, quod adhibuit preces & impetravit, quod ei possidere, aut quo uti liceat: veluti si me precario rogaveris per fundum meum vel agere liceat, aut in tectum meum stillicidium, vel signum in parietem immissum habeas. Cicero pro Cecinna: Nec id quidem satis est, nisi docet ita se posse sedisse, ut nec vi, nec clam, nec precario possederit. Idem in Verrem Actione septima: Quo tempore in tanta inopia navium, tantaq; calamitate Provinciae, et iam si precario essent rogandi, tamen ab his impetrarentur.
units.tr: Precario means by prayer or by prayers. And a person is said to hold something precario who has gained possession of a body or a right from this cause alone, that he has made entreaty and obtained permission to possess it or to use it. For example, if you have asked me by prayer for leave to pass through my farm, or to let your eaves drip onto my roof, or to keep a sign set into my wall. Cicero, Pro Caecina: "Nor is even that enough, unless he shows that he sat there in such a way that he possessed it neither by force, nor by stealth, nor precariously." The same, In Verrem, Action seven: "At a time of such great scarcity of ships and such calamity for the province, even if they had had to be asked by prayer, they would have been obtained from these men."

units.la: Deprecari porro aliquando est supplicare, vel precando impetrare. Aliquando vero significat recusare, detrectare, vel removere. Exempla igitur distinguenda sunt. Pro supplicare: Cicero epistolarum familiarium libro quarto: Hic te unius solitudines, unius etiam mulae & assidue lacrymae Caji Marcelli, fratris optimi deprecantur. Idem in Verrem Actione 7. Deprecatur a vobis, sum etiam pro suo juro contendet, ne patiamini talem Imperatorem Populo Romano Siculorum testimoniis eripi. Pro detestari,removeri,vel amoliri usurpatur istius loci. Cicerone in Verrem: Quid tot scelera commisit,ut nullam a se calamitatem poterit deprecari. Ibidem: Ne hoc quidem juris obtinuit, ut unius honestissimi atque innocentissimi civis mortem deprecaretur. Ibidem: Is non modo non hoc perfecit,ut virgarum vim deprecaretur : sed cum imploraret sepius, ufurparetq; nomen civitatis, crux,strux, inquam, infeliti & erumnoso comparabatur. Ovidius:
units.tr: Deprecari, moreover, sometimes means to supplicate, or to obtain by praying. But sometimes it means to refuse, to decline, or to remove, so the examples must be distinguished. For supplicate: Cicero, Letters to Friends, book four: "Here the loneliness of you alone, and the tears, constant tears, of Gaius Marcellus, the best of brothers, entreat you." The same, In Verrem, Action 7: "He begs of you, and will also contend for his own right, that you not allow such a commander to be snatched from the Roman people by the testimony of the Sicilians." For detest, remove, or ward off, this use applies: Cicero, In Verrem: "What crimes did he commit, so that he could avert no calamity from himself?" Ibidem: "He did not even obtain this right, that he might avert the death of one most honourable and most innocent citizen." Ibidem: "He not only did not bring it about that he might ward off the force of the rods, but when he implored more often and invoked the name of citizen, a cross, a gallows, I say, was made ready for the unhappy and wretched man." Ovid:

units.la: Sepe precor mortem,mortem quoq, depretor idem: Nemea Sarmaticum contegat offa solum.
units.tr: "Often I pray for death, and I also pray against death in turn: may Nemea's soil cover the Sarmatian bones."

units.la: Similes multæ locutiones occurrunt,quibus deprecari in vidiam,deprecari odium, deprecari iratos animos,atque horribiles impetus & similia dicimus,quæ videntur nocitura, vel nobis indigna : vel quæ nimium acerba & aspera appàrent : vel quæ sinstri ominis videntur.
units.tr: Many similar expressions occur, in which we say to deprecate envy, to deprecate hatred, to deprecate angry minds and dreadful assaults, and the like, which seem likely to harm us or to be undeserved by us, or which appear too bitter and harsh, or which seem to be of ill omen.

units.la: Hinc Deprecator vel pro eo,qui orat: vel pro eo,qui aliquid amolitur & removet. Cicero ad Atticum: Filium misit non solùm sui deprecatorem, sed etiam accusatorem mei. Idem pro Sextio: Omitto, quid ille Tribunus omnium rerum divinarum humanarumq, prædæ fecerit; qui adesse nobilissimos adolescentes,honestissimos Equites Romanos,deprecatores salutis meæ jusserit,eosque operarum suarum gladiis & lapidibus objecerit.
units.tr: Hence deprecator is used either of one who entreats, or of one who wards off and removes something. Cicero to Atticus: "He sent his son as an intercessor not only for himself but also as an accuser of me." The same, Pro Sestio: "I pass over what that tribune did, plundering all things divine and human; who ordered the most noble young men and the most honourable Roman knights to be present as intercessors for my safety, and exposed them to the swords and stones of his hired men."

units.la: Deprecatio similiter verbi sui varietatem retinet. Est enim obtestatio vel detestatio. Cicerone epistolarum familiarium quarto: Nos curâ & dolore proximi sumus,precibus tardiores,quod jus adeundi,cum ipsi deprecatione eguerimus,non habemus. Idem pro Rabirio: Huic afferec aliquam deprecationem periculi etas illa,quæ tum fuit. Idem in Partitionibus : Ad eius facti deprecationem ignoscendi petenda venia est. Et libro de Inventione : Deprecatio est,in qua non defensio factì, sed ignoscendi postulatio continetur.
units.tr: Deprecatio similarly keeps the variety of its word, for it means either entreaty or averting. Cicero, Letters to Friends, book four: "We are nearest in care and grief, but slower in prayers, because we do not have the right of approaching, since we ourselves have been in need of intercession." The same, Pro Rabirio: "That age which he then was brings some deprecation of danger for him." The same, Partitiones: "For the deprecation of that deed, pardon must be sought by asking forgiveness." And in the book De Inventione: "Deprecation is that in which there is contained not a defence of the deed but a request for pardon."

units.la: Imprecari denique, proprie mala & calamitatem dicimus. Quintilianus: Non imprecamur debilitatem, naufragia, morbos : pauper sit & amet quancunq, mcretricem,& amare non desinet. Hinc Imprecatio,Verbale: Exsecratio,de votio,dira,Græcè Ἀρὰ.
units.tr: Finally, imprecari we properly say of evils and calamity. Quintilian: "We do not curse with weakness, shipwrecks, diseases; may he be poor and love whatever prostitute he likes, and he will not cease to love her." Hence imprecatio, the verbal noun: execration, vow, dire curse, in Greek Ara [Ἀρὰ].

units.la: Precandi porrò aliô designatur etiam verbo obsecrandi ; quod Festus dicit esse opem a Diis petere ; sic dictum,quasi ob vos sacrare : quod in quibusdam precationibus ajt esse pro, vos obsecrare ; ut, sub vos placo, pro supplico. Cæterùm ejus usus & constructio hujusmodi est , ut modo absoluté ponatur pro eo,quod dicimus,Amabo ce:modo vero accusativum habeat simplicem:modo duplicem. Cicero ad Atticum: Obsecro, mi Pomponi,non vides ? Ibidem : Obsecro te , quod hoc miserius,quàm,&c. Idem pro Quincio : Nævium obsecravit per fratris sui mortui cineres per nomen propinquitatis,ut,&t. Idem in Verrem: Cùm multis lacrymis eum oraret atq, obsecret Heraclius,impetrare non potuit.
units.tr: Precandi is also designated elsewhere by the verb obsecrandi, which Festus says means to seek help from the gods; so called as if ob vos sacrare, which in some prayers is said to mean to beseech you, as sub vos placo means to supplicate. Its use and construction are such that sometimes it is put absolutely, in the sense of what we say, "I beg you"; sometimes it takes a simple accusative, sometimes a double one. Cicero to Atticus: "I beg you, my Pomponius, do you not see?" Ibidem: "I beg you, what is more wretched than..." The same, Pro Quinctio: "He besought Naevius by the ashes of his dead brother, by the name of kinship, that..." The same, In Verrem: "When Heraclius begged and besought him with many tears, he could not obtain it."

units.la: Obsecratio item signifiçat preces,deprecationem vel obtestationem. Cicero pro Fonteio: Cum rate ut nostris cestibus plus,quàm alienigenis credilisse videamini : plus saluti civium,quàm bonslium libidini consuluisse: graviorem duxisse ejus obsecrationem,quæ vestris sacris præsit , quàm eorum audaciam,qui cum omnium sacrus,delubris,bella gesserunt. Idem : Cavete,ne periculosum superbumq, sit,ejus vos obsecrationem repudiare , cujus preces si Dii aspernarentur,hæc salva esse non possent. Suetonius de Claudio Cæsare:Observavitq, sedulò, ut quoties terra in urbe movisset, ferias, advocata tonsione , Prætor indiceret : utq, ob dira aut in urbe, auc in Capitolio visa obsecratio haberetur : id est,venia a Diis peteretur.Est enim obsecrare etiam deprecari & quasi sacra facere,ut veniam impetremus.
units.tr: Obsecratio likewise signifies prayers, deprecation or obtestation. Cicero, Pro Fonteio: "Since you seem to have trusted our ships more than foreign ones, to have consulted the safety of the citizens more than the lust of the wicked, to have thought the entreaty of him who presides over your sacred rites more weighty than the audacity of those who waged war against all sacred things and shrines." The same: "Beware lest it be dangerous and proud to reject the entreaty of him whose prayers, if the gods should spurn them, these things could not be safe." Suetonius, on Claudius Caesar: "He also carefully observed that whenever the earth had moved in the city, the praetor should proclaim a holiday, a shaven ceremony being summoned, and that an obsecratio should be held on account of dire portents seen in the city or on the Capitol; that is, pardon should be sought from the gods." For obsecrare is also to deprecate and, as it were, to perform sacred rites, so that we may obtain pardon.

units.la: Sic verbo obtestandi actio ista pretandi exprimitur.Est autè non simpliciter pretari,sed deprecari, vel implorare, vel,quod vulgo dicitur , adjurare. Cicero familiarium epistol. libro quarto: Oro obtestorq, te,ut Quintum fratrem ames. Idem pro Quintio: Te obsecro obtestorq, per sinestutem & solitudinem meam.Idem ante exilium : Iure igitur vos obtestor, quos mihi & debere & posse intelligo opitulari. Terentius in Andria: Quod ego te per hanc dextram oro, & genium tuum:per tuam fidem,perq, ejus solitudinem te obtestor.
units.tr: In this way the act of praying is expressed by the verb obtestari. It is not simply to pray, but to deprecate, or to implore, or, as is commonly said, to adjure. Cicero, Letters to Friends, book four: "I beg and entreat you to love my brother Quintus." The same, Pro Quinctio: "I beseech you and entreat you by your good faith and my loneliness." The same, before his exile: "Rightly therefore do I entreat you, whom I understand both ought to and are able to help me." Terence, Andria: "Because I beg you by this right hand and your genius; I entreat you by your good faith and by her loneliness."

units.la: Hinc Obtestatio(inquit Donatus in Andria Terentii)dicitur , cùm eum adjuramus , quem rogamus:qualis est obtestatio apud Virgilium quarto Æneidos: Mène fugis ? Per ego has lacrymas dextramq, tuam te,, Per connubia nostra,per inceptos Hymeneos,
units.tr: Hence obtestatio (says Donatus on Terence's Andria) is said when we adjure the one whom we ask, as is the obtestatio in Virgil, Aeneid book four: "Do you flee me? By these tears and your right hand, I beg you, by our marriage, by the Hymeneal rites we began,"

units.la: Si bene quid de te merui, fuit aut tibi quicquam
units.tr: "If I have deserved well of you, or if anything was sweet to you with me,"
"Pity the falling house, and I beg you,"

units.la: Oro, si quis adhuc precibus locus,exue mentem.
units.tr: "If any place is still left for prayers, lay aside your mind."

units.la: Formaigitur hæc est. Dictionn exempla sunt ista. Cicero pro Cluentio: Mulier obtestatione viri domo exire non debet. Idem pro Domo sua: Quid ergo tua obtestatio tibicinis voluit? Celius Cicero familiarium ostavo: Meiofficii est, me meminisse,qua obtestatione decedens mihi,ne pater reret,mandaris. Titus Livius: Populus Romanus ad pueros & obtestationem versus est, ut sibi pœnam Magistri equitum Dictator remitteret.
units.tr: Such, then, is the form. These are examples of the word. Cicero, Pro Cluentio: "A woman ought not to leave the house at the obtestation of her husband." The same, Pro Domo sua: "What then did your obtestation to the flute-player want?" Caelius, in Cicero's Letters to Friends, book eight: "It is my duty to remember by what obtestation you entrusted to me, as you departed, that my father should not..." Titus Livy: "The Roman people turned to the boys and to entreaty, so that the Dictator would remit for them the punishment of the Master of the Horse."

units.la: Præterea Contendere,Flagitare,Exigere,& similia hanc precandi actionem designant. Ac Contendere quidem cum alia significat,tum instando petere. Cicero familiarium secundo: Verecundius a te, si qua magna res mihi petenda esset,contenderem.
units.tr: Besides, contendere, flagitare, exigere and similar verbs also express this action of praying. Contendere has several meanings, one of which is to seek by insisting. Cicero, Letters to Friends, book 2: "I would make my request to you more modestly, if I had some great matter to seek from you."

units.la: Flagitare autem est vehementer & instanter & quasi cum quodam clamore ac strepitu poscere. Quid acta tua vita,inquit Cicero familiarum quarto,quid sludia,quid artes,quibus a pueritia floruisti,a te flagitent,tu videbis. Idem de Legibus. Postulatur a te jamdiu vel potius flagitatur bistoria. Hinc Flagitator, qui flagitando instat. Cicero in Bruto: Non me hercule ti- bi repromittere istud quidem ausim. Nam hunc,qui negat,videor flagitatorem,non illum quidem tibi molestum. Sed assiduum tamen & acrem fore. Et Efflagitare est insolenter urgere,sicut Efflagitatio est vehementer instans postulatio. Cicero pro Milone: Eorum nos magis miseret, qui nostram misericordiam non requirunt,quam qui illam efflagitant.
units.tr: Flagitare means to demand vehemently and insistently, almost with a certain clamour and noise. Cicero, Letters to Friends, book 4: "What your life, what your pursuits, what the arts in which you have flourished since boyhood demand of you, you will see." The same author, On the Laws: "History has been demanded of you for a long time, or rather clamoured for." Hence flagitator, one who presses his demand by insisting. Cicero, Brutus: "Indeed, by Hercules, I would not dare to promise you that. For I seem to be a pestering demander to the man who refuses, not troublesome to you, but persistent and keen all the same." Efflagitare means to press insolently, just as efflagitatio is a vehemently insistent demand. Cicero, For Milo: "We pity more those who do not seek our pity than those who clamour for it."

units.la: Exigere poro significat flagitare vel requirere, aut flagitando extorquere. Cicero in familiaribus: Neid,quod petat, exigere magis,quam rogare,& in mercedis potius, quam beneficii loco numerare videatur. Idem de Oratore: Quo facilius id a te exigam, quod peto, nihil tibi po- stulanti negabo.
units.tr: Exigere means to demand or seek, or to extort by demanding. Cicero, Letters to Friends: "He seems to exact what he seeks rather than ask for it, and to reckon it as a wage rather than as a favour." Cicero, On the Orator: "So that I may the more easily get from you what I ask, I will refuse you nothing when you ask me."

units.la: Sunt alia nomina Latina,quibus hæc precandi actio exprimitur ut poscere,poscere,postulare, rogare,in vocare,implerare,& supplicare: a quibus implorare est voce miserabili,velut cum ploratu,ohem aliujus petere: supplicare vero, supplicem se ad aliujus pedes abjicere,vel manus alicui,vel ad aliquem tendere,pro aliquo precari vel deprecari. De supplicandi simul & adorandi significatione ita scribit Valla libro quinto,capite undecimo: Adorare,inquit,ab oro,quod est ore precor,componitur: supplicare a pleco,quod genu poplitemque,aut cervicem plicamus, cum a potentiore aliquo magnum quippiam precamur : & numeni adorare sine ore,hoc est, sine voce fit, non sine plicatione genuum ac gestu corporis. Supplicare sine plicatione genuum ac gestu corpores,non sine ore & voce. Hinc est, quare suppli..are tantum homini datur : adorare etiam mutis. Unde elephas & phœnix,& alia quaedam rationis expertia Solem adorare dicuntur: nosque rebus mutis & sensu carentibus non supplicamus,sed adorationis honorem exhibemus,ut Regum statuis,signis,vestibus,litteris aliusque similibus. Fiat Vaila.
units.tr: There are other Latin words by which this action of praying is expressed: poscere, postulare, rogare, invocare, implorare and supplicare. Implorare means to beg for someone's help with a piteous voice, almost weeping. Supplicare means to cast oneself as a suppliant at someone's feet, or to stretch out one's hands to someone, and to plead or entreat on another's behalf. On the meaning of supplicare and adorare together, Valla writes as follows in book 5, chapter 11: "Adorare," he says, "is compounded from ab oro, which means to pray with the mouth. Supplicare comes from plicare, because we fold the knees, the hams or the neck when we beg some great thing from someone more powerful. Adoring a divinity is done without the mouth, that is, without voice, but not without bending the knees and bodily gesture. Supplicating is not done without bending the knees and bodily gesture, nor without mouth and voice. Hence it is that one supplicates only a man, but one adores even dumb creatures. Whence elephants, the phoenix and certain other creatures lacking reason are said to adore the sun. We do not supplicate mute things that lack sense, but pay them the honour of adoration, as we do to the statues, images, garments and letters of kings and other such things." Thus Valla.

units.la: Caeterum quod ad supplicandi usum pertinet ; id diligenter observandum, perpetuo cum dativo jungi, nunquam cum accusativo. Dicimus igitur,supplicare alicui ; non supplicare aliquem: Cicero ad familiarum epistolarum libro sexto: Amicis ejus omnibus pro te libentissime supplicabo. Ibidem: Quibus ego supplicare non desiti. Idem pro Plancio: Ego tibi,Laterensis,Plancium non ante posui, sed cum esset is æqui boni viri,meum beneficium potius ad eam detuli, qui a me contenderetur, quam ad eum,qui mihi non nimis submisse supplicaret.
units.tr: Moreover, as regards the use of supplicare, it must be carefully observed that it is always joined with the dative and never with the accusative. We therefore say supplicare alicui, not supplicare aliquem. Cicero, Letters to Friends, book 6: "I will most willingly supplicate for you to all his friends." Ibid.: "To whom I have not ceased to supplicate." Cicero, For Plancius: "Laterensis, I did not put Plancius before you. But since he was a man of fair goodness, I transferred my kindness rather to the one who was seeking it from me than to the one who was not too humbly begging me."

units.la: Sed & voVere, votum,voti vus,de voVere, de voto vim quandam precandi habent. Quare ipsa quoque hic consideranda. Vovere proprie est votum suscipere vel facere,Deo aliquid sanctè promittere. Cicero in Verrem: Marcellus duo templa dedicaturum se Romæ voverat. Idem de Inventione: Naute voverunt,se Dianæ vitulum immolaturos. Idem de Divinatione: Qui cum sues pascerent,unde exitus amissa,vovisse dicitur,si recuperasset,unam se Deo daturam. Idem: Quid optamus a Diis immortalibus? Quid voVemus?
units.tr: But vovere, votum, votivus and de voto also carry a certain force of praying, so they too must be considered here. Vovere properly means to take up or make a vow, to solemnly promise something to God. Cicero, Against Verres: "Marcellus had vowed that he would dedicate two temples at Rome." Cicero, On Invention: "Sailors vowed that they would sacrifice a calf to Diana." Cicero, On Divination: "A man who was tending pigs, when he had lost them, is said to have vowed that if he recovered them he would give one to God." Ibid.: "What do we wish from the immortal gods? What do we vow?"

units.la: Votum deinde est proprie promissio factia Deo,quod aliquando sine conditione fit: aliquando addita conditione. Unde Voti reus is ; qui quid promisit,spopondit ve ac debet,inquit Festus. Inscrdum pro voluntate ac desiderio capitur,quoniam ea,quæ a Deo poscimus , vehementer desideramus: unde Voti compotem dicimus eum, qui desiderium suum consecutus est: & pro Voto nobis succedere,idem,quod,pro desiderio,ex animi sententia & voluntate nostra.Cicero pro Claentio: Nolumus illius sacrificia,sceleratas,s preces et nefaria vota eognoscimus. Idem pro Plan- cio:Deorum precer & vota de meo reditu audiri.Idem: Deus nihil sentiens nunquam nobis occurrit,neq; in precibus,neq; in optatis,neq; in votis. Virgilius: Et votum jam assuesce vocari:
units.tr: A votum is properly a promise made to God, which is sometimes made without condition and sometimes with a condition added. Hence Festus says that a voti reus is one who has promised or pledged something and ought to fulfil it. Votum is also taken for will and desire, since we earnestly desire what we ask of God. Hence we call a man voti compos who has attained his desire, and pro voto nobis succedere means the same as "to succeed according to our desire," that is, according to our wish and will. Cicero, For Cluentius: "We do not wish to know their sacrifices, their wicked prayers and impious vows." Cicero, For Plancius: "I pray and vow that the gods hear about my return." Cicero: "God, perceiving nothing, never meets us, neither in prayers, nor in wishes, nor in vows." Virgil: "And now grow accustomed to be called a vow."

units.la: Vbi elegans allusio ad voti nomen,quasi votum a voce,vel vocando fit derivatum:ad quam allusionem respiciens S. Augustinus dixit: Non vox, sed votum:non chordula Musica, sed eor: Non cantans, sed amans cantat in aure Dei.
units.tr: Here is an elegant allusion to the name votum, as if votum were derived from vox, or from vocare. Looking to this allusion, Saint Augustine said: "Not voice, but vow; not a musical string, but the heart. Not singing, but loving, sings in the ear of God."

units.la: Porro votum nuncupare, suscipere, facere,usitata & perelegantes formulae sunt loquendi: quarum omnium explicationem & nonnulla exempla subjungere libet. Vota nuncupare est Divus vota polliceri & destinare vel pro felici rerum eventu, vel pro alicujus salute et incolumitate,quae apud Antiquos non fiebat sine solenni ritu & religione: unde dicebantur nuncupata vota,quae Consules, Praetores, Imperatores,cum in Provincias proficiscebantur, faciebant ,eaq; in tabulas praescriptibus multis referebantur. Hinc Cicero in Verrem Actione septima:Cum paludatus exiisset,votaq; pro Imperio suo, communi Populi Romani nuncupasset,nobilu, flupri causa in urbem introferri solitus est. Suetonius in Claudio Caesare: Ieaq; & quasi pro aegro vota suscepta sunt. Plinius in Panegyrico: Nuncupare vota & pro aeternitate Imperii & pro salute ei vinm,immo pro salute principum, ac propter illos,pro aeternitate Imperii solebamus. Sic mos erat,ut Kalendis Ianuariis,solennis votorum nuncupatio fieret a Principe,Consulibus, Magistratum incuntibus, qui ibant,ut ajt Livius,in Capitolium ad vota nuncupanda. Horum erat minit Cornelius Tacitus his verbis: Quin & illa objectabat,principio anni vieare Thrasea solenne jusjurandum,nuncupationibus votorum non adesse. Suetonius in Nerone:Votorum nuncupatione magna jam ordinum frequentia vix repertae Capitolii claves: hoc est,cum Nero vellet ex ritu ire in Capitolium ad vota nuncupanda,habuit hoc dirum praesagium,quod claves vix repertae sunt: tanquam Dii recusarent votorum nuncupationem ferri a Nerone, qui illa nonefset soluturus.
units.tr: Furthermore, votum nuncupare, suscipere and facere are common and very elegant ways of speaking. I shall add an explanation of all of them, with some examples. Vota nuncupare is to promise and fix vows, either for a happy outcome of affairs or for someone's safety and well-being. Among the ancients this was never done without a solemn rite and religious observance. Hence vows made by consuls, praetors and emperors when they set out for the provinces were called nuncupated vows, and they were recorded in writing in many prescribed forms. Hence Cicero, Against Verres, Action seven: "When he had gone out in a military cloak and had nuncupated vows for his command, for the common good of the Roman people, he was accustomed to be brought into the city by a nobleman for the sake of debauchery." Suetonius, Life of Claudius: "These vows were also undertaken as if for a sick man." Pliny, Panegyricus: "We used to nuncupate vows both for the eternity of the empire and for the safety of the emperor, indeed for the safety of the princes and on their account, for the eternity of the empire." So the custom was that on the Kalends of January a solemn nuncupation of vows was made by the prince and by the consuls, and by magistrates entering office, who went, as Livy says, up to the Capitol to nuncupate vows. Cornelius Tacitus mentions this in these words: "Moreover he also objected that at the beginning of the year Thrasea was absent from the solemn oath, the nuncupation of vows." Suetonius, Life of Nero: "With the nuncupation of vows and a great crowd of the orders already present, the keys of the Capitol were scarcely found." That is, when Nero wished, according to custom, to go up to the Capitol to nuncupate vows, he had this dire omen: the keys were scarcely found, as if the gods refused to have vows made by Nero, who did not intend to pay them.

units.la: Suscipere votum est votis se obligare. Moris autem erat,ut vota suscipirentur a Romanis pro principibus in expedicionem enunciabus,ut solpites incolumes qi irent & reverterentur. Hinc ajt Seneca,olim Rufum, ordinis Senatorii virum inter coenam optasse, ne salvus Caesar rediret in ea peregrinatione,quam parabat : & adjecisse, idem omnes tauros & virulos optare. Sic Haractus voto prosequitur Caesarem,profectionem parantem in ultimos Britannos.Suetonius in Vesa Tyberii: Quam vis provincias quoq; & exercitus revisurum se saepe pronunciasset, & propquotannis profectionem praeparabat : vehiculus comprehensis,commeatibus per municipia & colonias disposites, vota pro itu & reditu suo, suscipere passus, &c.
units.tr: Suscipere votum means to bind oneself by vows. It was the custom for the Romans to undertake vows for princes setting out on an expedition, that they might go and return safe. Hence Seneca says that once Rufus, a man of senatorial rank, wished at dinner that Caesar might not return safe from the journey he was preparing, and added that all bulls and heifers wished the same. Thus Haractus follows Caesar with a vow as he prepares to set out against the remotest Britons. Suetonius, Life of Tiberius: "Although he had often announced that he would revisit the provinces and armies, and every year prepared for departure, having arranged carriages and supplies through the municipia and colonies, he allowed vows to be undertaken for his going out and his return, and so on."

units.la: Votum porro facere est idem,quod optare vel precari.Cicero in familiaribus: Nemo est, quin vota victoriae tuae fecerit. Sic votum debere,reddere,solvere, persolvere:item voto tenerī frequenter apud Ciceronem occurrunt.
units.tr: Votum facere is the same as optare or precari, to wish or pray. Cicero, Letters to Friends: "There is no one who has not made vows for your victory." So too votum debere, reddere, solvere and persolvere, and voto teneri, occur frequently in Cicero.

units.la: A voto hic votivus,id quod ex voto promittitur: unde vociva legatio,quae pro voto ac voluntate, vel voluntarie promititur:& voci va verba, quibus utimur in votis faciendis & votivae preces,quibus aliquid cum voto poscimus. Sic a voveo, Devovere ejusdem significatio- nem: quam vis etiam pro morte sese addicere, ut morte sua populus sive Respublica servetur : vel aliquando pro, diris imprecationibus malum alicui optare. Cicero post reditum : Me fortunas meas pro vestra incolumitate,concordia, devovi. Caesar de bello Gallico:Neq; adhuc hominum memoria repertus est qui quam,qui eo interfecto, cujus se amicitiae devovisset , mori recusaret. Titus Livius: Equidem mortem pro patria praeclaram esse fateor,ut me vel devovere pro populo Romano legionibus,q; vel in meos me mittere hostes paratus sim.Virgilius: Quorum se devovet aris
units.tr: From votum comes votivus, that which is promised by a vow. Hence votiva legatio is a embassy promised according to wish and will, or voluntarily; votiva verba are the words we use in making vows; and votivae preces are prayers by which we ask something with a vow. Devovere has the same meaning as vovere, though it also means to devote oneself to death, so that the people or commonwealth may be saved by one's death, or sometimes to wish evil on someone with dire curses. Cicero, after his return: "I devoted my fortunes for your safety and concord." Caesar, Gallic War: "Nor until now has anyone been found in human memory who refused to die when the man to whose friendship he had devoted himself was slain." Livy: "Indeed I confess that death for the fatherland is glorious, so that I am ready to devote myself for the Roman people to the legions, or to send myself into my enemies." Virgil: "Of whom he devotes himself to the altars."

units.la: Ovidius in Ibin: Illum ego devoveo,quem mens intelligit,Ibin.
units.tr: Ovid, in the Ibis: "Him I curse, whom my mind knows as Ibis."

units.la: Inde fit de votor, de votrix, & de votum, idem quod destinatum, modo ad prosperum, modo ad aduersum relatum. Cicero: Miloni de voto & constituta ista bostia videtur. Virgilius:
units.tr: From this come votor, votrix, and votum, which mean the same as destinatum, applied sometimes to a good outcome and sometimes to a bad one. Cicero: "This victim seems to be vowed and appointed for Milo."
Virgil: "The hostile troops pressed upon Decius, the one devoted."

units.la: Idem: Præcipuè infelix pesti de vota futurę.
units.tr: Idem: "Especially unhappy from the plague that is to be vowed."

units.la: Varro: Tu de voto tibi animo utere.
units.tr: Varro: "Make use of your own mind in regard to the vow."

units.la: Eandem significationem retinet De votio. Est enim destinatio, vel exsecratio. Suetonius in Caligula: Lenis adeo & innoxius, ut Pisoni, decreta sua rescindenti, non priùs succensere in animum induxerit, quàm veneficiis quoque & de votionibus impugnari se comperisset.
units.tr: The same meaning is kept by devotio, for it means either a dedication or a curse. Suetonius, in Caligula: "He was so mild and harmless that, when Piso rescinded his decrees, he did not bring himself to be angry until he learned that he was also being assailed with poisons and curses."

units.la: Denique a voveo, Conuoti, iisdem videlicet votis obligati, & voto vel votito frequentatitum, sunt orta.
