Votitum Veteres etiam ufurparunt, pro eo, quod est religione aliqua prohibitum atque interdictum. Plautus: Nolo illam habere caussam & votitam dicere. Quidam tamen a vetando, quasi vetitum dictum volunt.
units.tr: Finally, from voveo come conuoti, those bound by the same vows, and, by frequentative form, voto or votito. The ancients also used votitum for what is forbidden or prohibited by some religious scruple. Plautus: "I do not want to have her as a reason and say it is forbidden." Some, however, want it derived from vetare, as if it were called vetitum.
These are the Latin terms.

units.la: GRÆCA nomina atque verba, quibus precandi ista actio exprimitur, sunt primum ιυχὴ, ποιητικὰ ιυχαλὴν, ...
units.tr: The Greek nouns and verbs by which this act of praying is expressed are, first, prayer [εὐχὴ], to pray [εὔχεσθαι], making a prayer [ποιητικὰ εὐχήν]...

units.la: Nomina atque verba Græca precum. Ευχὴ, ιυχὴ, &c.
units.tr: Greek nouns and verbs of prayer: prayer [εὐχὴ], to pray [εὔχομαι], etc.

units.la: Descendunt inde ικεσια, supplicatio. (Plutarchus: ικεσίας χαριν ὑπὲρ τῆς ... supplicibus manibus orabant: ικέτης, supplex.)
units.tr: From these come supplication [ἱκεσία] (Plutarch: "for the sake of supplication... they begged with suppliant hands"); a suppliant [ἱκέτης].

units.la: Tertiò precandi actionem exprimunt Græci etiam verbo αιτεῖν, vel αἴτησις: quod posterius commune est verbum: nunc actiuè constructum, ut αἰτῶμαι τὸν ἀνθρωπον, rogo hominem.
units.tr: Thirdly, the Greeks also express the act of praying by the verb to ask [αἰτεῖν], or a request [αἴτησις]. The latter is a common word, now used actively, as "I ask the man" [αἰτῶμαι τὸν ἄνθρωπον].

units.la: 2. Ικέτης, ικε-σία, &c. 3. Αιτέω, αἴ-τησις. bola,quæ dantur ad canam : αἴτης, pauper,mendicus,qui semper petit : αἰτητικὸς, idem : αἰτητικός, propensus ad precandum:αἰτητὸς,petitus,ut αἰτητὸς αἰχμὴ, petitum imperium,& αἰτηθεῖσα quo quippiam petitum est. Thucydides libro secundo : αἰχμὴ λὼ αἰτηθεῖσα ut δοῦσα, halτησαι, μὴ τυχεῖν, deformius erat eum , qui posceretur,non dare , quàm eum , qui posceret non impetrare.
units.tr: 2. Suppliant [ἱκέτης], supplication [ἱκεσία], etc. 3. To ask [αἰτέω], a request [αἴτησις]. Alms given at a meal; a beggar [αἴτης], a poor man who always asks; likewise [αἰτητικός], one inclined to ask; [αἰτητός], asked for, as a dominion asked for; and a thing for which something has been asked. Thucydides, book 2: it was more shameful for the one who was asked not to give than for the one who asked not to obtain.

units.la: Quarto referendum huc est verbum Διομαι,ortum vel a Διος, hoc est, necessarium , quid a Deo non nisi necessaria,quorum vel maximè indigemus,petere debeamus: vel a ΔΘ, id est, timor,quid cum Dei timore et reverentia conjuncta nostra debeat esse supplicatio. Hinc autem Διομαι Διοπερηφος, imploro auxilii, Thucydides : Διομαι σὲ τοῦ, rogo te hoc, Aristophanes: Ἀλλὰ πάντα ἀποτ-σαι ἠιοψοποτ, omnes preces adhibere Plutarch dixere.Διοις enim petitio est vel preces.
units.tr: Fourthly, the verb to beg [δέομαι] should be referred here, derived either from [δεῖ], meaning necessity, since we ought to ask from God only necessary things, and especially those we most need; or from [δέος], meaning fear, since our supplication ought to be joined with the fear and reverence of God. Hence "I implore help" [δέομαι], and Thucydides: "I ask you this" [δέομαι σοῦ τοῦτο]. Aristophanes, and Plutarch, said "to bring every kind of prayer." For a petition [δέησις] is a request or a prayer.

units.la: His adde verba Λιασαι, vel Λιασθαι, et Λιτ-αι, vel Λιτεσθαι: item Λιτασ-ασθαι, idem quod ἱκετεύειν et ἱκέσ-σ: quorum priori aliquoties usus est Homerus: ut, Odyss. ο. Λιασομαι Ζεὺς, precor per sacra. Et Iliad. α. ἀλιστίου πάντας ἀχαιοὺς, ... Supplicavit omnibus Achivis: Et Iliad. τ. Λιασόμενοι ἀγελαττ-ες, rogantes,ut prandium funerent.
units.tr: To these add the verbs to entreat [λισσάσθαι] or [λίσσεσθαι], and the entreaties [λιταί] or [λιτέσθαι]; also to supplicate [λιτάζεσθαι], the same as to beseech [ἱκετεύειν] and supplication [ἱκεσία]. Homer used the first several times: Odyssey ο: "I beseech Zeus" [λίσσομαι Ζεύς], I pray by sacred things. Iliad α: he supplicated all the Achaeans. And Iliad τ: those beseeching that they might bury the dead at a feast.

units.la: Sic Apollonius Argonaut. 2. dixit Sjas Λιασθαι, Deos precari. Posteriori idem usus est iusti, Od. ξ.
units.tr: So Apollonius, Argonautica 2, used [λίσσασθαι] for to pray to the gods. Homer used the latter form too, Odyssey ξ.

units.la: Et Iliad. π. Οι αὐτὸ θέαντοι τε χρυσὸν ... ἄμφι Λιτέσθαι.
units.tr: And Iliad π: "those who ... with gold ... around to supplicate."

units.la: Hinc Λιτὰι, supplicatio, supplices preces, obsecratio, & Λιγαὶ Homero Dea praesides supplicationum, & Λιτ-σὶ & supplex: ut, Λιτ-σιος αὐχὴν, apud Nonn. supplex dorsum. Sic & verbo Λιγ-ευειν idem Homerus utiter, ut Iliad. χ. πάντας δ' ἀλλιτάνδας νυλυσδομένῳ κατὰ κόσμον Omnibus quidem supplicavit, volutus in cæno.
units.tr: Hence [λιταί], supplication, supplicating prayers, entreaty; and Homer's [Λιταί], goddesses presiding over supplications; and [λιτός], a suppliant, as in [λιτὸς αὐχήν], a suppliant neck, in Nonnus. So also Homer used the verb [λιτανεύειν] in Iliad χ: "he supplicated them all, rolling in the mud."

units.la: Sic Hesiod.in Theogn. —φίλης λιτάνδα τοκήας Μὴτ συμφιλιτασθε : amici supplica, &c.
units.tr: So Hesiod, in the Theogony: "the entreaties of dear parents..." and "let us not join in entreating with friends," and so on.

units.la: Hinc Λιτανεία, supplicatio, supplices preces, obsecratio,vulgo Litania.
units.tr: Hence [λιτανεία], supplication, supplicating prayers, entreaty, commonly called litany.

units.la: Denique huc refer ἀχαῖ, quasi ἀχαῖ, id est, supplicationes, vota, optata, & ἀποσθαι quæ supplicationes ad altaria Aristophanes in Nebulis exponit. Inde ἀποσθαι ιλαν apud Athenæum carmina, quæ canuntur, quum Diis supplicatur, & eorum altaria, ac pulvinaria precesfunt. Aliquando Svsias & ἀποσθαι sacrificia & supplicationes ab Ioscrate & Demostheme conjunguntur, ut τὰ ἀγαθὰ, ἰλάσκασθαι θεὸν ἀποσθαι, supplicationibus, sacrificiis, colere, vel placare Deum, supplicationibus, & sacrificiis.
units.tr: Finally, refer here [ἀχαί], as if from [ἀχαί], that is, supplications, vows, wishes; and [ἀποσθαι], which Aristophanes in the Clouds explains as supplications at the altars. Hence in Athenaeus [ἀποσθαι] are songs that are sung when the gods are supplicated, and the altars and cushions are the prayers. Sometimes sacrifices [θυσίαι] and supplications [ἀποσθαι] are joined by Isocrates and Demosthenes, as in [τὰ ἀγαθά, ἱλάσκεσθαι θεόν]: to worship or to appease God with supplications and sacrifices.

units.la: Hujusmodi fuerunt Græca nomina atque verba, quibus precandi actio exprimitur. Ayt.
units.tr: Such were the Greek nouns and verbs by which the act of praying is expressed. Thus far.

units.la: HEBRAEOS actio hæc exprimitur verbo שאל Schaal,quod petere,postulare,quærere, interrogare significat : nonnunquam etiam,mutuum petere:item,obtinere, quod petit. Esaiæ septimo, שאל לך אות מעם יהוה Scheal lechá oth mehim lehouá , Pete tibi signum à Iehova. Sic Deuteronomii decimo octavo idem Dei filiis tribuitur: Non inveniatur in te שאל ... ישׁאל Schóel ob veideHóni, interrogans Pythonem, aut sciolum (alii, interpretantur, Iconium.) Inde autem fit שאלה Scheelah, postulatio, petitio, &c. Et hæc de nominibus præcum, sive precationum satis sint dicta.
units.tr: Among the Hebrews this act is expressed by the verb [שאל], sha'al, which means to ask, to demand, to seek, to inquire; sometimes also to borrow, and to obtain what one asks for. Isaiah 7: "Ask for yourself a sign from the LORD" [שְׁאַל לְךָ אוֹת מֵעִם יְהוָה], Scheal lecha oth mehim Jehovah. Likewise, Deuteronomy 18 attributes the same to the children of God: "let there not be found among you one who asks [יִשְׁאַל] of the dead or consults a spirit of divination" (others render it differently). Hence [שְׁאֵלָה], she'elah, a request, a petition, and so on. Let these suffice as to the names of prayers, or entreaties.

units.la: Vt autem in sacrificiis, sita in precibus sacris, quæ vel in, vel cum, vel etiam extra sacrificia fiebant, confederabant diligenter, Quis precaretur, pro Quo, Quem, Quid, Vbi, Quando, Quomodo, & Cur.Quantum ad primum, is, qui precatur, precator, deprecator, aliusque nominibus a Latinis appellatur. Hoc autem cum omnium hominum, tum sacerdotum in primis et antiquitus cum rei divinæ, tum Reipublicæ munus esse existimabant.
units.tr: Now, just as in sacrifices, the sacred prayers, which were made either in, or with, or even outside the sacrifices, were carefully considered: who should pray, for whom, what, where, when, how, and why. As to the first, the one who prays is called a prayer-maker, an entreater, and other names in Latin. They thought this was the duty not only of all men but especially of priests, both in matters of divine worship and of the state.

units.la: Deinde non tantùm pro se, sed etiam pro aliis vel privatis hominibus, vel etiam pro universa familia, civitate, populo sibi precandum existimabant.
units.tr: Next, they thought that one should pray not only for oneself but also for others, whether private persons, or the whole family, city, or people.

units.la: Precum sacrarum,ut & sacrificiorum , objectum generale putabant esse cum Deos & Deas omnes,tum certos precantium Deos atq.Deas: principiò tamen precationis ad janum et Vestam dirigi solebat,quæ in omnibus sacris præcipua Numina habebantur, In totis enim nuncupandis perpetuam hi mensure praefationem. Hinc Fabius Seruilianus Pontifex M. disciplina traditum fuit ut alio die Manibus parentare non liceret, ne infesti Manes fierent: quia alio die nec Ianum, nec Vestam praefari licebat, sed tamen est Gyraldus. De Iano Fabius Pictor lib. a. Vnum, inquit, & far primus illos docuit Ianus, ad sacrificia & religionem magis, quàm ad esum & potum. Primus enim vas & pomaria & sacra docuit, & ob illum omnis sacrificio perpetua praefatio praemittitur, farg, it & vnum praelibatur. Illos tamen, qui ad aram Maximam sacra faciebant, alium, quam Herculem, Deum adorare non decebat. Cui vero Deo sacrum fuerat constitutum, id morus fuit, ut poi ipsum reliqui in vocarentur, ut volentes & propitii votis & precationibus adessent: Domitianus tamen Minervam genitricem & Ant. Heliogabalus suum Deum praeponi mandarunt. In Peloponnefo Melissa Nympha, quae vsum mellis illis dedisse creditur est, in sacrorum praefatione adhibebatur. Sane & cuique Deo sua carmina suaque precationes instituta erant, quae compositae verbis efferebantur: & neque praeponi forte duceretur, aut verborum aliquid praeteriretur, aliquis praeire sui solitus, rursusq, alius custos datus, qui attenderet sodalem: alius, qui favere linguis iuberet, & tibicen cecinit; ne quid infaustum exaudiretur: id quod Liuio & aliis scriptoribus patet. Materia precum generalis erat, quod vel precabantur a Dijs suis bona & animi & corporis 4. Quid. & fortunae, & publica & priuata: vel deprecabantur mala animi, corporis & fortunae, eaque similiter vel publica vel priuata. Preces autem hunc in modum in templis & ad altaria ante ora, sed fi, idolis atque simulacra suorum Deorum, item ad sepulcra, sibi potissimum faciendas esse putabant. Aliqui locum, quod hic obiter notandum, in quo ceteri petitores, & postulatores conuenire solebant, apud Romanos, erant pontes, & clivus Argivus propter confluentes ad templum Dianae, vt locus profecta dicebatur. Ἀπὸ τῶν ἀπο ποταμῶν: ἀπὸ ϑεῶν. Iuuenalis: Ad ... ubi consistas, in qua te quaero, proseucha. Quantum ad tempus; sacrificiorum potissimum tempore, sibi perfundebant preces suas Diis 6. Quando. suis esse gratas & acceptas. Habebant enim, ut sacrificandi, ita iuppiter Dei suis certa & definita tempora. Quantum ad modum attinet; certam ut animi: ita corporis affectionem ac dispositionem 7 Quomodo. precationibus requirebant. Habebant etiam certas precandi formulas, de quibus postea. Inde Asmouoicrune autem constat, modum precandi duplicem fuisse: alium animi & internum; alium corporis & externum. Quantum ad animi affectionem, seu modi internum; ut is esset piis, casus, mundus, sincerus, purus, a privatis obligationibus & cupiditatibus alienus & innocens necesse erat: quo tamen Gentiles carebant, cum animi ipsorum pravis imbuti atque infectis essent erroribus, & opinionibus; prava eorum esset mens, prava affectus, & vacui vera Dei scientia & cognitione. De hoc interno modo precandi vide Hesiodum, Platonem, Ciceronem. Quantum ad externum & corporum modum attinet; qui in voce, verbis, corporis cum tot Corpore exter status, sum singularum ejus partium, vestitu, latvatione, dispositione, situ, gestibus consistit, ei potissimum studebant, & in eo omnem fere pietatem sanctitatemq, collocabant. Quantum ad vocem; Voce. al quando voce utebantur submissa, aliquando alta, clara, intenta & clamosa. Hinc Pythagorei jubent cum voce precari. Non quod, ut mihi quidem videtur, existimarent, Deum non posse exaudire eos, qui tacite loquuntur, sed quod iustas vellent esse preces, quas non vereatur quis sun deri multis eas scientibus. Noti sunt etiam illi Baalitcorum sacerdotum clamores & vociferationes in sacris litteris, quas in precibus & supplicationibus suis adhibuerunt: quas Helias Prophetae sae perstrinxit & irrisit. Notum item illud, quod in decimo ab Vrbe condita apud Liuium legimus, Marcum Attilium Cos. cum ad versus Samnites atrox bellum esset, manus ad coelum tulisse, voce clara, ita ut exaudiretur, templum Iouis Statoris vouisse, si confistitisset a fuga Romana acies. Haec Liuius. Voce item usi fuerunt vel simplici, vel canora cantillantes. Quod ad verba, verbis plerunque, usi fuerunt barbaris, obscenis, obsoletis: cuiusmodi erant ple- Verbis. raque, verba, quibus in toto cultu atque religione suis fuit usi, quibus ipsi autoritatem quidem religionis suae confirmare fuerant conati, sed meram ejus barbariem & absurditatem, huiusmodi verborum barbarie & absurditate prodiderunt. P 2 Deinde in precibus suis aliquando βεχυλογία, Laconica, sed plerum·que ἀ... [illegible, ~40 letters] Ethnicus in sacris litteris tributit, ab eo ritu atq; more Ethnico dijsipulos suos debuerat...
units.tr: They thought the general object of sacred prayers, as of sacrifices, was all gods and goddesses, but also certain gods and goddesses chosen by the one praying. Yet prayer was usually first directed to Janus and Vesta, who were held to be the chief divinities in all sacred rites, for in all invocations they had a perpetual preface. Hence Fabius Servilianus, pontiff, was taught by tradition that it was not lawful to make parentalia to the Manes on another day, lest the Manes become hostile, because on another day neither Janus nor Vesta could be invoked first; but Gyraldus says so. Concerning Janus, Fabius Pictor, book 2: "Janus, he says, was the first to teach them spelt and salt, for sacrifice and religion rather than for eating and drinking. For he first taught the vessel, the fruit-bowl and the sacred rites, and because of him every sacrifice is preceded by a perpetual preface, and spelt and salt are offered first." Yet those who performed sacred rites at the Great Altar ought not to worship any god other than Hercules. Whatever god had been appointed to a sacrifice, it was the custom that the others were called upon along with him, so that they might be present, willing and favourable, to vows and prayers; Domitian, however, ordered Minerva his mother to be put first, and Antoninus Heliogabalus ordered his own god to be placed before all. In Peloponnesus the nymph Melissa, who is believed to have taught them the use of honey, was invoked in the preface to the sacred rites. Indeed, to each god their own songs and their own prayers were set down, which were uttered in fixed words; and lest anything be put in the wrong place or any word be omitted, one man was accustomed to lead the words, and again another was appointed as watchman to attend to his fellow, and another to bid them favour their tongues, while the flute-player played, so that nothing inauspicious might be heard. This is clear from Livy and other writers. The matter of prayers was general: they prayed to their gods for good things of mind, body and fortune, both public and private; or they prayed against evils of mind, body and fortune, likewise public or private. Moreover, they thought that prayers ought to be made especially in temples, at altars, before the faces of idols and images of their gods, and likewise at tombs, which is worth noting here in passing. Among the Romans the place where other petitioners and suppliants used to gather was the bridges and the Argive slope near the temple of Diana, from the place where it was said that they set out. Quantum ad tempus: at the time of sacrifices especially, they were eager that their prayers should be pleasing and acceptable to their gods, for they had fixed and defined times for sacrificing and for praying. As to manner, they required a fixed disposition of the mind and likewise of the body for their prayers. They also had fixed formulas of prayer, which will be discussed later. It is agreed that the manner of praying was twofold: one inward, of the mind; the other outward, of the body. As to the disposition of the mind, or the inward manner, it was necessary that the one praying be pious, chaste, clean, sincere, pure, free from private obligations and lusts, and innocent; but the Gentiles lacked this, since their minds were steeped and infected with wicked errors and opinions; their mind was wicked, their affections wicked, and they were empty of the true knowledge of God. On this inward manner of praying see Hesiod, Plato, and Cicero. As to the outward manner and the bodily aspect, which consists in voice, words, the whole external posture of the body, the individual parts of it, clothing, washing, arrangement, position, and gestures, they devoted themselves especially to these, and in them they placed nearly all their piety and holiness. As to voice: at times they used a subdued voice, at other times a loud, clear, intense and clamorous one. Hence the Pythagoreans bid one to pray with voice. Not, as it seems to me, because they thought God could not hear those who speak silently, but because they wished their prayers to be just, and not to be ashamed for many to know them. Those cries and shoutings of the priests of Baal in Holy Scripture are also well known, which they used in their prayers and supplications, and which the prophet Elijah lashed and mocked. Likewise known is what we read in Livy's tenth book from the foundation of the city: that Marcus Attilius, consul, when a fierce war was waged against the Samnites, lifted his hands to heaven and vowed, in a clear voice so that he could be heard, a temple to Jupiter the Stayer, if the Roman battle line should be re-established after its flight. So Livy. They also used a voice, either plain or singing and chanting. As to words: they mostly used barbarous, obscene, obsolete words, such as were most of the words by which they used in all their worship and religion; with these they tried to confirm the authority of their religion, but by such barbarism and absurdity of words they betrayed its utter barbarism and absurdity. Then in their prayers they sometimes used Laconian brevity... [the rest is illegible] ...the Gentile, in Holy Scripture, is given; from that rite and custom of the Gentiles his disciples ought to have been...

units.la: Praeterea ut in uniuerso suo culti, ita in precibus, & supplicationibus publicis usi aliquando corporis vestitu & habitu sordido, squallido, lugubri: aliquando splendido & nato. Nonnunquam etiam furiosorum ritu vestes suas scindere atque dilaceraire fuerunt: quod Ieremias in sua epistola ad Iudaeos, Babyloniorum etiam sacerdotes in more pium fuisse testatur.
units.tr: Moreover, in their whole worship, and in public prayers and supplications, they sometimes wore a dress and bearing that was squalid, filthy and mournful, and at other times splendid and festive. Sometimes, too, in the manner of madmen, they tore and rent their garments. Jeremiah, in his letter to the Jews, testifies that the priests of the Babylonians also did this as a pious act.

units.la: Corpora quoque & vestes suas, primsquam ad sacra & supplicationes accedebant, abluere, lebant. Hinc apud Homerum Penelope bausta aqua, mundas gestans in corpore vestes, ad preces dicitur venisse, de qua sic Eustathius: [Greek text] Sic Priamus: fit Telemachus ablutus manus pelu Minervae vota fecit; item alio in loco, nempe Illiad. 1. ad eundem morem alludens:
units.tr: They also used to wash their bodies and clothes before they approached sacred rites and supplications. Hence in Homer, Penelope, having drawn water and wearing clean clothes on her body, is said to have come to prayer. Eustathius says of this: [Greek]. So Priam... Telemachus, having washed his hands in water, made vows to Minerva. Likewise, in another place, namely Iliad 1, alluding to the same custom:

units.la: Φίτη ὁ χεῖρ' ὑδάρ, ὑπτηνων τε κλιάων, Οφθα δὲ Κεγίδ' αρπονίμεν' ἀχ' ἑλαύτρ...
units.tr: They washed their hands in water, and [took up the sacred barley] [Greek, garbled in the scan].
"Bring water," he says, "bring water, and bid them speak,

units.la: Vt jo'ri Saturnio supplicemus, si mijere aitur.
units.tr: So that we may supplicate Jove, son of Saturn, if the matter is spoken of mercifully."

units.la: Quo sane externo ritu lauandi manus, docent illi veteres, quam pure ad preces Deo fundendas accedendum sit, quem niorem Iudaeorum quoque iussse historia sacra testatur. Clemens ver Alexandrinus has corporeas utrorumque ablutiones perstringens ait: [Greek text] Asunt, nos oportere lotos, mundos [Greek] ... sed ad sacra precesque accedere. Addit: [Greek text] ... μετὰ ταῦτα τὸ ... [Greek text] id est, Non lavacro, sed animo & mente mundus esto. Emendatio enim, opinio perfecta animi est & operum & cogitationum sinceritas item perfectio monum, & innocentia in somniis. Sic idonea, fine dubio, homini lustratio est pœnitentia accurata, & constans, etc.
units.tr: Indeed, those ancient writers teach by this outward rite of washing the hands how pure one ought to be when approaching God in prayer, and sacred history testifies that the Jews also were commanded this cleanness. Clement of Alexandria, touching on these bodily washings of both peoples, says: [Greek]. He says that we ought to come to sacred rites and prayers washed and clean, [Greek]... but not by bathing; come clean in soul and mind. He adds: [Greek]..., that is, "Be clean not by washing but in soul and mind." For correction is the perfect opinion of the soul, and the sincerity of works and thoughts, likewise the perfection of manners and innocence in the affections. Thus, without doubt, the proper cleansing for a man is a careful and steadfast repentance, and so on.

units.la: Corporis item tam totius, tum singularum eius partium atque membrorum licet ✕ dispositionem habent, sed in terra, quam proftratione Hebraei verbo השתחוה Hifchtachave de quo supra, exprimunt, & Graeci verbo προσκυνεῖν: vel stantes aut sedentes vota facie bant, unde Pythagoras symbolum, καθ' ἡσυχίαν ... adoraturi sedeant: cuius symbolum tam expositionem vide in Adagiis Erasmi: vel corpus etiam totum vertebant in partes Mundi. Hinc Trismegistus Mercurius censuit, ut adorantes nudo die se ... recerent ad Austrum: occiduo ad Occasum: si vero primum oriretur Solis in Ortum. Fusi ... Tyanei opinio, sumnio dilui ulo cum Deus versandum, procedente mox die, de Deo ... Sic ex Graecis in Pindarum Commentarii constat, ad Orientem convertendo corpore Deus ... atque sacra fieri: berobus vero ad Occasum consuevisse. Porphyrius item Philosophus ... plorum flatuas & ingressus Orientem spectare debere statuit, ut adeuntes in occasum convert & in simulacrorum ora: id est, [Greek]... precesque effunderent: unde & Lucianus templa dii ad Orientem solem Veteres consuevisse testatur. Persæ quoque praeside ad Orientem oran sse docebant: quo pertinet pro verbum [Greek] apud Erasmum, & testimonium illud Apulei libro secundo: Tum in Orientem, inquit, ob versus, vel instrumenta So gusti tacitus imprecant.
units.tr: Likewise, of the whole body, and of its several parts and members, they had various postures. They expressed prostration on the ground by the Hebrew word השתחוה (hishtachaveh), mentioned above, and by the Greek word προσκυνεῖν. Or they made their vows standing or sitting; hence Pythagoras's symbol, [Greek]: "when about to worship, let them sit quietly." For the explanation of this symbol see Erasmus's Adages. Or they even turned the whole body toward the parts of the world. Hence Trismegistus Mercurius advised that those adoring at dawn should turn toward the south, at evening toward the west, and if the sun first rose, toward the east. The opinion of Apollonius of Tyana, that one must pray with the body turned to the rising sun as the day advanced, is well known. From the Greeks' commentaries on Pindar it is clear that they used to turn the body to the east when praying and performing sacred rites, and that they were accustomed to turn to the west when the rites were of the underworld. Likewise the philosopher Porphyry decided that the statues of the gods and their entrances ought to face east, so that those approaching should turn toward the west and the faces of the images, [Greek], and pour out their prayers. Hence Lucian also testifies that the ancients were accustomed to build temples facing the rising sun. The Persians also taught that they should pray facing the sun. To this belongs the Greek word [Greek] in Erasmus, and that passage of Apuleius in book 2: "Then," he says, "they silently invoke the gods facing east, turning their..."

units.la: Quod deinde ad corporis partes attinet; constat in precando certos gestus vel capitis, vel manuum vel pedum fuisse. Nam pretantes non solum caput totum huc vel illuc vertebant, & capite alias aperto: alias operto ut sacrificabant, ita precabantur: item illud oculos & tingere cum veneratione & honoris, tum precandi caussa solebant, id quod Homerus de Eumæo & Dolo. & Dolio, Vlyssis servis scribit, eos caput & humeros domini sui sculpatos, & item Vlyssem illo‑rum, Odyss.‑φ. Sed etiam vultus, partem nimirum capitis anteriorem, vel in altum tollebant, vel in terram dejiciebant; quo fortassis illud Ouidii: Os homini sublime dedit, cœlumque videre Iussit & erectos ad sidera tollere vultus.
units.tr: As for the parts of the body, it is clear that in praying there were certain gestures of the head, hands or feet. For those praying not only turned the whole head this way or that, and sometimes with the head uncovered, sometimes covered, as they sacrificed, so they prayed; they also used to touch their eyes, both in reverence and honour and for the sake of prayer. Homer writes this of Eumaeus and Dolius, the servants of Ulysses, that they kissed the head and shoulders of their master, and likewise Ulysses did to them, Odyssey φ. But they also raised the face, that is, the forepart of the head, either up on high or cast it down to the ground. Perhaps this is what Ovid means: "He gave man an upright face, and bade him behold the heavens and lift his face erect to the stars."
And that of Homer, Iliad τ:

units.la: Ἀρξαμένη δ' ἀ̈ες ἐἴπερ, ἰδὼν ὡς ὁ ἐγγὺς ὑψοῦ. Supplicans autem dixit suspiciens in cœlum laxum.
units.tr: [Greek, garbled] "Praying, she spoke, looking up at the wide heaven."

units.la: Sic Antiquos Græcos in supplicando mentum attingere solitos testatur Plinius libro undecimo, capite quadragesimo quinto.
units.tr: Thus Pliny, in book 11, chapter 45, testifies that the ancient Greeks were accustomed to touch the chin when supplicating.

units.la: Solitoque quoque fuerunt manus complicare, expandere, in altum tollere. Unde Lactantius
units.tr: It was also customary to fold the hands, to spread them, and to raise them on high. Hence Lactantius

units.la: 1. Manuum. Grammaticus, Altaria voluit esse dista, quòd circa illa manus in altum tollebantur. Hinc Virgilius quarto Æneid. Multa Iovem manibus supplex orâsse supinis Dicitur, &c.
units.tr: Book 1, on hands: a grammarian wished altars to be so called because hands were raised on high around them. Hence Virgil, in Aeneid 4: "Many times, as a suppliant, he is said to have prayed to Jove with upturned hands," and so on.

units.la: Et secunda Æneidos: Atque pater Anchises oculos ad sidera lætus Extulit & cœlo palmas cum voce tetendit: Iupiter Omnipotens, &c.
units.tr: And in the second book of the Aeneid: "And father Anchises, joyful, lifted his eyes to the stars and stretched out his palms to heaven with his voice: 'Almighty Jupiter,' and so on."

units.la: Sic Iliad. α. Chryses dicitur precatus esse Apollinem ἀναχθὼν τὰς χεῖρας, sublatis manibus, quod Eustathius interpretatur, ὡς ἀπείνας εἰς ἱερὸν.
units.tr: Thus in Iliad 1, Chryses is said to have prayed to Apollo, "lifting up his hands," which Eustathius explains as "as one who had come to the temple."

units.la: Legimus quinetiam, illos cùm sacrificantes, tum precantes, ut etiam jusjurandum (quod est species precationis, ut suo loco audiemus) facientes, manibus aram tenuisse. Nam nisi manu tenerentur, non licari putabatur. Hinc Varro lib. 5. aras ansas vult dictas, quòd esset necessarium a sacrificantibus eas tenere: cui opinioni Macrobium suffragari, ex quo verbum, quæ supra quoq; citavi, colligitur: Multifariam, inquit, legimus, quod litare sola non possit oratio, nisi is, qui Deos precatur, etiam aram manibus apprehendat, quam opinionem Virgilii auctoritate comprobat. Is 4. Æneid. sic canit: Talibus orantem dictis arasq; tenentem Audiit Omnipotens, &c.
units.tr: We read, moreover, that they, both when sacrificing and when praying, and also when swearing an oath (which is a kind of prayer, as we shall hear in its place), held the altar with their hands. For unless they were held by the hand, it was thought the prayer would not be heard. Hence Varro, in book 5, holds that altars (aras) were called "ansae" because it was necessary for those sacrificing to hold them. Macrobius agrees with this opinion, from which the word I cited above is also derived. He says: "We read in many places that prayer cannot be successful unless the one praying also grasps the altar with his hands," and he confirms this opinion by the authority of Virgil. In Aeneid 4 he sings thus: "The Almighty heard her, speaking such words and holding the altars," and so on.

units.la: Et alio loco: Tango aras, medios ignes, & Numina testor.
units.tr: And in another place: "I touch the altars, the middle fires, and call the divinities to witness."

units.la: Item 6. Æneid. Talibus orabat dictis arasq; tenebat.
units.tr: Likewise in Aeneid 6: "Speaking such words, he prayed and held the altars."

units.la: Hinc nonnulli aras, ut supra quoq; dictum, aprecationibus, sive etiam imprecationibus, quas Græci ἀρὰς appellant, volunt dictas.
units.tr: Hence some hold that altars, as said above too, are so named from prayers (aprecationes), or even from curses, which the Greeks call ἀραί.

units.la: Nec verò tamen, qui precabantur, manus complicabant, extendebant, in altum tollebant, sed etiam aliorum manus, a quibus quid petebant, partim tetigerunt, partim exosculati sunt. De prio‑ri Virg. Æneid. 7. Pars mihi pacis erit, dextram tetigisse tyranni.
units.tr: Yet those who prayed did not only fold, spread and raise their hands; they also touched the hands of others from whom they sought something, and some kissed them. Of the former, Virgil in Aeneid 7: "It will be a part of peace for me to have touched the right hand of the tyrant."

units.la: Deposteriori Homerus Iliad. α. —ἀγχὲ δ' ἄεα ς ας
units.tr: Of the latter, Homer, Iliad 1: [Greek, garbled].

units.la: Manibus Achillis tetigit genua, & manus osculatus est.
units.tr: He touched Achilles' knees with his hands and kissed his hands.

units.la: Cornelius Tacitus: Ad genua ipsius advolvi & dextram osculo fatigavi.
units.tr: Cornelius Tacitus: "I threw myself down at his knees and wore out his right hand with kisses."

units.la: Hic juvat in genere quædam de osculo subjungere. Osculum quasi os parvum dicitur Latinis. De osculo in nus, quia osculando os coaptamus atque minimum, & quasi ex ore osculum facimus: a quo Ofcu-lor, & Osculator, Osculatio; item, Exosculor & Exosculatio. Aliter Basium (unde Italicum Nomina osculi basiare, & Gallicum baiser) Basio, Basiator, Basiatio dicuntur. Suavium quinetiam osculum Latina vocatur a sua vitate: unde Suavio, Suaviator, Suaviatio; & Disuaviatio, Disuaviator. Quidam hac ita distinguunt, ut osculum sis officii, ut cùm e longinquo redeuntes, vel digredientes ali cundo salutamus atque osculamur: in quam sententiam Plutarchus in Vita Catonis Vticensis scribit, ipso de Provincia digrediente, milites reverenter manum osculatos fuisse: quod genus tamen non nisi Imperatoribus, quæ perpaucis cum temporis tributum fuit. Idem testatur Pomponius Latus in suo Compendio Romanarum historiarum. Basium porrò pudicorum erat, ut patris in filium, uxoris in maritum. Suavium vero voluptatis: unde idem quod dulce, & suavitas sive sua tudo, idem quod dulcedo. Plautus: Cor meum, spes mea, mel meum, sua vitudo mea, si gaudium.
units.tr: Here it is helpful to add some things about kissing in general. The Latins call a kiss osculum, as if it were a little mouth (os parvum). It is said to be named from os, the mouth, because by kissing we join mouths, and make, as it were, a small mouth out of the mouth; hence osculor, osculator, osculatio; also exosculor and exosculatio. Otherwise basium (whence the Italian baciare and the French baiser) gives basio, basiator, basiatio. Also suavium is called a kiss in Latin from suavitas, sweetness; hence suavio, suaviator, suaviatio, and disuaviatio, disuaviator. Some distinguish these as follows: osculum is a kiss of duty, as when we greet and kiss those returning from afar or departing. Plutarch, in the Life of Cato of Utica, writes to this effect: when he was leaving his province, the soldiers reverently kissed his hand; yet this kind of honour was granted only to commanders, and to very few at that time. Pomponius Laetus says the same in his Compendium of Roman History. Moreover, basium belonged to chaste people, as of a father to his son, a wife to her husband. Suavium, however, belonged to pleasure; hence suavitas or suavitudo means the same as dulcedo, sweetness. Plautus: "My heart, my hope, my honey, my sweetness, my joy."

units.la: Græce osculum dicitur φίλημα Απο φιλέιν, sive τὸς φιλίας, idest, amore dilectione, amo ria, cujus est symbolum. καὶ φρικε ἀπὸ φιλημα, mala mens, sua ve osculum. Inde osculum tale fuit.
units.tr: In Greek a kiss is called φίλημα, from φιλεῖν, or from φιλία, that is, love, affection, of which it is the sign. [Greek]. Hence such a kiss was...

units.la: Hebraicè oscula dicuntur נשיקות Neschehikoth. (Hinc Proverbior. 27. Fideliora sunt vulnera amantis, quàm Neschikoth, id est, oscula blanda osoris. Canico. 1. Osculetur me in oris sui) אנשק Naschåk, Osculatus est, quod affinis est verbo נשק Naschach per Caph, significanti, Mordere, Arrodere, uc serpens dentibus mordet & rodit. Oscula enim sunt quasi morsus culæ quædam; & sæpe quidem mortifere.
units.tr: In Hebrew kisses are called נשיקות Neschikoth. Hence Proverbs 27: "Faithful are the wounds of a lover, rather than the flattering kisses of one who hates." Canticles 1: "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth." The verb Naschak, "he kissed," is related to the verb נשק Nashach, with a Caph, which means to bite or gnaw, as a serpent bites and gnaws with its teeth. For kisses are in a way a kind of bite, and often a deadly one.

units.la: Germani osculum exprimunt per Kuß/ osculari per Küssen/a Græco κύσσω, quod idem, ἀ κύω, κυήσω, & κύω, quod item concipere, uterum vel partum ferre significat. Inde κύσσοι, osculum. Differunt autem γιλέιν & κυσίν, ὅπ τε μὲν κυσεν τὸ τοῖς χρείαις ἀσπᾶσ ... ἐ φιλεῖ ἀσπα- ζονται, Ammonius. Homerus, ἰόν κύσσε. Aristophanes κυσσον ως, κ' ἐλ ζ' ἐφ' ἃ δος φιλῶ ἀξιαν. Aristot. de animalibus lib. 6. κύσσι ἀλλ ἀλλ ἐξ ἐπιφαρ, se mutuo osculantur c lumbæ. Relle autem uno verbo contipere, graviam esse & osculari dixerunt, quia ex osculo se rumq; conceptio & uteri gestatio.
units.tr: The Germans render osculum by "Kuß" and osculari by "küssen." These come from the Greek κύσσω, which is the same as κυέω, κυήσω, and κύω, which also means to conceive, to carry in the womb or to bear a child. Hence κύσσος, a kiss. Ammonius distinguishes between φιλεῖν and κυσεῖν, saying that the one is used of those who greet with a kiss and the other of those who show love. Homer has "he kissed the earth." Aristophanes has a kiss given in a certain way. Aristotle, On Animals, book 6, says that doves kiss one another. Some have said that the same word means both to conceive and to kiss, because conception and carrying in the womb both come from a kiss.

units.la: Porrò osculum est gestus oris, quo os alterius oris admovemus, amoris & amicitiæ, vel sui reverentiæ, observantiæ, & honoris testificandi gratia, quod apud Orientales præsertim magno in usu fuit. De osculo vide pluraapud Sanctum Augustinum, qui illud in corporale & spiritu dividit, de quo hîc non agimus. Pomponius Lætus testatur Dioscoridanum & Cajum Caligu honoris & subjectionis pedes quoq; sibi osculandos præbuisse. Hæc obiter de osculo.
units.tr: A kiss is a movement of the mouth by which we bring our mouth to another's mouth, for the sake of showing love and friendship, or reverence, respect and honour. This was especially common among the Orientals. On the kiss, see more in St Augustine, who divides it into bodily and spiritual kisses; we do not treat that here. Pomponius Laetus reports that Dionysius and Caius Caligula offered their feet to be kissed as a sign of honour and subjection. These things, in passing, about the kiss.

units.la: Geniuum quoq, atq; pedum gestus iu precationibus cùm cristibus, & profanis, tum sacriss religiosis antiquissimus & creberrimus, ut eisa hodie, apud omnes feré gentes fuit. Is ab Hebræ quidem Bærech, a Græcis γονυ κλίσις, a Latinis supplicatio, sive genuum flexio & in ratio dicitur. Hinc Genuflectio, genibus flexus prerari, & Genuflexio precatio est, quæ si nculando, sive genuflectendo: quod verbum utrung, apud Tertullianum sæpe occurrit. Rhenanus: Genuflari, inquit, in adorando velut pœnitentes est: qui stans adonist, tanquam vensam tonsecutus, gratias agit. Plinius cur genuculationis ratio semper usus fuerit, rati reddens lib.11.cap.45.in hanc sententiam loquitur. Hominum genibus quædam & religio mel observatione Genium. Hæc supplices astringunt, ad hæc manus tendunt, hæc ut aras adorant ia sis quia inest in vitalibus. Namq; in ipsa genu utriusq; commissura de extra leyaque a p parte gemina quædam bucarum inanitas inest, qua perfossa, ceu ventulus spiritus fugit. In & in alijs partibus quædam religio, sicut dexira oculus a versa spiritu spiritus, in fide porro istur. Plinius:quibus adde, quæ de genibus, buic loco consentanee, Isidorus scribit originum libro Genua, inquit, sunt commissiones fémorum & cruri: & dicta genua, eò quòd in utero sint genu opposita. Coherent enim sibi ibi, & cognata sunt oculus Lacrymarum indicibus & misericordi Nam a genis genua dicuntur: deniq, complicatum gigni formariq, hominem dicunt, ut ut sur sursum sint, quibus oculi formantur, ut ea si & reconditi siant. Ennius, Atque genua compri arta genu. Inde est quod homines, dum ad genua se prosternunt, statim lacrymantur. Volu nimeos natura uterum maternum rememorari, ubi quasi in tenebris confedebant, antequam lucem perveniret. Hæc Isidorus.
units.tr: The bending of the knees and feet in prayer, both civil and sacred, was very ancient and frequent, and even today it is almost universal among nations. In Hebrew it is called ברך Berech, in Greek γονυ κλίσις, and in Latin supplicatio or genuum flexio, bending of the knees. Hence "genuflection," a bending of the knees, and "genuflexion," a prayer offered while kneeling; the word occurs often in Tertullian. Rhenanus says: "To kneel in worship is like penitents; one who stands and prays, as if he had obtained what he asked, gives thanks." Pliny, explaining why kneeling was always the custom, writes in book 11, chapter 45, to this effect: "Some religion and reverence resides in the knees of men. These are what suppliants embrace, to these hands are stretched, and these they worship as altars, because life is in them." Pliny adds that a certain hollow in the joint of the knee is like a breath of spirit that escapes when pierced. To this we may add what Isidore, in the same vein, writes in his Origins about knees: "The knees are the joints of the thighs and shins, and are called genua because they lie opposite one another in the womb. For they cling together there and are related to the eyes, which are indicators of tears and pity. For they are called genua from genae (cheeks). In short, they say that a man is conceived and shaped with his knees folded, and that what is above is formed as the eyes are formed, so that the eyes are hidden." Ennius: "and he pressed the knees tightly." Hence it is that men, when they throw themselves down at the knees, at once weep. Nature wished to recall the maternal womb, where they sat as in darkness before coming into the light. So Isidore.

units.la: Apud Homerum etiam, hujus gestus crebra fit mentio, qui eum exprimit vel per γόνυ κλίσω, id est, genuflecto, Iliad. 1. vel per γονυέσαι, id est, genua amplecti, vel per γούνα μαι, idem. Priora exemplum exstat, Iliad. φ. Γουνούμαί σ' Αχιλλεῦ, &c. Genua amplectens, idest, supplex oro te Achilles. Et Odyss. λ. πολλὰ δ' ἐμὲ γουνόμενον, Multa orans supplex Deos. Posteriores, Od. ρ. Nuū ἡ ὅτε πὰς ἐξ γουνάζομαι: Nunc quidem apud patrem te supplex oro. Eiusdem morus indicio sunt tritæ & usitatæ illæ formæ dicêdi apud eundem Homerum: γοῦναῤ, σὺ γε γουνᾶσαι ἀ-λ-φ-ί-ω-Θ-, λ-ε-ξ-ω-ν, ἰλάων, id est, attingens, sive, ut Virgilius exponit, amplexus genua, Æneidos tertio: —Et genua amplexus genibusq; volutus. Herebat, &c.
units.tr: Homer too often mentions this gesture, which he expresses either by γόνυ κλίνω, that is, to bend the knee (Iliad 1), or by γουνοῦσθαι, to embrace the knees, or by γούναμαι, the same. An example of the first is in the Iliad: "embracing your knees, Achilles," that is, "as a suppliant I beg you, Achilles." And in the Odyssey: "much supplicating the gods." Of the second, Odyssey ρ: "Now I beg you as a suppliant before your father." The familiar and common expressions in the same Homer are evidence of this custom: "touching the knees," and "by the knees," which mean attaching oneself or, as Virgil explains in Aeneid 3, "embracing the knees": "And clasping his knees and rolling at them, he clung..."

units.la: Quomodo & Plautus interpretatur in Ciftellaria: Anus ei amplexa est genua, plorans, obsecrans, Ne deserat se, &c.
units.tr: Plautus also explains it in the Cistellaria: "The old woman clasped his knees, weeping and begging him not to abandon her," and so on.

units.la: Pertinent hæc & ixαίνειν, sive ixαίνεσθαι γούναζε, ἀντὶ τῦ πρὸς γόνατα, id est, προσπίπτειν τῆς γούνα-τῶν, vel ἀπὸ γούνατος, accidere, procidere, procumbere, volvi ad genua, quod idem fere ac γοῦ-νᾶσθαι, genua attingere. Euripides in Hecuba: προσπιπτὶ δ' οἰκτρῶς τὴν ὀλυσσόμενον γόνυ.
units.tr: To this belong also the verbs ixαίνειν and ixαίνεσθαι γούναζε, used instead of "toward the knees," that is, to fall before the knees, from the knees: to fall down, to prostrate oneself, to roll at the knees, which is nearly the same as γουνάσθαι, to touch the knees. Euripides in the Hecuba: "falling piteously, clasping the knee."

units.la: Hinc verbum γονυκλιδὸν pro precari Deos apud eundem; & tritum illud: Ὑσὼν ὢν γούνατα κλῖ-ματα quod quidam interpretantur, Hæc nō sita sunt in nostra potestate sed sunt precibus & supplicibus votis a Deo petenda. Suetonius item in Tyberio meminit hujus moris: Defeendit, (ita quit de eo) e curru sed præsidenti patri ad genua summ{a}. Idem: Per genua orare conantur. Hit ritus supplicantium etiam hoc loco Homeri describitur Iliad.α. Καί ῥα πὰ σῶ' ἂν Διὸς κυδρὸς ἀλ-ε-ς-ε-ι-ν... ἐπ' ... Ὀ... ἐ, Σχαιὰ ἁζ... ... ... ἀ... ... ... ..., Λισσόμενος προσέειπεν... Ζῆν... ... ... ...: Et ante ipsum sedit & prehendit genua, Sinistraque manu dexteraque autem tab mento apprehendens, Supplicans allocuta est (Thetis) Iovem Saturnidem Regem.
units.tr: Hence the phrase "on bended knee" (γονυκλιδόν) for praying to the gods in the same author, and the well-known saying, which some interpret as: "these things are not in our power, but must be sought from God by prayers and suppliant vows." Suetonius, in his life of Tiberius, also mentions this custom: he got down from his chariot and, going to his father, fell to his knees. He also says: "they try to pray by the knees." The ritual of suppliants is also described by Homer in Iliad 1: "And so she sat before Zeus, the glorious son of Saturn, and touched his knees, and with her left hand his chin, and in supplication addressed Jove, the son of Saturn and king."

units.la: Vbi primum sedet Thetis ante jovem, cui erat supplicatura: quem morem supra quoq; observavit ex symbolo Pythagoræ: quo etiam illud referendum, quod interpretes Apollonii perhibent, solere supplices apud Larem tacitos sedere. Sic autem locutus erit Apollonius: τὸ δ᾽ αὖσο, ᾗ ἀναυδαῖ ἢ ἰχνιαν... ἐπ' εἰ ἔχει ... Sed illud non est hujus loci: nec videtur supplicem decere, ut sedeat, nisi hoc inter Deos propter affinitatem aut generis, aut dignitatis tolerari posset. Quæ sequuntur autem hic se habent, pro ut illa quod Rhodiginus libro decimo quinto, capite decimo ollavo, ex Eustathio & aliis Græcis interpretibus fluidiose collegit. Veteribus, inquit, post illos diu retenti fuit morus, ut supplicantes caput, dextram, genuaque ejus, cui se ingererent supplices, contingerent: nec totum tamen caput, sed mentum modo, ut naturæ Homerus videtur, vel barbæ mediusullum, quod probat Euripides. Id vero ὅ-τι τὸ -νὰ μὴ ἰκέτη, quia sit in nobis ea pars principalis: ut in qua ἀγέρωτα... id est, rationalis collocetur potentia. Dextra vero ὅ-τι τὸ ἀ-ρ-ε-τ-ι-κ-ο-ν, quoniam ut ubi maxima insit ad agendum facultas. Genua propter motus & progressiones necessitatem. Tria vero hæc, symbolice, conjunctum, actionem, progressum, ut veluti sinuosi ἐ-κ-ε-ι-α-ς τ-ό-σ-ι-δ-ε-ῖ-ς, euguria finis supplicandi. Hæc Calius: quibus addo, quæ Phurnutus in locum illum Homeri Iliad.1. Καὶ γάρ τε Λητα... ... Διὸς κούρας. Χωλαίτε... ... ... . Etenim Litæ sunt sorores filiæ magni, Claudaque, rugosæque strabæque oculis:
units.tr: Here Thetis first sits before Jove, whom she is about to supplicate. She also observed this custom earlier, from the symbol of Pythagoras; to this also belongs what the interpreters of Apollonius report, that suppliants were accustomed to sit silently before the household god. Apollonius speaks thus, but that is not the point here. Nor does it seem fitting for a suppliant to sit, unless this could be tolerated among the gods because of affinity of kin or of rank. What follows here is as Rhodiginus, in book 15, chapter 18, gathered at length from Eustathius and other Greek interpreters. "Among the ancients," he says, "the custom long remained after them that suppliants touched the chin, the right hand and the knees of the one to whom they came as suppliants. Not the whole head, but the chin only, as Homer seems to indicate, or the middle of the beard, as Euripides proves. They touch the chin because it is the principal part in us, the seat of reason. The right hand because it is the instrument of virtue and of the greatest power of acting. The knees because of the necessity of motion and progress." These three together signify symbolically action, progress, and the end of supplication. So Callius. To these I add what Phurnutus says on that passage of Homer, Iliad 1, where the Litae, daughters of great Zeus, are described as lame, wrinkled, and squint-eyed.

units.la: Pedes claudicantes a Poeta dici, quod se in ingenuas dejiciant, qui preces faciunt: quæ ejus ratio quoniam accommodatissima est huic de precibus loco, idcirco eam hic integram subjicio. Etiam Preces, inquit Phurnutus, Iovis esse filias dicit Poeta, & quidem claudas, quod se in genua dejiciant, qui preces faciunt. Deinde etiam eorum imbecillitas addit. Adhæc debili & obliquo esse visu, quod ad quædam semper conniveant. Postremo supplicandi necessitate devinctos esse. Amplius delineat Poeta Preces, eam quam Deas quasdam. Claudas quidem [?], quòd tarde & vix progrediatur, & hus suppl[?] esse, quos primò injuria leserint: rugosas certè & visa obliquo, quod affectos in juria egre & fren-te neutiquam laeta intueri possent, quos veniam poscunt. Adhaec jovis esse filias, quod venerande sint, secundum illud Orphei: ὁ δὲ ἀπὸ ἱ[?] Lῶ ὁ κυκλος ... Iovis autem filias dicit deo patet Natalis Mythol. lib. 2. cap. 1. quid Reges et potentiores magna semper rogantium aliquid frequentia tircumsistit.
units.tr: Phurnutus says that the poet calls their feet lame because those who make prayers throw themselves down on their knees. He adds their weakness. They are also weak-sighted and sidelong, because they always squint at certain things. Lastly they are bound by the necessity of supplicating. The poet further portrays the Prayers as certain goddesses. They are lame, indeed [?], because they advance slowly and with difficulty, and they are suppliants to those whom they first injured. They are certainly wrinkled and squint, because those who have been wronged can scarcely look with a cheerful face on those from whom they ask pardon. They are daughters of Jove, moreover, because they are venerable, according to the saying of Orpheus. That they are called daughters of Jove, Natalis Comes says in his Mythology, book 2, chapter 1, because kings and the more powerful are always surrounded by a great crowd of those asking for something [?].

units.la: Et haec quidem de modo precandi.
units.tr: And these are the things about the manner of praying.

units.la: SVPERest ut dicamus de precationibus fine, usu, vi & efficacia: de his primum hoc notandum, nullas ineffica-ces, otiosas aut vanas esse apud Homerum preces, si modo justè fuerint. Iamblichus deinde libro quinto, capite vigesimo septimo de mysteriis Aegyptiorum multa splendide hac de re disserit: Hanc enim astè esse cognitionis Deorum, rerumq; divinarum ducem atq; lucem, esse vinculum atq; copulam, qua homines cum Deo conjungantur, hanc claves insitae esse, quae hominibus Deorum penetralia & scrinia aperiantur, hac paulatim homines assuefieri ad divina, donec ad divinorum operum apicem provehantur, hac hominum mentes animosq; paulatim & tacite sursum rapi, donec in divinam naturam commutentur, & quasi in Deos evadant, hanc hac gratiam, amores, amicitiam aeternam hominum conciliare, hanc divinam animi partem accendere, & quicquid in ipsa omnino est contrarium, expiare, purgare, lustrare, quicquid facem & lutum mortalitatis redolet abstergere. Supplicatio, addit, mirifice prodest, quippe ipsum bonam & fidem perfidi ad lucis hausturi, ac ut omnia cumprehendam, familiares, ut ita loquar, domesticosque Deorum reddit eos, qui illa utuntur. Haec atque alia hujusmodi, quae de precibus loquuntur... non Ethnicorum, sed Christianorum veris precibus vere proprieque conveniunt.
units.tr: It remains to speak of the end, use, power and efficacy of prayers. First, it should be noted that in Homer prayers are never ineffective, idle or vain, provided they are made justly. Then Iamblichus, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-seven, of On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, discourses at length and brilliantly on this subject. Prayer, he says, is the guide and light of the knowledge of the gods and of divine things; it is the bond and join by which human beings are united with God; the keys implanted in us open to humans the inner sanctuaries and treasuries of the gods; through it people are gradually accustomed to divine things until they are carried up to the summit of divine works; through it human minds and spirits are gradually and silently lifted upward until they are changed into the divine nature and, as it were, become gods; it wins for humans this grace, love and eternal friendship; it kindles the divine part of the soul, and it expiates, purges and cleanses whatever in it is contrary to the divine, wiping away whatever smells of the torch and mire of mortality. Supplication, he adds, is wonderfully beneficial, for it makes those who use it, so to speak, intimate and domestic with the gods, since they draw good and faith from the faithless to the light. To sum up, these and other such things that are said about prayers agree truly and properly not with the prayers of the heathen, but with the true prayers of Christians.

units.la: Has adde, quod apud Platonem in Alcibiade secundo, Ammonius, precationem Lacedaemoniorum jucundiorem Deo esse, quam omnia Graecorum sacrificia. Locus inhigus & huic nostro propositio convenientissimus: quem idcirco totum hic subjungere placuit. Sic igitur habes: Τα ὑπὲρ Ἀμμων. Φησὶν ἂν ... Lacedaemonium faustam apprecationem sibi jucundiorem esse, quam omnia Graeca sacrificia. Haec tantum nec plura Deum refpon-dise fertunt. Non mihi quidem aliud, quàm precationem illam videtur Deus significasse. Illa enim revera aliis multo praestantior. Altenim Graeci curatis cornibus boves Dijs sistunt atque mactant: at ... Deos prosequentes, ita precantur uti fors tuleris, & temerè precantur vel bona, vel mala. Quoniam autem Dii illos sapenumero audiunt blasphemantes, utpote qui precantur per eram, opimas illas sumtuofas, sive pompas, sive boftias minime suscipiunt. Et paullo post, ... Ὅτι ... λόγον.
units.tr: Add to these what Ammonius says in Plato's second Alcibiades: that the prayer of the Lacedaemonians is more pleasing to God than all the sacrifices of the Greeks. The passage is remarkable and most suited to our present proposition, so I have thought it right to quote it here in full. So you have it: "Ammonius..." says that the Lacedaemonian's favourable prayer is more pleasing to him than all the Greek sacrifices. They report that the god answered nothing more than this. For my part, I think the god meant that prayer, for it is indeed far superior to the others. For the Greeks lead oxen with gilded horns to the gods and slaughter them, but ... following the gods, they pray as chance will have it, and they pray rashly for good or for evil things. Since the gods often hear them blaspheming, as they pray through their own wealth, they do not at all accept those costly and showy offerings, whether processions or victims. And shortly afterwards: ... (the rest of the passage).

units.la: {y} Lacedaemonium. Marginal references as printed in the left margin. si Dii ad nostra doua atq; sacrificia respicerent, non vero adani- mantis pius & justius nimirū fit, multo potiùs arbitror) quàm ad opiparas has pompas atq; quas nihil prohibet quo minus vel privatus homo, vel etiam Respubl. si quibus se scelestissimè si inxerint, illata impoenitentibus injuria, quotannis exsoluant. Verumenum vero Dii munerum, tribus minime capiuntur, ac proinde hæc omnia sesemè contemnunt, quemadmodum aste Deus & Deorum vates. Videtur igitur & apud Deos, & apud homines sanè mente præ- scientia & Sapientia pre ceteris omnibus rebus in primis esse. Sapientes vero & justissimo si quidem sint, quam illi, qui intelligunt, quid faciendum dicendumq́, sit, & apud Deos & apud homines oriri damnum: ita potiùs esse illos supersedendum precatione, quàm ut male & damno- sit precentur, donec didicerint precari.
units.tr: Lacedaemonian. Marginal references as printed in the left margin. If the gods looked to our gifts and sacrifices rather than to the soul of the one offering them, surely it would be more pious and just (I think, much more) than these splendid processions, which nothing prevents a private person, or even a commonwealth, from paying out yearly, even if they have sinned most wickedly, injuries having been inflicted on the unrepentant. But the gods are not moved by gifts of this kind, and therefore they utterly despise all these things, as the god and the prophets of the gods teach. It seems, therefore, that both among the gods and among human beings foreknowledge and wisdom are first of all things. Those who understand what must be done and said are wise and most just; and it would be a loss both among the gods and among humans if they did not refrain from prayer rather than pray badly and to their own harm, until they have learned how to pray.

units.la: Nunc, colophonis loco, precationum Ethnicarum aliquot formulas ex Poëtis & Oratoribus de promptas subjungemus. Harum apud Homerum, principem Poëtarum, exstant pene innumeræ, inter quas hæc ab Alcibiade apud Platonem, cum communem pro omnibus precationem con- ceperet, scitatur.
units.tr: Now, by way of a conclusion, we shall append some ready-made formulas of heathen prayers taken from poets and orators. Almost countless examples of these are found in Homer, the prince of poets, among which is this one, which Alcibiades in Plato uses when he frames a prayer common to all.

units.la: Ζεῦ Βασιλεῦ, τὰ μὲν ἰδ̀ ἀλλ' (φησί) ἢ εὐχομένοις Ϙ αἰνῶς ὁ̂ιο̂ς Αμμα δὲ ἰσὼ, τὰ ἡ δ̀ ἐστὰ ἡ εὐχομένοις ἀπαλίξῖν Καὶ αὐτοῖ, idest, Optima da nobis, vel si, pater, illa rogemus, Vel non: at damnum cæco si errore precemur, Tu damnum a nobis præsens averte, &c.
units.tr: "Zeus, King..." (he says) "give us the best things, or if, Father, we ask for those, or not; but if we pray in blind error for harm, you, present, turn the harm away from us," and so on. (Latin: Optima da nobis...)

units.la: Alia Chrysis exstat apud eundem Homerum Iliad. a. ΚΛΥΘΙ μάλ ἀργυρόπτοξ, ὃς χρύσιλω ἀμφιέλεπξ, Ἡ δ' ἀλλ' ἡ ἰμάν ἐπάξ ἀλλὰ ἡ ἐκ ἐπανίοιοι, Τιμῆσαι μὲν ἐμὲ ἡ ἐμὲ δὲ Ἀχαιῶν, Ἡ δ' ἐμ ἀλ ἐπαλλον, ἐν ἐπαλ ἐξ ἔλαβον ἀλ ἔλθο, Ἡ πνειν ἢ Δαναῶν ἀπο ἐκ λοιγὸν ἀμυνον. Audi me argenteum arcum habens, qui Chrysem tueris, Iam quidem aliquando me aneca exaudisti precantem, Honorasti quidem me: valde autem lesisti populum Achiworum. Item & nunc mihi hoc persice desiderium, jam nunc a Danais saeum exitium remove.
units.tr: Another prayer of Chryses occurs in the same Homer, Iliad book one: "Hear me, you who hold the silver bow, who protect Chryse and holy Cilla, and who rule Tenedos mightily, Smintheus. If ever I have built a temple pleasing to you, or if ever I have burned for you fat thighs of bulls or goats, fulfil this wish for me: let the Danaans pay for my tears with your arrows." (Latin rendering of the same.)

units.la: Et paullo post, hæc Thetydis formula legitur, eodem libro: Ζεῦ πατερ, ἐπίποτε Διὸς μὲν ἀθανάτοισι ὄνπτα Η τέα, ἡ ἰάργω, τοῦ δ μοι κρίνοι ἐλλὰ ἀμ, Τιμῆσον μοι ἰ ὑ ἀ ὡς ἀμυκρῶ τάλ ἃ ἄλλον Ἐπλιτ' ἀ ὑπ̓ μὲν νῦ ὀρ ἀε ἀ ἀρ ἀ Ἀχαιμένων Ἡ πιμοσινλᾶν ὃ ἰ ἰ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ. Αλλὰ σὺ ἀπὸ μὲν πίσον ὀλύμπιος μπηίλα ζιὺ. Τόφρα δ' ἐκ τρόποσι πίθει κρατ'ῷ, ὅρρ αἰ Αχαιοὶ Τιόν ἐμὸν πίσωσιν, ἀφίλλωσιν τι ἐπιω, id est, jupiter pater, siquando te inter immortales juvi, Vel verbo, vel opere, hoc mihi persice desiderium, Honora mihi filium, qui brevissimæ vitæ præ ceteris Est: sed ipsum nunc Rex virorum Agamemnon Inhonorāvit. Habet enim munus ejus ereptum, quod ipse si tepe, Sed tu ipsum honora, Olympie prudens Jupiter: Tandiu autem Trojanū adjice robur, donec Achi'vi Filium meum honorent, angeantq́ eum honore.
units.tr: And shortly afterwards, this prayer of Thetis is read in the same book: "Father Zeus, if ever among the immortals I have helped you by word or deed, grant me this wish: honour my son, who is destined to the shortest life of all. But now King Agamemnon has dishonoured him, for he has taken away his prize and keeps it. Yet you, Olympian Jupiter, wise one, honour him, and lend strength to the Trojans until the Achaeans honour my son and increase his glory." That is, Jupiter the Father, if ever I have helped you among the immortals by word or deed, fulfil this wish for me: honour my son, who is short-lived beyond all others; but now King Agamemnon has dishonoured him, taking away his prize. But you, Olympian Jupiter, honour him, and for a while give strength to the Trojans, so that the Achaeans may honour my son and increase his honour.

units.la: Similes precandi formulæ occurrunt etiam apud Poetas Latinos, qualis illa Anchisis, apud Virgilium Æneidos secundo: Iupiter omnipotens, precibus si flectleris ullis, Aspice nos, hoc tantum: & si pietate meremur, Da deinde auxilium pater, atq; hæc omnia firma.
units.tr: Similar formulas of prayer also occur in the Latin poets, such as that of Anchises in Virgil's Aeneid book two: "Almighty Jupiter, if you can be moved by any prayers, look upon us, this much only; and if we deserve it by our piety, Father, grant us help and make these things firm."

units.la: Et pro Turno iovem rogans iuno, hac precandi formula utitur Æneidos duodecimo: Illud te, nulla fati quod lege tenetur, Pro Latio obtestor, pro maiestate tuorum: Quuni iam concubius pacem felicibus (esto) Component, quum iam leges & fœdera iungent: Ne vetus indigenas nomen mutare Latinos, Neu Troas fieri iubeas, Teucrosq; vocari: Aut vocem mutare viros aut vertere vestes. Sit Latium, sint Albani per secula Reges: Sit Romana potens Itala virtute propago: Occidit, occideritq; sinas cum nomine Troja. Olli subridens hominum rerumq; repertor Es germana Iovis Saturnig; altera proles: Iturum tantos volvis sub pectore fluctus? &c.
units.tr: Juno, praying to Jupiter on behalf of Turnus, uses this formula of prayer in Aeneid book twelve: "This I beseech you, by what is not bound by the law of fate, for Latium, for the majesty of your own people: when they now make peace and join laws and treaties on happy terms, do not bid the ancient Latins change their name, nor the Trojans become Italians and be called Teucrians; do not bid them change their language or alter their dress. Let Latium be, let the Alban kings endure through the ages, let the Roman stock be mighty in Italian valour. Let Troy perish and be buried with its name." Jupiter, smiling on her, the discoverer of men and things, replied: "You are the sister of Jove and Saturn's other child; but why do you roll such great waves in your heart?" etc.

units.la: Exstant item apud Oratores multæ huiusmodi formæ insignes: qualis hæc Ciceronis in oratione antequam iret in exilium: Teq; anquit, iup iter Stator, quem vere huius Imperii Statorem Matrem iores nostri nominarunt, cuius in templo hostile in impetum Catilinæ repuli a muris, cuius tem-plum a Romulo victus Sabinis in palatii radice cum Victoria est collocatum, oro atq; obsecro fer-te opem pariter Reipublicæ cunctæq; civitati, meisq; fortunis, &c.
units.tr: There are also many outstanding formulas of this kind in the orators, such as this one of Cicero in the speech before he went into exile: "And you, Jupiter the Stayer, whom our ancestors rightly called the Stayer of this Empire, in whose temple I repulsed the hostile attack of Catiline from the walls, and beside whose temple, at the foot of the Palatine, Romulus placed the Victory after defeating the Sabines, I beg and implore you to bring help equally to the commonwealth, to the whole state, and to my fortunes," etc.

units.la: Talis hæc est Romuli suis fugientibus, apud Livium in primo ab Vrbe condita: At tu, Pater Diùm hominumq;, hinc saltem arce hostes, dene terrorem Romanos fugamq; fœdam fidei bio ego tibi templum Statori vovei, quod monumentum sit posterit, tuâ præsentiope servatam Vrbem esse voveo. Apud eundem, libro nono Decade tertia, Scipio, ubi illuxit, ante navigationem, im fastus ac di vinam & prætoria nam vi, silentio per præconem factio, hujusmodi precatione usus est Dii Deaq;, inquit, qui maria terraq; colitis, vos precor quæsoq;, quæ in meo Imperio geftaq; gerantur, positq; gerentur: ea mihi, populo, plebiq;, Romanæ, socius nominiq; Latino, qui populi Romani, quiq; meam fedam, imperium auspicium q; terra, nari, amnibusq; sequuntur, bene vertant eaq;, vos omnia bene juvetis: bonis auctibus auxitis: salvos incolumesq;, vitiis perduellibus vitiores fpolis decoratos; prædaq; onustos, triumphantesq; mecum domos reduces sistatis: inimicorum hostium q; uleis endorum copiam faxitis: quæq; populus Carthaginiensis in civitatem non vuam facere molitus est, ea, ut mihi populo, Romano in civitatem Carthaginiensium exempla edendi facultatem detis. Hæc Scipio.
units.tr: Such is Romulus's prayer to his fleeing men in Livy, book one of From the Founding of the City: "But you, Father of gods and men, at least drive back the enemy from here, and banish the terror and shameful flight of the Romans. I vow to you a temple to Jupiter the Stayer, as a memorial for posterity that by your presence the city was saved." In the same author, book nine of the third decade, Scipio, when the day dawned before his voyage, after a proclamation by the herald had enjoined silence in the praetorian tent, used this kind of prayer: "Gods and goddesses, you who dwell over the seas and lands, I pray and beseech you that whatever has been done and whatever shall be done in my command, may turn out well for me, for the people and commons of Rome, and for the allies and the Latin name, and for those who follow the Roman people and me, on land, in rivers and seas; and that you favour all these things with your help; that you increase them with good progress; that you return us safe and sound, having defeated our enemies, adorned with spoils, loaded with booty, triumphant, to our homes with me; and that you grant the Roman people power to take vengeance on the enemies and the peoples who strove to make war on us; and that you grant me and the Roman people the power to make an example of the Carthaginian state, as it sought to do to ours." Thus Scipio.

units.la: Porro & imprecationis multa pissim formulæ exstant: qualis hæc Atridis apud Homerum Iliad. τ. Ἰσσα τυὶ ἐλὸς πρόσω ἐπων ἐπὶ ἐπι ὧσ ἐτ ὧν ᾿ κ ἐγ ἀ τ. Γιπι, γαρ Ηλιος ἐις ἐεννητ, ἀπὸ ὑπο ἀιαν Ανθρώπων τὶ τὶ ὅμιλο, ὁ τὸν ὀ ῥ ὑπ. οὐ ὀα. ἀ ποτ. Καὶ μὴ ἑ ὠ ἠ ρ ἐ ἐ ἐπὶ ὁ ὡ ἐπὶ ὃ ἐ ἐπὶ ἔ ρ. Ουτ ἑ ἐ ἑ ἐ ἕ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἑ ἐ ἑ ἑ ἔ ἐ ἑ ἐ. Αλλ' ἰμὶν ἁπροῦ ὀ ἐ ἀ ἐν ἐ ἐ ἐ. Εἰ δ' ἡ ἐ ἐπ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ ἐ. Πολλ ἀ ἀ ἐ ἀ ἐ ὅ ὅ ἐ ἐ ἀ ἐ ὅ ἐ ἐ ἐ.
units.tr: Moreover, there are also many very wicked formulas of cursing, such as this one of the Atridae in Homer, Iliad 3, where the Greek is too garbled in the scan to be recovered with certainty: "Let Zeus now be witness, first and highest of the gods, and Earth and the Sun, and the Furies who punish men beneath the earth, ..."

units.la: Sciat nunc Iupiter primum, Deorum summus & praestantissimus Terraq; & Sol, & Furiae, quae sub Terram Homines puniunt, quicunq; perjurium juráric, Quod nequaquam ego puellæ Brifeidi manum inzuli, Neq; cubilis occasione usus, neq; alicujus alterius rei: Sed erat intacta in tentoriis meis: Si vero quid horum perjurum est, mihi Dii mala dent Multa admodum, quaecunq; dant ei, qui ipsos offenderit jurando.
units.tr: Let Jupiter now know, first, the highest and most excellent of the gods, and Earth and the Sun, and the Furies who punish under the earth whoever swears a false oath: that I did not lay a hand on the girl Briseis, neither in the occasion of a bed nor for any other purpose, but she remained untouched in my tents. If anything of these things is false and perjured, may the gods give me many evils, as many as they give to those who offend them by swearing.

units.la: Imprecationis autem simul & precationis exemplum exstat apud Livium, Decade quarta sic scribentem: Athenienses qui Philippo Regi bellum inferre conabatur, sacerdotes publici, quotiescunq; propopulo Atheniensi, socinq;, & exercitibus, & classibus eorum precarentur, cottes destetant, ex ferari Phtlippum, liberosq; ejus regnumq;, terrestres navales, copiac, Macedonum genius omne nomen, &c.
units.tr: An example of both cursing and praying at once is found in Livy, who writes in the fourth Decad as follows: the public priests of the Athenians, who were trying to wage war on King Philip, whenever they prayed for the Athenian people, their allies, their armies and their fleets, cursed and execrated Philip, his children and his kingdom, his land and sea forces, his troops, and the whole Macedonian name, and so on.

units.la: Votis ac precibus merito addenda & annumeranda sunt j VRAMENTA, juranda, & jusjurandum: cum hac nihil sint aliud quam precatio & imprecatio quaedam religiosa, in sacrisiciis vel jurejurando, sepissime adhiberi solita. Exerdium autem pro nostro more capiemus ab eorum nominibus & verbis.
units.tr: Vows and prayers rightly include and count among them oaths: things to be sworn, and the oath itself, since these are nothing other than a kind of religious prayer and curse, very often used in sacrifices or in swearing. We shall begin the discussion, after our custom, with their names and words.

units.la: Nomina & verba Latina, quibus hoc actis exprimitur, sunt, jurare, juratus, injuratus, jusjurandum, adjurare, dejurare, ejurare vel ejerare, perjurare, perjurus & perjurium: quibus adde Sacramentum, quod jusjurandum est militare. Æterni jurare est jurejurando devincire: dicitur jurare aliquid: jurare per aliquid: jurare vel in aliquid: vel absolute. Praeter haec dicunt Latini, conceptis verbis jurare, id est, dicere aliquid, & ex arbitrio adjurantis hoc est, digentia adjurandum praenotatis. Plautus in Pseudolo, jurare ne, te illam nulli vendicarum isi mihi? Bal. faeoer. Cal. Nemp: conceptu verbi. Bal. Etiam confulcus quod, id est, non modo dictum ate verbis, sed etiam cognicis & praemis: idem in Caelell. At ille conceptis juramentis verbis apud matrem ineam, me uxorem ducturum esse. Hunc velut ornatorem ex hoc verbo loquendi modum notant quidam. Notant quoq; alterum, lucet jurare in aliquid: ut jurare in leg. vel in verba. Unde Horatianum illud:
units.tr: The Latin names and words by which this act is expressed are: jurare, juratus, injuratus, jusjurandum, adjurare, dejurare, ejurare or ejerare, perjurare, perjurus and perjurium; to these add sacramentum, which is the military oath. To bind oneself by an eternal oath is jurejurando devincire. One says jurare aliquid (to swear something), jurare per aliquid (to swear by something), jurare in aliquid or absolutely. Besides these, the Latins say conceptis verbis jurare, that is, to swear by a formula of words, and, at the discretion of the one swearing, to swear what has been set down in advance. Plautus in the Pseudolus: "Swear that you will not sell her to anyone but me." "Bal. Faeoer. Cal. Nemp: by the formula of the words." "Bal. Yes, indeed, the very words," that is, not only spoken in words but also with gestures and signs. The same in the Caelius: "And he, having sworn the formula of words before my mother, that he would take me as his wife." Some note this way of speaking as an ornament. They also note the other usage, to swear in something, as jurare in leg(em) or in verba (to swear to the law or to the words). Hence that line of Horace:

units.la: Nullius addictus jurare in verba magistri.
units.tr: "Bound to swear to the words of no master."

units.la: Sic Cicero pro Cluentio: Nulliam petivit, quod in legem non jurâ, ec. Et pro Caelio: Is in legem, per vim lacam jurare noluit.
units.tr: So Cicero in the Pro Cluentio: "He sought nothing, which he would not swear to the law"; and in the Pro Caelio: "He was unwilling to swear to the law, by force."

units.la: A verbo jurare descendit juratus, id est, jurejuraudo devinctus, vel obligatus & licet passiv significationis videatur, deponentis tamen magis est: praesertim cum de persona dicitur. Cicero in Verrem Alione secunda: Nunc eo animo jum, ut eo judice, quàm praetore, hanc rem transfigi malim: & jurato juato, quam injurato aliorum cabellas conuinciere. Idem pro Flacco: Ernne ea sceleratissima coniunctata cocionis sed juratus Senatus. Et pro Syllà: Haec injuratus sum dictum, quae juratus in concione dixi.
units.tr: From the verb jurare comes juratus, that is, bound by an oath, or obliged by one. Although it seems to have a passive sense, it is rather deponent, especially when said of a person. Cicero in the second Verrine: "Now I am so disposed that I would rather have this matter settled by him as judge than as praetor, and I would rather convict others with a sworn judge than with an unsworn one." The same, in the Pro Flacco: "Did not that most wicked assembly ... of a sworn Senate?" And in the Pro Sulla: "I said these things unsworn, which I said sworn in the assembly."

units.la: Injuratus: jurato opponitur: de quo praeter modo citata testimonia, exstat cale apud eundem Ciceronem pro Roscio Comodo: Ego hoc ex contrario contendo: levior esset auctoritas Clurii, si diceret juratus, quàm nunc est, cùm dicit injuratus.
units.tr: Injuratus is opposed to juratus. Besides the testimonies just cited, there is also a passage in the same Cicero, Pro Roscio Comoedo: "I contend the opposite: the authority of Clurius would be less if he spoke sworn, than it is now, since he speaks unsworn."

units.la: jusjurandum porrò est sacramentum, fides, vel religio jurisjurandi. Cicero pro Roscio Comodo: Non ex pactione verborum, quibus jusjurandum comprehenditur, sed ex perfidia & malitia, per quam insidia tenduntur alicui, Dii immortales hominibus irascì & succenseře solent. Idem ostendit tertio: jusjurandum est affirmatio religiosa: quod autem affirmatur, quasi Deo se fleve promiserit, id tenendum est. Idem dixit jusjurandum dare, conservare, negligere vel violare, eodem libro tertio officiorum & de Aruspicum responsis. Ec Seneca, jusjurandum vel juramentum facere: O vocem, inquit, in concionem omnium mortalium mittendam! In tuus verba principes regasq, juramentum faciat, id est, jurent.
units.tr: Jusjurandum, moreover, is the sacred obligation, the faith, or the religious bond of an oath. Cicero, Pro Roscio Comoedo: "It is not from the agreement of words, by which an oath is comprehended, but from treachery and malice, by which snares are laid for someone, that the immortal gods are wont to be angry with men and to be provoked." The same shows in the third book: an oath is a religious affirmation, and what is affirmed, as if one had promised it to God, must be kept. The same author spoke of giving, keeping, neglecting or violating an oath, in the third book of De Officiis and in De Haruspicum responsis. And Seneca: jusjurandum or juramentum facere (to make an oath). "O what a voice," he says, "to be sent into the assembly of all mortals! Let the princes and kings make an oath by your words, that is, let them swear."

units.la: Adjurare quoq; est idem, quod jurare. Cicero familiarium libro nono: Ego tribus primis. Quid
units.tr: Adjurare is also the same as jurare. Cicero, Epistulae ad familiares, book nine: "I, with the first three ..."

units.la: Similes pretandi formulae occurrunt etiam apud Poetas Latinos; qualis illa Anchisis, apud Virgilium Aeneidos secundo: Iupiter omnipotens, precibus si flectëris ullis, Aspice nos, hoc tantum: & si pietate meremur, Da deinde auxilium pater, atq; haec omnia firma.
units.tr: Similar formulas of praying also occur among the Latin poets, such as that of Anchises in Virgil, Aeneid 2: "Almighty Jupiter, if you are moved by any prayers, look upon us, this only; and if we deserve it by piety, then grant help, Father, and make all these things firm."

units.la: Et pro Turno jovem rogans Juno, hac precandi formula utitur Aeneidos duodecimo: Illud te, nulla fati quod lege tenetur, Pro Latio obtestor, pro majestate tuorum: Quum jam concubitus pacem felicibus (esto) Component, quum jam leges & foedera jungent: Ne vetus indigenas nomen mutare Latinos, Neu Troas fieri jubeas, Teucrosq; vocari: Aut vocem mutare viros aut vertere vestes. Sit Latium, sint Albani per secula Reges: Sit Romana potens Itala virtute propago: Occidit, occideritq; sinas cum nomine Troja. Olli subridens hominum rerumq; repertor Es germana jovis. Saturnij altera proles: Inirum tanros volvis sub pectore fluctus? &c.
units.tr: And Juno, pleading with Jupiter on behalf of Turnus, uses this formula of praying in the twelfth Aeneid: "That one thing, which is not held by any law of fate, I beg you on behalf of Latium and for the majesty of your own people: when now they will join in peace with happy marriages, when now they will join laws and treaties, do not command that the native Latins change their old name, nor that they become Trojans and be called Teucrians, nor that they change their language or alter their dress. Let Latium be, let there be Alban kings through the ages, let the Roman line be powerful by Italian valour. Troy has perished; let it perish along with its name." Smiling at her, the father of men and things replied: "You are the sister of Jove, the second offspring of Saturn. Why do you roll such great waves in your breast?" etc.

units.la: Exstant item apud Oratores multae hujusmodi formae insignes: qualis haec Ciceronis in oratione antequam iret in exilium: Te, inquit, jupiter Stator, quem vere hujus Imperii Statorem Mariores nostri nominaverunt, cujus in templo hostile impetum Catilinae repulsa murus, cujus templum a Romulo vitas Sabinis in palatii radice cum Vitiosa est collocatum, oro atq; obsecro ferte opem pariter Reipublicae cunctae, civitati, meneq; fortunis, &c.
units.tr: There also exist among the orators many distinguished formulas of this kind, such as this one of Cicero in his speech before he went into exile: "You, Jupiter Stator, whom our ancestors truly named the Stayer of this Empire, in whose temple a wall repulsed the hostile attack of Catiline, whose temple was founded by Romulus at the foot of the Palatine when the Sabines were ... I pray and beseech you, bring aid equally to the whole Republic, the city, my own fortunes, etc."

units.la: Talis hac est Romuli, suis fugientibus, apud Livium in primo ab Vrbe condita: Ae tu, Pater Deum hominumq;, hinc [altera arce hostes, deme terrorem Romanis, fugamq; fedam fille: hic ego tibi templum Stator jovis, quod monumentum fit posteris, tuae praesentiae fer verbam esse vovere. Apud eundem, libro nono Decade tertiae, Scipio, ubi illuxit, ante navigationem, rem gaudia-tus divinam et praetoria nunc, silentio per praeconem facto, hujusmodi precationem ejus est: Dii Deaeq;, inquit, qui maria terrasq; tolitis, vos precor quaeso, quaeq; in meo Imperio gesta sunt, geruntur, posti, gerentur: ea mihi, populo, plebi, Romanae, locis nominis, Latino, qui populi Romani, quiq; meam fortunam, imperium auspiciumq; terra, mari, amnibusq; sequuntur, bene vertant; ea, vos omnia bene juvetis: bonis auctibus auxitis: salvos incolumesq; vitiis perduellibus vitiosos residuos dicoratos; praeda omniaqe, triumphantesq; mecum domos reduces sistis: inimicorum hostiumq; ulcisci: eorum copiam faxitis: quaeq; populus Carthaginiensis, ei vitasteaff nostram fasere molitur est, ea, ut mihi populo, Romano in civitatem Carthaginiensium exempla edendi facultatem det. Haec Scipio.
units.tr: Such is that of Romulus, when his men were fleeing, in Livy's first book from the founding of the city: "And you, Father of gods and men, drive the enemy from this citadel, take away terror from the Romans and stop their shameful flight. Here I vow to you a temple of Jupiter the Stayer, which shall be a memorial to posterity of your presence."
