In the same author, book nine of the third Decad: Scipio, when it dawned, before the voyage, performed a divine rite and then, with silence proclaimed by the herald, made this prayer: "Gods and goddesses," he says, "who protect the seas and lands, I pray and beseech you, and whatever has been done or is being done or will be done in my command, let it turn out well for me, for the people, for the plebs, for the Roman name, for the Latins, for those who follow the Roman people and my fortune, command, and auspices by land, sea and rivers; you, grant success in all things, increase them with good progress; bring us back safe and unharmed, victorious over enemies, rich in spoils, and triumphing home with me; grant that we may take vengeance on our enemies and their forces; and whatever the Carthaginian people are striving to do against us, let it be granted to me and to the Roman people to make an example of the Carthaginian state." Thus Scipio.

units.la: Porro & imprecationum multae pagrum formulae exstant: qualis haec Atridis apud Homerum Iliad. τ. Ἰσυ τὸ ζεύς παρὰς Ἑλλήνων ... ἀεὶς Θ᾽, Γνῶ τ᾽ Ἡλίου, εἴ ... αὐτὸ ὑπὸ ... αἴαν ... Ἀνθρώπων ... τὴν ... Καὶ μὴ ... ἱπέρ ... Οὐτ᾽ ... Ο ... ἀλλ' ... Ἀλλ᾽ ... τ' ... Εἰ δ᾽ ἰ ... Ε ... ἱ τὴ ... Πολλὰ μὲν ... ἀπὸ ... δὲ ...
units.tr: Moreover, there exist many formulas of curse and imprecation, such as this one of the Atridae in Homer, Iliad 3: "Zeus, first and greatest, and Helios, and Earth..." [Ζεὺς πρῶτος ... Ἥλιος ... Γαῖα]. The passage is garbled in the scan, and I have rendered only the sense that can be recovered.

units.la: Sciat nunc Iupiter primum, Deorum summus & praestantissimus Terraq; & Sol, & Furiae, quae sub Terram Homines puniunt, quicunq; per iurium iniurias, Quod nequaquam ego puella Brifeis manum in uli, Neq; cubilis occasione usus, neq; alicujus alterius rei: Sed erat intacta in tentoriis meis: Si vero quid horum perjurum est, mihi Dii mala dent Multa admodum, quaecunq; dant ei, qui ipsos offenderit jurando.
units.tr: "Let Jupiter first know it, the highest and most excellent of the gods, and Earth and the Sun, and the Furies who punish men beneath the earth, whoever perjure themselves by oath: that I did not lay hands on the girl Briseis, nor did I come to her bed, nor to anything else of the kind, but she remained untouched in my tents. If anything of this is false, may the gods give me many great evils, as many as they give to whoever offends them by swearing falsely."

units.la: Imprecationem autem simul & precationis exemplum exstat apud Livium, Decade quarta sic scribentem: Athenienses, qui Philippo Regi bellum inferre comabatur, sacerdotes publici, quotiescunq; propopulo Athenienses, socios, & exercitibus, & classibus eorum precarentur, toties detestarentur, precatae, execrari Philippum, liberos ejus regnumq; terresfres na valesq; copias, Macedonum nentium omne nomen, &c.
units.tr: An example of imprecation together with prayer is found in Livy, who writes in the fourth Decade: when Philip the King was preparing war against the Athenians, the public priests of Athens, as often as they prayed for the Athenians, their allies, their armies and fleets, so often they cursed and execrated Philip, his children and kingdom, and his forces, and the whole name of the Macedonians, and so on.

units.la: Votus ac precibus merito addenda & annumerandi sunt j VRAMENTA, jnranda, & jurandum: cum haec nihil sint aliud quam precatio & imprecatio quaedam religiosa, in sacrificiis adhiberi solita. Exordium autem pro nostro more capiemus ab eorum nominibus & verbis.
units.tr: Vows and prayers rightly have added to them, and are counted among, OATHS: the oath, the swearing of an oath, and the taking of an oath. For these are nothing other than a certain religious prayer and imprecation, customarily used in sacrifices. We shall begin, according to our custom, with their names and words.

units.la: Nomina & verba Latina, quibus haec actus exprimitur, sunt, jurare, juratus, injuratus, jusjurandum, adjurare, dejurare, ejurare vel ejerare, perjurus & perjurium: quibus adde Sacramentum, quod jnramentum est militare. Caeterum jurare est jurejurando devincire: dicimus, jurat aliquid: jurare per aliquid, vel in aliquid: vel absolute. Praeter haec duo Latini, concepti verbis jurare, id est, dictatus a defeccione juramentum, & ex arbitrio adjurantis hoc est, digentis adjusjurandum praenotatis. Plautus in Pseudolo: juras ne, se illam nullu venditurum si mihi? Bal.fateor. Cal. Nempe conceptu verbis. Bal. Etiam confulcis quoq; id est, non modictatis a te verbis, sed etiam iogunitas & praemeditatus idem in Caetell. At ille concepit jurare verbis apud matrem meam, me uxorem ducturum esse. Hinc velut ornatiorem ex hoc verbo quaeundi modum notant quidam. Notant quoq; alterius ilicet jurare in aliquid: ne jurare in legem, vel in verba. Unde Horatianum illud:
units.tr: The Latin names and verbs by which this act is expressed are: jurare, juratus, injuratus, jusjurandum, adjurare, dejurare, ejurare or ejerare, perjurus and perjurium. To these add sacramentum, which in the military sense means an oath. Now jurare means to bind oneself by an oath. We say that someone swears something, swears by something, or swears into something, or it is used absolutely. Besides these, there is the Latin phrase conceptis verbis jurare, that is, to swear according to a formula dictated by the one who swears, the oath being framed in the words of the one who swears or dictates it. Plautus in the Pseudolus: "Do you swear that you will never sell her to anyone but me?" "I do swear." "Of course, in the set form of words." "Yes, and even in the prescribed words, not merely in general terms but also deliberately and in advance." Likewise in the Casina: "He swore in set words before my mother that he would take me as his wife." From this, some note a more elegant way of swearing in this verb. They also note the phrase of swearing in aliquid, to swear into a law or into words. Hence that line of Horace: "Not bound to swear to the words of any master."

units.la: Nullius addictus jurare in verba magistri.
units.tr: Not bound to swear to the words of any master.

units.la: Sic Cicero pro Cluentio: Nullam petivit, quod in legem non jurejet. Et pro Caelio: Is in legem, per vim latam, jurare noluit.
units.tr: So Cicero in the Pro Cluentio: "He sought no one whom he did not bind by oath to the law." And in the Pro Caelio: "He was unwilling to swear to the law, which was passed by force."

units.la: A verbo jurare defendit juratus, id est, jurejurando devinctus, vel obligatus: & licet passive significationis videatur, deponentis tamen magis est: praeferunt cum deperjora dicitur. Cicero in Verrem Actione secunda: Nunc eo animo jam, ut eo judice, quam praetore, banc rem transfigi malim: & juratus suam, quam injurato aliorum tabellat conintuere. Idem pro Flacco: Ermi ea testimonia non concitare cocionis sed jurati Senatus. Et pro Sylla: Haec injuratus sum dilinquu, quae juratus in concione dixi.
units.tr: From the verb jurare comes juratus, that is, bound or obliged by oath. Although it seems to have a passive sense, it is rather deponent, as when it is said of a witness who has taken an oath. Cicero in the second Action against Verres: "Now my mind is so set that I would rather this matter be handled by him as judge than as praetor, and I would rather see his sworn word than the unsworn tablets of others." Again, in the Pro Flacco: "Those testimonies were not uttered at a public meeting, but by the sworn Senate." And in the Pro Sulla: "I was unsworn when I said these things, which I said under oath at a public meeting."

units.la: Injuratus jurato opponitur: de quo praeter modo citata testimonia, exstat tale apud eundem Ciceronem pro Roscio Comodo: Ego hoc ex contrario contendo: levior esset auctoritas Cluvii, si diceret juratus, quam nunc est, cum dicie injuratus.
units.tr: Injuratus is opposed to juratus. Besides the testimonies just cited, there is this one from the same Cicero in the Pro Roscio Comoedo: "I argue the opposite: the authority of Cluvius would be weaker if he were speaking under oath, than it is now, when he speaks unsworn."

units.la: jusjurandum porro est sacramentum, fides, vel religio jurisjurandi. Cicero pro Roscio Comodo: Non ex pactione verborum, quibus jusjurandum comprehenditur, sed ex perfidia & malitia, per quam insidiae tenduntur alicui, Dii immortales hominibus irasci & succenseri solent. Idem officiorum tertio: jusjurandum est affirmatio religiosa: quod autem affirmatiue, quasi Deo testes, promissi, id tenendum est. Idem dixit, jusjurandum dare, conferre, negligere vel violare, eodem libro tertio officiorum & de Aruspicum responsis. Et Seneca jusjurandum vel juramentum facere: O vocem, inquit, in concione omnium mortalium mittendam! In cujus verba principes regesq; jnramentum faciant, id est, jnrent.
units.tr: Jusjurandum, moreover, is the sacrament, the pledge, or the religious obligation of an oath. Cicero in the Pro Roscio Comoedo: "It is not from the agreement of words, by which an oath is framed, but from treachery and malice, by which snares are laid for someone, that the immortal gods are wont to be angered and incensed against men." The same author in the third book of the De Officiis: "An oath is a religious affirmation; and whatever is promised in an affirmative way, as if calling God to witness, must be kept." The same writer also speaks of jusjurandum dare, conferre, negligere, or violare, in the same third book of the De Officiis and in the De Haruspicum Responsis. Seneca too says jusjurandum or juramentum facere: "O voice," he says, "to be sent out before the assembly of all mortals! In whose words princes and kings make an oath," that is, swear.

units.la: Adjurare qnoq; est idem, quod jurare. Cicero familiarium libro nono: Ego tribus primis. Quid noster Patus? At ille adjurans nusquam se unquam libentius. Idem in Philippicis: Adjuras te in viro me non esse factu rum. Terentius in Andria: Per omnes tibi adjuro Deos, nunquam eam me deserturum: Et in Hecyra: Sanctè adjurat, non posse apud vos Pamphilo se absente perjurare.
units.tr: Adjurare too is the same as jurare. Cicero in the ninth book of the Letters to Friends: "I to the three first... What of our Patus? But he, swearing, said that he had never been more willing." The same in the Philippics: "You swear that I shall not be a man of action." Terence in the Andria: "I swear to you by all the gods that I shall never desert her." And in the Hecyra: "He solemnly swears that Pamphilus, in his absence, could not be proved to have sworn falsely before you."

units.la: Ejus & Dejerare idem, quod jurare. Cicero ad Herennium quarto: Iste oneratus auro clamat, & dejerat. Terentius in Eunucho: Illum licet mihi dejerare his mensibus sex, vel septem proꝑsus non vidisse proximis. Et in Hecyra: Phidippe Batchis dejerat persanctè. Plautus in Rudente: Tene aram banc. (Nota hît formam jurandi, ut jurans aram tenerer.) L. Teneo. G. Dejeth ie mihi argentum daturum eodem ipso die. Idem in Casin. Per Deos omnes & Deas dejeraverit, hac eum notte occisurum.
units.tr: Dejerare too is the same as jurare. Cicero in the fourth book to Herennius: "That man, weighed down with gold, cries out and swears." Terence in the Eunuchus: "I may swear that for six or seven months, or indeed for the last few days, I have not seen him." And in the Hecyra: "Phidippus swears solemnly by Bacchis." Plautus in the Rudens: "Hold this altar." (Note the form of swearing: the one swearing holds the altar.) "I hold it." "Swear that you will give me the silver on that very day." The same in the Casina: "He swore by all the gods and goddesses that he would kill him that night."

units.la: At vero Ejurare est id, quod desiderettur, non posse praestare: vel est, quod vulgo dicitur, renunciare. Cicero in Verrem Actione quinta: Negotiatores putant esse turpe forum sibi iniquum ejurare ubi negotiantur, Praetor provinciam suam totam sibi iniquam ejurat. Et Philippica decima: Ita ut alacres & leti spe pacis oblatatuer se impii cives, quasi victissent, gratulabantur: sit me iniquum ejurabant, de me querebantur, dissidebant etiam Servilio.
units.tr: Ejurare, however, means to deny that something which is demanded can be performed; or it means what is commonly called to renounce. Cicero in the fifth Action against Verres: "Businessmen think it shameful to renounce as unfair the court where they do business; the praetor renounces his whole province as unfair to himself." And in the tenth Philippic: "So the impious citizens, glad and joyful in the hope of peace which was offered them, rejoiced as if they had conquered; they renounced me as unfair, they complained against me, they even disagreed with Servilius."

units.la: Pejerare est fidem jus juranduma negligere, vel relinquere: vel est falso, & animo fallendi urare: unde pejerare est quasi in pejus jurare. Cicero pro Roscio Comoedo: Qui mentiri solet, peje jrare confuetui. Ibidem: Quem ego, ut mentiatur, inducere possum: ut pejeret, exorare facile poteris. Et pro Rabirio Posthumo: Vbi semel quis pejeravertit, ei credi postea etiam si per plures Deos jurent, non oportet.
units.tr: Pejerare is to neglect or abandon an oath, or it is to swear falsely and with intent to deceive; hence pejerare is, as it were, to swear for the worse. Cicero in the Pro Roscio Comoedo: "He who is accustomed to lie is accustomed to perjure himself." In the same place: "Whom I can induce to lie, you can easily persuade to perjure himself." And in the Pro Rabirio Posthumo: "Once someone has perjured himself, he ought not afterwards to be believed, even if he swears by several gods."

units.la: Perjurus est autem, qui pejerat, id est, qui fidem & jusjurandum negligit, in pejus jurat. Cicero pro Roscio Comoedo: Nihil interest inter perjurum & mendacem. Virgilius: Talibus insidiis, perjurij arte Sinonis.
units.tr: A perjurer, moreover, is one who perjures himself, that is, who neglects his pledge and oath, and swears for the worse. Cicero in the Pro Roscio Comoedo: "There is no difference between a perjurer and a liar." Virgil: "By such snares, by the art of perjury, of Sinon."

units.la: Et ipsa fidei vel jurisjurandi violatio est perjurium. Cicero in Verrem Actione sexta: Sunt erit cetera, qua modo integra reservare volut, ut quiam minimum dem illis temporis ad meditandum, confirmandumque perjurium. Et officiorum tercio: Id non facere perjurium est.
units.tr: The very violation of a pledge or of an oath is perjury. Cicero in the sixth Action against Verres: "There are other things which you wish to keep for now untouched, so that I may give them as little time as possible to plan and confirm their perjury." And in the third book of the De Officiis: "Not to do this is perjury."

units.la: Deniq; & Conjurare (unde Conjuratus & Conjuratio) hoc refertur: quod idem, ac conceptis verbis, sed data fide, factaq; coitione conspirare: capiturq, tam in bonam, quam malam partem. In bonam quidem; eo loco apud Livium ab Vrbe condita libro secundo: Trecenti conjuratissimi principes juventutis Romanae, ut te in hac via grassaremur: in malam vero, in qua saepius sumitur, apud Ciceronem pro Sylla: Catilina contra Rempublicam conjuravit. Livius quarto ab Vrbe: Servitia urbem ut incenderent, distiantibus locis conjuraverunt. Idem quinto belli Punici: Ferunt nobiles Tarentini conjuraverunt: quorum principes Mico & Philomenes erant.
units.tr: Finally, conjurare (whence conjuratus and conjuratio) is referred to this: it means much the same as to conspire in set words, but with a pledge given and an agreement made together; and it is used in both a good and a bad sense. In a good sense, as in Livy's second book from the founding of the City: "Three hundred of the most sworn leaders of Roman youth, that we might attack you on this road." In a bad sense, which is more often used, as in Cicero's Pro Sulla: "Catiline conspired against the Republic." Livy in the fourth book from the founding of the City: "The slaves conspired to set fire to the city, in places far apart." The same in the fifth book of the Punic War: "They say that the noble Tarentines conspired, of whom the leaders were Mico and Philomenes."

units.la: His adde Sacramentum, quod: ipsum jurandi species quaedam est, & jurisjurandi sacratione interposita geritur, teste Festo. Hinc Sacramentum militare; de quo ita scribit Vegetius libro secundo: Milites inquit, jurare solent: & ideo militiae sacramenta dicuntur: jurant autem, se omnia strenue factur os, quae praeceperit Imperator: numquam deserturos militiam pro Romana Republica. Haec ille: quibus adde ista, quae de forma hujus juramenti militaris, hoc est, sacramenti Polybius scribit: ...
units.tr: To these add the sacrament, which is a kind of oath, performed by interposing a solemn consecration of the oath, as Festus testifies. Hence the military sacrament, about which Vegetius writes thus in book two: "Soldiers," he says, "are accustomed to swear, and therefore they are called the sacraments of military service. They swear that they will carry out vigorously all that the commander has ordered, and that they will never desert the service for the Roman Republic." So he. To these add what Polybius writes about the form of this military oath, that is, of the sacrament: ...

units.la: Post metationem castrorum Tribuni convocantes omne topiam, tam liberos, quam servos, jurameneo adiguntur virtum, quod tale est: Nihil e castris furto tollere: immo si quis in venerit quidpiam, id ad Tribunos referatur. Cincius apud Agellium id plenius recitat libro duodecimo, capite quarto: Cum delessus, inquit, entiquitus fieret & milites scriberetur, ad jusjurandum eos Tribunus militaris agebat, in verba haec: In magistratu C. Lelii C.F. Consulis, L. Cornelii P.F. Consulis, in exertitu, decem; millia passuum prope, furtum non faciet dolo malo, solus, neq; cum pluribus pluris nummi argentesin dies singulos, exiraq; hastam, hastile, lignum, pomum, pabulum, utrem, follem, faculam, si quid ibi in vexeris, sustulerisq, quod tuum non erit, quod pluris nummi argentei erit, uti eu ad C. Lelium. C.F. Consulem, ad Cornelium P.F. Consulem sive quum ad utrum eorum jus erit, proferes prferes aut profitebere in triduo proximo, quicquid in venerij fuflulerit ve, fine dolo malo, aut domino suo, cujum id esse censebis, reddes, uti quod rectum factum esse voles. Hactenus Agellius. Nemmit porro hujus juramenti militaris Cicero primo officiorum: Cato ad Pompilium scripsit, ut suum pateretur in exercitu manere, secundo eum obligaret militiæ sacramento, quia, priore amissio jure pugnare cum hostibus non poterat. Sic Cæsar de bello Civili libro secundo, Desertos seu productos a vobis dicunt: prioris sacramenti mentionem faciunt.
units.tr: After the marking out of the camp, the tribunes summon the whole crowd, free and slave alike, and bind them by an oath to this effect: to take nothing from the camp by theft, but if anyone has found anything, he is to report it to the tribunes. Cincius, in Gellius, recites this more fully in book twelve, chapter four: "When a levy was held, as in ancient times, and soldiers were enrolled, the military tribune made them swear in these words: In the magistracy of Gaius Laelius, son of Gaius, consul, and of Lucius Cornelius, son of Publius, consul, in the army, within about ten thousand paces, he shall not commit theft by evil intent, alone or with others, of anything worth more than a silver coin a day, apart from a spear, spear-shaft, wood, an apple, fodder, a leather bottle, a bellows, or a torch. And if he has carried off anything there that is not his, and that is worth more than a silver coin, he shall bring it forward or declare it within the next three days to Gaius Laelius, son of Gaius, consul, or to Cornelius, son of Publius, consul, or to whichever of them has the right; or, without evil intent, he shall restore whatever he has carried off to its owner, whoever he judges that to be, as he would wish right to be done." Thus far Gellius. Cicero further mentions this military oath in On Duties, book one: Cato wrote to Pompilius that he should allow his man to remain in the army, but should bind him again by the military sacrament, because, having lost the earlier one, he could not fight with the enemy. So Caesar in the Civil War, book two: "They say that those deserted or dismissed by you..." they mention the earlier oath.

units.la: A sacramento porro natæ hæ loquendi formæ: Dicere sacramentum vel sacramento: Tenere vel teneri sacramento: solvere sacramento. Dicit autem sacramentum vel sacramento, qui semel litteræ sacramento astringit, solenniter, ut idem Vegetius docet, in verba Imperatoris jurans. Hinc Cæsar de bello civili primo: Milites Domitianos sacramentum apud se dicere jubet. Et Livius de bello Punico, quarto: Ego magnopere suadeo, eodem animo, quo, si fantibus in acie vobis armatus repente deligendi duo Imperatores essent, quorum ductu atque auspicio dimicaret is, bodie quoque Consules creetis: quibus sacramenta liberi nostri dicant, ad quorum edictum conveniant, sub quorum tutela atq; cura militent. Idem libro quinto, de bello Punico: Ad populum ferrent, ut, qui minores decem, & septem annis sacramento dixissent, iis perinde stipendia procederent, ac si ptem & viginti annorum, aut majores milites facti essent. Idem de locutione, Sacramento teneri: Itaq; quanquam per Dictatorem delectus habitus esset, tamen quia in Consulum verba jurant sacramento tenerimilitem rati, per causam renovati ab Æquis belli educi exurbe legio nes jussere. Et de locutione, Sacramento solvere ab Urbe condita libro secundo: Quo facto maturata est seditio: & primo agitatum dicitur de Consulum cede, ut solverentur sacramento: ductos solvere deinde nullam sceleris religionem exsolvi. Hæc de sacramenti militaris significatione.
units.tr: From the sacrament also arise these forms of speech: dicere sacramentum or sacramento; tenere or teneri sacramento; solvere sacramento. One is said dicere sacramentum or sacramento who once binds himself by the military oath, swearing solemnly in the words of the commander, as Vegetius also teaches. Hence Caesar in the Civil War, book one: "He orders the soldiers of Domitius to take the oath to him." And Livy in the Punic War, book four: "I strongly advise that, with the same spirit with which, if two commanders were suddenly chosen for you under arms in battle, under whose leadership and auspices you would fight, you should also today elect consuls, to whom our children may take the oath, under whose edict they may assemble, and under whose protection and care they may serve." The same, in book five of the Punic War: "They should bring it before the people that those who had taken the oath while under seventeen years of age should receive their pay just as if they were soldiers of twenty-seven or older." The same, on the expression sacramento teneri: "Therefore, although a levy had been held by the dictator, yet because they judged the soldiers still bound by the oath they had sworn to the consuls, they ordered the legions to be led out of the city for a war renewed against the Aequi." And on the expression sacramento solvere, from Livy, book two, From the Founding of the City: "On this being done, the sedition was hastened, and at first it was spoken of as the murder of the consuls, so that they might be released from the oath; those who were led away were then released, and no religious scruple of crime was loosed." So much for the meaning of the military sacrament.

units.la: Alius est sacramenti usus, forensis scilicet, ut cum dicitur sacramento contendere: quod sacramenti contendere ... non absimile fuisse sponsioni ex Varronis verbo intelligi potest. libro secundo de lingua Latina: Et qui enim petebat, inquit, & qui inficiabatur, de aliis rebus utrinq; quingentos æris ad pontem deponebant, de aliis item rebus certum numerum asserat ... Qui judicio autem vincerat, suum sacramentum a sacro auferebat: nilli ad erarium redibant: id est, nullus ea pecunia, quam deposuerat, multabatur in pænam injusta litigationis, quæ erarii cedebat. Pœnales igitur lites erant sacramentum & sponsio. Juxta autem sacramento contendere de Physiologia & reliquis Philosophiæ in tentis contendere oratorem licere dixit Scævola pro per præstantiam ingenii eorum hominum, qui fundatores autores sui, fuerunt magni nominis sectarum, quibus cum sacramento & vindicatione contendendo de physicæ speculationis explicatio ne, profesione, nullus sane orator litem vincere posset: vel propter tanti nominis præjudicium; vel quia impudentiæ daretur, si quis illis viris doctrinarum possessione non cederet, qui nomine suo professione earum rerum usq; adeo illustrarunt.
units.tr: There is another use of the sacrament, namely the forensic one, as when one says sacramento contendere (to contend by sacrament). That this was not unlike a wager (sponsio) can be understood from Varro's words in book two of On the Latin Language: "For he who sought and he who denied both deposited five hundred bronze coins at the bridge for other matters on each side, and likewise they asserted a fixed sum for other matters..." But he who had won the judgement took back his sacrament from the sacred treasury; nothing went to the public treasury. That is, no one was fined, in the penalty for unjust litigation, the money he had deposited, which went to the treasury. Therefore the sacrament and the sponsio were penal suits. Moreover, Scaevola said that an orator was allowed to contend by sacrament about physics and the rest of the subjects of philosophy, on account of the outstanding talent of those men who were the founders and authors of schools of great name. With them, contending by sacrament and vindication over the explanation of physical speculation, by profession, no orator could certainly win the suit, either because of the prejudice of so great a name, or because it would be thought impudence if someone did not yield to those men in the possession of their learning, who by their own name and profession had so illustrated those subjects.

units.la: Hæc de nominibus vel verbis Latinis, quibus juris jurandi actio exponitur.
units.tr: These are the Latin words and terms by which the action of swearing an oath is explained.

units.la: GRÆCA deinde nomina vel verba præcipua, quibus eadem actio exprimitur, sunt ὄρκος & ὀρκίζω.
units.tr: Next, the principal Greek nouns and verbs by which this action is expressed are ὄρκος [horkos] and ὀρκίζω [horkizō].

units.la: (unde ὁρκίζω, ὁρκίζω, ὅρκιον, ὁρκ. & ὁμνυμι, seu ὀμνύω: unde ἀμφιορκία & similia. ... ὅρκος porrò dicitur, quòd sit quasi ὁρκ. id est, coercendo, quòd nimirum eo homines contineantur ... verbum derivatum est ὄρκος τὸ εἴρχθαι, id est coercere ... ὅρος, finis, & terminus ...
units.tr: (Whence ὁρκίζω, ὁρκίζω, ὅρκιον, ὁρκ., and ὁμνυμι or ὀμνύω, whence ἀμφιορκία and similar words. ... Moreover, ὅρκος is said to be, as it were, from ὁρκ., that is, from coercing, because people are evidently held in check by it ... The verb is derived from ὄρκος, τὸ εἴρχθαι, that is, to restrain ... ὅρος, a boundary, and a limit ...)

units.la: Homines enim jurant per se majorem, ut sit, omnis contradictionis sive controversiæ finis: ad confirmationem jusjurandum, scilicet pertinet, sive spectat. Videtur ipse Apostolus ad vocis originem respexisse, quod ὅρκος sit quasi ὁρος, id est, terminus, finis & terminus omnis controversiæ: vel etiam quod ὀμνύοντες, id est, jurantes, δείζονται, hoc est, intra metas atq; terminos fui officii continentur. Adutr. amq; ipsam hujus vocis notationem respiciens Eustathius inquit: ὁρκος ὁ ὅρκος. ... Et Cicero de Legibus: Plurima, inquit, firmantur inter ipsos homines, Dius immortalibus interpositis, cum judicibus, tum testis
units.tr: For men swear by someone greater than themselves, so that an oath is, as it were, the end of every contradiction or controversy; it pertains, that is, looks, to confirmation. The Apostle himself seems to have regarded the origin of the word, since ὅρκος is as it were ὅρος, that is, a boundary, the end and limit of every controversy; or also because those swearing, ὀμνύοντες, that is, those taking an oath, δείζονται [deizontai], that is, are held within the bounds and limits of their duty. Eustathius, also looking at the very derivation of this word, says: ὅρκος is ὁ ὅρκος ... And Cicero in De Legibus: "Very many things," he says, "are confirmed between men themselves, with the immortal gods interposed, both with judges and with witnesses."

units.la: {y} Q. bus. Quid si ὅρκον dicatur quasi Orcus, quod iurisiurandi violatores ad Orcum fint detrudendi.
units.tr: {y} Q. bus. What if ὅρκον is said as if from Orcus, because violators of an oath are to be dragged down to Orcus?

units.la: Porro ab ὅρκος dicimus, ὅρκοσ δὲ ὄρκω, λαμβάνειν, ὀμνύναι, καὶ ὀμόσαι, ὀμόσαι, ὀμνύειν, ... iurejurando dum, & care ab aliquo iurejurando. Thucydides: ὅρκους τὰς σπονδὰς μὴ ἴσως ὅρκον, ad maximum iusiurandum adegerunt milites. Et Plutarchus: ἐξαίνῶς δὲ ἀφαυσιω ὅρκων ... μίαν ... ad iusiurandum adigere voluit Senatum. Hinc ὅρκωτὴς, legatus, qui iurejurando obligatur ... Xenophon: ... Demosthenes: ... Homerus Iliad. C.
units.tr: Further, from ὅρκος we say ὅρκον δὲ ὄρκῳ, λαμβάνειν, ὀμνύναι, καὶ ὀμόσαι, ὀμόσαι, ὀμνύειν, ... to swear an oath, and to bind someone by an oath. Thucydides: ὅρκους τὰς σπονδὰς μὴ ἴσως ὅρκον [horkous tas spondas], the soldiers compelled them to the most solemn oath. And Plutarch: ... he wished to bind the Senate to an oath. Hence ὅρκωτής [horkōtēs], an envoy who is bound by an oath. Xenophon: ... Demosthenes: ... Homer, Iliad 3:

units.la: Ὀρκία πιστὰ ταῦθ' ἵστε, ... Iso facere fido & firmo.
units.tr: "These oaths, pledged in faith, you know..." — that is, to make a thing faithful and firm.

units.la: Est enim frequens apud Homerum & Herodotum ὅρκια ζωστὰ, fœdus ferire, icere, cæsa scilicet sive mactatâ hostiâ: quod Eustathius exponit ... Iliad. ȝ. Interdum ὅρκια significat ea, quæ fœdera, iurejurando sancienda, pertinent, ut apud Homerum Iliad. γ.
units.tr: For in Homer and Herodotus ὅρκια ζωστὰ [horkia zōsta] is frequent, meaning to strike a covenant, to make a treaty, namely with a victim slain or sacrificed; Eustathius explains this ... Iliad 3. Sometimes ὅρκια signifies those things which pertain to covenants to be sanctioned by oath, as in Homer, Iliad 3.

units.la: —Θεῶν φίλεσ' ὅρκια πιστὰ, Ἀρνε δύω, καὶ οἴνον ἱερόν, etc.—Deorum ferebant fœdera firma Agnos duos, & vinum laetum, etc.
units.tr: "...the oaths of the gods, faithful pledges: two lambs, and holy wine, etc." — they brought firm covenants of the gods, two lambs and cheerful wine, etc.
And a little after:

units.la: —Ἀπ πῦρ κῆρυξ ὀμόσιο ὅρκια πιστά ... Ὅρκια πιστὰ Θεῶν σπονδὰς, πρὸς ἐκεῖ δὲ οἶνον Misso, etc.—Sed præconei splendidi Fœdera fida cogebant: sacrare autem vinum Misschebanc, etc.
units.tr: "...Then the heralds, splendid, swore faithful pledges..." Faithful pledges of the gods, libations, and wine poured out ... — they compelled the splendid heralds to make faithful covenants, and to pour out wine, etc.

units.la: Sumitur etiam nonnunquam pro ὅρκος, ut Iliad. C. apud Homerum;
units.tr: It is also sometimes used for ὅρκος, as in Homer, Iliad 3:

units.la: Πῶς δή σῶ ὅρκια ... Quo jam pactâ, & iuramenta ibunt nobis?
units.tr: "How then shall the pacts and oaths go on for us?"

units.la: Cæterum ab ὅρκος & composita sunt multa, quæ propositio nostro non parum inferviunt, ut ἀμφὶ ὅρκια, utring, datum iuramentum, Hesychio: ... iurejurando firmatum, secundum illud Pythagoræ, ἔχρο. Herodotus in Melpomene utitur: ὅρκος, & ἐνόρκων iurejurando obstrictus, iuratus, Aeschylus: ὅρκος εἰμι, iurejurando teneor. Et ἐνόρκιον ... Plutarchus in Thes. ... perjurus (unde ἐπιορκίζω, ἐπιορκῶ, idem quod ὀρκῶ) ... Demosthenes Con tra Conon.
units.tr: Moreover, many compounds are formed from ὅρκος which serve our purpose not a little: ἀμφὶ ὅρκια [amphi horkia], on both sides, an oath given, according to Hesychius; ... confirmed by an oath, according to that saying of Pythagoras, ἔχρο. Herodotus in Melpomene uses ὅρκος and ἐνόρκων [enorkōn], bound by an oath, sworn. Aeschylus: ὅρκος εἰμι [horkos eimi], I am held by an oath. And ἐνόρκιον ... Plutarch in Theseus ... perjured (whence ἐπιορκίζω [epiorkizō], ἐπιορκῶ, the same as ὀρκῶ) ... Demosthenes, Against Conon.

units.la: {ꝓ} varia com posita ab ὅρκος. dicor sem viola: πολύορκος, multum iurans: Ἐπίορκος, perjurus, qui falsò jurat. Eurypides, Ἐπιόρκῳ pro eodem dixit: unde ἐπιόρκιον, falsum juro, pejero, apud Aristophanem.
units.tr: {ꝓ} Various words compounded from ὅρκος: πολύορκος [polyorkos], one who swears much; Ἐπίορκος [Epiorkos], perjured, one who swears falsely. Euripides used Ἐπιόρκῳ [Epiorkō] in the same sense, whence ἐπιόρκιον [epiorkion], I swear falsely, I forswear, in Aristophanes.

units.la: Alterum deinde verbum, quo jurandi actio exprimitur a Graecis, est ὀμνύμι sive ὀμνύω, juro: unde Latinum Omen & Ominor. Nam jurantes sibi ipsis & alius vel bene vel male ominantur. Caeterum utrumq; & ὀμνύεσθαι Graecum, & Latinum Omen vel Ominor est ab Hebraeo שׁבע, Aman, seu Amen; quod fidem veritatem, certitudinem & confirmationem significat. unde Apostolus: Εἰς βεβαίωσιν ὅρκος, ad confirmationem, inquit, est jusjurandum.
units.tr: Next, the other verb by which the Greeks express the action of swearing is ὀμνύμι or ὀμνύω, I swear, whence the Latin omen and ominor. For those swearing invoke omens for themselves, and for another, either well or ill. Moreover, both ὀμνύεσθαι, a Greek word, and the Latin omen or ominor come from the Hebrew אמן [Aman, or Amen], which signifies faith, truth, certainty and confirmation. Whence the Apostle: "For confirmation, an oath is an end of all strife" [Εἰς βεβαίωσιν ὅρκος]; that is, he says, an oath is for confirmation.

units.la: Ab ὀμνύμι vel ὀμνύω descendunt ἀμφωμοσία, juramenti utrinq; praestatio, hoc est, cum utraq; pars litigantium jurat, apud Hesychium: ἀντομοσία, contrà juro, ἀντίορκος; apud Demosthenem (unde ἀντωμοσία) ἀντωμότης, injuratus, juramento non confirmatus apud eundem (unde ἀπωμοτεῖ, injurate, cura jusjurandum) ἀπομνύμι, vel ἀπομνύω, abjuro, jurejurando nego, apud Homerum, Herodianum, Demosthenem & alios (unde ἀπωμοσία, abjuratio, inficiatio per jusjurandum, & ἀπώμοτος, quasi dicas, abjurabilis, vitandus, fugiedus) ἐπίορκιμι seu ἐπιόρκιμαι, aut ἐπιόρκιον, quasi dicas, superjuro, de re aliqua juro: jusjurandi interpono, seu jurejurando confirmo: unde ἐπιομοσία, jusjurandum, quod additur ad confirmationem alicujus rei, quod exponitur & jusjurandum, quod debatur abeo, qui vel morbum, vel aliam causam jam justam, quare ad diem praescriptum judicio non adfuissent, afferebat. Similia plura passim apud autores profanos occurrunt, ad quae Lectorem remitto.
units.tr: From ὀμνύμι or ὀμνύω descend ἀμφωμοσία [amphōmosia], the giving of an oath by both parties, that is, when each side of the litigants swears, according to Hesychius; ἀντομοσία [antomosia], swearing against, ἀντίορκος [antiorkos]; in Demosthenes (whence ἀντωμοσία [antōmosia]) ἀντωμότης [antōmotēs], one not bound by an oath, not confirmed by oath, in the same author (whence ἀπωμοτεῖ [apōmotei], deny under oath, swear the oath); ἀπομνύμι or ἀπομνύω [apomnymi, apomnyō], to abjure, to deny by oath, in Homer, Herodian, Demosthenes and others (whence ἀπωμοσία [apōmosia], abjuration, denial by oath, and ἀπώμοτος [apōmotos], as one might say, abjurable, to be avoided, to be shunned); ἐπίορκιμι or ἐπιόρκιμαι, or ἐπιόρκιον, as one might say, to swear over, to swear about some matter: to interpose an oath, or to confirm by oath; whence ἐπιομοσία [epiomosia], an oath which is added for the confirmation of some thing, which is explained also as the oath which was owed by one who alleged an illness, or another cause already just, why he had not attended court on the appointed day. Many similar words occur everywhere among profane authors, to which I refer the reader.

units.la: Interdum ὅρκος & ὄμνυμι sive ὁμόνυμι, sive etiam ὁμνύμεσι, in unam coalescunt vocem, emphatice ὅρκοι causa: unde ὀρκωμότης, juramento adstringo ὁρκωμόσιος, idem quod ὀρκωτὸς, jurejurando adstrictus, ὁρκωμοτικὸς, adjus jurandum pertinens: ὁρκωμότιον, juro in sanciendis foederibus, & ὁρκωμότιον vel ὁρκωμοσία, jusjurandum. Plato in Phaed. ὁρκωμόσια, τὰ sacrificia, in quibus iebant fadera.
units.tr: Sometimes ὅρκος and ὄμνυμι, or ὁμόνυμι, or even ὁμνύμεσι, coalesce into one word, emphatically for the sake of the oath: whence ὀρκωμότης [orkōmotēs], to bind by oath; ὁρκωμόσιος [horkōmosios], the same as ὀρκωτὸς [horkōtos], bound by oath; ὁρκωμοτικὸς [horkōmotikos], pertaining to an oath; ὁρκωμότιον [horkōmotion], to swear in the sanctioning of covenants; and ὁρκωμότιον or ὁρκωμοσία, an oath. Plato in the Phaedo: ὁρκωμόσια [horkōmosia], the sacrifices in which covenants were made.

units.la: Haec de nominibus vel verbis Graecis jurandi.
units.tr: These are the Greek words and verbs for swearing.

units.la: HEBRAICE juramentum & jusjurandum dicitur שבועה Schebuahh, שבע, Nifchabhh, juravit: quod ipsum deducitur a שבע, Schaebahh, numero septenario; qui numerus est sacer religiosus, perfectionis, plenitudinis, saturitatis, sufficientiae, & quietis symbolum: quo significatur juramentum actionem esse sacram, et religiosam, quae non temere, sed certo confirmato animo atq; conscientia, certis testibus & argumentis fieri debeant. Hinc sacrosanctum ducebatur, teste Feste, quod jurejurando interpositio erat institutum, ut si quis id violasset, morte poenas penderet, cujus generis erant Tribuni plebis & Aedilles. GERMANI item & GALLI juramentum & hanc jurandi actionem certis nominibus vel verbis exprimit. Germanis quidem in genere jurare est Schweren / juramentum Schwur / quasi schwer / videlicet a gravitate & difficultate: quod res fit gravis, difficilis vel periculosa; & quod non temere, inconsulto, sine ratione, justa, legitima necessaria, causa, & cum gravitate fieri debeat. Alio nomine juramentum illius dicitur Eyd & Eydschwur / quod proprie est jusjurandum: forsan ab Hebraeo ערד Ed, testem vel testimonium significante, quod jusjurandu fit & esse debeat testimonium animi, conscientiae, veritatis, & quod is qui jurat, debeat esse testis veritatis, & quid Deus testis adhibeatur. Hinc Cicero pro Roscio Amer. Ut libentibus animis ad illius testimonium jusjurandum accommodetis. Et officiorum tertio: jusjurandum est affirmatio religiosa. Quod autem affirmati vel quasi Deo teste promiseris id tenendum est. Et de Legibus: Plurima firmantur jurejurando inter ipsos homines, Diis immortalibus interpositis, tum judicibus, tum testibus. Quid si Eyd ab Ita, voce affirmandi deducatur, quod juramentum fit affirmatio, ut ex modo citato loco Ciceronis patet, religiosa. GALLI vero jusjurandum Serment vocant, quasi seurement, eandem ob causam, quod juramentum fit affirmatio, ut dixi, religiosa. Et haec de nominibus vel verbis jurandi sive juramenti. Iureconsulti porro juramentum, sive jusjurandum definiunt, quod fit affirmatio, vel negatio rei alicujus facte, attestatione firmata. Unde Cicero eodem Officiorum tertio affirmationem religiosam vocavit. Et paullo post: Nullum vinculum ad stringendam fidem jurejurando Majores esse voluerunt: item: Qui jusjurandum violat, is fidem violat. Nam jusjurandum
units.tr: In Hebrew, oath and swearing are called שבועה [Shebuah], from שבע [Nishba', he swore], which itself is derived from שבע [Shaba', the number seven]: a number which is sacred and religious, and a symbol of perfection, fullness, satiety, sufficiency and rest. By it is signified that swearing is a sacred and religious action, which ought not to be done rashly, but with a settled and confirmed mind and conscience, with certain witnesses and proofs. Hence, according to Festus, it was regarded as sacrosanct, because it was instituted that the interposing of an oath, if anyone should violate it, should be punished by death; of this kind were the tribunes of the plebs and the aediles. The GERMANS likewise and the GAULS express this oath and this action of swearing by certain names or words. For the Germans, in general, to swear is schweren, and an oath is Schwur, as if from schwer, that is, from weight and difficulty: because a matter is weighty, difficult or dangerous; and because it ought not to be done rashly, without consideration, without reason, unless for a just, lawful, necessary cause, and with seriousness. By another name the oath of that kind is called Eid and Eidschwur, which properly means an oath: perhaps from the Hebrew עד [ʿEd], signifying a witness or testimony, because an oath is, and ought to be, a testimony of the mind, conscience and truth, and because he who swears ought to be a witness of the truth, and because God is called upon as witness. Hence Cicero, Pro Roscio Amerino: "that you may accommodate your minds, willingly, to the oath of that man." And in De Officiis 3: "An oath is a religious affirmation. What you have promised as if affirmed, or with God as witness, is to be kept." And in De Legibus: "Very many things are confirmed by oath among men themselves, with the immortal gods interposed, both with judges and with witnesses." What if Eid is derived from Ja, the word for affirming, so that an oath is an affirmation, as is clear from the passage of Cicero just cited, a religious one. The GAULS, however, call an oath Serment, as if seurement, for the same reason, that an oath is, as I said, a religious affirmation. And these are the words and names for swearing or an oath. Moreover, the jurists define an oath, or swearing, as an affirmation or denial of some fact, confirmed by attestation. Whence Cicero in the same third book of De Officiis called it a religious affirmation. And a little after: "Our ancestors wished that no bond should be used to bind faith except an oath"; likewise: "He who violates an oath violates faith." For an oath ...

units.la: afide, fidelitate, veritate apud Graecos quidè, appellari, supra dictum in voce ὅρκος. Unde Ethnici per Deum Fidium iurarunt. Et Dionysius Halicarnassensis testatur, Sacramentum (intelligi iusiurandum, quod dictum res sacra, sanctia, religiosa; & quia illud fiebat per Deos, res sacras; & in sacris sive sacrificiis; & sacro in loco; & quia sanctè in violateq, erat iurandum) Romanis gentilibus esse iurare per bonam suam fidem.
units.tr: ...is called, among the Greeks, by faith, fidelity and truth, as was said above in the word ὅρκος. Whence the heathen swore by Deus Fidius. And Dionysius of Halicarnassus testifies that for the Roman heathens, sacramentum (understood as an oath, which is called a sacred, holy and religious thing, and because it was made through the gods, sacred things; and in sacred rites or sacrifices; and in a holy place; and because it was sworn sacredly and inviolably) meant to swear by their good faith.

units.la: Caerum in hoc loco communi eadè fere observanda sunt, quae in precibus & votis, nempe primo personae iurantes: deinde formae & modi per quos iurarunt Ethnici: tertio locus, in quo iurarunt: deinde, quae iurisiurandi religio olim fuerit, sive religiosa observatio; quae item violatio, & ejus poena.
units.tr: Now, in this common topic, almost the same things must be observed as in prayers and vows: first, the persons swearing; second, the forms and manners by which the heathens swore; third, the place where they swore; then what the religion of an oath was in former times, that is, its religious observance; likewise its violation and the penalty for it.

units.la: Quod ad personas iurantes attinet: constat, quibusdam iurejurando fuisse interdictum. Sic enim, exempli gratia, viri iurabant Romae per Herculem: nunquam mulieres; quinetiam ab Hercules sacrificio abstinebant. Econtra viri non per Castorem & Pollucem: at mulieres, ut Thaïs in Eunucho. Sic Flaminis Diali apud Romanos iurare non licebat, cujus hac Plutarchus rationes adfert quaestione quadragesima quarta Romanarum, quae animad versione funi digna: Aut quia, inquit, tormentum liberorum est iusiurandum? Sacerdotes autem & animum & corpus oportet torture pesse expers. Aut quia non convenit de rebus parvis fidem non habere, cum sacra & maxima sunt creatae? Aut qua a omne iusiurandum in exsecrationem perjurio desiuit? Et autem exsecratio iustus res, & malominis: quae caujaest, ut dira imprecari alias sacerdotes per leges non possint. Et sanèlaudi datum est Athenis sacerdoti, quae populo jubente, Alcibiades de voto nere noluit, votorum se, non detestandi causa antistitiam esse inquiens. Aut ancia publicum est perjurii periculum, si homo impius ac perjurius pro civitate vota nuncupet, ac sacris operetur. Haec Plutarchus: quibus edde ista Varronis libro sexto de lingua Latina: Hoc, Cajo Poplilo rogante Sylla dictatore, sublatum, ne fieret, & omnes, qui bonam copiam iurarent, nec sient nexi, dissoluti. Ergo habitatione personarum, alia virorum, alia mulierum erant iuramenta. Alia horum: alia illorum sacerdotum.
units.tr: As for the persons who swore, it is clear that some were forbidden to swear. For example, men at Rome swore by Hercules, but women never did, and women even abstained from sacrifice to Hercules. On the other hand, men did not swear by Castor and Pollux, but women did, as Thais does in Terence's Eunuch. Likewise, the Flamen Dialis among the Romans was not allowed to swear. Plutarch gives reasons for this in his forty-fourth Roman Question, which deserve to be noted: "Is it because an oath is a torture of free men? Priests ought to be free of both mind and body from torture. Or is it because it is not fitting to distrust in small matters when sacred and great things have been entrusted to them? Or is it because every oath has come to be a curse on perjury? A curse is a grave and wicked thing, and for this reason priests cannot by law utter dire imprecations. And indeed the priest at Athens was rightly praised, who, when the people ordered Alcibiades to make a vow, refused, saying that he was priest for the sake of vows, not for the sake of cursing. Or is it because there is a public danger of perjury, if an impure and perjured man pronounces vows on behalf of the state and performs sacred rites?" This is Plutarch. To these add what Varro says in the sixth book of his On the Latin Language: "At the request of Gaius Poplilius, when Sulla was dictator, this was abolished, so that it should not happen, and all who swore by good faith were released from the bonds of their oath." Thus, by the condition of the persons, men's oaths were one kind, women's another, and those of the priests another still.

units.la: Iurandi deinde formulas varias Ethnici habuerunt. In genere quidem, omne iusiurandum fieri secundum iuris praescriptum atq. formulam debebat: unde etiam iusiurandum dictum, tanquam iustum, & legitimum, quod iure fit, iuramentum, sive, ut Plautus loquitur, iusjurandum. In Cistellaria: Verum haud metuo, ne iurandum nostrum quisquam culpiret.
units.tr: Next, the Gentiles had various formulas of swearing. In general, every oath had to be made according to the prescribed form and formula of law; hence the oath was also called iusiurandum, as if it were just and lawful, because it is made by right. In Plautus's Cistellaria: "But I am not afraid that anyone will find fault with our oath."

units.la: Et Paulus post: Abi quaerere, uti tuo iurando satis sit subsidii.
units.tr: And Paulus, afterwards: "Go and seek, so that your oath may be enough of a help."

units.la: Tametsi suo etiam hoc addam) iuramentum, iurare, & iusiurandum sic dicatur, quid sit solenne & publicum in iure & iudicio plerunque adhibeatur.
units.tr: (Although I will add this of my own as well.) The word iuramentum, iurare and iusiurandum is so used because it is solemn and public in law and judgment, and is commonly employed there.

units.la: Porro certa verborum formula iurare fuerit solita, quod dixerit, Conceptis iurare verbis (de qua phrasi supra i) cum videlicet iuraturo praebatur ei, qui iurameniti deferebat. Haec formula nem ex re obvia & contingenti, sed divina plane & augustissima arripuerunt: suitq. ab ipsis haec conceptae vel per Deos ac Deas: vel per homines: vel per animalia bruta: vel per tres inanimatas. Per Deos ac Deas quidem; iurabant vel per unum solum aut solam: vel per plures. Per solum, ut Iovem: vel alia per solam, ut Venerem, vel aliam. Hinc Grippus piscator apud Plautum in Rudente: Per Venerem banc iurandum est tibi.
units.tr: Moreover, it was customary to swear in a fixed verbal formula, which is why the phrase was "to swear in set words" (I mentioned this phrase above), namely when the words were offered to the one about to swear by the one who administered the oath. They did not take this formula from some ordinary and chance matter, but from what was plainly divine and most august. These set formulas were sworn by gods and goddesses, or by men, or by brute animals, or by three inanimate things. By gods and goddesses, they swore either by one god or goddess alone, or by several. By one alone, as by Jupiter; or by one goddess alone, as by Venus or another. Hence Grippus the fisherman in Plautus's Rudens: "By this Venus you must swear to me."

units.la: Caeterum per Iovem frequentissime iurabant. Unde ὅρκιον eum dictum singulari epitheto annotatum supra. Hinc in Elacis apud Pausaniam legimus, in Olympiae ΒυΑΩΝΙ, id est, Senatu, Iovis simulacrum fuisse, cognominatum ὅρκιον, quod utraque manu fulmen continebat, quasi ulturus ille fulmine qui fallerent iuramentum, & violaret: iuxta hoc simulacrum, qui ad certamen descendebant, eorum parentes & fratres, super immolati exta porci conceptis iurare solebant verbis, nihil se fraudis, nihil deceptionis ad certamen attulisse, aut fecisse, quam leges paterentur Olympiae commisisse. Hesychius ὅρκιον Δία, id est, Ephorcium Iovem in Titanii ordine fuisse scribit. Inde vero & Dius Fidius ide Iupiter a Romanis fuit dictus, quod ut iurimento praeerat, quo verum iustumq, esset: ita & fidei servandae, quae in iuramento dabatur, praeses esset. Cicero pro Fontejo: Ille jupiter, inquit, cujus nomine Majores nostri testimoniorum fidem sanctam esse voluerint. Et Apulejus: Trunci, idoneum non est, per quod adjures, nempe per dextram et telum, ut ve per ista jurent, cum sit summi Deorum bic bonos proprius. Nam et jusjurandum dicitur, ut ajt Ennius. Quid igitur juraboř Per Iovem Lapidem vetustissimo ritu? In quae verba sic justus Lipsius: Dicitur jusjurandum summi Deorum esse proprium, et id Ennii verbis probatum vult. Ubi ergo illa? Nam quae sequuntur, nihil ad eam sententiam. Censeo scribendum: Nam et jovis jurandum dicitur, ut ajt Ennius. Iurandu per Iovem esse, id est, summum Deorum, a verbo ipso colligit: quia formata vox quasi jovis jurandum sit. Ennii versus, quem intelligit, ecce apud Ciceronem est:
units.tr: Furthermore, they swore most often by Jupiter. Hence he was called [ὅρκιον], the Oath-keeper, a title noted above. Hence in Pausanias's Elis we read that in Olympia, in the council house (bouleuterion, which he calls the Senate), there was an image of Jupiter surnamed [ὅρκιος], holding a thunderbolt in each hand, as if that one would avenge with his thunderbolt anyone who broke or violated the oath. Beside this image, those who went down to the contest, together with their parents and brothers, over the entrails of a sacrificed pig, were accustomed to swear in set words that they had brought to the contest no fraud or deception, and had done nothing beyond what the laws of Olympia allowed. Hesychius writes that [ὅρκιον Δία], that is, Jupiter the Oath-keeper, was among the Titans in order. And from this also Dius Fidius, the same Jupiter, was named by the Romans, because as he presided over the oath, by which what was true and just was confirmed, so he was likewise the guardian of the good faith that was pledged in an oath. Cicero, in his speech for Fonteius: "That Jupiter, by whose name our ancestors wished the faith of witnesses to be holy." And Apuleius: "Trunce, it is not fitting to swear by what you use to adjure, namely by the right hand and the sword; rather, let them swear by those things by which the highest and proper god of the gods is sworn by. For it is called iusiurandum, as Ennius says. What then shall I swear? By Jupiter the Stone, in the most ancient rite?" On these words Justus Lipsius writes thus: "Iusiurandum is said to be proper to the highest of the gods, and he wants this proved by the words of Ennius. Where, then, is that? For what follows has nothing to do with that opinion. I think it should be written: Iovis iurandum is said, as Ennius says." From the word itself he gathers that the oath is by Jupiter, that is, by the highest of the gods, because the word is formed as if it were Iovis iurandum. Behold the verse of Ennius which he means, in Cicero:

units.la: Fides ala, apta pennis, jurandum Iovis.
units.tr: "Faith, a wing fitted with feathers, the oath of Jupiter."
He could also have cited the verse of Naevius:
"Sacred law, the oath of Jupiter by sacred herb."

units.la: Hac Lipsius in quibus notetur novitas et argutia hujus etymi.
units.tr: Thus Lipsius; in these matters the novelty and ingenuity of this etymology is to be noted.

units.la: Sed et obiter explicandum videtur, cur Iupiter Lapis dictus, per quem jurarunt. Nonnulli exstimant ab ipso Lapide, Iove vocato, qui Saturno oblatus fuit ab Ope. Nam et Eusebius in Chronicis ait: In Creta regnavit lapus. Lapidem Iovem interpretantur quidam, qui per tempora fuerit apta Proserpinae: vel certe dicitur a Lapide filice, quem in sanciendis foederibus juraturi tenebant, ut Festus docet, ea verba dicentes: Si sciens fallo, me Diespiter salvā urbe arcē, bonis ejiciat, ut ego hunc lapidem. Quidam antiquitatum studiosi haec concepta verba ita castigant et effecerunt: Si sciens fallo, qui me despicit, salvā urbe arcē, is me ejiciat, ubi ego hunc lapidem. De hoc vero juramento multa scribit Erasmus in Proverbiis, Iovem Lapidem jurare.
units.tr: But it also seems right to explain briefly why Jupiter was called the Stone, by whom they swore. Some think it is from the Stone itself, called Jupiter, which was offered to Saturn by Ops. For Eusebius also says in his Chronicle: "Lapus reigned in Crete." Some interpreters take Lapis Iovis to be a thing that was suited to the times of Proserpina; or certainly it is named from the flint stone, which those about to swear held when they ratified covenants, as Festus teaches, saying these words: "If knowingly I deceive, may Diespiter cast me out of the safe city and citadel, as I cast out this stone." Certain students of antiquity emend and correct these words thus: "If knowingly I deceive, may he who despises me, in the safe city and citadel, cast me out, where I cast out this stone." Erasmus writes much about this oath in his Proverbs, under "To swear by Jupiter the Stone."

units.la: Est et apud Pausaniam Iovis illud cognomentum Laete, quasi dicas lapidei Dei. Notisti jupiter dictum est enim apud Graecos λαος και λιθος lapides et saxa vocari: unde et populi fabulose a lapide dicti. Deucalionus et Pyrrhae jactus dicti sunt λαοι. Laete vero Iovis et Neptuni signa posita fuisse in Olympia testis est Pausanias in Eliacis libro priore. Hic videtur operaepretium, illud jusjurandum adscribere, quod primo foedere inter Romanos et Chartaginenses factum scribit Polybius, quod in tabulis aeneis inscriptum Aedilis in Iovis Capitolini templo diligentissime asservandum posuerunt. Hoc tale est: Si rectē ac sine dolo malo hoc foedus, atq; hoc jusjurandum facio, Dii mihi cunctā felicia praestent: sin aliter aut ago, aut cogito, ceterm omnibus salvis, in proprio patrii legibus, in proprio Laribus, in proprio templis, in proprio sepulchro, solus ego perear, ut hic lapis e manibus meis decidet. Nec plura locutus, manu lapidem dejecit. Hac Polybius:
units.tr: There is also in Pausanias the surname of Jupiter Laetes, as if you should say "of the stony god." Note Jupiter: for among the Greeks [λάος] and [λίθος] denote stones and rocks; hence also peoples were fabulously said to be named from a stone, since the stones thrown by Deucalion and Pyrrha were called [λάοι]. That statues of Jupiter Laetes and Neptune were placed in Olympia is attested by Pausanias in the first book of the Elis. It seems worthwhile here to add the oath which Polybius writes was made in the first treaty between the Romans and the Carthaginians, and which the aediles, having it inscribed on bronze tablets, placed to be most carefully kept in the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus. It runs thus: "If I make this treaty and this oath rightly and without evil intent, may the gods grant me all prosperity; but if I act or think otherwise, may I alone be cast out, with all others safe, from my own country, my own laws, my own household gods, my own temples, my own tomb, just as this stone falls from my hands." Having said no more, he threw the stone from his hand. Thus Polybius.

units.la: Per plures deinde Deos simul, jurare sunt soliti. Hujus formulae illustre exemplum apud Plautum in Bacchide: Ita me jupiter, (inquit Chrysalus) Iuno, Ceres, Minerva, Latona, Spes, Opes, Virtus, Venus, Castor, Pollux, Mars, Mercurius, Hercules, Summanus, Sol, Saturnus, Diiq; omnes ament, Vt ille cum illa neq; cubat, neq; ambulat, Neq; osculatur, neq; illud, quod dici solet.
units.tr: Then they were accustomed to swear by several gods together. A famous example of this formula is in Plautus's Bacchides: "So may Jupiter (says Chrysalus), Juno, Ceres, Minerva, Latona, Hope, Wealth, Virtue, Venus, Castor, Pollux, Mars, Mercury, Hercules, Summanus, the Sun, Saturn, and all the gods love me, if that man neither lies with that woman, nor walks with her, nor kisses her, nor does that which is usually said."

units.la: Sic Alcesimarchus adolescens in Cistellaria apud eundem Plautum: At ita me (inquit) Dii Deae, Superi atq; Inferi, et medioxumi, Itaq; me juno regina et Iovis supremi filia Itaq; me Saturnus patruus ejus, et Castor pater Itaq; me Ops opulenta, illius a via, etc.
units.tr: So too the young man Alcesimarchus in the Cistellaria of the same Plautus: "But so may I (he says) the gods and goddesses, the gods above and below, and those in between! So may Queen Juno, daughter of supreme Jove! So may Saturn, her uncle, and Castor, her father! So may bountiful Ops, by her way, etc."

units.la: Et paullo post: Enim vero ita me jupiter Itaq; me juno et Saturnus: Dei me omnes magni minuti, et patellarū
units.tr: And a little later: "Indeed, so may Jupiter! So may Juno and Saturn! May all the gods, great and small, and the dishes..."

units.la: Faxint,ne ego dem vivos hodie suavium Silenio: Nisi ego te tuamq; filiam meq; hodie obtruncavero.
units.tr: "May they grant that I never give a kiss today to a living Silenus, unless I today cut you and your daughter and me down."

units.la: Atq; haec illa est Ethnicorum per Deos alienos iurandi consuetudo, quam passim Deus in sacrosanctio suo verbo prohibet, per suum tantum nomen iurari volens: ut qui solus aeternus est, solus κορυφαῖος, rerum omnium conscius, & tam se verus faldi iustiq; ultor, quam veritatis custodiens videx & asserter. Vide Exodi caput vigesimum tertium, Deuteronomii sextum & decimo, Zephaniae primum. Plura item de antiquo iurandi modo per Deos ac Deas, & quam varium ac multiplex iusiurandum ipsud fuerit, vide apud Polydorum Virgilium, Caelium Rhodiginum, & Alexandrum ab Alexandro libro quinto, capite decimo.
units.tr: This is that heathen custom of swearing by strange gods, which God forbids throughout his most holy Word, wishing that men swear by his name alone, since he alone is eternal, alone is koryphaios [κορυφαῖος], the knower of all things, and both the true avenger of faith and justice and the watchful witness and defender of truth. See Exodus chapter 23, Deuteronomy chapter 6 and 10, and Zephaniah chapter 1. For more on the ancient way of swearing by gods and goddesses, and on how varied and manifold such oaths were, see Polydorus Virgilius, Caelius Rhodiginus, and Alexander ab Alexandro, book 5, chapter 10.

units.la: Porro per homines quando iurabant, partim per eos vivos iurare fuit solitum, vel salutem, vel calamitatem, vel nomina, vel genios: partim per defunctos. Per vivos quidem vel per integros, vel per certas eorum partes. Priores illustria exempla peti possunt cum ex aliis litteris tum monumentis, tum ipsud ex his Suetonii verbis in Claudio: Con versus hinc, atque, ad officia pietatis, iusiurandum neq; sanctius sibi, utq; crebrius inflicuit, quam per Augustum. In quibus sunt hoc quoq; notandum, Veteres solitos & iurare & obtestari nomen carissimi cuiusq; libis. Idem in Julio Caesare: Romae longo tempore sacrificare, vota suscipere, contra verfias quasdam, interposito per Caesarem iurejurando, distraherit perseveraverunt. Sic C. Caligula, ut Suetonius & Dio scripserunt, Drusillam divinis honoribus colvit, ac Veneri adquavit, & Pantheam vocavit, imperatumq; fuisse, ut per eam, tanquam Iunonem, in posterum iurarent. Sic Pythagoreos per Pythagoram, magistrum suum (cuius praeceptum exstat, Non iurandum per Deorum nomina, sed Iamblicho) iurare fuerunt soliti, non tanquam per Deum immortalem, aut Heroem, sed per hominem Deifimilem. Exempla, ex quibus constat, vel per salutem vel per calamitatem iurare fuisse solitos Veteres, plurima passim apud Homerum exstant. Pro alias illustre est Telemachus, qui per Deum & τὰ ἄλλα, id est, erumnas cum patris, tum propriae iurarvit. Sic Imperatores Romani pro insana sua ambitione ut alios honores divinos sibi vendicarunt, ut per nomina sua sus, perq; Genium suum iurari voluerunt. Hinc Tertullianus in Apologetico: Citius, inquit, apud vos per omnes, quam per unum Genium Imperatoris pejeratur. Vt in Pandectis admonetur lemigaressalem ei obtuisse, per genium Principis qui deieraffent. Religiofissimum enim id fuisse credunt, nominantur, quod iurandum habebatur. Ideoque Caligula, tum ob teviffimes causas nimirum plurimos quotiesdie affixi ceret, dicere sepe solebat, sicut Suetonius refert, Je illos panire, propterea quod nunquam per Genium suum iurassent, hoc pro seferentes, se ipsum contemnere, indignumq; censere coleretur.
units.tr: Further, when people swore by other people, some swore by the living, whether by their health, their misfortune, their names, or their guardian spirits; others by the dead. By the living they swore either by their whole persons or by certain parts of them. Illustrious examples of the former can be found both in other writings and in monuments, and in these words of Suetonius in the life of Claudius: "Turning from this to the duties of piety, he swore an oath, and swore it often, no more solemnly and frequently than by Augustus." On this point we must also note that the ancients were accustomed both to swear and to invoke the name of whomever each held most dear. In the life of Julius Caesar, Suetonius says: "For a long time the Romans went on sacrificing, making vows, and, under oath sworn by Caesar, settling certain disputes against their will." So too Caligula, as Suetonius and Dio have written, paid divine honours to Drusilla, put her on a level with Venus, and called her Panthea; and it was ordered that in future men should swear by her as by Juno. So too the Pythagoreans were accustomed to swear by Pythagoras their master, whose precept survives, "Not to swear by the names of the gods," in Iamblichus. They swore not as by an immortal god or a hero, but by a man made like a god. Examples showing that the ancients swore by their own well-being or by misfortune are found everywhere in Homer. Telemachus is a notable instance, who swore by Zeus and ta alla [τὰ ἄλλα], that is, by the sorrows of his father and of himself. So too the Roman emperors, in their mad ambition, claimed divine honours for themselves and wished men to swear by their names and by their genius. Hence Tertullian in the Apology: "Men swear more quickly, he says, among you by all the gods than by the one genius of the emperor." As is noted in the Pandects, certain men were compelled to swear by the genius of the Prince. For they believed it the most religious oath, the one that was thought most binding. And so Caligula, as Suetonius reports, when he had many men executed for very slight causes, used often to say that he would punish them because they had never sworn by his genius; by this he showed that he despised himself and thought himself unworthy of worship.

units.la: Partes vero hominis, per quas iurabant, fuerunt caput, ejusq; partes, oculi, dextra item. Ad consuetudinem per eapuf iurandi alludit Homerus Iliad. α. his verbis: Ἐι δ' ἄγα μι κεφαλὴ ταυτα ἰνεσσιν ὁτιν ἑώστως ταχίνδησ Sed age jam tibi capite annuam, ut confidas.
units.tr: The parts of the body by which they swore were the head and its parts, the eyes, and likewise the right hand. Homer alludes to the custom of swearing by the head in Iliad 1, with these words: "But come, I will nod my head to you, so that you may trust me" [ἀλλ' ἄγε τοι κεφαλῇ κατανεύσομαι, ὄφρα πέποιθς].

units.la: Ifie capitis nutus, ut egregie adnotat Spondanus, augustissime promissum Iovis confirmavit, sed Thetis de ipsius auxilio dubitare non potuit. Est autem caput pars in corpore praestantissima, in qua est rationalis anima sedes, secundum Platonicos: quia illic est cerebri conceptaculum, ac membrorum animalium, quae organa sunt & principia virtutis animalis, tam apprehendentis, quam eligentis, seu voluntarie moventis, ut observarit quoque ex illis Rhodiginus libro tertio, capite vigesimo tertio. Unde colligi potest, cur eam augustum sit capite Iovem annuere. Exeo enim, tanquam primo motore pendent voluntates nostrae, maxime, quae cum ratione conserventur. Nam hic non loquor de Δυμὼ aut ὄνδυμωθ, quorum illa est in corde; haec in iecore. Ideo, Iupiter subjungit pollicitum suum capitis nutu sanctum esse irrevocabile, omnifraudes catens, & cuius e eventus certissimus sit. Denique res sacra caput exaestimatum est: unde & sterutamenta sacra dixit Aristoteles in Problematibus sectione erigesima tertia, quaeffione nona. Iusiurandum ergo per caput pro sanctissimo & inviolabili habituum est apud Veteres. Alii dicunt, caput fuisse salutis symbolum. Itaque illud adjurare & devotare in fide praestanda teste primo. pium fuisse. Hinc Lyricus Latinus Iuliam Darinem perfidum caput votis obligare solitam dicit: Et κατὰ τωὶ ὀμνύσα, id est, in capica puerorum jurare, moris fuisse Budaeus testatur in Commentariis: id quod fiebat tallo ejus capite, in quem jurabant. Ita se sacrare caput ejus Diis infernis ac devovere significantes, si pejerasset. Hinc etiam Apulejus: Adjuro tuum caput, nulli me prorsus, &c. ubi Interpres addit, Hoc esse Gracorum jusjurandum, jurare per caput. Unde idem Homerus: —παῖδών κεφαλὴν μάγαι ὄρκον ὀμνύμεν.
units.tr: That nod of the head, as Spondanus remarks with care, most solemnly confirmed the promise of Jove, yet Thetis could not doubt his help. The head is the most excellent part of the body, in which, according to the Platonists, the rational soul has its seat, because there lies the receptacle of the brain and of the animal members, which are the organs and sources of animal power, both of perceiving and of choosing, that is, of voluntary movement. Rhodiginus also observed this, book 3, chapter 23. From this one can see why it was the most solemn thing for Jove to confirm with a nod of the head. For our wills depend, as on a first mover, on the head, especially those that are governed by reason. I am not speaking here of thymos [θυμός] or of the other word, of which the former lies in the heart and the latter in the liver. Therefore Jupiter adds that the promise he made by a nod of the head is sacred and irrevocable, excluding all deceit, and that its outcome is most certain. Finally, the head was regarded as a sacred thing; hence Aristotle in the Problems, section 23, question 9, also called it sacred excrement. So an oath by the head was held to be the most holy and inviolable among the ancients. Others say that the head was the symbol of safety; therefore to call it to witness and to bind oneself by it, as the first witness, in making good one's faith was held to be a pious act. Hence the Latin lyric poet says that Dareine, a faithless woman, was accustomed to bind her head with vows. And Budaeus testifies in his Commentaries that to swear "on the head of children" [κατὰ τῆς κεφαλῆς ὀμνύειν] was a custom: this was done by touching the head of the one by whom they swore. In this way they signified that they consecrated his head to the infernal gods and devoted it to them, should they perjure themselves. So too Apuleius: "I swear by your head that I am in no way..." where the translator adds, "This is the Greek oath, to swear by the head." Hence Homer again: "to swear the great oath by the heads of children" [παίδων κεφαλὴν μέγαν ὅρκον ὀμνύμεν].

units.la: Et Poëta alicubi: —Nondum Graecis jurare paratis, Per caput alterius.
units.tr: And a poet somewhere: "Not yet ready for the Greeks to swear, by the head of another."

units.la: A Virgilio quoq, dictum est: Per caput hoc juro, per quod pater ante fulebat.
units.tr: Virgil also says: "By this head I swear, by which my father once swore."

units.la: Pertinet huc imprecationis formula, malum aliquod in autorem retorquentis, Εις ἀφαλὴν σὺν ἐπὶ κεφαλὴν, apud Aristophanem.
units.tr: To this belongs the form of curse that turns some evil back upon the author, eis apsalen [Εἰς ἀφαλὴν] ... epi kephalēn [ἐπὶ κεφαλήν], in Aristophanes.

units.la: Per oculos deinde ut rogandi, ita jurandi consuetudo satis nota est, cum ex Petronio, Propertio, Ovidio, cujus amici per oculos leguntur jurasse, & infinitis aliis: tum ex Plauto. Hinc Menachmus in haec verba erumpit: Si volcus per oculos jurare, nihilo hercle ea caussa magis Facietis, ut ego hodie abjudicem pallium & pinter pessimae:
units.tr: Then, as to swearing by the eyes, the custom of entreating by the eyes is well enough known, and so is the custom of swearing by them: from Petronius, Propertius and Ovid, whose friends are read as having sworn by their eyes, and from countless others; and from Plautus. Hence Menaechmus breaks out with these words: "If you want to swear by your eyes, by Hercules, you will not make me any the more inclined to give up my cloak today and the pimp-and-worst-of-men..."

units.la: Ubi per oculos jurare dixit, quia nihil fere est oculus carius: jurabant autem per res carissimas.
units.tr: Here he said "to swear by the eyes," because nothing is almost dearer than the eye; and they swore by the things they held most dear.

units.la: De more vero jurandi per Ἠλίου sic Apuleius scribit: Verum, idoneum non est, per quod per dextram adjures, nempe per dextram: quod testimonium supra quod, a nobis fuit citatum.
units.tr: Concerning the custom of swearing by the right hand, Apuleius writes thus: "But it is not fitting to swear by that by which you swear, namely by the right hand"; this is the testimony cited by us above.

units.la: Nec vero tantum per homines vivos eorumq; partes certas jurare soliti sunt, sed etiam per defunctos defunctorum, genios: quod pra aliis gentibus imprimis Nasamones & Aegyptios sacrum defunctorum, per defunctos cis fuisse confiat. Sic quia religiose cinerem parentum & amicorum olim jurabantur, corporibus crematis, per illos etiam supplicabant & jurabant: est in Oratione Verrina Ciceronis quarta: Obsecratio per patris sui cinerem, & apud Horatium: Expedit matrib cineres opertos Fallere, &c. id est, Per matris manes filium jurare.
units.tr: Nor did they swear only by living men and certain parts of them, but also by the dead and by the spirits of the dead. Above all other peoples, the Nasamones and the Egyptians are known to have sworn by the dead, and by their dead, through a sacred rite of the dead. Thus, because the ashes of parents and friends were once solemnly sworn by, they also appealed to and swore by those whose bodies had been cremated. In Cicero's fourth Verrine Oration there is: "I beseech you by the ashes of his father"; and in Horace: "It is expedient to deceive mothers' covered ashes," etc., that is, to swear by the spirit of one's mother.

units.la: Per animalia icem rationis expertia jurebant, ut κατὰ γῆν, κατὰ κυνὸς καὶ νεὸς, id est, per anserem, per canem & arietem: quod triplex juramentum Eusebius refert Rhadamanthi primo reperisse, ne omnibus juramentis adhiberetur Dei nomen. Per anserem autem potissimum bruta.
units.tr: They also swore by animals that lack reason, as kata chēna [κατὰ χῆνα], kata kynos kai krious [κατὰ κυνὸς καὶ κριοῦ], that is, by the goose, by the dog and by the ram. Eusebius reports that Rhadamanthus first devised this threefold oath, so that the name of God would not be used in every oath. But they swore especially by the goose among the brute creatures.

units.la: Sic per porcum jurasse Agamemnonem apud Homerum legimus. Et pugiles certamen initurus Horatio, Hortis in Elide, maclato porco jurare solitos, sine fraude sese compararent Pausanias. Quin etiam ludices praefectos, certaminum eodem sacro, et apud eandem jurasse credit. Nulli vero porcum illum, per quem illi jurasset, ederet, licuisse. Quare Talibus Homericum porcum, quem Agamemnon pro juramento statuerat, arreptum in margine dedit.
units.tr: So we read that Agamemnon swore by a pig in Homer. Pausanias also reports that boxers about to fight Horatius in Elis, after a pig was slaughtered, used to swear that they would compete without fraud. Indeed, he believes the judges and officials of the games swore by the same sacrifice, and at the same place. It was never lawful for anyone to eat the pig by which he had sworn. Hence Talthybius placed the Homeric pig, which Agamemnon had set aside for the oath, in the margin after seizing it.

units.la: Per res porro inanimatas quoq; jurabant, ut per sidera & elementa, per gelum, per terram, per ventum & alia. Hinc Virgil. Aeneid. 12. Heu deam, Aenea, terramque, mare, sideraque Juno. Huc referendi illi versus Horatiani Ode octava, libro secundo: Expedit matris cineres opertos Fallere, & toto taciturna nocte Signa cum caelo gelidaq; Divos Morte carentes.
units.tr: They also swore by inanimate things, such as the stars and the elements, by the earth, by the wind, and by other things. Hence Virgil, Aeneid 12: "Alas, Aeneas, Juno swears by the goddess, the earth, the sea, and the stars." To this belongs the ode of Horace, Book 2, Ode 8: "It is worth while to deceive the covered ashes of a mother, and in the silent night, with the stars and the cold ..., the gods who have no death."

units.la: Sic jurabant quoque per Stygiam paludem; quod maximum & gravissimum fuisse juramentum apud Ethnicos, ex his versibus Homeri Odyss. conflat: Ἰσιῶ τόδ᾽ ὡ γαῖα, ὑπερ τόδε ὐπὸ ὕπερ Θαν, Καὶ τὸ ἀρχαϊκὸν ὕδωρ Στυγὸς ὕδωρ (ὡς μέγιστος Θ·
units.tr: They also swore by the Stygian marsh. From these verses of Homer in the Odyssey it is clear that this was the greatest and most solemn oath among the heathen: "Let earth be my witness, and the broad heaven above, and the water of Styx flowing beneath, which is the greatest and most solemn oath for the blessed gods." [Ἰσιῶ τόδ᾽ ὡ γαῖα, ὑπερ τόδε ὐπὸ ὕπερ Θαν, Καὶ τὸ ἀρχαϊκὸν ὕδωρ Στυγὸς ὕδωρ (ὡς μέγιστος Θ·]

units.la: ὅρκος δ᾽ αὐτοῖς τὸ πίλει μαχαίρας Στυγὸς)
units.tr: "And this is the oath for them, the water of Styx by the cliffs." [ὅρκος δ᾽ αὐτοῖς τὸ πίλει μαχαίρας Στυγὸς)]

units.la: Μήτί τοι αὐτὸ πῆμα κακὸν βυλόσιμον ἄλλο:
units.tr: "Lest some other evil shall befall you through this." [Μήτί τοι αὐτὸ πῆμα κακὸν βυλόσιμον ἄλλο:]

units.la: Sciat nunc iflud terra, & cælum latum supernum,
units.tr: Let now that earth know it, and the broad heaven above,
and the water of Styx flowing beneath (which is the greatest
and most solemn oath for the blessed gods).

units.la: Non ullum tibi ipsi damnum malum me confulturam aliud.
units.tr: That I will not counsel you any other evil harm to yourself.

units.la: Idem juramentum intelligit etiam hoc versu, Odyff. β.
units.tr: The same oath is also meant in this verse, Odyssey 2:

units.la: Ὡς δ᾽ ὁ̔ ὀρκος Ζεὺς ὁ Στυγὸς μέγα ὅρκον ἀπωμοσ:
units.tr: "As Zeus, the god of the Styx, swore the great oath." [Ὡς δ᾽ ὁ̔ ὀρκος Ζεὺς ὁ Στυγὸς μέγα ὅρκον ἀπωμοσ:]

units.la: Sic loquuta anus Deorum magnum juramentum juravit.
units.tr: So spoke the old woman; she swore the great oath of the gods.

units.la: Eàdem prorsus formulâ usa est etiam Latona, de templo condendo & lucis. Sic enim Homerus Hymno in Apollinem: —Ληυτὸ ἢ Στυγὸς μέλαν ὅρκον ὅμοασε Ἰσω τωῦ τόδ᾽ ἡ ἀὶα, ἢ ἡγαὶ θεοὶ ἀγὰς ὑπαρδὶν, Καὶ τὸ κατεισόμενον Στυγὸς ὕδωρ (ὃς ἐμιχυσος Ορκος ἀλευσόνατος τὸ πίλλ μαχαίρας Στυγὸς) Η μέλλ ψιλεσι τῆ ἢ Θνᾶς ἀνδ ἐστιν αὐτῆ Βωμὸς καὶ τιμὲν θ. τίνεῖ ἡ σε γ᾽ ἔξοχα πάντων:
units.tr: Latona used exactly the same formula, about the building of a temple and a grove. For Homer says in the Hymn to Apollo: "Then she swore the black oath of the Styx, by the water of Styx, that this earth and the broad heaven above and the sea-gods' ... (the greatest and most solemn oath for the blessed gods) [Ληυτὸ ἢ Στυγὸς μέλαν ὅρκον ὅμοασε Ἰσω τωῦ τόδ᾽ ἡ ἀὶα ...]; surely for you there shall always be an altar and a temple of Phoebus, and he shall honour you above all."
Latona, moreover, swore the great oath of the gods:

units.la: Sciat nunc hæc terra & cælum latum supernum
units.tr: Let now this earth know, and the broad heaven above,
and the water of Styx flowing below (which is the greatest
and most solemn oath for the blessed gods),

units.la: Certé uti, Phœbi bit odoriferum merit semper
units.tr: that surely, as the altar and temple of Phoebus will be fragrant with incense forever,

units.la: Altare & templum: honoratit autem te uti, maximè omnium.
units.tr: so he will honour you above all.

units.la: His adde, quæ apud eundem Homerum exfiant de eodem jureiurando, quod adeò illos sacrum erat, ut, qui ex Superis illud violassent, ab omni Deorum consortio aliquandiu depelleretur, ut copiosè docet Hesiodus in Theogonia. Sic igitur ille Iliad. ξ.
units.tr: To these add what is found in the same Homer about this same oath, which was so sacred that whoever among the gods had violated it was cast out from the fellowship of all the gods for a time, as Hesiod teaches fully in the Theogony. So Homer, Iliad 14: [Ἀγρετεῖ μοὶ ὁμοσον ὅσι τὸν Στυγὸς ὕδωρ]

units.la: Ἀγρετεῖ μοὶ ὁμοσον ὅσι τὸν Στυγὸς ὕδωρ,
units.tr: "Come now, swear to me by the inviolable water of Styx,"

units.la: Χειρὶ ἢ τῇ ἰτὴν μᾶν ἀλλ᾽ ὅρα πυλυξέστέγαν,
units.tr: "with one hand touching the earth, and with the other the shining sea,"

units.la: Τῇ ἢ ἰτὴν ἀλλ᾽ μηρίμην, ἵνα τοῖς ἀπαντᾶς
units.tr: Of this same thing, I pray you, that all of them may bear witness [Τῇ ἢ ἰτὴν ἀλλ᾽ μηρίμην, ἵνα τοῖς ἀπαντᾶς]

units.la: Μαρτυρίῳ οἱ εἴρδει Θεοὶ Κρίσοι ὁμοῖς ἰόντες,
units.tr: Let the gods who dwell on Olympus, the Greek gods, come together as witnesses [Μαρτυρίῳ οἱ εἴρδει Θεοὶ Κρίσοι ὁμοῖς ἰόντες,]

units.la: Η μὲν ἰκρὶ ἐδώσεν χάριτος μιαλόλοτερ᾽ αὐ,
units.tr: Let the one hand be raised in oath by the sacred water [Η μὲν ἰκρὶ ἐδώσεν χάριτος μιαλόλοτερ᾽ αὐ,]

units.la: Παρίβιλω, ὃς αὐτὸς ἰλλεῖ αἱ ἡ ἐματα πᾶσα:
units.tr: Beside the gods, the water by which all oaths are sworn [Παρίβιλω, ὃς αὐτὸς ἰλλεῖ αἱ ἡ ἐματα πᾶσα:]

units.la: Age nunc mihi jura inviolabilem Stygis aquam:
units.tr: Come now, swear to me by the inviolable water of Styx.

units.la: Manu verò altera quidem tape terram multipasiam;
units.tr: and with the other hand touch the wide-wayed earth;

units.la: Altera autem mare marmoreum: ut nobis omnes
units.tr: and with the other the marble-grey sea, so that all

units.la: Testes sint Inferi Dii, Saturnum circa existentes,
units.tr: the gods below, who surround Saturn, may be witnesses for us,

units.la: Certé te mihi daturum esse Gratiarum unam juniorum
units.tr: that you will surely give me one of the younger Graces
