as my wife, Pasithea, whom I desire every day.
And a little later:

units.la: Ὤμυσε δ᾽ ὡς ἀκὴ ἀλλιδ ἐκ Στυγὸς ἀπ᾽ ὀνόμνες ἀπασέας
units.tr: "He swore, as the goddess had said, by the water of Styx, all the gods" [Ὤμυσε δ᾽ ὡς ἀκὴ ἀλλιδ ἐκ Στυγὸς ἀπ᾽ ὀνόμνες ἀπασέας]

units.la: Τὰς ὑποταρτάρεσ ἀπ᾽ ἐξ ἰωσι Τιτῆνας κλέον:
units.tr: "the gods beneath Tartarus, who are called Titans." [Τὰς ὑποταρτάρεσ ἀπ᾽ ἐξ ἰωσι Τιτῆνας κλέον]

units.la: Iurabat autem, ut jubebat. Deos autem nominabat omnes Subtartareos, qui Titanes appellantur.
units.tr: He swore as he had been bidden. He named all the gods below Tartarus, who are called Titans.

units.la: Cæterum, cur per Stygiam aquam sive paludem jurare firmissimum Deorum habitum fuerit jusjurandum, Cœlius Rhodiginus libro vigesimo septimo, capite quinto has affert rationes: vel quia a Diis & hominibus odio habentur, qui ad dejurium proclivior sunt; vel quia juxta Hesiodum, omnibus elementis antiquior est aqua.
units.tr: But why swearing by the Stygian water or marsh was considered the firmest oath of the gods, Caelius Rhodiginus gives these reasons in Book 27, chapter 5: either because it is held in hatred by gods and men, and so one who swears by it is more prone to perjury; or because, according to Hesiod, water is older than all the elements.

units.la: Iurabant præterea iidem per plantas, ut Cramben, qui mos Ionicus fuit: & per Capparin, quo modo Zeno Stoicus sibi jurare permisit, per cibos omnis generis similiaq, multa. Hinc de more per cibos factidos jurandi ita Plinius libro secundo, capite septimo: Gentes verò quædam animalia, etiam aliqua obscæna pro Diis habent, ac multa dictu magis pudenda, per factidos cibos & alia
units.tr: They also swore by plants, such as the crambe, which was a Ionian custom, and by the caper-plant, by which Zeno the Stoic allowed himself to swear; and by foods of every kind, and many similar things. Hence Pliny, Book 2, chapter 7, on the custom of swearing by foul-smelling foods: "Some nations hold as gods certain animals, even some obscene ones, and many things more shameful to mention, swearing by foul-smelling foods and other

units.la: Forma iurandi per planta, & cibos. & alia similia iurantes. Sic per vinum mulieres iurasse legimus (unde Vino inscribere, mulieris per vinum iuramentum dici solet:) & per lapidem vel silicem Carthaginenses & Athenienses. De illis scribit Titus Livius libro primo tertiae Decadis. Inducitur enim Hannibal agnum laeva manu, dextra silicem lapidem retinens: Si falleret, Iovem castrosq; precatus Deos ita se mactarent, quemadmodum ipse agnum mactasset: & secundum precationem caput pecudis saxo elisit. Eadem formula, sed sub alia verborum conceptione repetitur, libro vigesimo secundo. Ejus quoque meminit Agellius libro primo, capite vigesimo primo, & Polybius libro tertio. Porro de Atheniensibus, ut ad lapidem iuramenta fecerint, Aristoteles in Republica Atheniensium & Philochorus scripserunt. Quo pertinet illud Demosthenis, Oratione in Canonem: Ὅρκοι ἀρρητοι καὶ ἐξορκώντες, id est, ad lapidem agentes et ejurantes: quod idem obscurat Harpocration.
units.tr: form of swearing by plants and foods. and others swearing similar things. So we read that women swore by wine (whence to inscribe the wine is commonly called a woman's oath by wine), and the Carthaginians and Athenians by a stone or flint. Titus Livy writes of them in Book 1 of the Third Decade. For Hannibal is introduced holding a lamb in his left hand and a flint stone in his right: if he should deceive, he invoked Jupiter and the gods of the camp, that they should slay him as he had slain the lamb; and in accordance with the prayer he dashed the animal's head against the stone. The same formula, but with different wording, is repeated in Book 22. Agellius also mentions it in Book 1, chapter 21, and Polybius in Book 3. Further, Aristotle in the Constitution of the Athenians and Philochorus wrote that the Athenians swore oaths at a stone. To this belongs the saying of Demosthenes in his speech against Kanon: "Oaths unspoken and swearing away," that is, taking and renouncing oaths at the stone; Harpocration explains the same thing obscurely.

units.la: Graecis etiam hoc in more positum fuisse legimus, ut ferrum tangentes tenentes iurarent: quod in sanciendis potissimum foederibus faciebant. Deos precantes, ut sanguis foedus perduraret, quemadmodum ferrum latuisset (id enim ferro ignito & candenti nomen) flatting in mare mydrum praecipitabant. Moris huius meminerunt Sophocles, Callimachus & Grammatici: qui mos posset a quo quosdam etiam in Livonia superstitiose potuit, quum pie per adiuramenta templi, fuit observatus. Nam sceleris alicujus accusati, ad ferri candentis iudicium vocabantur: & id subire nonnunquam vel invitii compellebantur. Id erat bu usmodi, ut crimius rem ferrum candens e medis prunis exemptum, in manus caperet, ac ut atorbund, & iudicibus offentaret, si ita adhuc ut nulla subsecuta illae fuisse, absolvere: si vi non eam passi non posset, obiecti criminis ita convicti damnaretur. Purgabant vero se prius iejunium, confessione & Eurhariis, mox ad horrifi cum illud experimentum accedebant. Id, quia periculosum erat, & insontes aliquando ex eo condemnabantur, praecipue vero contra Christianae pietatis mores erat, Denique tentari videbatur, Honorius lib. primo, fieri per gratiam sumptum edicto.
units.tr: We also read that it was a custom among the Greeks to touch iron while swearing an oath, especially when they were ratifying covenants. Calling on the gods that the covenant might last as long as the iron would remain unmelted, they threw the iron, heated and glowing (for the name comes from fire), into the sea. Sophocles, Callimachus and the grammarians mention this custom, which could have been used by some superstitiously in Livonia, though piously it was observed with oaths in the temple. For those accused of some crime were summoned to the trial by red-hot iron, and sometimes they were forced to undergo it even against their will. It was done in such a way that the accused took in his hands an iron glowing from the middle of the coals, and carried it for a certain distance, and showed it to the judges; if he came through without any injury he was acquitted, but if he could not bear it, he was condemned as convicted of the crime charged. They prepared themselves beforehand with fasting, confession and prayers, and only then approached that dreadful trial. Because it was dangerous, and innocent people were sometimes condemned by it, and especially because it was contrary to the practice of Christian piety, it was at last seen as a temptation; Honorius, in Book 1, ordered that it be abolished by an edict.

units.la: Pythagorei praeterea, teste Caelio Rhodigino libro vigesimo secundo, capite decimo, iurarunt per quaternitatem, sive numerum quaternarium, tanquam per numerum sacrum perfectum, quo conflat forma quadrata, omnibus numeris absolutissima.
units.tr: Moreover, the Pythagoreans, according to Caelius Rhodiginus in Book 22, chapter 10, swore by the tetrad, or the number four, as by a perfect sacred number, by which the square figure is formed, the most complete of all numbers.

units.la: Sic per Altare Veteres iurasse, conflat ex illo loco Matthaei, ubi Dominus perperam agere Pharisaeos inquit, qui non obligare iuramentum, quod per Altare fiebat, arbitrabantur, sed quod per donum fieret Altari illatum.
units.tr: That the ancients swore by the altar is clear from that passage of Matthew where the Lord says that the Pharisees were wrong, since they thought that an oath made by the altar did not bind, but only an oath made by the gift brought to the altar.

units.la: Per certa quinetiam instrumenta, eos iurasse ex multis probatis auctoribus constat; in primis vero per scepstrum. Id cum ex aliis locis, tum ex illo Homeri Iliad. x. dicit poetes: ΑΛΛ' ΕΚ ΤΟΙ ΧΕΙΩΝ, ΚΑΙ ΕΠΙ ΜΕΓΑΣ ΟΡΚΟΝ ΟΜΟΣΣΑΙ, Νῦ μὰ τὸ δὴ σκῆπτρον, τὸ μὲν οὐ ποτε φύλλα καὶ ὄζους: Φύσει, &c. Sed tibi edico, atque adeo magnum iuramentum iuro, Certe per hoc sceptrum, quod quidem nunquam folia & ramos Producet, &c.
units.tr: It is also established by many approved authors that they swore by certain instruments, especially by the sceptre. The poet says this both in other places and in that passage of Homer, Iliad 10: "But I swear a great oath, by this sceptre, which will never put forth leaves and branches..." But I declare to you, and indeed swear a great oath, surely by this sceptre, which never puts forth leaves and branches, and so on.

units.la: Hic ea quae Spondanus adnotat, quia propósito nostro serviunt, subiungere placet. Non assentior inquit, Eusebius, qui Achillem dicit ex re obvia & contingenti iurandi occasione arripuisse, quam illuc suggessit. Etenim si sceptrum Regium imperii, & iusticiae signum fuit (unde iusti nunc Philoricus ab origine rerum pro Diis immortalibus Veteres hastas coluisse dixit, ob cuius religionis memoriam, inquit, adhuc Deorum simulacris hastae adduntur. Hasta autem nihil aliud est, quam σκῆπτρον, sceptrum) non potest in rebus humanis are augustiori iusiurandum illis pete, quod Veteribus etiam usitatissimum fuit. Tale est illud Parthenopaei apud Euripidem: Ὀμνυσι δ' αἰχμὴ ὧν ἔχει, μᾶλλον Θεῶν Σιβέων πιστῶσ, ὀμνύειν δ' ὑπάρχει.
units.tr: Here I think it right to add what Spondanus notes on this point, since it serves our purpose. Eustathius, he says, does not agree that Achilles seized on an oath suggested by a chance occasion at hand. For if the sceptre was the sign of royal power and of justice (whence Philoricus says that in the beginning the ancients worshipped spears as the immortal gods, and that the memory of this religion is why spears are still attached to the statues of the gods), then in human affairs no more august oath could be sought than by it. The ancients used such oaths very commonly. So Parthenopaeus in Euripides: "The spear swears by what it holds, more trustworthy than the gods of the Sibyls, and it is possible to swear by it." [Ὀμνυσι δ' αἰχμὴ ὧν ἔχει, μᾶλλον Θεῶν Σιβέων πιστῶσ, ὀμνύειν δ' ὑπάρχει.]

units.la: Notum est etiam, quid de Cenei hastae proverbiali a Graecis interpretibus referatur. Sic apud Flaccum ex imitatione Homerica:
units.tr: It is also well known what is reported by the Greek commentators about the proverbial spear of Ceneus. So Horace, imitating Homer:

units.la: Hanc ego magnanimi splium Didymaonis hastam, Quae neque tam frondes virides, neq; proferet umbras, Vt semel est a vulsa jugis, ac matre peremptaFida ministeria & duras obit horrida pugnas,Testor.
units.tr: "By this spear of the great-hearted Didymaon I swear, which, once cut from the mountain and parted from its mother, will bear neither green leaves nor shade, and yet it serves faithfully and undergoes harsh battles."

units.la: Idem elegantissime Virgilius: Vt sceptrum hoc ( sceptrum dextra nam forte gerebat) Nunquam fronde leuis fundet virgulta, neq; umbram, Cum semel in sylvis imo de stirpe recisum Matre caret, posuitq; comas & brachia ferro Olim arbos, nunc artificis manus aere decoro Inclusit, patribusq; dedit gestare Latinis.
units.tr: Virgil says the same, very elegantly: "As this sceptre (for he happened to be carrying a sceptre in his right hand) will never put forth light shoots of leaves or shade, once it has been cut in the woods from its root and lost its mother; the tree once lost its hair and arms to the iron, but now the hand of the craftsman has enclosed it in fair bronze and given it to the Latin fathers to carry."

units.la: Iurat itaque per sceptrum Achilles duplici de causa, quasi dicat: Si sceptrum, ut lignum confidere res, quemadmodum illud nunc a motibus abscissum amplius non revirescet: sic nos, ubi dissitiemus in vicem, non sumus in illum gratiae & amicitiae florere reditur. Si vero ut divinum aliquid & sacrum hoc sceptrum intelligas, est, curjusjurandum augustum existimetur. Hoc enim sceptrum gerunt filii Graecorum Διοσκουροι. Quare δ' ... qui circa jura versantur, & Θεσμοφυλακες, quod erant Reges, quibus sceptrum erat justitiae symbolum, ut diximus, quemadmodum fortitudinis Hastam, inquit Eustathius: unde qui hastam collegerit distinguit τὸ ἀκρον ... contra quaemam ... Haltenus Spond.
units.tr: Achilles therefore swears by the sceptre for a twofold reason, as if he were saying: "If this sceptre, like wood, is cut off from its roots, it will never grow green again; so we, when we part from one another, shall never flourish again in that friendship and grace." But if you understand this sceptre as something divine and sacred, then it should be considered a most august oath. For the sons of the Greeks, the Dioscuri, carry this sceptre. Hence those who are concerned with law, and the Thesmophylakes, since they were kings to whom the sceptre was the symbol of justice, as we have said, just as the spear was the symbol of courage, says Eustathius; whence he who has gathered up the spear distinguishes the point... Thus far Spondanus.

units.la: Aliud exemplum hujus jurisjurandi per sceptrum extat apud eundem Homerum Iliad. 1. Ως φάτο· ὁ δ' ἐς χαρα σαπηλεγε βαλε κηρι δι ὀμοσας Ισαν νῦν ζεύς, &c. Sit dixit, hic autem in manibus sceptrum jetit & juravit Sciat nunc Iupiter, &c.
units.tr: Another example of this oath by the sceptre is found in the same Homer, Iliad 1. [Ὣς φάτο· ὁ δ᾽ ἐς γαῖαν σκῆπτρον βαλὼν κατώμοσε· ἴστω νῦν Ζεύς.] So he spoke, and he took the sceptre in his hands and swore: Let Zeus now know.

units.la: Hic idem Spondanus, Obser vandus est, inquit, mos antiquus juramento aliquid alicui fanciendi, a Rege videlicet injiciendo sceptrum in manus ejus, cui fit promissio.
units.tr: Here Spondanus also observes: the ancient custom of confirming a promise to someone by an oath is to be noted, namely, that the king places the sceptre in the hands of the one to whom the promise is made.

units.la: Pertinet hac, quod Agamenonis sceptrum Chaioneos tanquam Numen praesens veneratos legimus hastamq; votasse. Coluerunt vero illud non ut cetera colebantur Numina, templo arisq; constitutus, sed quotannis sacrorum antistes illud penes se domi suae habebat, singulis diebus hostias illi immolabat, remq; divinam faciebat: mensaq; illi variarum referta carnum, liborumq; & omnis generis placentarum semper adhabat. Nō mirū igitur est, Veteres per sceptrum jurare fuisse solitos.
units.tr: To this belongs what we read: the Chaioneans venerated the sceptre of Agamemnon as a present deity and vowed a spear to it. They did not worship it as the other gods were worshipped, established in a temple and on altars; rather, each year a priest of the rites kept it at home with himself, offered sacrifices to it daily and performed the divine service. A table laden with various kinds of meat, cakes and every sort of pastry was always set before it. It is no wonder, then, that the ancients were accustomed to swear by the sceptre.

units.la: Iurabant itemnonnulli per telum & acinacen, per mensam, aliaq; plurima instrumenta. Verum mos Scythicus fere est, cujus meminerunt Apuleius & Lucianus. Apuleius quidè loro illo supra citato, inquit: Vtrunq; tonò non est, per quod adjures, nempe per dextrā telum, &c. Haec fere sunt praecipua, per quae Ethnici jurare olim consuevorunt: quam consuetudinem, cum Iudei, ut alias Ethnicorum superstitiones, Iusserint imitari, Christus ipse perstrinxit Matth.5. in quiens: Ἐγω δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν μὴ ὀμόσαι ὅλως. μήτε ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ... Ego vero dico vobis, ne jurate omnino: neq; per coelum, quia thronus Dei est; neq; per terram, quia scabellum est pedum ejus; neq; per Hierosolyma, quia urbs est magni Regis; neq; per caput tuum jures, quia non potes unum capillum album aut nigrum facere. Esto autem sermo vester, etiam etiam, non non, &c.
units.tr: Some also swore by a spear and a scimitar, by a table, and by many other instruments. But the Scythian custom is almost the most common, and Apuleius and Lucian mention it. Apuleius, in the passage cited above, says: "Neither the one nor the other is a thing by which you may swear, namely by the spear in the right hand," and so on. These are almost the chief things by which the heathen were once accustomed to swear. When the Jews began to imitate this custom, as they did other superstitions of the heathen, Christ himself condemned it in Matthew 5, saying: "But I say to you, do not swear at all, neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God; nor by the earth, for it is his footstool; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. But let your speech be: yes, yes; no, no," and so on.

units.la: Porro ad formulas jurisjurandi referendum etiam hoc, quod ut praesentes; ita jurantes aram tangebant. Hinc Cicero pro Flacco: Ergo is, qui si aram tenens jumaret, trederet nemo, per epistolam quod volet, injuratus probabit. Plautus in Rudente: —G R. Tange aram hanc Venerii. L A. Tango. R G. Per Venerem hanc jurandum est tibi. L A. Quid jurem? G R. Quod jubeo. L . Prei verbus quid vis, id quod domi est, nunquam id i supplicabo. G R. Tene aram hanc. L A. Teneo. G R. Dejura te mihi argentum daturum. Eodem illo die, viduli ubi fis potius. Cicero quoque in oratione pro Cornelio Balbo scribit, Graecorum veterem hunc morem fuisse, ut post eam quis testimonium diceret jurandi deinde causa adamus accederet.
units.tr: Further, to the formulas of the oath belongs also this, that those who swore touched the altar, as those present did. Hence Cicero in the speech for Flaccus: "Therefore he who, holding the altar, swore, would be trusted by no one; a man who has not sworn will prove what he wishes by letter." Plautus in the Rudens: "G. R. Touch this altar of Venus. L. A. I touch it. R. G. You must swear by this Venus. L. A. What am I to swear? G. R. What I bid you. L. I shall never beg for what is at home, whatever you want by way of prayer. G. R. Hold this altar. L. A. I hold it. G. R. Swear that you will give me the money." On that same day, you will be more easily... Cicero also writes in the speech for Cornelius Balbus that this was the old custom of the Greeks: after someone had given testimony, he then came up to take the oath for the sake of the cause.

units.la: Loci item in jurejurando habitam fuisse rationem docet quaestio vigesima octava, Romanorum apud Plutarchum, quae sic habet: Cur pueros Herculem juraturos non fuisse jurejurando hoc intra domum facere, sed exire sub Dium jubent? Anea est vera quorundam opinio, quia Herculis non sit delectatus vitâ parietibus clausa, sed sub dio et pereregrinus degere? Aut quia Deus ille non indigena, sed peregrinus et hospes fuit? Nam Bacchum quoque, non juravit sub tecto, hunc quoque peregrinum. An vero haec joco tantum pueris dicantur? Aliis vero hac ratione co biberetur a levitate et jurandi temeritate voluerunt, sicut Favorino placet. Nam ille qui si apparatum cunctationem injicit, facultatem, deliberandi praebet. Hunc ritum nou communem, sed Herculi peculiarem fuisse cum Favorino aliqua affirmaret, is, quae de eo narrantur, confidentis. Adeo enim religiosum hac in re fuisse traduntur Herculem, ut ...
units.tr: The question of place in swearing, too, is shown to have been considered by the twenty-eighth question of Plutarch's Roman Questions, which reads: "Why do they bid boys who are about to swear by Hercules not to do this oath within the house, but to go out under the open sky?" Is the true opinion of some that Hercules did not delight in a life shut in by walls, but lived under the open sky as a stranger? Or because that god was not a native but a foreigner and guest? For they did not swear Bacchus under a roof either, and he too was a foreigner. Or are these things said to boys merely in jest? Others, however, by this rule wished to correct levity and rashness in swearing, as Favorinus thinks; for he who introduces a delay and a preparation gives opportunity for deliberation. Favorinus affirmed that this rite was not common but peculiar to Hercules, and what is told about him confirms it. For Hercules is reported to have been so scrupulous in this matter that...

units.la: Postremo considerandum hic est jurisjurandi conservatio quam religiosa olim apud Ethnicos fuerit: ...
units.tr: Lastly, we must consider here how religiously the keeping of oaths was once observed among the heathen: ...
His words are these: ...

units.la: Sed jura vis magnum jurumentum. Postea vero multum laesus est.
units.tr: But you may use a great oath. Afterwards, however, he was greatly harmed.
The same Carl...

units.la: Ex ipsis autem constat, Ethnicos vel naturae duce et magistra jusjurandum, ceu rem sacrosanctam, plurimi semper fecisse. juris jurandi religionem violassent. Hinc Pontifex Maximus apud Romanos (Maximus, scilicet esto, dicitus, quòd judex atque arbiter habebatur, rerum divinarum humanarumq;, sive, ut alibi ajt, quòd maximus rerum, quæ ad sacra religionesq; pertinent, judex sit, vindex q; contumaciæ privatorum, magistratuum q;) contro versias de perjurio, quo pietas ad versus Deos immortales violatur, disceptare & dijudicare solitus fuerat. Quò alludit apud Plautum in Rudente Labrax leno:
units.tr: From these very things it is clear that the heathen, guided and taught by nature alone, have always held the oath as something most sacred, and that the most (?) ... would have violated the religion of the oath. Hence the Pontifex Maximus among the Romans (called "Maximus" presumably because he was regarded as judge and arbiter of all divine and human affairs, or, as elsewhere it is said, because he is the greatest judge of the matters that pertain to sacred rites and religions, and avenger of the contumacy of private persons and magistrates) was accustomed to hear and decide disputes about perjury, by which piety toward the immortal gods is violated. To this Labrax the pimp alludes in Plautus' Rudens:

units.la: Libet jurare, tu n' meo Pontifex perjurio es?
units.tr: "Do you wish to swear? Are you my Pontifex in matters of perjury?"

units.la: Hoc est, Tuane, tanquam Pontificis Maximi, de meo perjurio arbitrandi, & judicandi potestas? Tune meo perjurio præesse, aut judex sedere postulas, tanquam Pontifex? Adde hus, quæ Xenophon scribit in istam sententiam secundo deexpeditione Cyri: ... Hoc primum & precipuum est, quod Deorum latere ... Ea verò si quis neglecta sibi conscius est, illum ego nequaquam beatum existimaverim. Divinitus enim illatum bellum, haud scio quæ quis aut celeritate effugere possit, aut quibus in tenebris latere, aut in quo monumento arcere. Etenim omnia Deis ubiq; sunt obnoxia, & æquali potentia reguntur ab ipsis omnia ubi vis gentium. Hæc Xenophon: quibus subjungi etiam hæc possunt que Nicolaus Leonicus Thomæus scribit, non tam de admirabili more jurandi apud Paliscorum fontem in Sicilia, quam de horrenda pœna eorum, qui dolo malo pejerassent. Ejus verba hæc sunt: jusjurandum autem tota insula et finitimus etiam Italiæ populo percelebre & horrendum eo loci fuisse perhibetur, cujus talis religionis fuerat modus. Juraturi illuc accedentes, quæcunq; affirmare volebant, tabellis antè conscripta, domo secum afferebant, bas posteaobsignatas in fontem dejiciebant: quæ si vera rectaq; fuissent, illa quæ juratus affirmasset, super aquas facile fluitare, & ferri videbantur. Sin vero secus esset, & dolo malo pejeranti quibusdam illas scripta esset, statim mergebantur & ima petebant, homoq; ille subitò correptus ignibus exuri illico, & in cineres verti cernebatur. Quamobrem sacerdotes ii, quibus sacri fontis erat cura, non prius aliquem ad id jusjurandum admittere dicebantur, quàm is sponsores præstituissent aliquos, qui expurgationis impensas, si quid sibi durius accidisset, pro se statim repræsentare tenerentur.
units.tr: That is: do you have the power, as if you were Pontifex Maximus, to judge and decide concerning my perjury? Do you demand to preside over my perjury, or to sit as judge, as if you were Pontifex? Add to this what Xenophon writes to the same effect in the second book of the Expedition of Cyrus: "This is the first and chief thing, that the gods are not hidden... If anyone is conscious of having neglected these things, I would by no means count him happy. For a war sent by the gods, I know not what man could escape by speed, or hide in what darkness, or shelter in what monument. For all things are everywhere subject to the gods, and all things in the world are governed by them with equal power." Thus Xenophon. To these may also be added what Nicolaus Leonicus Thomaeus writes, not so much about the admirable manner of swearing at the spring of the Palisci in Sicily, as about the terrible punishment of those who had sworn falsely with evil intent. His words are these: "An oath in that place was said to be very famous and dreadful throughout the whole island, and even for the people neighbouring Italy, and its manner of religion was as follows. Those coming there to swear took with them from home tablets on which they had written beforehand whatever they wished to affirm, and these, sealed afterwards, they cast into the spring. If what they had written was true and right, the tablets were seen to float easily upon the water and be carried along. But if it was otherwise, and anyone had written them with evil intent to swear falsely, they immediately sank to the bottom, and that man was at once seized by fire and seen to be burnt to ashes. Therefore the priests who had charge of the sacred spring were said not to admit anyone to this oath before he had furnished sureties who were bound to make good at once the costs of the purification, should anything harsher befall him." Thus far Leonicus.
So far Leonicus.

units.la: Postremò, ut hunc totum locum de juramento concludam, addere libet, memorabilem historiam, ceu congruentissimam huic loco, quæ apud Herodotum exstat libro primo Hist. (inquit ille) ex τινὲς ... Greek passage continues in the text.
units.tr: Finally, to conclude this whole discussion of oaths, I add a memorable story, which seems most fitting to this place. It is found in Herodotus, Book 1 of the Histories, where he says: [the Greek passage follows in the text].

units.la: Greek text as printed continues across the lower lines of the page. Fertur Archetimum ex Erythraea Ionica civitate in Tenedum venisse, & apud Cydiam bospitem suum auri magnum vim depositsse, nihil de homine sinistri aut violenti suspicatum, ne qui cum recens amicitiam init vissee. Tum Cydia malum consilium avaritia suggessit. Cum enim aurum apud se depositum ab ipso reposceretur, contumaciter negavit. Et cum inter se contenderent, tandem visum est, ut rorum negotium ad jusjurandū referretur. Cydias igitur cum certio postea die fidem suam seu Dei commissam jurejurando confirmaturus esset, reversus domū excogitavit dolum hujusmodi. Omne simul aurum in excavatam ferulam inclusit, & qua parte ferula manus amplectitur, faciebat circumvolvit undeque, ut dolus celaretur. Postquā verò praescriptus dies advenit, Cydias languidum gradu caussa morbi fingens, fulciendo ferula corpus, accessit: et stans ante templum, quod juramentum jui conscium esse volebat, ferulam, in qua omnis eius iniquitas latebat, Archetimo tenendum porrigie, donec absolverit juramentū: deinde manibus elevatis dixie, accepisse quidem se depositum ab Archetimo, sed id reddisse: quod mendacium erat arte confictum. His dictis graviter indignatus Archetimus, illu vehementi ferulam in pavimentum projecit: qua dirupta omnis auri moles effluxit. Haec quidem divinitus providentia adjutus est Archetimus. Cydias autem malum vite exitum habuisse dicitur. Hae ergo resticiens, quilibet sibi cavent ne sacramenta contemserit: utramvis enim in partem res incerta feratur, non sine periculo sunt. Hactenus Herodotus.
units.tr: It is said that Archetimus came from the Ionian city of Erythrae to Tenedos and deposited a large sum of gold with his host Cydias. Suspecting nothing dishonest or violent in the man, since he had only recently formed the friendship, he did not think to take precautions. Then avarice prompted Cydias to an evil plan. When Archetimus asked for the gold back, Cydias stubbornly denied having it. As they argued, it was finally agreed that the matter should be referred to an oath. Cydias was to confirm his good faith, or the trust placed in him before God, by swearing on a later day. He went home and devised a trick. He put all the gold into a hollow staff and wound the staff tightly wherever his hand would grip it, so that the fraud would be hidden. When the appointed day came, Cydias pretended to be lame from an illness, and leaned on the staff as he approached. Standing before the temple, which he wanted to be a witness to his oath, he held out the staff, in which all his wickedness was hidden, for Archetimus to hold while he swore the oath. Then, with his hands raised, he said that he had indeed received the deposit from Archetimus but had given it back. This lie was cleverly contrived. Archetimus, deeply indignant at these words, struck the staff hard against the pavement. It broke open, and the whole mass of gold spilled out. Archetimus was helped in this by divine providence. Cydias, it is said, came to a bad end. Therefore, Herodotus concludes, everyone should take care not to despise oaths: whichever way a doubtful matter turns, they are not without danger. Thus far Herodotus.

units.la: Atque hac quidem de precibus atque votis, quorum apud Homerum & Apollonium, in utrique, sacrificii de scriptione fit mentio: & simul de juramentis, quae precum quaedam sunt species, in sacrificiis, praesertim saederalibus, sape adhiberi solent, sint dicta.
units.tr: So much for prayers and vows, which Homer and Apollonius both mention in describing the sacrifice, and at the same time for oaths, which are a kind of prayer and are often used in sacrifices, especially covenant sacrifices.

units.la: N Y N C ad alia, quae ab utroque Poëta hic ordine recensentur, quaeq, actus sacrificialis fuerunt quasi σείδομεν, accedamus: Inter haec tertium est mola, sive frugum salsarū injuscfio, quae uno nomine Immolatio proprie a Veteribus fuit appellata, in omnibus, fere sacrificiis usurpatea.
units.tr: Now let us come to the other things which both poets list here in order, and which were parts of the sacrificial act, as it were their first steps. Among these the third is the mola, or the sprinkling of salted grain, which the ancients properly called by the single name immolatio, and which was used in almost all sacrifices.

units.la: Idest, interpreté Eustathio, ὅὰῖέὰῖέὰῖέὰῖ. Erant autem ὅλρχέὰῖ, ut inquit idem Eustathius, ὅὰῖέὰῖ. Nam ὅλρχέὰῖ usurpabant ante sacrificium &, ut Poëta inquit, ὅὰῖέὰῖέὰῖ. Quod si manifestius est loquendum, ὅλρχέὰῖ, sive ὅλρχέὰῖ etiam legie Hesychius ) id est, ὅὰῖέὰῖ (ita ille quoque ὅλρχέ interpretatur) ὅλρχέὰῖ, inquit, ὅὰῖέὰῖέὰῖ, id est, hordeā cum salibus, quae arte ante sacrificium igiruntur, infundebant. Dion vocat τὰ μὶὦὰ τὰ ὶὰῖὰῖ, mixtionem sive compositum ex hordeo & salibus. Hinc quic sufmodi primitias colligebant, ὶὰῖέὰῖ sunt dicti, te Plutarcho initio quaesti. Graec. oi ῖέὰῖέὰῖέὰῖέ roμὶὰῖέὰῖέὰῖέ omnes Graecorum ὰῖέὰῖέὰῖέὰῖέὰῖέὰῖέ.
units.tr: That is, according to Eustathius: [Greek]. Now the barley (hordea) were, as Eustathius says, [Greek]. For they used them before the sacrifice and, as the poet says, [Greek]. If we must speak more plainly, the barley-grains (which Hesychius also reads as [Greek]) are, as he explains, barley mixed with salt, which were scattered before the sacrifice. Dion calls it a mixture or compound of barley and salt. Hence those who gathered such firstfruits were called [Greek], as Plutarch says at the beginning of his Greek Questions, where all the Greeks [Greek].

units.la: Hujusce autem moris Eustathius aliquot causas enumerat. Velenim id faciebant ὰῖέὰῖέὰῖ, id est, abundantiam frugum abominandi gratia, quorum ceu primitiae quaedam hordea illa afferebantur. Hinc Caelius lib. 12. cap. 1. ait, fuisse auguriū futuræ frugum fertilitatis. Vel id faciebant suae erga Deum gratitudinis testificandae gratia, a quo hoc vitae subsidium acceperant. Nam quoniam glandium vitu asperiore liberati, ad meliore mitioremq;, vitu tradutti fuerant: atq; idcirco hordea projiciebant, ceu semen manufactum, quae primo hominibus ut antiquus est sermo, glandium esu liberatis subsidio fuerunt.
units.tr: Eustathius lists several reasons for this custom. First, they did it to ward off a shortage of crops, and barley was offered as a kind of firstfruits of abundance. Hence Caelius, Book 12, chapter 1, says it was a sign of future fertility. Second, they did it to show their gratitude to God, from whom they had received this sustenance. For when they had been freed from the rough diet of acorns and moved to a softer and gentler diet, they threw barley as if it were manufactured seed, since, as the ancient saying goes, it was the first help for men freed from eating acorns.
R

units.la: Atque hanc ipsam ob caussam hordea Graeci κριθαὶ dicta: propterea quod ipsis in vertiginem ἀνθρώπους τὴν ἀλέγων ζῳων αἵθεοπων, id est, homines a brutis animalibus fuerit distinctos et sequestrati. Hinc etiam κριθαὶ dicitur quasi κρίθος βαίνω. Appellat autem βάρβα etiam hodie Peloponnesii τὸν πυρῆς τόπον, id est, locum ignis, quem πυρῆας proprie appellamus. Inde apud Comicum κριθαιῶν dicti sunt panes caelum cribano, quem etiam Clibanum appellant per λ.ut κερασλαρχάς, κρατρελαλαγία. Ad gratam igitur memoriam antiqui vitibus hordea proiici solebant. Hoc olim, nondum molendi usu comperto, integra fuerunt de vorata: unde et hordea dicta, a fumo litterae v, quasi ἂλα, id est, tota, sive integra. Suidas similiter testatur ἄλαι vocari hordeum, eo quod olim integrum comederetur ante repertum molarum usum: in ejusmodi memoriam τῆς ἐπιθύων ἐπὶ τῆς ἀναμοῦ ἀλεύ. Quando autem deerant hordea pro illis quercus folia proiiciebantur: quo et ipso veteris diaeta atque tum ζῷ ἁβ δρυφαγον πραλαιοῦ ζοφῆς, id est, autiqui cibi glandibus memoriam replicabant. Sicin Odyss. Vfsdsv foeda defiruti sunt albo, decerptes teneris quercus solis supplicabant. Iidem cum deesse illis vinum ad libationem aquam libabant: qua ratione et libamenta et mole falsa illis erant ἐπιθῆκες, id est, paratu facilia. Atq. haec fuerunt causa hordei. Megaris vero, dum ad Terei sepulchrum sacrum fiebat, pro hordeo calculis utebantur: unde Pausanias Att. ἐκ τῆς ἀλῶν χαρφίν.
units.tr: For this very reason the Greeks called barley [Greek], because it distinguished men from the brute animals, [Greek]. Hence also [Greek] is said to be from [Greek], "to walk on barley." Even today the Peloponnesians call the place of the fire [Greek], that is, the hearth, which we properly call [Greek]. Hence in the Comic poet, loaves baked in an oven, which they also call clibanus, are called [Greek]. So, in grateful memory, the ancients used to throw barley on the victims. In former times, before the use of the mill was discovered, the grain was eaten whole, and so barley was called [Greek], from the alpha privative, as if [Greek], that is, whole or entire. Suidas similarly reports that barley was called [Greek] because it was eaten whole in earlier times, before the use of millstones was found; in memory of this, [Greek]. When barley was lacking, oak leaves were thrown instead, and this recalled the ancient diet, the acorn-eating of the old time, as in the Odyssey: [Greek]. The same people, when they lacked wine for libation, poured water instead; so both the libations and the salted meal were easy to prepare. These were the reasons for the barley. At Megara, when sacrifice was made at the tomb of Tereus, they used pebbles instead of barley; whence Pausanias, in the Attica, [Greek].

units.la: Porro sales hordeos miscebant non modo propter naturalem fertilitatem et repertam in alimonis gratiam, verum etiam quia sales amicitiae sunt symbolum, quam etiam ob causam hosp. tibus ante omnes alios cibos apponi consue verunt: vel ideo, ob amicitiae et redintegrationem et firmitatem. Sal enim multos corporibus firmitatis atque durationis causa exsistit: vel etiam ut esset symbolum τῆς κοινωνίας ἐκ θεῖος, id est, unitatem, quae est in amicitia. Nam ut sal ex multis aquis liquidis atque fusilibus in unum solidum corpus coalescit et concrescit; sic etiam qui ex diversis et longe a se invicem distinctis locum conveniunt in unum, et loco et amico habitu coalescunt: ὅτι γὰρ ἀλὸς ἐκ ὕδατων πολλῶν ῥυτῶν ὡς χυ πα γεὶς, εἰ ἡ γὴ ὁ πρίον τὸν ἀγγοι σῶμα ὀὗτος ἀμοῖ ἐν ἔτι· Sciendum autem est, quid cum Poeta οὐλοχύτας dicat, quidam posteriorum inter quos est Dion Romanus, non composite οὐλοχύτας, sed simpliciter οὐλὰς appellant.
units.tr: Moreover, they mixed salt with the barley not only for its natural fertility and its proven value in food, but also because salt is a symbol of friendship. For this reason salt is served to guests before all other foods, either to restore and strengthen friendship. Salt, indeed, gives firmness and durability to many bodies. Or it may be a symbol of the fellowship of unity, which is found in friendship. For just as salt is formed and solidified into one firm body from many liquid and fluid waters, so too those who come together from different places, far apart from one another, are joined into one in place and in friendly disposition: [Greek]. But it should be noted that, although the poet says [Greek], some later writers, among them Dion of Rome, do not say [Greek] but simply [Greek].

units.la: Licet etiam, ut idem Eustathius addit, alio modo breviss. simul et de mola falsa, et vini libatione sic disserere. Cum duplex sit nostrae vitibus necessarius, nimirum et ficus, qui conflat ex seminibus atq. aliis fructibus et humidus, qui conflatit primo quidem in aqua: secundario autem in vino, prinitias itaq, τῆς ἄλας ζωογόνου φορᾶς, id est, totius vitibus viviticis veteres illi et molas falsas in sacrificiis projiciebant, ceu ex sicco, atq. etiam libationes, quae modo in hoc, modo in illo humido fiebant pro tempore ratione.
units.tr: As Eustathius adds, one may also discuss the salted meal and the libation of wine briefly in another way. Our life needs a double nourishment: one dry, which consists of seeds and other fruits, and one moist, which comes first in water and second in wine. So the ancients threw salted meal, as the first of the life-giving produce of the whole vine, from the dry, and also made libations, which were offered in this or that moist form according to the circumstances of the time.

units.la: Post molas autem falsas secuta sunt sacrificia, et quae in illis fiebat κεισοφαγία, id est, scarnium manducatio. Idcirco post vitibus necessarium in ventionem consecuta est ἡ τῆς κρεωφαγίας τοῦ ἀπολῦειας, carnum magnificis sumptuosis apparatus atq. delitiae fuerunt excogitatae.
units.tr: After the salted meal came the sacrifices, and in them the keisophagia, that is, the eating of flesh. Hence, once the grain offerings were in place, the eating of meat followed, and magnificent, sumptuous preparations and delicacies of meat were devised.

units.la: Sciendum quod est nonnullos alia ratione οὐλοχύτας interpretari non θυμαῖος, ἡ σφαγὴ μυ, ἡ σφαγὴ ... hoc est, inter ea quae ante sacrificium fieri consuevesse, qualia etiam fuerunt evaporatio thuris, et id genus primitiae quaecunq, ut siligo, vel etiam placentulae, et similia: sed ipsa canistra, sive vasa, per quae hordea funduntur; cuiusmodi vasa οὐλοχόον, sive οὐλοχοῆον, alio nomine dicitur, hoc est, ἀγγεῖον, ἐκ δ' ἀλοῦλαι ἰμβάλλων ... ἀπαρχὰς τῇ θεῷ, Pascalum in quod molas sacrificaturi conjiciebant.
units.tr: It should be noted that some interpret the oulochytai in another way, not as the things done before the sacrifice, such as the burning of incense and similar first-fruits, like fine flour or small cakes. Rather, they mean the baskets or vessels themselves through which the barley was poured out. Such a vessel is called by another name, the oulochoon or oulochoeion, that is, a container, and the meal sprinkled on the victim was called the first-fruits offered to the god.

units.la: Apud Apollonium similiter hujusce cerimoniae expressa his verbis fit mentio: Primum: —οἱ δ' ἀρ' ὑπὸ εἰσί, ἀρχῆσθαι οὐλοχύτας τε παρίχων, id est, —Illi vero posiea
units.tr: Apollonius likewise mentions this ceremony in these words: "Then those who... began the oulochytai and..." The sense is obscure, but the text speaks of the beginning of the rite and of the offering of the grain.

units.la: Et aquam manualem et molam salsam praebebant,
units.tr: And they provided both the hand-water and the salted meal.

units.la: Sociu nimirum, qui et aquam manualem ad la vandas manus, et salsat illas fruges adferebant in canistris. Scholiastes in hec verba sic commentatur: οὐλοχύτας alii interpretantur τὰ κατα. ... ὑπὸ ὁ. ὑπὶ δ' ἀω ἢ φίρῃ) τα ϑεὸς ϑυσίαν, id est, calathos, sive taniftra (per metonymiam) quibus portabantur ea, quae ad sacrificium erant necessaria. Alii interpretantur τὰς κεδὰς, ὑπαὶ ὑμεὶ ὑλὰς ὀσὶ ἐαπλοὶ ὁὶς βωμοῖς, id est, hordea; quondam hordea inspergebant Altaribus.
units.tr: Namely, the attendants who brought both the water for washing the hands and the salted grain in baskets. The scholiast comments on these words thus: some interpret the oulochytai as the baskets, or wicker containers (by metonymy), in which the things necessary for the sacrifice were carried. Others interpret them as barley, with which the altars were once sprinkled.

units.la: Et paulli post: —ἢ κὰ ἀὑ ἰυχολη ϑεοχύτας βάλει.
units.tr: And a little later: "or throws the theochytai..."

units.la: Dixit (precatus est) & simul cum pretibus sparsit ϑεοχύτας.
units.tr: "He spoke (prayed), and at the same time he sprinkled the theochytai."

units.la: Per ϑεοχύτας intelligit Scholiastes τὰς κεδὰς, id est, hordea, vel, ut addit idem interpres, τὸ ὕδωρ, ὃ εἰωθαστν ἰυβάλλειν εἰς τὸ ὃς τὸ ἱερὸν ὅτι τὸ ὅ ἀπὸ τὸ ἱερὸν, id est, aquam, quam hostiae auribus infundere consuevernt, ejus nimirum recreandae, refi ciendaeq; gratia, ut ea facilius deinde caedi possent. Hesychius ϑεοχύτας exponit ὅλας κὴ ἀπαρχὰς. Ergo & ὅλαι & ὑλαὶ, & ὅλαι. item ἀλχὺ & ϑεοχύ) illa mole salsa Graecus dicuntur. Inde natum ὑλαῖ ἀροβάλ- λωσι & ϑεὸ ἀλλεν apud Homerum & Athenaeum, quod Suidas exponit κεδὰς ὅτι χιεῖς τὸς ϑύματα, id est, ut Virgilius & Horatius interpretantur, Spargere molam vitumis: & Cicero, Inspergere molam, aloco de Divinatione: Cor est, in extis, jam abscedet, simul ac molam & vitti mam inspergens. Item ϑεοϑυτεῖν immolare, mola inspersa sacrificare.
units.tr: By theochytai the scholiast understands barley, or, as the same commentator adds, the water which they were accustomed to pour into the ears of the victim, so that it might be refreshed and revived and thus more easily slaughtered afterwards. Hesychius explains theochytai as salted meal and first-fruits. So the Greeks call the salted meal by the names alphiton and theochytai. From this comes the Homeric and Athenaean phrase for sprinkling the god with meal; Suidas explains it as sprinkling the victims with meal. Virgil and Horace speak of "sprinkling the meal and the wine," and Cicero, in his book On Divination, has "to sprinkle the meal." Thus theothyteîn means to sacrifice, that is, to offer with meal sprinkled upon the victim.

units.la: Athenaeus scribit lib.7. Boeotios, scilicet Agartarchide, anguillas Copsadas (a Copaide lacu dictas) insuitate magnitudinis hostiarum more coronatas, molaq; etiam salsa conspersas cum precibus Diis immolare: accum peregrinus quispiam inusitato inopinato, hoc sacri genere obiisse conspiceret, cur id fieret, scisciretur, Boeotios nihil aliud respondere potuisse, quam servanda esse Majorum institutaaa: nec se decere, patriae consuetudinis ratione alius reddere. Ibidem scribit: Piscatores, quo tempore thynnos piscantur, post felicem retium jactum, sacrum Neptuno facere, eiq; thynnum captum immolare, quod sacrificium inde Thynnaeum vocane, & Phasielitas salsamentis quoq; tannis Cylabrae, quem tanquam Heroa venerantur, rem divinam facere. Hac Athenaeus.
units.tr: Athenaeus writes in book 7 that the Boeotians, following Agatharchides, adorned eels called Copsades (named from the Lake Copais) with garlands, as if they were sacrificial victims, sprinkled them with salted meal, and offered them to the gods with prayers. When a foreigner saw this unusual and unexpected kind of sacrifice and asked why it was done, the Boeotians could answer only that the customs of their ancestors had to be kept, and that it was not fitting to change the custom of their country. In the same place he writes that fishermen, when they catch tunnies, after a successful casting of the nets, make a sacred offering to Neptune and sacrifice a captured tunny to him; they call this the Thynnaean sacrifice. The Phaselites, too, with salted fish, perform a sacred rite for Cylabras, whom they venerate as a hero. So far Athenaeus.

units.la: Theocritus quoq; hujus cerimoniae, usitatae apud Graecos, expresse meminit his verbis: Ἀλφῖα τὸ φαῖῶν τας, ἀλλ' ὅτι τῶδε Θίσυλι ἀλεδισα, id est, Mola quidem primum igne frigitur in suffitum, sed inspergē O Theftyli misera, &c.
units.tr: Theocritus also expressly mentions this ceremony, customary among the Greeks, in these words: "The meal is first heated in the fire for the incense, but sprinkle it, O wretched Thestylis, etc."

units.la: Ἀλφιὸν definiunt farinam hordeaceam ex ϑεσὶ κεδὸν, ut ἀλλὰ ϑεσ ἐν τὸ τυρῶν farinam tritia tam: tamen eo distinguitur, quod ἀλφῑ πτον torreatur: ωλλ'ν ὁδεκ: quasi ex crudo hordeo fiat. Mola enim praeparata e farre tosto, sale & ture imponebatur capiti victimae, quae cum malla, id est, magis aulla credebatur & immolata, (Graeci pro his dicunt, τὸ ἰφελον, ϑάγον, ϑῦμα ϑῦμα- ταλαν, καὶ αἱ ἐπὶ & deinde vinum vel muslum eidem affundebatur, prius ab auspice degustatum, & a circumstantibus levitas delibatum, qui ritus dicebatur Libatio.
units.tr: Writers define alphiton as barley meal, made from grain that has been ground, as the flour of wheat is; but it is distinguished by the fact that alphiton is roasted, whereas the barley is not, as if it were made from raw barley. For meal prepared from roasted spelt, with salt and incense, was placed on the head of the victim, and the victim was believed to be more acceptable when sprinkled with it and then slain. (The Greeks call these things by other names.) Then wine or must was poured over the same victim, first tasted by the augur and lightly touched by the bystanders. This rite was called libation.

units.la: Vt autem apud Graecos, sic etiam apud Romanos hujusmodi hordei atque salis inspersio in sa crificiis fuit usitata. Appellata vero haec hordei atque mixtio Latine mola, mola salsa. libro trigesimo primo, capite septimo: Maximè tamen, inquit, in sacris intelligitur salis auctoritas, quando nulla conficiuntur fine mola salsa. Idem: Nec minus propitia erant mola salsa supplicantibus. Idem: Numa Pompilius Deos fruge coli & mola salsa supplicari instituit. Hac mola ex farre, sale & aqua fuit conspicua: sine qua mola nullum sacrificium ratum fieri existimans. Atque id far nisi tostum esset, ad rem divinam non esse purum statuit. Is & Forracalia & religiosas ferias, quibus far in fornacibus torrebatur, instituit. Meminit hujus molae quoq; Festus: Mola, inquit, sive mola salsa vocatur etiam far tostum & sale spartum, quod eo molto hostiae aspergantur. Idem: Immolare est mola, id est farre molito & sale hostiam perspersam confecture. Hinc Virgilius: Sparge molam, & fragiles, intende bitumine lauros; Et quarto Aeneidos: Ipsa molimanibus, pius, altaria juxta Vnum exuta pedem vinclis, in veste recincta Testatur, &c. Idem: Iam dies infanda aderat, mihi sacra parari, Et salsae fruges, & circum tempora vittae.
units.tr: As among the Greeks, so among the Romans the sprinkling of barley and salt was customary in sacrifices. This mixture of barley and salt is called in Latin mola, salted meal. In book 31, chapter 7, we read: "Most of all, however, the authority of salt is recognised in sacred rites, since nothing is performed without salted meal." Again: "Salted meal was no less propitious to those who prayed." Again: "Numa Pompilius instituted that the gods be worshipped with grain and supplicated with salted meal." This meal was made of spelt, salt and water. Numa thought no sacrifice valid without it, and held that spelt was not pure for divine service unless it had been roasted. He also instituted the Fornacalia and the religious holidays on which spelt was roasted in ovens. Festus also mentions this meal: "Mola, or salted meal, is also called roasted spelt sprinkled with salt, with which the victims are sprinkled." Again: "To immolate is to slaughter a victim sprinkled with ground spelt and salt." Hence Virgil: "Sprinkle the meal, and kindle the crackling laurels with pitch." And in Aeneid 4: "She herself, pious, near the altars, with her hands, one foot loosed from its fetters, her garment girded up, bears witness, etc." Again: "Now the accursed day was at hand; the sacred rites were being prepared for me, the salted grain, and the fillets around my temples."

units.la: Hic Servius: Salsa frages, id est, sal & far, quod dicitur mola salsa, qua & frontes victima. foci aspergebantur & cultri. Fit autem de horna fruge & horno sale, hoc est, fruge & sale suns anni. Unde Horatius tertio Carminum: Si thure placatis, & horna fruge Lares.
units.tr: Servius here: "salted grain" means salt and spelt, which is called salted meal, and with which the foreheads of the victims, the hearths and the knives were sprinkled. It is made from dry grain and dry salt, that is, from the grain and salt of the previous year. Hence Horace in Odes 3: "If the Lares are appeased with incense and dry grain."

units.la: Idem Servius illud Eclog. octavo: Sparge molam, id est, far & salem interpretatur.
units.tr: Servius, on that verse of Eclogue 8, "Sprinkle the meal," explains it as spelt and salt.

units.la: Horatius quoque expressit huius molae meminit secundo Sermonum, Satyra tertia: Tu quum pro vitulâ flatus dulcem Aulide natum, Ante aras, spargusque mola caput impiobe, salsa.
units.tr: Horace too mentions this meal in Satire 2.3: "When you, for a heifer, sacrificed the sweet child at Aulis, before the altars, and sprinkled his head with salted meal, impious man..."

units.la: Et Martialis: Consumpsi salsaque molas & thuris acervos.
units.tr: And Martial: "I have used up salted meal and heaps of incense."

units.la: Item Plautus in Amphitruo: —postquam experrecta es prodigiali sorti, Aut mola salsa, aut thure comprecaram oportuit.
units.tr: Plautus, in Amphitryo: "After you woke up to the lot of a portent, you ought to have prayed either with salted meal or with incense."

units.la: Prodigiali, id est, prodigiorum depulsori, qui prodigia amolitur. Mola salsa, id est, farre tosto, quisalse fit conspersus. Comprecari porro lovi, idem, quod a love aut Iunonem.
units.tr: "Prodigiali" means one who averts portents, who drives away omens. Salted meal means roasted spelt sprinkled with salt. To pray to Jove is the same as to pray from Jove or Juno.

units.la: Eiusdem meminit & Ovidius: Imponit libum miflaq; farra salè. Et alibi: Triticos factus passurah, farra bis igni.
units.tr: Ovid also mentions it: "He lays on a cake and spelt mixed with salt." And elsewhere: "Spelt made like wheat, passed twice through the fire."

units.la: Nam & torrebatur prius igni ex Numæ iustituto ad rem divinam: & postea rursus, quando in sacrificio adhibebatur. Nec solum far, quod adolebatur in sacris, bis ignem patiebatur, sed & quo Majores utebantur in cibo, cum vel panis, vel aliud cibi genus e farre, sicut nisi prius ro tosto conficeretur. Ita ergo torrebatur, primum cum telatum erat in horreo, deinde in sacris fixe in cibis.
units.tr: For it was roasted by fire beforehand, by Numa's institution, for divine service, and afterwards again when it was used in the sacrifice. Not only the spelt burnt in sacred rites underwent fire twice, but also the spelt the ancestors used for food, when bread or some other kind of food was made from spelt, unless it had first been roasted. So it was roasted first when it was stored in the granary, and then again in sacred rites and in foods.

units.la: Obiter hic notandum, molam a molendo dici. Hinc bordei granafrasta & contusa m, lu diffa, & uvarior, & imapiu dtoi, Dii molares, molarum praesides: de quarum usu & aniu molendi more sic Servius in illa verba Virgilii: —Frugesq; receptas
units.tr: In passing, it should be noted that mola is so called from molere, to grind. Hence the Greeks' words for barley ground and crushed, and the Molares gods, the guardians of mills. Servius, on those verses of Virgil, "and the gathered grains," speaks of their use and of the manner of grinding them:

units.la: Et torrere parant flammis & frangere ferro:
units.tr: And they prepare to parch them with fire and crush them with iron.

units.la: Et ista: Nunc torrete igni fruges, & frangite saxo;
units.tr: And that line: "Now parch the grain with fire, and crush it with a stone."

units.la: Nam & hodie, inquit, siccari ante frugesq; siccari, & sic frangi videmus. Et quia apud Majores nostros molarum non erat usus, frumenta torrebant & ea in pilas missa pinsebant: & hoc erat genus molendi. Inde & pinsores dicti sunt, qui nunc pistores vocantur.
units.tr: For, he says, we see even today that grain is dried before it is dried and then ground in this way. And since our ancestors did not use mills, they parched the grain and pounded it by putting it into mortars; this was the kind of grinding they had. From this, those who are now called bakers (pistores) were also called pounders (pinsores).

units.la: Ceterum illo farre Deos sibi constituere conjuveruni Veteres, eo quod, ut inquit Nonnius, epulis & immolationibus sacrum putabatur, ut Adorare verbum dictum putetur a farre, quod Adoreum Antiquos appellabant dictum supra, qui libus saepe adoreus farra Dijs exhibebant. Hinc Ovidius Fastorum primo: Ante Deos homini quod conciliare valeres Far erat & puri lucida mica salis.
units.tr: The ancients made gods for themselves out of that spelt, since, as Nonius says, it was thought to be sacred for feasts and sacrifices. Hence the word "to adore" (adorare) is thought to derive from far (spelt), since the ancients called it adoreum, as said above, because they often offered spelt to the gods. Hence Ovid in the first book of the Fasti: "Before the gods, what could win favour for man was spelt and the bright grain of pure salt."

units.la: Sed de farre, confarreatione, adorandi verbo, adorea, edor, & similibus dictum est supra: ad quae Lectorem remitto.
units.tr: But concerning spelt, confarreation, the word "to adore," adorea, edor, and similar things, I have spoken above; I refer the reader to those passages.

units.la: Hic postremo non est silentio praetermittenda, οὐλομαντεία, καὶ ἀλφιτομαντεία & ἀλφι— equarvia, hoc est, divinatio, quae per hanc molam salsam, ejusque materiam, hoc est, hor— deum, far atque farinam, qua victimae conspergebantur, fieri fuit solita. Nam haec ipsa in sacrificio [illegible, ~12 letters] suis tentatis scrutari, expendere, atque inde futurarum rerum scientiam capere con- [illegible, ~6 letters].
units.tr: Here, finally, must not be passed over in silence the oulomanteia, the alphitomanteia, and the alphi-[mantei]a, that is, divination which used to be practised through this salted meal, and its material, that is, barley, spelt, and flour, with which the victims were sprinkled. For in the sacrifice they would examine and weigh these very things, and from them seek knowledge of future events [several words lost].

units.la: Porro cum immolatione hoc est, mola salsa aspersione super hostiam, de qua modo dictum est, conjungi fuit quaedam batio, hoc est, vini super eandem hostiam effusio, cujus etsi neque meminerunt, neque Apollonius hoc in loco meminerunt, tamen eam aliis ex auctoribus colligere licet, ut videre licet apud Virgilium Aeneid.6. Quattuor hic primum nigrantes terga juvencos Constituit, frontique in vergit vina sacerdos.
units.tr: Next, joined to the immolation, that is, the sprinkling of the salted meal over the victim, of which we have just spoken, was a certain libation, that is, the pouring of wine over the same victim. Although neither they nor Apollonius mention this in this place, it may nevertheless be gathered from other authors, as can be seen in Virgil, Aeneid 6: "Here first the priest sets down four black-backed steers, and pours wine on their brows."

units.la: Et quarto medios: Ipsa tenens dextra paterum pulcherrima Dido Candentis vaccae media inter cornua fundit.
units.tr: And in the fourth place, from the middle: "Holding a bowl in her right hand, beautiful Dido pours it between the horns of a white heifer."

units.la: Ibi Servius: Non est sacrificium, inquit, sed hostiae exploratio.
units.tr: There Servius says: "It is not a sacrifice," he says, "but an examination of the victim."

units.la: Mediaminter cornua fundit. Fundere, ajt idem, est super ima manu libare, quod fit in sacris superum. Vergere autem est convertere in sinistram partem manu, ita fundere, ut patera convertatur, quod in inferas fit. Hinc apud Plautum in Curculione Lena anus ebriosa: ipsum expeto (inquit) Tangere, in vergere in me liquores tuos Sino dulcim.
units.tr: "Between the horns she pours." The same Servius says that to pour (fundere) is to make an offering with the hand held palm-down, which is done in the rites of the gods above; but to turn (vergere) is to turn the hand toward the left side, so as to pour while the bowl is turned, which is done for the gods below. Hence in Plautus, in the Curculio, a drunken old woman, the procuress, says: "I long (she says) to touch him, and I allow you to pour your liquors upon me."

units.la: Et Lucretius libro quinto: Illi imprudentes ipsi sibi saepe venenum Vergebant: nunc dant alis filertius ipsi.
units.tr: And Lucretius in book five: "Unwitting, they often poured poison for themselves; now they give it to others with their own hands."

units.la: Porro ista pertinent, inquit Servius, in locum illum Virgilii, ad vittimarum explorationem, (ex ceremonia hujus sumus) ut si non fluperint, aptae probentur. Hoc autem vinum depromebatur ex certo vase, quod Praeferculum sunt appellatum. Erat autem Praeferculum, inquit Festus, vas aeneum sine ansa patens summum, velut pelvis, quo ad sacrificia utebantur. Ejus effigiem videre licet apud Guilielmum du Choul in libro de antiqua religione Romanorum. Et tamen Festi descriptio hujus vasis non videtur respondere.
units.tr: Moreover, these things, says Servius, pertain to that passage of Virgil about the examination of the victims (from the rite of this sort), so that if they did not shudder, they were judged fit. This wine was drawn from a certain vessel which was called the praefericulum. Festus says the praefericulum was a bronze vessel without a handle, open at the top, like a basin, which they used for sacrifices. One may see its likeness in Guillaume du Choul's book on the ancient religion of the Romans. Yet Festus's description of this vessel does not seem to agree.

units.la: Porro antequam vinum illud fronti hostiae in vergeret, sive media inter ejus cornua funde-
units.tr: Moreover, before they poured that wine on the forehead of the victim, or between its horns...

units.la: Etsi vero Servius, optimus Virgilii antiquitatum interpres, hanc vinum super victimas ef- fionem vult ad earum exploationem fuisse factum solitam. Tamen aliae quoque hujus ceremoniae rationes probabiles admodum videntur afferri posse, ac eadem fere qui s Eustathius de immolatione id est, mola super hostiam aspersione, adfert. Nam quemadmodum illa ceremonia usufruct erga Deos suos.
units.tr: Although Servius, the best interpreter of Virgil's antiquities, holds that this pouring of wine over the victims was customarily done for their examination, other probable reasons for this ceremony also seem able to be given, and nearly the same ones that Eustathius gives concerning the immolation, that is, the sprinkling of the salted meal over the victim. For just as that ceremony [was used]... for their gods.

units.la: Deinde ut sales illi, Eustathio teste, hostiae aspersi, ex multis liquidis compactis unumque, corpus 1. Vtesset ami fusti, amicitia fuerunt symbolum: sic vinum quoque ex multis collectum acinis atque granis idem cuius symbola signe... sunt.
units.tr: Then, as those salts, according to Eustathius, were sprinkled on the victim, being made up of many grains compacted into one body, so also the wine, gathered from many grapes and berries, was a symbol of the same thing, [that is, of friendship/concord].

units.la: Quod ut hoc quoque addam, hac vini super frontem atque media inter cornua hostiae sive be- 3. Vini abusu stiae effusione significare voluissent, homines vini abusu, hoc est, immodice immoderatoque potu bestiae hominess effron tum cornigerarum ac cornupetarum fieri similes, et effrontes, hoc est, audaces, impudentes, in ve- tes fieri. recundos, temerarios, feroces et efferos. R 3
units.tr: To add this too: by this pouring of wine on the forehead and between the horns of the victim, they wished to signify that men, through the abuse of wine, that is, through immoderate and excessive drinking, become like horned and butting beasts, and shameless, that is, bold, impudent, unashamed, rash, fierce, and wild.

units.la: Postremo hic obser vandum,hac ipsa enim immolatione, hoc est, mole sragumq; salsa spersione,sum libatione,id est, vini effusione super hostias siue victimas, ipsas dicebatur, si fuisse mactari, hoc est, augeri atque cumulari: qua tamen voce etiam ad hostiarum cædem atque gulationem significandam usi fuerunt, de quo postea. Mactus, inquit Festus, dicitur magis auctus. Et Seruius in illa Virgilii:
units.tr: Finally, it must be observed here that by this very immolation, that is, the sprinkling of the salted meal, and by the libation, that is, the pouring of wine over the victims themselves, they were said to be "mactated," that is, increased and heaped up. Yet they also used this word to signify the slaughter and butchering of the victims, about which later. Festus says: "mactus" is said to mean "increased" more.
"...they slaughter the chosen two-year-old sheep, as is customary."

units.la: Verbum sacrorum ἱερουργικὸν dictum, ut Adorare, Nam mactare est magis augere. Addit vocem Lectas: Non vacat lecto. Nam mores fuerat, ut ad sacrificia eligerentur oves, quibus nihil deesset, ut in se o Æneidos:
units.tr: The word mactare is a sacred term of the rites, like adorare, for mactare means "to increase more." Servius adds the word "chosen": "It is not unnecessary to choose. For it was the custom that sheep were selected for sacrifice, that nothing should be lacking in them," as in the Aeneid: "Now I am to slaughter for you seven unbroken heifers."

units.la: Nunc ego te in intacto septem mactare juvencas.
units.tr: Now I am to slaughter for you seven unbroken heifers.

units.la: Bidentes autem dicta sunt, quasi biennes, quia neque minores aut majores lucebat hostias dari. Sunt autem ovibus duo emunctiores dentes inter osto, qui non nisi circa bienne apparent nec in omnibus, sed in his, quae sacrificia sunt aptae, inveniuntur. Hæc Seruius illa de hostiarum delectu addi possunt.
units.tr: Bidentes, moreover, were so called as if "biennes" (two-year-olds), since it was not permitted to offer victims either younger or older. Sheep have two more prominent teeth among the others, which do not appear until about the second year, and not in all, but are found in those which are fit for sacrifice. Servius says these things; they may be added to what he says about the choice of victims.

units.la: Idem in illa Virgilii libro nono Æneidos:
units.tr: The same Servius, on that line of Virgil in book nine of the Aeneid:

units.la: Mactæ nova virtute puer: sic itur ad astra,
units.tr: "Boy, slain in new valour: thus one goes to the stars."

units.la: Mactæ, inquit, quasi magis aucte: assectatæ gloriæ est sermo, et tractus a sacris. Quasi ties aut thus, aut vinum super victimam fundebatur, dicebant: Mactus est taurus vino vel thure hoc est, cumulatus est postea et magis auctus.
units.tr: "Mactae," he says, "as if magis auctae (more increased): the expression is taken from the language of glory and borrowed from the sacred rites. When wine or incense was poured over a victim, they said: 'The bull is mactatus with wine or incense,' that is, it was then heaped up and more increased."

units.la: Atq; hæc quidem de immolatione, id est, mola siue frugum salsarum in hostiam afferfa, et de Libatione, id est, vini in eandem effusione, prius le viter a sacerdote et lanatibus degust, siat dicta.
units.tr: And these things have been said about the immolation, that is, the sprinkling of salted meal or grain upon the victim, and about the libation, that is, the pouring of wine over the same, which the priest and the attendants first tasted.

units.la: SEQVITVR nunc alia cerimonia, ante hostiæ mactationem usurpari solita, cuius lucrua sentia in hoc Nestoris sacrificio, et in alijs sacrificijs apud Homerum fit mentio. Ea autem sunt villos de fronte victimæ evellere, quos postea cum molarum parte in ignem super aram tum a censum conjiciebant: et illa vocabantur prima libamina, si ve ἀπαρχαι. De hac igitur sic Homerus in hoc Nestoris sacrificio:
units.tr: Next follows another ceremony, customarily performed before the slaughter of the victim, of which mention is made in the sacrifice of Nestor and in other sacrifices in Homer. This consisted in plucking hairs from the forehead of the victim, which they afterwards cast into the fire upon the altar, together with a portion of the meal; these were called the first offerings (prima libamina), or aparchai. Homer speaks of this in the sacrifice of Nestor thus:

units.la: Ἐκ τῶν ἀπάρχεσθαι, κα ἐκ πάνων ιδρύσας ἐν πυρὶ βάλλεων.
units.tr: "From the head, beginning the first offering, and from all, he threw them into the fire."

units.la: Supplicavit initia facientes, ex capite pilos in ignem conjiciens.
units.tr: Making supplication as they began the offerings, casting hair from the head into the fire.

units.la: Et Virgilius Æneidos sexto in genere de omnibus sacrificiis:
units.tr: And Virgil, in book six of the Aeneid, speaks generally of all sacrifices:

units.la: Et summas carpens media inter cornua setas
units.tr: "And, cutting the topmost bristles from between the horns,"
"he lays them on the sacred fires as the first offering."

units.la: Hujus quidem moris Eustathius rationem hanc reddit: ὅτι ἢ ἀπαρχὴ πις, ἡ ἐκ ἀρχῆς ἢ ἐκ ἐκ ἐκ συ ... καὶ ἀποξόλλ... Idem celebrat illo sedere, quod a Trojanis atq, Achiuis sacrificio adhibito, contra suit, inter alia facti mentionem pilorum, quod ex capite agnorum immolandorum eruerunt; quæ postea præcones singulis Troianorum atq, Græcorum distribuerunt. Agamemnon enim suo gladio ... Eustath. Agamemnon, inquit, ... Idem sacrificium illud quod ad fœdus sanciendum spectabat, factens, pilos e capitibus agnorum exsectos per præconem optimatibus Trojanorum atque Græcorum distribui curaverit: qui suo signo abaturi ... malum in ejus caput esse redeunda omnia, qui sœdus illud violasset. Et verisimile videtur, Agamemnonem hujusmodi verbis usum fuisse: Sic exterminentur ex hac vita, hujusce fœderis qui violatores extiterint, quemadmodum ego disseco hostiæ istius pilos.
units.tr: Eustathius gives this reason for this custom: that the first offering is the beginning... Eustathius also records that the Trojans and Achaeans, in the sacrifice used for that purpose, made mention, among other things, of the hairs which they plucked from the heads of the lambs to be sacrificed; afterwards heralds distributed these to each of the Trojans and Greeks. For Agamemnon, with his sword... Eustathius says Agamemnon, making the sacrifice that pertained to ratifying the covenant, had the hairs cut from the heads of the lambs distributed by a herald among the Trojan and Greek leaders; and he declared with an oath that all things would return upon the head of whoever had violated that covenant. And it seems likely that Agamemnon used words such as these: "Thus let those who have been violators of this covenant be cast out of this life, just as I cut off the hairs of this victim."

units.la: Eras Erat praeterea illa pilorum differentia ἀναμυσις ἢ καλλωπισμός, id est, recordatio priqui olim dicitur fuisse, vestitus. Hujusce moris meminit Homerus etiā alibi, ut Iliad. τ. Κἀπρυ Χαῖτ' ἔχας ἀρξαμένῳ.
units.tr: Besides, there was that difference of hairs, which is called anamnesis or kallōpismos, that is, a recollection of ancient dress, which was made of animal hair. Homer also mentions this custom elsewhere, in Iliad 3: [Κἀπρυ Χαῖτ' ἔχας ἀρξαμένῳ].

units.la: Ex ἵνι. Ξ. Ἁπαρχόμδῳ καφαλῆς ἔχας ἐν πυρὶ βάλλει: Initia faciens, capitis pilos in ignem conjecit.
units.tr: In Iliad 3 he says: "Beginning from the head, he cast the hairs into the fire" [Ἀρξάμενος δὲ κεφαλῆς ἔχας ἐν πυρὶ βάλλει].

units.la: Quem versum: Dionysius Halicarnasseus cītans & inquiens, ἔχεσθαι ... ἀπὸ καφαλῆς τῶν ἔχας καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ πῦρ, id est, pilos quoque de capite victimæ resectos in ignem jeci, ejicit.
units.tr: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, quoting this line, says that the hairs cut from the head of the victim were thrown into the fire [ἔχεσθαι ... ἀπὸ καφαλῆς τῶν ἔχας καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ πῦρ].

units.la: ἀλλ' ὃν ἀπαρχόμδῳ καφαλῆς ἔχας ἐν πυρὶ βάλλει, Ardentes, focos raptus de vertice villis Sparsit, &c.
units.tr: "[Taking the hair from the head,] he cast it on the burning fires, and scattered the tufts of hair taken from the crown..., etc."

units.la: Hujusce igitur cerimoniae, quae, ut etiam alii Ethnicorum ritus atque cerimoniae, ridicula admodum & absurda videtur fuisse, standem fuit, quo tempore ante diversum rationem adferet Eustathius, ... in demolita illa sacra, ... Nam, ut illam ad antiquis vitiis, ita bant ad antiquos vestitus, qui pecorum pilis vestiebantur, ... ...
units.tr: Of this ceremony, which, like other rites and ceremonies of the Gentiles, seems quite ridiculous and absurd, there is a different explanation, which Eustathius gives at a time when... in those abandoned rites... For just as that practice refers to the ancient sacrifices, so it refers to the ancient clothing, which was made of the hair of flocks...

units.la: Sed praeter illam rationem ab Eustathio allatam, aliae quoque in cerimoniae ab Ethnicorum opinionibus ac superstitionibus non alienae adferri videntur, possunt rationes. Nam primum cum & illorum sacerdotes rasa plerunque, ut supra dixi, fuerunt capite atque barba, & reliquum etiam vulgus in sacris praesertim atque in funeribus capita barbaque pilos tondere, radere, atque etiam evellere consuev- erunt, quid miri est, si ex hostiarum quoque suarum capitibus pilos, villos atque setas evellere fuerunt solliti?
units.tr: But besides the explanation given by Eustathius, other reasons may be offered for this ceremony, not foreign to the opinions and superstitions of the Gentiles. For first, since their priests were, as I said above, usually shaved on head and beard, and since the common people too were accustomed to shave, cut and even pluck the hair of head and beard in sacred rites, especially at funerals, what wonder is it if they were also in the habit of plucking hair, wool and bristles from the heads of their own victims?

units.la: Deinde quemadmodum, ut supra fuit significatum, primos capitis barbaque pilos rasos sive sechatum de tonsos Dii suos, tanquam primitias, consecrarunt: sic mirum non fuisse hostiae unam mani, suarum (quas intensas esse oportebat, ut Servius annotat in illa Virgilii sententiis) jexto: Inconsumptae, bidentem) pilos, ἀπαρχὴν τῆς προθυσίας τῶν ζῴων, id est, primitias, sed primitiarum cum, ... (unde etiam Homerus, ἀλλ' ἀπαρχόμδῳ ait, ut Virgilius ea vocat Libaminaprima) Dixit suis obtulisse ac confecrasse.
units.tr: Next, as was pointed out above, they consecrated to their gods the first hair of the head and beard, shaved or cut, as firstfruits. So it is no wonder that from the head of the victim (which had to be unblemished, as Servius notes on Virgil's words "inconsumptae bidentem"), they took the first hair, as the "firstfruits of the sacrifice of the animals" [ἀπαρχὴν τῆς προθυσίας τῶν ζῴων]. This is why Homer says "beginning from the head", and why Virgil calls them the "first offerings" [libamina prima]; and they offered and consecrated them to their gods.

units.la: Praeterea satis superque confirmat, pilos atque villos, qui nihil sunt aliud, quam quaedam corporis excrementa, res esse viles, sordidas et abjectas: Unde ipsa quo, vox Latina villis a villus videtur dictus, quasi villis nihil sit villus; ... ut hoc nostra, ... Ut mammalium, ... pilo dignus, de homine villi: ... pilos et floccos legere, ... de rebus villibus et nihil ... are, quale est illud, De lana caprina. Hac cum ita se habeant, verisimile est, Ethnicos hac cerimonia significare voluisse, se quas vis res, etiam minimas, paratos esse Diis suis contrare: vel etiam significare voluerunt, nos res tantum pretiosas sectari: contra autem res viles sordidas contemnere ac Vulcano debere eradere.
units.tr: Moreover, it is more than sufficiently established that hairs and bristles, which are nothing other than certain excrements of the body, are vile, sordid and abject things. Hence the Latin word villus seems to be derived from something of no account, and the phrase "de lana caprina" is used of trivial matters. Since these things stand so, it is likely that the Gentiles meant by this ceremony to signify that they were ready to give to their gods whatever they had, even the smallest things, and perhaps also meant to signify that we pursue only precious things, while we despise vile and sordid things and ought to scrape them off for Vulcan.

units.la: Quid ? cum et morbus quidam sit pilaris, quem ψείας Graeci appellant (Est mammarum Quaria. ... ictum, quo mulieres corripiuntur, si pilum in poculo libertini) et verticuli quida sint, pilos arro-<bl>R</bl> ✣. dentes (qui ἐπιχθόνιοι, ἢ ἐπιχθονιώριοι Graecis appellantur, Germanice Vnholden) los Ethnici Dijs obtulerint, vt hujusmodi pilorum vitia atq; morbos velint a se avertuncare.
units.tr: Again, since there is a certain disease of the hair, which the Greeks call [ψείας], by which women are seized when a hair falls into a cup, and certain whorls on the head, which the Greeks call epichthonioi, and which in German are called "Unholden", the Gentiles offered hairs of this kind to their gods, so that they might avert such faults and diseases of the hair from themselves.

units.la: Ad hostiarum quinetia patientiam forsan explorandā ista pilorum e capite evulsio fiebat.
units.tr: Perhaps this plucking of hair from the head of the victim was also done to test the patience of the victims.

units.la: Postremo apud Ethnicos fuit quoddam Daemonum genus tenebrosum, ἀκάθαρτον, id est, mate√ria affixum, vt illud describunt, quos ὀνοκένταυροι, id est, asinos centauros, et a pilis ψίλοποδες, id est, pilosos, villos os, hirsutos appellarunt, quod uumnū talis specie atq; forma illis apparebant, qui idcirco Satyri Schirim, ab Hebraeis, et Satyri, ab eadem voce faerunt dicti. Hujusmodi igitur Daemonum iras, atq; furorem placandi et a se averruncandi gratia forsan istos hostiarum pilos ipsis obtulerunt.
units.tr: Finally, among the Gentiles there was a certain shadowy kind of demons, impure and attached to matter, as they describe them, whom they called onokentauroi, that is, ass-centaurs, and psilopodes, that is, hairy and shaggy, because they appeared to men in such a shape and form. For this reason they were also called Satyrs, from the Hebrew [שעירים] and from the same word, Satyrs. Perhaps they offered these hairs of the victims to such demons to appease their anger and fury and to avert them from themselves.

units.la: Sed de istis, ut ita loquar, tricis (quam ipsam vocem pilos, pedibus pullorum gallin accerumin volutos, proprie significantem Nonius Ἐκ τῆς ψιλῶν vult esse derivatam) satis de hoc iam, quam cum nimirum instituti hujus nostri ratio poflula vit; ne diutius, quam par sit, tricari et, ut Graeci loquuntur, ψιλολογεῖν videamur.
units.tr: But enough about these, so to speak, trifles (the word itself, which Nonius says derives from [ψιλῶν] and properly means the hair of the feet of young chickens). Enough on this now, since the plan of our undertaking requires it, lest we seem to linger on it longer than is fitting, and, as the Greeks say, to babble about trifles [ψιλολογεῖν].

units.la: NVNC quoniam ignis, in cuem ipsi hostiarum pilis fuerunt conjecti, ut eo absumerentur, fuisse mentio, de ipso quoq; igne sacrifico, sive sacrificali, in genere videtur esse dicendum, pro est tim tim is flatim ab initio inferri et accendi fit solitus. Fuit autem ignis in sacrificiis maxima ac plane necessarius usus, sine quo nullum sacrificium confici poterat. Atq; inde valde probabile ipsam Aram praes.puum sacrificiorum receptaculum, seu instrumentum, vel ab ardendo, quasi Ardeam, vel ab uerendo, quasi Vram (unde Vrinas animalium Arnobius per contemptum Gentilium aras appellavit) fuisse nuncupatam. Unde Virgilius Aeneidos duodecimo ara vota vitā fligrantes (quae etiam fragrantes propter odores, qui in illa incendebantur, dici puerunt.)
units.tr: Now, since mention has been made of the fire into which the hairs of the victims were thrown so that they might be consumed, something should also be said in general about the sacrificial fire itself, that is, the fire which was customarily brought in and kindled right from the start. Fire was used in sacrifices to a very great and entirely necessary degree, and no sacrifice could be performed without it. From this it is very probable that the altar itself, the receptacle or instrument of the sacrifices, was named either from burning, as if it were "Ardea," or from scorching, as if it were "Vra." Arnobius, in contempt of the Gentiles, called the altars the scorchings of animals. Hence Virgil, in the twelfth book of the Aeneid, calls the altars "blazing" (flagrantes), which were also called "fragrant" (fragrantes) because of the odours burned on them.
And he brought up the flock to the blazing altars.

units.la: Et Tibullus fulgentes vocavit, eiusdem ita canit: Cernite fulgentes ut eat sacer agnus ad aras:
units.tr: Tibullus also called them "gleaming" (fulgentes), and sings thus: "Behold how the sacred lamb goes to the gleaming altars."

units.la: Vrunq; autem hoc verbum Vrere et Arde re, cui dubiū, quin ut ante quod dixi, ab Hebraeo אור, Or, vel אור Vr et Chaldaeo אורא Orah, sive אורא, Orā, deriventur, quae et ignem lucemq; sive lumen, et splendorem, et focum quoq; an quo ignis fovetur, significant. Ara igitur quae Vrus, sive Chaldaice ארא, Orā dicta est. Ipsum quoq; nomen Graecum πῦρ, ignē ignificans (unde nostrum vernaculum feur) non dubito, quin ab Hebraeo אור, Or, sive Vr, fit deductum. Nam ablata littera π fit ὑρ.
units.tr: Now there is no doubt that this word, "vrere" and "ardere," is derived, as I said before, from the Hebrew אור [Or], or Vr, and from the Chaldee אורא [Orah], or אורא [Orā], which mean both fire and light, or lustre, and also the hearth on which the fire is kept burning. The altar, therefore, which is called "Vrus," or in Chaldee ארא [Orā], took its name from this. The Greek word itself, πῦρ [pyr], meaning fire (whence our own vernacular "feur"), I do not doubt is derived from the Hebrew אור [Or], or Vr. For when the letter π is removed, it becomes ὑρ [hyr].

units.la: Ad hunc ipsum ignis usum illud quoque videtur pertinere, quod a Vesta, quam tanquam ignis Deam et praesidem Ethnici colebant, quae vis illorum sacrificia incboari, et in eadem fere terminari consueverunt ut supra quod, dixum. et Celius Rhodiginus docet lib. 15. cap. 14. sub finem.
