Verderius: In sacrificiis, inquit, quae etiam aliis Diis offerebantur, semper Vestae nomē, ut etiam Iani praefabantur: cuius rei eam potissimum rationem adfert, quod vestibula, ubi olim sacrificabatur, Vestae erant sacra. Adfertur quoq; fabula, qua Vesta, post victoriam cōtra Titanes patram, a Iove impetrasse dicitur, ut vi, ut permaneret, at omnium sacrificiorum primitias sortiretur. Sed mihi eo potissimum ex illo veteres videntur, quod ea, quae in sacrificiis adhibebantur, ab illo igne, quem Vesta dei nat, habent, ut sint atq; permaneant. Adde quod nihil magis Deo ipsorum puritatem immortalitatemq; exprimeret, quam flamma, ideoq; nullum sacrificium sine igne conflabat: et hanc ob causam Vestae nomen caeteris omnibus praemittebatur.
units.tr: This use of fire seems also to pertain to Vesta, whom the Gentiles worshipped as goddess and guardian of fire, and with whom their sacrifices were customarily begun and almost always ended, as I said above; and Caelius Rhodiginus teaches this in book 15, chapter 14, near the end. Verderius says: "In sacrifices, which were offered also to other gods, the name of Vesta was always spoken first, as the name of Janus was too. For this he gives chiefly the reason that the vestibules, where they once sacrificed, were sacred to Vesta." A fable is also cited, that after her victory over the Titans Vesta obtained from Jove that she should have the firstfruits of all sacrifices. But to me the chief reason seems to be that the things used in sacrifices have their being and permanence from that fire which the goddess Vesta kept. Add that nothing expresses the purity and immortality of their god more than flame, and therefore no sacrifice was performed without fire; and for this reason Vesta's name was put before all the others.

units.la: Sed anteaquam ad ignis sacrificialis explicationem accedam, praemittenda quadam et superioribus adjicienda videntur in genere de πυρολατρεία, id est, ignis cultu antiquissimo, qui ob sen prifimum s i de s u cultu nibus fere gentibus valde fuit familiaris, ut ex sacris et profanis litteratum monumentis facile patet.
units.tr: But before I come to the explanation of the sacrificial fire, some things must be premised in general about pyrolatreia, that is, the most ancient worship of fire, which, on account of its usefulness, was very familiar to almost all nations, as is plain from sacred and profane written monuments.

units.la: At ipsi primum Chaldaei et Assyrii ignem coluerunt sub nomine Vr, quem nonnulli qui dem loci nomen fuisse autumant: alii vero ipsum ignem, quem gentes illae, tanquam Numen quoddam colebant, nomine ille volunt esse intelligendum, a quo locus quoq; ille fuerit denominatus.
units.tr: First, the Chaldeans and Assyrians worshipped fire under the name Ur. Some think this was the name of a place; others, however, want that name to be understood as the fire itself, which those nations worshipped as a certain divinity, and from which that place was named.

units.la: Deinde Aegyptii quoq; Ignem venerati sunt sub nomine Serapbim, quod illorum fuit N men a ⸗⸗⸗, Saraph, deductum, quod ardere, flagrare, splendere significat, quasi dicas flammeum, ignitum & lucidum quippiam; quo nomine Ignem significabant, quem perennem esse volebant Maiorum suo: um institute. His adde, quod Herodotus lib. 3. tradit, Aegyptios sibi persuasisse ignem, animatam quandam & voracissimam esse belluam, omnia, quae nascantur, devorantem, unde mortuorum corpora non passis sunt igne concremari: propterea quod ipsis absurdum & absonum rationem alienam esse videatur ignem, seu belluam, devorando expletam unā cum ipsa re devorata, atq; consumpta emori. Ut igitur aliarum bestiarum: ius ignis quoq; quem in bestiarum numero referebant, Aegyptiis colueruunt.
units.tr: Then the Egyptians also venerated fire under the name Serapbim, which was derived from their word Saraph, meaning to burn, blaze or shine, as if to say something flaming, fiery and bright. By this name they signified the fire that they wished to be kept perpetually burning in accordance with their ancestors' institution. To this add what Herodotus reports in book 3: the Egyptians persuaded themselves that fire is a living and most voracious beast that devours everything that grows, and for this reason they did not allow the bodies of the dead to be burned. They thought it absurd and incongruous that fire, or the beast, having been sated by devouring, should perish along with the thing it had devoured and consumed. So, as with other beasts, the Egyptians also worshipped fire, which they counted among the beasts.

units.la: Praeterea quanta superstitione Medi atq; Persae ignem coluerint passim historiae antiquae tenent. Coluerunt autem eum suo nomine Primasda, quae vox composita ex Or & Chasda, ignem sive lucem sanctam & divinam significat. Et hanc ipsam quidam ob causam noluerunt Persis, suorum corpora igne comburi, ut Herodotus refert libro tertio, propterea quod nefas ducebant ea depasci atq; consumi ab eo, quem Numinis loco haberent. Idem, Tyrio Maximo auctore, cum igni sacrificarent, praebito alimento, his utebantur verbis: EDE, DOMINE IGNIS.
units.tr: Moreover, the ancient histories widely record how great a superstition the Medes and Persians had toward fire. They worshipped it under the name Primasda, a compound word from Or and Chasda, signifying holy and divine fire or light. For this same reason, as Herodotus relates in book 3, some Persians refused to have their bodies burned with fire, because they judged it wicked for them to be eaten up and consumed by that which they held in the place of a deity. The same people, as Tyrius Maximus reports, when they offered sacrifice to fire, used to provide it with food and speak these words: EAT, LORD FIRE.

units.la: Porro a Chaldaeis, Assyriis, Aegyptiis, Medis atq; Persis, ut plurimae aliae superstitiones: ita ignis cultus, quoq; superstitiosissimus ignis cultus ad Graecos fuit propagatus. Nam hi quoque ignem vene ratis sunt Hyaslaos, id est, Vulcani, & Εσιας, id est, Vestae nomine: quae ipsa quoque duo nomina ab Hebraeis sunt deducta, nempe ab ⸗⸗⸗, Eleh vel ⸗⸗⸗, Esha vel ⸗⸗⸗, Eltha, Chaldaeorū. Ab eodem nomine Hebraeo, ⸗⸗⸗, Eich (ut hoc quoque obiter addam) & Graecum vocabulū ἱερὰ, forum significant, & nostrum vernaculum ⸗⸗⸗ est, Cinis (qui ignem est effectus) sine dubio profluxerunt. nisi quis ⸗⸗⸗ Germanicū, malit derivari ab Hebraeo ⸗⸗⸗ Duelschen; quae vox & pinguedinem & cinerem sonat: cuius soni similitudine nos sirum ⸗⸗⸗ est vicinum.
units.tr: Furthermore, as with many other superstitions, so the worship of fire was passed on from the Chaldeans, Assyrians, Egyptians, Medes and Persians to the Greeks, and the most superstitious worship of fire spread to them. For the Greeks too venerated fire under the names Hyaslaos, that is, of Vulcan, and Hesias, that is, of Vesta. These two names too are derived from the Hebrew words, namely from the Chaldean Eleh or Esha or Eltha. From the same Hebrew word, Eich (let me add this in passing), and the Greek word hiera, meaning sacred things, and our own vernacular word for ashes (which is what fire leaves behind) have undoubtedly descended. Unless someone prefers to derive the German word from the Hebrew word for tallow, Duelschen, which signifies both fat and ash; and by the similarity of that sound our word is close to it.

units.la: Ipsum quoq; ignis nomen, & in plurali numero, ignes ( quod nonnulli voluni esse compositum ab In, particula privandi, & gigno, ut dicatur ignis, quasi non gignens, quod ignis non quidem gignendi, sed cuncta potius consumendi vim obtineat,) mihi potius ab ⸗⸗⸗, Eich, Hebraeo videtur suam habere originem.
units.tr: The very name of fire, and in the plural ignes, which some think is compounded of In, a particle of privation, and gigno, to beget, so that ignis is as if "not begetting," since fire has the power not of begetting but rather of consuming everything, seems to me to have its origin rather from the Hebrew word Eich.

units.la: In Delphico templo Graeci perpetuum ignem fovebant: cuius custodia mulieribus, matrimonio solutis, fuit demandata.
units.tr: In the temple at Delphi the Greeks kept a perpetual fire burning, and its guardianship was entrusted to women who were released from marriage.

units.la: Attici in templo Palladis sive Minervae, unde ei Pallidio, id est, Palladis simulachro lychnum ignis inextinctus virginum opera atque ministerio custodiebant.
units.tr: In the temple of Pallas or Minerva at Athens, whence the image of Pallas is called Pallidium, unquenched lamps of fire were kept by the service and ministry of virgins.

units.la: Postremo postquam Romani omnium gentium atque nationum imperio fuerunt potiti, omnes simul superstitionum uni versi orbis terrarum sordes Romam, quasi in sentinam quandam conauxerunt: unde jure ac merito Theophilus Romam illam antiquam ⸗⸗id est omnis superstitionis epitomen sive compendium appellavit. Inter illas fuit hae ⸗⸗⸗, id est, ignis cultus. Nam illi quoq; igneni, seu Nunen quaddam, sub Vulcani & Vestae nominibus, Graecorum aliarumq; nationum more & exemplo superstitiosissime coluerunt.
units.tr: Finally, after the Romans had gained mastery of the empire of all peoples and nations, all the filth of superstitions from the whole world flowed together into Rome as into a sewer. Hence Theophilus rightly and justly called that ancient Rome an epitome or compendium of all superstition. Among these was the worship of fire. For they too worshipped fire, or a certain deity, under the names of Vulcan and Vesta, most superstitiously, after the manner and example of the Greeks and other nations.

units.la: Vulcani itaque sacrificia omnia fuerunt ignis ( Ignetum ante sacrificium Hebraice abigne ⸗⸗⸗, Ifchah, ab ascensu ⸗⸗⸗ Holah, Graece ὁλοκαύστου και ὁλοκαύτωμα, a Latinis Pyra, Latina ferti fuit appellatum) in quibus morte erat, ut quicquid ei fuisset oblatu, igni traderetur. Quinetiam victores, spoliatis hostium cadaveribus acia acervum fecerunt, aliusq; arma colle ta & pone incensus, Vulcano sacrificium offerre folebant, quemadmodum Virgilius lib. 8. Aeneidos Evandrum inducit, qui ait se,
units.tr: All the sacrifices of Vulcan were therefore by fire: burnt offerings (in Hebrew called ishah, from the ascent, olah; in Greek holokautou and holokautoma; by the Latins called pyra), in which the whole was consumed, so that whatever was offered to him was given to the fire. Moreover, the victors, having stripped the corpses of their enemies, made a heap of them, and having gathered up the other arms and burnt them, used to offer sacrifice to Vulcan, just as Virgil in book 8 of the Aeneid introduces Evander saying that he had
"Victor, under Praeneste itself,"

units.la: fecisse praedicat: quod Servius vult depromtum fuisse ex Romanorum historia, ubi legitur, Tatius quintum Prinum, de victis Sabinis, omnia eorum arma in Vulcani honorem combusisse, caeterosq; ejus exemplum secutos esse.
units.tr: claims to have done so. Servius holds that this was taken from Roman history, where it is read that Tatius, the fifth king, after the defeat of the Sabines, burned all their arms in honour of Vulcan, and that the others followed his example.

units.la: Qu intum ad Vestam attinet; observandum, duas apud Antiquos fuisse Vestas: quarum una Saturni fuit mater, quam pro terra posuerunt atque coluerunt (unde forsan nostrum ⸗⸗⸗ quod & virum nobile ac strenuum, unde ⸗⸗⸗ & quid vis, quod firmū est aq. stabile, terra nimirū ⸗⸗⸗ significat:) altera filiaque ignē significabat: qui Vestae nomē Latinū, & Graecū ἑστίας, in dubie a Chaldaeo ꝛɔɛ, Estcha sive Estha (de quo paullo antea) derivatu fuit. Ovid. in Fasti: Nec tu aliud Vestam, quàm vivam intellige flammam.
units.tr: As far as Vesta is concerned, it should be noted that the ancients had two Vestas. One was the mother of Saturn, whom they set up and worshipped as the earth (whence perhaps our word for a noble and vigorous man, and the Latin word for what is firm and stable, which certainly signifies earth). The other, the daughter, signified fire, and her Latin name Vesta, and the Greek hestia, are doubtless derived from the Chaldean Estcha or Estha (of which I spoke a little earlier). Ovid in the Fasti: "Do not understand Vesta to be anything other than the living flame."

units.la: Numa igitur Pompilius, qui Romanarum superstitionum primarius fuit auctor, & quasi architectus, præter innumeras alias superstitiones hanc quoq; ignis culturam in Romanam civitatem invexit. Is enim, ut ait Plutarchus in Camillo, ad Græcorum, adde etiam aliarum gentium, sturationem, ignem perpetuum atq; perennem in æde rotunda posuit, a certis virginibus custodiendum atq; colendum.
units.tr: Numa Pompilius therefore, who was the chief author and, as it were, the architect of the Roman superstitions, besides countless other superstitions, introduced this worship of fire into the Roman state as well. For, as Plutarch says in the Life of Camillus, he set up in the round temple a perpetual and everlasting fire, to be guarded and tended by certain virgins, to imitate the Greeks, and I may add other nations.

units.la: De hoc templo sic scribit Christophorus Landinus in illa Virgilii Aeneidos secundo, ubi Hestor Aeneæ Vestæ sacra commendat: Templum, inquit, erat sane magnum: in cujus medio eraçaltare, in quo ignis utreq; ex parte ardebat, cujus custodiæ binæ Vestales præerant. In templi culmine virgo erat effigiata, quæ ulnis infantem continebat, Jupiter enim a Vesta nutritus ferebatur. Huic Dea Antiqui vestibula consecrabant: unde & nomen ea a Vesta habere Ovidius. existimat. Hic sæpe comedere erant soliti, ad mensas suas Deos invitantes, quibus, tanquam altaribus utebantur, Diis videlicet penatibus consecratis. Cum autem nullum sacrificium absque igne fieret: ideo focus ei erat dicatus, qui & Lar dicebatur. Nam & ibi Dii Lares colebantur. Templum porro illud hodie adhuc forma circulari, rotundum in valle, quæ Palatino & Capitolino interjacet, visitur, nomine Sanctæ Mariæ de Gratia infignicum. Id interdiu ingredi vetabatur nemo: sub no- ctem fæminis quidem, sed masculis non licebat eo accedere. Nec effigiem in eo aliquam, nec simulacrum collocabant.
units.tr: Christophorus Landinus writes thus about this temple in his commentary on the second book of Virgil's Aeneid, where Hector commends the rites of Vesta to Aeneas: "The temple was indeed large; in the middle of it was an altar on which a fire burned on both sides, and two Vestals presided over its guarding. On the top of the temple a virgin was depicted who held an infant in her arms, for Jupiter was said to have been nursed by Vesta. To this goddess the ancients consecrated the vestibules, whence Ovid thinks she also has her name from them. Here they used often to eat, inviting the gods to their tables, which they used as altars, namely the household gods being consecrated. But since no sacrifice was made without fire, a hearth was dedicated to her, which was also called Lar, for the gods Lares were also worshipped there. Moreover that temple, of circular form, still today is seen in the valley that lies between the Palatine and the Capitoline, and is known by the name of Holy Mary of Grace. No one was forbidden to enter it by day; at night it was permitted to women but not to men to approach it. They placed no image or statue of any kind in it."

units.la: Hunc autem ignem sacrum, tanquam arcanum & cæleste depositum per virgines Vestales, Græcè Εςίαςδια dictas, conditum in penetralibus sacris & velut in sanctiore recessu templi Vestæ, cum Palladio & Diis Penatibus, Trojā advectis, custodiebant: quo nulli hominum, nisi Vestalibus & Pontificibus, ceu ἱερὸν ἀρχάς sædere fas erat.
units.tr: This sacred fire, as a hidden and heavenly deposit, was kept by the Vestal virgins, called in Greek Hestiades, established in the sacred inner shrine and, as it were, in the holier recess of the temple of Vesta, together with the Palladium and the household gods brought from Troy. No one among men was permitted to tend it except the Vestals and the Pontiffs, as sacred duties.

units.la: De harum autem virginum Vestalium collegio, numero, electione, tælibatu, vestitu, munere & officio, disciplina, dignitate, pœnis atq; supplicus, quando vel ignis illarum neglectæ erat extinctus: veliplæ incęstus constitut atq; damnatæ fuerant, vide post vetestos scriptores Peucerum, in libris de Divinatione, Gyraldum de Diis gentium, Florinium in libris Antiquitatum Romanarum.
units.tr: Concerning the college of these Vestal virgins, their number, election, celibacy, dress, function and office, discipline, dignity, punishments and penalties, and when their fire was neglected and went out, or when they were convicted and condemned for impurity, see the later writers: Peucerus in his books on divination, Giraldus on the gods of the nations, and Florinus in his books on Roman antiquities.

units.la: Nec verò publicè tantum, publicus in locis atq; templis, verùm etiá privatim, privatus in ædibus, ignis Romæ fuit cultus. Nam in omnibus ædibus culinæ erant quasi templa quædam, sic dictæ a colendo, ut Nonius et Varrone dotet, qui ad ignem ibi colebant & sacrabant: foci erant quasi ara sacra, in quibus ignis sovebatur (unde etiam foci a fovendo dicti, Ovidio teste:) Diu domestici & patrii, quos veneratur, Penates & Lares fuerunt appellati.
units.tr: Fire was worshipped not only publicly, in public places and temples, but also privately, in private houses. For in all houses the kitchens were, as it were, certain temples, so called from tending (colendo), as Nonius and Varro teach, because they tended and consecrated the fire there. The hearths were like a sacred altar on which the fire was kept alive (whence hearths too are so named from fostering, as Ovid testifies). The household and ancestral gods whom they worshipped were called Penates and Lares.

units.la: Hujusce autem τυχαίας, idest, cultus ignis & publici & privati, caussa fuerunt ignis ipsius divina quædam vis atq; natura, & innumerabilis utilitates. Unde Cicero lib. 2. de Natura Deorum rectè dixit: Quicquid magnam utilitatem generi affertre humano, id non sine divina bonitate erga homines fieri arbitrabantur. Itaq; tum illud, quod erat a Deo donatum, nomine ipsius Dei nuncupabant: ut cum fruges Cererem; vinum autem Liberum appellamus: um aute res ipse, in qua vis inest major aliqua sic appellatur, ut ea ipsa nominetur Deus, ut Fides, ut Mens, ut Virtus, ut Honor. Sic Ops, Salutis, Concordiæ, Libertatis, Victoriæ sunt templa consecrata. Quarum omnium rerum quia vis erat tanta, ut sine Deo regi non posset, aspæres Deoi ii nomen obtinuit. Item: Vitium magnitudine constituit sunt ii Dii, qui utilitates quasi gignerant: atque hæ quidem ipsis nominibus, quæ vis sit in quoq; declaratur. Eodem ex genere Cupidinus, Voluptatis, Lubentinæ Veneris vocabula consecrata sunt, vitiosarum rerum, neq; naturalium.
units.tr: Of this worship of fire, both public and private, the causes were the divine power and nature of fire itself and its countless uses. Hence Cicero rightly said in the second book of On the Nature of the Gods: whatever brings great benefit to the human race, they judged to happen not without the divine goodness toward men. So they named what God had given by the name of God itself, as we call grain Ceres and wine Liber. Again, when a thing in which some greater power dwells is named so that the thing itself is called a god, as Faith, Mind, Virtue, Honour. Thus Ops, Safety, Concord, Liberty and Victory have consecrated temples. Because the power of all these things was so great that they could not be ruled without God, they obtained the name of gods. Likewise: those are gods who, on account of the greatness of their vices, as it were produce benefits; and these are indeed declared by their very names, by the power that is in each. From the same class the names of Cupid, of Pleasure, and of Lubentine Venus were consecrated, for vicious things and not natural ones.

units.la: Verum cultus quoque hujus non minima caussa videtur fuisse cum ignis ille apud Iudæos, qui perpetuum ardebat in altari, quem sacerdos, subjectis lignis, muñé per jugul. dies nutriebat, ut Levitici sexto scriptum est: tum divina illa miracula, quæ legimus in sacris literis de gne cælitus delapso in Patriarchas um illorum prisci seculi sacrificia, quo illa fuerunt consumta, atque ita ipsius Dei testimonio comprobata. Atq; hinc quidem videtur promanasse illa de Prometheo fabula, quem Poetæ finxerunt ignem, e cælis surreptum, in terras detulisse.
units.tr: Yet this worship seems to have had no small cause in that fire which among the Jews burned perpetually on the altar, which the priest fed every morning by laying on wood, as is written in Leviticus chapter six. Add to this those divine miracles which we read of in Holy Scripture, of fire falling from heaven upon the sacrifices of the Patriarchs in the earliest age, by which those sacrifices were consumed and so confirmed by the testimony of God himself. And indeed from this seems to have flowed that fable of Prometheus, whom the poets feigned to have stolen fire from the heavens and brought it down to the earth.

units.la: Sed antequam ulterius progrediar; non videtur silentio prætereunda illa Ignicolarum quorundam, qui Dugbin fuerunt appellati, in insula 6 benerag, biso: 14 sestione administrationes, di- gna, qua in Beniamin Tudelensis itineratione continetur, quae quidem est talis: Insulae illius incolae, ignem colentes & Dugbun dicti, habent suos sacrificulos per singula loca in templis ipsorum superstitioni dicatos: sunt vero huiusmodi sacrificuli omnium ariolorum & incantatorum totius orbis terrae peritissimi in omni vanitatis bujus genere. Ante singula autem fana campus magnus & latus est, in quo ingens ignis omnibus diebus ardet, quem ipsi Elhotha vocant: solent autem filios suos per hunc ignem transmittere expiandi causa: mortuos etiam suos in medium rogum conjiciunt exurendos. Sunt praeterea ex terra magnatibus, qui se fe vivos igni devovent. Cum vero quispiam horum familiaribus & necessariis atq. propinquis suis huiusmodi sibi institutam devotionem indicat, continuo summa omnium gratulatione & communi voce audit: Beatus tu, & bene tibi erit. Igitur quo die votum exsolvendum est, magno concursu primum exceptus, si dives fuerit, equo vehitur; sin vero pauper, pedes suorum aliorumq; turba comitatus ad campi ufq; tum deducitur, unde cursu invito in ignem insilit: tum vero familiares cognati, omnes & consanguinei tympanis & choreis summa cum laetitia exsultant & ludunt, quoad ille omnino ambustus fuerit. Triduo autem post, duo expraeciputi sacrificuli illius domum adeuntes, familiae omni domum parari praecipiunt patri ipsorum, eadem die ipsis assuturo, atq; quid ipsos facere oporteat, declaraturo. Advocantur igitur ex civitate tres aliquot: & ecce Satan, illius speciem imitatus, adest, quem uxor & filii rogant quemadmodum cum illo in illo altero seculo agatur, quibus ille respondens: Veni, inquit, ad foetos meos, a quibus non excipior, donec ea exsolvam, quae familiaribus & propinquis debeo meis; ex templo filius res ad tributionem suas, jubet, debita omnia creditoribus persolvi, & a debitoribus quicquid debeatur exigi, testibus omnia ipsius verba et mandata excipientibus atq. describentibus, a quibus tamen non videtur, tum vero se viam repetere ascendere, evanuit. Huiusmodi itaq. errore, mendacio, & fraude sacrificulorum illorum callidiate & artibus magicis extructa, vanitatum suam gens haec tuetur ac mordicus tenet, sicque naufragium omnium terrae beatissimum esse jactat, &c. Haec Beniamin Iudaeus.
units.tr: But before I proceed further, I think that not be passed over in silence is that account of certain fire-worshippers, called Dugbin, on an island... which is contained in the itinerary of Benjamin of Tudela, and which runs thus: The inhabitants of that island, who worship fire and are called Dugbun, have their own priests in each place, dedicated to their superstition in their temples. These priests are most skilled in every kind of this vanity, of all soothsayers and enchanters in the whole world. Before each shrine there is a large and broad open space, in which a huge fire burns every day, which they call Elhotha. They are accustomed to pass their sons through this fire for the sake of purification, and they cast their dead onto the middle of the pyre to be burned. There are also among them men of rank who devote themselves alive to the fire. When one of them announces such a devotion to his household, his kin and his close relatives, he at once hears, with the general acclaim and common voice of all: Blessed are you, and it will go well with you. Then on the day on which the vow is to be fulfilled, he is first received with a great crowd; if he is rich, he is carried on horseback; but if he is poor, he is led on foot, accompanied by his family and a throng of others, to the open space, where he leaps unwillingly into the fire. Then his household, his kin and all his blood relations dance and make merry with drums and choruses, with great joy, until he is completely burned. Three days after this, two of the chief priests go to the house and order the whole household to prepare the house for their father, who is to come the same day and will declare what they ought to do. Then three or so men are summoned from the city, and behold, Satan, imitating his form, appears. His wife and sons ask him how matters stand with him in the other world. He answers: I have come to my followers, by whom I am not received until I have paid what I owe to my household and kin. Immediately his son gives orders for the distribution of his goods, that all his debts be paid to the creditors and whatever is owed to him be collected from his debtors, the witnesses taking down and recording all his words and commands. Yet from them he seems not to be seen; then, when he returns to his way up, he vanishes. By such error, lies and fraud, by the cunning and magical arts of those priests, this people defends its vanity and holds it tight with their teeth, and so it boasts that its shipwreck is the most blessed of all on earth, etc. Thus Benjamin the Jew.

units.la: His in genere de superstitioso ignis apud omnes feregentes culturam prae misi, nunc ad ignem sacrificalem, hoc est, in sacrificiis adhibitum, redeamus: in quo haec, quae sequuntur, sunt considerandi capita. Primum est de igne illius super aram accendendi tempore atq. modo.
units.tr: Having set forth in general these things about the superstitious fire-worship of all the peoples who practise it, let us now return to the sacrificial fire, that is, the fire used in sacrifices. In this connection the following points are to be considered. The first is the time and manner of kindling that fire upon the altar.

units.la: Quoad tempus, videtur ignis ille statim simul atq. hostia ad altaria fuerunt adductae, fuisse accensus, vel etiam paullo ante, secundum illa Virgilianae: Admovit ad pecus si ignarium aris.
units.tr: As to time, that fire seems to have been kindled at once, as soon as the victims were brought to the altars, or even a little before, according to that line of Virgil: He brought the unwilling beast near to the altar.

units.la: Quantum autem admodum attinet, tritus hic & usitatus erat apud Romanos, ut sacerdotes ac Sacrorum, minimi eum accenderent (cum, ut supra dictum, purgandi vis tributa fuit) facibus inhibitis ex tedae ligno, quas faces non nisi mares ferre fas erat.
units.tr: As to the manner, it was common and customary among the Romans that the priests of the rites, when they kindled it (since, as said above, it was held to have the power of purifying), used torches of pine wood, which only men were permitted to carry.

units.la: Sed, ut in sacris litteris legimus, prisci illis Patriarcharum temporibus sacrificia ignibus non manu atq. arte accensis, sed e caelo demissis fuisse consumpta: quo Deus festari voluit, sacrificia illa sibi grata fuisse & accepta: sic Ethnici idem de suis sacrificiis finxerunt: cujus quadam exempla subjiciam.
units.tr: But, as we read in Holy Scripture, in the early times of the Patriarchs the sacrifices were consumed not by fires lit by human hand and skill, but by fire sent down from heaven; by this God wished to show that those sacrifices were pleasing and acceptable to him. In the same way the heathen feigned the same about their own sacrifices; I shall set out some examples of this.

units.la: Apud Siculos in tolle Vulcanio iuxta flagnum quoddam, dum sacrum fieret, sarmentorum fasces super aram sua sponte iguem concepisse, & nullo flante anhelitu incendium fecisse fubulari sunt. Similiter quid de Seleuco proditum est, qui cum Iovis in Pollia victimam immolaret, ligna aris imposita ultro accensa sunt. Sicin ara Egnatia Nymphae, quae in Apulia culta fuit, lignis superpositis extra ustus, ignis sua sponte excitari incendique, ab Antiquis existimabatur. Plinius libro secundo miraculi meminit: non autem Nymphae. Servius in illa Virgilii Aeneidos duodecimo: Quia foedera fulmine sanxit,
units.tr: Among the Sicilians, in the Vulcanian lake near a certain pool, while a sacrifice was being made, they report that a bundle of brushwood on the altar caught fire of its own accord, and without any breath of wind a blaze was made. Similarly, it is recorded of Seleucus that when he was sacrificing a victim to Jupiter at Pollium, the wood laid on the altar caught fire of its own accord. Likewise, on the altar of the Nymph Egnatia, who was worshipped in Apulia, when wood was laid on top of it, the fire was, by the ancients' belief, kindled and ignited of its own accord. Pliny mentions this miracle in the second book, but not the Nymph. Servius, on that line of Virgil's twelfth book: because he sealed the covenants with a thunderbolt.

units.la: Certe, inquit, quia apud Majores are non incendebantur, sed igne divinum precibus elicie bat, qui incendebat altaria. Hinc forsan Iupiter Elicius dictus. Dubium non est, quin Diabolus hujusmodi ignes, Dei permissu, sepe, sacerdotum magicus incantationibus pro vocatus, ex aere, tanquam carcere illo suo turbido, in Gentilium sacrificia ut olim in Iobi greges deciderit: vel etiam sacerdotes fascinationibus quibusdam atq. praestigiis usi fuerint in ignibus illis accendendis, ita ut rudem imperitum, vulgus illos caelitus demitti arbitrarotur; idq. fecerint majoris sibi fuisse sacris fidei & auctoritatis conciliandae gratia.
units.tr: Certainly, he says, because among the ancestors altars were not kindled, but fire was drawn down by prayers from the divine, and it set the altars alight. Hence perhaps Jupiter was called Elicius. There is no doubt that the Devil, often summoned by the magical incantations of the priests, with God's permission, has dropped such fires from the air, his turbid prison, into the sacrifices of the Gentiles, just as once he fell upon the flocks of Job; or else the priests used certain enchantments and tricks in kindling those fires, so that the rude and unskilled crowd thought they were sent down from heaven; and they did this to gain greater respect and authority for their rites.

units.la: Verisimile etiam est, multas hujusmodi Ecbnicorum de ignibus,in sacrificia sua cœlitus dela-pfas,fabulas ex veris illis sacrarum litterarum historiis promanésse,quibus proditum est, ut paullo antea dixi, illa antiquissima sanctissimorum patrum sacrificia igne cœlitus delapso fubisco con-flagrâsse: quo miraculo Deus ceslabatur ipsos lites,seque sacrificiis illis placari. Nota est illa-stris illa de Heliæ & sacerdotum Baalliticorum sacrificiis historia, ubi legimus, Heliam quidem votis sui compotem factum fuisse, sacrificiumq; ejus, igne, e cœlis demisso, fuisse consumptum: adversarios autem ipsius, cum idem a Baale suo in sanis clamoribus, quos Helias irrisferat, contemdissent,ipse uotis, jussu cum maximo suo dedecore atq; exitio fuisse frustratos, ut scriptum est primo Regum libro, capite decimo octavo.
units.tr: It is also likely that many such fables of the Gentiles, that fires fell from heaven upon their sacrifices, arose from those true histories of Holy Scripture, in which it is recorded, as I said a little before, that those most ancient and most holy sacrifices of the fathers were set alight by fire that fell from heaven; by this miracle God showed that he was pleased, and that he was appeased by those sacrifices. Famous is the story of Elijah and the sacrifices of the priests of Baal, where we read that Elijah indeed obtained his request, and his sacrifice was consumed by fire sent down from heaven, while his adversaries, who had likewise appealed to their Baal with loud cries, which Elijah mocked, were frustrated of their hopes, to their great shame and ruin, as is written in the first book of Kings, chapter eighteen.

units.la: Ignem autem illum sacrificialem ex Flaminis domo adferri nonnunquam fuisse solitum illa Festi verba innuere videntur, quando ajt: Ignem ex domo Flaminis efferri non licebat, nisi tri-divinæ gratia. Dubium etiam non est, quin ex sacro & publico illo Vestæ igne apud Romanos ille sacrorum publicorum ignis fuerit accensus; do quo Vestæ igne idem Festus scribit: Vestæ ignis si quando interstinctus esset, Virgines verberibus afficiebantur a Pontifice, quibus mos erat tabulam felicis materiæ tandiu terebrare (verberare, alii legunt) quousq; excepium ignem cribro æneo Virgo in Ædem ferret.
units.tr: Festus's words seem to suggest that this sacrificial fire was sometimes brought from the house of the Flamen: "It was not permitted to carry fire out of the Flamen's house, except by the favour of the three gods." There is also no doubt that among the Romans this sacred public fire was kindled from the sacred public fire of Vesta. Festus writes of this Vestal fire that whenever the fire of Vesta went out, the Virgins were beaten by the Pontiff. They had the custom of boring a tablet of lucky wood for as long as it took (some read "beating") until a Virgin could carry the fire obtained into the temple in a bronze sieve.
These things concerning the sacrificial fire.
CONSEQUENTLY

units.la: nunc videtur, ut de lignis dicamus, quorum in igne illo sacrificiali usus erat. Nam ligna in genere cujusvis ignis sunt quasi alimenta acq; fomenta; & inde ligna Latini videtur dicta, quasi igna, ablatâ litera l. quia nimirū lignis pocissimum qui-vis ignis alitur, foretur ac conservatur. Varro cæmè ligna à legendo vulc dicta, quod ea caduco in agro legerentur.
units.tr: Now it seems right to speak of the woods that were used in that sacrificial fire. For wood in general is, as it were, the food and fuel of any fire, and hence the Latin word "ligna" seems to be derived as if from "igna", with the letter l dropped, because any fire is chiefly fed, nourished and kept alive by wood. Varro, however, thinks that "ligna" is so called from gathering (legendo), because it was gathered from fallen timber in the fields.

units.la: Ligna autem sacrificialia primum oportebat esse sicca & arida, Græcè ν π ο ν λ α, quasi dicat sobria dicta, quæ primum incendebantur, ut etiam ἀκαυτα, non fumida. Νυ λαν ξύλα alii pucant dicta, quæ in sacrificiis duntaxat Νηξάλλας ἐχι ποῦοις, id est, sobrius, & abs, vinò fieri solitus adhibebantur. Νηφαλία ξύλα, inquit Suidas, τα μὴ ὑπὸ ὑμί ἀλλὰ, μήτι οὐκ ἄχωπα, μὴ ἀμη ἀπ- Ἐκεί ἔστι ἐπὶ οἴνωων ἀπὸ ἡ ἀρχὴ ἀν ἄ ἑαυτῶν ἄ ἐν ὕδωρ. ἀλλ ἐν ᾧ ἀπ ἐν ϑ.
units.tr: Sacrificial wood had first to be dry and parched, in Greek "nēphalia xyla" [νηφάλια ξύλα], as if to say sober wood, the kind that catches fire first, and also "akapna" [ἄκαπνα], that is, not smoky. Some think that "nēphalia" wood was so called because only those woods that were sober, that is, free of wine, were used in sacrifices. Suidas says that "nēphalia xyla" are those that are not drenched or soaked, but dry and fit for burning; the passage in his text is corrupt.

units.la: Arida autem oportebat esse, quo facillime exardescerent, tanccq; celeriùs quæ vis, in ignem conjecta, conflagrarent: quod boni ominis loco habebatur. Quæ autem lignorum genera ad ignem quem vis maxime sint idonea, quæ item minimè apta, vide Curtium libro decimo octavo Hortorum capite decimo quarto, decimo quinto, & decimo sexto, ubi & de lapidibus, ex quibus ignis elicitur agic, & de arte ignaria, a Græcis αυγίον, ὑ ναυηκ vel μυν ξυλμα dicta: item, de facibus, earumq; materia, & de voce κόλον, lignum significante: unde καλοπόσσα, id est, calcei lignei, Claslus, id est fustis, sive clavalignea, & Calones, qui ligna militibus portabant, fuerunt dicti.
units.tr: The wood had to be dry so that it would catch fire most easily, and so that whatever was thrown on the fire would the more quickly burst into flame; this was regarded as a good omen. As for which kinds of wood are best suited to fire and which least suited, see Curtius, book 18 of the Hortorum, chapters 14, 15 and 16. There he also treats of the stones from which fire is struck, and of the art of making fire, which the Greeks call "auginon" and "nauēke" or "mynxylma". He also discusses torches and their material, and the word "kolon", which means wood. From this come "kalopodia", that is, wooden shoes; "clasis", that is, a club or wooden stick; and "calones", the men who carried wood for soldiers.

units.la: Eandem ob causam ligna prius illa in fragmenta minora aptè scindi, atq; secari solebant: cu-jus quidem ξυλοτομiac sæpe apud Homerum in sacrificiorum apparatu fit mentio; ut Odyss. ζ. in descriptione sacrificii sulli, ejusq; apparatu: —Κίαον ξύλα υπάλι χαλκός. Scidit ligna immiti ferro.
units.tr: For the same reason the wood was customarily split and cut into smaller pieces. Homer often mentions this woodcutting in the preparation of sacrifices, for example in Odyssey book 6 (ζ), in the description of the sacrifice of a bull and its preparation: "He split the wood with pitiless iron."

units.la: Est enim καίζειν dividere scindere, frangere, & proprie ligna secare, teste Eustathio: quod verbum magnam habet affinitatem cum verbo καίειν, id est, urere et accendere: forsan, quia ligna sedia facilius accenduntur & exuruntur, quàm ea, quæ non secta sunt. Respondet verbo καίζειν, verbum χίζειν, similiter scindere, findere, diffindere, secare significans: unde ligna scissa in sacrificiorum usum χίζα appellantur: & χίζα fragmentum, seu segmentum, sive fustum ligni scissi, sive lignum scissum sijumq;, quo ignis fovetur aut accenditur. Inde nostrum vernaculum Scheiten/vel Scheiten/id est, scindere, vel findere: & Schit/vel Schrit/id est, ligni fissi frustum sive segmentum. Σχίσαξ idem quod χίζα, hoc est, assula; velut Nazanzenus interpretatur, ἀλάσματα ξύλα, fragmentum ligni, quo in sacris utebantur.
units.tr: For καίζειν means to divide, split, break, and properly to cut wood, according to Eustathius. This verb has a great affinity with καίειν, to burn and set alight, perhaps because split wood catches fire and burns more easily than wood that has not been split. Corresponding to καίζειν is the verb χίζειν, likewise meaning to split, cleave, cut through and cut. From this, split wood used for sacrifices is called χίζα, and χίζα is a splinter, piece or chip of split wood, or the split stick with which the fire is fed or kindled. Hence our German "Scheiten" or "Scheit", that is, to split or cleave, and "Schit" or "Schrit", that is, a split piece or segment of wood. σχίσαξ is the same as χίζα, that is, a splinter or shaving; as Nazianzen explains it, "split pieces of wood, a fragment of wood used in the sacred rites."

units.la: Quoad Apollonium nostrum; meminit etiam hic hujus ξυλοτομίας, inquiens: —Καίον δ' ἐπὶ χίζαται,
units.tr: As for our Apollonius, he too mentions this splitting of wood, saying: "...and he burned it on the splinters."

units.la: Comburebant autem (carnes) super lignorum fragmenta. Caeterum non quaevis ex materia sive ligno ignem illum accendere licebat. In Arcadia in templo Deiphanae, quod quattuor fladiorum intervallo ab Acace distabat, ex olea, lauro, vel crassioris certiciis quercu, ignem facere nefas erat, quod diligna illa Arcades, cum ominosa detestaren-tur. Plinius libro decimosexto, capite sexto: Pestima, inquit, & carboni e materia Haliphloeos dicta, cui crassissimus cortex atque candex, & plerunque cavus fungosus. Nec alia putrescit ex hoc genere, etiam cum vivit. Quin & fulmine saepissime icitur, quam vix alia altitudine non excellat. Ideo lignorum nec ad sacrificia uti fas habetur. Addit: Hoc quoque inter reliqua negligere religionis est, quod emortuo carbone sacrificatur:
units.tr: They burned the flesh on the fragments of wood. However, it was not permitted to kindle that fire from any kind of wood. In Arcadia, in the temple of Diphanes, which was four stadia from Acacesium, it was unlawful to make fire from olive, laurel or the thicker oak, since the Arcadians detested these woods as ill-omened. Pliny, book 16, chapter 6: "The worst," he says, "is the wood and charcoal of the kind called haliphloios, which has a very thick and white bark and is usually hollow and spongy. No other wood of this kind rots so, even while it is alive. Indeed it is also struck by lightning very often, though it does not rise above other trees in height. Therefore it is held not lawful to use this wood for sacrifices." He adds: "It is also a matter of religious negligence, among other things, that sacrifice is made with charcoal that has gone out."

units.la: In Iovis Olympii sacris alba populo sacerdotes semper usi fuere. Elii etiam Jovi muscario (ut est Baal-Zebub) eandem arborem in sacrificiis adhibuerunt, ut scribit Pausanias in Eliacis.
units.tr: In the rites of Olympian Jove the priests always used white poplar. The Eleans also used the same tree in sacrifices to Jupiter the Fly-catcher (who is like Baal-Zebub), as Pausanias writes in his Eliaca.

units.la: Persarum Magi, ut autor est Herodotus, sacrificiis praefecti, carnes lanri myrtii, virgis impositas olim adurebant, ac latte & melle permisto, fasciculis myrteis apprehensis aspergebant.
units.tr: The Magi of the Persians, who had charge of the sacrifices, as Herodotus reports, used to burn the flesh on laid rods of laurel and myrtle; and after mixing milk and honey, they sprinkled it while holding bundles of myrtle.

units.la: Pini sacra in Cereris sacrificiis, tanquam eu apta & dicata adhibebatur, quod haec ad inveniligandam Proserpinam filiam, geminas pinus pro lampade accenderis, ut Ovidius testatur Fastorum quarto:
units.tr: Pine was used in the sacrifices of Ceres as especially apt and dedicated to her, because in seeking her daughter Proserpina she kindled two pine torches in place of a lamp, as Ovid attests in Fasti book 4:
There she lit two pines for a torch:

units.la: Hinc Cereris sacris nunc quoque tada datur.
units.tr: Hence even now torches are given in the rites of Ceres.

units.la: Sicyonii Veneri hostiarum coxas, finibus exceptis, sacrificarunt; reliquias autem in sacris altaribus juniperi lignis, & foliis herbae, quae Pederotus fuit nuncupata, combrebant.
units.tr: The Sicyonians sacrificed to Venus the thighs of the victims, with the entrails removed; the remains they burned on the sacred altars with juniper wood and the leaves of the herb called pederotos.

units.la: Iasides ex omni licet ligno aras incenderent; pinas tamen asparagi, aut stramina in sacris cremare nefas habebant.
units.tr: The Iasides, although they might kindle altars with any wood, considered it unlawful to burn asparagus or straw in sacrifices.

units.la: Apud Scythas autem, cum sacrum Martis fieret, hostiarum carnes ipsarum met ossibus adurebantur.
units.tr: Among the Scythians, when a sacrifice to Mars was made, the flesh of the victims was burned together with their bones.

units.la: Lapsitani autem lapidibus ignitis sacrificiorum earnas coquebant:
units.tr: The Lapsitani cooked the flesh of their sacrifices with red-hot stones.

units.la: Dubium etiam non est, quin in igni illo sacrificiali ligna adhibuerint exiis potissimum arboribus, quae Numini illi, cui rem dicabant, dicata & sacrata. Nam, ut supra dixi, singulis Diis certa quaedam arbores atque plantae ab Ethnicis fuerunt sacratae. De his, qui plura scripserunt, praeter ea, quae superius fuerunt explicata, cupis cognoscere, ut legat Benedicti Curtii Symphoris librum Hortorum quintum, qui ut etiam reliqui libri, lectione est dignissimae, cujus summa sacris arboribus sanctum capita hic recensebo. Primum est de quercu & jugulande, jovi sacris, et nonnulla de cibo. Pica corona, & adagio πολλῶν πάγκλιτη ἀργὴ ἰδ' ἐστὶ, multorum festorum Jovis glandes comedit, de sene & plurimarum rerum longo usu doctus, quem nos simili fere proverbio Eein alten bünerfreßer/id est, senem gallinarum devoratorem vocamus. Secundum est de lauro & loro, Apollini dicata: unde Apollo Daphnites a Syracusanis, teste Hesychio dictus: cujus templum primum apud Delphos lauri ramus aedificatum, et sacerdotes in templo quodam Daphnophoros, id est, laurifer fuit appellatus. Item Apollinis sacerdotes lauro coronari solitri: & Daphnophagi dicti lanriferi ab Aristophane: laurus item quae μαυκὸν, planta vaticinatrix, teste Dionysio Halicarnasseo, fuit appellata. Caput tertium est de Daphnes fabula, in laurum commutata. Quartum de olea, Minervae dicata, quod olea pacis & veniae fit index. Item de adagio: ἰδαίων ἐν ἐστὶν εἰς ἀνακύβην, Non est oleum in Lecytho, apud Aristophanem in Avibus: nbi precibus atque veniae jam non est locus. Sextum est de Minervae & Saturni super Athenarum nominis impositione, certamine. Septimum, de olea apud Athenas in arce Minervae. Octavum, de myrto, Veneri dicata. Nonum, de rosa & phylira, Veneri dicatis, et de naucinite corona. Decimum, de hedera, ferula & picea, Baccho dicatis: et de adagio, ἀνοφόρος, καὶ ἐπὶ Βάκχου. Multi feruligeri (sic dicti Bacchi ministri, qui initiati ferulans gestabant) sed pauci Bacchi. Undecimum, de cupressio, Diti sacra, & fabula Boreae & Cyparissi, Duodecimum, de pinu Cibele dicata, de Ida monte Troadis, et pinn, in eo pulcherrimae & Atys fabula. Decimumtertium, de populo Herculi, mali Punici fructu Mercurio, perfia Harpocrate dicatis.
units.tr: There is no doubt that in that sacrificial fire they used wood chiefly from those trees which were dedicated and consecrated to the deity to whom the sacrifice was offered, for, as I said above, certain trees and plants were consecrated by the heathen to each god. If you wish to learn more about this from those who have written at greater length, beyond what was explained above, read the fifth book of the Hortorum of Benedictus Curtius Symphorianus, which, like his other books, is most worth reading. I will list here the main chapters on sacred trees. The first concerns the oak and its acorns, sacred to Jove, with some remarks on food: "He has eaten the acorns of many festivals of Jove," said of an old man who is learned from long experience of many things, whom we call with a similar proverb "an old hen-devourer." The second concerns the laurel and the bay, dedicated to Apollo, whence Apollo was called Daphnites by the Syracusans, as Hesychius reports; the first temple of Apollo at Delphi was built of laurel branches, and certain priests in a temple were called Daphnophoroi, that is, laurel-bearers. Likewise the priests of Apollo were accustomed to be crowned with laurel, and Aristophanes called the laurel-bearers "Daphnophagi"; the laurel that is "mantikon", the prophetic plant, was also so named, according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus. The third chapter concerns the fable of Daphne changed into a laurel. The fourth concerns the olive, dedicated to Minerva, because the olive is a sign of peace and pardon; also the proverb "there is no oil in the flask" (ἐλαίου οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν λήκυθῳ), from Aristophanes' Birds, where there is no longer room for prayers and pardon. The sixth concerns the contest of Minerva and Saturn over the naming of Athens. The seventh concerns the olive at Athens in the citadel of Minerva. The eighth concerns the myrtle, dedicated to Venus. The ninth concerns the rose and the phyllyra, dedicated to Venus, and the crown of the nauclinite (?). The tenth concerns ivy, fennel and pitch-pine, dedicated to Bacchus, and the proverb "fennel-bearers, even for Bacchus": many are fennel-bearers (so called the ministers of Bacchus, who carried fennel-stalks when initiated), but few are Bacchus's own. The eleventh concerns the cypress, sacred to Dis, and the fable of Boreas and Cyparissus. The twelfth concerns the pine, dedicated to Cybele, on Mount Ida in the Troad, and the very beautiful fable of Attis. The thirteenth concerns the poplar, dedicated to Hercules, the pomegranate fruit to Mercury, and the persea to Harpocrates.

units.la: Haec idcirco subjicere libuit, propterea quod quibusvis vel cultissimum amanissimumque, hortis amaniora & jucundiora, quaeque ad institutum hoc nostrum maxime pertinent, complectitur. Quoniam igitur singulis Diis certi peculiaresq; flores, herbæ, folia, frondes, rami, arbores denique, atque plantæ integræ fuerunt consecratæ: idcirco in sacrorum quoq; & coronis, quibus & sacrificantes, & hostiæ, & simulacra, & altaria ornari consueuerunt; & templorum, altarium, simulacrorum, statuarum aliorumq; instrumentorum fabricatione; & denique in sacrificiorum lignis atque materiis diligens accuratáq; ab Ebraicis habita fuit ratio atque delectus. Et hæc pertinet ejusdem authoris liber tertius, seu totus: cujus hæc sunt capita. Primum, de arborum Numinibus & religione. Secundum, quid Antiqui sylvas, arbores, aut illarum genus unum coluerint: & de Galliarum Druidibus. Tertium, de ficu Ruminali, arboribus alijs arboribus Romæ & aliibi sacris. Quartum, Responsa Antiquos ex arboribus accepisse: & de oraculo Dodonæo: & adagio, Dodonæum humanum: quod in loquaces & in rebus frivolis garrulos dicitur. Quintum, de Deorum coronis & statuarum illorum ac sacerdotum & sacrificantium. Sextum, quod Dii ex arboribus cognominantur: & de inarculo, quod, teste Festo, fuit virga ex malo punico incurvata, quam regina sacrificans in capite gestabat: de Alboglero: de rege sacrificulo: de ejus uxore, quæ regina sacrorum appellata, & laurea Deorum & sacrificantium, & lauri in sacrificiis usu. Octavum, de arborum ad sacrificia usu. Nonum, de arborum apud Iudæos ad sacrificia usu & legibus. Decimum, de nonnullis ad sacrificia profanis arboribus. Undecimum, de arborum materia ad Deorum statuas: & quid delubrum & de adagio, Ne quovis ex ligno Mercurius fiat. Duodecimum, de feriis & festis ob arborum fructus institutis.
units.tr: I have thought it fit to add these matters, because they contain things more pleasant and delightful than any garden, for anyone most refined and fond of pleasure, and which pertain most to this undertaking of ours. Since particular and fixed flowers, herbs, leaves, fronds, branches, and indeed whole trees and plants were consecrated to individual gods, the Hebrews likewise took careful and exact account and selection of them for the sacred garlands with which sacrificers, victims, images and altars were customarily adorned; for the construction of temples, altars, images, statues and other implements; and finally for the woods and materials of sacrifices. The third book of the same author, or the whole of it, deals with this, and its chapters are these. First, on the divinities and worship of trees. Second, what the ancients worshipped: woods, trees, or one kind of tree; and on the Druids of the Gauls. Third, on the Ruminal fig tree and other trees sacred at Rome and elsewhere. Fourth, that the ancients received oracles from trees; on the oracle of Dodona; and on the proverb "a Dodonaean man", said of chatterers and babblers about trivial matters. Fifth, on the garlands of the gods and of their statues, and of the priests and sacrificers. Sixth, that gods are named after trees; on the inarculum, which, according to Festus, was a rod bent from a pomegranate tree that the sacrificing queen carried on her head; on the Alboglerus; on the king sacrificer; on his wife, who was called the queen of the rites; and on the laurel of gods and sacrificers and its use in sacrifices. Eighth, on the use of trees in sacrifices. Ninth, on the use of trees among the Jews for sacrifices and in their laws. Tenth, on certain profane trees used for sacrifices. Eleventh, on the wood used for statues of the gods; what a shrine is; and on the proverb "Let Mercury not be made of any wood". Twelfth, on the festivals and feasts instituted because of the fruit of trees.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem singulas arbores vel coluerunt tanquam Numina: vel vertis Diis atq; Numinibus dicarunt: sic etiam loca amplissima, arboribus consitas, et integras sylvas eisdem consecrarunt, atq; in iis, tanquam templis & sacrariis sacrosanctis eos coluerunt, quæ Græce ἄλσ-ον, Latinè Nemora et Luci fuerunt appellata. Nemorosa autem et umbrosa hujusmodi loca Pscherà a Græcis fuisse appellata Nicander testatur.
units.tr: Just as they worshipped individual trees as divinities, or dedicated them to the gods and deities, so also they consecrated very extensive places planted with trees, and whole woods, to them. In these places they worshipped the gods as in temples and holy sanctuaries. The Greeks called these alsos, and the Latins called them nemora and luci. Nicander testifies that the Greeks called such shady, wooded places Pschera.

units.la: De sacris hisce nemoribus atq; lucis idem Cursius sub finem libri tertii Hortorum, capite decimoquarto, & sequenti libro quarto toto egregie dissere, quibus ex hortis amœnissimis multisq; pulcherrimos ad rerum omnis generis, præsertim ad Gentilium super stitionem pertinentium, flores atque fructus nobis colligere atq; percipere licet, quorum hæc fere sunt capita: Libro tertio, caput decimum & quartum & ultimum est, de nemoribus sacris: de nemoru & luci diserimine. Libro deinde quarto Hortorum hæc tractaneur & explicantur, capite primo, de luco ejus religione: in lucis ac rebus publicis tractare & in illis, diebus sacris, epularî Veteres solitos: lucum esse sylvam Dijs, Heroibus, vel alicujus cineribus sacrum: Germanos veteres ... La Deorum templa habuisse præter lucos et nemora, teste Cornelio Tacito. Sacros, inquit Quintilianus, ex vetustate lucos adoramus: in quibus grandia et antiqua robora jam non tantam habent culturam, quantam religionem. Idem Horatii et Persii testimonio comprobat. In lucis Deorum simulacbra posita, quibus sacrificatum: in lucis Deorii sonitus et voces exaudite: lucos Manes, qui vitales Lares dicebantur, et Herorum animæ incolebantur, teste Servio: lucos et ædes Numinibus prunum consecrasse Faunum, a quo fana dicta, ut auctor Probus: In tuo luco fanoq; esse apud Plautum, adagiorum loco, teste Donato, id est, potestate & arbitrio: in agris habendos lucos, propterq; eos ferre oportere, Cicero de Legibus: luci nunquam cædui: ideo arborum verufiat veneranda: luci asylia, Livii, Virgilii, Ovidii testimonio probat: lucus Græcè etiam τέμενος: in ro antiquus fine templo lucus fuit, teste Servio: in lucis sepultos homines: in lucis de rebus publicis consultum: quæ in lucis decreta, sanctiora ob loci religionem habita: in lucis sacris diebus epulabantur: lucorum luculenta descriptio Lucani & Papinii carminibus.
units.tr: Curtius treats these sacred groves and woods admirably at the end of the third book of his Gardens, in the fourteenth chapter, and throughout the following fourth book. From these most pleasant gardens we may gather and take many beautiful flowers and fruits of every kind of thing, especially those pertaining to Gentile superstition. The main headings are these. In the third book, the tenth, fourteenth and last chapter concerns sacred groves, and the difference between a grove and a sacred wood. In the fourth book of the Gardens the following are treated and explained: in the first chapter, the grove and its religion; that the ancients were accustomed to hold feasts in groves and public places, and on sacred days to feast in them; that a grove is a wood sacred to the gods, heroes, or the ashes of someone; that the ancient Germans... had temples of the gods besides groves and woods, according to Cornelius Tacitus. Quintilian says: "We worship sacred groves from antiquity, in which great and ancient oaks now have not so much cultivation as reverence." Horace and Persius confirm the same by their testimony. Statues of the gods were set up in groves, where sacrifices were offered; sounds and voices of the gods were heard in groves. According to Servius, the groves were inhabited by the Manes, who were called the living Lares, and by the souls of heroes. According to the author Probus, Faunus was the first to consecrate groves and temples to the gods, from whom shrines (fana) are named. In Plautus, "in your grove and shrine" is a proverbial phrase, according to Donatus, meaning at one's power and discretion. In Cicero's On the Laws, groves ought to be kept in the fields and preserved there. Groves are never to be felled, and therefore the trees are to be venerated; groves were places of sanctuary, as the testimony of Livy, Virgil and Ovid proves. The Greek word for grove is also temenos. According to Servius, there was an ancient grove without a temple. Men were buried in groves; public matters were deliberated in groves; decisions made in groves were regarded as more sacred because of the religious character of the place; on sacred days people feasted in groves; and there is a splendid description of groves in the poems of Lucan and Papinius.

units.la: Secundo deinde capite agit de luci venerations: lucos fuisse invios, per quos etiam neq; in necessitate ipsa meare fas fuit: lucinuti ad venationem, & illorum animalia occidere, nisi sacrificii & Numinum eorundem causa non licebat: in lucis nonnullis animalia manfuetissima: lucis non homines tantum, sed etiam animalia peperisse. Capite tertio, lucus unde; & de vocabulo ab eo deductis: lucum alii dictum volunt per antiphrasin, quod umbrâ opacus parum luceat. Alii contra sentiunt, lucum pro luce usurpatum. Unde Terentius: Cum primo luci ibo hinc. Ibi enim ignes sacrificii & religionis causa sæpe apparebant. Lucani unde dicti. Festus a lu-cero, dere, quod a Graeco λόφος, Gellius ab αὐλὸς lucum vult dictum: a luco obluctinare, id est, mentem errare, hallucinari, lucullus, lucellus, lucar, lucaris, collucare, compescere lucum.
units.tr: In the second chapter he treats of the veneration of groves: that groves were inaccessible, and that it was not lawful to pass through them even in necessity; that one might not hunt in them, nor kill their animals, except for the sake of sacrifice and of the gods themselves; that in some groves the animals were very tame; and that in groves not only men but also animals gave birth. In the third chapter he asks whence the word lucus comes, and what words are derived from it. Some hold that lucus is so called by antiphrasis, because it is shady with foliage and scarcely lets in light. Others, on the contrary, think that lucus was used for lux, light. Hence Terence: "I shall go from here at first light (cum primo luci)". For fires of sacrifice and religion often appeared there. Whence Lucani are named. Festus derives it from lucere, to shine; Gellius holds that lucus is named from the Greek aulos; from luco comes obluctinare, that is, to lead the mind astray, to hallucinate; also lucullus, lucellus, lucar, lucaris, collucare, and to hold back the grove.

units.la: Capite quarto, a luco Lucina dicta: Lucus, lupercal dictus Romae: sylva densa constans Pani Deo Arcadiae sacra: luceres tertiae tribus homines, & nonnulla alia loca & oppida a luco denominata.
units.tr: In the fourth chapter, Lucina is so named from the grove; the Lupercal at Rome is named from a grove; a dense wood sacred to the god Pan in Arcadia; the Luceres, the third tribe of men, and several other places and towns named from a grove.

units.la: Quinto capite, Heroibus & praeclaris viris Veteres dicasse lucos. Sexto, Luci aliquot absque Numinum appellatione: palmetum continuum, in Arabiae aquis abundans: lucus sacer apud Senorias, teste Ammiano Marcellino, quem nemo nisi vinctus ingredi poterat. Quod si forte prolapsus corruisset, extollis ei minime licebat, verum per humum reptare conveniebat. Capite septimo, de poena & vindicta eorum, qui lucos violarunt, divina & humana; quae quidem capitalis constitutio. Nam violatoris caput expiandum erat, ideo gravissima, auctore Pompeio. Cajo Gabinio Cicero in oratione de provincia consul. lucorum Graeciae violationem exprobrat. Capite octavo, Deus lucorum Gentilium religionem exsecutus est, ac de poena eorum, qui eos coluerunt, ac venerati sunt. Nono, de lucis Iovi sacris. Decimo, de lucis Iunoni sacris. Undecimo de lucis, Apollini dicatis. Duodecimo, de luco Daphnes. Decimotertio, de lucis Minervae, Isidi, Latonae, Cybelae, Ofyridi & Aesculapio dicatis. Decimoquarto, de lucis Dianae sacris. Decimoquinto, de luco Aricino, omnium maximo, Dianae de voto: & adagio, Multi Momi Aricinae. Decimosexto, de luco Camenarum sive Musarum. Decimoseptimo, de lucis Vulcano, Veneri, Cupidini, Martii, Bellonae, Libero Patri, Pani & Sylvano dicatis. Decimooctavo, de lucis Neptuno dicatis. Decimonono, de lucis Cereri, Proserpinae, Plutoni, Vestae, Castori & Polluci dicatis. Vigesimo de lucis Feronia, a ferendis arboribus dicta, Alburneae fontium praesidi, Maricae (quam Cicero volunt fuisse) Laverna Deae furum (qui Lavernienses olim, teste Festo, appellari) Bellonae, Furinae, Suadelae dicatis. Vigesimo primo, de lucis aliquot Dis dicatis: ubi & de Dis meis iovis, id est, placidis, quibus nocturna sacrificia fiebant, &c.
units.tr: In the fifth chapter, the ancients dedicated groves to heroes and illustrious men. In the sixth, some groves are named without reference to any god: a continuous palm grove abounding in waters in Arabia; a sacred grove among the Senorians, according to Ammianus Marcellinus, which no one could enter unless bound; and if anyone chanced to fall and collapse there, it was not lawful for him to rise, but he had to crawl along the ground. In the seventh chapter, on the divine and human punishment and vengeance against those who violated groves, which indeed was a capital offence. For the violator's head had to be expiated, and therefore the penalty was most severe, according to Pompey. Cicero, in his speech on the provinces against Gabinius the consul, reproaches him for the violation of the groves of Greece. In the eighth chapter, Curtius pursued the religion of Gentile groves, and the punishment of those who worshipped and revered them. Ninth, on groves sacred to Jupiter. Tenth, on groves sacred to Juno. Eleventh, on groves dedicated to Apollo. Twelfth, on the grove of Daphne. Thirteenth, on the groves dedicated to Minerva, Isis, Latona, Cybele, Osiris and Aesculapius. Fourteenth, on the sacred groves of Diana. Fifteenth, on the grove at Aricia, the greatest of all, of Diana, from a vow; and on the proverb "many Momi of Aricia". Sixteenth, on the grove of the Camenae or Muses. Seventeenth, on the groves dedicated to Vulcan, Venus, Cupid, Mars, Bellona, Liber Pater, Pan and Silvanus. Eighteenth, on the groves dedicated to Neptune. Nineteenth, on the groves dedicated to Ceres, Proserpina, Pluto, Vesta, Castor and Pollux. Twentieth, on the groves dedicated to Feronia, named from bearing (ferre) fruit trees; to Albunea, guardian of springs; to Marica, whom Cicero holds to have existed; to Laverna, goddess of thieves (who, according to Festus, were formerly called Lavernienses); to Bellona, Furina and Suada. Twenty-first, on several groves dedicated to the gods; and there, on the gods called "my Jupiters", that is, the gentle ones, to whom nocturnal sacrifices were made, and so on.

units.la: Atque haec quidem operaepretium omnino duxi opusculo huic meo inferre, tanquam ei valde accommodata. Et sic quidem ab igne sacrificiali progressi sumus ad ligna, tanquam ignis pabula: a lignis ad arbores: ab arboribus denique ad lucos atque memora sacra, quae fuerunt loca, arboribus consita, Dis dicata.
units.tr: This I have thought wholly worth inserting in this little work of mine, as being very well suited to it. And so we have progressed from the sacrificial fire to the wood, as the fuel of the fire; from wood to trees; and finally from trees to the groves and sacred woods, which were places planted with trees and dedicated to the gods.

units.la: Nunc persequamur reliqua, quae ad ignem hunc sacrificialem pertinent, nempe usum & effectus ignis sacri ejus. Usus ejus fere quintuplex fuit. Primum, ut illo victimarum carnes, necnon flores, omnisque generis fruges atq; fructus, atq; etiam alia, in eum conjecta, concremarentur, Diis, quasi gratis, munera quaedam dona atq; munera offerrentur ac consecrentur.
units.tr: Now let us go on to the rest of what concerns this sacrificial fire, namely its use and its effects. Its uses were roughly five. First, the flesh of the victims, along with flowers, fruits and grain of every kind, and other things too, were thrown into it and burned, so that gifts and offerings were presented and dedicated to the gods, as if they were gifts.

units.la: Secundo, ut nidores inde atq; odores cum suavi, tum etiam mali olentes excitarentur, quibus Deos suos mirifice delectari, atq; ita leniri atq; placari posse arbitrabantur.
units.tr: Second, the fire gave off smoke and smells, both pleasant and foul, by which they believed their gods were wonderfully delighted, and so could be soothed and appeased.

units.la: Tertio igne illo ad carnes, earumq; partes, exta ad coquenda et assanda vero potissimum utebantur, quae postea vel Diis reddebantur, vel sacerdotibus & iis, qui ea obtulerant, dabantur, quo iisdem referrentur.
units.tr: Third, with that fire they cooked and roasted the flesh and its parts, and especially the entrails. These were afterwards either given back to the gods or handed to the priests and to those who had offered them, so that they might be returned to the same.

units.la: Quarto igne illo se purgari omnia purgari atq; lustrari credebant, cum igni vim ἁγνιστικὴν καὶ καθαρτικὴν id est, sanctificandi, lustrandi atq; purgandi Veteres tribuerint, unde etiam hominum cadaveria igne volunt olim fuisse consumata: de quo vide plura apud Eustathium Iliad. α. & Pierium in Hieroglyphicis, cujus haec sunt verba: Ignis aut, ut nostri veteres tradidere, purgat, aqua expiat, lustratq. Hinc ille Plantinus iocus in Aulularia: Quid impurato, quamquam Vulcano flades, —Coena ne caussa aut mercedis gratia. Nos nostras aedes possulas comburere?
units.tr: Fourth, they believed that by that fire all things were purified and cleansed, since the ancients ascribed to fire the power [ἁγνιστικὴν καὶ καθαρτικὴν] of sanctifying, cleansing and purging. This is why they wished human corpses to have been consumed by fire in former times. On this see more in Eustathius on the Iliad, book 1, and in Pierius's Hieroglyphics, whose words are these: "Fire, as our ancestors handed down, purifies; water expiates and cleanses." Hence that jest of Plautus in the Aulularia: "Why should I, though you blow on the fire of Vulcan for an unwashed man, burn my own house, not for the sake of a dinner or a wage?"

units.la: Et apud Lysophronem legas Thetin indignatur, se Deammortali Peleo in matrimonium collocatam, filios quotquot oriebantur in ignem excipiendos tonsicere solitare, quod ita rebatur mortalitatem exuri & quod immortale esset purgatum conservari, veluti aurum aere confusum ignis ope purgatur, postea quam quidquid admixtum erat erit, infumum & Scoriam verterit. Atq; ita sex jam filios abfumserat, donec ad Achillem venturn, quem pater superveniens ab igne exemit Chironiq. curandum commendavit.
units.tr: And in Lycophron you may read that Thetis was indignant that she, having been married to the mortal Peleus, had been in the habit of destroying whatever sons she bore by putting them into the fire. She reasoned that this burned away their mortality and kept what was immortal purified, just as gold mixed with bronze is purified by fire, once whatever was mixed in has turned to dross and slag. So she had already destroyed six sons, until Achilles came; his father, arriving in time, snatched him from the fire and entrusted him to Chiron to be raised.

units.la: Quintus usus fuit μαντικῆς, id est, divinatorius. Nam divinatio quae dapet ignem illum sacrificialem fiebat, quae a Graecis πυρομαντεία, et πυρομαντεία fuit appellata; a Latinis verò Ignisficium: cujus in ventorem primum & auctorem Plinius facit Amphiaraum libro sepiimo, capite quinquagesimo sexto. Is qui per ignē divinabat πυρομαντεῖᾳ & πυρομαντεῖα fuit dictus.
units.tr: The fifth use was for divination (μαντικῆς). For the divination that was carried out by means of that sacrificial fire was called by the Greeks pyromanteia (πυρομαντεία), and by the Latins ignisficium. Pliny makes Amphiaraus its first inventor and author, in book 7, chapter 56. One who divined by fire was called pyromantis (πυρομάντις) and pyromanteius.

units.la: Hunc usum Apollonius uoster in sacrificii Argonautici explicatione his verbis expressit, libationes prius, id est effusionis vini facta mentione super ignem: —γύθει δ' ὁ σίλας Ϸπνύμξω ἰδ μων Πλείστοι λαμπρόμενοι ὑψιον ἐπεὶ τοῖς λεγόν Πορφυρέως ἰλίκεσιν ἐκείσωμον αἰσωσι Αὐτ' δ' Ατπλησιος νοὸν ἰκαρτος λυτοὶ ὁ Hoc est, Idmon autem cum admiratione conspicatus Vndiq; insignem ex sacrificiis fulgorem Purpureas circumgyrationibus, & auspicati ominis emicantem E'uestigio Apollinis mentem aperuit.
units.tr: Our Apollonius expressed this use in his account of the Argonautic sacrifice, mentioning first the libations, that is, the pouring out of wine over the fire. Idmon, seeing with wonder the remarkable brightness rising from the sacrifices on every side, purple in its curling wreaths and shining with an auspicious omen, straightway revealed the mind of Apollo.

units.la: Vbi Scholiastes ἐ πορφυρίας ἰλίκεσι interpretatur ἐ τὸ χρὴ τῶν συγγροφῶς, ἐ ἐ πυρρὸς κίων πάλαι, ᾧ ἰλίκεσι οἷον πρὸ πορφυρίζουσαι, id est, purpureis fumi circulo volutionibus, sive cum ignis circumgyrationibus & circuvolutionibus, quasi purpureas, & boni ominis. Illius autem Scholiastes Scholiastes: id est, vaticinationis haec summa fuit. Sibi quidem mortem, quam jam antea ex augurin quibusdam intellexerit: socin vero reditum per multos varios, casus atque discrimina flammae ust atque sacrificio portendi.
units.tr: There the scholiast explains "purple in its curling wreaths" as "the swirling of smoke, purple and reddish, as it rose in circles, a good omen." The gist of this prophecy was that death, which he had already perceived from certain signs of birds, was portended for himself, but for the others a return, after many varied chances and dangers, was portended by the flame and the sacrifice.

units.la: Hujusce autem πυρομαντείας, id est, divinationis per ignem, rationem in genere Pencetus, libro illo suo de Divinatione veré di vino, his verbis exprimit: In sacrificiis igitur, inquit, si admota flamma victimas flatim corriperet, & diffusa repente totas occuparet ac consumeret: Si tranquilla, pura, perspicua, & nitida, nullis infecta coloribus allenus, aut nigro rutilo ve, aut pallido, nec permixta, vel sordibus, vel caligine fumi ve, junctu, strepitu, & fine egestione asq; ejaculatione favillarum turbulentia & crepitante recto ductu, turbinatę pyramidis inflar attolleretur & insurgeret: sic, non nisi tota victima depasta atq; exusta moreretur: placide Numen bostiam acceptare ac completi, annuere, quae requirebantur, conjiciebant.
units.tr: Pencetus, in his book On the True Divination, sets out the method of divination by fire, that is, pyromanteia, in general, in these words: "In sacrifices, then," he says, "if the flame, once applied, at once seized the victims and, spreading suddenly, wholly took hold of them and consumed them; if it was calm, clear, transparent and bright, not tinged with any colour at all, neither black, nor red, nor pale, nor mixed with filth or the murkiness of smoke; if it rose and soared straight up, in the shape of a whirling pyramid, without noise, without spitting out or flinging sparks, the victim being wholly eaten and burnt up, then they supposed that the god accepted the victim gently and nodded assent to what was asked."

units.la: Si tronta, multo vix excitari flatu possit, & cum exarsisset, non coiret, sed finderetur, atq; in hiatum dehisceret, nec in totam subito spargeretur ac penetraret victimam, sed viciniora sensim, veluti serpens, lamberet atq; ustularet: nec recto ductu viteretur sursum, sed in vertigines gyrosq; convoluta, atram secum & densam veheret caliginem, aut reperet dtorfum, qui dilaberetur ad latera, aulacienae nasceretur specie: sq; aut ventis disploderetur, aut restingueretur pluviis aut in solitum crepitaret, & circumquaq; multum eruditaret ad dextrum favillarum, aut si pallaret plus nimio, vel nigricaret, aut evanescerat ponte, priusquam tota conflagrasset victima aut si intacta aliqua partes remanerent & integra: lapsi infestiq; Numinis, & sacrificium respuentis, omen esse suspicabantur. Cognata huic erat χαπνομαντεία, quae notabat & scrutabatur fumos, quas vertigines facerent, quantumq; se attollerent, & quo motu, recto ne an obliquo, vel in orbes consorto aut complicato, agglomerationem quaedam in rotulas spiras & quo redolerat nidore, aliaone, an eo, qui ex carnibus usti effumaret.
units.tr: "If, on the other hand, the flame could scarcely be kindled even with much blowing, and once it had caught fire it did not gather itself together but split and gaped open, and did not spread at once through the whole victim and pierce it, but licked and scorched the nearer parts slowly, like a serpent; if it did not rise straight up but twisted in eddies and coils, carrying with it a black and dense darkness, or went down and slid to the sides, looking like a sort of shadow; if it was torn apart by the winds, or put out by rain, or crackled on as usual, and threw off much spark-dust on every side; or if it turned too pale or too black, or vanished, before the whole victim had been burned up; or if any parts remained untouched and whole, they suspected an omen of a god fallen away and hostile, refusing the sacrifice." Akin to this was kapnomanteia (χαπνομαντεία), which noted and examined the smoke: what whirls it made, how high it rose, and by what motion, whether straight or sideways, or turned and folded into circles; whether it gathered into little coils and spirals, and what smell it gave off, whether this or that, or the smell of flesh burnt.

units.la: Meminit τῆς πυρομαντείας Statius: Vincatur pietas, ponte ea altaria virgo, Quaramus superos: facit illa, acie, sagaci, Sanguineos flammarum apices, genitumq; per auras Ignem, & clara tamen medie fastigia lucis, Oria ducet, tunc in speciem serpentis inanem, Ancipiti gyro volui frango, rubore:
units.tr: Statius also mentions pyromanteia: "Let piety prevail: let the maiden sacrifice at these altars; let us seek the gods above. With keen sight she will perceive the blood-red tongues of flame, and the fire born in the air, and the bright summits of the light in the midst; then she will bring forth an empty image of a serpent, a fiery shape, twisting in a double coil."

units.la: Hæ Pencetus: quibus adde illa Pierii in Hieroglyphicis: Aruspices enim, inquit, igne in hujus-modi modi sæpe portentum accepere. Cujus non ignarus disciplinæ Virgilius de Lavinia, cujus caussa bellum adeò funestum excitandum erat, ita cecinit: Pretereà castis adolet dum altaria flammis Et juxta genitorem adstat Lavinia virgo, Visa (nefas) longis comprendere crinibus ignem, Atq; omnem ornatum flammâ crepitante cremari Regalesq; accensa comas, accensa coronam Insignem gemmis, tum fumida lumina fulvo Involvi ac totis Vulcanum spargere tectis. Id vero horrendum, ac visu mirabile ferri: Namq; fore illustrem famâ, fatisq; canebant Ipsam, sed populo magnum portendere bellum.
units.tr: So far Pencetus. To these add that passage of Pierius in the Hieroglyphics: "Haruspices," he says, "often received a portent from fire of this kind." Virgil, who was not unaware of this art, sang thus of Lavinia, for whose sake so deadly a war had to be stirred up: "Meanwhile, as she kindles the altars with pure flames, and the maiden Lavinia stands beside her father, she was seen (a horror!) to catch the fire in her long hair, and all her adornment to burn with crackling flame, and her royal locks and the crown set with jewels to blaze; then a smoky radiance wrapped her eyes in yellow light and scattered Vulcan through the whole house. This was thought a dreadful thing, and marvellous to see. For they foretold that she herself would be famous and renowned for her fates, but that she portended a great war for the people."

units.la: Nunc accedamus ad ea, quæ, ut cujus vis ingenere ignis: ita ignium horum sacrorum & sacrificialium fuerunt effecta. Hæc sunt fumi, carbones, prunæ, cineres, quæ & ipsa non secus atq; ignes sacra fuerunt habita & mystica.
units.tr: Now let us come to the effects of these sacred and sacrificial fires, which, just as the nature of fire is what it is, were also what they were. These are smoke, coals, embers and ashes, which were themselves regarded as sacred and mystical no less than the fires.

units.la: Quantum ad fumum attinet; est vapor niger ex igni exhalans, vel ignea exhalatio: sic Latinè a fui vo colore dictus, Græcè καπνὸς proprie vapor est e lignis, quasi καίοντα πῦρ, id est, ardens flatus, ὑγρὸς ab aqua, αὐλαῖα a lapidibus, λιγνὶς ab oleo vel cera, κρίσσα a carnibus. Inde καπνίζειν sæpe apud Homerum, Eustathio interprete, τὸ πῦρ ἀξιῶσι δὲ ἡ Θυσία ἡ ἀπὸ ὡς ἐν ...
units.tr: As for smoke: it is a dark vapour given off by fire, or a fiery exhalation. It is called in Latin fumus from its colour (fuscus). In Greek kapnos (καπνὸς) is properly a vapour from wood, as if from kaiont pyr (καίοντα πῦρ), that is, burning breath; hygros (ὑγρὸς) from water; aulaia (αὐλαῖα) from stones; lignis (λιγνὶς) from oil or wax; krissa (κρίσσα) from flesh. Hence kapnizein (καπνίζειν) is often used by Homer, as Eustathius explains, of the fire...

units.la: Germanicè fumus Rauch dicitur, ab Hebræo רוח Rúach, id est, Spiritus, sive רוח Reach, id est, spiratio, odor fragrantia, quæ excitatur motu & agitatione: unde etiam nostrum Riechen, quomod. ...
units.tr: In German smoke is called Rauch, from the Hebrew ruach (רוח), that is, spirit, or reach (רוח), that is, breath, a fragrance or odour which is stirred up by motion and agitation; whence also our riechen (to smell), and so on.
Smoke, going forth, and lightning ...

units.la: Hinc καπνομαντεία, magia, quæ ex fumo futura prævidet, & καπνομάντις, qui parvi im ex sumo, quos globos volveret, partim ex flamma, si lucidior, aut obtusior, & quæ specie foret, observabat. Ovidius libro quarto de Ponto: Surgat ad hanc vocem plenam pius ignis ad aram Detq; bonum voto lucidus omen apex.
units.tr: Hence kapnomanteia is the magic which foresees the future from smoke, and kapnomantis is one who observed, from the smoke, the globes it rolled into, partly from the flame, whether it was brighter or duller, and what shape it took. Ovid, in book 4 of the Epistulae ex Ponto: "At this voice the devout fire rises up at the altar, and the bright tip of the flame gives a good omen to the prayer."

units.la: Lucidus apex, id est, ipse ignis clarus & purus in apice & cacumine. Id enim maximè observabant. Hoc ignis augurium etiam uxori Cimonis contigisse legimus. Nam cum post peractum sacrificium libare vellet, in cinere visa est flamma, quæ eodem anno Consulem futurum offendit ejus maritum, cujus rei etiam Maro non ignarus ita cecinit: Aspice corripuit tremulis altaria flammis Sponte sua, dictum ferre moror, cinis ipse, bonum sit.
