units.tr: The bright tip means the fire itself, clear and pure at the top and summit of the flame, for this they observed above all. We read that this fire-omen also happened to the wife of Cimon. When, after the sacrifice was finished, she wished to pour a libation, a flame was seen in the ashes, which foretold that her husband would be consul in that same year. Maro, who was not ignorant of this, sang of it thus: "Look, the altars caught fire with trembling flames of their own accord. I hesitate to speak of it; let the ash itself say whether it is a good sign."

units.la: Ex earum item rerum, quæ injiciebantur, vario motu, sono acrepitu tatitinia captabant, ut supra dictum de igne.
units.tr: By the varied movement of the things thrown in, and by their sound and crackling, they likewise took omens, as was said above concerning fire.

units.la: Sed & fumorum istorum sacrificialium Hieremias quoque meminit in illa sua epistola ad Iu-daeos, ubi simulacrorum ipsorum facies dicit esse nigras propter fumos, qui in illorum templis af-fidue fieri soleant.
units.tr: Jeremiah also mentions these sacrificial smokes in his letter to the Jews, where he says that the faces of the images themselves are black from the smoke which was constantly made in their temples. ## Thus much on smoke.

units.la: Quin & de carbonibus, prunis & cineribus, tanquam ignis sacrificialis effectus hic quaedam dicenda. At carbo quidem & pruna, ut volunt Grammatici, sic differunt, quemadmodum favilla & cinis, videlicet quod pruna proprie sit carbo virens & candens, Graece Σπονδύλιον a perurendo (unde etiam pruina, meteoron exurens, & urtim herbas urens dicta) Carbo autem pruna explicatur, Graece à βεγζ, Germanice Kol: forsan a calore, sive colore, appellata. De carbonum utilitate, deleCtu, ex qua materie optimi fiunt carbones, de dendrophoris, qui arbores caedunt atque torrent, vide Benedictum Curtium libro decimo octavo, capite decimoseptimo. Carbones, inquit Plinius, libro trigesimo tertio, capite quinto, major vsus est, sterumque flagranti. Ibidem de carbonum vi & efficacia in medicinis multe disserit. Quae autem faciendi carbones sit ratio, & quae apta materia, idem agit libro decimosexto, capite septimo. Idem quod magis ad institutum nostrum pertinet, libro eodem, capite sexto, de quoque, inquit, inter reliqua neglecta religionis est, quod emortuo carbone sacrificatur.
units.tr: Something must also be said here about coals, embers and ashes as products of the sacrificial fire. The grammarians hold that coal and ember differ as ashes and cinders do: an ember is properly a coal that is glowing and red-hot, called in Greek σπονδύλιον, from burning (whence also pruina, a meteor that burns, and urtim, meaning burning herbs). Coal, however, is explained as derived from the Hebrew, and in German it is Kol, perhaps named from its heat or colour. On the usefulness of coal, from what material the best coals are made, and on the dendrophori who cut and roast trees, see Curtius, book 18, chapter 17. "Coals," says Pliny in book 33, chapter 5, "were found to have a greater use, and again when blazing." In the same place he discusses at length the power and efficacy of coal in medicines. What method of making coal is used, and what material is suitable, he treats in book 16, chapter 7. What bears more directly on our purpose is in the same book, chapter 6: "Moreover," he says, "among the other neglected parts of religion is this, that sacrifice is made with a dead coal."

units.la: Cinis porro Latine vel abigris, cujus est effectus, vel a cadendo, quod a re combusta cadat post humoris consumtionem: vel a Graeco xonis, quae vox & pulveres & cinerem significat, con-verso videlicet o in i, videtur derivari: Germanicum vero ⁊ Eschen, ut supra dixi, vel ab ᴠᴥ, Esch, igne, vel aγ, Dxschan, ablato Daleth, quae vox & cinerem & pinguedinem significat. Ide Graece etiam τεφρα est dictus a τέφω, id est, urere, incendere: sive τεφέω, quod & combustere & fumare sive fumigare significat. Cineres enim nihil sunt aliud quam pulveres, in quos materia adusta redigitur, sive lignorum, aliarumve rerum ustarum reliquiae. Inde etiam forsan τέφρα, id est, sepulchrum dictum, quod antiquitus mortuorum corpora cremari & in cineres redigeremus erat; unde vox cinerū per metonymiam saepe pro morte accipitur & mortalis conditione. Martialis Epigrammate trigesimo:
units.tr: Ash in Latin (cinis) is derived either from abigris, whose effect it is, or from cadere, to fall, because it falls from the burnt thing once its moisture is consumed; or it seems to come from the Greek κόνις, a word meaning both dust and ash, with the o changed into i. The German Eschen, as I said above, comes either from Esch, fire, or from the word Dschan, with the Daleth removed, which means both ash and fat. In Greek too, τέφρα is so called from τέφω, that is, to burn or set on fire, or from τεφέω, which means both to burn and to smoke or fumigate. For ashes are nothing other than the dust into which burnt matter is reduced, whether the remains of wood or of other burnt things. Hence τέφρα, meaning a tomb, is perhaps also so called, because it was once the custom to cremate the bodies of the dead and reduce them to ashes. For this reason the word cinis is often taken by metonymy for death and the mortal condition. Martial, in Epigram thirty:
Few poets have a name after their ashes.

units.la: Id est, post mortem. Elegans illud: τύμβος τάφος, id est, superbiae sepulchrum est finitimum.
units.tr: That is, after death. That elegant saying, "a tomb is the grave of pride," is closely related.

units.la: Esti vero cinerum & color atque faciei est vilis atque sordida, & sapor acerbus & amarus: tamen illorum maximus est in vita humana usus. Cinis enim vestium sordes abstergit, ignem regit atque fovet, carnium humores consumit. Sic, ut Conflantinus, & alii rerum phythearum perlittestantur, argentum vivum cum cinere salicis corpus repurgat atque mundat a pediculis. Eandem vim, ut idem testatur, habet cinis plumbi usti, mixtus cum oleo & aceto. Cinis ignem confervat atque tuetur, ne extinguatur. Unde Isidorus ait, Cinerem juniperi ignem Graecum reddere inextinguibilem. Idem acredine sua conjumit carnis humores. Is pellibus appositus, facit quidem pilos excidere, ac pelles ipsas conservat a corruptione & foetore. De cinerum usu quoque plura noscere cupit, legas (qui vult) Plinium libro decimo septimo, capite novo. At de cinerum usu apud Hebraeos vide Levitici caput sextum, Numerorum decimum nonum, & epistolae ad Hebraeos nonae. Sed apud Gentiles quoque cum corporum concrematorum cineres, tum etiam hostiarum quarumvis sacri habebantur.
units.tr: Although ashes are cheap and filthy in colour and appearance, and bitter and harsh in taste, their use in human life is nonetheless very great. Ash cleanses the dirt from clothes, governs and fosters fire, and consumes the moisture of flesh. Thus Constantinus and others who write about natural things attest that quicksilver with ash of willow cleanses and purifies the body from lice. The same power, as the same author testifies, belongs to the ash of burnt lead mixed with oil and vinegar. Ash preserves and guards fire so that it is not extinguished. Hence Isidore says that the ash of juniper makes Greek fire inextinguishable. Ash also consumes the moisture of flesh by its sharpness. Applied to skins, it makes the hair fall out and preserves the skins from corruption and stench. Whoever wishes to know more about the use of ashes may read Pliny, book 17, in the ninth chapter. On the use of ashes among the Hebrews see Leviticus chapter 6, Numbers chapter 19, and Hebrews chapter 9. Among the Gentiles, however, both the ashes of burnt bodies and those of any sacrificial victims were held sacred.

units.la: Caeterum ignus sacri & sacrificialis ut accendendi & fovendi, ita ejusdem exstinguendi vel exstinctis, integrandi rursus, accendedi magna apud Gentiles fuit religio, seu, ut verius dicam, superstitio. Hinc in Hieroglyphicis Pierius: Haec fuit, inquit, apud veteres super igne religio, ut eum porro extinguere nefas esset, quem potius per se languentem deficere sinebant. Hoc volu-ille significari, ne vitam animam exturbaremus, mortem nobis ipsis consciscentes. Idem: Ignis primas inter insignia Augustalia obtinebat. Hinc cautum erat lege, ne cui prorsus ignem exstinguere licetret: nec quidem alimenta adjiciebant, ne fructum nutriretur. Exstinctum porro nulli ex mulieribus intueri licebat. Volebant ita ignem simulacrum esse mortis, quae natura fieret. Porro de igne Vestalis, si forsan exstinctus esset, instaurari rursus, accendedi modo scripsit Plutarchus in vita Numae Pompilii. Ibidem multa reperies de virginibus Vestalibus: de quibus legere licebit etiam Dionysium. rystum Halicarnasseum, libro secundo. Fuit autem ignis ille Vestalis, quem tanta diligentia Romanae virgines nutriebant, sublimitoris diuturnaeque vitae symbolum, ut testatur Pierius in Hieroglyphicis libro quadragesimo sexto. Item: Incer portenta Vrbis periturae praesagium habebatur, si casu aliquo ignis ille exstingueretur. Hinc Camillus ad Quirites ait: Quid de acerrimo Vestae ignibus, signosque, quod Imperii pignus custodia ejus templi tenetur, loquar? Et Maro: Aeternumq; adyco esset penetralibus ignem.
units.tr: The religious observance of the sacred and sacrificial fire, both in kindling and tending it, and likewise in extinguishing it, or restoring it once extinguished, and kindling it again, was great among the Gentiles, or, to speak more truly, it was superstition. Hence Pierius, in his Hieroglyphics, says: "This was the ancients' religion concerning fire: it was wrong to extinguish it further, rather they let it die out when it languished of itself." This, he says, was meant to signify that we should not drive out life and soul, bringing death upon ourselves. Again Pierius: "Fire held first place among the Augustal insignia. Hence it was prohibited by law that anyone at all should extinguish fire, nor did they add fuel to it. No woman was permitted to look upon an extinguished fire. They wished fire to be an image of death, which comes by nature." Plutarch, in the life of Numa Pompilius, wrote that if the Vestal fire happened to go out, it was restored again simply by kindling it anew. In the same place you will find much about the Vestal virgins, and about them one may also read Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 2. That Vestal fire, which the Roman virgins tended with such diligence, was a symbol of a lofty and long-lasting life, as Pierius testifies in Hieroglyphics book 46. Again: among the portents of the doomed city, it was held a presage if by some chance that fire went out. Hence Camillus says to the Quirites: "What shall I say of the most sacred fires of Vesta, and of the signs? Her temple's keeping is held to be the pledge of empire." And Maro: "and the eternal fire in the innermost shrines."

units.la: Postremo ab ignis sacrificialis explicatione non aliena, sed potius perquis-accomodata videtur haec de certorum, lampadum, facum, lucernarum & candelabrorum apud Gentiles sacro usu, cujus passim apud autores profanos fit mentio. Faces Antiqui dicebant, inquit Festus, ut sides. Facem, inquit idem, novae nuptae in nuptiis praeferebant in honorem Cererus & aqua aspergebantur, sive uccasta purisque ad virum veniret: sive, ut ignem & aquam cum viro communicaret. Idem: Patrimi & matrimi pueri tres adhibebantur in nuptiis: Vnus, qui facem praeferret ex spina (sive pinu) alba, quia noctu nubebant: duo, qui tenebant nubentem. De hoc autem faces quinque per totidem pueros novae nuptae praeferendi more ejusque caussa, vide Plutarchum in quaestionibus Romanis & Pierium in Hieroglyphicis. De facum accensarum ludo Idibus Augusti in honorem Dianae vide Gyraldum & Curtium libro quarto Horcorum capite decimo quinto. Gyraldus tradit, eo die Romanos facibus accensis ab urbe in nemus Aricinum discurrisse, in quo nemore Dianae Nemorensis appellatae celebre templum fuerit. Curtii verba haec sunt: Cum autem Dianae Nemoralis sacrum inslaret, ab urbe in nemus Aricinum, accensis facibus discurrebatur. Propertius in secundo: Cum videt accensis devotam currere tedis In nemus, & Triviae Numina ferre Deae.
units.tr: Finally, it seems not out of place, but rather very fitting to the explanation of the sacrificial fire, to add here what is said about the sacred use among the Gentiles of certain torches, lamps, lights and candelabra, which is mentioned everywhere in profane authors. The ancients, says Festus, called torches faces. The new bride, he says, carried a torch in the wedding in honour of Ceres, and they were sprinkled with water, so that she came to her husband chaste and pure, or so that she might share fire and water with her husband. Festus again: three boys, patrimi and matrimi, were used at weddings. One carried a torch of white thorn (or pine), because they married at night, and two held the bride. On the custom of carrying five torches before the new bride, borne by as many boys, and its reason, see Plutarch in the Roman Questions and Pierius in the Hieroglyphics. On the game of lit torches on the Ides of August in honour of Diana, see Giraldus and Curtius, book 4, chapter 15. Giraldus relates that on that day the Romans ran with lit torches from the city into the Aricine grove, in which grove stood the famous temple of Diana called Nemorensis. Curtius's words are these: "When the sacred rite of Diana of the grove was being observed, they ran from the city to the Aricine grove with torches lit." Propertius, in book 2: "When she sees the devoted girl running into the grove with lit torches, and bearing the divinity of the goddess Trivia."

units.la: Ovidius in Fasti: Saepe potens voti frontem redimita coronis Foemina, lucentes portat ab urbe faces,
units.tr: Ovid, in the Fasti: "Often a woman, mighty in her vow, her brow crowned with garlands, carries lit torches from the city."

units.la: Hoc autem sacrificium simul atque dedicationem expressis Statius in sylui: Iamque dies aderat, cum Regibus alcum Firmat Aricinum Triviae nemus, & face multa Conscius Hippolytus splendet lacus.
units.tr: Statius, in the Silvae, expresses this sacrifice together with its dedication: "And now the day had come when, for the kings, the altar of the Aricine grove of Trivia is made firm, and the conscious Hippolytus shines over the lake with many torches."
Thus Curtius.

units.la: Fuit porro & in honorem Promethei lucernarum seu lampadum ludus, ab ipso Promotheo institutus, de quo Verderius sic scribit: Vt Numen (Prometheus) templo atque aris colui meruit, & quemadmodum Pausanias scribit, ei ara Athenis in Academia erat dicata, ad quam flatus temporibus homines confluebant, ubi, faces accendebant, quas gestantes versus civitatem currebant, serie quadam se sequentes: horum, qui accensam usque ad urbis ingressum conservassent, palmam ferebant: iis, qui praecedebant, si forti eorum faces fuissent inter currendum exstinctae, locum cedentibus illis, qui proximè sequebantur. Id boc etiam modo fieri solebat. Erat una tantum fax communis omnibus, quam currentes sibi mutuo tradebant; iis, qui ponè, in eorum locum, quierant ante, per successionem quandam subeuntibus. Sed hic ritus, si-ve ludos appellare placeat, non solum Promethei sacer erat (quanquam ab eo institutus legitur) sed in Vulcani quoq; ac Minervae cultum celebrabatur, neq; semper pedibus, sed interdum & equo currebant. Quare Adimantus apud Platonem, cum Socratem bortaretur, ne societatem quandam desereret, dicit, vesperi eam ludis equestribus interesse, mutuo sibi facem in Deae, boc est Minervae, honorem tradentibus. Herodotus cum Persicum morem narrat, quo celerrime nuntios mittebant (sicut etiam apud nos est in usu, cum aliquid per dispositos citatos, equos mittimus. Semper eum post aliquod decursum spacium in slathmis alii sunt in procinctu, qui alios currentes & ipsi continuando excipiant) dicit eos Graecorum consuetudinem imitari, cum currentes, facem quam Vulcano accensam gestant, per seriem sibi mutuo praebent. De his ludis quidam memoria prodiderunt,eos Promethei factum referre, cum igneme coelo sublatum in terras detulit: atque ideo ita ab eo institutos. Alii id ad humanae vitae cursum referunt: in quo,qui etate anteeunt, vitae lumine ius cedunt,qui pone sequuntur, ut est Platonis sententia, qui libro de Legibus bomines jussit inter se prolis grasia inire conjugia,ut vitam, quam a parentibus sunt mutuati, veluti ardentem facem,ipsi quoque apud filios ponant. Lucretius etiam de mortalium inter se successione loquens,sic inquit:
units.tr: There was also a game of lamps or torches in honour of Prometheus, instituted by Prometheus himself. Verderius writes of it thus: "Since the god Prometheus deserved to be worshipped with a temple and altars, as Pausanias writes, an altar was dedicated to him at Athens in the Academy. To it people flocked at certain times, and there they lit torches, which they carried while running back towards the city in a line, one following another. Those who kept their torch alight until they entered the city carried off the palm. Those in front, if their torches had gone out in the running, yielded their place to those who came next. This was done in the following way: there was only one torch common to all, which the runners handed on to one another, and those behind, coming up in succession, took the place of those who had stopped before." But this rite, if one likes to call it a game, was not sacred to Prometheus alone, although it is read to have been instituted by him. It was also celebrated in the worship of Vulcan and Minerva, and they ran not only on foot but sometimes on horseback. Hence Adimantus in Plato, when urging Socrates not to desert a certain fellowship, says that in the evening they attend the equestrian games, passing the torch to one another in honour of the goddess, that is Minerva. Herodotus, when he describes the Persian custom of sending messages most swiftly (as among us too, when we send something by relays of horses posted at intervals, there are always men at the stations ready to receive those running and to carry on in turn), says that they imitate the Greek custom, in which runners pass to one another in sequence the torch lit at Vulcan's altar. Some writers have recorded that these games refer to the deed of Prometheus, when he brought fire down from heaven to earth, and that they were therefore instituted by him. Others refer them to the course of human life, in which those who go first yield the light of life to those who follow. This is Plato's view, who in the book on the Laws ordered men to enter marriage for the sake of offspring, so that they might themselves pass on to their children, like a burning torch, the life they had received from their parents.

units.la: Et quasi cursores vitai lampada tradunt.
units.tr: Lucretius too, speaking of the succession of mortals among themselves, says: "And like runners they hand on the torch of life."

units.la: Haec Verderius: praeter quem legi possunt ad eodem ludo Aristophanis interpres in Ranis, Plato libro primo de Republica, Pausanias in Atticis,Herodosus in Vrania,Cicero in Rhetoricis ad Heren. Ad ludum illum ergo alludit Lucretius,ubi de animantibus agit, quae successione propagantur, vita per vices, ab alus in alia transfusa. Es Plato quidem libro sexto de Legibus,ubi animam lumini comparans cives ait oportere liberis generandis atque educandis operam dare,ut vitam, quam ipsi a Majoribus accepissent, vicissim quasi tedas ardentes posteris tradant.Cur Diis ofcilla et Saturno lampades dedicate, et in Saturnalibus praeter sigilla cereos missitare confuderint, egregie disserit idem Pierius libro ante citato, quadragesimo sexto, quem vide. Et de λαμπαδοχεία, id est, more ferendi faces in Promethets, Vulcanus et Panathenaicis sacris usitato, vide Erasmum in Chiliadibus. Inde et natum proverbium, Lampada tradere: et λαμπαδοδρομία, cursus,in quo faces seu lampades accensae manu gestabantur,certabantque, ouis primus ad scopum per veniret, non exstincta lampade: et λαμπαδηφορία, lampadum gestatio: et λαμπαδηφορεῖν lampadem gestare, lampadem gestantem cursu certare: λαμπαδοδρόμος Graece, qui lucernam gerit: λυχνοῦχος et λαμπαδοφόρος, idem: quem alio nomine διαδοῦχον, faciferum, tediferumque appellant a διαδοχή, faces praeferre. Sic λαμπαδοῦχοι Aristophanis interpres dixit, pro lampada tenentem cursu contendere.
units.tr: Thus Verderius. Besides him one may read about this same game the interpreter of Aristophanes on the Frogs, Plato in the first book of the Republic, Pausanias in the Attics, Herodotus in Urania, and Cicero in the Rhetoric to Herennius. Lucretius therefore alludes to that game where he treats of living creatures, which are propagated in succession, life passing from one to another in turn. Plato indeed, in the sixth book of the Laws, comparing the soul to a light, says that citizens ought to take care to beget and bring up children, so that they may in turn hand on to posterity, like burning torches, the life which they themselves received from their ancestors. Why lamps were dedicated to the gods Ops and Saturn, and why in the Saturnalia they threw candles along with little images, the same Pierius discusses excellently in the forty-sixth book cited above; see it there. On lampadochy, that is the custom of carrying torches, used in the rites of Prometheus, Vulcan and the Panathenaic sacrifices, see Erasmus in the Adages. Hence also the proverb "to hand on the torch" (lampada tradere). There is also lampadodromia [λαμπαδοδρομία], a race in which lit torches were carried in the hand, and the contestants strove to see who first reached the goal without his torch going out; lampadephoria [λαμπαδηφορία], the carrying of torches; lampadephorein [λαμπαδηφορεῖν], to carry a torch, to contend in a race carrying a lamp. In Greek, lampadodromos [λαμπαδοδρόμος] is one who carries a lamp; lychnouchos [λυχνοῦχος] and lampadophoros [λαμπαδοφόρος] mean the same; and they call him diadouchon [διαδοῦχον], torch-bearer and taper-bearer, from diadoche [διαδοχή], the bearing of torches in succession. So the interpreter of Aristophanes spoke of lampadouchoi, those who contend in a race holding a torch.

units.la: Lucernarum Apuleius meminit in descriptione pompae Isidis Aegyptiae: Magnus praeterea, inquit,utrimque, sexus numerus lucernas,tedas,cereos, et alio genere facis luminis sideri caelesium, stirpem propicitantes. Es paullo post: Quorum primus (scilicet antisfitum sacrorum et procorum) lucernam pramicantem porrigebat lumen non adeo nostris illis conspicilem,quae vesperisinas illuminare vi epulas, etc. In quae verba sic Beroaldus commentatur: Religionis Aegyptiae symbolum est lucerna, ut opinor pertinens ad Osyridis vestigationem, quem perditum cum lucerna quaerunt, mox in ventum magno gaudio prosequuntur, auctores Seneca, Lactantius, Augustinus et caeteri. Ob hoc videtur Seneca in libro de vita beata sic scripsisse: Cum laurum lintea senex et mediam lucernam de proferens exclamat, iratum aliquem Deorum concernitis et auditis. Apud nos hodie, in pompa sacrorum, Leroferarii conspiciuntur, ritu prope consimili atque Germano. Tersullianus denotat hunc ritum lucernarum solennium et improbat, inquiens: Cur die laeto nos laureis postes obumbramus,nec lucernis diem infi ingimus? Potest lucerna haec vide ri symbolum Solis, qui et Osyris dicitur,cujus hoc cunctia collustransur.
units.tr: Apuleius mentions lamps in his description of the procession of Egyptian Isis: "Moreover, on either side there was a great number of both sexes carrying lamps, torches, candles and other kinds of light-giving flames, propitiating the stars of heaven, the source of the race." And a little later: "The first of them (namely the chief priests of the rites and the attendants) held out a lamp shining forth, a light not so like those of ours which usually light our evening feasts," and so on. On these words Beroaldus comments thus: "The lamp is a symbol of the Egyptian religion, I think, pertaining to the search for Osiris, whom they seek when lost with a lamp, and soon afterwards they follow him with great joy as he is carried off into the wind. The authorities are Seneca, Lactantius, Augustine and others." For this reason Seneca seems to have written in his book On the Happy Life: "When an old man, bringing out laurel, linen cloths and a lamp in the midst, cries out that some god is angry, you all turn and listen." Among us today, in the processions of sacred rites, lamp-bearers are seen, in a rite nearly like the German one. Tertullian denotes this custom of solemn lamps and disapproves of it, asking: "Why on a happy day do we shade our doorposts with laurel, and do not illuminate the day with lamps?" This lamp may be seen as a symbol of the Sun, who is also called Osiris, by whom all things are illumined.

units.la: Praeterea autor est Herodotus, festivitatem solennem celebrari in Aegypto,cui nomen est, Accensio lucernarum, propterea quod noctu lusub dio per universam Aegyptium lucernas accendunt,imbutas sale et oleo plenas,cum multo illychno, quod tota nocte ardens perduret. Potest haec lucerna non solum esse symbolum inquisitionis Osyridis, verum etiam ad Vulcanum referri, quem in ventorem ignis primum in Aegypto regnasse sacerdotes affirmant. Lucernari apud eum dem Apuleium verbum vetus est, quod significat dispositis lucernus illuminare: Hinc illud: Tecta lucernantur florentia Numina fertis.
units.tr: Herodotus also records that a solemn festival is celebrated in Egypt called the Lighting of Lamps, because at night, under the open sky, throughout all Egypt they light lamps soaked in salt and full of oil, with a large wick which burns and lasts the whole night. This lamp may be understood not only as a symbol of the search for Osiris, but may also be referred to Vulcan, whom the priests affirm was the first to reign in Egypt, as the inventor of fire. The verb lucernari is an old word in the same Apuleius, meaning to light up with lamps set out; hence the line: "The flowery roofs are lit up with lamps, you bear the gods of the festival."

units.la: De more antiquo lucernas accensas diebus festis et in omni publica privatag; laetitia caseruulas suspendendi ad januas, ad fenestras (quae etiam lauro ornabantur) et ad arbores sacras vide Lipsium Electorum libro primo, capite tertio. Ibidem quoque docet, sacrificulos et vases lucernam ac laurum praeferre fuisse solitos,ut hoc festo quasi sacro ornatu augustiio: es se facerent, et lucernam solutam suspendi ad aedes lenonias, tanquam nor li lupanaris notam. Hac omnia Tertulliani, Senecae et Poetarum testimoniis confirmat et illustrat.
units.tr: On the ancient custom of lighting lamps on feast days and in all public and private rejoicing, and of hanging little lamps at doors, at windows (which were also decked with laurel), and on sacred trees, see Lipsius, Electorum book 1, chapter 3. There too he teaches that the little priests and the vessels were accustomed to carry lamps and laurel, so that by this festive, as it were sacred, adornment they might make the festival more august. He also teaches that a lamp was hung out at the houses of pimps as the mark of a brothel. He confirms and illustrates all this by the testimonies of Tertullian, Seneca and the poets.

units.la: Omnium porro istorum luminum et lucorum (Nam lux lucus etiam dicta propter ignes atque lumina, in iis perpetuo lucentia:) lampadum item, & facum, lucernarum, lychnorum, cereorum, tandelabrorum in templis Gentilium usus seu abusus potius, fuit fere quintuplex.
units.tr: Moreover, of all these lights and lamps (for lux is also called lucus, because of the fires and lights which shine perpetually in such places), the use, or rather the abuse, of lamps, torches, candles, lanterns, tapers and candelabra in the temples of the Gentiles was roughly fivefold.

units.la: Primus fuit naturalis; & quidem necessarius in illorum sacris noctumis, ad quae peragenda opus illis erat hujusmodi luminibus atque lucernis. His adde, quod cum quaedam sacra etiam interdiu in penitioribus & obscurioribus templorum suorum partibus facerent, luminibus hujusmodi indigebant.
units.tr: The first was natural, and indeed necessary, in their night rites, for which such lights and lamps were needed. Add to this that, since they performed some rites even by day in the more hidden and darker parts of their temples, they needed lights of this kind.

units.la: Secundus luminum lucernarumque usus fuit in a donatiuus, ut ita loquar, quod nimirum ut alia dona atque munera : sic luteruas quoque & candelabra magni pretii Dis suis, tanquam sua erga ipsos pietatis monumenta illoque placandi gratia dicabant: quas idcirco ante illorum simulacra collocare, suspendere, & accendere solebant. Id quod manefestum est, ut plurima alia ceremonia & exempla omittam, ex Baruchi, sive Hieremiae epistola ad Iudaeos, in qua B. chrysostomus idololatriam copiose describens haec quoque illis exprobat: Lucernas, inquit, illis (idolis seu simulacris) accendunt: & quidem plures: vel, ut alia exemplaria habent, plures, quam sibi ipsis, quarum nullam videre possunt. Sunt enim velut trabes in domo.
units.tr: The second use of lamps and candlesticks was, so to speak, as gifts. Just as they offered other gifts and presents, so they also dedicated lamps and candelabra of great price to their gods, as monuments of their piety towards them and to win their favour. Therefore they were accustomed to place them before the images, to hang them up and to light them. This is plain, to omit many other ceremonies and examples, from the Letter of Baruch, or Jeremiah, to the Jews, in which St Chrysostom, describing idolatry at length, also reproaches them with this: "They light lamps for them (the idols or images), and indeed many, or, as other copies have it, more than for themselves, though they can see none of them. For they are like beams in a house."

units.la: Tertius lucernarum & candelabrorum illorum usus speciebat ad ornatum: cum ista templorum religionis, sua magna existimarent esse ornamenta.
units.tr: The third use of these lamps and candelabra was for ornament, since they considered them great adornments of the worship of the temples.

units.la: Quartus illarum usus erat symbolicus & mysticus: cum illa ipsa interpretarentur varijs modis tenuissigna & symbola quaedam piectatis, religionis, puritatis, rerum sacrarum et divinarum, majestatis item suorum Deorum, & aeternitatis : maxime cum in basi alicujus simul icri essent positae. Apud Onirocritam lucernae ardens mulieris signum, lucubrationis erat signum.
units.tr: The fourth use of these lamps was symbolic and mystical. People interpreted the lamps in various ways as subtle signs and symbols of piety, religion, purity, of sacred and divine things, and likewise of the majesty of their gods and of eternity, especially when they were set together on the base of some statue. In Oneirocritus, a burning lamp was a sign of a woman, and a sign of late-night study.

units.la: Quintus usus erat μαντικός, quod ex iis, ut etiam ex multis aliis captabant augurla & cognitionem rerum futurarum. Verum, ut hoc postremo addam, hoc ipso lampadum lucernarumque in templis ante simulacra sua, vel in ipso meridie clarissimaque luce accensarum usu, significabant, se in tenebris maximis errorum & superstitionum versari maguamque animarum suarum prodabant tacitatem.
units.tr: The fifth use was mantic [μαντικός], since from these, as from many other things, they sought omens and knowledge of future events. To add this last point: by the very practice of lighting lamps and lanterns in temples before their images, or even at midday in the brightest light, they signified that they were living in the deepest darkness of error and superstition, and they revealed the great blindness of their souls.

units.la: Acq, haec quidem de ignibus, luminibus, lucernis, lampadibus, facibus, cereis, atque etiam lignis, carboibus, cineribus, fumis denique sacris & sacrificiis Gencilium satis sint dicta.
units.tr: Indeed, let this suffice on the fires, lights, lamps, torches, wax candles, and also the wood, coals, ashes, and finally the smoke of the sacred rites and sacrifices of the Gentiles.

units.la: NVNC praemissis iis, quae ad apparatum praeparationemque sacrificialem pertinent, quaeque sacrificium praecesserunt, quae ab Euflachio, ὑποτύποις, καὶ ἀπαρχαῖς Φόβος ... παραχαι, ἀπαρχαι, θυμάματα, & alii fere hujusmodi nominibus appellantur, ad ipsam ιερουργίαν cipali sacrificio, hoc est, actum sacrificialem, & quae eum fuerunt comitata, accedamus. Pro more autem nostro primum ipsius Homeri & Apollonii verba in utriusque sacrificii descriptione expendamus, & illorum quasi filum secuti, quid primo, quid secundo, quid tertio, quid deinceps fieri fit solitum, diligenter consideremus, simulque ea, quae ab ipsis fuerunt praetermissa, & apud alios auctores legantur in sacrificio fuisse usurpata, quae supplemeuci loco addamus.
units.tr: NOW, with those things set aside that pertain to the preparation and arrangement of the sacrifice, and that came before the sacrifice (which Eustathius and others call by such names as hypotypoi, aparchai, thymamata, and the like), let us come to the sacrificial act itself, the principal sacrifice, that is, the sacrificial action, and to what accompanied it. In keeping with our custom, let us first weigh the words of Homer and of Apollonius themselves in their descriptions of the sacrifice. Following their thread, as it were, let us carefully consider what was customarily done first, second, third, and thereafter, and let us add, as a supplement, those things which they omitted but which are read in other authors as having been used in sacrifice.

units.la: Ab utroque autem Poeta primum percussionis hostiae, ad aram stantis, fit mentio. Hostiam enim adductam ad aram oportebat stare primum : non autem humi jacere, priusquam secuti, bipenni, aut alio instrumento caesa profferneretur. Unde Standi & Statuendi verbum, quando de hostiis, ad animam adductis & admotis, sic sermo, saepe illi tribuitur, ut apud Virgilium: Et statuam ante aras aurata fronte juvencum.
units.tr: From both poets, mention is first made of the striking of the victim as it stands at the altar. For the victim, once brought to the altar, had first to stand; it was not to lie on the ground before it was struck down with an axe or some other instrument and laid low. Hence the verb "to stand" (stare, statuere) is often applied to animals brought up and placed for sacrifice, as in Virgil: "And I will set a bullock with gilded brow before the altars."

units.la: Et alibi: Et ductus tornu stabit sacer hircus ad aram.
units.tr: And elsewhere: "And the sacred goat, led by its horns, will stand at the altar."

units.la: Vbi Servius: Stubit, pro placebit interpretatur. Tunc enim aptum sacrificium esse, cum animal dedicatum vitiime patiens iu venisur. Quoties enim relictabatur, ostendebat se improbari: inprimis significabatur primum quidem hostia illam sana fuisse, deinde impavida & constantem quae non metu aliquo ab ara se proripuerit, quod mali erat omen. Notacumus est, auctore Plinio, non fere litari, trahente se ab ara hostia & aufugiente. Unde inter prisconum prodigia legimus aminofum fuisse, quotiescunque hostia fugisset ab ara. Hincintor ostenta Pharsalica clades hoc quoque numerat Lucanus: —Discussâ fugit ab ara Taurus.—
units.tr: Where Servius explains: "Stetit" is taken to mean "placuit" (was pleasing). For the sacrifice was then fit, when the consecrated animal stood patiently to be struck. For whenever it resisted, it showed that it was rejected. Chiefly this signified that the victim was sound, and then steady and fearless, not bolting from the altar in some fright, which was a bad omen. Pliny notes that sacrifice was almost never successful when the victim dragged itself away from the altar or ran off. Hence among the old prodigies we read that it was an ill omen whenever a victim had fled from the altar. Lucan also counts this among the portents before the defeat at Pharsalus: "The bull, having shaken off the axe, fled from the altar."

units.la: 'At Cajus Iulius Cæsar, qui, teste Suetonio, nullâ unquam religione ab incepto abstterritus vel retardatus esset, cùm immolanti aufugisset hostia, profectionem ad versus Scipionem & jubam non diffulit. Prolapsus etiam in egressu navis. (Ndalum enim omen putatur, quando quis in rebus obeundis prolabitur) versò ad melius omine: Teneo te, inquit, Africa.
units.tr: But Gaius Julius Caesar, who, as Suetonius testifies, was never deterred or delayed from any undertaking by any scruple of religion, when the victim ran away while he was sacrificing, did not postpone his expedition against Scipio and Juba. He also stumbled as he left the ship. (For it is thought a bad omen when someone stumbles in the course of an undertaking.) He turned it to a better omen: "I have you, Africa," he said.

units.la: His adde, quod hoc ipso, quod hostia stans ad aram subito illu percussa platim cadit, innuere videntur voluisse, eodem modo homines & cruentas res humanas, firmiter licet flare flabilesque videantur esse: tamen subito & ex improviso cadere atque corruere, secundum illa Ovidii:
units.tr: Add to this that by the very fact that the victim standing at the altar is suddenly struck and falls at once, they seem to intend to show that in the same way men and mortal human affairs, though they seem firm and strong, nevertheless suddenly and unexpectedly fall and collapse, in accordance with those lines of Ovid:

units.la: Omnia sunt hominum tenui pendentia filo, Et subito casu, quae valuere, ruunt.
units.tr: "All things of men hang by a slender thread, and what was strong suddenly falls in a sudden mischance."

units.la: Ita stans hostia modis illis, de quibus jam dictum, ad eadem praeparari, explorari & quasi consecrari confuerunt. Inter alia autem, quae, priusquam caderetur ac humi prosternetur, fieri solebant, hæc quoque cerimonia, cùm jam jam cadenda esset, ut superpari prius fuit solita: Nempe obliquum culerum ferreum a fronte hostiæ mactanda usque ad caudam ante immolationem ducere confuerant, quod Servius annotat in illa Virgilii Æneid. 12.
units.tr: Thus the victim standing at the altar was prepared, examined, and as it were consecrated, in the ways already described. Among the other things that were customarily done before the animal was cut down and laid flat on the ground, this ceremony was also in use, performed just before it was to be struck: they used to draw an iron blade obliquely from the forehead of the victim to be slain down to its tail before the immolation. Servius notes this on that line of Virgil in the Aeneid, book 12.

units.la: Illi ad surgentis conversi lumina SolisDant fruges manibus salsas & tempora ferroSumma notant pecudum paterïq;, altaria libant.
units.tr: "They, turned to the rising light of the sun, cast salted grain from their hands, and mark the topmost hairs of the beast's head with the iron, and pour libations on the altars."

units.la: Hunc ritum vult a Virgilio innui illis verbis:
units.tr: Virgil's words, "and mark the topmost hairs with the iron," are taken to refer to this rite.
"...and mark the topmost hairs with the iron," etc.

units.la: Videamus nunc, quibus verbis Homerus & Apollonius hanc hostiarum percussionem describant. Apud Homerum igitur Thrasymedes, audacia praditus, conjuncta cum consilio, fecur nomen ejus sonat, dicitur bovem percussisse, sumpta securi, propterea quod, ut Athenaeus annotat libro decimo quarto, Nestor ob senectutem id non poterat facere, quem reliqui fratres adjuvabant. Sic enim Homerus inquit: Αυτίκα Νέστορ ὡς ὑπ' ὀρθρομος θεσσαλιήσης Ηλασεν ἀγχι σὺν πελὶκος ἀπ' ἀσπίκος τίσοντας Αυχενιος, &c. Statim Nestoris filius generosus Thrasymedes Impulit prope stans: securis autem abscidit nervos Cervicales, &c.
units.tr: Let us now see with what words Homer and Apollonius describe this striking of the victims. In Homer, then, Thrasymedes, endowed with boldness joined to counsel (as his very name sounds), is said to have struck the ox, taking up an axe, because, as Athenaeus notes in book 14, Nestor could not do it on account of his age, and his other brothers helped him. For Homer says: "Straightway the son of Nestor, the noble Thrasymedes, struck it from close by, and the axe cut through the sinews of the neck, and so on."

units.la: Ἡλασεν hoc in loco, Eustathio interprete, idem est, quod πελίκες ἰδαλεξ, id est securi percussit. Rationem deinde percussionis exponit, cum inquit: —πελίκες δ' ἀπικοῦ τίσοντας Αυχένιος, &c. Securis autem abscidit nervos
units.tr: Here "struck" [ἤλασεν], according to Eustathius, means the same as "struck with the axe" [πέλεκυς]. He then explains how the striking was done, when he says: "...and the axe cut through the sinews of the neck..." That is, he struck, that is, cut off, cut through, and severed those two great sinews.

units.la: Cervicales, &c. id est, duos illos majores nervos percussit, hoc est, abscidit, resecuit, amputavit. Αυχένιος enim Eustathio est αὐχένημα. Intellegit autem illos nervos, qui sunt in ea parte, qua caput & cervix colliguntur, quibus interdum etiam cervix denotatur. Sic paullo ante: —πελίκεων ἡ μαν πελίκεως Θεσσαλικός Οξεως ἰχαν ἐκ χερὶ πνεύστο ... βοῦν ἔπλεξον: Securim autem bellicosus Thrasymedes Acutam gestans in manu adsilabat, bovem cæsuræ,
units.tr: For "auchen" [αὐχήν], according to Eustathius, is the neck. He means those sinews which lie in the part where the head and neck are joined, and by which sometimes the neck itself is designated. So a little before: "Thrasymedes, warlike, holding a sharp axe in his hand, leapt on to strike the ox." That is, according to Eustathius, he was trying to cut through the joints of the neck, whence also the ancients called the hollows of the joints the "salamoi" [σαλαμοί], which in a proper sense is called the kitchen table, on which meat is usually cut up, in Greek "hypochomous" [ὑποχόμους].

units.la: Id est, Eustathio interprete, ἰσαιῶν τῆς ζαχίλμ πλίξων, ὅθεν καὶ ἰαπόπον πηγὲ τὰς σαλαμοὺς τὸ ἐπιξώων: quod proprie mensa coquinaria dicitur, supra quam carnes concidi solent, Graecè ὑπιχόμου.
units.tr: That is, according to the commentator Eustathius, the word means the block on which the flesh is chopped up and cut into pieces, which is properly called the kitchen table, and in Greek is called by a word for the chopping-block.

units.la: Sic apud Apollonium in mactatione duorum illorum taurorum, quos Argonautæ sacrificafse iusserunt, Hercules ipse alterum quidem γόνατα λάβ μέσοτ κρῶρ ἀμφιμῆτ πτ Πλᾶξεν, δὲ' ἀθρίῳ αὖ̓ν πτ ... ἑπιφατ...ν Claramedium caput circa frontem Percussit: at ille totus confestim bumi prockbuit.
units.tr: So in Apollonius, when the two bulls are slaughtered that the Argonauts were ordered to sacrifice, Hercules himself struck one of them with his club on the forehead, between the horns, and the bull at once dropped to the ground.

units.la: Ancæus autem ―κατὰ ἀλλαν αὐχένα κόλας Χαλκεῳ πελίκεν κεραυρὼς ... νίκεροι πύσασσ latam cervicem percuriens Aerea securi fortes abscidis nervos.
units.tr: Ancaeus, in the same way, striking the broad neck of the other bull with a bronze axe, cut through the sinews.

units.la: Vbi autem securim pro ferro accipi Scholiastes admonet. Nam Veteres ferrò nondum reperti erant, sed in fine apud ferrum fuisse, conflat ex illo Hesiodi: Χαλκὸς δ' ἐίχαλ ... ὑπ ... ... σίδηρος. Aere operabantur, nigro nondum existente ferro.
units.tr: Mention of this kind of striking is made not only in the passages above but also, very vividly, in many other authors. Chiefly it appears in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, who, near the end of book 7 of his Roman Antiquities, briefly but very accurately describes, besides this striking, many other rites and ceremonies customarily employed in sacrifices, and so embraces the sacrifices in a single account. But since the words themselves help greatly toward understanding what precedes and what follows, it is worth setting them here:

units.la: Huiusmodi porro percussionem non tantum in praecedentibus iis locis, sed apud plurimos alios auctores luculenta admodum expressa, sit mentio: in primis vero apud Dionysium Halicarnassensem, qui sub finem libri septimi Antiquitatum Romanarum, praeter hanc percussionem, ritus plerosque alios atque caerimonias, in sacrificiis adhibere solitas, breviter quidem, sed accurate admodum describit, unoque quasi sacrificia complectitur. Sed verba ipsa, quia ad praecedentium, et eorum, quae sequuntur, intelligentiam maiorem facunt, hic subjicere libet: Σωπιαλεῖ ... ... ...
units.tr: Mention of this kind of striking is made not only in the passages cited above but in many other authors, described very clearly. Above all, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, toward the end of the seventh book of his Roman Antiquities, besides this striking, describes briefly yet very accurately many other rites and ceremonies customary in sacrifices, and embraces them, as it were, in a single account. But since his own words will help us understand both what precedes and what follows, I think it worthwhile to set them down here.

units.la: {a} Dionysius Halicarnassensis, lib. 7. Antiquit. Rom. de ritibus sacrificiorum in genere. communi & profano etiam vitæ humanæ vsu, pecora hominibus non nisi occisa feré, sive ad vestitum, sive ad victum prosunt: sic Ethnici in sacrificiis suis non nisi hostiis occisis ac mortuum letari, Dijs suis satisfieri, eosq; placari posse arbitrabantur.
units.tr: {a} Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 7 of the Roman Antiquities, on the rites of sacrifices in general. Even in the common and ordinary use of human life, livestock are useful to men scarcely except when they are killed, whether for clothing or for food. So the heathen, in their sacrifices, thought that their gods could be satisfied and placated only by victims that were slain and dead.

units.la: Porro ab hoc ritu cædendi, cædere sæpe synecdochicè pro sacrificare usurpatur, ut cædere bo- vem, id est, sacrificare, cædere victimam vel agnam, idem. Unde Virgilius, Cæsam victimam vocat sacrificatam: quod verbum, ut & nomen eadem, teste Festo, nonnulli putant ex Græco κτείνειν dici, quod apud illos significat interficere. Alii deducunt à cædendo. Quicquid fit, habet hoc verbum cædendi cum verbis cædere & cedere magnam affinitatem, quoniam plerunq; etiam ρίπτειν hæc sunt conjuncta, & ea, quæ cæduntur, id est, percutiuntur, sive sint homines, sive be- stiæ, sive etiam res inanimatæ, & cedere & cædere solent. Hinc Præcidere est ante cædere, & ante immolare, ut auctor est Festus: unde & agna Præcidanea, eodem teste, dicta, quæ ante alias immolabatur: item, porca Præcidanea, quæ Cereri cædebatur, id est, maétabatur ab eo, qui mortuo justa non fecisset, id est, glebam non objecisset, quod moris erat eis facere prius, quam novarum fruges gustarent, ut Festus inquit; vel, ut idem ajit, quam immolare erant solitæ, antequam novam frugem præciderent. Fordicidia quoque, festa, a cædendis fordis bubus, ex hoc ritu sunt dicta. Erat autem bos forda, quæ fuit in ventre: & eo die publicè immolabantur boves pragnantes in curiis complures. Victimam præterea nonnulli volunt dictam, quasi vi ictam, quod vi icta cadat. Jeere enim idem, quod percutere. Inde illius. Ab hoc eodem alluferias quoque volunt dictas, quod hostiæ in iis feriebantur. Feriæ, inquit Festus, a feriendis victimis appellatæ, & Feralia Diis Manibus sacrata, festa, vel a feriendis pecudibus appellata. Quid si ferire a ferro sit dictum, quia ferro ad feriendum opus est: vel a ferre; quia tollendum seu auferendum id, quod cæsum. Iude & Ferus, vox, sine dubio nata. His adde, quod hostia quoque dicta ab Hostire, verbo antiquo & obsoleto, quod ferire sive cædere significat, Festo teste. Idem verbum, ut idem auctor est, significat etiam æquare: unde Redhostire gratiam, idem, quod gratiam referre, sich nit cinem vergleichen.
units.tr: Furthermore, from this ritual of slaughtering, the verb caedere ("to cut down, slay") is often used by synecdoche for "to sacrifice": to caedere an ox means to sacrifice it, and to caedere a victim or a lamb means the same. Hence Virgil calls a slaughtered victim caesa, and some think that this verb, like the noun victima, comes, as Festus testifies, from the Greek κτείνειν, which among them means "to kill." Others derive it from caedere. Whatever the case, the verb caedere has a close affinity with the verbs cedere and cudere, since these are often joined with ῥίπτειν, and both cedere and caedere are used of things that are struck or beaten, whether they are men, beasts or even inanimate objects. Hence praecidere means to strike before, and to sacrifice beforehand, as Festus says. From this comes the agna praecidanea, as the same authority says, a lamb that was sacrificed before the others; likewise the porca praecidanea, a sow that was struck down for Ceres by the one who had not performed the due rites for the dead, that is, had not thrown earth on the body, which was the custom to do before they tasted the new fruits, as Festus says; or, as he says in the same place, a sow they were accustomed to sacrifice before they cut the new crop. The Fordicidia too, a festival, took its name from the striking of pregnant cows (fordae boves) in this ritual. A forda was a cow that was pregnant. On that day many pregnant cows were publicly sacrificed in the curiae. Some also want the word victima to be named as if from vi icta, "struck with force," because a victim falls when struck, for icere means the same as percutere. From this same root some also say the alluferia were named, because victims were struck in them. Festus says: "The feriae were named from the striking of victims, and the Feralia, consecrated to the spirits of the dead, are festivals named either from the striking of cattle." What if ferire comes from ferrum, because a blade is needed for striking? Or from ferre, because what has been slaughtered must be taken away or carried off? Hence also ferus, a word surely born of the same source. To these add that hostia too is named from hostire, an ancient and obsolete verb which, as Festus testifies, means to strike or to cut down. The same verb, as the same author says, also means to make equal; hence redhostire gratiam means the same as to return a favour (German: sich nit cinem vergleichen).

units.la: Verba Græca sunt πολέειν, πλήσσειν (unde forsan nostrum Germanicum Flopffen/id est, percutere) πλήσσειν, vel πλησσειν, quibus Homerus & Apollonius utuntur. Ab hac autem ipsa in sacrificiis fœderalibus, id est, quæ fœdera ineundi sanciendiq; caussa fiebant, bestias, seu hostias icuendi, feriendi, cædendi, atque demum jugulandi dissecandiq; consuetudine, nata sunt tritæ ille & usitate Hebræorum, Græcorum & Romanorum dicendi forma: Hebræorum quodem ברית Carath berith, scindere sive dissecare fœdus: Græcorum ὅρκια τέμνειν, fœdera ferire; quale illud Homeri: ὅρκια πιστὰ ταμόντες Fœdera fida ferientes.
units.tr: The Greek words are πολέειν and πλήσσειν (from which perhaps our German Flopffen, that is, to strike), and πλησσειν or πλήσσειν, which Homer and Apollonius use. From this very custom of striking, cutting down, slaughtering and finally cutting the throat and dissecting the beasts or victims in covenant sacrifices, that is, those performed for the sake of entering into and ratifying covenants, there arose those familiar and common forms of speech of the Hebrews, Greeks and Romans. Among the Hebrews it is carath berith [כרת ברית], to cut a covenant. Among the Greeks it is ὅρκια τέμνειν, "to strike covenants," like that line of Homer: "ὅρκια πιστὰ ταμόντες," "striking faithful covenants."

units.la: Et Latinorum: Fœdus icere, ferire, pro facere, inire, sancire, unde Cicero pro Cornelio: Lucius Marcius cum Gaditanis fœdus icisse dicitur. Idem pro Sestio: Tu scilicet homo religiosus, fœdus, quod meo sanguine in pactione provinciarū iceras, frangere voluisti. Idem: Id enim fœdus, meo sanguine illum, sanciri posse ducebat. Idem: Fœdera feriebantur provinciarum. Ferire fœdus cum aliquo, idem dixit pro Cornelio. Hinc fœdus ipsum Festus vult dictum, quod in paciescendo fœdere hostia necaretur. Unde Virgilius: Et casa jungebant fœdera porcâ.
units.tr: The Latins too: foedus icere or ferire is used for to make, to enter into, to ratify a covenant. Hence Cicero in the speech for Cornelius: "Lucius Marcius is said to have struck a covenant with the people of Cadiz." The same in the speech for Sestius: "You, of course, a religious man, wanted to break the covenant that you had struck with my blood in the settlement of the provinces." The same: "For he thought that covenant could be ratified with his blood." The same: "Covenants of the provinces were struck." Ferire foedus cum aliquo, to strike a covenant with someone, the same author used in the speech for Cornelius. Hence Festus holds that the word foedus itself was so called because a victim was slain in making a covenant. Whence Virgil: "And they joined their covenants over a slain sow."

units.la: Vel quia in fœdere interponantur fides; ad quod etymon posterius Cicero videtur alludere pro Domo: Gabinius fregit fœdus, Piso tamen in fide permansit. Idem in officiis: Fœdera, quibus cum hoste devincitur fœdus.
units.tr: Or because faith is put in place in a covenant. Cicero seems to allude to this later etymology in the speech Pro domo: "Gabinius broke the covenant, yet Piso remained faithful." The same in De officiis: "Covenants by which a bond is made with an enemy."

units.la: Porro in hac hostiarum victimarumve percussione (quæ magna caution e, religiosq; fiebat) hæc feré animad versione sunt digna, quæ a Gentilibus diligenter observabantur. Primum persona, quæ munus: hoc bestias feriendi, cædendi, maétandi, excoriandi, dividendi, atque etiam te- quendi obierunt. Apud Homerum quidem nominatur Thrasymedes, Nestoris filius: apud Apollonium vero Herculcs & Anceus, duo Argonauticæ illius navigationis socii. Hi a Latinis ab officio et instrumento ditti sunt Victimarii, sive Victimatores, Cultrarii, secundum illud Vir- gilii: Supponunt alii cultros, id est, victimas cædunt, interprete Servio: item Popa, sacrificium ministri, de quibus supra pluribus. Ælius Spartianus: Percussit, inquit, boftiam popa, nomine Antonius. Propertius:
units.tr: Furthermore, in this striking of sacrificial beasts or victims (which was done with great caution and religious care), the following points are worth noting, which the Gentiles observed carefully. First, the persons who performed the task. These offices of striking, slaughtering, cutting up, skinning, dividing and even roasting the beasts were carried out by: in Homer, Thrasymedes, son of Nestor; in Apollonius, Hercules and Ancaeus, two companions on that voyage of the Argonauts. The Latins named these men victimarii or victimatores, and cultrarii, from their office and their instrument, according to that line of Virgil: "Others set out the knives," that is, they struck the victims, as Servius explains. Likewise the popa, the minister of sacrifice, about whom more was said above. Aelius Spartianus: "A popa named Antonius," he says, "struck the victim." Propertius:

units.la: Succinctique calent ad noua sacra popæ.
units.tr: "The popae girded up glow for the new rites."

units.la: Apud Delphos vi, qui vitulum immolabat ὁσιωτὴρ dicebatur, ut Plutarchus scribit in quæstio- nibus Græcis statim ab initio, Οσιωτὴρ μὴ κα̃λòν τò ἀυ̃ρο̃ν ἱερεῖον (Stephanus pro Ṡυ- μο̃ρ, ἱ̃ρωτα ἀ̃ι ν̔ε putat legendum) ὅταν ὅσι ἀ̃ν ἀ̃ν ὅσι ἐ̃ζῆν. Quinq; autem ὅσιοι per omnem vi tam, qui ρατibus multis in rebus aderant, nunc etiam sacrificabant, cum se ex Deucalionis genere ortos arbitrarentur. Lactantius 4. Thebaid. Sacerdotum, inquit, consuetudo talis est, ut aut ipsi percutiat vitimas, & Agones appellatur: aut sic tenentes cultrum, alter impingat. Ideo dicit Stat.
units.tr: At Delphi the man who slaughtered the calf was called ὁσιωτήρ, as Plutarch writes at the very beginning of his Greek Questions: "The osiotes is not the fine... the victim... when the hosioi are living." (Stephanus thinks it should be read as ἱερώτατος or something similar.) Now the ὅσιοι, that is, those who were present at many sacred rites, sometimes even sacrificed themselves, since they believed they were descended from the race of Deucalion. Lactantius, in book 4 of the Thebaid: "It is the custom of the priests," he says, "either that they themselves strike the victims, and they are called agones, or that one holds the knife in such a way and the other strikes." Hence Statius says: "The cattle fell into the wound."

units.la: In vulnus cecidereгreges. Athenæus libro decimo quinto Dipnosophist. sub finem pluribus docet, has μαγειρον, id est, coquorum olim fuisse partes atq; munia. Ritus, inquit, sacrificiorum & cerimoniis coqui notas fuisse palam est ex Olympiadis ad Alexandrum epistola, qua mater illum hortatur, coquum ut emat in sacris faciundis excitatum his verbis: Perignum coquum missum a matre tuhabe. Scicille, omnia sacra patria tua quomodo peragantur, & αρχα (id est, pura, ut vulgo vertunt, proprie otiosa, inertia, in quibus hostiæ non immolabantur, sed frugum primitia tantum offerebantur) & διαχοιt (judicii alia fortasse, quæ a Rege fierent, cum jus diceret) & Bacchica, & alia prorsus omnia, in quibus mater tua vitimas immolat. Eum igitur ne contempseris, sed libenter excipe, & admemitte quam primum. Addit: Venerandam esse coquorum artem liquet ex Athenensium præconibus, quia dum res divina fieret, in ordine coquorū & vitti mariorum, boves cædentium, fieret Idem paulo post Demi ut in cadem tellimonio probat, Athenis fuisse tribum coquorum, qui ob artem suam magno essent in pretio & honore, qui curabant, ut plebs rice sacrificaret. Tandem artem coquinariam sive culinarium, liberalem esse disciplinam probat, ac coquum ipsum civem esse ostendit, nec sordidum, nec bum-micitus expertem. Inde μαγειρεῖν Græcis est mactare, quoniam coquus pecora coquenda mactat. Quid si igitur ipsum mactandi ver bum a Graeco μαγειρῶν & μαγειρεῖσ fue derivatum potius, quam a magis augere?
units.tr: Athenaeus, in book 15 of the Deipnosophists, near the end, shows at length that the μάγειρος, that is, the cooks, once had these duties and offices. "It is plain," he says, "that cooks were known for the rites and ceremonies of sacrifices, from the letter of Olympias to Alexander, in which the mother urges him to buy a cook who is skilled in performing sacred rites, in these words: 'Take the cook Perignus, whom I have sent. Know that all your ancestral sacred rites are carried out by him, and the ἄρχα (that is, the pure rites, as they commonly translate them, properly the idle or inert ones, in which victims were not sacrificed, but only the firstfruits of the crops were offered), and the διαχοί (judgements, perhaps, which were made by the king when he gave judgement), and the Bacchic rites, and absolutely all others in which your mother sacrifices victims. Therefore do not despise him, but gladly receive him, and send him back as soon as possible.'" He adds: "That the art of cooks is venerable is clear from the heralds of the Athenians, because while the divine rite was being performed, they were placed in order among the cooks and the victim-strikers who slaughtered the oxen." Shortly after, citing the same testimony, Demo proves that at Athens there was a tribe of cooks, who on account of their art were held in great esteem and honour, and who took care that the common people sacrificed properly. Finally, he proves that the culinary art is a liberal discipline, and shows that the cook himself is a citizen, neither base nor unversed in letters. Hence among the Greeks μαγειρεῖν means to slaughter, since the cook slaughters the cattle he is to cook. What if the very verb mactare was derived rather from the Greek μαγειρῶν and μαγειρεῖσ, than from magis augere?

units.la: Apud Homerum κὐρηξ, id est, præconibus, feré illa necessaria ad sacrificia adferendi vitimas, feriendi, carnes parandi, discindendi, vinum etiam libandi munia tribuuntur, ut idem Athenæus testatur. Sed Athenæus eodem in loco significat, magnæ quoque & illustris dignita- tis viros eadem hæc munia obiisse. Sic enim, exempli gratia, apud Homerum ipse quoq; Agamemnon, quamvis Rex, hostiam tamen percutit. Ajt enim Poeta: Agnorum senio ære stomachum proscindit Et alios quidem palpitantes adhuc humi sternit.
units.tr: In Homer, the duties of heralds (κήρυκες), namely to bring the victims for sacrifice, to strike them, to prepare the meats, to cut them up, and even to pour the wine for libation, are attributed to them, as the same Athenaeus testifies. But Athenaeus in the same place also shows that men of great and illustrious dignity performed these same duties. Thus, for example, in Homer even Agamemnon, though a king, strikes the victim. For the poet says: "He cut the throat of the lambs with the bronze, and laid out the others, still gasping on the ground."

units.la: Sic Thrasymedes adjuvantibus eum fratribus idem munus obiit.
units.tr: So Thrasymedes, with his brothers helping him, performed the same office.

units.la: Apud Romanos, Censores, qui magistratus summæ auctoritatis fuit, purpurati & coronati hostias mactabant. Sic in Pedalin gente Indica (testatur Nicolaus Damascenus, quod & Stro- bus repetit in sermone de justitia) non qui sacerdos esset, sed quin præsentia haberetur prudenti- tissimus, hostiam mactabat: nec a Diis nisi justitiam rogabat. Et hæc de personis quæ hostias ferire, percutere, mactare, excoriare atque dividere consuevere. Idem ergo fere illuṡim fuit munus, quod bodie apud nos est coquorum, laniorum, macellariorum: qui ab Italis beccari, forsan a pecoribus, junc dicti, & a Gallis bouchiers, quorum macellum vocatur boucherie, quasi, ut hoc joci causa addam, (la bouche rie) os hominis gaudeat & deleitetur macello. Ob illam autem causam, ut supra quoque attigi, Gentilium & templa atque delubra, macellis atque culinis, & altaria mensis macellariis ac coquinariis, & sacerdotes macellariis & coquis; & denique illorum sacrificia profanæ pecorum mactationibus atque laniensis merito comparari potuerunt.
units.tr: Among the Romans, the censors, who held the office of highest authority, in purple and crowned, slaughtered the victims. So among the Pedalian people of India (as Nicolaus Damascenus testifies, and Strabo repeats in his discourse on justice), the one who slaughtered the victim was not a priest, but the man who was considered most prudent among them, and he asked the gods only for justice. These are the persons who were accustomed to strike, slay, sacrifice, skin and divide the victims. Thus the office among them was almost the same as that which today among us belongs to cooks, butchers and meat-sellers, who are called beccari by the Italians, perhaps from pecora (sheep), and bouchiers by the French, whose shop is called boucherie, as if (I add this in jest) the mouth of man should rejoice and delight in the butcher's shop (la bouche rie). For this reason, as I have also touched on above, the temples and shrines of the Gentiles, and their altars, were fairly compared to butchers' shops and kitchens, with tables for meat-sellers and cooks, and their priests to butchers and cooks; and their sacrifices could rightly be compared to the profane slaughter and butchery of cattle.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem milites non, nisi signo dato, audent prælium inire, manuq; cum hostie vitimum per- conferere: sic illi sacrorum ministri, ac quibus modo dictum, injussu sacerdotum & eorum, qui sa- cutere non nisi crit præerant, minimè audebant hostias aggredi, cæsi, ferire, prosternere, atq; jugulare. Hoc Dionysius quoq; Halicarnassæus diserté in sacrificiis descriptione docet, cum ait, Tum demum (persilus scilicet ius, quæ sacrificium præcedebant) ministros eas Ἰνεον, id est, mactare, ferire, jugulare iubebant. Ideo succinctâ nutum imperium ve exspectantes dicebant Agôn', vel Agone? Hinc Seneca libro secundo Partitionum: Belle, iuquit, deridebat hac Asinius Pollio: Fikus, inquit, cervicem porrigat, carnifex manum porrigat: deinde respiciat ad patrem, & dicat Agôn'? quod fieri solet in vitulis. Idem docet Ovidius his versibus de Agonalibus: Nominis esse potest succinctus caussa minister Hostia caelestibus quo feriente cadit. Qui ealido striflos tinctiurus sanguine cultros Semper agâne rogat, nec nisi iussa agit.
units.tr: Just as soldiers dare not join battle or come to close quarters with the enemy unless the signal has been given, so those ministers of the sacred rites, and those mentioned just above, dared by no means to approach, strike down, throw down, or cut the throat of the victims without the command of the priests and of those who presided over the rite. Dionysius of Halicarnassus also teaches this plainly in his account of sacrifices, when he says: "Then at last (namely, the flute-players who went before the sacrifice) ordered the ministers to slaughter, strike, and cut the throat [σφάττειν]." Therefore, standing ready with their sleeves girded and awaiting a nod or command, they used to say "Agôn'" or "Agone?" Hence Seneca in the second book of his Partitions: "Asinius Pollio used to mock this wittily: 'Let the victim stretch out its neck, let the executioner stretch out his hand,' then he looks at the father and says, 'Agôn'?' which is commonly done with calves." Ovid teaches the same in these verses about the Agonalia: "The attendant is called the Succinctus for a reason: when the victim falls struck by him, he always asks 'Agen?' with his knives dipped in warm blood, and acts only on command."

units.la: Idem libro quarto de Ponto: At cum Tarpeja effet deductus in arces Dum caderet iussu victima sacra suo.
units.tr: The same poet in the fourth book of the Tristia from Pontus: "When, led up into the Tarpeian citadel, the sacred victim was falling at his command."

units.la: Atque hoc est primum membrum, nempe personae.
units.tr: And this is the first element, namely the person.

units.la: Alterum, quod in percussione victimae observari debet, est instrumentum, quod hostiis cedendis feriendisve adhibebatur. Hoc apud Homerum est πλαξ (ut etiam apud Apollonium) quod bipennem & securim vertunt: unde πλαξεῖν & πλαξεύειν, sive πλαξεῖον per iota, securi percutere, πλαξωτικε dolator, πλαξυφός; bipennifer, sive securifer. Apud eundem Homerum sic quoq; mentio φιζος ἀνοῦς, id est, sudis e quercu, qua hostia ista fuerit (id quod etiam apud Persas & Cappadoces in more fuit positum) ut in Enmai sacrificio: Κόλα, ἀταρχουύ & χιζή ἀνοῦς, λεῖ λῆνς κείων. Hostiam mola sparsam querna suda percutit.
units.tr: The second thing to be observed in striking the victim is the instrument used to fell or strike the victims. In Homer this is the pelex (as also in Apollonius), which they render as "double-axe" and "axe"; whence come the verbs meaning to strike with an axe, and the words for a carpenter and an axe-bearer. In the same Homer there is also mention of an oaken stake [ῥίζος ἀείρας], i.e. a stick of oak, with which the victim was struck; this too was the custom among the Persians and Cappadocians, as in the sacrifice to Enyo: "He strikes the victim, sprinkled with meal, with an oaken stake."

units.la: Dionysius Halicarnasseus locum hunc ipsum citans σαυτάλιον vocat instrumentum illud, quo victimae feriri fuerint fedite: cujus quidem vocis varia & diversa sunt significata. Nam & mirem araneum & scuticam, hoc est, flagellum, ex corio factum, & pteram corticeam & caeterum equestrem; & furculum loricatum (quod genus epistolae eras apud Lacedaemonios, de quo Gellius lib. 18. cap. 9.) & tabulam; in qua scripta fontium debita proponebantur, & baculum sive mirgam, & serpentis genus significat. Vide Erasmum in Chiliadibus, Triflis Scytale.
units.tr: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, quoting this very passage, calls the instrument by which the victims were struck a skytalion [σκυτάλιον]. The word has various and different meanings: a leather whip (scutica), that is a flail made of hide, a cork-bark club, and a horseman's whip; a forked stick bound with leather (the kind of letter used by the Spartans, on which Gellius writes in book 18, chapter 9); a tablet on which the debts of the debtors were posted; and it also means a staff or rod, and a kind of serpent. See Erasmus in the Adages, under "Laconian scytale."

units.la: Apud Apollonium porro Hercules ποπαλον alterum taurorum percussisse ac proftrasse dicitur. Est autem ρόπαλον sive ρόπαλον & idem quod ρόπλον, clava, fustis, malleus: quod ipsum instrumentum apud Latinos quoque in usu fuit. Is vero ligneus fuit sive ferreus: sicuti & bodie ligneo ad eundem effectum lanii utuntur, nempe ad boves similiter sternendos. Hic una cum securi a sacrificulo, seu ab uno ex Victimariis gestabatur: atq; coronatu victimarum capitibus (teste Plinio lib.16.cap.4. in his verbis: Postea Deorum honori sacrificantes sumpsere, victimis simul coronatis) malleo prius in ante aram percutiebant: deinde securi cervix abscindebatur: eum ad e'ssiferationem & extra rimanda, capiandaq; auspicia procedebant. Mallei hujus pissorum vide apud Gulielmum du Choul, libro ante citato de Religione Romana, & Bartholomaeum Marliannum in antiquitatibus urbis Romae.
units.tr: Further, in Apollonius, Hercules is said to have struck down the other bull with a rhopalon [ῥόπαλον]. The rhopalon, or rhoplon, is the same as a club, cudgel, or mallet; this instrument was also in use among the Latins. It was made either of wood or of iron. Even today butchers use a wooden one for the same purpose, namely to fell oxen in the same way. The sacrificer, or one of the victim-attendants, carried this along with an axe, and with the heads of the victims garlanded (as Pliny says in book 16, chapter 4: "Afterwards, when they sacrificed to the honour of the gods, they took up the victims at the same time as they were crowned"), they first struck them with the mallet in front of the altar; then the neck was cut off with an axe, and they proceeded to inspect the entrails and take the auspices. For pictures of this mallet see Gulielmus du Choul, in the book on Roman religion cited above, and Bartholomaeus Marlianus on the antiquities of the city of Rome.

units.la: Fuit deinde & securis apud Latinos, instrumentum ad boves ante aras Deorum perenciendos adhibitum: ideo Sacrificae dicta ab Ovidio duodecimo Metamorph. Elatumq; (scilicet funale) altè veluti qui candida tauri Rumpere sacrificâ (sacrificiis dicatâ) molitur colla securi.
units.tr: Then among the Latins there was also the axe, an instrument used for felling oxen before the altars of the gods. Hence Ovid in the twelfth book of the Metamorphoses calls it "sacrificial": "And the rope (namely the torch), raised high, as if he were striving with a sacrificial axe (dedicated to sacrifices) to break the neck of the white bull."

units.la: Hanc autem eneam fuisse constat ex Festo, & ideo Acierius dictam. Sic enim ille: Acieris securis anea, quain sacrificiis utebantur sacerdotes. Porro à secando dicta videtur, Germanice Axt, forsan a Graeco ἀξίνη, quae vox etiam securim sive bipennem significat. Unde ἀξιονζωτικὴ dicit: divinatio per fecuret; de qua Plinius lib.36.cap.19. Si vero sunt Veteres hoc instrumento ad varios usus; videlicet & ad ligna secanda, & etiam ad bellum. Virg. Aeneid. II. —eratam quatiens Tarpeja securim.
units.tr: That this axe was of bronze is clear from Festus, who for this reason calls it acierius: "An acierius is a bronze axe, which the priests used in sacrifices." Its name seems to derive from cutting, in German Axt; perhaps from the Greek axinē, which word also means an axe or double-axe. Hence the divination by axes [ἀξινομαντεία], which Pliny mentions in book 36, chapter 19. Ancient writers used this instrument for various purposes, namely for cutting wood and also for war. Virgil, Aeneid 2: "Tarpeia brandishing an iron-shod axe."

units.la: Visi ea sunt pariter ad fontes puniendos, quisque magistratibus capite plectendi erant, secuti percussi sunt. Cicero tertia Verrina: Agunt enim praecipitem poenae civium Romanorum, quos parsim percussit, partim in vinculis necavit, & Virg. 6. Aeneid.
units.tr: Axes were likewise used for punishing: those who were to be capitally punished by the magistrates were beaten and then struck down. Cicero, Third Verrine: "For the swift penalties of Roman citizens drive on, whom he struck with rods and partly killed in chains." And Virgil, Aeneid 6:
Consuls.

units.la: Ex Virg. Aeneid. Consulis imperium hic primus servasti, secures Accipiunt, &c.
units.tr: From Virgil, Aeneid 6: "Here he first preserved the authority of the consul; they receive the axes," etc.
And Lucan, book 1:
"Catiline set alight the axes of peace."

units.la: Hujus instrumenti in ventrix fuit Penchefilea Amazon, teste Plin. lib. 7. c. 56. Unde et Amazonei, securigera a Poëtis dicta sunt. Secures item magistratuum insignia erant, virgarum fasciculo loro illigatae. Cic. 6. Verr. Quamobrem fasces Praetoribus praeferuntur, cur secures datae? Secures demum, ut in nostram sententiam veniamus, licet grandiores erant, ad victimarum carnes secandas dividendas, prout libebat sacrificulis, vitimariis, & id genus hominibus, qui sacrificiis antiquorum praerant. Hodie Lanii in Urbe magno lato, cultro ad carnes dividendas, tuntur, quem spatagium vocant, &c.
units.tr: Penthesilea the Amazon is said to have been the inventor of this instrument, according to Pliny, book 7, chapter 56; hence the poets call the Amazons axe-bearing. Axes were also the insignia of magistrates, bound up with a bundle of rods. Cicero, Sixth Verrine: "Why are the fasces carried before praetors, and why were axes given?" Finally, to come to our own opinion: although the axes were larger, they were used to cut and divide the flesh of the victims, as the sacrificial attendants, victim-attendants, and that sort of men who presided over the sacrifices of the ancients pleased. Today the butchers in the great city use a broad knife to divide the meat, which they call a spatagium, etc.

units.la: De more porro securim, quae apud Athenienses primus bos mactatus fuit in sacrificiis, in jus vocandi quotannis vide Leonicenum libro 2. capite 3. Athenis, inquit, in Prytaneo judicum fuit locus, ubi ferrum & quaevis alia inanima, quibus patraca fuerat caedes, judicium quoq; illius, qua Erechtheo Athenis imperante, bos primus Athenis mactatus dicebatur, eanquam res causa quotannis magna cum solennitate agebatur. Cum enim sacerdos, quem illi Βουφόνον vocabant, bove percusso, humi, strato, relicta ibi securi, ocyus ex Attica aufugisset, non comparente homine, securim cunctis primum Athen. in judicio collocuerunt. Unde haec illa quotannis in jus vocandi consuetudo inolevit.
units.tr: Concerning the custom of summoning the axe to court each year, by which the first ox sacrificed at Athens was struck, see Leonicenus, book 2, chapter 3. "At Athens," he says, "in the Prytaneum, there was a place where judgment was given on iron and any other inanimate things by which a killing had been done; and also on that axe by which, when Erechtheus ruled at Athens, the first ox was said to have been slaughtered at Athens. This matter was carried out every year with great solemnity. For when the priest, whom they called the Bouphonos, had struck the ox, and it lay on the ground, he fled quickly out of Attica, leaving the axe lying there; and since no man appeared, they first brought the axe to trial in court before all the Athenians. Hence arose the custom of summoning it to court every year."

units.la: Tertium instrumentum, quo Latini utebantur in sacrificiis, erat Secespita, interprete Festo, culter ferreus, oblongus, manubrio eburneo, rotundo, filido, vinclo ad capulum argento, auro, fixo, clavis aeneis, aere cyprio, quo Flaminies, Flaminicae virgines, Pontifices, ad sacrificia utebantur, a secando, ficditi. Eadem aliàs dicitur, quia in sacrario ucuntur. Sacraria namq; in templis reticulo aeneo olim sepiebantur, in quo turbe reliqua sunt, per quas manibus sacra tangere licet. Et hoc in templo Bonae Deae, sed aliis in locis, qui sunt velut repascula quaedam, sica Secespita dicuntur duobus modis. Suetonius in Tyber. Nam & inter Pontifices sacrificanti simul, pro Secespita plembeum culerum subjiciendum cura vit. Idem alibi: Secespicam, alii securim, alii dolabram aeneam, alii cultellum putant.
units.tr: The third instrument which the Latins used in sacrifices was the secespita, according to Festus: a long iron knife with a round ivory handle, fixed to the hilt with silver or gold, with bronze nails of Cyprian bronze, which the flamens, the flaminicae (virgins), and the pontiffs used at sacrifices; it is named from cutting (secare). It is said elsewhere to be so called because it is kept in the sacrarium. For sacraria in temples were formerly enclosed with a bronze lattice, in which are left the remaining things through which it is lawful to touch sacred objects with the hands. This is so in the temple of the Good Goddess, but in other places, which are like certain feeding-places, a knife is called a secespita in two ways. Suetonius in Tiberius: "For among the pontiffs, when he was sacrificing, he took care that a lead knife be placed under in place of the secespita." Elsewhere he says: "Some think the secespita is an axe, others a bronze dolabra, others a little knife."

units.la: Aliud instrumentum, in sacrificiis adiberi solitum, fuit Dolabrum, sive Dolabra, quam Festus Pontificalem ab hoc usu vocat, & alio nomine Scenam, sive Scaenam. Fuit autem, ut ex formae patet, quam Marlianus in suis antiquicatibus expressit, Culer grandior, factorio perquam similis, quo olim reor in sacrificiis Veteres uti fuisse folicos, ad hostias, & victimas deglubendas, postquam malleo hae percussae, & jugulatae essent, a quo forte nomen funferic: seu potius a dolando, hoc est ab aequandis partibus carnium, quae arsa imponebantur, Dius immolandarum, sumpta mecaphora a dolabra, quae fabri lignarii est instrumentum, quo ligne dolancur, seu expoliuntur, quanquam & rusticum itidem fit instrumentum, cujus Columella lib. 3. meminit his verbis: Quae falce emputari non possunt, acute dolabra abrudito. Et & ejus diminutivum dolabella, de qua idem auctor lib. 5. sic inserit: Circa crus dolabella dimo venda est terra, &c. Plucarchus vero in vita Tiberii & Caji Graecchorum, de dolone, quod genus est gladii, sic memini: Ille vero (Tiberium intelligic) palam gladium, quem dolonem vocaut, accinctus ambulat, etc. Quid culter bujusmodi hoc nomine appellaretur, auctorem adhuc defidero; quod autem hac forma unum ex sacrificialibus instrumentis fuerit, nullis dubium esse puto. Nam pafim multis in locis marmore aut aliquo in sculptum cernere licet, & praesertim in arcu marmoreo, quem aurificum neminant, prope Ecclesiam S. Georgii in Velabro: ubi multae, quae ad antiqua sacrificia spectant, videre est, &c.
units.tr: Another instrument usually employed in sacrifices was the dolabrum, or dolabra, which Festus calls "pontifical" from this use, and by another name scena or scaena. It was, as its shape shows (which Marliani drew in his Antiquities), a fairly large knife, very like a carpenter's tool; I suppose the ancients used it at sacrifices to skin the victims and hostias after they had been struck with the mallet and their throats cut. Perhaps its name comes from this, or rather from dolare, that is from trimming the pieces of meat which were laid on the altar to be burnt, a metaphor taken from the dolabra, the carpenter's tool with which wood is hewn or smoothed; though it is also a rustic tool, which Columella mentions in book 3: "What cannot be cut off with the sickle should be hewn off with a sharp dolabra." Its diminutive is dolabella, of which the same author in book 5 writes: "Around the leg the earth is to be dug with a dolabella."
