Plutarch, in the lives of Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, mentions the dolon, a kind of sword: "He walks about openly, girded with the sword which they call a dolon." Which knife was called by this name I still lack an authority for; but that this shape was one of the sacrificial instruments I think is beyond doubt. For it can be seen carved in marble in many places, and especially on the marble arch which the goldsmiths call..., near the church of St George in the Velabrum, where many things pertaining to the ancient sacrifices are to be seen.

units.la: Ad instrumenta, quibus hostiae feriri, caedi & mactari solebant, referri quoq; debet lapis ille, sive silex, quo agni, porce, sive alterius bestiae caput in pangendis faederibus percuti atque feriri solebat. Exemplum hujus consuetudinis citatum a nobis fuit supra ex Livio, quod hic, quia ad rem maxime facit, repetemus. Apud Livium Annibal, magnus propositus promissis, milites suos ad fortitudinem adhortatus, ea, ut rata erunt fore, agnum leva manu, dextra filicem recinens, si fallerent, lovem, ceterosq; precatus Deos, ica se mactarent, quemadmodum ipse agnum mactavit: secundum precationem caput pecudis saxo elisit.
units.tr: To the instruments with which victims were struck, slaughtered and killed, that stone also belongs, or flint, with which the head of a lamb, pig or other beast was struck and beaten when covenants were made. We cited an example of this custom above from Livy, and since it bears most directly on the matter, we will repeat it here. In Livy, Hannibal, having set out his promises, encouraged his soldiers to courage. He took a lamb in his left hand and a flint in his right, and invoked Jupiter and the other gods: if the promises were kept, as they would be, then let them be struck as he struck the lamb, but if they broke faith, let them be slain in the same way. Following the prayer, he dashed the animal's head against a stone.

units.la: Tertio case vitimae casus quoque diserte exprimitur, qui & ipse diligenter, in hac percussione fuit obler vatus. De bove, ab Hercule caesa, sic ait Apollonius:
units.tr: In the third case, the manner of the blow is also clearly expressed, and this too was carefully observed in the striking. Apollonius says this of the ox slain by Hercules:
{T} a

units.la: —ὁ δ᾽ ἀθεῖς ἀῦθ᾽ πασὶν ἐπιφάνως ... γάλη,At illa totus confessim humi procubuit:
units.tr: "But it, all at once, sank down to the ground on every side" [ὁ δ᾽ ἀθεῖς ἀῦθ᾽ πασὶν ἐπιφάνως ... γάλη]. The line reads: "And the whole of it at once fell prone upon the earth."
So Virgil: "The ox sinks down to the ground."

units.la: De altero, quem Ancæus ferit, sic cecinit idem Apollonius:
units.tr: Of the other ox, which Ancaeus struck, the same Apollonius sang thus:

units.la: Ηρωτη δ᾽ ἀυροτίεσθαι ... Scholiastes, ... Eurymachus interpretatur ... Nunc autem significat ... eis τὸν ... est, cum pronus procubuisset.
units.tr: "But it began to ... " The scholiast explains ... Eurymachus interprets ... but now it signifies ... "when it had fallen forward, prone."

units.la: Quemadmodum autem mali omnino erat, si victima ductorem non sponte sequeretur, sed ut trahenda esset: vel si ex ductentium manibus se proripuisset: vel profugisset: sic mali auspicii erat si vel elapsa victima fefellisset, vel percussa aut exilii esset altius aut horridius exclamasset, aut non flatim; & quidem placide concidisset, & si supina & non prona cecidisset: vel si semianimis provoluta in terram eandem pedibus calcitrasset impotentius: vel difficulter exspirasset: vel jugulata non copioso diffluxisset sanguine: vel si inter jugulandum triste aliquid infausti ... oculis auribusque occurrisset, ut si locuta esset victima vel bostia: quod Roma fecisse bovem fœminam Livius refert Decad. 5. lib. 3. Unde libris a Decemviris aditum decretum ut supplicatio fieret, cum Æli magistratus circa omnia pulvinaria majoribus hostiis X L numero sacrificarent, ... coronatus esset. Quod ipsum & P. Volumnio & Servilio Sulpitio Cos. dot fœmina fecit: & item masculus inquient: Cave tibi Roma, quem bovem cum iura servari, aliqui arusticet fuisse. Signa hæc & alia, quæ inter percutiendum & jugulandum e venissent, offerri, & alienati Nummi penasque minitantes, e fe putabantur. Contra læti eminentes indicia & fortunæ Dei testimonia erant: cum emissa & ducta ad aram fonte acceleraret, & sine fremitu atque tumultu ut ilia utumpatienter perferret, collapsaque placide, sineque deformi fremitu aut pedum complosione animam exhalarit, & confossa tandem copiosum spirantemque, & cum impetu stridoreque prorumpentem effunderet cruorem. Talem læti & cum gratulatione exclamationeque excipiebant: ad alte: tus vero adstitum exponerentur, animusque suis conflernabantur, & trepidi fuspeētiāt arsis adbantur, ritusque absolvebantur cetero s, & sollicite, qua ratione Numen offensum reconciliarent, deliberabant. Pertinent huc, quæ Plinius scribit lib. 8. cap. 45. sub finem: Ex taurû & bobus victimæ inquit, optime, & lautissima Deorum placatio. Huic tantum animali omnium, quibus procerior e atuda, non flatim nato cusummate (ut cæteris) mensuræ crescit uni, donec ad vestigia ima per veniat. Quamobrem victimarum probatio in vitulo, ut articulum suffragium contigat, breviore non litant. Hoc quoq; notatum, vitulos ad aras humeris hominum allatos non fere litare, sicut nec clauditantem, nec aliena hostia Deos placari, nec trahente se ab ara. Est frequent in prodigiis prisco rum, Bovem locutum. Quo nunciato, Senatum sub dis vo haberi solitum. Hæc Plinius.
units.tr: Just as it was an altogether bad omen if the victim did not follow its leader of its own accord, but had to be dragged, or if it tore itself from the hands of those leading it, or ran away; so it was an ill omen if the victim slipped away and escaped, or if, when struck, it bellowed louder and more fiercely than it should, or did not fall at once; and if it fell calmly, but fell on its back and not on its front; or if, half-dead, it rolled onto the ground and kicked out with its feet too wildly; or if it died with difficulty; or if, when its throat was cut, it did not pour out much blood; or if during the slaughter something sad and unlucky appeared to the eyes and ears, as when the victim spoke, or the beast did. Livy relates that at Rome a heifer did this, in the fifth decade, book three. Hence the Decemvirs, consulting the books, decreed a supplication, and the magistrates of Aelius sacrificed larger victims, forty in number, at all the shrines, ... was crowned. The same thing was done by a female ox in the consulship of P. Volumnius and Servius Sulpicius, and likewise a male, which they said was an ox of the country, when the law was kept. These signs and others, which came about during the striking and slaughter, were thought to be offerings, and omens of anger, and threatening penalties from the gods. On the other hand, cheerful and outstanding signs were tokens of good fortune and of the favour of God: when the victim was led out and brought to the altar willingly, and endured the blows patiently without bellowing or tumult, and fell gently, and breathed out its life without any ugly bellowing or stamping of feet, and when, pierced at last, it poured out a copious and steaming blood with force and a gushing sound. The people received such a sign with joy, congratulation and shouting. But if the omens were ambiguous, the people were dismayed, and the magistrates, anxious and trembling with suspicion, performed the rites to the end and deliberated carefully by what means they might appease the offended divinity. To this belongs what Pliny writes in book 8, chapter 45, near the end: "The best and most sumptuous appeasement of the gods," he says, "comes from bulls and oxen. Of all animals this one alone, which has the taller stature, does not reach its full size at once when born, as the others do, but grows in size until it reaches the lowest parts of its feet. For this reason, in examining victims, a calf is not good for sacrifice unless its limbs are of the right length; a short calf does not give a favourable sign. It has also been observed that calves brought to the altars on men's shoulders seldom give a favourable sign, nor does a limping victim, nor a victim that is not one's own, nor a victim that pulls away from the altar. It is frequent in the portents of the ancients that 'the ox spoke.' When this was announced, the Senate was customarily convened in the open air." So Pliny.

units.la: In primis verò hic mugitum bestiæ observabant, & ex illo quædam vel læta, vel tristia consequebantur; id quod licet conjicere exillis Luciani verbis: Bestiam, inquit, sub Dei oculis jugulant, flebile quiddam emugientem, beneq; fuit licet conjicere, ominatam: denique voce jam leniore ad sacri tibias respondentem. Quo ex loco id quoq; colligere promtum est, tibias in percussione
units.tr: Above all, they observed the lowing of the beast, and from it certain happy or sad consequences followed. One may gather this from the words of Lucian: "They slaughter the beast," he says, "under the eyes of God, while it bellows with a mournful sound, and it is permitted to conjecture that it has forebodings; finally, with a softer voice, it answers the sound of the pipes." From this passage it is also easy to gather that pipes were used in the striking.

units.la: Quoniam autem tibiarum & tibicinum, præcæteris instrumentis Musicis antiquissimus in sacrificiis Gentilium, maximeq, tritus, per vulgatus, ac, ut ipsis videbatur, pene necessarius usus fuit, sine quibus nullum publicum sacrum satisfactum ve rite legitime, conficipossit existimabant, & idcirco creberrima illorum passim apud profanos scriptores, atq, etiam in sacris litteris ut sis mentio, non a ratione inflituitoque hoc meo alienum fore puta vi, si copiosius quædam de ijs hic seriam, initio factio ab ipsis nominibus, quæ multarum rerum ad instrumenti hujus cognitionem pertinentium notæ sunt atque symbola.
units.tr: Since the use of pipes and pipers was the most ancient of the musical instruments in the sacrifices of the Gentiles, and the most common and widespread, and, as they themselves thought, almost necessary, without which they believed no public sacrifice could be properly and lawfully completed, and since frequent mention of them is therefore made everywhere by profane writers, and also in Holy Letters, I think it will not be out of keeping with my plan and purpose to treat certain things about them here at more length, beginning with the names themselves, which are the marks and symbols of many things belonging to the knowledge of this instrument.
In Hebrew

units.la: Hebraice igitur hoc instrumentum חליל Chalil, appellatur,in plurali חלילים Chalilim, tibia Hebraea, quam votem septuaginta interpretes ἀυλὸν,id est,tibiam,verterunt,ut Isaiae quinto capite,quae quoque dragefimo octavo versu,& capite trigesimo, versu vigesimo nono. Thargum Isaiae quinto, versu duodecimo,& Genesis quarto, אבוּבא Abbubā interpretatur,quod siftula sit affinis. Rabbi Schelomōh hoc instrumentum sic vult dictum,quod sit concavum: unde curva tibia a Tibulo & Cava ab Ouidio appellatur.
units.tr: In Hebrew, then, this instrument is called חליל [chalil], in the plural חלילים [chalilim], the Hebrew pipe, which the Seventy translated as αὐλὸν [aulon], that is, pipe, in Isaiah chapter five, and in chapter thirty-eight, verse twenty-nine [sic]. The Targum of Isaiah, chapter five, verse twelve, and Genesis chapter four, interprets it as אבוּבא [abubba], which is akin to a flute. Rabbi Shelomoh holds that this instrument is so named because it is hollow: whence Tibullus calls it the curved pipe, and Ovid the hollow pipe.

units.la: Sicenim Tibullus Eleg. secunda: Obstrepit & Phrygio tibia curva sono.
units.tr: For Tibullus says in the second elegy: "The curved pipe drones with a Phrygian sound."

units.la: Et Ouidius sexto Fastorum: Queritur in scenā caua tibia, queritur aris.
units.tr: And Ovid in the sixth book of the Fasti: "The hollow pipe complains on the stage, it complains at the altar."

units.la: Aliquod mihi videtur verisimilius, sic volvit appellaetam,quod profanus illius & contamina tum in publicis epulis,con-viuiis atque choreis siue tripudiis fuerit usus. Hinc etiam מחול Mahol dictum,quod publicani & profanam,qualis fuit Gentilium,choream ,siue tripudium significat,in quo tibiā cani solebat:qui bodie quoque Christianorum communis ferè mos est. Tympanum enim atq; stilus,siue sistulis plurimq; Christianorum saltationes paragunture: qui quidem tibiarum usus in saltationibus manefeste colliguntur ex illis puerorum verbis Lucae 7. Ηυλήσαμεν ὑμῖν, καὶ οὐκ ὠρχήσασθε. Tibia nobis cecinimus; & non saltastis,&c. Inde & Hieremias cap. 3. מחול Mechōl meichachabim,eborum,siue choream ludentium dixit ab eodem instrumento חליל Chalil. seu tibiae: quem chorum Septuaginta sumou ἀυλὸν ἀυλοὶ sὶ καὶ ἀυλοὶ ἀφέκεσθαι, verterunt. Hinc חלילים Cholel, tibicen, & plurali חלילים Cholelim,tibicines,Psalmo octogesimo septimo. Eᴛ 1. Regum 1. versu 4. בחלילים Mechalelim Bā halelim , ludentes siue canentes tibias.
units.tr: It seems to me more probable that it was so called because it was used in profane feasts, banquets and dances or revels. Hence also מחול [mahol] is named, which signifies a profane dance, such as that of the Gentiles, or a revel, in which the pipe was played; and this is almost the common custom of Christians today. For many Christians accompany their dances with drums and pipes or flutes; and indeed this use of pipes in dancing is clearly inferred from those words of the children in Luke 7: Ηυλήσαμεν ὑμῖν, καὶ οὐκ ὠρχήσασθε [eaulēsamen hymin, kai ouk ōrchēsasthe], "We have piped to you, and you did not dance," etc. Hence also Jeremiah in chapter 31 [sic] speaks of מחול [mechol], the dance of those who play, from the same instrument חליל [chalil], or pipe; the Seventy render this dance with the words αὐλὸν αὐλοὶ [aulon auloi], and the pipers. Hence חלילים [cholel], a piper, and in the plural חלילים [cholelim], pipers, in Psalm 87. And in 1 Kings 1:4 בחלילים [mechalelim], [ba-chalelim], playing or sounding the pipes.

units.la: Græcè αὐλὸς tibia appellatur ἀπὸ τῶ αἰσω, id est, flando (unde & Germanicum fleutten) Tibia quomodo Hanc vocem & tibiam & sistulam & foramen interpretantur, ut alia ejus significata prater. ἀυλίω tibia canere; ἀυλέω, ut tibia canentem audire eos: cantu recrearicantum ad tibiam : ἀκροατὴς ἀυλῶ, tibiarum auditor: ἀυλίης, tibicina : ἀυλιτρὶς, theca tibiarum.
units.tr: In Greek the pipe is called αὐλὸς [aulos], from αἴω [aiō], that is, from blowing (whence also the German fleuten). This word is interpreted both as pipe, flute and hole, as are its other meanings: from it come αὐλέω [auleō], to play the pipe; the same verb also means to make them hear the pipe, or to delight the singers with the pipe' s sound; ἀκροατὴς αὐλῶ [akroatēs aulō], a listener to pipes; αὐλητής [aulētēs], a piper; αὐλητρίς [aulētris], a female piper; αὐλοθήκη [aulothēkē], a case for pipes.

units.la: Lariné tibia dicta ab osse cruris: & maxime cervorum, ut Plu archus memorat in libello, ut tibia Latinè sujus inscriptio est,Quod non liceat in unde vivere, fecundum E picuri sectam. Tibicen,nec Var. unde dicta, ro ait,a tibia & cantu dictus, & inde Tibicina, mulier cantans tibia. Unde Cicero de Oratore: Tibicen sine tibus canere non potest. Tibicines etiam stefle Festo, strabes in aedificiis dici existis stumantur,a similitudine tibia canentium,qui ut canentes sustineant ; ita illi aedificia, siue aedificatorum stella. Hinc Iuvenalis: Non urbem colimus tenui tibicine fultam.
units.tr: In Latin the pipe is called tibia from the bone of the leg, especially of deer, as Plutarch mentions in a little book whose title is That it is not possible to live pleasantly according to Epicurus' school. Tibicen, a piper, is said by Varro to be named from tibia and from singing, and tibicina is a woman singing to the pipe. Hence Cicero in De Oratore: "A piper cannot play without pipes." Pipers are also thought, according to Festus, to have been called strabones in buildings, from the likeness of pipers, who support the playing by blowing, so that these buildings support the stars, or the stars of the builders. Hence Juvenal: "We do not live in a city propped up by a thin piper."

units.la: Thuscorum lingua tibicines Subulones vocantur a Subula, vel potius Subulonis cornu similitudine. Sic Cornicen,qui cornu: Lituen, qui lituo: Siticen, qui apud sitos, id est, vita funēstos & sepultos canere solitum est.
units.tr: In the Tuscan language the flute-players are called subulones, from the subula, or rather from the likeness of the subulo's horn. So too the cornicen, who plays the horn; the lituus, who plays the lituus; and the siticen, who used to play at the funerals of those who had died and been buried.

units.la: De tibiarum origine & inventoribus varie fuerunt Veterum sententiae. Plutarchus in li. Origo tibiarū bro de Musica tradit,alios voluisse tibiam inventam esse a Marsya (quae communis ferē est opinio:) alios ab Olympo: alios ab Hyagnide: alios a Telpsichore. Plin lib.7. cap 56. tibiae oblīquae inventionem Midae in Phrygia tribuit: geminarum vero tibiarum,eidem Marsyae. Verba ejus hec sunt: Musicam Amphion (inuenit) sistulam Pan: monaulam Mercurius : obliquam tibiam Midas in Phrygia: geminas tibias Marsyas Scribit porrò Aristoteles lib. 8. Politicorum,tibiarum usum repudiassum fuisse,non tam propter oris deformitatem,quam ob caussam etiam a Pallade dicitur rejecta, quam quod inutilis videretur ad rerum intelligentiā. Pin dar us tamen Minervam facit tibiarum inventricem ad imitandum lamentationem, graviter sonantem. Plerij autem,ut dictum,tibiam a Marsya, sistulam (quam Hebraei נקאב Nεkab, vocant בקצ Nakab, id est perforare,nimirum a foraminibus,Graeci σύριγξ appellant ; quā tamen vox saepe pro tibia capitur) lyram ab Apolline aut Mercurio fuisse inventam.
units.tr: Among the ancients there were various opinions about the origin and inventors of flutes. Plutarch, in his book On Music, reports that some held the flute to have been invented by Marsyas (which is almost the common opinion), others by Olympus, others by Hyagnis, others by Telpsichore. Pliny, book 7, chapter 56, ascribes the invention of the oblique flute to Midas in Phrygia, and that of the double flute to Marsyas himself. His words are these: "Amphion invented music, Pan the pipe, Mercury the single pipe, Midas in Phrygia the oblique flute, Marsyas the double flutes." Aristotle, moreover, in book 8 of the Politics, writes that the use of the flute was rejected, not so much because of the distortion of the face it causes, as because, as is said, Pallas also rejected it, on the ground that it was useless for understanding things. Pindar, however, makes Minerva the inventor of the flute for imitating lamentation, which has a deep sound. Most people, as I have said, hold that the flute was invented by Marsyas, the pipe (which the Hebrews call nekab [נקאב], from nakab [נקב], to bore through, that is, from its holes, and which the Greeks call syrinx [σύριγξ], though that word is often taken for the flute) by Apollo or Mercury, and the lyre.

units.la: De tibiarum variis generibus & nominibus vide Seruium in nonum Æneid. versum illum.
units.tr: On the various kinds and names of flutes, see Servius on that verse of the ninth book of the Aeneid.
O truly Phrygian, etc.

units.la: Quantum ad tibiarum materiam attinet, illam conflat olim fuisse buxum, ex qua etiamnum bodie conficiuntur: unde Buxea a Poëtis appellatur. Ovidius duodecimo Metamorph. Non illos cithare: non illos carmina vocum: Longa, multifori delelit tibia buxi: Multiforis, id est, multa foramina habentis. Sic Mantuanus: Buxea quid letos modulatur tibia cantus?
units.tr: As far as the material of flutes is concerned, it is established that they were once made of boxwood, from which they are still made today; hence the poets call them "boxen." Ovid in the twelfth book of the Metamorphoses: "Not the lyres, not the songs of voices, but the long flute of many-holed boxwood dulled them." That is, "many-holed," having many holes. So Mantuan: "Why does the boxen flute sound out happy songs?"

units.la: Ex alia quoq; materia, preter buxum, tibiam confici fuisse solitam testantur Athenaeus, Plinius & alii. Athenaeus e loti ligno, quod in Africa nascitur, confectam docet lib. 4. (unde Lotina fit dita:) item ex ebore (unde elephantina quæ primum a Phænicibus fit pertusa) & ex calamo, unde Tityrina, Graece τιτυρινα: & τιτυρινος nuncupari, qui calamo canunt: quales feré sunt pastoralia, qui flipulas inflant. Idem docet, tibiam etiam ex eruribus hominis a Thebanis primum repertam esse. Plinius lib. 16. cap. 36. de materia tibiae sic scribit: Sed tunc ex sua quamque tantam barundine congruere perfusum erat: & eam, quae redicem antecessebat, laeve tibia conjungere: quae cacumen dextra. Nunc sacrifice Thuscorum e buxo; ludicra vero loto, ossibus, aliisque argento fiunt. Sic ex gruum quoq; tibiis eam confectam olim, dictum est supra.
units.tr: Writers such as Athenaeus, Pliny and others attest that flutes were also commonly made of other materials besides boxwood. Athenaeus, in book 4, teaches that they were made of the wood of the lotus, which grows in Africa (hence called "lotine"); likewise of ivory (hence "elephantine," which the Phoenicians first pierced), and of reed, whence the "tityrine," in Greek titurina, and those who play on reeds are called titurinoi; such are generally the pastoral pipers, who blow on stalks. The same author teaches that the flute was also first invented by the Thebans from the leg-bones of men. Pliny, book 16, chapter 36, writes thus about the material of the flute: "But at that time each flute was made of its own reed, and a smooth flute was joined to the root-end, and the one with the top end was joined on the right. Now the sacred flutes of the Tuscans are made of boxwood, while the playful ones are made of lotus, bone, and other materials, even silver." So it was said above that flutes were once also made from the bones of cranes.
So much for the material of flutes.

units.la: Quantum ad illarum usum attinet; Alcibiadem legimus duplicinomine omnem tibiarum usum damnasse, & quod sic mutet oris habitum, ut vix vel a familiarissimis aguoscipositi, qui tibiâ canit: & quod hominis propriam adimat vocem omnem, loquendi facultate præripiat. Nemo enim simul et tibiam inflare & loquipotest. Cantant igitur, dicere solebat, Thebanorum filii, qui loqui nesciunt: nobis autem Atheniensibus gentis nostræ principes sunt Pallas & Apollo: quorum illa flutulam coufregit, hic tibicinem excoriavit, qua quidem oratione, ut acutior est. Plutarchus in ejus vita, Atticæ juventuti perfusit, ut tibiarum usum rejiceret, atq; repudiaret. Porro proditum prisrorum fabulis est, Palladem ad speculum tibiâ canentem, offensam oris sui deformitate, quam in speculo confexerat, tibiam projecisse comminuisse. Apolloneum autem Marsyam, tibiae inventorem, canendo a se victum excoriasse. In eandem sententiam Plato in Protagora, sermone qui de Poësi habetur, similem esse dixit tibialium & plebeiorum concertationis, exbilarare ob insitam nequeunt, magnificiant tibicinas, & luculenta mercede tibiarum alienam vocem conducunt, quarum sono ad conviuium & congressum in vitantur, cum nusquam apud bonos, probos, ac eruditos convivas saltatrices, fidicinæ, citharedæ, citharicinæ, videantur, ut quiue citharistas et lusos ejusmodi, sibi sufficiant ad mutuam consuetudinem, sua ipsorum voce & loquentes vicissim, & sese audientes modestè, etiam complusculi si biberint. Idem & vos facitis, & Cynulce, dum bibitis, aut potius ebibitis, tibicine more vel saltricis voluptatem, quam hi sermones afferunt, interturbantes, vitamq; ut in Phileto idem Plato dixit, non hominem vivere sed pulmonis cujusdam marinis aut cujusdam ex illis corporibus, quæ animata teflis ostreorum assinguntur. Hæc Athenaeus: quibus addea, quæ apud Plutarchum habentur in quæstionibus sympo-
units.tr: As for their use, we read that Alcibiades condemned the whole use of flutes on two grounds: that it so distorts the face that the player is scarcely recognised even by his closest friends; and that it takes away the man's proper voice altogether and robs him of the power of speech. For no one can blow a flute and speak at the same time. "Let the sons of the Thebans, who do not know how to speak, play the flute," he used to say; "but for us Athenians, the leaders of our people are Pallas and Apollo, of whom she broke the flute, and he flayed the flute-player." That speech, as is more pointed, Plutarch in his Life of him says, persuaded the youth of Attica to reject and repudiate the use of flutes. Moreover, it is related in the old fables that Pallas, playing the flute before a mirror, was offended by the ugliness of her face which she saw there, and threw the flute away and broke it; and that Marsyas, the inventor of the flute, having been defeated by Apollo in playing, was flayed by him. To the same effect Plato in the Protagoras, in the discussion about poetry, said that the contest of those who cannot cheer themselves at drinking parties without flute-girls is like that of the common people: they hire flute-girls at a high price and buy another's voice, and they are kept away from conversation and company by the sound of the flutes; whereas among good, honest and learned guests, dancing-girls, harpists, citharists and players of the cithara are never seen, but they are content with their own voices for their mutual company, speaking and listening to one another in a moderate way, even when they have drunk a good deal. "You do the same," he says, "and you, Cynulcus, while you drink, or rather drain your cups, disturb with the flute-girl's pleasure the talk that these conversations bring, and you live, as Plato says again in the Philebus, not as a man but as some sea-lung or some one of those bodies that are attached, alive, to the shells of oysters." So far Athenaeus; to these may be added what is found in Plutarch's Table Talk.

units.la: iacus, lib. 2. quæst. 7. An tibicines sint adhibendi convivio?
units.tr: Book 2, question 7: Should flute-players be admitted to a banquet?

units.la: Aristoteles quoq; Politicorum libro 9. capite 6. tibiarum usum omnem videtur improbasse. Sic enim scribit: ὥστε ἀνδρὸς εἰς πολιτείαν ἀκήκοεν, ἵνα ἄλλο τεχνικὸν ὄργανον, οἷον κιθάραν, ἢ τι τοιοῦτον ἐτιδέον ἔστι, ἀλλ' ἔσται ποιεῖν ἀνθρώπ ἀκροατῶν ἢ ἄλλο, εἰς ἐστι. Neg, tibiae ad discipulos [?] sunt adducendae, neq; aliud quod vis organum artificiale, ut citharam, aut si quid aliud ejusmodi, sed quaecunque facunt auditores bonos. Vide eundem libro octavo, capite sexto: ubi de Musica canitur, agit, ibi multa organa Musicae veteris, ut psaltes, barbitos, & quae ad voluptates eorum pertinent, qui cantores audiunt, ut septangula, fi ve septagona, trigona, fambucas, & omnia, quae scientiam in manum opere munere, desiderant, repudianda esse existimat. Et hoc putat afferendam fabulam illam de Minerva, quam fiuxerunt, ut paulo ante dictum, tibiasa se repertas, o ut deformitate offensam & flomachatam abjecisse. Hoc significare volunt Veteres, tibiarum inflandarum disciplinam, cum nihil ad mentis agitationem conferat, ascernandam: cum Minervæ scientia & ars tribuatur.
units.tr: Aristotle too, in book 9 of the Politics, chapter 6, seems to have disapproved of every use of flutes. For he writes: "Nor are flutes to be brought in to the pupils, nor any other artificial instrument, such as the cithara, or anything of that kind, but whatever makes the listeners good" [ὥστε ἀνδρὸς εἰς πολιτείαν ἀκήκοεν, ἵνα ἄλλο τεχνικὸν ὄργανον, οἷον κιθάραν, ἢ τι τοιοῦτον ἐτιδέον ἔστι, ἀλλ' ἔσται ποιεῖν ἀνθρώπ ἀκροατῶν ἢ ἄλλο, εἰς ἐστι]. See the same author in book 8, chapter 6, where he discusses music, and where he thinks that the many old instruments of music, such as the psaltery, the barbiton, and those that serve the pleasures of those who listen to singers, namely the heptagon or seven-sided instrument, the trigon, the sambuca, and all that require skill in the hand and effort in the work, ought to be rejected. And he thinks that the fable that they invented about Minerva, which, as I said a little before, says that she invented the flute and threw it away, offended and disgusted by its ugliness, should be applied to this. The ancients wish this to mean that the discipline of blowing flutes, since it contributes nothing to the activity of the mind, is to be rejected, since skill and art are ascribed to Minerva.

units.la: Sic Pythagoras lyra organo usus esse dicitur: tibiae autem sonitum, tanquam illiberalem & tumultuarium explosisse, ut Nicolaus Scutellius testatur in descriptione vitae Pythagorae ex Iamblicho.
units.tr: So Pythagoras is said to have used the lyre as his instrument, but to have rejected the sound of the flute as vulgar and disorderly, as Nicolaus Scutellius testifies in his account of the life of Pythagoras, drawn from Iamblichus.

units.la: Legimus tamen apud Iudaeos tibiarum tantum magno fuisse in usu: & quidem maximè in publicis conviviis, & quae conviviia plurima, comitantur, tripudiis atque choreis profanis, quem admodum Deus per Prophetam Isaiam gravissimè reprehendit capite quinto verbis: Vae ius, qui mane surgunt ad sectandum ebrietatem, simul ac vesperi vinum ipsos incendit! Et quorum inconvivis sunt citharae, tympanum & tibia & vinum: & opus Domini non respiciunt, & factum manuum ejus non vident. Enexpressam nestrorum temporum morum imaginem.
units.tr: Yet we read that among the Jews the flute was in great use, and especially at public banquets, which were accompanied by very many feasts, dancing and profane choruses. God strongly rebukes this through the prophet Isaiah in chapter 5, in these words: "Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness, who stay up late until wine inflames them! Whose feasts have harps, timbrel, flute and wine; but they do not regard the work of the Lord, nor see the deed of his hands." This is a portrait of the manners of our own times.

units.la: Sed in Regum quoque unctione & inauguratione adhibitas fuisse tibias, vel illud unicum Samuelis exemplum satis docet primo Regum capite primo, versu quadragesimo. Nam cum is in Regem ungeretur, omnis populus magno tibiarum sono totam urbem reple visse dicitur.
units.tr: But that flutes were also used at the anointing and inauguration of kings is sufficiently shown by that single example of Samuel, in the first book of Kings, chapter 1, verse 40. For when he was anointed king, all the people are said to have filled the whole city with the great sound of flutes.

units.la: Prophetas quoq; tibiis usos fuisse ex primo Samuelis libro, capite decimo, versu quinto videlicet: Postea venies in collem Dei, in quo deorum sunt praefecti Palaestinorum. Quum autem ingressus fuerit illuc in urbem, obviam habebis coetum Prophetarum, descendentium de excelso, & ante eos erunt lyra, tympanum, & tibia, & cithara, & ipsi prophetantes.
units.tr: That the prophets also used flutes is shown from the first book of Samuel, chapter 10, verse 5, namely: "Afterwards you will come to the hill of God, where is the garrison of the Philistines. And when you come there into the city, you will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place, and before them there will be a lyre, a timbrel, a flute and a harp, and they themselves prophesying."

units.la: Rabbini volunt haec instrumenta musica adhibita fuisse a Prophetis, animos suos recreandi exhilarandi gratia, quod Spiritus Domini requirit animum latum & hilarem: maestum autem & triste mem fugiat.
units.tr: The rabbis hold that these musical instruments were used by the prophets to refresh and cheer their spirits, because the Spirit of the Lord requires a broad and cheerful mind, and flees a sad and gloomy one.

units.la: His adde, quod apud Israelem quidem fidelium gaudium, quo sint affici propter Assyriorum eladem: apud Hieremiam autem ira Domini & vindictae divinae adversus Moabitas comminatio tibiarum similitudine illustratur: ex quibus duobus locis patet, tibias & in laetitia & in luctu fuisse adhibitas. Idem luculentissimè colligitur ex miraculo illo Christi, Matthaei nono capite, verse tertio: Et quum venisset Iesus domum praefecti Synagogae, videns tibicines (&c.) & turbam tumultuantem, dixit eis: Recedite, &c. Hinc diserte conflat, tibias pertinere inter alia etiam ad funebrem usum: quem quidem morem tudei a profanis gentibus hauserant: ut et reliquas funerum pompas, licet inhibuisset Dominus in Lege.
units.tr: Add to this that among the Israelites there was the joy of the faithful, with which they were to be moved over the slaughter of the Assyrians. In Jeremiah, the wrath of the Lord and the threat of divine vengeance against the Moabites are illustrated by the likeness of pipes. From these two passages it is clear that pipes were used both in rejoicing and in mourning. The same is most clearly gathered from that miracle of Christ in Matthew chapter nine, verse three: "And when Jesus came into the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and saw the pipers (etc.) and the crowd making a tumult, he said to them: Depart, etc." From this it is plainly evident that pipes served, among other things, also for funeral use. The Jews had taken this custom from the profane nations, as they had also taken the other funeral pomps, although the Lord had forbidden them in the Law.

units.la: Apud Gentiles tibiarum usus latissimè patuit, ut etiam cotidie Musicae sive vocalis, sive organicae & instrumentalis. Earum igitur usus fuit & publicis & privatis, & scenicus sive theatricus, & bellicus, & pastoritius, & convivialis, & nuptialis, & denique funebris, & sacrificialis: de quo multa Athenaeus libro quarto & decimoquarto. Oratorius quoque tibiarii fuit usus. Non solum enim cantantes et Musici, sed etiam Oratores aliquando adhibendos sibi tibicines exiliam verunt: id quod docet Caji Gracchi, clarissimi sui aetatis Oratoris, exemplum, cui conscionanti, confliens posterum Musicus tibia, quam Tonariam vocant, modos ministrabat, quibus deberet intendi.
units.tr: Among the Gentiles the use of pipes was very widespread, as was music in general every day, whether vocal, or instrumental and played on instruments. Pipes were therefore used in public and in private, in the theatre and on the stage, in war, among shepherds, at banquets, at weddings, and finally at funerals and in sacrifices. Athenaeus writes much about this in books four and fourteen. The pipe was also used in oratory. For not only singers and musicians, but sometimes orators too, had pipers brought in to accompany them. The example of Gaius Gracchus, the most famous orator of his age, shows this: while he was speaking, a musician standing behind him with the pipe, which they call the Tonarian pipe, supplied him with the modes by which his voice should be pitched.

units.la: Sed nos hic de tibiarum usu sacrosanc, sive sacrificiali quodam addemus, quae institutio nostro mâ-ximè cenveniunt. Hinc tibiae sacrae dictae a Telesle Poëta, ut est apud Athenaeum libro decimo quarto. Ejus versus hi sunt, quibus tibiarum usus declaratur: Phrygum rex leniter personantium tibiarum sacrarum Cantum primus in venit, Dorice Musae equiparandum Aemulum: varie modulatum tenebrosi spiritus Aurum levem atque pernitem (unde aulos Graece a flatu volunt dictam) arum dine compellens.
units.tr: But here we shall add something about the use of pipes in sacred, or rather sacrificial, rites, which especially suits our purpose. Hence the pipes were called sacred by the poet Telestes, as is found in Athenaeus, book fourteen. His verses, in which the use of pipes is described, are these: "The king of the Phrygians was the first to come up with the sacred pipes, which sound softly, a rival to be matched with the Dorian Muses, playing in varied modes, drawing forth from the dark breath a light and swift air (whence some say the aulos was named from the blast)."

units.la: Ovidius ad hunc usum sacrum alludens sexto Fastorum sit canit: Quaeritur in scena tava tibia: quaeritur aris.
units.tr: Ovid, alluding to this sacred use, sings in the sixth book of the Fasti: "The pipe is sought on the stage; it is sought at the altars."

units.la: Hinc Sacrifia a Seneca appellata & a Plinio: Seneca: Sacrifica dulces tibia effundat modos Et Plinius loco ante citato: Nunc sacrificae Thusicorum tibia ex buxo &c.
units.tr: Hence pipes were called sacrificial by Seneca and by Pliny. Seneca: "Let the sacrificial pipe pour forth sweet strains." And Pliny in the passage cited above: "Now the sacrificial pipes of the Thusci, of boxwood, etc."

units.la: Apud Romanos tibicines sacrorum camsía plurimi siebant, magnusq; illa tribucus est bonos Idibus Ianuarij,ut scribit Plutarchus Quastione quinquagesima quinta,Romanarū. Illo enim die ipsis permissum erat vestem induti mulierem totam ut bene circuire, cuius mores bene rationem reddit Plutarchus. Cur Idibus Ianuarii tibicinibus permissum est per urbem circuire, vestem induti mulierem? An hoc fit propter caussam,quæ subiungitur; Magnos illos honores Numa rex religionis caussa contulerat. Quibus cum postea tribunis militum cōsulari potestate Rempub.administrantibus priuarentur,uniuersi Roma Tibur secesserunt,desiderata inde,quod religio animos tenebat Romanorū,neminēe sacrificium præcineret, accusatū, cum non obtemperarent, sed Tibure manerent,libertate quidam magistratibus promisit occulte, seeos Romam reduxurū. Instructo proinde pollustu, tanquam fi Dij rem sacram cessisset , inuitat tibicines, adhiberu etiam con- uiuium mulieribus,& per totam noctem compotatio,jocis choreaq;, protrahitur:tum subito sistis trepidatione,in proviso patroni super uenīle perturbatum est,persnademus tibicinibus, ut vehicula circumquaq; pedibus obstecla conscendant, Tibur se eos re veslurum dolose promittens: tibi circumastus, uehiculos eos, qui per tenebrulentes &t tenebras animad vertere, ubi locorum essent, nequibant, universos Romam primū luce perseverant autem pleriq; restibus florīdis & mulieribus amissi ob noctu rnam comessationem & conuiuium. Exinde cum magistraus tibicines s gratiam redierunt, decreuerūt, est ut tali habiuis istum diem eis per urbem vagari licaret. Hęc Plutarchus.
units.tr: Among the Romans there were very many pipers of the sacred rites, and on the Ides of January a great privilege was granted to them, as Plutarch writes in Roman Question fifty-five. On that day it was permitted to them to go about the city dressed as women, and Plutarch gives the reason for this custom: why on the Ides of January the pipers were allowed to go about the city dressed as women. Is it because of the cause that follows? King Numa had granted those great honours for the sake of religion. When later the pipers were deprived of them, while military tribunes governed the state with consular power, they all withdrew from Rome to Tibur. Since the religion which held the minds of the Romans was lacking, no one was left to sing at the sacrifices. The magistrates, accusing them because they would not return but stayed at Tibur, secretly promised them liberty and promised to bring them back to Rome. Then, as if the rites of the gods were being neglected, they prepared a feast, invited the pipers, and also brought in women to the banquet, and the drinking, jesting and dancing were kept up through the whole night. Then suddenly, with the pipers now drunk, they persuaded them to climb into carts, which were fastened about with wheels, falsely promising that they would be returned to Tibur. When the pipers had been taken away in the carts, they were carried through the night, and as they could not tell where they were, they were brought all the way to Rome at dawn. Most of them, however, were still wearing garlands and were dressed in women's clothes, worn out by the all-night revelry and banquet. Afterwards, when the magistrates had restored the pipers to favour, they decreed that they should be allowed to wander through the city in such dress on that day. Plutarch says this.

units.la: Ejusdem rei atq; secessionis tibicinum ex urbe Liuius quoq; meminit Decade prima,libro nono: Tibicines,inquit,quis prohibiti a prox mu censoribus erant in ede Ioui sesci, quod translu antiquitus erat, ægre passi Tiburno agminea abierunt: adeo ut nemo in urbe esset, quæ sacrificiū præcineret. Ejus rei religio tenui Senatum, legatosq; Tibur miserunt, ut darent operam, ut isti homines Romanis restitucerentur. Tiburtini benigne pollicit i,primū accitos in euriam hortati sunt,ut reuerterentur Romam, postquam perpelli nequibant,consilio habest abhorrente ab inge- nio hominum,eos aggrediuntur. Die festo alia alios per speciem celebrandi ritum canticum eorum canssa inuitant,& uino,cuius asuidum fermē genus est,suneratos sopiunt: atq; ita in plaustra somno uistos conjiciunt ac Romam deportant : nec prius sensere, quam planstrum in foro relistu plnos crapulæ eos lux oppressit. Tunc concursus populi sastius simperatuq; ut manerent,darum,ut triduum quotannis ornati cum cantu,atq; hac,quæ nunc solennis est li.en.ta per urbem vagarentur: restituturū, in æde rescendi ius isi,qui sacrū præcinerent. Eum refert ea quoq; illa,quæ Va- ro scribet libro quinto de lingua Latina: Quinquatrus,inquit,Minuscula dicta sunt sunt similitudine Maiorus quiđ tibicines tunc festiuissent ad aduersu Miner vaeum.
units.tr: Livy also mentions this same withdrawal of the pipers from the city, in the ninth book of the first Decade: "The pipers," he says, "who had been forbidden by the censors from the temple of Jupiter, where it had long been customary, took it badly and withdrew in a body to Tibur. So much so that no one was left in the city who could sing at the sacrifices. The Senate, troubled by the religious consequences, sent envoys to Tibur to see that these men were restored to the Romans. The Tiburtines promised kindly, and first invited them into their council and urged them to return to Rome. When they could not be persuaded, they resorted to a plan unworthy of the character of men: on a feast day they invited them one after another, under the pretext of celebrating a rite and to make use of their singing, and when they had overcome them with wine, to which they were almost universally addicted, they put them to sleep, loaded them asleep into wagons and carried them to Rome. They did not notice until the wagon had stopped in the forum, and the daylight overtook them, still oppressed by their drunkenness. Then a crowd of people gathered, and they were begged to stay; and they were granted that they should wander through the city for three days each year, dressed and singing, as is now the solemn custom. The privilege of performing in the temple was restored to those who sang at the sacrifices." Varro also records this, in what he writes in the fifth book of his work on the Latin language: "The Quinquatrus," he says, "were called the Lesser Quinquatrus by analogy with the Greater, because the pipers then held their festival in opposition to Minerva."

units.la: Hostias apud Romanos ad præconem & tibicinem immoluri fuisse solitas illa quoq; Ciceronis clare testantur in oratione contra Rullum: Erant, inquit, bostia majores,in foro constitutæ, quæ iis prætoribus de tribunali, ficuta nobis Consulibus de consilia sententia probata ad præconē & tibicinem immolabantur.Idem libro secundo de Legibus: Populare lætitiam,inquit,in cantu & fidibus,& tibiis moderanto eamq; cum Diuim honore jungunto.Idem eodem libro: iam ludi publici,inquit,cum sint carea,circoq; diuisi,sint corporum certatione,cursu & pugillatione, la- statione curriculisq; equorum usq; ad certam victoriam circo conslitutis:cantu,canticū, ac fidibus et tibiis, dum modo ea moderata sint,ut lege præscribitur. Assentior enim Platoni,nihil eam facilé in animos teneros atq; molles influere,quam uarios dicendi sonos,quorum dici vix potest,quam ta fit uis in utramq; partem. Namque & incitat languentes & languefacit exsistatos: & iuñ remittit animos,tum contrahit : eiuscatum hoc mulierum in Græcia interfuit antiquum nonum seruare modum:quarum mores lapsi, ad mollitiem parūter sunt inimicati cum cantibus:aut hac dulcedine corruptelaq; depravati,ut quidam putant.
units.tr: Cicero's clear testimony in his speech against Rullus also shows that animals were customarily sacrificed among the Romans to the herald and the piper: "There were," he says, "the greater sacrificial victims, set up in the forum, which under those praetors were sacrificed from the tribunal, just as for us consuls the sacrifices are offered, by the approved decision of the council, to the herald and the piper." The same author in the second book of the Laws: "Let them moderate the people's joy," he says, "with song, with the lyre and with the pipes, and join it to the honour of the gods." The same author in the same book: "Now, public games, since they are of two kinds, those in the arena and those in the circus, consist of contests of bodies, running, boxing, wrestling and chariot racing, with horses in the circus up to a fixed victory; of song, of singing, and of the lyre and pipes, provided only that they are moderate, as the law prescribes. For I agree with Plato that nothing flows more easily into tender and soft minds than varied sounds of speech, and it can hardly be said how great their power is in either direction. For they both stir up the languid and make the excited languid; and they both relax the minds and contract them. And this is the reason why the women in Greece once kept the ancient custom of a fixed measure: when their morals had slipped, they became hostile to softness along with the songs, or, as some think, were corrupted and depraved by this sweetness and corruption."

units.la: Tertera etiam in consecratione adhibitum fuisse tibicinem idem austor teslatur in Oratione pro Domo.
units.tr: The same orator also testifies in his speech for his house that a piper was used even in the consecration.

units.la: Matutinis quoq; vocum tibiarumq; cantionibus solitos fuisse Gentiles Deos suos salutare, illa Arnobii verba libro septimo satis ostendunt : Etiam ne Dii aera tinnitibus & quassationibus Cymbalorum ( afficiuntur? ) Etiamne tympanus? Etiamne symphonias? Quid assiduntur pius pitus Scabillorum? ut cum eos audierint Numina,bonorificè secum exi∫timent a∫ium, & ser̃ vero ues animos irarum obliviione deponant? An nunquid ut parvuli pu∫iones ab inepti᷑ vagitibus crepitaculis exterrentur auditus:eadem ratione & omnipotentia Numina tibiarū ∫tridore mulcentur & ad numerum Cymbalorum mollia indignatione flacefcunt? Quid ∫ibi volit,inquit, excitationes ille,quas canitis maturini,collatus ad tibiam vocibus? Condormi∫cunt enim Superi,remeare ut ad vigilias debeant? Quid dormitiones illæ, quibus bene ut ∫aleant,au∫picabili∫a lucatione mandatus? Somni enim quiete ∫ol'untur,occuparü ut hoc po∫sint lenes audienda ∫unt nene?
units.tr: That the Gentiles were accustomed to greet their gods with morning songs of voices and pipes is sufficiently shown by these words of Arnobius in the seventh book: "Are the gods moved by the clashing of bronze and the rattling of cymbals? By drums too? By harmonies? Why are the pipes of the shepherds' flutes played for them? So that when the divinities have heard them, they may think them honoured and lay aside the memory of their anger? Or, as small children are frightened into silence by rattles when they cry foolishly, are the gods, in the same way, quieted by the shrillness of pipes and softened, through indignation, to the rhythm of cymbals? What do those awakenings mean, which you sing at dawn, set against the voice of the pipe? Do the gods fall asleep, so that they must return to their watches? What do those slumbers mean, by which, so that they may be well, they are bidden to be lulled with auspicious singing? For the gods are loosed by the quiet of sleep; so are these gentle sounds to be heard, in order that they may occupy them?"

units.la: Hujus usus tibicinum in sacris meminit etiam Suetonius in vita Tiberii,his verbis: Et quo primum die post excessum Augusti curiam intravit,quasi pietati,simul ac religioni satis factur̃e, Minois exemplo, cure quidem ac vino, verum sine tibicine supplicavit, ut ille olim in morte filii. Id cur sactum sit cum a Minoe,cum a Tiberio, ejus exemplo, Beroaldus hanc rationem reddit, quod Musica in luctu importuna res sit: quanquam tibiisnes sacrificiis quidem praecinere solitos Historici tradiderunt. Unde O'vidius:
units.tr: Suetonius also mentions this use of pipers in sacred rites, in the life of Tiberius, in these words: "And on the first day after Augustus's death, when he entered the senate house, as if he had sufficiently satisfied both piety and religion, he prayed after the example of Minos, with a garland and wine, but without a piper, as Minos once did at the death of his son." Why this was done both by Minos and by Tiberius, after his example, Beroaldus gives this reason: that music is an unseemly thing in mourning, although the historians have handed down that pipers were accustomed to sing at sacrifices. Hence Ovid:
She sang at the temples, she sang with the pipe at the games.

Τὰ ἑ ταια ἡ τα ρ σ υ ε π ρ α ᾳ ηςτα ςὸ ἐν ἱ ἱ e Romanos ποῖ ἀ ταῖσ ε ἀ ἡ ἐ ἐκ ἐ ἑ ᾳ Halicar- nallum.
units.tr: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in the seventh book of his Roman Antiquities, describes the use of pipes in the sacred games and sacrifices of the Greeks and Romans, and writes thus: "After all the choirs, the lyre-players and the blind pipers were brought in [the Greek is too garbled in the scan to render exactly]." He says that the pipers and lyre-players also played at the sacrifices, both at the altars and in the sacred processions, and that their music was pleasing to the gods. [The Greek text in the scan is corrupt and only partly legible.] Dionysius writes this about the Romans.

units.la: Pleasing Roman gods and rites: see also Pachymer and Dioni. ille, Ibili Αἰδιλ tas porró sequebantur saltatorum chori, di𝔳isi trifariam; primò virorum, deinceps impuberum, postremò puerorū: post quos tibicines instantes antiqui morù tibias breves, quarum bursa permansit usus; cithariftaq, pulsantes eburneas septem fidium lyras, & quae vocantur baubitae; quorum vtus apud Graecos vsus meo tempore desiit: apud Romanos vero adhibentur omnibus ausiquis sacris. Hallenus Halicarnassaeus.
units.tr: Then came the choruses of dancers, divided into three companies: first the men, then the youths, and last the boys. After them came the pipers, who played the old short pipes, whose use still survives in the form of the bursa, and the citharists, who played seven-stringed lyres of ivory, and the instruments called baubitae. The use of these last among the Greeks ceased in my time, but among the Romans they are employed at all sacred rites. Thus far Dionysius of Halicarnassus.

units.la: His adde, quae Plutarchus in libello de Musica scribit: Quin & Hyperboreorum inquit, sacra adhibitis tibiis, citharis & fistulis in Delum missa referunt antiquitus. Sunt qui ipsum Deum tibia cecinisse autument: ut narrat optimus cantilenarum conditor Alcman. Carmina e Minerva didicisse tibiis canere Apollinem ajt: Iteaq veneranda prorsus est Musica, Deorum inventum cum sit. Et paulló ante, eodem libello: Sed quoniam simul veteres sibicinum et citharaedorum nomos reculimus, transfibimus jam ad tibicinum nomos. Traditum est enim Olympum, cum esset tibiten, e Phrygia, tibicinum nomum fecisse in Apollinem. Hunc Olympum ajunt a rum fuisse eorum, qui de fenderunt a primo Olympo, Marsyae discipulo, qui nomos in Deos fecit. Is enim cum amasius esset Marsyae, & ab eo artem tibia canenai didicisset, harmonicos nomos in Graeciam intulit, quibus nūc Graeci utuntur in ferijs Deorum. Ac omnino in toto illo libello Musicae digtatem in de probat, quòd non tam humanum, quàm divinum sit in ventum Musica, quod, in choreis, ludis & sacrificijs illa sit adhibita. Vide eadem de re etiam Apuleium: nec non Seruius illa Virgilij: Desidie tordi juvat indulgere choreis Et pacem assuetis biforum dat tibia cantum.
units.tr: To this add what Plutarch writes in his little book On Music: "Indeed, the sacred rites of the Hyperboreans, when sent to Delos, were traditionally performed with pipes, cithers and flutes. Some think that the god himself played the pipe, as the excellent composer of songs Alcman relates. Apollo, it is said, learned to play the pipe from Minerva; therefore music is truly to be venerated, since it is an invention of the gods." And a little before, in the same book: "But since we have at the same time treated the old nomes of the pipers and the citharists, let us now pass on to the nomes of the pipers. It is handed down that Olympus, who was a piper from Phrygia, composed a pipers' nome in honour of Apollo. They say this Olympus was one of those who descended from the first Olympus, the pupil of Marsyas, who made nomes to the gods. For he, being the beloved of Marsyas and having learned the art of playing the pipe from him, brought the harmonic nomes into Greece, which the Greeks still use at the festivals of the gods." Indeed, throughout that whole little book Plutarch shows that music is not so much a human as a divine invention, since it was used in choirs, games and sacrifices. See the same matter also in Apuleius, and Servius on those lines of Virgil: "The pipe grants the pleasure of indulging in the choruses of idle leisure, and gives peace with its two-fold song to those accustomed to it."

units.la: De eodem bor tibiarum, fistularum, citharārumq; usu antiquissimo in sacris videre licet etiā Leonicum de varia historia, u pite decimo quarto: ubi inter alia Deli antiquissimum Apollinis simulacrum, quod Herculei cum Meropibus colloca verit, dexterā quidem manu arcum; alterā vero tres cum Musicae instrumentis retinuisse Gratias tesătur: quarum una lyram; altera tibias; tertia vero inter has media fistulam manu gesta verit.
units.tr: The very ancient use of pipes, flutes and lyres in sacred rites may also be seen in Leonicus, On Varied History, book fourteen. There, among other things, he records that the most ancient image of Apollo at Delos, which was placed beside the Hercules and the Meropes, held a bow in its right hand, while in its left hand it held three Graces with musical instruments: one holding a lyre, another pipes, and the third, standing between them, holding a flute.

units.la: Ac hu jusmodi quidem tibiarum sacrificarum: & quidem geminarum, atq; tibicinum aliquot imagines cernere licet in sacrificiis illis, quae in nobili illa Tr. ijani columna sunt expressae, de qua supra.
units.tr: Images of this kind of sacred pipes, indeed of two pipes together, and of several pipers, can be seen in those sacrifices carved on the famous column of Trajan, which I mentioned above.

units.la: Porrò cum tibiis saepe conjunguntur fistulae, lyrae, citharae, fidra, cymbala, tympana, quae in Gentilium sacris fuerunt adhibita. Sed tubarum quoque, buccinarum, lituorum, cornuum usus non apud Iudaeos tantum, sed etiam apud Gentiles magnum fuisse in sacris & sacrificiis ipsorum usum passim antiqua litterarum monumenta testantur. Armilustrium, ut aje Festus, festum erat apud Romanos, quo res divinas armati faciebant: ac dum sacrificarent, tuba canebant. Tubilustrium, lustrium, ut auctor est Varro, dictum, quod eo die in atrio sutorio tubae lustrantur. Sic Festus: Tubilustria dies appellabatur, in quibus agná tubas lustrabant: quibus diebus adscriptum in Fasti erat, cum in atrio sutorio agná tubæ lustrantur, ab eis tubos appellant: quod genus lustrationis ex Arcadia Pallanteo translatum ac venisse dicunt. O vidius: Proxima Volcani lux est, Tubilustria dicunt Lustrantur purae, quas fuerit ille, tubae.
units.tr: Moreover, pipes are often joined with flutes, lyres, cithers, fiddles, cymbals and drums, which were used in the rites of the Gentiles. And ancient written records testify everywhere that the use of trumpets, horns, litui and cornets was great in the sacred rites and sacrifices not only of the Jews but also of the Gentiles. According to Festus, the Armilustrium was a Roman festival on which the men performed sacred rites under arms, and while they sacrificed, they sounded trumpets. The Tubilustrium, as Varro says, got its name because on that day the trumpets were purified in the Shoemakers' Court. Festus says: "The day was called Tubilustria, on which they purified the trumpets; on those days it was written in the calendar that the trumpets were purified in the Shoemakers' Court, and they call them tubae from the sound. This kind of purification, they say, was brought from Arcadia, from Pallanteum." Ovid: "Next after the day of Vulcan is the Tubilustria, when the trumpets, pure in whatever way they were made, are purified."

units.la: Et Tubicines, eodem teste, etiam ii appellantur, qui sacerdotes viri speciosi publicē sacra facibant, tubarum lustrandarum gratiā. Tubę, inquit Varro, a tubis, quos etiamnum ita appellant tubicines sacrorum. Tubicines sacrorum vocat, qui tubis in sacrarum administratione canebant.
units.tr: According to the same witness, those were also called tubicines who, as priests, publicly performed sacred rites for the purpose of purifying the trumpets. "Tubae," says Varro, "are named from the tubicines of the sacred rites, whom they still call by that name." He calls them the tubicines of the sacred rites, namely those who played the trumpets in the administration of the sacred things.

units.la: Calphurnius Eclogā prima. Altera regna Nume, quae primus o vantia cede Agmina Romulea & adbuc ardentia castris Paeis opus docuit, jussitq silentibus armis Iuter sacra tubas, non inter bella, sonare. Quemadmodum tuba andcum aliis instrumentis Musicis olim a Iudaeis ipsius Dei iussu in ipso-rum sacris fuerunt usurpata: ita Diabolus quoque, ceu Dei simia, praeter alia instrumenta Musica, tubas quoq; in sacerrimis sacrificiis, ac detestandis suis sacris eadem adhiberi & usurpari iussit, ut ex iis, quae supra astigi, & iis, quae mox sequentur, patet. Plutarchus in suis Sympo-siacis, ut Indaeos parvus tubis: ita Argivos quoq; in suis Dionysiis iisdem uti solitos fuisse scribit, ad Deum evocandum, libro quarto Problem. quinto. Eustathius Iliad. 2. sex tubarum genera enumerans, inter illas unam vocat Aegyptiam rotundam, quae κύρβυν sit dicta, qua Aegyptios ad sacra sua vsos fuisse, ejusq; clangore homines ad rem divinam convocasse scribit. Pollux similiter tubae ἀνὰ σάλπιγξ ἱερὸς ἡ τὴν ἐν σάλπιγξ dictae Suvias referit, id est, sonum sacrum sacrificialem, qui apud Aegyptios, Argivos, Tyrrhenos & Romanos in usu fuerit: indeq; tubicinem, qui in sacris tuba canebat (quod apud Iudaeos sacerdotum munus erat) ἱεροσάλπιγξ, sive melius, ἱερὸς σαλπιγξ, idest, tubicinem sacrum, & ἁλλομένη (forsan quia tuba clangore populum dimittebat) fuif-se appellatum.
units.tr: Calpurnius, Eclogue 1: "Numa, who first taught the Roman troops, still burning from their victories and camps, to be at peace, and ordered that trumpets should sound amid the sacred rites in silence of arms, not amid wars." Just as the trumpet, along with other musical instruments, was once used in the sacred rites of the Jews by God's own command, so the Devil, the ape of God, has likewise ordered that trumpets, besides other musical instruments, be employed and used in his most accursed sacrifices and in his detestable rites, as is clear from what I have touched on above and from what follows. Plutarch, in his Symposiacs, writes that the Argives also, like the Jews, customarily used trumpets in their Dionysia to call on the god; see book four, problem five. Eustathius, on the Iliad 2, enumerating six kinds of trumpets, calls one of them the Egyptian round trumpet, which was named kyrbis, and he writes that the Egyptians used it in their sacred rites and by its sound called men to divine worship. Pollux likewise tells of the trumpet called the sacred trumpet, and of the sacred sound made on it, which was in use among the Egyptians, Argives, Tyrrhenians and Romans. From this, he says, the trumpeter who played the trumpet in the sacred rites (which among the Jews was the office of priests) was called hierosalpinx, or better hieros salpinx, that is, the sacred trumpeter, and the sound was called [hallomene], perhaps because the trumpet's clangour dismissed the people.

units.la: Nunc de tibiarum ifflarum, nec non aliorum instrumentorum Musicorum, ut fistularum, lyrarum, cytharurum, cymbalorum, sistrorum, tympanorum, tubarum, buccinarum, litiorum, usus seu abusu potius Gentilium in sacris atq; sacrificiis quaedam sunt dicenda. Hasigitur ob causas, de quibus mox dicemus, instrumentorum istiorum Musicorum sono, seu strepitu potius usi fuerunt: Primum quidem ad sacra ista indicenda, & ad homines ad illa convocandos, ing, peractis ad illos rursus dimittendos, organorum istiorum flatu pulsuq; usi fuerunt.
units.tr: Now some things must be said about the use, or rather the abuse, of the Gentiles of pipes, and also of other musical instruments, such as flutes, lyres, cithers, cymbals, sistra, drums, trumpets, horns, litui, in their sacred rites and sacrifices. For these reasons, which we shall mention presently, they used the sound, or rather the noise, of these musical instruments: first, to announce these sacred rites and to summon men to them, and then, when the rites were finished, to dismiss them again, using the blowing and striking of these instruments.

units.la: Secundus illorum usus fuit, ut iis, qui sacris interessent, silentium, ut supra dixi, maxime necessarium indicerent, omnes ad taciturnam, diligensem, attentamq; sacrorum suorum administrationem meditationemq; excitarent.
units.tr: The second use of these instruments was to announce to those who took part in the sacred rites the silence which, as I said above, was most necessary, and to stir all of them to a quiet, diligent and attentive administration and meditation of their sacred rites.

units.la: Tertio ut quibus vis etiam aliis rebus asq; cerimoniis, quae in sacrificiis peragebantur; ita hoc quoq; suavi dulci, tibiarum aliorum q; instrumentorum sono, numero, modo Deos illos suos leni-ri, demulceri, placari, & ut ad se, quasi e caelo venirent, allici ac in vita ri posse sibi persuadebant.
units.tr: Thirdly, just as they used other rites and ceremonies in their sacrifices, so they also believed that by this sweet, pleasant sound of pipes and other instruments, sung in measure and mode, their gods could be soothed, softened and placated, and drawn to them as if they came down from heaven and were held there.

units.la: Quarto ut ebantur ista tibiarum, aliorumque organorum Musicorum cantu, eos, qui sacris intererant, exhilarandi, & ab omni tristitia ad laetitiam hilaritatemq; traducendi gratia, quam in sacris festisq; suis maxime requiri, Diis, quos colebant, placere arbitrabantur, secundum illa Ovidii: Dii quoq; ut a cunctis hilari pietate colantur, Tristitiam poni per sua festa jubent.
units.tr: Fourthly, by the singing of pipes and other musical instruments they were used to cheer those who attended the rites and to lead them from all sadness to gladness and cheerfulness. They thought the gods they worshipped especially required this cheerfulness in their sacred rites and festivals, following Ovid: "The gods too, that they may be worshipped with cheerful piety, command that sadness be put aside at their festivals."

units.la: Aristoteles οὕτως Politicorum ἱερὰ μάλλον, id est, sacros cantus dicit vim habere medicinae & pargationis ad animos componendos & sedandos.
units.tr: Aristotle, in the Politics, says that sacred songs have the power of a medicine and purgation for calming and settling the souls.

units.la: Quinto non deerant inter Gentiles, qui homines isti tibiarum, cymbalorum, aliorumq; instrumentorum sonis divinitus afflari & ad divinandum excitari opinabantur, ut Corybantes, Sa-baxio captos & eos, qui matrem Deorum furenter colebant. Hanc Porphyrii sententiam lamblichus in illo suo libro de mysteriis Aegyptiorum, segmento tertio, capite nono commemorat simul & refellit: ubi tamen Musicam magnam habere vim, & si soni, carmina atq; cantus, qui sin-gulis Diis sunt consecrati, atq; conveniunt, adhibeantur, ipsorum Deorum ad ventum atq; praesentiam effici posse confitetur.
units.tr: Fifthly, there were among the Gentiles some who believed that men were divinely inspired by the sounds of pipes, cymbals and other instruments and roused to prophesy, like the Corybantes, those possessed by Sabazius, and those who frenziedly worshipped the Mother of the gods. Iamblichus, in his book on the mysteries of the Egyptians, third section, ninth chapter, recalls and at the same time refutes this opinion of Porphyry. Yet there he admits that music has great power, and that if sounds, songs and chants that are consecrated to and fitting for each particular god are used, the coming and presence of the gods themselves can be brought about.

units.la: Sexto instrumentorum istiorum Musicorum sonitu atq; strepitu impedire conabantur, ne vel hostiarum, quae immolabatur, vel etiam hominum, ab iis, qui sacris interessent, voces lugubres, tri-stes & ominosae, quibus irrita possent fieri sacrificia, exaudirentur. Hujus rei clarum, manife-stum, exemplum & testimonium habemus in humanis illis sacrificiis; quae omnis humanitatis ex-pertia, immanitatum contra plenissima fuerunt: in quibus tympanorum, cymbalorum aliorumq; instrumentorum gravissimi soni pulsabantur, ne lamentabiles miseri funebrii illorum, quiligni cremabantur, fletus, ejulatus, clamores atque vociferationes, liberorum praesertim a parentibus exaudiantur, quibus illi (o horrenda, furiosam, monstrosam, prorsus Diabolicam impietatem!) ad commiserationem atq; tristitiam commoverentur. Idenim fieret, minime sacrificiis illis la-tari Numinaq; seu Daemonia potius sua placaripossel existimabant.
units.tr: Sixthly, they tried by the sound and din of these musical instruments to prevent the mournful, sad and ominous cries, of the victim being slaughtered or even of men, from being heard by those attending the rites, since these could render the sacrifices void. We have a clear, manifest example and proof of this in those human sacrifices, which were wholly without humanity and utterly full of savagery. In these the deepest sounds of drums, cymbals and other instruments were struck, so that the wretched lamentation, weeping, wailing and shrieks of the miserable victims who were burned, especially of children by their parents, should not be heard, lest the worshippers be moved to pity and sorrow. (O horrible, frenzied, monstrous, utterly diabolical impiety!) For they thought that unless this were done, the deities, or rather demons, would not delight in those sacrifices and could not be appeased.

units.la: Hūs adde posteremo, quòd hoc tibiarum aliorumq; organorum cantu, non solum Deos, quibus sacrificabant,net etiā homines tantum, qui sacrificiis illis intererant, sed ipsas quoq; bestias, immolabantur, lenire,demulcere,sicutare, & admmolationem mactationemq; patienter subeundam preparare quodam modo & aptas reddere conabantur.
units.tr: Finally, add to this that by the sound of pipes and other instruments they tried to soothe, soften and calm not only the gods to whom they sacrificed and the men who attended those sacrifices, but the very beasts that were slaughtered, and in some way to prepare them and make them fit to endure the immolation and killing patiently.

units.la: Atq; hæc quidem de tibiarum, aliorumq; instrumentorum musicorū usu sacrificialisfuit dicta, quibus admodum tonenunt ea, quæ apud Homerum sequuntur de mulierum quarundā, ut ipse loquitur, ὀλολυγῆ, id est, precatione quasi acclamatione, quæ bovum percussionem ac dejectionem in terram fuit consecuta. Nam postquam audax animosus ille & re & nomine Thrasymedes Nestoris filius securi feriit & abscidit cervicales bovis nervos, & idcirco bovis robur defecit, sequitur: —αἱ δ' ὀλόλυξαν Θυγατέρες τε νυοί τε καὶ αἰδοίη πεφνόντος Ipse verò ululabant. Filiæq; (Nestoris) nurus & pudica thori socia.
units.tr: These things have been said about the use of pipes and other musical instruments in sacrifice. Very well do they fit what follows in Homer about certain women who, as he says, [ὀλολυγή], a prayer or acclamation, followed the striking and felling of the ox. For after the bold and spirited Thrasymedes, son of Nestor, both in deed and in name, struck with an axe and cut through the neck sinews of the ox, so that its strength failed, the text continues: "But they ululated, the daughters and daughters-in-law and the venerable wife of the slain man." [αἱ δ' ὀλόλυξαν θυγατέρες τε νυοί τε καὶ αἰδοίη πεφνόντος]

units.la: Ὀλολύζειν, quid. Verbum ὀλολύζειν Eustathius adnotat τὴν γυναικείαν φωνὴν, id est, de precatione mulierbri dicta: eos vero, qui poëta Homerum vixerunt, verbum illud accipere pro κλαίειν (unde forsan nomen Flagen/id est, lugere: nisi quis malit clangore deducit) id est, plorare, sive pro ὁρκᾶν (unde forsan nostrum Grennen/vel Grinen/idem quod plorare.) Idem in illum versum Iliad. ζ. Αἰδ' ὀλολυγὴ πᾶσαι Ἀθηναῖαι ἀείχωι.
units.tr: What ololyzein means. Eustathius notes that the word ololyzein means a woman's voice, that is, a cry of prayer used of women. But those who came after the poet Homer took the word to mean weeping (whence perhaps the German Flagen, to lament, unless one prefers to derive it from clangor), that is, to wail, or to shout (whence perhaps our Grennen or Grinen, the same as to weep). The same is said on the verse of the Iliad, book six, "Then all the Athenian women ululated."

units.la: ὀλολύξει. Ὀλολυζῶ, inquit, Homerus mulierum precationem appellat: & ὀλολύζειν est σωὶ τοῦ εἶκτα τὴν ἄυδα, cum commiseratione quadam precari: at juniores illud capiunt pro κλαίειν, id est, plorare. Inde ἀὑτὸν quedam ὀλολυγμὸς... Herodoti testimonio probat, hanc ὀλολυγὴν, id est, precandi cum ululatu seu gemitu consuetudinem supra victimam, a Lybis primum ad Græcos promanasse. Lybiæ enim primos in sacris fuisse hujusmodi ὀλολυζειν, id est, precatione mulieb̄ri usos fuisse. Sed extra quoq; sacra ejus ut fuit fuisse. Eurypidem dicit κοκυτὸν opponere τῇ ὀλολυγῇ: unde conjiet ὀλολύζειν esse Θεὸς ἐπικαλέσθαι...
units.tr: Homer, he says, calls the prayer of women ololygē, and ololyzein is to pray with a certain pitiful cry, raising the voice. Later writers, however, take it to mean klaiein, to weep. Hence the ololygmos... Herodotus's testimony proves that this ololygē, that is, the custom of praying with a howl or groan over the victim, first passed from the Libyans to the Greeks, for the Libyans were the first to use this ololyzein, or women's prayer, in sacred rites. But outside sacred rites too... Euripides says that he opposed kokytos to ololygē, from which one may conjecture that ololyzein means to call upon God.

units.la: Hanc notam vide in sanctis vicinis.
units.tr: See this note in the neighbouring passages on sacred matters.

units.la: Διςηνὶ ἑῖ ἐντερ ὀλολύζω & ζειν per vulgatum illud Hippocratis significat: οἱ ἀσκαζομεν... Ac aliud quidem esse ὀλολύζειν differre ... Illi, quæ salutant, pollicentur, jubent, applaudunt, precantur, acclamant seu orant, faustia nunciante, ad omnem medicinam sunt apti. At qui gemunt, plorant, complicatas habet manus, curatu sunt difficiles.
units.tr: The familiar saying of Hippocrates, that ololyzein is different from [moaning], shows that those who greet, promise, command, applaud, pray, and shout or speak, announcing good news, are suited to every remedy. But those who groan, weep, and keep their hands clasped are difficult to cure.

units.la: Idem in illa Odyss. Δ. Ως εἰ πούσαι, ὀλόλυξε: Θέα δ' αἰ ἴκαυσε ἑῶς Sic locuta, ululavit: Dea autem ejus audivit preces.
units.tr: Likewise in Odyssey book four: "So she spoke and ululated, and the goddess heard her prayer."

units.la: Demonstratio hæc est precationis ἐπικαλέσεως, id est, efficacis, ὀλολύζειν γυναικεία ὑπὸ... ῥῶν, id est, precatio, quæ fit voce acuta, canora, strídula. Et paullo post: ὀλολύζει ἐπὶ... Ἐστὶ precari, Deos ἐπὶ invocare voce clara propter gaudium. Ibidem, ut illud obiter quod addam, non honestum, nec sanctum Græcis visum fuisset esse, supra viros occisos precari. Nam cum precatio Dei præsentiam postulet, Græcinon putabant fas esse Numen mortuis adesse.
units.tr: This is a demonstration of prayer as invocation, that is, of effective prayer: ololyzein is a woman's prayer, made with a high, clear, shrill voice. And a little after, it is to pray, to call upon the gods with a clear voice for joy. In the same place, as an incidental addition, the Greeks did not think it honourable or holy to pray over men who had been slain. For since prayer requires the presence of the god, they did not think it right for the divine power to be present with the dead.

units.la: Hoc igitur verbo hīc intelligenda est precatio cum oratione, gratulatione plausu, conjuncta propter felicem fausta||mq; mactationis percussionisve istius successum? Nā quando in victima percussione & mactatione bona laeta, signa atque omina apparebant, ea cum gratulatione, cum plausu laetaq; acclamatione excipiebant. At vero ad signa infausta & sinistra expavescere, animo; suis consternari solebant: ac nox aras suspectas trepide adibant, intusq; obser vabant ceteta, sollicitedq; quae ratione Numen offensum reconciliarent, ac cum eo in gratiam redirent, deli berabant. Nunc igitur cum in hac hostiae percussione & mactatione laeta omnia apparerent, mulieres he ὀλολύζειν acclamasse, & gratias Numeri ne eam ob eam ausam egisse dicuntur, tanquam re bene felicicerq; adhuc gesta: simulq; precate, ut reliqua etiam altio sacrificalis feliciter ipsis succederet.
units.tr: Should this word here be understood as prayer joined with speech, thanksgiving and applause, on account of the happy outcome of the striking and slaughter? For when good, joyful signs and omens appeared in the striking and slaughter of the victim, they received them with thanksgiving, applause and joyful acclamation. But at unfavourable and sinister signs they were wont to be dismayed and alarmed in their minds; they anxiously approached the suspect altars, observed the rest inwardly, and deliberated with anxiety how they might appease the offended deity and win back its favour. Now, since everything in this striking and slaughter of the victim appeared favourable, the women are said to have ululated and to have given thanks to the deity for this outcome, as if the thing had been done well and fortunately, and at the same time to have prayed that the rest of the sacrifice might succeed for them.

units.la: Voci ὀλολύζειν, ut hoc quoq; addam, & sono & significatione, affines fere sunt cum voces Hebraeae אלה Alah, id est, jurare, precari, imprecari, maledicere: הלל Hillel, id est, laudare: ולל jalal & הלל Hehil id est, ululare, clamare, vociferari: unde ילל jelel & ילל jelalah, id est, ululatus, vocis emissio, quae fit cum cordis dolore, interpretē R. Davide Kimchi: tum Latinae voces, ejulare & ululare: quae omnes ab Hebraeis vocibus fine dubio profectae sunt. Effet hic rursus dicendi locus de precibus & supplicationibus in sacrificiis adhiberi solitis: sed quoniam de illis supra satis est dictum, prolixiore illarum explicatione hic superfedeudum mihi esse existimo. Sed antequam a tibiarum & Musicae sacrificialis explicatione discedam, de Musica canctiq; vocali, de hymnis, cuiq; Deo proprijs ac dicatis, in illorum sacrificijs decantari solitis, denique de tripudijs, choreis, saltationibus, motibus incompositis, sive gestibus, seu gesticulationibus potius, in quibusdam sacris adhiberi solitis, hic quaedam adjiciemus: quae quidem Musicae illi artificiali & precibus cognata sunt & affinia.
units.tr: The word ololyzein, I may add, is close in both sound and meaning to the Hebrew words [alah], to swear, pray, invoke, curse; [hillel], to praise; and [yalal] and [hilel], to howl, cry out, shout; whence [yelel] and [yelalah], that is, a howling, a sound of the voice that is made from grief of heart, according to the interpreter R. David Kimchi. Then come the Latin words ejulare and ululare, all of which surely derive from Hebrew words. This would be a place to speak again about the prayers and supplications customarily used in sacrifices, but since enough has been said about these above, I judge that I should omit a longer explanation of them here. Before I leave the explanation of pipes and sacrificial music, however, I will add a few things here about music and vocal song: the hymns proper and dedicated to each god, customarily sung in their sacrifices, and finally the dances, choruses, leapings and unordered movements, or rather gestures and gesticulations, used in certain rites. These are akin and related to that artful music and to prayers.

units.la: Primo igitur observandum, singulis Diis certos dicatos fuisse hymnos, quos in illorum festis sacris, decantari confuerunt. Theodoretus sermone quarto, ad Graecos infideles de materia Deo dia & Mundo ad hunc morem hunc verbus pie eleganter alludic: Ne, inquit, cantentur jilum Cereri, ne, ipsi Rhea Lityer sam, ne Baccho Dithyrambum, ne Paeana Pythii Apollini, neve Diana continamus Hipoepum: sed rerum omnium conditori Deo hymnos Davidicos proferamus, cum eo pariter exclamemus: Quam magnificata sunt opera tua Dominel Omnia in sapientia fecisti. De hymnis ifiis & eorum generibus ac differentiis vide Caelium Rhodiginum libro septimo, capite quinto. Decantabant igitur alij Diis alios hymnos, Dianae Hypingos, Apollini Paeana Dionysio Dithyrambos, Cereri julos, Veneri hymnos ιεμνικούς, id est, amatorios. Graeci prae ter haec ἀφορωα ἐναιγίοσε, ἐξ χαρατα & σαιεξία. Athenaeus libro decimoquarto: Quas cantiones sive hymnos vocant julos, Cereri & Proserpinae sunt peculiares, Apollini Phi lelia, Hypingi Diane. Eodem in loco enumerat multarum cantionum genera atq; nomina, secundum varia vitae genera ac institutae: ut primum quidem ea, quae cum saltatione canebantur, dein de alia, quae voce pronunciari atq; cantari solebant: cujusmodi erant cautiones molentium in pistrino, textriarum, lanas tractantium, nutricum lactantium, messorum, mercenariorum in agro, ad opus commeantium, balneatorum, pinsentium fruges, eorum, qui pecora ducebant ad pabula, funerum & rerum aduersarum, nuptiarum, rerum felicium & laetarum.
units.tr: First, then, it must be observed that particular hymns were assigned to particular gods, which they were accustomed to sing at their festivals and sacred rites. Theodoret, in the fourth discourse, addressed to the unbelieving Greeks on the matter of God and the world, alludes to this custom piously and elegantly: "Let us not sing the iulos to Ceres," he says, "nor the lityerses to Rhea, nor the dithyramb to Bacchus, nor the paean to Pythian Apollo, nor let us chant the hyporchema to Diana; but let us offer the Davidic hymns to the Creator of all things, and cry out together with him: How magnificent are your works, Lord! In wisdom you made them all." On these hymns, their kinds and differences, see Caelius Rhodiginus, book seven, chapter five. So they sang different hymns to different gods: hyporchemes to Diana, the paean to Apollo, dithyrambs to Dionysus, iuloi to Ceres, and erotic hymns to Venus, that is, amatory ones. Besides these the Greeks had other kinds. Athenaeus, book fourteen: the songs or hymns called iuloi are peculiar to Ceres and Proserpina, the philelia to Apollo, the hyporchemes to Diana.
