In the same place he lists the many kinds and names of songs according to the various modes and conditions of life: first those sung with dancing, then others that were pronounced and sung with the voice, such as the songs of those grinding in the mill, of weavers, of those working wool, of nurses suckling infants, of reapers, of hired workers in the fields going to their labour, of bath attendants, of those pounding grain, of those who drove the flocks to pasture, of funerals and adversities, of weddings, and of happy and joyful events.

units.la: Sed ut ad Deorum hymnos redeamus, eos in epulis potissimum, quae post sacrificia agitabatur; & quidem in mensis plerunq; secundis in eorum honorem decantare solebant, quibus, antea sacra fecerant. Eum exemplum illustre extat apud Homerum Iliad. 1. post Hecatombem, a Chryse Apollini factum in epulo, quod sacrificium illud fuit consecutum: Οἱ ἢ παιῶν' ἀμφὶ ἀπόλλωνι θεᾷ μίζε ἐλαίσομαι ἀπολλο Καλὸν ἀείδοντες παιᾶνα ἀέσῃ ἀχαιοί Μίλπονται ἱκάνοντο δ' ἀντ' ἀυτοῦ ἀπολλὼν Hi autem totam diem cancu Deum (Apollinem) placabant Letum canentes Paeana pueri Achivorum Canentes longe operantem: is aucem mentem delectabatur audiens.
units.tr: But to return to the hymns of the gods: they used to sing them chiefly at feasts held after the sacrifices, and generally at the second course, in honour of the gods to whom they had first offered the sacred rites. A famous example is in Homer, Iliad 1, after the hecatomb which Chryses offered to Apollo, and which was followed by a feast: "They propitiated the far-darting god with the paean, the sons of the Achaeans singing beautifully and hymning the paean [ἰήιον ἀμφὶ ἑκάεργον ἀπόλλωνα μέλπον καλὸν ἀείδοντες παιήονα κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν]; and he was glad to hear them."

units.la: Hujus cantionis sacrae epularis, descriptione & cantores, nempe xoveς, id est, pueri, Achi vi, & tepus, παιηκαιον, id est, eorum die; & Deus, in cujus honorem cantabatur (ut fuit Apollinis) & cantionis genus atq; subjectum, nempe Paean, canentes longe operantem; et finis, ὀνὸν ιλ. communi & profano etiam vitæ humanæ usu, perora hominibus non nisi ortisfa fieri, sive ad vellitum, sive ad vitium prosunt: sic Ethnici in sacrificiis suis non nisi hostiis occisis ac mortuis litari, Diis suis satisfieri, eosque placari posse arbitrabantur.
units.tr: In this description of the sacred song sung at the feast we have the singers, namely the boys of the Achaeans; the time, the paean, that is, their day; the god in whose honour it was sung, Apollo; the kind of song and its subject, the paean, sung to the far-worker; and its purpose. In common and even profane human life too, nothing is obtained from men except by gifts, whether they are offered to win favour or to avert harm. So the Gentiles believed that in their sacrifices they could make propitiation only with slain and dead victims, and that in this way their gods could be satisfied and appeased.

units.la: Porrò ab hoc ritu cædendi, cædere sæpe synecdochicè pro sacrificare usurpatur, ut cædere bo- vem, id est, sacrificare, cædere vitulum nel agnam, idem. Unde Virgilius, Cæsam vitulamam vocat securitam: quod verbum, ut et nomen cædem, teste Festo, nonnulli putant ex Graeco κτείνειν dici, quod apud illos significat interficere. Alii deducunt a cædendo. Quicquid fit, habet hoc verbum cædendi cum verbo cædere et cædere magnam affinitatem, quonam plerunque etiam reipsa hæc sunt conjuncta, & ea, quæ cæduntur, id est, percutiuntur, sive sint homines, sive bestiæ, sive etiam res inanimatæ, & cedere & cædere solent. Hinc Præcidere est ante cædere, & ante immolarit, ut auctor est Festus: unde & agna Præcidanea, eodem telle, dicta, quæ ante alias immolabatur: item, porca Præcidanea, quæ Cereri cædebatur, id est, mactabatur abeo, qui mortuo justa non fecisset, id est, gleham non objecisset, quod morui erat in facere prius, quam novas fruges gustarent, ut Festus inquit; vel, ut idem ait, quam immolare erant solita, anteequam novam frugi gustarent. Fordicidia quoque, festa, a cædendis fordin bubus, ex hoc ritu sunt dicta. Erat autem hos forda, quæ fiunt in venire: & eo die publice immolabantur bones pregnantes in curiis complures. Vitulamam præterea nonnulli volunt dictam, quasi vitulam, quod vitula cadat. Iaere enim idem, quod percutere. Inde idus. Ab hoc eodem altu feriæ quoque vocant dictas, quod hostiæ in iis feriebantur. Feriæ, inquit Festus, a feriendis victimis appellatae, & Feralia Diis Manibus sacrata, festa, vel a feriendis pecudibus appellata. Quid si ferire a ferro sit dictum, quia ferro ad feriendum opus est: vel a ferre; quia tollendum seu auferendum id, quod cæsum. Inde & Ferus, vox, sine dubio nata. Hi n adde, quod hostia quoque dicta ab Hostire, verbo antiquo & obsoleto, quod fir.re sive cædere significat, Festo teste. Idem verbum, ut idem auctor est, significat etiam æquare: unde Redhostire gratiam, idem, quod gratiam referre, sich mit einem vergleichen.
units.tr: Moreover, from this rite of slaying, the verb "to slay" (caedere) is often used by synecdoche for "to sacrifice": to slay an ox, that is, to sacrifice it, or to slay a calf or a lamb, is the same thing. Hence Virgil calls the axe that slays the heifer "the axe of sacrifice". Some think that this verb, like the noun caedes, is derived, as Festus testifies, from the Greek κτείνειν, which among the Greeks means "to kill". Others derive it from caedere, "to strike". Whatever the case, the verb caedere has a great affinity with the verbs caedere and cedere; indeed these are often joined in fact, and things that are struck (caeduntur), that is, beaten, whether they are men, beasts or even inanimate things, are commonly said both cedere and caedere. From this comes praecidere, "to cut off beforehand", and "to sacrifice beforehand", as Festus says. Hence also the praecidanea lamb, so called from the same reason, which was sacrificed before the others; likewise the praecidanea sow, which was slain for Ceres, that is, killed by the man who had not performed the due funeral rites for the dead, that is, had not thrown earth upon the body. This was done before they tasted the new fruits, as Festus says; or, as the same writer says, it was a sacrifice customarily offered before they tasted the new grain. The Fordicidia, a festival, also took their name from the slaughter of pregnant cows (fordae) in this rite. Now the fordae are animals that are pregnant; and on that day many pregnant cows were publicly sacrificed in the curiae. Some also hold that the Vitulamia is so named as if it were "the calf-killing" (vitulam), because the calf falls (cadat), for cadere means the same as percutere, "to strike". From this same root the Ides are named. From the same origin, the holidays are also called feriae, because victims were struck (feriebantur) on them. Feriae, says Festus, are so called from the striking of victims, and the Feralia, festivals consecrated to the Manes, are called from the striking of cattle. What if ferire was derived from ferrum, because iron is needed for the striking, or from ferre, because the thing that has been slain is carried away or removed? Hence also the word ferus, which without doubt arose from this. Add that the hostia, too, is named from hostire, an old and obsolete verb which means to strike or slay, as Festus testifies. The same verb, as the same author says, also means to equal; hence redhostire gratiam means the same as to return a favour, to match it with something (sich mit einem vergleichen).

units.la: Verba Græca sunt πλήσσειν, κόπτειν (unde forsan nostrum Germanicum Flopffen / id est, percutere) πλάττειν, vel πλάττειν, quibus Homerus & Apollonius utuntur. Ab hac autem ipsa in sacrificiis fœderalibus, id est, quæ fœdera ineundi sanciendi, causa fiebant, bestias, seu hostias iciendi, feriendi, cædendi, atque demum jugulandi dissecandi, confuerudine, nate sunt trite ille & usitate Hebræorum, Græcorum & Romanorum dicendi forme: Hebræorum quidem ברית Carath berith, scindere sive dissindere fœdus: Græcorum vero, ὅρκια τεμεῖν, fœdera ferire; quale illud Homeri: —Ορκια πισά ταμόντες Fœdera fida ferientes.
units.tr: The Greek words are πλήσσειν, κόπτειν (whence perhaps our German "Flopffen", that is, to strike), and πλάττειν or πλήττειν, which Homer and Apollonius use. From this very custom of striking, slaying, killing, and finally cutting the throat and dismembering the beasts or victims in covenant sacrifices, that is, those made to ratify and confirm covenants, come those familiar and common expressions of the Hebrews, Greeks and Romans. The Hebrews say כרת ברית (karath berith), "to cut a covenant", that is, to split or divide the covenant; the Greeks say ὅρκια τεμεῖν, "to strike covenants", like Homer's line, "having cut the sworn pledges [ὅρκια πιστὰ ταμόντες]", that is, striking faithful covenants.

units.la: Et Latinorum: Fœdus icere, ferire, pro facere, inire, sancire, unde Cicero pro Cornelio: Lucius Martius cum Gaditanis fœdus icisse dicitur. Idem pro Sestio: Tu scilicet homo religiosus, fœdus, quod meo sanguine in pactione proviniciarū iceras, frangere voluisti. Idem: Id enim fœdus, meo sanguine illum, sanciri posse dicebat. Idem: Fœdera feriebantur pro vinciarum. Ferire fœdus cum aliquo, idem dixit pro Cornelio. Hinc fœdus ipsum Festus vult dictum, quod in paciescendo fœdere hostia necaretur. Unde Virgilius: Et cæsa jungebant fœdera porcâ.
units.tr: Among the Latins: foedus icere or ferire means "to make", "to enter into", "to ratify" a covenant. Hence Cicero, in the speech for Cornelius, says that Lucius Martius is said to have made a covenant with the people of Cadiz. Again in the speech for Sestius: "You, of course, a religious man, wanted to break the covenant which you had struck in the agreement about the provinces with my blood." And again: "For he said that the covenant could be ratified with his blood." And again: "Covenants were struck concerning the provinces." In the speech for Cornelius he also says "to strike a covenant with someone". From this Festus holds that the word foedus itself is named because in making a covenant a victim was slain. Hence Virgil: "And they joined the covenants with the slain sow."

units.la: Vel quia in fœdere interponatur fides; ad quod etymon posteriùs Cicero videtur alludere pro Domo: Gabinius fregit fœdus; Pisotamen in fide permansit. Idem in officiis: Fœdera, quibus cum hoste devincitur fœdus.
units.tr: Or it is because good faith (fides) is interposed in a covenant; and Cicero seems to allude to this derivation later, in the speech for his house: "Gabinius broke the covenant, but Piso remained faithful to his word." And again in the De Officiis: "covenants by which a treaty is bound with an enemy."

units.la: Porrò in hac hostiarum victimarum ve percussione (quæ magna cautione, religione, fiebat) hæc feri animad versione sunt digna, quæ a Gentilibus diligenter observabantur. Primum persone, quæ munus hoc bestias feriendi, cædendi, mactandi, excoriandi, dividendi, atque etiam coquendi obierunt. Apud Homerum quidem nominatur Thrasymedes, Nestoris filius: apud Apollonium vero Hercules & Anceus, duo Argonautica illius navigationis socii. Hi a Latinis ab officio et instrumento dicti sunt Victimarii, sive Victimatores, Cultrarii, secundum illud Virgilii: Supponunt alii cultros, id est, victimas cædunt, interpreti Servio: item Pope, sacerdos ministri,
units.tr: Furthermore, in this striking of the sacrificial victims (which was done with great care and religious scruple), the following points deserve attention, which the Gentiles observed carefully. First, the persons who performed this office of striking, slaying, killing, flaying, dividing and even cooking the beasts. In Homer, indeed, Thrasymedes, son of Nestor, is named; in Apollonius, Hercules and Ancaeus, two companions of that Argonautic voyage. The Latins called these men victimarii or victimatores, and cultrarii, from their office and their instrument (the knife), according to the line of Virgil: "Others place the knives," that is, they strike the victims, as Servius explains. Likewise the popa, the priest's attendant (sacerdotis minister),

units.la: victimarii. Cultrarii. Pope. ministri, de quibus supra pluribus. Ælius Spartianus: Percussit, inquit, bostiam popa, nomine Antonius. Propertius:
units.tr: victimarii (sacrificers), cultrarii (knife-men), popae (sacrificial attendants), ministri, concerning whom more has been said above. Aelius Spartianus: "The popa, named Antonius, struck the victim." Propertius:

units.la: Succinctique talent ad mortua sacra popae.
units.tr: "And girt up they came to the dead rites of the popa."

units.la: Apud Delphos is, qui victimum immolabat ὀσιωτὴρ dicebatur, ut Plutarchus scribit in quaestionibus Graecis flatum ab initio, Ὁσιωτῆρα μὲν καλᾶτο Σούμβυον ιερέων (Stephanus pro Σύμ-βορ, Ἰούντα alii vel putat legendum) ὅτως ἐπὶ ἐπὶ ἐπὶ ἐπὶ. Quinq, autem ὅσιοι per omnem ἐπὶ tam, qui ratibus multis in rebus aderant, unde etiam sacrificabant, cum se ex Deucalionis genere ortos arbitrarentur. Lactantius 4. Theb-eid. Sacerdotum, inquit, consuetudo talis est, ut aut ipsi percutiat victimas, & Agones appellantur: aut sic tenentes cultrum, alter impingat. Ideo dicis Stat.
units.tr: Among the Delphians the one who slew the victim was called hosiotēr (ὁσιωτήρ), as Plutarch writes in his Greek Questions, where he says that the men called hosioi were, in many matters, present at the sacred rites, and that for this reason they also performed the sacrifices, since they believed they were descended from Deucalion. Lactantius, in the fourth book of his commentary on the Thebaid, says: "The custom of the priests is such that either they themselves strike the victims, and these are called agones, or, holding the knife thus, another strikes the blow." Hence Statius says: "The flocks fell upon the wound."

units.la: In vulnus ciciderunt greges. Athenaeus libro decimo quinto Dipnosophist. sub finem pluribus docet, has μαγειρους, idest coquorum olim fuisse partes atque munia. Ritus, inquit, sacrificiorum & cerimoniarum coquis notas fuisse palam est ex Olympiadis ad Alexandrum epistola, qua mater illum hortatur, coquum ut emat in sacris faciundis excitatum his verbis: Perignum coquum missum a matre tu habe. Scit ille, omnia sacra patria tua quomodo peragantur, & αρχα (id est, puta, ut vnlgo vertunt, proprie otiosa, inertia, in quibus bostiae non immolabantur, sed frugum primitiae tantum offerebantur) & Ἰνάσχος (judicium forte fuisse, quae a Rege fierent, cum jus diceret) & Bacchica, & alia prorsus omnia, in quibus mater tua victimas immolat. Eumigitur ne contemperis, sed libenter excipe, & admemento quam primum. Addit: Venerandame esse coquorum artem liquet ex Atheniensium praeconibus, quia dum res divina fieret, in ordine coquorum & victi mariorum, boves cedentium, fieret idem paulo post Demi, usufrum testimonio probat, Athenis fuisse tribum coquorum, qui obarte suam magno essent in pretio & honore, qui curabant, ut plebs rectè sacrificaret. Tandem artem coquinariam sive culinariam, liberalem esse disciplinam probat, ac coquum ipsum civem esse ostendit, nec sordidum nec humanitate expertem. Inde μαγειρίζειν Graecis est maltare, quoniam coquus pecora coquenda maltat. Quid si igitur ipsum maltandi verbum a Graeco μαγειρεῖν & μαγείρειον fuerit deriuatum potuit quam a magis augere?
units.tr: In vulnus ciciderunt greges. Athenaeus, near the end of the fifteenth book of the Deipnosophists, shows at length that cooks [μάγειροι] once had these parts and duties. He writes: "It is plain that the rites of sacrifices and ceremonies were known to cooks from the letter of Olympias to Alexander, in which his mother urges him to buy a cook skilled in performing sacred rites, in these words: 'Take the cook Perignus, whom your mother has sent. He knows how all your ancestral sacred rites are carried out, both the archa (that is, as most translate it, the idle, inactive rites in which no victims were slain, but only the first fruits of the crops were offered), and the Inasch (perhaps the judicial business the king conducted when he dispensed justice), and the Bacchic rites, and altogether all the rites in which your mother sacrifices victims. So do not despise him, but gladly receive him, and see that he is sent as soon as possible.'" He adds: "That the art of cooking is venerable is clear from the Athenian heralds, since while the sacred rite was being performed, in the order of cooks and victim-slayers, oxen were slain..." and a little later the same happened. By the testimony of use, Demosthenes proves that at Athens there was a tribe of cooks, who on account of their skill were held in great price and honour, and who took care that the people sacrificed correctly. Finally, he proves that the culinary art is a liberal discipline, and shows that the cook himself is a citizen, neither base nor lacking in humanity. Hence among the Greeks μαγειρίζειν [mageirizein] means "to slaughter," because the cook slaughters the cattle to be cooked. What if, then, the Latin verb maltare was derived from the Greek μαγειρεῖν [mageirein] and μαγείρειον [mageireion] rather than from magis augere?

units.la: Apud Homerum κύρηξ, id est, praeconibus, fere illa necessaria ad sacrificia adferendi vi praeconcs. Eumas, feriendi, carnes parandi, dissecandi, vinum etiam libandi munia tribuuntur, ut idem Athenaeus testatur. Sed Athenaeus eodem in loco significat, magne quoque & illustris dignitatis viros eadem hac munia obiisse. Sic enim, exempli gratia, apud Homerum ipse quoq. Agamemnon, quam vis Rex, bostiam tamen percutit. Ait enim Poeta: Agnorum se voare stomachum proscindit Et alios quidem palpitantes adhuc humi sternit.
units.tr: In Homer the heralds (κύρηξ) generally brought up the things needed for sacrifice. Eumaeus is assigned the tasks of striking, preparing the meat, cutting it up, and even pouring the libation of wine, as Athenaeus also records. Athenaeus notes in the same place that men of great rank and distinction performed these same duties. Thus, for example, in Homer even Agamemnon, though a king, strikes down a victim. The poet says: "He slashes the throat of the lambs, and then lays down others still quivering on the ground."

units.la: Sic Thrasymedes adjuvantibus eum fratribus idem munus obiit.
units.tr: Thrasymedes, with his brothers helping him, likewise performed this office.

units.la: Apud Romanos, Censores, qui magistratus summae auctoritatis fuit, purpurati & coronati boftias maltabant. Sic in Padalis gente Indica (testatur Nicolaus Damascenus, quod & Stoeae repetit in sermone de justitia) non qui sacerdos esset, sed qui in praesentia haberetur prudentissimus, bostiam maltabat: nec a Diis nisi justitiam rogabat. Et hac de personis quae bostiae ferire, percutere, maltare, excoriare atque dividere confuevevunt. Idem ergo fere illorum suis munus, quod hodie apud nos est coquorum, laxiorum, macellariorum ve: qui ab Italis beccari, forsan a porcis, funs dicti, & a Gallis bouchiers, quorum macellum vocatur boucherie, quasi, ut hoc joci causa addam, (la bouche rie) os hominis gaudeat & delectetur macellis. Ob illam autem causam, ut supra quoque attigi, Gentilium & templa atque delubra, macella atque culinas, & altaria menses macellariis ac coquinariis, & sacerdotes macellarii & coquis; & denique illorum sacrificia profanis pecorum mactationibus atque lanienis merito comparari potuerunt.
units.tr: Among the Romans the censors, who held the highest magistracy, slaughtered the victims while wearing purple and crowned with garlands. So among the Padaei, an Indian people (Nicolaus Damascenus attests this, and Stobaeus repeats it in his discourse on justice), the one who slaughtered the victim was not the priest but whoever was judged the wisest at the time, and he asked the gods for nothing but justice. These are the sorts of persons who used to strike, smite, slaughter, flay and divide the victims. Their office was therefore much the same as that which among us today belongs to cooks, carvers and butchers: called by the Italians beccari, perhaps from porci (pigs), and by the French bouchiers, whose meat-market is called boucherie, as if (to add this in jest) "la bouche rie": the mouth of man rejoices and delights in the butcher's stalls. For this reason, as I touched on above, the temples and shrines of the Gentiles, their butchers' stalls and kitchens, and their altars were compared with butchers' and cooks' shops, and their priests with butchers and cooks; and finally their sacrifices could rightly be likened to the profane slaughterings and butcheries of cattle.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem milites non nisi signo dato, audent praelium inire, manusque cum hoste victimam conferere: sic illi sacrorum ministri, de quibus modo dictum, injussu sacerdotum & eorum, qui sacrificare non nisi cuere non nisi eru praerant, minime audebant bostias aggredi, ealque ferire, prosternere, atque jugulare. Hoc Dionysius quoq; Halicarnassens diserte in sacrificiis descriptione docet, cum ajt, Tum demum (perniis scilicet tis, quae sacrificium praecedebant) ministros eas ἱερεύς, id est, maltare, ferire, jugu-
units.tr: Just as soldiers dare not enter battle or bring the victim into hand-to-hand contact with the enemy until the signal is given, so those ministers of the sacred rites just mentioned, without the command of the priests and of those who presided over the sacrificing, scarcely dared to approach the victims and to strike, smite, slaughter, or... Dionysius of Halicarnassus also teaches this clearly in his description of sacrifices, when he says: "Then at last (namely after the prayers that preceded the sacrifice) they ordered the ministers to strike, to smite, to slaughter [ἱερεύειν]".

units.la: T lare jubebant. Ideo succinkti nutum imperium ve exspectantes dicebant Agon? vel Agone? Hinc Seneca libro secundo Partitionum: Belle, inquit, deridebat hac Asinius Pollio: Fiktus, inquit, cervicem porrigat, carnifex manum porrigat: deinde respiciat ad patrem, et dicat Agon? quod fieri feleterin vitiimus. Idem docet Ovidius his versibus de Agonalibus: Nominis esse potes succinctus causa minister Hostia caelestibus quo feriente cadit. Qui calido strictos tinctiurus sanguine cultros Semper agitne rogat, necnisi jussus agit.
units.tr: Hence the ministers, girded up and waiting for a nod or command, would say "Agon?" or "Agone?" So Seneca, in book two of the Partitions: "Pollio Asinius," he says, "used to mock this wittily: let the victim stretch out its neck, let the executioner stretch out his hand, then let him look to the father and say 'Agon?', which we spoil by rendering it 'fieri feliciter'." Ovid teaches the same in these verses about the Agonalia: "You may be called the girded-up attendant for the sake of the name, by whose striking the victim falls to the heavenly gods; who, about to dip the drawn knives in warm blood, always asks 'shall I drive?' and does nothing unless ordered."

units.la: Idem libro quarto de Ponto: At cum Tarpejas esses deductus in arces Dum caderes jussu victima sacra suo.
units.tr: The same author, in book four of the Pontic letters: "But when you were led up to the Tarpeian citadel, while you were falling as a sacred victim at his command."

units.la: Atque hoc est primum membrum, nempe persona. Alterum, quod in percussione victimae observari debet, est instrumentum, quod hostiis caedendis feriendisve adhibebatur. Hoc apud Homerum est πέλεκυς (ut etiam apud Apollonium) quod bipennem et securim vertunt: unde πελεκῖν et πελεκίζειν, sive πελεκίσεσθαι per iota, securi percutere, πελεκιστὴς dolator, πελεκυφόρος bipennifer, sive securifer. Apud eundem Homerum sic quod, mentio οἰκίας ἄνυδος, id est, sudus e quercu, qua hostia illa fuerit (id quod etiam apud Persium et Cappadoces in more fuit positum) ut in Eumaei sacrificio: Κόλα ἀπὸ αἱ ταρχόμενοι ἐκ χείρος ἀρυός, λοῦ λίτα κείων. Hostiam mola sparsam guerna sudo percutit.
units.tr: That is the first part, namely the person. The second thing to be observed in striking the victim is the instrument used to slaughter or strike the animals. In Homer this is the πέλεκυς (as also in Apollonius), which translators render as axe or hatchet (bipennis, securis); whence πελεκῖν and πελεκίζειν, or πελεκίσεσθαι with iota, to strike with an axe; πελεκιστής, a hewer; πελεκυφόρος, bearing an axe. In the same Homer there is also mention of an oak club (οἰκίας ἄνυδος, that is, a club of oak) with which the victim was struck, as was customary among the Persians and Cappadocians too, as in the sacrifice of Eumaeus: "Striking the victim sprinkled with meal with an oaken club [Κόλα ἀπὸ αἱ ταρχόμενοι ἐκ χείρος ἀρυός, λοῦ λίτα κείων]."

units.la: Dionysius Halicarnassensis locum hunc ipsum citans σκυτάλων vocat instrumentum illud, quo victimae feriri fuerunt: cujus quidem voces varia et diversa sunt significata. Nam et murem araneum et scuticam, hoc est, flagellum, ex corio factum, et peram coriaceam et caterva equestrem, et furculum loricatum (quod genus epistolae erat apud Lacedaemonios, de quo Gellius lib. 18. cap. 9.) et tabulam; in qua scripta fontium debita proponebantur, et baculum sive virgam, et serpentium genus significat. Vide Eratosthenem in Chiliadibus, Tristia Scytale.
units.tr: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, quoting this same passage, calls the instrument with which the victims were struck a σκυτάλη (scytale). The word has various and different meanings: it signifies a field mouse, a whip (scutica, a flail made of leather), a leather pouch, a troop of cavalry, a forked and armoured stick (a kind of letter among the Lacedaemonians, on which see Gellius, book 18, chapter 9), a tablet on which the debts of sources were set out, a staff or rod, and a kind of serpent. See Eratosthenes in the Chiliades, "Tristia Scytale."

units.la: Apud Apollonium porro Herculem ῥόπαλα alterum taurorum percussisse ac profusum vise dicitur. Est autem ῥόπαλον sive ῥόπαλον idem quod ῥόπαλος, clava, fustis, malleus: quod ipsum instrumentum apud Latinos quoque in usu fuit. Is vero ligneus fuit sive ferreus: sicuti et bodie ligneo ad eundem effectum lanti utuntur, nempe ad boves similiter sternendos. Hic una cum securi a sacrificulo, seu ab uno ex victimariis gestabatur: atq; coronatus victimarum capitibus (teste Plinio lib. 16. cap. 4. in his verbis: Postea Deorum honoris sacrificantes sumpsere, victimis simul coronatis) malleo primum ante aram percutiebant: deinde securi cervix abscindebatur: tum ad viscerationem et extra rimanda, caprandaq; auspicia procedebant. Mallei hujus pilluram vide apud Gulielmum du Choul, libro ante citato de Religione Romana, et Bartholomeum Marliani in antiquitatibus urbis Romae.
units.tr: Further, in Apollonius, Hercules is said to have struck one of the bulls with a ῥόπαλον and felled it. The ῥόπαλον or ῥόπαλος is the same as a club, cudgel or mallet, and this very instrument was in use among the Latins as well. It was made either of wood or of iron; even today wooden ones are used for the same purpose, namely to fell oxen in the same way. This was carried by the sacrificer or by one of the victimarii, and the victims were crowned with garlands (witness Pliny, book 16, chapter 4, in these words: "Afterwards they began to sacrifice in honour of the gods, with the victims crowned at the same time"). They first struck with the mallet before the altar; then the neck was cut with an axe; then they proceeded to the cutting up and inspection of the entrails, and to the taking of omens. For a picture of this mallet, see Guillaume du Choul, in the book on Roman religion cited above, and Bartolomeo Marliani, in his Antiquities of the City of Rome.

units.la: Fuit deinde et securis apud Latinos, instrumentum ad boves ante aras Deorum perentiendos adhibitum: ideo Sacrificia dicta ab Ovidio duodecimo Metamorph. Elatumq; (scilicet funale) altri veluti quicandida tauri Rumpere sacrificam (sacrificiis dicata) molitur colla securi.
units.tr: Then among the Latins there was also an axe, an instrument used to fell oxen before the altars of the gods. Hence, in Ovid's twelfth book of the Metamorphoses, the sacrificial (victims) are so called: "lifting up the (torch) — that is, the funeral torch — he strives to break the white neck of the bull, dedicated to sacrifice, with an axe."

units.la: Hanc autem aneam fuisse conflat ex Festo, et ideo Aciorin dictam. Sic enim ille: Acioris securis anea, qua in sacrificiis utebantur sacerdotes. Porro a securiando dicta videtur, Germanici ἀξιώματα ... forsan a Graeco ἀξίνη, quae vox etiam securim sive bipennem significat. Unde ἀξινομαντεῖα divinatio per secures; de qua Plinius lib. 36. cap. 19. Vis vero fuit Veteres hoc instrumento ad varios usus; videlicet et ad ligna secanda, et etiam ad bellum. Virg. Aeneid. II. —eratam quatiens Tarpeja securim.
units.tr: That this axe was of bronze is clear from Festus, and it was therefore called aciorin. For he says: "The bronze axe of Acior, which the priests used in sacrifices." It seems to be named from securiando (cutting), though perhaps it comes from the Greek ἀξίνη, which word also means an axe or double-axe. Whence ἀξινομαντεῖα, divination by axes, of which Pliny speaks in book 36, chapter 19. The ancients used this instrument for various purposes: both for cutting wood and also in war. Virgil, Aeneid II: "Tarpeia brandishing the axe."

units.la: Vis eâ sunt pariter ad fontes puniendos, quisque magistratibus capite plectendi erant, securi percutiebantur. Cicero tertia Verrina: Agunt eum praecipitem poenae civium Romanorum, quos parentem securi percussit, partim in vinculis necavit, et Virg. 6. Aeneid.
units.tr: Likewise, with this instrument those who were to be punished capitally by the magistrates were struck down with the axe. Cicero, in the third Verrine: "The punishments of Roman citizens drive him headlong, whom he struck with the axe as a parent, partly killed in chains..." And Virgil, Aeneid 6.

units.la: Consulis Consules imperium hic primus sceptrum secures Accipiunt,&c.
units.tr: "The consuls receive first the power, the sceptre, the axes, etc."
And Lucan, in book one.
"Catiline trembled at the peaceful axes."

units.la: Hujus instrumenti in ventrix fuit Penthesilea Amazon, teste Plin.lib.7.c.56. Unde et Amazones, securigera a Poetis dicta sunt. Secures item magistratuum insignia erant, virgarum fasciculo loro illigatae. Cic.6. Verr. Quamobrem fasces Praetoribus praeferuntur, cur secures detur? Securest demum ut in nostram sententiam veniamus, licet grandiores erant, ad victimarum carnes secandas dividendasque, prout libebat sacrificulis, victimariis, et id genus hominibus, qui sacrificiis antiquorum praerant. Hodie Lanii in Urbe magno lato cultro ad carnes dividendas, tuntur, quem spatagium vocant, &c.
units.tr: The inventor of this instrument was Penthesilea, the Amazon, according to Pliny, book 7, chapter 56. Hence the Amazons were called securigerae (axe-bearers) by the poets. Axes were also the insignia of magistrates, bound to a bundle of rods. Cicero, Verrines 6: "Why are the fasces carried before praetors, and why is an axe given?" Lastly, so that we may come to our own view: although they were larger, they were used for cutting and dividing the flesh of the victims, as pleased the sacrificing priests, the victimarii and that class of men who presided over the sacrifices of the ancients. Today the butchers in the city use a large broad knife to divide the meat, which they call a spatagium, etc.

units.la: De more porro securim, qua apud Atheniensis primus bos mactatus fuit in sacrificio, in jure vocandi quotannis vide Leonicenum libro 2.capite 3. Athenis, inquit, in Prytaneo judicium fuit locus, ubi ferrum et quaevis alia inanima, quibus patrata fuerat caedes, judicium quoque illius, qua Erechtheo Athenis imperante, bos primus Athenis mactatus dicebatur, tanquam rea causa quo tannis magna ex solennitate agebatur. Cum enim sacerdos, quae illi Buphonia vocabant, bovem percussum, humi, straro, reliqu, ibi sicuri, ocyus ex Attica aufugisset, non coparente homine, securim tunc primum Athen. in judicio constituerunt. Unde hac illa quotannis in jure vocandi consuetudo inolevit.
units.tr: On the custom of the axe with which the first ox was slaughtered in sacrifice at Athens, in the yearly legal summons, see Leonicenus, book 2, chapter 3. At Athens, he says, in the Prytaneum there was a place of judgment where the iron and any other inanimate thing by which a killing had been done was tried; and also the trial of that one by which, when Erechtheus ruled at Athens, the first ox was said to have been slaughtered at Athens, the thing on trial being brought each year with great solemnity. For when the priest, whom they called the Buphonia, had struck the ox, and fled quickly from Attica, leaving the axe lying on the ground, and the man could not be found, they then first placed the axe on trial at Athens. Hence this custom of the yearly summons in law took hold.

units.la: Tertium instrumentum, quo Latini utebantur in sacrificiis, erat Secespita, interprete Festo, culter ferreus, oblongus, manubrio eburneo, rotundo, filido, vinclo ad capulum argento, auroque, fixo, clavis aeneis, aere cyprio, quo Flaminies, Flaminicae virgines, Pontifices esse ad sacrificia utebantur, a secando sic dicti. Eadem aliter dicitur, quae in sacrario utuntur. Sacraria nam, in templis reticulo aeneo olim scipiebantur, in quo turbae relictae sunt, per quas manibus sacra tangere licet. Est in templo Bonae Deae, sed alius in locis, et sunt velut repacula quaedam, ita Secespita dicuntur duobus modis. Suetonius in Tyber. Nam et inter Pontifices sacrificantis simul, pro Secespita plumbeum cultrum subjiciendum curavit. Idem alibi: Secespitam, alii securim, alii dolabram aeneam, alii cultellum putant.
units.tr: The third implement that the Latins used in sacrifices was the secespita, which Festus describes as an iron knife, oblong, with a round ivory handle, filed smooth, its hilt bound with silver and gold and fixed with bronze nails of Cyprian copper. Flamens, Flaminicae (the priestesses of the Flamens) and Pontiffs used it at sacrifices, and it is so named from secare, to cut. The same instrument is called by another name among those who use it in the sacrarium. For in the temples the sacraria were once fenced off with a bronze latticework, through which the crowds were left to touch the sacred objects with their hands. There is one in the temple of the Good Goddess, and others elsewhere, and they are like little enclosures. The secespita is thus named in two ways. Suetonius, in his Life of Tiberius, says: "For he also had a leaden knife placed under the sacrificing Pontiffs in place of the secespita." The same author elsewhere says: "Some think the secespita is an axe, others a bronze mattock, others a small knife."

units.la: Aliud instrumentum, in sacrificiis ad hiberi solitum, fuit Dolabrum, sive Dolabra, quam Festus Pontificalem ab hoc usu vocat, et alio nomine Scenam, sive Scenam. Fuit autem, ut ex formata patet, quod Marlianus in suis antiquitatibus expressit: Culter grandior, furorio perquam similis, quo olim reor in sacrificiis Veteres uti fuisse solitos, ad bostias, et victimas deglubendas, postquam malleo hae percussae, et jugulatae essent, a quo forte nomen sumserit: seu potius a dolando, hoc est ab aequandis partibus carnium, quae arus imponebantur, Dius immolandarum, sumpta metaphora a dolabra, quae fabri lignarii est instrumentum, quo ligna dolantur, seu expoliuntur, quamquam et rusticum utidem sit instrumentum, cujus Columella lib.3. meminit hu verbis: Quae falce amputari non possunt, acuta dolabra abrudito. Est et ejus diminutivum dolabella, de qua idem auctor lib.5. sic infert: Circa crus dolabella dimovenda est terra, &c. Plutarchus vero in vita Tiberii et Caji Gracchorum, de dolone, quod genus est gladii, sic meminit: Ille veri (Tiberium intelligit) palam gladium, quem dolonem vocant, accinctus ambulat, &c. Quid culter hujusmodi hoc nomine appellaretur, auctorem adhuc desidero: quod autem hac forma unum ex sacrificialibus instrumentis fuerit, nulli dubium esse puto. Nam passim multis in locis marmore aut lapide in sculptum cernere licet, et praesertim in arcu marmoreo, quem aurificum nominant, prope Ecclesiam S. Georgii in Velabro: ubi multa, quae ad antiqua sacrificia pertinent, videre est, &c.
units.tr: Another implement that was customarily used in sacrifices was the dolabrum, or dolabra, which Festus calls pontificalis from this use, and which has another name, scena or scena. Its shape, as is clear from the picture that Marliani gives in his Antiquities, was this: a rather large knife, very like a mattock, which I suppose the ancients were accustomed to use in sacrifices to flay the beasts and victims after they had been struck with a mallet and their throats cut. It perhaps took its name from this, or rather from dolare, that is, from evening out the portions of meat that were laid on the altar for the offering. The metaphor was taken from the dolabra, a carpenter's tool with which wood is hewn or smoothed, although it is also a rustic tool. Columella, in book 3, mentions it in these words: "What cannot be cut off with a sickle should be stripped away with a sharp dolabra." There is also a diminutive, dolabella, of which the same author, in book 5, writes: "Earth must be cleared away around the leg with a dolabella, etc." Plutarch, in the life of Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, mentions the dolo, a kind of sword, thus: "He walked about openly girded with the sword that they call a dolo" (he means Tiberius). I still look for the author who gave a knife of this kind that name. But that it was one of the sacrificial instruments in this shape, I think no one can doubt. For in many places it can be seen carved in marble or stone, especially on the marble arch that they call the goldsmiths', near the church of St George in the Velabrum, where many things relating to ancient sacrifices may be seen, etc.

units.la: Ad instrumenta, quibus bostiae feriri, caedi et mactari solebant, referri quoq; debet lapis ille, sive silex, quo agni, porcae, sive alterius bestiae caput in pangendis faederibus percuti atque feriri solebat. Exemplum hujus consuetudinis citatum a nobis fuit supra ex Livio, quod hic, quia ad rem maxime facit, repetemus. Apud Livium Annibal, magnis propositis promissis, milites suos ad fortitudinem adhortatus, ea, ut rata fierent fore, agnum lactantem, dextra silicem retinens, fi falleret, Jovem, caeterosque precatus Deos, ita semactarent, quemadmodum ipse agnum mactasset: secundum precationem caput pecudis saxo elisit.
units.tr: To the instruments with which victims were struck, slain and killed must also be referred that stone, or flint, with which the head of a lamb, a sow or another beast was struck and smitten when covenants were being made. We cited an example of this custom above from Livy, and because it is very much to the point we repeat it here. In Livy, Hannibal, having held out great promises, urged his soldiers to courage. So that these promises might be fulfilled, he prayed to Jupiter and the other gods, holding a sucking lamb in his right hand and a flint in the other, that if he should deceive them, they should slay him as he himself had slain the lamb. In accordance with the prayer, he struck the beast's head against the rock.

units.la: Tertio caesae victimae casus quoque diserte exprimitur, qui et ipse diligenter, in hac percussione fuit obser vatus. De bove, ab Hercule caso, sic ait Apollonius:
units.tr: A third circumstance of the sacrificed victim is also expressly stated, which was carefully observed in this striking. Apollonius says thus of the ox felled by Hercules:

units.la: —’ὁ δ’ ἀθεὸς ἀλλ’ ἄτι πᾶσαν ἐπερέπουσι ... γαῖη,
units.tr: ὁ δ’ ἀθεὸς ἀλλ’ ἄτι πᾶσαν ἐπερέπουσι … γαῖη (He, the god-like one, ... over all the ... earth.)
But he, all at once, fell prone upon the ground.
So Virgil:
The ox falls prone to the ground.

units.la: De altero, quem Ancaeus ferit, sic ceciit idem Apollonius:
units.tr: Of the other, which Ancaeus strikes, the same Apollonius writes thus:

units.la: Ηρωσ δ’ ἀμφοτέρωσι ... posuit ἐπὶ τῷ ... ἐπὶ ... Eurymachus ... terpretatur ... ἐπὶ τὸ ... ἐπὶ τοῦ βοὸς ... Nunc autem significat ...
units.tr: Hero on both sides … laid … upon … Eurymachus … interprets … upon … upon the ox … But now it signifies …

units.la: Quemadmodum autem mali omnis erat, si victima ductorem non sponte sequeretur, sed retrahenda esset: vel si ex ductentium manibus sese proripuisset et profugisset: hi mali auspicii erat, si vel elapsa victima fefellisset, vel pertusa aut exilisset altius aut horridius exclamasset, aut nonne flatim; et quidem placide concidisset, si supina et non prona tecidisset: vel si semianimis provoluta in terram eandem pedibus calcitrasset importunius: vel difficulter exspiraffet: vel jugulata non copioso diffluxisset sanguine: vel si inter jugulandum triste aliquid infaustum, oculis auribusque occurrisset, ut si locuta esset victima vel hostia: quod Roma fecisse boverem feminam Livius refert Decad. 5. lib. 3. Unde libris a Decemviris aditu detectum ut supplicatio fieret...
units.tr: Just as it was a bad omen if the victim did not follow its leader of its own accord but had to be dragged, or if it tore itself from the hands of those leading it and ran away, so it was an ill omen if the victim, having slipped away, escaped the blow, or, when pierced, leapt higher or bellowed more horribly, or did not fall gently. A fall was good only if the victim fell on its back and not on its face. It was also bad if, half-dead, it thrashed its feet against the same ground more violently, or if it died with difficulty, or if, when its throat was cut, it did not pour out much blood, or if during the slaughter something sad and ill-omened met the eyes and ears, as if the victim had spoken. Livy reports that this happened at Rome with a cow-heifer, in the fifth decade, book 3. Whence the Decemvirs were consulted, and a supplication was made...

units.la: Et ita magistratus circa omnia pulvinaria majoribus hostiis X L. numero sacrificarent, ... coronatus esset. Quod ipsum et P. Volumnio et Servitio Sulpitio Cos. hos foeminae fecit: et hos item masculos, inquiens: Cave tibi Roma, quem bovem cum tura ferrent, aliqui arusp ... fuerunt.
units.tr: And thus the magistrates offered larger victims, forty in number, at all the pulvinaria... was crowned. This same thing a woman did when P. Volumnius and Servius Sulpicius were consuls, and these also were men; saying: "Beware, Rome, of which ox..." when they were carrying the incense, some haruspices ... were.

units.la: Signa haec et alia, quae inter percutiendum et jugulandum e vemissent, offerebant, et alienati. Nam minus panari minus... puta bantur.
units.tr: These signs and others that appeared during the striking and slaughter were offered, and they were disturbed. For they were thought less ... to be ...

units.la: Contra laeti eminus indicia et sacrificium Dei testimonia erant ... fine ... et flagrante ad aram ... Plinius scribit lib. 8. cap. 45.
units.tr: On the contrary, joyful omens from afar and the testimonies of a sacrifice pleasing to God were ... the end ... and blazing upon the altar ... Pliny writes in book 8, chapter 45.

units.la: In primis vero hic mugitum befliae observabant, et ex illo quaedam vel laeta, vel tristia conjectabant ... Tibiae etiam ad sacri ... Quae ex loco id quod colligere promtum est, tibiae in percussione ... ut in tota ioque ...
units.tr: Above all, they observed the bellowing of the beast, and from it they conjectured some things joyful, others sad ... Flutes too at the sacrifice ... What can readily be gathered from the place is that flutes were played at the striking ... as throughout ...

units.la: Quoniam autem tibiarum et tibicinum ... Gentilium maxime ... vulgatus ...
units.tr: Since, however, of flutes and flute-players ... of the Gentiles especially ... common ...

units.la: Habitasse Hebraicé igitur hoc instrumentum חליל Chalil, appellatur,in plurali חלילים Chalilim, Tibia Hebraïa quam vocem septuaginta interpretes αὐλὸν,id est,tibiam,verterunt,ut Isaiæ quinto tapite,quæ dragefimo octavo versu,et capite erigesimo,versu vigesimo nono. Thargum Isaia quinto, versu duodecimo,& Genesis quarto, אבוב Abbubá.interpretatur,quid sistula sit affinis. Rabbi Schelomoh hoc instrumentum sit vulg dictum,quod sit concavum: unde curva tibia a Tibulla & Cava ab Ovidio appellatur.
units.tr: The Hebrew name for this instrument is חליל Chalil, in the plural חלילים Chalilim, a Hebrew flute. The Seventy translated this word as αὐλὸν, that is, flute, as in Isaiah chapter 5, which is verse 48, and chapter 14, verse 29. The Targum on Isaiah 5, verse 12, and on Genesis 4, interprets אבוב Abbubá, which is akin to a pipe. Rabbi Solomon says that this instrument was so called because it is hollow; whence the curved flute is called tibia curva by Tibullus, and cava by Ovid.

units.la: Sicenim Tibullus Eleg. secunda: Obstrepit & Phrygio tibia curva sono.
units.tr: For Tibullus says in Elegy 2: "The curved flute drones with Phrygian sound."
And Ovid in Fasti book 6:
"On the stage the hollow flute complains, and complains."

units.la: Aliquod mibi videtur verisimilius, sic volunt appellacam,quòd profanus illius & tontamina tu in publicis epulis,conuiuiis atque choreis sive tripudiu fuerit usus. Hinc etiam מחול Machol dictum,quod publicani & profanam,qualis fuit Gentilium,choream,sive tripudium significat,in quo tibiâ cani solebat:quibodie quoque Christianorum communis fere mos est. Tympanum enim aliquando tibia,sive sistulis plurimis,Christianorum saltationes peraguntur : qui quidem tibiarum usus in saltationibus manęsse colliguntur ex illis puerorum verbis Lucæ 7. Hυλήσαμεν ὑμῖν, καὶ οὐκ ὠρχήσασθε: θρηνήσαμεν ὑμῖν, καὶ οὐκ ἐκλαύσατε 4: Tibia vobis cecinimus; & non sal- tastis,&c. Inde & Hieremias cap.3. מחול בשמחים Mechól meichachabim,cherum,sive choream ludentium dixit ab eodem instrumento חליל Chalil, seu tibiæ: quem chorum Septuaginta σὺν χοροῖς si ἐν τυμπάνοις, si ἐν χαρίζοντο, verterunt. Hinc חלל Chólel, tibicen, & plurali חלילים Cholelim,tibicines,Psalmo octogesimo septimo. Ezr.Regum 1. versu 4. בחלליים Mech-alelim Bas. halelim, ludentes sive canentes tibias.
units.tr: Something seems more likely to me: they think it was so called because it was used in profane and ... ways at public feasts, banquets and dances or tripudia. Hence also מחול Machol, because it signifies the profane dance, such as that of the Gentiles, in which the flute was played; and this custom is nearly common among Christians today, for dances are sometimes carried on to the tympanum or to many pipes. That the use of flutes in dances remained is gathered from those words of the boys in Luke 7: Ηὐλήσαμεν ὑμῖν, καὶ οὐκ ὠρχήσασθε· θρηνήσαμεν ὑμῖν, καὶ οὐκ ἐκλαύσατε ("We piped to you, and you did not dance; we wailed, and you did not weep"). Hence also Jeremiah chapter 3: מחול בשמחים Mechól meichachabim, he called a dance or a chorus of those playing, from the same instrument, חליל Chalil, or flute. The Seventy translated this chorus as σὺν χοροῖς, or ἐν τυμπάνοις, or ἐν χαρίζοντο. Hence חלל Chólel, a flute-player, and in the plural חלילים Cholelim, flute-players, Psalm 87. In 1 Kings, verse 5, בחלליים Mech-alelim Bas. halelim, those playing or sounding flutes.

units.la: Græcè ἀυλὸς tibia appellatur ἄνο τῶ αὐεῖ, id est, flando (unde & Germanicum fleiten) Tibia quomo- do dicta Græcè Hanc vocem & tibiam & fistulam & foramen interpretantur, ut alia ejus significata pratermittam. Hinc αὐλὸς,tibia canere: αὐλέω, ut tibia canen:em audire eos, cantu recreari: αὐλαρχος, cantus ad tibiam : ἀυσκεῖν ἀυλὸ , tibiarum auditor : ἀυλίεις,tibicina : ἀυλιοθὲκ, theca tibiarum. Aliquando tibia ludentes a Græcis χώρων εἰς ἀυλὸν dicebantur,id est, anserum modo tlangen- re,alt ut & flridulam vocem ed:re.
units.tr: In Greek the flute is called ἀυλὸς from αὐεῖ, that is, from blowing (whence also the German fleiten). The Greeks interpret this word as both flute, pipe and hole, to pass over its other meanings. Hence αὐλὸς means to play the flute; αὐλέω to play the flute, or to make the flute-player hear them and be refreshed by the song; αὐλαρχος a song to the flute; ἀυσκεῖν ἀυλὸ a listener of flutes; ἀυλίεις a flute-girl; ἀυλιοθὲκ a case for flutes. Sometimes those playing the flute were called by the Greeks χώρων εἰς ἀυλὸν, that is, to hiss like geese, or to give out a shrill voice.

units.la: Larmé tibia dicta ab osse cruris : & maximé cervorum, ut Plu archnis memorat in libello, Tibia Lælili eujus inscriptio est,Quod non licet ju unde viterct, secundum Epicuri seliam. Tibicen,ut Var- ro ait,a tibia & cantu dictus, & inde Tibicina,mulier cantans tibia. Unde Cicero de Oratore: Tibicen sine tibus tamen non potest. Tibiones set,tamen,teste Fesso,trabes in ædificiis dici existisstamentur,a similitudine tibiá canentium,quia ut canentes sussineant ; ita illi ædificia,sive ædificiorum testa. Hinc Juvenalis: Non urbem colimus tenuĭ tibicine fultam.
units.tr: The flute (tibia) is so called from the bone of the leg (os cruris), especially that of deer, as Plutarch recalls in his little book on the flute of Lælius, whose title is "That one cannot live pleasantly according to Epicurus." The tibicen, as Varro says, is named from the tibia and from singing, and from him the female flute-player, the tibicina. Hence Cicero in De Oratore: "The flute-player cannot perform without flutes." The tibiones, too, as Festus testifies, are said to be the beams in buildings, from the likeness to flute-players, who hold up their instruments as the beams hold up the structure. Hence Juvenal: "We do not inhabit a city propped up by a thin flute-prop."

units.la: Tbustorum lingua tibicines Subulones vocantur a Subulo, vel potius Subulonis cornu similitudine. Sic Cornicen,qui cornu: Lituen,qui lituo : Siticen,qui apud sitos,id est, vita funstos & sepultos tanere solitus ess.
units.tr: In the language of the Tuscans, flute-players are called subulones, from subulo, or rather from the likeness of the subulo's horn. So too cornicen, the horn-player; lituus, the trumpeter, from the lituus; and siticen, one who was accustomed to play among the sitos, that is, the dead and buried.

units.la: De tibiarum origine & inventoribus varie fuerunt sententiæ. Plutarchus in libro de Musica tradit,alios voluisse tibiam inventam esse a Marsya (quæ communis fere est opinio:) alios ab Olympo:alios ab Hyagnide : alios a Terpsichore. Plin lib.7.cap 56.tibiæ obliquæ inventionem Midæ in Phrygia tribuit : geminarum vero tibiarum,eidem Marsya. Verbæ ejus hæc sunt : Musicam Amphion (inventit) sistulam Pan:monaulam Mercurius : obliquam tibiam Midas in Phrygia: geminas tibias Marsyas Scribit porrò Aristoteles lib.8.Politicorum,tibiarum usum repudiatum fuisse,non tam propter oris deformitatem, quam ob caussam etiam a Pallade dicitur rejećta, quàm quod inutilis videretur ad rerum intelligentiam. Pindar us tamen Minervam facit tibiarum inventricem: ad imitandum lamentationem, graviter sonantem. Pleri ; autem,ut dissum,tibiam a Marsya, sistulam (quam Hebraei נזכרb, vocans נכב Nakab, id est. perforate,nimirum a foraminibus,Græci sυριγγα appellant ; quæ tamen vox sæpe pro tibia capitur) lyram ab Apolline aut Mercurio fuisse in ventam.
units.tr: Opinions about the origin and inventors of flutes have varied. Plutarch in his book On Music relates that some wished the flute to have been invented by Marsyas (which is almost the common opinion), others by Olympus, others by Hyagnis, others by Terpsichore. Pliny, book 7, chapter 56, ascribes the invention of the oblique flute to Midas in Phrygia, and that of the double flute to the same Marsyas. His words are: "Amphion invented music, Pan the panpipe, Mercury the monaulos, Midas in Phrygia the oblique flute, Marsyas the double flutes." Aristotle, moreover, in book 8 of the Politics, writes that the use of flutes was rejected, not so much on account of the deformity of the mouth, as for which reason Pallas is said also to have rejected them, but because it seemed useless for understanding things. Pindar, however, makes Minerva the inventor of the flute, for imitating lamentation, which sounds heavily. Most, as I said, hold that the flute was invented by Marsyas, and the pipe (which the Hebrews call nezkar [נזכר], and calling it Nakab [נקב], that is, "perforated," doubtless from its holes, the Greeks call syrinx [σύριγξ]; yet this word is often taken for the flute) and the lyre by Apollo or Mercury.

units.la: De tibiarum varii generibus & nominibus vide Serv ium in nonum Æneid. versum illum.
units.tr: On the various kinds and names of flutes, see Servius on that verse of the ninth book of the Aeneid.
O truly Phrygian, &c.

units.la: Quantum ad tibiarum materiam attinet, illam conflat olim fuisse buxum, ex qua etiamnum bodie conficiuntur: unde Buxea a Poëtis appellatur. Ovidius duodecimo Metamorph. Non illos citharae: non illos carmina vocum: Longa, multiforı delectat tibia buxi; Multiforis, id est, multa foramina habentis. Sic Mantuanus: Buxea quid latos modulatur tibia cantus?
units.tr: As far as the material of flutes is concerned, it is established that formerly they were made of boxwood, from which they are still made today; hence the poets call them "boxen." Ovid in the twelfth book of the Metamorphoses: "Not the cithara, not songs of the voice, but the long flute of many-holed boxwood delights them"; "many-holed," that is, having many holes. So Mantuan: "Why does the boxen flute sound out broad strains?"

units.la: Ex alia quoq; materia, praeter buxum, tibiam confici fuisse solitam testantur Athenaeus, Plinius & alii. Athenaeus e loti ligno, quod in Africa nascitur, confectam docet lib.4. (unde Lotina fistula dicta: ) item ex ebore (unde ebeanina quae primum a Phrygibus fistulae pertusa) & ex calamo, unde Tityrina, Graeci καλαμαύλακες, qui fistulas inflant. Idem docet, tibiam etiam ex eruribus hominum a Thebanis primum repertam esse. Plinius lib.16. cap.36. de materia tibiae sic scribit: Sed tunc ex sua quamque tamen harundine congruere perfusum erat: & eam, quae radicem antecesserat, levem tibiae convenire: quae cacumen dextra. Nunc sacrifice Tibicorum e buxo; ludicre vero loto, ossibus, aliis argentoque fiunt. Sic ex gruum quoq; tibiam eam confectam elim, dictum est supra.
units.tr: That flutes were commonly made of other materials besides boxwood is attested by Athenaeus, Pliny, and others. Athenaeus, in book 4, teaches that they were made of the wood of the lotus, which grows in Africa (whence they are called "lotus pipes"); likewise of ivory (whence the ebeanina, which the Phrygians first pierced), and of reed, whence the "Tityrine" ones; the Greeks call the players of pipes kalamaulakes [καλαμαύλακες]. The same author teaches that the flute was also first found among the Thebans, made from the shin-bones of men. Pliny in book 16, chapter 36, writes thus about the material of the flute: "But then each was made from its own reed, and the lighter part of the stalk, which had grown above the root, was suited to the flute, and the top part on the right. Now the flutes of sacrifices are made of boxwood, those for play of lotus, bone, and other materials, and silver." Thus it has been said above that a flute was also once made from a crane's bone.
These things concerning the material of flutes.

units.la: Quantum ad tibiarum usum attinet; Alcibiadem legimus duplici nomine omnem tibiarum usum damnasse, quod sic minuet ora habitum, ut vix vel a familiarissimis agnosci possit, quia tibia canit: & quod hominis propriam admirat vocem omnemq; loquendi facultatem praeripiat. Nemo enim simul & tibiam inflare & loqui potest. Cantantigitur dicere solebat, Thebanorum filii, qui loqui nesciunt: nobis autem Athenienses gentis nostrae principes sunt Pallas & Apollo; quorum illa fistulam confregit, hic tibicinem excoriavit, qua quidem oratione, ut aulos eicit. Plutarchus in ejus vita, Atticae juventuti persuasit, ut tibiarum usum rejecerit, atque repudiaret. Porro, prodeuntium prisco[rum] fabulas est, Palladem, ad spectandum tibia canentem, offensam oris sui deformitate, quam in speculo conspexerat, tibiam projectam commisisse. Apollinem autem Marsyam, tibiae interventorem, canendo a se victum excoriasse. In eandem sententiam Plato in Protagora, sermone qui de Poëtis habetur, similem esse dixit tibiam alterum & plebeiorum cibi vivis. Nam propterea quod inter poculo, mutua collocutione se invicem obligare aut oratione sua, & confabulatione, exhilarare ob infinitum nequeunt, magnificantur tibicinas, & luculenta mercede tibiarum alienam vocem conducunt, quarum sono ad convivium & congressum invitantur; cum nusquam apud bonos, probos, ac eruditos convivas saltatrices, fidicinae, tibicinae, videantur, ut quis citra nugas & lusus ejusmodi, sibi sufficiant ad mutuam consuetudinem, sua ipsorum voce & loquentes vicissim, & se audientes modeste, etiam complusculi sibi inherint. Idem & vos facitis, & Cynulce, dum bibitis, aut potius exhibetis, tibicina more vel saltricis voluptatem, quam bi sermones afferunt, interturbantes; vitamq; ait in Phileto idem Plato dixit, non hominem vivere sed pulmonis cuiusdam marini aut cujusdam ex illis corporibus, quae animata testis ostreorum affiguntur. Hac Athenaeus: quibus addea ea, quae apud Plutarchum habentur in quaestionibus symposiacis, lib.2. quaest.7. An tibicines sint adhibendi convivio?
units.tr: As for the use of flutes, we read that Alcibiades condemned all use of the flute on a double ground: first, because it so distorts the face that it can scarcely be recognised even by intimates, since it plays; and second, because it steals from man his own voice and the whole faculty of speech. For no one can at once blow a flute and speak. So he used to say: "The sons of the Thebans, who do not know how to speak, play the flute; but we Athenians have as the leaders of our race Pallas and Apollo; of whom the one broke the flute, the other flayed the flute-player." By which speech, as Plutarch relates in his life, he persuaded the youth of Attica to reject and repudiate the use of flutes. Moreover, the ancient fables tell that Pallas, while watching others play the flute, was offended by the ugliness of her face, which she had seen in a mirror, and threw the flute away. And Apollo, having defeated Marsyas, the inventor of the flute, in singing, flayed him. To the same effect Plato in the Protagoras, in the discourse on poets, said that the flute is like the food of the common people. For because at drinking parties they cannot, by mutual conversation, bind one another, or by their own speech and talk cheer themselves, they make much of flute-girls, and hire the voices of others at a splendid wage, by whose sound they are invited to the feast and the gathering; whereas among good, honest, and learned guests dancing-girls, harpists, and flute-girls are nowhere seen, since people who are not content with such trifles and games can, by their own voices, speaking and listening to one another modestly, keep up mutual fellowship, and even quite a few hold fast to themselves. You too do the same, Cynulcus, while you drink, or rather while you put on show, disturbing with the flute-girl's or dancer's pleasure the talk they bring. And in the Philebus the same Plato said that life is lived not by a man but by a kind of sea-lung, or one of those bodies which are attached, animated, to the shells of oysters. Thus Athenaeus; to which may be added what is found in Plutarch's Table Talk, book 2, question 7: Should flute-players be admitted to a banquet?

units.la: Aristoteles quoq; Politicorum libro 9. capite 6. tibiarum usum omnem videtur improbasse. Sic enim scribit: ἐν ἀνλὸς εἰς πνεῦμα ἀκοίμου, ἀλλὰ τεχνικὸν ὀργάνου, οἷον κιθάρα, ἢ ἐν ταῦτα ἐν τούτων δὲ ἐαυτῷ ἀπαρατὸν ἀρχοσι... Nec tibiae ad disciplinam sunt adducendae; neq; aliud quod vis organum artificiale, ut citharam, aut si quid aliud ejusmodi, sed quaecunque faciunt auditores bonos. Vide eundem libro octavo, capite sexto: ubi de Musica canticū, agit, ibi multa organa Musicae veteri, ut pectides, barbitos, & quae ad volutates eorum pertinent, qui cantores audiunt, ut septangulae, fi ve septagona, trigona, sambucae, & omnia, quae scientiam in manuum opere muneret, desiderant, repudianda esse existimat. Et huc putat afferendam fabulam illam de Minerva, quam fiuxerunt, ut paullo ante dictum, tibias a se repertas, oris deformitate offensam & flomachatam abjecisse. Hoc significare volunt Veteres, tibiarum instandarum disciplinam, cum nihil ad mentis agitationem conferatur, aspernandam: cum Minervae scientia & ars tribuatur.
units.tr: Aristotle also, in book 9, chapter 6 of the Politics, seems to have disapproved of the whole use of flutes. For he writes thus: "Nor should flutes be brought into education, nor any other artificial instrument, such as the cithara, or anything else of that kind, but whatever makes the listeners good" [ἐν ἀνλὸς εἰς πνεῦμα ἀκοίμου, ἀλλὰ τεχνικὸν ὀργάνου, οἷον κιθάρα, ἢ ἐν ταῦτα ἐν τούτων δὲ ἐαυτῷ ἀπαρατὸν ἀρχοσι]. See the same author in book 8, chapter 6, where, treating of music for singing, he holds that the many instruments of the old music, such as the pectides, the barbitos, and those pertaining to the pleasures of those who listen to singers, such as the seven-cornered (heptagonal), three-cornered, sambuca, and all those which demand knowledge in manual work, are to be rejected. He thinks also that the fable about Minerva should be brought in here, which they invented, as was said a little before, that she, offended and disgusted by the ugliness of her mouth, threw away the flutes she had discovered. The ancients wish to signify by this that the discipline of playing the flute, since it contributes nothing to the activity of the mind, is to be despised, since science and art are attributed to Minerva.

units.la: Sic Pythagoras lyrae organo usus esse dicitur: tibiae autem sonitum, canquam illiberalem & Pythagorā, tumultuarium explosisse, ut Nicolaus Scutellius testatur in descriptione vitae Pythagorae ex Iamblicho.
units.tr: Thus Pythagoras is said to have used the lyre, but to have rejected the sound of the flute as illiberal and disorderly, as Nicolaus Scutellius testifies in his description of the life of Pythagoras, drawn from Iamblichus.

units.la: Legimus tamen apud Iudaeos tibiarum cantum magno fuisse in usu: & quidem maximē in publicis conviviis, quae autem in via plarumque comitantur, triprodiem atque choreas profanas, quem absurdum Deus per Prophetam Isaiam gravissime reprehendit capite quinto his verbis: Vae vobis, qui mane surgunt ad sectandum ebrietatem, simul ac vesperi vinum ipsos incendit! Et quorum incon-vini sunt citharae, tympanum & tibia & vinum: & opus Domini non respiciunt, & factum manuum ejus non vident. Ex expressam nostrorum temporum mortuum imaginem.
units.tr: We read, however, that among the Jews the singing of flutes was in great use, and especially at public feasts, which were usually accompanied on the road by a profane triprodia and dances; God gravely rebuked this absurdity through the prophet Isaiah in chapter 5, in these words: "Woe to you who rise early in the morning to pursue drunkenness, who are inflamed by wine at evening! Whose feasts are with harps, tabret, flute, and wine; but they do not regard the work of the Lord, nor see the deed of his hands." This is an exact image of the dead of our own times.

units.la: Sed in Regum quoque, unctione & inauguratione adhibitas fuisse tibias, vel illud unicum Saulis exemplum satis docet primo Regum capite primo, versu quadragesimo. Nam cum is in Regem ungeretur, omnis populus magno tibiarum sono totam urbem repleuisse dicitur.
units.tr: But that flutes were also used at the anointing and inauguration of kings, the single example of Saul alone sufficiently teaches, in 1 Samuel chapter 10, verse 1 (in the Vulgate verse 40 of the first book of Kings, as numbered). For when he was anointed king, all the people are said to have filled the whole city with a great sound of flutes.

units.la: Prophetas quoq; tibius usos fuisse ex primo Samuelis libro, capite decimo, versu quinto videtur posse colligi, ubi Samuel ad Saulem, quemadmodum scriptum est: Posteā venies, inquit, in collem Dei, in quo deorum sunt praefecti Palaestinorum. Quum autem ingressus fueris illuc in urbem, obviam habebis coetum Prophetarum, descendentium de excelso, & ante eos erunt lyra, tympanum, & tibia, & cithara, & ipsi prophetantes.
units.tr: It seems that prophets too used flutes, and this can be gathered from 1 Samuel 10, verse 5, where Samuel says to Saul, as it is written: "Afterwards you will come to the hill of God, where the garrisons of the Philistines are. And when you enter the city there, you will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place, and before them there will be a lyre, a tambourine, a flute and a harp, and they themselves prophesying."

units.la: Rabbini volunt haec instrumenta musica adhibita fuisse a Prophetis, animos suos recreandi exhilarandi gratia, quod Spiritus Domini requirit animum laetum & hilarem: maestum autem & triste mensam fugiat.
units.tr: The rabbis hold that these musical instruments were used by the prophets to refresh and cheer their minds, since the Spirit of the Lord requires a glad and cheerful mind, while a sorrowful and gloomy one shuns the table.

units.la: Hinc adde, quod apud Israelitas quidem fidelium gaudium, quo sint affectiendi propter Assyriorum idolum, apud Hieremiam autem in Domini & vindicta divina adversus Moabitas comminatio tibiarum similitudine illustratur: ex quibus duobus locis patet, tibias & in laetitia & in luctu fuisse adhibitas. Idem luculentissime colligitur ex miraculo illo Christi, Matthaei nono capite, vergente tertio versu: Et quum venisset Iesus domum praefecti Synagogi, vidisset tibicines (θορυβοῦ ... ) & murmur tumultuantium, dixit eis: Recedite, etc. Hinc diserte constat, tibias pertinere inter alia etiam ad funebrem usum: quem quidem morem fuisse a profanis gentibus hauserant: ut & reliquas funerum pompas, licet inhibuisset Dominus in Lege.
units.tr: Add to this that among the Israelites the joy of the faithful, with which they were to be stirred against the idol of the Assyrians, and in Jeremiah the threat of divine vengeance against the Moabites, are both illustrated by the likeness of the flute. These two passages make clear that flutes were used both in joy and in mourning. The same is most clearly gathered from that miracle of Christ in Matthew 9, near the start of verse 23: "And when Jesus had come into the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and saw the flute-players and the crowd making a tumult (θορυβούμενον), he said to them: Depart, etc." From this it is plainly evident that flutes were used, among other things, at funerals. The Israelites had learned this custom from the profane nations, as they had also learned the other funeral pomps, although the Lord had forbidden them in the Law.

units.la: Apud Gentiles tibiarum usus latissime patuit, ut etiam cotes Musicae sive vocalis, sive organicae & instrumentalis. Earum igitur usus fuit & publicus & privatus, & scenicus sive cheatricus, & bellicus, & paftoritius, & convivialis, & saltatorius, & nuptialis, & denique funebris, & sacrificialis: de quo multa Athenaeus libro quarto & decimoquarto. Oratorius quoq; cibiarū fuit usus. Non solum enim cantantes et Musici, sed etiam Oratores aliquando adhibendos sibi tibicines existimarunt: id quod docet Caji Gracchi, clarissimi sui aetatis Oratoris, exempli, cui conciunanti, consistens post versum Musicus tibia, quam Tonarium vocant, modos ministrabat, quibus deberet intendi.
units.tr: Among the Gentiles the use of flutes extended very widely, as did the kinds of music, whether vocal, instrumental or accompanying an organ. Its use was therefore both public and private, scenic or theatrical, military, pastoral, convivial, for dancing, at weddings, and finally at funerals and sacrifices; on this Athenaeus writes at length in books 4 and 14. Flutes were also used in oratory. For not only singers and musicians, but also orators, sometimes thought flute-players should be engaged for themselves. This is shown by the example of Gaius Gracchus, the most famous orator of his age: when he was speaking, a musician stood behind him with a flute, which they call the tonarium, and supplied the modes by which his voice ought to be pitched.

units.la: Sed nos hic de tibiarum usu sacro, sive, sacrificiali quaedam addemus, quae institutio nostro mā-xime conveniunt. Hinc tibiae sacrae dictae a Telesle Poëta, ut est apud Athenaeum libro decimo quarto. Ejus versus bi sunt, quibus tibiarum usus declaratur: Phrygum rex leniter personantium tibiarum sacrarum Cantum primus in venit, Dorice Musa equiparandum Aemulum: varie modulatum tenebrosi spiritus Auram levem atq; pernicem (unde αὐλός Graeci a flatu volunt dictam) arundine completlens.
units.tr: But here we will add some things about the sacred, or rather sacrificial, use of the flute, which especially suit our purpose. Hence the flutes were called sacred by the poet Telestes, as is found in Athenaeus book 14. His verses, in which the use of flutes is described, are these: "The king of the Phrygians first came upon the sweet-sounding strain of sacred flutes, a rival to be matched with the Dorian Muse, playing variously a modulated tune, filling with reed the light and swift breath of a shadowy spirit (whence the Greeks wish the aulos to be named from its blast)."

units.la: O vidi tot ad hunc usum sacrum alludens sexto Fastorum sic canit: Queritur in scena cava tibia: queritur aris.
units.tr: Ovid, alluding to this sacred use, sings thus in book 6 of the Fasti: "The flute complains in the hollow stage; it complains at the altars."

units.la: Hinc Sacrifica a Seneca appellata & a Plinio: Seneca: Sacrifica dulces tibia effundat modos
units.tr: Hence Seneca and Pliny called them sacrificial flutes. Seneca: "Let the sacrificial flute pour forth sweet strains."

units.la: Et Plinius loco ante citato: Nunc sacrificae Thuseorum tibia ex buxo &c.
units.tr: And Pliny, in the passage cited above: "Now the sacrificial flutes of the Tuscans, made of boxwood," etc.

units.la: Apud Romanos tibicines sacrorum causa plurimi fiebant, magnumq; illud tributum erat bonos Idibus Ianuarii, ut scribit Plutarchus Quaestione quinquagesima quinta, Romanarum. Illo enim die ipsis permissum erat vestem induere muliebrem totam ut bem circuire, cuius moris banc rationem reddit Plutarchus. Cur Idibus Ianuarii tibicinibus permissum est per urbem circuire, vestem induere muliebrem? An hoc fit propter causam, quae subjicitur; Magnos illos honores Numa rex religionis causa contulerat. Quibus cum postea tribunus militum cusulari poeeflate Romanorum publ. administrantibus privarentur, uns versi Roma Tibur secesserunt, desiderata inde, quod religio animos tenebat Romanorum, neminine sacrificium praecinentes, accitiq; cum non obtemperarent, sed Tiburae manerent, libertus quidam magistratibus promisit occulte, fe eos Romam reductur um. Instructo proinde pollucto, tanquam fi Diuum rem sacram facissent, in vitat tibicines, adhibitis etiam conivis mulieribus, et per totam noctem compotatio, jocis chorea, protrahitur: tum subito sulla trepidatione, in provisio patroni super venu fe perturbatum at, perjuadentes tibicinibus, ut vebicula circumquaq; pedibus obtenta conscendant, Tibur se eos revertutum dolo promittentes: ibi circumaltis vehiculis eos, qui per tenebras animad vertere, ubi locorum effent; nequibant, universos Romam prima luce perfecerant autem plurimi vejibus floridis et mulierum amictis ob noctum mecum commissionem et conivium. Exinde cum magistratus tibicines in gratiam redierunt, decretum, est, ut tali habuisset illam diem ejs per urbem vagari licaret. Plutarchus.
units.tr: Among the Romans many flute-players were made for sacred purposes, and it was a great privilege that on the Ides of January they were allowed, as Plutarch writes in Roman Question 55, to dress in women's clothing and go round the whole city. Plutarch gives this reason for the custom: Why on the Ides of January were the flute-players permitted to go round the city dressed in women's clothing? Is it because of the cause that follows? King Numa had conferred these great honours for the sake of religion. When, afterwards, under the consulship of the Romans, the military tribunes and the public administrators deprived them of these, they all withdrew from Rome to Tibur. The Romans, whose religion held their minds, missed them, since no one was left to sing the sacrifice, and when they were summoned but would not obey and remained at Tibur, a certain freedman secretly promised the magistrates that he would bring them back to Rome. Accordingly, he provided wine and, as if they were celebrating a sacred rite of the gods, invited the flute-players, with women guests also included, and they spent the whole night in drinking, jokes and dancing. Then suddenly, with feigned alarm, he pretended to be disturbed by news that his patron was coming, and persuaded the flute-players to climb into carts that were hitched up on every side, promising them that they would be taken back to Tibur by a trick. There, when the carts had been driven round, they brought them, who could not tell in the dark where they were, all to Rome at first light. Most of them arrived wearing garlands and women's clothing, because of the night's joke and the banquet. Afterwards, when the magistrates and the flute-players were reconciled, it was decreed that they should have that day on which they might wander through the city in that dress. Plutarch.

units.la: Ejusdem rei atq; secessionis tibicinum ex urbe Livius quoq; meminit. Detade prima, libro no: Tibicines, inquit, quia prohibiti a prox mus censoribus erant in aede lovis velut, quod eradic antiquitus erat, aegre passi Tiburno agmine abierunt: adeo ut nemo in urbe esset, qui sacrificiu praecinteret. Ejus rei religio tenui Senatum, legatosq; Tibur misserunt, ut darent operam, ut ifli hominies Romanos restituerentur. Tiburtini benigne pollicit, primum accitos in curiam hortati sunt, ut revertentur Romam, postquam perpelli nequibant, consilio beud abhorrente ab ingenio hominum, eos aggrediuntur. Die fello alii alios per speciem celebrandarum canta opulatum causa invitant, et vino, cujus a vidum fermi genus est, mensatos sopiunt: atq; ita in plausitu lum no vitios conjiciunt ac Romam deportant: nec prius sentere, quam plaustris in foro relictis plenos trapula eos lux opprefit. Tunc concursus populi facile, impetratoq; ut manerent, dum tridum quotannis ornati cum cantu, atq; hac, quae nunc solemnis est li. en ia pes urbem vagantur: reflituntur in aedem velcendi us ut, qui satis praecinerent. Hinc referenda quoq; illa, quae Valerio scribit libro quinto de lingua Latina: Quinquatrus, inquit, Minusc ulae dictae Iunie Eidus ab similitudine Majorum quid ubicines tunc feriati per urbem vagantur et conveniunt ad aedem Minervaeum.
units.tr: Livy also mentions this same withdrawal of the flute-players from the city. In the first decade, book 9, he says: "The flute-players, because the censors had recently forbidden them to hold their banquet in the temple of Jupiter, as had been the custom of old, took it badly and departed in a body to Tibur, so that there was no one in the city who could sing the sacrifice. The religion of the Senate was troubled by this, and they sent envoys to Tibur to see that those men were restored to the Romans. The Tiburtines promised kindly; they first summoned the men into their council house and urged them to return to Rome. When they could not be persuaded, they turned to a plan that was far from their nature: on a festival day, some invited others, under the pretext of celebrating the festival, and with wine, of which there is a great store there, they lulled them into a stupor. In this way they threw them drunk into wagons and carried them to Rome. They did not notice until, with the wagons left in the forum, the light of day overwhelmed them, still full of drink. Then a crowd of people gathered easily, and when they had obtained that the men should stay, they were restored to the temple, so that they could sing the sacrifices. From this time they wander through the city each year, adorned and singing, on the day which is now celebrated as the festival of the Quinquatrus." Hence also what Valerius writes in book 5 of On the Latin Language: "The Quinquatrus, called Minor, was named from the Ides of June, in likeness to the greater, because on that day the flute-players are free from work and wander through the city and gather at the temple of Minerva."

units.la: Hostias apud Romanos ad praeconem et tibicinem immolari fuisse solitas illa quoq; Ciceronis clare testantur in oratione contra Rullum: Erant, inquit, hostiae majores, in foro constitutae, quae iis praetoribus de tribunali, sicut a nobis Consulibus de consilio sententia probatae ad praeconem et tibicinem immolabantur. Idem libro secundo de Legibus: Populares letitiam, inquit, in cantu et fidibus, et tibiis moderanto eam, cum Diuum honore jungunto. Idem eodem libro: Iam lundi publici, inquit, cum sint tria vea, circuq; divisi, sint corporum certatione, cursu et pugillatione, la Ratione curriculi, equorum usq, ad certam victoriam circo conflituitur: ea vua, caniu, ac fidibus et tibiis, dummodo ea moderata sint, ut lege praescribitur. Assentior enim Platoni, nihil tam facile in animos teneros atq, molles influere, quam varios dicendi sonos, quorum diu vix potest, quantum fit vis in utramq; partem. Namque et invitat languentes et languefacit excitatos: et tum remittit animos, tum contrahit: civitatum, hoc multarum in Graecia interfuit antiquum vetuum servare modum: quarum mores lapsi, ad mollitiem pater ut sunt immutati cum cantibus: aut hac dulcedine corruptela, depravati, ut quidam putant.
units.tr: Cicero clearly attests that the victims were usually sacrificed to the herald and the flute-player among the Romans, in the speech against Rullus: "There were the greater victims, set up in the forum, which, under those praetors, from the tribunal, just as among us the consuls with the advice of the Senate approved, were sacrificed to the herald and the flute-player." The same author in book 2 of On the Laws: "Let the people moderate their joy in song, lyre and flute, and join it with honour to the gods." The same book again: "Public games, since there are three kinds, divided into the circus, the contests of bodies in running and boxing, and the race of horses, which is run in the circus up to a certain goal: these are accompanied by song, lyre and flute, provided they are moderate, as the law prescribes. For I agree with Plato that nothing flows so easily into tender and soft minds as varied modes of speech, whose great power, in one direction or the other, is hardly to be grasped. For they both cheer the weary and weaken the excited, and they both relax and tighten the spirits. Therefore it was of great importance to many Greek states to keep the ancient rule of moderation, and when their morals slipped, they were changed into softness through songs, or were, as some think, corrupted by this sweetness."

units.la: Pauperem etiam in consecratione adhibitum fuisse tibicinem idem auctor testatur in Oratione pro Domo.
units.tr: The same author testifies in his speech for his house that a flute-player was also used at the consecration.

units.la: Matutinis quoq; vocum tibiarum, cantionibus solitos fuisse Gentiles Deos suos salutare, illa Arnobii verba libro septimo fatis ostendunt: Etiam ne Diu eris tinnitibus et quaflationibus Cymbalorum (afficiuntur?)
