Etiamne tympana? Etiamne symphonias? Quid efficiunt crepitus pitas Scabillorum? ut cum eos audirent Numina,honorificè secum existiment actum, & fervea tes animos irarum oblivione deponant? An nunquid ut parvuli pusiones ab ineptis Pagiribus crepitaculis exterrentur audiens: eadem ratione & omnipotentia Numina tibiarū stridore mulcentur & ad numerum Cymbalorum mollita indignatione flacefcunt ? Quid sibi volūt,inquit, excitationes ille,quas canitis matutini,tollatis ad tibiam vocibus? Condormiscunt enim Superi,remeare ut ad vigilias debeant? Quid dormitione ista illæ, quibus bene ut valeant,auspicabilis salutatione mandatas? Somni enim quiete sol vuntur,occuparig, ut hos possint lenes audiendæ fiunt nan:a?
units.tr: The words of Arnobius in book 7 sufficiently show that the Gentiles used to greet their gods each morning with the sounds of flutes and songs: "Are the gods also moved by the jingling and clashing of cymbals? By drums? By symphonies? What do the rattles of the castanets accomplish, so that when the divinities hear them they think themselves honoured, and put away the boiling of their anger in forgetfulness? Or, as little children are frightened by the rattles of foolish nurses, so are the almighty divinities soothed by the screeching of flutes, and, their indignation softened to the beat of cymbals, grow calm? What do those awakenings mean, which you sing in the morning, raising your voices to the flute? For do the gods fall back asleep, so that they must return to their watches? What is the purpose of those greetings sent with good wishes for their health, if their sleep is to be broken? Are they to be soothed, so that they may be able to hear the lullabies?"

units.la: Hujus usus tibicinum in sacris meminit etiam Suetonius in vita Tiberii,his verbis: Et quo primùm die post exeffum Augusti curiam intra vit,quasi pietati,firmul ac religioni fatis factũrus, Minor exemplo, ture quidem ac vino, verùm sine tibicine supplicavit, ut ille olim in morte filii. Idem fuit fuit fit cum a Minoe,tum a Tiberio, ejus exemplo, Beroaldus hanc rationem reddit, quod Musita in luctu importuna res sit: quanquam tibi,ines facrificius quidem præcinere solitos Historici tradiderunt, Unde Ovidius: Cantabat fanis,cantabat tibia ludis.
units.tr: Suetonius also mentions this use of pipers in sacred rites, in his life of Tiberius, in these words: "On the first day after Augustus's death, when he entered the senate-house, Tiberius, as if about to satisfy his duty to piety and religion, offered sacrifice with incense and wine, but without a piper, as Minos had once done at the death of his son." Beroaldus gives the reason for this same practice, both in Minos's case and in Tiberius's, which was that music is out of place in mourning. Yet the historians report that pipers were customarily employed in sacrifices too. Hence Ovid: "He sang in the temples, he sang at the games to the pipe."

units.la: De tibiarum in ludis sacris atq; sacrificiis apud Græcos & Romanos usu pulchrè sic Diony- fius Halicarnassens libro Antiquitatum Rom. scribit,Μετὰ ἡ τὰς ποσίας ταύτας,κιϑαρῳδοὶ πλ τὰ ἀδόμεια καὶ αὐλητὰι πολλοὶ παρεχόμενοι...
units.tr: Dionysius of Halicarnassus describes the use of pipes in the sacred games and sacrifices of the Greeks and Romans well in the seventh book of his Roman Antiquities: "After these processions, many citharodes singing hymns and many pipers were provided..." [Μετὰ δὲ τὰς πομπὰς ταύτας, κιθαρῳδοὶ πολλοὶ ᾄδοντες ὕμνους καὶ αὐληταὶ πολλοὶ παρεχόμενοι...]

units.la: {y} Dionysius Halicarnassensis, Antiquitatum Romanarum, lib. VII. tas porrò sequebantur [?] altatorum chori, diuisi trifariam; primò virorum, deinceps impuberum, postremò puerorum: post quos tibicines inflantes antiqui morù tibias breves, quarum bucula per-mansit usus; tibarifiaq̄, pulsantes eburneas septem fidium lyras, & quae vocantur baubita; quorum vsus apud Graecos usque meo tempore desiit: apud Romanos verò adhibentur omnibus autisquis sacris. Hactenus Halicarnasseus.
units.tr: {y} Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Roman Antiquities, book 7. "Behind them followed the choirs of the altar-attendants, divided into three companies: first the men, then the youths below puberty, and last the boys. After them came the pipers, who blew the old short pipes, of which a remnant of the practice still survives, and the lyre-players, who struck seven-stringed lyres of ivory, and those called baubita. The use of these among the Greeks ceased in my own time, but among the Romans they are employed in every kind of sacred rite." So far Halicarnassus.

units.la: His adde, quae Plutarchus in libello de Musica scribit: Quin & Hyperboreorum, inquit, sacra adhibitis tibiis, citharis & fistulis in Delum missa referunt antiquitus. Sunt qui ipsum Deum tibia cecinisse autumant: ut narrat optimus cantilenarum conditor Alcman. Carmina e Minerua didicisse tibiis canere Apollinem ajt: Ieaq; venerandae prorsus est Musica, Deorum in venerium cum sit, Et paulò ante, eodem libello: Sed quoniam simul veteres tibicinum et citharaedorum nomos retulimus, transfibimus iam ad tibicinum nomos. Traditum est enim Olympum, cum esset tibicen, e Phrygia tibicinum nomum fecisse Apollinem. Hunc Olympum ajunt à rum fuisse eorum, qui deserterunt a primo Olympo, Marsyae discipulo, qui nomos in Deos fecit. Is enim cum amasius esset Marsyae, & ab eo artem tibia canendi didicisset, harmonitos nomos in Graecium intulit, quibus nūc Graeci vsuntur in festis Deorum. Ac omnino in toto illo libello Musicae dignitatem inde probat, quòd non tam humanum, quàm diuinum sit in ventum Musica, quod in careis, ludis & sacrificiis illa sit adhibita. Vide eadem de re etiam Apuleium: nec non Seruium illa Virgilii: Desidiae cordi juvat indulgere choreis Et patem assuetis biforum dat tibia cantum.
units.tr: To this add what Plutarch writes in his little book On Music: "Indeed, they say the sacred rites of the Hyperboreans, performed with pipes, lyres and flutes, were sent to Delos in ancient times. Some hold that the god himself played the pipe, as the excellent composer of songs Alcman relates. Apollo, they say, learned to play the pipe from Minerva. Music is indeed worthy of reverence, since it belongs to the gods." And a little earlier in the same book: "But since we have related the ancient nomes of the pipers and the lyre-players together, let us now pass on to the nomes of the pipers. It is handed down that Olympus, when he was a piper, made from the Phrygian pipe-nome an Apollo-nome. They say this Olympus was one of those who came from the first Olympus, the disciple of Marsyas, who made nomes in honour of the gods. For he, being the lover of Marsyas and having learned from him the art of piping, introduced the harmonic nomes into Greece, which the Greeks now use at their festivals of the gods." In that whole little book he proves the dignity of music from the fact that it is not so much human as divine, since it has been employed in dances, games and sacrifices. See the same matter also in Apuleius, and Servius on the verse of Virgil: "The heart delights to indulge in idle dances, and the pipe of two reeds gives the accustomed song."

units.la: De eodem hoc tibiarum, fistularum, citharārumq̄, usu antiquissimo in sacris videre licet etiā Leo-nicum de varia historia, capite decimo quarto; ubi inter alia Deli antiquissimum Apollinis sima lacrum, quod Hercules cum Meropibus colloca verit, dextrā quidem manu arcum, altera vero tres cum Musicis instrumentis retinuisse Gratias tesletur: quarum una lyram, altera tibias; tertia verò inter has media fistulam manu gestavevit.
units.tr: On this same most ancient use of pipes, flutes and lyres in sacred rites one may also consult Leonicus, On Varied History, chapter fourteen. There, among other things, he relates that in the most ancient image of Apollo at Delos, which Hercules set up with the Meropes, the right hand held a bow, while the other hand held three Graces with musical instruments: one holding a lyre, another pipes, and the third, standing between these, carried a flute in her hand.

units.la: Ac hujusmodi quidem tibiarum sacrificarum: & quidem geminarum, atq; tibicinum aliquot imagines cernere licet in sacrificiis illis, quae in nobili illa Tripodum columna fuit expressae, de quae supra.
units.tr: Images of this kind of sacred pipes, indeed of two pipes, and of several pipers, may be seen in those sacrifices which were represented on that famous column of tripods, mentioned above.

units.la: Porrò cum cibis sepe conjunguntur fistulae, lyrae, citharae, sistra, cymbala, tympana, quae in Gentilium sacris fuerunt adhibita. Sed tubarum quoque, buccinarum, lituorum, cornuum usus non apud Iudaeos tantum, sed etiam apud Gentiles magnum fuisse in sacris & sacrificiis ipsorum usum pasum antiqua litterarum monumenta testantur. Armilustrium, ut ajt Festus, festum erat apud Romanos, quorum divinas armati facitabant: ac dum sacrificarent, tubis canebant. Tubilustrium, ut auctor est Varro, dictum, quòd eo die in atrio sutorio tubae lustrabantur. Sic Festus: Tubilustria dies appellantur, in quibus agnā tubae lustrabantur: quibus diebus adscriptum in Fastis erat, cùm in atrio sutorio agnā tubae lustrantur, ab eis tubas appellant: quod genus lustrationis ex Arcadia Pallanteo translatum ac venisse dicunt. Ovidius: Proxima Volcani lux est, Tubilustria dicunt Lustrantur purae, quas fecit ille, tuba.
units.tr: Moreover, pipes, lyres, cithers, sistra, cymbals and drums are often named together, being employed in the sacred rites of the Gentiles. But that the use of trumpets, horns, litui and cornets was great in sacred rites and sacrifices, not only among the Jews but also among the Gentiles, the ancient monuments of literature bear witness. The Armilustrium, as Festus says, was a festival among the Romans, on which the armed men purified their weapons, and while they sacrificed they sounded trumpets. The Tubilustrium, as Varro records, was so named because on that day the trumpets were purified in the Atrium Sutorium. So Festus: "The days are called Tubilustria, on which the trumpets were purified with a sacrificial lamb; on these days it was written in the calendars that, when the lamb was purified in the Atrium Sutorium, they called them trumpets. This kind of purification they say was brought from Pallanteum in Arcadia." Ovid: "The next day is Vulcan's; they call it Tubilustria, when the pure trumpets, which that god made, are purified."

units.la: Et Tubicines, eodem tepe, eciam ii appellantur, qui sacerdotes viri specio fi publicè sacra faciebant, tubarum lustrandarum gratia. Tuba, inquit Varro, a tubos, quos etiamnum ita appellant tubicines sacrorum. Tubicines sacrorum vocat, qui tubas in sacrarum administratione canebant.
units.tr: At the same time, those were also called tubicines who, as men chosen by public appointment, performed the sacred rites for the sake of purifying the trumpets. "Tuba," says Varro, "comes from tubos, which the tubicines of the sacred rites still call them by that name." He calls them tubicines of the sacred rites, who sounded the trumpets in the administration of sacred things.

units.la: Calphurnius Eclogaprima. Altera regna Numae, quae primus o'vantia cede Agmina Romuleis & adhuc ardentia caltris Paris opus docuit, jussit, silentibus armis Inter sacra tubas, non inter bella, sonare.
units.tr: Calpurnius, Eclogue 1: "The second kingdom of Numa, which first taught the Roman ranks, still burning with the spoils of the enemy, to rejoice in peace; he ordered that, with arms silent, trumpets should sound among the sacred rites, not among wars."

units.la: Quemadmodum tubæ unà cum aliis instrumentis Musicis olim a Iudæis ipsius Dei jussu in ipsorum sacris fuerunt usurpatæ: ita Diabolus quoque, seu Dei simia, præter alia instrumenta Musica, tubas quoque in sacerrimis sacrificiis, ac detestandis suis sacris eàdem adhiberi & usurpari curavit, ut ex iis, quæ supra attigi, & iis, quæ mox sequentur, patet. Plutarchus in suis Symposiacis, ut Indæos parvas tubas: ita Argivos quoq; in suis Dionysiis iisdem uti solitos fuisse scribit, ad Deum evocandum, libro quarto Problem. quinto. Eusthatius Iliad. 2. sex tubarum genera enumerans, inter illas unam vocat Ægyptiam rotundam, quæ χρῦσα fit dicta, qua Ægyptios ad sacra sua usos fuisse, ajunt, clangore homines ad rem divinam convocasse scribit. Pollux similiter tubæ πτιῶ ὀλίγα ἱσπορικὸν ἰπι Σωτίας refert, id est, sonum sacrum sacrificialem, qui apud Ægyptios, Argivos, Tyrrhenos & Romanos in usu fuerit: indeq; tubicinem, qui in sacris tuba canebat (quod apud Iudæos sacerdotum munus erat) ἰεροφάντας, sive melius, ὀρθὸς ἀνασκευάζειν, id est, tubicinem sacrum, & ἀγαυς ἀνὴρ (forsan quia tubæ clangore populum dimittebat) fuisse appellatum.
units.tr: Just as trumpets, along with other musical instruments, were once used in their sacred rites by the Jews at God's own command, so the Devil, the ape of God, besides other musical instruments, has also arranged that trumpets be employed and used in his most accursed sacrifices and his detestable rites, as is clear from what I have touched on above and from what follows. Plutarch, in his Symposiacs, writes that the Argives, like the Jews, customarily used small trumpets in their Dionysia, to summon the god; see book 4, problem 5. Eustathius on the Iliad 2, listing six kinds of trumpets, calls one of them the Egyptian round trumpet, which is named chrysa [χρῦσα], and which, he writes, the Egyptians used in their sacred rites, to call people to the divine service by its clangour. Pollux likewise describes a trumpet-sound [ὀλίγα ἱεροπρεπῆ] which, he says, was in use among the Egyptians, Argives, Etruscans and Romans, a sacred sound for sacrifice; and from this the trumpeter who sounded the trumpet in sacred rites (which among the Jews was the duty of the priests) was called a hierophant, or better a sacred trumpeter, and a man of... (perhaps because by the clangour of the trumpet he dismissed the people).

units.la: Nunc de tibiarum istarum, nec non aliorum instrumentorum Musicorum, ut fistularum, lyrarum, cytharurum, cymbalorum, sistrorum, tympanorum, tubarum, buccinarum, lituorum, ut seu abusu potius Gentilium in sacris atq; sacrificiis quedam sunt dicenda. Hæ igitur ob causas, de quibus mox dicemus, instrumentorum istorum Musicorum sono, seu strepitu potius usi fuerint: Primum quidem ad sacra ista indicenda, & ad homines ad illa convocandos, ius, perabilis adlo- ros rursus dimittendos, organorum istorum flatu pulsuq; usi fuerunt.
units.tr: Now some things must be said about these pipes, and about other musical instruments, such as flutes, lyres, cithers, cymbals, sistra, drums, trumpets, horns and litui, as used by the Gentiles in their sacred rites and sacrifices, or rather in their abuse of them. For these reasons, which we shall state shortly, they used the sound or rather the noise of these musical instruments. First, indeed, they used the blowing and striking of these instruments to announce the sacred rites, and to summon people to them, and then to dismiss them again.

units.la: Secundus illorum usus fuit, ut ius, quisacris intererant, silentium, ut supra dixi, maximè necessarium indicerent, omnes ad taciturnam, diligentem, attentamq; sacrorum suorum administrationem meditationemq; excitarent.
units.tr: The second use of these instruments was to announce silence, which, as I said above, was most necessary for those who attended the sacred rites, and to stir everyone to quiet, diligent and attentive administration and meditation upon their sacred things.

units.la: Tertio ut quibus eos etiam aliis rebus atq; cerimoniis, quæ in sacrificiis peragebantur; ita hoc quoq; suavi dulcij, tibiarum aliorumq; instrumentorum sono, numero, modo Deos illos suos leniri, demulceri, placari, & ut adsequaque et calos venirent, allicicas in vitæ posse sibi persuadebant.
units.tr: Third, as they soothed, softened and appeased their gods by other rites and ceremonies performed in the sacrifices, so too by the sweet and pleasing sound, rhythm and measure of pipes and other instruments, they were persuaded that those gods could be enticed to come and be present.

units.la: Quarto utebantur isto tibiarum, aliorumq; organorum Musicorum cantu, eos, qui sacris intererant, exhilarandi, & ab omni tristitia ad lætitiam hilaritatemq; traducendi gratia, quam iis sacris festisq; suis maximè requiri, Deisq;, quos colebant, placere arbitrabantur, secundum illa Ovidii: Dii quoq; ut à cunctis hilari pietate colantur, Tristitiaq; pòm per sua festa jubent.
units.tr: Fourth, they used the singing of pipes and other musical instruments to cheer those who attended the sacred rites and to lead them from all sadness to joy and gladness, which they thought was chiefly required in their sacred rites and festivals and pleasing to the gods they worshipped, according to Ovid: "The gods too, that they may be worshipped by all with cheerful devotion, command that sadness be put away at their festivals."

units.la: Aristoteles οἷα ἐν Politicorum ἰσχὺς μίλιν, id est, sacros cantus dicit vim habere medicinæ & parationis ad animos componendos & sedandos.
units.tr: Aristotle, in the Politics, says that sacred songs have [ἔχει ... δύναμιν] the power of medicine and purification to calm and settle the minds of men.

units.la: Quinto non dehorant inter Gentiles, qui homines istis tibiarum, cymbalorum, aliorumq; instrumentorum sonis divinitus afflari & ad divinandum excitari opinabantur, ut Corybantes, Sacerdotes & exaltati, baxio captos & eos, qui matrem Deorum furenter colebant. Hanc Porphyrii sententiam Iamblichus in illo suo libro de mysteriis Ægyptiorum, segmento tertio, capite nono commemorat, sed vnd & refellit: ubi tamen Musicam magnam habere vim, & si soni, carmina atq; cantus, qui sinulli Diis sunt consecrati, atq; conveniunt, adhibeantur, ipsorum Deorum ad ventum atq; præsentiam effici posse confirmat.
units.tr: Fifthly, the Gentiles did not shrink from the idea that men were inspired by the gods through the sounds of flutes, cymbals and other instruments, and were roused to prophesy, as the Corybantes, the priests of Cybele, and those who worshipped the Mother of the gods in a frenzy were thought to be seized by Bacchic rapture. Iamblichus mentions this opinion of Porphyry in his book on the mysteries of the Egyptians, section three, chapter nine, but he also refutes it. There, however, he affirms that music has great power, and that if sounds, songs and chants that are consecrated and suited to particular gods are used, the presence and coming of those very gods can be brought about.

units.la: Sexto instrumentorum istorum Musicorum sonitu atq; strepitu impedire conabantur, ne vel hostiarum, quæ immolabantur, vel etiam hominis, ab iis, qui sacris interemant, voces lugubres, tristes & ominosæ, quibus irrita possent fieri sacrificia, exaudiretur. Hujus rei clarum, manifestum, exemplum & testimonium habemus in humanis illis sacrificiis; quæ omnis humanitatis extinctam, pertubat, immanitatum contrà plenissima fuerunt: in quibus tympanorum, cymbalorum aliorumq; instrumentorum graviissimi soni pulsabantur, ne lamentabiles miseri funeris illorum, quiasi cremabantur, flesus, ejulatus, clamores atque vociferationes, liberorum præsertim à parentibus exaudiantur, quibus illi (o horrenda, furiosam, monstrosam, præ fuqq Diabolicam impietatem!) ad commiserationem atq; tristitiam commoverentur. Idenim fieret, minimè sacrificiis illis Iudæis Numinaq; seu Dæmoniapotius sua placaripoffe existimabant. propter felicem fauftamq; maftationis percussionisve istius successum? Na quando in victime percussione & maftatione bona laetaq; signa atque omina apparebant, ea cum gratulatione, cum plausu laetaq; acclamatione excipiebant. At vero ad signa infausta & sinistra expavescere, animiq; suis conflernari solebant: ac nox aras subpedas trepide adibant, intuiq; observabant cetera, follicitaq; quae ratione Numen offensum reconciliarent, ac cum eo in gratiam redirent, deliberabant. Nunc igitur cum in hac hostiae percussione & maftatione laeta omnia apparerent, mulieres h&e &lollo&ecl;ζκλαμαζεμεζ, & gratias Minervae eam ob caussam egisse dicuntur, tanquam re bene feliciterq; adhuc gesta: fimulq; precatae, ut reliqua etiam aftio facrificialis feliciter ipsis succederet.
units.tr: Sixthly, by the noise and din of these musical instruments they tried to prevent the mournful, sad and ominous cries of the victims being sacrificed, or even of the human being, from being heard by those who performed the rites, since such cries could render the sacrifices void. We have a clear and manifest example and proof of this in those human sacrifices, which utterly extinguish all humanity and were full of savagery. In them the deepest-sounding drums, cymbals and other instruments were struck, so that the lamentable groans, wailing, cries and shouts of those wretches as they were burned, especially of children by their parents, should not be heard, lest they be moved to pity and sorrow. (O horrible, furious, monstrous and, above all, diabolical impiety!) For they believed that the gods or demons could by no means be appeased by those sacrifices unless the slaughter or striking went well and auspiciously. For when good and joyful signs and omens appeared in the striking and slaying of the victim, they received them with congratulation, applause and joyful acclamation. But at unlucky and sinister signs they were wont to tremble and be dismayed in spirit, and then they hastily approached the altars, watched the rest closely, and deliberated carefully how they might reconcile the offended god and win back his favour. Now, when everything appeared favourable in this striking and slaying of the victim, the women are said to have shouted [ololyzein] and given thanks to Minerva for that reason, as if the matter had been well and happily accomplished so far, and at the same time to have prayed that the rest of the sacrificial action might also turn out well for them.

units.la: Voci λαλειν, ut hoc quoq; addam, & sono & significatione, affines fere sunt cum voces He-brae Alah, id est, jurare, precari, imprecari, maledicere: Hillel, id est, laudare: jalal & Hehil id est, ululare, clamare, vociferari: unde jelel & jelalah, id est, ululatus, vocii emissio, quae fit cum cordis dolore, interpretae Davide Kimchi: tum Latinae voces, ejulare & ululare: quae omnes ab Hebraeis vocibus fine dubio profectae sunt. Effet hic rursus dicendi locus de precibus & supplicationibus in sacrificiis adhiberi solitis: sed quoniam de illis supra fatis est dictum, prolixiore illarum explicatione hic supersedendum mihi esse existimo. Sed antequam a tibiarum & Musica facrificiali explicatione discedam, de Musica tantum vocali, de hymnis, cui Deo proprius ac dicatus, in illorum facrifitiis decantari solitus, denique de tripudiis, choreis, saltationibus, motibus incompositis, five gestibus, seu geftificationibus potius, in quibusdam sacris adhiberi solitis, hic quaedam adjiciemus: quae quidem Musice illi artificiali & precibus cognata sunt & affinia.
units.tr: To add this as well: the Greek word laleein [λαλεῖν] is in sound and meaning nearly akin to the Hebrew words alah, that is, to swear, pray, invoke a curse, or revile; hillel, that is, to praise; jalal and helel, that is, to howl, cry out, shout; whence jelel and jelalah, that is, a howling, an outpouring of voice that comes from grief of heart, as David Kimchi explains. Then the Latin words ejulare and ululare, all of which have undoubtedly come from Hebrew words. There would be occasion here again to speak of the prayers and supplications customarily used in sacrifices, but since I have said enough about them above, I think I should not go into a longer account of them here. Before I leave the account of flutes and sacrificial music, however, I will add a few remarks on purely vocal music: on the hymns, which were sung at their sacrifices to the god to whom they were proper and dedicated; and finally on the dances, choruses, leapings and unordered movements, or rather gestures and gesticulations, used in certain rites. These are related and akin to that artful music and to prayer.

units.la: Primo igitur observandum, singulis Dis certos dicatos fuisse hymnos, quibus illorum festis sacris decantari confuevenunt. Theodoretus sermone quarto, ad Graecos infideles de materia & Mundo ad hunc morem hos verbis pie eleganterq; alludit: Ne, inquit, cantemus julum Cereri, neq; ipsi Rhee Lityerfam, ne Baccho Dithyrambum, ne Paean Pythii Apollini, neve Dianae concinamus Hipoepum: sed rerum omnium conditori Deo hymnos Davidicos proferamus, cumq; eo pariter exclamemus: Quam magnificata sunt opera tua Domine! Omnia in sapientia fecisti. De hymnis istis & eorum generibus ac differentiis vide Caelum Rhodiginum libro septimo, capite quinto. Decantabant igitur alii Dii alios hymnos, Dianae Hypingos, Apollini Paana Dionysio Dithyrambos, Cereri julos, Veneri hymnos ερωτικουζ, id est, amatorios. Graeci prae-ter haec θρηνωδια accinebant, & χαριτων & στιχια. Athenaeus libro decimoquarto: Quas cantiones five hymnos vocant julos, Cereri & Proferpinae sunt peculiares, Apollini Philelia, Hypingi Dianae. Eodem in loco enumerat multarum cantionum genera atq; nomina, fecundum varia vitae genera ac instituta: ut primum quidem ea, quae cum saltatione canebantur, deinde alia, quae voce pronunciari atq; cantari folebant: cujusmodi erant cantiones molentium in piftrino, textrinarum, lanas tractantium, nutricum lactantium, meffiorum, mercenariorum in agro, ad opus commeantium, balneatorum, pinsentium fruges, eorum, qui pecora ducebant ad pabula, funerum & rerum aduersarum, nuptiarum, rerum felicium & laetarum.
units.tr: First, then, it should be noted that particular hymns were assigned to each god, to be sung at their festivals and sacred rites. Theodoret, in the fourth discourse to the unbelieving Greeks, On Matter and the World, alludes to this custom piously and elegantly in these words: "Let us not sing the iulos to Ceres, nor the Lityerses to Rhea, nor the dithyramb to Bacchus, nor the paean to Pythian Apollo, nor the hypoepus to Diana; but let us offer the Davidic hymns to the Creator of all things, and with him cry out together: How magnificent are your works, O Lord! In wisdom you have made them all." On these hymns and their kinds and differences, see Caelius Rhodiginus, book seven, chapter five. Different gods, then, had different hymns sung to them: the hypingi to Diana, the paean to Apollo, the dithyrambs to Dionysus, the iuli to Ceres, and erotic, that is, amatory, songs to Venus. Besides these, the Greeks also sang thrēnōdiai, and the songs called charites and stichia. Athenaeus, book fourteen: "The songs or hymns called iuli belong peculiarly to Ceres and Proserpina; the philelia to Apollo; the hypingi to Diana." In the same place he lists many kinds and names of songs according to the various modes and customs of life: first those that were sung with dancing, and then others that were customarily spoken and sung aloud, such as the songs of women grinding at the mill, of weavers, of those working wool, of nurses suckling infants, of reapers, of hired labourers in the field going to their work, of bath attendants, of those pounding grain, of those driving cattle to pasture, of funerals and misfortunes, of weddings, and of happy and joyful occasions.

units.la: Sed ut ad Deorum hymnos redeamus, eos in epulis potissimum, quae post sacrificia agitabatur; & quidem in mensis plerunq;, fecundis in eorum honorem decantare folebant, quibus, antea sacris fecerant. Eum exemplum illustre extat apud Homerum Iliad. 1. post Hecatombem, a Chryse Apollini factum in epulo, quod sacrificium illud fuit consecutum: Οι δ' παννυχιοι μολπη θεον ιλασκοντο Καλον αειδοντες παιηονα κουρους Αχαιων Μιλπουντες ικατρον, δια φοιβ' ιεπαντο ακουων Hi autem totam diem cantu Deum (Apollinem) placabant Latum canentes Paean pueri Achivorum Canentes longe operantem: is autem mentem delectabatur audiens.
units.tr: But to return to the hymns of the gods: they used to sing them especially at the feasts that followed the sacrifices, and indeed mostly at the tables, in their honour, to those gods to whom they had earlier offered sacrifice. A famous example is found in Homer, Iliad 1, after the hecatomb offered by Chryses to Apollo, at the banquet that followed that sacrifice: "But all through the night they propitiated the god with song, the boys of the Achaeans singing the paean well, hymning the far-darting one; and he was glad at heart as he listened." [Greek]

units.la: Hujus cantionis sacra epularia, descriptione et cantores, nempe xouegi, id est, pueri, Achivi, & tepus, paeanismus, id est, tota die; & Deus, in cujus honore cantabatur (is fuit Apollo) & cantionis genus atq; subjectum, nempe Paean, canentes longe operantem; et finis, Ἰησοῦ
units.tr: In this description of the sacred feast and its song we have the singers, namely the youths [kouroi], the Achaeans; the time, the whole day, that is, all day long; the god in whose honour it was sung, Apollo; the kind of song and its subject, the paean, sung to the far-working god; and the effect, in the words "he was glad at heart".
An example of a hymn from Homer.

units.la: ὅντερ, idest, Deum placabant; & effectus, at ille mentem delestabatur, exprimitur. Spondanus in illa verba Homeri sic commentaetur est: Varia sunt, inquit, canteleneratum species, quas Eustathius & post eum Rhodiginus enumerant: τ αττιgit etiam Epitome Athenæi libro primo. Alia igitur est σποφορικὴ, qualis est vatis illius, quem Clytemnestræ reliquit discedens Agamemnon, qui primum mulierum laudes percurrens, desiderium quoddam honoris, gloriæ, probitatis, in eius animo impressit: unde Aegysthus non priust Clytemnestra potiust est, quam dolo & silium in insulam desertā obtruncarit. Alia est ὑμνοποιικὴ, qua virorum præstantium laudes recinebantur, ut de Achille aliquando, Homerus dicet. Alia ὄπλωτικὴ: quam etiam Philostratus Achilli tribuit his verbis: Hδη δ', inquit, τους ἀρχαίους ἱλλαας & Τυλύσσον, καὶ Ναρθικαδιος. Spondanus. Hactenus Spondanus.
units.tr: The words mean "they propitiated the god", and the effect, "he was glad at heart", is expressed. Spondanus comments on those words of Homer thus: "There are various kinds of song," he says, "which Eustathius, and after him Rhodiginus, enumerate; the Epitome of Athenaeus, book one, also touches on them. One kind, then, is the sposphorikē [σποφορική], such as that of the singer whom Agamemnon left behind with Clytemnestra when he departed, who, first running through the praises of women, impressed on her mind a certain longing for honour, glory and virtue; whence Aegisthus did not possess Clytemnestra until he had cunningly killed her husband on a deserted island. Another is the hymnopoiikē [ὑμνοποιική], by which the praises of outstanding men were sung, as Homer at one point tells of Achilles. Another is the hoplōtikē [ὁπλωτική], which Philostratus also attributes to Achilles in these words: 'Already the ancients...'" Thus far Spondanus.

units.la: Simile exemplum habemus apud Apollonium nostrum in Argonauticis istius sacrificii, & quod sacrificium illud fuit consecutum, epuli descriptione in quo Orpheus citharædus cecinisse dicitur. Fit etiam eodem in epulo mentio saltationum. Sed de hac & aliorum hymnorum decantatione, & choreis, saltationibus atque tripudiis, quæ in epulis nonsantum profanis, sed etiam sacris, siue sacrificialibus celebrari a Gentilibus confuse verunt, copiosè admodum in meo Antiquitatum Conuiuialium opere disserui. Illuc itaque Lectorem benevolum remitto.
units.tr: A similar example is found in our Apollonius, in the Argonautica, in his account of that sacrifice and of the feast that followed it, at which Orpheus the citharist is said to have sung. Mention of dances also occurs at the same feast. But I have discussed at considerable length the singing of this and other hymns, and the choruses, dances and leapings which the Gentiles were accustomed to perform at feasts, not only profane but also sacred or sacrificial, in my work on the antiquities of banquets. I therefore refer the kind reader there.

units.la: Veruntamen mentio muliebris istius ἰάλυγμὸς, id est precationis, siue orationis & acclamationis, nobis quædam cum de clamoribus & vociferationibus plerumque insanis, tum corporibus quoque, motibus, gestibus, seu gesticulationibus potius incompositis & ridiculis, quibus Gentiles in quibusdā suis sacris & sacrificiis usi fuerunt, scribendi occasione, meo iudicio, satis oportunam atq; commodam præbuit.
units.tr: However, the mention of that womanly ialygmos [ἰάλυγμος], that is, of prayer or speech and acclamation, has, in my judgement, given me a fairly suitable and convenient occasion to write both about the clamours and shouts, often frenzied, and also about the bodies, movements and gestures, or rather the disordered and ridiculous gesticulations, which the Gentiles used in some of their rites and sacrifices.

units.la: Quanti igitur ad prius attinet, tamen si plerunq; Gentiles in sacris seu sacrificiis suis silentio fuerunt usi summo: seqz sibi necessarium utendum esse censuerunt; de quo supra plurib. tamen nonnunquam & sacerdotes & reliqui, qui adstabat sacrificantis, intererant verba nonnunquam, & voces quasdam sacris suis aptas & accommodatas ediderint. Huiusmodi fuit exempli gratia, vox illa Vistimarii, AGONE? Acinprecibus præcipue & supplicationibus suis sacrificialibus usi fuerunt verbis voce, clara & sonora.
units.tr: As far as the former is concerned, although the Gentiles for the most part kept the deepest silence in their sacred rites and sacrifices, and thought this silence necessary, I have said above that priests and the others who stood by the sacrificer sometimes spoke words and uttered certain cries suited and fitting to their rites. An example is that cry of the Victimarii, "Agone?" They used spoken words, loud and clear, above all in their sacrificial prayers and supplications.

units.la: Ac omnino ut in omnibus actionibus, ita in sacrificio alia actione tempus erat tacendi: tempus etiam erat fandi & loquendi. Sic enim, exempli gratia, inter casa & porresta fari licebat: at vero, quando exta vel cadebant, vel porriciebantur, sari non licebat. Hinc intercidi dies sunt inquit Varro, per quos mane & vesperi est nefas (id est, quibus fari non licet:) medio tempore inter hostiam casam & exta porresta fas: id est, fari licet: a quo quod fas tum intercidit, intercisi dies aut quod tum intercisum, nefas.
units.tr: In general, as in all actions, so in sacrifice there was a time for silence for one action, and a time for speaking and talking for another. For example, it was lawful to speak between the casting of the sacrificial cake and the sprinkling of the grain, but when the entrails were either falling or being offered, it was not lawful to speak. Hence, says Varro, "the days are cut off in which it is wrong (that is, when it is not lawful to speak) from morning and evening; in the middle time, between the cake and the offering of the entrails, it is right, that is, it is lawful to speak." From this, the period in which it was right was cut off, and the days are called 'intercisi,' cut off, or because what was then cut off was wrong.

units.la: Sed observandum prateterea hic quædam Gentilium sacra non nisi in sacris furiosis, clamoribus atq; vociferationibus, partim læts, partim eristibus & gemebundis fuisse celebrata: cuiusmodi fuerunt illa sacra Baalitica, sacra Corybantum, Saturnorum: itē Lupercalia, Bacchanalia, Organia Panos, & aliaq generis.
units.tr: But one should further observe here that some Gentile rites were celebrated only in frenzied rites, with shouting and outcry, partly joyful, partly mournful and wailing. Of this kind were those Baalite rites, the rites of the Corybantes and of Saturn, likewise the Lupercalia, the Bacchanalia, the Orgies of Pan, and others of the same kind.

units.la: Quod dico de clamoribus & vociferationibus, idem intelligendum de vario multiplicij corporis, vel totius, vel singularum eius partium situ, motu, atq; gestu, quo in sacrificiis & supplicationibus suis usi fuerunt. Nam modo sedere (qui corporis situs Gentilibus, maxime adorantibus & supplicantibus videbatur conveniens, de quo supra) modo stare, modo cubare, humi iacere, modo statim, modo euntere, modo saltare, modo corpora sua nunc in hanc, nunc in aliam partem vertere, plurimos deniq; motus incompositos bistrionicos & ridiculos (quos enumerare omnes difficile limum foret) edere consueverunt: de quibus supra in loco precationum & supplicationum nonea fuerunt commemorata. Seruius in illa Virgilii Æneidos tertio:
units.tr: What I have said about shouting and outcry must be understood equally of the varied and manifold posture, movement and gesture of the whole body or of its individual parts, which they used in their sacrifices and supplications. For they were accustomed to sit (a posture which seemed to the Gentiles, especially when adoring and supplicating, suitable, as I said above), or sometimes to stand, sometimes to lie down, to lie prostrate on the ground, sometimes to leap, sometimes to walk, sometimes to turn their bodies now this way, now that, and finally to make very many unseemly, theatrical and ridiculous movements (too many to list), of which I mentioned some above in the place on prayers and supplications. Servius, on that passage of Virgil's Aeneid, book three:

units.la: Ante ora Deum (simulacrorum) pingues statiatur ad aras, (id est, pinguib. hostiis plenas) Matronæ enim ingt, sacrificaturæ circa aras, faculas tenentes, datur quasi si quodam gestu. Huc etiā pertinent illa ejusdē Poëtæ, Georgic. 1.
units.tr: "Before the faces of the gods (the images) they feed the fat altars" (that is, full of fat victims). For he says the matrons, about to sacrifice around the altars, holding torches, are given, as it were, by a certain gesture (a signal).

units.la: Terá, no vas circum felix eat hostia fruges
units.tr: Here also belong those lines of the same poet, Georgics 1:

units.la: Addit de Cereris sacrificio: Omnis quam chorus & socii comitantur o vantes Et Cererem clamore vocent in tecta: neq; ante Falcem maturis quisquam supponat aristis, Quàm Cereri torta redimitus tempora quercu Det motus incompositos & carmina dicat.
units.tr: "Then let the victim go round the fields, a happy offering," and he adds on the sacrifice to Ceres: "All the chorus and companions following, singing and calling Ceres with a shout into the homes; and let no one put the sickle to the ripe ears before, crowned at the temples with twisted oak, he has performed the incomposed movements to Ceres and recited songs."

units.la: Hujusmodi motus incompositos false perstringit Arnobius septimo adversus Gentiles, his ver- bis: jam vero si viderint in foeminas mollitudines enervantes se viros vociferari hos frustra sine causa alios cursitare, amicitiarum fide salva contundere se alios, & crudis mutilare se caesibus, certare bos spiritu, buccas vento distendere, votisq; inanibus concrepare, manus ad coelum tollue, rebus admirabilibus motiprofiluunt, exclamant, in gratiam cum hominibus redeunt. Haec si Dius immortalibus oblectionem afferunt simultatum, si ex comoediis, atellanis, mimis, ducunt lascivire, saltare, obscenas compingere cantiones, & clunibus fluctuare crispatis? Quid enim dissere aut interesse, faciant ne haec ipsi, an ab iis fieri in amoribus atq; in delitiis ducant? Haec Arnobius.
units.tr: Arnobius, in book seven against the Gentiles, rightly criticises such incomposed movements, in these words: "Now if they see men, made soft like women, shouting, running about vainly and without cause, others beating themselves with friendship's trust intact, and mutilating themselves with raw blows, vying with one another in spirit, puffing out their cheeks with wind, clattering with empty vows, lifting their hands to heaven, leaping forward with wondrous movements, shouting, returning to favour with men: if these things bring the immortal gods the pleasure of quarrels, if they take delight in comedies, Atellan farces and mimes, to frolic, to dance, to compose obscene songs, and to ripple with curled buttocks? For what difference is there, whether they themselves do these things, or whether they think they are done by others in their loves and pleasures?" Thus Arnobius.

units.la: Porro quid dicam, quid in illis suis sacris, praesertim noctur nis, nonnunquam stupra, adulte- ria, caedes, homicidia, furta aliaq; scelera atque flagitia turpia & foeda perpetrarunt atq; designarunt? De sacris illis Bona, seu Mala potius Deae nocturnis, Chodii stupro violatis, quid crebrius quaeso apud Ciceronem legitur? Quid? Antiquissima illa, & omnibus fere gentibus familiaris fima sacrificia humana, quid fuerunt al.ud, nisi homicidia, seu parricidia potius tetra, dira & immania?
units.tr: Moreover, what shall I say of how, in those rites of theirs, especially the nocturnal ones, they sometimes committed and practised fornication, adultery, murders, homicides, thefts and other crimes and shameful and foul disgraces? Of those nocturnal rites of the Good, or rather Bad, Goddess, in which the Chodii violated women with fornication, what is read more often, I ask you, in Cicero? And what of those most ancient human sacrifices, familiar to almost all peoples, what were they but foul, dire and monstrous homicides, or rather parricides?

units.la: Apud Samios, quando Mercurio χαρίδοτη, id est, Munificio, sacrificabant, permissum erat furari, & aliorum vestes sufurari, ut testatur Plutarchus Quaestionum Graecarum quaestione quin- quagesima quinta. Ejus Plutarchus hanc rationem reddit, quod nimirum Samii, quando oraculum secuti ex insulain Mycalen migrarunt, decem annos vixerunt et latrocinio, quibus finitis cum rursus in insulam suam navigassent, hostes suos devicerunt. Theodoretus sermone septimo ad Graecos infideles de sacrificiis: En ἡ ταῦτας, ἡ ὀϋν ὑρ̈όσι, παν ἐδ̈ & ἀναλογίας ἀνὸ ὑτ̈ιαλ- μάτο. Και ἰδ̈ ἀ̈ ταλίαι, ἐ τὰ ὀρχηστὰ τ̈ῶν ἐπλ ἀνιγμάτα. ἢ κ̈ιγα μὲν ἡ Ἑλλόσιν, ἡ φαλλα- ϙωγία ἡ φαλλόν, ἀπαρ δ̈ἡ ἡ ἐπα ἡ ὀργασῶν δρώμενα, εἰς πᾶ- ἑ̈ὰ & ἀσ̈λ̈γεῖας τοὺς ὁρῶντας ἀ̈ροίζει, hoc est, Lu ejusmodi autem con venticula & omne flagitiorum genus patrabatur. Initia enim Cereris, & Liberi Patris Orgia, eorum scelerum involuera quaedam praetendebant. E leusis nam, pectinem ostentabat. Veretrum autem Phallagogia Libero dedicata. Sed enim citra enigmatum haec in volucra, ipsa quoque Orgia, quae a celebrantibus fieri cernebantur, ad omne flagitiorum genus spectantes facile incitabant.
units.tr: Among the Samians, when they sacrificed to Mercury as "Charidotes" [χαριδότης], that is, the Giver of Gifts, it was permitted to steal and to pilfer one another's clothes, as Plutarch attests in the fifty-fifth question of his Greek Questions. Plutarch gives this reason for it: when the Samians, following an oracle, had migrated from their island to Mycale, they lived for ten years by robbery, and when these years were ended and they sailed back again to their island, they defeated their enemies. Theodoret, in the seventh discourse to the unbelieving Greeks, on sacrifices: "Such things, or rather others like them, are done in their rites, and the dances of the Mysteries are full of enigmas. In Eleusis the rite of the Pecten (comb) was displayed; the phallus was dedicated to Liber by the Phallagogia. But these things, apart from the enigmas, the very Orgies themselves, which were seen to be performed by the celebrants, easily stirred the onlookers to every kind of shamefulness and impiety." That is, such gatherings and every kind of wickedness were carried out. For the initiations of Ceres and the Orgies of Father Liber were pretexts for certain covers of these crimes.

units.la: Atq; haec quidem de victimae percussione, & de iis, quae eam fuerunt comitata, ac de tibiarum aliorumq; instrumentorum musicorum in sacrificiis usu sint dicta.
units.tr: So much then has been said about the striking of the victim, about those things which accompanied it, and about the use of pipes and other musical instruments in sacrifices.

units.la: PORRO victimam prostratam humi, jacentem, apud Homerum quidem, ex terra dicun- sur sustulisse. Verba Poëtae haec sunt: Οἱ μὲν ἴπεντ' ἀνεδ̈λόντες ἀ̈ο̈ οὐ̈ χοῦνος ἐ̈φαλοιο ἐήν Ἐ̈ρ̈ν.— Hi quidem deinde corripientes a terra spatiosa Tenebant, &c.
units.tr: NEXT, in Homer, they are said to have lifted the victim, lying prostrate and stretched on the ground, from the earth. The words of the poet are these: "They then, rushing up, lifted and held him from the wide earth," etc. [Οἱ μὲν ἔπειτ' ἀναδραμόντες ἀπὸ χθονὸς εὐρείης ἔχον]

units.la: Vocatè terram spatiosam, quam Veteres μεγαλάμφοδον dixerunt.
units.tr: Note the "wide earth," which the ancients called "megalampholon" (of great sound?) [μεγαλάμφοδον].

units.la: Ανάλυτος Eustathius αἰαζας̈ ἐ̈ουτ̈ε, sursum ferentes sive portantes interpretatur: cui contrarium καθάλλητε, id est, dejicientes, seu prosternentes. Hostiam igitur percussam, quae ceciderat, a terra sublatam manibus tenebant. Verisimile autem est, ipsos hostiam illam deinde reposuisse in mensa sacrificiali: in qua illam deinde jugulare, excoriare ac dissecare solebant. Apud Guiluel-
units.tr: Eustathius explains the Homeric word as "lifting up" or "carrying upward" [ἀναφέροντες]; its opposite is "letting down" or "casting down" [καθιέντες], that is, dejecting or prostrating. So they held in their hands the struck victim, which had fallen, lifted from the ground. It is likely that they then placed that victim on the sacrificial table, on which they were accustomed to cut its throat, flay it and cut it up.

units.la: mum de Choul Victimarii victimam maftatam humeris suis bajulantis pictuam videre lint. Menfa autem, in qua hoftiae & maftari, feu jugulari, & excoriari, & diffecari feu diffindi, exea educi ac infpici folebant, Latinè Anclabrio dicta eft, miniftertis di vinu apta, ab anculando, hoc eft, miniftrando. Vnde vafa quoq; aenea, quibus facerdotes utebantur, Anclabria fuerunt appellata.
units.tr: In Guillaume du Choul, the Victimarii are seen carrying the slaughtered victim on their shoulders in a picture. The table on which the victims were slaughtered, or cut their throats, and flayed, and cut up or split, and were carried out and examined, was called in Latin "anclabrium," suited to divine service, from "anculare," that is, to minister. Hence the bronze vessels also which the priests used were called "anclabria."

units.la: POSTQVAM vero beftia five hoftia (quarum fimiliter vocum notanda obiter affinitas eft & fimilitudo) percuffa, cefa, ifta, ac in terram defecta fuit, confecuta ftatim fuit σφαγη, id eft, jugulatio five maftatio: cujus poft percuffionem apud Homerum, Apollonium, ut etiam apud alios auctores in facrificiorum defcriptionibus fit mentio.
units.tr: AFTER the beast or victim (the similarity and affinity of these words is to be noted in passing) has been struck, cut, felled and fallen to the ground, immediately follows the "sphagē," that is, the throat-cutting or slaughter. Mention of this after the striking is made in Homer, Apollonius, and also in other authors in their descriptions of sacrifices.

units.la: Ac apud Homerum quidem in Neftoris iftius facrificii defcriptione hac actio hiis verbis expreffa primitur:
units.tr: In Homer, in the description of that sacrifice of Nestor, this action is expressed in these words:
"But he slew Peisistratus, the leader of men."

units.la: Ἀτ' ἀπ' ἴντεὶ ἐκ μέλαν αἵμα ἐν χθῶν, ἔ ἀν τ' ὅβλας ἀγ'.
units.tr: "And from him the black blood flowed on the earth, and..."

units.la: At vero (at & attamen, forfan a Graeco ἀτάρ) jugulavit (hoc maftavit) Piftratus dux (Graece ὅρχαμος, quafi praefultor, five praefes) virorum:
units.tr: But (at, and yet, perhaps from the Greek ἀτάρ) he cut the throat (that is, slew) Peisistratus, leader (in Greek "orchamos," as it were the leader in front, or president) of men.

units.la: Exilla (fcilicet hoftia jugulata) poftquam niger fluxit fanguis, reliquit offa animus.
units.tr: When the black blood had flowed from it (namely the victim whose throat had been cut), the spirit left the bones.

units.la: Apud eundem Poetam praemittitur aliquando verbum αἰφνέειν, ut Iliad. Σ.
units.tr: Elsewhere in the same poet the verb aiphneein is sometimes placed before the action, as in Iliad Σ.
"Indeed they slew him and cut his throat" [ὑσφαξαν].

units.la: Sed de hoc verbo ἀνιέναι poftea.
units.tr: But I will discuss this verb ἀνιέναι later.

units.la: Apollonius in Argonauticis facrificii defcriptione eandem actionem hoc verbis explicat.
units.tr: In his description of the sacrifice in the Argonautica, Apollonius explains the same action in these words.

units.la: Τοὺς δ' ἱέρευσαν ζῶντ' Ἰφέ: (fcilicet tauros proftratos humi, jacentes, vele terra forfan flatim fublatos & in menfa aliqua collocatos) fofi confeftim, quafi dicas curfim, curriculo, ut Plautus loquitur (nam Σφάζειν a Ἠίεν id eft, currendo eft derivatum) jugulantes. Hi confimilia fere funt illa Virgiliana de eadem actione:
units.tr: "And they sacrificed them alive, [the bulls]" [τοὺς δ' ἱέρευσαν ζῶντ']. That is, the bulls were thrown prone on the ground, lying down, or perhaps lifted at once from the earth and placed on some table; then they were quickly slaughtered, as we might say, "at a run," in haste, as Plautus puts it. For σφάζειν is derived from a word meaning running (currendo), so the sense is "cutting the throat." Virgil's words about the same action are very similar:
Some set knives beneath,
and catch the warm blood in bowls.

units.la: Dionyfius Halicarnafseus inejufdem cerimoniae defcriptione primo quidem generaliter verbo ϑύειν ufus, inquit: σφαζάλιας τὰ παιοῖας τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν τὴν ἱερῶν, & τὰ πὸν τὰ θύσιας, hoc eft Veftibus frientes hoftias (fcilicet Homerus introducit) & collapfas humi, jacentes facrificantes. Et paullo antea: Miniftrorum five victimariorum alii quidem ftatim etiamnum hoftiam recte feriebant in tempora: alii, ἀπ' αὐτῶν ὑπνιθέντας ἐλέους χειρέα, ἀδεῖς, cadenti hoftiae culleros fupponebant, qua dicendi phrafi etiam Virgilius ufus eft, ut paullo ante diftum in verfu: Supponunt alii cultros, &c.
units.tr: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in his description of the same ceremony, first uses the general word θύειν and says: slaughtering (σφαζάλιας) the victims, which the priests... and those that were sacrificed, that is, striking the victims with axes (as Homer introduces them), and those lying prone on the ground, sacrificing. A little earlier he says: some of the ministers or victim-slayers struck the victim at once on the head while it was still standing; others, holding out the hand under it, set basins beneath the falling victim. Virgil too used this phrase of speaking, as was said a little before in the line: Some set knives beneath, etc.

units.la: Ex locorum iftorum diligenti confideratione atq; collatione colligi facile intelligi, poteft, quas jugulationis maftationes veftius ritus fuerit atq; modus. Non minus enim fluidiose atque accurate quam reliquae, actio quoq; iftae facrificialis, atq; cerimonia fieri & obfervari fuis folita.
units.tr: From a careful consideration and comparison of these passages it can easily be gathered what the manner and method of this ancient rite of slaughtering and cutting the throat was. For this sacrificial action too was customarily carried out and observed no less fluently and accurately than the others.

units.la: Primum igitur ipfa verba dicendiq; phrafes diligenter notis expendende funt, quae non ad ipfam rei atque moris iftius faciliorem notitiam intelligentiamq; deduxunt. Vtuntur igitur fere verbo σφάζειν five σφάσις, cujus σφαγὴ, ut a μικρῶ, σμικρὸν, a ὑφδί suidas; a μὲ ὀλίγῳ. Porro hujus verbi ejufdem derivatorum quafi finu atq; coplexu omnia fere, quae ad actionem illam pertinent, fummatim comprehenduntur. Id vero jugulare, tu acidare, maftare fignificat. Nam & ipfa actio, id eft, maftatio feu jugulatio σφαγή dicitur: & hoftia feu victima σφαγιον (ut hoftia Latinè ab hoftire, ideft, ferire: & victima, quafi victa: & Graece ϑυμα, ἀπὸ τῶ ϑύειν:) & σφαγεὺς vel σφαγεὺς, maftator feu victimarius: & σφάγελα maftatrix feu facrificula: et σφακλον, tributigenne, quod pro maftata hoftia perfolvebatur (de quo Pollux: τὸ ἱερὸ οὖν ὁ ὀμπλί τῆ πρῷος, Ἡρ & τὸ ἡμέρας ὑμω ἀγ 'τὸ) & σφαγὴ, jugulum feu pars colli, quae feriebatur, item couca vitae illa fub pectore: & σφαγῖον vel σφάγιον, vas, quo jugulata pecudes fanguine excipitur: & σφάγιον, locus, quo excipitur fanguis pecudum: & σφάγιον ipfe, qui colligitur, vafculo fuppofito pecudi jugulatae: & σφάγαρον, five σφάγις & σφαγίδιον, enfis, vel culter quo jugulatio illa perquatur. agitur, secundum illud Virgilii: Eufe ferit, &c: & σφαγὴν, ἢ ἱεροργίας πωίεας, dies, quo sacra fiunt mactatus jugulatus, victimus: & σφαγῖτις φλὸν jugularis vena, aliud, similia apud Hesychium, Pollucem, Suidam, Eustathium & alios.
units.tr: First, therefore, the words themselves and the modes of speaking must be carefully weighed, since they lead to an easier knowledge and understanding of the thing and its custom. They mostly use the verb σφάζειν or σφάσις, whose noun σφαγή (as Suidas says, from μικρόν, small, or from ὀλίγον, little) ... Moreover, nearly everything that pertains to that action is briefly comprehended in the embrace and compass of this verb and its derivatives. It means to cut the throat, to slaughter, to butcher. For the action itself, that is, the slaughter or cutting of the throat, is called σφαγή; the victim or sacrificial animal is σφάγιον (as in Latin hostia comes from hostire, that is, to strike, and victima, as if "conquered," and in Greek θύμα from θύειν); σφαγεύς or σφαγεύς is the slaughterer or victim-man; σφάγελα is a female slaughterer or small sacrifice; σφάκλον is a tribute payable for a slaughtered victim (of which Pollux speaks); σφαγή is also the throat or part of the neck that was struck, and likewise the vital spot beneath the breast; σφάγιον or σφάγιον is the vessel into which the slaughtered animal's blood is received; σφάγιον also names the place where the blood of the animals is received; σφάγιον itself is the blood collected by setting a vessel under the slaughtered animal; σφάγαρον, or σφάγις and σφαγίδιον, is the sword or knife with which that cutting of the throat is done, according to the line of Virgil: He strikes with the sword, etc.; σφαγή, or the day on which sacred rites are performed with the slaughtered, killed and sacrificed victims; and σφαγῖτις, the jugular vein. Similar words are found in Hesychius, Pollux, Suidas, Eustathius and others.

units.la: Ceterum illud φῶ, cujus antea mētio facta, Eustathius in Odyss. μ, vult idem significare, quod φοντύο, id est, occido, per paragogen, sive pleonasmum litterae σ. φῶ autem sive φῶ & λάω λαλέω, id est, dicere, & facere. & φαίνειν, id est, lucere, & φανεῖν, id est, necare atq; occidere, significat numirum a φῶς (quod derivatur ab Hebraeo ורא, Or) quae vox lucē sive lumen significat, cujus maximus est usus planè, necessarius ad dicendum agendumq. Idem autē verbi occidere significat per antiphrasin, quasi lucē, id est, vitam adimere, eripere, extinguere: ut nos quoq; vernaculano nostra lingua loquimur, Einem das licht auslöschen/ id est, lucem alicujus extinguere, pro, vitā aliquem privare. Alibi verbum hoc deducit Eustathius a φάεσιν, id est, lucere, apparere, (unde fax dicta) & occidere, addita litterā σ. Idem loco antē citato plurima recensent secundum triplicem hujus verbi significationem ejusdem derivata; quae non est δ'ἀεσ ut ipse loquitur, id est, injucundum legere atq; cognoscere, Sed nos hic de una tantum ejus significatione loquimur, quae est φονεύειν, occidere, jugulare, necare. unde φθάω, teste Eustathio, idem, quod φθεῖρω, id est, corrumpo, perdo, & φάζω, & additā litterā σ. σφάζω: unde ἀπιφάτ, id est, in praelio occisus, & ἐπισφάτ, id est, ὀλεθρὸς permitiosus, & περιφαγίδος τας apud Lycophronem, id est, taurus mactatus, & πέφευται id est, ἰφοντο, occisi sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, Eustathius, on Odyssey μ, holds that the word φῶ, mentioned earlier, means the same as φονεύω, that is, I kill, by the addition (paragoge) or pleonasm of the letter σ. φῶ, or φῶ together with λάω and λαλέω, that is, to speak and to do, and φαίνειν, that is, to shine, and φανεῖν, that is, to kill and slay, signify indeed from φῶς (which is derived from the Hebrew אור, Or), a word meaning light, which is most plainly necessary for speaking and doing. The same verb also means to kill by antiphrasis, as if to take away, snatch or extinguish the light, that is, life; just as we in our own vernacular say, "Einem das Licht auslöschen," that is, to extinguish someone's light, meaning to deprive someone of life. Elsewhere Eustathius derives this verb from φαίνειν, that is, to shine or appear (whence fax is said), and "to kill," with the letter σ added. In the same passage he lists many derivatives according to the threefold meaning of this verb, which is not ... as he himself puts it, "unpleasant to read and learn." But here we speak only of one of its meanings, which is φονεύειν, to kill, to cut the throat, to slay. Hence φθάω, according to Eustathius, is the same as φθείρω, that is, to corrupt or destroy, and φάζω, and with the letter σ added, σφάζω; whence ἀπιφάτ, that is, slain in battle, and ἐπισφάτ, that is, destructive, pernicious; and περιφαγίδος in Lycophron, that is, a bull slaughtered; and πέφευται, that is, they were slain.

units.la: A σφάζω porro sive σφάζων fiunt composita, ἀπαπροσφάζων, seu ἀπορσφάζων, idem quod σφάζων: Composita varia a τύφειν: ἀπέσφαξν, jugulum differre seu aperire: unde ἀπερπάσ, ἀπαφάζων, ἀπαφάζων. Denique: subtus jugulare, jugulum succedere. Inde fiunt quoq; σφαγιάζω, σφαγιάζω, & ejus composita varia. Quid si a σφαγιάζω, vel σφαγιάζω ablata litterā σ, σφάζω, id est, somedere, per contractionem sic derivatum: quoniam pecudes nisi mactate et necatae prius fuerint, non possunt comedi, & hae praecipuē sunt hominum ejus atq; cibus. Deniq; hic quoq; differentia inter σφάζω & θύω est notanda, quam Ammonius affert his verbis: Θύειν inquit, τὸ σφάζειν ἀληφεῖς. Θύειν μὲν γὰρ ὅταν τιμὴ Θεῶ, καὶ τὸ μηνιστὴν ἐπὶ ἐνδίξω, καί τοιοῦ ἱεροῦ ἰσχύει. Σφάζειν δὲ τὸ μὴ πνεῦσαι... hoc est, θύειν, (sacrificare vulgo) differt a σφάζειν, id est, mactare: quod illud quidem fit in honorem Dei: utem significat futura praedicere in ejus honorem per extra. Mactare verō, occidere est ob quam vis aliam caussam. Et illud quidem de irrationali; hoc verō de rationali accipitur victima. Sed, pace Ammonii dixerim, ipsum quoq; θύειν vel θύεσθαι de profanis usurpatur mactationibus: nec tam victimarum humanarum, quam etiam brutarum: id quod cum ex aliis tum ex duobus illis sacrae scripturae locis colligere promtum est. Prior habetur Matthaei vigesimo secundo, versu quarto: Idū τὸ ἄρισιον μου ἑτοίμασα, οἱ ταῦροι μου καὶ τὰ σιτιστὰ τεθυμένα: Ecce prandium meum paravi, taurimei & altilia mactata sunt. Alter habetur Lucae decimoquinto versu vigesimo tertio, septimo & trigesimo: ubi θύειν verbum, est proprie de sacrificiis dicatur, secundum Ammonii sententiam tamen ad alias etiam, nempe profanas mactationes traslum, ter expresse repetitur. Haec de solennisio verbo σφάζειν, vel σφάζειν.
units.tr: Moreover, compounds are formed from σφάζω or σφάζων: ἀπαπροσφάζων, or ἀπορσφάζων, the same as σφάζων; various compounds of τύφειν: ἀπέσφαξεν, to cut the throat apart or open it; whence ἀπερπάσ, ἀπαφάζων, ἀπαφάζων. Finally, to cut the throat from below, to succeed to the throat. From these also come σφαγιάζω, σφαγιάζω, and various compounds of them. What if σφάζω was derived from σφαγιάζω or σφαγιάζω, by removing the letter σ, to mean "to eat," by contraction? For animals cannot be eaten unless they have first been slaughtered and killed, and these are especially the food of men. Finally, here too the difference between σφάζω and θύω must be noted, which Ammonius sets out in these words: "Θύειν," he says, "is truly different from σφάζειν. For θύειν is when honour is paid to a god, and when it is done for an end, and when it is done for such a sacred purpose. But σφάζειν is to not breathe..." That is, θύειν (to sacrifice, commonly) differs from σφάζειν, that is, to slaughter: the former is done in honour of God, and it signifies foretelling future things in his honour through entrails. But to slaughter is to kill for some other cause. And the former refers to irrational victims, the latter to rational ones. Yet, with due respect to Ammonius, θύειν or θύεσθαι is also used of profane slaughters, and not only of human victims but also of brute ones; this can be readily gathered both from other passages and from two places of Holy Scripture. The first is Matthew 22, verse 4: "Ἰδοὺ τὸ ἄριστόν μου ἑτοίμασα, οἱ ταῦροί μου καὶ τὰ σιτιστὰ τεθυμένα," Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and fatlings are slaughtered. The other is Luke 15, verses 23, 27 and 30, where the verb θύειν, which is properly said of sacrifices, is expressly repeated three times for profane slaughters, according to Ammonius' opinion. So much for the solemn verb σφάζειν or σφάζειν.

units.la: Hanc ipsam autem actionem tristem, & cruentam, id est, peculum jugulationem & necationem, in sacrificiis, κατ᾽ υἱρημαμὸν, boni omnis ergo, lenioribus verbis designarunt Graeci. Nam primum ipsi non tam verbo φονεύειν (quo tamē Lucianus utitur, sed per contemptum et ironiam pro more suo) aut κτάνειν, & bisce similibus, quam σφάζειν & σφαγιάζειν, seu σφαγιάζεσθαι sunt usi: necnon verbo θύειν, de quo modo dictum, & quo Dionysius Halicarnasseus, usus est. Vt sunt etiam hat discendi phrasi, ἱεροθύειν τὰς σφαγὰς ac: cui respondet illa Virgiliana, Supponere cultros.
units.tr: But the Greeks designated this very sad and bloody action itself, namely the slaughter and killing of animals in sacrifices, by gentler words, as a kind of good omen. For they did not primarily use the verb φονεύειν (which Lucian does use, but with contempt and irony, after his manner), or κτάνειν and similar words, but σφάζειν and σφαγιάζειν, or σφαγιάζεσθαι, and also the verb θύειν, of which we have just spoken and which Dionysius of Halicarnassus used. So also in this phrase, ἱεροθύειν τὰς σφαγάς..., to which corresponds that Virgilian phrase, to set knives beneath.

units.la: Latini similiter ad hanc actionem exprimendam usi sunt verbo Mactandi, de quo supra plurivibus, quod proprie magis augere, sive auctare significat: itē verbo Immolandi, quod proprie magis ... Lam salsam est victimae aspergere. Item, Supponere cultros, idem est, quod tadere. Unde Servius illa Virgiliana:
units.tr: The Latins likewise used, to express this action, the verb mactandi, of which more above, which properly means to increase or magnify; also the verb immolandi, which properly means... It is indeed to sprinkle the victim with salted meal. Likewise, supponere cultros means the same as to slaughter. Hence Servius, on that Virgilian line:

units.la: Supponunt alii cultros, &c. sic interpretatur, Victimas cadunt. Est autem, inquit, sacrorum, in quibus mali omines verba vitantur. Hinc est, quod & maßare dicunt, id quod magis augere sive außare significat. Idem Poeta Georgicorum tertio, eandem repetens phrasin, inquit:
units.tr: Servius, commenting on the line "Supponunt alii cultros, &c.", explains it thus: "They cut the throats of the victims." He adds that these are sacred rites, in which ill-omened words are avoided. Hence they also say mactare, which means to increase or augment (magis augere). The same poet, in the third book of the Georgics, repeats the same phrase and says:
But scarcely are the knives placed beneath them stained with blood.

units.la: Similis huic phrasi videtur esse illa ejusdem Poeta dicendi forma, Falces supponere arista, pro eas demittere, in illis versibus:
units.tr: A form of speech similar to this phrase seems to be that other expression of the same poet, falces supponere arista, meaning to lower the sickles to the ears of grain, in these verses:

units.la: Et Cererem clamore vocent in tesla, neq; anteFalcem messuris quisquam supponat aristis, Quam Cereri, &c.
units.tr: And let them call Ceres with a shout upon the threshing-floor, and let no one set the sickle to the ripe ears before they have offered to Ceres, etc.

units.la: Huc quoq; videtur pertinere illud ejusdem Poeta, Iuguli demittere cruorem, quod est jugulationis periphrasis.
units.tr: That other phrase of the same poet, iuguli demittere cruorem (to let blood flow from the throat), also seems to belong here, being a periphrasis for slaughtering by cutting the throat.

units.la: In hac ipsa autem jugulationis cerimonia, ut ab Homero & Apollonio hic describitur, haec sa- ri sunt consideranda. Primum personae, qualis fuit apud Homerum Pisistratus: apud Apollonium socii naviigationis Argonauticae. Hoc ipsum autem poparum, victimariorum & cultariorum opus muniuq; fuit: &, ut Cultrarius a cultro; ita σφαγεὺς Graece ἀπὸ τοῦ σφαγῆ &, vel σφαγα- νὸ, id est, ense vel cultro, cetera instrumento, dictus fuit.
units.tr: In this very ceremony of throat-cutting, as Homer and Apollonius describe it, the following points are to be considered. First, the persons: in Homer, such a man as Pisistratus; in Apollonius, the companions of the Argonautic voyage. This task was itself the work and duty of the cooks, the victim-slayers and the knife-men. Just as cultrarius is named from culter, so the Greek sphageus is named from sphagē, or sphaganon, that is, a sword or knife, after the instrument.

units.la: Deinde considerandum certa bostia bestiae ve jugulanda atq; mactanda disposi- tio, quae verbo ὡς αἷμα definitur. Sic enim Homerus Iliad. a. Ἀνίπυσαν μὲν σφαγάς, καὶ ἴφαξαν: Prius sursum traxerunt, & mactarunt,
units.tr: Next one must consider the particular placing of the victim, the beast to be cut and slaughtered, which is expressed by a verb. For Homer, Iliad 1, says: [ἀνέσπασαν μὲν σφαγάς, καὶ ἔσφαξαν]: "They first drew them up and slaughtered them."

units.la: Est enim, Euftathio interprete, τὸ ἀπάρειν quasi a sum ιρίνειν, sursum trahere. Ac τὸ ἀπὸ Συμβούλην τόπον ἀπὸ τοῦ σφαγῆς ἢ τῆς ἰδ/ας. Idem ιεύων interpretatur ἕλκειν, trahere, liberare, eruere eximere. Et eodem loco Iliad. a. ἐξ ἡμῶν ἀπὸ ἐξώσεως ἔναιρον ἴσσι. Hoc dicebatur ἱερὰ ἀπὸ αὐτῶν εἰς ἡ, ἀπὸ τῶν εἰς ἡμῶν ἀφέλειν, ἐν ἀπὸ ἡμῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ πρέπειν. ὁ δ' ἐν ἄλλοις ἐν ἀφαιρεῖν ἡ ἀμφιτέρα οὖν ἐν ἤτοι ἑτέρω...: Quando, inquit, Superū sacrificabant, Victime collum reflectere solebant trahendo illud retrorsum, ita ut quasi telum contorqueretur: id quod Sophocles videtur interpretari, cùm inquit, Sursum flectendo mactantur. Nam quando Heroibus, aut prorsus vita sunt fundus sacrificabant, tum victima deorsum respicie- ns mactabatur. Ad modum hunc duplicem mactandi videtur alludere etiam Apollonii Scholia in illa de tumulo Dolopis:
units.tr: For, according to Eustathius, apareïn is as it were sursum trahere, to draw upward, from the word for lifting up. Eustathius also explains the verb as meaning to pull, to drag, to free, to rescue, to take away. In the same passage of the Iliad the text reads: [ἐξ ἡμῶν ἀπὸ ἐξώσεως ἔναιρον ἴσσι]. Such language was used when the gods above were sacrificed to: the victims used to bend their necks back, pulling them backward so that the neck was twisted as if a weapon were turned. Sophocles seems to explain this when he says: "They are slaughtered by bending upward." When they sacrificed to heroes, or to those who were altogether dead, the victim was then slaughtered looking downward. The scholia of Apollonius on the mound of Dolops seem to allude to this double manner of slaying, in the verse:

units.la: Καὶ μιν χυδ' αἵνοτεν τυπ' ξυρια ἐξ τομα μαλων,Κέιαν, &c.
units.tr: [Καὶ μιν χυδ' αἵνοτεν τυπ' ξυρια ἐξ τομα μαλων, Κέιαν, &c.]

units.la: Errorem inquit, tu σφάγια χυρίως τὰ τοῖς τεθνεῦσι ἐπαγόμενα ἀλλ' ἡ τὸ ἐν τῇ γῇ ἀντιτυπ- τὰς καφάλας. Ut τὸ δὲ Θυσίαν τοῖς χθονίοις, τοῖς ὑπὸ ἡγεμόνι ἀπὸ ἀπὸ ἐπορεύετο τὸν ὑπέρ ἐπ' ἀντ ἀπὸ ἐπαγεῖς σφαγ. Αλλοις ἡ ἐπ' ἄρεως τοῖς τυφλῶσιν ἐπ' ἀν- ἱνον ἕως τοῖς ἀγανοῖς, τοῖς ἡ ἡγιοῖς Ἠ αὐτ' ἑ ἰδ/σ Ἀνοῖς, boc est, Caeftratas victimas putaremus, id quod in terra ipse- rum amputentur capita. Sic enim sacrificat terrestribus: exlestribus vero sursum reflexo oo- ollo mactant. Alii dicunt, caestratas mortuis offerri, cui fferiles ferilibus et infecundis.
units.tr: He says, in error, that the sphagia are properly those offered to the dead; but the heads of those on the ground were struck down. For when they sacrificed to the gods of the underworld, the victims were led down into the pit, and their throats were cut with the head turned down. For the victims with which they sacrifice to the earthly gods are slaughtered with the head lowered, while those for the heavenly gods are slaughtered with the neck bent back upward. That is, we would think the victims castrated, which have their heads cut off on the ground. Others say that castrated victims are offered to the dead, and barren ones to the barren and infertile.

units.la: Tertio considerandum instrumentum, quod σφαγεὺς a Graeco, & σφαγίδιον: item σφάγιον, ἀπὸ τῆς σφαγῆς ἐπὶ diffum, Latinis culter, vel ensis, Festo Clunadum, hoc est culter sanguina- rius, vel quia clunes bostiarū dividit, (in dividendis enim & secandis bostiis: quotx ritu Gra- cum ὁ σύνοψις natum, certis utebantur cultris,) vel quia ad clunes dependet. Inde autem cul- trarius, qui eo cultro vel ense bostiam jugulaverat & ferierat: sicut, qui victimas mactabat, Vi- timarius, Θυμάτος Graece, est dictus: cujus quidem cultri sacrificialis seu mactatoris pillulam, quā cum ejus vagina sive theca videre licet & apud Guilielmum de Choul, libro illo citato, & apud Bartholomaeum Marlianum: quorum hic de vagina ita scribit: Vagina, adeo note signi- fications est, ut nulla prorsus alia indigeat declaratione, nisi dixerimus fuisse thecam gladiorū, quam (ut in Sacrificio diximus) bullis aneis auratis, aut etiam argenteis ornatam fuisse exstitisse mandunt. mandum sit, in qua cultri omnes, nempe dolabrum, secespisa, & alii omnes cultri ad varios usus sacrificiorum recondebantur, peraëtis sacrificiis, quam unus e victimarus, seu sacrificulis de so-ma pendentem gestabat, ut patet in arcu insculptum, superius citato, in quo ordo ipse pene totus sacrificantium more antiquo; ibiq; simulacra L. Seprimii, Severi Imp. ac Iulia Augusta nxoa tis, Antonini, seu Geta eorum filiorum insculpta videntur.
units.tr: Third, the instrument must be considered. The Greek sphageus, and sphagidion, and likewise sphagion, from sphagē, is called in Latin culter or ensis, a knife or sword. Festus gives clunaculum, that is, a bloodletting knife, either because it divides the victim's buttocks (for in dividing and cutting up the victims, according to the Greek rite, certain knives were used), or because it hangs down at the buttocks. Hence the cultrarius, who had slain and struck the victim with that knife or sword, just as the one who slaughtered victims was called victimarius (in Greek thymatos). Of this sacrificial or slaughtering knife, a small image with its sheath or case can be seen, both in Guillaume du Choul, in the book already cited, and in Bartolomeo Marliani. Of the sheath Marliani writes thus: "The sheath has a meaning so clear that it needs no other explanation, unless we say it was the case of the swords, which, as we said in the discussion of sacrifice, they say was adorned with golden or even silver studs." In it were stored all the knives, namely the axe, the secespita, and all the other knives for the various uses of sacrifice, once the rites were finished. One of the victimarii, or sacrificial attendants, carried it hanging from his shoulder, as is shown carved on the arch cited above, on which almost the whole order of the sacrificers according to the ancient custom is depicted. There too appear the images of L. Septimius Severus the emperor, of Julia Augusta his wife, and of Antoninus, or Geta, their sons.

units.la: Quartum in hac hostiarum jugulatione inprimis animad versione dignum, fuit hostiæ sanguis, tanquam res velmaxime sancta & sacra. Et certè a sanguine vox sancti & sancire videtur esse deducta, propterea quod sanguine res quæ vel sanctificari aut sacri aliquid sic pertinent, sanguis, qui, ut Servius ait in Virgilium, vitæ sedes est, vel, ut alii volunt, vita ipsa, & quibusdam anima, Hebraicè רם Dam appellatur: unde homo videtur dictus אדם Adam, partim ab אדמה Adamâh, id est, terra, sive humo: unde ortus est secundum corpus, & quo tandem redit, ut Homo Latinè ab humo; partim a דם Dam, id est, sanguine, quia vita ejus consistit in sanguine: ad quod etymon ipse Spiritus Sanctus pulchrâ elegantiâ, & quidem gemina, paronomasia utitur alludere hîc verbis, Genesis nono capite, sexto versu: שפך דם האדם באדם דמו Schophek dam haâdam baadam, damo schâphek, Quiessuderit sanguinem hominis in homine, sanguis ejus effundetur. Ac ab eadem quidem Hebraea voce דם Dam, sive Chaldaea דמא Dama, vox Græca αἷμα videtur deducta. Nam alludit litterâ ו fit ama, & interjecta jota cum aspiratione & accentu xiua.
units.tr: The fourth point to be noticed above all in this throat-cutting of victims is the victim's blood, as a thing most holy and sacred. Indeed the word sanctus and sancire seems to be derived from blood, because by blood things are made holy, or in some way belong to sacred matters. Blood, which, as Servius says on Virgil, is the seat of life, or, as others hold, life itself, and for some the soul, is called in Hebrew dam (דם). From this the man seems to be called Adam (אדם), partly from adamah (אדמה), that is, earth or ground, from which he arose according to the body and to which he at last returns, just as homo in Latin is from humus; and partly from dam, that is, blood, because his life consists in blood. The Holy Spirit himself, with beautiful elegance and indeed with a double paronomasia, alludes to this etymology in the words of Genesis 9, verse 6: Shophek dam ha'adam ba'adam damo schaphek ("Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed"). And from this same Hebrew word dam, or the Chaldee dama, the Greek word haima seems to be derived, since the letter vav is turned into a sound like ama, with an interposed iota with aspiration and accent.

units.la: Porro in hoc sanguine sacrificiali hostiarum tria sunt consideranda. Primò ejus effluxus atque color. Secundo ejus excipiendi suscipiendisve modus. Tertiò ejusdem effundendi super altare aspergendiq; mos ac consuetudo.
units.tr: Further, three things are to be considered in this sacrificial blood of the victims. First, its outflow and colour. Second, the manner of catching and receiving it. Third, the custom and practice of pouring it out and sprinkling it upon the altar.

units.la: Primoigitur ex hostia jugulata sanguis effluebat, secundum illa Homeri verba: Τῆς δ᾽ ἀκ μελάνος ἀῖμα ρύη.
units.tr: First, then, blood flowed out of the slain victim, according to Homer's words: [Τῆς δ᾽ ἐκ μελανος αἷμα ῥύη], "and from it the black blood flowed."

units.la: Exilla autem (hostia jugulata) sanguis niger (Virgilius etiam atrum vocat) erumpebat seu prorumpebat.
units.tr: Out of it (the slain victim) black blood (Virgil also calls it ater) burst out or gushed forth.

units.la: Non utitur verbo ῥέει, id est, fluere, sed ὑεν (quod verbum de sacrificiis proprie efferri Pausanias ait) quod violentiam significat, & cum impetu quodam prorumpere: unde ουςωξοντο, & υσαξω, violo. Odyss. π. Hic observandum, Veteres mali omnium loco duxisse, si victima jugulata non copiosè diffluxisset sanguine: vel si inter jugulandum triste quid infaustumq; asslancium oculis auribusve occurrisset; quale istud fuit, quod ante mortem Sergii Galbæ, quum oppidatim victimæ caderentur, staurus securis ictu consternatus, rupto vinculo, essedum ejus in vaste, & totum cruore perfudit. Contrà saufli letiq; omnis ac propitii Dei testimonium esse existimabant, quando hostia confossa, copiosum spirantem, & cum impetu stridoreq; prorumpentem ef-fundebat cruorem.
units.tr: He does not use the verb for flowing, but a stronger verb (which Pausanias says is properly used of sacrifices), which signifies violence and bursting forth with some force. Hence the verb for violent pouring out, as in the Odyssey, book π. Here it should be observed that the ancients regarded it as a bad omen if the slain victim did not pour out its blood copiously, or if something sad or unlucky struck the eyes or ears of the bystanders during the slaughter. Such was the event before the death of Sergius Galba: when victims were being killed in the towns, a bullock, stunned by an axe-blow, broke its bond, and in the entrance hall it drenched his chariot and everything with blood. On the contrary, they held it to be a testimony of a favourable, joyful and propitious god when the pierced victim poured out copious blood, gushing forth with force and a hissing sound.

units.la: Dubium etiam non est, quin sanguinis quoq; colorem, quem Homerus hic nigrum appellat, diligenter observarint: & inde vel læta & jucunda; vel tristia & funesta conjecerint.
units.tr: There is also no doubt that they carefully observed the colour of the blood, which Homer here calls black, and from it they drew conclusions, either joyful and pleasing, or sad and ominous.

units.la: Hunc autem hostiarum sanguinem effluentem, seu potiùs prorumpentem, cum rem factam, stridore fixto: Supponunt alii cultros, tepidumq; cruorem Succipiunt paterîs, &c.
units.tr: When the thing was done, this blood of the victims flowed out, or rather burst forth with a fixed hissing sound: "Some place the knives beneath, and catch the warm gore in bowls, etc."

units.la: Succipiunt: Antiquum hoc, inquit Servius. Modo, suscipiunt, dicimus, ut supra; Suscepit, ignem foliis, &c.
units.tr: Succipiunt: Servius says this is an old form. Now we say suscipiunt, as above; suscepit, ignem foliis, &c. ("he caught the fire in the leaves").

units.la: Donatus addit, Ne consecratæ sanguis funderetur in terram, banc paterîs suscipiebant.
units.tr: Donatus adds that, so that the consecrated blood should not be poured out on the ground, they caught it in bowls.

units.la: Vas porrò, quo sanguinem istam succipiebant, Græcè distum fuit αἷμα-ιον, quod Perseus dicitur manibus tenuisse, nimirum ad sanguinem e bove mastato profluentem excipiendum. Eust. quia exceptus in hanc vocem sic commentatur: Αιμαιον, inquit, ut ajunt, est τὸ ᾿ἐκ ἀίματ ὅ ὅτ ἐς τὸ ἱερὸς ἀγυμ ἱερὸς ἀμαιον ἴσ. Διοτυνον ἀγγεῖον, id est, vas aptum ad recipiendum mastatæ bestiæ sanguine, sic distum, quasi ἀπ ἱίμης, hoc est, ἰμαῖος robur, id est, sanguinis ςῳρήτικον. Cretenses autem αἷμαιον dicunt esse vas eis ἐτὸ αἷμα τ ἱερὸν ἐγχεῖ, in quod excipiebat hostiarum sanguinem: sic distum, αἷμαιον n ὃν, id est, sanguineum, ὅτι τὸ ἀιμα ἕος, sanguine nimirum Perfius Hierapytnius testatur banc vocem adhuc esse in usu apud Hierapytnios & ἁιμῶν dici ὅτι τὸ ἀιμῶν. Apollodorus existimac verisimile esse, ab Homero similiter illam vocem prolatam esse : iota autem a nonnullis suisse ademium. Nicander & Theodorides ἁιμῶν vocant, πα̈ῤ τὸ ἀιμα̈ ἃ τὸ σφαξόμενον ζῷον, id est, quód occisum animal domabatur. Attici verò hujusmodi vas ἀγγεῖον appellarunt, εἰς ὃ ἀφῶν ἂμμα ἀιγύθμοι τῆ Cοιμὴ ἐσείνεον, id est, in quod primùm sanguinem excipientes illum are infundebant. Hoc autem nomen semel ajunt apud Poëtam reperiri, five ἀιμῶν, fi- ve ἁιμεῖον, five ἁιμῶν fit legendum. Sanguinem autem illum & Euftathius loco paullo ante citato, & Lucianus libro de sacrificiis, testantur are fuisse infusum, seu circumfusum. Ad hunc morem alludit Virg. Æglog.s.
units.tr: The vessel in which they caught this blood was called in Greek haimaion [αἷμαιον], the one Perseus is said to have held in his hands, no doubt to catch the blood flowing from the slaughtered ox.
