Eustathius, commenting on this word, says: "Haimaion, as they say, is the vessel... that is, a vessel fit for receiving the blood of a slaughtered beast, so called as if from haima, that is, blood, and haimatos, of blood." The Cretans, he adds, call the haimaion the vessel into which the blood of the victims was poured and received. Perseus the Hierapytnian testifies that this word is still in use among the Hierapytnians, and that haimōn is said of the blood. Apollodorus thinks it probable that Homer also used this word, though some have held that the iota was added. Nicander and Theodoridas call it haimōn, from haima, because the animal was tamed when slaughtered, that is, was subdued by the killing. The Attic writers called such a vessel angeion [ἀγγεῖον], into which they first received the blood and then poured it on the altar. They say this word is found only once in the poet, and that one should read either haimōn, or haimeion, or haimōn. Both Eustathius in the passage cited just before and Lucian in his book on sacrifices testify that the blood was poured or sprinkled around the altar. To this custom Virgil alludes in Eclogue 5:

units.la: Sæpe tener nostris ab ovilibus imbuet agnus.
units.tr: Often the tender lamb from our folds will stain it.

units.la: Imbuet, id est, perfundet seu madefacient.
units.tr: "Imbuet", that is, will drench or moisten.

units.la: Homerus hoc in loco, postquam inquit Pififtratus eam jugulavit, addit:
units.tr: Homer, in this place, after Pisistratus (as he says) cut its throat, adds:

units.la: Τῆς δ' ἰπεὶ ἐκ μέλαν ἅιμα ρύν, λίπε δ' ὁσ ἐκ θυμός.
units.tr: "From her the dark blood flowed out, and the spirit left her bones" [Τῆς δ' ἐκ μέλαν αἷμα ῥύη, λίπε δ' ὀστέα θυμός].

units.la: Sanguis quidem fit mentio, qui effluxerit. Subincello ergo reliqua: hunc nimirum sanguinem fuisse vase excepcum, illo, altaria conspersa five perfusa.
units.tr: Mention is made of the blood which flowed out. I therefore pass over the rest: namely that this blood was received in a vessel, and that the altars were sprinkled or drenched with it.

units.la: Latiné verò vas hoc Patera di&tum fuit : unde Virgilius loco citato:
units.tr: In Latin this vessel was called patera, whence Virgil in the passage cited:
"—and they catch the warm blood in bowls,
etc."
The same poet:
"...and of the sacred bowls of blood, etc."

units.la: Festus: Pateram pelvlo vere in sacris cum dicerent, significabant pertusam esse. Idem: Parellæ, vasa picata parva, sacrificiis faciendis apta. Marlianus hujus quoque vasis pictuam & descriptionem posuit. Descriptio est talis : Patera fuit poculi genus latum ac patens, de quo Virg.1. Aeneid.
units.tr: Festus: "When in sacred rites they said patera for a pelvis, they meant it was pierced through." The same Festus: "Parellae: small pitched vessels, fit for making sacrifices." Marlianus also gave a picture and description of this vessel. The description is this: the patera was a kind of broad, open cup, of which Virgil says in Aeneid 1:
"—eagerly he drank
the foaming bowl, etc."

units.la: Cic.6. Verrina ajt : Patera, quâ mulieres adres divinas uterentur. Macrobius verò Saturnallibro quinto, capite vigesimo primo, de poculorum generibus loquens, cum de Carchesio loquutus fuisset, sic infert de patera : Sed Plautus insuetum nomen relinquit, aitque an fabula Amphycrione pateram datam, cum longè vetiusq; poculi figura di ver sa sit. Pacer enim, ut et ipsum nomen inditio est, planum ac patens est, Carchesium verò procerum, & circa mediam partem compressum, ansatum mediocriter, ansis a summo ad infimum pertingentibus, & prosequitur. Asclepiades autem inter Græcos apprimè doctus, ac diligens, Carchesia navali re existimat dicta. Ait enim navalis veli partem inferiorem, Pateram vocari : At circa mediam fermé partem, Τρᾶχλον, dici : fuminam verò partem Carchesium nominari, & inde diffundi in utrumq; veli latus, eaque cornua vocantur, &c. Virgilius autem offenden. pateras libare lovi solitum, sic infert:
units.tr: Cicero in the sixth Verrine speech says: "a patera, which women used in the divine rites." Macrobius, in the fifth book of the Saturnalia, chapter twenty-one, speaking of the kinds of cups, after treating of the carchesium, goes on about the patera thus: "But Plautus leaves the unfamiliar name, and says that in the Amphitruo a patera was given, though the shape of the cup was quite different and much older. For the patera, as its very name shows, is flat and open, whereas the carchesium is tall and somewhat compressed around the middle, moderately handled, with handles reaching from top to bottom." Asclepiades, a very learned and careful man among the Greeks, thinks the carchesia were named from ships' rigging. For he says the lower part of a sail is called patera, the part about the middle is called trachelos, and the upper part is called carchesium, and from it the sail spreads out to each side, and these are called the horns, etc. Virgil, however, having noticed that they were accustomed to pour libations of the bowls to Jove, goes on:
"Then pour libations from the bowls to Jove, etc."
But so much for the patera.

units.la: Hunc postremò sanguinem effundebant super altaria, atque ita Diis eum offerebant ac confecrabant. Unde Virgilius:
units.tr: Finally they poured this blood over the altars, and so offered it to the gods and consecrated it. Whence Virgil:
"—of that altar

units.la: Sæpe tener nostris ab ovilibus imbuet agnus.
units.tr: often the tender lamb from our folds will stain it."

units.la: Lucianus irridens Gentilium sacrificia : Οἱ ἰχθύες ἀντες ἴςκεσθ ἡμαγ μὲν ὁ̓ κεὶ ὧσπερ ἀνυ λαι, ἱκεῖσ ἀνατιμαῖ, τὸ ἰς κατὰ αὐτοτελείως ἐ πειρ ἡ ἄλλα τοῦ σώματος αἱ τἀτ ιλ. Ἐ τὸ μὲν ἐσῆς, id est, Atqui sacrificus, inquit ipse sanguine facdatus, neque aliter, quàm cyclops ille pecudum incidit, inceflina educit, cor revellit, cruorem are circumfundit. Et quid eandem non abiens, peragensq, quod ad pietatem sacrorum, ritum pertineat ?
units.tr: Lucian, mocking the sacrifices of the Gentiles: the sacrificer, he says, is himself smeared with blood, and cuts up the animal no differently from that Cyclops of the flocks: he draws out the entrails, tears out the heart, and pours the blood around the altar. "And what, pray, did he not do, finishing everything that pertains to the rite of pious sacrifice?"

units.la: Addit Homerus, postquam sanguinis effluxum animam reliquisse ossa, id est, torpus hostiæ. Vi- de rursus colligi potest, vitam esse in sanguine. Periphrasis est Morcus, quæ est discessus, megratio, separatio animæ a corpore. Corpus synecdochice ossium nomine hic intelligitur. Ossa pro corpore , quia sunt corporis quasi columna fulcra atque robur : unde הרצומים Hatzumim ab Hebreis, a רצם Hatzam, id est, robore, quasi robur corporis dicuntur.
units.tr: Homer adds, after the outflow of the blood, that the spirit left the bones, that is, the body of the victim. From this too it can be gathered that life is in the blood. "Death" (mors), which is the departure, migration and separation of the soul from the body, is a periphrasis. The body is here understood by synecdoche through the name of the bones, since the bones are as it were the pillars, supports and strength of the body. Whence the Hebrews call them hatzumim [עצמים] from hatzam [עצם], that is, strength, as if they were called the strength of the body.

units.la: Postremo in hac actione observatione quoque est digna particula Θοῶς, id est, celeriter, currim: ex qua colligimus, in sacris peragendis summam alacritatem, agilitatem celeritatemque a Gentilibus fuisse adhibitam, ne diuturniore mora & cunctatione, sinistra quadam minusque laeta accideret, quo minus litari posset. Idem antemex alius quoque, ad verbus celeritatem significantes bus, ut ἀντίκης, καρπολίμους, κίνδα (quibus Homerus in sacrificiis hujus descriptione utitur) collegi potest. Unde festa ipsa a festinatione videntur dicta, quod in iis erat festinandum, festinanter, res divina faciendu. Inde quoq; Confestim videtur dictum, id est, celeriter, e vestigio, extem plo, quasi dicas, cum festo, sive cum festinatione: non possit festum, ut est in pro verbio, hoc est, nimis tarde atque sero.
units.tr: Finally, in this action the particle thoōs [Θοῶς], that is, quickly, is also worth noticing. From it we gather that in performing sacred rites the Gentiles used the greatest eagerness, briskness and speed, lest through a longer delay and hesitation something unlucky and less favourable should happen, by which the sacrifice could not be made propitious. The same thing can be gathered from other words signifying speed, such as antikēs, karpolimous, kinda (which Homer uses in his description of this sacrifice). Whence the festivals themselves seem to be named from haste, because in them one had to hurry and perform the divine rite quickly. Hence too "confestim" seems to be said, that is, quickly, on the spot, at once, as if you said "with festival", or with haste; a festival cannot be delayed, as the proverb has it, that is, too slow and too late.

units.la: Atque haec quidem de hostiarum σφαγή, id est, mactatione & jugulatione, ejus modo, instrumentis, de sanguinis exhostiis effluxu, signis, suscepctione & asperione super aram sint dicta.
units.tr: These things have been said about the slaughter (sphagē), that is, the slaying and cutting of throats: its manner, its instruments, the outflow of blood from the victims, the signs, and the receiving and sprinkling of the blood over the altar.

units.la: NUNC progrediamur ad alias actiones atque cerimonias, quae hostiarum jugulationem sedemq; fuerunt consecutae : inter quas prima apud Homerum & Apolloniam occurrit: bestiae hostiae ve jugulatae atque mactatae excoriatio, hoc est, cutis, tergoris, pellis cutis ve detractio, cujus arsi Homerus hoc in loco non meminit: credrant tamen ejus pasti in aliis sacrificiorum descriptionibus mentionem facit, hoc fere tria, nempe ἀπρῶν, σφαγεῖον & Ἰδρων, sive σωφρονίου, conjungeni, ut Iliad. Ἀνίωτον μὲν πρῶτα καὶ ἱστέξαν καὶ ἰδλείπαι: Primam quidem sursum traxerunt, tum mactarunt, & excoriarunt. Sic Iliad. ι. —Τὸν βοῦν ἄρα ἀ, τιτταιτάεγον Διεγ, Ἀμφὶ ἴπος, καὶ μὲν δίχ ἔλεν ἀπιτοῦ Bouem masculum, quinquennem
units.tr: Now let us proceed to the other actions and ceremonies which followed the slaughter and cutting of the victims. Among these the first to occur in Homer and Apollonius is the flaying of the beast or victim after it has been cut and slaughtered, that is, the removal of the hide, the back, the skin. Homer does not mention this in this passage, but in other descriptions of sacrifices he does mention it, generally joining three actions: the drawing up, the slaughtering, and the flaying. So in the Iliad: "First they drew it up, then they slaughtered it, and flayed it." Likewise in the Iliad, book 1: "...the bull, a five-year-old male, of Zeus..."

units.la: Excoriarunt, &c. Loquitur de Bove, quem Rex virorum Agamemnon Apollini ἐφθολλ, id est, sacrificavit. Sed quid attinet: plura testimonia proferre? Paśim apud Homerum funcobria. Sic Apollonius Τοὺς δ' ἀνορέ ξ ἀκαξαν ἀλεγ ἀλθιγτα βοῖτε.
units.tr: "...they flayed it, etc." He speaks of the bull which Agamemnon, king of men, sacrificed to Apollo. But why bring forward more testimonies? Everywhere in Homer flaying is mentioned. So Apollonius: "They quickly slew those who..." and of the bulls.

units.la: Illos autem (tauros) fuci mactarunt celeriter, & pelles detraxerunt.
units.tr: They slew those bulls quickly and stripped off their hides.

units.la: His similia sunt illa Virgilii, ceu periphrasis excoriationis:
units.tr: Similar to these are the words of Virgil, a periphrasis for flaying:
"They tear the hides from the ribs and strip the flesh from the entrails."

units.la: Servius : Tergus tergoris. Unde & tergora, corium significat: tergum vero tergi dorsum.
units.tr: Servius: tergus, tergoris. Whence tergora also means the hide; tergum, however, means the back.

units.la: Graece Δέρειν & Δέρειν, excoriare seu pellem detrahere significat. Iude Δερματ, δέρω, δερμα, δέρω, pellis, ut nonnullis volunt, proprie animalium, ratione carentium. Hinc δέρω: χρυσαλλοῖς, pellus aureas Suidas dixit. Eustathius tamen hic distinguere videtur Iliad, Βιλ. μὲν ἄλλης αὐτὸ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀπόδα ἐρωτήσεως καλλιστα ἄ πονα ... ἀλλὰ εἰ... (quietia xoras & βωμολόχος appellatur) nugator, homo garrulus & loquax videtur deducere. Ἀπε Polluci & Hesychio culter est, excoriationi destinatus; Latinè Dolabra: de quo instrumento: usu fuisse dictum est satis, cum in genere de omnibus instrumentis, ad perlustrationem & similes cerimonias adhiberi solitis, agereatur.
units.tr: In Greek derein and derein mean to flay or strip off the skin. Whence derma, from dero, derma, a skin, as some hold, properly of animals, which lack reason. Hence Suidas spoke of "golden skins". Eustathius, however, seems here to distinguish... (the one who is called a buffoon) a trifler, a chatterer and talker, seems to derive... According to Pollux and Hesychius the knife is intended for flaying; in Latin it is the dolabra. About this instrument enough has been said, since we treated in general of all the instruments usually employed for the sprinkling and similar ceremonies.

units.la: Latina deinde nomina sunt, Pellis, Tergus, Corium, Cutis. Pellis (unde forsan nostrum fel, litter a media in densam mutata) a pellendo est dicta, quod externas injurias tegendo pellas. Pellicula, diminutivum. Pellex postquam concinnata est ad calceos et cetera facienda aluta dicitur. Inde alutamen, sive alutamentum Veteres dixere opus ex concinnatis pellibus factum. Item Alutarii sive Corsarii, hoc est, pellium, sive coriorum concinnatores. Propriè tamen ea: Alutaris tenuiorum pellium dicuntur : Coriarii crassiorum. A pelle fit pelliceum, quod ex pelle est, Germanicé Bels: pellarius vel pellio, qui pelles conficit & concinnat: versipellis, idem, qui sal lax & inconstans. Suppellex etiam inde dicta: item pellex, id est, concubina, quae cum eo rem habet, qui habet uxorem: unde pellicatus, pellicere, quod Servio interprete, est blandiendo elici re vel decipere: & pellax, per blanditias decipiens, quales re veras sunt pellices.
units.tr: Next are the Latin names: Pellis, Tergus, Corium, Cutis. Pellis (whence perhaps our "fell", the middle letter having changed into a denser one) is so called from pellendo, to drive away, because by covering the body it drives off external injuries. Pellicula is its diminutive. Pellex, once it has been prepared for making shoes and other things, is called aluta. From this the ancients called a work made of prepared skins alutamen or alutamentum. Likewise there were alutarii, or corsarii, that is, makers of skins or hides. Strictly speaking, however, alutarii are said of thinner skins and coriarii of thicker ones. From pellis comes pelliceum, that which is made of skin (in German "Bels"); and pellarius or pellio, one who makes and dresses skins; and versipellis, the same, a man who is slippery and inconstant. Suppellex is also derived from it; so too pellex, that is, a concubine, who has relations with a man who has a wife; whence pellicatus and pellicere, which, according to Servius's explanation, means to be coaxed or deceived by flattery; and pellax, deceiving by flattery, as concubines truly are.

units.la: Corium proprie animalum est, praesertim eorum, quae crassiorem pellem habent ac duriorem, quod Scortum dicitur. Inde excorio, id est, corium detraho, sicut a cortice decortico, id est, detraho cortices. Inde etiam excoriatio & decorticatio.
units.tr: Corium properly means the hide of animals, especially of those with a thicker and harder skin, which is called scortum. From it comes excorio, that is, I strip off the hide, just as from cortex comes decortico, I strip off the bark. From it also come excoriatio and decorticatio.

units.la: Scortum etiam dicitur pellis crassior & densior. Unde Scorta appellatae sunt meretrices, vel quod sicut pellicula subiungantur (unde etiam pellices dictae) cum solum calciamentum omnibus subjectum sit; vel quod in grabatulis pellitis stratas tenere consuevèrunt. Ee Scorteum; quicquid ex pelle est, & Scortor, meretricor, & Scortea aricetinorum testium pelles. Scortum alias amen a Graeco σκύτος deducunt, quod pellam significat, & inde Scutum, vel Scutum, quod non fine pellibus fit. Inde Scutula quoque dicta, quasi parva scuta & scutulata vestis, & Scutra, vasis genus, quod & Scutula dicitur: & Scutilum tenue ac macrum; in quo tamen exili pellicula cernitur.
units.tr: Scortum is also said of a thicker and denser skin. Whence prostitutes were called scortae, either because, like a thin skin, they are placed under (whence also they are called pellices), since footwear is placed under everyone; or because they were accustomed to lie on pallets of hide. Hence scorteum, whatever is of skin; scortor, to whore; and scortea, the skins of rams. Others derive scortum from the Greek σκύτος, which means a skin, and from it scutum (a shield), or scutum, which is not made without hides. Hence scutula too is so called, as if small shields, and a checked garment; and scutra, a kind of vessel, also called scutula; and scutilum, thin and lean, in which, however, a slight skin can be seen.

units.la: Tergus idem, quod corium, tergum, dorsum. Inde Tergiversari & Tergiversatio.
units.tr: Tergus is the same as corium: the back. Hence tergiversari and tergiversatio.

units.la: Cutis (unde nostrum vernaculum but/ vel bani) idem quod pellis, & corium, a Graeco σκύτος.
units.tr: Cutis (whence our vernacular "but" or "bani") means the same as pellis and corium, and comes from the Greek σκύτος.

units.la: Hebraicé עוֹר Hhor (unde forsan Latinum, Corium, deductum est) pellem fiv e cutim significat, five illa a corpore fit detracta, five non: & tam de hominis, quam animalium pelle dicitur, nomenq; habere videtur a pilis.
units.tr: In Hebrew, עוֹר ['or] (whence perhaps the Latin corium was derived) signifies skin or hide, whether it is stripped from the body or not, and is said of the skin of man as well as of animals; it seems to have its name from the hairs.

units.la: Sunt autem pellium tot genera, quos sunt animalia: unde etiam denominantur: ut apud Eu-flathium exemplagratia, sic legimus Iliad. γ. Deinceps, inquit, etiam alios Heroas legimus pellibus animalium fuisse amictos. Alium quidem Λεοντέων, id est, Leonina: alium λυκέων, id est, lupina. Est etiam ταράδαλίνδορον, pellis pardi, ut λεοντήν leonis, λυκήν lupi, τεργίν hirci, sive capri, αἰγέην, pellis humana, ταύρεων taurina, αἰγέιν caprina, κυνέων canina. Desin: unde habet voces apud Graecos in eis, vel in. Pellis agnina Graeci etiā ἀρνακίς, ... vestis pellis. Sed infinitum esset omnia generatim numerare.
units.tr: There are as many kinds of skins as there are kinds of animals, and they are named after them. So we read in Eustathius, on Iliad book 3, for example: "Next, he says, we read that other heroes too were clothed in animal skins: one indeed in lion skins (Leontea), another in wolf skins (lykea)." There is also the skin of a leopard (pardus); as leontē [λεοντή] is a lion's, lykē [λύκη] a wolf's, tragin [τραγῆ] a he-goat's or goat's, aigeē [αἰγέη] a goat's, taureon [ταύρεον] a bull's, aigeion [αἰγεῖον] a goat's, kyneon [κυνέον] a dog's. The Greeks have words of this kind ending in -eis or -in. Greek writers also call a lamb's skin arnakis [ἀρνακίς], a garment of skin. But it would be endless to list all of them by kind.

units.la: Porro pellium usus varius olim ac multiplex fuit cum facerent, tum profanus. Sed nos de sacris potissimum loquamur, qualis quidem erat apud Gentiles, ducemus: unde excoriationis huius hostiarum ratio atque cuius tanto facilius intelligi poterit.
units.tr: Moreover the uses of skins were in former times varied and manifold, both in making things and in profane affairs. But we shall speak chiefly of sacred uses, such as they were among the Gentiles; from this we shall derive the account of the flaying of the sacrificial victims, and by it this will be understood all the more easily.

units.la: Primo igitur ipsis hostiarum mactatarum pellibus eanquam sacris, ipsos sacerdotes earum vestes minisfros legimus vestiri jussi solitos. Quemadmodum igitur vicitum sic vestitum quoq; habitum, corporis suimebant a victimis ipsis sive hostis, quo minimum sanctiores augustioresque habuerentur.
units.tr: First, then, we read that the priests and ministers were ordered and accustomed to dress in the skins of the slaughtered victims themselves, as sacred things, as their garments. Just as they fed on the victims, so they also took on the dress and, as it were, the bodily habit of the victims, so that they might be held the holier and more august.

units.la: His autem bestiarum mortuarum pellibus recentibus, & adhuc sanctis maleq; olentibus, quibus eanquam sepulchro quodam erant involuti, eos procul dubio admonere voluit, partim pecunie beluaneq; sua natura, in qua, amissa illa Dei imagine, degenerarint (unde etiam peccare mibia pecore sive pecude videtur dictum, propterea quod peccando homo, exuta quasi ratione natura, humana pecori fit similis) partim mortalis sua conditionis atq; mortis, quam peccato illo suo promoverat.
units.tr: By these skins of dead beasts, still fresh and holy yet foul-smelling, in which they were wrapped as in a sort of sepulchre, he doubtless wished to remind them, partly of their brutish and beastly nature, in which, the image of God lost, they had degenerated (whence also to sin, peccare, seems to be named from pecus, a beast or flock animal, because by sinning a man, his reason as it were stripped off, becomes like the beast), and partly of their mortal condition and of the death which they had brought on by that sin.

units.la: Pelles itaq; illae mortuorum animalium cum peccati, tum etiam mortis fuerunt symbola ac quae testimonia: unde vestis, Latinum vel ἱμάτιον Graecum, a quo Latinum descendit sicut ab Εσθης fit vestis, seu peccati poena, ideo Heid Germanis ablata litteral. lobi idest, luctus, vel tanquam pestis est ditta. Sed ufdem simul, tanquam munimentis quibusdam, ipsos adversus saeviens peste... flatim.
units.tr: Those skins of dead animals were therefore symbols and witnesses both of sin and of death. Whence vestis, in Latin, and himation in Greek, from which the Latin descends, as vestis comes from esthēs; so among the Germans the garment, as a punishment for sin, was called Leid, that is, grief, or was named as if it were a plague. But at the same time, as with certain defences, he wished to cover them against the raging plague...

units.la: {·} Vestes ex pellibus mortuorum animalium. flatumque inclementiam atque injurias, quibus propter peccatum erant obnoxii, tectos esse vo- luit.
units.tr: Garments made from the skins of dead animals. He wished them covered against the inclemency and the injuries of the winds, to which they had become subject on account of sin.

units.la: Has autem pelles negnaquam novas, vel ex nihilo, vel ex terra creavit, sed ex animalibus mortuis & occisis (sive id ἀπὸ τοῦ & per se, sive per Angelos beatos fecerit, in dubio alias dijudicandum relinquo) detraxit, huicque exuvias recentibus, omnino foetidis ac putidis, ut pauló antea quoque attigi, cum peccati, tum mortis factorem, atque putorem ipsum, ut ita loquar, naribus objecit & exprobravit.
units.tr: These skins, however, he did not create anew, from nothing or from earth, but drew them from animals that were dead and slain (whether he did this himself [ἀπὸ τοῦ], or through the blessed angels, I leave to be decided elsewhere), and he set before their nostrils, as I touched on a little earlier, the very stench of sin and death, as it were, and rebuked them with it.

units.la: Non igitur vestibus ex arborum foliis, ut ficus, vel palmae Christi, quae vocatur Cucurbita terrestris (qualem vestem Hieronymus libro primo Epistolarum, Epistola de vita Pauli Eremitae, Paulum illum Monachum gestasse scribit) sed ex animalium pellibus primos illos nostros parentes vestivit, propter causas jam commemoratas, & quod haec vestium materia admonere cœli injurias robustiores ac dinturnior. Hinc addi potest, Deum hoc ipso facto significare voluisse, licitum esse atque concessum hominibus, ipsius nimis ut bonitate atque beneficio, animalibus brutis & ad vestitum & ad victum uti.
units.tr: Therefore he clothed our first parents not with garments of tree leaves, like the fig leaves or the palm of Christ, which is called the earthly gourd (a garment such as Jerome, in the first book of his Letters, in the letter on the life of Paul the Hermit, says that the monk Paul wore), but with animal skins, for the reasons already mentioned, and because this material of clothing reminds one of the injuries of the sky more strongly and lastingly. From this it may be added that God meant by this very act to signify that it is lawful and permitted to men, by his own goodness and kindness, to use brute animals both for clothing and for food.

units.la: Hinc etiam verisimile videtur, Ethnicorum sacerdotes, quoniam de hac antiquissima bifloria aliquid audivera nt, tanto libentius hisce mactatorum jugulatorumque animalium pellibus indui atque vestiri voluisse. Iulius Caesar libro sexto Commentariorum de bello Gallico, hujusmodi rudes & impolitum vestis pellicea genus, quod ex pellibus animalium, nondum concinnatis & expolitis, & pilo nudatis, texebatur, Rhenones Germanica voce Belgica a pelle, ut supra dictum appellat, quod ex Iohannis Baptistae Zona pelliceas, hoc est, vestis ex pilis fuisse creditur.
units.tr: Hence it also seems likely that the priests of the Gentiles, since they had heard something of this most ancient history, were all the more willing to be dressed and clothed in the skins of the animals slaughtered and killed. Julius Caesar, in book six of his Commentaries on the Gallic War, calls a rough and unpolished kind of skin garment, woven from the skins of animals not yet dressed and smoothed, and stripped of hair, by the Belgic German word rhenones, derived from pelle, as said above. It is believed that from the girdle of John the Baptist these are pelliceae, that is, garments of hair.

units.la: Secundus pellium istarum, quae mactatis bestiis detrahebantur, usus fuit cubitorius, cubitarius, ad cubandum. Paufanias de Amphiamo verba facientes, illum vult interpretandorum somniorum arte excelluisse, & in Deos relatum, eundem artem posterus tradidisse. Ad cujus oraculum, inquit, qui pergit, tum purgari prius oportet. Purga.io autem est, ut Deo res sacra peragatur: cui, ut omnibus, quorum nomina in ara sculpta sunt, sacrificant. Hu peractis mactati arietis pellem substernit, atque ita solitos dormire, ut aptanter somniorum significationes. Sic Lacedaemoniis in fano Pasiphae somniandi causa excubabant: et quoniam Aesculapium nudi videre somnia credebant: sicut ejus templum frequeus Graecia adiit atque coluit. Sic Calabri quoque Podalyrium, Aesculapii filium, consulturi, ad ejus sepulchrum agninis iuftratum pellibus ipsi quoque cooperti decumbebant. De his fit Calius Rhodiginus libro vigesimo septimo, capite decimo quarto: Legimus icem D. uiss vel Calabris in more fuisse pellibus incubare; quas melotas dicunt, id est, Ovillas, in Podalirii sepulcro: sicque per quietem oraculi influi. Hu addit: Traditum illud quoque, ejusdem in Alibeno amne propinquo, cum pecoribus lotos ab vulneribus perfusa ri Podalirio (ὀλίγως λήσιον) unde datum fluvio nomen, quia ἀλθαί-ων medebat est, (forsan quasi ἀλθῆ ὁμοίως) sicut vituliginem curae Alpheus & Cycnus, pedibus item aegros.
units.tr: A second use of those skins, which were stripped from the slaughtered beasts, was for lying on, cubitorius or cubitarius. Pausanias, speaking of Amphiaraus, says that he excelled in the art of interpreting dreams, was taken up among the gods, and handed this art down to posterity. "Whoever goes to his oracle," he says, "must first be purified. Purification is the performance of the sacred rite for the god; to him, as to all whose names are carved on the altar, they sacrifice. When these things are done, they spread under them the skin of a slaughtered ram, and so they were accustomed to sleep, that they might grasp the meanings of dreams." So too the Lacedaemonians kept watch in the temple of Pasiphae for the sake of dreaming; and because they believed that dreams are seen by those who sleep naked, many Greeks went to, and worshipped at, the temple of Aesculapius. Likewise the Calabrians, consulting Podalirius, son of Aesculapius, lay down at his tomb, covered with lambskins. Of these things Caelius Rhodiginus writes in book 27, chapter 14: "We read that the Calabrians had the custom of lying on skins, which they call melotae, that is, woolly, at the tomb of Podalirius, and so oracular answers flowed in through sleep." He adds: "There is also the tradition that Podalirius, in the nearby river Alibenus, washed the cattle with the water of their wounds ... and that the river got its name from this, because he was a healer, [ἀλθαίων]..., just as Alpheus and Cycnus cured calves and, likewise, the sick in their feet."

units.la: Ad hunc autem pellibus animalium in Deorum templis atque sepulchris incubandi, dormiendique, et pernoctandi somniaque, eanquam rerum futurarum praenuncia explorandis morem atque consuetudinem Virgilius manifestè alludit, cum ita canit Hinc Itala gentes omnes, Oenotria tellus (Servius, Proprie Sabinorum troas, ab Oenotrio Rege.) In dubiis responsa petunt: huc dona sacerdos Quum tulit & caesarum oviumque sub nocte silenti Pellibus incubuit stratis, somnoque petivit Multa modis simulacra videt volitantia mirus, Et variae audit voces, fruituraque Deorum Colloquio, atque imis Acheronta affatur averni, Hic et tum pater ipse petens responsa Latinus Centum lanigeras mactabat rite bidentes, Atque harum effultus tergo, stratisque jacebat Velleribus: subito ex alto vox reddita luco est. Seruius in illud, Incubuit: Incubare, inquit, proprie dicuntur hi, qui dormiunt ad accipiendum responsa. Vnde est, Ille incubat Iouis, id est, dormit in Capitolio, ut responsa possit accipere: quae phrasi Plautus est vsus: Incubare te satius fuerat Ioui, qui tibi auxilio in iurejurando fuit. Donatus in eadem verba Virgilii sic commentatur: Morem dixit illius luci dum dixit, responsa accipi scuntur, venit saterdos ad lucum: aut dona, pecudes taedit, et eorum stratis pellibus incubant, inde dormiens futura somniat, et futura cognoscit.
units.tr: Virgil clearly alludes to this custom of lying down, sleeping and spending the night on animal skins in the temples and tombs of the gods, in order to seek out dreams as forecasts of future events, when he sings: "From here all the nations of Italy and the land of Oenotria seek answers in doubtful matters. When the priest has brought gifts there, and in the silent night has lain down on the fleeces of slaughtered cattle and sheep, and sought sleep, he sees many strange visions flitting about, hears various voices, enjoys conversation with the gods, and addresses Acheron in the depths of the underworld. Here too Latinus himself, seeking answers, sacrificed a hundred woolly sheep in the proper way, and leaning on their backs and lying on their fleeces, a voice suddenly came back from the high grove." Servius, on the words "he lay down", says: "Those are said to lie down properly who sleep in order to receive responses. Hence 'he lies down to Jove', that is, sleeps in the Capitol so that he may receive responses." Plautus also used this expression: "It would have been better for you to lie down to Jove, who helped you in your oath." Donatus, commenting on the same words of Virgil, writes: "He spoke of the custom of that grove: when they wish to receive responses, the priest comes to the grove, bringing gifts or sheep, and lies down on their skins; there, asleep, he dreams of the future and comes to know it."

units.la: Ad horum explicationem melioremq; intelligentiam mirifice conducunt illa Plautina in Curculione, vbi Cappadox et Coquus sic inter se colloquuntur. Cappadox leno suum natrans somnium, quod in Aesculapii fano, in quo pernoctarat, viderat, sit ait: CAP. Hac nocte insomnis visus sum tuerier Procul sedere longe a me Aesculapium, Neque eum ad me adire, neque me magnipendere Visu'st. COQ. item alios Deos fasturos scilicet. Sane illi inter se congruunt contorditer. Nihil est mirandum meliùs finibil fit tibi. Nanque incubare satius te fuerat Iovi, Tibi qui auxilium in iurejurando tulit. CAP. Siquidem incubare velint qui pejura verint, Lotus non praeberi potis est in Capitolio. COQ. Hoc animum advorte, patem ab Aesculapio Petas, ne forte tibi evenit magnum malum, Quod in quiete tibi portentum fi.CAP. bene facis. Ilo atque orabo. COQ. quae res mali vortat tibi.
units.tr: Plautus's lines in the Curculio are wonderfully useful for explaining and better understanding these matters, where the pimp Cappadox and the cook speak to each other as follows. Cappadox, recounting the dream he had seen in the temple of Aesculapius, where he had spent the night, says: "CAP. This night I was troubled by a sleepless vision: Aesculapius sat far off from me, and would neither come near me nor give me any regard." "COQ. Doubtless he will act likewise towards other gods. Indeed these things agree with each other most awkwardly. Nothing is to be wondered at; it will turn out better for you. For it would have been better for you to lie down to Jove, who gave you help in your oath." "CAP. Surely those who have sworn falsely may lie down there, but a bath cannot be provided for them in the Capitol." "COQ. Take note of this: go and seek your ease from Aesculapius, lest some great misfortune befall you, which is a portent in your sleep." "CAP. You do well. I will go and pray." "COQ. May whatever evil there is turn out for your good."

units.la: Hinc colligi potest, aegrotos olim in fano Aesculapii solitos esse pernoctare, ut etiam ex praecedentibus ejusdem lenonis verbis liquet: Migrare certum fi jam nunc e fano foras Quando Aesculapii ita sentio sententiam: Vt qui me nihil faciat, nec salvum velit. Valetudo decrescit, atcrescit labor. Nam jam quasi zonae liene cinctus ambulo. Item: Ideo fit, quia hic leno aegrotus incubat In Aesculapii fano.
units.tr: From this it can be gathered that the sick used in former times to spend the night in the temple of Aesculapius, as is also clear from the earlier words of the same pimp: "I am resolved to leave the temple now, since I feel that Aesculapius does nothing for me and does not wish me to be well. My health is declining and my distress increasing; for now I walk about as if girdled with a spleen-wrap." Again: "This is why it happens, because this sick pimp lies down in the temple of Aesculapius."

units.la: In quae verba Lambinus sic commentatur:
units.tr: On these words Lambinus comments as follows:

units.la: Qui a Diis aliquid petere cogitabant, cubabant in eorum Deorum, quorum ope egebat, fanis aut templis, tanquam responsa ab iis vel vigilantes, vel in somnis accepturi. Notat Servius ad illud Vergil. Aeneid. 7. et eesdem o'uium subnocte silenti Pellibus incubuit stratis, somnos petivit. Vl. Tullius lib. 1. de Divinat. Atque etiam qui praerant Lacedaemoniis non contenti Tegulantibus turis, in Pasiphae fano, quod est in agro propter urbem, somniandi causa excubabant, alibi incubabant, quia vera quietu oracula ducebant. Eodem pertinent illa Strabonis, lib. 16, ubi de Mose loquitur, ... Idem, sed docebat ille, omnem flatuarum fabrica tionem omittere oportere, et fanum, ac templo Augusto certus finibus eircumscripto quod Deo consecraretur, eum Deum tolendum: et in eo templo pro se quemq;, vel alios, qui essent ad bene somniandum apti natura, pro aliis incubare oportere: et iis, qui tempe ranter, et iusle vivunt a Deo donum aliquod, aut ignum esse expectandum: alias vero nihil tale expectandum, etc. Sic igitur aegri in templis Aesculapii incubabant, ut saltem in somniis monitti, aliquod morbi laxamentum, aut levamentum, ab eo consequerentur.
units.tr: Those who intended to ask something of the gods lay down in the temples or shrines of those gods whose help they needed, as if they would receive answers from them either while awake or in dreams. Servius notes this on the passage of Virgil, Aeneid 7: "and in the silent night he lay down on the fleeces of slaughtered sheep, and sought sleep." Cicero, De divinatione, book 1: "Moreover, the rulers of the Lacedaemonians, not content with burning incense, kept watch in the temple of Pasiphae, which is in the fields near the city, to obtain dreams; elsewhere too they lay down, because they held that true oracles were received in sleep." To the same purpose belong those words of Strabo, book 16, where he speaks of Moses: "... but he taught that every construction of images ought to be omitted, and that a temple, a sanctuary circumscribed by fixed bounds, should be set up and consecrated to God, and that in this temple each man, or others who were by nature apt for dreaming well, should lie down on behalf of themselves or of others; and that those who live temperately and justly should expect some gift or sign from God, but that nothing of the kind should be expected otherwise," and so on. Thus the sick used to lie down in the temples of Aesculapius, so that, at least while warned in their dreams, they might obtain from him some relief or alleviation of their illness.

units.la: Sed eundem morem ex Arnobio quoque cognoscere licet, cujus haec sunt verba: Et quoniam beneficia salutis data aliorum Numinum comparatis, et Christi: quot millia vulnis a nobis debilium vobis ostendi, quot tabifitis affectos morbis, nulla omnino retulisse meditinam, tum per omnia supplices irent templa? Cum Deorum ante ora prostrati, limina ipsa converterent oscenlos? Cum Æ. Sculapium ipsum datorem,ut prædicant sanitatis,quoad illis superfuit vita,& precibus fatigarent,& miserrimus votis in vitarent? Nonne alios scimus malis suis commortuos? Cruciatibus alios consenuisse morborum? Perniciosius alios sese habere cæpisse,postquam dies ne ulcis in continuus precibus & sanitatis expectatione triverunt? Quid ergo prodest? offendere, unum,aut alterum fortasse cunctos,cum tot nullibus subvenerit nemo,& plena sint omnia miserorum infelicium,desubra?
units.tr: But this same custom may also be learned from Arnobius, whose words are these: "And since the benefits of health given by the other deities are compared with those of Christ: how many thousands of the men weakened by wounds have we shown you, how many afflicted with wasting diseases, who in no way obtained a remedy, although they went as suppliants to the temples in every way? Prostrate before the faces of the gods, they kissed the very thresholds; they wore out Aesculapius himself, the giver of health, as they proclaim him, with prayers and most wretched vows, as long as life remained to them. Do we not know of others who died with their ills? Others who grew old in the torments of diseases? Others who began to be worse after they had spent days and nights in continual prayer and in expectation of health? What, then, is the use? That one or perhaps two were helped, while so many thousands of miserable and unhappy men, and all things full of them, were helped by no one?"

units.la: Ad hunc Gentilium in sepulchris atque templis Deorum pernoctandi, & per somnia rerum futurarum præsagia aucupandi morem atque consuetudinem Esaias quoque alludit,eamque suæ ætatis idololatriæ exprobrat.
units.tr: Isaiah also alludes to this custom of the Gentiles of spending the night in tombs and temples of the gods, and of seeking omens of future events through dreams, and he reproaches it as the idolatry of his own age.

units.la: Noti alienum autem forsan a proposito & instituto hoc nostro fuerit,hic quædam de bellico ac militari pellium usu antiquo dicere. Nam quoniam & tentoriorum experimenta, & militum vestitus,cubilia atq; strata,atq; etiam omnis generis arma atq; organa pellibus constabant,idcirco sub pellibus esse & vivere milites dicebantur. Tacitus Annalium quarto scribit Phrisius in Germaniæ tributum injunctum a Druso pro angustia rerum, ut in usus militares coria bovum penderent,non intenta cujusquam curâ,quæ firmitudo,aut quæ mensura. Cicero quæstionum Academicarum secundo: Vt non multum,inquit,Imperatori sub ipsis pellibus otn relinquatur. Livius libro quinto: Militem Romanum in labore & opere pruinis, obrutum sub pellibus durare. Idem libro trigesimo septimo: Aut sub pellibus habendo milites. Sub pellibus,metonymice,id est, tentoriis,quæ pellibus obtegebantur: tametsi vestitus quoq; atq; strata possunt intelligi. Porphyrio illa Horatii Sermonum primo: Quoniam in propria non pelle quiescam, Inde sumptum,inquit,quod duriores in pellibus dormirent.
units.tr: It may perhaps seem foreign to our purpose and plan to say here something about the ancient warlike and military use of skins. For since the tents, the soldiers' clothing, beds and coverings, and indeed all kinds of arms and equipment, were made of skins, soldiers were therefore said to be and to live "under skins". Tacitus, in the fourth book of the Annals, writes that the Frisians were ordered by Drusus to pay as tribute, because of the straitened state of affairs, ox hides for military uses, without anyone's concern as to what the quality or what the measure should be. Cicero, in the second book of the Academic Questions: "so that," he says, "little is left to the general under the very skins." Livy, book 5: "that the Roman soldier, buried under skins amid frost and toil, should endure." The same, book 37: "or keeping the soldiers under skins." "Under skins" is a metonymy for tents, which were covered with skins, although clothing and bedding may also be understood. Porphyrio, on that line of Horace's Satires, book 1, "since I shall not rest in my own skin," explains that the phrase was taken from this, because the harder men slept in skins.

units.la: Arrianus libro primo de gestis rebus Alexandri: Pelles sub quibus milites hybernabant,lævi & sicca herba complevit. Idem fermé legitur libro tertio.
units.tr: Arrian, in the first book of the Deeds of Alexander: "The skins under which the soldiers wintered were filled with smooth and dry grass." The same is read almost word for word in the third book.

units.la: Hinc autem Supellectilem novimus pellem dictam. Celsus Iurisconsultus Digestis de Supellectili legata: Labeo,inquit,originem fuisse supellectilis putat, quòd olim in usu,qui in legionem proficiscerentur, locari solerent quæ sub pellibus usui forent: alii tamen a supplendo: alii a suppetendo supellectilem volunt dictam. Sed prior etymologia mihi videtur probabilior, quippe cum utensilia atque supellex cum bellica,cum p tesi maxima ex parte pellibus atque coriis constet. Sed de pellibus,de centoriis, de iis quæ remiggibus fuerint subfratæ,de pellibus hircinis,ovillis, aliisq; vide plura apud Cælium Rhodiginum libro 27. capite 14.
units.tr: From this we know that the furniture was called "supellex" from "pellis". The jurist Celsus, in the Digest, on the bequest of furniture: "Labeo," he says, "thinks that the origin of supellex was that in former times those who set out for the legion were accustomed to have set out things which would be useful to them under their skins; others, however, want supellex to be named from 'supplying' or from 'sufficing'. But the former etymology seems to me more probable, since equipment and furniture, like military gear, consisted for the most part of skins and hides." On skins, tents, the things that were covered with rowers' ... and on goatskins and sheepskins and others, see more in Caelius Rhodiginus, book 27, chapter 14.

units.la: Sed ut ad sacrum pellium usum redeamus, observandum finulacra quoq; Gentilium nonnulla pellibus,animalium nimirum immolatorum,tecta atq; indutæ fuisse. Cicero de Natura Deorum Sospita Deacum pelle caprina,hasta & scutulo. Huc referenda alia quoq; sacrorum vasa,ornamenta atq; instrumenta,quæ ex pellibus atq; coriis confecta fuerunt folia: quo pertinent pelles aries tum taxorum,rubricatæ,quibus tabernaculum illud vere sacrum, apud Iudæos Dei jussu fuit tectum,de quo Exodus 25.& 36.
units.tr: But to return to the sacred use of skins, it should be noted that some images of the Gentiles were also covered and clothed with skins of the animals that had been sacrificed. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods: "Sospita of the Argives, with a goatskin, spear and small shield." To this should also be referred the other sacred vessels, ornaments and instruments made of skins and hides, among which are the rams' skins dyed red, with which that tabernacle, truly sacred, was covered by the Jews at God's command, of which Exodus 25 and 36.

units.la: Denique pelles illæ,animalibus mactatis detractæ,eraut anathemata quædam,quæ Gentiles in Deorum suorum templis suspindere solebant,tanquam dona quædam atq; munia, ipsis gratiffima. Huc referendus commemoratione sané diquisimus clypeus ille ligneus,bovis mactati pelle obductus,qui Romæ in templo Fidei, tanquam perpetuum monumentum illi inter Romanos & Gabinos fœderis, fuerat suspensus: de quo sic scribit Dionysius Halicarnassensis: ... Ρώμη κεφάλαιον ... Ex quibus verbu apparet, ad ipsam usq; Dionysii tempora Federis inter Romanos,& Gabinos illi monumentum,in templo Dei Fidei,quæ & Sanctum Romani vocant, servatum esse, clypeo ligneo bovis, qui tum in confirmationem fœderis mactatus est, corio inctéto, antiquis etiam inscripta litteris, quæ leges fœderis indicarent, inter ipsos initi. Sed minimè hic silentio est prætereunda religiosa illa pellium apud Scythas observatio: quibus pellis iurisiurandi sacrosancti loco erat. Mos verò talis fuit: Quando quis injuria a quodam erat affectus, cui altiùs tendo se neq̃uaquam videbat esse parem, immolato bovis carnes quidem tocuchat aqua: pellem verò extendens, in ca ipse confedebat; manibus verò addutis, ut ex iis unus, qui cubitus collocarentur. Hic verò modus est, illis gentibus supplicandi maximus. Adjacentibus igitur, hostiæ carnibus edeunt domestici familiaresque primum, deinde cui collibuerit. Accepta verò carnis portione, dextroque super corium illato pede, pollicetur pro virili, unus quidem ol. ratus est: nullis cibariis, nullaque item mercede: nonnulli gravius armaturæ milites: quoniam trifamum esset, offerre se ipsum, fitque ad eum modum haud contemnenda in bovis cutium exercitatio, eique ea rum firmissima, cum hosti prorsus inexpugnabilis, ut quæ jurejurando fit obstrictus. Inde cutem sæpe legitur in historia cultum exercitum ex corio esse conflatum.
units.tr: Finally, those skins, stripped from animals once slaughtered, were certain offerings (anathemata) that the Gentiles used to hang up in the temples of their gods, as gifts and tributes most pleasing to them. To this belongs, to be mentioned here, that wooden shield covered with the skin of a slaughtered ox, which was hung up at Rome in the temple of Faith as a lasting memorial of the covenant between the Romans and the Gabii. Dionysius of Halicarnassus writes about it thus: ... [Ῥώμη κεφάλαιον ...]. From these words it appears that, down to Dionysius's own time, the monument of the covenant between the Romans and the Gabii was kept in the temple of God Faith, which the Romans also call Sancus. It was a wooden shield of an ox, slaughtered at that time to confirm the covenant, covered with its hide and also inscribed with ancient letters setting out the terms of the agreement entered into between them. But the religious custom of the Scythians concerning skins must not pass unmentioned here: for them a skin took the place of a sacred and inviolable oath. The custom was this. When someone had been wronged by another whom he saw he was in no way equal to in power, an ox was slaughtered and its flesh touched with water. Then he spread out the skin and sat down upon it, and joined his hands, as it were, with the elbows placed together. This was the most solemn form of supplication among those peoples. Then, with the flesh of the victim set before them, the household and close friends ate first, and then anyone else who wished. Having taken a portion of the meat, and with the right foot placed upon the hide, each pledged himself as far as he was able: one as a horseman, without provisions and without pay; others as heavily armed soldiers, since it was regarded as disgraceful not to offer oneself. In this way the ox-hide was no small exercise, and the most binding of oaths, so that the man bound by it was utterly invincible to the enemy. Hence it is often read in histories that an army was equipped with leather.

units.la: Hīs adendum & illud, novam nuptam apud Romanos in lanca pelle considere solitam, vel ob verecundiam morem, quòd antiquitus homines pellibus confoprinentur, vel ut attestarentur sacrifi cium se prædicturum viro. Lugentes quoque diebus luctus in pellibus erant. Unde M. Tullius in Pisonem: Ecquid recordaris, cum omni totius provinciæ petore compulso pellium nomine, omnem quæstum illum domesticum paternumque reno vasti. Et Festus: Pellem habere Herculeis fingitur, ut hominem cultus antiqui admoncantur: lugentes quoq; diebus luctus in pellibus sunt. Ex hoc ipso autem cum sacro, tum prophano, & quidam antiquo & per vulgato pellium usu, multa in omnibus fere linguis nata sunt proverbia, quorum inter innumera hæc fere sient prætextatum: Hauten/ein gute Haut/ Haue und belz dran setzen/ auff der Haut bevmb wer ffen/ an ß anderen beiten oder leder ri ennen schneiden: Alieno ludere corio, pellem alienam Leonis, Vulpis, &c. Sen balg setzbe zum Kürschner tragen. Quiescere in propria pelle, id est, contentum esse sua forte, nec quicquam supra vires tentare. Horatius.
units.tr: To these may be added that among the Romans a new bride was accustomed to sit on a ram's skin, either from a sense of modesty, since men were of old clothed in skins, or to signal that she would bear sacrifices for her husband. Mourners also wore skins during the days of mourning. Whence Marcus Tullius, against Piso: "Do you recall at all, when, with the whole herd of the province driven together under the pretext of skins, you wasted all that domestic and paternal gain?" And Festus: "To have a skin is said to be like Hercules', so that men of ancient worship are reminded of it; mourners also during the days of mourning are in skins." From this very custom of skins, both sacred and profane, and of ancient and widespread use, many proverbs have arisen in almost all languages. Among countless others, these are almost the same: [German proverbs: "Hauten/ein gute Haut/ Haue und belz dran setzen/ auff der Haut bevmb wer ffen/ an ß anderen beiten oder leder ri ennen schneiden"] (to risk one's skin; a good skin; to stake one's hide and fur; to be on the hide; to cut into another's leather or hide); "Alieno ludere corio" (to play with another's hide), "pellem alienam" (the lion's skin, the fox's skin, etc.); "Sen balg setzbe zum Kürschner tragen" (to take one's skin to the furrier). "Quiescere in propria pelle", that is, to be content with one's own lot and not to attempt anything beyond one's strength. Horace:

units.la: Vel merito, propria quoniam sub pelle quiescat.
units.tr: And rightly so, since he rests under his own skin.

units.la: Sic, pellem tanquam rodere, pelle pre te ferris, ceu non dicas, proverbialiter Latini dixerunt.
units.tr: In the same way, the Latins proverbially said "to scrape the skin" and "to be carried out of one's skin," as if to say.

units.la: Et hæc quidem de excoriatione hostiarum in sacrificiis & pellium hostiis deiectarum usu sacro apud Gentiles sint dicta.
units.tr: These remarks must suffice concerning the flaying of victims in sacrifices, and the sacred use among the Gentiles of skins cast off from the victims.

units.la: Sed postremo observandum, nonnunquam hostias sive bestias matatas una cum pelle hostiis ignem fuisse conjectas, coque concrematas, ut in holocaustu fieri consueverit. Lucianus libro ca. sacrificus: Post incensio, inquit, igni, caprum ipsum pariter cum pelle deportatam imponas (sacrificios) ipsam item cum lanis o'rum.
units.tr: But lastly it should be observed that sometimes the slaughtered victims or beasts were thrown on the fire together with their skins, and so were burnt, as is customary in a holocaust. Lucian in his book on the sacrificer: "After the burning," he says, "lay the goat itself, carried along with its skin and wool, upon the fire."

units.la: Post excoriationem autem sequitur apud Homerum & Apollonium hostiarum bestiarumve excoriatarum ἀσκωτόν, ut ita loquar, id est, dissectio, quam Homerus quidem hoc in loco, ut etiam multis aliis in locis, verbo διχόδας exprimit, quod sacrorum videtur fuisse proprium. Αὐλὰ δ' ἀφ' ὑμῶν διχόδας· ἀφαρ ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐναιέϊα τόμον.
units.tr: After the flaying, Homer and Apollonius describe the cutting up of the flayed victims or beasts, which I may call the askoton, that is, the dissection. Homer expresses this in this place, as in many others, by the word dichadas, which seems to have been peculiar to sacrifices: "They cut them up at once" [Αὐλὰ δ' ἀφ' ὑμῶν διχόδας· ἀφαρ ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐναιέϊα τόμον].

units.la: Hic primum ad ἀσκός, id est, flatim, continuo, confestim, ut etiam aliis, idem significantibus, ἀντίος, ἀφαναῖος, significat summamin cærimoniis istis omnibus paragendis dexteritatem simul & celeritatem fuisse adhibitam. Verbum autem διχόδας. Eustathius interpretatur εἰς μιλλὰ ἐξ ἐκ θυσιῶν ἀληθῶς ἀναχρῷ ὠκα· id est, in membra seu fruita crassa bovem sedebant adhuc integram. Idem Pœta Iliad. v. in descriptione sacrificii similiter ex bove, quod Agamemnon Apollini fecerat, eodem uritur verbo διχόδας:
units.tr: Here, first, the word askos, that is, at once, immediately, forthwith, is to be noted; and other words with the same meaning, such as anti and aphanai, show that the greatest skill and speed were applied in carrying out all these ceremonies. The word dichadas, Eustathius explains as "into limbs or thick pieces," while the ox still lay whole. The same poet in the fifth book of the Iliad, in describing a sacrifice of an ox which Agamemnon made to Apollo, uses the same word dichadas:
[Ἐ μὲν διχόδας ἄπαντα]
And they cut all of them into pieces.

units.la: Quod Eustathius sit distinguit a verbo μισχάλλω, de quo positea: Διχόδας ἐστι τὸ μισχάλλω ἀποκόπτω ἐκ τῶν μελῶν ἐξ, ὡς ὁ καὶ ἢ ο ἐις τὸν εἴς ἑκάστου ἄμα εἶναι· Hoc est, Διχόδας est membratim, sive in membra dividere, sive, ut alibi quoq; fuit explicatum, in partes sive partesculas concidere, & quasi imminuere, id est, minutim concidere. Idem Eustath. Odyff. z. eandem
units.tr: That Eustathius distinguishes it from the verb μισχάλλω, which I will discuss below, is shown by his words: διχόδας is to cut off piece by piece from the limbs [Διχόδας ἐστι τὸ μισχάλλω ἀποκόπτω ἐκ τῶν μελῶν]. That is, dichodas means limb by limb, that is, to divide into members, or, as is explained elsewhere too, to chop into parts or small portions, and so to diminish, that is, to cut into small bits.

units.la: verbi utrinque, differentiam sic definit: Διαχάνιλαι τὸ ιερὸν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐομαρὸς: μισυλλαβὰ ἢ εἰς βραχέα ποα, Hostia dicitur διαχείαξ, quando in partes seu membra crassiora et majora: μισυλλαθαι autem, quando in partes breves et minutas secatur. Item Odyss. ξ. in illa Homeri:
units.tr: Eustathius defines the difference between the two words in the same place as follows: a victim is said to be diachaeax [διαχείαξ] when it is cut into larger parts or thick members, but mischallai [μισχάλλω] when it is cut into small and minute pieces. He says the same in his commentary on Odyssey 22, on that line of Homer.

units.la: Αἶλα δ᾽ μὲν διχεῖα, idem Scholiastes interpretatur, κατὰ μέρη ἀνέλκει, ὑχίερ... in partes diviserunt, dissecuerunt: et volunt metaphoram ductam esse ἀπὸ τῆς ὑγρῶν, id est, humidis seu liquidis, quae diffundi atq; ita dispari solent.
units.tr: The same scholiast explains the Homeric phrase "Αἶλα δ᾽ μὲν διχεῖα" as meaning that they divided and dissected the parts in pieces. He thinks the metaphor is taken from liquids, that is, moist or fluid things, which are usually poured out and so scattered.

units.la: Eandem actionem Apollonius his verbis expressit: Κοπτον ... Κέλλ᾽ ...
units.tr: Apollonius expressed the same action in these words: "They chopped..." [Κοπτον ... Κέλλ᾽ ...].

units.la: Apollonius hic pro verbo διχάζω duobus utitur, nempe κόπτειν et ἀμφιτύπειν, quae cadere, secare, dividere significant. Eustathius in illa supra: Βουῶν διχάζων, id est, ἐπάνω ... quod proprie διχοτομεῖν dicitur. A verbo τέμνω... Lune si verbo ... truncum sive membrum ... proprie διχοτόμωσ sit dictum, Germanice ein meer gerbaneck.
units.tr: Here Apollonius uses two words in place of the verb dichazo, namely kopteîn and amphitypein, which mean to strike, to cut, to divide. Eustathius, in the passage above, speaks of "dividing the oxen" [Βουῶν διχάζων], which is properly called dichotomein. From the verb temnō ... the piece or limb ... is properly called dichotomōsis, in German "ein meer gerbaneck."

units.la: Homeri et Apollonii descriptionibus similia sunt illa Dionysii Halicarnassei: Καὶ μετὰ τοῦτο ... Hoc est, Post id jugulationem videbant, excoriatam condeibant membrum. Quod igitur Homero est διχάζειν, Apollonio κόπτειν, id Dionysio est μαλίζειν, id est, interprete Eustathio, εἰς μέλαν ἄφρος... in membra crassiora secare. Lucianus item de sacrificiorum ritu: Pecudem, inquit, ... id est, incidit, intestina eduxit, cor resellit, etc.
units.tr: Similar to the descriptions of Homer and Apollonius are those of Dionysius of Halicarnassus: "And after this..." [Καὶ μετὰ τοῦτο ...]. That is, after this they saw the slaughter, and they cut up the flayed limb. What is dichazein for Homer and kopteîn for Apollonius, is for Dionysius malizein, that is, according to Eustathius, "to cut into thick limbs." Lucian likewise, on the ritual of sacrifices: "He cut up the animal," he says, "drew out the entrails, cut away the heart," and so on.

units.la: Haec porro hostiarum vilmimarum, sive in majores et crassiores, sive in minores et tenuiores partes dissectio, dextro, soleter, rite accurate, hebat: unde saepe apud Homerum illae partes sicut ... est, scienter, ... Nota, accuratam, hostiarum cum in Judaeorum, tum etiam Gentilium sacrificiis nitatam dissectionem atque divisionem Sanctum Paullum volunt alludere illo verbo ... id est, aptè et accommodatè personis, locus et temporibus praedicare, explicare et interpretari verbum Dei.
units.tr: Moreover, this division of the victims, whether into larger and thicker or into smaller and finer parts, was done dextrously, carefully and duly. Whence in Homer those parts are often described as ... (knowingly ...). Note that the careful dissection and division of victims, practised both in the sacrifices of the Jews and in those of the Gentiles, is thought by Saint Paul to allude to that word ... that is, to preach, explain and interpret the Word of God aptly and fittingly to persons, places and times.

units.la: Haec ipsa porro hostiarum hostiarumve dissectio fuit duplex: prior quidem in partes seu membra διχάζειν, ut sape Eustathius loquitur, id est, majora et crassiora, quem idem interpres verbo διχάζειν, Homero familiarissimo proprie vult esse intelligendam. Posterior, quae in partes, seu particulas potius, minores, breviores et tenuiores fuit, quam verbo μισυλλαβεῖν, quo et ipso Homerus in omnibus fere sacrificiorum descriptionibus utitur, Eustathius vult exprimi, de quo postea plurimus. Hostiarum igitur partes primo secundum quantitatem fieri dividi possunt, quod illarum aliae fuerunt majores et crassiores: aliae minores et tenuiores.
units.tr: This dissection of victims or of the victim was twofold. The first was into parts or members, dichazein, as Eustathius often calls it, that is, larger and thicker pieces; this the same interpreter wishes to be understood properly by the word dichazein, which is very familiar to Homer. The second was into smaller, shorter and finer parts, or rather particles, which Eustathius wishes to be expressed by the word mischallein, which Homer also uses in almost all his descriptions of sacrifices, and of which more will be said later. Thus the parts of victims may first be divided according to quantity, since some of them were larger and thicker, others smaller and finer.

units.la: Deinde secundum situm, quod aliae fuerunt externae, aliae internae, ut intestina, viscera, exta, de quibus postea, possunt dividi.
units.tr: Next, according to position, they can be divided into external parts and internal parts, such as the intestines, the viscera and the entrails (exta), of which more later.

units.la: Tertio illarum divisio est secundum usum, quod nimirum illarum quaedam in aram focum-ve fuerunt porrectae, id est, projectae, igni concrematae, atq; ita Diis redditae, consecratae et oblatae: aliae vero refertur ad epulum, quas sacrificantes comederunt.
units.tr: Third, they are divided according to use. Some of them were placed on the altar or hearth, that is, thrown in and burned by fire, and so were given, consecrated and offered to the gods. Others were set aside for the feast, which the sacrificers ate.

units.la: Sed quoniam apud Homerum non in hujusce tantum Nestorei, sed in omnium sacrificiorum descriptionibus, et apud Apollonium in Argonauticis hujus sacrificii narratione, prae ceteris hostiarum immolatarum partibus omnibus, coxarum in primis, seu femorum tam clara et illustris fit mentio, idcirco de iisdem, justa de causa primo loco mihi videtur esse dicendum. Incipiam autem pro mere meo primum ab ipsis nominibus.
units.tr: But since in Homer, not only in this Nestorean sacrifice but in all his descriptions of sacrifice, and in Apollonius's account of this sacrifice in the Argonautica, the thighs, above all the coxae or femora, are mentioned clearly and conspicuously before all the other parts of the slain victims, it seems right, for good reason, to treat them first. I shall begin, as is my custom, with the names themselves.

units.la: Ac vamen quidem Graecum, quo pars sive membrum istud, de quo nunc agimus, insignitur, est μηρος, sive μηρός, et μηρος ... apud Homerum legitur quod Latini et coxam, et coxendicem, et femur, et femen, et crus pertunt ac interpretantur. Est quoque alia vox Graeca, quae coxam seu femur significat. nempe igitur. Meiσς autem, sive unσn, sive μηρον, quod nomen in sacrificiis potissimum usurpatur, videtur dici quasi μηρις, sive μηρον, hoc est pars xat' ἐξοχὴν, propterea quod ista animalis pars eximia, selecta, & in primis sacra Dimque grata fuit habita: unde ἱερα μηρα, id est cosse, seu femora sacra hic ab Apollonio appellantur. Hinc μηροῦ tueri femur caedere, & μηροτμητης, id est femur cedens, fodiens, effodiens & καλλιωπ coxis seu femoribus pulchris praeditus, & Lacaena μηροκοιλης nuncupata, quod incisu parcem hanc registerent, tosse Celio Rhodigino libro 4. capite 10. Ibidem ὀξυμηρια vult dici femora inter coxas, & μηρουόμηρον, quod coxas interjacet.
units.tr: The Greek word by which this part or limb, which we are now discussing, is designated is μηρος or μηρός. In Homer, μηρος is read, and Latin writers render it as coxa, coxendix, femur, femen and crus. There is also another Greek word meaning coxa or femur. The name μηρον, which is especially used in sacrifices, seems to be derived as if from μηρις or μηρον, that is, the part above all others, because this part of the animal was regarded as choice, selected, and especially sacred and pleasing to the gods. Hence Apollonius here calls them ἱερα μηρα, that is, sacred thighs or femora. From this come μηροῦσθαι, to cut the thigh, and μηροτμητης, thigh-cutter, one who cuts or digs out; also καλλιμηρος, having beautiful thighs. The Spartan woman is called μηροκοιλης, because by cutting they expose this part, as Caelius Rhodiginus says in book 4, chapter 10. In the same place, ὀξυμηρια is said to mean the femora between the thighs, and μηρουόμηρον, that which lies between the thighs.

units.la: Vocem autem Graecam μηρον, sive unεjus alii, ut modo dixi, coxam, alii coxendicem, alii femur, alii crus, nonnulli eciam inguina reddunt.
units.tr: The Greek word μηρον, as I have just said, some render as coxa, others as coxendix, others as femur, others as crus, and some even as the groin.

units.la: Ac coxa quidem & coxendix pro eodem accipiuntur, quam nonnulli volunt dictam a cogendo, quod ibi femur cum superiore parte cogatur ac coarctetur. Sunt autem coxae sive coxendices duo, sacro ossi intrinque adstrictae, carumque quaedam habentia acceptabula, quibus ossium femoris capitula inseruntur. Graece ἰσχία appellantur. Unde Ischiadicus morbus, qui coxendires infestat: & Ischiadici dicuntur, a coxendicibus laborantes. Plinius libro vigesimo quinto coxendicibus art.culis omnibus cum axungia utilissima. Cato incantamentum dolet ad sanandas coxendices luxas, hoc est, loco suo motas. Suetonius de Augusto, Coxendice, & femore & crure sinistro non per ire valebat: ut saepe etiam inde claudicaret. Plinius in Epistola: Hunc dum sequitur colligi que per laevem & lubricum paviementum, fallente vestigio cecidit, coxamque fregit, quae parum apte collocata, reluctante aetate, mali colit.
units.tr: Coxa and coxendix are taken to mean the same thing. Some say the name comes from cogere, to compel, because there the femur is compelled and constricted together with its upper part. There are two coxae or coxendices, joined on each side to the sacrum, and some of them have sockets into which the heads of the femur bones are fitted. In Greek they are called ἰσχία. Hence ischiadic disease, which afflicts the hips, and those who suffer from the hips are called ischiadici. Pliny, in book 25, speaks of all the joints of the hip being treated with axungia, a most useful fat. Cato gives a charm for healing hips that are sprained, that is, dislocated from their place. Suetonius says of Augustus that he could not walk well with his hip, thigh and left leg, so that he often limped because of it. Pliny, in a letter: as he followed him, slipping on the smooth, slippery pavement, he fell and broke his hip, which, set badly, resisted his age and remained a source of trouble.

units.la: A coxa fit verbum incoxare, id est, cosim, quasi incoxim, sive in coxam sedere. Pacuvius. Adeo incoxante mihi pes obstupuit.
units.tr: From coxa comes the verb incoxare, that is, to sit on the hip, as if incoxim, or to sit in the hip. Pacuvius: "So, while I was sitting on my hip, my foot went numb."

units.la: Sub coxa femur est ad genu usque deductum, & ex lato in angustum definens. Pes autem dicitur, quod est a femore ad calcem & dividitur in coxam, sive coxendicem, femur, genu. Femur femoris, & femen feminis, inquit Festus, dicti potest, ut fenero & femen, vero utrumque nomen, in eadem fere significatione fit: tamen a nonnullis ita distinguunt, & quidem bifariam: vel quod femen pars sit posterior & crassior; femur anterior. Femur autem sive femen a seren do volunt dici, quia dies praecipue partibus suslineacur animal atque feracur. Hinc femoralia dicta sunt: sub gaclus, quibus partes pudende teguncur. A femoris item sive feminae mollicie nonnulli feminam volunt nomen sumtraxisse: quod quidem etymon ab ipsis sacris litteris non videtur abhorrere, in quibus primam feminam sive mulierem, Evam postea nominatam, ex Adami, viri ac maritii sui dormientis, costarumque a Deo fuisse aedificatam (Hebraea dicendi formā) hoc est, sictum & formatam legimus: unde Adamus illam vitae sue adjutricem atque socian sed a Deo additam, sibique connubio flabili junctam propriam, dicatam ישׁה Ichah, id est, Virilem, sive Viram ac viraginem, & os ex ossibus, acg. carnem ex carne sua di vino infinitu afflatuque appellavit. Costa ibi צלע Tzelahh, appellatur, quae vox & costam sive lapsum significat: eo quod claudicatio sive lapsus in alterum sic latus. Costa & coxa magnam inter se habent affinitatem. Quid si igitur coxae dicta sunt quasi costa, quae corporis totius sunt quasi columnae quedam?
units.tr: Below the hip is the femur, which extends down to the knee and narrows from broad to slender. The leg (pes) is so called because it runs from the femur to the heel, and is divided into coxa or coxendix, femur, and knee. Festus says femur (of femoris) and femen (of feminis) may be named as fenero and femen are; both words come to nearly the same meaning, yet some distinguish them in two ways: either because femen is the hinder and thicker part and femur the front part. Femur or femen, they say, comes from serere, to sow, because the animal is chiefly sustained and made fruitful by these parts. Hence femoralia, the breeches, are named: the undergarments by which the private parts are covered. Some also want the name femina (woman) to have been taken from the softness of the femur, and this etymology does not seem to clash with Holy Scripture itself, in which we read that the first woman, afterwards named Eve, was built by God from the rib of Adam, her husband, while he slept (a Hebrew way of speaking), that is, shaped and formed. Whence Adam called her his helper and companion, given by God and joined to him in a bond of marriage as his own, named [ישׁה] Ishah, that is, Woman, or Wife, and virago, and bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh, by divine inspiration. The rib there is called [צלע] Tzelah, a word that means both rib and a fall or lapse, because of the limping or falling to the other side. Rib and hip have a great affinity. What if, then, the hips are named as if they were ribs, since they are, as it were, columns of the whole body?

units.la: Denique hic inter nomina coxae sive coxendicis referri debent, etiam Hebraea: quorum duo ferē sunt. Primum est ירך jarech, proprie quidem coxam, sive femur significans: translatē vero ad multa pro latere cujuslibet res transfercur; quia videlicet femur est in latere, ut supra quoque dictum. Exemplum posterioris significationis illustre exstat Exodi quadragesimo capite, versu trigesimo, ubi ירך jarech hammisechcan, femur tabernaculi, latus ejus appellatur. Alterum nomen, quod coxam infigninit, est שׁוק Schók, ut Proverbiorum vigesimo sexto capite, versu septimo dicitur: Elevate שׁוקיכם Schokim, id est, coxas a claudo. Voces hujus etymon ignoratur: quidam tamen voci שׁוק Schuk, affinem faciunt, quae vicum, platea significat, quod excurrat coxa a corpore, sicut vicus a platea. Galli ab hac Hebraea voce שוק Schok vel שוק Schuk, mutuati sunt vocem Choquer, quae femoribus sive coxis collidere significat.
units.tr: Finally, here the Hebrew names for the hip or haunch must also be listed, of which there are about two. The first is [ירך] yarech, which properly means the hip or thigh, but figuratively is transferred to the side of any thing, because the thigh lies at the side, as said above. A famous example of this latter meaning occurs in Exodus chapter 40, verse 30, where [ירך] yarech hammishkan, the thigh of the tabernacle, is called its side. The other name, which denotes the hip, is [שוק] shoq, as in Proverbs chapter 26, verse 7: "Lift up your [שוקיכם] shokim, that is, your hips, from the lame." The etymology of this word is unknown. Some, however, relate it to [שוק] shuq, which means a street or broad way, because the hip runs out from the body as a street runs out from the square. The French borrowed from this Hebrew word [שוק] shok or shuq the word choquer, which means to strike together with the thighs or hips.
And this is enough.
And these things concerning the names.

units.la: Nunc, quod attinet ad coxarum sive femorum isiorum sacrificium, quod diligenter accuratius ab Homero describitur, in eo hæc sunt observanda, sed quæ dum ipsius Homeri & aliorum describionem. Horum primum est ipsa τομὴ, id est, sectio seu amputatio illorum, quod Græci uno verbo compositio μηρὸς-τομεῖ exprimunt. Homerus: Αχαρ ἀ'ς ὠμογον ἴσχειν Πάντα κατὰ μηρὸν, Statim autem (nota rursus celeritatem & agilitatem, quæ fuit adhibita) coxas excideruntomnia rite.
units.tr: Now, as regards the sacrifice of the hips or thighs (femora) of the victims, which Homer describes carefully and in more detail, the following points are to be observed, though these are to be taken from Homer's own description and that of others. The first is the cutting itself (τομή), that is, the section or amputation of these parts, which the Greeks express in one compound word, from μηρός and τέμνειν [μηρὸς-τομεῖ]. Homer: "...to cut away all things at the thigh [κατὰ μηρόν]." Straightaway (note again the speed and agility that were employed) they cut away the hips, and all things were done duly.

units.la: Illud πάντα Eustathius interpretatur ὅλα, seu ὁλόκληρα, id est, tota, integra, solida. Alioquin enim (addit) vox πάντα esset super vacanea, cum duæ tantum sint costæ sive femora. Mihi perículum illa πάντα videtur generaliter ad totam actionem referenda, ut significetur, omnia hæc κατὰ μέρη, ut addit, hoc est, rite atque legitime fuisse peracta. Iliad. α. μηρὸς τι ὀξίζει μὴ. Scholiastes Homeri reddit ὀξυκόλ.
units.tr: Eustathius takes the word "all" (πάντα) to mean "whole" or "entire" (ὅλα, ὁλόκληρα), that is, complete, unbroken, solid. Otherwise (he adds) the word "all" would be superfluous, since there are only two hips or thighs. To me, however, that "all" seems to refer generally to the whole action, so as to signify that all these things were done κατὰ μέρη, as he adds, that is, duly and lawfully carried out. Homer, Iliad 1: the thigh... Homer's scholiast renders the word as "sharp-cutting" (ὀξυκόλ...).

units.la: Apollonius quoque hujus exsectionis meminit: ἠ ἰσχία ὑπὸ ἰτάμωνο: Et sacra femora excidebantur.
units.tr: Apollonius also mentions this cutting out: "the hips were cut out from beneath..." that is, the sacred thighs were cut away.

units.la: Verbo hoc σκτίμωστ, quo Homerus & Apollonius utuntur, non simpliciter coxarum femorumque exsectio, abscisio & amputatio, sed præstantia simul eorundem videtur intelligenda, quæ verbo Græco cum ca, & Latino cum ex sæpe designatur: ut sensus sit, illas potissimum partes primo omnium, tanquam eximias, selectas, Diis inprimis gratas & acceptas fuisse amputatas, sive abscissas, quæ primæ Diis offerrentur: unde ἀγλαὰ, id est, splendida ab Hesiodo appellantur: Ἐπεὶ δ' ἀγλαὰ μηρία καίειν: Postea autem splendida femora sive coxas adurito, adoleto.
units.tr: The verb σκτίμωστ, which Homer and Apollonius use, should be understood not simply as the cutting out, excision and amputation of the hips and thighs, but also as their preeminence, which is designated by the Greek ca and by the Latin ex so often. The sense is that these parts were especially, before all others, cut away as choice, select and especially pleasing and acceptable to the gods, and were offered first to the gods; hence Hesiod calls them "splendid" (ἀγλαά), that is, shining: "Then burn the splendid thighs" (ἐπεὶ δ᾽ ἀγλαὰ μηρία καίειν), that is, afterwards burn and offer up the splendid thighs.

units.la: Secundo coxas sive femora ista adipe sive pinguedine operierunt, sive obduxerunt.
units.tr: Second, they covered these hips or thighs with fat or grease, or wrapped them in it.

units.la: Homerus: —κατὰ τε κνίσσῃ ἐκάλυψα, Insuper omento operierunt.
units.tr: Homer: "...and they covered them over with fat (κνίσση)." They wrapped the thighs in omentum.

units.la: Apollonius: Κα'λ'υ'ψαν ἀ'ν'ν'δ' πάντα κα'λυ'ψαντες πύ'ντ'ε Δ'ν'ν'ω Simulq; hæc omnia (ἀρά ικέες, facta femora) operientes sive tegentes, videlicet ornate, affabre, prudenter, (id enim sibi vult nomen πύ'ντα) densa pingue-dine.
units.tr: Apollonius: "They covered over all things, wrapping the thighs..." Here, covering all these things (the thighs being made) and wrapping them, namely finely, skilfully and prudently (for this is what the word πύντα signifies), with thick fat.

units.la: Apollonii Scholiastes Δ'νω interpretatur, τὸ ἔ'σ'ιλ' ν'ε'ι'λ'ν'ιλ' ἀπ'α' ἔ' ἐ' ἐ'κ' κα'ι' ἀ'ν'ι' ἀ'ι'ο'υ'α' ἰ'σ' ἐ' ἀ' ἔ'ο'υ' ἐ'ρ'ν' ἐ'ν' ἰ'ο'ν'ε'ν' ἀ'ν' ἀ'ν'ι', id est, omento invo-lvunt hostias, ut facillime exardescant atque consentiant. Homeri Scholiastes Δ'νω vertit τὸ ἐ' τέ'. Εἰ'ς autem Δ'ω' populus, & Δ'ν'ω', pinguedo. Eustathius Iliad. α. τὰς ἡ ὠμο'υ'ς' ἰ'σ'η' πυ'σ'ι'ς, inquit, ποσὶν κα'λ'υ'σ'τον' ἱ'ε'τ' : coxas autem sive femur, pinguedine cooperta, comburunt. Ibidem indicat, pro κνίσσῃ bodie vocem κνισσάζει' ὑ'φ'ο'υ'ρ'ι'.
units.tr: Apollonius's scholiast explains the word (Δ'νω) as meaning that they wrap the victims in the caul so that they may catch fire and burn together most easily. Homer's scholiast renders the word as "the thigh" and the word for "poplar" and "fat." Eustathius, on Iliad 1, says: "they burn the hips or thighs, covered with fat." In the same place he notes that for κνίσση the modern usage is κνισσάζει, to be sprinkled with fat.

units.la: Vox κνίσσα autem sive κνίσα, per simplex σ, ἀ'ν'ο' κνίσ', id est, κνίζω, duo apud Homerum significat, Eustathio auctore, nempe ἀ'ν'ι'σ'ε'ι'σ, id est, pinguedinem, & τὸ ἀ'ν'ι'σ' χ'ρ'ά'σ'ι'ν ὀ'πῶ' μὸν κ'ά'ν' ἀ'ν'ο' ἀ'ν'σ', id est, evaporationem, fumum, nidorem ex carnibus assatis, Eustathius ἀ'ιλ'ε'ι'σ' ἀ'ι' ἀ'ι' ἀ'ι'σ' ἀ'ι' ἀ'ι' ἀ'ι' ἀ'ι' Odyss. p. ἀ'ι'σ' ἀ'ι'σ' ἀ'ι'σ'. Sic Arnobius sæpe Cnisse voce Græca pro vapore atque nidore utitur. Hoc in loco κνίσσα dixit, λίπ&, sive μ'ε'λ'ν' id est, sumum, adipem sive pinguedinem significat, quæ coxæ sive femur obduci atque in volvi solebant, quæ & majoris id est flamma, vapor atque nidor excitarentur, & illa tanto facilius conflagrarent: id quod aufficatur & boni omnis loco habebatur. Et hoc ipsum quidem summo fludio, riteque sieri consuevisse particula illa ἀ'ν'ε'ω', quæ Apollonius utitur, satis ostendit. Eodem fere pertinet tertium membrum, cuius Homerus in omnibus fere sacrificiis meminit: [Greek, illegible, ~12 letters], id est, duplicia, sive bifariam facienti, scilicet femoris, sive coxae. Quid autem sit, [Greek, illegible, ~10 letters], malo ipsius Eustathii verba proferre, cuius haec sunt: [Greek, illegible, ~40 letters], ut ipsorum femorum, sive coxarum binarum, tum adipis sive pinguedinis, quibus sacrificium obducebantur, duplicationem, quae utraque in sacrificiis usitata erant, ita dicendi forma intelligi. Eustathius verba Odyss. E. haec sunt: [Greek, illegible, ~30 letters].
units.tr: The word κνίσσα, or κνίσα with a single σ, from κνίζω, has two meanings in Homer, according to Eustathius: smoke, fat or grease, and the evaporation, savour and smell of roasted meats. Eustathius (in Odyssey) relates these senses. So Arnobius often uses the Greek word cnisse for vapour and savour. In this place he means by κνίσσα the fat or grease with which the thighs were wont to be covered and wrapped, so that the flame, vapour and savour would be stirred up more strongly and the thighs would burn all the more readily; this was thought to be a desirable and good result. That this was done with the greatest care and in the proper manner is clearly shown by the particle that Apollonius uses. Almost the same applies to the third element, which Homer mentions in nearly all sacrifices: [Greek, illegible], that is, doubled, or folded in two, namely of the thigh or hip. What this means I prefer to give in Eustathius's own words, which are: [Greek, illegible], that the doubling of the thighs themselves, both of the two hips, and also of the fat or grease with which the sacrifice was covered, both of which were customary in sacrifices, is understood by this manner of speaking. Eustathius's words on Odyssey 5 are: [Greek, illegible].

units.la: Idem Eustathius hic eodem loco ait: duplicare, id est complicando, atque ita duplici facere significat vel pinguedinis unam partem supra femora, alteram sub illis ponere. Vel ea duplicare unum supra alterum collocando. Idem Eustathius Odyss. Γ. Τὸ δὲ διπλοῦν ...
