Duplicia sive duplicata, facere etiam aliam significationem habet: scilicet Veteribus maxime placet hac dicendi forma significari pinguedinis duplicationem, cuius una pars supra femora, altera infra ponatur. Sed copiosius ... hic idem Scholiastes ... de consuetudinem his verbis exprimit Iliad. α.
units.tr: The same Eustathius says in the same place: to double, that is, by folding, and so to make double, signifies either placing one part of the fat above the thighs and the other below them, or doubling them by laying one over the other. The same Eustathius, on Odyssey 3, says that the word "double" (τὸ διπλοῦν) has another meaning as well: the Ancients most approve of understanding by this manner of speaking a doubling of the fat, one part of which is placed above the thighs and the other below. But more fully... this same scholiast... expresses the custom in these words in Iliad 1.

units.la: Hoc est, Duplicia facientes, vel duplicationem, coxas sive femora alia super alia ponentes: vel potius pinguedinem dilorum duplicantes. Id enim omnii fluidi cl. borabant, ut femora claro luculentoque conflagrantia igni tota absumerentur: quoniam id nisi fieret indispicatum Graecis esse videbatur nec se putabant litare, quando terrore aliquo religionis injectio, coxae seu femora ex pinguedine, qua erant in voluta, excidebant.
units.tr: That is: making them double, or doubling, placing the hips or thighs one upon another; or rather doubling the fat over them. For they took care to do all this, so that the thighs would be wholly consumed, burning in a clear and bright fire; for unless this were done, it seemed to the Greeks unlawful, and they did not think they had properly sacrificed, when, with some religious dread, the hips or thighs were cut out from the fat in which they had been wrapped.

units.la: Ilud autem Homerus exprimit verbo [Greek, illegible, ~10 letters], quod de verbo ad verbum significat crudum imponere: de quo Eustathius disserit Odyss. Γ. [Greek, illegible, ~60 letters].
units.tr: Homer expresses this by a verb which, word for word, means "to place raw" (the Greek verb), concerning which Eustathius discourses in Odyssey 3: [Greek, illegible].

units.la: Hoc est, Ex reliquis ... aut ea duplicia [?] ... [Greek, illegible, ~25 letters], id est, humerum ponebant.
units.tr: That is: from the remaining... or doubled [?]... [Greek, illegible], that is, they placed it on the shoulder.

units.la: Hu pene similia sunt illa Scholiastis in Homerum Iliados α. in illa [Greek, illegible, ~30 letters], καὶ ... Hoc est, Ab ipsis autem hostiis crudis incipientes partium quaedam ex omnibus earum membris patem abscindebant, eamque coxis imponebant: ita ut sortem hostiae membris sibi viderentur fruì.
units.tr: Similar to this are those statements of Homer's scholiast on Iliad 1, in those lines, where: "But beginning with the raw victims themselves, they cut off a portion from all their members and placed it on the thighs, so that they seemed to enjoy the lot of the victim's members."

units.la: Hīc consentanea sunt illa Hesychii: ὠμοβρῶτες, inquit, δὲι τὸ ἀρ᾽ ἱκαταμίχια τῷ ἱσφαγ- ιον ιερὸν ἀ᾽ ὀ ἀμφ... οὐ... ἀ ἀλλ... μὴ... ἁμὸν, ἐπὶ..., ἡ ἐ ἀπ... ἁ... Hoc est ... ab unoquoque, hostiæ mactatæ membro adhuc crudo aliquid decerpere, & id sacrificio imponere. Nec ὠμοφάγων tantum, sed etiam ὠμοφάγ... dicitur, ut Odyss. ξ. Αἶψα δ᾽ ἱ μὲν ... Πέκτ... Καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐν πυρὶ βάλλα παλλύν... Statim autem ipsum (porcum nimirum mactatum & usulatum) diviserunt: crudaque autem posuit subjicere. Undiq; initio facto a membris in pinguem adipem, Et partim quidem in ignem jecit, ubi commiscuisset farinæ flore Vel, ut ea carmine eleganti reddidit Fridericus Sylburgius: Crudaq; de cunctis delibans frustula membris Pingui conspersit flammæq; adolend a Vernicibus indit
units.tr: Consistent with this are the words of Hesychius: "raw-eaters" (ὠμοβρῶτες), he says, is the term for when from each victim, while the animal is still alive, something is plucked from the limb and placed on the sacrifice. Not only the word "raw-eaters" (ὠμοφάγων) but also the other is used, as in Odyssey 14: "Straightaway they divided the pig (slaughtered and slit open), and laid the raw pieces upon it. Having made a beginning, they took portions from all the limbs and laid them upon the fat; and partly they threw them into the fire, after sprinkling them with barley meal." Or, as Friedrich Sylburg rendered it in elegant verse: "Taking raw morsels from all the limbs, he sprinkled them with fat and put them on the flame to be burnt."

units.la: Hic Scholiastes ὠμοβρῶτες exponit ... quod crudas carnes, primitias Dijs offerebat. Resté. Ex omnibus enim membris primitias Diis credebant apponebant, quæ postea in ignem conjecta adolerentur. Eustathius in hunc locum, ...
units.tr: Here the scholiast explains "raw-eaters" as meaning that they offered raw flesh, the firstfruits, to the gods. For they believed they placed firstfruits from all the limbs before the gods, which were afterwards thrown into the fire and burnt. Eustathius, on this passage...

units.la: Adhæc postremò magis illud ... Dionysii Halicarn. lib. septimo: ... ... Omnia ... ex singulis ... ex ...
units.tr: Moreover, finally, what is more: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 7: ...... All ... from individual ... from ...

units.la: Postquam verò coxas sive femora & exsecuerunt, & exsecta omento, adipe sive pinguedine operuerunt ac in volverunt, & eo, quo dictum est, duplicarunt, & denique crudas illas partes ex omnibus hostiæ membris resectas & farrenvolutas ... ... Καὶ (Scholiastes, ἱκαιρ) ... Adolebat ea super ligna senex, id est, Nestor. Καὶτ... Adolevérunt super lignis cui similiter subjungit mori effusionem.
units.tr: After they had cut out the hips or thighs and cut away the fat, they covered them with fat, wrapped them, and doubled them in the way already described; and finally they placed those raw parts cut from all the members of the victim, sprinkled with barley meal... The scholiast (...). The old man, that is Nestor, burned them upon the wood. ... They burned them upon the wood, and similarly he adds the pouring out of the wine.

units.la: Sic Homerus de Eumæi sacrificio: Καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐν πυρὶ βάλλα: Et hæc in ignem conjecit.
units.tr: So Homer, on the sacrifice of Eumaeus: "And these he threw into the fire" [Καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐν πυρὶ βάλλα].

units.la: NVNC postremò, antequam ulterius progrediar, dicendum aliquid est de fine, cur Græci veteres tanto studio, atq; cerimonia coxas in primis sive femora bestiarum Diis suis consecrarint, & in illorum honorem concremarint. Ejus rationem hanc reddit Eustathius Iliad. α. hisce verbis: ἔτω μὲν τοὺς ὀμφαλοὺς τῆς ὑπὸ Διὸς ... Hoc est, Ea hoc quidem modo ritu, coxas siue femora tota in solidum concrematbant, ea tanquam pretiosum quid ex reliquis hostiæ membris deligentes, propterea quòd ea conferunt atq; conducunt ad animæ ingressum & egressum atq; generatione ejectione seminis. Ex his Eustathius verbis eonstat, Ethnicos, quinon nisi eximia, selecta ac pretiosa Diis suis offerenda sibi atq; consecranda esse putabant; idcirco hæc quoque potissimum animalium membra ipsis, tanquam munera pretiosissima sacrasse & adolevisse. Duplicem autem & quidem maximum istarum partium usum esse docet. Vnum est, quòd totius corporis sunt quasi columina atq; fulcra ad illud sustentandum, & ad illius motū incessumq; omnino sunt necessaria. Alterum earundē usus cernitur in generatione: unde femina quasi femina dicta: unde etiā femina, id est, mulier videtur denominata. Huc referenda vetus juramenti forma, qua soliti sunt illi, qui se juramento obligabant, manus ejus femori, cuius se obligabant, subjicere, Genesis 24. & 28. Hanc jurandi consuetudinem sunt, qui inde professam tantum, quòd ex femore fit procreatio; unde Genesis 46. capite, anima diuntur progressæ de femore Iacob. Sed de hoc partium istarum, ut etiam aliarum omnium, usu consulendi sunt Physici atque Medici.
units.tr: Now, before I go further, something must be said about the purpose for which the ancient Greeks burned the thighs, or rather the haunches, of their beasts to their gods with such care and ceremony, and consumed them in honour of those gods. Eustathius, on the first book of the Iliad, gives this reason in these words: "In this way they burned the thighs whole, choosing them from the rest of the victim's limbs as something precious, because they contribute and conduce to the soul's entering and leaving, and to generation and the emission of seed." From these words of Eustathius it is clear that the heathen thought that only what was outstanding, chosen and precious should be offered and consecrated to their gods. For this reason they especially dedicated and burned these parts of the animals to the gods as the most precious gifts. He teaches that these parts have a double and very great use. One is that they are, as it were, the pillars and supports of the whole body, and are wholly necessary for holding it up and for its motion and walking. The other use of these parts is seen in generation, and from this the word for thigh (femur) seems to be derived, as is the word for woman (femina). To this belongs the old form of oath, by which those who bound themselves by an oath were accustomed to place their hand under the thigh of the person to whom they bound themselves (Genesis 24 and 28). Those who explain this custom of swearing say that it arises from the thigh's being the source of procreation; hence in Genesis 46 the souls are said to have come forth from the thigh of Jacob. But concerning the use of these parts, as of all the others, physicians and natural philosophers must be consulted.

units.la: Præter hanc verò rationem, quam Eustathius adfert, verisimile est Ethnicos, superstitiosè bujus suæ circa coxas siue femora hostiarum occasionem partim ex altera illa historia de coxa siue femoris Iacobi Patriarchæ, in admirabili illa cum Angelo luctâ, luxatione. & quæ illam consecuta fuit, claudicatione arripuisse. Et quoniam, ut sacrum litteris prodirum est, Iudæi in rei illius memoriam abstinuerunt ab esu nervi ex contractione, quia est in pala femoris: id probabile est, Gentiles quoq; κοκοζωλία quadam, ut etiam in aliis sastiatur unt, in sacrificiis suis hostiarum coxas atque femora Diis suis malu isse adolere, & in illorum honorem con-remare, quamea comedere. Aliastamen in profanis epulis, ut vel ita, id est, dorsa siue terga, sic quoq; ιστε, id est, femora, Eustathius Odyss. 9. docet fuisse, ut ipse loquitur, ὁρὼ ὧν ἐπὶ ἔσχα, id est, mãnopen expesita: idq; Posidonii testimonio comprobat, qui in epulis publicis optimum & so-rissimum quemq; υπρὸ, id est, femoris portione fuisse honoratum testatur: de qua parte monomachia nonnunquam atq; duella inter con-vivas exiterint. Et hæc de coxis siue femoribus sint dicta, quorum in sacrificiis, ut ex Homero & alijs scriptoribus constat, tam diligens super stitiosaq; in sacrificiis a Gentilibus habita fuit ratio & observatio, ut pluribus fuit explicatum.
units.tr: Besides this reason, which Eustathius gives, it is likely that the heathen, in their superstition, took the occasion for this practice concerning the haunches or thighs of victims partly from that other story, of the dislocation of the thigh of the patriarch Jacob in his wonderful wrestling with the Angel, and of the limping that followed it. And since, as Holy Writ records, the Jews, in memory of that event, abstained from eating the sinew that shrinks, which is in the socket of the thigh, it is probable that the Gentiles too, with some misguided zeal, as also happens in other matters, were accustomed to burn the thighs and haunches of their victims in their sacrifices to their gods and to consume them in honour of those gods, while they themselves ate the rest. Yet in ordinary feasts, Eustathius teaches on the ninth book of the Odyssey, the backs or loins were served in the same way, and the thighs too, as he himself puts it, "the piece of the thigh" [ὁρὼ ὧν ἐπὶ ἔσχα]. He confirms this by the testimony of Posidonius, who says that at public feasts the best and most distinguished man was honoured with a portion of the thigh (ὑπρόν). Over this portion there sometimes arose single combats and duels among the guests. Let these remarks on the haunches or thighs suffice; as Homer and other writers make clear, so diligent and superstitious a regard and observance was paid by the heathen to these parts in their sacrifices, as has been explained at length.

units.la: CONSEQVENS nunc videtur esse, ut de aliis quoq; hostiarum partibus, earumq; in Gentilium sacrificiis usu, seu abusu potius superstitiosissimo dicamus. Quemadmodum igitur Gentiles coxas atq; femora hostiarum suarum, quæ motus generationis stimulis, ammalis sunt instrumenta, Diis suis potissimum sacrificarunt: sic capita quoque atq; linguas immolatorum bestiarum iisdem consecrarunt.
units.tr: It now seems right to speak in the same way of the other parts of the victims, and of their use, or rather their most superstitious abuse, in the sacrifices of the heathen. Just as the heathen offered especially to their gods the thighs and haunches of their victims, which are the instruments of the stimulus of generation and motion, so they also consecrated to the same gods the heads and tongues of the sacrificed animals.
a. Heads.

units.la: Ac quantum ad capita attinet, quæ principem inter corporis membra locum obtinent, taurorum & arietum capita, detractis carnibus, cum ornatu culto, illo suo sacrificiali in templo assigi atq; suspendi suisse solita legimus, tanquam testimonia atq; monumenta ipsorum vel gloriæ atq; pietatis erga suos Deos. Illorum quoq; pilaturæ & imagines ibidem vi sebantur, ut in pilaturis antiquis, quas Guilhelmus de Choul in libro suo ponit, cernere licet. Ægyptiorum mos mirus hic non est tacendus. Illi hostiæ capua dirè devorabant, & cum precatione, seu imprecatione potius solenni in flumen deiiciebant, ut, si quid ad versi acciderat, in caput illud redundaret.
units.tr: As for the heads, which hold the chief place among the members of the body, we read that the heads of bulls and rams, with the flesh removed and finely decorated, were customarily fixed and hung up in their sacrificial temples, as witnesses and memorials of their glory and piety towards their gods. Carvings and images of these were also set up there, as one may see in the ancient carvings which Guillaume du Choul includes in his book. The strange custom of the Egyptians must not be passed over here. They would terribly curse the heads of the victims, and with a solemn prayer, or rather a curse, cast them into the river, so that if any evil had befallen them, it might fall back upon that head.
a. Tongues.

units.la: Linguarum autem, quæ peraftis sacrificiis in epulo sacrificiali ante con-vivarum discessum in focum conjectæ comburebantur, frequentissima apud Homerum & alios scriptores sic mentio, cum qua linguarum concrematione conjungebatur libatio, de quibus vide mea Con- vivialia. Athenaus libro primo. Post cænam, inquit, cum jam cætus dissoluerentur, libabant antiqui Mercurio, nõ ut posteritas soli Teleo (τελέου Hεsychius τελεσφόρος, ὀλόκληρος exponit) idest, sacrorum. perfectum & integrum, quoniam Mercurius somno præfuit. Libabant & eidem a cœna discesuri ob linguæ commercium. Mercurio namq; sacre linguæ sunt ob eloquentiam & orationis pspicuitatē.
units.tr: Of tongues, which, once the sacrifices were finished, were thrown into the fire and burned at the sacrificial feast before the guests departed, there is very frequent mention in Homer and other writers. The burning of the tongues was joined with a libation; on these matters see my Convivialia. Athenaeus, book one: "After supper," he says, "when the company was breaking up, the ancients made libations to Mercury, not as to Teleius (which Hesychius explains as 'perfect' and 'whole', τελέου, τελεσφόρος, ὀλόκληρος), that is, of the sacred rites, perfect and entire, since Mercury presided over sleep. They also made libations to him as they were about to leave the supper, on account of the exchange of tongues; for the sacred tongues belong to Mercury because of eloquence and clarity of speech."

units.la: Cœlius Rhodiginus Lectionum antiquarum lib.13. cap.5. Ionum vel Atticorum hunc morem fuisse ait, rationem huius rei afferens varias, vel quia inter membra reliqua bonitate lingua præstat: optima vero Diis reddi par sit: vel quod linguæ & verbi parcant somnum petentes: vel quia in convivijs prolata, silentio sint obruenda (unde est illud, ὑπὸ ὀρὸς ὑπάοτ ... Odi memorem compotorem) vel quoniam linguas amburendo (amburi autem solebant, juxta illud Homeri Odyss. γ. λιλάνας ...) perperam dictorum labes expurgarent. Addit Sponda nus, hoc fieri solitum in fine convivii, quia post multas confabulationes significabatur, tunc illius esse finem imponendum: nec poterat melius ullum silentii symbolum usurpari quam ista linguarum adustio, cum lingua sit orationis instrumentū. Sed & apud Aristophanem in Pluto adhæc verba ... Theophrastus de Characteribus ... Diana quoq; libationes illas fieri solitas. Sed de linguarum immolatione in ... 2 ... Vnde fur fan coligi possit, linguam Mercurio, ob illius præconium, quo Dijs inservit, deberi.
units.tr: Caelius Rhodiginus, Ancient Lessons, book 13, chapter 5, says that this was the custom of the Ionians or Athenians, giving various reasons for it: either because among the other members the tongue excels in goodness, and the best things ought to be given to the gods; or because those who seek sleep spare both tongue and speech; or because things spoken at feasts ought to be drowned in silence (whence the saying, "I hate a drinking companion who remembers"); or because by burning the tongues (they were burned, as in Homer, Odyssey 3) the blemish of words spoken amiss was purged away. Sponda­nus adds that this was done at the end of a feast, because after much talk it was signalled that the end should now be put to it, and no better symbol of silence could be used than the burning of the tongues, since the tongue is the instrument of speech. But also in Aristophanes, in the Plutus, these words... Theophrastus, in the Characters... Libations of this kind were also customarily made to Diana. But concerning the sacrifice of tongues in... 2 ... From this one may gather that the tongue is owed to Mercury, on account of his office as herald, by which he serves the gods.

units.la: NVNC vero ab externis hostiarum præcisio progrediamur ad partes atq; membra interna, quæ a Græcis ... generatim, a Latinis viscera & exta appellantur, quorum in sacrificijs gentilium maximum usus fuit. Eustathius Iliad. explicata cox arum seu femoris cerimonia ... Iungit.
units.tr: Now let us move from the external parts of the victims to the internal parts and limbs, which the Greeks call in general σπλάγχνα and the Latins call viscera and exta, and which were of very great use in the sacrifices of the Gentiles. Eustathius, having explained the ceremony of the thighs or haunches... Continues.

units.la: Viscera Hebraice ... Kerabin appellatur a singulari Kæræb, quod intimū, interstinum, medium significat, a Karab, appropinquare, adjungere ... membra. Eandem ob causam etiam Mehim, & in duali Mehim, appellantur: quæ voce Rabbi David Kimhi in Psal.21. docet intelligi ... cal haaperim hapenī nim, omnia membra interiora. Hinc Psal 46. dicitur: Lex tua est in medio visceram meorum ...
units.tr: The viscera are called in Hebrew Kerabin, from the singular Kerab, which means inmost, interior, middle; from Karab, to draw near, to join... the limbs. For the same reason they are also called Mehim, and in the dual Mehim. Rabbi David Kimhi, on Psalm 21, teaches that this word is to be understood as "all the inner parts" (kal haaperim hapenim). Hence Psalm 46 says: "Your law is in the midst of my bowels..."

units.la: Generalis deinde & communis vox apud Græcos, quæ viscera, exta significat ... σπλὰγχνα ... Eustathius viscerum tria genera enumerans, nempe splen, cor, & jecur ... ἔνδοσθεν ... nimirum a situ seu loco appellantur.
units.tr: Next, the general and common Greek word, which means viscera or entrails, is σπλάγχνα [splanchna]... Eustathius, listing three kinds of viscera, namely the spleen, the heart and the liver... (inside) ... they are named from their situation or place.
Hebrew names of the viscera.

units.la: Dicuntur etiam χορδαί, item τομία ἀπὸ τοῦ τέμνειν a sectione, in qua significatione Demosthenes quoq; & Aeschines hoc nomine τομίων utuntur, quasi dicas secta, sive refecta, exsecta, profecta: quia sectione e victima eximebantur, super quæ exsecta manus imponere, vel etiam sive, atque ita jurare solebant, ut docet Dionysius Halicarnassensis, libro septimo: de qua jurandi consuetudine postea. Possunt tamen voce τομίων etiam aliæ partes, quæ ex victimis recidebantur intelligi.
units.tr: They are also called χορδαί [chordai] and likewise τομία [tomia], from τέμνειν [temnein], to cut, from the sense of cutting. In this sense Demosthenes and Aeschines also use the term τομίων [tomion], as if you should say "cut," "cut off," "cut out," "set apart," because they were removed from the victim by cutting; and people were accustomed to lay their hand on these cut-out parts and so to swear, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his seventh book. More will be said of this custom of swearing later. Yet by the word τομίων other parts also cut from the victims may be understood.

units.la: Ἐντομα etiam dicuntur & exta, sive etiam aliæ victimæ partes, & fædera (quæ sacrificium interpositis gradibus fiebant) & expiationes Hesychio. Nam ἐντέμνειν & incidere, & cæsa femur ἀτάλαταs hostias immolare atq; sacrificare significat. Thucydides libro quinto, ὡς ἐπιμεν ἐντόμωτοι, quæ impiis ὑπὸ δώρων τῶν, id est, tanquam Heroi cedunt victimas sive sacrificant, & bona res tribuerunt: unde ἐντομὴ & incisuram sive incisionem, & sacrificium, quod cæsa seu intisa sit victima, significat.
units.tr: Entoma are also called the entrails and other parts of a victim, and also covenants (which were made by sacrifice with pieces cut and placed between them) and expiations, according to Hesychius. For entemnein means to cut into, and also to slaughter or sacrifice a victim whose thigh has been cut. Thucydides, in book five, speaks of those who cut up victims for the gods, as if they sacrificed to a hero and gave good things to the dead [ὡς ἐπιμεν ἐντόμωτοι]. Hence entome signifies both an incision and a sacrifice, because the victim has been cut or slashed.

units.la: Non est hic silentio prætereundum, σπλάγχνον, de quo modo dictum, præter propriam significationem, capi sæpissime in sacris & profanis litteris, ut etiam viscera apud Latinos, pro amore, misericordia, & alio affectu intimo, maximo & flagrantissimo: quoniam σπλάγχνα seu viscera membra sunt corporis intima, corporis ipsius penetralia (unde etiam in omnibus fere linguis suum nomen habent) maxime vitalia, mollia, tenera, quibus cibi digeruntur, utilia retinentur, superflua emittuntur: quoniam ut magis elluum sunt sedes & instrumenta: unde per metonymiam sæpe pro ipsis affectibus sumuntur. Et sic apud Euripidem in Medea vox σπλάγχνον miserationem significat. Unde verbum σπλαγχνίζεσθαι in sacris præsertim litteris, Veteris & Novi Testamenti sæpissime accipitur pro, Ex intimis visceribus et medullis misericordia affici atq; moveri, quod Deo creberrime atque Christo ἐσπλαγχνισθη, tribuitur & hominibus: ut Lucæ primo σπλάγχνα ἐλέους, viscera misericordiæ, p quæ Deus exoriens ex alto nos visitavit. Sic 2. Corinth. 7. σπλάγχνα ἀπέστιλλε, ... tanto vos magis ex animo, ex intimis animi visceribus amat. Sic Philipp. 1. μάρτυς γάρ μου ἐστὶν ὁ θεός, ὡς ἐπιποθῶ πάντας ὑμᾶς ἐν σπλάγχνοις Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, Deus enim mihi est testis, quod vehementer omnes vos desidero in visceribus Iesu Christi, Hoc est, me ex intimis planè, Christiano affectu per & propter Christum maximo vestium flagrare desiderio. Et capite secundo: Ei σπλάγχνα ... οἰκτιρμοί, siquidem viscera et miserationes: ubi οἰκτιρμοὶ adduntur ἐσπλαγχνίσκος. Pauli gratia obtestatio: si quis est animorum vestrorum ergo mea affectus, amor, miserationes, &c. Sic Colossen. 3. ἐνδύσασθε σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμοῦ, induite viscera miserationum, id est, fludete sincero ergo fratres vestros aviori & misericordiæ, date operam, ut ornati, tis et instructi vero sincero et ardente amore atq; misericordia ergo fratres vestros. In epistola ejusdem Apostoli ad Philemonem ter σπλάγχνον, id est, viscerum: fie mentio. Primo dicit σπλάγχνα, id est, viscera sanctorum per Philemonem fuisse refocillata. Secundo: Refocilla, inquit, τὰ ἐμὰ σπλάγχνα, mea viscera suscipe: ubi ipsum Onesimum vocat sua viscera (ut Titus amor & delitiæ gentis fuit appellatus) id est, sibi carissimum: Sic Penelope apud Homerum: τὰ σπλάγχνα, id est, viscera nostra, tuæ dilaniantur opes, id est, quæ sunt, tanquam viscera uostra, quibus alimur & sustentamur quæq; nobis sunt carissima. Τὰ σπλάγχνα a porro claudere ab aliquo, est, Nulla ergo ipsum misericordia tangi, quæ sensui. Iohan. 3. prohibemur viscera claudere a fratre egente, hoc est, nulla commiseratione affici ad ejus inopiam fuble vendam ac sustentandam: quod idem, ac esse ἀνσπλάγχνος, seu ἀπλάγχνος, ut Græci loquuntur, imitatem, immisericordem esse: ecui opponitur εὐσπλάγχνος, humanus, mitis, misericors, benignus, & πολύσπλάγχνος, qui valde est misericors. Aliquando εὐσπλάγχνος etiam animosus dicitur, ut Ephesiorum 4. εὐσπλάγχνος, animositas, animus ad misericordiam promtus, Sophoclis interpreti. Et hæc de nominibus Græcis.
units.tr: It must not be passed over in silence that splanchnon, which I have just mentioned, is used very often in sacred and profane writings, apart from its proper meaning, just as viscera is used by the Latins for love, pity, and any other inward, very great and burning feeling. For the splanchna, or viscera, are the innermost parts of the body, its inmost recesses (which is why in almost all languages they have their own name), the most vital, soft and tender parts, by which food is digested, useful things are retained and superfluous things expelled. Since they are the seats and instruments of the emotions, they are often taken by metonymy for the emotions themselves. So in Euripides' Medea the word splanchnon signifies pity. Hence the verb splanchnizesthai, especially in sacred writings of the Old and New Testament, is very often used for being moved and stirred with pity from the inmost bowels and marrow; it is ascribed very frequently to God, and Christ was moved with compassion [ἐσπλαγχνίσθη], and to men too. So in Luke 1 the splanchna eleous, the bowels of mercy, by which God, rising from on high, has visited us. So 2 Corinthians 7: his splanchna perissoteros, he loves you all the more from the heart, from the innermost bowels of his mind. So Philippians 1: "For God is my witness, how greatly I long for you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ" [σπλάγχνοις Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ]; that is, I burn with the greatest longing for you from the depths of a truly Christian affection, through and for Christ. And in chapter 2: "if there is any splanchna and mercies," where the mercies are added to the bowels of compassion. Paul's entreaty by grace: if there is any affection, love, or pity of your minds, and so on. So Colossians 3: "put on the bowels of mercies" [ἐνδύσασθε σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμοῦ], that is, show sincere kindness and mercy to your brethren, take care to be adorned and furnished with true, sincere and burning love and mercy toward your brethren. In the same apostle's letter to Philemon the word splanchnon, in the plural, is mentioned three times. First, he says that the splanchna, that is, the bowels of the saints, were refreshed by Philemon. Second, he says: "Refresh my bowels" [τὰ ἐμὰ σπλάγχνα], receive my own heart; where he calls Onesimus himself his bowels, as Titus was called the love and delight of the nation; that is, most dear to him. So Penelope in Homer: "our bowels," that is, our possessions which are like our bowels, by which we are fed and sustained and which are most dear to us, are torn apart by your wealth. To close the bowels against someone (ta splanchna apo klein) is to be untouched by any mercy toward him. In 1 John 3 we are forbidden to close our bowels against a brother in need, that is, to be moved by no compassion toward his poverty, to relieve and support him. This is the same as being an-splanchnos, or aplanchnos, as the Greeks say, that is, unmerciful and pitiless. Opposed to this is eusplanchnos, humane, gentle, merciful, kind, and polysplanchnos, who is very merciful. Sometimes eusplanchnos is also taken to mean spirited, as in Ephesians 4, eusplanchnos (spiritedness, a mind readily inclined to mercy), in the words of the interpreter of Sophocles. These are the Greek terms.

units.la: Latinè Viscera interiora omnia dicuntur, ut jecur, cor, pulmo, renes, lien & reliqua, quæ pellegantur, quæ etiam intestina & interanea dicuntur, quibus respondent nomina Græca, paulo autè commemorata: quæ Plinius uno nomine Præcordia vocat, quia cordi prætenduntur. Sed sunt in illa Virgilii: Illi se prædæ accingunt dapibusq; futuris Tergora deripiunt costis & viscera nudant: Viscera, inquit, non tantum inteslina dicimus, sed quicquid sub corio est. Vt in Albano Latinus visceratio dabatur, id est, caro. Visceratio enim carnis crudae diltributio fuit, quae fieri solebat vel in solenni festivitate & praecipue in funere excellentus alicujus persona. Hinc viscerari, car nempopulo distribuere. Idem Servius in illa Virgilii Aeneidos sexto:
units.tr: In Latin, viscera is the name for all the inner organs, such as the liver, heart, lungs, kidneys, spleen and the rest, which are also called intestines and entrails, and which correspond to the Greek words mentioned a little above. Pliny calls them all by one name, praecordia, because they lie before the heart. But in that line of Virgil: "They gird themselves for the booty and the coming feast; they strip off the hides from the ribs and lay bare the viscera," viscera, he says, is not only the intestines but whatever lies beneath the skin. So in Alba, a visceratio (distribution of meat) was given to the Latins, that is, of flesh. For visceratio was the distribution of raw meat, which was customarily made at a solemn festival or especially at the funeral of some eminent person. Hence viscerari means to distribute meat to the people. Servius, on that line of Virgil's Aeneid book six, says the same:

units.la: Et solida imponit taurorum viscera flammis:
units.tr: "And he lays the solid viscera of the bulls upon the flames."

units.la: Non exta dicit, sed carnem. Nam viscem sunt, quicquid inter ossa & cutem est: unde etiam viscus ratio dicitur communium de carnibus factu. Ergo solida viscera holocaustum significat, quod detractis extis are super imponebatur, quae nonnunquam ablata: elixa etiam ipsa reddebantur. Unde infert:
units.tr: He does not say exta, but flesh. For viscera are whatever lies between the bones and the skin; hence also the viscus is said to be a mixed dish made of meats. So "solid viscera" signifies the burnt offering, which was placed on the altar after the entrails had been removed, and these were sometimes taken away, and were given back boiled as well. Hence he adds:

units.la: Pingue super q; oleum fundens ardentibus extis.
units.tr: "Pouring rich oil over the burning entrails."

units.la: Quanquam alii pro parte totum velinc, ut per exta totum animal intelligatur. Vifenea videtur di quasi vescum (ut Vescum, papaver) a vescendo, quia hominibus viscera vescuntur, tanquam cibus delicatus: vel quia visceri insiliant cenacum acq, sequacus corpori adherent & quasi agglutinata sunt. Hinc vox viscerum mecaphorice saepe pro re quavis abdita, abstrusa, penicus infixa & inhaerente accipitur: ut Cicero in quaestionibus. Tusculus. Haret in visceribus id malum. Item: Periculum autem residebit & erit inclusum penitus in venis atq; vt ceribus Reipublicae. Ite: Sed nolime pucare, ὑγιήσ ἐι ὄσμα, illa cua abjecisse, quae mihi in visceribus haerent. Item de Oratore: Haec non extrinsecus ulcinde quarendo, sed ex ipsis visceribus causa fumeuda sunt, in medullis & visceribus. Viscera tamen erant a vivendo dicta, ut vita in corporis muembra.
units.tr: Although some take the whole for the part, so that the whole animal is understood through the exta. Viscera seems to be named as if from vescum (as vescum, poppy), from vescendo (eating), because the viscera are eaten by men as a delicate food; or because they cling to the entrails like a glue and adhere closely to the body, as if glued together. Hence the word viscera is often used metaphorically for any hidden, concealed matter, deeply fixed and clinging: as Cicero says in the Tusculan Disputations, "that evil sticks in the viscera"; again: "the danger will remain and be shut up deep in the veins and viscera of the commonwealth"; again: "but I do not wish to cast away those things that cling to my viscera"; likewise in On the Orator: "these causes are to be drawn not from outside, but from the viscera themselves, from the marrow and inmost parts." Yet viscera were so called from living (vivendo), as life is in the limbs of the body.

units.la: Exta porro proprie fuerunt dicta, quae ex visceribus Dijs sacrificabantur, & in quibus harum species suctura praenoscebantur, sic cista, quod ad hunc usum praeciperet ur, quod exstarent & eminerent, propterea quod cor olim non solebat inter exta numerari: postea pinguicudo illa, quae in summo corde est, laeta exta facit. Extaigitur quasi exsecta, & exstantia, vel quasi extra dicta.
units.tr: Exta, properly speaking, were those parts that were sacrificed to the gods from the viscera, and by which the outcome of things was foreknown; so called (cista) because they were set apart for this use, because they stood out and projected, for the heart was not formerly counted among the exta; later that fat which lies on the top of the heart made the exta cheerful. Exta therefore is as if exsecta (cut out), and standing out, or as if extra (outside) said.

units.la: HIS PRAEMISSIS nunc ad viscerum ifiorum sive mitum sacrificiis proprie appellata fuerunt, extorum usum seu abusum potius idolatricum, qui Gentilibus valde fuit familiaris, explicandum accedamus: cujus crebra frequentia in omnibus fere Gentium sacrificiis fit mencio. Sic enim sapissime apud prophanos auctores exta inspici, consuli, coqui, profecari, porrici, reddi, eome di quoq, fuisse solita legimus; de quibus singulis dicemus ordine.
units.tr: Having made these preliminaries, let us now proceed to explain the use, or rather the idolatrous abuse, of the inner parts of animals, which were properly called exta, a practice very familiar to the Gentiles and which is mentioned in almost all the sacrifices of the nations. For we read that in profane authors the exta were very often inspected, consulted, cooked, cut up, offered, given back, and also eaten by the sacrificers. We shall discuss each of these in order.

units.la: PRIMO igitur dicamus de u'u uavreia, id divinatorio, qui primus fere & praecipuus isto rum vitorem extorum sacrificialium usus apud Gentiles fuit. Ex ullorum enim inspectione res & eventus futuros sive bonos sive malos praenoscere atq, praedicere consueverunt. Divinatio nem, a Divis, teste Cicerone, dictam, quam Graeci μαντικὴν a furore appellat, Cicero definit earum rerum, quae forcuita putantur, praedictionem acq, perfusionem. Eandem Chrysippo definit his verbis: Vim cognoscentem & videncem, & explicantem signa, quae a Diis bonitatibus portendantur. Officium autem ejus esse, praenoscere Diierga homines quae menie sint; quid, significent. Idem Divinationem facit duplicem: Aliam naturalem, quae arte careat: aliam artificiosam, quae artis fit particeps, ut est divinatio extorum, fulgurum, ostentorum, prodigiorum, coelestium. Divinationem igitur ex extis Cicero fecit artificiosam. Sic enim idem lib. 2. de Divinatione, artificiosa divinationis illa fere genera ponebat, Extispicii, corum, quae ex fulguribus, stentis, praedixerunt.
units.tr: FIRST, then, let us speak of divination (manteia), which was almost the first and chief use of inspecting sacrificial entrails among the Gentiles. For by inspecting them they were accustomed to foreknow and foretell future events and outcomes, whether good or bad. Divination, according to Cicero, is named from the gods (a divis), which the Greeks call mantike from madness (furor). Cicero defines it as the foretelling and foreseeing of things that are regarded as accidental. Chrysippus defines it in these words: a power that knows, sees and explains the signs that are portended by the gods' goodwill. Its office, he says, is to foreknow for men what things will come and what they signify. The same author divides divination into two kinds: one natural, lacking art; the other artificial, which shares in art, such as the divination of entrails, lightnings, omens, prodigies and celestial signs. Cicero therefore counted divination from the entrails as artificial. For in the second book On Divination he gives this same kind of artificial divination, listing the haruspicy, and the things that are foretold from lightnings and portents.

units.la: Haec divinatio a Graecis ἀστραλογοσκοπία, seu ἀστραλογομαντεία, exceptio inspectione per exta divinatio: quo pertinet ἀστραλογολογία, extorum sectio: nec non ἐπυροσκοπία, id est, epatis inspectio, sive Ruplenia. Haec autem Graeci per fynecdochen idem sic nominarunt, quod quanquam explorarent ea omnia, quae visceris nomine continentur, ut epar, lien, cor, renes & caetera: jecur tamen vaticinationi istius sedem & quasi fontem constituebat: quo tese constitutio & optime temperato pro vitiatu natura laeta promisit, eo ancem vitiato aut mutilato ad versa portendi opina narentur, sive refragarentur caetera, sive consenserit: & quid inde initium inspectionis considerationem vel istius sciebat. Latine divinatio ista vix extitisis, seu extaris: nec non extispicina, & haruspicina dicta fuit.
units.tr: This divination is called by the Greeks astragalo-skopia or astragalo-manteia, that is, divination by inspection of the entrails. To it belongs astragalo-logia, the cutting up of the entrails, and also epyroskopia, that is, inspection of the liver, or ruplenia. The Greeks named the whole art by synecdoche after these parts, though they examined everything included under the name of viscera, such as the liver, spleen, heart, kidneys and the rest. The liver, however, was regarded as the seat and, as it were, the fount of this prophecy. If its constitution was sound and well tempered, it promised a happy outcome; if it was vitiated or mutilated, adverse things were portended, whether the other parts agreed with it or contradicted it. From this, inspection of the liver came to be the main consideration of the art. In Latin this divination was scarcely called extispicium or extaris, and was also called extispicina and haruspicina.

units.la: Ipsi vero extorum inspectores & aestimatores, qui caesa victima exta inspiciebant, & ex eorum colore aut qualitate futura conjiciebant & praedicebant Graece & ἀστραλογόλογοι, quo nomine & juppiter fuit dictus, teste Athenaeo, ab extorum sectione qui viscera ἰερόσκοποι qualem Enslathius dicit nullum in Cypro hostiae mactatae cultro resolvebant & eximebant. fuisse cultum & αλλαξγοσκόποι, ab eorum inspectione, & speciales ἀπολλοπόποι, interior: inspectores (causam nominis antea attigi) & generatim Συσκόποι, & ingenium Gorκόποι, facitores sacrificiorum inspectores (quia non exta tantum, sed etiam alia in sacrificiis observabantur, & ex iis futura prædicebant) a Latinis extispices & harupices, a victimis in aram spiciendis fuerunt appellati. Hesychius τοὺς δὴ ἀλλαξγοσκόπους ... quo ea, quæ ex ignibus sacrum, sive hostiis, significantur, prænoscunt, appellat: utera Συσκόπους παρὰ τὸ θύω, id est, sacrificia, inspicere, intelligere. Idem etiam ἱμπυρομαντεῖοι dicitur esse Eustathio Iliad. ultimo.
units.tr: The inspectors and assessors of the entrails themselves, who examined the entrails once the victim was slain and from their colour or quality conjectured and foretold the future, were called by the Greeks astragalologoi. From this Jupiter too was named, as Athenaeus witnesses, from the cutting of the entrails. Eustathius says that there was a cult of Jupiter in Cyprus whose priests cut out and removed the viscera with a knife once the sacrificial animal was killed. There were also allaxoskopoi, named from their inspection, and the special apollopoi, the inner inspectors (I touched on the cause of the name earlier). In general they were called sysko-poi and gorkopoi, the makers and inspectors of sacrifices, because in sacrifices not only the entrails but also other things were observed, and from these they foretold the future. The Latins called them extispices and haruspices, from looking at the victims on the altar. Hesychius, who calls them allaxoskopoi, says they foreknow what is signified by the fires of sacrifices or by the victims, and derives syskopous from thyo, that is, to inspect and understand sacrifices. Eustathius, in his commentary on the last book of the Iliad, says the same practice is also called impyromanteia.

units.la: De hoc autem Divinationis genere ex extis sin in genere Plutarchus in lib. de Orat. Pyth. ai ἐπὶ τὰ ἀλλαξγοσκοπῶ, & ποιοῦται ... Hoc est, Vsfcernum sive extorum forma & qualitates hominibus futura significant. Cicero de Divinatione libro primo: Democritus autem, inquit, censet, Iapienter instituisse veteres, ut hostiarum immolatarum inspicerentur exta: quorum ex habicu atque colore tum salubritatus, tum pestilentiæ signa perspicere nonnunquam etiam, quæ sit vel sterilitas agrorum, vel fertilitas futura.
units.tr: Plutarch, in his book on the Pythian oracle, speaks of this kind of divination from entrails in general terms: the forms and qualities of the entrails signify future things to men. Cicero, in the first book of On Divination, writes: "Democritus, moreover, thinks that the ancients wisely instituted the inspection of the entrails of slain victims. From their appearance and colour they perceived signs of both health and pestilence, and sometimes even whether the fields would be barren or fertile in the future."

units.la: Verba, quibus divinationis iflius actio atq; munus exponitur sunt, αλλαξγοσκοπεῖν, αλλαξγοσκοπεῖν, πανσκοπεῖν, (Hinc Extispicina a Græcis ἀπολλοπόσυνια nominatur, quod quanquam exploratur omnia, quæ vise... Vaticinii hujus fontem esse existimabant, & ab illius contemplatione exordiebantur) Συσκοπεῖν, vel Συσκοπεῖν, ἱμπυρομαντεῖν, item ζυλαπιῶν τὰ ἀλλαχα apud Æschinem in Ctesiphontem, id est, observare exta, quid significent, quid ve portendant.
units.tr: The words by which the action and function of this divination are described are allaxgoskopein, allaxgoskopein, panskopein [ἀλλαξγοσκοπεῖν, ἀλλαξγοσκοπεῖν, πανσκοπεῖν]. (From this the Greeks call extispicy [ἀπολλοπόσυνια], because although they examine everything, they believed it was the source of this prophecy and began from the observation of it.) Also suskopein or suskopein [Συσκοπεῖν, Συσκοπεῖν], impyromantein [ἱμπυρομαντεῖν], and, in Aeschines against Ctesiphon, zylapion ta alla [ζυλαπιῶν τὰ ἀλλαχα]. That is, to observe the entrails, what they signify or what they portend.

units.la: Latinibus feré verbus utuntur: Viscera aperire. Ovidius Aflorum primo: Hic qui nunc aperi: percusti viscera tauri In sa..is multum culter babebat opus.
units.tr: The Latins for the most part use the phrase viscera aperire, "to open the entrails". Ovid in the first book of the Fasti: "He who now opens the entrails of the struck bull, had a knife with much work to do in the sacrifice."

units.la: Item, Nudare viscera. Virgilius: —Et viscera nudant Culi ris. Hic respondet Græcum αλλαξγοσκοπεῖν.
units.tr: Likewise nudare viscera, "to lay bare the entrails". Virgil: "And they lay bare the entrails." This corresponds to the Greek allaxoskopein.

units.la: Item, Viscera inspicere: quo illud et felli ve ille apud Plautum in Aulula. ia: Quiolla atq; pelle totus est, tota vara macet. Quin exta inspicere in Sole etiam vivo licet. Ita enim pellucet, quasi laterna Punica.
units.tr: Likewise viscera inspicere, "to inspect the entrails", to which that saying of Plautus in the Aulularia applies: "He is all skin and hide, all bones and rags. Yet one may inspect his entrails even in the living sun; for they shine through like a Punic lantern."

units.la: Item, Viscera consulere. Virgilius Aeneidos tertio: Instaurata, diem donis, pecudumq; reclusfo Pectoribus, inhiansq; pirantia consulit exta Heu vatum ignara mentes, quid vota furentem, Quid delubra juvant?
units.tr: Likewise viscera consulere, "to consult the entrails". Virgil in the third book of the Aeneid: "Having renewed the days with gifts, and the breasts of the beasts laid open, they gaze eagerly and consult the still-breathing entrails. Alas, ignorant minds of the seers! What do vows or shrines avail a raging man?"

units.la: Donatus in illa: Spirantia consulit exta, idem sunt, inquit, ac quaerebat futura in interioribus eorum: sic posuit quasi exta possent revocare respondere: sed videntur respondere, dum consulentibus ostendunt. Servius, Auspicalem, inquit, artem intelligi, victibus signa commissæ consultationis oflendunt. Servius, Auspicalem, inquit, artem intelligi.
units.tr: Donatus, on the line "consults the still-breathing entrails", says that it means the same as seeking the future in their inner parts; the poet wrote it as if the entrails could answer, but they seem to answer while they show themselves to those consulting. Servius says that the art of augury is meant, and that the signs in the victims show the outcome of the consultation. Servius says the augural art is meant.

units.la: Mensa huic actioni, hoc est, hostiarii partim dufsectioni, partim inspectioni destinata, Latinè Ara clabra fuit dicta, scilicet Festo, de qua supra. Sacerdos igitur sive harupex culero, ad id deflituato, viscera sive exta ex inmolate hostiæ corpore evellebat, eaq; diligenter attente explorabatur ac rimabatur, quomodo singula essent affecta, & nunquid deesset: unde, vel bona vel mala significantur, perlustrantur ne e'let, nec ne? Erat in culter ferreus & oblongus, manubrio eburneo, clavis anxis, aere Cyprio & capulo argenteo ornatus. Non enim licebat manibus contrectare viscera, quæ offensa polluerint sacris interciderent. Sed de his cultris & aliis victimariorum instrumentis quibus victimæ cædi, percuti, jugulari, matari, dissecari ac divisi folebant, supra dictum est.
units.tr: The table set for this action, that is, destined partly for the cutting and partly for the inspection of the victim, was called in Latin ara clabra, as Festus says, which I mentioned above. The priest or haruspex therefore, with a knife prepared for this purpose, tore out the viscera or entrails from the body of the slain victim, and these were carefully and attentively examined and probed, to see how each part was disposed and whether anything was missing; from this good or bad signs are indicated. They checked whether something was absent or not. The knife was iron and elongated, with an ivory handle, nails of bronze, Cyprian copper, and a silver hilt. For it was not permitted to handle the entrails with the hands, lest they be polluted by touch and become unfit for the sacred rites. But concerning these knives and the other instruments of the victim-slayers, by which the victims were accustomed to be struck, stabbed, cut at the throat, sprinkled, and dissected and divided, I have spoken above.

units.la: Secundum haec ergo divinationes et extorum inspectiones sacrificia et exta alia appellabat ...
units.tr: Accordingly, by these divinations and inspections of the entrails, they called sacrifices and other entrails...

units.la: Latinè Muta, in quibus nulla instant signa: alia Argua, quæ cospicuas & illustres notantur ... bebant: alij Regalia, apud Festum, quae potentibus inspe ratum bonorem pollicentur: privatis et humi oribus credit ates, filio familiae dominationem: a lia lustralia, quae praepinguia fuerant, eo quod lu ustralis, id est, quinquennalis bos ducitur esse perfecta aetatis; de quibus Poeta: Flexaque verba greges lustralia, exta.
units.tr: In Latin, muta, those in which no signs appear; others argua, which are marked as conspicuous and illustrious... others regalia, according to Festus, which promise an honour of rule to the powerful, and to private and humble persons the rule of a household over its sons; others lustralia, which had been very fat, because a lustralis, that is, a five-year-old ox, is considered to be of perfect age. Of these the poet says: "Flock of lustral entrails and words of divination."

units.la: Alia item piacularia: alia clivia: alia pestifera auspicia secundum illam divinationem appella- bant Piacularia quidem; quae sacrificantibus trifita portendebant: Clivia, quae aliquid fieri probant. Omnia enim difficilia clivia vocabant. Unde colivi loca ardua difficilia adiu. Pestifera, sicut dentes, cum cornua extis, aut caput in jecinore non fuisset; quo modo pestiferum fulgur dicebatur, quod mors exilium ve significaret: folebat, fasto teste.
units.tr: Others also were called piacularia, others clivia, others pestifera, as auspices in accordance with that divination. Piacularia were those which portended sorrows for those sacrificing; clivia those which proved that something was to be done, for they called all difficult things clivia, whence hard and difficult places are called colles. Pestifera were such as when the teeth, or the horns, or the head were not in the entrails or in the liver; in the same way a lightning bolt was called pestiferum because it signified death or exile, as Festus relates.

units.la: Et cum quidem sicebant haec divinationes Romani, ut et libri describerent confulen- tes, et erga in ipsis oraculorum custodiri publice, et in ea disciplina suos exercent a teneris curarint libri magnificatio. Ceperint autem moverint, nisi sacrificiis diligenter perluftratio et examinatus. Affici ium. Y similiter, notas, monitoribus eventorum subito seu consignari abiis Numinibus, quae adesfent, eorum vocata, et ritus spectarent, perfusissimum habebant.
units.tr: The Romans not only practised these divinations, but also had books describing them for those consulting, and kept the oracles themselves publicly, and from childhood they trained their sons in that discipline. They held that nothing could be moved or begun without diligent purification and examination of the sacrifices, and the prodigies and monsters of events, which were recorded and reported, and that the gods who were present should be summoned by name and their rites observed, as a most established practice.

units.la: Hanc item a Romulo primum fuerunt institui, ut auctor est Dionysius Halicarnassensis libro secundo. Primum autem haruspices omnes Etruscis fuerunt, in quorum patria haec disciplina manifesta viguit. Unde Cicero libro secundo de Legibus: Prodigia, portenta ad Hetrusos et Harufpices, si senatus jussit, deferunto. Et secundo de Divinatione: Vere rear inquit, in extis totam Etruriam desinere.
units.tr: This was also first instituted by Romulus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus witnesses in the second book. Now all the haruspices were originally Etruscans, in whose country this discipline flourished openly. Hence Cicero says in the second book of On the Laws: "Let prodigies and portents be reported to the Etruscans and haruspices, if the senate so orders." And in the second book of On Divination: "Truly, I think, in the entrails all Etruria is at an end."

units.la: Postea vero Senatus decrevit, ut Principum filii sex singulis Hetruriae populis in disciplina traderentur, teste Cicerone libro primo de Divinatione: id quod et Valerius Maximus libro primo confirmat, qui tamen non sex docet, verum decem Principum filios mitti solitos in Hetruriam. Verba ejus haec sunt: Tantum autem fundum Antiquis non solum observandae, sed et in amplificandae, vel gloria fuit, ut et florentissima, tum etiam opulentissima civitate decem Principum filii Senatusconsulto singulis Hetruriae populis percipiendae sacrorum disciplinae tanquam tradeantur. Ho. in loco, ut et apud Ciceronem, non sex vel decem, sed duodecim, Glareanus legendum censet: ut, cum duodecim Hetruriae populi fuerint, singulis unus fuerit traditus. Huc Lex Illa Ciceronis pertinet: Hetruriae principes disciplinam doceto.
units.tr: Afterwards the Senate decreed that the sons of the chief men should be taught the discipline, six from each of the peoples of Etruria, as Cicero witnesses in the first book of On Divination. Valerius Maximus in the first book confirms this, though he does not teach six but says that ten sons of chief men were usually sent into Etruria. His words are: "So great was the honour and glory the ancients took not only in observing but also in extending their sacred rites, that even when the state was most flourishing and wealthy, the sons of ten chief men were handed over by senatorial decree, one to each people of Etruria, to learn the discipline of the sacred rites." Glareanus thinks that in this place, as also in Cicero, one should read not six or ten but twelve, so that, since there were twelve peoples of Etruria, one was handed over from each. To this belongs that law of Cicero: "Let the chiefs of Etruria teach the discipline."

units.la: Hi aruspicum igitur munus erat victimas in ara inspicere considerare, et exitus futura, arte Dea monum divinare. Considerabant autem haruspices aut bobias ipsas, priusquam jugularetur: aut e in n. possiquam dissecta erant, exta; de quo officio bos in loco agimus: aut flammam, quae ex incensis et ordinatis evolabat victimis, atq; etiam fumum: aut farinam et farinae materiam, ex quibus libi percipiebantur et mole: aut thus, quod adolebatur, aut vina et aquas. Haec in genere.
units.tr: The office of these haruspices, then, was to inspect and consider the victims on the altar, and to foretell outcomes by an art given by the gods. The haruspices considered either the ox itself before it was struck down, or the entrails after they had been dissected, a duty about which we speak in its place; or the flame that rose from the victims set alight and arranged, and also the smoke; or the meal and the material of the meal, from which the cakes were offered; or the incense that was burnt, or the wines and waters. These are the general points.

units.la: NUNC speciatim de extorum iuspectione et divinatione, quae quidem huius loci propria est, quaedam addamus ex Peucero, qui tum in genere de omnibus Divinationum generibus, tum de Extispicio et extispicum divinatione sic scripsit: In dissectis jam victimis ex signis salubribus, nexo, ex habitu colore extorum et fibrarum, defectu aliquarum particularum in praecipuis organis, aut praeter naturam adnatus, collectu vel ex humorum affluxu absccessibus, sumebant conjecturas de eventum conditione, et in quam partem Numen, cui fiebat sacrificium, inclinatum esset ac propenderet: ut quando exta, aut etiam quid vis aliud e manibus exciderat, id negocium et triste videbatur. Unde Plutarchus in Crasso: ... Haec sunt, quae Romani caduca auspicia vocabant. Festus: Caduca auspicia dicunt, cum aliquid in templo excidit, veluti virga e manu: ut virga Flaminis Commentacu- lum dicta.
units.tr: Now, more specifically, on the inspection and divination of entrails, which is the proper subject of this place, let us add some points from Peucer. He wrote both in general about all kinds of divination and about extispicy and the divining of entrails as follows: "When the victims had been cut open, they drew conjectures about the outcome from the favourable signs, the connection, the appearance and colour of the entrails and fibres, from the lack of some small part of the principal organs, or from a growth beyond the natural form, from a gathering or accumulation of humours, or from abscesses. They judged the state of the outcome, and in which direction the deity to whom the sacrifice was offered was inclined and leaning. If the entrails, or indeed anything else, slipped from the hands, that matter seemed ominous and sad." Hence Plutarch in the Life of Crassus: "These are what the Romans called falling omens." Festus: "They speak of falling omens when something falls in a temple, such as a rod from the hand, whence the rod of the flamen is called the commentaculum."

units.la: Inter visera autem sive exta, quoniam praecipuum illius videbatur Epar, ab eorum extorum contemplatione incboabant: unde etiam uniuersa extorum inspectio et divinatio hepatoscopia fuit a, pellata.
units.tr: Among the viscera, or entrails, the liver seemed the chief, so they began their observation from the examination of the entrails. Hence the whole inspection and divination of the entrails was called hepatoscopy.

units.la: Sillud grata et nativa purpura ruberet nulla, effet contaminatum labe vel si caput jecinoris duplicatum vel aut geminum jecur reperiretur: vel si extremae fibrae, versus interiora, replicatae, ac convolutae viderentur hae eximiae felicitatis argumenta certissima dare et magnas accessiones, poteritae amplificationem, prolationem finem, triumphos, summa dignitatis fastigia, designare augurabantur: Cōstitutis etiam in epate geminis capitibus, unum bofti, alterū ꝓ, so ea- ius gratiam instituebatur divinatio, destinabat: alterum eorum, si vel corrugatum emarcuisset, vel colorem, babitumq; suum quo ⁊ vs modo mutasset, ruinam aut inclinationem, ad versa, omnia minitari: si velut inflatum atq; distensum intumuisset & florido enituisset colore moitu, alacri & continuo micasset, victoriam certam spondere, & successus felicissimos illi putabatur, cujus nomine sedebatur. Lucanus exta Cæsarem victorem renunciasse contra Pompeium, annotat ita:
units.tr: If the caul was not reddened with its natural, pleasing purple, or was stained with a blemish; or if the head of the liver appeared doubled, or the liver was found to be double; or if the outermost fibres were seen to be folded back and curled toward the inside, they took these as very certain signs of extraordinary good fortune, and they foretold great increases, the growth of power, the extension of territory, triumphs, and the highest peaks of dignity. When there were two heads on the liver, the divination was made by the good omen of the one for whom it was undertaken, and the other head was assigned to the opposing side. If that head shrank and withered, or changed its colour and condition in any way, they believed it threatened ruin or decline and every kind of disaster. But if it swelled as though inflated and stretched, grew bright with a flourishing colour, and quivered with a lively and continuous motion, they believed it promised certain victory and the most fortunate success to the man in whose name the sacrifice was being made. Lucan records that the entrails announced Caesar as victor over Pompey, in these words:

units.la: Quodq; nefas nullo impune apparuit extis.
units.tr: And that the crime, committed by no one, showed itself unpunished in the entrails.

units.la: Ecce videt capiti fibrarum increscere molem
units.tr: Behold, the seer sees the mass of the fibres growing on one head,

units.la: Alterius capius pars ægra & martida pendet
units.tr: part of the other head hangs sick and withered,

units.la: Pars micat, & celeri venas movet improba pulsu
units.tr: part gleams, and the wicked vein stirs with a quick pulse.

units.la: Si vero aut obsitum vlceribus pustulisve aut livore deforme aut duritie contractū corrugatumve abscissibus aut humoribus vitiosis imbutum asset, atq; obstructum: vel si in sua non conspiceretur sede, sed aut a præcordiis avulsum subsedesset, aut permutatis sedibus lienis locum occupasset, illo in dexteram regionem translato aut procidisset in anteriora: vel si tentabuisset, aut aliquain gracilius justo aridiusq; appareret: vel si totum defuisset, aut solo caruisset capite: denique si incir coquendū, purulenta inquinaretur sanie: aut adeum exaresceret modū, ut inter exta non eminēret, aut colliquatum dissoluereturq; in pultem: hæc piacularia esse funestaq; adeo persuasum erat, ut factus accidere, atq; ab his demonstratū erat, ubi posse affirmaretur. Anno Vrbis 6:6 Catoni Cæjuli immolanti exta emarcuerunt & caput jecinoris evanuit. Cajo principi & M. Marcelliose cur subico extabuisse annotatum est. Lucilio Luco inter exta caput jecinoris non in ventum est: Quare prælio perjisse existimatus est.
units.tr: But if the liver was covered with sores or pustules, or was disfigured by a livid colour, or was contracted and wrinkled by hardness, or was filled with diseased humours and blocked; or if it was not seen in its proper place but had been torn from the diaphragm and had sunk down, or had taken the place of the spleen with the two organs exchanging positions, the spleen having moved to the right side, or had fallen forward; or if it appeared thinner or drier than is right, or if it lacked its whole substance or was without its head altogether; finally, if it was polluted with pus-like matter when it was being cooked, or dried up to such an extent that it did not stand out among the entrails, or melted and dissolved into a mash: they were firmly persuaded that these signs were ominous and deadly, and that they came about as they were predicted, wherever they were said to portend something. In the year of the city 566, when Cato Caelius was sacrificing, his entrails withered and the head of the liver vanished. It is recorded that the entrails of the emperor Gaius and of Marcus Marcellus wasted away. In the case of Lucilius Lucus, no head of the liver was found among the entrails; for this reason he was thought to have perished in battle.

units.la: A jecinore Cor inspiciebant: idsi palpitaret, aut exiliret aut flaccesceret, aut minus justo appareret, aut omni destitueretur pinguedine, aut toi risset in rugas, aut inter exta omnino non vi-ere tur, existit, direq; atq; infeste fortune omina præbebat. Nam & Julio Cæsari, quo die purpurea veste processit, & a conjuratis interfectus est, cor bis in opimis bobus defecit, & Cajo Mario, Vi ca inmolanti. Pertinaci Cæsari utriusq; viscerus epatis, et cordis defectus in ea, quam ante morte mallari iussit, victima interitū portendit. In ara Veneris Paphie, ubi pro igne & præcibus altaria adolebantur tercifima semper fibras hadorum fidesest habita. Si vero aut solico grendium, aut pulmam ginoruim, & humellum nec flaceidum , nec ex ariditate implica nugasq; cotractum in ventretur, aut si in summa basi Largiore pinguedine vestium foret, aut abriperetur ab aquila propitios hæc Deos, & cæpcn annuentes flatusq; secundos aspiraturos confirmabant.
units.tr: From the liver they inspected the heart. If it throbbed, or leapt or went flabby, or appeared smaller than it should, or was deprived of all its fat, or was wrinkled into folds, or was not seen among the entrails at all, this indicated and offered omens of dire and disastrous fortune. For in the case of Julius Caesar, on the day he came forth in a purple robe and was killed by the conspirators, the heart was missing twice in fat oxen; and in the case of Gaius Marius, when he was sacrificing... The Emperor Pertinax, in the victim which he ordered to be sacrificed before his death, had a defect of the heart and of both lobes of the liver, which foretold his destruction. On the altar of Paphian Venus, where the altars were burnt with fire and prayers, the fibres of kids were always held most trustworthy. But if the heart was found to be a little larger, or the lungs of the heart full, and the small lobe neither flaccid nor shrivelled into a dry knot, or if in the upper part there was more fat than usual, or if an eagle snatched it away, they affirmed that these gods were favourable, would grant assent, and would breathe prosperous winds.

units.la: Cordeexploratō ad fellis, lienis, pulmonum, & membranaru viscera ambientiū considerarionē se vertebat. Si υδσ ψ ολ ⁊ dyo geminam, qualē Augusto exhibita ferunt, eodem, quæ Antonii profligaret ad Actiū, aut topiosa bile turgentē atq; effluentē notassent, atria & felici a prelia expectabat. Si suo loto positum lienē sine pustulis duritie torrugatione sineq; alieno colore cospex ifsent, felicia propositæ rei ominabatur.
units.tr: Once the heart had been examined, they turned their attention to the gall, the spleen, the lungs and the membranes surrounding the viscera. If they had noticed the gall swollen and overflowing with abundant bile, such as they report appeared for Augustus and for Antony's defeat at Actium, they expected victory and successful battles. If they saw the spleen lying in its proper place, without pustules, hardness, wrinkling or an unnatural colour, they prophesied a favourable outcome for the matter in hand.

units.la: Si contra in dextrum lien vergeret, aut antrorsum propenderet, aut reperet deorsum, anū notas alienas a natura sua habuerat. Si exta ex sacrificatusi manibus decidissent: si viscera aut eruore saduis aspersa, aut liquido sedata colore, aut macula variata forent, superiore enim ruptum alicubi hiaret, aut sanguine suffusum esset, si phlystiemis & ampulla, pure aut salsi lagine referti scatrent intestina, aut lacerata essent minus, vel rupta at divulsa: Si dracones inter exta serperent, Si scaterent viscera, aut patrilagiñem redolerent, fatalium hæc et jam imminencium malorum indicia erant, quæ pro condicione earum rerum, de quibus vistumæ consulebantur, vates interpretabantur.
units.tr: If, on the other hand, the spleen leaned to the right, or hung forward, or sank downward, they took it to have marks foreign to its nature. If the entrails fell from the hands of the one sacrificing; if the viscera were sprinkled with blood or stained with a liquid colour or varied by a spot; if some part gaped as if broken on the upper side, or was suffused with blood; if the intestines were covered with blisters and bubbles filled with pus or salty fluid; if they were lacerated, or broken, or torn apart; if serpents crept among the entrails; if the viscera leapt or smelled of the stench of the grave, these were signs of deadly and impending evils, which the seers interpreted according to the nature of the matters about which they were consulted.

units.la: Pulmones bifidi incifiq; moras adferebant rebus et tunstationes simplices, & solidi, mora rupta tontinuabant rerum currituta & exetutionem maturabant, &c. Hæc Peucerus, quibus addit, quæ Plinius scribit lib. xi, cap. 37. inquiens: In corde summo pinguitudo est quædam lætitæ extu. Non semper hoc autem in parte extorum habitum ast. L. Posthumio Albino, rege sacrorum post, centesimam vicēsimam tertiam Olympiadem, cum rex Pyrrhus ex Italia discessisset, leor in excus aruspices aspicere cœperunt. Cæsari dictatori, quo die primum veste purpurea discessit, atque in sella aurea injecit sacrificatum bis in extis desuit. Vnde quaestio magna de divinatione argu- mentan. ment.mtibus,potuerunt sine ullo viscere hostia vivere,an ad tepus admiserit? Ide lib.28.cap.2, ubi similiter bujus extifpicinæ meminit: Vidimus,inquit,certus precationibus obfecraffe fummos magistratus. Et ne quid verborum prætereatur, aut præposterum dicatur, descripto præire aliquem,rursus,alium custodem dari,qui attendat; alium vero præponi,qui favertlinguas jubeat: tibicinem canere,ne quid aliud exaudiatur:utraq; memoria insigni,quoties ipsæ diræ obstrepentes nocuerint,quoties ve precatio erraverit,fi repente extis adimi capita, vel corda,vel geminari vi ftima stante accideriit. Hactenus Plinius.
units.tr: Lungs that were split or cut signified delays for affairs, and simple and solid ones signified obstruction; when the lungs were broken, they foretold the quick running and speedy execution of affairs, and so on. These are Peucer's words. He adds what Pliny writes in Book 11, chapter 37: "In the upper part of the heart there is a certain fatness of joy and exultation. This is not always found in that part of the entrails." Under Lucius Posthumius Albinus, king of sacred rites, in the 123rd Olympiad, after King Pyrrhus had left Italy, the haruspices began to inspect the heart in the victims. For Caesar the dictator, on the day he first came forth in a purple robe and sat on a golden chair, the sacrificed victim lacked a heart twice in the entrails. Hence arises the great question about the arguments of divination: could victims live without any viscus, or did it admit a temporary absence? The same author, in Book 28, chapter 2, where he similarly mentions this extispicy, says: "We have seen the highest magistrates beseech with prayers, and, lest anything of the words be omitted or said out of order, one was appointed to go before and read the written text, another was assigned as a guard to watch, and another was placed in front to order the tongues to be silent, while a flute-player played so that nothing else might be heard. Both of these were remarkable memorials, whenever the ill omens themselves, by their clamour, had interfered, or whenever the prayer had gone wrong, or if suddenly the heads or hearts were taken from the entrails, or the victim was found to have two of them, while the victim was standing." Thus far Pliny.

units.la: NEC vero animalium tantum brutorum, sed hominum quoq; maƈtatorum maximé capi?orum, visceribus atq; extis divinare fuerunt soliti,fagus fe velantes: inde ubi plaga infligebatur ab intestinis sub haruspice primùm ad hominis casum vaticinabatur: quæ aƈtio ab ὁ ὀνομάζεται Græcè su t appellata,qua & Heliogabalus,sesse Ælio Lampridio, & Iulianus Apostata,ut au tor est Eusebius lib.7.cap.9. Ecclesiastica historie, ut suerunt. Sed de humanis hostiis supra,quibus pauca hæc adderelibet,quæ ad illam languinis hostiarum aspersionem,de qua supra,pertinet. Arelatein Galliis,quæ Aera la:a Priscus fuit appellata,prope civitatè,quæ Rochette dicebatur,duæ columnæ erant extructæ & super eas ara imposita: ubi quotannis ad KL. Majas frequens undique populus humanas hostias pro sua solutate maƈtare consueverat. Itaque tres juvenes emtos anno toto saginabant, quos constituto die ad ipsam aram immolabant, victimarum sanguine circumstantem populum aspergentes. Quem ritum Trophimus, unus ex L X X I I. discipulus Christi,istuc ex Iudæa missus,sustulit,dorens,non cruore mortalium hominum,sed Christi sanguine debere aspergi: testis huius rei est Robertus Gaguinus lib.19.historiæ Francorum. Porphyrius quoq; huius si ϑεὸς τοῖς τοῖς ἐς ἀ sitenta: sæ ἔ si cos s's ἀ θ θ ἀ ἀ ἀ, sed est,per viscera hominum sugurari. Plura vide lib.ejus 2.
units.tr: Nor did they divine only from the entrails and viscera of brute animals, but also from those of men who were slaughtered, especially of captives; they were accustomed to foretell the fall of a man by a wound inflicted in the intestines under the haruspex. This practice is called by the Greeks by a name derived from the entrails; by it Heliogabalus, as Lampridius tells us, and Julian the Apostate, as Eusebius reports in Book 7, chapter 9 of his Ecclesiastical History, were accustomed to practise. But I have said above about human victims; I wish to add a few things here which pertain to that sprinkling of the blood of victims mentioned above. At Arles in Gaul, which was called Aelia Pricia by Priscus, near the city that was called Rochette, two columns were erected and an altar placed upon them. There, every year near the Kalends of May, the people from everywhere, in fulfilment of their vows for safety, were accustomed to slaughter human victims. Thus they fattened three young men bought for the whole year, and on an appointed day they sacrificed them at the altar itself, sprinkling the surrounding people with the blood of the victims. Trophimus, one of the seventy-two disciples of Christ, who had been sent there from Judaea, abolished this rite, teaching that the people should be sprinkled not with the blood of mortal men but with the blood of Christ. Robert Gaguin attests this in Book 19 of his History of the Franks. Porphyry also, in his work on the gods, says that by the entrails of men they performed divination; see more in his second book.

units.la: Hic adde populorum Indiæ Occidentalis,qui Cariines appellantur, immanem consuetudinem. Ii enim ad bella Chiappem,idolum suum,deferunt,siq; prufquam expeditionem suscipiunt, lesas humanas, victimas ex captivis maƈtantes pluribus sacrificiis litant, totumq;, ipsius simulacrum sanguine oblinentes carnes inter se ipsi epulantur. Hæc Benzo in historia novi orbis.
units.tr: Add here the monstrous custom of the peoples of the West Indies called Cariines. When they go to war, they carry Chiappe, their idol, with them. Before they undertake the expedition, they sacrifice human captives, slaughtering many of them as offerings and smearing the image itself with their blood. Then they feast among themselves on the flesh. Benzo reports this in his history of the New World.

units.la: Nunc ut ad extorum inspeƈtionem redeamus adjungam hic quædam ex Ciceronis libris de Divinatione depromta,quæ ad superiora illa illustranda & confirmanda nou parum faciunt: Quid sissum,inquit,quid sibra valeat accipiat:quæ causa sit nescio. Atq; horum quidem vita plena est. Extis enim omnes feré muntur. Exhis verbis constat, extispicium Ciceronis ætate valde fuisse celebratum. Idem: Nihil feré quondam majoris rei,nisi auspi- cato,ne priv atim quidem gerebatur: quod etiam nunc nuptiarum auspices declarant,qui re amissa,nomen tantùm tenent. Namuc ut extis, quanquam idipsum aliquanto minus, quam clim sicium avibus magnæ res impertiri solebant. Idem: Etrusci autem,quod religione imbuti studiosius & srebrius bollias immolabant, excorum cognitioni se maximè dediderunt. Idem: Omitto nostros, qui nihil in bellis sine extis agit, nihil sine auspiciis domi habent. Hinc Dionysius Halicarnasseus libro tertio de Metio Fufetio, Albanorum imperatore: ἡ ςἁ ἑ , πόσ ἐ ν, ἡ πρ ἡ ἡ ὁ ἡ ἔ. Extæ, de pugnæ exitu consulta nihil fausti portendere. Idem de eodem: α ἡ ἡ , ν ἡ ἡ ἐ ἁ ἐ ἡ , ἐ extasuper pugnam consulerem, & divi- na signa dissic hoc esse animad verterè. Idem: ἐ ν ἡ ἐ ἡ ἡ , ἡ ἐ, ἐ ἀ . Et quoties bellica pegimus sacrificia,exta nos pugnæ auspicari veiueriste.
units.tr: Now, to return to the inspection of entrails, I will add here some passages from Cicero's books On Divination. They help not a little to illustrate and confirm what was said above. "What the cleft and the fibre of the liver signify," he says, "he understands; what the cause is, I do not know. Indeed, the life of these people is full of such things, for almost everyone is ruled by entrails." From these words it is clear that augury from entrails was very widely practised in Cicero's day. Again: "In former times almost nothing of great importance was undertaken, even privately, without taking the auspices. Even now the augurs of marriages show this, who keep only the name when the thing itself has been lost. And, although it is now done to a somewhat lesser degree than of old, great affairs were once commonly referred to the entrails and to the birds." Again: "The Etruscans, because they were steeped in religion, sacrificed animals more eagerly and more diligently than others, and they devoted themselves especially to the study of entrails." Again: "I pass over our own people, who do nothing in war without entrails and have nothing at home without the auspices." Hence Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in the third book, on Metius Fufetius, the Alban commander, says that the entrails, when consulted about the outcome of the battle, portended nothing favourable. Of the same man he says that when he consulted the entrails about the battle and observed the divine signs, he took this to be the meaning. Again: whenever we have offered sacrifices for war, the entrails have shown us that we should begin the battle.

units.la: Porro & de eadem extispicina Cicero agit hæ quoque verbis: Ad hostiam deligendam posest dux esse vis quedam sentiens, quæ est toto corpue ipsam cum immolare velit, extorum fieri mutatio potest, ut aut absit aliquid, aut supersit : par vis enim momenti multa natura aut affingit, aut mutat , aut detrahit:quod ne dubitare possimus,maxime est argumento,quod paullo ante interitum Cæsaris contigit: qui cum immolaret illo die,quo primo in sella aurea sedit, & cum purpurea veste processit,in extis bovis opimi cor non fuit. Num igitur eenses ullum animal,quod sanguinem habeat,sine corde esse posse? Qua ille ei non vitate percussus cum Spurina diceret, timendum esse,ne & consilium,& vita deficeret: eorum enim rerum utrumq; a corde proficisci: postero die caput in jecore non fuit , quæ quidem illi portendebantur,a Diis immortalibus,ut videret interitum,non ut caveret. Cum igitur ea partes in extis non reperiuntur, fine quibus victima illa viuere nequisset: intelligendum est, in ipso tempore immolatio ne eas partes, quæ absint interiisse. Hallenus Cicero. Idem porrò & contra existimicinam, & alia diuinationum naturalium & artificiosarum generra ropiosè disserit lib. 2. de Diuinatione: cuius verba quia huius loco cõ venientissima sunt, eumq; summopere illustrant, quippe ab augure ipso, & in disciplina hac exercitatissimo Cicerone videliceet profecta, integra inserere placuit. Vt igitur ordiar, initiū, ab baruspicina, quam ego Reipub. causa, communisq; religionis colendam esse cen- seo: sed solū sumus: liceat verum exquirere sine invidia, mihi præsertim de plerisq; dubitanti: inspi- ciamus, si placet, exta primum. Persuaderi igitur cuiquā potest, ea quæ significari dicuntur extis, cognita esse ab baruspicibus obseruatione ecquam diuturna istia fuit? aut quam longinquo tempore obseruari potuit? aut quomodo est collata inter ipsos, quæ pars inimici, quæ pars familiaris esset, quod issum periculum, quod compodum aliquod ossenderet? Anhæc inter se ha- ri spicis Etrusci, Elij, Ægyptij, Pœni contulerunt? Aliosenim alio more videmus exta interpretari, nec esse unam omnium disciplinam. Et certè, si est in extis aliqua vis, quæ declaret futurinecesse est, eam aut cum rerum natura esse conjunctam, aut conformari quodam modo numeni deorum. Atqui diuina cum rerū natura tanta, tamq; præclara in omnes partes, motusq; diffusa, quid habere potest commune, non dicam gallinaceum sel (sunt enim, qui hæc arguissima exta esse dicant) sed tauri opimi iecur, aut cor, aut pulmo, quid habet naturale, quod declarare possit, quid suturum sit? Democritus tamen non inscite nugatur, ut Physicus: quo genere nihil arrogantius: Quod est ante pedes, nemo spectat: cœli scrutantur plagas. Verum u tamen habitus extorum, & colore declarari censet, hoc duntaxat, pabuli genus, & earum rerum, quas terra procreet, vel vbertatem vel tenuitatem: salubritatem etiam aut pestilentiam extis significari putat, O mortalem beatum! cui certo scioludum nunquam desuisse. Huccine hominem tantis delectatum esse singit, ut non videret, tum futurum id verisimile, si omnium pecudum extra eodem tempore in eundem habitum se, coloremq; conuerterent? Sed si eadem hora aliæ pecudis iecur nitidum, atq; plenum esset, aliæ borridum exile: quid est quod declarari possit habitu extorum, & colere? an hoc ejusdem modi est, quale Phereycedeum illud, quod est ante distum? qui cum aquam vidisset ex puteo haustam, terræ motum dixit futurum. Parum, credo, imprudenter, quod cum factus essent motus, dicere audent quæ vis id efficerit: etiamne futurum esse, aquæ tugus colore præsentium? multa istiusmodi dicuntur in scholis: sed credere omnia vide, ne non sit necesse. Verum sint sane ista Democritea vera. Quando nos ea extis exquirimus? aut quando aliquid ejusmodi ab baruspicis inspectis extis audiuimus ab aqua, aut ab igne pericula monent: tum hæ diuates, tum damna denuntiant, sissum familiare, & vitalit tractant: caput ieiore ex omni parte diligentissimè confederant: si vero id non est in ventu, nihil putant accidere potuisse tristius.
