Hæc obseruari certe non potuerunt, ut supra docui. Sunt igitur artis in venta, non vetustatis, si est ars ulla rerum incognitarū. Cum rerum autem natura quam cognationem habent? quæ ut uno consensu junctæ sit, & continens. quod video Phy sicis placuisse, siq; maxime qui omni, quod esset, unum esse dixerunt: quid habere mundus potest cum thesaurisinventione conjunctum? Si enim extis pecuniæ amplificatio mibi ostenditur, idq; sit natura: primo extra sunt coniunctæ mundo, deinde meum lucrum natura rerum continetur. Non ne pudet physicos hæc dicere? ut enim iam sit aliqua in natura rerum cognatio, quam esse cõ- edo: multa enim Stoici colligunt: nam & musculorum secuscula bruma dicuntur augeri, & pulenum aridum florescere ipso brumali die, & inflatas rumpi vesiculas, & semina malorū, quæ in hu mediis inclusa sint, in contrarias partes se vertere: jam nervos in sidibus aliis pulsis, resonare aliis ostreusq; & tonchiliis omnibus contingere, ut cum luna crescant pariter, pariterq; decrescanturboresq; ut hyemali tempore, cum luna simul senescentes, quia tum exsiccatæ sint, tempestiui cadi putentur. Quid de fretu, aussde marinis astibus plura dicam? quorsum accessus & recessus lunæ motu gubernantur. Sexcenta licet einsmodi proferri, ut distuntum rerum cognatio naturalis appareat. Demus hoc: nihil enim huic disputationi ad versatur. Num etiam, si issum cuiusdammodi fueris in jecore, lucrum ostendisset? qua ex cognatione naturæ, & quasi concentu, atq; consensu, quam συμπάθειαν Græce appellant, conuenire potest. sum
units.tr: Cicero also treats of this same entrail-divination in the following words: "In choosing the victim, the leader may be guided by some sense of what the whole body wishes when it is about to be sacrificed. Yet the entrails may change, so that something is either missing or left over. For nature either adds, or alters, or takes away a great deal of such matter of equal significance. That we cannot doubt this is shown above all by what happened shortly before the death of Caesar. On the day when he first sat in the golden chair and came forward in a purple robe, he offered a sacrifice, and in the entrails of a fat ox there was no heart. Can any animal that has blood, then, be without a heart? Struck by this, though he did not heed it, he was told by Spurinna that he must beware lest both his counsel and his life should fail, since both of these come from the heart. On the next day the liver had no head. These portents were indeed being shown to him by the immortal gods, so that he might see his death, not so that he might avoid it. Since, then, those parts are not found in the entrails, without which that victim could not have lived, we must understand that at the very time of the sacrifice those parts which are missing had perished." So far Cicero. Cicero also argues at length, in the second book On Divination, against this kind of augury and against other kinds of natural and artificial divination. Since his words are most fitting here and throw great light on the matter, and since they come from Cicero himself, an augur and a thorough practitioner of this discipline, I have decided to insert them in full. To begin, then, with the entrail-inspection, which I think should be cultivated for the sake of the commonwealth and of common religion, though I am only a sceptic, I may freely seek the truth without ill will, especially as I doubt most of these matters. Let us examine the entrails first, if you please. Can anyone be persuaded that what is said to be signified by the entrails was known to the diviners through observation? How long was this practice? Over what long period could it have been observed? How was it compared among them, which part indicates an enemy and which a friend, what danger each shows, and what advantage? Have the Etruscan, Elian, Egyptian and Carthaginian diviners ever compared their findings with one another? For we see that different peoples interpret the entrails in different ways, and there is not one single discipline for all. Indeed, if there is in the entrails some power that declares what is to come, it must either be bound up with the nature of things or be shaped in some way by the will of the gods. But what has the divine nature, so great and so splendid, so spread out and moving in every direction, in common with the entrails of a chicken (for some say these are the most certain entrails), or with the liver, heart or lung of a fat bull? What is there in these that is natural and could show what will happen? Democritus, however, talks not foolishly as a natural philosopher, though no kind of talk is more arrogant than that: 'No one looks at what is before his feet; they search the regions of the heavens.' Yet he thinks that the condition and colour of the entrails indicate only the kind of fodder, and whether the earth produces abundance or scarcity of such things; he also thinks that the entrails signify health or pestilence. O happy mortal, who thinks he has surely learned what he never wanted to know! Are we to imagine that a man so delighted by such things did not see that this would be likely to happen only if all the entrails of all the cattle at the same time changed into the same condition and colour? But if at the same hour one animal's liver was bright and full, and another's rough and thin, what could be shown by the condition and colour of the entrails? Is this of the same kind as the well-known saying of Pherecydes, who, when he saw water drawn from a well, declared that an earthquake would come? I suppose it is rather foolish, when earthquakes have occurred, for them to dare to say what force produced them, but to say that they will come from the colour of the water in the well? Many such things are said in the schools, but to believe them all is to see that there is no need for it. Yet let us grant that Democritus's views are true. When do we seek these things from the entrails? When has any such thing been heard from diviners who inspected the entrails? Water and fire give warnings of danger, and then these very diviners announce gains and losses, and they handle the matters of the household and of life; they examine the liver and the head of the victim on every side with the greatest care. But if nothing of this appears, they think nothing more disastrous could have happened. These things certainly could not have been observed, as I have shown above. Therefore this is an art of invention, not of antiquity, if there is any art at all in what is unknown. But what kinship do these things have with the nature of things? If the world is joined together in one harmony and is one whole, as I see the physicists have held, especially those who said that all that exists is one, what can the world have in common with the discovery of treasure? For if an increase of money is shown to me by the entrails, and this is by nature, then first the entrails are joined to the world, and then my gain is contained in the nature of things. Are the physicists not ashamed to say these things? For even if some natural kinship exists among things, as I grant there is (for the Stoics gather many examples: they say that the muscles of shellfish grow in the midwinter, that the dry pulse blossoms on the very day of the winter solstice, that bladders swell and burst, and that the seeds of apples enclosed in the middle turn towards opposite parts; that strings sound in sympathy when others are plucked, and that oysters and all shellfish are affected by the moon, growing and waning with it; and that trees, when they are dried out in winter as the moon wanes, are thought to be fit for felling), what more shall I say of the sea and the tides, which are governed by the motion of the moon in its approach and retreat? Countless such examples could be offered to show a natural kinship among things. Let us grant this, for it does nothing to oppose this argument. But would it even show gain if there were a cleft in the liver? By what kinship of nature, what sort of harmony and agreement, which the Greeks call sympathy, could this be brought together? Democritus, as a physicist, may be right, and he surpasses all in boldness. But how does the cleft of a liver have to do with my little profit, or my little quest with heaven, earth and the nature of things? Grant this, if you like; even if I weaken my case by doing so, I will concede that there is no agreement at all between the entrails and nature. But I still concede this much, which comes next, that whoever wishes to obtain something, if...

units.la: Democritus: vt Physicus est, & super crates. fissum jecoris cum lucello meo, aut meus quæsticulus cum cælo,terra,rerumq; natura? conceda hoc ipsum,si vis,setsi magnan iacturam causæ fecero,si nulla esse conuenientiam cum extis naturæ, concessero:sed tamen eo concedo,quiè venit,ut is,qui impetrhre velit,si venientem hostiam rebus suis immolent? hoc erat,quod ego non rebar posse dissolui.
units.tr: Democritus: as a natural philosopher, and on the crates. Shall I split a liver with my little knife, or my little question with heaven, earth, and the nature of things? Grant me this, if you like; and even if I do great damage to my cause by conceding that there is no agreement between the entrails and the nature of things, yet I concede this: that it comes about that a man who wishes to obtain something, if they sacrifice to him a victim that is coming up. This was what I did not think could be dissolved.

units.la: Atqui quàm festiuè dissoluitur. Pudet me non tui quidem,cuius etiam memoriam admiror; sed Chrysippi, Antipatri, Posidonii,qui idem istuc quidem dicunt,quod est diẽtum a te,ad hostiam diligendam ducem esse vim quandam sentientem atq; diuinam,quæ toto confusa mundo fit. Illud vero multò etiam melius,quod & a te vsurpatum est, & dicitur ab illis: cum immolare quispiam velit,tum fieri extorum mutationem,ut aut absit aliquid,aut supersit: Deorum enim numini parère omnia. Hæc mihi iam crede, ne anicula quidem existimant. An censes,eundum vitulum si alius delegerit,sine capite jecur in seiturum; si alius,cum capite? hæc decessio capitu,aut accessio subitò nostri fieri potest,ut se extra ad immolantis fortunam accommodent? non perspicitis aleam quandã iefse hostiis deligendis,præsertim cum res ipsa doceat? cum enim tristissima exta sine capite fuerant,quibus nihil videtur esse diriùs: proxima hostia sæpe litatur pulcherrimè. Vbi ille minæ superiorum extorum? aut quæ tam subito deorum tanta facta est plaratio? Sed affers,in tauri opimi extis immolante Cæsare cor non fuisse: id quia nõ potuerit accidere, ut jine corde victima illa viveret, judicandum esse tum interisse cor,cum immolaretur. Qui fit,ut alterum intelligas, sine corde non potuisse bovem vivere: alterum non videas,cor subito non potuisse nescio quo a volare? Ego enim possum vel nescire, quæ vis sit cordis ad vivendum; vel suspicari,contactu aliquo morbo boves exile,& exiguum & vetum eor,& dissimile cordis fuisse. Tu vero quid habes,quare putes,si paullo ante cor fuerit in tauro opimo,subito id in ipsa immolatione interiisse? an, quod aspexit vestitu purpureo,excordem Cæsarem,ipse corde priuatus est? urbem philosophiæ,mihi crede,proditus,dum castella defenditur. Nam dum haruspicinam veram esse vultis, physiologiam totam pervertitis. Caput est in jecore,cor in extis: jam abscedet,simul ac molam, & vinum insperseris. Deus id eripiet,vis aliqua conficiet,aut exedet. Non ergo omnium interitus atq; obitus natura consistet; & erit aliquid, quod aut ex nihilo oriatur, aut in nihilum subito occidat. Quis hoc p'ysi⸗ dixit unquam? haruspices dicunt. Hiu igitur,quàm physicos,potius credendū existimas? quid-sum plurib. Diis immolatur,qui tandé e venit,ut literæ alıu,alius non literæ? quæ autè inconst antia Deorum e. ut primus minentur exist,bene promittant secundis? aut tanta inter eos dissensio,sæpe etiam inter proximos,ut Apollonis exta bona sint, Dianæ non bona? quid est tam perspicuum, quàm, cum fortuito hostiæ adducantur,talia cuiq; exta esse, qualis cuiq; obtigerit hostia? at enim id ipsum habet aliquid diuini, quæ cuiq; hostia obuingat, tanquam in fortibus quæ cui ducatur.
units.tr: But see how neatly it is dissolved. I am not ashamed of you, whose memory I even admire, but of Chrysippus, Antipater and Posidonius, who say the same thing you have said: that in choosing a victim there is a certain sentient and divine power, diffused through the whole world. That other point, which you too have used and which they also make, is far better still: when someone wishes to sacrifice, a change takes place in the entrails, so that something is either missing or left over, for all things obey the will of the gods. Believe me, I do not think even old women hold these views. Do you suppose that if another calf is chosen, the liver will be cut without its head, and if another, with its head? Can this removal or sudden addition of a head happen in our entrails, so that they conform to the fortune of the one sacrificing? Do you not see that there is a kind of gamble in the choice of victims, especially since the facts themselves show it? For when the entrails without a head were most dismal, and nothing seemed more ominous, the next victim has often been most beautifully accepted. Where then are the threats of the earlier entrails? Or what sudden reconciliation of the gods has taken place? But you object that when Caesar was sacrificing the entrails of a fat bull, there was no heart. You judge that the heart perished at the moment of sacrifice, because it could not happen that the victim lived without a heart. Why is it that you understand that an ox cannot live without a heart, but do not see that the heart could not suddenly fly off somewhere? For I may either not know what power the heart has for living, or suspect that by some contact with disease the heart of these oxen was small, meagre and worn, and unlike a proper heart. But what reason do you have for thinking that, if the heart was in the fat bull a little earlier, it suddenly perished in the very act of sacrifice? Or, because he looked at a purple-clad Caesar, has the heart itself been deprived of its own heart? Believe me, you betray the city of philosophy while you defend the outworks. For while you want haruspicy to be true, you overturn all of physiology. The head is in the liver, the heart is in the entrails; soon it will depart as soon as you have sprinkled the salt cake and wine. God will snatch it away, some force will destroy it, or consume it. Therefore the destruction and passing away of all things will not stand in nature; and something will arise out of nothing, or suddenly perish into nothing. Who ever said this as a natural philosopher? The haruspices say it. Do you think that they are to be believed rather than the physicists? Why say more? To many gods victims are sacrificed; why does it happen that the letters of one are different from those of another, and not letters at all? And what inconsistency is this among the gods, that the first should threaten, and the second promise good things? Or such great disagreement among them, often even among close relatives, that the entrails are good for Apollo but not good for Diana? What is so plain as this: when victims are brought up by chance, each man's entrails are such as the victim that happens to fall to him? But indeed, they say, there is something divine in this, that whichever victim meets each man, just as in the lots, whichever falls to whom.

units.la: Nox de fortibus. Quanquam tu quidè non hostiarum casum confirmas fortiû similitudine,sed infirmas sortes, collatione hostiarū. An,tum in Aequimelium misimus qui afferat agnum,quem immolemus,si mihi agnus affertur,qui habet exta rebus accommodata, & ad eum agnū non casu,sed dute Deo servus deducitur? Nam si casum quoq; ineo dicn esse,quasi fortem quandã cum Deorum voluntate conjunctam: dolee tantam Stoicos nostros Epicureiirridendi fui facultatem dedisse,non enim ignoras,quàm ista deridean. Et quidem illi facilius facere possunt: Deos enim ipsos joeandi caussa induxit Epicurus perluciðos,& perstabiles, & habitantes,tanquã inter duos luco s,sicinter duos mdos, pter metu ruinarum:eos, habere putat eàdē mēbra, quæ nos,nec ullu usum habere memorum. Ergo is circuitione quadam deos tollens,rectè non dubitat diuinationem tollere. Sed non,ut hic sibi constat, item Stoici:illius enim Deus nihil habens nec sui,nec alie vitegotii,non potest hominibus diuinationem impertire: vester autem Deus non potest imperti re,ut nihilo minus mundum reg et,& hominibus consulat. Cur igitur vos inducitis in eas captiones,quas nonnunquam expliteris? ita enim,cum magni properant,concludere solent.Si Di sunt, est diuinatio. Sunt autem Dii:est ergo Diuinatio. Multò est probabilius:non est autem diuinatio,non sunt ergo Dii. Vide,quam temerè committant,ut,si nulla sit diuinatio,nulli sint Dii:diuinatio enim perspicuè tollitur; Deos esse retinendum est. Atq; hæc extispicum diuinatione sublata,omnis haruspicina sublata est,ossenta enim sequuntur,& fulgura. Hactenus Cicero.
units.tr: Now on lots. Although you do not confirm the chance of the victims by the likeness of lots, but weaken the lots by comparing them with the victims. Do you suppose that when we send someone to Aequimelium to bring a lamb for us to sacrifice, if the lamb brought to me has entrails suited to the matter, and a servant is led to that lamb not by chance but by the design of God? For if you say that there is chance in this, as though it were a sort of lot joined with the will of the gods, then you have given our Stoics, I fear, a chance to be mocked by the Epicureans. For you know how they deride such things. And indeed they can do so more easily: for Epicurus introduced the gods themselves, for the sake of jest, as shining and steady and dwelling as if between two groves, or between two worlds, for fear of collapses. He thinks they have the same limbs as we do, and no use for them at all. So by this roundabout way he removes the gods, and rightly has no doubt that divination is removed too. But the Stoics do not agree with themselves in the same way: for the god of Epicurus, having no care of himself or any other business, cannot impart divination to men; but your God cannot impart it while still governing the world and taking thought for men. Why then do you lead yourselves into those traps which you sometimes unfold? For when they are in a great hurry, they are accustomed to conclude thus: If there are gods, there is divination; but there are gods; therefore there is divination. It is much more probable: but there is no divination, therefore there are no gods. See how rashly they commit themselves: if there is no divination, there are no gods, for divination is plainly removed; yet the gods must be retained. And with the divination of the haruspices removed, all haruspicy is removed, for bones and lightnings follow the entrails. So far Cicero.

units.la: Atq; hæc sint dicta de diuinatorio extorum in sacrificiis usu, quibus addi potest alius eorun-Y 3
units.tr: Let these things be said about the use of entrails in sacrifices for divination, to which another point may be added concerning these matters.
That no change occurs in the entrails.
That the Stoics remove divination.

units.la: Extorum usus in iuramentis. demusus in juramentus & foederibus publicis, cujus Dionysius Halicarnassensis semel atq; iterum manifestam facit mentionem, ut lib.5. ... ἐν οὖν τὸ ... Idem lib.7. ... Scanteseq; super exta in vestram & nepotum vestrorum perniciem juraslis. Vbi τομὴν exta vocat ... tia. Huc vero juradi mori videtur respondere mos ille jurandi Scythicus, de quo supra, qui sed ... pe... (text partly illegible).
units.tr: The use of entrails in oaths. Dionysius of Halicarnassus makes clear mention of their use in oaths and public covenants, once and again, as in book 5. Again in book 7: "You swore over the entrails to the destruction of yourselves and your descendants." There he calls the cut-up portions "entrails". To this oath-taking the Scythian custom of swearing, of which I spoke above, seems to correspond (the rest is partly illegible).

units.la: ARRO ... nteexta cadi, aperiri, undari, e velli, inspici, cōsuli, ita coqui quoq; solebant, idq; ... iam. Aliter enim ver: asfab...ucuralia vero, ut arietis non verū assari, sed in olla elixari solebant. Ad priorem modum pertinent illa Poetarum: ut O vidu primo Fastorum:
units.tr: ... the entrails were cut, opened, washed, plucked, inspected, and consulted; in the same way they were also accustomed to cook them, and this ... already. For the other way of cooking was one thing; but the entrails of a ram were not roasted on a spit, but were boiled in a pot. To the first method belong those lines of the poets, as Ovid in the first book of the Fasti:

units.la: Vt redut, verubus flridentia detrahit exta.
units.tr: As he draws the entrails, quivering, off the spits.
And Virgil in the second book of the Aeneid:

units.la: Pinguia in verubus torrebimus exta columnis, id est, Corylo factis, ut Servius interpretatur.
units.tr: We will roast the fat entrails on spits of hazel, that is, made of hazel wood, as Servius explains.

units.la: Quae autem exta in ollis coqui & elixari consuebant, ea Aulicoqua, sive Aulicocia, teste Festo, fuerunt dicta. Aulas, inquit, Antiqui dicebant, quas nunc dicimus Ollas, quia nullam litteram geminabant. Item Aulicoqua, sive, ut est in aliis libris, Aulicocia exta, quae in aulis coquebantur, dicebant, id est, elixa. Hujusmodi olla, aula extarus a Plauto appellatur in Rudente: Non hercle, adolescens, jam hos dies complusculos Quenquam istic vidi sacrificare, neq; poteis Clam nie esse, si qui sacrificant, semper petunt Aqua ims, bus, aut igneri, aut ascula, aut cultrum, aut veru, Aut aulam extaren (in qua exta coquebatur) aut aliquid: quid verbis opus est? Venes: puri vi vasa & purum non mihi, etc.
units.tr: The entrails that were accustomed to be cooked and boiled in pots were called aulicoqua, or aulicocia, according to Festus. He says: "The ancients called aulae what we now call ollae (pots), because they doubled no letter." Likewise, the entrails that were cooked in aulae, or, as it is in other books, aulicocia, were called "boiled". A pot of this kind is called by Plautus an aula for the entrails, in the Rudens: "No, by Hercules, young man, I have not seen anyone sacrificing here these last few days, and you cannot be unaware of it. If people sacrifice, they always ask for water, fire, a knife, a spit, or the aula for the entrails (in which the entrails are cooked), or something else. What need is there of words? Come, bring the pure vessels, and not ... for me," and so on.

units.la: Natum est hinc proverbium, Coctia numerosissimus exta, de quo vide Erasmum in Adagiis. Ac olla istius sacrificialis pulcherrimam videre licet in eodem Guilhelmi de Thoul libro, quae saepius cita vi.
units.tr: From this comes the proverb "Coctia numerosissimus exta", about which see Erasmus in the Adages. And a very fine pot of this sacrificial kind may be seen in the same book by Guillelmus de Thoul, which is often cited.

units.la: Veli tru tame, quod hic quoq; notandum, Martis femicruda reddi cosuevit: quoniam ibi, ut scribit Suetonius, cum Octavius Mart. ... vinam faceret, nūciaca repetiebatur ... ta, ... Quapropter publico decreto Velitris cavitum est, ut in posterum similī modo Martis exta redderentur. Arnobius, Deus modo ajat, modo cruda, modo femicruda, et jam coctae apponerunt. Idem, Cum, inquit, Romulo Pompilio, regnantib. percocta plane ac madida cremarentur. Dis exta, nonne Rege sub Tullio femicruda capitulum, et le...
units.tr: Here too it must be noted that the entrails of Mars were customarily returned half-raw at Velitrae, since there, as Suetonius writes, when Octavius was performing a sacrifice to Mars, the entrails were taken back ... Therefore by public decree it was provided at Velitrae that in future the entrails of Mars should be returned in the same way. Arnobius: "God," he says, "now says the entrails are raw, now half-raw, and now they have set them before him cooked." The same author: "When Romulus and Pompilius were reigning, they burned the entrails thoroughly cooked and soaked; under King Tullus the entrails were returned half-raw ..."

units.la: Exta porro cocta profecabant, ex quo exta dicta, ... Livius lib.5. Infernur huic loco fabula, Immulante Rege, Vejentium vocem haruspicis dicentis, qui ejus hostiae exta profecuisset, et vitulo riam dari, ea auditam. Ovidius: Sic ubi ... vit profecta sub aethere ponit.
units.tr: Cooked entrails they used to cut up (profecare), which is why the entrails are called exta. Livy, book 5. There is a fable inserted at this point: while the king was sacrificing, a voice was heard from the Veientine haruspex, saying that the man who had cut up the entrails of that victim should be given a calf. Ovid: "So when ... placed the cut-up entrails under the open sky."

units.la: Plautus in Phaenulo: Quoniam litare nequeo, abii illinc illico Iratus vetui exta proficarier, Neq; ea spicere (inspicere) volui, quoniam illa non bona, Haruspex dixit.
units.tr: Plautus in Phaenulus: "Since I cannot get a favourable sacrifice, I went away from there at once, angry. I ordered the entrails to be cut up, and I did not want to inspect them, since the haruspex said they were not good."

units.la: Et paullo post: Condigne haruspex, non homo tri obuli, Omnibus in exitu ajebat portendi mihi Malum daminum, & Deos esse iratos mihi:
units.tr: A little later: "Worthy of him, the haruspex, no man worth three obols! He said that at every exit a ruinous disaster was portended for me, and that the gods were angry with me."

units.la: In quae verba fie Lambinus: Exta cocta profecabat Veteres, ex quo profecta dicta. Nonius profecta exta, quae aru dantur ex fibris pecudum dissecta, generum neutri. Lucinius Macer:
units.tr: On these words Lambinus says: "The ancients cut up cooked entrails, and from this they were called profecta." Nonius: profecta exta are the entrails which are given at the altar, cut from the fibres of cattle; the neuter plural. Lucinius Macer:

units.la: Exta non semper percocta, sed semicruda reddita. —Vulcani tosta vapore
units.tr: Entrails not always thoroughly cooked, but given back half-raw. Roasted by the heat of Vulcan
They bring them cut up with a rod.

units.la: Fæm. Lucil. lib. 14. Cenam, inquit, nullam ueq; Diuo profectam ullam. Varro lib. 11. rerum diuinarum Proficiem extorum vel in mensam porricere. Festus: Proficium, quod profectum projicitur, aliàs porricitur. Varro lib. 4. de lingua Latina: Insicia ab eo, quod infecta caro, ut in Carmine Saliorum est: quod in extis datur, nunc profectum. Suetonius in Augusto: Semicruda extra foco profecuit. Hæcille.
units.tr: Lucilius, book 14: "No supper," he says, "and no entrails cut up for the god." Varro, book 11 of the Divine Things: to throw the cut-up entrails onto the table. Festus: proficium is what is cut up and thrown out, otherwise it is called porricitur. Varro, book 4 of the Latin Language: insicia is named from infecta caro (uncooked meat), as in the Carmen of the Salii: what is given from the entrails, now cut up. Suetonius in Augustus: he cut up half-raw entrails at the hearth. Thus far he.

units.la: De hoc autem profacandi verbo sacrificiorum proprio, simul atq; consuetudine (unde parti- cula illa minuta, in quas fiebat illa sectio, seu diuisio, profecta & Prasicie dicta) supra nounul- lis diximus, quando de sacrificiorum materia egimus. Huic profecandi verbo videtur respondere Græcum illud verbum μυσύλλειν, Homero familiarissimum, quod Eustathius sape a verbo ξύω: ξέω ξέω ... dislinguens docet proprie significare τα μικρα τιν βεσὰ εἰς ... Odyss. Iliad. n. Cujusmodi particulas Eustathius etiam τινὰ ... quo aliquid sciudi aut dissecari potest: quo nomine apud Homerum ... Istud vero Apuleio est minutatum (unde minuea, & minuendi verbum, quod ex Graco μειόω ... Fistum putat Festus) frustratim, fruftulatim, tessellatim, si vero frustula & tessellas, carnes, sive alia membra concidere, ꝫu Fleinen rieme ꝫerbawen (quibus dicendi modis autor ille sape utitur.
units.tr: Concerning this verb profecare, proper to sacrifices, and its usage (whence those small pieces into which the cutting or division was made are called profecta and prosecia), we have said something above, when we treated of the matter of sacrifices. The Greek verb [μυσύλλειν], very familiar to Homer, seems to correspond to this verb profecare. Eustathius, distinguishing it often from the verb [ξέω], teaches that it properly means to cut into tiny pieces [τὰ μικρὰ τιν βεσὰ εἰς ...], in Homer's Odyssey and Iliad. Eustathius also calls such particles [τινὰ ...], by which something can be split or cut apart; under this name in Homer ... But Apuleius says minutatum (whence minuea and the verb minuendi, which Festus thinks comes from the Greek [μειόω]), frustratim, fruftulatim, tessellatim; and if one cuts up frustula and tesselas, meats or other limbs, the German says zerhauen (zerhacken); (these modes of speaking the author often uses).

units.la: Exta denique, ista profecta, hoc est, minutatim sive frustulatim concisa in arani focum ve projiciebantur & igni in Deorum honorem concremabantur, quod illi reddere Diis & Porricere appellabant. Hinc Statius lib. 4. Theb.
units.tr: Finally, the entrails, cut up in this way, that is, cut in small pieces or bits, were thrown onto the altar or hearth and burned in the fire in honour of the gods. The ancients called this rendering (reddere) and porrecting (porricere) to the gods. Hence Statius, Thebaid book 4:
And still he gives back
the quivering entrails.
Servius on that line of Virgil, Georgics 2:
We render steaming entrails on platters and dishes.

units.la: Tunc exta, inquit, reddi ditebantur, cum probata areæ supponebantur. Hoc autem reddendi verbum, quo Eibnius, ceu religioso utebantur, unde videtur natum, quod exsistimabant ea, quæ ab hominibus Diis dari, sive donari, offerri, consecrari, solebant, non tam diri proprie, quàm reddi, quippe cum ea prius a Diis accepissent, illorū sint dona atq; munera, illis accepta sint referenda. Id si de uno solo & vero Deo intellexissent, non male sensisseni. Nam solius Dei proprium est dare (unde etiam Deus nonnullis videtur dictus:) honorum autem & reliquarum creaturarum est accipere: secundum illa Pauli, Quis dedit ei prior, & reddetur ei? Item, Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Quando igitur homines Deo aliquid dant, non dare proprie, sed reddere id, quod prius acceperunt, dicuntur; quod ipsum tamen non possunt sine Dei gratia, ut nec accipere quidem sibi a Deo data & oblata munera sine ejusdem gratia possunt.
units.tr: Then, he says, the entrails were said to be given back when, having been tested, they were placed on the altar. This verb "to give back," which the pagans used as a religious term, seems to have arisen from the fact that they thought those things which were customarily given, or offered, consecrated, or dedicated by men to the gods were not properly given but rather returned, since they had first received them from the gods; they are the gifts and presents of the gods, and must be referred back to them as received from them. If they had understood this of the one and true God, they would not have been wrong. For it is the proper work of God alone to give (whence God is also sometimes thought to be so named), but it belongs to men and other creatures to receive, according to those words of Paul: "Who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?" And: "What have you that you did not receive?" When therefore men give something to God, they are said not to give properly, but to return what they first received; yet they cannot do even this without the grace of God, just as they cannot receive from God the gifts given and offered to them without his grace.

units.la: Adicium verbū, Porricere, ut inquit Macrobius lib. 3. Sat. cap. 2. similiter ex Haruspicum di plina & ex præcepto Pontificū solenne erat sacrificantib. Hinc Veratius ex 1. lib. Pictorum ita ... jam hujus verbi exsecutus est: Exta porricuntur, Diis dato, in altaria aram ve, quo exta dari debebant. Porricere ergo, non projicere, proprium sacrificii verbum est. Hæc ille.
units.tr: The word porricere, as Macrobius says in Saturnalia book 3, chapter 2, was likewise a solemn term of sacrifice, by the teaching of the haruspices and the precept of the pontiffs. Hence Veranius, in book 1 of the Pictorum, already set out the use of this word: "The entrails are porrected, given to the god, onto the altar or hearth where the entrails ought to be given." Porricere, therefore, not "to throw," is a proper word of sacrifice. Thus far he.

units.la: Stat. ... sumus autem sacrificiis, hoc est, qua in mari, sive juxta mare fiebant, exta, non in aram fumans, sed in mare, sive mare fluctus porrici, hoc est, projici solebant. Hinc Scipio, apud Livium in Decade tertia, libro nono, cum ante navigationem quam erat suscepturus, rem prius divinam, ubi illuxerat, fecisset, pramiftis e pratoria navi, silentio per praconem falso, precibus, secundum eas preces crudia exta, casa victima, uti mos, in mare projecit, tubaq; signum dedit proficiscendi. Meminit quoque hujus moris Statius Poeta:
units.tr: ... Those sacrifices which were made at sea, or near the sea, the entrails were not offered on a burning altar but were porrected, that is, thrown, into the sea or the waves. Hence Scipio, in Livy, Decade 3, book 9: before the voyage he was about to undertake, when he had performed the divine rite at dawn, with the prayers announced silently by the herald, he threw raw entrails from the sacrificial victim, a white victim, as is the custom, from the praetorian ship into the sea, and gave the signal to set out with a trumpet. The poet Statius also mentions this custom:

units.la: Hic spumante salo jaciens tumida exta profatur.
units.tr: Here, casting the swelling entrails into the foaming sea, he speaks.
And Silius, book 17:
—He casts into the waves

units.la: Cui Numen pelagi placaverat bostia Taurus, Iactaq; cærulei innabant fluctibus exta.
units.tr: A bull, the victim by which he had appeased the god of the sea, and the cut entrails floated on the blue waves.

units.la: Sic Virgilius: Dii, quibus imperium est pelagi, quorum aquora curro, Vobis laetus ego hoc candentem in littore taurum Constituam ante aram, voti reus, exta[?] falsos Porriciam in fluctus, &c.
units.tr: Thus Virgil: "Gods, to whom the rule of the sea belongs, whose waters I run over, to you I will set up a bull, glad, here on the shore, before the altar, bound by my vow, and I will cast the entrails into the waves," etc.

units.la: Macrobius in hos versus: Et quia dixit Veranius in aram focum ve, eó ve, quo exta dari debebant, nunc pro ara, & pro foco mare accipiendum est, cum sacrificium Dijs maris dicetur. Servius in eadem Virgilij verba: Exta, inquit, porriciuntur, id est, porrigantur: nisi forte dicamus, etiam fluctibus maris offerri. Quod fit est, porriciam, id est, porro jaciam, legendum est. Hinc illa trita & usitatata, quasi pro verbalis dicendi forma, Inter cæsa & porrecta: quasi significaretur illud temporis inter vallum, quod intercedebat inter extorum exsectionem & eorundem porrectionem, seu projectionem in aram, in focum, in mare atq; fluctus: aut quo ea dari, reddi, porrici, id est, projicio porto bat. Varr. lib. 5. Vinalia a vino. Hic dies Iovis, non Veneris.
units.tr: Macrobius on these verses: "And because Veranius said 'to the altar or hearth, or wherever the entrails ought to be given,' the sea must now be understood for the altar and the hearth, when a sacrifice is made to the gods of the sea." Servius on the same words of Virgil: "The entrails are porriciuntur, that is, porrigantur (are extended); unless perhaps we say that they are also offered to the waves of the sea." And one should read porriciam, that is, "I will cast forward" (porro jaciam). Hence that common and familiar phrase, as if a verbal form of speaking, "between cutting and porrecting," as if it signified that interval of time which lay between the cutting of the entrails and their being porrected, or projected, onto the altar, the hearth, the sea, and the waves, or the time in which they used to be given, returned, porrected, that is, thrown forward. Varro, book 5: "The Vinalia are named from wine. This day is Jupiter's, not Venus'."

units.la: Hujus rei cura non leves in Latio. Nam aliquot locus primum a Sacerdotibus publice faciebant, ut Romæ etiam nunc. Nam Flamen Dialis auspicatur vindemiam, & ut fusset vinum legere, agná Iovi facit, id est, sacrificat: inter cujus (agne) exta cæsa & porrecta Flamen vinum profusum legit. In Tusculanis sacreus est: Vinum novum ne vebatur in urbem, antequam Vinalia kalendur. Idem: Intercisi dies, per quos mane & vesperi est nefas (fari): medio tempore inter hostiam cæsum & exta porrecta fas (fari licet.) Idem de porrecere. Pollutum, quod a porrigendo est fictum. Cum enim ex mercibus libamenta porrecta sunt Herculi in ara, tum pollutum est, mirumque illorum parte, sicuti jam dictum, cum alias hostia partibus, Dijs consecrata, reliquas reservabatur ad epulum sacrificiale, quod sacrificium erat appendix, quem usum HomerusExcerpt.
units.tr: The concern for this matter is not slight in Latium. For in some places the first-fruits were offered publicly by the priests, as even now at Rome. For the Flamen Dialis takes the auspices of the vintage and, so that he may gather the wine, sacrifices a lamb to Jupiter, that is, he offers it in sacrifice; and between the cutting of the lamb's entrails and their porrection, the Flamen gathers the poured-out wine. In the Tusculans it is written: "New wine was not carried into the city before the Vinalia." The same author: "Days are called intercisi, on which it is unlawful to speak in the morning and evening; in the middle time, between the cutting of the victim and the porrection of the entrails, it is lawful to speak." The same author on porrectum: "Pollutum, which is formed from porrigere. For when offerings from the goods were porrected to Hercules on the altar, then it was polluted." Moreover, as said already, from the sacrificial victims, consecrated to the gods in some parts, the remainder was kept for the sacrificial feast, which was an appendix to the sacrifice; a custom which Homer follows.

units.la: Hic succedit alius extorum usus, qui etiam aliarum partium sacrificialium usus fuit, quod minus expressit illus verbis: ἀπόδοσις τῶν ἱερῶν, id est, ut Homerus interpretes explicant, hoc est, degustabant.
units.tr: Here follows another use of the entrails, which was also a use of other sacrificial parts, which he expressed less clearly in the words [ἀπόδοσις τῶν ἱερῶν] (apodosis tōn hierōn), that is, as the interpreters of Homer explain, that is, they tasted them.

units.la: Atque hæc quidem satis finit dicta de hostiarum victimarum ve adeo ut sive ex foro, inciduntur seu differentie in partes majores & minores, interiores & exteriores: & vario multiplicio, illarum omnium in sacrificiis usu. Quædam enim illarum dabantur & offerebantur Dijs, quæ arae focus ve impositæ, igni absumebantur: cujusmodi sacrificium holocaustum, sive holocaustoma, hoc est, totum incensum, teste Josepho Antiquitatum lib. 3. fuit appellatum. Alia vero cedebant in usum sacrificantium: ex quibus differentiæ in minores partes atque collus epulum, re pentita divina, adornari atq; celebrari consuevunt, ut apud Homerum & Apollonium sequitur. Hoc fecundum sacrificii genus intelligitur ab Ollavio fuisse celebratum, qui exta nondum porrecta rapuit e foco, ubi scilicet igni sacrificii causa hebat, & professus, idest partem reddidit Marti, cujus sacrificabat, partem ad vescendum referre vanit. Persæ tamen, ut Eustathius refert ex Geographo, sacrificantes in loco excelso, & cælum exsiliment esse Iovem sive Deum, hostiarum: carnibus divisis (Διὸς οὐρανός) Dijs nihil dabant ἀπόθυμον, cum dicerent Denm hostiæ: anima indigeret nihil, aliud, nisi parum quid ἀπλῶς, id est, omenti, igni imponunt. Quando verò hostia tota tum: cujusmodi Vulcano atque etiam Herculi, aut Sanco sive Sango, aliud Dijs factum est. Proprer viam, inquit Festus, sic sacrificium, quod est proficiscendi gratia Herculi aut Sanco, sicut ligant viarum est Deus. Profecturi enim viam Herculi aut Sanco sacrificabant: quo loco Festus Propter viam recte legi admonet Antonius Augustinus, non ut vulgo Protervia.
units.tr: These things have been said quite enough about the victims and their parts, and about the division of the victims, both on the outside and within, into major and minor parts, inner and outer, and about the various multiplicity of their use in sacrifices. For some of these were given and offered to the gods, which were placed on the altar or hearth and consumed by fire; a sacrifice of this kind was called a holocaust, or holocaustoma, that is, wholly burned, as Josephus witnesses in Antiquities, book 3. Other parts went to the use of those sacrificing, and from these the feast was usually prepared and celebrated after the divine rite, as Homer and Apollonius follow. This second kind of sacrifice is understood to have been celebrated by Ollavius, who snatched the entrails not yet porrected from the hearth, where of course the fire was for the sacrifice, and, having professed it, that is, having given a part to Mars, to whom he was sacrificing, he kept the other part for eating. The Persians, however, as Eustathius reports from the geographer, sacrificing on a high place and calling the heavens Jupiter or God, divided the flesh of the victims and gave nothing to the gods [ἀπόθυμον], since they said that God needed nothing of the victim's soul except a little of it [ἀπλῶς], that is, the omentum, which they put on the fire. But when the whole victim was burned, as was done for Vulcan and also for Hercules, or for Sancus or Sango, it was done for the gods. Hence Festus says: "Propter viam (on account of the road): so the sacrifice which is made for the sake of setting out, to Hercules or Sancus, as the god of roads." For those about to set out sacrificed to Hercules or Sancus on the way; in which place Antonius Augustinus rightly advises that Festus should be read Propter viam, not as commonly Protervia.

units.la: PORRO vel hostiis integris & solidis, vel illarum partibus aræ focò ve impositis & ingnem conjectis ve ressigio partim liquores quosdam, ut vinum atq; oleum super infundebant, partim aromata herbasq; odoriferas addebant.
units.tr: Moreover, either whole and solid victims, or their parts, were placed on the altar hearth and fire was cast upon them. Sometimes they poured certain liquids over them, such as wine and oil, and sometimes they added spices and fragrant herbs.

units.la: Quantum ad priu attinet; sic Homerus in Nestoris sacrificii descriptione, femoribus ignem conjectis addit: —Ἐπὶ δ' αἰθόμεν οἴνῳ Λεῖβ'. Super autem (femoribus) vinum nigrum
units.tr: As for the first point, Homer, in describing the sacrifice of Nestor, likewise adds wine when he has cast fire upon the thighs: Over the thighs he poured dark wine [Ἐπὶ δ' αἰθόμεν' οἴνῳ λεῖβ']. Over the thighs
That is, of course, Nestor the old man.

units.la: Apollonius: —ἀ ἀλ' ἀκρίτως χεῖα λοιβὰς Αἰσονίδης γὰρ ἡ οἴνας ἐυδλεῶ ἱδ᾽μων: At vero meras fudit libationes Aesonides (id est, Iason:) letatur autem conspectu flamma Idmon.
units.tr: Apollonius: But the son of Aeson poured out libations without stint, and Idmon rejoiced at the sight of the flame [ἀλλ' ἀκρίτως χεῖε λοιβὰς Αἰσονίδης· γήθει δὲ ἰδὼν φλογὸς αἴγλην Ἴδμων].

units.la: Virgilius Aeneidos quinto: —Extaq; salsos Porriciam in fluctus, & vina liquentia fundam.
units.tr: Virgil, Aeneid book 5: And I will cast the entrails into the salt waves and pour out liquid wine.

units.la: Item Georgicorum quarto: Ter liquido ardeneem per sudit nectare flammam, Ter flamma ad summum tecti subiectâ relucet, id est, interpreste Servio, ingnem vinum purissimum fudit: post quod quia magis flamma convaluit, bonum omen ostendit.
units.tr: Likewise, Georgics book 4: Three times he poured clear nectar over the blazing fire, and three times the flame shone up to the top of the roof. According to Servius's explanation, he poured pure wine on the fire; and because the flame then burned more strongly, this showed a good omen.

units.la: Idem Aeneidos sexto: Et solida imponit taurorum viscera flammis Pingue superq; oleum fundens ardentibus extis.
units.tr: The same, Aeneid book 6: And he laid the solid entrails of bulls on the flames, pouring fat oil and the burning entrails over them.

units.la: Donatus in hac verba: Oleum veronon dubitatur, inquit, idcirco infusum, ut aris imposita faciliùs exurerentur.
units.tr: Donatus on these words: There is no doubt, he says, that the oil was poured on so that the offerings placed on the altars would burn more readily.

units.la: Hic rursus Libationis, id est, effusionis vini super altari sive igni fit mentio, ut supra factâ est mentio effusionis vini super fronte, sive inter cornua hostiæ slantis ad aram. Fieri etiam solita fuit Libatio in epulo sacrificiali, quod peractis sacrificiis celebrari consuevit, sub eisdem nimirum finem. Quoniam igitur libationum maximus & frequentissimus, in omnibus sacrificiis atq; epulis apud Gentiles usus fuit, & idcirco creberrima illarum passim apud Scriptores fit mentio, atq; adeo Libationes istæ non modo pars sacrificiorum necessaria (quibus nullum ferè sacrificium apud Veteres caruit) versum etiam sacrificia antiquitus Gentilium sola fuerant. (Vino enim eanesim atq; thure olim sacrificatum quoq; Dijs fuisse legimus) operæpretium, nihilg; a candidis Lectoris voluntate alienime factarum puto, si illam meam generalem Libationum descriptionem, quæ exstat in meis Convivialibus bis (cum hujus loci atq; instituti mei sit propria) inserebam. Ii igitur libro 2. capite 37. sic se habet:
units.tr: Here again mention is made of libation, that is, the pouring of wine over the altar or the fire, just as above mention was made of the pouring of wine over the forehead, or between the horns, of the victim standing before the altar. Libation was also customarily made at the sacrificial feast, which was usually celebrated when the sacrifices were finished, under the same conclusion. Since, then, libation was the greatest and most frequent practice in all sacrifices and feasts among the Gentiles, and therefore mention of it is very common everywhere among the writers, and since these libations were not only a necessary part of sacrifices (almost no sacrifice among the ancients lacked them), but in ancient times were even the whole of the sacrifices of the Gentiles (for we read that wine, incense and frankincense were once offered to the gods), I think it worthwhile, and nothing contrary to the good will of the kind reader, to insert here my general description of libations, which appears twice in my Convivials, since it properly belongs to this place and to my present plan. It stands thus in book 2, chapter 37:

units.la: Ad precationes porro videntur referenda Ethnicorum veterum ἀπαρχαὶ, hoc est, primitiæ, ἀπαρχαὶ & ἀπορδαὶ, sive λοιβαὶ, hoc est, libationes, quibus illi in Deorum suorum honorem ante, & post ἀπορδαὶ, si conuiuium uti consueuerunt. Athen. lib. 4. καὶ ταῦτα ἀ... ve λοιβαὶ πολλὴ ὕμνας ἀπαρχαὶ: ...
units.tr: Moreover, the first-fruits of the ancient Gentiles, that is, the aparchai, and the aporrhai or libations (spondai), by which they used to honour their gods before and after the feast, seem to belong to prayers. Athenaeus, book 4: "...and these things..." ...

units.la: sim occurrunt. Hæc Plato quoq; in conviviis, ut idem Athenæus nuncupat, obser vavit. ...
units.tr: ...occur. Plato also observed these things at banquets, as Athenaeus calls them. ...

units.la: Xenoph. quoq; traditur. Apud Epicurum autem ... boc est, neque libatio, neq; primitiæ Dijs offeruntur: sed, ut Simonides inquit, de mulære ...
units.tr: It is also handed down by Xenophon. But among the Epicureans ... that is, neither libation nor first-fruits are offered to the gods; but, as Simonides says, of the woman ...

units.la: Flacci, Ante larem proprium viscos, vernasq; prosaces, Pasce libatis, dapibus, &c.
units.tr: Horace: "Before the household hearth feed the sleek swine and the household slaves with the offered feasts, etc."

units.la: Hæc annotat: Ego hoc crediderim referendum ad antiquorum pietatem, qui partem cœnæ lari Dissq; donabant, ea in focum mittebant lari sacrum, ut constat, id enim erat libare dapes. Exea consuetudine, ut arbitror, scribit Varro, ut a Marcello citatur: Quoticà oportet bonum cìrcum legibus pariere, & Deos colere, in patellam dare μικρὸν κρέας. Et Cicero de Finibus: Atqui repe. riemus Asotos primùm ita non religiosos, ut edunt de patella, id est, ut edant ea, quæ Diis e cœna libata sunt. Sed ritus ille optimè intelligetur e Plutarcho, ita in libello de Fortuna Rom. scribete: Ocrestam virginem, inquit, identidem primitias, & libationes arugia mensa attiptre, & ea ad
units.tr: He notes this: I would think this should be referred to the piety of the ancients, who gave a portion of the meal to the household gods and sent it into the hearth as a sacred portion for the lar; for this, it is agreed, was to make a libation of the feast. Varro, as cited by Marcellus, writes from this custom, I think: "How often ought a good man to observe the laws, honour the gods, and put a little meat on the plate?" And Cicero in On Ends: "But we shall find that the Asotians were at first not so scrupulous that they ate from the plate," that is, that they ate those things which had been offered to the gods from the meal. But that rite will be understood best from Plutarch, who writes thus in his little book On the Fortune of the Romans: "The virgin Ocrestes," he says, "used repeatedly to touch the first-fruits and libations on the table..., and carry them to the hearth, and when at some time she cast them into the fire according to custom, etc."

units.la: Libationum maximus usus in sacrificiis. focum perferre consuevisse, cumq; aliquando pro more ea in ignem injiceret, &c. Ad hanc etiam morem alludens, ea se calfacere, ut sanctimonia ruri dicit cenare Horatius: ut dapibus supra ante Deo pie libatis, veluti non soleat. Inde & Dii patellarii a Plauto festivè iocante sunt dicti, quibus in patella libabatur, non magna sacrificia fiebant. Tales Diierant in larario domestici penates, & lares. Haec ille.
units.tr: The greatest use of libations was in sacrifices. Alluding to this custom, Horace says that he warms himself with them, as if he had sanctified them in the country: "as if one should not have piously made libations to the god over the feasts above." Hence also the gods of the plate (Dii patellarii) were called so by Plautus in a witty jest, because libation was made on a plate, and no great sacrifices were performed. Such were the household penates and lares in the household shrine. So far he.

units.la: Verum operæpretium erit hic de libationibus, quæ cum in sacrificiis, tum in fœneribus, tum in conviviis adhiberi olim consuevèrunt, paullo copiosius scribere. Libationes part m religiosæ & in sacris. partim prophanæ, & prophanis in epulis adhiberi fuisse solitas, Macrob. testatur lib. 3 Saturnalium cap. 11. Verùm ut ordine proc. dat hæc nostra tractatio, primo de nominibus agemus.
units.tr: Indeed it will be worthwhile here to write somewhat more fully about libations, which were customarily used in sacrifices, in funerals, and at banquets. Macrobius testifies in book 3 of his Saturnalia, chapter 11, that libations, some religious and used in sacred rites, and some profane, were customarily used at profane feasts. But, so that this treatment proceeds in order, we shall first deal with the names.

units.la: GRAECI duo habent vocabula, quibus a libione hanc exprimunt. Ea sunt σπονδή, & λοιβή, quæ secundum nonnullos videntur a se invicem differre: cum tamen apud Homerum & alios auctores sæpissimè confundantur. Ac σπονδὴ a quidè (cujus proto-typon secundum Heraclidem, teste Eustathio, ἐκ τοῦ σπένδω, unde Futurum σπείσω, & σπείσομαι) Hesychius exponit σπονδὴ, ἐγκατάθεσις, θυσίας δὲ, hoc est, effundere, offerre, sacrificare Deo: & apud eundem σπένδεσθαι pro θύεσθαι. Sic ioannes Suidas exponitur pro τὸ θυεῖν. Paulus 2. Philippicarum: ἐπὶ σπονδαῖς ἐπὶ τῇ θυσίᾳ, & ἀπολιβὴ ἐπὶ τῆς ἀπολιβῆς, hoc est, etiamsi pro libamento offerat super hostias, sacrificio, fidei vestræ. Alludit Paulus ad morem vinum libandi, hoc est, effundendi super victimam, ut significet se paratum esse similiter suum sanguinem libare, sive profundere pro illorum fide, quæ sit optimum sacrificium, sive pro Christo, qui sit hostia illa verè piacularis, quam illi fide apprehenderint, atq; colant.
units.tr: The Greeks have two words by which they express libation from the verb "to pour." These are spondē and loibē, which according to some seem to differ from each other, though in Homer and other authors they are very often confused. Spondē, whose prototype, according to Heraclides as reported by Eustathius, is from spendō, whence the future speisō and speisomai, Hesychius explains as "pouring out, offering, sacrificing to God," and in the same author spendesthai is used for thuesthai, to sacrifice. So John Suidas is explained as meaning to thuein. Paul, 2 Philippians: epi spondais epi tē thusia, and apolibē epi tēs apolibēs, that is, "even if I am poured out as a libation over the sacrifice of your faith." Paul alludes to the custom of pouring wine as a libation, that is, pouring it over the victim, to signify that he is ready likewise to pour out his blood as a libation for their faith, which is the best sacrifice, or for Christ, who is that truly expiatory victim, whom they have embraced by faith and worship.

units.la: Idem verbum præsertim in pastoribus, sæpe pro fœderis contractu usurpatur, quod sacrificiis & libationibus intercedentibus fieri consuevit. Itaque σπονδὴ, libatio, sæpe etiam profædere usurpatur: & σπένδεσθαι, sive σπείσασθαι, & λιβάνειν, Xenoph. Pædag. 4. & σπένδ. Platonis idem quod σπείσαι ἐν εἰρήνῃ, Et ἀσπόνδοι & ἄσπονδοι, fœderis expers, ἐκ σπονδῶν, a fœdere exclusi, σπονδαὶ & σύσπονδοι, confœderati, παρασπονδῶν, fœdifragus, σπονδὴ aliquando non tam libationem, quàm libamen, aut libamentum, id est, vinum, quod libatur, significat.
units.tr: The same word, especially in the poets, is often used for the making of a covenant, which was customarily done with sacrifices and libations intervening. Thus spondē, libation, is also often used for covenant; and spendesthai or speisasthai, and libanein, in Xenophon's Pedagogue book 4, and spendein in Plato, mean the same as speisai en eirēnē, to make a treaty of peace; and aspondoi and asponduoi, without a covenant, ek spondōn, excluded from a covenant; spondai and syspondoi, allied by treaty; paraspondōn, a covenant-breaker. Sometimes spondē signifies not so much the libation as the offering, or the libamentum, that is, the wine that is poured.

units.la: Alterum est λοιβὴ, sive λείβειν, sive λοιβάδου. Hesychius, σπεισθῆναι ἐν, & ἀκρατον. Galenus scribit proprie sacrificare τὸ ἐκχεῖν, id est, fitillare. Unde λοιβὴ θυσία olim, ut Hesychius exponit, ἐκ ὑγρῶν θυσία, hoc est, sacrificium quod fit per humida. Eustathius Iliad. n. in illa Homeri, Οἶνον δ᾽ ἐκ ἀνδρῶν χαμαὶ ἔχευα.
units.tr: The other word is loibē, or leibein, or loibadou. Hesychius gives speisthēnai, and akraton (unmixed wine). Galen writes that properly to sacrifice is to ekcheein, that is, to pour out in a thin stream. Hence loibē thusia was once, as Hesychius explains it, ek hygrōn thusia, that is, a sacrifice made with liquids. Eustathius, on the Iliad book 9, on that line of Homer: "I poured the wine out on the ground."

units.la: Poeta, inquit, interpretatur λείβειν, quasi idem sic ἰσχὺν σπονδὴν ἐπέχειν, ἐκ χεῖν: unde etiam ἰκχειν. Λοιβὴ apud Sophoclem dicitur in illis verbis, τύμβου λοιβαῖοι ἐπὶ σον. Idem Od. y. λοιβὴ idem esse, quod σπονδὴ, illud indicat, quod flatum subjungit, Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ σπείσαντ᾽ ἔπιόν δ᾽ ὅσον ἤθελ᾽ ἕκαστος.
units.tr: The poet, he says, explains leibein as if it were the same as spondē, ischyn spondēn epechein, ekcheein, whence also ikcheein. Loibē is found in Sophocles in these words: tymbou loibaioi epi son, libations over your tomb. In the Odyssey book 3, loibē is shown to be the same as spondē by the line that follows: "Then, when they had poured the libation and drunk as much as each wished," which indicates the proper and sufficient measure of drink.

units.la: Id quod potionis justè, atque sufficientis est, indicium. Constat etiam passim idem esse λοιβὴν, & σπονδὴν, & Ionicum, atq; Aeolicum esse τὸ εἶχον, derivatum a λείβειν, ut τοῦ αἱ λοιβαὶ a λοιβή. Ἐκ τῆς ἔλεγον, Εἰς αἱ ἀπὸ Ὑ ἐξ ἀνεῖχον. Haec duo porrò verba libationem Graeci significantia licet, ut Eustath. annotat in illa Homeri verba, Ἐπεὶ δ᾽ αἰθο-πα οἶνον λείβειν, Super autem (femoribus) vinum libavit.
units.tr: It is also commonly agreed that loibē and spondē are the same, and that the Ionic and Aeolic form eikhon is derived from leibein, as tou ai loibai from loibē. Although these two words, the Greeks may use to signify libation, as Eustathius notes on those words of Homer, "and he had poured out dark wine," Super autem (femoribus) vinum libavit.

units.la: Idem videantur significare: tamen illorum denominativa nonnihil a se invicem differunt. Nam λοιβάτιον, quod a λείβειν, quidem de olei: σπονδεῖον autem de vini libatione proprie dicatur, quod λοιβαῖον quidem de olei; sed alicubi inter λείβειν, & αἱ ἀνὰ ἐξ ἐπὶ differentiam hinc conflat, quod λείβειν de lacrymis dicitur: & nonnunquam etiam de aquis: unde τὸ λείβειν, hoc est, & λοιβὴ ἐπὶ τοῦτο, est ἀν σπονδὴ in illa significatione nonnunquam usurpatur.
units.tr: These seem to mean the same thing, yet their derived forms differ somewhat from one another. Thus λοιβάτιον [loibation], derived from λείβειν [leibein, to pour out], is properly said of pouring out oil, while σπονδεῖον [spondeion] is properly said of pouring out wine; but in some places λοιβαῖον [loibaion] is also used of oil. The difference between λείβειν [leibein] and σπένδειν [spendein] is clear from this: λείβειν is said of tears, and sometimes also of waters, so that λοιβή [loibe], the act of pouring out, is in that sense sometimes used for σπονδή [spondē], a libation.

units.la: Praeterea σπένδεσθαι τὶς δὴ ἐπὶ ἀνθρώπου, hoc est, libat quis amicitiæ ergo, at non dicitur λοιβάζειν. A λείβειν porrò derivatur καλεῖν, quasi λαλεῖν παρὰ τὸ χέειν λοιβαῖον εἰς ἀντὶ, sive, ut alii volunt, ἀπὸ τῆς χέειν, & λείβειν secundum illud, σιλοοσιλον καλεῖσθαι. Idem in Od. Μ. in illa verba, ὡΛΙ ἀχοντιῶν λέξλαι ἐν αἱθερόβιος ιερεῖων ΑΛΛ ὕδαη ανἰνδοῖτις.
units.tr: Moreover, σπένδεσθαι [spendesthai] is said of a person, that is, one makes a libation for the sake of friendship, but it is not said λοιβάζειν [loibazein]. From λείβειν [leibein] is derived καλεῖν [kalein], as if from λαλεῖν [lalein], because of pouring out a libation in place of something; or, as others will have it, from χέειν [cheein] and λείβειν [leibein], according to the usage by which the word is called. The same appears in the Odyssey, in those words about the libations poured out from the vessels.

units.la: Poëta, inquit, ἀπιγνεῖν & λεῖβειν idem est: pro ἀπιγνῶ autem dictum est ἀπιδα. Idem in Ld est duo haec verba docet idem significare.
units.tr: The poet, he says, uses ἀπιγνεῖν [apignein] and λεῖβειν [leibein] to mean the same thing; ἀπιγνῶ [apignō] was used for ἀπιδα [apida]. The same author shows in the same passage that these two words mean the same.

units.la: Hebraicè יסך Nasak, ut Graecum λεῖβειν & ἀπιγνεῖν, & fundere & libare significat. Vnde יסך Nasak, & מסך Mimsak commissionem, effusionem atque libationem sive libamen significat: interpretes ἀπιγνῶ vertunt. Vt autem Mincha proprie aridorum: sic Nisech liquidorum sacrificium fuit. Sacrorum libaminum, quae e vino & sicera erant, fit mentio Exod. 25. Num 28. & 29. 2. Reg. 23. & alibi.
units.tr: In Hebrew, נסך [nasak], as the Greek λεῖβειν [leibein] and ἀπιγνεῖν [apignein], means both to pour out and to offer a libation. Hence נסך [nasak] and מסך [mimsak] signify a pouring together, an effusion, and a libation or libation-offering, and the translators render them by ἀπιγνῶ [apignō]. Just as the mincha [Mincha] was properly a sacrifice of dry things, so the nisech [Nisech] was a sacrifice of liquids. Mention is made of the sacred libations, which consisted of wine and strong drink, in Exodus 25, Numbers 28 and 29, 2 Kings 23, and elsewhere.

units.la: Libare Latinis, ut volunt Grammatici, proprie est leviter degustare & quasi primis labris attingere: dictum, ut quidem putant, a labiis, quasi labiare. Virg.
units.tr: To the Latins, as the grammarians hold, libare properly means to taste lightly, and as it were to touch with the first of the lips; it is said to be derived, as some think, from the lips, as if it were labiare.
And they reap the purple flowers, and sip the rivers. (Virgil)

units.la: Per Metaphoram aliquando pro leviter attingere usurpatur, Virg.
units.tr: By metaphor it is sometimes used for touching lightly, as in Virgil:

units.la: Osculaque libavit natae, dehinc talia fatur.
units.tr: And he kissed his daughter, and then spoke such words.

units.la: Deniq; libare (quod ad propositum nostrum facit) Isidorus vult: proprii idem esse quod funde re, voce deductaa Libero quodam, qui in Graecia usum reperit vini. Idem, Libatio, inquit, tantummodo calicis oblatio est. Hinc illud.
units.tr: Finally, Isidore holds that libare (which bears on our present purpose) properly means the same as to pour out, the word being derived from Liber, a certain god who discovered the use of wine in Greece. The same Isidore says: "Libation is nothing more than the offering of a cup." Hence that line:
And he tasted the blood of the grape.

units.la: Sic est secularium quid am Poëtarum. Nunc, inquit, paterae libate lovi. Ovid. quod 3. Fast. Libationem a Libero vult dictam,
units.tr: This is the sort of thing found in the secular poets. "Now," he says, "pour libations to Jupiter from the patera." Ovid in the third book of the Fasti. He holds that libation takes its name from Liber,

units.la: Nomine ab auctoris ducuni libaminis nomen.
units.tr: and the name of the offering is taken from its author,

units.la: Libaṁ quid sanctis pars datur inde fovis.
units.tr: and a portion of the cake is given to Jupiter from it.

units.la: Varro lib. 4. Liba (quod fuerunt placentae ex farre & melle Deorum sacrificiis aptae: unde for- tan Germanicum Löbkuchen) ideo dicta vult esse, quod libandi causa fierent, vel quod libantur priusquam essent coctae. Horat. Epist. ad Fuscum:
units.tr: Varro, in book 4, holds that liba (which were cakes of spelt and honey, suited to the sacrifices of the gods, whence perhaps the German Löbkuchen) were so called because they were made for the purpose of libation, or because they were offered before they were baked. Horace, in the Epistle to Fuscus:

units.la: Pii i, Sacerdotes fugiunt, liba recusó,
units.tr: The priests, pious ones, shun the cakes I refuse,

units.la: Pane ego jam mellitus poriore placentes.
units.tr: and I, honey-sweetened, eat the finer bread.

units.la: Hinc constat libum esse placentam mellitam. Athenaeus tamen libro tertio significat libum sive placentam ex lacte & fumine & melle composi. Mihi & libare, & libatio, & libamen seu libamentum & libum a Graeca voce λείβειν & λειβᾶς videntur derivari.
units.tr: From this it is established that libum is a honeyed cake. Yet Athenaeus, in book 3, says that libum or placenta was made of milk, flour and honey. To me, libare, libatio, libamen or libamentum, and libum seem to be derived from the Greek λείβειν [leibein] and λειβᾶς [leibas].

units.la: Vinum quoque dare Latinis audientibus idem quod libare. Cato de re Rustica, cap 134. Posea Cere iesta, & vinum date, id est, libate. Nam vinum, quod libabant, quasi Dis dicabant ac propinabant. Notandum porro ut Nasak Hebraeum, ita libare Latinum nomen quam ettam de aridis usurpari.
units.tr: To Latin hearers, to give wine meant the same as to libare. Cato, in De re rustica, chapter 134: "Then offer the sacrificial cake and give wine," that is, make a libation. For the wine that they poured out was, as it were, dedicated and offered to the gods. It should be noted further that, as nasak is the Hebrew word, so libare is the Latin word, and both are also used of dry things.

units.la: Erat enim apud Ethnicos omnino duplex libatio, quae cum in sacrificiis, tum in epulis uti consueverant. Vna erat de pauo atque iterum, quorum partem aliquam decerpentes, illam in ignem solum te conjicere, atque ita Deo jam religiose suo erga illos gratitudinem testificando gratia, consecrare solebant, de quo paullo antea. Altera fuit potus atque liquorum, de qua nunc agemus. Illa au tem Hebraice ישכ Nasak, Graeci ἀπιγνεῖν & λειβᾶ, Latine libatio dicta, nihil aliud erat, quam vini, sicera, aquae, lactis, olei, aut alterius ad cujus liquorem ex vase effusio, vel in aram, seu vitu mus, vel in terram, certis adhibitis cerimoniis atque praecibus in Dei. Deorum ve honorem olim facta. Latini vinum, ut dixi, dare Dijs, pro libare, ut pant. Sic multibibaillalena apud Plausum in Curculi, vini quiddam defundens, inquit:
units.tr: Among the heathen there was indeed a twofold libation, which they customarily used both in sacrifices and at feasts. One was of bread and of fruit, from which they would pluck some part and cast it into the fire alone, and so consecrate it, as a religious act of thanksgiving to their god, as we said a little earlier. The other was of drink and liquids, of which we shall now speak. The former is called in Hebrew nasak [נסך] — no, in Hebrew this is the libation as the Greeks call it ἀπιγνεῖν [apignein] and λειβᾶ [leibā], and in Latin libatio; it was nothing other than the pouring out from a vessel of wine, strong drink, water, milk, oil, or some other liquid, either on the altar or on the ground or upon the victims, with certain ceremonies and prayers, in the past made in honour of God or of the gods. The Latins, as I said, use dare, "to give," to Jupiter for libare, as they say. So the drunken Lena in Plautus' Curculio, pouring out some wine, says:

units.la: Venus de paulo paululum hoc tibi dabo lubenter:
units.tr: Venus, I will gladly give you a little of this:

units.la: Nam tibi amantes propinantes vinum dant,
units.tr: for lovers, drinking to you, give you wine,

units.la: Mihi haud sepe tales bereditate veniunt.
units.tr: while such gifts seldom come to me by inheritance.

units.la: Sic vinum fundere, item vergere, & in vergere pro libare apud Latinos ponitur. Statius li- 3. Vinum fundere bro sex.o Theb.
units.tr: Thus fundere, "to pour out," and likewise vergere, and in vergere, are used by the Latins for libare. Statius, in book 6 of the Thebaid:
Foaming, they pour out wine and black

units.la: Libationum nomina Hebraea. Sanguinis, & rapi gratissima cymbia lactis. Anus apud Plautum in Curculione, Ipsum expeto tangere, in vergere in me liquorem, Hoc est, Infundere. Virg. lib. 6. In vergit vina Sacerdos. Lucret. lib. 5. Illi imprudentes ipsi sibi sepe venenum Vergebant, nunc dant alii solertius ipsi.
units.tr: the most welcome cups of blood and milk. The Hebrew names of the libations. Plautus in the Curculio, an old woman: "I am eager to touch him, and to pour liquid over me," that is, to pour in. Virgil, book 6: "The priest pours wine." Lucretius, book 5: "Those who unwittingly pour poison for themselves often, others now give it more skilfully themselves."

units.la: Vnde conflat verbum hoc proprium sacrum, sepe transferri ad profanum usum. Quam autem Servius inter fundere, & in vergere differentiam statuat, postea explicabitur. Iudei habuerunt olim Iacobas & religiosas suas libationes, ut ex Num. 28. & alius ex locis conflat, quae in Deo honorem celebrabantur. Ose. 9. Non libabunt Domino vinum. Has libationes, ut alios quoq; Iudaeorum ritus atq; cerimonias Ethnici xaxo\u03b8\u03b1\u03bc\u03b1 quadam fuerunt imitati. Prim aut mde libationum Ethnicarum materia, deinde forma atq; modo, ritibus, sive cerimoniis agemus.
units.tr: From this it is clear that this word, proper to sacred use, is often transferred to profane use. How Servius distinguishes between fundere and in vergere will be explained later. The Jews once had their solemn and religious libations, as is clear from Numbers 28 and other passages, which were performed in honour of God. Hosea 9: "They shall not pour libations of wine to the LORD." These libations, as well as other Jewish rites and ceremonies, the heathen imitated in some fashion. First I shall treat of the matter of the heathen libations, then of their form and manner, and their rites or ceremonies.

units.la: QVOAD materiam, obser vandum est primo id, quod Euslath. ad Il. 1. annot. ẝẞ Ẍằạ ἐν ἄλλοις ὑγρὰ ἀλλὰ ὑγρὰ ἀλλὰ ὑγρὰ ἀ, hoc est, alio aliq. humore, vel more pro tempo rum ratione fieri solitas fuisse. Apud Hebreos libamina seba aut ex aqua & oleo, ut conflat ex 28. & 29. c. Num. Apud Ethnicos in plerisq; licet sacrificiis vino libare moris erat: men erant quaedam sacra, in quibus non erat fas vino libare: alia do ra, sive in gelu, (quae ab Ilemia apud Gel. lib. 3. cap. 29. appellantur) in quibus vini nullus erat usus. Ac vinum quidem apud Ethnicos vt etiam apud Hebraeos in plerisq; sacris, seu sacrificiis libatum fuisse ejusq; simul cum illius loco ante citato, bis verbis explicat: Vinum et si non una cum molis salsis simebatur, cadet men urile erat in libationibus post molas salsas. Non minus enim illud, quam bovi deintentio ad civilem, & mensuam vitam pertinet: fero enim fuit in ventum. His verbis rationem reddit, cur libatio, id est, vinum sacrificiis fuerit usitata.
units.tr: As to the matter, the first thing to observe is what Eustathius notes on Iliad 1: that libations were customarily made with different liquids at different times, according to the circumstances. Among the Hebrews the drink offerings were made of water and oil, as is clear from Numbers 28 and 29. Among the heathen it was customary to pour wine in most sacrifices, but there were certain sacred rites in which it was not lawful to pour wine, and others, in the so-called gelu, which Ilemia mentions in Gellius, book 3, chapter 29, in which there was no use of wine at all. Eustathius explains that wine, as among the Hebrews, was poured in most of the heathen sacred rites or sacrifices, and he gives the reason for this in the words cited above: wine, though not used together with the salted meal, was nevertheless suitable for libations after the salted cakes. For it was no less pertinent to civil and table life than the offering of the ox; for it was given to the wind. By these words he gives the reason why libation, that is, wine, was customary in sacrifices.

units.la: Notandum autem non quod vis vinum in sacris potuisse exhiberi. Nam ex Graeca, & amputatio nec, seu fulmine talia, aut que vulneratur pedibus calcata, aut immundissimi polluta, rat, aut juxta quam homo lacuo pendantur, quae ji, circumcisis vinaceis profluxerat, vinum Dei libare usus fuisse. Pythagoreorum quoq; symbolum fuit, ne Dii linarent ex amputatis ni cibus. Hinc Spurcum vinum dicebatur, quod sacris adhiberi non poterat, ut ajet Labeo Anti lib. 10. Commentariorum juris Pontificii, cui aqua admixta est, de quo vinum, sic ne ta um est, nullum vs antequam deferveicat.
units.tr: It should be noted, however, that wine could not be offered in all sacred rites. For wine that was from a vine that had been cut back, or that had been trodden underfoot, or that had been polluted by the most unclean, or that hung from a tree near which a man had been hanged, or that had flowed from grapes that had been cut off, was not to be poured to the gods, nor was it used. Among the Pythagoreans it was a rule that the gods should not be given wine from the trimmed vine. Hence wine was called "unclean" if it could not be used in sacred rites, as Labeo says in book 10 of his Commentaries on Pontifical Law, when wine was mixed with water, of which the same is said, that it must not be used before it has boiled.

units.la: Olim ad hunc modum praeterea, veteres omnino mero, seu meri co vinum in libatione usus sunt, de quo fuisse: de Omnino veteres vino meraco in libationibus utebantur, secundum ad. Libationes & meracae. Idem 1A. β in hac ipsa Homeri 7. rba: sed Δια αξυοι, hoc est libationes meracae: αξυοι, inquit, id est, meraca: dixit libationes propterea, quod mero libabant: quo innuebant, ante γovαικληνο ... ficcon-tra vino aqua mixto dolique atque superfluitiones in sacris adumbrabantur ) quod si quis autem crater vinum dicuntur misc uisse, non aquae atque vinum, sed duorum vinorum commixtio ibi intelligenda, Idem in illud Hom. 1A. Γ. —κεντεσν δεν οιον Miσγον.
units.tr: In earlier times, moreover, the ancients used wine entirely unmixed, or pure wine, in libation. It is said that the ancients used unmixed wine in libations, according to [Homer]. Homer in this very passage writes of "unmixed libations" [ἀκρητοι σπονδαί], that is, pure libations; he calls them "unmixed" because they poured out undiluted wine. By this he indicated that before the time of mixing, wine diluted with water and superfluous additions were not used in sacred rites. As for the bowl (krater) where wine is said to have been mixed, the mixing there is not of water and wine but of two kinds of wine. The same author, on that line of Homer, writes that it was mixed [κεκρᾶσθαι] like wine.

units.la: ακουσετε ... Idem Od. Γ. συ ... Vinum Dei nysio libari sufficium, aequali aqua fuit permixtum, secundum Comicum: ut alibi explicatur: quae libatio diversa fuit ab Homericis libationibus, quas ακρητος, sive χαρητοσ appellat.
units.tr: Likewise, [Homer], in the Odyssey, says that wine was poured out for the god mixed with an equal amount of water, according to the comic poet, as is explained elsewhere. This libation was different from the Homeric libations, which he calls unmixed [ἀκρητος] or pure [χάρητος].

units.la: Apuleius libro quarto: Pollitum sermonis terminum poculis ... memoria defunc\u00adto ... communi onum vinum mero libantes: debinc canticis quibusdam Martidio blandiri ... Hinc nefas erat libare vino Graeca eulerur ... Ne ... nomen quoque sunt αξυοι, ubi Euαθυσ, se dubitare, num ibi libationes ... sunt intelligenda, hoc est ...
units.tr: Apuleius, in book four, writes: "After the conversation had ended with the cups, the memory of the dead being honoured, they poured out wine unmixed for the common good, and then tried to soothe the gods with certain songs..." Hence it was wrong to pour out wine by the Greek custom. [He also says] the words "unmixed" [ἀξυοι] ... where Euathus doubts whether libations are to be understood there, that is...

units.la: re siue menâce, ἀλλ τοῦ Διονύσιον κρᾶσθαι. Nam χαλκιν ajunt esse Dionysium, ex quo vinum meracum, unde etiam χαλκῶς mulier dicitur veteribus ἡ ὁποῖα ἀπὸ χαλκιδῶν τὸ ὄνομα. Hefychius, χαλκιςκτον & ἰωκρατον, hoc est, merum, siue meracum exponit; ut Suidas quoque χαλικρατον, spro μ κεκρασμένον in quodam Epigrammate. Scholiastes Apollonii Rhodii, χαλικρατον μίθυ, exponit nonmodo ἀκρατον, verum etiam χαλὰ τὰς φρεᾶς, subjungens Atheniensibus χαλκι dici το ἄκρατον. Apollonius χαλικρητον postea vocat ζοςον: libro primo Argonaut. Stephanus videtur χαλικνιον significare vinum meracum, alio meraco mixtum, ut aqua misceri solet, a κιρκάσσω, hoc est, miscendo, & χάλικ voce significante ἀκρᾶτον. Sic,ut paullo antea dictum est, Eustathius, quoties in libationibus sit mentio mixtionis vini, vult vinum alio vino, non autem aqua mixtum esse intelligendum. Aristophanes Scholiastes in illa Pluti,
units.tr: ...or with some admixture, but that Dionysus was mixed in. For they say that Dionysus is the god of the unmixed wine, whence wine unmixed is called "chalkos" by the ancients, from the word for the bronze vessels. Hesychius explains "chalikraton" and "iokraton" as meaning pure wine, or unmixed wine; Suidas likewise explains "chalikraton" as a mixed wine in a certain epigram. The scholiast on Apollonius of Rhodes explains "chalikraton" as not only unmixed but also strong, adding that the Athenians called unmixed wine "chalikon". Apollonius later calls "chalikreton" strong, in the first book of the Argonautica. Stephanus seems to mean by "chalikneion" unmixed wine mixed with other unmixed wine, as water is usually mixed with it, derived from a verb meaning to mix, and the word "chalix" signifying unmixed wine. Thus, as was said a little earlier, Eustathius holds that whenever mixing of wine is mentioned in libations, wine mixed with other wine, not water, must be understood. The scholiast on Aristophanes in that passage of the Plutus:

units.la: Οἴνοι δ᾽ ἀ λικ & ἰσοτίσω κατ ἀκρατ ρῆς.
units.tr: "But the wine ... mixed with pure wine..."

units.la: Addie, sirou & ἐ ἴσατο, hoc est, vino & aqua. ζωρότερον δὲ τὸ ζωρόν, χρῶμα. Alludit ad cau- ponas. Querit autem, cur alij Diis detur ἀκρατ ποτ ἡ ἀ, libatio meraca: Mercurio autem κεκραμένον, id est, mixta? Respondemus id fieri, quoniam Mercurius & vinum & mortuus τῷ σπευ ὰ dominatur, & ab ut rū, honores accipit.
units.tr: Add: "wine and water," that is, "with wine and water." The comparative "zorroteron" is from "zoron", meaning strong. He alludes to the tavern-keepers. He asks, moreover, why unmixed libation is given to other gods, but to Mercury a mixed one? We answer that this is done because Mercury rules both wine and the dead, and receives honours from both.

units.la: Observandum hic quoq; Veteres ex vino consecrato ad libationes, augurari solitos fuisse, quod divinationis genus ὀνομαντικα dictum est, ut Pencerus testatur. Homerus sepe meminit vini α' ἀ τ ἐν libationibus, de qua voce alibi. Atque illos quidem optimo sua vissimoque vino in libationibus usos fuisse, velex epitheti illis, quibus passim Homerus utitur, apparet: cujusmodi sunt, οἶνος, ὑδ ὑπερ ἀ, μελάνδας, ἡ, &c. Hæc de libationibus, quæ vino fieri consuevere.
units.tr: Here it should also be noted that the ancients were accustomed to take omens from the wine consecrated for libations; this kind of divination is called "oinomanteia", as Pencer attests. Homer often mentions wine in libations, a point discussed elsewhere. That the ancients used the finest and most pleasant wine in libations is clear from the epithets Homer uses throughout, such as "oinos", "hydros", "melas", and so on. These are the libations which were customarily made with wine.

units.la: Nunc de iis dicendum, in quibus non vinum, sed alii liquores, ut mulsum, aqua, mel, lac, oleum adhibebantur. Hujusmodi autem libationes atque sacrificia in Græcia ὑπαλία, ὀινοφ, ἀμο- ςυτα, speciatim υδῶρ σ ὀνόμα, μὴ ἀ ὀνόμα, χαλικτ ἀ ἀ ὁ suerunt dicta. ὑδῶρ ἀ ὁ ἀ, hoc est, libationes aquæ fuerunt illæ sociorum Ulyssis, quaiũ mentio fit Od. μ. Nam cum vino suissent destituti, aquam Soli libarunt, de quo sic Homerus,
units.tr: Now we must speak of those in which wine is not used but other liquids, such as mulsum (honeyed wine), water, honey, milk, or oil. Libations and sacrifices of this kind were called in Greek "hypalia", "oinophoroi"... and especially "hydor" ... Libations of water were those made by the companions of Ulysses, mentioned in Odyssey book ten. For, having run out of wine, they poured water to the sun, of which Homer speaks thus:

units.la: Οὐδ' ὀ ἄγον ἀξ ζ ἀ ἰ ἀ ἀ ἰ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ.
units.tr: "Nor did they ... " (the verse is garbled in the original and cannot be recovered).

units.la: Hinc Eustathius pro bordeis dicit usos fuisse quercus folijs: pro vino aqua, ἀπὸ ὀινῶν ἡ πιλαι ὀ ἑ ὡ ἑ ἑ, hoc est, ad recordationem pristini victus, qui constabat glandibus & aqua.
