units.tr: Hence Eustathius says that, instead of wine, they used water, with oak leaves for barley, in memory of their former diet, which consisted of acorns and water.

units.la: Idem Th.Z. Omnino libationes antiquitus mero celebrabantur: sit tamen quarundam libationum mentio, quæ plane fuerunt ἀοινοι, hoc est, vini expertes, ut libatio, quæ Soli fiebat melle. Idem Od.ν. ex Atheneo docet, Græcos Soli sacrificantes, solitos fuisse nel libare, vinum non infe- rentes altaribus. ἀ ὁ ὠ ὀ, ἀ, sed &c. Plutarchus Sympos. 4. ὑπαλία ταῦτα & υλίτωσ τῷ ὑ ὡ, id est, sacra sobria, & quæ mellu li- bamenta habent. Idem in libro περὶ ὄ ὀ: ἀ ὁ ν ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ. Hinc suta sacra usi. Hujusmodi erant Cereris sacra, de quibus primo in libro. In sacris siviliter Deæ Ruminæ inserre vinum expiatione dignum fuit: quippe illis sacrum sacientes bostie lac,non vinum inspergebant. Et in sacris Bonæ Deæ,cum vinum libabant, lac esse dicebant. Vestæ quoq; non vino, sed de Numico flumine,ut ait Servius, libabant, quibus diebus mense Iunio molæ frumentariæ & asini festis & pane coronabantur. Prodítum quoque memoriæ est, Romulum nunquam vino in sacris, sed latte libasse.
units.tr: Again, Eustathius: in general libations were celebrated with wine in ancient times; yet there is mention of certain libations which were entirely without wine, such as the libation made to the sun with honey. The same author, on the Odyssey, teaches from Athenaeus that the Greeks, sacrificing to the sun, used to pour libations without bringing wine to the altars. Plutarch, in the fourth book of the Symposiacs, calls these "sober sacrifices", which have honey offerings. The same author, in his book on ..., and hence they used sacred rites without wine. Of this kind were the rites of Ceres, of which he speaks in the first book. In the rites of the goddess Rumina, it was a crime to pour in wine, for in sacrifices to her they poured milk, not wine. And in the rites of the Good Goddess, when they poured libations, they said it was milk. The Vestals also poured not wine but water from the Numicus river, as Servius says, and on those days in June, mills, asses, and bread were garlanded. It is also recorded that Romulus never poured wine in sacrifices, but milk.

units.la: Quia etiam Athenienses Mnemosynæ, Aurorae, Soli, Lunæ, Vranie, Nymphis non vino, sed aqua, melle diluta, sacrificarunt, esse Suida. Pausanias tamen ait, Eleos thure cum tritico melle sibasio, addito ne ramis, aras suffire solitos et uti vino. Solus autem Nymphis, ὸ τοῖς ὅραι s ἀ , ἰ ὅ, ἀ τοῖς Cereri & Proserpine vinum minime libare consuevisse, nec ad aram omniū Deorum. Sunt & quibus sacrum Dionysio interdum, & Erechthei silaus exhibitum tradunt, ut testatur Philochorus. Plutarchus in libro de Sanitate: αὐτοὶ τοῦ Διονύσου πολλάκις ὑπαλία θύεται, ἰ ἂ ἱ ἀ ἀ ἀ. Silius Italicus lib.13. Punic. Corpora lanigerum procumbunt lecta bidentum, Fundunt mella super Bacchiq;, & lactis honorem.
units.tr: The Athenians, moreover, did not sacrifice to Mnemosyne, Aurora, the Sun, the Moon, Urania, or the Nymphs with wine, but with water mixed with honey, according to Suidas. Pausanias, however, says that the Eleans were accustomed to burn incense on altars with wheat and honey, adding branches, and to use wine. Only to the Nymphs ... it is said that wine was never poured for Ceres and Proserpina, nor at the altar of all the gods. There are also those who report that a sacrifice to Dionysus was sometimes offered without wine, and to Erechtheus a sacrifice of olive oil, as Philochorus attests. Plutarch, in his book on health, says that sacrifices to Dionysus were often offered without wine. Silius Italicus, in the thirteenth book of the Punica: "The bodies of the chosen two-year-old sheep fall down; they pour honey upon Bacchus and the honour of milk."

units.la: Ex his conflat, in libationibus sacrificiorum inferorum Antiquos, non vinum tantum, sed etiam mella, atq; lac in vergere fuisse solitos. Idem ex Virgilio conflat: tametsi in ferum vina Numa lege libare vetitum aliquando fuerit, juxta illud: Vino rogum ne aspergito. Oleo quoque nisi sint. Virgilius: Pinguè super oleum fundens ardentibus extis.
units.tr: From these it is clear that the ancients were accustomed to pour into libations for the lower gods not only wine but also honey and milk. The same is clear from Virgil, although at one time Numa's law forbade pouring wine on the funeral pyre, according to that line: "Do not sprinkle wine on the pyre." Oil also ... Virgil: "pouring rich oil over the burning entrails."
These things concern the matter of libations.
III. The rite of libations. The washing of hands.

units.la: NVNC de earum ritibus atq; cerimoniis varijs dicamus. Ac primo quidem cùm manuum ablutionem, tum etiam libationibus adhibitas fuisse, cùm ex aliis auctoribus, tum ex Homero satis conflat, ut In Z. Hector ad matrem: Χειρὶ Δ' ἀ·ίπ·ὸσιν ἀλ ἔ·βειν ἀ· ἔοπα ἴ. τεν Αἴ ἴουα ; ἰάν ἴ ἰσι κ ἑλα ιτ ἐ ᾗ κ ἐ ἔ ἴ ἴ ἴ ἰ
units.tr: Now let us speak of their various rites and ceremonies. First, that both the washing of hands and libations were employed is sufficiently clear, from other authors and from Homer, as in Iliad Z, where Hector tells his mother to wash her hands before offering the wine: "With hands washed clean, pour the bright wine to Zeus..."

units.la: Hîc utrumq; vides conjungi. Sic In I. antequam biberent.
units.tr: Here you see both joined together. So in Iliad I, before they drank.

units.la: Et Od. γ. nec non Od. ... eadem lotionis manuum, quæ ante libationem facta fuit, ... ut ille lib. 2. de op. & die.
units.tr: And in Odyssey γ, and in the same way as the washing of hands that was done before the libation, as that author says in book 2 of his Works and Days.

units.la: Apud Homerum patrisimum creberrima fit mentio hujusmodi precum in libationibus adhibitis.
units.tr: In Homer especially, mention is very frequent of prayers of this kind used in libations.

units.la: Apud Homerum patrisimum creberrima fit mentio hujusmodi precum in libationibus adhibita-rum, ut Il. I. inquit Nestor ad Graecos:
units.tr: Again, in Homer, where prayers are very frequently mentioned as used in libations, as in Iliad I, where Nestor speaks to the Greeks:

units.la: Sic Od. Γ. Lisistratus Nestoris filius, cùm Telemacho atq; Minervæ hospitibus partem vini & poculorum vini dedisset, Minervam his verbis alloquitur:
units.tr: Likewise in Odyssey Γ, when Lysistratus, son of Nestor, had given Telemachus and Minerva, his guests, a portion of wine and cups of wine, he addresses Minerva with these words:

units.la: Sequuntur postea preces, quas Minerva ad Neptunum fundit, quibus peractis, deinde Telemacho poculum tradidit, ut ille libaret simul. Sic Od. II. in fine.
units.tr: Prayers follow, which Minerva pours out to Neptune. When these were finished, she handed the cup to Telemachus so that he too might libate. So Odyssey II at the end.

units.la: Virgil. lib. 4. Georg. describit con vivium magnificum, quo Cyrene filium loco festivo excepit, libationi quoq; memoriæ verbis: —Panchæa adolescunt ignibus aræ, hoc est, thure aræ illato. Et matur, Cape Mæonii Carchedia Bacchi Oceano libemus, ait.
units.tr: Virgil in Georgics book 4 describes a magnificent banquet at which Cyrene received her son in a festive place, and mentions the libation in these words: "Panchaean altars blaze with fires", that is, the altar is loaded with incense. And again: "Take the Maeonian wine of Bacchus, let us pour it to Ocean," he says.

units.la: Idem, Hoc Carchedio vinum præstantissimum in honorem Oceani libemus, & in hanc aram sacrum sacrificium defundamus. —Simul ipsa precatur Oceanumq; patrem rerum, Nymphasq; sorores Centum, quæ fyl vas, centum quæ flumina serrant.
units.tr: Again: "We pour this excellent Carchedonian wine in honour of Ocean, and pour out a holy sacrifice on this altar." "And at the same time she herself prays to Ocean, father of all things, and to the sister Nymphs, a hundred who guard the groves and a hundred who guard the rivers."

units.la: En preces quas fundunt ad Oceanum, ac Nymphas sorores, quibus aut fyl varum & rivorum credia aut fluviorum & aquarum cura commissa erat. Sequitur ipse libationis allum. Ter liquido ardentem perfudit nectare Vestam:
units.tr: Behold the prayers they pour out to Ocean and the sister Nymphs, to whom was entrusted either the care of groves, springs and streams, or of rivers and waters. Then follows the libation itself: "Three times she poured clear nectar over the burning Vesta."

units.la: Idem, Ter vinum ardenti foco asperserat. Sequitur omen: unde πυεμαντια: Ter flamma ad summum tecti subiecta reluxit. Omine quo firmans animum, sic incipit ipsa.
units.tr: Again: "Three times she had sprinkled wine on the burning hearth." Then follows the omen, whence the art of divination: "Three times the flame, rising, flashed up to the top of the roof." Strengthening her spirit by this omen, she begins thus.

units.la: Idem, Ter flamma ad summum conclavis tectum ferebatur, ibi relucebat. Unde bono omine capto animo, confirmato Cyrene, sic ad filium loqui incipit. Virgil. in Aeneid. In menfani laeti libant, Diuosq; precantur.
units.tr: Again: "Three times a flame was carried up to the top of the chamber's roof, and there it shone." Whence, having taken the omen with a good heart, and Cyrene's spirit being confirmed, she begins to speak thus to her son. Virgil in the Aeneid: "Joyfully they pour libations on the tables and call upon the gods."

units.la: Sic libans Dido in conuiuio precatur: Iuppiter, hospitibus nam te dare iura loquuntur. Et apud Horat. Et alteris, te mensis (mensa fecunda, in qua solet libatio fieri et Deorum precatio) adhibeo Deum:
units.tr: So Dido, pouring a libation at the banquet, prays: "Jupiter, for they say that you give laws to guests." And in Horace: "and I call upon the god at the table" (the fruitful table, at which libation and the invocation of the gods are usually made):

units.la: Idem, Te ut Deum obsecrant, et tibi ut Laribus libant, Iteq; mox libatio sequitur. Te multa prece, te prosequitur nero, Defuso paterus.
units.tr: Again: "they pray to you as to a god, and pour libations to you as to the Lares; and soon after the libation follows. With much prayer they follow you, with the cup poured out."

units.la: Quoniam autem in sacris hujusmodi libationibus voce, morosa et cunctabunda usi sunt, hinc Σπονδαιος, boc est, sfundens pes dictus est, consistans duabus syllabis longis, quod ex tali pes dictus ex ri ορουδαισεις ινοιοντο αρξεσθαι ... teste Hephaest. Schol. Arnobius de tu libationis.
units.tr: Since in such sacred libations they used a slow and lingering voice, the spondaic foot was therefore named from pouring, consisting of two long syllables. The foot is so named from this, as the scholiast on Hephaestion testifies; Arnobius also speaks of the libation.

units.la: Sacrificiis verba facienti, operaepretium, inquit, est etiam verba ipsa depromere, quibus cum vinum datur, (id est, libatur) uti, ac supplicare consuetudo fuit.
units.tr: When speaking of sacrifices, he says, it is worth while to bring out also the very words with which wine is given, that is, poured out, and by which it was customary to pray.
Here there is nothing about wine poured out for the gods below.

units.la: Inferio, inquit Trebatius, verbum ex cuius additum eadem ratione profertur, ne vinum omne ominio, quod in cellis et Apothecis est conditum, ex quibus illud, quod effunditur, promptum est esse sacrum incipiat, et ubibus eripiatur hunianis. Additio ergo hoc verbo, solum erit, quod infertur sacrum, nec religione obligabitur, ut inferiuni videlicet viuum dicatur sacrum, quod Diuus inferunt vinum infer-fercur. Et hac de manuum ablutione et precibus verbis conceptis ec sacris, quibus clim libantes rium quid usi fuerunt.
units.tr: "Inferio," says Trebatius, is a word added on the same principle, so that all the wine stored in cellars and pantries, from which what is poured out is taken, should not begin to be sacred and be snatched from human use. The addition of this word therefore means only that what is poured below is sacred and not bound by religion; so that wine poured for the gods below is called sacred. And so much for the washing of hands and for the prayers, the words and sacred formulas which libating men at times used.

units.la: Nunc ut reliquos libationum ritus atq; cerimonias persequar, primo quidem muniftri seufa-muli (qui idcirco distli sunt αρχεδαφοι) libamina, hoc est, liquores, quibus libabatur (incer liquorum, quos praecipuum erat vinum) afferebant usque craterasq; ad summum implebant (quod Homero est ... Virgil. coronare, de quo alibi) quos deinde in medio collocabant. Hinc sepe Homerus, Κωσι ... Od. I. Iuuenes autem crateres coronarunt vino. Item, Collocarunc crateres coronatos vino. Od. B. sub finem. Libabant autem immortalibus Diis sempiternis.
units.tr: Now, to pursue the remaining rites and ceremonies of libations: first, the ministers, the cupbearers (who for this reason were called archedapoi), brought the libamina, that is, the liquids with which one libated (of liquids, the chief was wine), and filled the kraters right up to the brim (as Homer has it; Virgil speaks of crowning them, which I shall discuss elsewhere), and then set them down in the middle. Hence Homer often says: "The young men crowned the kraters with wine" (Odyssey I). Also: "They set down the kraters crowned with wine" (Odyssey B, near the end). And they libated to the immortal, everlasting gods.

units.la: Athenaeus lib. 14. Cyacho enim tunc non utebantur, neq; cotyla, sed cratera Diis flatuebant non argenteum, neq; lapillis disiiniectum, sed ex terra coctae: hunc quoties imple riffent, libantes Diis ex phiala vinum possea fundebant, cymbio nuper mysium tingentes, ut etiam nunc apud nos in Phiditis fieri solet, Plutarchus Polic. praecepta. Τὸ κρατῆρ ἀγκεμαπυς ὅπ ταῖς αποσλαῖς.
units.tr: Athenaeus, book 14: For they then did not use a cyathus or a cotyle, but set up a krater for the gods, not of silver nor adorned with jewels, but made of baked earth. Whenever they had filled it, they poured out the wine from a phiale as a libation to the gods, dipping a cymbium in the mixture, as is still customary among us in the Phiditia, as Plutarch says in the Precepts of Politics. The krater...

units.la: Hic quoque usitata fuit vini mixtio, cuius sepe apud Homerum fit mentio, non cum aqua (non enim licebat antiquitus Diis vinum aqua dilucum dare, sive libare) sed cum alio vino miscere, de quo supra.
units.tr: Here too the customary mixing of wine was used, of which Homer often speaks. It was not with water (for it was not allowed in antiquity to give or pour undiluted wine to the gods, nor to pour it mixed with water), but with other wine, as stated above.

units.la: Ex crateri porro deinde vina in minora pocula infundebant, quae Homerus οἰνοχοαι fere vocat aureas: ex quibus deinceps pars vini effundebatur. Homerus lx. K. in fine. Liquorum infusio in pocula minora. Σπονδ. Αθλων.
units.tr: From the krater they then poured the wines into smaller cups, which Homer mostly calls golden oenochoai; from these a part of the wine was then poured out. Homer, near the end of book K. Pouring of the liquids into the smaller cups.

units.la: Πλάτω ... Hoc est, ex crater pleno haurientes, scilicet in minora pocula, libabant mellitum vinum. Eu-stach. Od. θ.
units.tr: Plato... that is, drawing from the full krater, namely into smaller cups, they libated honeyed wine. Eustathius on Odyssey θ.
And a two-handled cup, a double cup...

units.la: Αἴπος Hesych. ... Et Athen. lib. 1. ... rium, Od. θ.
units.tr: Hesychius, Aipos... and Athenaeus, book 1... in Odyssey θ.

units.la: Ω ( Ylyβii) ... Ἀλκίνοος ... Homerus quod nominat ...
units.tr: Homer names... Alcinous...

units.la: Εἶς ἀλεισον & Suidae ... Hesychio poculum ... Euftathio ... Athen. lib. ... ex Clearcho ... Pollux libro 10. ... ἀλλοτι ...
units.tr: Into the aleison... and Suidas... Hesychius, a cup... Eustathius... Athenaeus... from Clearchus... Pollux, book 10... another...
Virgil: "We libate with bowls and gold."

units.la: Patera, inquit Harro, dicta, quia pateant: quibus etiam nunc in publico con vivio antiquitus ... fiunt potio circumfertur: & in sacris ... ita hoc poculum appellatur.
units.tr: Harro says the patera is so called because it lies open (pateant), and with it even now the drink is passed round at public banquets, and in sacred rites... and thus this cup is so named.

units.la: Et Vaticano fugi es de monte patellas.
units.tr: And "from the Vatican hill, the dishes."

units.la: Arnobius similiter de Libus verba faciens: Date quaeso, inquit per Iovem ... Sympuvium ... Epicharis ... Pausanias populo Rom. ... Athenaeus ... Sympuvium fuit vocatum.
units.tr: Arnobius, likewise speaking of libations: "Give, I beg you, he says, through Jupiter..." The sympulium... Epicharis... Pausanias to the Roman people... Athenaeus... The sympulium was so called.

units.la: Sympuvium videre Numae, ni rumq; caeteris. Sed hoc quoq; suprá dictum Varro inter vasa vinaria ... numerat ut etiam Guttum, aguttis ... Sympulum nomina verum.
units.tr: Varro, among the wine vessels, lists the sympulium, the guttus and the others. The names are truly given.

units.la: Porro libationis unus quidem quasi praesultor videtur fuisse, qui deinceps singulis ex ordine pocula dedit plena vini ad libandum ... Homeri locis videtur posse colligi, ut Od. Γ. fere ab initio: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ... ἐξέτα Δὸς καὶ τῷ ... οἶνο.
units.tr: Moreover, one of them seems to have been a kind of leader of the libation, who in turn handed each of them a cup full of wine to libate. This can be gathered from the passages of Homer, as in Odyssey Γ near the beginning: "But when... pour out a libation... wine."
To pour out (Greek σπένδειν).

units.la: Hic Pisistratus jubet Telemachum, postquam ipse libaris, alteri quoque poculum ... similiter libet. Vel etiam famulis singulis pocula vini plena dederunt, ex quibus libarent. Hinc appellatur illud occurrit apud Homerum:
units.tr: Here Pisistratus bids Telemachus, after he himself has libated, to hand the cup to the other also, who likewise libates. Or they gave each of the attendants a full cup of wine from which to libate. Hence that name occurs in Homer:

units.la: Νόωνδεας ... Hesychio ... Sic Od. θ. Alcinous ad Pontonoum,
units.tr: Hesychius... So in Odyssey θ, Alcinous to Pontonous:
"All..." "Having drunk..."
Epicharis... Epichysis and ejathus.

units.la: Expaní posƐ Potonous hoc[?] mandatum sic dicitur fuisse exsecutus.
units.tr: Pontonous, having executed this command, is said to have done so.
Pontos... honeyed...
"He distributed the cups to all."

units.la: Notabis verbum κεραννύω, siue χεῖσαι, significare non modo miscere, sed etiam infundere vi-num, ut multis in locis Eustath. annotat.
units.tr: Note that the verb kerannymi, or cheo, signifies not only to mix but also to pour in wine, as Eustathius notes in many places.

units.la: Vinum porrigitur antequam sundebat sacerdos in sacra (aut vdixes inde hujusmodi sacrorum dona vocantur, οἶνος σπονδας χοῖες, Hesychius sprius simpuliogneo propinabat, vel si-quod etiam ἱερον vinum vocatum est. Portio siue guttæ vini aut cuiuscunque alterius liquoris, quæ inter libandum et pateris fundebatur, a Græcis σπονδαὶ s*ὰ, hoc ἐ[?]stillalibatio stia dicta est.
units.tr: Wine was poured out before the priest drank in the sacred rites. Hence such offerings are called in Greek libations [σπονδαί], and Hesychius says the priest made the libation with a ladle. Any portion or drop of wine, or of some other liquid, poured out between the drinking and the cups, which the Greeks called spondai, was called a libation of drops.

units.la: Hæc ipsa autem effusio varia fuit & multiplex. Et ut olim in veteri Testamento, quemadmodum coustat ex 25. & 30. Exod. Num. 28. vinum libari, hoc est, effundi cousueuit super omnes victimas: ita Ethnici quoq; in suis sacrificiis huiusmodi vini super victimas effusionibus plerunq; nisi fuerunt. At primo quidem vinum inter cornua hostiæ, antequam illa esset mactata, spargere solebant. Vnde Virg. lib. 4. Aeneid, Ipsa tenens dextra pateram pulcherrima Dido, Candentis vaccæ media inter cornua fundit.
units.tr: This pouring out was itself varied and manifold. As in the Old Testament, as is clear from Exodus 25 and 30 and Numbers 28, wine was poured out, that is, offered as a libation, over all the victims, so the Gentiles also, in their sacrifices, mostly poured out wine of this kind over their victims. But first they used to sprinkle the wine between the horns of the victim before it was slain. Hence Virgil, Aeneid book 4: "Dido herself, the most beautiful, holding the cup in her right hand, pours it out between the horns of the white heifer."

units.la: Ibi Seruius: Non est, inquit, sacrificium, sed hostiæ exploratio, utrum apta sit. Item Aeneid. 6. Quatuor hic primum nigrantes terga iuvencos Constituit, frontiq; in vertgit vina sacerdos.
units.tr: There Servius says: "This is not a sacrifice, but a test of whether the victim is fit." Likewise in Aeneid 6: "Here the priest first sets four black bullocks, and pours wine on their foreheads."

units.la: Seruius in illum locum, in Quarto: —Medias inter cornua fundit,
units.tr: Servius on that passage, on book 4: "He pours it between the horns."

units.la: Et fundere est iupina manu illud scire quod fit in sacris supernis: Vergere autem est conversa in si-nistram partem. Ut si fundere, ut partem in vertatur quod inferius est. (Notabis diversos libandi gestus, Vergere.
units.tr: To pour is to do this with the hand turned upward, as is done in the upper rites; but to turn (vergere) is to pour with the hand turned to the left side. As when one pours so that the part lower down is turned. (Note the different gestures of libation, the turning.)

units.la: Plutarchus de Oraculis: ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τοῖς ἐκτὸς ἀπολυθεὶς. Est autem pertinens ad victimarum explorationem, ut si nou lupuerint, apte probentur. Plutarchus de Oraculis: ἐκεῖ semper ὁ σπονδὸς ... Hoc est, nec Verbum, causae pilorumque Vest. Rus. in Plutarchus eodem in ... Ex his ergo colligitur, hostiam primo fuisse vino aliquo super perfusam, ut probaretur. Hinc Ovid. testimonia Fast. 1. Rode caper vitem, tamen hinc cum stabit ad aram, In tua quod sparsi cornua post erit. Vera s de sequitur s Veri nec est in si dedicus hostis, Sparsa s s a s Veri nunc cornua Bacche mero.
units.tr: Plutarch, On the Oracles: "but being released outside..." This pertains to the examination of victims, so that if they do not shake, they are approved as fit. Plutarch, On the Oracles: "there the libationer always..." That is, neither the word nor the cause... Varro in Plutarch, in the same place... From these things, therefore, it is gathered that the victim was first sprinkled over with some wine, so that it might be tested. Hence Ovid, Fasti 1: "Gnaw the vine, goat; yet when you stand by the altar, the horns on which I sprinkled wine will be yours." And from this follows the true...; the horns of the victim are now sprinkled with wine, O Bacchus.

units.la: Deinde super exta alia s s partes hostiæ in iguem conjectat, vina fundere confuserunt.
units.tr: Then, over the entrails and the other parts of the victim, which he casts into the fire, they agreed to pour wine.
Hence Homer, Iliad book 9:
Greek verses, of which only fragments survive: wine...

units.la: Et ... Οὐδ' ... ἐπ' ... Cui seile illud Virgilii de sacrif. 10. Et solida imponit tauroꝛum viscera flammis, Pingue super oleum fundent ardentibus exta.
units.tr: And the verse of Virgil on sacrifice, book 10: "And he places the solid entrails of the bulls on the flames, and they pour fat oil over the burning entrails."
So Apollonius, Argonautica: "the unmixed..."

units.la: Scilicet super s mora, quæ paullo ante dixerat fuisse concremata. Hinc Ioban. Grammat. in Hesiodum libatio ... nem definit vini effusionem in id, quod immolatur.
units.tr: Namely, over the fire, which he had said a little before had been burned up. Hence John the Grammarian, on Hesiod, defines libation as the pouring of wine upon that which is sacrificed.

units.la: Aliter s ext s puta sacrificta, vinum in bunum effundebant, secundum illud Homeri Ἰλιαδ', n. sub s em. Οὐ τον δ' ἐκ ἀπιῶν χαμάδις λάον,ἀλλ' ὅτι ὅ[?] ... [illegible, ~20 letters] Πεῖν πίει', σφὶν λάλα ... [illegible, ~20 letters] Et Virg. Aeneid. lib. 6. Hic duo riuë mero libans carchesia Baccho, Fundit humi.
units.tr: In another way, when they sacrificed on the ground, they poured wine onto the earth, according to that line of Homer in the Iliad: "Not drinking, he threw himself down on the ground..." [partly illegible]. And Virgil, Aeneid book 6: "Here he, pouring a libation from two bowls of pure wine, pours it onto the ground."

units.la: Apud Virgilium Aeneid. lib. 5. et exta, et vina in mare spiciuntur: Stans procul in puppi (Aeneas) pateram tenet, extaq; salso Porricit in fluctus, ac vina liquentia fundit. Ieem, —Extaq; fluctus Porriciam in fluctus, et vina liquentia fundam.
units.tr: In Virgil, Aeneid book 5, the entrails and the wine are cast into the sea: "Aeneas, standing far off on the stern, holds the bowl, and casts the entrails into the salt waves and pours out the liquid wine." Again: "I will cast the entrails into the waves and pour the liquid wine."

units.la: Apud eundem quoq; lerter virti. Sub iudex pate a defundebant in mensa mit. Dixit, et in mensa lacticum libavit honores Ieem, In mensam laticis, Diuos, precantur
units.tr: In the same author, likewise, the bowls were poured out on the table: "He spoke, and poured libation of honey-sweet wine on the table." Again: "They pray to the gods, pouring on the table..."

units.la: Sed operæ pretium est Arnobii verba hic subjicere, qui Rivebujusmodi ... de hac re ... ordo tamen, nec cur id
units.tr: But it is worth while to add here the words of Arnobius, who, speaking of this kind of thing... Nevertheless the order, and why this is done...

units.la: bis simul, et irridet: Nerum, inquit, thuris est, quoque explanarium est. Sed, cur id superfundatur incensioni? Si enim vatio, cur fiat, non ostenderetur, nec haberent ... ausam, non illud jam erroris objiciendum est ludicro, sed (ut dicatur expresse) ... cecitati. Vt enim jam ... dicium est, debent omnes quod geritur, caussa ... nec caliginis alicuius objici ... conte'tam. Si ergo fidius ... [illegible, ~30 letters]

For, as has already been said, everything that is done ought to have a cause... nor should any darkness of some kind be objected... If, indeed..." [partly illegible]

IV. The manifold use of libations.

units.tr: Now, last of all, let us add some things about the varied and manifold use of libations. First, ... chapter 17.

units.tr: Next, libations were most customary at the seats (of the diners). Hence also among the Greeks ... "Sacraments sanctioned by a libation of wine, and give right hands." Hellenica 3.

units.la: In exequiis quoque libationes multiplices adhibitas fuisse libro primo ostendsum est in tit. de Conviviis funeralibus.
units.tr: Multiple libations were also used at funerals, as was shown in the first book, in the title on funeral banquets.

units.la: Denique in conviviis cum sacrificialibus, hoc est, in quae sacra facta sunt, tum etiam in aliis omnibus libationes ꝑ solitas fuisse, passim ex auctoribus colligitur. Præcipua exempla in Alexandro magno, & Macedonibus. Nam Alexander M. dicitur, quod inter Persas & Macedonas exarserat, compositas quo Dijs gratias ageret, sacrificio facto, cum vinum poposcit, [illegible, ~10 letters] Macedones accubuere, deinceps Persae ... eosque, ut vsitatum erat, dispersi ...
units.tr: Finally, it is gathered from authors everywhere that libations were customary at banquets, both sacrificial ones, that is, those at which sacred rites were performed, and all others. The chief examples concern Alexander the Great and the Macedonians. For Alexander the Great, when the quarrel that had flared up between the Persians and the Macedonians had been settled, is said to have arranged a feast to give thanks to the gods. After the sacrifice was made, he called for wine, ... the Macedonians reclined, and then the Persians ... and, as was customary, they were scattered ...

units.la: Τῶν ὀνομάτων ... Apud Homerum etiam pro ... Ἐν μ ... Et Achilles ... Unde apud Virgilium Dido: Dixit, & in mensa lætitiam ... Et alibi, In mensa lœti libant, Diuini precantur.
units.tr: Greek word ... Also in Homer, pro ... And Achilles ... Hence in Virgil Dido: "She spoke, and at the table joy ..." And elsewhere: "At the table the cheerful pour libations; they pray to the gods."

units.la: Sed ... Ser ... privatim Romanos legimus apud Dionem Cassium, qui inter alios honores Augusto decreta, in conviviis,
units.tr: But ... we read that the Romans in private (made libations), in Dio Cassius, who among the other honours decreed for Augustus (had them) at banquets,
V. The time of libations.

units.la: Ἀλλ' ἄγε (inquit Minerva ad Nestorem) τάμωμεν μὴ γλώσσας ...
units.tr: "Come then," said Minerva to Nestor, "let us cut the tongues ..." [Greek]

units.la: V. Libationum tempus, quo potissimum vti debeat.
units.tr: V. The time of libations, which ought to be used especially.

units.la: Κούοσι ἡ κρητῆρας ἐπεςιλασ̈λο ποτοῖο. Νώυνσαε δ' ἀρχ πάσι ἱπαρξαμένοισ ἀπιπασιν Γλώσσας δ' ἐν τυσὶ βάλλοι, ἀλεξιμόρος δ' ἰπίλλξεοι, idest.
units.tr: They mixed the bowls and poured the wine to each one, and when they had made the first libations and drunk as much as their hearts desired, they threw the tongues into the fire, and rose to their feet. [Homer, Od. 3, garbled Greek]

units.la: Sed agite di vidite quidem linguas, miscete vinum, Vt Neptuno & aliis immortalibus Vt biliba verimus, lectum curemus: ejus enim hora adest, jam enim lumen vit sub occasum, neq; decet Diu Deorum in epulo sedere, sed redire Dixit sane jovis filia, hi vero audi verunt locutam. His quidem praecones aquam manibus infuderunt, juvenes autem craterem coronarunt vino. Diviserunt autem omnibus, mitium sumentes a poculis. Linguas in ignem conjecerunt, surgentesq; illi arunt.
units.tr: "But come, divide the tongues, mix the wine, so that we may pour to Neptune and the other immortals, and then attend to our rest, for the hour is at hand; the light has already sunk toward evening, and it is not fitting to sit long at the feast of the gods, but to go home." The daughter of Jove spoke, and they heard her speaking. Heralds poured water over their hands, and young men crowned the mixing bowl with wine, and distributed it to all, first pouring from the cups. They threw the tongues into the fire, and rising, poured libations. [Latin rendering of Homer]

units.la: Hinc Athenaeus lib. v. Libabant enim e coenis discedentes, quae libationes Mercurio vocabant, non autem, ut postea, Iovi τελείῳ perfecto, sive adulto. Mercurius enim, τῶν ἀγεσσόνιος etiam, idest, somno videtur praesse. Libanae etiam side linguas a coena discedentes, eo quod linguae ... cum Deorum, hominumq; interpreti atq; internuntio tribuuntur. Eustathius eadem de re in verbis Homeri paulo ante allegatos, eleganter sane hunc in modum disserit: quae quia vetilia simul sunt & jucunda lectu, subjiciam. His verbis,
units.tr: Hence Athenaeus, book 5. For they made libations when leaving dinners, which they called libations to Mercury, not, as later, to Jupiter Teleios, that is, perfect or grown. For Mercury, the messenger of the gods, is also thought to preside over sleep. They also offered tongues when leaving dinner, because tongues are attributed to Mercury as interpreter and go-between of gods and men. Eustathius, treating the same matter in the words of Homer quoted a little earlier, argues elegantly in this way; since these are both useful and pleasant to read, I shall add them. In these words:
"Divide the tongues, mix the wine," etc.

units.la: Homerus antiquam consuetudinem indicat. Veteres enim post sacrificium cubitum se receperunt vitilimarum prius linguas sacrificabant, illas in ignem conjicientes: idq; de Ionum, sive Aeoliūm more. Hac Eustathius ius. Cur autem illas dederint atq; confecerint Diis, copiose supra d est exeodem: quibus adde quod ea quoq; decaulla sacrificabantur linguae, ut in ... sed fer vetur idem solum, quod in illa est optimum, ut de illa, cum ... tem velinante, propter mi iorum hominum ... ... tiam cubit, gorsari merito posit. Is autem fuit, quibus ... cherrimum linguam mi it: deinde rursus interrorasus, quod nomin ... imis et determinu, ... rum guam mit. Hoc ... possit carevolunt, multi ... prode et obe ... ... esset ... gladius ... ceps, controversiam vim labent, nimirum & nocend, ... ... modandi. (Hic similiter sunt, quae hac lus ... rabant sub vesperam, ut supra quod dictum, ceu iam tacituri, & loquam, ceu d posseit cu ... dium: & idcirco illas Mercurio dedicabant, ceu λόγου δοτῆρες hoc est ... datori sermonis. Forte etiam, ut omni... loquacitate, ... sed garrulitate liberarentur ... ... ... ... ... et ... ... ... ...
units.tr: Homer indicates an ancient custom. For the ancients, after the sacrifice, withdrew to bed; they first sacrificed the tongues of the victims, casting them into the fire, and this was according to the custom of the Ionians or Aeolians. Thus far Eustathius. Why they gave and burned these to the gods has been discussed fully above in the same place; to these add that tongues were also sacrificed ... [garbled] ... Here likewise are those things which were sacrificed toward evening, as was said above, as if about to be silent and about to speak; and therefore they dedicated them to Mercury, as givers of speech (logou dotēres), that is, giver of speech. Perhaps also, that they might be freed from every ... loquacity, but from garrulity ...

units.la: Vt pra ... ... ... ... ... ... Mercurius ... ... ... potabilis, quo Dipnosophista, qui dicit Epulas esse ... ... genus potionis apud Stratidem. Et paulo post: Praeter haec fuiendum iosecrat ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ... ut bona audirent, quibus profere dus lingua ... Mercurio autem illas sacrificabant, ... ... ... ... ... ... cui sermonis praesidi. Unde Comicus Mercurio Iuγαπα... ... ... ... quod perinde est, ac si diceret, & ruftra linguae sacrificantur ... Aristophanes in Pace,
units.tr: ... as Mercury ... drinkable, which the Deipnosophist, who says the feasts are ... a kind of drink, with Stratis. And a little later: Besides these ... that they might hear good things, by which the tongue ... But they sacrificed those to Mercury, ... to whom the guardianship of speech belongs. Hence the comic poet, Mercury ... which amounts to the same as saying that tongues are sacrificed in vain ... Aristophanes in Peace,

units.la: Interpres admonet pro ... ... ... dictum, Sumptum autem ex Homero Od. γ.

units.la: Epist Eiusq; sententia Caelestratum esse auctorem. Rursum in Pluto, ὁ λωτὸς τὸ κηρυκεῖον τῶν τῷ τι-μωλλαι, id est, Praecombus horum praetidi solet. Callisthratus: ut essent interpres, tradit olim in sacerdotium linguam exeitam praeconibus dari solitam. Nam aliquando iunt qui dicant, ex rivimus Mercurio deberi linguam. Est autem in Aristophanis verbis ἀκαταξθῶνε non infacete, qualitergua utrolibet referri poterit, vel ad boves, vel praecones. Interpres admonet alium esse ad proverbiale dictum, ὁ λωτὸς τοῦ κηρυκος, Lingua praeconi. Quo recte videbimur ujus: , cum praemisi nonnihil debere fieri, sacrificiis, qui incensiendo, ne ostio profisa ... ad umeros fuit, aut ... ὁ λωτὸς δ' πεδ. Dictum erat eodem nunciantis. Sic enim vocat Homerus mercedulam, quae ausi conjungi vi letum adferentibus nuntium. Apud Plutarchum Antigonem, ut incidisse ... tu enim de Demade iam senio imperii fra ... Velut, inquit, ex immolatis vitulas, sed rex ... ua superesti. Apparet lingnam, ceu prophetarum membrum sacrificu ... tacus Amasidi regi mittit et vitulam linguam, ut membrum pescumus, ... sayant. Praecones autem linguam habent venalem, et in sacrificiis adnonebant aut populum ut ... ... favent. Plautus in Prologo Poenuli,
units.tr: Epistle; and its meaning, Callistratus is the author. Again in Plutus, "the tongue is the herald's portion among the ...," that is, the herald of these is usually ... Callistratus records that the tongue of the sacrificial victim was once customarily given to the heralds, that they might be interpreters. For some say that the tongue is owed to Mercury, since he is the messenger. In the words of Aristophanes, "ἀκαταξθῶνε," the phrase may not be unhappily referred either to the oxen or to the heralds. The commentator warns that there is another proverbial saying, "the tongue of the herald," a tongue for the herald. By which we shall rightly be guided, since it has been said before that something ought to be done at sacrifices ... to the shoulders ... "the tongue of the herald" was said of the same ... For Homer calls the little reward which was added to those bringing the news of joy the messenger's portion. In Plutarch, Antigonus, when ... for Demades, now old in rule ... "Just as," he says, "from the sacrificed calves," but the king ... the tongue remains. It appears that the tongue, as the member of the prophets sacrificed ..., Amasis the king sends the calf's tongue, as the member we ..., they say. The heralds, however, have a tongue for sale, and at sacrifices they warn the people to ... be favourable. Plautus in the prologue of the Poenulus:

units.la: Exerte votem per euam vivis et coles, Nam uti clamabo, Latim, e obstum fomes.
units.tr: "Stretch out your voice through the ears of the living and attend, for as I shout, ... Latin ..., the ..."

units.tr: These things Erasmus has in his Adages. Erasmus added ...

units.la: Obser vandum etiam praeter libationem poti ... ... ... ... pocultum, ut Aelius Dionysius tradit, ... ... ... ... remotis mensis proserebatur, de quo infra. Hac Eusebius de libationibus vitus, quae post epulas olim fieri consueverunt, Horatius, Et venerata Ceres, ut culmo surgeret alto, Explicuit vino contractam ferit fronte.
units.tr: It is also to be observed that, besides the libation of drink, ... the cup, as Aelius Dionysius records, ... was brought forth with the tables removed, of which below. Thus Eusebius on libations of wine, which were customarily performed after feasts. Horace: "And venerated Ceres, that the grain might rise on a tall stalk, unfolded her brow, contracted with wine."

units.la: In quae verba Turnebus in suis Adversariis, jugum ... ... ... ... in honorem Cereris, venerantes praesentes, fundebant, ... ... ... cum fuisse convivium veneratum Cererem, vinum posse canam bibisse, et contractam frontes ... ... ... ... Apollonium in Argonautica.
units.tr: On these words Turnebus, in his Adversaria, says ... in honour of Ceres, the guests venerating her, poured out ... that the banquet had venerated Ceres, and the guests had drunk wine ... and their brows were contracted ... Apollonius in the Argonautica.
Nor is there ... [Οὐδ' ἔσθ' ...]

units.la: De Argonautis convivium sacrorum Apollinis celebrantibus. De his sic Scholiastes, ... ... ... hoc est, si fas est. Quoniam, inquit, mos erat veterum, ut dormituri craterem miscerent, et hospitarum linguas Mercurio sacrificarent, vinumque libarent, idque forsan naturali quadam ratione dictum. Nam quoniam Mercurius sermo esse dicitur, alius autem instrumentum est linguae, quae somno irruente quiescit, idcirco meritò illam Mercurio immolant. Directe hidas autem in Megara ut ... ... litteris memoriae prodidit. Alcathus Pelopis filius, ob Chrysippi caedem, Megara pulsus in exilium, in aliam quandam urbem se retulit. Is cum incidisset in leonem quendam, qui Megaram depopulabatur, ad versus quem etiam alia a rege Megarensium missi fucraut, illum prosternit, siusq; lingua supra rogum posita, Megaram rediit. Cum vero illi, qui ad Κνανdum missi fuerant, a se profratam illam feram esse diceren[t], allata pera illos mendacii coarguit. Quamobrem rex Dius sacra faciens, postremo linguam altaris impositam: unde mos ille ... gara semper permansit. Philoborus autem in lib. de Sacrificiis hanc affert causam, quod lingua optima sit & princeps pars corporis: & Homerus, ἀλλ' ἀγα τὰ μετὰ λόγους, pro πάντα τοὺς λόγους, dixit Hesiodus:
units.tr: On the Argonauts celebrating a feast in honour of Apollo. The Scholiast says of these things: "... that is, if it is lawful. Since, he says, it was the custom of the ancients, when they were about to sleep, to mix a bowl and to offer the tongues of their guests to Mercury, and to pour a libation of wine; and perhaps this was said on some natural principle. For since Mercury is said to be speech, and the tongue is the instrument of speech, which rests when sleep comes on, they rightly offer it to Mercury." Moreover, Hidas ... in Megara, as ... has handed down in writing. Alcathous, son of Pelops, driven from Megara into exile for the killing of Chrysippus, withdrew to another city. When he had met a certain lion that was laying waste Megara, against which other men had also been sent by the king of the Megarians, he struck it down, and, placing its tongue upon the pyre, returned to Megara. When those who had been sent to Cnossus said that they themselves had slain the beast, he refuted them by producing the pouch ... Therefore King Dius, when sacrificing, at last placed the tongue upon the altar; whence that custom ... has always remained. Philoborus, in his book On Sacrifices, gives this reason: that the tongue is the best and chief part of the body. And Homer [says] "but all else after words," meaning "all the words"; Hesiod said:

units.la: Ἄλλοτε δ' ἂ αὐτοῦ δ' ἡς ἔνθεν ... ἱλά... Ἡ μὲν τὸ· ὑπὸ ζώη ... ἱερὸν ἐλθῆ.
units.tr: "At other times ... [Ἄλλοτε δ' ... ἱερὸν ἐλθῆ.]" (the verse is garbled in the scan; the sense is a line of Hesiod about the time of the rite, which cannot be recovered with certainty)

units.la: Obseruabis hic cum tempus duplex, quo libationibus atq; sacrificiis operam dabant, matutinum nimirum atq; vesperum: cum finem, qui erat, ut Deos placarent, sibi propitios redderent. Scholiastes in vocem ἀποδ' ἡς addit, Hic erat alter modus cultus, & ille quotidianus libationibus constans in conviviis & compotationibus. Eustathius in illa Homeri Od. ν. ω ποτὲ ἀπ' ... Plutarchus in Sympof. 7. Sapientum: ... Idem 7. Sympof. Probl. citans versum illum Homeri, Σπίνδοντες δ' ἀπὸ αἴσιν ... Ωσπερ... ἀπὸ τὸν... —Vlimo. Mercurio libant cum iam dare corpora somno Et animus.—
units.tr: Here you will observe the double time at which they devoted their labour to libations and sacrifices, namely morning and evening, the aim being, as it was, to placate the gods and make them favourable to themselves. The Scholiast adds on the word "apodes": "This was the other mode of worship, the daily one, consisting of libations at banquets and drinking parties." Eustathius on that line of Homer, Od. ν ... Plutarch in the Symposiacs, book 7, On the Seven Wise Men: ... The same, in the Symposiac Problems, book 7, citing that line of Homer: "Pouring libations from ..." ... "They pour libations to Mercury when now they give their bodies and minds over to sleep."

units.la: Nonne conjungunt, inquit, cum vino rationem, quando ut praesenti, ... una disjicienti prudentissimo Deo vota faciunt (... ) iam discefsuri. Athenaeus libro decimo quinto. Cum consurrexissent atque libabant, reliquum quod erat meri, dederunt femulo, qui illis poculum porrexerat exhauriendum. Aristophan. ... quum videlicet bono ge- nio libatur, ut prosperam mittat fortunam. Verum de hoc poculo Daemonis alibi in loco plura dicentur.
units.tr: Do they not, he says, join reason with wine, when they make vows to the most prudent god, one who scatters cares, just as they are about to depart? Athenaeus, book fifteen: "When they had risen and were making libations, they gave the remaining neat wine to the servant who had handed them the cup, to drain." Aristophanes ... namely, when a libation is poured to the good spirit, so that he may send prosperous fortune. But more will be said about this cup of the Daemon in another place.

units.la: Notandum quoq; quod Eustathius scribit. ... inquit, οἶνον ... ἄπο ... ἀλλὰ ἔχει ... ὅτι ... ἐξίας ... ὅσα ταῦτα.
units.tr: It should also be noted what Eustathius writes: "... he says, wine ... but has ... that ... these things."

units.la: Mos quoq; fuit veterum Romanorum, ut vinum non nisi libarent Diis immortalibus, priusquam ipsi gustarent: cujus rei exemplum habes in Od. 31. lib. 1. —Quid orat, de patera nō rum Fundens liquorem ? Et Odyss. 5. lib. 4. Temulta prece, te prosequitur mero Defuso patera. Ad eundem modum idem Poeta alludit, lib. 2. Satyr. 2. Ac nisi mus. tum parcit defundere vinum:
units.tr: It was also the custom of the ancient Romans not to take wine except to pour libations to the immortal gods before they themselves drank. An example of this you have in Odes 1.31: "What does he pray for, pouring the liquor from the patera?" And in Odes 4.5: "With much prayer he follows you, pouring out wine from the patera." The poet alludes to the same custom in Satires 2.2: "Unless he sparingly pours out the wine ..."

units.la: Vbi cepdices alii, ut vulgati, habent diffundere: alii defundere, quae scriptura Lambino verior videtur, ut fit sensus: Tantum abest ut hic Avidienus vinum non rum Dius liberet, deinde ipse bibere, ut non nisi corruptum & acidum defunderet, &c.
units.tr: Where some manuscripts, like the printed editions, have "diffundere," others have "defundere," which reading seems truer to Lambinus. The sense is: far from this Avidienus pouring out wine to the gods and then drinking it himself, he pours out nothing but spoiled and sour wine, and so on.

units.la: Dii postremo, quibus convivantes libare solebant, a Graecis dicti sunt Dii παρα... Mercurius, bonus Daemon, &c. Pisidae, teste Nicolao de mor. gent. convivantes patentibus, ut alii Dius parasphondiss... sed primitias libare solebant.
units.tr: The gods to whom those at table used to pour libations were called by the Greeks gods ... Mercury, the good Daemon, and so on. The Pisidians, according to Nicolaus, On the Customs of the Nations, when feasting with open doors, as others ... but used to offer first-fruits as libations.

units.la: Atq; haec quidem dicta sint in genere de Libationibus, quas proprie ac uno verbo liquidorum sacrificia possit appellare: quae quidem varia fuerunt, ut dictum, etiam Porphyrio teste, quibus libro fecundo de sacrificiis sic scribit: Τὰ ᾶρ ἀχαῖα τῷ ἀρῶν ἀ αρέ... [Greek line illegible, ~60 letters]
units.tr: And these things may be said in general about libations, which one might call, in a single word, sacrifices of liquids. These were indeed various, as has been said, also according to the testimony of Porphyry, who in the second book of On Sacrifices writes thus: [Greek line illegible in the scan].

units.la: POSTQVAM vero, ut influxum hoc vsurpum per sequamur et ad finem perducamus, partium animalia, prius cesa et mactata, eadem vel tota et integra, vilcertas illorum partes atque membra, sive exteriora, sive interiora, in aram focum ve projecta ignibus tradita fuerunt, vel Apulejo teste, in super fluctus libarunt minitum, id est, ut Herodianus explicat, ad influxum interitus minutatim: partim vero vinum, thus, oleum, omnis generis liquores, herbas atque plantas similiter super fuerunt infusae, atque impositae: inde excitatae fuerunt flammae, fumi, nidores, vapores, odores cum bene, cum male olentes, denique cineres atque pulveres: quae quidem omnium illorum sacrificiorum, victimarum, hostiarum, libationumque fuerunt quasi effectus. Verisimile itaque possumus dicere omnia Gentilium vel augustissima, magnificentissima, fumosissima sacrificia tandem in flammas, in sumos, in nidores atque odores tetros ac putidos, denique in favillas atque cineres vilissimos et abjectissimos abiisse.
units.tr: But now, to follow this subject through and bring it to an end: after the animals had been slain and slaughtered, the same whole and entire, or certain of their parts and limbs, external or internal, were placed upon the altar or hearth and given over to the fires; or, as Apuleius testifies, libations were poured over them, that is, as Herodian explains, gradually, as the victim perished. Partly, too, wine, incense, oil, every kind of liquid, herbs and plants were similarly poured over and laid on. From these arose flames, smoke, steam, vapours, odours, pleasant and foul, and finally ashes and dust. These were, as it were, the effects of all those sacrifices, victims, offerings and libations. It is therefore fair to say that all the most august, most magnificent, most smoky sacrifices of the Gentiles finally passed into flames, smoke, steam and foul, stinking odours, and at last into the most worthless and abject ashes and cinders.

units.la: Debus ipsis igitur, de quibus supra pauca quaedam attigimus, leviter, perfrinximus, consequens nunc videtur esse, et instituto nostro ordini conveniens, ut fusius quaedam et copiosius dicamus. Nam hos ipsos, ut inde ordiar, fumos, suffumigia, seu suffimenta, hosce nidores, odores, odoramenta atque aromata, exhalantur res esse Divinas suas valde gratas atque jucundas, quibus illi gaudeant, magnoque opere deleCTentur, quibus placari reddantur atque propitii, quibus denique res quae vis pollutae et contaminatae expientur, atque lustrentur. Quamobrem suffitionum istarum ac suffumigationum, incensorum atque thymiamatum creberrima apud scriptores profanos fit mentio, ita ut proram et puppim, ut ita loquar, cultus divinus atque religiosus suae in illis collocasse videantur. Id autem ex ipsis primum nominibus apertum est atque manifestum, a quorum explicatione incipiemus.
units.tr: Since we touched only lightly, above, on some of these matters, it now seems the proper next step, and in keeping with our plan, to speak of some of them more fully and at greater length. For these very fumes, these smokings, or perfumings, these steams, odours, scents and spices: we say they are exhaled as things very pleasing and delightful to their divinities, in which they rejoice and take great delight, by which they are made placated and propitious, and by which, finally, things polluted and contaminated are expiated and purified. Therefore very frequent mention is made among profane writers of these fumigations and suffumigations, of incense and thymiamata, so that divine and religious worship seems to have placed, as it were, its prow and stern in them. This is clear from the very names, and we shall begin with an explanation of those.

units.la: Nam primum Fumi nomen non tam a furno vel a furo, ut Grammatici volunt, quam ἀπὸ τῶ θυμίαμα, voce Graeca videtur derivari, quae aram sive altare significat: unde ara seu altaria e Poëtis Latinis fumida, fumosa, fumantia, fumiferi, rendentia, vaporata dicuntur. Sic enim Ovidius tertio Tristium: Fumida cingantur florentibus ara coronis.
units.tr: First, the name "fumus" (smoke) seems to derive not so much from furnus or furo, as the grammarians want, as from the Greek word thymiama, which signifies an altar. Hence Latin poets call altars smoky, fumid, smoking, smoke-bearing, steaming, vaporous. So Ovid in Tristia, book 3: "Let the smoking altar be garlanded with flowering wreaths."

units.la: Et secundo Elegiarum: Ipse ego thura dabo fumosis candidus aris.
units.tr: And in the second book of the Elegies: "I myself, gleaming white, will give incense upon the smoking altars."

units.la: Sic Faustus: Qualia fumantes fragrant pia thura per aras. Idem alibi: Et dabo fumiferas fragrantia thura per aras. Sic Statius libro primo Theb. Thure vaporatis lucent alii aribus ignes.
units.tr: So Faustus: "Such as the devout incense breathes through the smoking altars." Elsewhere the same: "And I will give fragrant incense through the smoke-bearing altars." So Statius, Thebaid, book 1: "With incense-steamed altars the other fires shine."

units.la: Et libro quarto: Thurea nec supra volitante altaria fumos.
units.tr: And in book 4: "Nor do incense altars send up smoke above the flying ..."

units.la: Quoniam igitur fumi res habita fuerunt sacrae et divinae, rei divinae aptae, convenientes; idcirco Fumus ἀπὸ τῶ Θυμιᾶ (fumus et θυμός voces sunt sibi invicem affines) recte videtur deduci. Hinc frequentissime etiam arae ab Homero θυμίατ, id est, odore sive odorata fuerunt dictae, de qua voce postea pluribus. Virgilius in Aetna: Surgit odoratu sublimis fumus ab ara.
units.tr: Since, therefore, smokes were held to be sacred and divine things, fitting and suited to divine worship, "fumus" (smoke) is rightly derived from thymos (the Greek for the burnt offering and spirit), since "fumus" and "thymos" are words akin to each other. Hence very often Homer calls altars thymiatai, that is, fragrant or odorous, of which word more later. Virgil in the Aetna: "Rises the smoke, sublime with fragrance, from the altar."

units.la: Fumosa igitur re vera fuerunt Gentilium et altaria et templa, et sacerdotes, et simulacra, et omnia denique illorum sacra fumi atque fuci fuerunt plenissima.
units.tr: Thus the altars, temples, priests and images of the Gentiles were truly smoky, and all their sacred rites were full of smoke and reek.

units.la: Aromata praeterea Graeci, et Latini aromata appellarunt, et odores, sive odoramenta (unde Aromatitum, herba sic dicta, quod myrrhae odore habeat) a qua voce ara Latine videtur dicta. (Possunt enim unius ex ipsdem vocis plures etymologiæ afferri probabiles, quas deinde lectori hos doctus dijudicandæ relinquuntur) propterea quod aromata odores, sive odoramenta super alia creberrime incendi fuerunt solita. Quoniam igitur aris aromata fuerunt potissimum destinata, inde veri similiter aras fuisse appellacas. Ἀρώματα autem Græcè videntur dicta ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀάρω, id est, tollendo, propterea quod odores tollantur in altum, ac superiora petunt. Cicero: Omnis odor ad superiora fertur, unde etiam nares sursum iunt. Fortasse ἀρώμα, sic dicitur ab ἀρ seu ἀρ. particula intensiva, et ὀζω, fœtor, seu odor, unde et a Suida exponitur ὑπεδύμενα ὑψωμένα ἀπὸ καπνοῦ, aromaticos odoratus: ἀρώματα ὀσμὴ aromata redolens, odoratus: ἀρωματίζειν, aromata resipere, aromatis seu odoramentis imbuere. Apuleius lib. 11. Tunc cunctis popatis, cum religiosis, quam profani, variis onustos aromatis et hujusmodi supplicium certatim congerunt: supplicii, id est, sacrificiis, juxta illud Festi: Supplicio Veteres quedam sacrificia a supplicando vocabant.
units.tr: The Greeks and the Latins called these things aromata, and also odores or odoramenta. From this comes aromatitis, an herb so named because it has the smell of myrrh, and the Latin ara (altar) seems to be derived from the same word. (Several probable etymologies of this one word can be offered, and I leave the learned reader to judge between them.) Aromatic substances, that is, odours or perfumes, were burned more often than anything else, and since they were chiefly destined for altars, it is likely that altars were named from them. The Greek aromata seems to be named from aarō [ἀάρω], that is, lifting up, because odours are carried aloft and seek higher places. Cicero: "Every odour is carried upwards, whence the nostrils also turn upward." Perhaps aroma is so called from ar or ar, an intensive particle, and ozō, to smell or give off an odour. Hence Suidas explains it as "rising up from smoke" [ὑπεδύμενα ὑψωμένα ἀπὸ καπνοῦ], "aromatic fragrance" [ἀρώματα ὀσμή], "smelling of spices, fragrant" [ἀρώματα ὀσμὴ], and "to be seasoned with spices, to be steeped in aromatics or perfumes" [ἀρωματίζειν]. Apuleius, book 11: "Then all the people, the religious no less than the profane, eagerly heap up offerings laden with various spices and such things, for the supplicium, that is, the sacrifices." This accords with Festus: "The ancients called certain sacrifices supplicia from supplicare, to supplicate."

units.la: Veniamus nunc ad ipsum odoris nomen, ex quo similiter ad institutum nostrum pertinentia colligi possunt. Non dubium est, quin illud deriveturā Græco ὀζειν, id est, olere, unde ὀδμή et ὀδωδή vel ὀδωδη, olus, inde ὀδωδη, et Latinum odos sive odor ut nidos, sive nidor, etc. Ab odore ficodorari, odoratus, odorator, odoratus, odoratum (unde odorata canum ut sundo, apud Virgilium, et odorata ara, ut supra) odoriscus, odoribilis, id est, odorem reddens, et odoramentum, quod odore gracia tenemus, ut unguencum, quod unguenti causa odorares, odoris sequuntur, quod est canum epitheton: quam ut etiam gulosis hominibus possit accommodari.
units.tr: Let us now come to the word odor itself, from which things pertinent to our purpose can likewise be gathered. There is no doubt that it derives from the Greek ozein [ὀζειν], that is, to smell, whence osmē [ὀδμή] and odōdē [ὀδωδή], and the Latin odos or odor, as nidos or nidor, and so on. From odor come odorari, odoratus, odorator, odoratum (whence the odorata of hounds, as in Virgil, and the odorata ara, as above), odoriscus, odoribilis, that is, giving off a smell, and odoramentum, which we hold to be a thing that is pleasant by its smell, as unguentum is a thing used for the sake of ointment. Odoris follows, which is an epithet of hounds, and which may also be applied to greedy men.

units.la: Etsi igitur adorandi et adorationis nomen, ut plerique Grammaticorum non male sentiunt, ab ore videtur dictum: tamen non alicnum plane, sed vero simile videtur esse, adorare quasi odorari, et adorationem quasi odorationem esse dictam (unde Ador etiam videatur appellatum) propterea quod Veteres adorationis maximam fere partem in odorum sive odoramentorum incensionibus posuerunt.
units.tr: Although the words adorandi and adoratio are, as most grammarians rightly think, derived from os (mouth), it does not seem altogether unlikely but rather probable that adorare is as it were odorari, and adoratio as it were odoratio, so named (whence ador also seems to have been called), because the ancients placed almost the greater part of their worship in the burning of odours or perfumes.

units.la: Hinc quoq; pertinent verbum olere et ejus compositæ. Olere plerisque Grammaticorum videtur derivatum a Græco ὀλέω, Latine oleum: quoniam olei maximus et præstantissimus est odor, sed ἐλάιον autem non abs, ratione dixerunt ab Hebræa voce, id est, Dei, dicuntur, propterea quod oleum habita fuit res sacra et divina, et in omnibus sacrificiis frequentissime fuit adhibita. Oleo tamen nonnullis non ab Gleum deductum volunt, sed ὀζω ... quod olere significat, a quo et odoror videtur dictum, ut supra. Oleo autem, propter quod Veteres etiam Olere dixerunt, significat bonum et malum odorem emittere: unde Redolere, quod in bonam fere semper partem accipitur: Olentica, mali odoris loca: Olidum, quod odorem habet: Olectio, pro flercore hominis, quod male olet. Inde olfacio, quod et olfactio Veteres dixerunt, et olfactus.
units.tr: Hence also comes the verb olere (to smell) and its compounds. Most grammarians think olere is derived from the Greek oleō, Latin oleum (oil), since the odour of oil is the greatest and most excellent. But elaion [ἐλάιον] they rightly derived not from oleum but from a Hebrew word, meaning "of God" (?), because oil was regarded as a sacred and divine thing and was used very frequently in all sacrifices. Some, however, prefer to derive olere not from oleum but from ozō, which means to smell, from which odorari also seems to be named, as above. Olere, which the ancients also used, signifies to give off a good or bad smell: whence redolere, which is nearly always taken in a good sense; olentia, places of bad smell; olidum, that which has a smell; olectio, for the dung of man, which smells badly. Hence olfacio, which the ancients also called olfactio, and olfactus.

units.la: Sed verbum Adolere hic imprimis consideratione dignum, quod modo significat accrescere: quia crescentes pueri, cum primum puberes fiunt, olere hircum (quod Græcis est ἐμίγεσθαι) incipiunt, unde Hirquitali sunt appellati: et inde adolescentior, adolescentulus, adolescentia, adultus. Idem verbum quando de sacris dicitur, et odores incendere, adurere, et in genere sacrificare atq; colere significat. Virgilius: Verbenasq; adole (id est, incende, ure) pingues et mascula thura.
units.tr: But the verb adolere deserves particular consideration here. It now means to grow up, because boys growing up, as soon as they become pubescent, begin to smell of the goat (which the Greeks call emigesthai), whence they were called hirquitales; and hence adolescentior, adolescentulus, adolescentia, adultus. The same verb, when said of sacred things, means to burn odours, to set on fire, and in general to sacrifice and worship. Virgil: "Burn (that is, set fire to, cook) the crackling verbena and the male frankincense."

units.la: Idem Æneid. 1. Quinquaginta incus famulæ, quibus ordine longo Cura penum struere et flammis adolere Penates.
units.tr: The same in the Aeneid, book 1: "Fifty household maids, to whom in long order it is a care to arrange the store and to burn the Penates in the flames."

units.la: Servius: Adolere, id est, Colere. Sed adolere proprie est augere. In sacris quidem Adolere per hominem omen dicitur. Nam et in aris non adolentur aliqua, sed cremantur. Ergo ex hoc quoq; adolere colligitur odores in aris incendendi Vecerum consuetudo: unde adolere pro uerere sacrificare. Varro. Cum inteflina (Nota hic rursus inteflinorum extorum, in sacrificiis usum) adole missent partem Dijs obtulerunt, partem ipsi consumserunt. Virgilius: —Adolescunt (id est, accenduntur, ardent) ignibus ara.
units.tr: Servius: Adolere means to worship, but adolere properly means to increase. In sacred rites, to adolere is said of a man's omen. For nothing is adolentur on the altars, but burned up. Therefore from this too it is gathered that the custom of the ancients was to burn odours on altars; whence adolere is used for to sacrifice. Varro: "When they had sent up the entrails (note here again the use of the entrails in sacrifices), they offered part to the gods and consumed part themselves." Virgil: "The altar grows with flames" (that is, is kindled and blazes).

units.la: Sed verbum quoq; Fio huc pertinet, et ejus compositæ. Fio a facio videtur dici per synærefin. Nam sublatus litteris a et c ex Facio, sit Fio, pasta rum. Ut igitur Facere Latine κοτ' ἐξοχὴν sacrificare significat, sacrificio, operam dare (cui respondet Græcum ποιεῖν in eadem significatione) ut etiam.
units.tr: The verb fio also belongs here, and its compounds. Fio seems to be derived from facio by synaeresis. For when the letters a and c are removed from facio, fio results, as the grammarians say. Therefore, as facere in Latin signifies, par excellence, to sacrifice, and to give effort to a sacrifice (to which the Greek poiein corresponds in the same sense), so also...
Whence the word odor is derived.
The verb adorandi from the verb adorare.
Olere.
Adolere.

units.la: Fio. ut etiam operari, propterea quod nullum factum operatione est praestantior, quàm res diuina: sic Fieri quoq; ea potissimum & proprie dicuntur, quae fiunt in Dei honorem.
units.tr: Fio: as also operari (to work), because no deed is more excellent in its working than the divine worship; so the things said to be "done" (fieri) most especially and properly are those done to the honour of God.

units.la: A Fio autem suffio componitur, quod est suffumigo, quasi fur sum fumum ago. Plinius: Hippocrates ruta vt varum causa naturam suffire debet. Idem: Alis carnem recente hordorum pilo suffiunt, eodemq; nidore fugant serpentes. Idem: Quidam citrei sunt fumo bujus millura suffire vineas secundo flatu continuo triduo. Virgilius: At suffite thymo, &c. Hinc suffitum dicimus suffumigatum. Plinius: Anufum dolorem capitis le nigas, suffitum naribus. Quarta declinatione suffitum, quemadmodum suffimentum, Plinius dixit: Et vulnarum conventionem suffitu excitant. Idem: Quod & suffimentis quibusdam facere conjuerunt. Idem: Ob has causas equidem crediderim honorem lauro habitum in triumphis potius, quàm quia suffimentum fit cadis hostium & purgatio.
units.tr: From fio is compounded suffio, which is to fumigate, as it were fur sum fumum ago (to drive smoke upward). Pliny: "Hippocrates ought to fumigate the womb with rue for the sake of..." Again: "They fumigate flesh with the fresh hair of hogs, and with the same smoke they drive away serpents." Again: "Some fumigate vines with the smoke of this millet, with a continuous second wind for three days." Virgil: "But fumigate with thyme, etc." Hence we speak of suffitum, a fumigated thing. Pliny: "Pain of the head is eased by the nostrils with suffitum." Pliny used suffitum in the fourth declension, as also suffimentum: "They excite the joining of wounds by suffitus." Again: "Which they also used to make with certain fumigations." Again: "For these reasons I would believe the laurel was honoured in triumphs rather than because a fumigation is made from the slaughter of enemies and a purification."

units.la: Suffitio etiam aliquando dicitur. Plinius: Orpheus & Hesiodus suffitiones commendavere.
units.tr: Suffitio is also sometimes used. Pliny: "Orpheus and Hesiod commended fumigations."

units.la: Suffitor autem dicitur, qui buccis infuffiat iguem. Plinius: Lycius & ipse pinxit suffitorem. Idem: Lycius Myronis discipulus, qui fecit dignû praeceptore disciputi suffitantes languidos ignes.
units.tr: A suffitor is so called who blows fire with his cheeks. Pliny: "Lycius himself also painted a fire-blower." Again: "Lycius, a pupil of Myron, who made, worthy of his teacher, the fire-blowers stooping over the weak fires."

units.la: Suffimenta etiam a vtteribus dicta sunt, quae fieri solebant ex faba, milio, molito, mola spar-fo. Hac Dies eo tempore dicebantur, quo vna calcata pilo imprimebantur: testis est Festus.
units.tr: Suffimenta were also called by the ancients those things that were customarily made from beans, millet, and meal sprinkled on salted cakes. These were called dies at the time when, a single sacrifice having been trodden with the pestle, they were pressed in; Festus is a witness.

units.la: A Fio etiam fit Exfio, quod est purgo, a quo Exfitus, id est, purgatus. Exfir Veteres pro purgamento posuerunt. Festus: Exfir purgamentum: unde adhuc manet suffitio.
units.tr: From fio also comes exfio, which means to purge, whence exfitus, that is, purged. The ancients used exfir for refuse. Festus: "Exfir is refuse"; whence the word suffitio still remains.

units.la: His postremo adde Fimi nomen. Fimus sive fimum in neutro genere, proprieletamen fignificat & excrementa animalium, quibus agri dercortantur. Graece κόπρος, ἀπὸ τοῦ κόπη, ὁ πυ Ἀρρ. Dijt Germanice, āmiflura, vel a fumo videtur derivari, quia fimi fumant, sive fumum edunt: vel a fio. Cui autem dubium, quin in Gentilium sacrificiis multitudo atq; copia hujusmodi fimorû atq; fumorum fuerit: unde templa illorum sinuera atq; sterquilinia meritò potuerunt appellari.
units.tr: Finally, add to these the noun fimus. Fimus or fimum in the neuter gender properly signifies the excrement of animals with which fields are manured. In Greek kopros, from kopē... In German it is called Mist. It seems to be derived either from fumus, because dung steams or gives off smoke, or from fio. Who can doubt that in the sacrifices of the Gentiles there was a great multitude and abundance of such dung and smoke, whence their temples could rightly be called stables and dunghills?

units.la: Et haec dicta sint de nominibus Latinis ex quibus ipsis frequentissimus istorum fumorû, suffumigationum, suffimentorum, odorum, atq; odoramentorum in sacris usus facile possit colligi.
units.tr: And let these things be said of the Latin names, from which the very frequent use of these fumes, fumigations, fumigated offerings, odours and perfumes in their sacred rites can easily be gathered.

units.la: Idem ex nominibus Graecis clarius: adhuc patet. Suffimentum enim sive suffitus, suffitio, &, quod idem significat, suffumigium seu suffumigatio, id est, odorum sive odoramentorum excitatio, Graeci θυμίαμα, ἀπὸ θυμίαμα, ἀπὸ θυσία, ἡ θυσία ἀπὸ θυμίασις appellatur ἀπὸ τῶ θυ-μός, sive θυμιάω ἀπὸ θυμός, ἀπὸ θυμίαμα, ἀπὸ θυμ., ἡ ἀπὸ θυμιασις, id est, suffitus, vaporare, evaporare, exha-lare, suffitum emittere, odores incendere, seu adolere: unde θυμιητήριον, acerrum, sive thuribulum, ἀπὸ θυμιάδες ferta florida, quae collo appendebantur, sic dicta, quod cerebri sua fragrantia quasi suffiunt & refocillani: Plutarchus fympos.lib.3.cap.1. Ea etiam ἀπὸ ἀπὸ τὸ θυμίαμα eandem ob causam appellantur.
units.tr: The same is still more clearly shown from the Greek names. For suffimentum or suffitus, suffitio, and, which means the same, suffumigium or suffumigatio, that is, the kindling of odours or perfumes, is called by the Greeks thymiama, from thymos, or thymiaō from thymos, and thymiasis, that is, fumigation, evaporating, exhaling, sending up incense, burning odours or perfumes, or worshipping. Hence thymiētērion, a censer or thurible; and thymiadés, flowery garlands hung about the neck, so called because by their fragrance they as it were fumigate and refresh the brain; Plutarch, Symposiaca, book 3, chapter 1. These, too, are named from thymiama for the same reason.

units.la: Hoc ἀπὸ verbum θυμιᾶν derivatur παρὰ τὸ θύω, quod verbum, ut Eustathius pluribus in lo θυμιᾶν is ostendit, duo significat, nempe idem quod θυμιᾶν, id est, suffire, suffumigare, suffimentum, suffi-. unde dictum tum, suffumigium edere, odores sive odoramenta Dius incendere. Deinde idem verbum sacrificaEustathius apud Homerum docet, partim θυμιᾶσαι, id est, suffitum seu suffimentum, partim θύμα, sive θυσίαν, seu ἱερεῖον, id est, victimam, bostiam sive bestiam sacrificis destinatà significat: unde & θυσίαν Porphyrius & Grammatici sacrificium volunt dictum, quod primi mortalis ex combustis arboribus sive plantis, earumq; partibus & fructibus θυμιᾶσαν, id est, suffimentis sive suffitus Dius impenderint, sita ut ἀπὸ ὁ θυμιᾶσαν θυσίαν fit appellata. Islib.2.in quo multa de sa-crificiis disserit: Ex ἡ τῆς θυμιάσεως, inquit, τὸ ἀπὸ γῆς θυμιᾶτήριον ἐκάλουν, τὸ θύειν, θυ-σίαν: ἀ ἀνόμασεν οἱ ἢ ὑπὸ πάρτα, ἐπὶ ἡ ἀπὸ ὁ πλαντὸς ἀποκαλλοῦσι τὴν ἐκείνη κοὶ ἀφ' ἡ ἀπὸ ἔλαξ κομίζοι.
units.tr: This word θυμιᾶν is derived from θύω [thyō], which verb, as Eustathius shows at length on Homer, has two meanings. It means the same as θυμιᾶν [thymiān], that is, to fumigate, to burn incense, to make a fumigation, and from this it is said to give off a fume and to set odours alight. The same verb, Eustathius teaches on Homer, also signifies in part θυμιᾶσαι [thymiāsai], that is, incense or a fumigation, and in part a θύμα [thyma], or θυσία [thysia], or ἱερεῖον [hiereion], that is, a victim, a beast set apart for sacrifice. Hence Porphyry and the grammarians hold that θυσία (sacrifice) is so called because the first mortals offered up to the gods a burning of incense made from trees or plants and their parts and fruits, so that sacrifice is named from the burning of incense. Eustathius, in the second book, where he discusses sacrifices at length, says: from the fumigation, he says, they called the altar of earth a thymiaterion, and to sacrifice, thysia; and what they named this, all the others, from the plant, have called by the same name, and from the fruit they bring it.

units.la: Idem eodem lib.τὸ ἡ πολλὰ δὲ πολὺ ἐκείνη παρὰ μὲν χεῖρα ἀπὸ τὸ ἀρχαῖον ἡ ἄγαιον, ἀρὸ ἡ ἀπὸ θυσία. Idem: Vetus mos Deos colendi fiebat per placentas sive liba (a voce πόπανον forsan Popa dicta) & fructus. Unde sacrificia illa θυσίαι, θυλάκι & θυμίαμα dicta, & verbum θύειν ἰδεῖ, quod θυμιᾶν, id est, suffire, quod nunc appellamus θυθύῃ, id est, sacrificiū addere. Quod autem nunc appellamus Θύλη, id vocabant ipsi. Euflathius Odyff.o. in illa ἀγυμα ῥάιν ἀλλ᾽ ἀν ἐπρέξαμον, interpretatur ἀπαρχὰς Θύος Σύσι, quae primias Dij sacrificavit: addit, Sive secundum Veteres θυμίαμα, id est, suffitus, suffimenta fecie Nusquam enim apud Poetam verbum Θύειν legi pro σφάζειν, τὸ ἱερεῖον, id est, mactare victimam. Hic suffragatur ὑσ, qui scripsit σφάζειν μὲν τὸ ἱερὸν χοῖρον, Θύσαι δὲ τὸ συμμαχον. Hoc est Verbum σφάζειν significat mactare animal: Θύσαι autem idem, quod suffumigare. Nam Θύη sunt thymiamata sive suffimenta. Ibidem, Theoeriti quoque testimonio probat, verbum Θύειν pro θυμιᾶν, id est, suffire accipi. Hinc vīc Θύος καὶ κολαυτὸν Θυώδης, id est, nubes odorata, & fumus odorifer, sive odorem exhalans. Idem Ιλιο. Θύω, inquit, unde Θύσαι, non solum θυμιατυς, id est, suffimentum, sed incensum (unde Θυμιαστικος dicta) sed etiā θύμα, id est, hostiam seu victimam significat. Idem Iliad. Ἐτοιμάσαν ἵνα ἐπιθύμα μένος τι ἐν πᾶτα οἴκῳ. Διὸ Θύνον ... id est, Τίμον δὲ autem boc in loco appellatur locus abscissus & separatus a loeis circumcirca jacentibus, cujus pars est altare: in quo sacrificata comburebant: unde etiam θυσίς appellatur: quoniam Θύσι appellatur id, quod sacrificatur. Idem Odyff. ... appellatur ... Compositae enim est ἥν ex ἐν ὤ(ν)... Θυσκόν igitur ... Θυσκόσ inquit, secundum Veteres sunt, qui per suffimenta φαινόμενον... Hic adde, quod Θύσει est facere odorari, adolere, adorare & odorari: Θύει mactare, sacrificare, sacra facere, sufficere... Εὐλήματα, Sic Θυλήματα sunt simul farra melle imbuta & suffimenta, quae in aris adolebantur: vel farina vino & oleo aspersa in sacrificium, apud Aristophanem in Pace.
units.tr: The same author, in the same book, says: the ancient custom of worshipping the gods was carried out by cakes or offerings (perhaps the word popanon gives the name popa) and by fruits. Hence those sacrifices are called thysiai, thylakia and thymiamata, and the verb thyein, which is to burn incense, which we now call thyein, that is, to add to the sacrifice. What we now call thyle, they themselves called that. Eustathius, on the Odyssey, on the line "but we would have made an offering," explains that the first-fruits which the gods were offered by the sacrifice; he adds that, according to the ancients, these were thymiamata, that is, incense or fumigations. For nowhere in the poet is the verb thyein read in place of sphazein, that is, to slaughter a victim. Here he is supported by the one who wrote that sphazein means to slaughter a sacred pig, but thysai the offering of smoke. That is, the verb sphazein means to slaughter an animal, while thysai means the same as to fumigate, for thye are thymiamata or fumigations. In the same place, he proves by the testimony of Theocritus also that the verb thyein is taken to mean thymian, that is, to burn incense. Hence also thyos and the cloud of incense, the fragrant one, that is, a scented cloud and a fume giving out fragrance. The same author, on the Iliad: thyō, he says, whence thysai, signifies not only thymiatus, that is, a fumigation, but something burned (whence thymiastikos is named), and also thyma, that is, a sacrificial victim. The same author, on the Iliad, "a place prepared, which is set apart"; here it is called a place cut off and separated from the surrounding lands, of which the altar is a part, on which they burned the sacrificial offerings; whence it is also called thysia, since that which is sacrificed is called thysia. The same author, on the Odyssey, says that it is called... for it is compounded... Thyskos therefore... he says, according to the ancients, are those who through fumigations appear... Add here that thyein means to cause to smell, to burn, to worship and to smell; thyei means to slaughter, to sacrifice, to perform rites, to offer incense. Thylemata: thus thylemata are at once spelt grains soaked in honey and fumigations which were burned on the altars, or meal sprinkled with wine and oil for sacrifice, as in Aristophanes' Peace.

units.la: Odores porrὸ fācti fiunt sacrificiales generatim primo dividi possunt, quod alii illorum sunt sua vestes, jucundi, bene & suavē olentes: alii infausti, injucundi, tetri, fætidi, putidi: quo modo & Theophrastus alia sunt vīsiqnia in... id est, male graviterq; olentia.
units.tr: The sacrificial odours which are made can be divided generally, first, into two kinds: some of them are pleasant, agreeable, sweet-smelling and fragrant; others are unlucky, unpleasant, foul, stinking, rotten. Theophrastus also divides them in this way: some are sweet-smelling, others strong-smelling, that is, badly and heavily scented.

units.la: Odores boni & jucundi fragrantes quoq; appellantur: unde Fragnonnulli volūt dicta quasi fragrantia, id est, bene suaveq; olentia: tametsi ea a frangedo quoq; videantur appellata, quasi fragilia. Fragrare autem est in bona plerung, parte accipitur pro, odorem bonū reddere, ut Redolat.
units.tr: Pleasant and good odours are also called fragrances, and some want fragrantia to be named as if from fragrance, that is, giving off a sweet and pleasant smell, although these also seem to be named from frangere (to break), as if they were fragile. To fragrare, however, is generally taken in a good sense, to give off a good odour, as in redolere (to smell sweet).
Thylema: to eat, to spread, a sin of error.
"Fragrant honeycombs smell strongly of thyme," (Vergil-style line as quoted).
Catullus: "The house is fragrant with Assyrian perfume."

units.la: Tamen in malam quoque partem nonnunquam accipitur, pro, odorem malum emittere; ut Martialis:
units.tr: Yet it is sometimes taken in a bad sense too, to give off a bad smell, as Martial has it:
"You stink of yesterday's Fescennine wine."

units.la: Et Valerio Argonaut. quarto: Odor fragrat aeerbus.
units.tr: And Valerius, Argonautica, book four: "A bitter odour rises."

units.la: A fragrare fit Fragrans, quod odorem emittit: Fragrantia, odoris emissio, sive odor ipse. Verbum autem fragrare Seruius vult a fragrando dictum, qu[od] specie fracta odor redditur major. Forsan derivatum est ab ὀσφραίνεσθαι, vel ὀσφραΐσθαι, id est, odorari, per synaeresin. Οσφραίνεσθαι autem videtur dictum, quasi ὀσμῆς ἀϊσθάνεσθαι, id est, odorem sentire, sive percipere, vel ὀσὸ τοῦ ὀσμῆ ἱσφαίνεσθαι, id est, odore delectari et recreari. Non etiam a vero ratione, videtur abhorrere, si verbum fragrare mutatione unius tantum litterae dicamus a flagrare, id est, ardere, quoniam ex rerum flagratione seu conflagratione fragrantia exsistit. Nam ignis atque calor odoris causa est efficiens. Flagro autem, id est, ardeo, et conflagro, id est, ardendo consumor a Flamma videtur nomen suum trahere: flammas autem ὁπὸ τοῦ φλογίζ, id est, ardere: unde φλόξ, id est, flamma.
units.tr: From fragrare comes fragrans, which gives off a smell, and fragrantia, the emission of a smell or the smell itself. Servius holds that the verb fragrare is named from frangere, because by the breaking of the species a greater odour is given off. It may perhaps be derived from osphrainesthai or osphresthai, that is, to smell, by synaeresis. Osphrainesthai seems to be named as if it meant to perceive a smell, that is, to sense an odour, or to be delighted and refreshed by the odour. Nor does it seem out of keeping with reason if we say that fragrare is changed by a single letter from flagrare, that is, to burn, since fragrance comes into being from the burning or conflagration of things. For fire and heat are the efficient cause of odour. Flagro, that is, to burn, and conflagro, that is, I am consumed by burning, seem to draw their name from flamma (flame); flammae in turn come from phlogizein, that is, to burn, whence phlox, flame.

units.la: Odores vero mali et tetri generatim factores et putores appellantur, quorum species multae sunt, ut pedor, rancor, murcor, situs et similia. Factor autem dicitur a facteo, id est, malè oleo: unde factidum male olens. Facteo autem a fatu, quoniam mulieres fastendo, id est, fatum emittendo mulies modis polluuntur et inquinantur: unde Facio verbum, id est, polluo, inquino, et Fadum nomen; quod deforme et crudele significat.
