Sunt qui Faedus inde dictum volunt a porca Faedi, id est, crudeliter casa et interfecta. Alioquin et sus confecta dicta a Veteribus quae cum omni faeu adhibebatur ad sacrificium, teste Festo.
units.tr: Bad and foul odours are generally called stenches and rot, of which there are many kinds, such as stink, rancidity, mustiness, mould and the like. Factor is said from faeteo, that is, to smell badly, whence factidus means ill-smelling. Faeteo, moreover, comes from fatus, since women are defiled and polluted in many ways by breaking wind, that is, by emitting fatus; whence the verb facio, that is, to pollute or defile, and the noun foedus, which means what is ugly and cruel. Some want foedus to be named from the sow of Faedus, that is, a sow cruelly slain and killed. Otherwise, the sow sacrificed was called by the ancients a sus confecta, which was used with all its foulness for sacrifice, according to Festus.

units.la: Pedor squalorem proprie significat atq; omnem immunditiem.
units.tr: Pedor properly means filth and every kind of uncleanness.
Lucan: "and a stench in the long body."

units.la: Cicero Pedores mulubres dixit. Item barbam pedore horridam: unde pedicosum, quod malì est odoris a pedore sive pediculo, foedo illo capitis animaculo. Hinc etiam Pedo verbum, quod est crepitum ventris emitto quod ut facere in cenvivo licat, Claudius Princeps edicto statuit, quod periclitatum quendam pro pudore et continentia reperiret. Inde et Pedicosus deducitur, id est, squalidus: quod a pedibus deductum scribitur cum e simplici, ut apud Festum, quasi: Pedes dicuntur, quos diminuti vel dicimus pediculos. Ab his pedicosi appellantur, ut est illud: Pedicosus squalidus ubi me videt, caput scabit, pedes legit.
units.tr: Cicero called them foul-smelling worms (pedores). Likewise a beard bristling with stench; whence pedicosus, which is of bad smell, from pedor or from the pediculus, that foul little creature of the head. Hence also the verb pedo, to let out a fart, which Emperor Claudius by edict ruled should not be done at a dinner, since he found a certain man endangered for lack of modesty and restraint. From this too pedicosus is derived, that is, squalid, which is written as derived from pedes (feet), with a single letter, as in Festus, as if: they are called pedes, which we diminutively call pediculi. From these pedicosi are named, as in the line: "a squalid pedicosus, when he sees me, scratches his head and picks his feet."

units.la: Putor porro idem, quod foetor, a Puteo, quod foetere est. Inde Putidum, Putulentum, quod est odoris mali, a pus, puris, quod est sanies, et quicunq; humor, in putrednem versus. Unde Putulentum: plenum sanie, locus Purulentus, in quem factus est humorum malorum concursus: qui fit in sanie veritur maturari et maturescere dicitur, sin minus, discuti sive resolvi. Hinc Putreo, Putresco, quod in purem vertitur, et Putredo Putrefactio, id est, corruptio. Putridum ite, quod corruptum. Quin et Purgo a pure dictum, quasi purem agor, id est, extrabo, promeo. Sic a putore Puteus: quia putet, id est, foetet, quando cavatur.
units.tr: Putor, moreover, is the same as foetor, from puteo, which means to stink. Hence putidum, putulentum, which is of bad odour, from pus, puris, which is matter, and any humour turned to putrefaction. Whence putulentum: full of matter; locus purulentus, where a concourse of evil humours has been made, which, when it turns to matter, is said to ripen and mature; if not, to be dispersed or dissolved. Hence putreo, putresco, which turns into pus, and putredo, putrefaction, that is, corruption; putridum, what is corrupt. Indeed purgo too is named from purus, as if I drive out the pus, that is, extract and bring forth. So also puteus (well) from putor, because it stinks, that is, reeks, when it is dug.

units.la: Deinde odores isti sacri atque sacrificiales dividi possunt secundum materiam sacrificiorum duplicem, de qua supra. Ea fuerunt partim animalia, partim plantae omnis generis et utrorumq; parees et effecta. Ex utroq, autem horum genera odores exhalarunt partim graves, tetri atq, fastidii, partim suaves, jucundi et fragrantes. Vtraq, autem miseri isti idololatrae Deos illos suos alienos seu daemonas potius (idi, illorum ipsorum suggestione, monitus atq, oraculus) delectari atque placari putarunt.
units.tr: Next, these sacred and sacrificial odours can be divided according to the twofold matter of the sacrifices, mentioned above. That matter was partly animals and partly plants of every kind, along with their parts and products. From both sources arose odours, some heavy, foul and loathsome, others sweet, pleasant and fragrant. Those wretched idolaters believed that their foreign gods, or rather demons, who by their own suggestion gave warnings and oracles, were delighted and appeased by both kinds.

units.la: Quantum ad animalia attinet; ex illorum primum adhuc vivorum, postquam in templa et aras adulta fuerunt, percussione, jugulatione, mactatione, excoriatione atque dissectione, flerceribus denique, et excrementis, cui dubii; quin multi graves, odiosi foetidi, in templis (ut in macellis atq, laniensis videretur) odores exsisterent et sacrificantium oculos fuerint objecti.
units.tr: As far as animals are concerned, first the living creatures, once they had been brought into the temples and altars when fully grown, were struck, cut at the throat, slaughtered, flayed and dissected. Finally their blood and excrement, which there is no doubt about, were added. Indeed many heavy, hateful and foul odours arose in the temples, as if in a meat market or a butcher's shop, and were presented to the eyes of the sacrificers.

units.la: Deinde vero ex iisdem animalibus sive integris, sive eorum partibus membrisve, inq, cum internum, ut sanguinibus, intestinis, visceribus, praecordiis, extis; tum externis, ut carnibus pellibus, tergoribus, femoribus, caudis, testiculis, pilis; et hiis omnibus vel adustis et ustulatus, vel coctis, lium. vel combustis & tonitrematis, quales quantosq; fumos atq; nidores extitisse, in aërem ascendisse ac longe latèq; templa, in quibus sacrificabatur, locaq; vicina omnia complevisse existimandus est. Hujusmodi autem fumi atq; nidores Graecè ϰνίσεαι, sive ϰνίσωμ, Latinè Nidores appellantur. De vocenuisnis (quae partim pinguedinem sive adipem & omenti, partim nidoré significat) supra fuit explicatum.
units.tr: Then, from the same animals, whether whole or in their parts and limbs, both internal parts such as blood, intestines, viscera, entrails and innards, and external parts such as flesh, skins, hides, thighs, tails, testicles and hair, and all of these either scorched, or boiled, or roasted, or burnt, there must have risen into the air such great and varied smoke and savours, filling the temples where the sacrifices were made and all the surrounding places far and wide. Such smokes and savours are called in Greek knisēsai or knisōma, and in Latin nidores. The word knisis, which signifies partly fat and the omentum and partly savour, was explained above.

units.la: Nidor autem proprie carnis, ut cujuscunq; aluerius edulii cotti vel etiàm rei aduesta odorem proprié significat. Est & alius quidem Nidor suavis & jucundus, quiĥominiĥ nares ita vel benè, ut appetitum quandoq; excitet secundum illud Catulliani:
units.tr: Nidor properly means the smell of cooked flesh, or of any other cooked food or burnt thing. There is also a nidor that is sweet and pleasant, which pleases the nostrils and sometimes even stirs the appetite, as in that line of Catullus:
When you smell it, you will pray to the gods

units.la: Totum ut te faciant, Fabulle, nasum.
units.tr: to make you all nose, Fabullus.

units.la: Alius vero est nidor carnium aliarumq; rerum adustarum teter ac sœtidus, ut apud Virgilium: Occupat & flammas, illi ingens barba relinxit, Nidoremq; ambusta dedit.
units.tr: Another nidor, of burnt flesh and other burnt things, is foul and stinking, as in Virgil: "He seized the flames too; his great beard was left behind, and the scorched body gave off a burnt stench."

units.la: Nidorem autem, quoniam proprie dicitur odor sirnis, aut cujuscunque rei adustæ Grammatici vulgo volunt distum à nitore ignis, vel quasi nimium odor: unde & Nidere & Renidere aliquando odorem, aliquando fulgorem significant emittere. Cicero: Paulsper stetimus uti illo sanearum tuarum nidore atque fumo. Juvenalis: Captum te nidore suæ putat esse culinæ.
units.tr: Grammarians commonly hold that nidor, since it properly denotes the smell of smoke or of any burnt thing, is derived from the brightness (nitor) of fire, or else is as it were "too much odour." Hence nidere and renidere sometimes mean to give off a smell and sometimes to give off a gleam. Cicero: "We stood a little while enjoying the stench and smoke of your sausages." Juvenal: "She thinks you are captivated by the smell of her kitchen."
Martial:
You feed on the black smell of the kitchen alone.

units.la: Mantuanus ad Martialis imitationem: Fumifice motus crasso nidore culinæ.
units.tr: Mantuan, imitating Martial: "moved by the thick, smoky smell of the kitchen."

units.la: Idem alibi Nidores fumiferos vocat. Plautus: Tota renidet domus.
units.tr: The same poet elsewhere calls them smoky nidores. Plautus: "The whole house gleams."

units.la: Sunt qui Nidum distum volunt a nidore, quod sædi & mali odoris sint avium cubilia. Mihi quidem nidor videtur deduci a Graco ϰνίσεαι, sive ϰνίσωμ, tùm est sidem fere sint significationis. Ablatâ enim litterâ prima, videlicet ν, fit νίσσε vel νίσις, & inde Nidor. Et hinc quod Arnobius crebro vocat Cnisse, tanquâ Latina, pro nidore utitur. Finxerùt igitur Graeci Deos suos ϰνίσσοι ( quos Germani Bratenschmäcker appellant) bocest gulæ dedit os, qui carnium alierum, edulio rum coctorum nidoribus atq; fumis capiantur. Hinc saltem Arnobius illos perstringit libro septimo his verbis: Nisi forte hostiarum Deus animis de vorat, aut ex aris ardentibus nidorem consectatur & fumos, pafciturq; de cnislis, quae e vomunt ardentia visceris, seabuc uda sanguine, & prioribus humectatae satiis. Idem: Quod est honoris genus, signa cum struibus incens-te telum fumo subtexere et effigies Numinum nigrore offus-care?
units.tr: Some hold that nidus is named from nidor, because birds' nests are foul-smelling. To me, however, nidor seems derived from the Greek knisēsai or knisōma, since they have nearly the same meaning. For when the first letter, namely ν, is removed, one gets nisēsai or nisis, and from that nidor. This is why Arnobius often uses knisse, as if it were Latin, for nidor. So the Greeks invented gods of the knisai (whom the Germans call Bratenschmäcker), that is, gods given a mouth for gluttony, who are caught by the savours of roasted meats and cooked food and by smoke. Arnobius censures them in book seven with these words: "Unless perhaps the god of the victims devours their spirits, or from the burning altars pursues the savour and smoke, and feeds on the knisai which the burning entrails vomit forth, moistened with blood and soaked with the former fats?" The same writer says: "What kind of honour is it to overlay the statues with smoke from burning torches, and to obscure the effigies of the gods with blackness?"

units.la: VENIO ad odores, odoramenta, suffitus, seu suffumigia ex omni plantarii & e terra nascen-tium genere fieri solita. Atq; hæc quidem Gentiles putarunt antiquissima & prima fuisse sacraficia (de quo pauso antea) ut Porphyrius plurimus docet libro secundo de non necandis animalibus. Eodem in libro, antiquitus herbas simplices, domesticas, patrias adsacros illos suffitus conseciendos adhibitas fuisse docet, qui posse ex thure, ex myrrha, ex costo, ex croco & cinnamomo & aliis hujusmodi aromatibus pretiosis transmarinis, e longinquis ad vetus fieri sint foliis. Ei suffragatur Ovidius libro primo Fastorum his versibus: Nondum portabane lacrymatas cortice myrrhas Asta per aquoreat bofpita navis aquas: Thura nec Euphrates, nec miserat India fostum: Nec fuerant nobis cognita fila croci. Aru dabat fumos, herbis contenta Sabinis, Et non exiguo laurus adusta sono.
units.tr: I come now to odours, perfumes, and fumigations, which were customarily made from every kind of plant that grows on the earth. The Gentiles believed these to be the most ancient and first sacrifices, of which I spoke a little earlier, as Porphyry teaches at length in the second book of his work On Abstinence from Killing Animals. In the same book he teaches that in antiquity simple herbs, domestic and native, were used to make those sacred fumigations, which in later times were made from frankincense, myrrh, costus, saffron, cinnamon and other such precious spices brought from overseas and distant lands. Ovid supports this in the first book of the Fasti with these verses: "Myrrh in tears of bark had not yet been carried over the Aegean waters by ship; neither had the Euphrates nor India sent frankincense; nor were the threads of saffron known to us. The altar gave smoke, content with Sabine herbs, and the laurel burned with no small crackling."

units.la: Huc referenda illa Plinii, sui secus luxum atq; luxuriam reprehendentis, verba lib.12. cap.74: Nosnet Indicarum Arabicarumq; mercium aut externi orbis attigimus madicinas. Non plescent remedia tam longè nascentia. Non nobis gignuntur, immo ne illis quidem: alioquin nō ven-derent odorum eaussâ unguentorumq; & deliciarum, si placet etiam superstitionis gratia emantur, quoniam thure supplicamus & costo. De costo & nardo vide eundem scriptorem lib.12.cap.39. Ovidius inter herbas in sacris antiquitus suffiri & incendi solitas numerat atq; nominat herbas Sabinas atque laurum. Propertius similiter verbenarum herbæq; Sabinæ bis verbis meminit: Florè sacella tego, verbenis compita velo, Et crepat ad veteres herba Sabina focos.
units.tr: To this belong the words of Pliny, who censures the luxury and extravagance of his own age, in book 12, chapter 74: "We ourselves have touched the Indian and Arabian wares, and the medicines of the outer world. Remedies grown so far away do not please us. They are not grown for us; indeed, not even for those who grow them. Otherwise they would not sell them for the sake of perfumes, ointments and luxuries; they are bought, if you like, even for the sake of superstition, since we supplicate the gods with frankincense and costus." On costus and nard, see the same author, book 12, chapter 39. Ovid, among the herbs formerly burned and kindled in sacred rites, names the Sabine herbs and laurel. Propertius likewise mentions verbena and Sabine herb in these words: "I cover the shrines with flowers, I veil the crossroads with verbena, and the Sabine herb crackles at the old hearths."

units.la: Hic observandum, Verbenarum & herbarum Sabinarum nomen bifariam apud authores propriè sanos usurpari: Aliquando pro certo herbarū genere, quæ in sacrificiis fuerunt adhibitæ: aliquādo verò pro quibuscunq; herbis, quarum in sacris usus fuit creber & frequens.
units.tr: It must be observed here that the names verbena and Sabine herbs are used in two ways by authors who write with proper precision: sometimes for a certain kind of herb used in sacrifices, and sometimes for any herbs that were frequently and commonly used in sacred rites.

units.la: Quantum ad verbenas attinet, de iis iam supra fuit dictum, quibus hæc adjungam. Verbena multis nominibus à Medicis solet insigniri: duobus quidem a Græcis, ιερὰ βοτάνη id est, herba sacra, quod in sacris & lustrationibus adhiberetur, ideoq; ab Apuleio Lustrago vertitur: quia jovis mensa, id est, ara verrebatur, domus purgabatur, convivæ exhilarabantur, legati deniq; mittebantur clarigatum, id est indictâ hostilibus bellum. De hac vide plura apud Plinium lib.22.cap.2.& lib.25.ca.9. Περιστερέων & hoc quoq; dicitur, quod columba sie familiaris, vel περιστερεὼν, de qua lege Dioscoridem lib.4.cap.10. A Latinis bis nominibus appellatur Cincinnalis, Saguntalis, Betonica, Licinia, Columbina, Militaris, Verbenaca, Vertipedium, postremò etiam ab Aetio Herba Veneris. Horatius lib.1. Odarum oda decima nona hujus mentionem faciens herbæ, sic canit: Hic vivum mihi cespitem, hic Verbenas pueri ponite, thuraq́, Bimi cum patera meri. Mallata veniet lenior hostia.
units.tr: As far as verbena is concerned, I have already said something above, to which I will now add. Physicians commonly designate verbena by many names. Two are Greek: hiera botanē, that is, sacred herb, because it was used in sacrifices and purifications, which is why Apuleius translates it as lustrago; and peristereōn, because it is so familiar to doves, on which see Dioscorides, book 4, chapter 10. Its purpose was that Jupiter's table, that is the altar, was swept, the house was purified, the guests were cheered, and finally envoys were sent to declare war on the enemy (clarigatio). On this see more in Pliny, book 22, chapter 2, and book 25, chapter 9. Latin writers call it by these names: cincinnalis, saguntalis, betonica, licinia, columbina, militaris, verbenaca, vertipedium; finally even Aëtius calls it herba Veneris. Horace, mentioning this herb in Odes, book 1, ode 19, sings: "Here, boys, set down for me a living turf, here verbena and incense, and a cup of undiluted wine. A gentler victim will come, softened."

units.la: Et hinc Veneris herba dicta, eamq; ob rem ejus in hac ode ab Horatio fit mentio, ut in Pharmacenteria, ad Glyceram, ab se alienatam, revocandam: quòd ea herba crederetur vim habere conciliandi petita impetrandi. Unde apud Virgilium: Verbenasq; adole pinguesq; et masculâ turâ.
units.tr: Hence it is called the herb of Venus, and for this reason Horace mentions it in this ode, as in the Pharmaceutria, to win back Glycera, who had become estranged from him, because this herb was believed to have the power of winning affection and obtaining requests. Hence in Virgil: "Add verbena, and fat frankincense, and male incense."

units.la: Apuleius: Exin gaudio delibuti populares, tales verbenas corollas ferences exosculati vestigiis Deæ, &c. Verbenarum fasciculi teste Festo, Deorum capita fuerunt appellati. Ex quo ipso confiat, quod his herbis veteres in sacris fecerint.
units.tr: Apuleius: "Then the people, delighted and overflowing with joy, wearing such garlands of verbena, kissed the footprints of the goddess, etc." According to Festus, bundles of verbena were called heads of the gods. From this itself it is clear what the ancients did with these herbs in their sacred rites.

units.la: Verbenas porrò nonnulli volunt dictas, quasi Herbenas, quoniam generatim significatur illo vocabulo omnes herbæ frondesq;, sacræ, & festæ, quibus vel arae ( unde Donatus eas ararum redimicula vocat) vel sacrificantes, vel etiam simulacra redimi atq; coronari solebat: ex quibus etiam incensis suffitus fiebant, secundum illa Virgilii in Bucolicis, quæ modo citata: Verbenasq; adole, &c. Verbenæ etiam sagmina dicta, de quibus supra.
units.tr: Some hold that verbenae are so called as if they were herbenae, because that word generally signifies all herbs and fronds, sacred and festal, with which altars (whence Donatus calls them garlands of altars), sacrificers, or even images were wont to be wreathed and crowned. From these, when they were burnt, fumigations were also made, according to the lines of Virgil in the Bucolics quoted just now: "Add verbena, etc." Verbenae are also called sagmina, of which I spoke above.

units.la: Servius in illa Virgilii Aeneidos 12. Fontemq; ignemq; ferebant, Velati lino & verbena tempora vinctí:
units.tr: Servius, on that line of Virgil's Aeneid 12: "They carried water and fire, their temples veiled with linen and bound with verbena."

units.la: Verbena, inquit, proprie est herba sacra, sumta de loco sacro Capitolii, qua coronabantur Faciales & Pater patratus, fœderà facturi vel bella indicturi. Abusive tamen etiam verbenas vocamus, omnes frondes sacratas, ut est laurus, oliva, & myrtus. Terentius: Ex ara hinc verbenas desume.
units.tr: Verbena, he says, is properly a sacred herb, taken from the sacred place of the Capitol, with which the Fetiales and the Pater patratus were crowned when they were about to make covenants or declare war. Loosely, however, we also call all consecrated leaves verbenas, such as laurel, olive and myrtle. Terence: "Take verbenas from the altar here."

units.la: Nam myrtum fuisse Menander testatur, de quo Terentius traustulit.
units.tr: For Menander testifies that there was myrtle, which Terence transferred into his play.

units.la: Ut autem verbenarum, sic Sabinarum similiter nomine cum certa herbae species, tum quaevis herba frondesq; sacrate intelliguntur, ut ille, de quibus jam dixi, olea, laurus & alia id genus, de quibus paullo post. De Sabina herba & ejus usu in suffitu sic scribit Plinius lib.24.ca.11. Herba Sabina, bratby appellata a Græcis, duorum generum est. Altera tamaricæ similis folio est, altera cupressō. Quæ ex re quidam Creticam cupressum dixerunt. A multis in suffitibus pro thure assumitur. In medicamentis vero duplicato pondere eosdem effectus habere quod cinnamum traditur. Colliectiones minuit, & nomas compescit. Illa ulcera purgat. Partus emortuos appositâ extrahit & suffitu. Plinius igni sacro & carbunculus. Cum melle & vino pota, regio morbo medetur. Gallinaceigeneris puiu: as sumo eius herbæ fanari tradunt. Similis huic herbæ Sabinæ est
units.tr: As the name verbenae is used, so the name sabinae is likewise used for a certain kind of herb, and for any herb or consecrated leaves, as with those I have already mentioned, olive, laurel and the like, which I will discuss shortly. Pliny writes as follows about the Sabine herb and its use in fumigation, Book 24, chapter 11: "The Sabine herb, called brathy by the Greeks, is of two kinds. One has a leaf like the tamarisk, the other like the cypress. For this reason some have called it the Cretan cypress. Many use it in fumigations in place of incense. In medicines it is said to have the same effects as cinnamon, but at twice the weight. It reduces swellings and checks ulcers of the nose. It cleanses sores. Applied and also used as a fumigation, it draws out dead foetuses. Taken with honey and wine, it cures the king's disease (jaundice). Men say that the chicks of hens are cured by the smoke of this herb." The herb Selago is similar to this Sabine herb.

units.la: Selago appellata. Legitur sine ferro dextra manu per tunicam quae sinistra exuitur, velut a furao te, candida veste vestito, pureq; lotis nudis pedibus, sacro facto prius quam legatur, pane vinoq; Praeferturin mappa nova. Hanc contra omnem perniciem habendam prodidere Druidae Gallorum, & contra omnia ostulorum vitia fumum ejus prodesse. Idem lib.17. cap.13. Sabina ipsius herbae mentionem facit, quam propagine tradit fui & a vulsione.
units.tr: Selago is gathered without iron, with the right hand, passing under the tunic, which is taken off on the left side, as if by a thief; the gatherer is dressed in a white garment, with clean and bare feet, and before it is gathered a sacrifice is made of bread and wine, and it is carried in a new cloth. The Druids of the Gauls declared that it should be held as a remedy against every destruction, and that its smoke helps against all diseases of the eyes. Book 17, chapter 13, of the same author also mentions the Sabine herb itself, which he says is propagated from a shoot and by pulling up.

units.la: Sabina herba quia in sacris adhibita nonnullis videtur ἀπὸ τῆς σίδηρος ... idest, tolendo dicta: unde & Sabaeos & Sabinos populos, tanquam religiosissimos Deorum cultores, & Sabinum Deum, & Sabbatium, de quibus supra, nonnulli volunt appellatos.
units.tr: Since the Sabine herb is used in sacred rites, some think it is so called from the Greek word meaning "to pull out" (ἀπὸ τῆς σίδηρος...), that is, from pulling it up. For this reason some also think that the Sabaeans and Sabines, as the most religious worshippers of the gods, and the god Sabinus and Sabbatius, of whom I spoke above, were named after it.

units.la: Quoniam autem cum Verbenarum, tum Sabinarum herbarum nominib. laurus, myrtus, olea & alia herbae sacratae in sacris ad suffitus usurpari solitae, nunc quaedam addida. Ade lau ri quidem, olea at q, myrti usu sacro plurima passim in antiquis litterarum monumentis ceftimonia exstant, ita ut eorum commemoratio videatur esse supervacanea. Solam quidem laurum suffiri solitam apud Delphos scribit Plutarchus. Casaubonus, vir doctissimus, in doctissimo suo Commentario in Theophrasti characteres in illum locum de superstitione: Δάφνης εἰς τὸ σωμα ... hoc est eodem interprete, Folium lauri ore prehensum tenensita commentatur: Scimus namq; Veteres in purgationibus, lauri foliis uti solitos. Clemens Alexandrinus in Protreptico, ... Sic & Romani, ut ait Festus, omnibus suffitionibus laurum adhibebant. Mortis praeterea fuit Graecis baculum laureum prae manibus habere, tanquam ἀλεξικακον φρόυρκτον, ut ait Sudas, quod crederent lauro inesse quandam malum a verruncandi. Inde natum pro verbum ... quod negat se sibi ab alicuius insidiis metuere. Eodem etiam ipsestat, quod observare aliquando meminimus, solitos Graecos pro foribus laurum statuere. Autor Hesychius in voce κωλυσις. Quid ait Theophrastus laurum in os capi solitam e superstitiosis, nescio an huic simulis sit superstitio, quam apud Hieronymum in Marcelle vidua epitaphio annotavimus. Sic ille, Nec mirum si in placetis & in fororum venalium festus ariolus fultorum verberat nates, & obtorto fulte dentes mordentium quatiat. Nam ariolorum consuetudo fuit (colligi potest ex Seneca de vita beata) laurum gestare cum per urbem incederent, quam fuffiem videtur Hieronymus vocare, quia erat, credo, virga laurea. Sane poetae dicuntur laurum mordere Juvenalis, & Calpandrus Δάφνης & Lycophron appellatur: quod quomodo Critici explicent non est obscurum. Hasellus ille.
units.tr: Since laurel, myrtle, olive and other sacred herbs, which were commonly used in sacred rites for fumigation, have been mentioned under the names of verbenae and sabinae, let me now add some things. Indeed there are very many ceremonies about the sacred use of laurel, olive and myrtle scattered through the ancient monuments of literature, so that to recall them would seem superfluous. Plutarch writes that laurel alone was customarily burned at Delphi. Casaubon, a most learned man, in his very learned commentary on the Characters of Theophrastus, on the passage about superstition, "Holding a laurel leaf in the mouth" (Δάφνης εἰς τὸ σῶμα...), comments, in the words of the same interpreter: "We know that the ancients were accustomed to use laurel leaves in purifications." Clement of Alexandria in the Protrepticus... Thus also the Romans, as Festus says, used laurel in all fumigations. Moreover, it was the custom among the Greeks to carry a laurel staff in their hands, as a "protection against evil" (ἀλεξικακον φρόυρκτον), as Suidas says, because they believed there was some power in laurel to ward off evil. From this came the saying that a man fears no one's ambush. The same thing is indicated by the fact, which I recall observing, that the Greeks used to set up laurel before their doors. Hesychius is the authority, under the word "prohibition". What Theophrastus says, that a laurel leaf was commonly put in the mouth, is one of the superstitions; I do not know whether this is similar to the superstition which I noted in Jerome's epitaph for the widow Marcella. He says: "Nor is it surprising if, in the squares and in the markets of the sellers, a fortune-telling fool beats his buttocks with a cudgel and shakes the teeth of those who bite with a twisted stick." For it was the custom of soothsayers (as may be gathered from Seneca, On the Happy Life) to carry laurel when they walked through the city; Jerome seems to call this a fustis, because it was, I believe, a laurel rod. Indeed poets are said to bite laurel, as Juvenal does, and Calpurnius is called "of the laurel" and Lycophron too; how the critics explain this is not obscure. Thus that man (Hasellus).

units.la: Cur vero adiguem sempiternum de omnibus lignis sola uratur abies, cur sola laurus suffiatur Plutarchus rationem reddit in Commentariis de Isi inscripto foribus templi Delphici. Plinius de lauri sacro usu & profano sic scribit lib.15.cap.ultimo: Ipsa laurus pacifera, ut quam praesentes etiam inter armatos hostes quoties sit inductum. Romanis praecipue laetitiae victoriarum, nuncia additur litiis, & militum lanceis pilisq. Fasces Imperatorum decorat. Ex his in gremio lovis, Opt. Max. deponitur, quoties laetitiam victoria novam attulit, id, non quia perpetuo viret, nec quia pacifera est, praeferenda utique myrto & oleae sed quia spectatissima in monte Parnaso. Ideoque etiam gratia Apollini, ut ejus ea dona mittere jam & Regibus Romanis, teste L.Bruto. Foriafis etiam ita argumentum, quomam ibi libertatem publicam ut meruisset, lauriferam tellurem illam oculatus ex respoenso: & quia manu sacrorum recepta mque in domomos, fulmine sola non icitur. Oh has causas equidem crediderim, honorem eis habitum in triumphis potius, quam quia suffimentum sit caedis boflium, & purgatio, ut tradit Massurius. Adeoque in profanus usibus pollui laurum & oleam fas non est, ut ne propitiandis quidem Numinibus accendi ex his altaria are ve debeant. Laurus quidem manifesto abdicatignes crepitu & quadam detestatione, interaneorum etiam vitia & nervorum ligno torquente. Tiberium principem sonante caelo coronari solitum ferunt contra fulminum metus.
units.tr: Why only fir is burned as a perpetual fire from all woods, and why only laurel is used for fumigation, Plutarch gives a reason in his Commentaries on Isis, inscribed on the doors of the Delphic temple. Pliny, on the sacred and profane use of laurel, writes thus in Book 15, last chapter: "Laurel itself, the bringer of peace, since it is carried even among armed enemies whenever it is presented; it is especially a sign of joy for the Romans at victories, and is attached to the lictors' fasces and to the lances and javelins of soldiers. It adorns the fasces of the commanders. From these, whenever it has brought news of a new victory, a sprig is laid in the lap of Jupiter Best and Greatest. This is done not because it is always green, nor because it bears peace, since myrtle and olive ought surely to be preferred for that, but because it is most esteemed on Mount Parnassus. And so it is also a gift to Apollo, as is said to have been sent to the Roman kings too, as Lucius Brutus testifies. It is also a sign of this, since the Pythian oracle, when Brutus asked how the public liberty might be obtained, answered him that it would be obtained when the land of laurel was kissed. And because it is received by the hand of priests, and is brought into houses, it alone is not struck by lightning. For these reasons I would indeed believe that it was honoured in triumphs rather than because it is a fumigation for slaughtering enemies and a purification, as Maccius (?) relates. And indeed it is not lawful to pollute laurel and olive in profane uses, so that they must not even be lit as altar fires for propitiating the divinities. Laurel is clearly rejected from the fire on account of its crackling and a certain abhorrence, since it also twists the entrails and nerves with its wood." They say the emperor Tiberius was accustomed to be crowned with laurel when the sky thundered, as protection against the fear of lightning.

units.la: Idem lib.16.cap.32. Circa Bosphorum Cimmerium in Panticapea urbe, omni modo laboravit Mithridates Rex, ut caeteri incolae, sacrorum terte caussa laurum myrtumq; haberent. Idem lib.15.cap.30. Laurus triumphis proprie dicatur, velgratissima domibus: janitrix Casarum Pontifitumq; quae sola & domos exornat & ante limina excubat.
units.tr: The same author, Book 16, chapter 32: "Around the Cimmerian Bosphorus, in the city of Panticapaeum, King Mithridates took every trouble so that the other inhabitants might have laurel and myrtle for the sake of sacred rites." The same author, Book 15, chapter 30: "Laurel is properly dedicated to triumphs, or is most pleasing to houses; it is the doorkeeper of the Caesars and the Pontiffs, which alone both adorns the houses and keeps watch before the thresholds."

units.la: De myrtoidem scriptor libro 15.cap.29. inter alia, quae ad institutum nostrum faciunt, sic scribit: Quippe ita traditur, Myrcea verbena Romanos Sabinosq; cùm propter raptas virgines dimicare voluissent, depositis armis pacificatos in eo loco, quinunc signa Veneris Cluacinae habet. Cluere enim antiqui pugnare dicebant. Et in ea quoq; arbore suffimenti genus habetur. Ideo tum electa, quoniam conjunctioni & buic arbori praest Venus. Haud scio, an prima ea etiam omnium in loco publico Romae sata sit, fatidico quidè & memorabili augurio. Inter antiquissima nanq; delubra habetur Quirini, hoc est ipsius Romuli: in eo sacrae myrti fuere duae ante aedem ipsam per longum tempus. Altera patritia appellata: altera plebeia, exuberans ac laeta, quamdiu senatus quoq; floruit, illa vigens, plebeia torrida ac squalida. Quae postquam eveluit, flavescente patricia, Martio bello languida authoritas Patrum salta est, ac paulatim in sterilitatem emarcuit majestas. Quin & ara vetus suit Veneri Myrteae, quam nunc Murtiam vocant.
units.tr: On the myrtle: the same writer, Book 15, chapter 29, among other things that bear on our purpose, writes thus: "For it is handed down that the Romans and Sabines, when they wished to fight on account of the raped virgins, laid down their arms and were reconciled in that place, which now has the image of Venus Cloacina. For the ancients used to say cluere for to fight. And in this tree too there is a kind of fumigation. It was then chosen because Venus presides over marriage and this tree. I do not know whether it was also the first of all to be sown in a public place at Rome, though by a prophetic and memorable omen. For among the most ancient shrines is that of Quirinus, that is, of Romulus himself; in it there were two sacred myrtles before the temple itself for a long time. One was called patrician, the other plebeian, lush and cheerful. As long as the senate also flourished, the patrician one was vigorous, the plebeian one parched and squalid. But after the patrician one was uprooted, and the myrtle turned yellow, the authority of the Fathers was languid in the Martian war, and gradually the majesty withered into barrenness. Moreover there was also an old altar to Venus Myrtea, which they now call Murtia."

units.la: De olea idem libro 15.capite ultimo, de quo antea.
units.tr: On the olive: the same author, Book 15, last chapter, which I mentioned before.

units.la: Nidor porro est proprie rei adustae odor nonnullis videtur distus a nitore ignis, sive a nitio odore, sive a Graeco νιτοσα seu νιτοσα: tamen de odore etiam plantarum vocabulum hoc usurpari indicant illa Plinii libro decimo tertio: Cedri tantum & Citri suorum fructuum in sacris sumum convolutum nidorem veriùs, quàm odorem noverant.
units.tr: The smell (nidor) properly means the odour of a burned thing; some think the word is derived from the brightness (nitor) of fire, or from a word for shining, or from the Greek νιτοσα or νιτοσα; yet the word is also shown to be used of the odour of plants by that passage of Pliny, Book 13: "Only the smoke of the fruits of the cedar and citron in sacred rites was known to them as a smell (nidor) rather than as an odour."

units.la: Verum de herbis antiqui & odoramentis ex herbis odoriferis earumque differentiis in genere vide eundem Plinium libro vigesimo primo, capite septimo, ubi lotos, trocon, byacintum flores ab Homero ait celebrari. Idem de fructuum suttis arborumque coloribus & odoribus scripsit libro 15.cap.28.
units.tr: On herbs in general, and on the perfumes made from fragrant herbs and their differences, see the same Pliny, book 21, chapter 7, where he says that the flowers of the lotus, the trochus and the hyacinth are celebrated by Homer. He wrote on the juices of fruits and on the colours and odours of trees in the same work, book 15, chapter 28.

units.la: Ficus quoque pro ture olim in sacris adoleri solitas, manifeste illa Iuliani Imp. testantur in epistola ad Sarapionem, quae ficuum pariter atque numeri centenarii egregiam laudationem continent. Verba ejus haec sunt: Καθάπερ αὐτ' ἄλλης τινὸς ἀλεξήσεως ἰσχὺς ταῖς τῶ βεσμάτοις ἀδυνάτως εἰς ἀναπαυομένου... ... Ficus etiam pro ture in sacris adhibitae. Tandem hoc unum (ficus) pro omnibus sacrum remedium ad versus ciborum injurias exhibebatur. Enimverò Diis eam consectari omnibus, ars adhiberi, & quo vis thure ad odores aptioreni esse, non mea est oratio, sed quisquis usum ejus didicit, a sapiente aliquo homine, sacrorumque antistite intelligat.
units.tr: Figs too were once commonly burned in sacred rites in place of incense, as the Emperor Julian clearly attests in his letter to Sarapion, which contains high praise both of figs and of the number one hundred. His words are: "Just as the power of other remedies is of no avail to those who..." [Καθάπερ αὐτ' ἄλλης τινὸς ἀλεξήσεως ἰσχὺς ταῖς τῶ βεσμάτοις ἀδυνάτως εἰς ἀναπαυομένου...] ... Figs were also used in sacred rites in place of incense. Finally, this one thing, the fig, was offered as a sacred remedy against the harms of foods, above all others. That figs are to be sought by all the gods, that an art is to be applied to them, and that they are better suited to odours than any incense, is not my claim; but whoever has learned their use will understand it from some wise man, a priest of the sacred rites.

units.la: His addantur tedae atque sulphuris suffimenta, olim usitatissima ad quasvis respurgandas seu purificandas: Tedae Virgilius memiнит in Bucolicis: Hic focus, & pingues tedas: hic plurimus ignis. Ovidius primo Fastorum: Exspectat puros pinea taeda dies. Idem Virgilius Aeneidos septimo: Praeterea castis adolet dum altaria tedis. Castis, id est, piis, interprete Servio.
units.tr: To these may be added the fumigations of torch-pine and sulphur, once very widely used for cleansing and purifying of every kind. Virgil recalls torches in the Bucolics: "Here a hearth, and fat torches, here a great fire." Ovid in the first book of the Fasti: "The pure days await the pine torch." The same Virgil in the seventh book of the Aeneid: "Meanwhile he burns the altars with chaste torches." Chaste, that is, pious, as Servius explains.

units.la: Sed & tedae cum sulphure sape conjunguntur, ut apud Satyrographum illo versu: Cuperent lustrari, si quae darentur Sulphura cum tedis.
units.tr: But torch-pine is also often joined with sulphur, as in the satirist's line: "They would wish to be purified, if sulphur were given with torches."

units.la: Sic Plinius libro 16.cap.10. inter arbores, quae resinam ferunt, ponit & tedam, quam flammis ac luminibus sacrorum dicit esse gratam, & libro 25.cap.15. Habet, inquit, & in religionibus locum sulphur ad expiandas suffitu domos. Apuleius libro 11.in descriptione pompae & sacrorum Isidis Aegyptiae: Ibidem simulacrus rite dispositis, navem faberrime factam, pictura nurus Aegyptiorum circumseptus variegatam sumnius sacerdos tedā lucida, & ovo, & sulphure, solemnissimas preces de casto praefatur ore, quàm purissimè purificatam Deae (Isidi) nuncupavit dediaque siuque. Exhoc loco liquido conslat, tedam, sulphur, & ovum in purificationibus fuisse adhibita. Ovidius triplitem banc purgationem signat illo versu: Terg,senem Flamma,ser Aqua,ter Sulphure lustrat.
units.tr: So Pliny, book 16, chapter 10, among the trees that yield resin, lists also the torch-pine, which he says is pleasing to the flames and lights of sacred rites; and in book 25, chapter 15: "Sulphur also has a place in religious rites, for purifying houses by fumigation." Apuleius, in book 11, describing the procession and rites of the Egyptian Isis: "There, with the images duly arranged, the chief priest, wrapped in a variegated robe, with a shining torch, an egg and sulphur, utters the most solemn prayers from a chaste mouth, and having purified the ship most thoroughly, dedicates it to the goddess Isis." From this passage it is clear that torch, sulphur and egg were used in purifications. Ovid marks this threefold purgation in the line: "Thrice he purifies with flame, thrice with water, thrice with sulphur."

units.la: Sed ovis quoque lustrationes purgatione sque fieri solitas fuisse, non tantum illa Apulei, sed & Iuvenalis testatur: —Nisi se tentum lustra veris ovis. De ovis in lustrationibus ad bibitas.
units.tr: But that eggs too were customarily used for purifications is attested not only by Apuleius but by Juvenal: "Unless he purifies himself with eggs." We shall speak below of eggs in lustrations.
And Ovid in the Art of Love:

units.la: Et veniat, quae lustret anus, dellumque locumque,
units.tr: Let there come an old woman to purify the house and the place,
and let her bring sulphur and smoke in a trembling hand.

units.la: Lucianus in Dialogo, cui titulus, Καταπλους ἢ τυφανος, τα εἰς τὰ καθαρσίων ὀναμα, id est, purgationum ova vocat, quo ostendit ova esse lustralia et purgatoria. Sic legimus apud Macrobium, initiatos sacris Liberi patris magna cum ratione ovum coluisse, Ovidii similia cum mularum vocantes. De ovis vide Plinium libro 10. cap. 13. et de angariis eorum (ὠὸν-τεια dicta) capite 55. Ergo purificationes illae Veterum, aqua, et igni, et tedae, et sulphure, et ova fiebant.
units.tr: Lucian, in the dialogue entitled The Voyage Down, or The Tyrant, calls them purgation-eggs, by which he shows that eggs were used for lustration and purgation. So we read in Macrobius that those initiated into the rites of Father Liber reverenced the egg with great reason, as Ovid's similar lines about the mules show. On eggs see Pliny, book 10, chapter 13, and on their offerings, chapter 55. Therefore the purifications of the ancients were performed with water, fire, torch-pine, sulphur and eggs.

units.la: Vt ad sulphur redeam, Proclus nobilis Platonicus scribit, sacerdotes in purificationibus, uti solitos sulphure atque asphalto, id est, bitumine aqua marina aspergentes, quoniam ut ille inquit, purificat sulphur propter odores acumen, aqua vero marina propter igneam portionem.
units.tr: To return to sulphur: the noble Platonist Proclus writes that in purifications priests were accustomed to sprinkle with sulphur and asphalt, that is, bitumen, mixed with sea water; for, as he says, sulphur purifies because of its sharp odour, and sea water because of its fiery part.

units.la: Quoniam igitur sulphur res hal ita fuit sacra et divina, magnaque ei quae vis purificandi tribuitur, Graeci illud Θειον, quasi dicas divinum et Latini sulphur, a suffiendo (ut videtur) appellarunt: unde Exsir, purgamentum esse telle appellatum.
units.tr: Since, then, sulphur was regarded as so sacred and divine, and so great a power of purifying is ascribed to it, the Greeks called it theion, as if to say "divine," and the Latins called it sulphur, from suffiendo (as it seems). Whence the word for a purgation was also derived.

units.la: Denique hiceferenda est duplex illa Veterum consuetudo expiandi lustrandique, fe, cuius meminit idem Caesaubonus eodem Commentario in Theophrastichamcleres. Verbaeius adhaec Theophrastii σχολιαν ὁ σχολακα κελευσαι αυτον ἀποκαθαρσαι, sunt ista: Tangis duplicem Veterum consuetudinem explicandi lustrandique, sc. Altera erat circumacta circa corpus scilla: alterus catulo similiter circa corpus ducto. Hoc enim significat ἀποκαθαρσαι. De scilla, quod expiandi rim crederetur habere, notum vel ex Plinio, et medicorum libris. Artemidorus Euodius, ὁ σιλλα καθαρσεις τῶν νοσων. Lucianus Ἐλλησπονικος. Εκ Φατητ τα ἐξ ἀπεσαν, καὶ ἀποκαθαρσεῖν. Vide amplius Theochriti Scholiasten Thalysius. De catulo, res minus vulgo, ut videtur, nota: quare etiam ejus ritus ignoratione interpretes minus modus hunc locum depravarunt: in quo nihil erat prorsus mutandum. Nam verum est quod diximus, veteres catulo solitos lustrare se eum circumferentes circa corpus: eam, lustrationem voc.ant ἀποκαθαρσιον. Plutarchus in Καθαρσιοις Romanorum institutorum. Τὸ δὲ κυνὶ πάντες ὡς τὸν ἐν κατέλ ἀγαλμα τοῦτο τοῦ ἐξω ἀπὸ τὸ ὅλον. Idem repetit in Romulo. Fuerunt et alii tum Scillae, tum catulorum in feebrutationibus usus, quos prudens emitto.
units.tr: Finally, here should be mentioned that double custom of the ancients of expiating and lustrating, which the same Casaubon recalls in his commentary on Theophrastus' Characters. The words of Theophrastus, with the scholium, are these: "You touch on the twofold custom of the ancients of expiating and lustrating: one was to carry a squill around the body, the other to lead a puppy around the body in the same way. For this is what apokatharsai [ἀποκαθαρσαι] means." That the squill was believed to have expiatory power is known even from Pliny and the medical books. Artemidorus Euodius says that the squill is a purgation of diseases; Lucian in the Hellenes' Lament... Consult also the scholiast of Theocritus, Thalysius. The matter of the puppy is less known to the common reader, as it seems; therefore interpreters, through ignorance of this rite, have corrupted this passage, where nothing at all needed changing. For it is true, as we have said, that the ancients used to purify themselves by carrying a puppy around the body, and they called this lustration apokatharsion. Plutarch, in the Roman Questions, says that all carried the dog around the body and away from the whole. He repeats this in the Life of Romulus. There were also other uses of both squill and puppies in purifications, which I prudently pass over.

units.la: Idem, Αὐτὸ ἀποκαθαρσαι significat hoc verbum applicare aliquid corpori expiandi causa, id in orbem ducere: quod et circumferre dicitur: Latinus circumferre. Vergilius: Idem ter fociosis pura circumtulit unda. Servius, circumtulit, purgavit. Antiquum vel huius est: Plautus, Pro laevato te circumferam id est, purgabo. Nam lustratio a circumlatione dicta est vel tedae vel sulphuris. Juvenalis: Si qua darentur sulphura cum tedis. Recte exprimit Servius circumlationem illam, quae in luftrationibus fieri solebat. Similiter et urbes, et agri lustrabantur, hostiis in orbem circumlatis. Polybius libro quarto de Mantinensibus, ὡς γὰρ ἀπὸ ἀρχῆς ... Ideo Latinus ea Sacra ambarualia dita. Atque hinc ἐξ, quod νῦν ἐξ fere in verbis eo pertinentibus reperitur, ut in ἀναπαύειν, ἀποβαίνει... xii. Sic et ἀποβαίνει apud Aristotelem in sexto Historiarum, de lustratione galatarum, quae ἐκκαρθειν Plutarcho nuncupatur. Sed et ἕκαστος ἐν εὖ ἐστι νομοσ... Demosthenes pro corona καθαρσιον ... Sic accipiendum et in illo Callimachi ut puto, versiculo, initio Athenaei.
units.tr: The same author: the verb αὐτὸ ἀποκαθαρσαι [apokatharsai] means to apply something to a body for the sake of expiation, to lead it around in a circle. This is also said "to carry around," in Latin circumferre. Virgil: "The same, three times, with pure water sprinkled [circumtulit] his companions." Servius on circumtulit: "purified." There is an older use of this in Plautus: "Pro laevato te circumferam," that is, "I will purify you." For lustration took its name from carrying something around, either a torch or sulphur. Juvenal: "If any sulphur were given with torches." Servius rightly explains that carrying around, which was customary in lustrations. In the same way cities and fields were purified, with victims carried around in a circle. Polybius, in book four, on the Mantineans: "for from the beginning..." For this reason the Latins called those rites the Ambarvalia. Hence also ἐξ, which is found almost in words belonging to this, as in ἀναπαύειν and ἀποβαίνει... xii. So too ἀποβαίνει in Aristotle, in the sixth book of the Histories, on the lustration of the Galatians, which Plutarch calls ἐκκαρθειν. But also ἕκαστος ἐν εὖ ἐστι νομοσ... Demosthenes, in the speech for the crown: καθαρσιον [katharsion]... In the same way, I think, that little verse of Callimachus at the beginning of Athenaeus should be understood.

units.la: Τὸς ἐνσύμεξ ἀμάνοντα ἐν ἀδελφ ἀλλ' ἔνῳ.
units.tr: Τὸς ἐνσύμεξ ἀμάνοντα ἐν ἀδελφ ἀλλ' ἔνῳ. [A line of Greek verse, too garbled in the scan to be rendered reliably.]

units.la: Quem locum Erasmus et alii non rectè conati sunt trabere, cum ex hoc ritu fit explicandus. Hinc dictae sunt mulierculae illae, quarum hic Theophrastus meminit, ἀγαμάχαι, ut est, apud Pollucem vel ἀποκαθαρσιας, ut vocat eas Plutarchus, de superstitione. Latinis piatrices, et fumulatrices, vel potius fimpulatrices, vide Festum. Talem fuisse ait Demosthenes Glaucothean sive Empusam Aeschinis matrem. Haec enim Caesaubonus.
units.tr: Erasmus and others have not rightly tried to draw this passage out, since it must be explained from this rite. From it are named those little women, mentioned here by Theophrastus, the ἀγαμάχαι [agamachai], as they are called in Pollux, or the ἀποκαθαρσιας [apokatharsias], as Plutarch calls them in his work On Superstition. Among the Latins they were called piatrices and fumulatrices, or rather fimpulatrices; see Festus. Demosthenes says that Glaucothea, or Empusa, the mother of Aeschines, was such a woman. So Casaubon.

units.la: Quemadmodum igitur suffimentorum ac suffitionum iflarū, quae ex omni rerum genere fieri solent, maximus est in medicina usus, ut docent Medici, ut docet ipsa ratio et experientia quotidiana: sic Ethnici quoque in sacris suis maximam eindem purgandi, purificandi, lustrandi, expiandi reatū, ipsos placandi vim tribuerunt, ut passim in authorum libris licet legere. Iamblichus de mysteriis Aegyptiorum, segmento 3. ca. 24. Suffimigationes, inquit, adhibite affinitate et cognatione hoc usu. nem habent cum Deo ipso, cui offeruntur, non cum anima vidente. Idem segmeto 5. cap. 1. Ajunt, inquit, Hypophetas sacrificulos abstinere debere ab animantibus, ne Dij sanis exhalantibus ex mactatione animalium inficiantur. Sed huic sententiae repugnat fama communis, et vox omnium gentium, Numina nidoribus maxime delectari, capiq; inescata. Hanc quaestionem sol vit, capitibus etiam sequentibus. Cicero quoq; horum suffimentorum meminit de Legibus, inquiens: Nam etiam fine ullius suffimentis expiari sumus.
units.tr: Just as, therefore, fumigations and suffumigations made from every kind of material are of the greatest use in medicine, as physicians teach and as reason itself and daily experience show, so the heathen too in their sacred rites attributed the greatest power to cleansing, purifying, lustrating and expiating guilt, and to appeasing the gods themselves, as one may read everywhere in the books of the authors. Iamblichus, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, section 3, chapter 24: "Fumigations, he says, which are used, have affinity and kinship with God himself, to whom they are offered, not with the seeing soul." The same, section 5, chapter 1: "They say," he says, "that the Hypophetes, the minor priests, ought to abstain from animals, lest the gods be contaminated by the exhalations from the slaughter of animals." But this opinion is opposed by common report and the voice of all nations, that the deities take the greatest delight in savours and are caught by baits. He resolves this question also in the following chapters. Cicero too mentions these fumigations in his On the Laws, saying: "For we are also purified even without any fumigations."

units.la: Porphyrius in libro, qui sunt quattuor, ἀπο ἀπέχεσθαι ... ut ipse, ab abstinentia ab animalibus, malibus, sive de non vescendo ad epulas veterum animalibus, libri duo pluribus disputat, Herbarum quidem et plantarum sacrificia ac suffimenta antiquitus fieri solita Dijs esse grata et acceptata: at animalium sacrificia, et quae exi(sunt) fumigatio, sen suffimenta, atq; etiam vaticinia non item. Lucianus in Dialogo, qui inscribitur Prometheus sive Caucasus, hanc Gentilis in sacrificiis odores incendendi et suffitus omnis generis faciendi consuetudinem manifestè indicat, falsè, simul irridet atq; perstringit, sub Prometheo sese designe farsepto excusantis personae. Ejus verba habet sunt: Οἱ ἄνθρωποι κ.τ.λ. ... Lucianus.
units.tr: Porphyry, in the work that is in four books, On Abstinence from Animal Food, discusses at length, as he himself does, the eating of animals in the feasts of the ancients, in the two books. He holds that herbs and plants were anciently offered in sacrifice and burned as incense to the gods, and were pleasing and acceptable to them. But sacrifices of animals, and the smoke or fumigation of them, and even their divinations, were not so. Lucian, in the dialogue entitled Prometheus, or the Caucasus, plainly indicates the Gentile custom of burning odours in sacrifices and making every kind of fumigation. Yet he at once mocks and lashes it, though falsely, by putting these excuses in the mouth of Prometheus. His words are: The men, and so on [Οἱ ἄνθρωποι κ.τ.λ.]. Lucian.

units.la: Sed non opus est in re nota ad modum et manifesta plura proferre testimonia, quae passim apud Poetas aliosq; scriptores profanos sunt obvia. In libro quoq; Sapientiae et illa Jeremiae sive Baruch epistola de Babyloniorum aliarumque gentium idolol(atria) fumorum ut sacrificiorum ac suffimentorum fit mentio, quibus significantur idola ipsorum acq; simulacra fumis ... ut infici ac denigrari fuisse solita, ad idololatrarum ipsorum fulcitiam demon(s)trandum.
units.tr: But there is no need to bring forward many testimonies on a matter that is well known and plain, since they are everywhere to be met with in the poets and other profane writers. In the book of Wisdom too, and in that letter of Jeremiah, or Baruch, about the idolatry of the Babylonians and of other nations, mention is made of the smoke of sacrifices and of fumigations, by which their idols and images were said to be customarily stained and blackened by the smoke. This is done to show the idolaters' own folly.

units.la: Nec tamen mirum est, Gentiles odoribus suffimentis, istis in illis suis sacris usos fuisse, tantum tres quarum purificandi, Deosq; suos propitiandi vim tribuisse, cum odores, si vim illorum atq; naturam in genere spectemus, vel ipsa ratione experientiaq; esse locupletissima. Et sint maximē tenues, subtiles, ignes ac spiritus naturam habentes, esse etiam Plutarchoin commentario de Ei foribus templi Delphicis inscripto: unde celerrime fur sum feruntur, longe late, diffundantur, hominum animalium, cerebrum penetrandi, et varii afficiendi vel ledendi, vel retrenandi et reficiendi maximam vim habent.
units.tr: Yet it is no wonder that the Gentiles used such odours and fumigations in their sacred rites, and attributed to them the power of purifying and of propitiating their gods, since, if we consider the force and nature of odours in general, they are proved by reason and experience to be most abundant. Even though they are most fine and subtle, and have the nature of fire and spirit, as Plutarch also says in his commentary on the inscription on the doors of the temple at Delphi, they are carried most swiftly upwards and spread far and wide. They have the greatest power to penetrate the brain of men and animals, and to affect them variously, either to harm or to restrain and refresh them.

units.la: Atq, hac quidem illorum vis subtilis ac spiritualis magis adhuc patet, si cum reliquorum sensuum objectis conferantur: cujusmodi sunt colores, soni, saporis, et tactiles qualitates, quae crassae magis et corporeae sunt subjiciant. Ipsa quoq; flandi seu effiandi, halandi seu exhalandi, spirandi verba, quae odoribus sepe tribuuntur, ipsos significant flatus, halitus et spiritus quosdam esse. Quamobrem Deorum sive Daemonum, potius illorum suorum naturae odores, suffimentaq; ista sua maxime convenire, et idcirco plurimum illis placere, maximam illos placandi vim habere arbitrabantur.
units.tr: Indeed, this subtle and spiritual power of theirs appears still more clearly if we compare odours with the objects of the other senses, such as colours, sounds and tastes, and tactile qualities, which are grosser and more bodily. Moreover, the words used of odours, such as blowing or breathing out, inhaling or exhaling, and breathing, show that they are certain puffs, breaths and spirits. Therefore they thought that odours and such fumigations were especially fitting to the nature of the gods or demons, and that for this reason they were most pleasing to them, and had the greatest power to appease them.

units.la: His rationibus congruunt illa Plutarchi in libro de Iside et Osiride, ubi significat, Graecos illos suis suffimentis sacris non pietatis tantum, sed etiam sanitatis rationem habuisse. Verba ejus sunt ista: Quod si est, sicuti in me recepere aliquid, etiam dicendū de iis, quae quotidie adolentur: illud primo cogitandi videtur, viros ipsos fluidum rerum ad sanitatem conducentium nunquam non secisse maximè in sacrificiis autem, caeteris moniis ac vita quotidiana nfu no minore pietatis duxisse quam sanitatis rationem sentiebant videlicet neq; corporibus neq; animis morbi suffectus aut vitii redi- coli eam, posse naturam, quae undiquaq; pura in pollura, atq; illaesa est. Ergo quoniam aer quo affluduo utimur, sinq; eo degimus, non eodem semper affectus, temperatusq; est, modo: sed nostrum den- satur, corpus comprimit, animamq; compellit ad mestitiam quandam & solicitudinem velut caliggine ei quadam & gravedine indutam: flatim ut a somno surrexere, rejiciunt adolent reficientes aerem & secretione purgantes, spirituq; qui concretus cum corpore languorem contraxit refusitantes, habet enim odor resinae vehementiam quandam & vim percellidi. Rursum meridie sentientes Solem e terra attrahentem vi sua admodum multum ac gravem vaporem, & aeri admiscem myrrham suffiunt, nam calor dissoluit atq; dispitat turbulentas faeces quae in aere coeunt. Itanim medici censent ad versus pestem remedio esse coprosam flammam, utpote quae aerem attenuet, hoc aut fit rectius, si odorata ligna urantur, ut cupressis, tuniperi picea & acre medicus Achenis tempore magnae pestis gloriam sibi parat vi iubendo ignem pone aegrotantes accendi: nam jussit non paucos. Aristoteles etiam affirmat unguentorum, florum, pratorum, sua vi es fragrantias non minus ad sanitatem facere quam ad voluptatem: quod ea cerebrum natura frigidum & ad concretionem proclive, seninn suo calore lavitate relaxent. Id quod, ad rationem causae reddendae non nullum adfert testimonium, quod myrrham Aegyptii Bal, nominant quae vox si interpretetur de lirationis significat amplitudinem. Kyphi porro mixtura est sedecim rerum in unum compositarum, mellis, vini, uvae passae, cyperi, resinae, myrrhae, aspalathi, seselis, sinci odorati, bituminis, folii ficulni, rumicis, juniperi, urriusq; (duas enim nominant maiorem, ac minorem) cardamomi, & calami. Has autem species non temere componunt, sed seplafiari scura sicut haec miscent, sacra recitantur litere. Ipse numerus aliquid videtur habere, quod ut murum, quadratus est a quadrato procreatus, solus talium pariter par, & aree quantitatem cum ambitu numero eandem. Sed ad hoc rouducunt plurima eorum quae miscentur, aromatici praedita facultatibus. Itaq; Kyphi sua vem emittu utilem, exhalationem, qua aer mutatus spiritu suo etiam corpus efficit temperiem, blandam adipisci tur & molestiam ac vehementiam diurnarum curarum quasi vinculu quaedam animi citra ebrietatem relaxat: facultatem q; animi imaginatricem & somninorum capacem laevigat inflar speculi, purioremq; reddit non minus id quidem efficaciter, quam lyrae strepidus quibus ante somnum Pythagorei utebantur brutam mortibus q; subitis obnoxiam animae partem ea ratione excantantes atq; sedantes. Odores enim sepe sensum deficientem revocant sepe etiam contra heretant ac sopiunt, dissufis ob levitatem, per corpus exhalationibus, sicut medicorum non nullis somnis oboriri ajunt, quando alimenti vapor velut serpens leniter circum intestina & ea contrellans titillationem quandam inducit. Kyphi porro Aegyptii etiam ad bibendum temperatur, potum enim videtur ob vim mollientem suam interiora purgare praeter haec, resina. Solis est opus; & myrrha lachryma est ad lunam a stripibus edita. Eorum porro quae in Kyphi componitur, sunt quae nocle magis gaudent ut quae spiritibus frigidis, umbris, rore & humoribus alantur. Nam dicit hanc una est, & simplex & Solem Pindarus cerni aiet per vacuum aetherem. Nocturnus autem aer mixtus temperatus, est e variis luminibus atq; facultatibus quae velut semen in unum ab omnibus stellis confluent. Ergo non abs re illa ut simplicia a sole procreata; interdum haec & mixta & omnigenis qualitatibus praedita se & veniente nocte adolent. Hactenus Plutarchus.
units.tr: Plutarch's words in his book On Isis and Osiris agree with these reasons, where he indicates that those Greeks, in their sacred fumigations, took account not only of piety but also of health. His words are these: "If it is as they have taken it up in me, something must also be said about those things which are burned daily. First, it seems worth considering that the men themselves never failed to use the things that bring health, and especially in sacrifices; in other matters, in their daily life, they held that the consideration of piety was no less than that of health. They judged that neither bodies nor souls can be affected by disease or defect, since nature, which is pure and unharmed on every side, cannot be corrupted. Therefore, since the air we breathe and live in is not always the same in its condition and temperature, but is thickened by our breath, it presses on the body and drives the soul into a certain sadness and anxiety, as if wrapped in a kind of mist and heaviness. So, as soon as they rise from sleep, they burn incense to refresh the air and to purify it by its scent, and to revive the spirit which, being thickened with the body, has contracted weariness; for the odour of resin has a certain strength and power to drive away heaviness. Again, at midday, when they perceive that the sun draws from the earth a great and heavy vapour by its force, they burn myrrh and mix it with the air, for heat dissolves and disperses the turbulent dregs that gather in the air. Thus physicians think that a burning flame is a remedy against plague, since it thins the air; and this is done better if fragrant woods are burned, such as cypress, juniper, pine and cedar. The physician Acheas won glory for himself in a time of great plague by ordering fires to be lit beside the sick, and he ordered not a few of them." Aristotle also affirms that the scents of perfumes, flowers and meadows, by their own force, serve health no less than pleasure, because they relax the brain, which by nature is cold and prone to thickening, by their own warmth and lightness. This also gives some witness to the reason for the cause: the Egyptians call myrrh Bal, and if that word is interpreted as 'expansion', it signifies its breadth. Now kyphi is a mixture of sixteen things put together into one: honey, wine, raisins, cyperus, resin, myrrh, aspalathus, seseli, fragrant reed, bitumen, fig leaf, sorrel, juniper, two kinds of... (for they name one greater and the other less), cardamom and calamus. They do not compose these ingredients at random, but as they mix them, the sacred letters are read out. The number itself seems to have some meaning, since, like a square, it is produced from a square, and alone among such numbers is even in pairs, and its area equals its perimeter in number. But most of the things mixed in it have aromatic qualities. So kyphi sends forth a useful exhalation, by which the air, changed by its breath, also gives the body a pleasant temperature, and it relaxes the annoyance and violence of the day's cares, like a kind of bond of the mind, without drunkenness. It smooths the imaginative faculty of the mind and makes it fit for dreams, and renders it purer like a mirror; and it does this no less effectively than the lyre's sound, which the Pythagoreans used before sleep, charming and calming in this way the brutal part of the soul, which is liable to sudden passions. For odours often revive a failing sense, and often on the contrary weigh down and lull it to sleep, when their exhalations are scattered through the body because of their lightness; just as some physicians say that sleep arises when the vapour of food, creeping gently round the intestines, tickles and stirs them. Moreover, the Egyptians also mix kyphi for drinking, for it seems to purge the inner parts by its softening power. Besides these, resin is the work of the sun, and myrrh is a tear shed by the moon from the trunks of trees. Of the things compounded in kyphi, some delight more in the night, such as those nourished by cold spirits, shadows, dew and moisture. For Pindar says that the sun is seen through the empty ether, but that the night air, mixed and tempered, is made of various lights and powers which flow together, as from a seed, from all the stars. So it is not without reason that kyphi is compounded from simple things produced by the sun, and sometimes from mixed things endowed with all kinds of qualities, and is burned when night comes." So far Plutarch.

units.la: Praeterea ex iisdem fumis & suffumigiis, tanquam praesentiae & voluntatis Deorum suorum signa atq; symbola miseri hominis alios quasi fumos, hoc est, res eventus, futuros praenoscendi praedicendi; octaginta captabant. Et huc referenda ΚΑΠΝΟΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ, ΛΙΒΑΝΟΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ, ΟΙΩΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ, ΚΕΦΑΛΟΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ, ΑΙΘΟΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ, & ipsa in genere ΨΥΧΟΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ, de qua addere placet ea, quae de hac Pencerus adnotavit libro suo de divinatione: ΨΥΧΟΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ, inquit, facitane, pice, quae ex tedis colligitur, comminuta in pulverem, et hoc in ignem coniecto. Quod si exardescens inde flamma eoit, nec dispergitur, faufla si divititur, aut dissilit, infausta designare creditur. Sic pugnantem, diducitur, in diversa procumbentem in focum, crepitantem, aegrum malum, e vanescentem, indem mortem minitari immo & simulatra formare, eruptione agitationeq; lucentis flammae, sed no conspici, nisi ab impolluti, falso persuadet credulis Pyromancum genus.
units.tr: Moreover, from these same smokes and fumigations, as signs and tokens of the presence and will of their gods, wretched men sought other omens, as it were from smoke, that is, to foreknow and foretell events that are to come. Here belong kapnomanteia [ΚΑΠΝΟΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ], libanomanteia [ΛΙΒΑΝΟΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ], oiomanteia [ΟΙΩΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ], kephalomanteia [ΚΕΦΑΛΟΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ], aithomanteia [ΑΙΘΟΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ], and in general psychomanteia [ΨΥΧΟΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ], about which it is worth adding what Pencer noted in his book on divination: "Psychomanteia," he says, "is practised with pitch, which is gathered from torches, crushed into powder, and this thrown into the fire. If the flame that blazes up from it burns steadily and is not scattered, it is believed to signal good fortune; if it is divided or bursts apart, it signals misfortune. If it struggles, is drawn apart, falls to the hearth in different directions, crackles, or fades away, it is believed to threaten sickness or death. Indeed, the kind of pyromancy deceives credulous people into thinking that, by the eruption and motion of the shining flame, it even forms images, which, however, can be seen only by the unpolluted." That is the false persuasion of the pyromancers.

units.la: ΚΑΠΝΟΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ instituunt granulis papaveris aut sesami, projectis in candentes prunas, & fumo, qui inde nascitur, observato. Sed has praefigias omitto.
units.tr: They establish divination by kapnomanteia: grains of poppy or sesame are thrown onto glowing coals, and the smoke that rises from them is observed. But I omit these prognostications.
Pyromanteia [πυρομαντεία]

units.la: ΚΑΠΝΟΜΑΝΤΕΙΑ Ἀλλαγοματεία ex incēto ture,divinabat. Si ignis mox illud attreptum diffolutumq́, verteret in fumum & suffitum cieret gratum,læta: Si refugeret, aut odorem exprimeret inde sædum, & natura turis dī versum,abominanda osteudi putabantur.
units.tr: By kapnomanteia (allagomanteia [ἀλλαγομαντεία]) they divined from incense that had been burned. If the fire at once seized it, dissolved it and turned it into smoke, raising a pleasant, fragrant fumigation, the omen was cheerful. If it shrank back, or gave off a foul odour, and the nature of the incense was reversed, they were thought to show abominable things.

units.la: Meminit loci cujusdā Dion,in historia Romana,quem Nympheum appellat,in quo, hoc modo,ex suffito thure,præscita de omnibus rebus petita fuerunt,præterquam de morte,& coitu.
units.tr: Dion, in his Roman History, mentions a certain place which he calls the Nympheum, where in this manner things foreknown about everything were sought from burnt incense, except for death and sexual intercourse.

units.la: Οἰνομαντεία ex vinto confectâ ad libationes, ὑδρομαντεία, ex sacra aquâ, qua abluebantur & decoquebantur vitâ me,coloribus,sapore,motu,strepitu,subitâ mutationibus argumēta cucneuum colligebat. Virtusq́ meminit Virgilius in historia Didous: Vidit thuricremū cum dona imponeret aras, (Horrendum dictu) latices nigrescere sacros Fusaq́ue ob scæuum,se vertere vina cruorem.
units.tr: Oinomanteia was practised with wine prepared for libations, and hydromanteia with holy water, in which they had washed and boiled the victims' entrails. From its colours, taste, motion, sound and sudden changes they gathered signs of the outcome. Virgil also mentions this in the story of Dido: "She saw, as she laid the gifts on the altars and the incense burned (horrible to tell), the sacred liquids turn black, and the poured wine change into blood." [Virgil, Aen. 4.]

units.la: Κεδωμαντεία & ἀπαδομαντεία molas & libamenta & præcipuè materiâ eorum, ut hordeum, sar, & inde confectas farinas, quibus victimæ couspergebantur, scrutabantur, & expendebant. τέφ.
units.tr: Kedromanteia and apalomanteia [κεδρομαντεία, ἀπαλομαντεία] examined and weighed the cakes and libations, especially their ingredients, such as barley and spelt, and the meal made from them with which the victims were sprinkled.
So far Peucer.

units.la: Atq; hæc quidem de uidoribus,odoribus,fumis, suffumigiis & suffimentis istis sacris & sacrificiis libus sint dicta.
units.tr: And so much has been said about these winds, odours, smokes, fumigations and sacred and sacrificial suffumigations.

units.la: De cineribus quoq;,de quibus supra,nunc rursus esset dicendi locus,ad quos taudem Gentilium sacrificia fuerunt redacta. Unde Arnobius: Autsi aliquod viscus aris fuerit tradi-tum, ratione ardescit pari,& dissolutum in cinerem labitur. Hæc Arnobii verba ad sacrificiorum istorū Geutilium contemtum spectant,dum significat,omnem illorum pompam & magnificentiam, tandem in fumos,in saviillas atq; cineres abiisse.
units.tr: Concerning ashes, of which I spoke above, there is now again room to speak, since it was to ashes that the sacrifices of the Gentiles were finally reduced. Hence Arnobius: "Or if some matter has been handed over to the altars, it burns with equal reason, and, dissolved, it slips away into ash." These words of Arnobius bear on the contempt for those sacrifices of the Gentiles, since they signify that all their pomp and magnificence finally passed into smoke, vapour and ashes.

units.la: His ipsis autem cineribus,tánquam sacris,dubiū non est, quiu Gentiles multifariam ad idololatriam & ad divinationem (quæ τεφρομαντεία,sive ασοδομαντεία, sive etiam κονιομαντεία Græcè appellari potuit) abusi fuerint:ac, quemadmodum,ut de fumis paullo antè, atq; suffimentis dixi,iu meditatus cinerum maxima est vis & facultas,de qua consulendi Medicinâ cineribus quoq; istis sacris maximam vim lustrandi,purgandi De-sq́ suos placaudi tribuerunt.
units.tr: There is no doubt that the Gentiles also abused these very ashes, as if they were sacred, in many ways for idolatry and divination (which could be called tephromanteia, spodomanteia, or also koniomanteia in Greek). And just as I said a little earlier about smokes and fumigations, the power and efficacy of ashes is very great, a matter to be consulted in medicine. The Gentiles also ascribed the greatest power of cleansing, purifying and appeasing their gods to these sacred ashes.

units.la: Adde,quod cineres in sacris & profanis litteris fragilitatis mortalitatiq́, sunt symbola: quæ spectat antiqua illa Iudæorum & Gentilium cineres capiti vestimentiq́, aspergendi,vel etiam in cineribus volutandi consuetudo: cujus passim in sacris & profanis litterarū monumentis fit mentio; ut memiuissent se esse cinerem,pulvisculum,in cinerem & pulverem reversuros, secundum illud Pessanum: —Cinis & manes & sabula sies.
units.tr: Add that in sacred and profane writings ashes are symbols of frailty and mortality. To this belongs the ancient custom of the Jews and Gentiles of sprinkling ashes on head and clothing, or even rolling in ashes, which is mentioned everywhere in the monuments of sacred and profane literature. They did this so that they might remember that they are ash and dust, and will return to ash and dust, according to Persius: "You shall be ash, and shades, and a tale."

units.la: Et illud Horatianum: Pulvis & umbra sumus.
units.tr: And the line of Horace: "We are dust and shadow."

units.la: His igitur cineribus & pulveribus, ad quos vel maximè, robustissimæ, magnificentissimæq́, bostiæ rationales & irrationales temporis momento redigebantur,cinereæ,sive cinerosæ (quo verbo Apuleius utitur) bocesi,fragilis,caduce,ac mbrtalis hominum rerum,humanarum omnium naturæ admoneri poterant. Sed eo ipso Deus illis sacrificiorum isporū uduviav exprobrare & demonstrare voluit,ut intelligerent,quæ vis illorū vel magnificentissima sacrificia uibi esse aliud, quàm sumus,quàm cineres,atq́ pulveres vautissimos & vilissimos.
units.tr: By these ashes and dust, into which the most robust, most magnificent rational and irrational victims are reduced in a moment, men could be reminded of the fragile, transient and mortal nature of all human affairs. But by this very thing God wished to rebuke the vanity of sacrifices and to show it to them, so that they might understand that those most magnificent sacrifices were nothing other than what we are, namely ashes and dust, most worthless and vile.

units.la: Atq́ hæc quidè,de quaadhuc verba fecimus,fuit communis, trita & vulgata inter omnes feré gentes sacrificandi ratio,ritus,modus,atq́ methodus,qualis ab Homero, ab Apollonio,a Luciano,a Dionysio Halicarnasseo & ab aliis antiquis scriptoribus litteris memoriaq́, est prodita.Incereà tamen si singularia & particularia spectemus,non est diffitendum,tam varios,multiplices, diversos ac dispares,pro Deorum,locorum,temporum, personarū,atq́ gentium diversitate,fuisse sacrificiadi ritus atq́ ceremonias, ut ipsas enumerare omnes infinitoperis atq́ laboris esse videatur,summo plane ἀδ ὠπαίτων. Sic etenim,exempli gratia,ut ex innumeris uuum atq́ alterū proseram,etsi secundum communē & per vulgatam Græcorum,Romanorum,aliarumq́ gentium consuetudinem, hostiæ seu victimæ post mastationem vel totæ, vel integræ (quæ quidem teste Festo idcirco Proterviæ, Prodigæ, Græcè Holocausta seu Holocaustomata fuerunt appellata) vel cerea illarum partes ignī fuerunt tradite,eoq́ consumtæ,reliquæ ad epulandum & ad sacrificandum usum fuerunt refertæ: tameu, ut Lucianus, postquam communem Gentilium sacrificandi morem descripsit, simul atque deriuit, subjungit sub finem illius sui libelli de sacrificiis, peculiarem hunc Aegyptiorum: Sacrorum, inquit, peragendorum idem fermé apud illos (Aegyptios) ritus, nisi quòd boftiam lu&ta prosequuntur: jamq; ma&ate ejus circumfusi membra laniant. Sunt qui sepeliunt duntaxat, postea quam occiderunt. Ejusdem autoris libellus exstat de Syria Dea, quam Atergatin vocant, quae etiam Gatis dicta Syrorum Regina fuit, ac post mortem pro Dea habita atq; culta, quam Graeci Derceto appellant, de qua vide Athenaeum lib. 9. In illo libro Dea istius templum, fignaq; statuas, sacerdotes, sacra, ritus atq; ceremonias, quibus culta fuit, lacum deniq; & pisces sacros commemorat atq; describit. Sub finem autem illius libelli hos recenset singula res sacrificandi ritus. Haec, inquit, ab iis, qui folennes ad cetus veniunt, factitantur. Is, qui in civitatum Sacram abit (hanc Assyriorum urbem, in Coelofyria sitam, Stephanus Hieram, id est, sacram, Strabo & Plinius Hierapolim vocant, quae Bambyre quoq;, & Edessa, & Magog a Syrus fuit appellata, ut iidem authores testantur) caput ille quidem & superciliis tondere solet, po-ftea autem mafata o've cetera quidem in frustra concidit & convivatur. Vellus autem humi flernens, super hos in genua procumbit. Pedes autem & caput animantis suo ipsius eupi imponit & simul precando, postulat ut prefens sacrificium acceptu sit, majusq; aliud in posterum politicetur. His ita peractis, caput suum corona induit iisdemq; aliorum omnium, qui, eandem cum ipso viam proficisciuntur, atq; ita attollens se ex terra sua profici scitur, utens & frigidis aquis, lauandiq; cau-sa pariter & potus, & omnino buius quoq; dormiens. Nec enim fas illi est conscendere lectulo, do-nec iter illud peregerit domumq; suam reversus iterū fuerit. In Sacra autem civitate recipit ipsum publicus hospes ignotum. Certi enim uniusque, civitatis hospites ibi sunt, & quod ex patria cujusq; venit id denuo apud se recipit. Appellantur autem ab Affyrus ipsi doctores, quoniam ipsi omnia exponunt, & enarrant. Sacrificant autem non in ipso templo, sed postquam ad duxit ad altare hostiam libatione insuper factâ rursus eandem domū ducit. Deinde vero ubi redit, faciunt ipse domi sacrificat & precatur. Ef autem & alius quidam sacrificandi ritus talis. Postquam animalia immolationi destinata coronarunt ex vestibulis templi ea demittunt: illa vero praecipitata, ex casu moriuntur. Quidam autem, & pueros suos ex eodem loco admittunt, non tamen eodem modo, quo pecudes, sed in peram si ve saccum inclusos manu deducunt. Simul autem & aterdo in-crepantes illos ditendoq; non puer, sed boves sint. Certi autem notis compungunt ut omnes, alii quidam in volamanus, alii autem in terzvite. Et inde est, quod cunsti Affyri notas inustas habent. Faciunt eutem & aliud quiddam, in quo cum solus Graecorum Traeznis consentiunt. Dicum autem etiam, quae illi faciunt. Traezenii virginibus et adolescentibus legem statuerunt, ut quis ipsorum cōrubo sese illigaret, priusquam Hyppolito comas totondisset faciunt, hoc pacto. Ideus igitur & in Sacra civitate fit. Ac adolescentes quidem barbas sua: confecrana. Iuuenibus autem tapillos sacros a naturitate usq; consecratos demittunt, quos postquam in temple iunt, resecant, & in vasa deposita alii quidem argentea, multi vero etiam aureas in aede assignant atq; ea-dem inscripto utriusq; nomine. Atq; hoc ego quoq; cum juvenis ad huc essem, feci, & intemplo meus capillus ad huc meum, nomen restat. Hac Lucianus.
units.tr: These things, of which we have so far spoken, are the common, familiar and widespread manner, rite, mode and method of sacrificing among almost all peoples, as it has been handed down in writing and memory by Homer, Apollonius, Lucian, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and other ancient writers. Yet if we look at particular and individual cases, it must not be denied that the rites and ceremonies of sacrifice were so varied, manifold, diverse and dissimilar, according to the differences of gods, places, times, persons and nations, that to enumerate them all would seem an endless labour and a task utterly beyond our powers.
