For example, to bring forward one or two out of countless instances: although, according to the common custom of the Greeks, Romans and other nations, the victims were either wholly burnt after slaughter (which, according to Festus, were therefore called Proterviae or Prodigae, and in Greek holocausts or holocaustomata), or their parts were given to the fire and consumed there, while the rest was kept for feasting and for sacrificial use; nevertheless, Lucian, after describing the common custom of the Gentiles and finishing it, adds at the end of his little book on sacrifices this peculiar Egyptian practice: "The rite of performing sacred rites among them (the Egyptians) is almost the same, except that they follow the victim with mourning; and once it is struck, they gather round and tear its limbs. Some only bury them after they have killed them." There is also a book by the same author about the Syrian goddess, whom they call Atargatis, who was also called Gatis and was queen of the Syrians, and who after her death was regarded and worshipped as a goddess, and whom the Greeks call Derceto; on her see Athenaeus, book 9. In that book he mentions and describes the temple of this goddess, her images and statues, her priests, sacred rites and ceremonies by which she was worshipped, and finally the lake and sacred fish. Near the end of that little book he recounts the individual features of the rite of sacrifice: "These things," he says, "are done by those who come to the solemn festivals. The one who goes into the Sacred City (this Assyrian city in Coelosyria, which Stephanus calls Hiera, that is, Sacred, and which Strabo and Pliny call Hierapolis; it was also called Bambyce, Edessa and Magog by the Syrians, as the same authors attest) usually shaves his head and eyebrows. Afterwards he cuts the other sacrificed animals into pieces and feasts on them. Spreading a fleece on the ground, he kneels upon it. He places the feet and head of the animal on his own head, and at the same time prays that the present sacrifice may be accepted and that a greater one may be offered in future. When this is done, he puts a garland on his head, and then, lifting himself from the ground, he sets out on his journey, using cold water both for washing and for drinking, and he even sleeps on the ground. For it is not lawful for him to climb onto a couch until he has completed the journey and returned home again. In the Sacred City a public host receives him as a stranger; for there are certain hosts of each city, and he receives again in his own house whoever comes from his homeland. Those Syrians who teach are called doctors, because they explain and expound everything. They sacrifice not in the temple itself, but after leading the victim to the altar and pouring a libation, they lead it back to the house. Then, when they return home, they sacrifice and pray at home. There is also another rite of sacrifice of this kind. After they have crowned the animals destined for slaughter, they let them down from the porches of the temple; they are thrown headlong and die from the fall. Some also admit their boys from the same place, not in the same way as the cattle, but they lead them down, enclosed in a bag or sack, by hand. At the same time they call out to them with a harsh shout, pretending that they are not boys but oxen. The Syrians also mark them with certain signs, pricking all of them, some on the hands and others on the throat. And from this it is that all Syrians have marks branded on them. They also do one other thing, in which the Troezenians alone of the Greeks agree with them. I will tell you what they do. The Troezenians have made a law for their young men and maidens, that none of them shall marry before they have offered their hair to Hippolytus; they do this as follows. The same is done in the Sacred City. The young men shave their beards there. The young women let down their hair, consecrated from birth, and when they have entered the temple they cut it off and deposit it in vessels, some of silver and many of gold, and assign it in the temple with the name of each inscribed. I too did this when I was still young, and in the temple my hair still remains, with my name." These are Lucian's words.

units.la: Eusta|bius similiter ex Strabone in Homerum Iliad. a. descriptionem illam suam ritus moris, communis sacrificandi concludit commemoratione ritus atq; ceremoniae peculiaris Persarū: quae talis fuit: Persae, inquit, nec statuas, nec aras erigunt, sacrificant in loco excelsi. Calum lovem putant, colunt Solem, quem Mithram vocant. Item Lunam, & Veneré, & Iguem, & Terlurem, & Ventos, & Aquam. Sacrificant in loco inundato ἀπιγυ , id est, cum imprecationibus, & coronatam hostiam statuunt. Vbi autem Magus, qui sacrificiis praeest, hostia car-nē in portiones distribuit, sua quisq; accepta parte abeunt, nulla parte Diis relictā. Dicunt Deum nihil velle, praeter hostiae animam. Quidam tamen ut fertur, omenti partem igni.
units.tr: Eusebius similarly, following Strabo on Homer's Iliad, concludes his account of the common manner of sacrificing with a mention of the peculiar rite and ceremony of the Persians. It was this: the Persians, he says, erect neither statues nor altars, but sacrifice on high places. They think of the heavens as Zeus, worship the sun, which they call Mithras, and likewise the moon, Venus, fire, earth, winds and water. They sacrifice in a flooded place [ἀπιγυ] with imprecations, and they set up a crowned victim. When the Magus who presides over the sacrifice divides the flesh of the victim into portions, each person takes his share and goes away, no part being left for the gods. They say that God wants nothing but the soul of the victim. Some, however, as is reported, burn a portion of the omentum in the fire.

units.la: Precipue Igni & Aquae sacrificant: Igni quidem ligna arida imponentes, adempto corio, & anima (ψυχη) superimela: deinde infusio oleo sutendunt, non inspirantes, sed ventilantes. Si quis inspirat, aut mortuum quid cenum ve in ignem injicit, morte privatur. Aquae sacrae peragunt hoc modo. In lacum, vel flumen, vel fontem venientes, ferobem faciunt, ibiq; hostia ingu-lant (σιωγαδοντες) cautione summa adhibita, ne quid proxima aquae sanguine contingat: sic enim omnia pollutum iri. Postea carnibus myrto laurog; impofitu, eas Magi gracilibus ur-pu com. gis comburunt, & saltis imprætationibus quibusdam oleum laße & melle muxtum inspergunt, (Χοοαπἰσθουεσ)non in ignem,nec in aquam, sed in terram. Imprecationes diu faciunt (ιπιοδιϱ πο:ουωταγ) fasciculum virgarum myricinarum tenuium manibus tenentes. In Capadocia (cenim maxima ibi est Magorum multitudo,qui Pyrrhi vocantur,& multa Persicorum Deorum templa) non cultro,sed flipite (κοπτω) mactant (θυουσι) tanquam malleo(υπτω) ferientes. Sunt & Pyrathæia (πυρασθεια) septa (σηοει) quædam ingentia,in quorum medio ara est. Inea Magi & cinerem (ασοδον) mulcum & ignem perennem feruant, & eò quotidiè ingeffi,imprecationes faciunt per horam fere ante ignem virgarum fasciculum tenentes,pileis infulis velati (πιλεος ςεχμειωαγοι πλ ωτις) ex utraque parte dependentibus ,adeo ut vittæ labia contegant ac malas. Hæc in Anaitidis & Omani delubris fiunt. Nam & horum ibi delubra sunt,& Omani statua in pompa ducitur. Ista nos vidimus :quæ sequuntur historici memoriæ mandaverunt,In fluvium Persæ non immejunt,nec lavant,nec abluunt,nec cadaver injiciunt,nec alia,quæ immunda esse videntur. Cuicunq; Deo sacrificent ,primùm igni imprecationem faciunt (ιυχορται.)
units.tr: They sacrifice especially to fire and water. To fire they lay dry wood, having removed the skin, and place the soul [ψυχή] on top; then they pour on oil and kindle it, not by breathing on it but by fanning it. If anyone breathes on it, or throws a corpse or dung into the fire, he is deprived of life. They perform the water sacrifices in this way. Coming to a lake, river or spring, they dig a trench and there slaughter the victim [σφάζοντες], taking the greatest care that nothing touch the water with blood, for everything would thereby be polluted. Then, laying the flesh on myrtle and laurel, the Magi burn it with slender rods, and with certain imprecations sprinkle over it oil, milk and honey mixed [χοαί], not into the fire nor into the water, but onto the earth. They make their imprecations for a long time, holding in their hands a bundle of slender tamarisk twigs. In Cappadocia (for there is a very great multitude of Magi there, who are called Pyrathei, and many temples of the Persian gods) they slaughter the victims not with a knife but with a club [κόπτω], striking as with a hammer [τύπτω]. There are also certain great enclosures [πυραθεῖα], in the middle of which is an altar. In these the Magi keep much ash and a perpetual fire, and, bringing wood to it daily, make imprecations for about an hour before the fire, holding the bundle of rods and covered with felt caps [πίλοι] with fillets hanging down on each side, so that the ribbons cover their lips and cheeks. These things are done in the temples of Anaitis and Omanus, for there are temples of these deities there too, and a statue of Omanus is carried in procession. These things we have seen; what follows is what the historians have recorded. The Persians do not urinate in rivers, nor wash, nor bathe in them, nor throw a corpse or anything else that seems unclean into them. Whichever god they sacrifice to, they first make an imprecation over the fire [ἐπιχοραί].

units.la: PORRO, ut hunc mèo de trito & usitato feré apud omnes gentes sacrificandi more, ritu, forma atque ordine explicationi finem imponam: quemadmodum ad sacrificia illa conveniendi, sciendi a sacrificio illa se præparandi,ad illa homines convocandi, illa inchoandi celebrandiq.; sit quoq; ab illis erificiu̇ apud Veteres. discendi,illa deniq; finiendi terminandiq; certa fuit ratio atq; cerimonia.
units.tr: Furthermore, to bring my account of the manner, rite, form and order of sacrificing, which is almost common and familiar among all nations, to a close: among the ancients there was also a fixed rule and ceremony for how to gather for those sacrifices, how to know and prepare oneself for them, how to summon people to them, how to begin, celebrate and finally bring them to an end.

units.la: Sacrificiis itaq; peractis atq; confectis, quasi receptui per sacerdotes sive præcones certis vocibus dicendis, formulis cauebatur,ac populus dimittebatur, eiq; discedendi venia dabatur. At apud Græcos quidem usitata erat hæc dicendi forma : Λαοῖς ἀφιστε, id est, populus missus : cujus Apulejus libro 11. meminit his verbis : Tunc ex his (sacerdotibus) unus,quem cunctis Grammatea (scribam) dicebant pro foribus assistens,cætu Pastophorum (quod sacrosancti collegii nomen est) velut in concionem vocato , iudicem de sublimi suggestu, in libro de litteris saluta vota præfatur, principi magno Senatuique & equiti cotiq; Romano populo nauticis navibus quæque sub Imperio Mundi nostratis regunter,renunciat sermone ritusque Græcensi ( Gracanico more & lingua) λαοῖς ἀφιστε,id est,populus missio.Quam vocem felicitèr cunctis e venire fgna vit populi clamor insecutus.Exin gaudio delibuti populares,talos,verbenas,corollas ferentes,exofcu-latci vestigiis Deæ,ad suos descendunt Lares. Hæc Apulejus,quibus adde,quod Festus ait:Dici mos erat Romanis in omnibus sacrificiis precibusque POPVLO ROMANO QVIRITIBVS Q. quod est Cureuibus, quæ civitas Sabinorum potentissima fuit.
units.tr: When the sacrifices had been performed and completed, the people were dismissed, as it were at a signal given by the priests or heralds with certain set words and formulas, and leave to depart was granted. Among the Greeks this form of words was in common use: "Λαοῖς ἄφιστε", that is, "the people are dismissed." Apuleius, in book 11, mentions it in these words: "Then one of these priests, whom everyone called the Scribe, standing before the doors, the company of the Pastophori (which is the name of that sacred college) being called together as to an assembly, from a high platform, in a book about letters, first offers greetings and prayers for the great prince, the Senate, the knights and the whole Roman people, and for the sailors and all who are governed under the empire of our world; and he announces in the Greek manner and language, 'Λαοῖς ἄφιστε', that is, 'the people are dismissed.' When this word was spoken, a shout from the people followed, signifying that it had been favourably uttered for all. Then the people, rejoicing, carrying palm-branches, verbena and garlands, went down to their homes from the footsteps of the goddess." Thus Apuleius. To this add what Festus says: it was the custom of the Romans in all sacrifices and prayers to say "POPULO ROMANO QUIRITIBUS Q.", which means "Curibus", since Cures was the most powerful city of the Sabines.

units.la: Redeo ad Missionem populus. Hic subinde tellige, est, vel datur ; ut tum demum omnibus abire fas sit. Inde ἀπολύειν Græcis dicitur cum vel equi emittuntur ad currum,alio nomine ϑυοαι ιπιοδοιυ,id est,Ianus. Hippodromius. Sunt autem ἀφετηρια, teste Suida, ὅρμαται πολτοχητηριαι, id est,instrumenta ad urbes expugnandas accommodata,cujusmodi fune illa, quæ Petarn Gallice a petendo,vel impetendo appellantur.Populus igitur,qui sacris sive sacrificiis intereratt, quasi septus atq; carcerbus quibusdam continerì atque coerceri consueverat, donec illa finita esset ; et absoluca,cum ante discedere nefas duceretur.
units.tr: I return to the dismissal of the people. Here understand "est" or "datur", so that at last it is lawful for everyone to leave. Hence the Greeks say "ἀπολύειν" when horses are let loose from the chariot, and the starting-gates of the hippodrome are also called by another name. According to Suidas, the "ἀφετήρια" are "ὁρμητήρια", that is, instruments adapted for storming cities, of the kind that the French call "petard" from "petere" or "impetere". So the people who were present at the sacred rites or sacrifices were customarily kept enclosed and confined, as if fenced in and held in certain barriers, until the rites were finished and they were released, since it was considered wrong to leave beforehand.

units.la: * Vox præterea Latina, quæ vel per sacerdotes ipsos,vel per præcones iis, qui sacris interant dicet abeundi signum ac poscellas dabatur, fuit ILICET ,id est,Ire licet : cujusmodi eraut antiqua illa verba,Ite,Mifla est; quibus significabatur,tempus esse abeundi. Eadem vox in judicis quaque & in exsequiis fuit usitatissima. Hac enim per præconem pronunciata judices de Concilio dimittebantur. In exsequiis & justis omnibus perfectis Præfica familiter novissimum illud verbum, Ilicet,pronunciabat. Quo dicto, qui funus comitati erant,domum abituri,extremum alta voce pronunciabant hoc modo : Vale,Vale, Vale. Nos te ordine,quo Natura permiserit,prosequemur. Varro scribit,ideo mortuo Vale & Salve dici:uon quod Valere,aut Salvi esse possint, sed quod ab his recedamus,eos nunquam revisuri. Servius in illum Virgilii versum:
units.tr: Moreover, there was a Latin word that was given as the signal for departure and dismissal to those who attended the sacred rites, either by the priests themselves or by heralds. This word was ILICET, that is, "it is permitted to go." Such were the old words "Ite, missa est," by which it was signified that it was time to leave. The same word was also very commonly used in courts of law and at funerals. For when it had been proclaimed by a herald, the judges were dismissed from the council. At funerals, once all the rites had been completed, the mourner-woman would customarily utter that final word, "Ilicet." At this word, those who had accompanied the funeral, as they were about to go home, would call out a last farewell in a loud voice in this way: "Farewell, farewell, farewell. We shall follow you in the order that Nature allows." Varro writes that "Vale" and "Salve" are said to the dead, not because they can be well or safe, but because we withdraw from them, never to see them again.
"Straightway we are overwhelmed by numbers, and first Choroebus," (Virgil, Aeneid 2.)

units.la: Ilicet,inquit,ubicunq; ponitur,extrema omnia accidere vel accidisse significat.Idem in hunc versum Virg. Ilicet ignis edax summa ad vestigia venit:
units.tr: "Straightway," he says, "wherever it is placed, signifies that all extremities happen or have happened." The same author, on this verse of Virgil: "Straightway the devouring fire came up to the highest point."

units.la: Sumptum,inquit,a more judicium.Nam cum actus suos explessent,hoc voce per præconé utebantur. tur, ut dicerent, Ilicet, hoc est, ire licet, ut omnes, qui aderant, obsequio ac veneratione sollicitudine solverentur. Idem in illa Virg. Æneid. 6. Idem ter socios pura circumtulit unda. Spargens rore leui, & ramo felicis oliuæ, Lustrauit, uiros dixitq́; nouissima verba:
units.tr: "It is taken," he says, "from the custom of judgment. For when they had completed their business, they used this word through the herald, to say 'Ilicet,' that is, 'you may go,' so that all who were present were released from obedience, reverence and anxiety." The same word appears in that line of Virgil, Aeneid 6: "Thrice he led his comrades round with pure water, sprinkling them with light dew and a branch of the happy olive; he purified them, and spoke the final words."

units.la: Idest, Ilicet. Nam Vale dicebatur postquam tumuli peracta solemnia. Quoniam igitur & in sacrificiis, & in iudiciis, & in exequiis atq; iustis uox hæc Ilicet usurpari fuit solita: idcirco illa dicendi forma Ilicet, actum seu conclamatum est, de desperatis deplorandis quibusdam rebus pro verbalicer usurpatur.
units.tr: That is, "Ilicet." For "Vale" was said after the solemnities of the tomb were finished. Since this word "Ilicet" was customarily used in sacrifices, in courts, and at funerals and rites, that form of speech, "Ilicet, actum seu conclamatum est" (it is done, or it is given up for lost), is used proverbially of certain desperate matters that are to be lamented.

units.la: Est autem, ut supra quoq; attigi uox hæc Ilicet composita ex I. boc est, uto, seu abi, & Licet: boc est, quia licet tibi iam abire sacris, iudicijs, sine peracta, quod antea non licebat, non concessum erat, sed illicitum. Sic Videlicet quoq; & Scilicet uoces sunt compositæ ex Vi de & Licet, quasi videre licet, & Scilicet, Scire licet: quibus respondet Italicum Cosa, & Gallicum Ceftasceauoir, vel, per maniere de dire, quæ idem sunt ac Germanicum Ylemlich / vel Ylamlich, hoc est, perspicere licet, vel nominare: quando rei alicuius planius & diuersius explicandæ & confirmandæ adhibentur.
units.tr: As I touched on above, the word "Ilicet" is compounded of "I", that is, "go" or "depart", and "licet", that is, "it is permitted": because it is now permitted for you to leave, now that the sacrifices, judgments or funerals are finished, which before was not permitted, was not allowed, but was forbidden. So too "Videlicet" and "Scilicet" are compounded of "videre licet" and "scire licet", "one may see" and "one may know." To these correspond the Italian "Cosa" and the French "c'est-à-dire" or "per maniere de dire," which mean the same as the German "Ylemlich" or "Ylamlich", that is, "one may perceive" or "one may name", when they are used to explain and confirm some matter more plainly and fully.

units.la: Huic vero voci solemne in sacris respondet uox sacra & augurales EXTEMPLO, quæ idem significat, quod illico, e vestigio, confestim, concinuo, quasi ire diuina peracta & absoluta tum demum confessim: extemplo esse dicebantur: vel quod hominum rei diuinæ iam per eos, Nam rerum diuinarum facile eos flatimq; cadum capit) properè, magna celeritate e templo se proripuint, Idomumq; vel alio ad res negociaq; sua necessaria properant. Deboc verbo sic scribit Varro: Extemplo est continuo, quid omne templum debet esse circa septum, nec plus, quam unum introitum habere: sive quod posti templi factum illico capcuntur augurla: seu quod augures flatim visis auspiciis vel a templo cæli oculos a vercebant, vel e templo terra discedebant. Quidam tamen inter Ilicet & extemplo discrimen flatuunt, ut Ilicet non nisi judiciorum sic: hoc sacrorum verbum. Vt enim iliud dimissio Senatu, jic hoc sacrificio peracto a præcone pronuntiatum fuisse volunt: sed atrium, sacrorum esse vocem, supra a nobis est ostensum.
units.tr: To this word "Ilicet", in sacred matters, corresponds the solemn sacred and augural word "EXTEMPLO", which means the same as "illico", "at once", "on the spot", "forthwith", as if, when the divine rites were finished and completed, people were said to go forth "extemplo", at once. Or it is because the people, once the sacred rite was over, hurried out of the temple with great speed, and hastened home or elsewhere to their necessary affairs. Varro writes thus about this word: "Extemplo" means "continuo", since every temple ought to be enclosed by a boundary and to have no more than one entrance; or because, as soon as the temple was made, the augury was taken on the spot; or because the augurs, as soon as the auspices were seen, turned their eyes away from the heavenly temple, or left the earthly temple. Some, however, make a distinction between "Ilicet" and "extemplo", holding that "Ilicet" is used only of judicial matters and "extemplo" only of sacred ones. Just as "Ilicet" was announced when the Senate was dismissed, so, they say, this word was announced by the herald when the sacrifice was completed; but we have shown above that "Ilicet" is also a word of sacred usage.

units.la: Hucrei.oq; videtur accommodari posse ad verbii CONFESTIM, id est, flatim, quasi cum festus sive quod sollo jam est, sed pro ea, penitus flatim discedebatur. Huic opponitur, Post sollum: ut, Vt nire post sollum, quod pro verbi loco dicitur de cunctabundis, nimiamq; morantibus, quia, ut nil... aut atione sic magnas quarumvis rerum gerendarum agendarum necessitas, moras ministrat.
units.tr: This also seems applicable to the word CONFESTIM, that is, immediately, as if it came from festus, a festival, though in that sense they used to depart at once. Opposed to this is post solum, "after the ground," which is used in place of a verb for those who delay and linger too long, since, as the necessity of any affairs to be done or transacted brings delays, so too does a great reason for deferment.

units.la: Tremo quoniam plerunq;, sacrificiorum, præsertim solenniu & publicorum, quasi confetta, sed vulg. colophones sive appendices fuerunt epulæ atq; convivia, quæ sacrificantes peractis sic ipsis cum in loco, in quo sacra fecerant, in Deorum, quibus sacrificaverant, honorem, agnatos inter se conjuncti aut: idcirco de iis, quoq;, nobis quadam sunt dicenda. Horum convivorum sacrificialium Homeri in omnibus fere sacrificiorum descriptionibus luculentam faciet mentionem, quæ quidem sacrificia flatim fuerunt consecuta. Sic Apollonius quoque nostrum in hac ipsa Argonautica sacrificii descriptione poslremo subjungit prolixam admodum epuli, quod Argonautæ latì atque hilares peracta re divina inter se celebratorum, descriptionem.
units.tr: Furthermore, since sacrifices, especially solemn and public ones, were for the most part followed by feasts and banquets as their appendices, which the sacrificers held after the rites were finished, in the same place where they had sacrificed, in honour of the gods to whom they had offered, with their kinsmen gathered together, some things must also be said about these. Homer makes a splendid mention of these sacrificial banquets in almost all his descriptions of sacrifices, and they immediately followed the sacrifices. So too Apollonius, in his own description of a sacrifice in the Argonautica, at the end adds a very long account of a feast, in which the Argonauts, glad and cheerful, celebrated together after the rite was done.

units.la: His ipsis autem epulis atque convivijs partim Deos suos colendi atq; venerandi, partim ex rerum, quibus operati fuerant, divinarum feriarum, (quales ipsi vitæ fuerunt) mediationibus et actionibus animos suos reficiendi recreandiq; gratia usi fuerunt. Harum epularum Paulus quoq; in epist. priori ad Cor. meminit et ab illarū comunione Christianos sedulo servo, vocat ac deterret.
units.tr: By means of these feasts and banquets they used partly to worship and honour their gods, and partly to refresh and restore their spirits after the divine holidays and the labours of the things they had done (such as their life was). Paul too mentions these feasts in his first Epistle to the Corinthians, and he carefully warns, calls and deters Christians from fellowship with them.

units.la: Illarum autem erebra, diligens, accurataq; descriptio apud Homerum his fere membris conflat, quæ paucis percurram. Primum est illarū APPARATVS, quem Græci κάλλισται & ὀρχηστὸν appellant, Homerus πέλεν, id est, laborem: quem his fere verbis exprimit. Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ παύσαντο πόνου, τεύχοντο δ᾽ ἄριστα. Postquam cessarunt a labore (scilicet, carnes coquendi & cuncta ad convivium necessaria præparandi) & adornarunt epulum.
units.tr: Homer's frequent, careful and exact description of them consists of the following parts, which I shall briefly run through. The first is the PREPARATION, which the Greeks call by a word I cannot read clearly, and which Homer calls labour (ponos), expressing it in these words: [Αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ παύσαντο πόνου, τεύχοντο δ᾽ ἄριστα]. That is, when they had ceased from labour (namely, roasting the meats and preparing everything necessary for the banquet), they made ready the feast.

units.la: Idem ἐτοιμάσαν δ᾽ ἄρισ(αν). id est, instruere, parare, adornare epulum.
units.tr: Likewise, [ἐτοιμάσαν δ᾽ ἄριστον], that is, they set out, prepared and furnished the feast.

units.la: Hic ipse autem epularū istarum sacrificialium apparatus in his fere consistebat. Primum earnes, quæ scilicet sacrificiorum fuerant reliquiæ, quæque sacrificantibus data & ad vescendum servatæ fuerant, in partes minores fetuerunt; quod Homerus voce μαςύλλειν, a μείω (unde minute dicta, id est, frusta, de quibus Virgilius: Pars in frusta secant) crebrerrime exprimit. Ha ipse autem carnes Dius quoq; antea oblate et consecrate fuerunc. Unde Paulus illas εἰδωλόθυτα, id est, idolis sacrificata vocat. Homerus quidem Od. 2. hujusmodi sectionis meminit his verbis:
units.tr: This preparation of the sacrificial feasts consisted mainly of the following. First, the meats, which were of course the remnants of the sacrifices, given to the sacrificers and kept for eating, were cut into smaller pieces. Homer very often expresses this by the verb mastyllein, derived from a word meaning "smaller," whence the pieces are called "minute," that is, morsels, of which Virgil says: "Some cut it into pieces." These meats had also been offered and consecrated to the gods beforehand. Hence Paul calls them [εἰδωλόθυτα], that is, things sacrificed to idols. Homer, in the second book of the Odyssey, mentions this cutting in these lines:

units.la: —ἰρύσαντό τ᾽ ἐπάντα. Βάλλον δ᾽ ἐς ἱλοῖσιν πολλία αὐ ἡ συβώτης Ισχυτο ἀλαβόσσων ( ὃ ἢ ἢ ἢ φρεῖν αὐτιμα ἡδῆ ) Καὶ τὰ μὲν ἑπτάζα πάντα διαμοιρέωτο δαίζων. Τῶν μὲν ἴκει Νύμφησι καὶ Ἑρμῇ Μαίᾳ υἱῷ Θύκεν ἐπὶ ξέ ἐμενος, πὸς δ᾽ ἄλλας νέμων ἐχίς ω Να᾽τοισιν δ᾽ ὁ δυσκ διλωκέασ γ᾽ ἐμαρν.
units.tr: They flayed it all. The swineherd, standing ready, threw the fat portions onto the flames... and cut everything up, dividing it into seven portions. One portion he set aside with prayer for the Nymphs and for Hermes, son of Maia, and he distributed the rest to each; to the backs he gave the whole honour to Vulcan.
They drew out everything.

units.la: Posiuerant autem in diffis primul omnia, subulcus vero Surrexit in quadram di videns (valde enim mentibus aequa sciebat) Atque quidem septifariam omnia partitus est divident, Partem quidem unam Nymphis, & Mercurio Maiae filio Posuit apprecatus, alias distribuit singulis, Dorsis autem Vulcanum integrus honoravit.
units.tr: They had first laid everything out on the spits. The swineherd, rising up, divided everything into seven parts (for he knew well how to do it), setting one part aside for the Nymphs and for Mercury, son of Maia, with prayer, and distributing the rest to individuals. To the backs he gave entire honour to Vulcan.

units.la: Deinde carnes illas minutas differias verbibus affigebant, quae ἱβολοι & πυτυβόλα ab illo appellabantur, cujusmodi verua antiquorum erant, instar craticula, quasi tuspides plures connexae, quibus carnes affigebantur, & a flamma adurebantur. Spiß Germanice, ab ultima Cuspe. De hoc aliu sic Homerus:
units.tr: Then they fixed those small pieces of meat on skewers, which Homer calls by names I cannot read clearly, and which were like the spits of the ancients: a sort of grating, as several spikes joined together, on which the meats were fixed and roasted by the flame. In German it is called Spiess, from the sharp point.
...and around the hearth, on the coals,
and they pierced others with spits.

units.la: Tertio, carnes illae verubus affixas ἐμεπ ξὸ Φιος, ut Homerus saepe loquitur, id est, summa cura diligenter, assabant. Sic autem ille:
units.tr: Third, the meats fixed on the spits were roasted with the greatest care and diligence, as Homer often says. He says:

units.la: Ὤπτων δ᾽, ἀκεσπόεσυς ὀβελοῖς ἐκ χερὸς ἀμέσθα ἐσες:
units.tr: Roasting them, and taking them from the hands with the spits...

units.la: Assaruncautem acuta verua in manibus tenentes.
units.tr: They roasted them, holding the sharp spits in their hands.

units.la: Quarto, posiquam satis assae fuerant, eas verubus detractas ἱλοῖς, id est, mensis culinarijs, ad id paratis ac destinatis imposuerunt, ibiq; in certas portiones singulis deinde contributis distribuendas dispensarunt: unde huius dicta ἀπὸ τῶν ἀμέσθων, a dividendo, dilaniando, discerpendo. Et haec de apparatu.
units.tr: Fourth, when they were roasted enough, they drew them from the spits and laid them on the kitchen tables, prepared and set aside for this purpose, and there divided them into fixed portions to be distributed to each guest. Hence the name, from the dividing and tearing apart of the meat. And this is what I have to say about the preparation.

units.la: Secundum membrum, cujus in convivantium istorum facrificialium fit mentio fuit certa CONVIVARUM COLLOCATIO, & ipsa Convivarum confessio seu accubatio.
units.tr: The second member of these sacrificial banquets, mentioned in the accounts, was a fixed PLACING OF THE GUESTS, and the reclining or lying down of the diners.

units.la: Tertium membrum & fere praecipuum fuit ipsa MANDVCATIO atque POTATIO, eibi potusq; sumptio.
units.tr: The third member, and almost the chief one, was the EATING and DRINKING itself, the taking of food and drink.

units.la: Quartum membrum fuerunt Convivarum SERMOCINATIONES atque colloquia, quae cibi potusq; sumptionem, postquam nimirum ex eo expleti fatiatiq; fuerant, consequi, sicut alia, quae sequuntur membra, solebant.
units.tr: The fourth member was the conversations and talk of the guests, which, once they had eaten and drunk their fill, normally followed the taking of food and drink, as did the other members that come after.

units.la: Quintū CANTVS aut Carmina, Musica partim vocalis, partim organica seu instrumentalis, V. Cantus.
units.tr: The fifth was SONG or singing, music partly vocal and partly instrumental.

units.la: Sextū fuerūt TRIPVDIA, saltationes et alii ludi, quorū Homerus aliū frequenter meminerit. VI. Tripudia.
units.tr: The sixth was DANCES, leaps and other games, which Homer often mentions.

units.la: Septimum LIBATIONES, quae in ipsis sacrificiis & in epulis fuerunt usitatissime. VII. Libationes.
units.tr: The seventh was LIBATIONS, which were most commonly used both in the sacrifices and at the feasts.

units.la: Octavum fuit LINGVARVM, quae ex hostiis immolatis excisae fuerunt in Mercurii honorem CONCREMATIO. VIII. Linguarum concrematio.
units.tr: The eighth was the BURNING of the tongues cut from the slaughtered victims, in honour of Mercury.

units.la: Nonum, PRECES, quae sacrificia atque epulas & antecedere & consequi fuerunt solitae. IX. Preces.
units.tr: The ninth was PRAYERS, which were customarily said both before and after sacrifices and feasts.

units.la: Decimum fuit LAVATIO & aquarum asperso, quae similiter & in principio & in fine sacrificiorum epularum facrificialium fuit celebrata. X. Lavatio.
units.tr: The tenth was WASHING and sprinkling with water, likewise observed at the beginning and at the end of the sacrificial feasts.

units.la: Undecimum fuit ipsa convivarum discussus atque SOMNVS. XI. Somnus.
units.tr: The eleventh was the breaking up of the guests and SLEEP.

units.la: Sed de his omnibus quoniā fufissime topiosissimeq; partim in Convivialib.mei, partim supra in hac ipso tractatu facrificiali ego, ne actum agere videar, illue equit bene volumus, Lectore remitto.
units.tr: But since all these matters have been treated very fully and at length, partly in my Convivialia and partly above in this very treatise on sacrifices, I leave them to the reader, lest I seem to be going over old ground. Let him turn there, if he is willing.

units.la: Hactenus de sacrorum sacrificiorumq; Gentilium & objecto & subjecto sive materia, & tempore, De sacrificiorum fine.
units.tr: So far the object, the subject or matter, the time, the place, the persons, the manner, the rite and the order of the sacred sacrifices of the Gentiles have been explained.

units.la: pore, & loco, & personis, & modo, ritu atq; ordine fuit explicatum: restat nunc ultimum bonum stri tractatus membrum explicandum, nempe FINIS, quem Gentiles in hisce suis sacrificiis spectare statuerunt, qui quidem in omnibus actionibus potissimum spectari considerari, s s utpote ad quem omnes actiones referuntur & accommodantur.
units.tr: It remains now to explain the last principal part of this treatise, namely the END, which the Gentiles resolved to aim at in these their sacrifices. This is to be looked at and considered above all in every action, since all actions are referred to it and adapted to it.

units.la: In utroq; igitur hoc sacrificio & Nestoris & Argonautarum Homerus & Apollonius utrinq; finem nequaquam silentio prætermiserunt, sed disertis verbis expresserunt.
units.tr: In each of these sacrifices, both that of Nestor and that of the Argonauts, Homer and Apollonius have by no means passed over the end in silence, but have stated it in plain words.

units.la: Ac apud Homerum quidem Nestor ipse, quem Poeta loquentem inducit, sacrificii sui finem sic exprimit: Οφρα ιλασσομαι, Ut placeat, &c.
units.tr: In Homer, Nestor himself, whom the poet introduces speaking, states the end of his sacrifice thus: "That I may propitiate" [Ὄφρα ἱλάσσωμαι].

units.la: Sensus est, Minervæ sacrificare statui, ejus nimirum placandæ gratia, Idem finis & idem verbis exprimitur in descriptione Hecatombes, quæ Apollini fuit oblata, Iliad. α. Οἰ δ᾽ ιερὰ ἔρεζον ἑκατόμβας Ἀπλιζ ὑπὲρ ἀκλεων ὀῖ ἱλασάμενοι ἀνακτα Οἱ ἐγὼ ἀρχοῖοι πολύσωτε κινδ᾽ ἀρῆκεν: Et Apollinis sacram Hecatombem Facere pro Danaïs, ut placemus Regem (Apollineum) Qui nunc Argivos lugubria valde immisit funera.
units.tr: The sense is: "I resolve to sacrifice to Minerva, namely in order to appease her." The same end and the same words occur in the description of the hecatomb offered to Apollo in Iliad 1: "And they offered sacred hecatombs to Apollo on behalf of the Danaans, to propitiate the king, who had now sent grievous deaths upon the Argives." The Latin of the Vulgate reads: "and to perform a sacred hecatomb of Apollo for the Danaans, that we may appease the king (Apollo) who has now sent very mournful deaths upon the Argives."

units.la: Qui autem Nestoreus, idem Argonauticus quoque sacrificii finis fuit, quem Apollonius his verbis exprimit:
units.tr: The end of the Argonauts' sacrifice was the same as Nestor's, and Apollonius expresses it in these words:

units.la: Σπεισθεὶς δ᾽ εἰξεῖν τι πόορυς ἀλὸς ἐν κοθυνλαις:
units.tr: "Having poured libations, to yield some passage through the gulfs of the sea" [Σπεισθεὶς δ᾽ εἴξειν τι πόρους ἁλὸς ἐν κολπίαις].

units.la: Vt nobis in his sacrificiis monstret viam per mare.
units.tr: That is: so that he might show us the way through the sea by means of these sacrifices.

units.la: Hic primum expressit finis μεριπος. Nam ἐπος θυμὸν & sacrificium, sive primitias, & arculam in qua odoramenta reconduntur, & denique, teste Eustathio, τῶν δὲ θυσιῶν μετ᾽ ζ, id est, divinationem, quæ fit per sacrificia, significat. Deinde finis quoq; alter, siempe ἱλασικὸς s primitur bis verbis: Νῦν γε μὲν ἀξθ, ἡ ἡ δ' ἐντουμί... Hoc est, ut Apollini sacrificiis nostris placato con tingant illico paremus.
units.tr: Here the end is first expressed by the word [μέρι]. For the word signifies both the heart or spirit (thymos) and a sacrifice or first-fruits, and also a chest in which perfumes are stored, and finally, according to Eustathius, divination, which is done through sacrifices. Next, another end is also stated, namely propitiation, in these words: "Now indeed..." The meaning is: that once Apollo has been appeased by our sacrifices, we may at once make our way.

units.la: Ἀρίστειας quid & quæ s conjugata Vitur hic verbo ἀρίστειος, quod significat gratiam ab aliquo ini e, gratiam alicujus capta te: unde ἀρετὴ & dicitur, gratia captator & aucupator, qui omnibus suit pl... ut spud omnes cupit esse gratiosus, si omnium gratiam sibi conatur insinuare, qualem Aristoteles dicit 4. Ethicorum, quiq; a Paulo αὐθεντικιν appellatur. Hinc etiam cer... sicut si ve lib genus ἀρίσωρια... Diis dicatum, quod Diis placet. S s si genere placenta & libum omne videatur dissum, quod Diis placeat, & altubescat. Lustratio ... Iliad. γ. τιμαι ἐ... id est, libum quoddam sacrum vocat. Et Iliad. ... τὸ θεῖον ἀρισκέ... id est, per quod Numini divino quis potest placere. Deniq; ab eodem ... derivatur quod, ὑκρισέις pro placari, Heb. 13. ... Toχντες ... Huiusmodi enim sacrificiis Deus placatur, ejusq; gratia communicatur.
units.tr: Here ἀρέσκειν, the verb from which the word ἀρίστεια is derived, means to win the favour of someone or to seek someone's favour. Hence the ἀρέσκος is called a favour-hunter and fawner, who wishes to be agreeable to everyone and tries to insinuate himself into everyone's good graces, as Aristotle describes in the fourth book of the Ethics. Paul calls such people men-pleasers [ἀνθρωπάρεσκοι]. From the same root comes the word for what is dedicated to the gods, that is, what pleases the gods. So a cake or any kind of cake-offering that seems to be made to please and appease the gods is called by this name. In the Iliad the author calls it a certain sacred cake, and elsewhere he speaks of that by which one can please the divine power. Finally, from the same root comes the verb meaning to be pleased or well pleased, as in Hebrews 13: "for with such sacrifices God is well pleased" [εὐαρεστεῖται]. For by such sacrifices God is placated, and his favour is bestowed.

units.la: Finis sacrificio s quadruplex. His præmissis nunc generatim & aliquanto copiosius de sine, quem Gentiles sibi in suis sacris sacrificiis atque religionibus in universum proposuerunt dicamus. Is autem seré fuit triplex, nempe etiam quadruplex, nempe ἱλασικὸς, id est, placatorius sive propitiatorius, καθαρτικὸς sive αγιαστικὸς, id est, expiatorius sive lustratorius, ἀγαθικὸς, gratitudine testandi, et ut ἐξος ... id est, divinatorius, sive vaticinatorius. Secundum quod ... Gentiles alia dicuntur ἱλασικὰ, id est, propitiatoria: alia καθαρτικὰ sive ἀγαθὰ... id est, lustratoria seu expiatoria: alia ἐυχαριστικὰ, sive χαρίςεια, gratitudinis testificandæ causa: alia denique μαντικὰ, id est, vaticinatoria. Nam sacris sive sacrificiis ... Diis suis sallistarunt partim illos iratos placandi, & pacis, gratiæ atque veniæ ipsorum impetrandæ, partim peccata sua, quibus eos offenderant, expiandi & res atque personas ... lustrandi purgandique gratia, partim ipsos de ... ebus futuris, & de iis, quæ sibi ... non aut non agenda essent, tonsulendi, partim denique gratias ipsis pro acceptis beneficiis agendi, atque ita gratitudinis testificandæ gratia. Etsi vero omnes hi quattuor fines in omnibus vel plerisque certè sacrificiis atque cerimoniis Gentilium simul fuerunt propositi; tamen seorsim separatim, de singulis verba satiemus.
units.tr: The end of sacrifice is fourfold. Having said this, we now speak in general, and somewhat more fully, about the end which the Gentiles set before themselves in their sacred rites, sacrifices and religions. This end was in fact threefold, or rather fourfold: the propitiatory [ἱλαστικὸν], that is, placatory or appeasing; the purificatory [καθαρτικὸν], that is, expiatory or purifying; the eucharistic [εὐχαριστικόν], for testifying gratitude; and the divinatory [μαντικόν], that is, for seeking prophecy. Accordingly, the Gentiles' sacrifices are called propitiatory, purificatory or expiatory, eucharistic, and finally divinatory. For by their sacred rites and sacrifices they sought, partly, to placate their angry gods and to obtain their peace, favour and pardon; partly, to expiate the sins by which they had offended them and to cleanse and purify themselves and their things; partly, to consult the gods about future events and about what should or should not be done; and finally, partly, to give thanks to them for benefits received, and so to testify gratitude. Although all these four ends were proposed together in all, or at least most, of the Gentiles' sacrifices and ceremonies, we will treat each one separately and in turn.

units.la: Quantum igitur ad primum finem attinet, qui propitiatorius, placatorius, pacatorius, sive pacificatorius est dictus, & institutus ideo ut Deos placarent, sibi propitios redderent, eorum gratiam, pacem, veniam consequerentur, sibique conciliarent: illius, ut apud Homerum & Apollonium, sic apud reliquos auctores profanos crebrerrima fit mentio, et apud Græcos ἱλάσκεσθαι sive ἱλασμὸν nominibus feré exprimitur, quæ quidem ab ἱλεὼς dedu-cta sunt, quod est propitium esse, & Eulathio dictum ἵλεως τῷ ἱερῷ, quod idem ac ἰφίλεως, id est, cupio, & λάεων, quid est, videre: quod ii, qui sunt propitii, libenter eos videant, quibus sunt propitii, qui precibus aliquid petitum accedunt. ἱλάσασθαι & ἱλάσκεσθαι est propitium reddere: item expiare. Inde ἱλασμὸς propitiatio, placatio, ἱλαον & Attice ἵλεω propitius, unde ἱλεῶ & ἱλασμῷ, gratia & misericordia: item ἱλαρὸς, hilaris: quoniam qui propitii sunt hilares: contrà irati & infensi verbi vultu, tristitiam præ se ferunt, de qua voce ἱλαρὸς, ἱλαρῶ, ἱλαρὸς vide pulchram apud Schabotum in epistolarum Homeri librum.
units.tr: As for the first end, which is called propitiatory, placatory, pacatory or pacificatory, it was instituted so that men might placate the gods, make them favourable to them, and obtain and win over their favour, peace and pardon. Of this end the most frequent mention is made, not only in Homer and Apollonius but in the other profane authors. Among the Greeks it is expressed mostly by the words ἱλάσκεσθαι and ἱλασμός, which are derived from ἵλεως, meaning propitious. Eustathius says that ἵλεως is said of the god as if from ἵφιλεως, that is, "I desire," and λάεων, "to see," because those who are propitious gladly look upon those to whom they are propitious, namely those who approach them with prayers asking for something. ἱλάσασθαι and ἱλάσκεσθαι mean to make propitious; likewise to expiate. Hence ἱλασμός means propitiation or placation; ἵλαος, and in Attic ἵλεω, means propitious; whence come ἱλεῶς and ἱλασμῷ, meaning grace and mercy; likewise ἱλαρός, cheerful, because those who are propitious are cheerful, whereas the angry and hostile, with a stern look, show sadness. For the beautiful discussion of the words ἱλαρός, ἱλαρῶς and ἱλαρότης, see Schaefer's book on the letters of Homer.

units.la: Latini hunc finem exprimunt multis verbis, cujusmodi sunt placare, propitiare, patare, piare, &c. Placare est mitem & placidum facere, unde O vidus: Est bonos & tumulus animas: placare paternas.
units.tr: The Latins express this end with many words, such as placare, propitiare, patare, piare, and so on. To placare is to make mild and gentle; whence Ovid: "It is an honour to appease the souls of the dead at their tombs."

units.la: Et: Munera (crede mihi) placant homines, Deos. Placatur domus Iuppiter ipse datus.
units.tr: And: "Gifts, believe me, appease men and gods. Jupiter himself is appeased when he is given a house."

units.la: Hinc placamina & placamenta appellabantur vel sacrificia, ut supplicamenta Apulejo, vel animalia: quibus Deos suos placare se posse existimabant. Livius 7. ab Vrbe: Ludi quoq; scenici, nostra res bellicosi populo, inter alia cælestia iræ placamina instituti dicuntur. Plinius lib. 20. cap. 7. Hoc veluti placamento terra blandiuntur. Idem libro 8. cap. 47. Magna & pecori gratia vel in placamentis Deorum, vel in usu vellerum. Tacitus lib. 15. Non largitionibus Principis aut Deum placamentis decedebat infamia.
units.tr: Hence the appeasements [placamina and placamenta] were called either sacrifices, like the supplications in Apuleius, or the victims by which men thought they could placate their gods. Livy, book 7 from the founding of the City: "The stage games too, though a warlike matter for a warlike people, are said to have been instituted among other heavenly appeasements of anger." Pliny, book 20, chapter 7: "By this kind of appeasement they flatter the earth." The same, book 8, chapter 47: "Great is the favour of wool, both in the appeasements of the gods and in its use." Tacitus, book 15: "Infamy did not yield to the Prince's largesses or to the appeasements of the gods."

units.la: Sed & Placere a placandi verbo videtur derivari: qua quidem duæ voces magnam inter se habent cognationem, ita ut una ab altera videatur esse derivata. Nam & ea, qua vel Deo, vel hominibus placent, ea utrosque placant: & nicilum ea, quæ vel Deum vel homines placant, ea vel Deo, vel hominibus placent necesse est. Inde et Placenta dicta, libum farinaceum, ex farina, caseo, melle, vel quod nobis placeat, vel quod ea folerent Deos placare, eaque Dis placeret: nisi malimus a Græco πλακοῦς, idem significante derivare. Sic Placatio ab eodem dedu-cta. Cicero de Divinatione: Nunquam civitas nostra sine placatione Deorum immortalium tanta esse potuisset. Idem & Placatum dixit. Dii, inquit, vel placati jam, vel etiam satiati esse debent. Et in officiis: Deos placatos pietas efficit. Item: Tu Deiocrum de votionibus placatos esse Deos censes. Placatores quoq; ab eodem verbo sunt dicti. Plinius lib. 13. cap. 18. Nec minus propitii erunt Dii mola salsa supplicantibus: immo verò, ut palam est, placatores.
units.tr: But placere also seems to be derived from the verb placare. These two words have a close kinship, so that one seems to be derived from the other. For whatever pleases God or men, does appease them both; and conversely, whatever appeases God or men must please God or men. Hence placenta is also so called, a flour cake made of flour, cheese and honey, either because it pleases us, or because people were accustomed to appease the gods with it and it pleased the gods; unless we prefer to derive it from the Greek πλακοῦς, which has the same meaning. So placatio is derived from the same root. Cicero, On Divination: "Our state could never have been so great without the appeasement of the immortal gods." The same also used placatum: "The gods, he says, ought already to be appeased, or even satisfied." And in On Duties: "Piety makes the gods appeased." Again: "Do you think that the gods were appeased by the vows of Diagoras?" Placatores too are named from the same verb. Pliny, book 13, chapter 18: "The gods will be no less propitious to those who supplicate them with salted meal; indeed, as is plain, they are appeasers."

units.la: Hoc ipsum placari di verbum magnum cum verbo pacandi affinitatem habet. Placare enim unius tantum littera l interpositione a pacare differt; significatione est cum eo idem. Placare est, pacare, hoc est, pacificare, pacem dare vel impetrare: quod ipsum a Virgilio hac periphrasi est expressum: Hic Helenus cæsis primum de more juvencis Exorat pacem Divum vittasq; resolvit.
units.tr: This very verb placari has a close affinity with the verb pacari. Placare differs from pacare only by the insertion of one letter, l, and in meaning it is the same. Placare is pacare, that is, to pacify, to give or obtain peace. Virgil expresses this by a periphrasis: "Here Helenus, first, after the slaughter of young bullocks in the customary way, begs peace of the gods and unties the fillets."

units.la: Servius: Orare est petere, exorare est impetrare.
units.tr: Servius: "To orare is to ask; to exorare is to obtain."

units.la: Sed & idem verbum sæpe ad Deos referetur, ut apud Tibullum libro 4. Elegia 1. Parvaq; cælestes placavit mica, nec illis Semper inauratio taurus cadit hostia cornu.
units.tr: But the same verb is also often referred to the gods, as in Tibullus, book 4, elegy 1: "With a little salted meal he appeased the heavenly ones; nor did a bull with gilded horns always fall as the victim."

units.la: Seneca: Sed tu domitor magnæ ferarum Orbis, simul placator adest.
units.tr: Seneca: "But you, conqueror of the great circle of wild beasts, are at once their appeaser."

units.la: Sic Pax pro venia, gratia, & propitiatione Deorum. Virgilius quarto Æneidos: —pacemque per aras Exposcunt. Et 3. Æneid. Sed voti precibusq; iubent exposcere pacem. Cicero pro Rabirio: Ab Iove paceni & veniam peto. Idem in Officiis: Peccavit igitur pace vel Quirini vel Romuli dixerim.
units.tr: So pax is used for pardon, grace and the propitiation of the gods. Virgil, Aeneid book 4: "and they seek peace through the altars." And Aeneid book 3: "but they bid them seek peace by prayers and vows." Cicero, for Rabirius: "From Jupiter I seek peace and pardon." The same, in On Duties: "He sinned, then, I would say, against the peace of Quirinus or of Romulus."

units.la: Propitiandi verbum in eadem significatione & ad eundem sacrorum finem saepe a profanis scriptoribus usurpatur. Propitius, id est, placidus, placatus, sive pacatus nonnullis videtur dictus a Prope & ito, itas, &c. eo quod is, qui nobis favet, prope nos ire consuevit: vel quod prope ad illum audemus accedere. Vel dicitur Propitius aut prorsus pius, aut porro, id est, valde pius, auctore Nonnio. Plautus in Merc. Tam propitium reddam, quam cum propitia est Iuno. Idem in Amph. Et tibi, & tuis omnibus propitius caeli cultor advenit. Cicero pro Caelio: Huic homini ego, fortasse & pauci Deos propitios: plerique autem iratos putabant. Idem in epistola ad Octavium: Perque Fortunam populi Romani, quae pestquam nobis infesta est, fuit aliquando propitia. Idem in Pisonem: Quid est, Caesar, quod te supplicationes toties decreta tot diersum tantopere delectent: in quibus homines errore ducuntur, quos Dii negligunt: qui, ut nofferlo divinus dixit Epicurus, neque propitii cuiquam esse solent, neq; insti. Idem in Verrem Actione prima: Ita Deos mihi velim propitios, ut cum illius temporis mihi venit in mentem, &c. Plaut. Menach.
units.tr: The verb propitiare, in the same meaning and for the same end of sacrifices, is often used by the profane writers. Propitius, that is, mild, placated or pacified, is thought by some to be derived from prope and ire, because he who favours us is accustomed to come near us, or because we dare to approach him closely. Or propitius is said to be simply pius, or porro, that is, very pious, on the authority of Nonnius. Plautus, in the Merchant: "I will make her as propitious as Juno ever was." The same, in the Amphitryon: "And the heavenly worshipper has come to you and all yours, propitious." Cicero, for Caelius: "For this man, perhaps a few thought the gods propitious, but most thought them angry." The same, in a letter to Octavius: "and by the Fortune of the Roman people, which after it was hostile to us, was once propitious." The same, against Piso: "What is it, Caesar, that so many supplications and so many days of thanksgiving, decreed so often, delight you so much? In these men are deceived by error, whom the gods neglect; who, as the divine Epicurus said, are wont to be propitious to no one, nor angry." The same, in the first action against Verres: "So may I have the gods propitious to me, as when that time came into my mind, etc." Plaut. Menach.

units.la: Prologo. Salutem primum iam a principio propitiam Mihi atque vobis Spectatores nuntio.
units.tr: Prologue. Greeting, first of all, already favourable to me and to you, spectators, I announce.
The same author, in the Pseudolus:

units.la: AD. Egone in edem Veneris? AG. Quid eo? AD. Ut Venerem Propitiem. AG. Ebo, an irata est? AD. Propitia hercle est.
units.tr: AD. Am I to go into the temple of Venus? AG. Why would you go? AD. To make Venus favourable. AG. Ebo! Is she angry? AD. Favourable, by Hercules.

units.la: Idem in Panulo: Dii illum infelicitent omnes, qui pot hunc diem Lenonem illam Veneriunquam immolarit boftiam: Quin ve ullum turus granum sacrificaverit. Nam ego hodie infelix, Dis meis instissimis Sex agnos immolavi: nec potui tamen Propitiam Venerem facere, ut esset mihi, Quoniam litare nequeo abs illinc illico.
units.tr: The same author, in the Poenulus: May all the gods curse that pimp, who on this day has never offered Venus a sacrifice, nor even thrown a grain of incense on the altar. For I, unhappy today, sacrificed six lambs to my most just gods, yet I could not make Venus favourable to me, since I cannot get a favourable sign from the sacrifice straightway.

units.la: sacrificando a Diis, quod volo impetrare.
units.tr: By sacrificing to the gods, to obtain what I wish.

units.la: apud eundem Charmidem senex ad Neptunum: At que ego, Neptune, tibi ante alios Deos gratias ago atq; habeo summas. Nam pol placido te & clementi, meo usque modo, ut volui, usus sum.
units.tr: In the same author's Charmides, an old man speaks to Neptune: "And I, Neptune, give you and hold the greatest thanks before all the other gods. For indeed I have found you gentle and merciful, just as I wished, all the while."

units.la: Et penul 'o pesl: Nitua pax propitia foret praeflo.
units.tr: And in the Penulus: "Unless a favourable peace were to be ..."

units.la: Pinnas quoq; vel bani huic sacrificiorum sini est accommodatum, quatenus videlicet idem est, quod placare sive propitiare. Horatius: Tellurem porcos Syl vanum lactae piabant, id est placabant.
units.tr: The word piare too is suited to this kind of sacrifice, inasmuch as it means the same as placare or propitiare. Horace: "The fruitful sows propitiated (piabant) the earth and the woodland god," that is, appeased (placabant).

units.la: Propitiare est idem, quod placare, placatum reddere, conciliare. Suetonius in Othone: Per omnia piaculorum genera manes Galbae, a quo deturbari expellit, se videret, propitiare tentat. Curtius lib. 4. Ille capite velato, verbenas manu preferens praebat precos Regis, Iove Minervaque vitio riam propitiante. Propitiabilis inquit Nonius, est prosus ad propitiandum. Ennius: Animus huic est propitiabilis hostia, id est, apta propitiationi.
units.tr: Propitiare means the same as placare: to make placated, to win over. Suetonius in Otho: when he saw the ghost of Galba, by whom he was thrown down, he tried to propitiate it by every kind of expiatory rite. Curtius, book 4: "He, with head veiled and holding sacred boughs in his hand, offered the king's prayers, Jupiter and Minerva being favourable to the sacrifice." Nonius says propitiabilis means fit for propitiating. Ennius: "The victim is propitiable for him," that is, suited to propitiation.

units.la: Sequitur secundus sacrificiorum cerimoniarum, Gentilium finis, videlicet lustratorius, purgatorius, expiatorius, seu februatorius, qui primum magna affinitate attingit, & ad illum refertur. Nam quoniam vel personis, vel rebus, quocunq; modo pollutis & contaminatis credebant Deos sibi adversos esse, infensos & infestos: idcirco contra personarum rerum ve lustratione & purgatione eo fdem rursus sibi placari ac propitios reddi: ac in gratia secum redire arbitrabantur. Erant etiam sacrificia atque cerimoniae huiusmodi lustratoriae & purificatoriae quasi praeparatae quaedam ad majora solennia, sacrificia, quae non, nisi praemissa huiusmodi rerum personarumque lustratione, rite celebrari a sepossel existimabant. Hic finis secundum a Latinus his verbis exprimitur: Piare sive Expiare, Lustrare, Purgare, Purificare, Februare.
units.tr: Next comes the second end of the Gentile sacrificial ceremonies, namely the lustral, purgative, expiatory, or februatory rite, which touches the first very closely and is referred to it. For since they believed that the gods were hostile, angry and unfriendly to persons or things polluted and defiled in any way, therefore by purifying and cleansing those persons or things they thought the gods could again be placated and made favourable, and return to grace with them. There were also lustral and purificatory sacrifices and ceremonies of this kind, prepared as it were in advance for the greater solemnities, which they believed could not be rightly celebrated unless such a lustration of persons and things had been carried out beforehand. This end is expressed in Latin by these words: piare, or expiare, lustrare, purgare, purificare, februare.

units.la: Piare significat etiam idem quod purgare, expiare, ἁγνίζειν, Virg. 3. Aeneid. E Et culpam miserorum morte piabant.
units.tr: Piare also means the same as purgare or expiare, to cleanse (ἁγνίζειν). Virgil, Aeneid 3: "And they expiated the guilt of the wretched by death."

units.la: Cicero: Antiqui si quid a se in Deos peccatū vel admissum arbitrarentur, falsa religione piabant, vel expiabant delictum. Et pro Domo sua: Si quid tibi piandum, aut instituendum fuisset religio ne domestica. Idem de Legibus: Hetruriæ Principes fulgura atq; ostenta pianto.
units.tr: Cicero: The ancients, if they thought they had sinned against the gods in any way, either by a false religion expiated (piabant) or atoned for the offence. And in the speech for his house: "If anything had to be expiated for you, or instituted, in the domestic rites." The same, in On the Laws: "The leaders of Etruria expiate (piant) lightnings and portents."

units.la: Aliquando significat piū amare. Naevius apud Nonium: Nemo est, qui magis suos pios liberos. Aliquando in genere colere significat. Plautus in Amphit.: Ubi piem pietatem si stultus more morata tibi postulem placere.
units.tr: Sometimes it means to love dutifully. Naevius, quoted by Nonius: "There is no one who loves his dutiful children more." Sometimes it means to honour in general. Plautus in the Amphitryon: "Where, if I, a fool, wish to please you by dutiful conduct."

units.la: Hinc ergo Pius & Pietas: cui opponitur Impius & Impietas. Quando, idem verbum contaminare, polluere contraria significatione est, quod & Iuspiare dicuntur Sacrum etiam pro exsecrabili ponitur.
units.tr: Hence pius and pietas, to which impius and impietas are opposed. Since the same word, to contaminate or pollute, has an opposite meaning, they are also called iuspiare. Sacer is also used for what is detestable.

units.la: Hinc sacrificia, cultus & quicquid agitur seu praebetur ... ti flatione peccati Piaculum di citur: unde sacrificium piaculare & auspicium piaculare ... ficantibus tristia portendebat, cum aut hostia ab ara profugisset, aut percussa magis ... Virgilius sexto Aeneidos: ea prima piaculi sunto.
units.tr: Hence sacrifices, worship, and whatever is done or offered ... by the expiation of a sin is called piaculum; whence a piacular sacrifice and a piacular omen ... foretold sad things to those sacrificing, when either the victim had fled from the altar or had been struck ... Virgil, Aeneid 6: "let this be the first atonement (piaculi)."
Piaculum.
Horace, Odes book 2:

units.la: Te quoque piacula nulla resolvent hoc est, nullis hostiis te expiabis.
units.tr: "No expiations will release you either," that is, you will not be atoned for by any victims.

units.la: Plautus: Me ne piaculum oportet fieri propter ... iultuiam tuam,
units.tr: Plautus: "Must I be made an expiation (piaculum) because of your folly,

units.la: Ut meum tergum fulcire tuae subdat: fuccidaneum: id est, oportet ne tuam stultitiam mea poena expiari?
units.tr: so that my back may be a prop for yours, a substitute? That is, must your folly be expiated by my punishment?"

units.la: Interdum etiam ponitur pro ipso peccato, crimine & flagitio: unde idem Virgilius eodem sexto Aeneidos:
units.tr: Sometimes it is also used for the sin itself, crime and disgrace. Whence Virgil in the same sixth book of the Aeneid:

units.la: Diffulit in seram commissa piacula mortem. Ubi Servius crimina, propter quae piacula debentur, interpretatur.
units.tr: "He deferred to a late death the crimes (piacula) he had committed." Where Servius explains piacula as the crimes for which expiations are owed.

units.la: Et Plautus: Piaculum est miserere nos hominum, male rem gerentium, id est, trimen, fla g:tium est.
units.tr: And Plautus: "It is a piaculum, have mercy on us men who manage our affairs badly," that is, it is a crime, a disgrace.

units.la: Sic apud Hebraeos vox חטאת, Chattā, cum peccatum, tum sacrificium pro peccato, ejus expiandi causa oblatum significat: ut apud Hosaam Pharisaeos: Comedunt peccata populi mei. Sic Paulus Christum vocat peccatum, id est, hostiam pro peccato. Sed de hoc verbo & ejus compositis vi de supra.
units.tr: So among the Hebrews the word חטאת, chattā, means both sin and the sin offering offered for its expiation: as in Hosea, the Pharisees: "They eat the sins of my people." So Paul calls Christ sin, that is, a sacrifice for sin. But of this word and its compounds see above.

units.la: Piabile porro id, quod expiari & purgari potest. Oridius:
units.tr: Piabile is what can be expiated and cleansed. Ovid:

units.la: Cui Deus nimium terrere pi ... le sul ... ens, Est ait & saevi flectitum ira Dei.
units.tr: "To whom God, too much to be feared ... that is, expiable, and the anger of the cruel God can be bent."

units.la: Idem Expiabile, de quo infrā: cujus contrarium Inexpiabilis, inexpiabile bellum apud Cicero nem, quod Graeci πόλεμον ἄσπονδον: dov η ἀκατάλλακτον. Tu- pid. bre dixerunt.
units.tr: Expiabile is discussed below, whose opposite is inexpiabilis, as in Cicero's "inexpiable war," which the Greeks called πόλεμον ἄσπονδον, or ἀκατάλλακτον, that is, a war without truce, irreconcilable.

units.la: Poëtice Piamen quoq; & Piamentum dicitur id, quo (Expiatio, vel actus expiandi; vel id ipsum, quo ad expiationem utimur. Sunt autem, teste Festo, actiones magis Poëticae, quam Oratoriae. Ovidius secundo Fastorum:
units.tr: In poetic language piamen and piamentum are also used for that by which expiation is made, or the act of expiating, or the very thing by which we use for expiation. According to Festus, these are rather poetic than oratorical terms. Ovid, Fasti book 2:
Piamen and piamentum.
"The Roman fathers called the februa piamina."

units.la: Plinius lib.25. cap.4. Haec vulsa ferobem repleri vario genere frugum religio est, & terra pia mentum. Apuleius: Tandem perrantes plateis omnibus & in modum eorum, qui lustralibus pia mentis minas portentorum hostias circumforantes expiant. Circumforanea hostia dicuntur, quae circūagros & urbes in ambarvali amburbalive sacrificio circumducuntur, seu circūaguntur, a circumforendo dicta. Inde Piamenta lustralia dicta eide Apuleyo, quibus urbes agrosve lustrantur.
units.tr: Pliny, book 25, chapter 4: "When this plant is pulled up, it is a religious duty to fill the pit with various kinds of grain, and that is the expiation of the earth." Apuleius: "At last they wandered through all the streets, and in the manner of those who go about with lustral expiations of portents, carrying victims around, they purify." Victims are called circumforanea when they are led around the fields and cities in the ambarvalis or amburbalis sacrifice, or driven around, named from circumforare. Hence Apuleius calls piamenta lustralia those by which cities or fields are lustrated.

units.la: Expiare porro est procurare, placare, vel mallare, purgare, purumfacere. Accipitur etiā pro punire: ut, expiare scelera. Cicero ad Atticum; Quae violata sunt, expiabuntur. Idem: Mari omnia, quae violata sunt, expiari putantur. Idem: Ceres in Numen istius supplicio expiari vole b.ant. Livius, Ita, ut caedes manifesta aliquo piaculo lueretur, imperatum est patri, ut filium ex piaret pecunia publica. Plinius lib.33. cap.11. Eadem quoq; ratione luxum populi expiare solent bella.
units.tr: Moreover expiare means to take care of, to appease, or to make good, to purge, to make pure. It is also taken for to punish, as expiare scelera, to expiate crimes. Cicero to Atticus: "What has been violated will be expiated." The same: "All things that have been violated are thought to be expiated by the sea." The same: "They wished Ceres to be expiated by the punishment of that man." Livy: "So that a manifest murder should be atoned for by some expiation, it was ordered that the father should expiate his son with public money." Pliny, book 33, chapter 11: "For the same reason wars are wont to expiate the luxury of the people."
Explare.

units.la: Expiabile, quod expiari potest, vel quod in expiatione positum est, vel, quod ad expiationē perti net. Inexpiabile contra. Cicero Tuscul. 2. Itaq; unū illud erat turpis prisci illis, quos Cascos ap-
units.tr: Expiabile is what can be expiated, or what lies in expiation, or what pertains to expiation. Inexpiabile is the opposite. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 2: "Therefore that alone was the shameful thing for those ancient men whom Ennius calls Cascos, to hold that there is feeling in death and that a man is not so destroyed by the passing of life that he perishes utterly."

units.la: Expiabile. pellat Ennius, esse in morte sensum, neq; excessu vitæ sic deleri hominem, ut funditus interiret. id cum multis aliis rebus, tum e Pontificio jure & cerimoniis sepulcrorum intelligi licet: quas maximam ingenii prædicti nec tanta cura tolluissent, nec violatas tam expiabili religione Janxissent, nisi befsiffet in eorum mentibus mortem non interiu esse omnia tollentem atq; delenem, sed quandam quasi migrationem, commutationemq; vitæ.
units.tr: Expiabile. This may be understood from many other things, and from the Pontifical law and the ceremonies of sepulchres: men of great and distinguished intellect would neither have undertaken such care for them, nor joined the violated tombs with such expiatory religion, unless it had been fixed in their minds that death does not destroy and wipe out all things, but is a kind of migration and change of life.

units.la: Caterum & Expiatio & Expiamentum inde compositu. Cicero: Diis violatis expiatio debetur. Et de Legibus. Scelerum in homines atq; impietatum nulla expiatio est.
units.tr: Moreover, both expiatio and expiamentum are formed from this. Cicero: "Expiation is owed to the gods when they have been violated." And in On the Laws: "There is no expiation for crimes against men and for impieties."

units.la: His addenda purificandi, lustrandi, lucendi, februandi verba, quibus similiter facta sacrificiorum, fine Ethnici expresserunt. Purgandi verbo non tam usi sunt Veteres in sacris, quam verbo purificandi. Purificare igitur est mundu seu purum facere. Plinius lib.10.cap.41. Villaribus gallinis & religio inest: inborrefcunt edito ovo, excutiuntq; fe, & circumactu purificant ac fefsu ea aliqua sese & ova lustrant. Idem lib.8.cap.1. de elephantis: Autores sunt, inquit, in Mauritanie saltibus ad quendam amnem, cui nomen est Amilo, nitescente Luna novæ greges eorum defcedere, ibiq; fe purificantes folenniter aqua circumspergi, atq; ita salutato fidere in fylvas reverti.
units.tr: To these should be added the words purificandi, lustrandi, lucendi, februandi, by which the Gentiles likewise expressed the acts of their sacrifices, or their ends. The ancients used the word purgandi in sacred matters less than purificandi. To purify, therefore, is to make clean or pure. Pliny, book 10, chapter 41: "Hens also have a religious scruple: they shudder after laying an egg, shake themselves, and by turning around they purify themselves, and with a sort of sneeze they lustrate themselves and their eggs." The same, book 8, chapter 1, on elephants: "Authors say," he says, "that in the woods of Mauritania, at a certain river called Amilo, when the moon is shining, their herds go down, and there, purifying themselves, they are solemnly sprinkled with water, and so, having greeted the star, they return to the forests."

units.la: Hinc Purificatio, id est, Purgatio, καθαρσις, ἁγισμος. Plinius lib.15.cap.30. de lauro loquens: Eadem & purificationibus inquit, adhibetur. Ibidem, Lauro, quam pacifetam & gratam Apolli nitovocat, in profanis quoq; usibus ut & oleam pellui fas non fuisse: ita ut ne propitiandis quidem Numinibus accendi ex his altaria areve debuerint.
units.tr: Hence "purificatio," that is, purgation [καθαρσις], [ἁγισμος]. Pliny, book 15, chapter 30, speaking of the laurel: "It is also used for purifications," he says. In the same place: the laurel, which he calls peaceful and pleasing to Apollo, was not lawful to use even for profane purposes, just as with the olive. For this reason, they ought not to be burned on altars or hearths even to propitiate the gods.

units.la: Lustrandi deinde verbum in sacris magis fuit usitatum pro, Purgare, Purificare, Expiare: quod vel ἀπὸ τῆς λούω, id est, lavare, eluere, ablucre, diluere: vel a lucido, Varroni, id est, folvedo; unde λύτρον & αὐτιλύτρον: ideo, quia quinto quoq; anno vectigalia tributa exigebatur. Luftrum a Latinis dictum est; de quo ita Varro: Lustrum nominatu tempus quinquennale a lucendo, hoc est, folvedo, quod quinto quoq; anno vectigalia et tributa per Censores persolvebatur. Tempus hujusmodi fuerit apud Græcos Olympiades, quæ similiter erant quinquennales. De hoc ante lustrandi verbofie Virgilius, in Bucolicis: —Et cum folennia verba Reddemus Nymphis & cum lustrabimus agros. Et 6. Æneid. Idem ter socios pura circumtulit unda Spargens rore levi & ramo felicis oliva.
units.tr: Next, the verb "lustrare" was more commonly used in sacred contexts to mean purge, purify, or expiate. It derives either from λούω, that is, to wash, cleanse, rinse, or dilute, or, as Varro says, from "lucidus," that is, to loosen (solvere). Hence λύτρον and ἀντίλυτρον, because taxes and tributes were exacted every fifth year. The Latins called this "lustrum." Varro says of it: "Lustrum is the name of a five-year period, from lucendo, that is, loosening, because every fifth year the taxes and tributes were paid through the censors." Among the Greeks the Olympiads were a similar five-year period. Virgil, in the Bucolics, speaks of this before the word lustrare: "And we shall render the solemn words to the Nymphs, and when we purify the fields." And in Aeneid 6: "He carried his companions three times around in pure water, sprinkling them with light dew and a branch of the fortunate olive."

units.la: Lustra vitæ, viros dixit, a novissima verba. Idem fecundo: Lustramur a loris, notiq; intendimus aras. Vbi Servius: Aut lustramur, inquit, id est, purgamur, ut Sacra faciamus, aut certe lustramur levi, id est, expiamur.
units.tr: He spoke of the lustra of life, of men, from the final words. The same poet in book 2: "We are purified with thongs, and we raise the altars we know." Servius there: "Either we are purified, that is, cleansed, so that we may perform sacred rites, or at least we are purified by a light sacrifice, that is, expiated."

units.la: Sic Ovidius: Ego lustror ab illis Et purgante nefas novies mihi tarmine dicto, Pellora fluminibus jubent supponere centum.
units.tr: So Ovid: "I am purified by those, and with the formula spoken nine times, which purges the wrong, they bid me place a hundred rivers beneath me."
The same, book 10: "You will be purified with a magic rite."

units.la: Lustratum ac purgatum Capitolium dixit Livius lib.2. ab Vrbe, & lustratum corpus divino odore idem Ovid.12. Metamorph. Et Martialis in praefatione libri 8. meminit non nisi religionis purificatione lustratos accedere ad templa debere.
units.tr: Livy, book 2 from the founding of the city, speaks of the Capitol as purified and cleansed; Ovid in Metamorphoses 12 speaks of a body purified with divine fragrance. Martial, in the preface to book 8, mentions that only those purified by religious lustration ought to approach the temples.

units.la: Hinc & Luftrame Flacco, & Luftramentu at Luftratio dicta: & Luftratio quidē velut expiatio: qua quid solvitur ac liberatur: unde & λύτρον, λύτρον, id est, solutione auri, inquit Festus. Columella lib.2, cap.27. Hoc loco cerui habeo, quosfa, quum folennia festorum percensuerint, desideraturos luftrationi, ceterorum, sacrificiorum, quae pro frugib. fiunt, morè prisco vfur parum.
units.tr: Hence also "lustrame" in Flaccus, and "lustramentum" and "lustratio" are used. Lustratio is, as it were, expiation, by which something is loosened and freed; whence λύτρον, a ransom, "that is, a payment in gold," says Festus. Columella, book 2, chapter 27: "Here I have stags, which, when they have recounted the solemn festivals, will need lustration, and the other sacrifices that are made for the crops, in the old custom, are used too little."

units.la: Erat aute mos apud Romanos folennis exercitus auc populi lustrandi. Cicero de Divinatione: Cum Impator exercitu, Censor populi lustraret, qui hostias ducerent, eligebantur: id est, Cum vel Populi Censores, vel Imperatores exercitum lustrarent, cetera & flatus quibufda cerimonia omnes omnes aut a populo, aut ab exercitu deprecarentur & in hunc modu populum vel exercitum expiarent. Hinc Festus: Lustrum, inquit, significat nunc tempus. nunc populi luftrationem. Et Livius lib.3. Omnes Centuriæ & equites in campum Martium convocatisue, ove, tauro casis immolarunt, quod Lustrum est dictum, fitq; a sacrificio illo census obtinuit nomen lustri.
units.tr: Among the Romans there was a solemn custom of lustrating the army or the people. Cicero, On Divination: "When the commander lustrated the army, or the censor the people, those who would lead the victims were chosen," that is, when either the censors of the people or the commanders lustrated the army, all the rites and prayers were offered by the people or the army, and in this way they expiated the people or the army. Hence Festus: "Lustrum," he says, "signifies sometimes a period of time, sometimes the lustration of the people." And Livy, book 3: "All the centuries and the knights were called together into the Campus Martius, and they sacrificed a sheep, a pig, and a bull, which is called the lustrum; and from that sacrifice the census took the name lustrum."

units.la: Dictum hinc fuit Tubilustrium, & Armilustrium: illud quidem quod eo die in atrio Sutorio sacrorum tubae lustrantur: hoc vero quod in armilustrio armati sacra faciebant: nisi locus potius dictus ab hostis, sed quod de hostibus prius id ab ludebo aut lustrio id est, quod circumbant ludentes ancilibus armati.
units.tr: From this were named the Tubilustrium and the Armilustrium: the former because on that day the sacred trumpets are purified in the Sutorian atrium; the latter because in the Armilustrium armed men performed sacred rites, unless the place is named rather from the enemies, but because the armed men, dancing around with the ancilia, were called by the name of the lustrum.

units.la: Sed & sacrificium lustrale hinc dictum, quod in lustrationis, id est expiationis, ad Lustrale sacrificium...
units.tr: But the sacrifice called "lustrale" is also named from this, because in the lustration, that is, the expiation, ...

units.la: Ideo fuit pinguia, interprete Festo: quoniam morus fuerat completo lustro, id est, quinquennii tempore victimas sacrificari, id est, piscatio aetatis: & idcirco pingue. Huic & Lustrici dies in tumultu dicti, quibus pueri lustrarentur, & nominaeis imponerentur, quia Macrobius, & Tranquillus: Ejusdem futurae in felicitatis signum eximiae dies lustrico exunt. Qui infantes lustrabant Lustratores; feminae lustratrices fuerunt appellatae. Festus: Lustro dies infantium appellantur puellarum octavus, puerorum nonus: quia hos lustrantur aeq. nomen a eis imponuntur: cujusmodi dies ferculum religionem Christianam sunt dies Baptismales.
units.tr: Hence the "pinguia," according to Festus: because it had been the custom, when the lustrum was completed, that is, in the period of five years, to sacrifice victims, that is, in the fifth year of life, and therefore they were fat. Hence also the "lustric" days, named in the ancient tongue, on which boys were purified and given their names. Macrobius and Suetonius (Tranquillus) say: "Of the same future good fortune, the extraordinary days of lustration are the signs." Those who purified infants were called lustratores; women who did so were called lustratrices. Festus: "The days of infants are called lustric: the eighth day for girls, the ninth for boys, because on these days they are purified and their names are given. Such days, among us Christians, are the baptismal days."

units.la: His addit, quod verbum lustrari & nomen Lustri ab qui id. Ni. lam in parte accipitur. Lustra ri quidem pro Inlustris agere, id est lustrare. Plautus Lu...
units.tr: To these he adds that the verb lustrari and the noun lustrum are also taken in another sense: lustrari indeed means to make bright (inlustrare), that is, to light up. Plautus, Lu...

units.la: Lustra ergo dicentur lupanaria, luparum, id est, meretricium latibula. Festus Lustra, inquit, significant lacunas lutosas, quae sunt in sylvis, apo eum cubilia, aquae similitudine, qui in locis ab dimes & sordidis ventri & defidae operam dant, dicuntur in lustris agere.
units.tr: Therefore lustra are called brothels, the dens of wolves, that is, the hiding places of prostitutes. Festus: "Lustra," he says, "signify muddy pools, which are in the woods, and are beds like water; those who do base and filthy work for the belly and idleness are said to work in lustra."

units.la: His postremo addendum Februandi verbum antiquum, quod ipsum quoq. lustrationem significat; de quo sic Festus: Februarius, inquit, mensis dictus, quod cum, id est, extremo mense anni purgatur, id est, lustrari et purgaretur: vel a Iunone Februata, quam alii Februalem, Romani Februlum vocant, quod eo ipso mense sacra fiebat, eas quae feriae erant Luperealia, quo die mulieres februabantur a lupercis amicula. Iuvenes, id est, pelle caprina: quam ob causam ut quoq. dies Februatus appellabatur.
units.tr: Finally, to these must be added the old verb februare, which also signifies lustration. Of it Festus says: "The month of February was named because at the end of the year, that is, in the last month, it is purged, that is, lustrated and cleansed; or from Juno Februata, whom some call Februalis and the Romans Februlum, because sacred rites were performed in that very month. On the feast days that were the Lupercalia, the women were purified (februabantur) by the Luperci with the amicula, that is, a goatskin. For this reason the day too was called Februatus."

units.la: Februus autem, verbum Sabinum, id est, lustro purgo sunt, qui volunt dictum a Februo, proprie ea quod hoc adoleudo & flammis fer ventibus fieri solebat.
units.tr: Februus, a Sabine word, means to purify or cleanse. Some want it named from Februus, properly because this used to be done by burning and by the flames of fire.

units.la: Februus dictus est hinc Pluto, vel Dis pater, Inferorum Deus: quod de mense Februario facrificaretur: Vide Macrobium lib.2. Et Februa eorum, dici batur quaecunq. purgamen cau, a in quibusdam ritibus, Graece Καθαρμός.
