Plinius: Vulgata prima tempore opimo obtinuit, Februa esse omnia, quibus mala fatorum confessentia purgarentur, delerentur, peccata, aut manes defunctorum placidi redderentur accensis videluntur circa sepulchra facibus cereis. Ovidius secundo Fasti.
units.tr: From this, Pluto or Dis Pater, god of the underworld, was called Februus, because sacrifice was offered to him in the month of February. See Macrobius, book 2. Their februa were called whatever means of purgation was used in certain rites, in Greek καθαρμός. Pliny: "The common view, from earliest times, held that all things were februa by which the evils of fate were purged and sins were blotted out, or by which the spirits of the dead were appeased, when torches of wax were lit around the tombs." Ovid, Fasti, book 2.

units.la: Februa Romani dixere piamina patres: Nunc quoq. dant verbo plurima signa fidem. Et paulo post Deniq. quodcunq. est, quo carmina nostra piantur, Hoc apud incolas nomen habebat avos.
units.tr: "The Roman fathers called purifications februa; even now many signs confirm the word." And a little later: "Finally, whatever it is by which our songs are purified, among the natives this had the name avos."

units.la: Sed & Februatio idem, quod purgatio. Plutarchus 4. Rom. 68. An quia Lupercalia urbis sunt Februatio. lustratio & sunt mense Februario, an ab expiando nomen, ipsorum dies Februatus dicitur, cum Februatio purgamentum significet? Haec de nominibus Latinis.
units.tr: But februatio also means the same as purgatio. Plutarch, Roman Questions 68: "Is it because the Lupercalia are a lustration of the city and fall in the month of February, or is the name from expiating, so that their day is called Februatus, since februatio signifies a purgation?" These are the Latin names.

units.la: Verba Graeca, quibus idem fines exprimitur sunt ἁγνίζειν & ἁγίζειν, sanctificare, confectare, ἁγισμὸς, item sanctificare, & peragere, quae ad sacrificium pertinent: ἁγνίζομαι, purificari, expiari: ἁγνισμὸς purificatio, expiatio: ἁγνισμὸς purificatio, lustratio: ἁγνισμα, idem: ἁγνιζω expiandi seu lustrandi rim habent. ἁφαγνίζειν purificare, expiare: καθαίρειν, purgare, mundare, expiare, lustrare: καθαρτὸς purgari, expiari: καθάρσιον, purgamentum, piamen.
units.tr: The Greek words by which the same things are expressed are ἁγνίζειν and ἁγίζειν, to sanctify, to consecrate; ἁγισμός likewise, sanctification, and the carrying out of what pertains to sacrifice; ἁγνίζομαι, to be purified, expiated; ἁγνισμός, purification, expiation; ἁγνισμός, purification, lustration; ἁγνισμα, the same; ἁγνίζω, to expiate or lustrate. ἀφαγνίζειν, to purify, expiate; καθαίρειν, to purge, cleanse, expiate, lustrate; καθαρτός, purged, expiated; καθάρσιον, purgation, piacle.

units.la: tum: καθαρσιν, purgatio, expiatio: καθαρσις, purgatorium, vel purgatrix, purgatorium, b. ubi expiatorium, ut καθαρσις ὑδωρ, lustralis aqua: καθάρσιος Svcia, lustralis victima. καθαρσις et καθαρμος, expiatio, lustratio, piaculum: καθαρσια sacra expiatoria, piacula Luciano, Plutarcho, Paufanie: καθαρτης, purgator, expiator, lustrator, Sophocli et Plutarcho: καθαρτικος purgativus: καθαρσιευς, idem quod καθαρσιος, purgatrix: καθαρσια purgare, mundare, purificare: καθαρσιμος, purificatio, purgatio, explamentum, piaculum, pro καθαρσιον Luciano.
units.tr: Also καθαρσιν, purgation, expiation; καθαρσις, a purgatory or purifying thing, expiatory, as in καθαρσις ὕδωρ, lustral water; καθάρσιος σῦς, a lustral victim. καθαρσις and καθαρμος, expiation, lustration, a piacle; καθαρσια, expiatory sacred rites, piacles, in Lucian, Plutarch, Pausanias; καθαρτής, purger, expiator, lustrator, in Sophocles and Plutarch; καθαρτικός, purgative; καθαρσιεύς, the same as καθάρσιος, a purger; καθαρσια, to purge, cleanse, purify; καθαρσιμος, purification, purgation, expiation, piacle, used for καθάρσιον in Lucian.

units.la: Similia fere sunt ostia, ιερεια, καθαρσιον, αφοσιοι, piare, expiare, lustrare, sanctum et purum fce leris reddere, case crare sacrificare: unde ωσπερ, qui hostia immolabat apud Delphos. Plutarch.
units.tr: Similar in meaning are ὁσια, ἱερεια, καθάρσιον, ἀφοσιοῦν: to pierce, expiate, lustrate, to make sacred and pure, to consecrate, to sacrifice. Whence ... the one who sacrificed a victim at Delphi, in Plutarch.

units.la: His addi potest verbum λοιβη, λοιβαζω: unde Latinum Luo, eluo, et inde frequentativum, Lustro, quod quidem ipsum λυειν, vel a λυκος, lux, ignis, videtur aeri vari. Duo enim praecipua, quib. lustrandi vis tributa, aqua fuerunt et ignis: et aqua inprimis marina: adigne refuntur teda, et sulphur: quae ignem facillime excipiunt. Hoc ipso ergo verbo λοιβη, unde luere, et lustrare, aliaq; conjungi ea quaeq; fasce praecipuus lustrationis modus atq; materia comprehenditur. Atq; haec etiam de numinibus vel verbus apud Graecos.
units.tr: To these may be added the word λοιβή, λοιβάζω, whence the Latin luo, eluo, and from it the frequentative lustro, which itself seems to derive from λύειν, or from λύκος, light, fire. For the two chief things to which the power of lustrating was assigned were water and fire, and especially sea water; and the fire is supplied by torches and sulphur, which take fire most readily. So by this very word λοιβή, whence luere and lustrare, and other words joined with them, the chief mode and matter of lustration is comprehended. And this is what I have to say about the gods or words among the Greeks.

units.la: Porro ad duos hoc priores fines, Propitiatorium nimirum et lustratorium illustrados, antequam ad tertium et quartum accedam, lubet excipla quaedam atq; testimonia subjungere. Romani, quia pra teteris ferè gentib. omnib. religiosissimi haberi atq; dici volebant, quæ do vel bellis aliquod, nova praesertim et periculosum suscipiebant, vel pestilentia, morbus, epidemia, vel fame et annona ita ritate laborabant, vel alia gravi aliqua calamitate premebantur, vel etiā prodigia, porteta, monstra, ostenta nunciabatur, quib. Diuiram suam gravem, calamitatem portendere videbatur, nihil illis prius et antiquius erat, quam ut cōjultus priut librum oraculo, divinum, et eorum interpretibus, sacrificiis, supplicationibus, lectisternium, votis, jejuniis, donis, ludis, aris, tēplisq; novis, novandis, fabricandis, ac dedicandis Deos illos suos irator placaret, ibi reconciliarent. Hujusce moris atq; consuetudinis exempla quaedā ex Livio depromta, libet bis subjungere, quae non solum ad hunc sacrificiorum finem, sed ad ritus cerimoniasq; reliquas ontinet, de quibus supra dictum illustran dat non parum conducent.
units.tr: Before I come to the third and fourth ends, I want to add some excerpts and testimonies that bear on these first two purposes, propitiation and purification. The Romans wished to be regarded and called the most religious of almost all peoples. Whenever they undertook something, especially a new or dangerous enterprise such as a war, or were troubled by pestilence, disease, epidemic, famine or dearth, or were oppressed by some other grave calamity, or when prodigies, portents, monsters or omens were announced that seemed to foretell some serious disaster to the state, nothing was more important or urgent to them than to consult the oracle books and their divine interpreters, and to appease and reconcile their angry gods by sacrifices, supplications, lectisternia, vows, fasts, gifts, games, altars, and new or renewed temples built and dedicated. I think it will help not a little to add two examples of this custom from Livy. They concern not only this purpose of sacrifice but also the other rites and ceremonies I mentioned above.

units.la: Tullo regnante, cum post de vitiosa Sabinor Regi Patribusq; nunciatum esset in monte Albano lapidibus pluisse, et nisi etiā esset audire vocem ingentis ex summo cacuminis luco, ut patrio ritu Albani sacra facerēt, quae velut Dim quod, simul cū patria relictis, obliviōne dederent: aut Romana sacra suscepenant, aut Fortunae (ut sit) obtrati cultū reliquerunt. De m. Romanis quod, ab eode prodigio (scilicet plu vie lapidea, et vocis audiea, quae fuerit potestatem aeratum praestigia, ludibria) Novendiale sacra publice suscepit est: seu voci celestis (daemoniaca vel ruis, seu diabolica dixerū) seu aruspicis monitu. Manifestum certe solenne, ut quandocunq; idem prodigium nunciaretur, feriae per novem dies agerentur. Haec Livius lib. Decadis primae. Novem diale ergo hoc sacrum tra Deum platandae causa (quam prodigium illud portendere videbatur) a Romanis suscep tum fuit ac institutum.
units.tr: In the reign of Tullus, when it was reported to the King and the Fathers that stones had rained on the Alban mountain, and a loud voice was also heard from the summit of the grove, commanding the Albans to perform the sacred rites in their ancestral manner, which they had neglected and forgotten along with their homeland, they either took up Roman rites or abandoned the worship of Fortune (as is likely). Concerning the Romans, from the same prodigy (namely the rain of stones and the hearing of the voice, which was either a deceit or a trick of the enemy's power), the nine-day sacrifice was publicly undertaken, whether at the bidding of a heavenly voice (which they called demonic, or rather diabolical) or of the haruspices. It is clear that it was the customary practice that whenever the same prodigy was announced, holidays were kept for nine days. Livy reports this in the first book of the first decade. So this nine-day sacrifice was undertaken and instituted by the Romans for the sake of appeasing God, whom that prodigy seemed to portend.

units.la: Idem vero Rex Tullus, cum nihil ante ratus esset minus regium, quam sacris dedere animum (utinam no hodie quod principium quorunda Christianorum in versu Sacris eadē essent meus atq; sententia) morbo longiusq; implicitus, quo fracti simul cum corpore spiritus illius erant ferociores, repetē omnib. pravis magnis, superstitionibus degere, religionibusq; etiam populū implere caepit, teste eode Historico, eode in loco. Notabus in hoc exemplo τα καθαρματα esse μαθημα ea hominem praesertim illustris fortune vix posse tenere medium: quin aut sint alios, aut superstitiosi: demū exemplis regum et principum populum trahi facillime vel ad bona, vel ad mala, vel ad religiones veram, vel ad superstitionem.
units.tr: King Tullus himself, when he thought nothing less royal than to devote himself to sacred things (would that today the beginnings of some Christians were of the same mind and opinion!), was then caught by a long illness, and since his spirits were made fiercer along with his weakened body, he began to live in all kinds of vain superstition and to fill the people with religious observances, according to the same historian in the same place. Note in this example that τὰ καθάρματα are a lesson: a man, especially one of illustrious fortune, can hardly keep to the middle way, but is either lax or superstitious. Finally, by the examples of kings and princes, the people are drawn most easily either to good or to evil, either to true religion or to superstition.

units.la: Sic cum eodem tempore morbus epidemius graviter fuissēt laboratum, vulgo jam homines cum flatum rerū, qui sub Numa Rege fuerat (Hic Rex superstitionū Romanarū primus autor fuit et architectus) requirentes, una opem egris corporibus relicta, Si pax veniā, ab Diis impetrare esset (utinam sit de vero Deo sensisset) credebant. Teste idem Livius eodem in loco.
units.tr: Thus, when at the same time a widespread epidemic had grievously afflicted them, the people, now recalling the ancient state of things under King Numa (who was the first author and architect of Roman superstitions), believed that the only help left for the sick bodies was to obtain from the gods, if peace and pardon could be obtained (would that they had thought of the true God!). Livy reports this in the same place.

units.la: Ipsum etiam Regem Tullum tradunt, inquit Livius, volventem commentarios Numae, licet de religione: utinam tanto studio hodie nostri reges, et principes atq; magistratus volumine ad re-
units.tr: Livy says that they relate that King Tullus himself, while reading the commentaries of Numa, concerning religion... Would that our kings and princes and magistrates today were as eager to read these books.

units.la: Veteres Deorum iram quomodo placare sint soliti. ex Livio.
units.tr: How the ancients were accustomed to appease the anger of the gods, from Livy.
They undertook the nine-day sacrifice.

units.la: Agri corporis remedium pax et venia Dei.
units.tr: Peace and the pardon of God are the remedy for bodily sickness.

units.la: Iram Dei sollicitat pravatc. lud veteris & novi Testamenti vol verent atq; re vol verent) cum ibi quedam ac ulta solennia sacrificia Iovi Elicio falla in venisset operatum his sacris se abdidisse: sed non nisi initum aut curatum id sacrum esse, nec solum nullam ei oblatam caelestium speciē, sed ira Iovis solicitata, prava religione, fulmine ipsum cum domo conflagrasse. Fuit hæc Proter via, sive Holocaustum tetrum, funestum, & horrendum, quod miser ille Rex fecit.
units.tr: How they provoke the anger of God by wrong worship, both of the Old and of the New Testament. There, when certain strange and unusual solemn sacrifices had been offered to Jupiter Elicius, he had retired to these rites, as if by hiding in them he had carried out the act; but it was not performed or completed properly, and not only was no heavenly sign given him, but the wrath of Jupiter was stirred up, and by a wrong worship he was struck by lightning together with his house. This was a foul, deadly and horrible holocaust, which that unhappy king offered.

units.la: Hujus Regis successor, Aucus Martius, Numæ ex filia nepos, cum aut neglectis religionibus
units.tr: The successor of this king, Ancus Martius, grandson of Numa through a daughter, when the religions had been either neglected

units.la: Hoc exemplum principes & magistratus Christiani sibi, quod verum Dei cultu, ad imitationem proponant, ut neglecta, vel prave culta religione, nihil illis prius sit & antiquius, quam dare operam ut sacra nova Numa, aut hominibus sed ab ipso Deo instituta rite fiant ac celebrentur, & omnia, quæ ad religionem veram pertinent, ex fasorum antiquitate illius Regis regum commentariis per sacrorum antistites publicè populo proponantur ac inculcentur.
units.tr: Christian princes and magistrates should take this example as a model for the true worship of God: when religion is neglected or wrongly observed, nothing should be more important and urgent to them than to take care that the sacred rites instituted not by men but by God himself be duly performed and celebrated, and that everything pertaining to the true religion be publicly set before the people and impressed upon them from the ancient records of the sacred things, through the bishops of the sacred rites, as that king of kings did with the commentaries of Numa.

units.la: Roma T. Æmilio, & Q. Fabio Consulibus anno urbis conditæ 585. cum ut testis est Livius Tempore cla-Decade prima, l. b. 3. & siccum magnam cladem accepissent, & non minor hominum fragies morbo
units.tr: At Rome, in the consulship of T. Aemilius and Q. Fabius, in the year 585 from the founding of the city, as Livy witnesses in the first decade, book 3, when they had received a great disaster, and no less a loss of men from disease

units.la: Hoc autem illustrius adhuc exemplum extat apud eundem autorem Decade prima, lib. 5. Cum
units.tr: There is an still more illustrious example of this in the same author, first decade, book 5. When

units.la: Sic anno Vrbis conditæ 357. prodigia multa nuncupata, quorum pleraq;, & quia singuli autores Desperat ope erant, parum credita ip sæ ad, & quia hostilibus Hetruscis. per quos ea procurarunt, arupices non
units.tr: Thus in the year 357 from the founding of the city, many prodigies were announced. Most of them were scarcely believed, both because individual authors despaired of help and because the Etruscan haruspices, through whom they were to be expiated, were hostile.

units.la: Præterea anno urbis conditæ 537. Cn. Servilio, & C. Flaminio Coss. Romæ circa urbem ea Romæ quoque, & lectisternium in vrbe, & supplicatio ad ædem Herculis, nominatim deinde vniuerso populo, circa omnia pulvinaria indicta: & Genio majores hostia cæsa quinq; vel C. Attilius Serranus prætor vota suscipere iussus, Si in decem annos R.P. eodem statu stetisset statu. Hæc procurata votaq; ex libris Sibyllinis magna ex parte leuerant animum religione.
units.tr: Moreover, in the year 537 from the founding of the city, under the consuls Cn. Servilius and C. Flaminius, at Rome and around the city, a lectisternium was held in the city and a supplication at the temple of Hercules; then the whole people was summoned by name, and a sacrifice of five large victims was offered to the Genius, and C. Attilius Serranus the praetor was ordered to make vows that the state would remain in the same condition for ten years. These things, procured and vowed largely from the Sibylline books, greatly relieved their minds of religious anxiety.

units.la: Quæ porrò sacra a Cos. Romæ consulatum ineuntibus fieri sint solita, ex his Patrum verbis patet, quibus C. Flaminium novum Consulem insectati sunt, qui sacra terimonii si, illi negle&tis in Prouinciam profectus fuerat, nec cum seniatu modo sed cum Diis immortalibus C. Flaminium bellum gerere consulem ante inauspicato factum, reuocantibus ex ipsa acie diis atq; hominibus non paruisse: & nunc comitia prætorum & capitolium & solennem votorum iuncupationem fugisse: ne die iniiti magistratus Iouis Optim.max. templum adiret: ne senatum in uisus ipse, et sibi uni inuisum, uideret consuleretq; ne Latinas indiceret, Iouiq; Latiali solenne sacrum in monte Albano faceret: ne auspicato profectus in Capitolium ad vota nuncupanda, paludatus inde ad prouinciam iret. Lixæ modo sine insignibus, sine litioribus, profectum clam, furtim, haud aliter quam si exsilii causa solum vertisset: magu pro maiestate vidisset imperii Arimini, quam Romæ magistratum initurum, & in diuersorio bospitali, quam apud penates suos prætextam sumpturum.
units.tr: What sacred rites the consuls were usually accustomed to perform at Rome on entering office is clear from these words of the Fathers, with which they attacked the new consul C. Flaminius, who, neglecting the sacred ceremonies, had set off for his province: not only had he disregarded the senate, but he had waged war against the immortal gods as well, since, when the gods and men had called him back from the very battle line, he had not obeyed. He had shunned the elections of the praetors, the Capitol, and the solemn taking of vows, so that on the day he entered office he might not go to the temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest; he had avoided looking at the senate, which was hateful to him alone, and consulting it; he had not proclaimed the Latin festival, nor performed the solemn sacrifice to Jupiter Latialis on the Alban mountain; he had not, after taking the auspices, gone up to the Capitol to make his vows, and then set out for the province in military cloak. He had departed secretly and furtively, in a mere cloak without insignia or lictors, as if he had gone into exile, and he had seen the majesty of empire at Ariminum, which he would enter upon at Rome, and had assumed the praetexta in a hospitable inn, which he should have taken up at home among his household gods.

units.la: Et paulló pòst: Paucos post dies magistratu initi, (C. Flaminius in prouinciā) immolantiq; ei vitulus iam ictus a manibus sacrificantum se cum proripuisset, multos circumstantes cruore respersit. Fuga procul etiam major apud ignaros quid trepidaretur, & concursatio fuit: id a plastrisq; in omne magni terroris acceptum.
units.tr: And a little later: a few days after he had entered office, while C. Flaminius was sacrificing in the province, a calf already struck by the hands of the sacrificers broke loose and splashed many of the bystanders with blood. Then a flight, even greater, arose among those who did not know what the alarm was, and there was a stampede; and this was taken, from the carts and everywhere, as a sign of great terror.

units.la: Per idem tempus Cn. Seruilius Consul Romæ Idib. Martis magistratu initi. Ibi cum de Repub. retulisset, redintegrata in C. Flaminiū ( eius collegam) inuidia est. Duos se consules creasse unum habere. Quod enim illi iussuri imperium, quod auspicium esset magistratus: id a domo, publicis priuatisq; hominibus Latini feriæ atq; sacrificio ut moræ per secto, votoq; ritum Capitolio nuncupatus, secum serre. Nec priuatum auspicia sequi: nec sine auspicis profectum in externo eo solo noua atq; integra concipere posse. Augeban̄ mecum prodigia, ex pluribus simul locis nunciata.
units.tr: At the same time Cn. Servilius, the consul at Rome, entered office on the Ides of March. When he had reported on the state, the ill will against C. Flaminius, his colleague, was renewed. They said that the consuls had created two men, one of whom had... what the consul-elect was to command, what the auspices of his office were, he took these from home, from the public and private sacred rites of the Latin festival, from the delay of the sacrifice, and from the vows made at the Capitol; he carried them with him. Nor could he follow private auspices, nor, having set out without auspices, conceive new and untouched plans in that foreign land. Meanwhile prodigies, announced at several places at once, were increasing.

units.la: Deinde ut sicut erant nunciata, ex postis, autoribusq; in Curiam iatroduxit, Cosul de religione patres consuluit. Decretum, ut ea prodigia partim maioribus hostiis, partim lactentibus proscurarentur: & ut supplicatio per triduum ad omnia pulvinaria haberetur. Cætera cum decem viri libros inspexissent, ut ita fierent, quæ mandabantur, pro hac sacris statuerunt: iouis institutum est. Iouiq; primum donum fulmen aureum pondo quinquaginta fieret, Iunoni Mineruæ, ex argento daretur, & Iunoni regina in Aventino, Ioniq; Sophia sacris, numerare hostiis sacrificaretur, matronæq; pecunia collata, quantum conferre cuiq; commodum esset, donum Iunoni Reginæ in Aventinum ferrent, lectisterniumq; fieret: quin & liberti ne, & ipse, unde Feroniæ donum daretur, pecuniam professuratibus suis conferrent. Hæc ubi factā, decem viri Ardeæ in foro majoribus hostiis sacrificarūt. Postremò ex libris Decembris ammense ad ædem Saturni Romæ immolatum est, lectisterniumq; imperatum; (& eum lectum senatores strauerunt) & conuiuium publicum ac per urbem Saturnalia die ac nocte clamatum, populusq; eum diem festum habere, ac seruare in perpetuum jussus. Dum consul placandus Romæ diuis, habendoq; delectus dat operam. Annibal profectus ex hybernis.
units.tr: Then, just as the reports had been given, he brought the informants and their authorities into the Senate, and the consul consulted the Fathers about religious matters. It was decreed that these prodigies should be expiated, partly with larger victims and partly with sucklings, and that a supplication lasting three days should be held at all the couches. As for the rest, when the decemvirs had consulted the books, they laid down that the following should be done as they directed: a rite was instituted for Jupiter. First, a golden thunderbolt of fifty pounds was to be made as a gift to Jupiter, a silver gift was to be given to Juno Minerva, and a sacrifice was to be offered to Juno Regina on the Aventine and to Juno Sospita with the customary number of victims. The matrons were to collect money, each as much as she could conveniently give, and carry it as a gift to Juno Regina on the Aventine, and a lectisternium was to be held. Moreover, the freedwomen too were to contribute money, through their patrons, for the gift to Feronia. When this was done, the decemvirs offered sacrifices with larger victims in the forum at Ardea. Finally, according to the Sibylline books, a sacrifice was offered at the temple of Saturn at Rome, and a lectisternium was ordered; the senators spread the couch themselves. A public feast was held, and Saturnalia were proclaimed by day and night throughout the city, and the people were ordered to keep that day as a festival forever. Meanwhile, the consul was occupied with appeasing the gods at Rome and with holding the levy, while Hannibal set out from his winter quarters.

units.la: Post Cannensem autē illā Romanorū cladem, valde insigniē & funestam, supplicationes priuatæ quoq; p domos vulgatæ sunt, adeoq; tota urbe opplete lectus, ut sacrum annuerfarium Cereris intermissum fuit: qa neclugebit. id facere est sas, nec ulla in tempestate matrona expers lectus fuerat. Itaq; ne ob eandem caussam alia quoq; sacra publica aut priuata desererentur, senatusconsulto lectus triginta diebus finitus est. Liuius Decade 3. lib. 2. Ac paulló post: Territi etiā super tantas clades, cum ceteris prodigiis: tum quod dua Vestales eo anno, Opimia & Floreniæ slupri comperte: & altera sub terram, ut mos est ad portam Collinam neccata fuerat: altera sibimet ipsa mortem consciuerat. L. Cantilius scriba Pontificum, quos nunc minores pontifices appellant: quia cum Floreniâ slupruum fecerat, a Pont. max. eo vsq; virgis in comitio cæsus erat, ut incer verbera exspiraret: Hoc nefas cum inter tot, ut fit, clades in prodigiis versum esset, decem viri libros adire jussi sunt. Et Q. Fabius pictor Delphos ad oraculum missus est sacrarum, quibus precibos supplicationibusq; deos posset placare, & quanā futura finis tantus cladibus foret. Interim ex fatalibus libris
units.tr: After that very notable and deadly defeat of the Romans at Cannae, private supplications were also proclaimed throughout the households, and the lectisternium was spread so widely through the whole city that the annual sacred rite of Ceres was suspended, because it is unlawful to mourn during that rite, and in no time of mourning had any matron been excluded from the lectisternium. So, lest other public or private sacred rites be abandoned for the same reason, a decree of the Senate limited the lectisternium to thirty days. Livy, Decade 3, book 2. And a little later: the people were also terrified, above such great disasters, by the other prodigies; and especially because two Vestals that year, Opimia and Floronia, had been found guilty of unchastity, and one of them had been buried alive by the Colline Gate, as is the custom, while the other had taken her own life. L. Cantilius, a scribe of the pontiffs, whom they now call the lesser pontiffs, had committed unchastity with Floronia, and for this the Pontifex Maximus had him beaten with rods in the Comitium until he died under the blows. Since this crime, as usually happens amid so many disasters, was counted among the prodigies, the decemvirs were ordered to consult the books. And Q. Fabius Pictor was sent to Delphi to the oracle, to learn with what prayers and supplications the gods could be appeased, and what end would come to such great disasters. Meanwhile, from the fatal books

units.la: Sacrum Cereris anniuersarium quando intermissum. libri sacrificia aliquot extraordinaria facta: inter quae Gallus & Galla, Graecus & Graeca in foro Boario sub terra vivi demissi sunt in locum saxo consceptum, ibi antea hostium humanarum minimè Romano sacro imbuntur. Placatu fatis, ut rebantur, Deis.
units.tr: When the annual sacred rite of Ceres was suspended. From the books, several extraordinary sacrifices were performed; among them, a Gaul and a Gaulish woman, and a Greek man and a Greek woman, were buried alive in the Forum Boarium, in a pit lined with stone. Human sacrifices had formerly never been stained upon the Roman rites. The gods, as they believed, were thus placated by fate.

units.la: Anno quinto decimo belli Punici, Q. Fabio Maximo quartum, M. Claudio tertium Cos. f. proa digia mnita nunciata sunt, quae quo magis credebant simplices ac religiosi homines, eo plura num. tabantur. Haec prodigia hostiis majoribus procurata sunt ex aruspicum responsis, & supplicatio omnibus Diis, quorum pul vinaria Romae fuit, indicta est. Perpetratis quae ad pacem Deum pertinebant, de Rep. bello, gerendo, & quantum copiarum & ubi quaeque, offuse, Cos. ad Senatum retulerunt. Idem Livius Decade 3. lib. 4. Observationem dignum Cos. primum de religione ad sena tum retulisse, et perpetratis primum in, quae ad pacem Dehm pertinebant, tum demum de Repub. & bellogerendo reculisse. Quanto magis igitur Christiani principes ac magistratus ea, quae ad religionem verram pertinent, quae ad verum Deum placandum spectant, prius curare debent, quam ea crastent, quae ad res bellicas, & ad Remp. pertinent. Id si fieret, multo felicior profecto domi, militiaeque rerum & publicarum & privatarum offet status.
units.tr: In the fifteenth year of the Punic war, when Q. Fabius Maximus was consul for the fourth time and M. Claudius for the third, many prodigies were reported, and the more credulous and religious people were, the more they reported. These prodigies were expiated with larger victims according to the responses of the haruspices, and a supplication was proclaimed to all the gods whose couches were at Rome. When the things pertaining to the peace of the gods had been completed, the consuls reported to the Senate about waging war, and how many troops there were, and where each force was. Livy, Decade 3, book 4, notes that it was worthy of observation that the consul first reported to the Senate on religion, and only when the matters pertaining to the peace of the gods had been completed did he report on the state and on waging war. How much more, then, should Christian princes and magistrates first take care of those things that pertain to the true religion and to appeasing the true God, before attending to those that concern warfare and the commonwealth! If this were done, the condition of public and private affairs, both at home and in the field, would surely be far happier.

units.la: Simile fere superiori exemplum Livius refert Decade tertia lib. 7. Q. Fabio Maximo quinquam, Q. Fulvio Flacco quartum Cos. Prodigia, inquit Livius, priusquam ab Urbe Cos. proficerentur, procurari placuit. Enumeratis deinde ipsis prodigiis, ea dicit hostiis majoribus fuisse procurata, & supplicationem circa omnia pulvinaria, & obsecratione in unum diem indicta: & de creti: ut, C. Hostilius, Praetor, ludos Apollinis facere, ut annis votis factis erant, voverat facere.
units.tr: Livy relates an example much like the previous one in Decade 3, book 7, when Q. Fabius Maximus was consul for the fifth time and Q. Fulvius Flaccus for the fourth. "It was decided," says Livy, "that the prodigies should be expiated before the consuls set out from the City." After listing the prodigies themselves, he says they were expiated with larger victims, and a supplication was proclaimed around all the couches, and a prayer lasting one day. It was also decreed that C. Hostilius, the praetor, should hold the games of Apollo, as he had vowed in the annual vows that had been made.

units.la: M. Marcello, & T. Quintio Crispino Cos. ut ceterur Livius Decade 3. lib. 7. Consules illos religio tenebat, quod prodigium aliquod nunciatum, non facile licebant. Per dies aliquot hostiis majores sine litatione case, diu, non impetrata pax Deum, in eapsa consulum Repub. incolumi ex sacrabilis prodigiorum eventus vertit. Indi Apollinaris Q. Fulvio, Ap. Claudio consul. a P. Cornelio Sulla praetores urbis primum facti ierant inde omnes deinceps praetores urbani fecerant, sed in unum annum vovebant, diu, incerta faciebant. Eo anno pestilentia graves incidit per urbem, a rosa, quae tamen magis in longos morbos, quam in perniciales evasit. Eius pestilentiae causa & supplicatum per compita tota urbe est, & P. Licinius Varus praetor urb. legem ferre ad populi jussus, ut hi ludi in perpetuum in flatam diem moverentur. Ieaq; ipse primus ita mo vit, facta ad III. Nonas Quinctiles. Is dies deinde solemnis fer vetus.
units.tr: Under the consuls M. Marcellus and T. Quinctius Crispinus, as Livy says in Decade 3, book 7, scruple held those consuls back, since, when a prodigy had been reported, they could not easily proceed. For several days sacrifices with larger victims were offered without favourable omens, and the peace of the gods was not obtained for a long time. In that very year, however, the state remained intact, and the outcome of the prodigies turned favourable. Thereafter the Apollinarian games, first vowed under the consuls Q. Fulvius and Ap. Claudius, were held by P. Cornelius Sulla as praetor of the city; afterwards all the urban praetors held them, but they vowed them only for one year, and they often made them uncertain. That year a grievous pestilence fell upon the city, which, however, turned more into long illnesses than into deadly ones. For its cause a supplication was held at the crossroads throughout the whole city, and by the people's order P. Licinius Varus, praetor of the city, was to propose a law that these games be moved to a fixed day in perpetuity. He himself first did so, and the games were moved to the third day before the Nones of Quinctilis. That day later became a solemn festival.

units.la: Item C. Claudio Nerone & M. Licinio iterum Cos. primique Cos. proficerentur, Nov. en diale sacrificium fuit, quia Vejus de caelo lapidaverat. Sub unius prodigii (ut sic) mentioni, alia quoq; nunciata: Ecpaullo posit: Haec procurata hostiis majoribus prodigia, & supplicatio diem unum fuit ex decreto Pontificum: inde iterum Novendiale inflauratum, quod in armilustro lapidibus visum pluere. Libertas religione mentes turbavit rursus nunciacui, Frutione infantem natum esse quadrimo parem: nec magnitudine tam mirandum, quam quod ei quoq; ut Sinthesse biennio an te, intertus mas an femina essent, nacus erat. Id vero arspices ex Hetruria accitis sedit ac corpus prodigium ditere: extorrem agro Romano procul terrae contactu alco mergedum. Virum in aeram condidere, pro vetustum, in mare proiecerunt. Decreverat tum postificeis ut virgines ter novena peruerbum cantes carmen canerent. Id enim in Iovis Statoris aede disserere conditum ab Livio pacta carmen, tacta de caelo aedes in Aventino Iunonis Reginae, prodigiumque id ad matronas pertinere arspices cum respondissent, donoq; dicam placandans esse, aedilium currulium edictio in Capitolium convocate, quibus in urbe Roma, intra, decimam lapidem ad urbe domicilia esse, ipsae inter se quinq; & viginti delegarunt, ad quas ex dotibus stipem conferrent. Inde donum pelvis aureaque talia, lata, in Aventinum pures, & caeca a matronis sacrificasti. Confectum ad aliud sacrificium eadem dirvo ab decem virus edicta dies, cujus ordo talis fuit. Ab ade Apollinis boves famine albae duae porta Carmentalis in urbem ducta. Post eas duo signa cupressea Iunonis regi na portabantur. Tum sepcem & viginti virgines longam indutae vestem carmen in Iunonem regnam canentes ibant, illa campestrate forsitan laudabile rudibus ingenio, nunc abhorrens & incorditum, st referatur.
units.tr: Likewise, when C. Claudius Nero and M. Livius were consuls for the second time, and before the consuls set out, a Novendiale sacrifice was held, because at Veii it had rained stones from heaven. Along with the mention of this one prodigy, others were also reported. A little later: these prodigies were expiated with larger victims, and by decree of the pontiffs there was a supplication for one day; then the Novendiale was renewed again, because it had been seen to rain stones in the Armilustrium. Religious scruple troubled minds once more when it was reported that at Frusino an infant had been born, about three years old in size, and it was not so remarkable for its size as because, like the one two years before, it was doubtful whether it was male or female. The haruspices summoned from Etruria declared this a portent and a prodigy of the body, and ordered that it be carried out of Roman territory and drowned in the sea, far from any contact with land. They shut the infant alive into a chest, and threw it into the sea. The pontiffs then decreed that twenty-seven maidens should go through the city singing a hymn. For that song, composed by Livius, was preserved in the temple of Jupiter Stator. The temple of Juno Regina on the Aventine had been struck by lightning, and when the haruspices answered that this prodigy pertained to the matrons and must be appeased by a gift, the curule aediles, by edict, summoned the matrons to the Capitol. Those who had homes in the city of Rome, within the tenth milestone, chose among themselves twenty-five women to whom they would contribute alms from their dowries. Then a gift of a golden basin and such things was carried to the Aventine, and the matrons made their offerings. By edict of the decemvirs, another day was appointed for a further sacrifice, and its order was as follows. From the temple of Apollo two white cows were led into the city through the Carmental Gate. Behind them were carried two cypress statues of Juno Regina. Then twenty-seven maidens in long robes went singing a hymn to Juno Regina. That hymn, perhaps praiseworthy in the rustic simplicity of its time, would now, if it were repeated, seem absurd and uncouth.

units.la: L. Pecuaris, Q. Caecilio Cos. (quia M. Livio dictatore creati fuerat) in civitate tanto disceptione belli fallucia, eius omnium fecundorum ad versorum, cau sas in Deos vertere ent, multa prodigia nunciabantur. Et post illorum enumerationem prodigia illa Consules majoribus hostiū procurare jussi, & supplicationem unum diem habere. Ea ex senatusconsulto facta. Plus omnibus aut nunciatis peregre, aut visis domi prodigiis, terruit animos hominum ignis in aede Vestae extinctus. Ob quam causam tafa flagro est Vestalis, cujus custodia noctis eius fuerat, jussu P. Licinii pontificis. Id quoque nihil portendentibus dei, caeterum negligentia humana actiderat, amen & hostiis majoribus procurari, & supplicationem ad Vestae haberi placuit.
units.tr: In the consulship of L. Pecuarius and Q. Caecilius (who had been appointed after M. Livius the dictator), when the state was in such great turmoil from war and treachery, and all the unfavourable events were attributed to the gods' causes, many prodigies were reported. After these were listed, the consuls were ordered to make expiation with larger victims and to hold one day of supplication. This was done by decree of the Senate. More than all the prodigies reported from abroad or seen at home, the fire that went out in the temple of Vesta terrified people's minds. For this reason the Vestal whose duty it was to watch that night was scourged by order of P. Licinius, the pontiff. Although the gods were sending no portent by this, it had happened through human negligence; nevertheless it was decided that it should be expiated with larger victims and that a supplication be held to Vesta.

units.la: L. Cornelio Lentulo, P. Villio Tappulo Coss. Prodigiorum, quae nunciata fuerunt tauffa fe natus ceufuit, ut Consul majoribus hostiis, quibus Diis videretur, sacrificaret: ob hoc unum prodigium aruspices in senatum vocati, atq; ex responso eorum populo in diem unum edicta, & ad omnia pulvinaria res divina facta. Livius Decade 4. lib. 2. Hic etiam obser vatione dignum, iisdem Coss, aedilem curulem creatum, C. Valerium Flaccum, qui quia Flamen Dialis erat, jurare in leges non poterat: magistratum autem plus quinq; dies, nisi qui jurasset in leges, non lice bat gerere. Tandem datus, qui juraret pro fratre L. Valerius Flaccus, Praetor designatus, Tribuni ad plebem tulerunt, plebs, scilicet, ut perinde esset, ac si ipse aedilis juraffet. Hinc patet, quanta jurijurandi apud Romanos religio fuerit.
units.tr: In the consulship of L. Cornelius Lentulus and P. Villius Tappulus, when the prodigies that had been reported were thought to be of great significance, the consul was ordered to sacrifice larger victims to whichever gods seemed right. Because of this one prodigy alone, the soothsayers were summoned to the Senate, and on their response a day of public prayer was proclaimed and a sacred rite performed at all the cushions of the gods. Livy, Decade 4, book 2. Here is also something worth noting: in the same consulship a curule aedile, C. Valerius Flaccus, was elected, who, because he was Flamen Dialis, could not swear to the laws; yet no one could hold office for more than five days unless he had sworn to the laws. At last L. Valerius Flaccus, the praetor-designate, was given to swear on behalf of his brother, as the tribunes proposed to the plebs, and the plebs agreed that it should be the same as if the aedile himself had sworn. From this it is clear how great was the Romans' religious regard for the oath.

units.la: Coff. creatu Sexto Aelio Peto, & T. Quinctio Flaminino, T. Quintium habito dilectu, propterea in provinciam, prodigia nunciata, atq; eorum procuratio Romae retinuerunt. Eorum prodigiorum causa supplicatio unum diem habita, & Consules rebus divinis operam dederunt placatiq; Dis profecti in provinciam sunt. Livius eadem Decade 4. lib.
units.tr: When Sextus Aelius Paetus and T. Quinctius Flamininus were created consuls, and T. Quinctius was holding a levy, prodigies were reported, and on that account they kept him in Rome, and the procuration of the prodigies was entrusted to him. Because of these prodigies a supplication was held for one day, and the consuls attended to the sacred rites; the gods being appeased, they set out for their province. Livy, same Decade 4, book ...

units.la: Cn. Cornelio Cethego & Q. Minutio Rufo Coss. creatis, profusquam Coss. Praetores, in provin tias profiticerentur, prodigia procurari placuit, Livius Decade 4. lib. 2. Sic L. Furio Purpurio renitur, aut ipsi Coss. ab urbe moverent, procurari, ut assolet, prodigia, quae nunciabantur, jussis. Livius Decad. 4. lib. 3.
units.tr: When Cn. Cornelius Cethegus and Q. Minucius Rufus were created consuls, before the consuls and praetors set out for their provinces, it was decided that the prodigies should be expiated. Livy, Decade 4, book 2. So when L. Furius Purpurio was ... or when the consuls themselves were to leave the city, the prodigies that were reported were ordered to be expiated, as is customary. Livy, Decade 4, book 3.

units.la: P. Cornelio Scipione Africano iterum, & T. Sempronio Longo Coss. creatis prodigia visa & nunciata Romae ex Pontificum decreto procurata, & sacrificium Novendiale factum, quod Adriani nuncia verant, in agro suo lapidibus pluisse. Livius Decade 4. lib. 4.
units.tr: When P. Cornelius Scipio Africanus (for the second time) and T. Sempronius Longus were created consuls, prodigies seen and reported at Rome were expiated by decree of the pontiffs, and a novendial sacrifice was made, because the people of Adria reported that it had rained stones on their land. Livy, Decade 4, book 4.

units.la: M. Acilio & P. Cornelio Coss. prodigiorum causa libros Sybillinos ex S.C. Decemviri cum adiissent, renunciarunt jejunium institutum Cereri esse, & id quinto quoque anno ser vandum: quoniam Tarracinae & Amiterni nunciatum est aliquot is lapidibus pluisse, novendiale sacrum fieret, & unum diem supplicatio esset, torònari supplicarunt: & Coss. P. Cornelius, quibus Diis quibusq; hostiis edidissent, decemviri sacrificant. Placatis Diis, cum vonis rite solvendis, tum prodigiis expiandis (procurandis) in provinciam proficisciur Consul.
units.tr: When M. Acilius and P. Cornelius were consuls, the decemvirs, having consulted the Sibylline books by a decree of the Senate on account of the prodigies, reported that a fast had been instituted for Ceres and was to be kept every fifth year. Since it had been reported that it had rained stones at Tarracina and at Amiternum, a novendial sacrifice was to be made, and a day of supplication held; they performed the supplication at the temples. The consul P. Cornelius sacrificed to whatever gods and with whatever victims the decemvirs had prescribed. With the gods appeased, the consul set out for his province, both to pay the vows duly and to expiate (or procure) the prodigies.

units.la: L. Cornelio Scipione, & C. Lelio Coss. creatis, prusquam Coss. in provincias profitisc erentur, prodigia per Pontifices procurari placuit. Ea procurata, Latinis instaurata, quod Laurentibus carnes, quae dari debebat, data non fuerant. Supplicatio quoque earum religionum tauffa fuit, qui bus Dii Decemviri, ex libris, ut fieret, ediderunt, Decem ingenui, decem virgines, paerimi omnes matrimi, ad sacrificium adhibiti, & decem viri nocte laetantibus rem divinam fecerunt. Livius lib. 7. Decad. 4.
units.tr: When L. Cornelius Scipio and C. Laelius were created consuls, before the consuls set out for their provinces, it was decided that the prodigies should be expiated through the pontiffs. They were expiated, and the Latin festival renewed, because the meat that ought to have been given to the people of Lavinium had not been given. A supplication was also held for these rites, which the decemvirs, according to the books, had ordered to be done: ten freeborn boys and ten girls, all with both parents living, were admitted to the sacrifice, and the ten men performed the sacred rite while the people rejoiced. Livy, book 7, Decade 4.

units.la: Q. Martio et Q. Servilio Coff. publicorum prodigiorum causa, libri a Decemviris, aditi, XL. majoribus hostiis, quibus Dii Coff. sacrificarent: & addiderunt, ut supplicatio fieret, eundem ma gistratus circa omnia pulvinaria victimis majoribus sacrificarent, populusq; coronatus essent, om nia, ut Decemviri praeerunt facta. Livius Decade 5. lib. 5.
units.tr: When Q. Martius and Q. Servilius were consuls, on account of public prodigies the books were consulted by the decemvirs, and they ordered forty larger victims to be sacrificed to whichever gods the consuls should choose; and they added that a supplication should be held, and that the same magistrates should sacrifice larger victims at all the cushions of the gods, and the people should be crowned with garlands; all these things were done as the decemvirs directed. Livy, Decade 5, book 5.

units.la: Denig, quanta cura atq; religione Romani prodigia procurarö Deum, suorum iras, quae illis portendi videbantur, placare fluderint, satis patet ex illa Ciceronis oratione de Aruspicum re sponsis, cujus haec sunt verba ultima: Quod eodem fere tempore factus in agro Piceno potentia nunciatur terraemotus horribilis cum quibusdam multis meminerunt, rebus: hac eadem profecto quae futura prospicimus, impendentia pertimescetis, etenim haec deorum immortalium vox, has pone oratio judicanda est, cum ipse mundus, cum agri terraemotu quoda novo contremiscens, & in visitato aliquid sono incredibili, praedicunt, in quo cosistuenda nobis quidem sunt procurationes & obseruatio, quemadmodum monemur: sed facilas sunt preces apud eos, quibus utro nobis viam fa luta huius ostendunt: nostræ nobis fuut inter nos ire, difcordiæq; placeude. Et paullo ante: Exauditus in agro propinquo & suburbano est strepitus quidam reconditus, & horribilis fremitus armorū, quis est ex gigantibus illis, quos poeta ferūt bellū diis immortalibus iuuulisse, cam impius, qui hoc iam novo tautoq; metu nou magnū aliquid deas populo R. prænionstrare, & præcinere fateatur? de ea re scriptum est, postulationes decretas esse Iovi, Saturno, Neptuno, Telluri, diis tale stibus, audio, quibus diis violatū expiatio debeatur.
units.tr: Finally, how great the care and religious devotion with which the Romans set about expiating the prodigies, and appeasing the anger of their gods, which seemed to be foreshadowed to them, is clear enough from that speech of Cicero On the Responses of the Haruspices, whose final words are these: "That an horrible earthquake of great force is reported to have happened in the Picene country at about the same time, many remember; and you will surely fear these things that we foresee as impending, for this voice of the immortal gods, this speech, must be judged, since the world itself, trembling with a new earthquake in the fields, and announcing something with an incredible sound, which indeed we must regard with expiations and observance, as we are warned; but the prayers to those by whom the way is shown are easy, and the gods show us the way to appease them by ourselves: we must go among ourselves and appease discord." And a little before: "A certain hidden noise and a dreadful clamour of arms has been heard in a nearby and suburban field. Who is the impious man, in so new and so great a fear, who would not admit that these things foreshadow something great to the Roman people, and foretell it? About this matter it is written that supplications were decreed to Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune, Earth, and the celestial gods; I hear that expiation is owed to whichever gods have been violated."

units.la: Plura bis similia leguntur apud Livium, ut de aliis scriptoribus taceam, prodigiorū portento rumq; exempla, quib. Dæmones Dei permissu, Romanos ut ecciā alii mortalib. sucū fecerunt, eosq; exēslis fascinatos jam antea & exceatos, terrūq; erroribus imbutos majori indies superstitioni amore atq; studio inflammarunt. Quibus autē ritibus atq; cerimoniis illa, quæ irę Deorū ac proiudę magnarū cladium calamitatumq; illis videbuntur esse præsagia, procurare & expiare fuerunt soliti ex Livio sacis intelligitur. Vtinam vero nos Christiani tanto studio atq; zelo, pdigia, signa, ostenta, monstra illa ferē quotidiana in cælo, in terra, in mari, in suustiš deuiq; creaturis apparētia quibus Deus justissimam nobis suam iram atq; furorem, propter essreuem & indomicam uostram peccandi libidinem, porteudist, significant, monstrat & ostentat assidui, verā seriaq; pœnitentia expiare, & iram illam diuinam placare sludeteimus!
units.tr: Many similar examples are read in Livy, not to mention other writers, of portents and prodigies, by which the demons, with God's permission, made the Romans, as well as other mortals, more superstitious, and inflamed with an ever greater love and zeal for superstition those whom they had already bewitched and deceived by their illusions and steeped in errors. From Livy it is clear with what rites and ceremonies they were accustomed to procure and expiate those things which seemed to them to be omens of the anger and wrath of the gods and of great disasters and calamities. Would that we Christians, with such zeal and eagerness, would constantly expiate by true and earnest repentance those portents, signs, omens, and monsters which appear almost daily in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in all creatures, which show, mark, and display God's most just anger and fury, which he foretells because of our wicked and unbridled lust for sinning, and would strive to appease that divine wrath!

units.la: Atq; hæc quidem de duplici sine priori sacrorum & sacrificiorum.
units.tr: And so much for the first and second ends of their sacred rites and sacrifices.

units.la: NVNC duos reliquos sines, quos Gentiles in sacris illis suis & sacrificiis spestaruut, paucis persequamur.
units.tr: NOW let us briefly pursue the two remaining ends which the Gentiles aimed at in their sacred rites and sacrifices.

units.la: TERTIVS ergo finis fuit ὐχαριστία: unde sacrificia propter illū finem suscepta & factā III. De sine. ὐχαριστία & χαριςεια fuerunt appellata; quæ pro acceptis beneficiis, voti aliusue sui facti compotes, & victoria, aut alijs rebus speratis & optatis potiri Diis, quib. ea accepta ferebāt, gratitudinē suæ erga ipsos testificandæ gratiæ faciebant. Ob hunc finē & victimæ dicte fuerunt χαριςια. Hinc Dionysius Halicarnasseus: Θυσιας, inquit, & ὑπερ suoις χαριςμεις ὅπη ἡ ὠφελις ἡ ὁμοιος slgoλλαγειε, victimas Diis offerre, quib. illis agerentur gratiæ pro recōcliatione plebis. Idē: θυσιας τα χαριςηκοις τοις θεοις υπολυντα, ἡ sκύλον αἰλαθιες τὰς πως, ἡ τας ἁ ροας ςυ-ωσιν, & ὅτας ὁ ἀ ὠναύ sὰ ἐ ὀ ὁ ... ἰορτας ἐ ὑ ρε θεοις, s stpicɔ, pla forad, sua suspensis ornabāt hostiis spoliis, vacauter epulis & hilaritatiḃ. Idē: Romani post ui Horiam de Volscis reportacā τοις θεοις χαριςηε ἱ ἰν ἀ ἀ ... sacrificia decreuerunt. Sic lib.10. ejusdē suum idem meminit: Romani peste liberati Ѳuơιαν χαριςιον τοις θεοις ὑπολλυτο δηπο sia, ad ageudas Diis gratias publicē peractā sacrificia. Idem fatūm post reportacam victoriam. Hinc idem Dionysius: Post trigemiuorum puguam Romani in castrā θυσιαν τα τα θειας τοις θεοις ἐ ἐ ταθειας ἡσαι, mactatis pro victoria, hostiis, genio epulisq; indulgebant. Hæc de sine tertio.
units.tr: The third end, then, was thanksgiving [εὐχαριστία]; for which reason sacrifices undertaken and made for that end were called eucharistic and charistic [εὐχαριστία, χαριστία]. These were made by those who, having received benefits, or having obtained their vow or other wish, and having gained victory or other hoped-for and desired things, bore witness to their gratitude toward the gods to whom they attributed these gifts. For this end the victims too were called charistia. Hence Dionysius of Halicarnassus: "Sacrifices," he says, "were offered to the gods, to whom thanks were given for the reconciliation of the plebs." The same author: "Sacrificing victims to the gods in thanksgiving, they decorated their temples with spoils and hostages, and they celebrated festivals with feasting and cheerfulness." The same: "The Romans, after the victory over the Volsci, decreed sacrifices to the gods in thanksgiving." Thus in book 10 of the same author he recalls the same: "The Romans, freed from plague, offered sacrifices in thanksgiving to the gods, to give thanks publicly." The same author records the same after the victory won. Hence the same Dionysius: "After the battle with the Tricarnians the Romans, in camp, offered sacrifices of thanks to the gods, and, with victims slain for the victory, indulged in feasting and a banquet for the gods." These things concern the third end.

units.la: QVARTVS finis fuit ὠχαριςια, diuinatorius. Etbuici enim ex victimarū rerūq; IV. De sine divinatorio. sacrificatarū, extorum præsertim, variis qualitatib. & circum stanciis Deorum suorū mentem ut voluntatem ac res eventuq̃, suturos sognoscendi occasioné seuabantur. Hucpertinuet tota Haruspicina, quam Cicero Reipub. communiq; religiouis caussa colendam esse eensuit lib..de Nat. Deorum: de qua satis dictum supra.
units.tr: The fourth end was the divinatory one. By means of the various qualities and circumstances of the victims and of the things sacrificed, especially the entrails, people sought to learn the mind and will of their gods and to discover the occasion for knowing future events. To this belongs the whole of haruspicy, which Cicero in his book On the Nature of the Gods thought should be cultivated for the sake of the commonwealth and common religion. Enough has been said of it above.

units.la: Preter quatuor autē illos generales ac prinitipes omniū sacrificiū fines, alii quoq, fuerūs fines particulares, ferē iusuiti ac diuersi, pro Deorū, rerū, lororum, temporū, personarumq; diuersita- te, quos enumerare imēnse effet opere ac laboris. Ac sacerdotum quidē seu sacrificulorū pleriq;, dubiū nou est, quim, id quod ex antiquis bistoriis est manifestū, in illis sacrū ac religionib. suis, sua passissimum privata comoda atq; emolumenta, ut diguitates, honores, opes ac diuitias, delicias & voluptates, pro ambitione, avaritia & libidiue sua, religioues specie atq; simulatioue quesierunt. Fuerunt itaq; hæc illorū sacra atq; sacrificia nihil ferē aliud, quam gratiæ et savoris, gloriæ et diguitatis, pecuniæ atq; diuitiarum denig; delitiarum, voluptatumq; aucupia.
units.tr: Besides these four general and principal ends of all sacrifice, there were also other particular ends, almost infinite and varied according to the diversity of gods, things, places, times and persons. To enumerate them would be an immense labour. Now most priests, or minor sacrificers, there is no doubt (as is clear from ancient histories), in their sacred rites and sacrifices sought their own private advantages and profits: dignities, honours, power and riches, pleasures and delights. They pursued these out of ambition, greed and lust, under the appearance and pretence of religion. So their sacred rites and sacrifices were little else than a hunting after favour and goodwill, glory and dignity, money and riches, and finally delights and pleasures.

units.la: Porro quando sines bolce suos sibi visi fuerunt consecuti, & sacrificia ipsis bene et ex auimi seutentia successerunt, hoc est, Deos placarunt, sibiq; propitios reddiderunt, tunc Latiui Litasse, & Impetri vilse seu Impetrasse: Gratē vero ιαλλαγοναι ditebantur: de quibus verbis & distudi formis operæ pretium fuerit quædam his attingere.
units.tr: When they thought they had attained these ends, and the sacrifices had gone well and according to their wishes, that is, when they had placated the gods and made them favourable, then the Latins said they had litated (sacrificed successfully) and had obtained (impetrasse). Such sacrifices were also called reconciliations [διαλλαγαί]. It will be worth while to touch briefly on these words and their forms.

units.la: Quantum ad prius, Litare nimirum, nihil aliud id olim fuit quàm ritè sacrificio factò Deos placare, votumq; impetrare. Macrobius 3. Saturnal. in illud Virgilii: —animaq; litandum Argolica, &c.
units.tr: As for the first, to litare, nothing else was formerly meant than to placate the gods by a sacrifice rightly performed, and so to obtain one's vow. Macrobius, in Saturnalia book 3, comments on the line of Virgil about the soul that must be propitiated with Argive blood, and so on.

units.la: Litare, inquit, est sacrificio factò placare Numen, legimusq; quòd litare non potest sola oratio, nisi is, qui Deos precatur, etiam aras manibus apprehendat. Suetonius in Galba: Ante paucos quòq; periret mensés, attendit & extispicio, nec unquam litavit, id est, nunquam placata exta, sed dira semper observavit. Plautus in Poenulo: Si, Hercule, isthuc unquàm factum est, tunc me Iuppiter faciat ut semper sacrificem, neq; unquam litem. Sacrificiorum enim finis erat propitiatio seu placatio Numinum, quo qui erant potiti litare dicebantur. Inter litare igitur & sacrificare hoc differimus: Non enim esse significat, quod illud significet veniam petere, hoc verò propitiare, & votum impetrare. Plinius in Trajani Panegyri: Ergo ista quidem aerea, & pauca manent, munebuntq; quaendam templum ipsum. Illae autem (icilicet statuae) aureae & innumerabiles, strage & ruina publico gaudio litaverunt. Ibi interpres, Litaverunt, id est satisfecerunt. Nam non omnis inquit, qui sacrificat, litat: tum sacrificare fit veniam petere: litare verò propitiare & veniam impetrare. Dicimus autem Lito te, & Lito tibi. Lucanus: —Neq; enim tibi summe litavi, Iuppiter, &c.
units.tr: "To litare," he says, "is to placate the divine power by a sacrifice performed. We read too that prayer alone cannot litare, unless the one who prays to the gods also lays hands on the altars." Suetonius in Galba: "A few months before he perished, he attended to the entrails but never litated, that is, the entrails were never favourable, but always showed ill omens." Plautus in the Poenulus: "If, by Hercules, that has ever happened, may Jupiter grant that I always sacrifice and never litate." For the end of sacrifices was the propitiation or placation of the divine powers, and those who obtained it were said to litare. Between litare and sacrificare, then, we make this distinction: the one means to seek pardon, the other to propitiate and obtain one's vow. Pliny in the Panegyric of Trajan: "So those bronze statues, few in number, remain and serve as a kind of memorial of the temple itself. But those others, the golden and innumerable statues, by their destruction and ruin litated to the public joy." There the commentator glosses litaverunt as "satisfied," for, he says, not everyone who sacrifices litates; to sacrifice is to seek pardon, but to litate is to propitiate and obtain pardon. We say "lito te" and "lito tibi." Lucan: "For I have not litated to you, highest Jupiter," and so on.

units.la: Cicero Div. 2. Cùm pluribus Dijs immolatur, qui tandem evenit, ut litetur aliis, alijs non litetur (id est, facta fiat?) Plinius de viris illustribus: Dum Numam Pompilium sacrificijs imitatur, Iovi Elitio litare non potuit. Apuleius lib. 2. Solenni dies a primo cunabulis hujus urbis condite crastinus advenit, quo die folio mortalium sanctissimum Deum Risum hilaro atq; gaudia li-ritu propitiamus. Hunc tua praesentia nobis efficiet graciorem. Atq; utinam aliquid de proprio lepore relatificum honorando Deo commiscere: quo magna plenius, & tanto Deo litemus, id est, Risum Deum propitiemus, placemus. Idem: Tunc illa: Et tu Fortuna, inquit, durior iam satis esse define: fas tibi miserò istis cuitatibus meis litatum est. Sic dicitur Lito Deos extis, sacrificiis, & bostijs: non, lito exta, vel sacrificia, vel bostias. Deos enim placabant Gentiles, non exta: sed extis Dii placabantur, ut Galeotus Martius nota vit. Cicero eodem ills libro: Cùm tristissima exta sine capite fuerint, quibus nihil videtur esse dirius, proximá bostiá litatur saepe pulcherrimè. Suetonius in Caesare: Dein pluribus caesis quàm litare (id est, extis Deos placare) non posset, introiit Curiam. Hit Beroaldus: Mos fuit, inquit, Principibus Senatum ingredientibus ab ingressu fl atim sacrificare: quem morem cùm usurparet Caesar, nec tamen litare posset, ingressus est Senatû, dicitansque illud celebratum: Necesse est, quod necesse est, evenire Caesari. Addit L. Florus quia centurio vitimis perlitare non potuit.
units.tr: Cicero, On Divination book 2: "When sacrifice is made to several gods, how does it come about that one is litated and another is not litated?" (that is, the sacrifice does or does not turn out well). Pliny in On Illustrious Men: "While he imitated Numa Pompilius in his sacrifices, he could not litate to Jupiter Elicius." Apuleius book 2: "The solemn day, the day after the first cradle of this city was founded, has come, on which we propitiate with cheerful rites the most holy god Laughter, and with joy. May your presence make him more gracious to us. And would that you might add something of your own charm to honour the god, so that we might litate more fully and to so great a god, that is, propitiate and placate the god Laughter." The same author: "Then she said: 'And you, Fortune, cease now to be so hard. It was lawful for you to litate to my wretched misfortunes.'" Thus one litates to the gods with entrails, sacrifices and victims; one does not litate the entrails, or the sacrifices, or the victims. For the Gentiles placated the gods, not the entrails, but the gods were placated by means of the entrails, as Galeotus Martius observed. Cicero in the same book: "When the entrails have been most gloomy and without a head, than which nothing seems more ominous, the next victim often litates most beautifully." Suetonius in Caesar: "Then, after more victims had been slain than he could litate with (that is, than he could placate the gods with the entrails), he entered the Senate-house." Beroaldus: "It was the custom," he says, "for princes entering the Senate to sacrifice at once upon entering; and when Caesar kept to this custom and yet could not litate, he entered the Senate and, repeating the saying, declared: 'What must happen, must happen to Caesar.'" L. Florus adds that a centurion could not litate with the last victims.

units.la: Ab hoc Litandi verbo dicimus Litans, Litatum, Litatio, Litatò & Perlito: ut Litans sacrificium apud Suetonium in Augusto: Cirro Perusiano, sacrificio non litante, id est, non placante Numen conflitit inter Arusites, &c. Beroaldus in haec verba: Morus erat, inquit, ut prima bostia non litante alteri, dein tertia plures ve adhiberentur; & ita numerus bostiarum augeretur, donec litatum foret. Hinc legimus P. Aemilium olim sacrificantem nō litasse usq; ad vigesimam bostiam: in vigesima vero prima apparuisse signa, vilioriam promittentia.
units.tr: From this verb litare we say litans, litatum, litatio, litato, and perlito. Thus Suetonius in Augustus: "When the sacrifice at Perusia by Cirrus was not litating, that is, the divine power was not placated, he fought among the Arusites, etc." Beroaldus on these words: "It was the custom," he says, "that if the first victim did not litate, then a second, and a third, or more were brought, and so the number of victims was increased until it litated. Hence we read that P. Aemilius, sacrificing long ago, did not litate until the twentieth victim; but with the twenty-first the signs appeared, promising victory."

units.la: Sit Litatum, teste Festo, vel solutum est, vel dedit um Deo, quasi luitatum: quod tamen alii ex Graeco deducunt a precibus, quas illi Λιτας dicunt: quas quidem maximam arbitrabantur Deos placandi vim habere. Quid si Litatum, ut & ipsum verbum Litare a lite fit dictum, quod sit litem & inimicitiam inter Deos & homines tollere, Deorumq; gratia hominibus conciliare. Virgilius: Tu modo posce Deos veniam sacrisq; litatis, id est, ritè factis, venia per sacrificia impetrata, vel felicem e ventum promitteute victima:
units.tr: Litatum, according to Festus, means either "released" or "given to the god," as if from luitatum (paid off). Others, however, derive it from the Greek, from the prayers which they call litai [λιταί], which they thought had the greatest power to placate the gods. But perhaps litatum, like the verb litare itself, comes from lis (strife), because it removes the strife and enmity between gods and men and wins the favour of the gods for men. Virgil: "Only ask the gods for pardon and for favourable sacrifices," that is, sacrifices rightly performed, with pardon obtained through the sacrifices, or with a happy wind promised by the victim.
"Be indulgent to the hospitality," etc.

units.la: Litatio porrò est votis per casam victimam impetratio, vel victimae, laeta promittentis mactatio. Plautus in Poenulo: Vt bodie ad litationem huic suppetat satias (satiętas) Iovi: Livius lib. 7. de bello Punito: Per dies aliquot hostia sine litatione caesa: diuq; non impetrata pax Deum.
units.tr: Litatio, moreover, is the obtaining, by a fitting victim, of what was vowed, or the slaughter of a victim that promises joy. Plautus in the Poenulus: "So that today there may be enough of satiety for Jupiter for the litatio." Livy book 7 on the Punic war: "For several days a victim was slain without litation, and for a long time the gods' peace was not obtained."

units.la: Ditunt Latini & Litató, id est, additentibus victimis, sicut auspicato, id est, additentibus avibus, bos est, latum rei inflituta exitum promittentib. Livius quinto ab Vrbe: Non Deorum salte m.fi non hominum memores, nec auspicato, nec litato inflruunt aciem didu&am in tortuna.
units.tr: The Latins also say litato, that is, with the victims given, just as auspicato, that is, with the birds given, is said, promising a happy outcome for the thing undertaken. Livy, book 5 from the founding of the city: "Not mindful of the gods, nor of men, neither after taking the auspices nor after litating did they draw up their line in battle, and it turned out to their misfortune."

units.la: Compositum hinc est Perlito, quod est perfecte Lito. Gellius: Si bares divina facta, riteque perlitata essent, auspices dixerunt, omnia ex sententia processura esse.
units.tr: From this is compounded perlito, which means perfectly litated. Gellius: "If the birds had given divine signs and the sacrifices had been rightly perlitated, the augurs said that everything would go according to their wish."

units.la: Impetrire quoque verbum antiquum ex Hetruscorum disciplina, idest, quod Litare, et significat impetrare seu obtinere id, quod petimus. Cicero de Divinatione: Ut nunc extis (quanquam sed ipsum aliquanto minus, quam olim) sic tunc avibus magne res impetrari, id est, impetrari solebant. Idem: Quieveniit, ut is, qui impetri verit, conveniente bostiam rebus suis immolet? Plautus in Amphitr. Impetrium (id est, impetratum, interprete Festo) inauguratio est, quo avis admittunt aves: Unde Admissi aves, teste Festo, ab Auguribus dicta, quae consulentem juvarent, seu juberent.
units.tr: Impetrire is also an old word from Etruscan discipline, which, like litare, means to obtain or secure what we seek. Cicero, On Divination: "As now great matters are obtained by entrails (though to a rather lesser degree than formerly), so then great matters were obtained by birds, that is, they were usually obtained." The same: "How does it come about that he who has obtained something should sacrifice a victim fitting to his affairs?" Plautus in the Amphitryon: "Impetrium (that is, impetratum, as Festus explains) is the inauguration by which birds admit birds. Hence admissi aves, as Festus says, were so called by the augurs, because they would assist or order the one consulting."

units.la: Graeci porro καλλισφέυς idem, quod Latinis Litare, et καλλίερα, sacrificium rite perattum, quod ipsi aliter τα καλά ίερα appellant. Xenophon lib. 6. de Cyri minoris expeditione: Θυομένης ἱ ὑπὸ τῆ ιφόδω, ὅτι ἱ ὑ ἐγίγνετο τα ἱερὰ καλά. Et paulo post: Θυομένων πάλιν εἰς τρόπον τὴ ἐν τῷ. Et lib. 4. rerum Graecarum: ἐν ὁ ἱ τοῦ ἱερά καλά. Et bæc de finis consecutione.
units.tr: The Greeks, moreover, use kallisphageisthai (καλλισφάγειν) for what the Latins call litare, and kallierai (καλλιέρα) for a sacrifice rightly completed, which they otherwise call ta kala hiera (τὰ καλὰ ἱερά, the good sacrifices). Xenophon, book 6 of the Expedition of Cyrus the Younger: "While the sacrifice was being made, because the omens were not good..." and a little later: "When the sacrifices were again made in the manner..." And book 4 of the Greek History: "...in which the sacrifices were good." And these are the points about the attainment of ends.

units.la: Arnobius lib. 7. ad versus Gentes pluribus docens, nullam esse causam aut rationem, cur Diis sint sacrificandum, et fines, quos ipsi praetendebant, in suis sacrificiis refellens, tandemillos per anacephalaeosin uno quasi fasciculo his verbis completitur: Satis igitur, inquit, ut opinor, ostendi mus, frustra Diis immortalibus hostias cum consequentibus admoveri, quod neq; his alantur, aut pascantur, neq; ullam inde percipiant voluptatem (quam eleganter corporis quasi adulationem vocat) neq; ut iras aut animos ponant: neque ut tribuant faustam, neq; ut abigant, a verruncuntq; contraria. Addit hus sextam causam finalem, eamq; similiter nullam esse docet, nempe dum ajunt, se illa bonorum ergo Dius facere, et hoc facto Numinum potentias, ut Arnobius loquitur, auctiorare, sive auctiscare.
units.tr: Arnobius, in book 7 of Against the Gentiles, teaches at length that there is no cause or reason why sacrifices should be offered to the gods, and refutes the ends the pagans themselves put forward for their sacrifices. At last he sums them up, as it were in a single bundle, in these words: "I think I have now shown well enough that victims and their accompaniments are offered to the immortal gods in vain: they are not nourished or fed by them, they take no pleasure from them (which he neatly calls a kind of flattery of the body), they do not lay aside their anger or their moods, they do not grant prosperity, and they do not drive away or avert what is contrary." He adds a sixth final cause and likewise shows that it is nothing: namely, when they say that they make these offerings for the sake of blessings, and by this act they increase the powers of the divinities, as Arnobius puts it, or make them greater.

units.la: Idem ab initio libri 7. Varronis hanc sententiam de sacrificiis proponit: Quid ergo dixerit qui- piam, sacrificia censetis nulla esse omnino facienda? Ut vobis non nostra, sed Varronis vestri sententia respondeamus, nulla. Quid ita? Quia, inquit, Dis veri nec desiderant ea, neq; depositi: ex are autem facti, stella, gypso, vel marmore multo minus bac curant. Carent enim sensu, nque nulla contrabitur, si ea non feceris, culpa: neque ulla, si feceris, gratia: Hac Varro. Addit Arnobius: Sententia reperiri nulla potest integrior, quam quivus possit, quam vis ille fit favos et difficillimus, occupare. Quis enim est pectoris tam obtusi qui aut reb. nullu babentib. sensum bostias cedat et victimas, aut eas existimet dadas, qui sunt ab his lege natura et beatitudine destigati.
units.tr: At the beginning of book 7, Arnobius also sets out Varro's opinion on sacrifices: "What, then, might someone say? Do you think sacrifices should not be offered at all? So that I may answer you not from my own view but from that of your Varro: none. Why so? Because," he says, "the gods neither desire them nor need them, and those made of bronze, wood, plaster or marble care for them even less. For they lack sense, and no blame is incurred if you do not offer them, nor any favour if you do." Thus Varro. Arnobius adds: "No more sound opinion can be found than this, one which anyone, however dull and slow, could grasp. For who is so dull of heart as to offer sacrifices and victims to things devoid of sense, or to think they are owed to those who by their nature and blessedness are removed from such things?"

units.la: Praeter Lucianum autem, qui peculiari libro Gentilium sacrificia irrisit, Porphyrius quoque libro de sacrificiis et aliiinter Ethnicos ea contemperunt: de quibus praeter Arnobium libro citato, vide Eusebium lib. 2. et 4. Praeparat. Evangelica, Augustinus lib. 8. de Civitate Dei cap. 13. et 14. Theodoretum ite ad versus gentes, et Cyrillum, qui ex eo Daemonas colligit impuros esse in festos et crudeles, quod sacrificiis delectentur.
units.tr: Apart from Lucian, who mocked Gentile sacrifices in a special book, Porphyry too, in his book On Sacrifices, and others among the heathen, have criticised them. On these matters, besides Arnobius in the book cited, see Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, books 2 and 4; Augustine, City of God, book 8, chapters 13 and 14; Theodoret, Against the Gentiles; and Cyril, who from this concludes that the demons are impure and cruel, since they delight in sacrifices.

units.la: De superioribus vero istis suibus quatuor, atq; etiam aliis (namunius ejusdem rei plures pofsunt esse fines) Jamblichus in libro de Aegyptiorum religione copiose admodum disserit. Ac fegmento quidem tertio de fine sacrificiorum vaticinatorio; et in genere de divinationibus et rationationibus agit pluribus. Primo segmento, cap. 11. eodem teste, Heraclitus sacrificia medicavsenta vota vit, quae medeantur morbis, quaq; animos reddant immunes. Segmento autem quinto, ubi de reliquis tribus sacrificiorum finibus, et in genere de sacrificiorum Gentilium origine, praeftatia dignitate, vi et efficacia, malo, fine, usu et utilitate multiplici mulga verba, inter alia sacrificii perfectionem docet in eo consistere, ut omnibus Numinibus litetur, omnes, Diipropitii reddantur, et cap. 23. docet sacra unire et ligare: et cap. 24. sacrificia facta lustrare, purgare, defacare, perficere, ponere in ordine, sol vere vincula. Cap. 25. docet, grata cuiq; Deorum munera, opera atq; sacra secundum locorum praefecturas et distributionem esse tribuenda. Et cap. 26. sacra docet non esse hominum commenta, sed habere auctores, duces, spectatores Deos, Angelos, Genios. Quamobrem in sacris admodum esse dendum, summamq; adhibendam cautionem, ne quid superis indignum, ne quid minus proprium minusq; gratum litetur. Capite ultimo de precum et supplicationum vi, virtute atq; energia disputat.
units.tr: As for the four ends mentioned above, and others too (for one and the same thing can have several ends), Iamblichus discusses them at considerable length in his book on the religion of the Egyptians. In the third section he treats of the prophetic end of sacrifices, and more generally of divinations and oracles. In the first section, chapter 11, by the same witness, Heraclitus called sacrifices remedies and vows that heal diseases and make the soul free from its passions. In the fifth section, where he deals with the remaining three ends of sacrifices and, more generally, with the origin, dignity, power and efficacy, value, purpose, use and manifold usefulness of Gentile sacrifices, he says many things. Among them he teaches that the perfection of a sacrifice consists in this: that offerings are made to all the divinities, so that all of them are rendered favourable. In chapter 23 he teaches that sacred rites unite and bind; in chapter 24, that the sacrifices offered purify, cleanse, perfect, put in order and loose bonds. In chapter 25 he teaches that the gifts, works and rites pleasing to each god should be assigned according to the regions and districts of the gods. In chapter 26 he teaches that sacred rites are not human inventions but have authors, leaders and overseers: gods, angels, and genii. For this reason great care and caution must be taken in sacred rites, lest anything unworthy of the superior beings, anything less proper or less pleasing, be offered. In the final chapter he discusses the power, virtue and energy of prayers and supplications.

units.la: Ibidem disserit, cur sacra & sacrificia fuerint instituta, eorum causam esse occultam, sacra autem eanorum esse imaginec, in sacramentis formas visibiles significare occultas. Nec si suffitus, & alia res ad, cerimonia corporea in sacrificiis adhibeantur, idcirco flatuendum Genios & alios Deos esse patibiles, & capi atq; affici rebus istis corporeis. Segmenco 1.cap.12.contra Porphyrium disputat Genioc atq; Deos non tangi affectibus humanis, eo quod in vocationibus atq; preculis moveantur & flectantur. Et segmento 1.cap.12.docet, qua ratione nobis supplicantibus de omni immortali lum irascundia, ipsis tamen immotis placentur. De expiationibus & lustrationib.ibidē. Ec ca.25. Sacrorum lex, inquit, jubet sacra faciētes liberos esse ab affectibus et quicquid in sacrificiis pre se fert, aut sapit sensum, aut corpus, symbolu esse significanc aliquid occultum, divinū & intellectuale. Que sint dona, qui ve fructus ornatur ex Numinis apparitionibus docet segmento 2.cap.6. ut toto tertio segmento de vaticiniis eorum, generibus; & quarto, de precibus ac Deorum invocationibus, cur & quomodo in vocantium precec exaudiant. Quinto segmenco,cap.6.quas ob causas divinae res & sacrificia offerantur, opinionem eorum recensentur, qui affirmant sacrificari bonorum, gratiarum habendarum & primitiarum gratia. Ide per facta affirmat noceripi a cladibus & malis, ut fame, peste, inopia, vinculis, ea conferre ad lustrationem animorū, ad perfectionem & liberationem. Horum sacrificiorum altiorem & praestantiorem rationē sumptam ajt ab harmonia & conspiratione magni animalis, scilicet Mundi, eodem segmēto 5.cap.8. Et cap 10.ac 11. Sacrificiorum usum & fructum dicit esse bonimum cum Dijs conjunctionē: sacrificia esse vinicula amicitiæ & societatis conjunctionis, hominū cum Dijs. Et cap.13. Sacrorum opus esse purificare, mollire, attollere, illustrare, ad divinum ignem traducere: cumq; ni Numinū & igne consumatur sacrificiorum materia, quomodo Genii inde pascantur, docet cap.12. Idem ca.15. duo genera Divum flatuit, materiales alios, alioc immateriales. Cultum itaq; materialibus materialem, immaterialibus immaterialem adhibendum censet. Idē cap 16. cum duplex sit animi statu, divinus & corporatus inde duplicem colligit cultum, & duplex sacrificium: materiale unum, alterum immateriale. Idem cap.19. secundum tria vitæ & hominum genera, ut sunt naturales, divini, medii, tria statuit sacrorum genera. Idem cap.20, trec facit essentias divinas, ut quaedam sint animales, quaedam abstractae, alias medias: unde colligit triplicem cultum suum cuiq; tribuendum, nempe naturalibus naturalē, secretis arcanum, medijs medii. Hæc Iamblichus: quæ quia cēm in speciē fines sacrificiorum, tum generatim totam eorum doctrinam illustrant, ideo prioribus addere juvabat.
