units.tr: In the same work he discusses why sacred rites and sacrifices were instituted: their cause is hidden, but the sacred rites are images of it, and in the sacraments visible forms signify hidden things. Nor, if incense and other bodily ceremonies are used in sacrifices, should one therefore conclude that the genii and other gods are subject to passions and are moved and affected by such bodily things. In section 1, chapter 12, arguing against Porphyry, he maintains that the genii and gods are not touched by human emotions, although they are moved and turned by invocations and prayers. In the same section and chapter he teaches by what reasoning the gods, though they remain unmoved, are placated when we supplicate them, and expiations and lustrations are treated there too. In chapter 25 he says: "The law of sacred rites orders those who perform them to be free from passions; and whatever in sacrifices has the appearance of sense or body is a symbol signifying something hidden, divine and intellectual." What gifts and fruits come from the manifestations of the gods he teaches in section 2, chapter 6; the whole third section treats of the kinds of their prophecies, and the fourth of prayers and invocations of the gods, why and how they hear those who call upon them. In the fifth section, chapter 6, he enumerates the reasons why divine things and sacrifices are offered, recounting the opinion of those who affirm that they are offered for the sake of blessings, to give thanks, and as firstfruits. He also affirms that by these rites calamities and evils such as famine, plague, poverty and imprisonment are averted, and that they contribute to the purification, perfection and liberation of souls. He says that a higher and more excellent reason for these sacrifices is drawn from the harmony and concord of the great living being, namely the World (same section, chapter 8). In chapters 10 and 11 he says that the use and fruit of sacrifices is the good of union with the gods: sacrifices are bonds of friendship and fellowship between men and gods. In chapter 13 he says that the work of sacred rites is to purify, soften, lift up, illuminate and lead up to the divine fire; and since the matter of sacrifices is consumed by the divine fire, he teaches in chapter 12 how the genii are fed by it. In chapter 15 he posits two kinds of gods, some material and others immaterial, and therefore thinks that material worship should be given to material gods and immaterial worship to immaterial ones. In chapter 16, since the soul has a twofold state, divine and embodied, he infers a twofold worship and a twofold sacrifice: one material, the other immaterial. In chapter 19, according to the three kinds of life and of men, natural, divine and intermediate, he establishes three kinds of sacred rites. In chapter 20 he makes divine essences threefold: some are animate, some abstract, and others intermediate; whence he concludes that each should be given its own threefold worship: natural worship to natural beings, hidden worship to hidden ones, and intermediate worship to intermediate ones. Thus Iamblichus. Since these passages illustrate both the particular ends of sacrifices and their whole doctrine in general, it was helpful to add them to the previous ones.

units.la: Verum quicquid Ethnici de Deorum suorum cultu atq; religione, ritibus, sacris, sacrificiis, eo rumq; finibus garrierint atq; nugati sint: tamen qui inter eos fuerunc sapientiores & cordatiores. Numen divinum vel ipsa natura duce & magistra, non tam rebus, ritibus, ac gestibus excernit & corporeis, quam animo, mente & affectu bono, casto & sincero, precibus, virtutumq; quarum vis fludio colendum atq; placandum esse duxerunt. De hoc multa exinde in ipsorum scriptis extant sententiae, quae sunt quasi scintillulae quaedam luminis naturae, quarum nonnullas hic citabo. Persius Sat.2. O cur va in terris anima & cælestium inanæ c Quid juvat hoc, templis nostroc immittere mores Et bona Dijs ex hac scelerata ducere pulpa?
units.tr: But whatever the Gentiles chattered and babbled about the worship and religion of their gods, their rites, sacred things, sacrifices and their ends, those among them who were wiser and more discerning have judged that the divine power, with nature herself as guide and teacher, is moved and propitiated not so much by things, rites and bodily gestures as by the mind, the soul and a good, chaste and sincere disposition, by prayers, and by the strength of virtues, which should be cultivated with zeal. Many such opinions survive in their writings, and they are like little sparks of the light of nature. I will cite some of them here. Persius, Satire 2: "O wretched souls on earth, empty of heavenly things! What good is it to bring these customs into our temples, and to offer the gods good things from this wicked flesh?"

units.la: Item: At hoc Pontificec in templis quid facit aurum, Nempe hoc, quod Veneri donate a virgine puppe? Quin damus id superis, de magna quod dare lance Non possit magni Messalae lippa propago Compositum jus, fasq; animi sanctosq; recessus Mentis & incoltum generoso pectus honesto. Hæc cedo ut admoveam templis, & farre litabo.
units.tr: Likewise: "But what does gold do in the temples of the pontiffs? Namely this, which a maiden gives to Venus as a doll? Rather let us give the gods what the bleary-eyed offspring of great Messalla could not give on a great dish: a mind's right and law, composed, the holy recesses of the mind, and a breast uncultivated by noble honour. Shall I bring these to the temples, and sacrifice with spelt?"

units.la: Sic ille apud Plautum: Atq; hoc scelesti in animum inducunt suum, Iovem se placare posse omnibus hostiis, Ecoperam & sumptum perdunc: ideo Fit, quia nihil ei acceptum est a perjurio Supplici facilius, si qui pius est a Diis supplicans, Quim Quàm qui scelestus est, in veniet veniam sibi.
units.tr: Thus that character in Plautus: "And these wicked men put it into their heads that they can appease Jove with all kinds of victims; they waste their expense and effort. That happens because nothing is more readily accepted by the gods from a perjurer than from a pious suppliant; he who is wicked will not find pardon for himself."

units.la: Idcirco moneo vos ego hæc: quiestis boni,
units.tr: "So I warn you: you who are good,"

units.la: Quique ætatem agitis cum pietate & cum fide
units.tr: "and who spend your lives with piety and with faith,"
"keep to it. Afterwards, when fate has come, rejoice."

units.la: Parva petunt Manes: pietas pro diuite grata est
units.tr: "The spirits of the dead ask for little; piety is pleasing in place of a rich"

units.la: Munere: non auidos Styx habet ima Deos.
units.tr: "gift. Styx does not hold the gods below as greedy."
"The heavenly powers do not delight in the slaughter of an ox,"

units.la: Sed quæ præstanda est, vel sine teste, fide.
units.tr: "but in the faith that must be rendered, even without a witness."

units.la: Sed tamen ut fuso taurorum sanguine centum,
units.tr: "But just as a hundred bulls with poured-out blood"
"do not win a god so much as a little incense does with its small honour."
"Set aside the gods, and the sacred things that you profane by touching them;"
"a hand that is not clean does not worship the heavenly gods well."
"Impious incense is offered on altars that are unwilling."
"—It is no concern of yours"
"to try many things, as you slaughter ..."
"crowning the little gods"
"with nizarine dew, with a fragile myrtle."
"If a hand that is not clean has touched the altar,"
"no victim, however costly and more inviting,"
"will soften the Penates who turn away,"
"though it be with pious spelt and crackling salt."

units.la: Si Deus est animus, nobis ut carmina dicunt,
units.tr: "If God is a mind, as the poets say,"

units.la: Hic tibi præcipuè sit pura mente colendus.
units.tr: "then he must be worshipped by you above all with a pure mind."

units.la: Cùm sis ipse noceris moritur cur victima pro te?
units.tr: "Since you yourself are guilty, why does a victim die for you?"
"It is folly to hope for salvation by the death of another."

units.la: His consentaneè Cicero ait libro 2. de Nat. Deorum, Cultum Deorum esse optimum, sundemq; castissimum, ut eos semper purè, integrè, incorruptè & mente & voce veneremur. Et Seneca: Optimus animus pulcherrimus Dei cultus est. Sic Eubulus ille apud Clementem Alexandrinum irridet superstitiosos homines, sacrificiis illis externis numium addiftos & deditos: interim negligentes virtutem. Ait enim, Θυμιατα ἀλλα καὶ κὺπτικὰ κὰρδια, μηδὲ ζῶπολαιον, id est, sacrificant sanguinem & vesticam: cordis autem ne supersiciem quidem. Plinius item scribit libro 18. cap.6. ad vbertatem frugum plurimùm innocentium agricolarum valere. Honestis, inquit, Mabibus omnia lætiùs pro veniunt. Idem docet Plato in Alcibiade, Deos integritate animorum ac precibus placari, nec precibus rerum ipsis oblatarum, sed purâ offerentis manu capi.
units.tr: To the same effect Cicero says in the second book of On the Nature of the Gods that the best and purest worship of the gods is that we always venerate them purely, wholly, and uncorrupted, in both mind and voice. And Seneca: "The best mind is the most beautiful worship of God." So that Eubulus in Clement of Alexandria mocks superstitious men, who are given over and devoted to external sacrifices, while meanwhile they neglect virtue. For he says: "They burn incense and sacrifice ... and hearts [θυμιάματα ἄλλα καὶ κρύπτικα καρδία]", that is, they sacrifice blood and entrails, but not even the surface of the heart. Pliny likewise writes in the eighteenth book, chapter 6, that the fertility of crops depends very much on the innocence of farmers: "Everything turns out more happily," he says, "for honest hands." Plato teaches the same in the Alcibiades, that the gods are placated by the integrity of souls and by prayers, and are won not by prayers or by the things offered, but by the pure hand of the one offering.
And these things concerning the purposes of sacrifices.

units.la: NVNC POSTREMO, ut huic meæ lucubratiunculæ finem tandem aliquando imponam, su-
units.tr: Now at last, so that I may finally bring this little work of mine to an end, I

units.la: perioribus lubet colophonis quasi loco, Gentilismi, siue, ut alium vocant, Ethnicismi, vel Paganismi & Christianismi drn siu quandam, hoc est, oppositionem subjicere, quæ merito nos Christianismi. Christianos incitare atq; impellere debet ad gratias Deo immortali & agendas & habendas animis nostris immortales & perpetuas, quid pro infinita sua gratia atq; misericordia Filii sui unigeniti unicè, adamari ad ventu in carnem atq; morte, Evangelii prædicatione Catholica & Apostolica, Sanctis fui spiritus virtute & efficacia, ex tetris fumestiq; illis errorum superstitionum, tenebris in admirandam hanc, serenam & salutarè Christiane religionis lucem nos traduxit. Eris simul hæc ἀἡ εὐρονο quasi ἀπαιτιάλλον, hoc est, summaria & compendiosa omnium penè eorum, quæ supra copiosius fuerunt explicata, repetitio quædam & complexio, quam pio candidoq; Lectori spero non ingratam futuram & injucundam.
units.tr: Now at last, to bring this little work of mine to an end at some point, I would like to add, as it were by way of a conclusion, a contrast between Gentilism, or as others call it Ethnicism, or Paganism, and Christianity—that is, a juxtaposition, which ought rightly to incite and drive us Christians to give thanks to the immortal God, and to have immortal and perpetual gratitude in our hearts, because by his infinite grace and mercy, through the coming of his only-begotten Son into the flesh and his death, through the Catholic and Apostolic preaching of the Gospel, and through the power and efficacy of his Holy Spirit, he has brought us out of those foul and smoky darknesses of errors and superstitions into this wonderful, serene and saving light of the Christian religion. At the same time this will be a kind of summary and compendious recapitulation of nearly all those things that have been explained more fully above, which I hope will be neither unwelcome nor disagreeable to the pious and candid reader.

units.la: PRIMVM igitur Gentiles pro cæco mentis suæ errore Deos siue Diuos coluerunt numero in-numerabiles, visibiles et invisibiles, rationales & irrationales, animatos & inanimatos, bonos et malos, nominibus, sexu, ætate, tempore, ordine, dignitate, locis, muneribus, officiis, aliisq; rebus di-spares atque diuersos, quos enumerare omnes tam difficile fuerit, quam numerare vel cœli stellas, vel arenas maris, vel pulvérem terræ. Quot enim in hac uni versitate rerumq; natura res sunt, tot illos fuere Dii atq; Numina; atq; adeo multa, quæ nunquam in rerum natura fuerant, tanquam mem cerebri sui figmenta, pro Diis habuerunt, ac divinis affecerunt honoribus. Pro Diis ergo atq; Numinibus istis Gentilium (quae nomina veriùs, nulla subjecta re, vel vanissima dixerint) alieni, sitiis, commentitiis, adulteriis, prodigiosis, ridiculis, absurdis (quos Daemonas, atq; Daemonia, saepe sacra scriptura appellat) nobis Christiani Deus, què colimus & veneramur, est unus, unus hoc, trinus Τριασθενσον, Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus, caeli, terrae, maris, omniumq; rerum visibilium & invisibilium Conservator, Rector, atq; Moderator, aeternus, immortalis, omnipraesens, omniscius, omnipotens, clementissimus & justissimus.
units.tr: Now in this crowd, or as it were jumble, of gods, the Gentiles also imagined a certain chief son, or supreme God, whom they called the father of gods and men. The Greeks called him Zeus and Zan, the Latins Jovis and Jupiter, as if you were to say "Jovis pater," or "helping father." The Assyrians, Chaldeans and others called him Baal, that is, Lord. To him they also attached a certain Juno as his sister, wife and the queen of heaven, of gods and goddesses. Yet, as Augustine proves from the testimony of Varro, they worshipped about three hundred Jupiters, or Jupiteres (as Tertullian calls them). For us Christians, however, there is one true Jehovah (from whom the Gentiles seem to have borrowed the name of that fictitious Jove). Since he has been from eternity, is, and will be forever, he has his being from himself, and he gives being to all things. Rightly, then, he is called Jehovah, that is, being, essence, or the one who gives essence. It seems that the name "Ei," which was inscribed on the doors of the Delphic temple, alludes to this, and Plutarch wrote a special book about it.

units.la: In hac autem Deorum turba & quasi colluvie, Ethnici etiam finxerunt quendam summum filium, ve supremum Deum, quem Deum hominumq; patrem appellarunt, qua a Graecis Zeus & Zan a Latinis Jovis & Jupiter, quasi dicas, Jovis pater, sive juvans pater, ab Assyrijs, Chaldaeis & aliis Baal, id est, Dominus fuit appellatus (cui etiam lunonem quandam ceu sororem, conjugem & Coeli, Deorum Dearumq; reginam affinxerunt) tamen iidem, ut Parronis testimonio S. Augustinus probat, circiter trecentos Jovis, sive Jupiteres (ut eos Tertullianus vocat) colucrunt. Nobis vero Christianis unus est & verus Jehova: (unde Gentiles Jovis illius fuicomnientitii nomen videntur mutuati) qui quoniam fuit ab aeterno, est & erit in aeternum, esse suum habet a seipso, esse denique dat rebus omnibus rectè Jehova, id est, ens, essentia, sive essentiator appellatur. Huc videntur allusisse nomine illo Ei, quod templi Delphici foribus fuit inscriptum, de quo Plutarchus peculiarem librum scripsit.
units.tr: Besides, they called these gods of theirs, along with very many other august and magnificent titles and names (though some of these became ridiculous through their deeds), by names that were nearly common to all: their fathers, patrons, lords, guardians, presidents, helpers, or helpers and saviours. But we Christians acknowledge only the one supreme God as our truest Father, Patron, Lord, Guardian, Helper and Saviour, the author and fountain of all salvation, both temporal and eternal. Likewise we acknowledge and believe that Christ, the natural and proper Son of God, is the only Saviour of us, who is true God and man, and that he is the Saviour, the leader and author of salvation, the guide and author of our salvation. Hence also he was called by the Hebrew name Yeshua, that is, Jesus, or the Lord who is Saviour, because, as we read in 1 John 4, "God sent his Son as the Saviour of the world."

units.la: Hos praeterea suos Deos cum plurimis alijs augustis & magnificis titulis atq; nominibus (quo rumtamen nonnulla factis fuerunt ridicula) tum, quae communia fere fuerunt, suos patres, patronos, dominos, tutores, praesides, opitulos, seu opitulatores & servatores appellarunt. At nos Christiani Deum solum agnoscimus summum, verissimoq; nostrum patrem, patronum, dominum, tutorem, opitulatorem, servatorem, omnis & temporalis & aeternae salutis auctorem atq; fontem. Christum item, Dei filium naturalem & proprium Σωτῆρα, id est, verum Deum & Hominem agnoscimus atq; credimus solum & unicum uostrum σωτῆρα, σωτῆρα, σωτῆρα, ἀρχηγὸν καὶ αἴτιον σωτηρίας, servatorem seu salvatorem, salutem ipsam, salutis nostrae ducem & auctorem. Hinc etiam ΥΝΨ Ιεʃchuah, id est, Iesus, seu servator dominus mittus fuit appellatus, quoniam, ut habetur 1. Joh. 4. σωτήρ Deus misit filium suum σωτῆρα τοῦ κόσμου.
units.tr: Moreover, the Gentiles invented and worshipped countless middle gods, or middlemost gods, as they call them, mediators, go-betweens, interpreters, intercessors and agents between gods and men, such as Mercury, and those whom the Greeks called Diamesoi (from being in the middle) and the Latins called Genii. But for us Christians there is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who, as Paul says, "gave himself a ransom [ἀντίλυτρον], that is, a price of redemption, for all" (1 Tim. 2). This same Jesus Christ is our Advocate and Patron before the Father [παράκλητος], and the propitiation [ἱλασμός] for our sins, as John says in his first epistle, chapter 2. He is so not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world.

units.la: Finxerunt praeterea atque coluerunt Gentiles innumeros Deos medios, seu medioxumos, ut eos appellant, Deorum hominumq; mediatores, internuncios, interpretes, intercessores, sequestros, ut Mercurii et eos, quos Graeci Διάμεσος ut a scientia, Latini Genios appellarunt. At nobis Christianos unus ut est Deus, sta unus est Dei hominumq; μεσίτης, id est, Mediator, homo Christus Iesus, qui dedit semetipsum αντίλυτρον, id est, redemptionis pretium pro omnibus, ut Paulus locutur. 1. Tim. 2. Idem etiam Iesus Christus justus noster est μεγαλωτορ, id est, advocatus et patronus apud Patrem, & Ιλαστὴς, id est, propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, ut inquit Iohannes priore epistola, cap. 2., nec pro nostris tantum, sed etiam totius Mundi.
units.tr: Likewise, in place of those Genii of the Gentiles, we have the angels, those spirits described by Paul in Hebrews 1 as ministering spirits, sent out to serve (namely by God) for the sake of those who are to inherit eternal salvation. We do not worship and adore these as gods, in the manner and ritual of the Gentiles. Rather, as servants of God, his attendants, guards, messengers, envoys and faithful guardians who love our salvation and were assigned to us by divine decree, we revere, look up to, admire and imitate them. As for that Angel of great counsel, that is, Christ, to whom all the angels bow in service, we adore him alone, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and call upon him alone.

units.la: Pro Genijs item illis Gentilium nos habemus Angelos, Spiritus illos, ut a Paulo describuntur Hebr. 1. ministratorios, qui ad ministerium mittuntur (scilicet a Deo) propter eos, qui salutis suae aeternae haereditatem adiuunt atque cernent. Hos nos non Gentilium more ritu, tanquam Deos veneramur, & adoramus, sed tanquam Dei ministros, famulos, satellites, apparitores, legatos, nuncios, noftrę salutis amantes & custodes fidelissimos, divinitus nobis assignatos ꝑmus, suspicimus, admiramur, imitamur, Angelum illum magni consilii, id est, Christum, eius Angelo omnes inservuntur, quem adorant, solum adorantes ac invocantes cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto.
units.tr: Therefore, in place of those countless gods of the Gentiles, we Christians (to conclude this point with the splendid words of Arnobius from the third book Against the Gentiles) in performing the worship of divinity, hold to God first, who is the first God, the father and lord of things and the ruler of all these things. Whatever is to be worshipped, we worship in him. Whatever is to be adored, we adore. Whatever demands the homage of reverence, we honour with reverence. For since we hold to the head of divinity itself, from whom all divinity and all the divine beings that exist are derived, we think it unnecessary to go through the individual persons, since we do not know who they are, what names they have, or how many they are, and we cannot have any clear, comprehended or certain knowledge of them. Just as in earthly kingdoms, no necessity compels people to worship the princes of the royal households by name along with the king, but in worshipping the king, whatever is attached to him is honoured by a tacit sense of respect and included in it, so, whatever these gods are that you say we should have, if they are a royal and principal offspring sprung from the head, then even though they receive no separate worship from us, they understand that they are honoured together with their king and are contained in his veneration. And this indeed we have set forth in such a way, provided it is clear and certain that the king and the princes are the other heads, which, being arranged and separated by number, make up a kind of people, as it were a multitude of common folk.

units.la: Pro Diis igitur illis innumeris Gentilium nos Christiani (ut hunc locum primùm illis pul-cher rimis Arnobii verbis ex libro 3. ad versus Gentiles concludam) ad cultum divinitatis obeundum: Deum primum, qui Deus primus est, pater rerum ac dominus, consistuntur moderatorq; cum storum in hoc omne, quod colendum est, colimus: quod adorari eon venit, adoramus: quod obsequiij veneraționis exposcit, veneracionibus prorumeramur. Cum enim divinitatis ipsius teneamur caput, a quo ipsa divinitas di vinorum omnium, quaecunq; sunt ducitur: super sacuum putamus personas ire per singula: cum & ipsi, qui sint, & quae habeant nomina, nescsamus: & cujus sunt praeterea numeri, neq; liquidum, neq; comprehensum, nec exploratu habere possimus. Atq; ut sic terrestribus regnis necessitate nulla compelliuntur, regalibus in familiis constituor nominatim cum principi-bus adorare, sed in regnũ ipsorũ cultu, quicquid illis annexũ esset, tacita ui se sentir honorificentia: comprehendi. non alia ratione (quicunque hi dii sint) quos esse nobis proponitis: si funcprogenies regia, et principalis oriuntur e capice, etiamsi nullos accipiant nominarum a nobis cultus intelligunt: se tamen honorari communiter cum suo rege, atq; in illis veneratione contineri. Et hoc quidem a nobis ita fuerit prolacum, si modo liquet et constat praeceptum ipsum regem et principes esse non alia capita, quae digesta et separata per numerum, veluti quendam populum plebeiae multitudinis faciant.
units.tr: Instead of those countless gods of the Gentiles, we Christians (to begin this point with the fine words of Arnobius from book 3 against the Gentiles) worship the divinity: first God, who is the first Father and Lord of things, and the ruler of all these, we honour in everything that is to be honoured; what is due to adoration we adore, and what the duty of reverence demands we pay in acts of reverence. For since we hold to the head of divinity itself, from whom divinity and all divine beings that exist are derived, we do not think it necessary to go through the gods one by one, since we do not know who they are, what names they bear, or how many they are, and cannot have any clear, comprehended or certain knowledge of them. And just as in earthly kingdoms people are not compelled of necessity to name each prince when they pay homage in a royal household, but whatever is given to the king's own person includes, by a tacit kind of honour, whatever belongs to him: so, whoever these gods are that you set before us as ours, they are not honoured by any separate worship of ours, yet if they are of royal lineage and spring from the chief, they understand that even though they receive no separate cult from us, they are nonetheless honoured together with their king and included in his reverence. And this indeed we have said, provided it is clear and certain that the king and the princes themselves are not other heads, which, arranged and separated by number, would make up a sort of people of common multitude.

units.la: Porro Deorum illorum innumerabilium innumera Gentiles habuerunt idola, simulacra, animo gines, effigies atq; statuas; eaq; multiplicis et materiae et formae, quas nunc secus ipsi atq; Deos ipsos di vinis colurunt honoribus. Et fuerunt hac idola illis, tanquam Dii quidam ἐπιφανεῖς, ἀρτιφιλοσ, hominum nimirum artificio, ope atq; manu elaborati, unde Opera manuum sapientissime in sacris litteris appellancur. Pro his nos Christiani vivas habemus veracis, Dei imagines. Prima quidem et principalis Dei imago est, Christus, Dei filius unigena, qui, ut Paulus Christianorum loquitur ad Colossenses, εἰκὼν θεοῦ ἀοράτου, id est, imago Dei invisibilis, ut idem Apostolus imagines. ait ad Hebr. 1. ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ, id est, splendor gloriae et character, id est, expressa effigies et imago substantiae ipsius. Sic ad Philip. 2. dicit Christum, cum esset in μορφῇ θεοῦ, in forma Dei, non rapina duxisse esse similem Deo, sed formam servi sumpsisse, ἐν ὁμοιώματι, id est, in similitudine factum hominis, et σχήματι, id est, figura, in venium, tanquam hominis. Hanc imaginem abiit ut incuri, nobis ance meritis nostrae oculos proponere, colere deni, atq; venerari debemus. Deinde meminisse nos abiit ut recordari decet, primos nostros parentes fictos a Deo atq, formacos fuisse ad Dei imaginem atq, similicudinem, quam quidem, sua culpa, sua perfidia et apostasia amissa, et ipsi et nos eorum posteri, falsi sumus Diaboli imago. Ac Deus nos pro infinita sua misericordia praedestinavit συμμόρφους τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ, ut Paulus testatur ad Rom. 8. id est, conformes fieri imagini sui filii, ut ipse sit primogenitus, id est, primus, seu principatum censet, incer multos fratres. Quamobrem, ut idem Paulus nos fidelissime monet et confulacur 1. Cor. 15. Quemadmodum porca vinus imaginem terreni hominis, sic porcabimus imaginem coelestis, id est, Christi, et ut idem inquit 2. Cor. 3, nos omnes facie aperta Domini gloriam, tanquam in speculo intuentes, τὴν αὐτὴν εἰκόνα μεταμορφούμεθα, eandem imaginem, Christi scilicet, ἀπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν, transformamur a gloria in gloriam, tanquam a Domini spiritu. Praeterea uni 3. Universus versus hic Mundus atq; Nacura, et singula creatura, maxima, media, minima clarissima sunt Mantua. Dei in visibilis imagines. Denique, splendidissimum et illud Trinitatis Dei simulacrum sunt sacra 4. Sacra litteratura et sacramenta; in quibus Deus, et Christus, verus Deus atq; homo ad verum exprimitur viraq; coloribus depingitur, secundum illa Pauli ad Gal c. 3. ἐν ὑμῖν προεγράφη Ἰησοῦς Χριστός, id est, quibus Christus Iesus proscriptus est, ante oculos oft descriptus atq; depictus. Haec sunt vera, viva, solidae, ut vitae majestatis voluntatisq; imagines: quibus adde illa Arnobii lib. 3. adversus Gentes: Neque e sol in aedibus sacra effigies pro diis, et illa simulacra Veluti ostendere: quae intelligicus vos quoq;, et rerum conciteri, vilissimi esse formas luti, et fabrorum figmenta puerilia, et cum de re loquimur vobis cum divina, hoc ut ostendatis expositum esse deos alios natura, vi, nomine, non in simulacris propositos, quos videmus, sed in ea subsistentia, in qua conveniat aestimari tanci esse nominis oporcere vircutem.
units.tr: Moreover, the Gentiles had countless idols, images, likenesses, effigies and statues of those countless gods, made of many kinds of material and in many forms, which they now worship with divine honours, no differently from the gods themselves. And these idols were for them as if they were certain illustrious gods, lovers of man, worked out by human craft, labour and hand; hence in Holy Scripture they are most wisely called the works of men's hands. In place of these we Christians have the living images of the true God. The first and principal image of God is Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who, as Paul speaks to the Colossians, is [εἰκὼν θεοῦ ἀοράτου] the image of the invisible God; and as the same Apostle says in Hebrews 1, he is [ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ] the brightness of glory and the express image of his substance, that is, the splendour of glory and the character, that is, the expressed figure and image of his substance. So in Philippians 2 he says that Christ, though he was in [μορφῇ θεοῦ] the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but took upon himself the form of a servant, [ἐν ὁμοιώματι] being made in the likeness of men, and [σχήματι] found in fashion as a man. This image we ought to set before our eyes, to cherish, honour and reverence, not as a thing to be neglected. Next, we ought to remember, as is fitting, that our first parents were created and formed by God in the image and likeness of God; which image, lost through their own fault, their own faithlessness and apostasy, both they and we, their posterity, have become an image of the devil. Yet God, in his infinite mercy, has predestined us [συμμόρφους τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ], to be conformed to the image of his Son, as Paul testifies in Romans 8, that he might be the firstborn, that is, the first, or chief, among many brethren. Therefore, as the same Paul most faithfully warns and exhorts us in 1 Corinthians 15, as we have borne the image of the earthly man, so shall we bear the image of the heavenly, that is, of Christ. And, as the same writer says in 2 Corinthians 3, we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, [τὴν αὐτὴν εἰκόνα μεταμορφούμεθα] are changed into the same image, namely that of Christ, [ἀπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν] from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord. Furthermore, this whole world and nature, and every single creature, greatest, middling and least, are most clear images of the invisible God. Finally, the most splendid likeness of the Trinity of God is the sacred Scripture and the sacraments, in which God and Christ, the true God and man, are expressed and painted in their true colours, according to Paul's words in Galatians 3: [ἐν ὑμῖν προεγράφη Ἰησοῦς Χριστός] Jesus Christ was openly set forth among you, that is, Jesus Christ was set forth before your eyes, described and depicted. These are true, living and solid images of his majesty and will. To these add the words of Arnobius in book 3 against the Gentiles: "Nor do you show, in your temples, sacred effigies as gods, and those statues as if to display them; which, as you yourselves understand and confess, are the basest forms of clay and childish figments of craftsmen; and when we speak with you of divine matters, you do this to show that other gods have been set forth by nature, power and name, not in the images we see, but in that substance in which it is fitting to judge that virtue of the name ought to be present."

units.la: Nec vero Ethnici concenti patrii et praesentibus suis Dius atq; idolis, peregrinationes praeceptores arduas, difficiles et periculosas, maximas cum molestiis, laboribus, sumtibus, vita q; periculis suscepetunt in loca peregrina et longinqua, ad certorum Deorum templa, idola atq; oracula, eos nimirum consulendi, comprecandi gratiamq; eorum sibi conciliandi gratia. Sic Israelitas quoq; legimus post apostasiam illam a rege et religione avita, Ethnicorum exemplo et imitatione, ad aureos illos viculos, ad Baalim, aliaq; idola Dan, Bethel, Gilgal, Bethaven, Beerseba (quod Prophetae illis saepe exprobrant) atq; etiam extra regionem Israelitarum ad aliarum quarumvis Gentium idola Deos, cucurrisse, eos illorum locus cōprecandi veneradiq; gratia. Ac nos Christiani unus veru mq; no Christianorum flrum Deu, tanquam Spiritus immensum, infinitum et omnipraesente, passim ubiq;, locorū, secundū peregrinatio fidelissima ipsius Christi admonitione, in spiritu et veritate reli adoramus. Sic Paulus quoq; hortatur et scripsit 1. Tim. 2. ut omni in loco sublatis sanctis manibus, supplicemus Deo. Cogicundi etiā in spiritu et veritate, omni nob. sepenumero, omnē nostrum vitam in huc seculo esse quasi perpecui, quandam peregrinationem a Domino, nosq; in hoc mundo peregrinos esse et viatores: unde vera fide atque ipse toto pectore ad
units.tr: Nor indeed did the heathens, leaving their native land and the gods they had at home, undertake arduous, difficult and dangerous journeys to distant places, enduring great troubles, labours, expenses and risks to life, merely to reach the temples, idols and oracles of certain gods, namely to consult them, to pray to them and to win their favour. So we read that the Israelites too, after their apostasy from their king and ancestral religion, following the example and imitation of the Gentiles, ran to those golden calves, to Baal and the other idols at Dan, Bethel, Gilgal, Bethaven and Beersheba (which the prophets often reproach them for), and even outside the land of Israel to the gods and idols of other nations, to pray to them and venerate them in their places. We Christians, however, worship the one true God, who is a spirit, immense, infinite and omnipresent, everywhere and in every place, following the most faithful admonition of Christ himself, in spirit and truth. So Paul also exhorts and writes (1 Tim. 2) that in every place we should pray to God, lifting up holy hands. We should also often reflect, in spirit and truth, that our whole life in this age is as it were a continual pilgrimage away from the Lord, and that in this world we are strangers and wayfarers. Hence, with true faith and with our whole heart, we ought to long for, aspire to and strive towards that heavenly and eternal Father and fatherland.

units.la: Ethnicorum peregrinatio ad idola. cælestem & æternum illum Patrem atque Patriam ambelare, aspirare atq; contendere debemus. Porrò falsos & fucatos hosce suos Deos, sive naturales, sive artificiales coluerunt partim me- terné, hoc est, animo, meute, affectu, amore, ipsé, fiducia vana & inani: partim externè, innumeris cùm rebus externis & corporeis, tum ritibus, gestibus & cærimoniis, de quibus suprà. Nos autem Christiani non Deos alienos, sed verum Deum, tanquam spiritum invisibilem & immensum colimus, atq; veneramur; & quidè colere atq; venerari debemus, autore Christo, in spiritu potissimum & veritate, toto animo, tota mente, toto corde et affectu, verâ vigentiq; fide, spe & charitate. Externé autè adulterinos et siculneos illos suos Deos superstitiosissimè coluerunt parcim rebus donis, atq; muneribus, quibusdá externis & corporeis, partim certis quibusdá ritibus, gestibus, atq; cærimoniis.
units.tr: The pilgrimage of the Gentiles to idols. Moreover, these false and counterfeit gods of theirs, whether natural or artificial, they worshipped partly inwardly, that is, with mind, soul, affection, love and vain and empty trust; and partly outwardly, with countless external and bodily things, and with rites, gestures and ceremonies, of which I have spoken above. We Christians, however, do not worship alien gods but the true God, as an invisible and immense spirit, and we ought to worship and venerate him, at the bidding of Christ, chiefly in spirit and truth, with the whole soul, the whole mind, the whole heart and affection, and with true, living faith, hope and love. The spurious and counterfeit gods of the Gentiles, on the other hand, they worshipped most superstitiously outwardly, with certain external and bodily gifts and offerings, and partly with certain rites, gestures and ceremonies.

units.la: Res quibus Deos suos honorarunt, quasq; illi obtulerunt (quæ sacrificia oblationes, offerimenta, dona sive donaria, anathemata et alias uominibus fuerunt appellata) alia quidem fuerunt animate: alie inanimes: Animatæ; ut animalia, plantæ: Auimalia verò, quæ Diis suis obtulerunt & immolarunt, fuerunt alia ratione uteutia, ut Homines: alia rationis expertia: quæ animalia sive animantia bruta appellantur: quorum alia fuerunt aerea, seu volatilia, alia terrestria, alia aquea, alia amphibia. Pro innumeris ergo illis sive hominü, sive animaliū brutorum sacrificiis, hostiis atq; victimis Ethnicis, unicum habemus (ut uno verbo atq; generatim dicam) Christi sacrificium, Christi hostiam atq; victimam, semel in ara crucis oblatam, quæ ad universi generis huma ni salute sufficiens est, fatriq; idonea: secundum illa Pauli Eph. 5. Sicuti & Christus nos amavit & tradidit semetipsum pro nobis προσφορὰν καὶ θυσίαν τῷ Θεῷ εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας, id est, obla eionem & victimam pro nobis in odorem fragrantiæ, id est, fragrantissimum, Deo sacratissimū & gratissimum. Hoc est sacrificium veré sacrum, veré sanctum, veré proinde sacro sanctum, quod Christus ipse per se, fine cujusquam alterius ope et auxilio fecit: in quo simul & hostia fuit & sacerdos. Hoc demum sacrificium veré & hostia & victima poterit appellari, quippe quo solo semel, satio omnes Dei hominumq; hostes, tam visibiles quam invisibiles, ut peccatum, iras Dei, legis ma- ledictio, mundus caro, diabolus, mors, inferuus, vinculi, vitti, atque profrati fuerunt.
units.tr: The things with which they honoured their gods and offered to them (which were called by various names: sacrifices, oblations, offerings, gifts or donaria, anathemata and others) were of two kinds, some animate and some inanimate. Animate things were animals and plants. Of the animals which they offered and sacrificed to their gods, some were endowed with reason, like men, and others were without reason, which are called brute animals; and of these some were aerial or flying, some terrestrial, some aquatic, and some amphibious. In place of those countless sacrifices of men or brute animals made by the Gentiles, we have, to put it in one word and in general terms, the sacrifice of Christ, the victim and offering of Christ, offered once on the altar of the cross, which is sufficient for the salvation of the whole human race and fit to atone for it, according to Paul's words in Eph. 5: "Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour" [προσφορὰν καὶ θυσίαν τῷ Θεῷ εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας], that is, an oblation and victim for us, for a fragrant odour, that is, most fragrant, most holy and most acceptable to God. This is truly a sacred sacrifice, truly holy, and therefore most holy, which Christ himself accomplished by himself, without the help or aid of anyone else; in it he was both victim and priest. This sacrifice alone can truly be called both victim and offering, since by it alone, once for all, all the enemies of God and of men, visible and invisible, such as sin, the wrath of God, the curse of the law, the world, the flesh, the devil, death, hell, chains and vices, were overcome and laid low.

units.la: Humana illa Gentilium sacrificia, quæ & antiqua & per vulgata fuisse legimus, fuerunt immanissima, ab ipsa lege nature, omnið humanitate abhorrentia. Ipsi quoq; parentes, deprofita abjectæ naturali illa sua φιλοστοργία, exuta omni humanitate, non dubitarunt suos liberos, vificera atq; pi gnora sua charissima Dius illis suis, seu demonib, potiùs madante miserrimè atq; cremanda offer re. O seclus horrendū, immane, detestandū ac inexpiabile. Sed quemadmodū sacrificiorū istorum immanitatē meritò detestamur & exsecrmur: sic contra Patris illus nostri cœlestis charitatem satiò admirari non possumus, qui filio illi suo unigenito et charisimo non pepercit, sed eum pro no bis, nob. inquā, suis inimicis morti, et quidē morti gratissimæ, acerbissimæ, ignominiosissimæ, tradidit, secundū illa Christi verba: Sic Deus dilexit Mundū, ut filium suum unigenitū traderet pro Mundo, ut omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternā. Verum ut Patris, ita Filii quoq; ipsius incredibilē amorus erga nos vim ac magnitudinē æstiduē, gratia memorig, menee, nos bonuncione mortales, qui ejus quoq; inimici eramus, colere, recolere, volvere atq; volvere de hemus, de quo ille duētius sometipsum pro nobis obtulit, corpus animumq; suum humanū crudèlissimè affligi & excruciari, crucis denig, supplicio horrendo mactari passus est pro nostra salute. Fuit hoc illius jacrificii immane quidè & inhumanū, si cruciatus, tormenta, crucē atq; mortem, item eorum, qui bis tormētis atq; supplicius eum affecerunt, sævitia, crudelitatem, spectaculo sua. Fuit simul illud sacrificiū, veré humanū, quod a Christo, ceu veró homine, nobis consubstantiali & animo et corpore pro humani generis salute factū est. Fuit etiā sacrificiū humanissimū, quia ab infinita illa Dei patris atq; filii φιλανθρωπία seu charitate erga genus humanum profectum est.
units.tr: Those human sacrifices of the Gentiles, which we read were both ancient and widespread, were most monstrous and abhorrent to the very law of nature and to all humanity. Parents themselves, casting off that natural storge of theirs and stripped of all humanity, did not hesitate to offer their children, their offspring and their dearest pledges most miserably to be burned, at the command of their gods or rather demons. O horrible, monstrous, detestable and inexpiable age! But just as we rightly detest and curse the monstrousness of those sacrifices, so on the other hand we can never sufficiently admire the charity of our heavenly Father, who did not spare his only begotten and most beloved Son, but handed him over for us (for us, I say, his enemies) to death, and indeed to the most bitter, most shameful and most ignominious death, according to Christ's words: "God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son for the world, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." But, as we should honour the Father's love, so we should honour also the Son's incredible love and its immensity towards us; we who were mortal by nature and also his enemies ought to worship, recall, turn over and meditate in our grateful memory on how he offered himself for us, suffering his human body and soul to be most cruelly afflicted and tortured, and at last put to death by the horrible punishment of the cross, for our salvation. That sacrifice was indeed monstrous and inhuman, if one considers the torments, the cross and death, and likewise the cruelty of those who inflicted these torments and punishments upon him, as a spectacle. Yet it was also truly human, made by Christ as true man, consubstantial with us in body and soul, for the salvation of the human race. It was also the most humane of sacrifices, because it proceeded from the infinite philanthropy, that is, the charity, of the Father and the Son towards the human race.

units.la: Quantum verò adilla animaliū pecorumq; sacrificia attinet, quæ varia fuerunt et multiplicia crificii, qui non Hecatombas, nō Chiliombas, non alia animalia atq; pecora, sed seipsum, seipsum, in quā, pro generis humani salute Deo patri suo cælesti libentissimè patientissimeq; obtulit. Legimus apud quosdā Indiæ populos solitos fuisse nonnullos furore quodā seipsos Dijs fui, eos nimirū placandi gratia, mactandos offerre. At Dei filius non quodā furore, sed ardentissimo erga Deum genus, humanūq; amore adductus et impulsus seipsum, ire divinæ placanda generiq; humani redi mendi gratia, Patrisq; suo cælesti in ocorem suæ vitatis obtulit.
units.tr: As for those sacrifices of animals and cattle, which were various and manifold, Christ, the author of this sacrifice, offered not hecatombs, not chiliombs, nor other animals and cattle, but himself, to God his heavenly Father, most willingly and most patiently, for the salvation of the human race. We read that among some peoples of India it was customary for some, in a kind of frenzy, to offer themselves to be slaughtered to their gods, in order to placate them. But the Son of God, moved and impelled not by any frenzy but by the most ardent love towards God and the human race, offered himself to his heavenly Father, to appease the divine wrath and redeem the human race, in place of his own life.

units.la: SumpuoSumptuosißimorum pretiosißimorumq; sacrificiorū ex omni animalium genere exempla passim occurrunt in profanis litteris. Ex quibus colligimus miseros illos Gentiles nullis vel laboribus vel sumtibus in falso illo falsorum Deorum suorum cultu perecisse: qui tamen illis non falutem, sed mortem potius & exitium sempiternum peperit. Quanto igitur majori studio, zelo, feduliitate, labore atq; opera nos manus veri Dei vero, justo, legitimoq; cultu versari, & illud Christi sacrificium salutiferum, quod non sine sudore & sanguine factum est, dies noctesq; meditari decet: unde vita nobis & salus aeterna parta est.
units.tr: Examples of the most sumptuous and precious sacrifices, from every kind of animal, occur everywhere in profane writings. From these we gather that those wretched Gentiles perished in that false worship of their false gods, sparing no toil or expense; yet it brought them not salvation but death and eternal ruin. How much greater, then, ought our eagerness, zeal, diligence, labour and effort to be, to be occupied day and night in the true, just and lawful worship of the true God, and to meditate on that saving sacrifice of Christ, which was accomplished not without sweat and blood, and by which eternal life and salvation have been won for us.

units.la: Inter alia animalia, quae Gentiles falsis sitis, illis suis Diis immolarunt, fuit Agnus, qui, Festo autore, a Graecis ἀγνὸς dicitur, quod castum significat: eo quod hostia fit pura & inimolatio nisi apta, vel, ut ibidem addit, a Graeco ἁμνὸς deduci videtur, quod nomen apud Majores communis erat generis. Vsitatissimum fuit hoc sacrificii genus apud Gentiles. Unde Plinius lib. 8. cap. 47. Magna & pecori gratia vel in placamentis Deorum, vel in usum vellerum. Sed revera illi Gentilium agni, quos sitis illi suos Diis sacrificarunt, non fuerunt ἀγνοί sive ἁγνοί, id est, casti, sive sancti, sed polluti potius et contaminati in confectu Dei. At nobis Christianis Christus est agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccata Mundi, quem admodum Johannes Baptista, ejus προφῆτης, id est, Praevius, seu Praecursor, digito suo illum demonstrando loquentem, testatus est. Christus est Agnus ille occisus ab origine Mundi, habens librum vitae, cui inscripta sunt nomina sanctorum, de quo Apoc. 13. Christus est Agnus ille stans in medio throni coelestis, tanquam occisus, septem praeditus cornibus & oculis immensa ejus cum potestas, tum sapientia defigitur. Is est, qui accepit e dextera Patris sui, sedentis in throno, librum scriptum intus et a tergo, & septem signatum sigillis, quem nemo praeter ipsum aperire et resignare potuit, hoc est, qui patefaciat simul et exsequatur mysteria atq; judicia divinae providentiae. Hunc Agnum quatuor animalia, & viginti quatuor seniores, coram illo prostrati, hoc est, universa Ecclesia novo celebrat carmine, dicens: Dignus es, accipere librum, & aperire signacula ejus: quoniam occisus es, & redemisti nos Deo, per sanguinem tuum, ex omni tribu, & lingua & populo & natione, et fecisti nos Deo Reges & Sacerdotes, et regnabimus super terram. Eundem Angelorum quoq; myriades tanunt et celebrant magna voce, dicentes: Dignus est Agnus, qui occisus est, accipere virtutem, et divitias, et sapientiam, et sortitudinem, et honorem et gloriam et benedictionem. Hunc denique Agnum cum Patre laudant et celebrant omnes creaturae coelestes, terrestres, subterraneae, maritimae, tribuentes uni, honorem, gloriam et potestatem in secula seculorum, de quo, ut ejus sanguine, electis, nuptiis, sponsa vitae, vide plura Apoc. cap. 5. 11. 12. 14. 19. et 21. quae omnia mysteriorum salubberrimorum sunt plenissima. Hic Agnus appellatur Leo de tribu Juda, victor, radix David, Christus est ἀμνὸς ἄμωμος καὶ ἀσπίλος.
units.tr: Among the other animals which the Gentiles sacrificed to their false gods was the lamb, which, according to Festus, is called by the Greeks hagnos [ἀγνὸς], which means chaste, because the victim is made pure and unblemished unless it is fit; or, as he adds in the same place, it seems to be derived from the Greek amnos [ἁμνὸς], a word which among the ancients was common to both genders. This kind of sacrifice was very widespread among the Gentiles. Whence Pliny, book 8, chapter 47: "The sheep is of great value both for placating the gods and for the use of its wool." But in truth those lambs of the Gentiles which they sacrificed to their gods were not chaste or holy, but rather polluted and defiled in the sight of God. For us Christians, however, Christ is that Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world, as John the Baptist, his forerunner, that is, his herald, bore witness, pointing him out with his finger. Christ is that Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, who has the book of life in which the names of the saints are written, concerning which see Rev. 13. Christ is that Lamb standing in the midst of the heavenly throne, as if slain, endowed with seven horns and eyes, by which his immense power and wisdom are signified. He is the one who received from the right hand of his Father, who sits on the throne, a book written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals, which no one but himself could open and unseal; that is, he both reveals and carries out the mysteries and judgments of divine providence. The four living creatures and the twenty-four elders, prostrate before him, that is, the whole Church, sing to this Lamb a new song, saying: "You are worthy to take the book and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you have redeemed us to God out of every tribe and tongue and people and nation, and have made us kings and priests to our God, and we shall reign upon the earth." The myriads of angels also sing and celebrate him with a loud voice, saying: "Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honour and glory and blessing." Finally, all creatures, in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea, praise and celebrate this Lamb together with the Father, ascribing to the one honour, glory and power for ever and ever. Concerning his blood, the elect, the marriage and the bride of life, see more in Rev. chapters 5, 11, 12, 14, 19 and 21, which are all full of most wholesome mysteries. This Lamb is called the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the victor, the root of David. Christ is the lamb without blemish and without spot [ἀμνὸς ἄμωμος καὶ ἀσπίλος].

units.la: Apud Gentiles fuit praeterea tertium sacrificii genus (quod quoniam ejus supra mentio fa-ta non est, hic silentio non est praetermittendum) Ἑπτάυα Graece ἑ & βοσκούσας appellatum, de quo Eustathius in Homerum Odyss. Δ. et Λ. Ac ἑπτάῦα quidem fuit dictum a tribus animalibus, quibus conflabat, nempe duabus ovibus et bove, teste Epiharmo: vel bove, capra et ove: vel, ut alii volunt, capro, hirco et tauro. Sit enim alia quoque non onnulla sacrificia ab animalium numero nomina fuerunt sortita, ut, exempli gratia, δωδεκάτος, sive δωδεκάς dictum est sacrificium duodecim animalibus constans, Hecatombe a centum, Chiliombe a mille animalibus. Idem sacrificium dictum etiam est βούβροσ, eo quod in eo bos reliqua animalia, non ferus atque nativa prora, praecedebat.
units.tr: Among the Gentiles there was also a third kind of sacrifice. Since it was not mentioned above, it should not be passed over in silence here. It was called in Greek heptaya [Ἑπτάυα] and boskousai [βοσκούσας], as Eustathius explains on Homer, Odyssey Delta and Lambda. The heptaya took its name from the three animals of which it consisted: two sheep and an ox, according to Epicharmus; or an ox, a goat and a sheep; or, as others hold, a he-goat, a billy-goat and a bull. Other sacrifices likewise took their names from the number of animals: the dodekatos, or dodekas, was a sacrifice of twelve animals, the hekatombe of a hundred, and the chiliombe of a thousand. The same sacrifice is also called the boubrosos, because in it the ox went before the other animals, which were not wild and native to the place.

units.la: Nobis autem Christianis Christus est ille, qui, ut Isaias de eo vaticinatus est, cap. 53. ουκ ἴσταρ ad mactationem fuit ductus, et qui tanquam agnus coram tondente se obmutuit, et os suum non aperuit, hoc est, nullam emisit vocem, indicem vel minimam ejus impaenitentiae. Christus est agnus ille mansuetus, qui portatus fuit ad victimam, et non cognoverunt, quia cogitarunt sic per cum consilia, dicentes: Mittamus lignum, cum, ut Jeremias cap. 11. multis ante seculis de eo cogitare. cinit. Christus est hircus ille, qui, conjectus in eum peccatis totius populi, non Baccho, sed Deo ex- tra urbem pro peccatis fuit immolatus, de quo Le v. vici 16. & Num. 15.
units.tr: For us Christians, however, Christ is the one who, as Isaiah prophesied in chapter 53, [ouk anoigei] was led to the slaughter, and who, like a lamb before its shearer, was silent and did not open his mouth, that is, uttered no sound, showing not the least sign of impenitence. Christ is the gentle lamb who was brought to be a victim, and "they did not know," because "they devised such plans against him, saying: Let us put wood on his bread," as Jeremiah wrote in chapter 11 many centuries before. Christ is also that goat which, with the sins of the whole people laid upon it, was sacrificed for sins outside the city, not to Bacchus but to God; see Leviticus 16 and Numbers 15.

units.la: Sed ne, quod longum nimis foret & prolixum, singula animalium genera, quae Gentiles Diis suis immolarunt, perscquar: illorum quidem corpora, ex toto grege electa, ad aras adducere, coro-nare, vincire, immolare, mactare, cædere, jugulare, excoriare, membratim dissecare, tandem, vel cota, vel integra, vel certas illorum partes, in Deorum suorum honorem concremare consuevere. Pro infinitis illis animalium corporibus nos Christiani Christi hostias. Hemus corpus: corpus, inquam, electum, eximium, purum, putum, sacrosanctum, quod ut ipsemet Christus in sacrosancta sua Cœnae institutione locutus est, pro nobis fuit traditum: hoc est, quod pro nobis captum, vinctum, ab uno tribunali & judice injusto, ad alterum raptum, consputum, flagellatum, corona spinea fasciatum, horrendis miserandis modis a vertice capitis ad plantas usque exträciatum ac deformatum fuit. Hoc ipsum corpus jam fere ex sanguine & examine, gravi crucis onere eius impositio, extra urbem, tanquam χρῖσμα, ad locum supplicii, Golgatha dictum, quasi ad macellum quoddam ductum, vestibus per iudibrium & contumeliam summam exutum, nudum, erneci affixum, atque post multos cruciatus enecatum fuit. Ex hoc ipso autem corpore, vere licet mortuo, & militis cuiusdam lancea confossô sanguis & aqua (o miraculum ac mysterium ingens!) profluxit, hoc est, ut uno verbo dicam, peccatorum remissio, vita & salus in universum genus humanum redundavit. Unde Petrus epist. 1. cap. 2. Corpore suo super lignum pertulit peccata nostra, ut peccatis mortui justitiae viveremus, cujus vibice sanati sumus. Hoc ipsum Christi corpus sepultum, & ad vitam revocatum, ad dexteram Patris, cui nostra quoq. corpora candem reddentur conformia, secundum illa Pauli verba ad Philip. 3. cap. Christus, inquit, corpus nostrae humilitatis transfigurabit, & reddet ut suam gloriae. Hoc ipsum igitur Christi corpus, vere Σῶμα, hoc est, Dei carnis, vita & salus nostra potest appellari, quod nobis fide manducandum in sacra illa synaxi panis symbolo porrigitur: Unde panem illum, quem frangimus, Paulus κοινωνίαν corporis Christi appellat 1. Cor. 10. Sed Christi quoq. corpus mysticum est, & appellatur Ecclesia, cujus ipse est caput. Eph. 1. 4. 5. 1. Cor. 11. Memineritis ergo & cogitemus assidue, qui nos Christianos profiterimur, nos Christi esse corpus, in unum nos omnes baptizatos esse corpus & sanguinis, ut Paulus ait 1. Cor. 10. nos Christi esse membra: unde memores semper simus ejus, studiosi cum puritatis atque innocentiae, tum obedientiae erga Christum, tum charitatis mutuae ac sincerae erga nos invicem. Postremo cum Christus corpus suum pro salute nostra tradiderit, & obtulerit in ara crucis, nos quoq. invicem ... Ergo ... ( fieri Paulus nos per Dei miserationes obsecrat ) corpora nostra debemus ...
units.tr: But lest I pursue at excessive and tedious length each kind of animal which the Gentiles offered to their gods, I will say only this. They were accustomed to bring to the altars bodies chosen from the whole flock, to crown them, bind them, slaughter them, kill them, cut their throats, flay them, cut them limb from limb, and at last to burn them, whole or in part, in honour of their gods. In place of those countless animal bodies, we Christians have the sacrifice of Christ's body: the body, I say, chosen, outstanding, pure, spotless and holy, which, as Christ himself said in the institution of his most holy Supper, was given up for us; that is, which was seized for us, bound, dragged from one judgment hall and unjust judge to another, spat upon, scourged, crowned with a crown of thorns, and torn and disfigured in dreadful and pitiable ways from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet. This same body, now almost drained of blood and worn out by the heavy weight of the cross laid upon it, was led outside the city like a sacrificial offering to the place of execution, called Golgotha, as if to a kind of slaughterhouse. In mockery and great contempt it was stripped of its clothes, and naked it was fastened to the cross and, after many tortures, put to death. From this same body, truly dead though it was, when a soldier's lance had pierced it, blood and water flowed out (O miracle and immense mystery!). That is, to put it in one word, the forgiveness of sins, life and salvation, poured out upon the whole human race. Hence Peter, 1 Peter 2: "He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, might live to righteousness; by whose stripes you were healed." This same buried body of Christ, restored to life and raised to the right hand of the Father, will make our own bodies conformed to it, according to Paul's words in Philippians 3: "Christ," he says, "will transform the body of our humiliation and make it like his glorious body." This very body of Christ, truly the Body, that is, the flesh of God, can be called our life and salvation, which is offered to us to be eaten by faith in that holy communion under the sign of bread. Hence Paul calls the bread which we break the communion [κοινωνία] of the body of Christ, 1 Corinthians 10. But the body of Christ is also mystical, and it is called the Church, of which he himself is the head: Ephesians 1, 4, 5; 1 Corinthians 11. Remember, then, and constantly consider, you who profess yourselves Christians, that we are the body of Christ, that we all baptized into one body and blood, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10, are the members of Christ. Let us therefore always be mindful of him and eager for purity and innocence, and for obedience towards Christ, and for mutual and sincere love towards one another. Finally, since Christ gave up his body for our salvation and offered it on the altar of the cross, we too ... Therefore ... (Paul begs us, by the mercies of God, to do so) we ought to present our bodies ...

units.la: Porro & carnes animalium macatorum Gentiles partim igni comburere atque consumere, partim comedere in sacrificiis suis fuerunt soliti: quae quidem carnes Deo fuerunt exosae, in- & exsecrabiles. At nos Christiani pro sacrificiis illis Gentilium carnibus Christi habemus carnem purissimam & verificam; de qua Christus ipse multa praelare disseruit, in illa quondam clarissima urbe Capernaum, ut Joan. 6. Scriptum est. Idem Evangelista cap. 1. ἦν λόγος ... Verbum illud, quod fuit in principio, quod fuit apud Deum, quod est Deus; factum est Caro: cui re fundentilla Pauli 1. Tim. 3. ὃς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκί, id est, Deus apparuit, sive manifestatus est in carne. Et ut idem scribit ad Hebr. 2. Quoniam pueri participes fuerunt carnis et sanguinis, ipse (Christus) similiter facilius est participes eorundem, ut per mortem ener v ret ... Cujus ... Hoc ipsum ... Caro est panis, vere cibus, ut Christi ... Christus ... carnem edit, bibit ejus sanguinem, vitam habet aeternam, manet, in Christo, & Christus in ... ipso, qui eum excitabit in extremo die. Atq; horum quidem omnium ipsum Christum ceteri habemus & doctorem loquentissimum & veritatis summam Ioan.6. Hac ipsa igitur caro cassissima Christi Caro, tanquam salutis nostrae causa unica, carissima nobis esse debet. Hujusce carnis, tanquam panis atq; cibi veri, vereq; salutaris, simus quasi helluones, hoc est, avidis semper & appetentes, illis esuriamus, illam manducemus, quae solae ad vitam aeternam pascit atq; satiari possumus. Hac Christi caro facit, ut simus caro de carne ejus, os de ossibus ejus: esse, hac purissima Christi caro putissime corruptissimaeq; nostrae carnis optima medicina. Quemadmodum autem Christus purissimam illam suam Carnem pro Mundi vita & salute dedit, Patri, suo obtulit, illam multis modis excruciari, crucifigi ac tandem enecari passus est: sic nos impuram nostram carnem crucifigere atque mortificare debemus, secundum illa Pauli ad Gal.5. Qui Christi sunt, carnem suam crucifixerunt cum vitiis & concupiscentiis. Ex Sanctus Petrus 1.epist.4.cap.4. ... Atq; hac ipsa quidem carnis nostrae, hoc est, naturae impurae & corruptae, crucifixio & mortificatio & spiritus vivificatio (quae una est, solidaq; poenitentia) sacrificium est Deo gratissimum.
units.tr: Moreover, the Gentiles were accustomed to burn and consume the flesh of the slaughtered animals in part with fire, and in part to eat it in their sacrifices. That flesh was hateful and abominable to God. But in place of those Gentile sacrificial meats we Christians have the flesh of Christ, most pure and true, of which Christ himself spoke at length in that once famous city of Capernaum, as is written in John 6. The same evangelist in chapter 1 says: "The Word, which was in the beginning, which was with God, which is God, was made flesh." To this agrees Paul's word in 1 Timothy 3, [hos ephanerōthē en sarki], that is, God appeared, or was manifested, in the flesh. And as he writes in Hebrews 2: "Since the children were partakers of flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same, that through death he might destroy ..." ... This very flesh is bread, truly food, as of Christ ... Christ ... eats the flesh and drinks his blood, has eternal life, abides in Christ, and Christ in ... him, who will raise him up on the last day. And of all these things we have Christ himself as our most eloquent teacher and the highest truth, John 6. This very most pure flesh of Christ, as the sole cause of our salvation, ought to be most dear to us. Let us be like gluttons for this flesh, as for true and saving bread; let us always be eager and hungry for it, let us eat it, for it alone can nourish us to eternal life and satisfy us. This flesh of Christ makes us flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones. It is the most excellent remedy for our most foul and corrupt flesh. But just as Christ gave his most pure flesh for the life and salvation of the world, offered it to his Father, and suffered it to be tormented in many ways, crucified and finally put to death, so we ought to crucify and mortify our impure flesh, according to Paul's words in Galatians 5: "Those who are Christ's have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires." And Peter, 1 Peter 4: ... Indeed, this very crucifixion and mortification of our flesh, that is, of our impure and corrupt nature, and the quickening of the spirit (which is one and the same, and solid repentance) is a sacrifice most acceptable to God.

units.la: Praeterea ut carnes, sic sanguines quoq; illi hostiarum Gentilium impuri fuerunt & immundi, ita ut non tam sanguines, quam sanies quaedam purulentae, putridae ac putidae dici meruerint. Quamvis igitur illis sanguinibus, quibus altaria, simulacra, sepulcra ac ... quam fuerunt soliti, sanctificandi, expiandi, lustrandi, divinandi, foedera sanciendi vim tribuerunt: tamen revera nihil fuerunt aliud, quam sanguines, hoc est (in qua quidem significatione saepe in sacris litteris nomen hoc usurpatur) tetra & nefaria quaedam scelera atque flagitia. Pro illis igitur Gentilium sanguinibus atq; cruoribus impuris & immundis nos Christiani Christi sanguinem sanctissimum & purissimum, qui pene nobis cumulatus, ad salutem nostram praestitit omnia illa, quae Gentes impuris illis sacrificiis fuerant sanguinibus affinxerunt. Nam, ut Iohannes inquit epist.1.cap.1. Sanguis Iesu Christi, filii Dei, ... purgat & emundat nos ab omni peccato. Sic Apocal.1. Christus dilexit nos, ... in sanguine suo ... ut sanctificaret populum, quemadmodum Paulus testatur ad Hebr. 12.cap.item, nono, in hunc modum: ... in sanguine omnia purificantur secundum legem. Sic ad Col.cap.1. ... in quo (filio Dei) habemus redemptionem per sanguinem, remissionem peccatorum. ... in quo (Christo) habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ejus remissionem peccatorum, secundum divitias gratiae divinae. Et hac Hebr.9. ... Sanguine ergo Christi ... Ideo Christi sanguinem conferens cum sanguine taurorum & hircorum & cum cineri juvencae: Quanto magis, inquit, sanguis Christi, qui per spiritum aeternum seipsum obtulit inculpatum Deo, purgabit conscientiam nostram a mortuis operibus ad serviendum Deo vivo, quo toto capite ... Haec Christi, tanquam agni immaculati & incontaminati, sanguine pretiosi redemti sumus, ut Petrus ait, epist.1.cap.1. Eodem in loco ... id est, aspersionem sanguinis Iesu Christi opponit sanguinis brutorum animaliam ... Hoc crucis Christi sanguine in cruce profusso, Paulus ad Colos. dicit, Deum placasse atque pacasse tam ea, quae in coelis sunt, quam quae in terris: et idcirco, ut idem Apostolus ad Hebraeos ait, aspersio sanguinis Christi melius loquitur, quam Abelis sanguis. Hoc Christi sanguine nos justificari Deo, reconciliari docent illa Pauli verba ad Rom.3. Qui justificamur gratis ejus gratia per redemptionem in Christo Iesu quam proposuit Deus propitiatorium per fidem in ejus sanguine. Et cap.5. Multo igitur magis justificati, nunc in sanguine ejus servabimur ab
units.tr: Furthermore, just as the flesh, so also the blood of those Gentile victims was impure and unclean, so that they deserved to be called not so much blood as a kind of purulent, putrid and stinking pus. Although they attributed to that blood, with which they were accustomed to consecrate, expiate and purify altars, images, and tombs, to make predictions, and to ratify covenants, the power of sanctifying, expiating, purifying, divining and sealing covenants, in truth it was nothing other than blood, that is (in which sense this word is often used in the Holy Scriptures) foul and wicked crimes and shameful deeds. In place of those impure and unclean blood-offerings and gore of the Gentiles, we Christians have the most holy and pure blood of Christ, which, poured out for us almost to the full, has brought about for our salvation all those things which the Gentiles falsely attributed to their impure sacrifices of blood. For, as John says in 1 John 1: "The blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, ... cleanses us and purifies us from all sin." So Revelation 1: "Christ loved us ... in his blood ... that he might sanctify the people," as Paul testifies in Hebrews 12; likewise in chapter nine, in this manner: "... in blood all things are purified according to the law." So Colossians 1: "in whom (the Son of God) we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins. ... in whom (Christ) we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of the grace of God." And in Hebrews 9: "... By the blood of Christ therefore ..." Hence, comparing the blood of Christ with the blood of bulls and goats and the ashes of a heifer: "How much more," he says, "will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God," and so on through the whole chapter ... By the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot, we have been redeemed, as Peter says in 1 Peter 1. In the same place ... that is, he sets the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ against the blood of irrational animals ... By the blood of Christ poured out on the cross, Paul says in Colossians, God has reconciled and pacified both things in heaven and things on earth; and therefore, as the same Apostle says in Hebrews, the sprinkling of the blood of Christ speaks better than the blood of Abel. That we are justified before God and reconciled by the blood of Christ is taught by Paul's words in Romans 3: "Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood." And in chapter 5: "Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from his wrath."

units.la: Dd ejus ira. Idem ad Col. 1. Hic Christi sanguis, ipso teste, vere est potus (ut ejusdem caro vere est cibus) quem qui bibit, vitam habet aeternam, manetque in Christo et Christus in ipso. Hujusce sanguinis xoinwnia, id est communio, sive communicatio, est calix seu poculum illud Dominicum, Paulo teste, 1.Cor. 10. Hic denique, sanguis is est, cujus Iohannes meminit, priore epist. 5. cap. Christus venit per aquam et sanguinem. Item: Tres testes in terra, spiritus, sanguis, aqua. Hujus etiam Agni, multi Christi, sanguine Martyres Apoc. 7. flolas suas dicuntur dealbasse. His diuinis sanguinis in Christi elogiis addatur illud Cypriani pulcherrimum ejusdem sanguinis encomium in epistola ad Fortunatum de duplici martyrio, unde mirificam quoque, qui peccatorum suorum conscientia et irae judicium di vini metu anguntur, consolationem haurire possunt: Nimirum, inquit, hoc est efficax illud sacrosanctum sanguinis testimonium, dicens, Ecce agnus Dei, ecce qui tollit peccatum mundi. Plus est tollere peccatum, quam peccata: et peccatum non hujus aut illius, sed mundi. Quia pus enim peccati mundum uni verbum occupavit, hoc per Christum esse sublatum, sanguis ipsius pro nobis effusus, reddit videns testimonium, melius pro nobis loquens, ut magis Apostolus, quam sanguis Abel. Si quidem ille clamans, pacem loquitur et reconciliatione. Quin idem sanguis quia a nobis bibitur, si modo digne bibitur, clamat in cordibus nostris verba pacifica et soluti plena. Et hic triplex est testimonium licet spirituale quodammodo. Clamat spiritus, qui nobis arrhabonis loco datus est Abba pater testificans: quod jumus filii Dei: clamae aqua per quam renati fumus, quod edonata sunt nobis omnia peccata: et si quis adhuc dubitat accedit sanguinis testimonium, calamitatis. Quid adhuc haesitas? quid apud te patritas syrinmis Satanae? ecce praecium, qui te redemit Dei filius. Nisi te salvum voluisset Deus, non tradidisset unigenitum suum in mortem. Nemo majorem charitatem habet, quam ut animam suam ponat pro amicis suis. Si non est majus exemplum bene volentiae testimonii, quum si quis vitam impertiat, amico gratuito est Domini sanguis testimonium, qui pro iniquis effusus est. Effusus pro inimicis fecit amicos ac filios Dei, atque ut consideremus hanc fore perpetuam amicitiam, vel quit nobis edendam carne suam, reliquit bibendum sanguinem, ut per eadem alterum jus, per quae, unus redempti. Sanguinis asperso ne confirmatum est vetus Testamentum, quemadmodum Hebraeis scribens praeclare docet beatissimus: Pulsus: Christi sanguine consignatum et corroboratum est novum Testamentum, hoc est Testamentum, gratiae et remissionis peccatorum, per sanguinem agni immaculati, qui in se peccata gestavit totius mundi peccatu, quod omnes ex Adamo contrahunt, qui prodeunt in vitam et cujus cuteagio peccant quicunque peccant. Christi ergo sanguis sanctissimus (ut haec vid., ut addam multi ita pro nobis praesertim in ara crucis profusus, quod nobis per spiritum sanctum per Sacramenta aspergitur, et ad postanda propinantur, fide, a nobis propositus omnes impiorum nostros sanguines, hoc est, peccata clucidexpiandi, perfectum Iesum obtinet.
units.tr: ...his anger. Again, in Colossians 1: here the blood of Christ, by his own testimony, is truly drink (as his flesh is truly food). Whoever drinks it has eternal life and abides in Christ, and Christ in him. The communion [κοινωνία] of this blood, that is, the sharing or participation in it, is the cup or the Lord's chalice, as Paul testifies in 1 Corinthians 10. Finally, this is the blood of which John speaks in the fifth chapter of his first epistle: "Christ came by water and blood," and again: "There are three witnesses on earth: the Spirit, the blood, and the water." Of this Lamb, many martyrs, by the blood of Christ, are said in Revelation 7 to have washed their robes white. To these divine descriptions of Christ's blood let us add the beautiful praise of this same blood by Cyprian in his letter to Fortunatus on the twofold martyrdom. From it, those who are tormented by the awareness of their sins and by fear of God's judgment of wrath may draw a wonderful consolation. "Surely," he says, "that most sacred testimony of the blood is powerful, saying: Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sin of the world. It is more to take away sin than sins, and sin not of this or that man, but of the world." For since the sin of the world had filled the whole world with one word, that this has been taken away through Christ, his blood poured out for us gives a true testimony, speaking for us better than the blood of Abel. For that blood, crying out, speaks of peace and reconciliation. Indeed, the same blood, since it is drunk by us, if it is drunk worthily, cries out in our hearts words of peace and full of absolution. And here there is a threefold testimony, though in some way spiritual. The Spirit, who has been given to us as a pledge, cries out, "Abba, Father," testifying that we are children of God. The water through which we have been born again cries out that all our sins have been forgiven us. And if anyone still doubts, there comes the testimony of the blood, of our redemption. Why do you still hesitate? Why do you still, in yourself, feed the snares of Satan? Behold the price, the Son of God, who has redeemed you. Unless God had wished you saved, he would not have handed over his only begotten Son to death. No one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends. If there is no greater example of good will than when someone gives his life, the blood of the Lord, shed for the unrighteous, is a testimony to a friend who is free with his love. Poured out for enemies, it made us friends and sons of God. And so that we may consider that this friendship is perpetual, he who gave us his flesh to eat has left us his blood to drink, so that by the same means by which we were redeemed, we might be made one. The Old Testament was confirmed by the sprinkling of blood, as the most blessed Peter writes clearly to the Hebrews. Likewise, the New Testament is sealed and strengthened by the blood of Christ, that is, the testament of grace and of the remission of sins, through the blood of the spotless Lamb, who bore in himself the sins of the whole world, the sin which all draw from Adam, who are born into life and by whose contagion all who sin, sin. Therefore the most holy blood of Christ (as these things are seen, and as I may add, poured out for us, especially on the altar of the cross) is sprinkled upon us by the Holy Spirit through the sacraments, and is offered to us to drink by faith. Thus it obtains for us, the perfect Jesus, the cleansing and expiation of all the impious blood of our sins.

units.la: Sed et Animalium immolatorum coxas sive femora exsecta, et adipe sive pinguedine obdurata, ignem Ethnici (ut supra dixi) porricere atque conceperunt in Deum suorum honorem consecrare: Nos contra gloria praeter ne, illis superstitionibus contemptis, illis tradit sacrificium: sanguis et medicinam illud Christi festus ... . Quod apud Apoc. cap. 19. legimus, in scriptis fuit augustissimum illæ titulus, REX REGVM ET DOMINVS DOMINANTIVM: qui cum majestatis Christi, tum justae debitae, nostrae obedientiae, et, quod est consequens, nostrae salutis est symbolum.
units.tr: But the Gentiles, as I said above, also burned on the fire the thighs or hips cut from the sacrificed animals, and the fat hardened into tallow, and they consecrated them to the honour of their gods. We, on the contrary, having set aside those superstitions, are given by Christ a sacrifice, his blood and body, ... What we read in Revelation 19 was written as the most august title upon his garment and thigh: KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS. This is a symbol both of the majesty of Christ, and of our due obedience, and, as a consequence, of our salvation.

units.la: Linguas praeterea hostiarum suarum, peraëlo sacrificio, in Mercurii honorem superstitiose concremarunt, antequam discederent ac somnum caperent. At nos Christiani, non Mercurio, sed Deo linguas, ut et reliqua corporis nostri membra, conficerat, linguas nostras cohercere et refrenare, ea idem, brutas, belluinas, et impuras S. Spiritus igne exurere atque purgare debemus.
units.tr: Moreover, the Gentiles, in the sacrifice they offered, superstitiously burned the tongues of their victims in honour of Mercury before they departed and went to sleep. But we Christians, consecrating our tongues, like the other members of our body, not to Mercury but to God, ought to restrain and bridle our tongues, and to burn and purify them with the fire of the Holy Spirit, which makes them brutish, beastly and impure.

units.la: Quid dicam, quod pilos quoque, ex hostiarum suarum capite evulsos, ceu primitias quasdam Diis suis consecrare, et in ignem conjicere atque comburere consueverunt? de qua similiter ri- monia futili atque superstitiosa supra dictum. Nos vero Christiani pilos ipsos pecorum, hostiarum, rumi, Gentilium ne pili quidem facientes, cogitemus saepe, capitis nostri pilos quoque, ut Christus considera- tur, a Deo patre nostro coelesti esse numeratos, ei esse cordi, ut nullus eorum jure ejus voluntate in terram decidat. Meditemur etiam illos Christi capillos, atque ut nos vitam, in candidos, quorum unus illa Christi profopographia Apoc. cap. 1. fit mentio: qui partim candoris, id est puritate. puritatis & innocentiæ Christi, partim remissionis nostrorum peccatorum symbola sint: quò ac commodari possunt illa verba Isaiæ cap.1. Si peccata vestra fuerint, quasi coccinum, tanquam nix dealbabuntur: et si fuerint rubra instar vermiculi, erunt tanquâ lana. Ac meo quidem judicio non inepté & absurdè per illos Christi capillos piæ ac fideles possunt intelligi, qui Christi, tanquam capitis, sunt quasi pilis: quipilos licet viliores in hoc Mundo censeantur: tamen Christus illos habet in numero, illorum curam gerit, eos sanctisui Spiritus gratiâ niveatque lanâ candidiores reddit.
units.tr: What shall I say of how they also plucked the hairs from the heads of their victims, consecrated them as it were as firstfruits to their gods, and cast them into the fire and burned them? In a similar way, they set the hairs of their victims at nothing, as a futile and superstitious ceremony, as said above.
