But we Christians, not making even the hairs of animals, victims, or cattle of any account, should often reflect that the hairs of our own head, as Christ says, are numbered by God our heavenly Father, that they are dear to him, so that none of them falls to the earth without his will. Let us also meditate on those white hairs of Christ, mentioned in the vision in Revelation 1, which are symbols partly of his brightness, that is, of the purity and innocence of Christ, and partly of the remission of our sins. To these fit the words of Isaiah 1: "If your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and if they are red like a worm, they shall be as wool." In my judgment, not foolishly or absurdly, through those hairs of Christ may be understood the pious and faithful, who are, as it were, the hairs of Christ, the head: though they are regarded as of little worth in this world, yet Christ keeps them in his count, takes care of them, and by the grace of his Holy Spirit makes them whiter than snow and wool.

units.la: Nec verò partes tantum hostiarum externas, sed etiam internas, ut viscera, intestina, precordia,exta, Dij suis consecrabant. Illa enim fluidiosæ curioseq; intueri, rimari, atque scrutari, ex iis de rebus futuris prædicere,ea coquere, coëla prosecare, prosesta in aram focum ve porricere,hoc est, projicere atque ita comburere solebant: qua ceremonia magnam se putabant a Dijs suis inire gratiam. Unde exta hæc sua vocabant Lustralia. Nobis contrà Christianis viscera atque præcordia Dei patris cœlestis, & Fili ejus unigeniti, diligenter, assiduè attenteq; sunt consideranda & contemplanda cum ad doctrinam, tum ad consolationem nostram, secundum illa Luc.1. Per viscera misericordiæ Dei visitavit nos Oriens ex alto, hoc est, Christus Dei filius, Sol ille justitiæ, ex alto, id est, e cœlo oriens,nos miseros hominiones pro initima,& quasi viscerali Dei patris misericordia ( quæ αλλαγ; Iνσὸ ἐλεῆου appellat Paulus ad Philip.1.) visitavit,in carne venit, adnos scilicet redimendos. Viscerum Christi crebrain Evangelio sit mentio:quorum assiduè meminisse debemus,quibus visceralis,& cordialis,ita loquar,hoc est,summa & infinita ejus erga genus humanum charitas atque misericordia designatur. Hæc exta sunt verè lustralia, quibus lustnamur: hæc sunt certissima æternæ nostræ salutis præsagia atque indicia: hujusmodi ἀπολύτρωσιν οικτιρμῶν, viscera misericordiarum, nos quoque debemus ἐοῦ ὑστ-ρον sit, idest, induere, Christi videlicet exemplo & imitatione misericordes esse, benigni atque beneficci ergaproximum : non συγκλειστὰ ἀλλαγὰ, præcludere viscera nostra atque præcordia fratri,qui opus est indigus, sed ejus commiseratione tangi,eiq;opem ferre: ut nos Paulus hortatur surs,Colos.3.
units.tr: Gods were consecrated not only the external but also the internal parts of the victims, such as the viscera, intestines, the heart-region, and the entrails. For they were accustomed to examine these carefully and curiously, to inspect, probe and scrutinise them, to foretell future things from them, to cook them, to cut the sinews, and to offer them, that is, to cast them, on the altar or hearth, and so burn them. By this ceremony they thought they gained great favour from their gods; and so they called these entrails of theirs "lustral." On the contrary, we Christians ought to consider and contemplate diligently, attentively and continually the viscera and bowels of God the Father in heaven and of his only begotten Son, both for our teaching and for our consolation, according to Luke 1: "Through the tender mercy of our God, the dayspring from on high has visited us," that is, Christ, the Son of God, that Sun of righteousness, rising from on high, that is, from heaven, has visited us wretched men out of the innermost and, as it were, visceral mercy of God the Father (which Paul calls "the bowels of Jesus Christ" in Philippians 1), and has come in the flesh, to redeem us. In the Gospel there is frequent mention of the bowels of Christ, which we ought always to remember, since by them his visceral and heartfelt, if I may so speak, that is, his supreme and infinite love and mercy towards mankind, is signified. These are truly the lustral entrails by which we are cleansed; these are the most certain presages and signs of our eternal salvation. Such bowels of mercies we too ought to "put on" [ἐνδύσασθε], that is, to be merciful, kind and beneficent towards our neighbour, following the example and imitation of Christ; not to "shut up" [κλείσῃ] our bowels and hearts against a brother who is in need, but to be moved by his distress and bring him help, as Paul exhorts us in Colossians 3: "put on bowels of mercy" [σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμοῦ].

units.la: Et hæc de animalium sacrificiis, quæ non nisi animalibus verè mortuis, Dijs suis placere, eosq;placare existimabant.Hiigitur animalium, atque etiam hominum mactatorum mortes magnam Deos propitiandi & peccata expiandi vim habere sibi persuadebant,cùm illa sacrificiari-tibus contra essent reverâ mortifera,hoc est,non vitam,sed mortem potiùs illis æternam adserrent. At nos Christiani solam Christi mortem credimus atque confitemur vitam nobis & salutem æternam peperisse,uosq; morte illa æterna,quæ peccatis est stipendium, liberasse.Unde Paulus i. Thess.5. Mortuus est, inquit, Christus pro nobis,ut sive vigilemus, sive dormiamus, unà cum illo viv amus. Idem ad Rom.5. Christus pro nobis adhuc infirmis,& suis inimicis mortuus est. Si igitur cùm essemus inimici, Deo reconciliati sumus per mortem filii ejus, multò magis, nunc reconciliati, servabimur in vita ejus.Idem Apostolus Christi mortem nostram vocat ἀπολύτρωσιν, id est redemptionem, ad Hebr.9. Et ad Colos.1. Christi corpus, carnem atq; mortem conjungens,iis Deo nos reconciliatos esse ait. Verba ejus hæc sunt: Ἀποκατηλλάξεν ( scilicet Deus nos) ἐν τῷ σώματι τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ διὰ τοῦ θανάτου, hoc est, reconciliavit nos in corpore carnis suæ (corpore verè humano & mortali) per mortem. Sic idem Christum dicit factum esse obedientem Deo ad mortem usque: & quidem mortem crucis. Quemadmodum autem Christus pro nobis nostrâ salute mortuus est, sic nos quoq; peccatis mori,& justitiæ Deo si verè,et mortemoppetere,ac vitam sanguinem ἡ, nostrum pro Christo profundere parati semper esse debemus.
units.tr: These things concern the sacrifices of animals, which they thought pleased their gods, and appeased them, only when the animals were truly dead. So they were persuaded that the deaths of animals, and even of men slaughtered, had great power to propitiate the gods and expiate sins, although those sacrifices were in truth deadly to those who offered them, that is, they brought them not life but rather eternal death. But we Christians believe and confess that Christ's death alone has brought us life and eternal salvation, and has freed us from that eternal death which is the wages of sin. Hence Paul says in 1 Thessalonians 5: "Christ died for us, so that whether we wake or sleep, we should live together with him." The same in Romans 5: "Christ died for us while we were still weak and his enemies. If, therefore, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, now reconciled, we shall be saved in his life." The same Apostle calls Christ's death our redemption [ἀπολύτρωσιν], that is, redemption, in Hebrews 9. And in Colossians 1 he says that by the body of his flesh and by death, we have been reconciled to God. His words are: "He has reconciled us [ἀποκατήλλαξεν] in the body of his flesh [ἐν τῷ σώματι τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ] through death [διὰ τοῦ θανάτου]," that is, reconciled us in the body of his flesh (truly human and mortal) through death. Likewise, the same Apostle says that Christ was made obedient to God even unto death, and indeed the death of the cross. And just as Christ died for us for our salvation, so we too ought always to be ready to die to sin and to live to God, if truly, and to face death, and to pour out our life and blood for Christ.

units.la: Persæ,ut suprà ex Strabone & Eustathio diximus,non putabant fas esse Dijs animalia corpora atq; carnem immolare:quippe quos animalium tantum anima putabant esse contentos,& in ea acquiescere. At nos Christiani dicere possumus, Christum Dominum nostrum & corpus atque sanguinem & animam suam pro nobis Patri suo cœlesti obtulisse,secundum illa Ioh.1.epist.c.4.3. Lustue animam suam pro nobis posuit.Vt igitur corpus: sic animam quoq; suam, verè humanâ san guissimam,multis doloribus,priusquam ex corpore ipsius sacrosanctâ exceederet,angi,afflgi, atq; excruciari voluit: ne sustantur illa ejus verba: Anima mea contristata est,usq; ad mortem.Sic ipse tur & anima & corpore pro nobis patì volúit, ut perfestissimus esset & animarum & corporum nostrorum Servator.
units.tr: The Persians, as we said above on the authority of Strabo and Eustathius, did not think it lawful to offer the bodies and flesh of animals to the gods, since they held that the souls of animals alone were enough and were content with that. But we Christians can say that Christ our Lord offered to his heavenly Father his body, his blood and also his soul for us, according to 1 John 3 ("Ille animam suam pro nobis posuit"; "he laid down his soul for us"). So, just as he willed his body, he also willed his soul, which was truly human, to be troubled, afflicted and tormented by many sorrows before it departed from his most holy body, so that those words would stand: "My soul is sorrowful, even unto death." Thus he willed to suffer for us in both soul and body, so that he might be the most perfect Saviour of both our souls and our bodies.

units.la: Porró praeter Animalia Ethnici Dius suis etiam e terris nascentia, hoc est, omnis generis plantas, ut herbas, gramina, flores, arbores, fruticés, suffrutices, fruges atq; fructus obtulerunt. Atque haec quidem Gentes omnium antiquissima Diisq; gratissima, ac prima censuerunt esse sacrificia, de quo Porphyrius libro 2. de sacrificiis. Nos in sacris literis prima sacrificia fuisse legimus Abelis & Caini, fratrum germanorum: quorum unus, Abel nimirum, ex primogenitis sui gregis: Cainus ex fructibus terrae Deo munus obtulit: ac Abelis quidem munus, licet cruentum, tamen propter fidem Deo gratum fuit. Cains autem, quia malus erat, nec animus fidei expers, ei fuit odiosum: unde postea horrendum & immane illud fratricidium fuit consecutum.
units.tr: Besides animals, the Gentiles also offered to their gods what grows from the earth: plants of every kind, such as herbs, grasses, flowers, trees, shrubs, undershrubs, grains and fruits. The Gentiles judged these to be the most ancient of all sacrifices, the most pleasing to the gods, and the first, as Porphyry says in book 2 of his work On Sacrifices. In the sacred letters we read that the first sacrifices were those of Abel and Cain, full brothers. One of them, Abel, offered from the firstborn of his flock, while Cain offered a gift to God from the fruits of the earth. Abel's gift, although bloody, was pleasing to God because of his faith. But Cain, because he was evil and his mind was not free of unbelief, was hateful to God; and from this there followed afterwards that horrible and monstrous murder of his brother.

units.la: De utroque sacrificio scribit Tertullianus libro ad verses Iudaeos: Sic & sacrificia terrenarum oblationum, & spiritualium sacrificiorum praedicta oflendimus. Et quidem a primordio majoris filii, id est, Israel, terrena fuisse: in Cain praeoffensa sacrificia: & minoris filii Abel, id est, populi nofiri (Christiani) sacrificia de versa demonstrate. Nam, major natu Cain de fructu terrae obtulit munera Deo: minor vero filius, Abel, de fructu ovium suarum. Respexit Deus in Abel & munera ejus: in Cain autem & munera ejus non respexit. Ex hoc igitur duplicia duorum populorum sacrificia praefigurata jam nunc a primordio animad vertimus. Sacrificia carnalia veteris populi reprobata legimus Esaias, Malach, Psalm 50. & alibi: quae non nisi in terra promissionis & sanctae offerre fas erat. Sacrificia autem non terrena, sed spiritualia nobis populus nostri, Testamentum, quibus Deo litandum, sunt sacrificia laudis, vota (Psal. 50.) cor item contritum sacrificium Deo acceptabile (Psal. 49.) de quibus sacrificiis spiritalibus Malach. 1. Et omnis loco sacrificia munda offerentur nomini meo.
units.tr: Tertullian writes about both kinds of sacrifice in his book against the Jews: "So also we have shown beforehand the sacrifices of earthly offerings and of spiritual sacrifices. Indeed, from the beginning, the sacrifices of the elder son, that is Israel, were earthly; in Cain the sacrifices were foreshadowed, and in the younger son Abel, that is our people (the Christians), the sacrifices were shown to be spiritual. For Cain, the elder by birth, offered gifts to God from the fruit of the earth, but the younger son Abel offered from the fruit of his sheep. God looked upon Abel and his gifts, but he did not look upon Cain and his gifts. From this we have already observed from the beginning that the twofold sacrifices of the two peoples were prefigured." We read that the carnal sacrifices of the old people were rejected by Isaiah, Malachi, Psalm 50 and elsewhere; these could be offered lawfully only in the land of promise and in the holy place. But our people, the new Testament, offer not earthly but spiritual sacrifices, with which God is to be honoured: sacrifices of praise, vows (Psalm 50), and likewise a contrite heart, a sacrifice acceptable to God (Psalm 49). Of these spiritual sacrifices Malachi 1 says: "And in every place sacrifices shall be offered to my name, pure."

units.la: Ethnici autem ut certa animalium: sic plantarum quoq; arborumq; genera singula Diis consecrarunt, de quo supra. Nos autem Christiani et animalia, & plantas, & omnia reliqua vitae bona atq; subjecta, atq; adeo vitam ipsam soli Deo vero, seu bonorum omnium creatori & largitori, unico acceptum merito referimus & consecramus. Herbas, quas Dius sui offerre, & inilar. Nam cultu adhiberi fuerunt soliti, vulgo & Verbenas, quasi Herbenas, & Salvia, Xero & olea, id est, colendo, per synecdochen appellarunt (cum tamen haec ambo certarum herbarum sint nomina atq; genera) & in his potissimum numeraverunt myrtum, laurum, abeam, quae amoris, victoriae, pacis, aeternitatis symbola: quorum trium frequentissimum olim in sacris Gentium usus fuit. Nostra autem myrtus, laurus, oleum, id est, charitas, victoria, pax (ut paucis multa complectar) est Christus.
units.tr: The Gentiles consecrated to their gods not only certain kinds of animals but also single kinds of plants and trees, as said above. We Christians, however, refer and consecrate to the one true God, the Creator and Giver of all good things, the animals, the plants, all the other goods of life and subsistence, and life itself, as his gift alone. The herbs which the Gentiles offered to their gods, and the like, were commonly used in worship; they called verbena "herbena" by a kind of synecdoche, as if from cultivation (colendo), and likewise sage and olive, although these two are names and kinds of certain herbs. Among these they especially counted myrtle, laurel and olive as symbols of love, victory, peace and eternity. Of these three, the most frequent use in pagan rites was in former times. But our myrtle, laurel and oil, that is love, victory and peace (to embrace much in few words), is Christ.

units.la: Hi, ut modi autem herbas atq; plantas, earumq; partibus partim suffitus atq; thymiamata, earum prae-tendendo Diis suis fecerunt, partim in sis templis, altaria, fimalacra, victimas, & se denique ipsos in Deorum suorum honorem, conspergere atque ornare confuevernunt.
units.tr: Thus, just as they offered herbs and plants, and parts of them, partly as fumigations and incense, holding them before their gods, so they were accustomed partly to sprinkle and adorn with them the temples, altars, images, victims and finally themselves, in honour of their gods.

units.la: Ac quantum ad odores & odorimenta, chymiamata Graeci dicta attinet, Pagani ea, tanquam ad Deorum suorum honorem cultumq; maxime pertinentia, & quasi antiquitus ante animalium mactationes atq; sacrificia usurpari solita, plurimi fecerunt, usq; maximam Deos placandi vim assignarunt. Verum omnes huiusmodi cum foetidi & male olentes (cujusmodi fuerunt illi carnium, sanguinum, pinguium, foemorum, viscerum, aliarumq; hostiae partium adustarum, seu combustarum nidores atq; fumi) tum vel fragrantissimi & suavissimi quique ex herbis plantis, odoriferis, ex ture, ex cosio, ex cinnamomo, ex myrrha, ex casia, ex flarte & aliis id genera, suffitus & odores Deo ingratissimi fuerunt & odiosissimi. Nos contra Christiani firmissime credimus minime dubitamus, odorem, odorumentum atq; thymiama Deo gratissimum nobis, falsiferumesse Christum ejus sacrificium, qui, ut Paulus loquitur, παρέδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν προσφορὰν καὶ θυσίαν εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας, tradidit semetipsum pro nobis oblationem & sacrificium in odorem suavissimum et fragrantissimum.
units.tr: As for odours and perfumes, which the Greeks call thymiamata, the pagans made much of them, as pertaining most of all to the honour and worship of their gods, and as if they had been used of old before the slaughter of animals and sacrifices; they assigned to them the greatest power of appeasing the gods. But all such things, both the foul and ill-smelling (such as the stench and smoke of the flesh, blood, fat, thighs, entrails and other burnt or scorched parts of victims) and also the most fragrant and sweetest odours from aromatic herbs and plants, from frankincense, cassia, cinnamon, myrrh, cassia, nard and the like, were most unpleasing and hateful to God. We Christians, on the contrary, firmly believe and do not doubt that the odour, perfume and incense most pleasing to God for us is Christ, and his sacrifice, who, as Paul says, "gave himself up for us as an offering and a sacrifice for a fragrant odour" [παρέδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν προσφορὰν καὶ θυσίαν εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας]: he delivered himself for us as an offering and sacrifice of most sweet and fragrant odour.

units.la: Et igitur antiquissimum illud Noachi sacrificium, quod ex omni fere animalium genere post horrendum funestum, illud diluvium, Deo obtulit, ex dicitur fuisse sacrificium boni odoris: sed multo magis hoc Christi sacrificium (cujus illud Noachi sacrificium umbra quaedam tantum fuit, sed admirabilis) qui non animalia, non homines, sed seipsum Deo patri suo obtulit pro Mundi vita, sacrificium fuit Deo suavissimi odoris, quo ille placatus est generis humano: cui propter peccata inimicissimus merito ac infensissimus fuerat. Hoc ipsum autem Christi et sacrificii ejus praeconium sive praedicatio Evangelica, credentibus quidem; eis, qui jam ita fiunt, εἰς ἐνωδία, id est, odor bonus & suavis, & odor vitae ad vitam, id est, vitalis & salutaris: non credentibus autem & iis, qui pereunt, odor est mortis ad mortem, id est, mortifer & exitialis, ut Paullus docet 2. Cor. 2. Unde hunc locum Gregorius Nyssenus scite admodum sic explicat: Quemadmodum, inquit, unguenta columbis addunt robur, fcarabaeos autem necant: sic Christi & Evangelii de Christo divinus odor pius quidem est salutis: impius autem exitio. Huc quoque referri possunt illa Cantici quarto, ubi odor vestimentorum & unguentorum Sponsi, id est, Christi, dicitur suavitate sua superare quaevis tura & aromata. Et 7. cap. eiusdem libri, Odor oris ejus dicitur esse quasi odor malorum. Propter hoc ipsum Christi thymiama & odoramentum Deo gratissimum, grata Deo sunt Christianorum quoque thymiamata spiritualia: cujusmodi sunt, Collectae & eleemosynae, boni operis, & fideles, tum in pauperes & inopes conferuntur, ex misericordia profectae: unde etiam eleemosynae dicuntur τὰ ἰλάσεις appellantur. Sic Paullus ad Philipp. 4. hujusmodi dona atque munera vere pia religiosa oblatio, id est, odorem suavitatis, odoris suavitatis, ad Deum, id est, odorem suavitatem, & hostiam Deo gratam & acceptam vocat. Unde idem ad Hebr. ult. ... Beneficentiae & liberalitatis, inquit, nolite oblivisci. Talibus enim sacrificiis placatur Deus. Preces similiter piorum odores, odoramenta sive thymiamata Deo gratissima appellantur Apocal. 5. Unde etiam Paullus ad Hebr. 13. ... Per ipsum (Christum) offerimus sacrificium laudis semper & ubique Deo, hoc est, fructum labiorum (Psal. 50. vitulis labiorum vocantur) confitentium nomini ejus. Echae de thymiamatis seu odoramentis Gentilium sacris; quibus non incommode subnecti possent unguenta, atque coronae sive corollae. Gentes igitur varia habuerunt & multiplicia ἀρώματα unguina, sive unguenta sacra, prosperitate & odorata, quibus in personarum, templorum, altarium, & idolorum initiationibus & consecrationibus fuerunt usi. Nos Christiani ἰσμα nostrum habemus a Sanctospiritu, ut Iohannes epist. 1. cap. 2. aic. Unde etiam nomen nostrum habemus. Christus nostrum, hoc est, unguentum, sive unctio nostra est Spiritus sanctus & χρίσματα nostra sunt Spiritus sancti ἀρώματα, id est, dona atque munera, quibus initiamur, inauguramur consecramur Deo. Unde Iohannes loco illo citato: ὑμεῖς τὸ χρῖσμα, ὃ ἐλάβετε ἀπ' αὐτοῦ, ἐν ὑμῖν μένει ... Sed unguentum, quod accepisties ab eo (Christo) in vobis manet: et non opus vobis est, ut quis vos doceat: sed sicut illud ipsum unguentum sive unctio (id est, Spiritus sanctus) docet vos de omnibus. Sic Christus, qui ab ipso unguento nomen habet, eodem Apostolo teste, in Evangelio promittit suis suum spiritum, ceu doctorem atq; doctorem fidissimum. Coronarum similiter apud Gentes in sacrificiis, in ludis in festivitatibus quibusvis maximus & frequentissimus usus fuit, de quo legere licet Tertulliani librum de Corona militis. Fuerunt autem coronae illae sacrae Gentilium antiquitus graminea, florea, herbidae, ex graminibus floribus herbis, ex arboribus frondibus, ramis, foliis, praesertim ex myrto, lauro, oleo confici fuerunt solitae. Hisce autem coronis sive corollis & idolis, & sacerdotes, & altaria, & foci, & hostiae ornari, decorari ve confuerunt. Has etiam in ignem nonnunquam conjicere atq; comburere fuerunt soliti. In Actis Apostolicis legimus Iovis sacerdotem, qui erat ante civitatem, una cum populo taurus & στέμματα, id est, coronas attulisse, quos Paullo & Barnabae, tanquam Diis, immolare volentes impium ipsorum conatum sanctissimi illi Apostoli sciss vestibus, magna contentione repellerunt. Ipse denique fores, inquit Tertullianus, ipse arae & hostiae, ipsi ministri & sacerdotes eorum (Ethnicorum) coronantur. Idem: Caeterum a sacrato coronantur & lupa, varia & lares, & piscinae, & carceres, & ludi, & ipsa amphitheatra, & ipsa spolia, ipsaeque lumina. Sed de hoc antiquo coronarum apud Gentes usu, & sacro & profano, sive superstitioso & luxurioso & libidinoso vide multa apud eundem Tertullianum eodem in libro. Vnum hic tantum addam de foribus, ostia sive ianuis, & sacrarum & profanarum adium, quas sacras habitas, sanctè religioseque cultas ac Dijs quibusdam fuisse consecratas apud Gentes constat. Tertullianus eodem libro: At enim Christianus, inquit, nec ianuam suam laurea infamabit, si noris, quantos Deos etiam ostiis Diabolus affixerit. Ianum a janua, Limentinum a limine, Forculum & Cardeam a foribus & cardinibus, ut apud Graecos Thyreum Apollinis & Dii coelios daemones. Idem in libro de Idololatria: Ergo, inquit, Deihonos est lucerna pro foribus, & laurus in postibus, non utiq, quod Dei bonor est, sed quod eius, qui pro Deo eius modis officium bonorature: quantum in manifesto est, salva operatione, quae est in occulto ad Daemonia pertinens. Certi enim esse debemus, si quos latet per ignorantiam literaturae secularis, etiam ostiorum Deos apud Romanos, Cardeam a cardinibus appellatam, & Forculum a foribus, & Limentinum a limine, & ipsum Ianum a janua, & utiq, scimus, licet nomina inania atq; conficta sint, cum tamen ad superstitionem deducuntur, rapere ad se Daemonia et omnem spiritum immundum per conspectus obligamentum. Aliquin Daemonia nullum nomen habent singulatum, sed ibi nomen inveniunt, ubi & pignus. Etiam apud Graecos Apollinis Supaicv, & aneleos Daemonas ostiorum praesides legimus. Haec igitur ab initio praevidens Spiritus sanctus, etiam ostia in superstitionem ventura praecinuit per antiquissimum prophetam Enoch. Nam & alia ostia in balneis adorari videmus. Sin autem sunt, quae m ostiis adorentur, ad eos & lucernae, & laureae pertinebunt. Idolo fecerit, quidquid ostio fecerit. Et haec de forum, ostiorum, januarum, superstitioso apud Gentes cultu. Nobis vero Christianis Christus, ut ipsemet testatur, unica est Janua, ostium, porta, fores, cardo atq, limen ad regnum coelorum, vitam & coelestem & aeternam.
units.tr: And so that most ancient sacrifice of Noah, which he offered to God from almost every kind of animal after that horrible and deadly flood, is said to have been a sacrifice of sweet savour. But Christ's sacrifice is far more so. Noah's sacrifice was only a shadow of it, though a wonderful one. Christ did not offer animals or men but himself to God his Father for the life of the world. This was a sacrifice of most sweet savour to God, by which God was appeased toward the human race, which had deservedly been most hostile and bitterly angry toward it because of its sins. Now this very proclamation of Christ and of his sacrifice, the preaching of the Gospel, is to believers, and to those who are being made believers, "a good and sweet odour" [εἰς εὐωδίαν], "and the odour of life unto life," that is, vital and saving. But to unbelievers and to those who perish it is "the odour of death unto death," that is, deadly and destructive, as Paul teaches in 2 Cor. 2. Gregory of Nyssa explains this passage very aptly: "Just as ointments give strength to doves but kill beetles, so the divine odour of Christ and of the Gospel concerning Christ is indeed a pious thing for salvation, but for the impious it is ruin." This passage may also be related to what is said in the fourth chapter of the Song, where the odour of the garments and ointments of the Bridegroom, that is, of Christ, is said by its sweetness to surpass all incense and spices. And in the seventh chapter of the same book, the odour of his mouth is said to be like the odour of apples. For this very reason, the incense and fragrance of Christ, most pleasing to God, make the spiritual incense of Christians also pleasing to God. Of this kind are collections and alms, the works of goodness and faith, which are bestowed upon the poor and needy, proceeding from mercy; whence alms are also called "propitiations" [τὰ ἱλάσεις]. Thus Paul, in Phil. 4, calls such gifts and offerings, truly pious and religious, "an odour of sweet smell," and a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God. Whence the same Apostle, in the last chapter of Hebrews, says: "Do not forget beneficence and liberality, for with such sacrifices God is appeased." Likewise the prayers of the pious are called the most pleasing odours, fragrances or incense to God, in Rev. 5. Whence Paul also says in Heb. 13: "Through him (Christ) let us offer the sacrifice of praise always and everywhere to God, that is, the fruit of lips (called 'calves of the lips' in Psal. 50) of those confessing his name." Next, concerning the incense or fragrances of the sacred rites of the Gentiles, to which ointments and garlands or wreaths could not inappropriately be joined. The Gentiles therefore had various and manifold sacred anointings and perfumed ointments, which they used in the initiations and consecrations of persons, temples, altars and idols. We Christians have our anointing from the Holy Spirit, as John says in his first epistle, chapter 2. Whence we also have our name. Our Christ, that is, our ointment or anointing, is the Holy Spirit, and our chrisms are the spiritual fragrances of the Holy Spirit, that is, the gifts and benefits by which we are initiated, inaugurated and consecrated to God. Whence John, in the passage cited: "The anointing which you have received from him abides in you... But the anointing which you received from him (Christ) abides in you, and you have no need that anyone teach you, but as that same anointing (that is, the Holy Spirit) teaches you concerning all things." [ὑμεῖς τὸ χρῖσμα, ὃ ἐλάβετε ἀπ' αὐτοῦ, ἐν ὑμῖν μένει] So Christ, who has his name from the ointment itself, as the same Apostle testifies, promises in the Gospel his Spirit to his own, as their teacher and most faithful counsellor. Likewise among the Gentiles there was the greatest and most frequent use of garlands in sacrifices, in games and in all kinds of festivities, about which one may read Tertullian's book On the Soldier's Garland. Those sacred garlands of the Gentiles were in ancient times commonly made of grass, flowers or herbs, of leaves or boughs, branches and foliage from trees, especially of myrtle, laurel and olive. With these garlands or wreaths, the idols, priests, altars, hearths and victims were used to be adorned and decorated. Sometimes they were also in the habit of throwing these into the fire and burning them. In the Acts of the Apostles we read that the priest of Jupiter, who was before the city, brought oxen and garlands [στέμματα] to the gates, together with the people, wishing to sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas as gods; but those most holy Apostles, tearing their clothes, with great vehemence drove back their impious attempt. Tertullian says: "Indeed the very doors, the altars and the victims, the very ministers and priests of the Gentiles are crowned." And again: "Moreover, by the same token, the wolf, the crossroads, the lares, the fishponds, the prisons, the games, and the amphitheatres themselves, the spoils themselves and the lamps themselves, are crowned." But concerning this ancient use of garlands among the Gentiles, both sacred and profane, or superstitious, luxurious and lustful, see much in the same Tertullian in the same book. I will add only one thing here about doors, gates or thresholds of sacred and profane buildings, which it is established were regarded as sacred among the Gentils, and were devoutly and religiously worshipped and consecrated to certain gods. Tertullian in the same book: "But the Christian, he says, will not disgrace his door with laurel, if you know how many gods the Devil has fastened even to doors. Janus from janua (door), Limentinus from limen (threshold), Forculus and Cardea from the fores and cardines (hinges), as among the Greeks Thyreus of Apollo, and the heavenly gods are demons." The same in his book On Idolatry: "Therefore, he says, the lamp before the doors and the laurel on the door-posts are an honour to a god, not indeed because it is the honour of God, but because of him who by such means claims the office of honour for himself in the place of God, while his operation, which pertains to demons, lies hidden. For we must be certain that if anyone is ignorant of secular literature, the Romans also have gods of doors: Cardea, named from the hinges, and Forculus from the doors, and Limentinus from the threshold, and Janus himself from the door; and we know that although these names are empty and invented, yet when they are drawn into superstition, demons and every unclean spirit are drawn to themselves through the bond of sight. Otherwise demons have no single name of their own, but they find a name where also they find a pledge." We read also that among the Greeks there were the demons of Apollo, Thyraeus and Aneleos, guardians of doors. Therefore the Holy Spirit, foreseeing these things from the beginning, also foretold through the most ancient prophet Enoch the doors that were to come into superstition. For we also see other doors worshipped in baths. But if there are things which are worshipped at doors, the lamps and laurels will pertain to them too. Whatever is done to a door is done to an idol. And these things about the superstitious worship of doors, gates and thresholds among the Gentiles. But for us Christians, Christ, as he himself testifies, is the one door, gate, porta, fores, hinge and threshold to the kingdom of heaven, to heavenly and eternal life.

units.la: Pro coronis autem illis Gentium atque fertis, sive gnaminis, floreis, herbidis, frondosis, sive etiam aureis, argenteis, gemmatis, aut ex quacunque alia vel pretiosissima materia confectis, nos primum Christi habemus coronam spineam, quae nobis aeternam ac coelestem illam coronam peperit. Quemadmodum autem spineam primum gesta est coronam, ac deinde coelestem illam coronam sunt consecutus (Unde Apostolus ad Hebr. 2. Christum dicit fuisse ἀνάστασιν τὸ ἀπόλυσον δόξη καὶ τιμῇ ἐστεφανωμένον, per passionem gloria & honore coronatum & ornatum:) sic nobis quoque portantibus primum in hoc Mundo spineam illam Christi coronam, hoc est, pie patienterque quasi afflictionem, hoc est religionis nomine ferentibus confecto tandem vitae huius curriculo atque certamine, repositae est in coelis, certoque speranda & exspectanda ἀναμένειν illa δικαίας, id est, immarcescibilis & aeterna gloriae ac beatitudinis corona, ut eam Petrus vocat 1.ep. 4. cap. Sic Paullus epist.2. ad Tim.4. Certamen bonum certavi, inquit, cursum consumavi, fidem servavi. Reliquum est, quod repositum mihi est corona justitiae, quam reddet mihi Dominus in illo die justus judex, nec mihi tantum, sed omnibus, qui amant ejus adventum. De eadem corona loquitur Apostolus Jacobus in sua epistola cap.1. Beatus, inquit, vir, qui suffert tentationem. Nam tentatione probatus coronam vitae accipiet: quae tamen corona spinae illi Christi corona, hoc est, mortis atque passioni acerbissimae & divinae gratiae atque miserieordiae accepta est ferenda. Sic ille quoque Ecclesiae Apostolice ac primigenie Protomartyr Stephanus (quod nomen coronam sonat) lapidea primum corona oneratus & afflictus, idest, lapidibus obrutus, ac demum illi ornatus fuit. His adde, quod pii quoque & fideles ipsi pastorum & doctorum Ecclesiae Corona, id est, decus & ornamentum appellantur (sic enim Paullus Philippensis suam vocat coronam:) unde vicissim doctores atq, pastores Ecclesiae (siquidem probe fungantur suo munere & officio) ipsae Ecclesiae corona, hoc est, ornamentum, verissime dici possunt.
units.tr: Instead of those garlands and wreaths of the Gentiles, whether of grass, flowers, herbs or leaves, or even of gold, silver or jewels, or made of any other most precious material, we first have the thorny crown of Christ, which brought us that eternal and heavenly crown. Just as Christ first bore the thorny crown and afterwards obtained that heavenly crown (whence the Apostle in Heb. 2 says that Christ was "crowned with glory and honour" [δόξῃ καὶ τιμῇ ἐστεφανωμένον] through suffering), so for us too, who first bear in this world that thorny crown of Christ, that is, who piously and patiently endure affliction, and who bear it in the name of religion, when the course and struggle of this life is at last finished, there is laid up in heaven, to be surely hoped for and awaited, that unfading [ἀμάραντον] and eternal crown of righteousness and blessedness, as Peter calls it in 1 Ep. 4 chap. Thus Paul in 2 Ep. to Tim. 4: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day, and not to me only, but to all who love his appearing." The Apostle James speaks of this same crown in his epistle, chapter 1: "Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been proved by temptation he will receive the crown of life." Yet that crown of life is to be received only by bearing that thorny crown of Christ, that is, through death and most bitter suffering, and through divine grace and mercy. So also Stephen, the first martyr of the apostolic and primitive Church (whose name means "crown"), was first burdened and afflicted with a stony crown, that is, overwhelmed with stones, and at last was adorned with that crown. To these things add that the pious and faithful themselves are called the crown, that is, the glory and ornament, of the ministers and teachers of the Church (for so Paul calls the Philippians his crown). Whence, conversely, the teachers and ministers of the Church (provided they discharge their office and duty well) may most truly be called the crown, that is, the ornament, of the Church itself.

units.la: Sed ut ulterius hoc ex plantis sacrificiorum genus persequamur, panes quoque, placentas, luba, aliaque id generis edulia, ex frugibus atque fructibus confecta, Ecbnici Dijs suis supplices perstitiosissimè obtulerunt. Pro illis omnibus nos Christum habemus, qui seipsum panem, panem verum, panem coelestem, e coelis delapsum, panem vitae, panem virum & vivificum appellavit, quem qui manducant, in eum nimirum credendo, vitam habent aeternam. Christus igitur solus nostrer est panis, quo vere pascimur ad vitam aeternam: est sua placenta, quae sola Deo placet, ejusque iram placavit, & idcirco sola, tanquam unica salutis nostrae causa nobis placere debet, ut in illa sola acquiescamus. Libam quoque eandem ob causam (sive a Libet nomen illud volimus esse deductum) potest appellari, propterea quod ille pro nostra salute in ara crucis libatus, nobis merito solus, si salus nostra nobis cure est, debet allubescere.
units.tr: But let us pursue this kind of sacrifice further. The Ethnici also offered to their gods, with superstitious devotion, loaves, cakes, luba, and other such foods made from grain and fruit. For all these we have Christ, who called himself the bread, the true bread, the heavenly bread come down from heaven, the bread of life, the living and life-giving bread. Those who eat it, that is, who believe in him, have eternal life. Christ alone, therefore, is our bread, by which we are truly fed to eternal life. He is also the cake that alone pleases God and has appeased his wrath, and for that reason he alone, as the sole cause of our salvation, ought to please us, so that we may rest in him alone. He may also be called the libum for the same reason (whether we prefer to derive that name from libet, "it pleases"), because he was offered as a libation on the altar of the cross for our salvation, and so, if our salvation is a concern to us, he alone ought rightly to attract us.

units.la: Porro ut & carnibus & frugibus & fructibus & plantenis atq; edulijs variis, inde confectis, surdè eorundem situm, liquorum quorundam profusionibus (quæ Libationes dicta) extinguere voluerunt, secundum illa Lactantii Institut. divin. lib. 6. cap. 2. Malunt igitur, inquis, opimas & pingues bostias Deo, quasi furenti, profundunt vina, tanquam sitienti, accendunt lumina, velut in tenebris agenti. Libationum istarum (de quibus supra pluribus) materia fuit aqua, lac, mel, vinum, oleum. Omnium illarum libationum superstitiosum usum loto nobis Christianos ad sultancem nostram satis superq; est ac sufficit unica illa, ut summatim dicam, Christi L. barto, hoc est, sanctissimi Scriptis sanguinis in ara crucis profusio, qui sanguis, & aqua, & vinum, & oleum, & lac, & mel nostrum est suavissimum & saluberrimum, & ad salutem nostram invincem. Verum operæpretium erit sigillatim singula persequi.
units.tr: Moreover, the Gentiles wished to quench their thirst, as it were, with the pouring out of certain liquids (called libations), and also to satisfy the meats, grains, fruits, plants and various foods made from them. So Lactantius, Divine Institutes book 6, chapter 2: "You say that they prefer to offer rich and fat victims to God, as if he were raging; they pour out wines, as if he were thirsty; they kindle lights, as if he were acting in darkness." Of these libations (discussed at length above) the matter was water, milk, honey, wine, and oil. For us Christians, the one thing, to put it briefly, is enough and more than enough to replace the superstitious use of all those libations: the washing of Christ, that is, the outpouring of his most holy blood on the altar of the cross. This blood, together with water, wine, oil, milk and honey, is most sweet and most healthful for us, and is for our salvation. But it will be worthwhile to go through each of these one by one.

units.la: Ac ut aqua exordiar, quibus primitus libationes sistere fieri fuisse solitas Ethnici tradiderunt, illarum olim apud Gentiles in sacrificiis & toto illorum cultu summum maximum fuit usus (ut ex superioribus patet, quibus magnam personas, acres quasque lustrandi atq; purgandi & peccata expiandi vim tribuerunt: unde etiam Lustrales & Lustrice ab illis fuerunt appellata. At Christiana norum aquæ verè lustrales, lustricæ, purgatoriæ, vivæ & vivificæ, corpora animosq; ipsorum purgandi sanctificandi, lustrandi, reficiendi & recreandi, vivificandi, peccata, eluendi & expiandi reste facta scripturæ, vim habentes, sunt sanguis Christi, Spiritus sanctus, Verbum Dei, quorum sacramentum atq; sigillum est sacrosanctâ illa aquæ Baptismalis & initialis, quam & ipsam ideo verè aquam lustralem, sexlustricam appellare possumus, secundum illa verba Petri epistolæ prio re cap. 3. ὁ ἐκ ἀρὼ φαρμιοῦ ἀπὸ ... Christ. Cui rei nunc correspondens existat Baptismus nos quoq; servat (non quo carnis sordes abjiciuntur, sed stipulatio bonæ conscientiæ apud Deum) per resurrectionem Iesu Christi.
units.tr: To begin with water, with which the Gentiles reported that libations were first made: among the Gentiles, water had the highest and greatest use in their sacrifices and in their whole worship, as is clear from what was said above, where they attributed great power to water to cleanse and purify persons and places and to expiate sins. For this reason they also called it lustral and lustric. But the true lustral, purifying, cleansing, living and life-giving waters of Christianity, which have the power to cleanse and sanctify, purify, restore and refresh, quicken, wash away and expiate sins, both bodies and souls, are the blood of Christ, the Holy Spirit and the Word of God. The sacrament and seal of these is that holy baptismal and initiatory water, which we may rightly call the true lustral water, lustric water, according to the words of Peter in his first epistle, chapter 3: "which also now saves us, as an antitype, baptism" [ὃ καὶ ἡμᾶς ἀντίτυπον νῦν σῴζει βάπτισμα]. Corresponding to this, baptism now saves us also, not by the removal of the filth of the flesh, but as the pledge of a good conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.

units.la: Vina quoq; Gentes Dijs suis libare atque profundere consueverunt (de quorum delectu supra dictum.) Nostra vina, verè vitalia ac salutaria sunt sanguis Christi (cuius sacramentum sanguinis est vinum atque poculum illud Dominicum) ceu vitis verè, quæ vitam nobis æternam conciliant, cujus nos sumus palmites: est Spiritus sancti gratia: est Verbum divinum: quæ vina solum nostra æterne vitæ atq; salutis sitim explere atq; satiare, animosq; nostros peccatorum nostrorum conscientia senstuq; ire divinæ, pistratos & conflernatos recreare ing exhilarare possunt.
units.tr: The Gentiles also customarily poured out and offered wines to their gods (on the choice of which we have spoken above). Our wines, which are truly life-giving and salutary, are the blood of Christ (of which the sacrament is the wine and the Lord's cup); they are the true vine, which wins us eternal life, and of which we are the branches; they are the grace of the Holy Spirit and the divine Word. These wines alone can satisfy and quench the thirst for our eternal life and salvation, and can refresh and cheer our souls, which are crushed and dismayed by the consciousness of our sins and the sense of divine wrath.

units.la: Præterea pro latte illo ab Ethnicis in sacrificiis atq; libationibus adhibiti solito, quo sup pos, ut ita loquar, quasi ipse quadam vana & inani lactarunt, dum magni existimarunt sea Dijs suis inire posse gratiam, nos Christiani habemus lac illud λογικον & ἀδολον, id est, rationale, dolo expers; quod est Verbum Dei, quodq; S. Petrus epistola prioris, cap. 2. nos jubet ὡς ἀρτι ... hementer desiderare, ut in eo resecamus, &c.
units.tr: Furthermore, in place of the milk that the Gentiles used in their sacrifices and libations, supposing, as it were, that by some vain and empty means they had been nursed by their gods, while they thought they could gain the favour of their gods by it, we Christians have that milk which is logikon and adolon, that is, rational and free from guile, which is the Word of God. Peter in his first epistle, chapter 2, bids us to desire it earnestly, "as newborn babes" [ὡς ἄρτι γεννηθέντα βρέφη ἐπιποθήσατε], so that we may grow by it, etc.

units.la: Similiter pro melle, mulso atque favis Ethnicorum, quibus Deos suos delinire atque demulce re sepolcre existimabant, nobis Christianis est mel a ipsum nomen Iesu Christi, quo vis melle, mulso, atq; favis dulcius ac salutarius, in quo solo nostra salus est posita, secundum illa Petri verba in Actis Apostolicis cap. 4. ... Nec est in alio quoquam salus. Nec enim aliud nomen (quam Christus) sub cœlo, quod datu hit inter homines, p quod oporteat salvari.
units.tr: Likewise, in place of the honey, mead and honeycombs of the Gentiles, with which they believed they could soothe and sweeten their gods, we Christians have the honey, which is the very name of Jesus Christ, sweeter and more healthful than any honey, mead or honeycomb, in whom alone our salvation is laid up. So Peter's words in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 4: "Neither is there salvation in any other. For there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved."

units.la: De oleo quoq; ut apud Ethnicos in sacrificiis, libationibus, ac toto illorum cultu per vulgato supra satis multa. Pro illo itaq; Ethnicorum oleo olido, nos Christiani habemus oleum illud lætitiæ, quod est Spiritus sanctus: unde & Christus, qui est noster caput, & nos, qui sumus ejus corpus atq; membra Christiana appellamur: propterea quod ipse quidem plenè perfecitq;, nos autem ad mensura spi ritualis, lætifico salutarij, illo oleo delibuti atq; unbuti sumus, secundum illa Psalmi 102. quæ ad Hebr. cap. 1. allegantur: διὰ τοῦτο ἔχρισέν σε ὁ θεὸς ... Iudex in Deus, Deus tuus oleo exultationis supra consortes tuos. Oleum quoque sanans vulnera nostrorum peccatorum est Verbum Dei.
units.tr: As for oil, we have said enough above about its use among the Gentiles in sacrifices, libations and their whole worship. In place of that foul oil of the Gentiles, we Christians have that oil of gladness, which is the Holy Spirit. For this reason Christ, who is our head, and we, who are his body and members, are called Christians, because he indeed was fully anointed, while we, by the measure of the spiritual and joyful gift of salvation, are anointed and smeared with that oil. So the words of Psalm 102, which are cited in Hebrews chapter 1: "Therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows" [διὰ τοῦτο ἔχρισέν σε ὁ θεός, ὁ θεός σου, ἔλαιον ἀγαλλιάσεως παρὰ τοὺς μετόχους σου]. The oil that heals the wounds of our sins is also the Word of God.

units.la: Sal postremò, ut omnium ciborum condimentorum est pene necessarium: sic Ethnici quoq; il- lud omnium sacrificiorum suorum quasi condimentum duxerunt necessarium, quo sine Dijs litari minime possit. Pro illo autem Gentilinm sale insulso, insipido, ac tartaro, nobis Christianis sal sa- lucare est Verbum Dei, fidei ejus pracones. Sic Christus enim Apostolos suos Sal, terra appellavit. Matth. 5. Hoc sale, veré sapido ac salutifero quasi conditi atque conspersi, fideles immunes possunt esse ab æterna illa pnetredine atq; corruptione. Sic quoq; secundum fidelißimam Sanctii Panlli admonitionem sermo noster non insulsus & insipidus, sed est, insipiens, debet esse, sed sal ἐν ἑαυτῷ ἀλατι πρυρεῦ..., id est, gratiâ sanctis spiritus, tanquam sale conditus.
units.tr: Lastly, salt: as it is almost necessary for seasoning all foods, so the Gentiles also regarded it as a necessary seasoning for all their sacrifices, without which they could by no means make an offering to their gods. In place of that tasteless, insipid and saltless salt of the Gentiles, we Christians have the salt that saves, which is the Word of God, and its heralds of faith. For Christ so called his apostles the salt of the earth (Matt. 5). Seasoned and sprinkled, as it were, with this salt, which is truly savoury and salutary, believers can be free from that eternal putrefaction and corruption. Likewise, according to the most faithful admonition of St Paul, our speech should not be unsalted and insipid, but should be seasoned, as it were, with salt: "let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt" [ἐν χάριτι ἄλατι ἠρτυμένος]; that is, seasoned with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Pro mola item illa falsa Gentilinm atq, casta (sic enim illam falsò vocarit: cùm insulsareverâ fuerit & incèsta) nobis est Christus, pronobis immolatus, nostrum Pascha. 1.Cor. 5. Unde, ut ibidem nos monet Apostolus, expurgato veteri fermento, novæ simus conspersio. (ζύμωμα) & ἀζύμοι, id est, infermentati, hoc est, snoveiac x, καινῆς improbitatis & malitiæ experters, & contrà εἰλικρινείας, ἀληθείας, sinceritate & veritate praditi.
units.tr: Likewise, in place of that false and so-called chaste meal of the Gentiles (for it was falsely called so, since it was really unsalted and impure), we have Christ, who was sacrificed for us, our Passover (1 Cor. 5). Hence, as the Apostle admonishes us in the same place, having purged out the old leaven, we should be a new lump, unleavened [ἄζυμοι], that is, free from the old leaven and from malice and wickedness [κακίας καὶ πονηρίας], and on the contrary endowed with sincerity and truth [εἰλικρινείας καὶ ἀληθείας].

units.la: Inter Gentium antem sacrificia numerantur etiam Decimæ & Primitiæ cùm frugum, tum pecorum. Ac decimas quidem quarnm vè rerum Gentes Herculi tanquam pollucere (quod verbum proprié in hoc Herculis cultu antiquitus suic nsurpatum) hoc est, so vere atq; offerre consuevernnt. Unde Terinllianus in Apolog. De Decima, inquit, Herculi, nec tertiam partem in arum ejus imponitis. Plin. lib. 12. cap. 19. de Cinnamomo verba facit: Primumingę significant, illud in Æthiopia Troglodytide non meti, nisi Deus permiserit, quem lo'vem aliquâ intelligunt, illi Assabinum vocant: & 44. boum caprarnmq, & arietum exitu impetrari veniam metendi. Non tamen ante ortum Solis, aut post occasum metere licebat. Deinde sarmenta, inquit, hastâ dividiti sacerdos, Deoq; partem ponit: reliquam mercatorin nassas condit. His addit: Est & alia forma, cum Sole divisidi, cernatq; partes fieri, deinde sorte germina discerni. Quod Soli cesserit, relinqui, ac sponte conflagrare. Hinc rei Solinus quoque mentionem facit. Idem de ture Plinius scribit lib. 12. cap. 15. cujus pars decima Deo erat consecrata, ꝑ quam nisi sacerdos priist accepisset, illud mercatoribus vendere nō licebat. Plinii verba sunt: Ibi decimas Deo, quem vocat Sabin, mensurâ, non pondere, sacerdotes accipiunt: nec ante licet mercari. Credebantur autem augeri diviiatis illorum, qui decimam Herculi vovissent, teste Dionysio lib. 6. Macrob. 3. Saturn. cap. 12. Alexandro Neapolitano lib. 3. cap. 12. Hac persuasione Lucullus, Crassus, Sylla, auctore Plutarcho, & Orestes fenerator, ut testatur Cicero 2. Offic. bonis æstimatu decimam partè Hercnli confecrarunt. Et hæc de decimis Gentilium; quæ superioribus possunt addi. Nos verò Chri- stiani nostrarum frugum, fructuum, aliorumq; bonorum decimam, partemq; aliquam, secundum legem & mandatum diviinum recte pieq. pollucemus, offerimus & consecramus Christo, qui plusquam Herculeos pronostra salute labores atq, dolores exantla vit, adipsius ministros, quasi, vicariōs, hoc est, cùm ad Ecclesia sacrorum, antistites, tnm ad pauperes & inopes benigne liberàliter, aleudos ac fovendos. Deinde Christum ipsum Dominum & Servatorem nostrum relig& Decimam nostram appellare atq, consiteri possumus, quippe cum Deus pater illam pro uni versi genere- ris humani salute, quod peccato mortiq, æterna eræ obnoxium, quasi decimam, hoc est, Crucis gravissimum, ignominiofissimmq, supplicium subire sibi, sacrificium hoc modo fieri voluerit. Atq, adeo Christus ipse sua sponte lubenterq, Patris sui cœlestis voluntati obsecutus se ex toto genere hnmano, illud redimendi liberandiq, gratiâ, ad supplicium sacrificiumq, illud decimari sustinuit. Ergo nos quoq, demus operam, ut toti simus Dei decima, hoc est, ei de voti, addisti & consecrati.
units.tr: Among the sacrifices of the Gentiles are counted the tithes and first-fruits, both of crops and of livestock. The Gentiles were accustomed to offer, as it were to Hercules (a word used in antiquity specifically in this worship of Hercules), that is, to dedicate and present, the tenth of their goods. Hence Tertullian in his Apology: "Of the tithe, you give not even a third part to Hercules." Pliny, book 12, chapter 19, speaks of cinnamon: the first who enter there, they say, in the Troglodyte land of Ethiopia may not reap unless God permits it, whom they understand as some Jupiter, and whom they call Assabinus; and by the going out of forty-four oxen, goats and rams, they obtain pardon for reaping. Yet they were not allowed to reap before sunrise or after sunset. Then, he says, the priest divides the twigs with a spear and sets aside a portion for God; the rest the merchant stores in baskets. He adds: "There is also another form: when the sun has divided them, they see the parts made, and then the shoots are separated by lot. What falls to the sun is left and burns of its own accord." Solinus also mentions this matter. Pliny writes the same about frankincense in book 12, chapter 15, of which a tenth part was consecrated to God, and unless the priest had first received it, it was not lawful to sell it to merchants. Pliny's words are: "There the priests receive the tithes for God, whom they call Sabis, by measure, not by weight; nor is it lawful to trade before this." It was believed that the wealth of those who had vowed a tenth to Hercules would increase, as Dionysius witnesses in book 6; see also Macrobius, Saturnalia 3, chapter 12, and Alexander of Naples, book 3, chapter 12. By this belief Lucullus, Crassus and Sulla, according to Plutarch, and the moneylender Orestes, as Cicero attests in De Officiis 2, dedicated a tenth part of their goods, valued at what they were worth, to Hercules. So much for the tithes of the Gentiles, which may be added to what was said above. But we Christians, according to the law and command of God, shall rightly and piously offer, present and consecrate a tenth of our crops, fruits and other goods to Christ, who for our salvation endured far more than the labours and sorrows of Hercules, and to his ministers, as to his vicars: that is, both to the leaders of the Church's sacred things, and to the poor and needy, to be kindly, liberally, and faithfully supported. Further, we may call and confess Christ himself our Lord and Saviour to be our tithe, since God the Father willed that, for the salvation of the whole human race, which was liable to sin and eternal death, he should undergo as a tithe, that is, the most grievous and ignominious punishment of the cross, and that sacrifice be made in this way. And indeed Christ himself, willingly and of his own accord, obeying the will of his heavenly Father, endured to be tithed from the whole human race for the sake of ransoming and freeing it, enduring that punishment and sacrifice. Therefore let us also take care that we may be wholly God's tithe, that is, vowed, offered and consecrated to him.

units.la: Sed & Primitias (quas Hebræi רֵאשִׁית Reschith, Græci ἀπαρχὰς vocant) frugum, frustuum pecorum Deus suis gratitudinis suæ ergà ipsos testificande gratia Ethnici offerebant, quarum pars cedebat in usum sacrificantium. At verò nostræ Primitiæ prima ac principes Christus est, ut eum Paullus appellaet. Cor. 15. cujus hæc sunt verba: Nunc verò Christus surrexit e mortuis, ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων, primitiæ eorum, qui obdormiunt. Quoniam enim per hominem mors, etiam per hominem resurrectio mortuorum. Nam quemadmodum in Adamo omnes moriuntur: sic in Christo omnes ζωοποιηθήσονται, sive ad vitam revocabuntur, unusquisq; in pro- prio ordine atq, statu. Ἀπαρχὴ χριστὸς, ἔπειτα οἱ τοῦ χριστοῦ ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ αὐτοῦ, id est, Primi- tiæ Christus: deinde ii, qui sunt Christi in adventu ejus. Eandem ob caussam Christus ἀφεστοῦχ̈ρ, id est, primogenitus, πᾶσιν πρωτότοκος, omnis creatura dicitur, Hebr. 12. & ἀπαρχὴ πνευμάτων, Apocal. 1. primogenitus mortuorum. Deinde primitiae etiam Dei sunt omnes pii & fideles 1. Thess. 2. Primitias nos Deus elegit ad salutem: cui & gratias agere debemus. Sic Apoc. 14. Primitiae Deo & Agno, id est, Christo, appellantur, in quorum ore non est inventus dolus, qui sine macula sunt ante thronum Dei, qui empti sunt ex hominibus de terra, id est, redemti pretio Christi sanguine, qui virgines sunt, mulieribus non polluti, qui sequuntur Agnum, eiὰ in omnibus obsequuntur. Sic Hebr. 12. Ecclesia primogenitorum, qui in caelis scripti sunt, appellantur. Hi sunt, qui, ut idem Apostolus testatur ad Rom. 8. aut filii Dei, & per consequens, haeredes Dei, coheredes Christi, ᾿Απαρχὴν τῆς πνεύματος, id est, primitias Spiritus habentes in seipso, exspectantes adoptionem, liberationemq; sive redemptionem corporis sui. Honoremus item Deum, non Deos alienos, ut Salomon Prov. 3. docet, de nostra substantia & primitiis cunctis nostri proventus, ut impleatur horum nostra saturitate, & eorcularia quasi rumpantur prae nimia copia musti: id fit, quando partem illorum conferimus ad Dei cultum externum, ad eorum, qui sacris praesunt, & ad pauperum atq; inopum sustentationem.
units.tr: But the Gentiles also offered first-fruits (which the Hebrews call reshith and the Greeks aparchas) of the crops and the flocks, to show their gratitude toward God; part of these went to the use of those who sacrificed. Our first-fruits, however, are Christ, the first and chief of them, as Paul calls him, 1 Cor. 15, whose words are: "But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep [ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων]. For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead has also come through a man. For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive [ζωοποιηθήσονται], or called back to life, each in his own order and rank: Christ the firstfruits [ἀπαρχὴ χριστὸς], then those who belong to Christ at his coming." For this same reason Christ is called the firstborn [πρωτότοκος] of all creation, Heb. 12, and the firstfruits of the spirits, Apoc. 1, and the firstborn of the dead. Next, all the godly and faithful are also the firstfruits of God, 1 Thess. 2: "God chose us as firstfruits to salvation, for which we also ought to give thanks to him." So in Apoc. 14 the firstfruits are named as belonging to God and the Lamb, that is, Christ: "in whose mouth no deceit was found, who are without blemish before the throne of God, who were bought from among men, from the earth, that is, redeemed by the blood of Christ's price, who are virgins, not defiled with women, who follow the Lamb wherever he goes." So in Heb. 12 they are called the church of the firstborn, who are written in heaven. These are, as the same Apostle testifies in Rom. 8, either sons of God, and consequently heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, "having the firstfruits [ἀπαρχὴν] of the Spirit in themselves, waiting for adoption and the liberation or redemption of their body." Let us also honour God, not alien gods, as Solomon teaches in Prov. 3, with our substance and with the firstfruits of all our produce, so that our barns may be filled and our presses may burst with the excess of new wine. This is done when we contribute a part of these things to the external worship of God, to those who preside over the sacred things, and to the support of the poor and needy.

units.la: Omnibus ergo, ut alterum hoc meae Antichefeos membrum concludam, & quidem infinitis ac innumeris illis Ethnicorum sacrificiis, victimis, hostiis, oblationibus libationibus decimis, primitiis, donis, anathematis, atque muneribus quibus alienos & adulterinos illos suos Deos egregie fecolere, sibi, demereri exisfumabant, nos Christiani optimo meritissimo, jure non anteponimus folim infinitis partibus, sed etiam opponimus unicum illud Christi sacrificium, unicam illam victimam, hostiam, libationem, oblationem, quae semel certo definitoq; a Deo tempore facta, Christus tanquam sacerdos summus & maximus pro universi generis humani salute perlita vit: ut perspicue docet Apostolus in epistola ad Hebr. capite praesertim 9. & 10. Hoc ipsum perfectum, omnibusq; suis numeris absolutum sacrificium, ut & sacerdos ipse (quisimul & sacrificium & sacerdos fuit) herie est, & hodie: in ejus virtifica ac salutifera perpetua est ac perennis: quae se ad omnes omnium temporum atq; aetatum homines in Christum credentes & pie sanctèque viventes extendit atq; diffusa est. Huic uni & soli sacrificio (cujus quidem memoriam corde, ore atq; opere perpetuo colere atque celebrare debemus) in solidum verissime competunt atque conveniunt, & a nobis tribui debent illa, quae Paganifucata, adulterinis atque sacrilegis illis suis sacris & sacrificiis affinxerunt; de quibus supra in explicatione finium dictum est.
units.tr: So, to conclude this second member of my Antichefeos, all those countless sacrifices of the Gentiles, the victims, offerings, oblations, libations, tithes, first-fruits, gifts, votive offerings and presents, by which they used to worship their alien and counterfeit gods and try to win their favour, we Christians rightly and most deservedly not only prefer, by infinite degrees, but also set against them that single sacrifice of Christ, that single victim, offering, libation and oblation, which was made once, at a time fixed and determined by God, when Christ, as the supreme and greatest priest, was offered for the salvation of the whole human race. The Apostle teaches this clearly in his Epistle to the Hebrews, especially in chapters 9 and 10. This same sacrifice, perfect and complete in all its parts, is and remains today the same priest (who was at once both sacrifice and priest). Its life-giving and saving power is perpetual and everlasting, and it extends and is spread to all men of every time and age who believe in Christ and live piously and holily. To this one and only sacrifice (which we ought to honour and celebrate with perpetual memory in heart, mouth and deed) belong and fit in full, most truly, those things which the Papists have attached to their adulterous and sacrilegious sacrifices and rites, and which must be ascribed to Christ's sacrifice, as was said above in the explanation of the boundaries.

units.la: Hoc etenim Christi sacrificium verè perfectum, est ἱλαστήριον, id est, propitiatorium, seu placatorium: quo solo Christus nobis fuit propitiatus: unde & Christus ipse passim in sacris litteris ἱλαστικόν, & ἱλαστήριον est, propitiatio, propitiatorium, placatio, seu placamentum appellatur, & verbum ἱλάσκεσθαι, id est, propitiare ei sapissime tribuitur. Hoc Christi sacrificium verè perfectum, est εἰρηνικόν, sive εἰρηνοποιόν, id est, pacificatorium, pacificum: quo Deus nobis fuit placatus: unde Christus ipse saepe ειρην & εἰρηνοποιός, id est, pacificator, & pax ipsa appellatur, & cunctis in caelis & in terris εἰρηνοποιητικόν, pacificasse dicitur. Hoc Christi sacrificium verè est καταλλακτικόν, id est, reconciliatorium; quo homines Deo, & Deus hominibus reconciliatus fuit, cujus quidem ut apud Paulum ἀλλαγὴν, id est, reconciliationis, quae Christo tribuitur, crebra in scriptura litteris ita mentio. Deinde hoc Christi sacrificium verè est ἁγιαστικόν, ἁγνιστικόν, καθαρτικόν, sive καθαρτικόν, λυτρωτικόν, hoc est, sanctificatorium, purgatorium, purificatorium, expiatorium, sive lustricum, seu lustratorium, quo cuncta mundi peccata plene perfecte expiata atque lustrata sunt, quo cuncti mortales, qui illum vera fide ample ... sanctificantur, purgantur, lustrantur, expiantur. Hoc solum & unicum Christi sacrificium est nostrum λυτρωτικόν ... ἀπολύτρωσις, quo perfecte ex omnium nostrorum malum... visibilium et invisibilium, manu potestate redemti sumus. Hoc Christi sacrificium verè σωτηρικὸν ... σωτήριον, id est, salutare: quod Christus partim salutem generi humano peperit, partim pro parte salute Deo patri suo gratiae egit. Hoc Christi sacrificium verè ευχαριστία, vereq; χαρισμάτων, sive gratitudinem testificacum est, eius & suo nomine justas merito gratias habuit, egit, reddit ac persolvit.
units.tr: For this sacrifice of Christ, truly perfect, is the hilastērion, that is, the propitiatory or appeasing sacrifice, by which alone Christ was made propitious to us. Hence Christ himself is everywhere in the sacred letters called hilastikon and hilastērion, propitiation, propitiatory, appeasement, or means of appeasement, and the verb hilaskesthai, to propitiate, is very often ascribed to him. This sacrifice of Christ, truly perfect, is the eirēnikon, or eirēnopoion, that is, pacifying and peacemaking, by which God was reconciled to us. Hence Christ himself is often called eirēnē and eirēnopoios, that is, peacemaker, and peace itself, and is said to have made peace, eirēnopoiētikon, in heaven and on earth. This sacrifice of Christ is truly katallaktikon, that is, reconciling, by which men were reconciled to God and God to men; of this reconciliation, which in Paul is called allagē, which is ascribed to Christ, there is frequent mention in the Scriptures. Further, this sacrifice of Christ is truly hagiastikon, hagnistikon, katharktikon or katharTikon, lytrōtikon, that is, sanctifying, purging, purifying, expiating, or cleansing and atoning, by which all the sins of the world have been fully, perfectly expiated and cleansed, and by which all mortals who embrace him with true faith are sanctified, purged, cleansed and expiated. This single and only sacrifice of Christ is our lytrōtikon ... apolytrōsis, by which we have been perfectly redeemed by his hand and power from all the evils of ours, visible and invisible. This sacrifice of Christ is truly sōtērikon ... sōtērion, that is, saving: Christ partly brought salvation to the human race, and partly offered thanks for that salvation to God his Father. This sacrifice of Christ is truly eucharistia, and truly a testimony of thanksgiving (charismatōn); in his own name and ours he has rightly rendered, offered, paid back and fully discharged the thanks that are due.

units.la: Hoc denig, Christi sacrificium verè μαντεῖον, id est, divinatorium dici & censeri debet: propterea quod illud est certissimum, verissimum adde laetissimum omnibus credentibus, caelestium.
units.tr: Finally, this sacrifice of Christ ought to be called and considered truly manteion, that is, prophetic, because it is most certain, most true, and most joyful to all believers, a token of heavenly things.

units.la: Ethnicorum sacrificiis ... opponimus unicum illud Christi sacrificium. fui æterna, vita, gloriæ, & beatitudinis, per illud ipsum Christi sacrificium parta, indicium ac testimonium. Ac propter hoc ipsum quidè ac solum Christi sacrificium omnia (Christianorum, hoc est, priorum & fidelium sacrificia, spiritualia & Eucharistica, cujusmodi sunt preces, eleemosynæ, benignitas atq; beneficentia erga pauperes, jejunia, pœnitentia vera ac solida, veritatum operum, & honorum illud um, martyria aliaq; similia Deo grata sunt & accepta.
units.tr: We set against the sacrifices of the Gentiles that single sacrifice of Christ, the sign and testimony of eternal life, glory and blessedness, obtained through that very sacrifice of Christ. And because of this alone, the sacrifice of Christ, all the sacrifices of Christians (that is, of the early and faithful, spiritual and eucharistic ones, such as prayers, almsgivings, kindness and beneficence towards the poor, fasting, true and solid repentance, works of mercy and of honour, martyrdoms and other similar things) are pleasing and acceptable to God.

units.la: Porrò ad sacra sacrificia vel ista sua (quæ sacrilegia sæpe Lactantius, Arnobius, Tertullianus & alii Patres appellarunt) conficiendas atq; celebranda Gentiles certa habuerunt loca, ædificia templa, personas tajtigumenta, ritus atq; cæremonias: unde magnæ adhuc, quantumq; inter Gentilismum & Christianismum sit interyallum, apparet. Gentiles igitur innumeris illis vanissimis, fuisse Deas plurimas, & quidem splendidissimas magnificentissimasq; ædes, templa, fana, delubra, sacraria, sacella, cellas, altaria, idola venerare, extruere, dedicare, initiare atq; consecrare consueverunt, Deos ut in fabulis colendi, & idolatriæ atq; superstitionibus vacandi gratia.
units.tr: Moreover, for performing and celebrating their sacred sacrifices, or these their own (which Lactantius, Arnobius, Tertullian and other Fathers often called sacrilegious rites), the Gentiles had fixed places, buildings, temples, persons, vestments, rites and ceremonies. From this it is evident how great and how wide is the gap still between Gentilism and Christianity. The Gentiles, therefore, used to honour, erect, dedicate, initiate and consecrate, for the sake of those most vain gods, countless most splendid and magnificent shrines, temples, sanctuaries, chapels, cells, altars and idols, so that they might be worshipped as gods in the fables and be given over to idolatry and superstitions.

units.la: Atq; hæc quidem ut apud ... ipsa quæ sententiarum & vanitatis, vanissimaq; ... originem, suam bufla atq; sepulchra, & propter idola Deorum, alienos & adulterinos in iis solos solitos (qui sæpe portiis & adulteris in sacris litteris comparantur) atque etiam bolaciones... scelera & flagitia, quæ in illis fiebant, lupanaria atque lustra, & propter animalium mutationes, excoriationes, dissectiones que, in iis sæpe solitas, carnaria, sirvemas cella, & propter carnium, aliarumque partium collationes, adultiones seu concremationes, culinæ sive coquinæ, & quoad computationes, commessationes, quæ in illis postfacticia celebrabantur, tri-linia, caupona atque popina, & denique propter ipsos Dæmonas, quos in illis colebant, quibus illis sæpe visibili aliqua species in iis apparebant, ad illos verba faciebant, drorsoria Dæmonum sive Dæmoniorum, receptacula & habitacula a veteribus Patribus pure mericog, fuerunt appellata.
units.tr: And these things, as ... the very ... of opinions and of vanity, and of most vain ... their origin: their altars and sepulchres; and because of the idols of the gods, the alien and adulterous ones who were usually kept in them (and who in Scripture are often compared to harlots and adulterers), and also the ... crimes and disgraceful acts which were committed there, brothels and stews; and because of the cutting up, flaying and dissection of animals, which was often practised in them, butcheries and slaughterhouses; and because of the sharing out and the burning of meats and other parts, kitchens and cookhouses; and as to the banquets and feasts which were celebrated after the sacrifices, dining-rooms (triclinia), taverns and cookshops; and finally, because of the demons themselves, whom they worshipped in those places, and to whom, in them, some visible appearance sometimes showed itself, to whom they spoke, the ancient Fathers rightly and purely called them the inns (diversoria) and dwellings of demons.

units.la: Christianorum templa. Pro templis ipsis Gentilium templum primum nostrum est sacratissimum Christi corpus, de quo ipsemet locutus est ad Iudæos: Iohan. 2. Destruite hoc templum, & intra triduum illud reædificabo, atque adeo Christus ipse totus: in quo, ut Paulus ait, habitat plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter. Deinde templum nostrum est universalis & catholica Ecclesia, quæ est Sanctorum communio, in qua Deum assidue contemplari possumus & debemus. Huc respiciens Paulus, ad Ephes. 2. ita scribit: Ἐν ᾧ (ᾧ) πᾶσα οἰκοδομὴ συναρμολογουμένη αὔξει εἰς ναὸν ἅγιον ἐν Κυρίῳ. Et ἐν ᾧ ὑμεῖς συνοικοδομεῖσθε εἰς κατοικητήριον τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν πνεύματι, id est, In quo (Christo) totum ædificium congruenter coagmentatum crescit, ut fit templum sanctum Domino: in quo & vos ipsi ædificamini, ut sitis domicilium Dei per Spiritum. Præterea singula Ecclesiæ membra, singuli fideles, ac illorum cum animi, tum corpora Spiritus sancti templa atque sacraria infantes litterarum appellantur; & quidem esse debent. An ignoratis, inquit Paulus 1. Cor. 16. corpus nostrum templum esse Spiritus sancti, habitantis in vobis, nec esse vos vestri juris? Hinc Hebr. 3. idem ait: οἶκός & οἰκουργίη, cujus (Dei) domus nos sumus. Templum etiam, quo aspiramus, nostrum æternum est cœlum. Item Dei templum augustissimum & amplissimum est universæ hic Mundus: in quo Deus quotidie se nobis contemplandum præbet. Unde Cyprianus: Quod vero templum habere possit Deus, cujus templum totus est Mundus, & cum homo latius manet, intra unam ædiculam vim tanti majestatis includat? In nostra dedicandum est mente, in nostro consecrandus est pectore. Denique præter templa illa σύγκρισις & spiritualia, templa habemus, Dei beneficio, γενέσεις inter sese, humano opere manuque facta: in quibus verba & oraculas divina audire, sacra & sacramenta divinitus instituta celebrare, vota precesq; nostras ad Deum fundere, eleemosynas pauperibus elargiri, Deum denique colere atque venerari possumus & debemus.
units.tr: Christian temples. As for the temples themselves, the first and most sacred temple of ours is the body of Christ, of which he himself spoke to the Jews: John 2. "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up," so that Christ himself, in his whole person, is the temple, in whom, as Paul says, the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily. Next, our temple is the universal and catholic Church, which is the communion of the saints, and in which we can and must constantly contemplate God. Paul, looking to this in Ephesians 2, writes thus: "In whom all the building, fitly framed together, groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord" [Ἐν ᾧ πᾶσα οἰκοδομὴ συναρμολογουμένη αὔξει εἰς ναὸν ἅγιον ἐν Κυρίῳ], and "in whom ye also are builded together for an habitation of God through the Spirit" [ἐν ᾧ ὑμεῖς συνοικοδομεῖσθε εἰς κατοικητήριον τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν πνεύματι]. That is, in Christ the whole building, joined together in good order, grows into a holy temple for the Lord, and you yourselves are built up in him to be a dwelling place of God through the Spirit. Moreover, the individual members of the Church, the individual faithful, both their souls and their bodies, are called temples and shrines of the Holy Spirit, and indeed they ought to be. "Do you not know," says Paul, 1 Cor. 6, "that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, and that you are not your own?" Hence in Heb. 3 he says the same: "whose house we are" [οἶκος αὐτοῦ ἐσμεν ἡμεῖς], namely of God. Our eternal temple, toward which we aspire, is also heaven. Likewise the most august and most spacious temple of God is this whole world, in which God presents himself daily for us to contemplate. Whence Cyprian: "What temple can God have, whose temple is the whole world, and when man dwells in a wider space, can he enclose the power of so great a majesty within one little shrine? In our mind must he be dedicated, in our breast must he be consecrated." Finally, besides those spiritual temples, we have, by God's goodness, temples made by human work and hand, which are the product of human craft; in them we can and must hear the divine words and oracles, celebrate the sacred rites and sacraments divinely instituted, pour out our vows and prayers to God, distribute alms to the poor, and in short worship and venerate God.

units.la: Quidam Ethnicorum Deorum nomen: Etsi vero plerique Gentilium Deos suos templis, ædificiis atque simulacris sibi colendos esse putarunt: eamen multi inter illos templa, ut etiam simulacra, a Deorum natura & majestate exsistimantes esse alienas, in sylvis atque nemoribus consecrarunt (quæ Luci vulgo fuerunt appellata) & in iis idolatriam superstitionesq; illas suas celebrarunt. Unde Plinius lib. 12. cap. 1. & ut Fuerunt, inquit, occulta ejus (naturæ) beneficia, summumq; munus homini datum, arbores sylvæque putabant. Et cap. 2. Hæ (arbores et sylvæ) fuerunt Numinum templa, prisco que ritu simplicitas. simplicia: sed etiam nunc Deo praecellentem arborem dicane. Non magis auro fulgentia atque ebore simulacra, quàm lucos & in iis Silentia ipsa adoraruné. Arborum genera Numinibus suis dicata perpetuò seruantur.
units.tr: The groves of the heathen gods. Although most of the Gentiles thought that their gods were to be worshipped with temples, buildings and images, many of them, judging that temples as well as images were foreign to the nature and majesty of the gods, consecrated them in woods and groves (which were commonly called luci), and there they carried on their idolatry and those superstitions of theirs. Hence Pliny, book 12, chapter 1: "They thought," he says, "that the hidden benefits of nature, and its highest gift to man, were trees and woods." And chapter 2: "These trees and woods were the temples of the divinities, and by ancient custom simplicity worshipped them rather than images. Even now they call a tree excelling in the god's honour... Not images gleaming with gold and ivory, but groves and the very silences within them were adored. The kinds of trees dedicated to their divinities are preserved to this day."

units.la: Iuter alias autem Gentes, quæ Diis suis lucos atque arbores dicarunt, atque in iis illas coluerunt, fuerunt prisci Germani, ut Tacitus in suis Annalibus & in lib. de moribus Germanorum clarissimè testatur. Petrus Albinus ex Ernesto Brotusio scribit lib.1. cap.6. civitatem Merseburgum (quæ sic dicta, quasi Martiburg) antiquitus ad Carolisque M. tempora Martiem atque Zutiberum (quem Dendrodæmona, Germani den Holtzteufel appellant) coluisse in quercetō, siveluco, quernis arboribus confito, ad quem certis temporibus, sacra ei faciebat gen- tia, maxima hominum multitudo confluxerit. Hujusmodi autem sylvas lucosve sacros (in quibus & equos sacros aluerunt, e quibus de futuris diuinabant) Bagen siue Bayn appellarunt (vnde multi pagi atq. oppida fuerunt denominata) a nomine Græco βαγὸς, vt nonnulli putant. Erant cuim sacrosanctii: in quibus arbores tædere, aut earum ramos amputare tapitus suppliciò erat interdictum. Quoniam autem antiquitus ad hujusmodi lucos atque nemora magna hominum copia confluebat, etiam ex locis remotissimis, inde peregriuatio Germanis wall/ quasi waltsart/hoc est, profectio ad sylvam videtur dicta. Sed de Germanorum veterum Diis cum paucis, ut tris & proprijs, ut fuerunt Taufan, Hertus siue Herta, Teutones siue Teutates, Alemann, Irmenseul siue Armeseul, siue Henneseul, Crodo, Triglà, Flinitz, Pronesive Prouo, Radegast siue Redegast, siue Ridegast, Seba siue Syba, Zermebock, Suanteniz, Podan siue Guodan: tum quiillis tum Romanis & aliis gentibus fuerunt communes, ut fuerunt Iupiter Hamuonius, Sol, Luna, Vulcanus, Isis, Mars, Mercurius, Venus, Castor & Pollux, & alii, de quorum imaginibus, slatuis, templis, sacerdotibus, sacrificiis cum pecorum, tum hominum cultu atq. veneratione, itemque divinationibus vide Erpoldum Lindenbruchium in{ ~ } chronicis Germanicis de Carolo M. Hæc omnia ille confirmat atq. comprobat autorum cum veterum, ut C. Iulii Caesaris, Lastantii, Plinii, Straboni, Tacitij tum recentiorum, ut Alberei Cranzii, Petri Albini, Alexandri Sardi, Irenici, Middeudorpii, Holmoldi, Adami Bremensis, Diaconi, Methodii Picnensis, Sabini, Euzelii, Emferi & aliorum historicorum testimonis & autoritatibus. De iisdem vide etiam Iunium in historia Batauorum. Vnum tantum hic addam, quòd Emserus de idolo siue de- mone potiùs illo Schmanteuiz (quem alij sanctum Vitum: alij sanctum lumen: alij sanctum fundamentum interpretantur: Vitz enim & lumen & fundamentum priscā linguā significat) prodidit.
