Cùm Magorum, inquit, constans sit seuentia, Dæmonia sanguine vitari: sacerdos tamè Schmanteuiz persuadebat suis hunc nisi Christiano cruore placari non posse. Vnde quotannis illi homiuem Christianum, quemcunq. sors obiecerat, litare consueuerunt. Ejusdem meminit Helmoldus lib.1.cap.6.& lib.2.cap.12.
units.tr: Among the other nations who dedicated groves and trees to their gods and worshipped them there, were the ancient Germans, as Tacitus clearly attests in his Annals and in his book on the manners of the Germans. Petrus Albinus, following Ernst Brotuse, writes in book 1, chapter 6, that the town of Merseburg (so called as if it were Martiburg) in ancient times, down to the time of Charlemagne, worshipped Mars and Zutiberus (whom the Germans call Dendrodaemon, den Holtzteufel) in an oak grove, or lucus, planted with oak trees, to which at certain times a very great crowd of people flocked to perform sacred rites for him. Such sacred woods or groves (in which they also kept sacred horses, from whose behaviour they drew omens about the future) they called Bagen or Bayn, whence many villages and towns took their names; the name, some think, comes from the Greek βαγὸς. For they were held sacrosanct: it was forbidden, on pain of punishment, to cut the trees there or to lop their branches. Since in ancient times a great throng of people flocked to such groves and woods, even from the most distant places, the German word wallfahrt, as if waltsart, that is, a journey to the forest, seems to have been derived from this. But of the old German gods, I shall mention only a few, those that were peculiar to them: Taufan, Hertus or Herta, Teutones or Teutates, Alemann, Irmensul or Armeseul or Henneseul, Crodo, Triglaf, Flinz, Prone or Provo, Radegast or Redegast or Ridegast, Seba or Syba, Zermebock, Suanteniz, Podan or Guodan; and those that were common both to them and to the Romans and other nations, such as Jupiter Hamuonius, Sun, Moon, Vulcan, Isis, Mars, Mercury, Venus, Castor and Pollux, and others. For their images, statues, temples, priests, sacrifices, both of beasts and of men, and their worship and veneration, as well as their divinations, see Erpold Lindenbruch in his German chronicles, on Charlemagne. He confirms and proves all these things by the testimonies and authorities of ancient authors such as Gaius Julius Caesar, Lactantius, Pliny, Strabo, Tacitus, and of more recent historians such as Albert Krantz, Petrus Albinus, Alexander Sardus, Irenicus, Middendorp, Helmold, Adam of Bremen, the deacon, Methodius of Pícen, Sabinus, Eucel, Emser and others. On the same matters see also Junius in his history of the Batavians. I shall add only this one point: Emser has reported concerning the idol or rather demon Schmantewiz (whom some interpret as St. Vitus, others as holy light, others as holy foundation, for vitz in the old language means both light and foundation). "Since," he says, "it is a constant tradition of the Magi that demons are driven off by blood, the priest Schmantewiz nevertheless persuaded his people that this god could be appeased only by Christian blood. Whence every year they used to sacrifice a Christian man, whomever the lot had pointed out." Helmold also mentions the same, book 1, chapter 6, and book 2, chapter 12.

units.la: Pro omnibus porrò istis Gentilium lucis luctuosis & opacis, in quibus vanissima ista sua Numina tolurunt, uiuersus hic Mundus nobis est quasi lucus quidam lucidissimus: in quo diuinae Maiestatis lux passim resplendet ac refulget, & in quo not verum Deum perpetuò secundum ejus voluntatem colere atq. venerari decet.
units.tr: In place of all those gloomy and shadowy groves of the Gentiles, in which they worshipped their most vain divinities, this whole world is for us a sort of most bright grove, in which the light of the divine majesty shines and gleams everywhere, and in which it is always fitting to worship and venerate the true God according to his will.

units.la: Præterea pro Geutilium aris & altaribus altare nostrum est Christus: est crux; in qua pro nobis suit iuimolatus: est meusa Domiuica: est Ecclesia; in qua mortis & sacrificii Christi sa- lutiferi memoria perpetuò celebratur: sumus deinque nos singuli, nostraq. cum corda, tum corpora; quibus spirituales illas bodias, de quibus supra, sine cessatione & intermissione Deo offerimus. Hinc Augustinus Sermone 152 de tempore: Duo, inquit, in nobis sunt altaria confisitura, corporis scilicet & cordis nostri. Vnde & duplex a nobis sacrificium quarie Deus. Vnum; ut simus casto corpore: aliud, ut mundo corde esse debeamus. Ergo in extetriori altare, idest, in corpore nostro offeremus opera bona: in corde odorem suavissatis redoleat cogitatio sancta.
units.tr: Furthermore, in place of the altars of the Gentiles, our altar is Christ; it is the cross, on which he was sacrificed for us; it is the Lord's Table; it is the Church, in which the memory of the death and saving sacrifice of Christ is constantly celebrated; and finally we ourselves, each of us, both our hearts and our bodies, on which we offer those spiritual victims, of which I spoke above, to God without ceasing and without intermission. Hence Augustine, Sermon 152 on the season: "Two altars," he says, "are within us, of our body and of our heart. Hence God also requires a double sacrifice from us: one, that we should have a chaste body; the other, that we should have a clean heart. Therefore on the outer altar, that is, in our body, we shall offer good works; in the heart, holy thought shall send up a most sweet fragrance."

units.la: Sic & pro socus illis Gentilium cum publicis, tum priuatis & domesticis: in quibus sacros perpetuò ignes seruabant, Focus noster maximus & amplissimus est Ecclesia: in qua ignis ille sancti Spiritus, verbi, divini ad salutem nostram perpetuò souetur atq. colitur.
units.tr: Likewise, in place of the hearths of the Gentiles, both public and private and domestic, in which they kept perpetual sacred fires, our greatest and most spacious hearth is the Church, in which that fire of the Holy Spirit, the divine Word, is constantly kept alive and tended for our salvation.

units.la: Pro iguibus item illis sacrificialibus sacris & perpetuis, quos superstitiosissimè coluerunt in altaribus atq. focis publicis & priuatis diligentissimè souerunt, ad sacrificia sua adhibuerunt, Ee 2 quibus quidem ignem illum tartareum & inextinguibilem promeruerunt, ignis primum nostri perpetuus & aeternus, quem solum colimus, & iure quidem optimo ac merito maximo, esse Deus Opt. Max. est Spiritus sanctus verus Deus, qui saepe ignis partim consumens, partim illuminans & illustrans, salutaris denique in sacris literis appellatur. Erat Deus ipse, sic verbum quoq; ejus ignis est illuminans nostras mentes atq; animos, exurens atq; consumens pravos nostros affectus & errores, inflammans nostra corda charitate gemina erga Deum atq; proximum. Atq; hoc quidem geminae charitatis igne inflammati, apti reddimur & idonei ad sacrificia illa spiritualia facienda, quae spectant ad Dei gloriam & ad nostram salutem. His postremo addendus ignis crucis & afflictionis: quo non secus atq; aurum & argentum igni pii atque fideles probantur & purgantur. De his Gentilis luminibus superstitiosis sic Lactantius disserit lib.6. Instit. divin. cap.2. Accendunt, inquit, lumina, velut in tenebris agenti. Quod si sufficari, aut percipere animo possent, quae sunt bona illa caelestia, quorum magnitudinem terreno adhuc corpore obvoluti sensu capere non possumus, jam se cum bis officiis inanibus stultissimos esse cognoscerent vel ficaelestem lumen, quod dicimus solem, contemplari velint, jam sentiant quod non indigeat lucerna eorum Deus, qui in suum hominis tam candidam lucem dedit: & tamen cum in tam parvo circulo, qui propter longinquitatem non amplius, quam humani capitis videtur habere mensuram, tantum sit fulgoris, ut eum mortalium luminum acies non queat contueri: & fipaxlifper intenderis, bebetatos oculos caligo, ac tenebrae consequantur: quid tandem luminis, quid claritatis apud Deum, penes quem nulla nox est, esse arbitremur? qui hanc ipsam lucem sic moderatus est, ut neq; nimio fulgore, neq; colore vehementi noceret animantibus: tantumq; iflarum rerum dedit ei, quantum ad mortalia corpora pati possunt, aut fragum mauritas possultaret. Numigitur menti compos putandus est, qui authori, & datori luminis candelarum, ac cerarum lumen offert pro munere? Aliud vero ille a nobis exigit lumen, & quidem non fumidu, sed (ut ait Poeta) liquidum, aq; clarum mentis scilicet. Propter quod a poetis quoq; nuncupatur: quod exhibere non potest, nisi qui Deum agno verit. Illorum autem Dis, quia terreni sunt, egent luminibus ne in tenebris sinat: quorum culto res, quia caelestis nihil sapiunt, etiam religiones quibus deservient, ad terram ne vocante. In ea eum lumine opus est: quia ratio eius, & natura tenebrosa est. Itaq; Dijs no caelestem sensum humanum potins attribuunt. Ideo quod necessaria illis, & grata credunt esse, quae nobis, quibus aut ufurientibus opus cibo, aut sitientibus potu, aut vestle algentibus, aut cum sol deceperit, lumine, ut videre possimus. Nullis igitur ex rebus tam probari, ac intelligi potest, Deos ipsos, cum aliquando vixerint, mortuos esse, quam ex ipso ritu, qui est totus e terra: Haec Lactantius.
units.tr: As for those fires of the sacrifices, sacred and perpetual, which they worshipped most superstitiously, and which they tended most diligently on altars and hearths, both public and private, and used for their sacrifices, and by which indeed they merited that fiery and unquenchable hell, our perpetual and eternal fire, the one we worship, and rightly and most justly as the greatest, is God Most Good and Most Great; the Holy Spirit is the true God, who is often called in the sacred letters a fire, partly consuming, partly illuminating and enlightening, and in short a saving fire. He is God himself; so also his Word is a fire, illuminating our minds and souls, burning up and consuming our wicked affections and errors, and kindling our hearts with a twofold love toward God and our neighbour. And it is by this fire of twofold love that we are inflamed, made apt and fit to perform those spiritual sacrifices which concern the glory of God and our salvation. Finally, to these must be added the fire of the cross and of affliction, by which, no less than gold and silver, the pious and faithful are tested and purified. Lactantius discourses thus on these superstitious lights of the Gentiles, book 6 of the Divine Institutes, chapter 2: "They light lamps," he says, "as if to someone walking in darkness. But if they could grasp with their minds, or perceive, what those heavenly goods are, whose greatness we, still wrapped in an earthly body, cannot grasp by sense, they would already recognise that they are most foolish in these empty duties. If they wish to contemplate that heavenly light which we call the sun, they would already perceive that their God, who gave to man so bright a light, has no need of a lamp. And yet within so small a circle, which because of its distance seems to have no more than the measure of a human head, there is so much brilliance that the sight of mortal eyes cannot bear to look upon it, and if you gaze at it a little too long, darkness follows and your dimmed eyes are blinded. What light, then, what brightness must we suppose there is with God, with whom there is no night? He who so tempered this very light that it harms living creatures neither by excessive glare nor by intense heat, and gave to these things only so much of their power as mortal bodies can bear or as the weakness of the eyes can endure. Is he to be thought sane who offers the light of candles and tapers as a gift to the author and giver of light? He demands from us another light, and indeed not a smoky one but, as the poet says, a liquid and clear one, namely of the mind; on account of which he is also called by the poets... This only the one who knows God in truth can offer. But the gods of those people, because they are earthly, need lights lest they remain in darkness; their worshippers, because they savour nothing of heaven, also have religions which, calling them down to earth, serve them. There they need light, because their reason and nature are dark. Thus they attribute to their gods not a heavenly but a human sense, because they believe that the things which are necessary and pleasing to us are also necessary and pleasing to them: food for those who hunger, drink for those who thirst, clothing for those who are cold, and light, when the sun has set, so that they can see. Therefore from nothing can it be proved so well and understood that the gods themselves, though they once lived, are dead, as from the very rite itself, which is wholly of earth." Thus Lactantius.

units.la: Praeter ignes autem illos sacros, sacrificiales ac perpetuos, quos habuerunt in aris aeq; focis, praeterea sunt Gentiles in templis, atq; etiam extra templa, diebus praesertim festis, multis ac variis luminibus, lampadibus, facibus ac lucernis, de quibus supra. At nostrum lumen luminosissimum fonsq; omnis luminis est Deus Opt. Max. pater ille luminum, uti a S. Iacobo appellatur, lucem habitans in accessum: est Christus, Dei filius, qui seipsum Mundi lumen sive lucem appellat in eandem sententiam Iohannes primi epistolae cap.1, inquit: Deus lumen est & tenebrae in eo nulla. Et ut Deus ipse sic lux ejus atq; verbum, lumen est, atque lucerna lucidissima pedum & semitarum nostrarum: ut pulchre David cecinit Psal.19. Praeterea cum omnes pii atque fideles, cum inprimis Ecclesiae doctores atque pastores Ecclesiae Mundi, lumina atque lucernae sacrae literis appellantur; & quidem esse debent alii hominibus, cum vere doctrinae, cum vitae puritate relucentes. Unde Paulus in epistola ad Philippenses cap.2. Inter quos lucetis, tanquam luminaria in Mundo. Et Christus ad Apostolos suos Matth.5. Sic luceat, inquit, lux vestra inter homines, ut homines videant bona vestra opera, et glorificent patrem vestrum, qui est in caelis. Hiisi autem in caelo, in caelesti illa et aeternali luce fulgebunt, tanquam stellae totius firmamenti hujus affabilis. Postremo cum uniuersa hic Mundus est quasi lux sive lumen quoddam splendidissimum divinae majestatis, tum singulae ejus partes, singulae creaturae maximae, mediae, minimae ejusdem sunt lumina, lucernae, scintillae denique clarae & illustres.
units.tr: Besides those sacred fires, sacrificial and perpetual, which they kept on altars and hearths, the Gentiles also have many and various lights in their temples, and outside their temples too, especially on feast days: lamps, torches, flares and lanterns, as I said above. But our most luminous light, and the fountain of all light, is God Most Good and Great, that Father of lights, as St James calls him, "dwelling in light unapproachable." It is Christ, the Son of God, who calls himself the light of the world. John says to the same effect in the first chapter of his first epistle: "God is light, and in him is no darkness." And as God himself is light, so his light and word is a lamp and a most bright lantern to our feet and paths, as David sang beautifully in Psalm 19. Moreover, since all the pious and faithful, and above all the teachers and ministers of the Church, are called lights and lamps in Holy Scripture, they ought indeed to be lights to other men, shining both with true doctrine and with purity of life. So Paul in Philippians 2: "Among whom you shine as lights in the world." And Christ to his apostles, Matthew 5: "So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven." These will shine in heaven, in that heavenly and eternal light, as stars of this whole firmament. Finally, since this whole world is as it were a light, a most splendid lamp of the divine majesty, so each of its parts and each creature, greatest, middling and least, are its lights, lanterns, and finally bright and illustrious sparks.

units.la: Ut autem lucernas, cereos atque lumina illa sacra oleo, teda, pice, bitumine, sulphure aliaq; materia, ex quibus lignis impiis, certis & pecuniis ...
units.tr: But as for the lamps, candles and those sacred lights made of oil, pine torch, pitch, bitumen, sulphur and other material, and of what impure woods, certain and ... [the rest of this sentence is too garbled in the scan to be rendered].
Which lamps belonged to the Gentiles, and which to the Christians.

units.la: Ethnicorum quae ligna sacrificia & quae Christianorum. liaribus foverunt: in quorum deleētu valde fuerunt superstitiosi, sicuti supra pluribus fuit explicatum. Verum pro omnibus istis Gentilium ligum sacrificialibus atq; etia (ut hoc addam) arboribus sacris; quas Dius suis sacrarunt nos habemus Christum, arborem sive lignum illud viva, ut in sacris litteris appellatur, lignum viride, semper virens ac vigens, ut seipsum appella vit: quod quidem ligno illo vitæ in medio Paradisi fuit præfigurantum. Cogitemus igitur miseros nos mortales nostrapte natura quasi ligna quædam esse infelicia, mortua, arida, inutilia & infrugifera, digna, quæ in illum Gehennæ ignem horrendum & inextinguibilem conjiciamur, eoque perpetuo excruciemur: ac proinde non nisi ligno illi vitæ atq; viridi, vuli illi atq; olex frugifera, idest, Christo, per Spiritum sanctum, veramq; fide insitos, ejus nimirum ligna posse fieri viva, virentia atq; fructuosa ad proferendos justitiæ & bonorum operum fructus. Meditemur etiam ad doctrinam consolationemq; nostram diei noctesq; lignum illud Crucis, cui Christus, lignum vitæ atq; viride, idest, salutiferum, pro nobis affixus, in quo pendens pro nobis factus est maledictio ut nos redimeret ex maledictione legis, in eoq; horrendis modis excruciatus tandem validissima voce exspiravit: cujus quidem ligni ille lignorum fastitulus, quem Isaacus patriarcha humeris suis portavit, illustris typus fuit. In hoc ligno Christus ut S. Petrus sancti Spiritu afflatu dixit, peccata nostra portavit ut justitiæ, ut eandem in sententiam S. Paulus ejusdem Spiritus infinitum locutus est, affixit, atq; ita delevit Chirographum illud nostrum, quod fuit adversus nos, id est, contrarium, & adversum nostra salus, nos accusans nosq; mortis reos peragens.
units.tr: Which sacrificial woods belonged to the Gentiles, and which to the Christians. They cherished them in household shrines, and in choosing them they were very superstitious, as was explained at length above. But in place of all those sacrificial woods of the Gentiles, and even (to add this) the sacred trees which the gods consecrated to themselves, we have Christ, that tree or wood of life, as Scripture calls him, a green wood, always green and flourishing, as he called himself, which was prefigured by the wood of life in the middle of Paradise. Let us therefore consider that we miserable mortals, by our own nature, are like unfortunate wood, dead, dry, useless and unfruitful, fit to be cast into that dreadful and unquenchable fire of Gehenna and tormented there forever. Therefore we cannot become living, green and fruitful wood, bearing the fruits of righteousness and good works, except by being grafted into that wood of life and greenness, that is, into Christ, through the Holy Spirit and true faith. Let us also meditate, for our teaching and comfort, day and night, on that wood of the Cross, on which Christ, the wood of life and greenness, that is, the wood that saves, was fastened for us. Hanging on it he was made a curse for us, to redeem us from the curse of the law, and there, tormented in dreadful ways, at last breathed out with a very strong voice. Of that wood, the bundle of sticks which the patriarch Isaac carried on his shoulders was a notable type. On this wood, as St Peter said under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, Christ "bore our sins," and, as St Paul, speaking of the same Spirit in the same sense, says, he fastened them to it, and so blotted out that handwriting of ours which was against us, that is, contrary to and hostile to our salvation, accusing us and making us guilty of death.

units.la: Sed cinerum quoq;, (qui sacrificiorum erant reliquiæ) hic non prætermittenda est mentio. Legimus in Olympo monte quotannis sacrificium solenne & magnificum, fieri fuisse solitum, & rerum concrematarum cineres in ara illa per integrum annum, donec aliud sacrificium fieret, inter gros semper permansisse, nec ventorum aliarumve tempestatum vi & injuria fuisse dissipatos: unde nonnulli montis illud altitudine, quæ reliquos terræ montes omnes superet, conjiciunt. Huic simile est illud, quod Epiphanius lib. 1. con. 1. hæresi 18. prodidit de magnificentissimo illo Noachi patriarcha sacrificio, quod ille ex omni animalium mundorum genere Deo, ευχαριστιας gratia, post horrendum illud diluvium, pro data sibi fuisse salute obtulit: nempe ejus & cinerum & Altarum reliquias adhuc loco fecit in Armenia montibus extisisse. Sed nos pro vanissimis illis Gentilium cinerib[us], ad quos illorum victima vel sumtuosissima & pretiosissima quæ tandem fuerunt tedæda, animus nostros volvere atq; revolvere assidue debemus sanctissimum purissimumq; illum Christi cinerem, id est, mortem ac passionem, cujus afferfione purgamur ab omnibus carnis nostræ peccatorum, sordibus, qui cineres vitulæ sive vaccæ illius rufæ Veteris Testamenti, extra urbem combustæ fuerunt adumbrati: unde Paulus ad Hebræos 9. cap. ως δωδεκα, inquit, λεγω, λεγει ... Cinis vitulæ asperæ sanctificat inquinatos: quod de vitula illa Veteris testamenti terimonialiter cantum, de Christo autem proprie & vere est intelligendum.
units.tr: But we must not pass over here the mention of ashes too, which were the remains of the sacrifices. We read that on Mount Olympus a solemn and magnificent sacrifice used to be made every year, and that the ashes of the burnt offerings remained on that altar throughout the whole year, until another sacrifice was made, never scattered by the force or violence of the winds or other storms. From this some conjecture that the mountain is higher than all the other mountains of the earth. Similar to this is what Epiphanius reports in Book 1 against heresies, Heresy 18, about the most magnificent sacrifice of the patriarch Noah, which he offered to God after the dreadful flood, in thanksgiving (eucharistia) for the salvation granted to him, from every kind of clean animal. He says that remains of both its ashes and its altars still existed in the mountains of Armenia. But instead of those most vain ashes of the Gentiles, to which their victims, even the most costly and precious, at last came to be only ashes, we must continually turn over and over in our minds that most holy and pure ash of Christ, that is, his death and passion, by the sprinkling of which we are cleansed from all the filth of the sins of our flesh. Of this the ashes of that red heifer of the Old Testament, burnt outside the city, were a shadow. Hence Paul to the Hebrews, chapter 9: "The ashes of a heifer sprinkling the unclean sanctify." This was spoken of that heifer of the Old Testament in a ceremonial sense, but of Christ it must be understood properly and truly.

units.la: Iam vero ni Deos, ut simulatam, ut sacrificia, ut templa, ut altaria atq; focos: sic sacrorum quoq; sacerdotes & ministros sive sacrificiales... (continued) sacerdotes, & bona, sed ut... ordine, dignitate, corporis tutus atq; habitu, ritibus et cerimoniis dissentes valde ac diversos. Nobis autem Christianis Christus primum ut sacrificium, sic sacerdos quoq; nostrum est summus & maximus: de cujus sacerdotali dignitate, munere atque officio, eiusq; effectus & fructibus salutiferis Apostolus in epistola ad Hebræos praclare disserit: Christum, inquit, oportuit secundum omnia fratribus similem fieri, ut misericors fieret et fidelis pontifex ... Idem cap. 3. initio: Οθεν ἀδελφοι ἁγιοι... Et paullo post Christum cum Mose comparando, inquit: ... Idem cap. 4. sub finem: ... Idem cap. 5. Christum comparans cum summo alijs sacerdotibus eandē concludit: [illegible, ~40 letters] Idem ca.6. de eodem Christi sacerdotio differens, quòd diuinitus interposito ipsius Dei iurejurando fuerit constitutum & stabilitum, tandem hac clausula, consolationis plenissimâ mutitur: Et [illegible, ~60 letters] Capite deinceps: septimo, eandem; & quidem nullem ac salutarem canens de hoc Christi sacerdotio exantilenam Apostolus, cum Melchisedeco, Rege simul & sacerdote singulari & extraordinario primùm, deinde cum sacerdotibus ordinarijs comparat, tandemq; sermonem hunc suum his verbis concludit: [illegible, ~50 letters]
units.tr: Now indeed, as the Gentiles had their gods, their sacrifices, their temples, altars and hearths, so they also had their sacred priests and ministers, differing greatly from one another in order, dignity, dress, bearing, rites and ceremonies. For us Christians, Christ is first, as the sacrifice, and so also he is our priest, the highest and greatest, of whose priestly dignity, office and function, and of whose saving effects and fruits, the Apostle speaks splendidly in his epistle to the Hebrews: "It behoved Christ," he says, "to be made like unto his brethren, that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest..." The same, at the beginning of chapter 3: "Wherefore, holy brethren..." And shortly after, comparing Christ with Moses, he says: ... The same, at the end of chapter 4: ... The same, in chapter 5, comparing Christ with the other high priests, he concludes: [illegible in the scan]. The same, in chapter 6, discussing the same priesthood of Christ, that it was established and confirmed by God's own oath, ends with this most comforting clause: [illegible in the scan]. In the following chapter, the seventh, the Apostle sings the same most excellent and saving song about this priesthood of Christ, first comparing him with Melchizedek, at once king and priest, singular and extraordinary, and then with the ordinary priests, and he concludes this discourse with these words: [illegible in the scan].

units.la: Vt igitur Ethnici habuerunt suos ἀρχιερεῖς, archisacerdotes, archiflamines, archigallos, pontifices maximos, reges sacrorum: sic nobis Christianis Christus est noster ἀρχιερεὺς, id est, sacerdos summus, sacerdotum princeps, ille pontifex noster maximus, qui suo sacerdotio, sanguine atque sacrificio quasi pontem nobis per Mundi huius pelagus fecit, straravit & munivit ad coelestes illas sedes atq; templo, ad vitam & beatitudinem illam aeternam. Ille est verus noster Rex sacrorum secundum ordinem Melchisedech, ut saepe S. Paullus loquitur, ὁ ἀρχων τῆς βασιλείας Σαλήμ, qui impense Regib. serrae. Idem, ut statim subjungit, pro suo ergo nos amore, nos sanguine suo ablui a peccatis nostris, nosq; Deo & patri suo reges & sacerdotes constituit. Ergo post Christum omnes quoq; veri Christiani reges sunt & sacerdotes, a Christo ipso, summo rege & sacerdote suo constituti: unde Petrus quoq; epistola priore cap. 2. eos appellat ἱεράτευμα ἅγιον, βασίλειον ἱεράτευμα, ἔθνος ἅγιον, λαὸν εἰς περιποίησιν, hoc est, sacerdotium sanctum (Exod. 19. unde haec verba defuncta sunt) est regale sacerdotium ad offerendii Deo spiritualia sacrificia. Hinc in illa Apoc. 20. Sederunt sacerdotes Dei & Christi, & regnabunt cum eo, Aug. lib. 20. de Civ. Dei c. 10. sic scribit: Non utiq; de solis Episcopis & Presbyteris dictum est, qui proprie jam vocantur in Ecclesia sacerdotes: sed sicut omnes Christianos dicimus propter mysticum Christi, sic omnes sacerdotes, quoniam membra sunt unius sacerdotis, de quib. Apostolus Petrus: Plebs, inquit, sancta, regale sacerdotium, &c. Etsi vero omnes Christiani & reges & sacerdotes sunt, quod & seipsos & alios, sue praesertim fidei concreditos bene sapienter, secundum Dei verbum regere, & hostias illas spirituales, de quibus supra dictum, Deo offerre debent, tamen ex ipsius Dei instituto atque praecipiuo, ut omnia in Ecclesia, tanquam domo Dei fiant ἐυσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν, et contra confusionis ac perturbationis evitandae gratia, non quibuslibet hominibus, sed iis, qui juste legitimeq; ad id sunt electi & vocati, & ad id apti sunt atq; idonei, publice in Ecclesia docendi sacramenta & disciplinam rite rel gioseq; administrandi jus ac potestas permittitur.
units.tr: Just as the Gentiles had their high priests, archpriests, archflamens, archgalli, chief pontiffs and kings of sacred rites, so for us Christians Christ is our high priest, that is, the chief priest and prince of priests, our greatest pontiff. By his priesthood, blood and sacrifice he made for us, as it were, a bridge across the sea of this world, and paved and fortified the way to those heavenly seats and temple, to that eternal life and blessedness. He is our true king of sacred rites, after the order of Melchizedek, as St Paul often speaks, "the king of Salem," who, as he says, is most excellent among kings. The same, as he goes on to add, out of his love for us, washed us from our sins by his own blood, and made us kings and priests to God and his Father. Therefore, after Christ, all true Christians too are kings and priests, appointed by Christ himself, their supreme king and priest. Hence Peter also, in his first epistle, chapter 2, calls them "a holy priesthood," "a royal priesthood," "a holy nation," "a people for a possession," that is, a holy priesthood (words taken from Exodus 19), a royal priesthood to offer spiritual sacrifices to God. Hence, in Revelation 20: "They sat as priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him." Augustine, in Book 20 of The City of God, chapter 10, writes thus: "It is not said of bishops and elders alone, who are now properly called priests in the Church; but just as we call all Christians by reason of the mystical Christ, so all are priests, since they are members of the one priest, of whom the Apostle Peter says: 'a holy people, a royal priesthood,' etc." Although all Christians are both kings and priests, because they ought to rule themselves and others committed to their faith wisely and according to God's word, and to offer to God those spiritual sacrifices of which we spoke above, nevertheless, by God's own institution and command, so that everything in the Church, as in the house of God, is done decently and in order, and to avoid confusion and disturbance, the right to teach the sacraments publicly in the Church and to administer discipline rightly and religiously is not granted to just anyone, but to those who have been justly and lawfully chosen and called to this, and are fit and suitable for it.

units.la: Perro ut loca, ut per sonat, sic a tempora quoque Gentiles certa singulos Dies colendis destinarunt, quae festa, festivitates, ferias, solennitates appellarunt. In hac ab operibus & actionibus suis quotidianis ac necessariis vacantes, eii cerimoniis ac superstitionibus multis vanissimis, cum convivis & compotationibus intemperantissimis, tum tripudiis atq; ludis turpissimis, tum denique omnis generis sceleribus atq; flagitiis operam dederunt. Pro feriis istis Gentilium feralibus atq; suriosis solennitatibus atq; festis funestissimis nos Christiani habemus diem Dominicum; habemus nos etiam dies sacros & festos Christianae nostrae religionis colendae, ac operum divinorum memoriorum, Christi memoriam recolendi gratia institutos. His utinam nos Christiani ad divini Numinis cultum & honorem, sicuti pietatis ratio postulat, sanctae religionis, uteremur: ac non potius ut plerunq; fieri solet, Ethnicorum illorum priscorum ritu & exemplo, ad idololatriam & superstitionem, ad iguanum otium, ad convivia luxuriae, ad ludos obscoenos, ad Venerem & libidinem, ad avaritiam, ad faenerationes & alia opera profana exercenda, denique ad quaevis maleficia atq; flagitia impie nefarie, perpetranda abuteremur? Unde illa Tertulliani verba libro 2. ad Versus Marcionem de festorum apud Iudaeos abusu nobis quoq; Christianis recte meritoq; accommodari possunt: Et solennitates & dies festos, & vestra sabbata dicenda (Isa. cap. 1.) quae secundum libidinem suam: non secundum religionem Dei celebranda, sua jam, non Dei fecerant. Duplicem autem illum Sabbatismum, de quo egregie copiose, Apostolus in epistola ad Hebr. cap. 4. disserit nobis semper ante mentis nostrae oculos proponere a sidueq; meditari debemus. Unus est καταπαυσις, id est, cessatio, vacatio, abstinentia a nostris operib. ut quemadmodum Deus κατέπαυσεν ἀπὸ τῶν ἰδίων ἔργων, requievit & cessavit a proprio operib. quae fuerit bona: sic nos quoq; a proprio nostro natura operib. hoc est, peccatis et vitiosis, quae opera carnis appellantur, abstinere amus nobis, & semperemus. Et hic sabbatismus in hac vita nihil est aliud, quam ut uno verbo dicam, vera solidaq; poenitentia, cui per eorum vitae curriculum nobis est studendum. Alter deinde sabbatismus post hanc vitam, qui certe nobis sperandus, patienterq; est expetendus, est coelestis, aeterna & beatissima illa quies, hoc est, vacuitas seu requies ab omnibus malis atq; miseriis, & tuta, tranquilla ac secura caelestium & aeternorum illorum bonorum usura, ad quam omnes toto aspiramus pectore.
units.tr: Indeed, just as they set aside certain places, so too the Gentiles appointed certain days for worshipping their gods, which they called festivals, feasts, holy days and solemnities. On these days they abstained from their daily and necessary work and devoted themselves to many most vain ceremonies and superstitions, to the most intemperate feasting and drinking parties, to the most shameful dancing and games, and finally to every kind of wickedness and disgrace. In place of those Gentile holidays, which were given over to frenzied solemnities and most deadly feasts, we Christians have the Lord's Day. We also have holy and festive days, set apart for worshipping our Christian religion and for recalling the works of God and the memory of Christ. Would that we Christians used these days for the worship and honour of the divine Power, as the duty of piety and holy religion requires, and did not, as often happens, follow the custom and example of those ancient heathens and misuse them for idolatry and superstition, for lazy idleness, for banquets of luxury, for obscene games, for lust and sensuality, for greed, for usury and other profane business, and finally for every kind of evil deed and disgrace, committed impiously and wickedly. Hence the words of Tertullian in the second book Against Marcion, about the abuse of feasts among the Jews, can rightly and fitly be applied to us Christians too: "Solemnities and festal days, and your sabbaths" (Isa. 1), which they were celebrating according to their own lust, and not according to the religion of God, were already theirs and no longer God's. We must always keep before the eyes of our minds, and constantly meditate on, that double Sabbath-keeping about which the Apostle discourses so excellently and fully in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 4. The first is rest [καταπαυσις], that is, cessation, release, and abstinence from our own works, so that just as God rested [κατέπαυσεν] from his own works, that is, ceased and rested from his own works, which were good, so we too must abstain from our own natural works, that is, from sins and vicious deeds, which are called the works of the flesh, and must keep on abstaining. And this Sabbath-keeping in this life is nothing other than, to put it in one word, true and solid repentance, which we must strive for throughout the course of our lives. The second Sabbath-keeping comes after this life. This we must certainly hope for and eagerly and patiently seek: it is that heavenly, eternal and most blessed rest, that is, freedom and rest from all evils and miseries, and the safe, tranquil and secure enjoyment of those heavenly and eternal goods, towards which we all aspire with our whole heart.

units.la: Inter Gentilium autem sacra atque cerimonias, quas diebus festis celebrarunt, principem fere locum obtinebant preces atq; supplicationes, quibus potissimum Deos suos placari posse putabant: unde etiam vox supplicationis saepe pro uni verso cultu atq; religione ujurpatur. Nec vero preci-bus tantum bonis & faustis, sed etiam imprecationibus & maledictis utebantur in Herculis sa-cris, secundum haec Lactantii verba de falsa religione libro 1. cap. 21. Herculis sacra, inquit ille, (quae sacrilegia veriùs dixeris) non ιυχηυλα, ut Graeci appellant, sed maledictiis & exsecrationes apud Lindum, quod est oppidum Rhodi, celebrari solita, eaq; pro violatis habebant, si quando inter folennes ritus vel imprudenti alicui extidisset banum verbum.
units.tr: Among the sacred rites and ceremonies which the Gentiles performed on their feast days, prayers and supplications held almost the chief place, by which they especially believed their gods could be placated. Hence the word "supplication" is often used for the whole worship and religion. Nor did they use only good and auspicious prayers, but also imprecations and curses in the rites of Hercules, according to these words of Lactantius in the first book of On False Religion, chapter 21: "The rites of Hercules" (you would more truly call them sacrileges), "which are celebrated not with [ἰυχηυλα], as the Greeks call them, but with curses and execrations, at Lindus, a town of Rhodes; and they held that the rites were violated if at any time during the solemn ceremonies some ill-omened word had slipped out from someone, even inadvertently."

units.la: Sed pro omnibus ipsis Gentilium publicis & privatis precibus, precationibus (quas imprecationes veriùs dixeris) supplicationibus, obsecrationibus, postulationibus (ut a Cicerone, Livio, & aliis scriptoribus appellantur) superstitiosissimis, quas ad commentitios illos suos Deos, illorum gratiam, veniam, pacem opemq; exposcendi ac impetrandi gratia adhibendas censuerunt, nos Christiani ad solum verum Deum, per Christum, Dei filium, Θεανθρωπον, Dei hominum, mediatorem unicum, preces nostras, non tam ore, quam ex pectore & animo nostro fundimus, partim ei pro accepta salute & innumeris beneficiis gratias agendi, partim jus gratiae, misericordiae, pacis ac veniae impetrande gratia. Sed potissimum ac precipue Domini nostri Iesu Christi, sedentis nunc ad dextram patris intercessione ac deprecatione perpetuo ad salutem nostram utimur.
units.tr: But instead of all those public and private prayers of the Gentiles, their entreaties (which you would more truly call imprecations), supplications, obsecrations and demands (as Cicero, Livy and other writers call them), most superstitious, which they thought must be used to seek and obtain the favour, pardon, peace and help of those fabricated gods of theirs, we Christians pour out our prayers to the only true God, through Christ, the Son of God, the God-man [Θεανθρωπον], the one mediator between God and men. We pour them out not so much with the mouth as from our heart and soul, partly to give thanks for the salvation received and for countless benefits, and partly to obtain the right of grace, mercy, peace and pardon. But above all and especially we rely constantly, for our salvation, on the intercession and entreaty of our Lord Jesus Christ, who now sits at the right hand of the Father.

units.la: Supplicationes Gentilium publicae, ut scriptores profani passim testantur, fiebant ad Deorum, vel omnium, vel quorundam, pulvinaria: fiebant lectisternia, in quibus ipsos saepe Consules Romanos lectos strafsise legimus. At lectisternia & pulvinaria, non superstitiosa, qualia fuerunt illa Gentilium, sed sancta & religiosa, Deo, gratissima sunt illa, quando Christi quasi caritas in hoc Mundo, hoc est, pauperibus & peregrinis, ipsius Christi mandato, atque nomine lectos & pulvinos sternimus, hoc est, illos hospitio excepimus, illuq; quae vis hospitalitatis, humanitatis, benignitatis, officia pro nostra virili praestamus.
units.tr: Public supplications of the Gentiles, as profane writers testify everywhere, were made at the couches [pulvinaria] of the gods, either of all of them or of some. There were lectisternia, in which we read that the Roman consuls themselves often spread the couches. But lectisternia and couches that are not superstitious, such as those of the Gentiles, but holy and religious, are most pleasing to God, when, at the command and in the name of Christ, we spread couches for Christ's love in this world, that is, for the poor and for strangers, that is, when we receive them into our homes and show them the duties of hospitality, humanity and kindness, as far as we are able.

units.la: Vota similiter Gentiles vanissimus illis suis Diis voverunt, diligenterq; perfol verunt. Nos Christiani soli Deo vota devota, pia ac religiosa facere & persolvere debemus, secundum illa Davidis Psalm. 50. Sacrificia laudem & redde Altissimo vota tua. Sed vori inprimis nostri maximi & sanctissimi, quod in sacrosanctio Baptismo, in lustrali illo lavacro, fecimus, quo, nos Deo obstrinximus (nos nimirum Satanae ejusq; pompe renunciaturos, & Imperatori Christo per omnem vitam militaturos) semper meminisse, & sanctè in violateq; illud per totam nostram vitam persolvere debemus.
units.tr: Likewise the Gentiles made vows to their vain gods and carefully paid them. We Christians ought to make and pay devout, pious and religious vows to God alone, according to that saying of David, Psalm 50: "Offer to the Most High a sacrifice of praise and pay your vows." But above all we must always remember and faithfully and inviolably perform, throughout our whole life, the most great and holy vow which we made in holy Baptism, in that cleansing bath, by which we bound ourselves to God (namely, that we would renounce Satan and his pomp, and fight for Christ our Emperor all our life).

units.la: Sic juramenta quoq;, quae votis & precibus sunt annumeranda, Gentiles sua fecerunt per sal-fos fucatos, illos suos Deos, per Caelum, per Terram, per Stygiam paludem, per singula fere corporis membra, ut per caput, per oculos, per dextram, per genua, per omnes fere creaturas, & per multa turpia & foeda dicitu. Nos Christiani per solum Deum, tanquam solum χαρδιοχρωστον, omniscium et omnipotentem, justa legitima, nostra juramenta facimus, quem solum agnoscimus ac coluimus esse ορκιον, hoc est, jurisjurandi praesidem & assertorem, piumq; vindicem & ultorem. Quod si Gentiles superstitiosa illa sua juramenta, summa fide religionis coluerunt & servarunt, quanto majori fide & religione nos Christiani vera nostra juramenta servare minime, violare debemus? Quemadmodum autem Gentiles Deos quoq; suos finxerunt juraffe: sic nos Christiani sec undum sacras litteras Dei, per seipsum propter nos jurantis, juramenta, tanquam salutis nostrae sigilla, initia atq; testimonia certissima plurimi facere, sitq; fidem indubitatam adhibere debemus.
units.tr: Likewise the Gentiles also made their oaths, which are to be counted among vows and prayers, by their false and feigned gods, by heaven, by earth, by the Stygian marsh, and by almost every part of the body, such as the head, the eyes, the right hand, the knees, by almost all creatures, and by many things that are foul and shameful to mention. We Christians swear our lawful and just oaths by God alone, as the one [καρδιογνώστης], heart-knowing, all-knowing and almighty, whom alone we acknowledge and worship as the [ὅρκιος], that is, the guardian and witness of oaths, and the pious avenger and punisher. If the Gentiles kept and observed those superstitious oaths of theirs with the greatest faithfulness in religion, with how much greater faithfulness and religion ought we Christians to keep, and in no way violate, our true oaths? And just as the Gentiles also imagined that their gods had sworn, so we Christians, according to the holy writings of God, who swears for our sake by himself, ought to hold oaths in great esteem, as seals, pledges and most certain testimonies of our salvation, and to give them undoubted faith.

units.la: Preterea sicut Gentiles suos Deos coluerunt sacrificiis, votis, precib. supplicationib. lectisterniis, juramentis: sic habuerunt superstitiosa quaedam jejunia, et suas quasdam abstinentias a certo alimentorum genere; idq;, vel ad tempus aliquod, vel perpetuum ac semper, quibus magna se putabant a Diis suis inire gratiam: de quibus supra & in Conviualibus meis epi pluribus. Talia fuerunt, quae superioribus addi possunt, illa Cybeles, qui Galli fuerunt appellati, jejunia, qui, ut Hieronymus de iis scribit, per dies aliquot inediam perferebant, ut deinde phasianis avibus vicis sim tanto majori cum voluptate impleri possent. Tale quoq; fuit superstitiosum illud apud Romanos jejunium, quod, teste Livio, Decemvirie libris Sibyllinis Cereri, quod quinto quoq; anno servaretur, instituendum esse renunciarunt: idque ad expianda prodigia, & averruncandum iram caelestem.
units.tr: Moreover, just as the Gentiles worshipped their gods with sacrifices, vows, prayers, supplications, lectisternia and oaths, so they also had certain superstitious fastings and their own abstentions from a certain kind of food, either for some time or permanently and always, by which they thought they would win great favour from their gods. Of these I have written above and in my Convivalia, in more detail. Among such practices, which may be added to the above, were the fastings of the priests of Cybele, who were called Galli. As Jerome writes of them, they endured fasting for some days so that afterwards they could be filled with pheasant birds and other delicacies with all the greater pleasure. Such also was that superstitious fast among the Romans which, as Livy testifies, the Decemvirs, consulting the Sibylline books, declared should be instituted for Ceres, to be observed every fifth year, and this to expiate portents and to avert heavenly anger.

units.la: At nos Christiani secundum Christi, Prophetarum, Apostolorum aliorum, Sanctorum cum jejunia Christi precepta, tum exempla sanctius religiosius, jejuniis & abstinentia a cibis necessariis aliquando & sitiatorum, publice & privatim, tempore praesertim difficili & periculosso, rebus fludemus, carnis nostrae lasciviam domandi & reprimendi, tantoq; ardentiore studio atq; animo sanctis precibus rerumq; divinarum meditationibus vacandi gratia. Sed inprimis perpetuum nostrum jejunium, quod Deus praecipue a nobis requirit, fit perpetua sobrietas, & temperantia vitae, denique abstinentia a carnis operibus, hoc est, vitiis & peccato.
units.tr: But we Christians, following the precepts of Christ and the examples, more holy and religious, of Christ, the Prophets, the Apostles and other Saints, shall strive from time to time for fasting and abstinence from necessary foods, and from the thirsty, both publicly and privately, especially in a difficult and dangerous time, to tame and restrain the lasciviousness of our flesh, and to devote ourselves with all the greater zeal and eagerness to holy prayers and meditations on divine things. But above all, the perpetual fast which God especially requires of us is perpetual sobriety and temperance of life, and finally abstinence from the works of the flesh, that is, from vices and sin.

units.la: Quae vero jejunio rum, eadem caelibatus quoque Gentilium superstitiosissima fuit ratio. Talis fuit & virginum vestalium apud Romanos, & virginum Dianae apud Gracos caelibatus, & sacerdotum Cybeles insana castratio: de quibus multa licet legere apud profanos autores. Nos Christiani & caelibatum atque virginitatem, tanquam singulare & coelestie Dei donum, cujus ea men non omnes sunt capaces, plurimi merito facere, magnis, laudibus efferre, & conjugium, followed by bolis procreanda & fortationis vitandae gratia divinitus institutum, jus, qui caelibatus non sunt capaces, concessum esse arbitramur, secundum illa Apostoli ad Hebr. 13. Honorabile inter omnes conjugium, & cubile impollutum: fornicatores autem & adulteros judicabit Deus. Idem Apostolus virginitatem quidem suadet iis, qui caste in caelibatu vivere possunt: sed qui se continere nequeunt, eos ad conjugium idem hortatur. Bonum est, inquit, 1. Corinth. 7. hominem uxorem non attingere: attamen stupra vitandi causa suam quisq; uxorem habeat, & suum quaeq; virum. Et paullo post: Nam velim omnes homines esse, ut & ipse sum: sed unusquisq; proprium donum habet ex Deo; alius quidem sic: alius autem sic. Dico autem in conjugatis, & viduis: bonum eis est, si manserint, ut & ego. Quod si se non continent, contrahant matrimonium.
units.tr: The celibacy of the Gentiles was as superstitious as their fasting. Such was the celibacy of the Vestal virgins among the Romans, of the virgins of Diana among the Greeks, and the mad castration of the priests of Cybele. Much about these can be read in the profane authors. We Christians, however, rightly hold celibacy and virginity to be a singular and heavenly gift of God, which not all are able to receive, and we praise them greatly and esteem them highly. We believe that marriage was instituted by God for the procreation of children and the avoiding of fornication, and that it is permitted to those who are not capable of celibacy, according to the words of the Apostle in Hebrews 13: "Marriage is honourable among all, and the bed undefiled; but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge." The same Apostle commends virginity to those who can live chastely in celibacy, but urges those who cannot contain themselves to marriage. "It is good," he says in 1 Corinthians 7, "for a man not to touch a woman. Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband." And a little later: "For I would that all men were even as I myself am; but every man has his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that. But I say to the unmarried and the widows, it is good for them if they abide even as I do. But if they cannot contain, let them marry."

units.la: Nam satius est matrimonium contrahere, quam uri. Sic Christus Servator apud Matthaeum, quo loco eunuchos aliquos esse testatur, qui se castraverint propter regnum caelorum, ibidem mox addit: Qui potest capere capiat: ostendent caelibatus donum pauciis contingere divinitus, nec quibusvis esse datum. Vere igitur Chrysostomus, Primus, inquit, gradus castitatis est fyncera virginitas: secundus fidele conjugium. Sed & Christus ipse, ut ostenderet se utrumq; & caelibet est matrimoniale vitae genus ac institutum approbare, cum in matrimonio sanctissimo & casti simo, tuni ex virgine aeterna, id est, intemerata & perenni abstinentia, femine virili, secundum carnem nascitur atq; procreari voluit. Praecipuus autem Deo, gratissimus caelibatus, virginitas atq; castratio est, perpetua sive in conjugio, sive extra conjugium pudicitia, corporis animique integra castitas & puritas.
units.tr: For it is better to marry than to burn. So Christ the Saviour, in Matthew, where he says that there are some eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven, adds immediately after: "He that is able to receive it, let him receive it." This shows that the gift of celibacy is granted by God to few, and is not given to everyone. Chrysostom rightly says: "The first degree of chastity is pure virginity; the second is faithful marriage." Christ himself, moreover, to show that he approves both celibacy and the married state of life, was willing to be born, according to the flesh, of a most holy and chaste marriage, and of a virgin who was eternally a virgin, that is, of an undefiled and perpetual abstinence, a man-child. Yet the celibacy most pleasing to God, and most acceptable to him, is virginity and the purity of body, a perpetual chastity and integrity of body and soul, whether within marriage or outside it.

units.la: Quin in vestitu etiam Gentiles, habituq; corporis partim vili & sordido, partim splendido & ornato sanctitatis religionisq; partem non minimam collocarunt, eusque speciem quandam apud rude & imperitum vulgus prae se tulerunt. At nos non in externo & corporis, sed in interno & spirituali ipsius animi cultu atq; habitu pietatem sanctissimam confiteri arbitramur: de quo Paullus ad Coloss. cap. 3. Exuite, inquit, veterem hominem, cum actionibus ejus, qui renovatur in cognitionem, secundum ejus, qui eum condidit. Idem ad Galat. 3. Quicunq; baptizati estis, Christum induistis. Quantum autem ad cultum habitumq; corporis attinet, in eo necessitatis, moderati & mediocritatis, mores confuetudinisq; patriae, honestatis, generis ac institutae vitae tenendus habendam esse rationem.
units.tr: Indeed, the Gentiles also placed no small part of holiness and religion in their clothing and bodily dress, partly plain and dirty, partly splendid and adorned, and they displayed some image of this before the rude and unlearned crowd. We, however, believe that the most holy piety is professed not in external and bodily worship and dress, but in the inward and spiritual worship and dress of the soul itself. Concerning this, Paul says in Colossians 3: "Put off the old man with his deeds, who is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him." The same in Galatians 3: "As many of you as have been baptized have put on Christ." As far as the worship and bodily dress are concerned, however, in this one must observe a regard for necessity, moderation and mediocrity, for the customs and usages of one's country, for decency, for one's rank and for the manner of life one has chosen.

units.la: Praeter haec omnia, quae hactenus a nobis recitata sunt, Gentiles tantu quoq; cum vocali, tum instrumentali, ut ribis, tubis, fistulis, sistris, citharis, cymbalis, crotalis, tympanis & aliis instrumentis Deo; suos coluerunt ac venerati sunt. At nostra tuba vere argentea, immo quo vis argento pretiosior, organum nostrae salutis vocalissimum, nostra melodia quo vis melle suavior, nostra Musica dulcissima est Verbum Dei, sunt oracula & eloquia divina, quae hominis animos mentesq; versa, solida, salutaris, voluptate afficiunt & perfundunt, quaeq; & doloribus ad molestias quibusvis efficacissime vehementer ac recreant. Horum eloquiorum divinorum admirabilis, suavissimus, saluberrimus est concentus & harmonia, quae cujusvis sive vocalis, sive instrumentalis Musicae atq; cantus symphoniam suavitatis utilitatisq;, quae pondere longe superat. Hanc tubam atq; organum salutare Deus semper in Ecclesia sua resonare & a minus fris suis instari, hoc est, decantari praedicariq; voluit: unde Verbi divini praecones et interpretes vere tubicines spirituales possunt appellari.
units.tr: Besides all these things which we have recited so far, the Gentiles also honoured and worshipped their gods with vocal and instrumental music, with pipes, trumpets, flutes, sistrums, lyres, cymbals, rattles, drums and other instruments. But our trumpet, truly silver, or rather more precious than any silver, our most vocal organ of salvation, our melody sweeter than any honey, our most sweet music, is the Word of God. These are the oracles and divine sayings, which turn, strengthen and refresh the minds and souls of men with a healthful and solid delight, and most effectively and vehemently console them in any sorrows or troubles. Admirable, most sweet and most wholesome is the harmony and concord of these divine sayings, which far surpasses in weight the symphony of pleasure and usefulness of any vocal or instrumental music and song. God willed that this trumpet and saving organ should always resound in his Church, and be sounded, that is, sung and preached, by his people. Hence the heralds and interpreters of the divine Word may truly be called spiritual trumpeters.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem fuguliis suis Dijs certos quosdam cecinerunt hymnos, illorum laudes celebrandi gratia: ficnos Christiani multo justiore de caussa & corde & ore, Deo vero & Christo Immanueli ac Seruatori hymnos atque psalmos canere debemus: quales sunt Psalmi illi, Dauidici & aliorum sanctorum hominum, secundum Paullinam illam admonitionem, nostris his temporibus valde necessarium: Καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ, ἐν ᾧ ἐστιν ἀσωτία, ἀλλὰ πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι, λαλοῦντες ἑαυτοῖς ψαλμοῖς, καὶ ὕμνοις, καὶ ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς, ἀδοντες καὶ ψάλλοντες ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν τῷ κυρίῳ. Idem Col. 3. Ὁ λόγος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐνοικείτω ἐν ὑμῖν πλουσίως ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ, διδάσκοντες καὶ νουθετοῦντες ἑαυτοὺς ψαλμοῖς, ὕμνοις, ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς, ἐν χάριτι ᾄδοντες ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν τῷ κυρίῳ. Idem priore ad Concap.14. precum sinimul & cantus Ecclesia astici in sacris coetibus luculentam mentionem facit.
units.tr: Just as the Gentiles sang certain hymns to their gods to celebrate their praises, so we Christians, for a much more just cause, ought to sing hymns and psalms with heart and mouth to God and to Christ Immanuel and Saviour: such as those psalms of David and of other holy men, according to that Pauline admonition, which is very necessary in our times: "And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord" [Καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ, ἐν ᾧ ἐστιν ἀσωτία, ἀλλὰ πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι, λαλοῦντες ἑαυτοῖς ψαλμοῖς, καὶ ὕμνοις, καὶ ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς, ἀδοντες καὶ ψάλλοντες ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν τῷ κυρίῳ]. The same in Colossians 3: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord" [Ὁ λόγος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐνοικείτω ἐν ὑμῖν πλουσίως ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ, διδάσκοντες καὶ νουθετοῦντες ἑαυτοὺς ψαλμοῖς, ὕμνοις, ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς, ἐν χάριτι ᾄδοντες ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν τῷ κυρίῳ]. The same Paul, in the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 14, makes clear mention of prayer and singing together in the Church's sacred assemblies.

units.la: Ludos praeterea & spectacula omnis generis in circo, theatris & amphitheatris in Deorum suorum gratiam & honorem instituerunt atq; celebrarunt, quae superstitionum, immanitatis, scelerum flagitiorumq; fuerunt plenissima, de quibus peculiares exstant & Tertulliani & Cypriani libri, quibus fuz aetatis Christianos ab hujusmodi ludorum spectaculorumq; studio auocarunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the Gentiles instituted and celebrated games and spectacles of every kind in the circus, theatres and amphitheatres, for the favour and honour of their gods. These were full of superstition, savagery, crimes and disgraceful deeds. There are special books on them by both Tertullian and Cyprian, by which they called the Christians of their own time away from the zeal for such games and spectacles.

units.la: ne ijs interesserent. Nostrum autem Theatrum, Amphitheatrum Circensq; maximus & amplissimus est Ecclesia: in qua ludi nobis & spectacula non rerum superstitiosarum, turpium & impium, sed sacrarum, diuinarum, caelestium & aeternarum nostrum salutem pertinentium exhibentur.
units.tr: So that they would not attend them. Our own theatre, amphitheatre and circus is the Church, the greatest and most ample of all. In it, games and spectacles are offered to us not of superstitious, shameful and impious things, but of sacred, divine, heavenly and eternal things, which pertain to our salvation.

units.la: Ludis addi possunt tripudia & saltationes superstitiose & obscenae, quibus in sacrificiis, epulis sacris Gentiles fuerunt usi, quibus ipsis se Deorum suorum gratiam demereri sibi, coucinare putabant. Sed nos reiectis repudiatis, tripudiis illis atq; saltationibus laseiuis, quae superstitionum libidinum, sunt irritamenta, in Domino, sancta salutarisque laetitia propter fidem & spem aeternae vitae, exsilire, gestire atque tripudiare debemus, secundum illa S. Petri epistola 1. cap.1. Quem ( lefum scilicet) nunc non videntes amatis, in quem nunc non intuentes: sed credentes gaudio ineffabili, & reportantes finem fidei vestrae, salutem animarum. Χαρὰ ἀνεκλάλητος καὶ δεδοξασμένῃ, id est, exultatis atque tripudiatis gaudio ineffabili, reportantes finem fidei vestrae, salutem animarum.
units.tr: To the games may be added the superstitious and obscene dances and leapings with which the Gentiles used to indulge in their sacrifices and sacred feasts, by which they thought they could win the favour of their gods for themselves. But we, having rejected and renounced those dances and lascivious leapings, which are incitements of superstitious lusts, ought to leap, exult and dance in the Lord, with a holy and saving joy, on account of faith and the hope of eternal life, according to that passage of the first epistle of St. Peter, chapter 1: "Whom, though you have not seen, you love; in whom, though now you see him not, yet believing, you rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory, receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls" [Χαρὰ ἀνεκλάλητος καὶ δεδοξασμένῃ]. That is, you exult and dance with unspeakable joy, receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls.

units.la: Peractis porro sacrificiis Gentiles plerunq; epulas atq; conuiuia in Deorum suorum honorem magna cum laetitia, seu lascivia potius atq; luxuria agitarunt. Nostrum vero Conuiuium atq; epulum, vere vitale & salutare est, autore & teste ipso Christo, Regnum caelorum, ad quod diuina gratia & clementia in vitam & vocati sumus, in vitamur & vocamur quotidie. Iu hoc epulo non tam corpora, quam animi nostri pascuntur ad vitam aeternam in hoc quidem seculo, fide atq; spe: in altero vitione atq; re. Epulum item nostrum spirituale est verbi divini, quod verum salutare, est animarum nostrarum pabulum atq; cibus. Habemus quoq; epulum illud Dominicum & sacrosanctum: in quo similiter, ut & in verbo Christus cum totus, tum ejus & caro sive corpus, tanquam panis vivificus ad manducandum porrigitur atq; proponitur, tum sanguis, tanquam vinum atq; potus salutaris ad bibendum propinatur: quorum manducatio & potatio salutifera fide fit: ideo spiritus sancti virtute & efficacia. Epulae deniq; atq; dapes, Deo gratissimae & jucundissimae sunt, quaudo pauperes atq; inopes alimus ac pascimus. Mos olim apud Ethnicos fuit locuplete cuiusdam viri, qui singulis mensibus Hecatae sive Lunae sacrificarent panem, et in trivis proponerent, quae non ab inopibus & egenis raperentur: quae, Suida teste, Hecatea coena appellabatur. Quanto magis igitur nos Christiani in Dei honorem panes alios, cibos atq; potus pauperibus & egenis ad famem sitimq; illorum sublevandam praebere debemus?
units.tr: Furthermore, after their sacrifices the Gentiles usually held feasts and banquets in honour of their gods, with great merriment, or rather with lasciviousness and luxury. Our banquet and feast, however, is truly life-giving and saving, as Christ himself is both author and witness: the kingdom of heaven, to which by divine grace and mercy we have been called into life, and are called every day. In this feast it is not so much our bodies as our souls that are fed for eternal life, in this age by faith and hope, and in the next by sight and enjoyment. Our spiritual feast is also the Word of God, which is the true saving food and nourishment of our souls. We also have that Lord's and most holy feast, in which, just as in the Word, Christ is set forth and offered as the living bread for eating, both his flesh and body, and his blood is offered to drink as the saving wine and drink; the eating and drinking of these is accomplished by faith, and so by the power and efficacy of the Holy Spirit. Finally, feasts and banquets are most pleasing and delightful to God when we feed and nourish the poor and needy. Among the heathen there was formerly a custom that certain wealthy men, every month, would offer bread to Hecate or the Moon and place it at the crossroads, where it was not to be snatched up by the poor and needy; according to Suidas this was called the Hecatean supper. How much more, then, ought we Christians, to the honour of God, to offer other breads, foods and drinks to the poor and needy, to relieve their hunger and thirst?

units.la: Oracula Gentiles babuerunt sua Delphica, Dodonea, Hammonia atq; etiam aliorum Deorum, seu potius Daemonum: quae publice & privatim magnis in periculis, ac quibusdam de rebus publicis & sacris agendis adire atq; consulere consueuerunt: quibus Daemones illis mirifice suas, fallacibus, obscuris, perplexis, flexiloquis & falsiloquis illis Daemonum oraculis habemus Θεόπροπος; & quidem certissima, veritatem, saluberrima, Christi, Prophetarum, & Apostolorum oraculo, ex ipso Dei ore, id est, inspiratione prophetica, viva voce pronunciata, litterisque memoriae consecrata, quae quotidie adire, audire, legere atq; consulere, iis fidem adhibere, secundum illa vitam religionemq; nostram conformare atq; componere debemus.
units.tr: The Gentiles had their oracles: at Delphi, Dodona, Hammon, and also those of other gods, or rather demons. Publicly and privately, in great dangers and when certain public or sacred matters were to be undertaken, they were accustomed to approach and consult them. By these ambiguous, obscure, perplexed, equivocal and deceitful oracles of the demons, the demons wonderfully deceived them. But we have the most certain oracle of God, most true and most wholesome: that of Christ, the prophets and the apostles, from the very mouth of God, that is, by prophetic inspiration, pronounced by the living voice and consecrated to memory in writing. We ought to approach, hear, read and consult it every day, give it our faith, and shape and order our life and religion according to it.

units.la: Pro divinationibus similiter alius atq; vaticinius Gentilium innumeris, variis, et multiplicibus. tibus non diuinis, sed humanis & daemoniacis, fallaciarum, errorum mendaciorum, plenissimis, Pro nos Christi habemus ac Prophetarum, Apostolorum, diuinationes, vere diuinas ac caelestes, & vaticinia non dubia, ambigua, obscura, pestifera (cuiusmodi fuerunt illa Gentilium) sed vera, perspicua, certa & salutifera. Haec partim malorum miseriarum, nostrorum sunt solatia, partim religionis & vitae morum, nostrorum documenta, partim rerum futurarum praesagia; quaerum alia quidem iam venerunt & acciderunt: aliarum vero enentum & exitum certissimum fide, nostra patienter expectamus.
units.tr: Likewise, in place of the countless, varied and manifold divinations and prophecies of the Gentiles, which were not divine but human and demonic, and most full of deceits, errors and lies, we have the divinations of Christ, the prophets and the apostles, truly divine and heavenly, and prophecies that are not doubtful, ambiguous, obscure or pestilential (such as those of the Gentiles were), but true, plain, certain and salutary. Some of these are comforts for our evils and miseries, some are instructions for our religion and way of life, and some are predictions of future things; of these, some have already come and happened, and the outcome and end of the others we await patiently in faith.

units.la: Sic prodigiis, signis atq; miraculis Gentilium fictis atq; fallacibus, quorum pleraque fuerunt Pro Daemonum praestigiae, nos merito opponimus Christi, Prophetarum, Apostolorum & Martyrum plurima, ut ipsa miracula, diuina virtute edita; quae quidem doctrinae, religionis, vere, quam illi praedicarunt, testimonia fuerunt & sigilla.
units.tr: Thus, against the prodigies, signs and miracles of the Gentiles, which were made up and deceptive, and most of which were tricks of demons, we rightly set the many miracles of Christ, the prophets, the apostles and the martyrs, which were wrought by divine power; these were indeed witnesses and seals of the teaching and religion which they preached, and of its truth.

units.la: Postremo, ut hanc Antithesin tandem concludam, Gentiles volumina librorum habuerunt plurimos sacros, diuinos, ceremoniales, rituales, pontificales, augurales, haruspicinos, fatales, fa- Pro libris Ethnicorum, quae sunt dicos (nti vulgo fuerunt appellati) vanissimas illorum de Dijs opiniones, seu errores potius, atq; deliria, somnia atque fabulas, totam religionum, superstitionum diuinationum, illorum rationem complectentes. Atq; hos quidem libros diligenter asservare magni in periculis, rebus, ad versis, adire, consulere atque legere, & ex illis Deos suos colendi atq; placandi rationem depromere solebant. Nostri vero libri, vere sacri, sancti, sacrosancti, diuini, religiosi, pontificales, rituales, ceremoniales sunt illa, quae ςρ ἐξοχὴν merito Biblia, id est, Libri appellantur, libri videlicet veteris et novi Testamenti, quibus quae de Deo, deejus natura, cultu atq; religione, de nostro proximum, sive Hominem officio credituri, cognitu, dicta fuerunt, ad salutem nostram sunt necessaria, plene perfecte conti nentur.
units.tr: Finally, to bring this antithesis to a close, the Gentiles had very many books that were called sacred, divine, ceremonial, ritual, pontifical, augural, haruspical and fatal (as they were commonly called), containing the most vain opinions, or rather errors, delusions, dreams and fables of theirs about the gods, and the whole system of their religions, superstitions and divinations. In great dangers, adversities and affairs, they were accustomed to keep these books carefully, to approach, consult and read them, and to draw from them the manner of worshipping and appeasing their gods. Our books, however, which are truly sacred, holy, most holy, divine, religious, pontifical, ritual and ceremonial, are those which are rightly called the Bible, that is, the Books par excellence: namely, the books of the Old and New Testament, which fully and perfectly contain everything said about God, his nature, worship and religion, and about our duty to our neighbour and to man, which is to be believed and known, and which are necessary for our salvation.

units.la: Atque haec quidem de Paganismi & Christianismi Antithesi satis sint dicta; quae, si quis singula vellet perseqvi, crescoret in immensum oratio. Ex hac ipsa autem apparet, quanta in utrumq; sit differentia, & quanta nobis curae studio, sit elaborandam, ut Ethnicam quidem superstitionem omnem vitemus atq; fugiamus (cum, ut recte Livius dixit, Pra va religione nihil in sue ciem sit fallacius) Christianam autem religionem illibatam ac puram puram constanter tueamur ac conservemus. Domino nostro Iesu Christo (ut hunc meum Tractatus finiam, & unde exorsus sum, in eodem terminem) Redemptori, Seruatori & Mediatori nostro unico, qui pro nostra salute factus & Sacerdos simul & sacrificium pacificum ac salutiferum, cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto, sit honor, laus & gloria in secula seculorum, AMEN.
units.tr: Let these things be said about the antithesis of paganism and Christianity; if anyone wished to pursue each point, the discourse would grow to an immense length. From this very thing, however, it is clear how great the difference is between the two, and how much care and zeal we must expend to avoid and flee all Gentile superstition (since, as Livy rightly said, nothing is more deceptive for a show of piety than a false religion), and to hold fast and preserve the Christian religion unimpaired and pure. To our Lord Jesus Christ (so that I may end this my treatise where I began), our sole Redeemer, Saviour and Mediator, who for our salvation has been made both priest and a peace-giving and saving sacrifice, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit be honour, praise and glory for ever and ever. AMEN.
THE END.
